1A.13 Interview questions

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is the difference between a CPU register and a device register?
    Model answer

    A CPU register is internal storage used by instructions and invisible outside the core. A device register is a control/status location in a device, reached through an address (MMIO or config space), and may have side effects when read or written.

  2. Beginner What does “memory-mapped I/O” mean?
    Model answer

    Device registers are assigned addresses in the physical address map, so ordinary load/store instructions to those addresses reach the device instead of DRAM.

  3. Beginner Why is memory called volatile?
    Model answer

    DRAM loses its contents without power; storage such as NAND retains them.

  4. Beginner What is a cache line?
    Model answer

    The unit in which caches hold and transfer memory, commonly 64 bytes; coherence is tracked per line.

  5. Beginner What is the role of the root complex?
    Model answer

    It bridges the CPU/memory system to the PCIe hierarchy: turns CPU accesses into TLPs and device memory requests into memory accesses.

  6. Intermediate Why is a register read more expensive than a write?
    Model answer

    Reads are non-posted: the core must wait for the round trip and completion. Writes are posted: the core continues once the store is handed off.

  7. Intermediate What is a read “flush” of posted writes?
    Model answer

    Because a read's completion cannot pass earlier posted writes in the same path, reading a device register after writes guarantees those writes have reached the device.

  8. Intermediate What does Bus Master Enable control?
    Model answer

    Whether the function may issue memory and I/O requests upstream — i.e. do DMA and send MSI/MSI-X.

  9. Intermediate Why must a barrier precede the doorbell write?
    Model answer

    So the SQE stores are visible in memory before the device is told to fetch; otherwise the device might read stale bytes.

  10. Intermediate Why is write-combining unsafe for control registers?
    Model answer

    WC can merge, reorder or delay stores, breaking side-effect semantics and ordering.

  11. Advanced How does a 64-bit register read appear on PCIe, and what risk exists?
    Model answer

    Either one 2-DW MRd or two 1-DW MRds depending on CPU/driver; split reads can tear if the register changes between them.

  12. Advanced What does an all-ones read tell you?
    Model answer

    Usually that the read failed (UR, CA, completion timeout, link down) and the platform returned all ones; check Vendor ID in config space to confirm.

  13. Advanced How do NUMA effects show up in NVMe performance?
    Model answer

    Higher latency and lower IOPS when queues, buffers or interrupt targets are on a different socket from the device's root port.

  14. Advanced What does CAP.TO govern?
    Model answer

    Worst-case time, in 500 ms units, for CSTS.RDY to transition after CC.EN changes.

  15. Advanced Why does NVMe use per-core queues?
    Model answer

    To avoid cross-core locking and cache-line bouncing on a shared queue, allowing linear scaling with cores.

  16. Senior A customer reports 50 µs latency spikes in the driver's interrupt handler. How do you proceed?
    Model answer

    Profile which instructions stall; look for MMIO reads in the handler; correlate with link power states and with analyzer capture of slow completions; test with ASPM disabled and with polling mode; form a hypothesis per evidence.

  17. Senior How would you prove a missing barrier caused corruption?
    Model answer

    Capture the fetched SQE bytes on an analyzer and compare with the driver's intended SQE logged after the fact; reproduce under stress on a weakly ordered platform; show the fix eliminates mismatches over a statistically meaningful run.

  18. Senior How would you design register-access validation for a new controller?
    Model answer

    Reset values, RO/RW/RW1C behaviour, access widths and alignment, reserved bits, side effects, behaviour during reset and when disabled, concurrency with DMA, error responses for unimplemented offsets.

  19. Senior What is the risk in a driver timeout shorter than CAP.TO?
    Model answer

    Spuriously declaring a healthy but slow controller dead, especially after unsafe shutdowns when initialisation is longer.

  20. Senior How do you tell a host hang from a device hang?
    Model answer

    Host hang: cores stuck (watchdog, NMI backtraces), possibly in an MMIO read waiting for a completion; device hang: link alive, device responds to config reads but not to commands. Analyzer or root-port completion-timeout logs discriminate.

1A.14 Teach-back

  • To a child: explain why the harbour master prefers sending messages to asking questions.
  • To a junior engineer: explain how writel() to a doorbell becomes a TLP and why it does not wait.
  • To a senior engineer: argue whether an all-ones CSTS should trigger an immediate controller reset or a link investigation first.
✅ Mastery gate — Module 1A
  • I can explain the path of an MMIO read and an MMIO write, naming every actor.
  • I can draw Figure 1A.1 from memory.
  • I can identify host MMIO reads/writes and their completions in a trace.
  • I can debug an all-ones register read and a never-ready controller.
  • I can distinguish MMIO from DMA, and posted from non-posted.
  • I can cite which specification defines the NVMe register offsets and which defines posted semantics.

1B Deep Dive — DMA and Address Translation

← 1A Deep Dive — CPU, Memory and I/O Foundations1C Chapter 1 Wrap-Up — Views, Lab, Quiz and Gate →

Every byte an NVMe SSD moves goes by DMA. Every DMA uses an address that someone had to compute, translate and permit. Most of the scariest storage bugs — silent corruption, “impossible” data in the wrong buffer, a system that hangs only with the IOMMU on — live in this module. It builds on §1.7 Virtual memory, §1.8 Physical memory and §1.15 DMA.

1B.1 Learning objectives by level

LevelObjective — you can…
BeginnerExplain DMA as “the device reads and writes memory itself” and name the three address kinds (virtual, physical, device-visible).
IntermediateExplain how a driver turns a user buffer into a list of device-visible addresses (pin, map, describe).
AdvancedExplain IOMMU translation, IOTLB misses, ATS (Address Translation Services) at a conceptual level, and bounce buffering.
SeniorDiagnose use-after-unmap, stale-mapping and wrong-address DMA bugs from indirect evidence.
Trace analysisMap a TLP's address back to which buffer, queue or PRP list it belongs to.
DebuggingRead IOMMU fault logs and decide whether the device or the driver is at fault.
ValidationDesign DMA tests: boundary crossings, unaligned buffers, 4 GiB crossings, IOMMU on/off, high memory addresses.

1B.2 A fresh story — the delivery robot and the address book

🧒 Kid analogy

A delivery robot (the device) brings parcels to an enormous apartment building (memory). The robot cannot read people's names — it only understands door numbers. Families use nicknames for their rooms (“Mia's bedroom”) — those are virtual addresses. The building manager (the OS) keeps the book that says which nickname is which door.

Before a delivery, the family asks the manager to write down the door numbers on the delivery slip (mapping) and promises not to move rooms until the parcel arrives (pinning). In some buildings, a security guard at the entrance (IOMMU) holds a second list: the robot is given “guest door numbers” and the guard translates each one to a real door — and refuses entry to any door not on the list.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks
  • Represents: devices cannot use virtual addresses; pinning; mapping; IOMMU translation and protection.
  • Hides: translation is per page, not per room; the guard caches translations (IOTLB) and cache misses cost time; a parcel can be split across many doors.
  • Misleads: a refused robot usually does not know it was refused — a posted write blocked by the IOMMU is typically just dropped and logged by the host, while the device believes it delivered impl.

1B.5 Mechanism — a 16 KiB O_DIRECT read, step by step

#Who actsWhat changesWhereEvidence
1ApplicationCalls pread(fd, buf, 16384, off) with an aligned buffer, O_DIRECTUser spacestrace
2Kernel (block/direct I/O)Pins the 4 user pages backing bufPage structsTracepoints / bpftrace on GUP functions impl
3NVMe driver via DMA APIMaps pages: gets 4 DMA addresses (or 1 IOVA range if the IOMMU merges)IOMMU page tablesIOMMU tracepoints impl
4NVMe driverWrites PRP1 = first DMA address; since > 2 pages, PRP2 = address of a PRP list holding the remaining entriesSQE in SQ memory; PRP list pageAnalyzer: SQE bytes 24–39 in the fetched command
5DriverBarrier, doorbell writeMMIOAnalyzer: MWr to SQ tail doorbell
6ControllerFetches SQE, then fetches the PRP listDevice → host MRdAnalyzer: MRd to SQ address, then MRd to PRP list address
7Controller DMAWrites 16 KiB via MWr TLPs to the 4 DMA addressesHost memoryAnalyzer: MWr TLPs whose addresses match the PRP entries
8IOMMUTranslates each MWr address; checks write permissionRoot complexFault log if denied
9ControllerPosts CQE, MSI-XHost memoryAnalyzer: MWr 16 B to CQ; MWr to MSI-X address
10DriverUnmaps, unpins, completes requestKernelIOMMU unmap; request completion tracepoint
💡 Senior insight — step 10 is where corruption is born

If the driver unmaps (step 10) before the device's last write (step 7) lands — for example after a timeout and abort race — a later mapping may reuse the IOVA for a different buffer, and the device's late write lands in somebody else's data. No error is reported anywhere. This is why reset and abort paths must guarantee the device has stopped DMA before memory is released.

1B.6 Specification discipline

📘 Specification — sources

NVMe Base Specification Rev. 2.4 and NVM Command Set Rev. 1.3 define data pointers (PRP, SGL), memory page size (CC.MPS) and queue base addresses. PCI Express Base Specification defines memory request TLPs, Bus Master Enable, and (optional) ATS. IOMMU behaviour is defined by platform architecture documents (Intel VT-d, AMD IOMMU, Arm SMMU), not by NVMe. Linux behaviour is defined by kernel documentation (DMA API) and source impl.

CategoryExamples
Normative (NVMe)PRP entry format and offset rules relative to memory page size; SGL descriptor formats; queue memory must be physically contiguous when CAP.CQR (Contiguous Queues Required) is set verified
Normative (PCIe)Memory request formats, 32- vs 64-bit addressing headers; requests must not cross a 4 KiB address boundary verified
OptionalSGL support (advertised in Identify Controller); ATS/PRI; IOMMU itself
Implementation-dependentIOMMU page-table format, IOTLB size, whether passthrough mode is used, bounce-buffer policy
Version-dependentSGL feature details and requirements across NVMe revisions; Linux DMA API internals

1B.7 Hardware view

  • Must participate: device DMA engine, PCIe link, root complex, memory controller, DRAM.
  • May participate: IOMMU and its IOTLB; device-side ATC (Address Translation Cache) if ATS is used; switches; inter-socket links.
  • Observable: TLP addresses and lengths on the link; IOMMU fault logs; kernel DMA debug output (CONFIG_DMA_API_DEBUG on test kernels).
  • Unobservable without special tools: IOTLB hits/misses, cache snoop behaviour, device-internal DMA queues.

1B.8 Protocol view

OperationRequesterTLPCompletionOrdering note
Device reads host memory (SQE, PRP list, write data)DeviceMRd (32- or 64-bit address)One or more CplD; large reads may be split into multiple completions on Read Completion BoundaryMultiple outstanding reads distinguished by tag
Device writes host memory (read data, CQE, MSI-X)DeviceMWrNone (posted)Default ordering keeps data writes ahead of the later CQE write
Host-to-device MMIORoot complexMWr / MRdFor MRd onlyUnrelated to DMA ordering
Failed DMA readDeviceMRdCpl with UR/CA, or completion timeout at the deviceDevice must report error (NVMe status / AER)

Candidates: IOTLB misses on scattered 4 KiB mappings, remote-NUMA memory, memory bandwidth contention. Disambiguate: repeat with IOMMU in passthrough mode on a test box; repeat with huge-page buffers; pin the workload to the device's node.

Synthetic trace G — failed: DMA write to an unmapped IOVA
tSourceEventNote
0.0 µslink ↑MWr to 0x0000_0000_FFFF_F000, 64 DWread data from SSD
0.0 µsIOMMUNo translation → write blocked, fault recordeddevice unaware (posted)
0.4 µslink ↑MWr CQE: status successcontroller believes data delivered
+mskernel logIOMMU/DMAR fault: write, device 01:00.0, address 0xfffff000 (paraphrased)evidence

The application gets “success” and a buffer of stale bytes. The first bad event is the address in the PRP entry; root cause is either the driver (wrong/expired mapping) or the controller (computed a wrong address, e.g. mis-handled a PRP offset). Compare the fetched SQE/PRP list bytes in the capture with the faulting address.

Synthetic trace H — ambiguous: data and CQE close together after a timeout
tSourceEventNote
0 shostRead CID 0x1A submitted
30 shostTimeout; Abort issued; driver later resets controller and unmaps buffershost gave up
30.002 slink ↑MWr data to old IOVA of CID 0x1Alate data
30.003 slink ↑CQE CID 0x1A, status: Command Abort Requested

Ambiguous because whether the late write landed harmlessly (IOVA unmapped → blocked), harmfully (IOVA reused → corruption) or correctly (still mapped) depends on timing the trace alone does not show. You need the IOMMU fault log and the driver's unmap timestamps to decide.

1B.11 Labs

🧪 Lab 1B.1 (beginner) — Is my IOMMU on? SAFE

Objective: determine translation mode for your NVMe device. Procedure: run the Linux-view commands above. Questions: which IOMMU (if any)? which group type? Expected reasoning: group type “DMA”/“DMA-FQ” → translated; “identity” → passthrough; no groups → IOMMU disabled or absent.

Solution

Answers are platform-specific. Many distributions default to translated mode on some platforms and passthrough on others impl. Record it — it matters for every performance and fault analysis later.

Extension: find the other devices in the same IOMMU group and explain why grouping matters for device assignment to VMs.

🧪 Lab 1B.2 (intermediate) — Predict the PRP layout SAFE

Objective: apply page rules. Setup: paper. Memory page size 4 KiB. For each case give PRP1, PRP2 meaning: (a) 4 KiB buffer at offset 0; (b) 8 KiB buffer at offset 0; (c) 8 KiB buffer starting at offset 0x200 in its first page; (d) 64 KiB at offset 0.

Solution

(a) PRP1 = page address, PRP2 unused. (b) PRP1 = page 1, PRP2 = page 2 address (exactly two pages). (c) The data spans three pages (3.5 KiB + 4 KiB + 0.5 KiB): PRP1 = page1+0x200, PRP2 = pointer to a PRP list with two entries. (d) 16 pages: PRP1 = page 1, PRP2 = pointer to a PRP list with 15 entries. Full PRP rules are in Part XII. derived

Extension: how many PRP-list entries fit in one 4 KiB list page, and what happens when more are needed?

🧪 Lab 1B.3 (advanced) — IOMMU cost on throughput CAUTION

Objective: measure translation overhead. Setup: dedicated test box, a spare NVMe namespace or file, ability to change kernel boot parameters. Procedure: run fio --name=r --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=64 --numjobs=4 --direct=1 --runtime=60 --time_based --readonly with IOMMU translated mode and with passthrough. Record IOPS, mean and p99 latency, CPU usage.

⚠️ Warning

Use --readonly and a non-system device. Changing IOMMU modes affects every device on the machine; do not do it on a production host.

Solution

Differences range from negligible to significant depending on platform, IOTLB behaviour and mapping strategy impl. The skill is attributing a difference to translation by changing exactly one variable.

Extension: repeat with 128 KiB blocks and explain why the relative cost changes.

🧪 Lab 1B.4 (senior forensic) — Who produced the bad address? SAFE

Setup: synthetic evidence. The SQE fetched for CID 0x33 (Read, 10 KiB = 2 KiB + 4 KiB + 4 KiB across three pages) contains PRP1 = 0x3_1000_0800, PRP2 = 0x3_2000_0000 (list). The list contains 0x3_1100_0000, 0x3_1200_0000. The IOMMU logs a write fault at 0x3_1000_1800.

Question: driver bug or controller bug?

Solution

With PRP1 offset 0x800, the first page holds only 0x800 bytes (0x800–0xFFF); the controller must then move to the first list entry. A write to 0x3_1000_1800 means the controller kept incrementing linearly past the end of the first page instead of following the PRP list — a controller PRP-offset handling bug (confidence medium-high, pending confirmation that the driver's mapping for page 1 really is a single 4 KiB page). The driver's structures were correct per the PRP rules.

Extension: design a validation test that would have caught this before shipping (unaligned PRP1 offsets × transfer sizes).

1B.13 Interview questions

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is DMA?
    Model answer

    A device reading/writing system memory directly as a bus master, without the CPU copying each byte.

  2. Beginner Why can't a device use a virtual address?
    Model answer

    Virtual addresses are translated by the CPU's MMU with per-process page tables the device cannot access.

  3. Beginner What is pinning?
    Model answer

    Preventing pages from being moved or swapped while a device may access them.

  4. Beginner What is an IOMMU?
    Model answer

    Hardware that translates and permission-checks device memory accesses.

  5. Beginner Is a CQE write a DMA?
    Model answer

    Yes — a device-initiated Memory Write into host memory.

  6. Intermediate Coherent vs streaming DMA mappings?
    Model answer

    Coherent: long-lived, shared by CPU and device concurrently (queues). Streaming: per-transfer, ownership handed to device then back (data buffers).

  7. Intermediate Why do PRP lists exist?
    Model answer

    To describe buffers spanning more pages than PRP1/PRP2 can directly, since buffers are physically scattered.

  8. Intermediate What is a bounce buffer and when is it used?
    Model answer

    A reachable intermediate buffer used when the device cannot access the real buffer (addressing limits, encrypted guest memory); costs a copy.

  9. Intermediate Why must PCIe memory requests not cross 4 KiB boundaries?
    Model answer

    It is a PCIe rule for requests; DMA engines split transfers at 4 KiB address boundaries, which also matches page granularity.

  10. Intermediate What happens to a posted write blocked by the IOMMU?
    Model answer

    Typically dropped and logged by the host; the device generally receives no indication impl.

  11. Advanced What is ATS?
    Model answer

    Address Translation Services: a device can request translations from the IOMMU and cache them in its own ATC, then issue pre-translated requests.

  12. Advanced How does an IOTLB miss show up in a trace?
    Model answer

    Indirectly — as longer latency for some MRd completions; the walk itself is not on the PCIe link.

  13. Advanced Why are reset paths dangerous for DMA?
    Model answer

    The device may still DMA after the host considers commands dead; memory must not be freed/reused until DMA has provably stopped.

  14. Advanced What does CAP.CQR imply?
    Model answer

    Contiguous Queues Required: I/O queues must be physically contiguous in memory (no PRP-list-based queues).

  15. Advanced Why is the low part of an address the same in VA and PA?
    Model answer

    Translation replaces only the page number; the in-page offset is preserved.

  16. Senior Silent corruption on a fleet — how do you start?
    Model answer

    Characterise the corruption (size, alignment, content source), correlate with resets/timeouts, enable IOMMU to convert silent wrong writes into faults, collect fault addresses, map to commands.

  17. Senior How would you validate a controller's PRP engine?
    Model answer

    Sweep PRP1 offsets × sizes × list chaining, random page placements, above-4 GiB addresses, IOMMU-on fault detection, compare captured addresses with expected ones.

  18. Senior Passthrough IOMMU in production: pros/cons?
    Model answer

    Pro: lower overhead. Con: no protection from errant DMA, harder to detect device addressing bugs, security exposure to malicious devices.

  19. Senior Device reports Data Transfer Error. Host or device?
    Model answer

    Check whether the device received UR/CA/timeouts for its DMA reads (host side) versus internal errors; AER on both ends and capture discriminate.

  20. Senior How would you design the abort/reset path to be DMA-safe?
    Model answer

    Quiesce the controller (disable, or reset with confirmation via CSTS), optionally clear Bus Master Enable, only then unmap/free buffers; never reuse IOVAs before quiescence.

1B.14 Teach-back

  • To a child: why must the family promise not to change rooms before the delivery robot arrives?
  • To a junior engineer: walk through pin → map → PRP → DMA → unmap for one read.
  • To a senior engineer: argue whether IOMMU translation should be mandatory on storage servers.
✅ Mastery gate — Module 1B
  • I can explain virtual, physical and DMA addresses and when each is used.
  • I can draw Figure 1B.1 and the steps of a mapped read.
  • I can locate the DMA addresses of a command in a trace and match data TLPs to PRP entries.
  • I can debug an IOMMU fault and a late-DMA corruption scenario.
  • I can distinguish MMIO from DMA, pinning from mapping, and coherent from streaming.
  • I can cite which documents govern PRP/SGL (NVMe), memory requests (PCIe) and IOMMU behaviour (platform).

1C Chapter 1 Wrap-Up — Views, Lab, Quiz and Gate

← 1B Deep Dive — DMA and Address Translation2 What Is Storage? →

Specification view

Chapter 1 concepts are mostly general computer architecture and are not defined by NVMe. Where NVMe relies on them, it names them precisely: controller registers and their offsets (NVMe Base 2.4, register map specifics in NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4), memory page size via CC.MPS, PRP/SGL data pointers, queue base addresses, interrupt vectors associated with CQs. PCIe defines the transaction types, posted/non-posted semantics, Bus Master Enable and interrupt capabilities. version Always check the revision you are working to.

Protocol view — the five transactions you will see forever

PurposeTLPInitiatorDirectionPosted?
Doorbell / register writeMWrHostDownstreamYes
Register readMRd → CplDHostDown, then upNo
Command / PRP list / write-data fetchMRd → CplDDeviceUp, then downNo
Read data / CQEMWrDeviceUpstreamYes
MSI/MSI-X interruptMWrDeviceUpstreamYes

Worked example — counting TLPs for one 4 KiB read

Assume Max_Payload_Size = 256 bytes, Max_Read_Request_Size irrelevant for a read command (the device writes), PRP1 only, one MSI-X vector, no coalescing. derived

  1. Doorbell: 1 MWr down.
  2. SQE fetch: 1 MRd up (64 B), 1 CplD down (64 B, possibly split by the root complex — typically not for 64 B).
  3. Data: 4096 / 256 = 16 MWr up.
  4. CQE: 1 MWr up (16 B).
  5. Interrupt: 1 MWr up (4 B).
  6. CQ head doorbell: 1 MWr down.

Total ≈ 21 TLPs: 3 host-initiated, 18 device-initiated (plus 1 completion). Data efficiency: each 256-byte data TLP carries roughly 20–30 bytes of framing, header, sequence number and LCRC overhead on Gen3–5 derived, so about 90% of link bytes in the data phase are payload. Doubling MPS to 512 B halves the data TLP count and nudges efficiency upward.

Code — a tiny simulation of a queue, doorbell and DMA

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Toy model: host memory, a submission queue, a doorbell, a 'device' that DMAs.
Runs anywhere; touches no hardware. Teaches who owns what, and when."""
MEM = bytearray(1 << 16)             # 64 KiB of pretend host memory
SQ_BASE, SQ_ENTRIES, SQE = 0x1000, 8, 64
DATA_BASE = 0x8000
sq_tail_doorbell = 0                   # lives "in the device" (MMIO register)

def host_submit(slot, opcode, lba, buf):
    sqe = bytearray(SQE)
    sqe[0] = opcode                     # CDW0 byte 0: opcode
    sqe[24:32] = buf.to_bytes(8, "little")   # PRP1 at bytes 24-31
    sqe[40:48] = lba.to_bytes(8, "little")   # CDW10-11: starting LBA (NVM Read)
    MEM[SQ_BASE + slot*SQE : SQ_BASE + (slot+1)*SQE] = sqe   # 1) write SQE in host memory
    return (slot + 1) % SQ_ENTRIES                           # 2) new tail for the doorbell

class Device:
    def __init__(self): self.head = 0; self.media = {7: b"HELLO-NVMe".ljust(64, b".")}
    def doorbell(self, tail):                # 3) host MMIO write lands here
        while self.head != tail:
            sqe = MEM[SQ_BASE + self.head*SQE : SQ_BASE + (self.head+1)*SQE]   # 4) DMA read (fetch)
            prp1 = int.from_bytes(sqe[24:32], "little")
            lba  = int.from_bytes(sqe[40:48], "little")
            if sqe[0] == 0x02:               # Read
                MEM[prp1:prp1+64] = self.media.get(lba, bytes(64))           # 5) DMA write (data)
            self.head = (self.head + 1) % SQ_ENTRIES

dev = Device()
sq_tail_doorbell = host_submit(0, 0x02, 7, DATA_BASE)
dev.doorbell(sq_tail_doorbell)
print(bytes(MEM[DATA_BASE:DATA_BASE+16]))   # b'HELLO-NVMe......'

The model is deliberately incomplete (no completion queue, no phase tag, no interrupt). Lab 1.1 asks you to add them.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing CPU registers with device registers.
  • Putting a virtual address where a DMA address belongs.
  • Assuming an interrupt means success.
  • Assuming KB = KiB, or that a 0's-based field holds the real count.
  • Believing the SSD “receives” commands — it fetches them.
  • Treating an all-ones register value as real data.
  • Forgetting the barrier between writing an SQE and ringing the doorbell.

Debugging connection

Every NVMe failure investigation later in this book starts with three Chapter 1 questions: Who was supposed to act? (host CPU, device, IOMMU, link) At which address? (which space, which mapping) Was the action posted or non-posted? (does a missing response mean failure, or is no response expected?). Answering these three correctly eliminates most wrong hypotheses before you open a single specification.

💡 Senior insight

Juniors look for the error message. Seniors look for the first deviation from expected behaviour, which is usually silent: a doorbell with no fetch, a fetch with wrong bytes, a data write to an address no PRP entry named. Error messages are almost always downstream consequences. Train yourself now to ask “what should have happened next, and did it?”

Lab 1.1 — the first lab of the book

🧪 Lab 1.1 — Meet your NVMe device from the outside in SAFE

Objective: connect every Chapter 1 concept to an observable artefact on your own machine, and extend the toy model.

Setup: Linux with pciutils and nvme-cli; an NVMe SSD (or a QEMU guest with -device nvme). Python 3 for part B. All commands are read-only.

Part A — steps:

lspci -nn -d ::0108                              # 1. find the function and its class code
lspci -tv                                        # 2. where it sits in the tree
sudo lspci -vv -s <BDF> | grep -E "Control|Region|MSI-X|LnkCap|LnkSta"   # 3. decode/DMA/link
lspci -k -s <BDF>                               # 4. which driver claimed it
sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H | head -40      # 5. CAP, VS, CC, CSTS
grep nvme /proc/interrupts                       # 6. interrupt vectors and CPUs
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:<BDF>/numa_node    # 7. NUMA locality
sudo nvme list                                   # 8. controllers and namespaces

Observations to record: class code; BAR0 address and size; Mem+/BusMaster+; MSI-X vector count; link speed/width (capability vs status); CAP.MQES, CAP.DSTRD, CAP.TO; CC.EN, CSTS.RDY; number of nvme interrupt lines; NUMA node.

Part B — extend the simulation: add a 4-entry completion queue with 16-byte entries, a phase tag that flips each time the queue wraps, a CQE carrying the command identifier and SQ head, and an “interrupt” callback. Make the host consume completions by checking the phase bit, not by counting.

Questions:

  1. Is your link running at its capable speed and width? If not, why might that be?
  2. How many interrupt vectors are in use versus available? Relate this to your CPU count.
  3. From CAP.DSTRD, compute the doorbell address for I/O SQ 1 and CQ 1.
  4. In your simulation, what goes wrong if the host reads a CQE slot before the device has written it, and how does the phase bit prevent it?
Solution

1. LnkSta below LnkCap can be normal (power saving at idle on some platforms, or a slot wired narrower) or a sign of signal-integrity problems; compare under load and check the slot's wiring impl. 2. Linux typically creates one I/O queue (and vector) per CPU up to the device's limits, plus the admin vector; fewer vectors than CPUs means queues are shared. 3. SQ1 tail = BAR0 + 1000h + 2 × (4 << DSTRD); CQ1 head = BAR0 + 1000h + 3 × (4 << DSTRD); with DSTRD = 0: BAR0+1008h and BAR0+100Ch. 4. Without a phase bit, stale entries from the previous lap look valid; the host compares the entry's phase with its expected phase (which starts at 1 and flips on each wrap), so old entries are ignored.

# Sketch of the completion side (add to the toy model)
CQ_BASE, CQ_ENTRIES, CQE = 0x2000, 4, 16
class CQ:
    def __init__(s): s.tail = 0; s.phase = 1          # device-side producer state
    def post(s, cid, sqhd, status=0):
        e = bytearray(CQE)
        e[8:10]  = sqhd.to_bytes(2, "little")          # DW2: SQ head pointer
        e[12:14] = cid.to_bytes(2, "little")           # DW3 bits 15:0: command identifier
        e[14:16] = ((status << 1) | s.phase).to_bytes(2, "little")  # DW3 bit 16 = phase
        MEM[CQ_BASE + s.tail*CQE : CQ_BASE + (s.tail+1)*CQE] = e
        s.tail += 1
        if s.tail == CQ_ENTRIES: s.tail, s.phase = 0, s.phase ^ 1
host_head, host_phase = 0, 1
def host_poll():
    global host_head, host_phase
    e = MEM[CQ_BASE + host_head*CQE : CQ_BASE + (host_head+1)*CQE]
    if (int.from_bytes(e[14:16], "little") & 1) != host_phase: return None   # not new
    host_head += 1
    if host_head == CQ_ENTRIES: host_head, host_phase = 0, host_phase ^ 1
    return int.from_bytes(e[12:14], "little")                              # CID

Extension: make the device complete commands out of order and confirm the host still matches completions by CID.

Quiz — Chapter 1

  1. How many bytes are in an NVMe submission queue entry and a completion queue entry?

    Answer

    64 and 16 bytes.

  2. What is 0x1000 in decimal, and what NVMe register region starts at that offset?

    Answer

    4096; the doorbell registers.

  3. A drive is sold as 2 TB. Approximately how many GiB will a binary-reporting tool show?

    Answer

    2 × 1012 / 230 ≈ 1,863 GiB.

  4. Why is a register read on the I/O fast path a performance problem?

    Answer

    Reads are non-posted; the core stalls for the full round trip (often ~1 µs), wasting thousands of cycles per access.

  5. Name the three address kinds involved in a DMA from a user buffer.

    Answer

    Virtual (user), physical, and device-visible DMA address/IOVA.

  6. Which PCI Command register bit must be set before a device can DMA?

    Answer

    Bus Master Enable.

  7. What does a CPU see when it reads a register of a device whose link is down?

    Answer

    Typically all ones (e.g. FFFFFFFFh), synthesised by the platform after the failed request impl.

  8. True or false: an MSI-X interrupt is a special wire.

    Answer

    False — it is a posted Memory Write TLP to an address programmed by the OS.

  9. What NVMe class code identifies an NVMe controller?

    Answer

    Base class 01h, sub-class 08h, programming interface 02h.

  10. Why do PRP lists exist?

    Answer

    Because a virtually contiguous buffer may be physically scattered, so the device needs a list of page addresses.

  11. What is a 0's-based value? Give the real count for MQES = 0x3FF.

    Answer

    A field storing count − 1; 0x3FF means 1024 entries.

  12. Compute raw per-direction bandwidth of a PCIe Gen4 x4 link.

    Answer

    16 GT/s × 4 × 128/130 ÷ 8 ≈ 7.88 GB/s.

  13. Why must a barrier be placed between writing an SQE and writing the doorbell?

    Answer

    So the SQE contents are visible to the device before it is told to fetch them.

  14. What is the difference between polling and interrupts?

    Answer

    Polling repeatedly checks for completion (low latency, CPU cost); interrupts notify the CPU asynchronously (efficient, adds handling latency).

  15. Which component translates device-visible addresses to physical addresses?

    Answer

    The IOMMU (when enabled).

Interview questions — Chapter 1

  1. Beginner Explain DMA to a non-engineer.
    Model answer

    The storage device copies data straight into the computer's memory by itself, so the processor doesn't have to carry every byte.

  2. Beginner What does a device driver do?
    Model answer

    It configures and operates a specific kind of device and presents it to the OS through a standard interface.

  3. Intermediate Walk me through what happens between read() and the data arriving.
    Model answer

    Syscall → filesystem maps offset to LBA → block layer request → driver builds SQE with DMA addresses → barrier + doorbell → device fetches SQE → reads media → DMAs data → posts CQE → MSI-X → ISR consumes CQE, rings CQ head doorbell → request completes → syscall returns.

  4. Advanced Why did NVMe avoid register reads in the submission path?
    Model answer

    MMIO reads are non-posted and stall the CPU for a round trip; at millions of IOPS they would consume whole cores. Doorbell writes are posted and cheap.

  5. Senior An SSD returns success but the data is wrong. Where do you look?
    Model answer

    Characterise corruption; check for resets/timeouts; enable IOMMU to catch stray DMA; capture SQE/PRP and data TLP addresses; check end-to-end protection info if available; distinguish media/FTL corruption (wrong data at right address) from DMA corruption (right data at wrong address).

Teach-back challenge

Without looking, explain the busy-school story to a friend, then retell it replacing every story word with its real name. Then explain to a colleague why “the device writes completions and interrupts into memory” is the key to understanding NVMe traces.

Chapter summary

  • A computer is a collection of workers moving information: cores compute, memory holds, devices specialise, buses connect.
  • Addresses only make sense inside an address space; devices use DMA addresses, not virtual addresses.
  • Device registers have side effects; reads are expensive, writes are posted.
  • Drivers set up devices through registers; devices then do the bulk work by DMA and report via interrupts, which are themselves memory writes.
  • Every later NVMe/PCIe concept is a structured use of these primitives.

Further reading

  • Linux kernel documentation: “Dynamic DMA mapping Guide” and “DMA API” (Documentation/core-api/).
  • Linux kernel documentation on PCI drivers (Documentation/PCI/).
  • NVM Express Base Specification Rev. 2.4 and NVMe over PCIe Transport Rev. 1.4 — controller registers and initialisation (nvmexpress.org).
  • Your CPU vendor's IOMMU architecture specification (Intel VT-d, AMD IOMMU, Arm SMMU).
  • Any computer-architecture textbook chapters on memory hierarchy and virtual memory.

  • I can convert hex/binary/decimal and handle KB vs KiB and 0's-based values without errors.
  • I can draw the host architecture and the DMA translation chain from memory.
  • I can list the TLPs for one 4 KiB NVMe read and say which are posted.

PART II

Storage Fundamentals

We walk down the corridor and open the library door. Spinning disks, the interfaces built for them, flash memory and the hidden machinery — the Flash Translation Layer, garbage collection, wear leveling — that makes flash behave like a disk. By the end you will know exactly why a new interface was needed, and which parts of an SSD's behaviour no interface will ever show you.

2 What Is Storage?

← 1C Chapter 1 Wrap-Up — Views, Lab, Quiz and Gate3 From SATA/SAS to NVMe →

Why this chapter exists

An NVMe trace tells you when the device answered. It never tells you why it took 80 µs one time and 9 ms the next. The why is inside the SSD: NAND page reads, program and erase operations, garbage collection, a full write buffer, a read retry on a weak cell. A protocol engineer who does not understand the media will misattribute media behaviour to the protocol — and spend weeks hunting a PCIe bug that is really garbage collection.

Learning objectives

  • Explain how HDDs and SSDs store data and why their performance profiles differ by orders of magnitude.
  • Compare SATA, SAS and NVMe at the level of link, command set and queueing.
  • Explain NAND pages, blocks, planes, dies and channels and why erase-before-write forces an FTL.
  • Compute write amplification, endurance (TBW/DWPD), over-provisioning, IOPS↔throughput and use Little's law.
  • Convert namespace sizes from logical blocks to bytes and handle KB/KiB/GB/GiB exactly.
  • Interpret NVMe SMART data-unit counters using their defined units.
  • Separate host-visible protocol behaviour from implementation-dependent media behaviour.

Prerequisites

Chapter 1, especially §1.2 bits and bytes (units), §1.3 memory (hierarchy) and §1.11 controllers.

Story

🧒 Kid analogy — two libraries

The old library keeps its books on a giant spinning record player. To read a page, a robot arm swings to the right ring and waits for the right spot to spin round. It is cheap and enormous, but every new page means waiting for the arm and the spin.

The new library keeps its words in millions of tiny jars of marbles. Reading a jar is quick. But there is a strange rule: you can only fill an empty jar, and you can only empty jars a whole shelf at a time. So when you want to change a word, the librarian writes the new word into a fresh jar somewhere else, crosses out the old jar in a big index book, and later — during quiet time — copies the still-good jars off a messy shelf so the whole shelf can be emptied. Also, each jar wears out after being emptied too many times, so the librarian spreads the work around evenly.

🌍 Real-world analogy

An SSD is like a hotel with a strict rule that rooms can only be cleaned floor by floor. Guests (data) who “change rooms” are simply given a new room; the front desk (FTL) updates its register; housekeeping (garbage collection) periodically moves the remaining guests off a mostly-empty floor so the whole floor can be cleaned (erased). A hotel that keeps spare floors (over-provisioning) never makes guests wait while housekeeping works.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Hotels do not have rooms that wear out after a few thousand cleanings, nor rooms whose contents slowly fade (NAND charge leakage/retention). And the front desk register in a real SSD is itself data that must survive sudden power loss — a hard engineering problem the analogy hides.

Beginner explanation

Storage is where data lives when the power is off. The host does not see platters or flash cells; it sees a numbered array of fixed-size logical blocks (typically 512 bytes or 4 KiB), addressed by Logical Block Address (LBA) 0, 1, 2, … The device's job is to make that simple array fast and durable, whatever the media underneath.

2.1 HDD — the hard disk drive

An HDD stores bits as magnetic orientation on spinning platters. A head on an actuator arm moves to a track (seek), waits for the sector to rotate under it (rotational latency) and then transfers data. Every random access pays mechanical time:

taccess ≈ tseek + trot + txfer, trot,avg = ½ × 60 / RPM
  • tseek — head movement time, several ms average impl
  • trot,avg — average rotational wait in seconds: half a revolution
  • RPM — spindle speed (5,400 / 7,200 / 10,000 / 15,000)
  • txfer — media transfer time, tiny for 4 KiB

For 7,200 RPM: trot,avg = 0.5 × 60/7200 = 4.17 ms. With ~8 ms seek, a random 4 KiB access takes ~12 ms → ~80 random IOPS per disk derived. Sequential transfer, by contrast, can reach a few hundred MB/s because no seeks are needed. HDDs therefore love sequential I/O and hate random I/O; an HDD with queue depth 32 helps a little because the drive can reorder commands to shorten head travel (that is what Native Command Queuing was for).

Misconception: “Interface speed limits an HDD.” A single HDD cannot saturate even a 3 Gb/s SATA link on random I/O; mechanics dominate.

2.2 SATA — Serial ATA

SATA (Serial AT Attachment) replaced parallel ATA in the early 2000s for consumer and many enterprise drives. Key facts:

  • Link rates 1.5, 3.0 and 6.0 Gb/s (SATA I/II/III), 8b/10b encoding → 6 Gb/s carries at most 600 MB/s of raw data, ~550 MB/s achievable after protocol overhead derived.
  • Half-duplex at the protocol level: one frame direction at a time per link.
  • Uses the ATA command set (READ FPDMA QUEUED, WRITE FPDMA QUEUED for NCQ).
  • NCQ (Native Command Queuing): up to 32 outstanding commands per device (tag 0–31) verified.
  • Host side normally uses an AHCI (Advanced Host Controller Interface) controller, a PCI device that bridges system memory to SATA ports (Chapter 3).

For HDDs, SATA was more than enough. For SSDs, the 600 MB/s ceiling was reached by mainstream SATA SSDs within a few years — the ceiling, not the flash, became the limit.

2.3 SAS — Serial Attached SCSI

SAS carries the SCSI command set over serial links and targets enterprise systems:

  • Link rates 3, 6, 12 Gb/s and “24G” SAS (22.5 Gbaud with a more efficient encoding) version.
  • Full-duplex; dual-port drives connect to two controllers for high availability.
  • Expanders allow hundreds of drives behind one HBA; SAS controllers can also attach SATA drives.
  • Rich SCSI features: deep command queues per device (depth is device- and HBA-dependent impl), task management, protection information (T10 PI), mature error recovery.

SAS SSDs exist and are fast, but each I/O still traverses an HBA, its firmware and a SCSI protocol stack. NVMe adopted several SAS-world ideas (dual-port, end-to-end protection information, reservations) while removing the HBA in the middle.

PropertySATASASNVMe over PCIe
Command setATASCSINVMe (designed for NVM)
Host controllerAHCI HBASAS HBA / RAID controllerNone — controller is in the SSD
Typical max link per device6 Gb/s12 / 22.5 Gb/s per portPCIe x4: ~3.9 GB/s (Gen3) … ~15.8 GB/s (Gen5)
DuplexHalfFullFull
Queues × depth1 × 32 (NCQ)Device/HBA-dependentUp to ~64 K × ~64 K
Dual-portNoYesYes (multi-port / multi-controller subsystems)
Typical use todayConsumer, boot, bulk HDDEnterprise HDD and legacy SSDMost SSDs, client to hyperscale

2.4 SSD — solid-state drive

An SSD has no moving parts: a controller system-on-chip (Figure 1.4), NAND flash packages, usually DRAM for the mapping table and buffers (or a Host Memory Buffer borrowed from host DRAM on DRAM-less designs), power-loss protection capacitors on enterprise drives, and a host interface. Form factors include 2.5-inch, M.2, U.2/U.3 and the EDSFF family (E1.S, E1.L, E3.S, E3.L).

The SSD's essential trick is parallelism. A single NAND die is not fast — one page read takes tens of microseconds — but an SSD contains dozens to hundreds of dies operating at once. The controller's job is to keep them all busy. Feeding that parallelism needs many commands in flight, which an interface with a single 32-deep queue cannot supply efficiently.

The picture below is the map for the rest of this chapter. Commands arrive over PCIe at the controller; the FTL decides where each logical block lives; the ECC engine protects every page; and the flash interface spreads the work over channels and dies. Sections 2.5–2.12 zoom into each box.

HostSSD controller and NANDSSD-internal memoryPCIe link

2.5 NAND flash

A NAND cell stores charge in a floating gate or charge-trap layer; the stored charge shifts the cell's threshold voltage, which the read circuitry senses against reference voltages. Storing more bits per cell means distinguishing more voltage levels:

TypeBits/cellVoltage statesRelative read/program speedTypical endurance (P/E cycles)
SLC12Fastest~tens of thousands to 100 K
MLC24Fast~3 K–10 K
TLC38Medium~1 K–3 K
QLC416Slower, especially program~hundreds to ~1 K+

Endurance and speed values are broad industry ranges impl; they vary by vendor, generation and how the controller manages the cells. Modern NAND is 3D: hundreds of layers of cells stacked vertically. Many SSDs also run part of their TLC/QLC NAND in SLC mode as a fast write cache — which is why a long sustained write can suddenly slow down when that cache fills.

🔧 Hardware — why bits fade

Charge leaks over time (retention), reading neighbours disturbs cells (read disturb), and each program/erase cycle damages the oxide (wear). The controller fights back with strong ECC, read-retry with shifted reference voltages, periodic refresh (rewriting data), and wear leveling. All of this is invisible to NVMe — except as latency outliers and, eventually, SMART statistics.

2.6 NAND pages

A page is the smallest unit NAND can program (write) and the usual unit it reads. Modern page sizes are commonly 16 KiB of data plus a spare area for ECC and metadata impl. Constraints: a page can be programmed only when erased; within a block, pages are typically programmed in order; a programmed page cannot be partially rewritten.

Consequence: when the host writes 4 KiB, the controller must buffer and combine writes to fill pages (and often multiple planes' pages at once), and a 4 KiB host overwrite cannot modify the old page in place.

2.7 NAND blocks

A block (erase block) is the smallest unit that can be erased, containing hundreds to thousands of pages — block sizes in modern 3D NAND are many MiB impl. Erase is slow (milliseconds) and each erase wears the block. This mismatch — write in pages, erase in blocks — is the single most important fact about flash. It is the reason the FTL, garbage collection, write amplification and over-provisioning exist.

2.8 Channels

A channel is an independent bus between the controller and a group of NAND packages, using a NAND interface standard (ONFI or Toggle) at a rate measured in MT/s. Controllers commonly have 4 to 16 channels impl. Data transfers on different channels proceed in parallel; on one channel, transfers to different dies are time-multiplexed.

2.9 Dies

A die (often called a LUN in NAND interface terminology — not to be confused with a SCSI LUN) is the unit that executes array operations independently. While die 0 is busy for tens of microseconds sensing a page, the channel can be used to send commands to or move data from die 1. This die interleaving is the main source of SSD parallelism.

2.10 Planes

A die is split into planes (commonly 2 to 6 impl), each with its own page buffer. Multi-plane operations read or program one page in each plane at once, multiplying a die's throughput — subject to addressing restrictions defined by the NAND vendor.

PNAND = channels × dies per channel × planes per die
  • PNAND — maximum number of page operations that can be in progress simultaneously (an upper bound)

Example: 8 channels × 4 dies × 4 planes = 128 page operations in flight. If a page read (tR) takes ~50 µs and a page is 16 KiB, the array-side read bound is 128 × 16 KiB / 50 µs ≈ 42 GB/s — far above a PCIe Gen4 x4 link (~7.9 GB/s), so the link, channel transfer rates, ECC throughput or firmware become the limit instead derived (numbers synthetic). The crucial engineering point: to keep 128 operations busy with 4 KiB random reads, the host must keep enough commands outstanding — a queue depth of 1 uses only one die at a time.

2.11 Flash Translation Layer (FTL)

The FTL is controller firmware (often with hardware assists) that makes NAND look like a rewritable block device. Its core is the logical-to-physical (L2P) map: for each logical unit (commonly 4 KiB), where its current copy lives (channel, die, plane, block, page, offset).

  • On write: data goes into an open (erased) page, the map entry is updated to the new location, the old location is marked invalid (stale).
  • On read: look up the map, read the physical page, run ECC, return data.
  • On deallocate/trim (NVMe Dataset Management with the Deallocate attribute): the map entry is removed, the old copy becomes invalid without new writes — making garbage collection cheaper.

Here is an overwrite step by step, including the garbage collection it eventually causes (Section 2.12). Pages are shown as 8 per block to keep the picture small; real blocks have hundreds to thousands. Click a step to follow it. synthetic

Host starts itInside the SSD (FTL, never visible on PCIe)
  1. The host writes LBA 7 again

    LBA 7 already holds data "B", stored in block 12, page 3. The host now sends new data "B′" for the same LBA. The host only knows the LBA number; it never sees blocks or pages.

    Where: host → SSD (an NVMe Write command)PCIe: Yes. The command and data cross the link as in Chapter 40.
    Write LBA 7, 1 block, data = B′
  2. The FTL programs B′ into the next erased page

    NAND cannot rewrite page 3 of block 12 in place: a programmed page can only be changed by erasing its whole block. So the FTL puts B′ into the next erased page of the block it is currently filling (the "open" block): block 40, page 5.

    Where: Inside the SSD (NAND program)PCIe: No.
    Program B40·P5 ← B′ (hundreds of µs; often done later from the write cache)
  3. The map entry for LBA 7 is updated

    The logical-to-physical (L2P) map now points LBA 7 at the new location. Every later Read of LBA 7 goes to block 40, page 5.

    Where: L2P map in controller DRAM (saved to NAND periodically)PCIe: No.
    LBA 7: B12·P3 → B40·P5
  4. The old page is marked stale

    Block 12, page 3 still physically contains the old data B, but nothing points to it any more. The FTL marks it stale (invalid) and lowers block 12's count of valid pages. Nothing in the NAND itself changes in this step; it is bookkeeping.

    Where: FTL metadataPCIe: No.
    Block 12 valid pages: 2 → 1 (only LBA 5 left)
  5. Later: garbage collection copies the last valid page

    When free blocks run low, garbage collection picks a victim: a block with few valid pages. Block 12 has only one (LBA 5). GC copies it to a free block. This copy is extra NAND writing the host never asked for: write amplification.

    Where: Inside the SSD (NAND read + program)PCIe: No. The host cannot see GC, only its effect on latency.
    Copy B12·P1 → B77·P0 (LBA 5) Host wrote 1 page, NAND programmed 2 → WAF = 2 for this tiny example
  6. The map entry for LBA 5 is updated

    The moved data has a new home, so its map entry changes too. The host's LBA 5 is unchanged from its point of view.

    Where: L2P mapPCIe: No.
    LBA 5: B12·P1 → B77·P0
  7. Block 12 is erased and becomes free

    With no valid pages left, the whole block is erased (milliseconds, and one more program/erase cycle of wear) and returns to the pool of free blocks, ready to become a future open block.

    Where: NAND erasePCIe: No.
    Erase B12 → all 8 pages erased; P/E count of block 12 + 1
DRAML2P ≈ (C / G) × E
  • DRAML2P — memory needed for a flat page-level map
  • C — capacity in bytes
  • G — mapping granularity (e.g. 4 KiB)
  • E — bytes per entry (e.g. 4)

For 4 TB at 4 KiB granularity with 4-byte entries: 4×1012 / 4096 × 4 ≈ 3.9 GB — the origin of the rule of thumb “about 1 GB of DRAM per 1 TB of flash” derived. DRAM-less SSDs cache part of the map in SRAM and/or use the NVMe Host Memory Buffer (HMB) feature, borrowing host DRAM over PCIe. Some high-capacity drives use larger indirection units (e.g. 16 KiB or more) to shrink the map — which then makes small random writes more expensive impl.

2.12 Garbage collection (GC)

As data is overwritten, blocks accumulate invalid pages. To reclaim space, GC picks a victim block, copies its still-valid pages to a new location (consuming NAND bandwidth and causing extra writes), then erases the victim. GC competes with host I/O; when free blocks run low, host writes must wait for GC — producing the famous SSD write cliff and read tail-latency spikes.

WAF = NAND bytes written / host bytes written
  • WAF — write amplification factor, ≥ 1 without compression
  • NAND bytes written — includes host data, GC relocation, metadata, refresh
  • host bytes written — bytes the host asked to write

A simplified steady-state model for greedy GC under uniformly random overwrite: if a victim block is on average a fraction u valid, reclaiming it to free (1−u) of a block costs u of a block in copies, so WAF ≈ 1/(1−u) derived conceptual. More spare space → emptier victims → lower u → lower WAF. Sequential writes invalidate whole blocks together, giving WAF ≈ 1.

2.13 Wear leveling

Each block survives a limited number of program/erase (P/E) cycles. Dynamic wear leveling steers new writes to the least-worn free blocks. Static wear leveling also moves cold (rarely changed) data off low-wear blocks so those blocks can share the burden — at the cost of extra writes. The goal is that all blocks wear out at about the same time rather than a hot few failing early. NVMe exposes the consequence, not the mechanism: the SMART Percentage Used estimate and Available Spare.

2.14 Over-provisioning (OP)

OP = (physical NAND capacity − user capacity) / user capacity
  • physical NAND capacity — raw flash available for data (excluding ECC spare area)
  • user capacity — capacity exposed to the host

Example: 512 GiB of raw NAND (549.8 GB) sold as 512 GB → OP ≈ 7.4%, the “free” OP from the GiB/GB difference. Enterprise drives often expose 3.84 TB from ~4.4 TB of NAND (higher OP, more endurance, steadier latency) impl. Hosts can add effective OP by leaving space unwritten and deallocated, or by creating smaller namespaces.

2.15 Endurance

TBW ≈ (C × PE) / WAF · DWPD = TBW / (C × 365 × Y)
  • TBW — terabytes written (host writes) the drive is rated for
  • C — user capacity in TB
  • PE — rated program/erase cycles of the NAND
  • WAF — expected write amplification for the rating workload
  • DWPD — drive writes per day over the warranty
  • Y — warranty years

Example: 3.84 TB, 1 DWPD, 5 years → TBW = 3.84 × 365 × 5 ≈ 7,008 TB ≈ 7 PB derived. Vendors rate endurance against specified workloads (for example JEDEC client/enterprise workloads); a different workload yields a different WAF and different real endurance impl.

2.16 Latency

Latency is the time from submission to completion of one I/O. For an NVMe 4 KiB random read it decomposes roughly as:

ComponentOrder of magnitudeVisible where
Application + kernel submission path1–5 µsperf, bpftrace
Doorbell, command fetch over PCIe~1 µsAnalyzer
Controller processing, FTL lookupa few µsNot visible (inferred)
NAND array read (tR) + channel transfer + ECC~40–100 µs TLC; less for SLC-class mediaNot visible (inferred)
Data DMA + CQE + interrupt~1–2 µs for 4 KiBAnalyzer
Interrupt handling + completion to app1–5 µsperf, bpftrace

All values are typical orders of magnitude impl. Writes often complete faster than reads because the controller acknowledges them once data is in a protected buffer — until the buffer fills. Tail latency (p99, p99.9, p99.99) matters more than the average in real systems: a read that lands on a die busy programming or erasing can wait milliseconds unless the controller supports program/erase suspend impl.

2.17 IOPS

IOPS — I/O operations per second — measures how many commands complete per second, usually for small random I/O (4 KiB). It depends on queue depth, parallelism and latency, linked by Little's law:

L = λ × W ⇒ IOPS = QD / latency
  • L — average number of I/Os in the system (outstanding = effective queue depth, QD)
  • λ — throughput in I/Os per second (IOPS)
  • W — average time each I/O spends in the system (latency, in seconds)

Example: QD 1, 80 µs latency → 12,500 IOPS. QD 32 at the same latency → 400,000 IOPS, if the device has the parallelism to keep latency flat. When parallelism saturates, latency rises instead of IOPS — the knee of the curve. Little's law holds for averages in steady state; it says nothing about tails. It is previewed here and used heavily in Part XXVIII.

2.18 Throughput

Throughput = IOPS × I/O size
  • Throughput — bytes per second (state decimal MB/s or binary MiB/s explicitly)
  • IOPS — completed operations per second
  • I/O size — bytes per operation

Examples: 1,000,000 IOPS × 4 KiB = 4.096 GB/s (3.81 GiB/s); 7 GB/s at 128 KiB = ~53,400 IOPS derived. Small I/O is usually IOPS-bound (controller, CPU, interrupt rate); large I/O is bandwidth-bound (PCIe link, NAND channels). A Gen4 x4 drive cannot exceed ~7.9 GB/s raw link bandwidth whatever its IOPS.

Engineering explanation — the whole SSD in one model

 host cmd ─▶ NVMe front end ─▶ FTL ─▶ scheduler ─▶ ch0: die0 die1 die2 die3
 (LBA, len)  (queues, DMA)    (L2P)  (per-die    ch1: die0 die1 die2 die3
                                       queues)    ...
                               ▲                  chN: die0 die1 die2 die3
                               └── GC / wear leveling / refresh compete for the same dies

Host commands and background work share dies. Everything the host sees as “latency variance” is the result of this shared scheduling, which is implementation-dependent and not specified by NVMe.

Storage media reality — what the protocol does not expose

📭 What the spec does not say

The NVMe protocol defines the host-visible contract: logical blocks, commands, status, log pages, features. It generally does not expose or mandate: where an LBA is physically placed in NAND; the FTL mapping scheme or granularity; the garbage-collection algorithm or when it runs; the wear-leveling policy; the size of the write cache or SLC cache; how read retries are performed. Some features let the host influence placement or observe aggregates (for example Zoned Namespaces, Flexible Data Placement, Endurance Group and SMART log pages, predictable-latency features) version, but the mechanisms remain the vendor's.

Host-visible protocol behaviourInternal flash behaviour (generally hidden)
Command accepted, completed, status codeWhich die served it; whether it waited behind GC
Namespace size, LBA formatRaw NAND size, OP, block/page geometry
SMART: Percentage Used, Available Spare, Data Units Read/Written, Media and Data Integrity ErrorsPer-block P/E counts, retry rates, ECC margins
Deallocate (trim) acceptedWhen/if the mapping entries are actually discarded
Latency distribution (measurable)The causes of each outlier
🏭 Implementation-dependent

When you see a latency outlier in a trace, “the SSD was doing GC” is a hypothesis, not a finding. Support it with evidence: correlation with sustained writes, free-space level, deallocate history, vendor telemetry logs — or label it as uncertain.

Hardware view

Controller SoC with CPU cores, NVMe/PCIe front end, DMA, ECC engines, encryption, NAND channel controllers; DRAM (or HMB); NAND packages each holding several dies; power-loss-protection capacitors (enterprise); temperature sensors feeding thermal throttling. When temperature exceeds thresholds the controller slows itself — another non-protocol cause of performance changes, visible through SMART temperature fields and thermal-management features.

Specification view

NVMe Base 2.4 and NVM Command Set 1.3 define namespaces, logical block formats, the SMART / Health Information log page, Endurance Group information, and Dataset Management deallocate semantics version. Key well-established definitions you will use in this chapter's labs:

  • NSZE / NCAP / NUSE (Identify Namespace): namespace size, capacity and utilisation, all in logical blocks.
  • FLBAS selects the active LBA Format; each LBA format gives LBADS — the LBA data size as a power of two (9 → 512 B, 12 → 4096 B) — and the metadata size.
  • Data Units Read / Written (SMART log): reported in thousands of 512-byte units, i.e. a value of 1 = 1,000 × 512 bytes = 512,000 bytes, rounded up verified — confirm in your revision of the Base specification.

SPECIFICATION BASELINE: NVMe Base Specification 2.4; NVM Command Set 1.3. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: in NVMe 1.x the NVM command set and Identify Namespace fields were in the single base document; field names are stable but locations moved in the 2.0 refactor version.

Protocol view

From the link's perspective a 4 KiB read and a 4 KiB read that waited 5 ms behind an erase look identical except for the gap between command fetch and the first data write. The protocol transports the consequences of media behaviour as time. That is why latency histograms are the main window into the media.

Trace view

Synthetic trace — read tail latency during sustained random writes (host + PCIe correlated)
t (ms)EventCIDFetch → first data (µs)Note
0.000Read 4 KiB fetched0x010178normal
0.050Read 4 KiB fetched0x010281normal
0.120Write 128 KiB ×64 burst begins——background writer saturates
3.400Read 4 KiB fetched0x011096slightly elevated
3.900Read 4 KiB fetched0x01112,850outlier: die likely busy (program/erase/GC) uncertain
4.100Read 4 KiB fetched0x01123,120outlier
9.000Writes stop——
9.300Read 4 KiB fetched0x012080recovered

No PCIe error, no NVMe error — just time. The protocol is healthy; the media scheduler is the suspect.

Linux view

sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -E "^(mn|fr|tnvmcap|unvmcap|nn) "
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H | grep -E "nsze|ncap|nuse|flbas|LBA Format"
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/logical_block_size /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/physical_block_size
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/size          # always in 512-byte sectors, regardless of LBA size!
lsblk -b -o NAME,SIZE,LOG-SEC,PHY-SEC
⚠️ Unit trap

/sys/block/<dev>/size is in 512-byte units even on a 4 KiB-formatted namespace, while nsze from nvme id-ns is in logical blocks of the active LBA format. Mixing them up gives an 8× error.

Code — Little's law and WAF calculators

#!/usr/bin/env python3
def iops_from_littles_law(qd, latency_us):          # L = lambda * W
    return qd / (latency_us * 1e-6)

def throughput(iops, io_bytes):                    # returns (GB/s, GiB/s)
    b = iops * io_bytes
    return b / 1e9, b / 2**30

def waf_greedy(valid_fraction):                    # conceptual steady-state model
    return 1.0 / (1.0 - valid_fraction)

def dwpd(tbw_tb, cap_tb, years):
    return tbw_tb / (cap_tb * 365 * years)

print(iops_from_littles_law(32, 80))               # 400000.0
print(throughput(1_000_000, 4096))                 # (4.096, 3.81...)
print(waf_greedy(0.75))                            # 4.0
print(round(dwpd(7008, 3.84, 5), 2))               # 1.0

Worked example — a capacity, from identify data to bytes

Synthetic Identify Namespace values: NSZE = 0x1BF1F72B0, FLBAS selects LBA format 1, LBAF1: LBADS = 12, MS = 0. synthetic

  1. NSZE = 0x1BF1F72B0 = 7,501,476,528 logical blocks.
  2. Logical block size = 212 = 4,096 bytes.
  3. Capacity = 7,501,476,528 × 4,096 = 30,726,047,858,688 bytes.
  4. In decimal units: ≈ 30.73 TB. In binary units: ÷ 240 ≈ 27.94 TiB.
  5. In Linux /sys/block/.../size units (512 B): 7,501,476,528 × 8 = 60,011,812,224.

Had the same namespace been formatted with 512-byte blocks (LBADS = 9), NSZE would be 8× larger for the same capacity. Always multiply by the active format's size.

Common mistakes

  • Assuming an SSD overwrites data in place.
  • Treating SSD latency as a constant; ignoring tails.
  • Measuring a fresh-out-of-box drive and calling it steady state (no GC yet).
  • Comparing MB/s numbers computed with different units.
  • Reading Data Units Written as bytes or as 512-byte sectors (it is thousands of 512-byte units).
  • Blaming PCIe for latency spikes with no PCIe errors and no protocol anomaly.
  • Believing trim/deallocate guarantees the data is erased (it does not, by itself; sanitize does — Part XVIII).

Debugging connection

When performance changes without errors, ask in order: Did the workload change (size, mix, QD)? Did media state change (free space, preconditioning, SLC-cache exhaustion, temperature/throttling)? Did the host change (CPU, interrupts, NUMA)? Only then: did the link change (speed/width downgrade, retraining, errors)? The first two are invisible to the protocol and are the most common causes.

💡 Senior insight

Always precondition before measuring: fill the drive (sequentially, then randomly for random workloads) until performance stabilises, and report steady-state numbers with percentiles. A benchmark on an empty SSD measures the FTL's best case, not the product.

Labs

🧪 Lab 2.1 — Capacity and LBA lab SAFE

Objective: compute capacity exactly from Identify data and reconcile it with every tool. Setup: Linux, nvme-cli, any NVMe namespace (read-only commands only).

Steps:

  1. sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H — record NSZE, NCAP, NUSE, FLBAS and the LBA format marked “in use” (LBADS, MS).
  2. Compute bytes = NSZE × 2LBADS. Express in B, KB, KiB, MB, MiB, GB, GiB, TB, TiB.
  3. Compare with lsblk -b, /sys/block/nvme0n1/size × 512, and nvme list.
  4. Record tnvmcap from nvme id-ctrl (total NVM capacity, in bytes) if reported, and compare.

Questions: (1) Do all tools agree once units are normalised? (2) What does NUSE < NSZE mean? (3) Why might tnvmcap exceed the namespace size?

Solution

(1) They should agree exactly in bytes; disagreements are unit errors (decimal vs binary, 512 B sectors vs logical blocks). (2) Fewer blocks are currently allocated than the namespace size — e.g. after deallocate, or thin provisioning; NUSE semantics depend on features supported version. (3) Capacity may be reserved, unallocated to namespaces, or the controller may support multiple namespaces; tnvmcap counts the NVM capacity of the controller/subsystem as defined in the spec, not just this namespace.

Extension: list all supported LBA formats and their “relative performance” hints; explain why a 4 KiB format may perform better (no read-modify-write for 4 KiB-aligned I/O).

🧪 Lab 2.2 — Data unit lab SAFE

Objective: interpret SMART counters using their defined units. Setup: sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 and, separately, sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 -o json.

Steps: record data_units_read, data_units_written, host_read_commands, host_write_commands, percent_used, avail_spare, temperature. Note whether the human-readable output already converts units (nvme-cli versions differ impl).

Compute: bytes written = data_units_written × 512,000. Average write size = bytes written / host_write_commands. Daily write rate = bytes written / power-on days.

Questions: (1) What is the TB written? (2) What is the average write size and what does it tell you about the workload? (3) Is the drive on track for its rated DWPD?

Solution

Example (synthetic): data_units_written = 12,345,678 → 12,345,678 × 512,000 = 6.32 × 1012 B ≈ 6.32 TB. With 98,000,000 write commands, the average is ≈ 64.5 KB — a mixed workload. Dividing TB written by capacity and days gives observed DWPD; compare with the vendor rating. Note: “data units” count data transferred by the host, not NAND writes; WAF cannot be computed from the SMART log alone. Some devices expose media-written counters in the Endurance Group Information log page or in vendor-specific logs version impl.

Extension: take two readings an hour apart during a known fio write job; check that the delta matches the bytes fio reports (allowing for the rounding rule).

🧪 Lab 2.3 — Little's law on a real device CAUTION

Objective: observe IOPS vs queue depth vs latency. Setup: a spare NVMe namespace or a scratch file on a non-system drive. Read-only workload.

for qd in 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128; do
  fio --name=qd$qd --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --readonly --direct=1 --ioengine=io_uring \
      --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=$qd --runtime=20 --time_based --group_reporting \
      --output-format=terse | awk -F';' '{print "'$qd'", $8, $40}'   # field numbers vary by fio version
done
⚠️ Warning

Never point fio write workloads at a device holding data. --readonly protects against typos. Terse field positions vary by fio version — verify with --output-format=json if unsure.

Questions: (1) For each QD, does IOPS ≈ QD / mean latency? (2) Where is the knee? (3) What happens to p99 past the knee?

Solution

Little's law should hold within a few percent for steady runs (deviations come from host overhead counted differently). IOPS grows almost linearly at low QD (parallelism unused), then flattens; past the knee, mean and p99 latency grow roughly proportionally to QD because requests queue inside the device. The knee position reveals effective internal parallelism and controller limits impl.

Extension: repeat with --numjobs=4 --iodepth=qd/4 to spread load over more submission queues and compare.

🧪 Lab 2.4 — Write amplification thought experiment SAFE

A drive has 1,000 blocks; user data occupies the equivalent of 800 blocks; the rest is OP. Under uniformly random 4 KiB overwrites with greedy GC, assume victim blocks are on average 75% valid. (1) Estimate WAF. (2) If the NAND is rated at 3,000 P/E cycles and capacity is 1 TB, estimate host TBW. (3) How would sequential writes change the answer?

Solution

(1) WAF ≈ 1/(1−0.75) = 4. (2) Raw NAND writes available ≈ 1.25 TB × 3,000 = 3,750 TB of NAND writes (using total physical capacity 1,000 blocks for 800 blocks of user data → physical ≈ 1.25 TB); host TBW ≈ 3,750 / 4 ≈ 940 TB. (3) Sequential overwrite invalidates whole blocks → victims nearly empty → WAF ≈ 1, host TBW ≈ 3,750 TB. derived conceptual model.

Why NVMe was needed

Put the chapter together:

  1. NAND SSD performance comes from parallelism across channels, dies and planes — dozens to hundreds of concurrent operations.
  2. Exploiting it requires many outstanding commands (Little's law) — far more than one 32-deep queue comfortably supplies, and supplied from many CPU cores at once.
  3. SSD latency is tens of microseconds, so every microsecond of host-interface overhead (HBA firmware, register reads, locks) is now a large fraction of the total.
  4. Bandwidth outgrew SATA's 600 MB/s and SAS's per-port rates; PCIe lanes, already wired to the CPU, offered gigabytes per second.

The next chapter tells the story of how the industry got from AHCI to NVMe — and quantifies each of these points.

Quiz — Chapter 2

  1. Average rotational latency of a 15,000 RPM drive?

    Answer

    0.5 × 60/15000 = 2 ms.

  2. Smallest unit NAND can erase? program?

    Answer

    Erase: block. Program: page.

  3. Why can't an SSD overwrite a page in place?

    Answer

    NAND pages must be erased before reprogramming, and erase works only on whole blocks.

  4. Define WAF and give a value for purely sequential writes.

    Answer

    NAND bytes written / host bytes written; ≈ 1 for sequential.

  5. A drive does 600,000 IOPS of 4 KiB reads. Throughput in GB/s and GiB/s?

    Answer

    2.4576 GB/s; 2.29 GiB/s.

  6. Mean latency 100 µs at QD 16. Predicted IOPS?

    Answer

    160,000.

  7. Data Units Written = 2,000,000. Bytes?

    Answer

    2,000,000 × 512,000 = 1.024 × 1012 bytes ≈ 1.02 TB.

  8. NSZE = 1,000,000 with LBADS = 9. Capacity?

    Answer

    512,000,000 bytes (512 MB, ≈ 488.3 MiB).

  9. What is a NAND die and why does it matter for performance?

    Answer

    The independently operating unit; interleaving operations across dies provides SSD parallelism.

  10. Name two things NVMe does not expose about NAND.

    Answer

    Any two of: physical placement, FTL map, GC algorithm/timing, wear-leveling policy, cache sizes.

  11. What is NCQ's maximum queue depth?

    Answer

    32 commands.

  12. Why does a longer warranty at the same TBW reduce DWPD?

    Answer

    The same total writes are spread over more days.

Interview questions — Chapter 2

  1. Beginner Why are SSDs faster than HDDs for random I/O?
    Model answer

    No mechanical seek or rotation; flash reads take tens of µs and many dies work in parallel.

  2. Beginner What is TRIM/deallocate for?
    Model answer

    Telling the SSD that LBAs no longer hold useful data so GC need not copy them, reducing WAF.

  3. Intermediate Explain the SSD write cliff.
    Model answer

    When free blocks/SLC cache are exhausted, writes must wait for GC and native TLC/QLC programming, so throughput drops and latency rises sharply.

  4. Intermediate How does over-provisioning improve performance and endurance?
    Model answer

    More spare space means GC victims hold fewer valid pages, lowering WAF, which reduces both background work and NAND wear.

  5. Advanced Use Little's law to explain why QD 1 latency benchmarks do not predict QD 32 throughput.
    Model answer

    At QD 1 only one die works; IOPS = 1/latency. Higher QD exploits parallelism until internal resources saturate; the relation depends on how latency changes with load.

  6. Advanced How would you estimate an SSD's internal parallelism from the outside?
    Model answer

    Sweep QD for random reads; IOPS × latency gives the effective concurrency at the knee, an estimate of usable parallel units (with caveats about controller limits).

  7. Senior A customer reports p99.9 read latency spikes every few minutes with no errors. Approach?
    Model answer

    Correlate with write activity, free space, temperature and power-state transitions; check SMART and vendor telemetry; reproduce with controlled preconditioning; consider host causes (interrupt affinity, CPU frequency); only then inspect PCIe for retraining/errors. Report GC as a hypothesis with evidence.

  8. Senior How do you test for endurance-related behaviour changes without waiting years?
    Model answer

    Accelerated write workloads on test drives, monitoring percent used, spare, error counters and latency drift; vendor-assisted pre-aged samples; retention bake tests per vendor methodology impl.

Teach-back challenge

Explain to a child why the marble-jar library writes changed words into new jars. Explain to a junior engineer why WAF rises as the drive fills with random overwrites. Explain to a senior engineer which latency outliers you can attribute to media with evidence, and which you must label as hypotheses.

Chapter summary

  • HDD performance is mechanical; SSD performance is parallel flash managed by firmware.
  • NAND programs pages and erases blocks; the FTL hides this with an L2P map, GC and wear leveling, at the cost of write amplification.
  • OP, WAF and P/E cycles determine endurance; TBW and DWPD express it.
  • IOPS, throughput and latency are linked: Throughput = IOPS × size; IOPS = QD / latency.
  • Units matter: logical blocks vs 512-byte sectors; KB vs KiB; SMART data units of 512,000 bytes.
  • The protocol exposes time and aggregates, not media mechanisms.

  • JEDEC SSD endurance workload and requirements standards (JESD218/JESD219 family).
  • ONFI specifications (NAND interface) — onfi.org.
  • SNIA Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification (preconditioning and steady state).
  • fio documentation (fio.readthedocs.io).
