PART III

Why NVMe Exists

Every interface is an answer to a problem. NVMe's problem was simple to state and hard to solve: flash had become parallel and fast, and the interfaces in front of it were single-file and slow. This Part tells the story from SATA and AHCI through the first proprietary PCIe SSDs to NVMe 1.0, the 2.0 refactor and the August 2026 release — and quantifies, with formulas you can check, exactly what changed.

3 From SATA/SAS to NVMe

← 2 What Is Storage?4 The PCIe Mental Model →

Why this chapter exists

Engineers who know why a protocol is shaped the way it is can predict its behaviour and its failure modes. NVMe's queue pairs, doorbells, phase tags, fixed-size entries and per-queue interrupts are not arbitrary; each removes a specific cost that AHCI and SATA imposed. Knowing those costs also tells you what NVMe still cannot fix — media latency, host software overhead, and interrupt handling — which is where real performance work happens.

Learning objectives

  • Describe AHCI's architecture: one command list of 32 slots per port, PRD tables, FIS areas, port registers.
  • Explain command serialization, queue limits and CPU overhead in the SATA/AHCI path, with numbers.
  • State NVMe's queue limits precisely (up to 65,535 I/O queues; up to 65,536 entries each; admin queue up to 4,096 entries) and why a ring of N slots holds N−1 commands.
  • Compare per-command register-access cost of AHCI and NVMe and compute its CPU impact.
  • Compare SATA, SAS, NVMe/PCIe and NVMe-oF protocol stacks layer by layer.
  • Narrate the history SATA → AHCI → PCIe SSDs → NVMe → NVMe 1.x → NVMe 2.0 family → NVMe 2.4, labelling dates by confidence.
  • List NVMe's design goals and connect each to a mechanism you will study later.

Prerequisites

Chapter 1 (registers, MMIO cost, interrupts, DMA — especially §1.4 and §1.14) and Chapter 2 (parallelism and Little's law — §2.17).

Story

🧒 Kid analogy — the restaurant

An old restaurant has one order spike by the kitchen door that holds 32 tickets. Every waiter in the restaurant must queue at that spike, and only one waiter may touch it at a time. After pinning a ticket, the waiter must also lean into the kitchen and ask the cook a few questions (“Did you see my ticket? Which orders are ready?”) and wait for each answer. When food is ready, the cook rings one bell for the whole restaurant, and somebody has to go and find out whose food it is.

The new restaurant gives every waiter their own order rail and their own pickup shelf, each with room for thousands of tickets. A waiter clips tickets on their own rail, flips a little flag to say “new tickets up to here”, and walks away — no questions, no waiting. The cooks (dozens of them now) take tickets from all rails at once. When a dish is ready, the cook puts it on that waiter's shelf with the ticket number, and buzzes that waiter's own pager.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In NVMe the “cook” (controller) walks to the waiter's rail to fetch tickets — the tickets live in host memory, not in the kitchen. The “flag” is a doorbell register write. And dishes are delivered by the cook writing directly into the waiter's memory (DMA), not by handing a plate across a counter. The restaurant analogy also hides that cooks may finish orders out of order, which is why every ticket carries a command identifier.

Beginner explanation

SATA drives are controlled through a host-side chip called an AHCI controller. AHCI was designed in the era of hard disks, when a disk could handle a few hundred operations per second and nobody cared about a few microseconds of overhead. It offers one queue of 32 commands per drive, needs the CPU to read device registers to learn what finished, and funnels everything through a single shared structure. SSDs made the drive thousands of times faster, so the overhead that used to be invisible became the bottleneck. NVMe replaced the whole design with many deep queues in host memory, written without locks and signalled with a single register write.

3.1 Limitations of SATA

LimitationDetailConsequence for SSDs
Bandwidth ceiling6 Gb/s, 8b/10b encoding → 600 MB/s raw, ~550 MB/s achievable derivedMainstream SATA SSDs hit the ceiling around 2012–2013; flash could go faster
Half-duplex transportFrames flow one direction at a time on the linkMixed read/write workloads cannot use both directions simultaneously
Single queue of 32NCQ tags 0–31 per device verifiedCannot express enough concurrency for many-die SSDs from many cores
ATA command set heritageCommand delivery via FIS (Frame Information Structure) transfers; many legacy modesExtra translation and protocol steps per command
Extra hopCPU → PCIe → AHCI HBA → SATA link → drive controllerAdditional latency and a second controller in the path

3.2 AHCI — the Advanced Host Controller Interface

AHCI is a register-level interface specification (Intel, first released in 2004 version) for SATA host controllers. The AHCI HBA is itself a PCI function, class code 01h/06h/01h (mass storage, SATA, AHCI) verified. Its memory-mapped registers live in a BAR (ABAR). Per port it uses:

  • a command list of up to 32 command headers (“slots”) in host memory, each pointing to a command table containing the command FIS and a Physical Region Descriptor Table (PRDT) — AHCI's scatter-gather list;
  • a received-FIS area in host memory where the HBA deposits frames from the device;
  • port registers including PxCI (Command Issue — bit per slot), PxSACT (SATA Active — bit per NCQ tag), PxIS (Interrupt Status), PxIE (Interrupt Enable), and a global IS (Interrupt Status per port).

3.3 Command serialization and queue limitations

With AHCI, all CPU cores issuing I/O to one drive must allocate slots from the same 32-slot command list and update the same PxSACT/PxCI registers. The driver therefore serialises submission with a per-port lock. On a many-core server, cores contend on that lock and the cache lines holding the command list bounce between cores. The queue limit compounds the problem: at most 32 commands can be in flight per drive, and Little's law says

IOPSmax ≤ QDmax / Wmin
  • IOPSmax — upper bound on completions per second for one device
  • QDmax — maximum outstanding commands (32 for NCQ)
  • Wmin — minimum per-command latency (seconds)

With W = 80 µs: 32 / 80 µs = 400,000 IOPS as an absolute ceiling, before any overhead derived. A modern NVMe SSD can exceed 1,000,000 random-read IOPS, which at 80 µs requires at least 80 commands in flight — more than NCQ allows. (In practice SATA's 600 MB/s caps 4 KiB IOPS at ~146,000 anyway: 600×106 / 4096 derived.)

3.4 CPU overhead — the register-access cost

From §1.4: an uncached MMIO read stalls a core for a full round trip (~1 µs order impl); a write is posted. Compare the shape of a typical submit/complete cycle:

// AHCI-style (conceptual; real drivers differ in detail)
submit(cmd):
    lock(port)                          // serialise all cores
    slot = find_free_bit(issued_mask)   // shared 32-bit bookkeeping
    build command header + command table + PRDT in memory
    write PxSACT |= 1<<slot              // MMIO write (NCQ)
    write PxCI   |= 1<<slot              // MMIO write
    unlock(port)
irq():
    is   = read IS                      // MMIO READ  (which port?)
    pis  = read PxIS                    // MMIO READ  (why?)
    write PxIS = pis                    // MMIO write (ack, RW1C)
    sact = read PxSACT                  // MMIO READ  (which tags still active?)
    done = issued_mask & ~sact          // infer completions by difference
    write IS = is                       // MMIO write (ack)

// NVMe-style (conceptual)
submit(cmd):                            // per-CPU queue: no lock shared with other cores
    copy 64-byte SQE into sq[tail]; tail = (tail+1) % depth
    wmb(); write SQyTDBL = tail         // ONE posted MMIO write (can cover many commands)
irq():                                  // per-queue MSI-X vector, ideally on the submitting CPU
    while cq[head].phase == expected_phase:     // plain memory reads, cache-friendly
        complete(cq[head].cid, cq[head].status)
        advance head (flip expected_phase on wrap)
    write CQyHDBL = head                // ONE posted MMIO write per batch
Per command (typical driver shape)AHCINVMe
Uncached MMIO readsSeveral (on completion path)0 on the fast path verified design property
MMIO writesSeveral≈1 submission doorbell + ≈1 completion doorbell, both amortisable across batches
Shared lockPer-port lock across all coresNone between cores (per-core queues)
Command formatCommand header (32 B) + command table (FIS + PRDT entries, variable)Fixed 64 B SQE; data pointer PRP/SGL
Completion discoveryRead status registers, compute bit differencesRead CQE in memory; phase tag says “new”
Interrupt steeringPer HBA or per portPer completion queue, MSI-X vector per queue/CPU

NVM Express overview material from NVMe's introduction commonly summarised this as AHCI needing about four uncacheable register reads per command (on the order of 2,000 CPU cycles) versus none for NVMe uncertain — treat the exact counts as illustrative of a typical driver, not a protocol constant. The derived consequence is robust:

CPUstall = IOPS × R × tread
  • CPUstall — core-seconds per second spent stalled on MMIO reads (1.0 = one whole core)
  • IOPS — commands per second
  • R — MMIO reads per command
  • tread — stall per read (seconds)

1,000,000 IOPS × 4 reads × 0.7 µs = 2.8 cores doing nothing but waiting derived (synthetic tread). Interrupt batching reduces R per command, but the structure cannot reach zero. NVMe removes the term entirely from the fast path.

3.5 Latency

For HDDs, 10 µs of host-interface overhead was 0.1% of a 10 ms access. For a 70 µs flash read it is 14%; for low-latency media (SLC-class or storage-class memory with ~10 µs reads impl) it is half the total. NVMe shortens the path: no HBA, no SCSI/ATA translation layer, no register reads, interrupt delivered to the submitting core. What remains — the kernel block layer, the interrupt and context switch — is why polling modes and io_uring exist for the lowest-latency use cases.

3.6 Parallelism

QuantityAHCI/SATANVMe (PCIe transport)
Queues per device1 (per port)1 admin + up to 65,535 I/O submission queues (and completion queues) verified
Commands per queue32I/O queues up to 65,536 entries (CAP.MQES, 0's-based, device-limited); admin queue up to 4,096 entries verified
Max commands in flight (theoretical)32~65,535 × 65,535 ≈ 4.3 × 109 derived (a ring of N slots holds N−1 commands)
Typical real configurationNCQ depth 31 or 32One SQ/CQ pair per CPU core (device-limited, often 32–128+ queues), depths of 1,024 or more impl
Submission/completion pairingFixedSeveral SQs may share one CQ
📘 Specification — why a ring holds N−1

NVMe queues are circular. The queue is empty when head equals tail, and full when tail + 1 (modulo size) equals head. One slot always stays unused so that “full” and “empty” are distinguishable verified. A 1,024-entry queue holds at most 1,023 outstanding commands.

3.7 PCIe as the transport

PCIe was already the CPU's native high-speed I/O fabric, with lanes coming directly from the processor. Attaching flash directly to it removed the HBA and offered scalable bandwidth (x1 to x16, doubling per generation), full duplex, low latency, and a mature software model (enumeration, BARs, MSI-X) every OS already understood. The missing piece was a standard host interface, so one driver could run every PCIe SSD. Early PCIe SSDs (late 2000s) used proprietary interfaces and vendor drivers; competing standardisation paths included SATA Express (AHCI over PCIe) and SCSI Express (SCSI over PCIe, SOP/PQI). NVMe became the dominant one version.

3.10 Historical timeline

The story in one sentence: disks got an interface designed for disks; flash outgrew it; vendors bolted flash to PCIe with private drivers; the industry standardised one queue-based interface; then it grew features, transports and management until it needed to be split into a family of specifications.

The readable version of the story. In the disk era, AHCI was a sensible design: one drive could only do a few hundred operations per second, so a 32-slot queue and a few register reads per command cost nothing measurable. Flash broke every one of those assumptions within a few years. Vendors first attached flash directly to PCIe with their own interfaces — fast, but every product needed its own driver, and enterprises dislike unique drivers. A consortium of companies wrote a clean-sheet interface instead, designed around the costs we quantified above: never read a register on the fast path, give every core its own queues, make commands fixed-size, let completions arrive out of order. NVMe 1.0 shipped in 2011. Over the 1.x years it grew enterprise features (namespaces, reservations, multi-path, sanitize, power and thermal management), went beyond PCIe to fabrics, and gained a management interface. By 2021 the single document had become unwieldy and was refactored into a family. Each release since has added command sets, transports and management capabilities, up to the August 2026 set that this book uses as its baseline.

Hardware view

SATA SSD: chipset AHCI controller (a PCIe function), SATA PHY, cable or M.2 SATA, drive controller. NVMe SSD: CPU root port lanes (or chipset lanes), M.2/U.2/EDSFF connector, NVMe controller with PCIe endpoint, NVMe queue engine, DMA. One less controller and one less serial link in the data path. Note that an M.2 slot may be wired for SATA, PCIe, or both — the connector shape does not tell you the protocol.

Specification view

SPECIFICATION BASELINE — DOCUMENTS: NVMe Base Specification Rev. 2.4 (queue model, admin commands, limits); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification Rev. 1.4 (register-based doorbells, PCIe-specific queue and interrupt rules). AHCI is governed by Intel's AHCI specification; SATA by SATA-IO; SAS by INCITS T10. STATUS: NVMe baseline current as of August 4, 2026. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: in NVMe 1.x, PCIe-specific content and the NVM command set lived in the base document version. What you must check in the specification: exact limits for queue identifiers and sizes; the definition of CAP.MQES and CAP.CQR; which queues the admin queue can be; how SQ head is reported in CQEs.

The AHCI sequence is conceptual — real drivers vary in which registers they read and how they batch impl — but the structural difference is visible: AHCI's completion path contains non-posted reads (rows 7, 8, 10), each a full round-trip CPU stall; NVMe's contains none.

Linux view

lspci -nn | grep -i -e "SATA controller" -e "Non-Volatile"   # [0106] AHCI vs [0108] NVMe
cat /sys/block/sda/device/queue_depth 2>/dev/null            # SATA NCQ depth (often 32 or 31)
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/ | wc -l                           # number of NVMe hardware queues mapped
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/0/cpu_list                        # which CPUs use hw queue 0
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x07 -H                 # Number of Queues feature (read-only Get)
sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H | grep -i -A2 "Maximum Queue Entries"
OutputProvesDoes not prove
Count of mq/ directoriesHow many hardware queues blk-mq is usingHow many the device supports (see Number of Queues feature)
Number of Queues featureI/O SQs/CQs allocated by the controller (0's-based)That all are in use
CAP.MQESMaximum entries per I/O queue (0's-based)The depth Linux chose

Worked example — sizing queue depth for a target

Target: 1.5 M random-read IOPS on one SSD whose loaded latency is 120 µs, from 16 cores.

  1. Little's law: required outstanding = 1.5×106 × 120×10−6 = 180 commands.
  2. Per core: 180 / 16 ≈ 12 outstanding per queue.
  3. With AHCI: impossible — 32 max total, and SATA bandwidth caps 4 KiB at ~146 K IOPS.
  4. With NVMe: 16 queues of depth ≥ 13 suffice (remember N−1); Linux defaults (e.g. 1,024-entry queues impl) give ample headroom.
  5. Bandwidth check: 1.5 M × 4 KiB = 6.1 GB/s → needs at least a Gen4 x4 link (~7.9 GB/s raw), and the TLP overhead must still fit derived.

Common mistakes

  • Saying “NVMe supports 64 K queues of 64 K commands” without the precise limits (65,535 I/O queues; up to 65,536 entries, N−1 usable; device-advertised maxima).
  • Assuming every NVMe device supports many queues — the controller grants a number via the Number of Queues feature.
  • Believing M.2 means NVMe.
  • Attributing NVMe's speed only to PCIe bandwidth; the protocol overhead reduction matters as much for small I/O.
  • Assuming NVMe removes all host overhead — interrupts, block layer and context switches remain.
  • Citing AHCI-vs-NVMe register-read counts as specification facts; they describe typical driver behaviour.

Debugging connection

Chapter 3's ideas become debugging tools: if a device advertises few queues, many cores share them — expect lock contention and lower IOPS; if completions arrive out of order, the host must match by CID — a driver that assumes order will corrupt request state; if one doorbell write covers several commands, a lost or mis-addressed doorbell stalls them all; if queue depth exceeds what the device can parallelise, latency rises with no errors.

💡 Senior insight

Interfaces carry their history. NVMe's admin/I/O split, its 64-byte command and its doorbell model come from 2011 assumptions about PCIe and host memory. When you see a newer feature that looks awkward — doorbell buffer configuration for virtualised guests, controller memory buffers, fabrics capsules — ask which original assumption it is compensating for. That question tells you its likely corner cases.

Labs

🧪 Lab 3.1 — SATA vs NVMe on the same machine SAFE

Objective: observe queue structure differences. Setup: a machine with an AHCI controller (most PCs) and an NVMe SSD; or a QEMU guest with both -device ahci/ide-hd and -device nvme. Steps: run the Linux-view commands; record class codes, queue depth for the SATA disk, number of NVMe hardware queues and their CPU lists, CAP.MQES and the Number of Queues feature.

Questions: (1) How many queues and what depth for each device? (2) How are NVMe queues mapped to CPUs? (3) Is the NVMe queue count limited by CPUs or by the device?

Solution

(1) SATA: one queue, depth ~32 (Linux often reports 32 or 31). NVMe: typically one hardware queue per CPU (or per group of CPUs) with large depth. (2) Each mq/N/cpu_list lists the CPUs mapped to hardware queue N. (3) Compare queue count with CPU count and with the Number of Queues feature value (+1 since 0's-based); the smaller one wins impl.

Extension: in QEMU, change the emulated NVMe device's maximum queue count (consult your QEMU version's documentation for the property name) and observe how Linux adapts.

🧪 Lab 3.2 — Register-access budget SAFE

Objective: quantify CPU cost. Assume tread = 0.8 µs, twrite (CPU-side) = 0.05 µs. Driver A (AHCI-like): per command 3 MMIO reads + 4 writes. Driver B (NVMe-like): per command 0 reads + 2 writes, with doorbells batched 8 commands per write.

Questions: CPU time per command and cores needed for 1 M IOPS, for each.

Solution

A: 3×0.8 + 4×0.05 = 2.6 µs/command → 2.6 cores at 1 M IOPS just for register access. B: (2×0.05)/8 = 0.0125 µs/command → 0.0125 cores. Ratio ≈ 200× derived (inputs synthetic). Real totals include block layer and interrupt costs, which dominate for NVMe.

🧪 Lab 3.3 — Verify the timeline yourself SAFE

Objective: practice source discipline. Steps: open the NVM Express specifications index and revision-changes pages; for each row in the timeline labelled uncertain, find a primary source (the specification's own revision history, or an NVM Express announcement) and record the exact date and document. Deliverable: a corrected timeline with a source per row.

Solution

There is no single answer key on purpose: the skill being tested is refusing to cite a date you have not verified. A good deliverable cites the document title, revision and its own history table for each row, and marks any row still unverified.

Quiz — Chapter 3

  1. How many command slots does an AHCI port's command list have?

    Answer

    32.

  2. Maximum number of NVMe I/O submission queues?

    Answer

    65,535 (queue ID 0 is the admin queue).

  3. Maximum entries in an NVMe admin queue? an I/O queue?

    Answer

    Admin: 4,096. I/O: 65,536, limited by the device's CAP.MQES.

  4. Why can a 256-entry queue hold only 255 commands?

    Answer

    Full is defined as tail+1 = head; one slot stays empty to distinguish full from empty.

  5. What is the theoretical IOPS ceiling of NCQ at 100 µs latency?

    Answer

    32 / 100 µs = 320,000 IOPS.

  6. Which AHCI registers indicate issued and active NCQ commands?

    Answer

    PxCI (Command Issue) and PxSACT (SATA Active).

  7. How does an NVMe host learn which commands completed?

    Answer

    By reading CQEs in host memory, identified as new by the phase tag, each carrying the CID and SQ ID.

  8. What major structural change came with NVMe 2.0?

    Answer

    Refactoring into a family: base specification, separate command-set specifications and transport specifications.

  9. Name three highlights of the August 2026 NVMe release.

    Answer

    Any three of: Post-Quantum Cryptography, PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration, Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting, Restore Manufacturing Default Settings.

  10. Why does NVMe avoid a lock shared across cores?

    Answer

    Each core gets its own SQ/CQ pair, so cores never contend on a common submission structure.

  11. What class code does an AHCI controller report?

    Answer

    01h/06h/01h.

  12. Why did proprietary PCIe SSDs not become the standard?

    Answer

    Each required its own driver and management tools; the industry wanted one standard interface with in-box OS drivers.

Interview questions — Chapter 3

  1. Beginner Why was NVMe created?
    Model answer

    SATA/AHCI, designed for HDDs, limited SSDs with one 32-deep queue, high per-command CPU overhead and a 600 MB/s link; NVMe offers many deep queues over PCIe with minimal overhead.

  2. Beginner What is AHCI?
    Model answer

    The register-level interface for SATA host controllers, using per-port command lists of 32 slots.

  3. Intermediate Explain why NVMe needs no register reads to submit or complete a command.
    Model answer

    Submission: host writes SQE to memory and the tail to a doorbell (posted). Completion: device writes CQE with phase tag to memory, host polls memory, then writes the head doorbell (posted). SQ head progress is reported inside CQEs.

  4. Intermediate How does out-of-order completion work in NVMe?
    Model answer

    Each command has a CID unique within its SQ; CQEs carry CID and SQ ID, so the host matches completions regardless of order.

  5. Advanced If NVMe allows billions of outstanding commands, why do devices advertise far fewer?
    Model answer

    Each queue/command costs controller resources (state, doorbells, interrupt vectors, fetch bandwidth); devices size limits to their parallelism and silicon budget.

  6. Advanced Compare the SATA and NVMe software stacks in Linux.
    Model answer

    SATA: blk-mq → SCSI mid-layer → libata translation → ahci → HBA → SATA. NVMe: blk-mq → nvme-core/nvme → PCIe → device. Fewer layers and no translation.

  7. Senior Where does NVMe over PCIe still spend host CPU per I/O, and how would you reduce it?
    Model answer

    Block layer, request allocation, DMA mapping/IOMMU, interrupts and context switches; reduce with batching, interrupt coalescing, polling queues, io_uring with registered buffers, user-space drivers, IOMMU passthrough where acceptable.

  8. Senior A team wants to keep SATA for a new low-latency product “because it's simpler”. Argue the trade-offs.
    Model answer

    SATA: cheap, mature, adequate for low-IOPS. But QD 32 cap, 600 MB/s, HBA latency and CPU overhead; NVMe offers lower latency, scalability, richer features (namespaces, telemetry, management) and is now the commodity interface. Quantify with Little's law and the target workload.

Teach-back challenge

To a child: explain why giving every waiter their own order rail makes the restaurant faster. To a junior: explain the N−1 rule and phase tags. To a senior: present Lab 3.2's numbers and argue where NVMe's remaining host overhead lies.

Chapter summary

  • SATA/AHCI suited disks: one 32-slot queue per port, shared locks, register reads on completion, 600 MB/s.
  • Flash needs concurrency (Little's law) and low overhead; AHCI could supply neither.
  • NVMe: up to 65,535 I/O queues, up to 65,536 entries each (N−1 usable), admin queue up to 4,096; fixed 64 B/16 B entries; doorbell writes; no fast-path reads; per-queue MSI-X; out-of-order completion.
  • History: SATA → AHCI → proprietary PCIe SSDs → NVMe 1.0 (2011) → 1.x features → 2.0 family (2021) → 2.4 set (August 4, 2026).

PART IV

PCIe From Zero

An NVMe SSD is, electrically and logically, a PCI Express (PCIe) Endpoint. Every doorbell write, every Submission Queue Entry fetch, every data transfer and every interrupt you will meet later in this book is carried by PCIe packets over PCIe lanes. This Part builds PCIe from nothing: why it replaced shared parallel buses, how the topology is wired (Root Complex, Root Ports, Switches, Endpoints), what a lane physically is, how the generations differ in signaling and encoding, how the three-layer protocol stack divides responsibility, and how two chips that have never met agree on a link width, a speed and a set of equalization coefficients through the Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM). If an NVMe drive "disappears", "runs at half speed" or "throws AER errors", the root cause very often lives in the material of this Part.

📘 Specification baseline for Parts IV–VI

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG). REVISION: concepts in these Parts are stable across revisions 3.0 through 6.x unless labelled; PCIe 6.0 (released January 2022) introduced PAM4 signaling and FLIT mode; PCIe 7.0 (128 GT/s) was released in 2025 version. STATUS: PCI-SIG specifications are member-access documents; the learner should obtain the revision matching their hardware. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: 1.x/2.x (8b/10b only, 8-bit tags by default, no equalization handshake), 3.x (128b/130b, equalization phases), 4.0 (10-bit tags, 16 GT/s), 5.0 (32 GT/s), 6.0 (FLIT mode, 14-bit tags in FLIT mode, new header formats in FLIT mode). SOURCE: PCI-SIG; this book does not quote section numbers, because section numbering moves between revisions — search the specification by topic name (e.g. "Transaction Ordering", "Flow Control", "Link Training and Status State Rules").

📭 Source discipline used throughout Parts IV–VI

Every statement in these Parts belongs to one of four worlds, and we keep them separate: (1) PCIe normative behavior — what the PCIe Base Specification requires (e.g. a Memory Read is non-posted and must be completed); (2) NVMe behavior — what the NVMe specifications layer on top (e.g. the host writes a doorbell register in BAR0 with a Memory Write); (3) device implementation behavior — what a particular SSD controller, switch or root complex chooses to do inside what the specs allow (e.g. how many reads it keeps in flight, how many credits it advertises); (4) protocol analyzer presentation — how a tool chooses to draw and name what it captured. A conclusion drawn from world 4 must be checked against world 1 before it is believed.

4 The PCIe Mental Model

← 3 From SATA/SAS to NVMe5 PCIe Physical Architecture →

4.1 Why this chapter exists

Before bit fields, before state machines, you need a correct picture in your head of what is connected to what. Engineers who carry the wrong picture — "PCIe is a bus that every device listens to" — make predictable mistakes: they expect broadcast behavior, they misread lspci trees, they blame the SSD for a problem in an upstream switch, and they cannot explain why one device's link failure does not take out its neighbors. This chapter builds the right picture: PCI Express (PCIe) is a packet-switched, point-to-point, serial interconnect organized as a tree, whose software model deliberately pretends to be the old PCI bus so that operating systems did not need to be rewritten.

4.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain why a shared parallel bus stopped scaling and what "point-to-point" means.
  • Intermediate: name and place Root Complex, Root Port, Switch (upstream and downstream ports), PCI-to-PCI bridge, Endpoint, link, lane, width and generation on a diagram.
  • Advanced: explain how the hierarchy is enumerated as buses/devices/functions (Bus:Device.Function, BDF) and how a switch routes a TLP by address, by ID, or implicitly.
  • Senior: reason about shared-uplink bottlenecks, failure domains, and peer-to-peer paths in a multi-SSD system.
  • Trace-analysis: given a capture point on one link, state which traffic you can and cannot see.
  • Debugging: use lspci -tv and sysfs to locate an NVMe device in the tree and identify every link between it and the CPU.
  • Validation: design a test that proves a reported bottleneck is in a switch uplink rather than the SSD.

4.3 Prerequisites

Only basic computer architecture: a CPU, memory, and the idea that devices are accessed through addresses (Parts I–III of this book). No PCIe knowledge assumed. Physical details are deferred to Chapter 5; packets to Chapter 10.

4.4 Story: the railway that replaced the high street

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine a town where every shop delivers goods along one single high street. Only one truck may drive on it at a time; everyone else waits. When the town grows, the street jams. So the town builds a railway: each shop gets its own private track to a station. Big stations (switches) connect several tracks to one larger track heading to the central station (the Root Complex) near the town hall (the CPU and memory). Trains carry sealed parcels with an address label. Two shops can ship at the same time, on their own tracks, in both directions at once.

🌍 Engineering analogy

PCIe is closer to a small, lossless, credit-controlled packet network (think switched Ethernet with guaranteed delivery on each hop) than to a bus. Each link is a full-duplex pipe between exactly two ports. Switches forward packets using routing information inside the packet header. The difference from Ethernet: PCIe guarantees per-hop reliable, in-order delivery (with replay) and never drops a packet because a buffer is full — the sender simply is not allowed to send until the receiver has granted buffer space (credits, Chapter 16).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The railway analogy represents private point-to-point tracks, stations as switches, and addressed parcels. It hides three things: (1) a "track" is really a bundle of 1–16 lanes, each a pair of one-way differential wires per direction; (2) the stations do not inspect parcels at leisure — forwarding is cut-through or store-and-forward in hardware in hundreds of nanoseconds; (3) the parcel service has a strict rulebook about which parcels may overtake which (ordering). It becomes misleading if you conclude that PCIe has no shared resources: the uplink from a switch to the root port is shared by every device below that switch, and the root complex's internal fabric and memory controller are shared too.

4.5 Beginner view: bus versus point-to-point

Conventional PCI (1990s) was a shared parallel bus: 32 or 64 data/address wires plus control wires, routed to every slot. At any moment one bus master owned the bus after arbitration; every other device listened and ignored addresses that were not theirs. Its weaknesses compound as speed rises:

  • Clock skew: 32+ signals must arrive within the same clock window. At hundreds of MHz the differences in trace length across a motherboard consume the whole timing budget.
  • Electrical loading: every extra slot adds capacitance and reflections to every wire, so faster buses support fewer slots.
  • Half duplex and shared bandwidth: 133 MB/s (32-bit, 33 MHz) was shared by all devices, in one direction at a time.
  • Pin count: wide parallel buses need many pins per device.

PCI Express (first released 2003) answered with serial, differential, point-to-point links. Each lane has one differential pair transmitting and one receiving, so a lane is full duplex. The clock is embedded in the data stream and recovered by the receiver (Clock and Data Recovery, CDR), which removes the skew problem within a lane; skew between lanes is removed by the receiver's lane-to-lane deskew logic. To gain bandwidth, PCIe either clocks faster (new generations) or bundles more lanes (wider links).

PropertyConventional PCI (shared bus)PCI Express (point-to-point)
Physical mediumParallel, single-ended, shared by all slotsSerial, differential, one link per pair of ports
DirectionHalf duplexFull duplex (independent TX and RX pairs per lane)
Bandwidth sharingAll devices share one busEach link dedicated; sharing only at switches/root complex
Transfer unitBus cycles with address/data phasesPackets (TLPs, DLLPs, ordered sets)
Error handlingParity, limitedLCRC + per-hop replay, optional ECRC end-to-end, AER
Software modelConfig space, BARs, Bus/Device/FunctionSame (backward-compatible), extended to 4 KiB config space
📌 Remember

PCIe changed the wires completely but kept the software model (configuration space, Base Address Registers, Bus/Device/Function numbering). That is why lspci still shows "buses" even though no physical bus exists: each link and each switch's internal routing fabric is modeled as a "virtual PCI bus".

4.6 Engineering view: the components

Root Complex (RC)

The Root Complex is the interface between the CPU/memory subsystem and the PCIe hierarchy. It is not one standardized chip: in modern systems it is a block inside the CPU package (or the chipset/PCH for chipset-attached lanes). It generates configuration, memory and I/O requests on behalf of the CPU, and it accepts DMA requests from devices and turns them into memory-controller transactions — often after translation by an IOMMU. Its internal structure is impl; the spec defines its externally visible behavior.

Root Port (RP)

A Root Port is a PCIe port on the Root Complex that begins one hierarchy branch. Software sees it as a PCI-to-PCI bridge (Type 1 configuration header) with a secondary bus number. Each Root Port owns exactly one link. When an NVMe drive is directly attached to the CPU (typical for an M.2 or U.2 slot wired to CPU lanes), the chain is CPU → Root Port → link → NVMe Endpoint.

Switch

A switch has one Upstream Port (toward the root) and multiple Downstream Ports (toward devices). Software sees it as a set of virtual PCI-to-PCI bridges joined by an internal virtual bus: one bridge for the upstream port, one per downstream port. The switch forwards TLPs between ports by examining routing fields: address routing (memory and I/O requests, compared against each bridge's base/limit windows), ID routing (configuration requests and completions, compared against secondary/subordinate bus number ranges), and implicit routing (some messages, e.g. "route to root complex" or "broadcast from root").

Bridge

"Bridge" in PCIe software terms means any function with a Type 1 header that forwards between a primary and secondary bus: root ports, switch ports, and real PCIe-to-PCI(-X) bridges for legacy devices. Bridges hold the Primary/Secondary/Subordinate Bus Number registers and memory base/limit windows that make routing work.

Endpoint (EP)

An Endpoint is a function that is the requester or completer of transactions on its own behalf — a leaf of the tree. It has a Type 0 configuration header with Base Address Registers (BARs). An NVMe SSD controller is a PCIe Endpoint whose class code is 01h (mass storage) / 08h (non-volatile memory controller) / 02h (NVM Express) verified. One physical device may expose multiple functions (multi-function devices, and with SR-IOV, many virtual functions).

Link, lane, width, generation

  • Lane: one differential TX pair plus one differential RX pair — four wires — carrying one bit stream in each direction.
  • Link: the connection between two ports, made of 1, 2, 4, 8 or 16 lanes (x32 and x12 existed in older specs and were later removed or rarely implemented version).
  • Width: the number of lanes the link actually trained to (e.g. x4). It can be lower than the maximum either side supports.
  • Generation / speed: the data rate per lane, in gigatransfers per second (GT/s): 2.5, 5, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 GT/s for Gen1–Gen7 (Chapter 6).

4.7 Hardware view

🔧 Hardware

Must participate in any NVMe transaction: the root complex (and its root port), every switch on the path, every link's PHY on both sides, and the SSD's PCIe controller IP. May participate: retimers (a retimer is a physical-layer device that is LTSSM-aware and re-drives the signal; it is not a switch and has no configuration-space bus of its own), redrivers (analog amplifiers, protocol-unaware), and the IOMMU. Observable: configuration space of every port and function, link status registers, AER error logs, traffic on a link if you insert an interposer/analyzer. Generally unobservable: the root complex's internal fabric queues, switch internal buffer occupancy (some switches expose vendor counters impl), and the SSD controller's internal request scheduling.

4.8 Specification and protocol view: how packets find their way

📘 Specification

The PCIe Base Specification defines three routing methods for TLPs verified: address-based (Memory and I/O requests), ID-based (Configuration requests, Completions, ID-routed Messages), and implicit (certain Messages: routed to Root Complex, broadcast from Root Complex, local — terminate at receiver, gathered and routed to RC). Enumeration software assigns bus numbers depth-first and programs each bridge's Secondary and Subordinate Bus Number so ID routing works, and programs memory base/limit windows so address routing works.

Mechanism, step by step — an NVMe doorbell write from CPU to the SSD behind Switch DSP 2 in Figure 4.1:

  1. CPU core executes a store to an uncached MMIO address inside the SSD's BAR0 + 1000h region. What changes: a write leaves the core. Evidence: none externally yet.
  2. Root Complex decodes the address as belonging to Root Port B's memory window and builds a Memory Write TLP (posted). Evidence: visible on the Root Port B link with an analyzer.
  3. Switch Upstream Port receives the TLP, checks it, and compares the address against each downstream bridge's memory base/limit. It matches DSP 2. Evidence: switch-internal; usually only inferable.
  4. DSP 2 transmits the TLP on its link. Evidence: visible on the DSP 2 link.
  5. SSD receives the TLP, its BAR decode hits the doorbell register, and the NVMe controller updates its tail pointer. Evidence: later behavior (it starts fetching SQ entries — Memory Read TLPs going upstream).

The SSD's subsequent DMA read of the Submission Queue travels upstream: address-routed toward the root (because the address is not inside any downstream window, the switch forwards it upstream). The completions coming back are ID-routed to the SSD's Requester ID (its BDF).

4.9 Trace view: what a single capture point can see

🔍 Trace visibility rule

An analyzer on a link sees only that link. On the DSP 2 link above, you see the doorbell write, the SSD's reads, completions, and the SSD's interrupt write, but not traffic of the other two SSDs — even though their traffic competes for the same uplink. A "slow" trace on DSP 2 with long gaps between a Memory Read and its completion therefore does not prove the SSD or root complex is slow: the delay may be uplink contention invisible from this capture point.

4.10 Linux view

# Tree view: shows root ports, switches and endpoints with their bus numbers
lspci -tv

# Find NVMe controllers (class 0108) and their BDF
lspci -d ::0108

# Walk the sysfs path: every directory component is a port on the way to the root
readlink -f /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device

# Inspect a bridge's bus numbers and windows (read-only)
lspci -vv -s 00:01.1 | grep -E 'Bus:|Memory behind|Prefetchable'

What these can prove: the logical hierarchy as enumerated (which bridge sits above which device), bus-number assignments, memory windows. What they cannot prove: physical retimers/redrivers (invisible to config space), the actual bandwidth delivered, or whether two "sibling" devices are electrically independent. Example of what readlink returns, illustrative only: a path like /sys/devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:01.1/0000:01:00.0/0000:02:02.0/0000:04:00.0, meaning root port 00:01.1 → switch upstream 01:00.0 → switch downstream 02:02.0 → SSD 04:00.0 synthetic.

4.11 Code: modeling routing

# Simulation: how a switch chooses an egress port (address and ID routing)
class Bridge:
    def __init__(self, name, sec, sub, mem_base, mem_limit):
        self.name, self.sec, self.sub = name, sec, sub
        self.mem_base, self.mem_limit = mem_base, mem_limit

dsps = [Bridge("DSP1", 3, 3, 0xFE000000, 0xFE0FFFFF),
        Bridge("DSP2", 4, 4, 0xFE100000, 0xFE1FFFFF),
        Bridge("DSP3", 5, 5, 0xFE200000, 0xFE2FFFFF)]

def route_memory(addr):
    for b in dsps:
        if b.mem_base <= addr <= b.mem_limit:
            return b.name
    return "UPSTREAM"            # not claimed below us: send toward root

def route_id(bus):
    for b in dsps:
        if b.sec <= bus <= b.sub:
            return b.name
    return "UPSTREAM"

print(route_memory(0xFE101008))  # DSP2 (doorbell)
print(route_memory(0x123400100)) # UPSTREAM (DMA to host memory)
print(route_id(4))               # DSP2 (completion to bus 4 device)

4.12 Worked example: oversubscription math

Three Gen4 x4 SSDs sit behind a switch whose uplink is Gen4 x8. Per direction, Gen4 delivers 16 GT/s × 128/130 ÷ 8 = 1.969 GB/s per lane derived. Downstream aggregate: 3 × 4 × 1.969 = 23.6 GB/s; uplink: 8 × 1.969 = 15.75 GB/s. Oversubscription 23.6 / 15.75 ≈ 1.5:1. If each SSD can read at 7 GB/s, three concurrent sequential readers want 21 GB/s, but at most ~15.75 GB/s raw link rate (and less after TLP overhead, ≈ 13–14 GB/s with 256-byte payloads, see Chapter 10) can reach the host. The SSDs are not "slow" — the topology is.

4.13 Common mistakes

  • Calling a switch a "hub" and expecting broadcast. Switches route; only specific message types are broadcast.
  • Reading the bus number in lspci as a physical bus. Bus 03 is just the number assigned to the link below some bridge.
  • Assuming the CPU's root port and the SSD negotiate the link "through the OS". Link training is hardware; the OS only observes and can request retraining.
  • Ignoring the switch uplink when computing aggregate bandwidth.
  • Assuming chipset-attached M.2 slots have the same path as CPU-attached ones; chipset lanes share the CPU–chipset link impl.

4.15 Senior insight

💡 Senior insight

Topology is a performance and a reliability decision. Two SSDs under one switch form a shared failure domain: a switch firmware hang or uplink retrain hits both. In storage servers, architects deliberately spread mirror pairs across root ports and sockets. When someone reports "NVMe latency spikes", the first diagram you draw is the tree from the CPU socket to the drive, annotated with each link's width and speed — before you look at a single NVMe command.

🧪 Lab 4.1 — Map your NVMe path to the CPU SAFE

Objective: draw the exact PCIe path from each NVMe controller to its root port. Prerequisites: Linux machine with an NVMe SSD, pciutils. Setup: none; all commands read-only.

  1. Run lspci -tv and locate devices with "Non-Volatile memory controller".
  2. For each, run readlink -f /sys/class/nvme/nvmeN/device and split the path into BDFs.
  3. For every BDF on the path run lspci -vv -s BDF | grep -E 'LnkCap|LnkSta'.
  4. Draw the tree with width and speed on every link.

Observations: count links between the SSD and the root. Questions: Is any link narrower or slower than the SSD's own link? Do two SSDs share an ancestor? Expected reasoning: the minimum bandwidth along the path bounds throughput; a shared ancestor bounds aggregate throughput.

Solution

A directly attached drive shows two components in the sysfs path after the host bridge: the root port and the endpoint. A drive behind a switch shows root port → switch upstream port → switch downstream port → endpoint (three bridges). The narrowest link along the path determines the ceiling; if two drives share the switch upstream port, its link bounds their sum.

Extension: repeat on a dual-socket server and note which socket's root complex each drive hangs off (cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device/numa_node).

🧪 Lab 4.2 — Senior forensic: prove an uplink bottleneck CAUTION

Objective: distinguish an SSD limit from a shared-uplink limit. Prerequisites: ≥2 NVMe drives behind one switch, fio, test drives with no valuable data (use read-only workloads: --rw=read --readonly). Procedure: run 128 KiB sequential reads, QD 32, on drive A alone; then B alone; then A+B concurrently; then A plus a drive C under a different root port. Observations: per-drive GB/s. Expected reasoning: if A+B ≈ uplink limit while A+C ≈ A + C, the shared uplink is the bottleneck.

Solution

Compare the A+B sum against the derived uplink ceiling (lanes × per-lane rate × TLP efficiency). Within ~10% of that ceiling with each drive below its solo number is strong evidence of uplink saturation; A+C scaling linearly rules out a CPU/memory limit.

Extension: measure P99 latency at QD1 during the concurrent run to show contention effects on latency, not just bandwidth.

Quiz

  1. Why does lspci show bus numbers if PCIe has no shared bus?

    Answer

    PCIe preserves the PCI software model; each link and each switch's internal fabric is presented as a virtual PCI bus behind a PCI-to-PCI bridge so enumeration and ID routing work unchanged.

  2. Which routing method is used for a completion returning to an SSD?

    Answer

    ID routing, using the Requester ID (bus/device/function) copied into the completion.

  3. A Gen4 x8 switch uplink serves four Gen4 x4 SSDs. Oversubscription ratio?

    Answer

    16 lanes downstream / 8 lanes upstream at equal speed = 2:1.

  4. Is a retimer visible in lspci?

    Answer

    Normally no; retimers participate in link training but do not appear as functions in configuration space (some expose sideband management interfaces, implementation-dependent).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is the difference between a lane and a link?
    Model answerA lane is one TX differential pair plus one RX differential pair; a link is the set of lanes (x1–x16) connecting two ports and operating as one logical connection.
  2. Beginner What is a Root Complex?
    Model answerThe entity connecting the CPU/memory to the PCIe hierarchy, containing root ports; it issues requests for the CPU and services device DMA to memory.
  3. Beginner Why is PCIe full duplex?
    Model answerEach lane has separate transmit and receive differential pairs, so both directions carry traffic simultaneously.
  4. Beginner What header type does a switch port have?
    Model answerType 1 (bridge); endpoints have Type 0.
  5. Beginner Name the three TLP routing methods.
    Model answerAddress, ID, implicit.
  6. Intermediate How does a switch decide to forward a Memory Write upstream?
    Model answerIf the address does not fall into any downstream port's memory base/limit (or prefetchable) window, and arrives on a downstream port, it is forwarded upstream; arriving on the upstream port and matching no window it is handled as unsupported.
  7. Intermediate Explain bifurcation.
    Model answerA root port's lanes split into multiple narrower independent links (e.g. x16 → 4×x4), each its own root port/link, configured by platform firmware; no switch involved.
  8. Intermediate What happens to a config read to an empty slot?
    Model answerThe downstream port with link down returns a completion with UR (or the RC synthesizes all-ones); software reads FFFFh Vendor ID.
  9. Intermediate Why might two drives in the same chassis have different latency?
    Model answerDifferent paths: switch hops, chipset vs CPU attach, NUMA distance, link speed.
  10. Intermediate What is a multi-function device?
    Model answerOne device number exposing several functions (0–7, or more with ARI), each with its own config space.
  11. Advanced How does ACS affect peer-to-peer NVMe traffic?
    Model answerACS Source Validation/P2P Request Redirect can force P2P requests upstream to the root complex for IOMMU checks, adding latency or blocking P2P if the RC does not forward.
  12. Advanced Can a switch reorder TLPs?
    Model answerOnly within ordering rules: e.g. posted may pass non-posted; relaxed-ordering-marked traffic may be reordered as permitted. It must not violate required orderings.
  13. Advanced Why does enumeration use depth-first bus numbering?
    Model answerSo each bridge's descendants occupy a contiguous range [secondary, subordinate], enabling simple range-based ID routing.
  14. Advanced What is a Root Complex Integrated Endpoint?
    Model answerAn endpoint built into the RC with no physical link; it appears on the root bus and has no link status of its own.
  15. Advanced Where would you insert an analyzer to see all traffic of 3 SSDs behind one switch?
    Model answerOn the switch uplink; but that view loses per-downstream timing inside the switch.
  16. Senior Design an 8-SSD server for redundancy and bandwidth.
    Model answerSpread drives across sockets/root ports, avoid oversubscribed switches for hot paths, put mirror pairs in different failure domains, align NUMA of application threads with drive locality.
  17. Senior A customer says "drive X is slow". What topology evidence do you request?
    Model answerlspci -tvvv with LnkSta for every port on the path, NUMA node, concurrent workloads on siblings, AER logs.
  18. Senior When is a switch preferable to bifurcation?
    Model answerWhen more devices than root ports are needed, for hot-plug isolation, P2P locality, or when the platform cannot bifurcate; at the cost of latency (~100+ ns per hop, implementation-dependent) and oversubscription.
  19. Senior How would a switch firmware bug manifest differently from an SSD bug?
    Model answerAffects multiple downstream devices, correlates with upstream link events, often visible as completion timeouts on several BDFs simultaneously.
  20. Senior What can configuration space never tell you about topology?
    Model answerPhysical retimers/redrivers, cable/board quality, signal margin, and actual delivered bandwidth.
🎯 Exercise

Draw Figure 4.1 from memory. Then annotate: (a) routing method used by the doorbell write, the SQ fetch and its completion, the MSI-X interrupt write; (b) the link an analyzer must sit on to see each.

📌 Teach-back

To a child: "Each gadget gets its own train track to the big station." To a junior: "PCIe is a tree of point-to-point serial links; switches route packets by address or by ID; the software still sees PCI buses." To a senior: "The hierarchy defines bandwidth ceilings, failure domains and P2P paths; config space shows the logical tree but not physical retimers or contention."

4.16 Summary

PCIe replaced a shared parallel bus with point-to-point serial links arranged as a tree: Root Complex at the top, root ports beginning branches, switches fanning out, endpoints (such as NVMe SSDs) at the leaves. Packets are routed by address, ID, or implicitly. The software model of buses, bridges and BDFs survives unchanged. Throughput and failure domains are properties of the whole path, not just the device.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain point-to-point vs shared bus and why PCIe kept the PCI software model.
  • I can draw a hierarchy with RC, root ports, switch (upstream/downstream ports) and endpoints.
  • I can identify which link an analyzer must be on to see a given transaction.
  • I can debug "missing device" and "aggregate throughput plateau" using the topology.
  • I can distinguish a switch from a bifurcated root port and from a retimer.
  • I can cite the PCIe Base Specification as the source for routing rules.

Further reading: PCI Express Base Specification (topology and routing sections); Linux kernel documentation Documentation/PCI/. Next: Chapter 5 — what a lane physically is.

5 PCIe Physical Architecture

← 4 The PCIe Mental Model6 PCIe Generations →

5.1 Why this chapter exists

The physical layer is where "the SSD only runs at x2" and "the link keeps retraining" are born. You need to know what a lane is made of, how a receiver recovers a clock from data, how width and speed are negotiated, and which compatibility rules let a Gen5 x4 SSD work in a Gen3 x16 slot.

5.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: describe a lane as two differential pairs and a link as 1–16 lanes.
  • Intermediate: explain differential signaling, AC coupling, embedded clocking, lane reversal, polarity inversion.
  • Advanced: explain width and speed negotiation outcomes and how the "lowest common denominator" rule works.
  • Senior: diagnose degraded links from LnkCap/LnkSta and correlate with signal integrity, reference clock and retimer issues.
  • Trace/debug/validation: know which physical events an analyzer can record (ordered sets, electrical idle, speed changes) and how to validate that a link meets its expected width/speed under stress.

5.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 4 (link, lane, width).

5.4 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Two friends talk with flashlights across a valley. Each has a flashlight pointed at the other (TX) and eyes watching the other's flashlight (RX). If they want to talk faster, they can add more flashlight pairs side by side (more lanes) or blink faster (higher generation). They first agree how many flashlights both can see and how fast both can blink before chatting.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Real lanes use differential signals — two wires carrying opposite voltages, where only the difference matters — not a single light. Bits on separate lanes are not independent messages: one packet is striped byte-by-byte across all lanes of the link. And "blinking faster" requires both sides to equalize — pre-distort and filter the signal — which a flashlight never does.

5.5 Beginner: lane, differential pair, TX, RX

A differential pair is two wires, D+ and D−, driven with complementary voltages. The receiver looks only at (D+ − D−). Noise that hits both wires equally (common-mode noise) cancels. Swings can be small (hundreds of millivolts), which saves power and allows high rates. A lane = one TX pair from this side to the other + one RX pair in the opposite direction. One device's TX connects to the other's RX. The pairs are AC coupled through series capacitors (on the transmitter side of the channel), so the two chips need not share a DC common-mode voltage — and that capacitor is exactly what the receiver-detect circuit in Detect probes.

5.6 Engineering: how bits cross a lane

Serialization and embedded clock

The transmitter serializes symbols into a bit stream at the line rate. No separate data clock is sent; the receiver's CDR locks a local clock onto the transitions in the data. To guarantee enough transitions and DC balance, data is encoded (8b/10b for Gen1–2) or scrambled with a sync header (128b/130b for Gen3–5); Gen6+ uses PAM4 with FLIT encoding (Chapter 6). A 100 MHz reference clock (REFCLK) is commonly distributed to both sides so their PLLs run at matching frequencies; architectures include common clock, separate reference clocks with no spread spectrum (SRNS), and separate with independent spread spectrum (SRIS) verified. Clocking mismatches between what the platform provides and what the device was configured for are a classic cause of link instability.

Byte striping across lanes

On a multi-lane link, consecutive bytes of a packet go to consecutive lanes: byte 0 on lane 0, byte 1 on lane 1, ... byte 4 on lane 0 again for x4. Every lane carries a share of every packet. That is why a single bad lane corrupts packets on the whole link, and why the link must deskew lanes (align them using ordered sets that are sent simultaneously on all lanes).

Lane reversal and polarity inversion

Polarity inversion: if D+ and D− of a pair are swapped on the board, the receiver detects inverted training sequences and inverts internally — mandatory support verified. Lane reversal: if lane 0 of one side is wired to lane 3 of the other (board routing convenience), the link can still train with reversed lane numbering; support is optional for one side as long as the pair can resolve it impl.

Link width negotiation

During Configuration the downstream port proposes link and lane numbers in TS1 ordered sets on lanes where it detected a receiver; the upstream port echoes those it can accept. The result is the largest supported width that both sides and the detected, working lanes allow. If lane 2 of an x4 link is broken, the link cannot form an x3 (non-standard) and typically falls back to x2 using lanes 0–1, or x1 derived.

Speed negotiation

Every link first trains at 2.5 GT/s (Gen1). Each side advertises supported rates in TS1/TS2 "data rate identifier" fields. After reaching L0, if both support higher rates, the LTSSM goes through Recovery to change speed (and for 8 GT/s and above, performs equalization). Speed is therefore negotiated after the link already works at Gen1 — a key debugging fact: a link that "comes up at Gen1 but never Gen4" has a problem in the speed-change/equalization path, not in basic detection (Chapter 9).

Compatibility

  • Speed: every generation must support all lower data rates, so Gen5 devices interoperate with Gen3 ports at Gen3 verified.
  • Width: a x4 card in a x16 slot trains to x4 ("up-plugging"); a x16 card in a physically open-ended x4 slot trains to x4 ("down-plugging") if the device supports narrower widths — all PCIe devices must support x1 verified.
  • Result: link = min(speed both support, signal quality permits) × min(width both support, working lanes).

5.7 Hardware view

🔧 Hardware

Per lane, the transmitter has a serializer, a de-emphasis/FIR equalizer (pre-cursor, main cursor, post-cursor taps from Gen3), and a driver; the receiver has termination, a CTLE (continuous-time linear equalizer), often a DFE (decision feedback equalizer), CDR and a deserializer. Channel loss grows with frequency and trace length: as rates double, the allowed channel loss budget is consumed faster, so Gen5/Gen6 platforms often need retimers for long traces or risers. Form factors: M.2 (up to x4), U.2 (x4, or 2×x2 dual-port), U.3, EDSFF E1.S/E1.L/E3 (x4/x8/x16) impl.

5.8 Linux view

# Capability vs status: what could be vs what was negotiated
sudo lspci -vv -s 0000:04:00.0 | grep -E 'LnkCap:|LnkSta:|LnkCtl2:'

# Same through sysfs (no root needed)
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/max_link_speed
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/max_link_width
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/current_link_speed
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/current_link_width

Illustrative, abbreviated output synthetic: LnkCap: Port #0, Speed 16GT/s, Width x4 and LnkSta: Speed 8GT/s (downgraded), Width x2 (downgraded). Recent pciutils versions annotate "(downgraded)" version. Can prove: what was negotiated at the moment of reading. Cannot prove: why — signal integrity, BIOS speed caps (LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed), retimer limits, or a slot wired with fewer lanes all look identical in LnkSta. Always compare both ends of the link: the endpoint and its parent port.

⚠️ Warning

Do not use setpci writes to force speeds or retrain links on a system with mounted filesystems or valuable data. A retrain that fails takes the device offline; a write to the wrong register can hang the machine. Read-only commands are always safe.

5.9 Worked example

An SSD reports LnkCap 16 GT/s x4; LnkSta 16 GT/s x2. The parent root port reports LnkCap 16 GT/s x4, LnkSta 16 GT/s x2. Both ends agree and speed is full, so equalization at Gen4 succeeded on the working lanes. Width x2 points to lanes 2–3: either physically not routed (slot wired x2 — check motherboard manual: some M.2 slots share lanes with SATA ports), a damaged connector, or a receiver that was not detected on lanes 2–3 during Detect. Expected throughput ceiling: 2 × 1.969 = 3.94 GB/s per direction — matches a user complaint of "~3.5 GB/s instead of 7 GB/s".

🧪 Lab 5.1 — Capability vs status audit SAFE

Objective: find every degraded link in your system. Setup: none. Steps: loop over /sys/bus/pci/devices/* and print max vs current speed and width where both exist. Observations: devices with current < max. Questions: Is it degraded on purpose (ASPM does not change width; but some GPUs downclock link speed at idle)? Which end limits?

for d in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*; do
  [ -r "$d/current_link_speed" ] || continue
  printf '%s  max=%s x%s  cur=%s x%s\n' "${d##*/}" \
    "$(cat $d/max_link_speed 2>/dev/null)" "$(cat $d/max_link_width 2>/dev/null)" \
    "$(cat $d/current_link_speed 2>/dev/null)" "$(cat $d/current_link_width 2>/dev/null)"
done
Solution

Expect many devices legitimately below max (e.g. a Gen4 device on a Gen3 port shows max 16 GT/s, current 8 GT/s: the port limits). Compare with the parent port's max values; the link runs at the minimum of both ends. Some devices (notably GPUs) change speed dynamically for power; NVMe SSDs normally hold their trained speed.

Extension: repeat under heavy I/O and after suspend/resume to see whether anything changes.

Quiz

  1. How many signal wires in a x8 link?

    Answer

    8 lanes × 2 pairs × 2 wires = 32.

  2. At what speed does every link initially train?

    Answer

    2.5 GT/s (Gen1); higher speeds are reached later via Recovery.

  3. Why can't a x4 link with one broken lane run as x3?

    Answer

    x3 is not a defined width; the link falls back to a supported width such as x2 or x1 using contiguous working lanes starting at lane 0 (or reversed).

  4. What does AC coupling enable?

    Answer

    Different DC common-mode levels at each end, and the charge-time-based receiver detection.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a differential pair?
    Model answerTwo complementary wires; the receiver uses their voltage difference, rejecting common-mode noise.
  2. Intermediate What do LnkCap and LnkSta mean?
    Model answerLink Capabilities (max speed/width the port supports) and Link Status (currently negotiated).
  3. Advanced Why are retimers needed at Gen5?
    Model answerHigher Nyquist frequency increases channel loss; long traces exceed loss budget; retimers recover and retransmit, splitting the channel into two compliant segments.
  4. Advanced What is SRIS?
    Model answerSeparate Reference clocks with Independent Spread spectrum; requires larger elastic buffers and more frequent SKP ordered sets.
  5. Senior Both ends show Gen3 although both support Gen4. Investigate.
    Model answerCheck Target Link Speed in LnkCtl2 (BIOS cap), equalization status bits in Link Status 2 / 16 GT/s capability, AER history, riser/retimer support, try forcing a retrain at Gen4 in a lab setting.
💡 Senior insight

"Negotiated" is not "healthy". A link at full width and speed can still be marginal, logging thousands of correctable errors that each cost a replay. Always pair LnkSta with error counters.

📌 Teach-back & summary

Child: "two flashlights per lane, one each way." Junior: "a lane is TX+RX differential pairs; links of x1–x16 stripe bytes across lanes; width and speed are negotiated, speed after first training at Gen1." Senior: "negotiated state lives in LnkSta at both ends; cause analysis requires channel, clocking and equalization evidence."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can draw a x4 link with TX/RX pairs and AC coupling.
  • I can explain byte striping, deskew, polarity inversion and lane reversal.
  • I can predict the negotiated width/speed for any device/slot combination.
  • I can find a downgraded link in Linux and state what the evidence does not prove.
  • I can cite the PCIe Base Specification (Physical Layer) and the form-factor spec (e.g. M.2/EDSFF) as separate sources.

Further reading: PCIe Base Specification, Physical Layer Logical and Electrical chapters; PCI-SIG CEM and form-factor specifications. Next: Chapter 6 — generations and bandwidth math.

6 PCIe Generations

← 5 PCIe Physical Architecture7 PCIe Layer Model →

6.1 Why this chapter exists

"Gen4 x4" is the most common phrase in NVMe product sheets, and the most commonly mis-computed. Engineers confuse GT/s with Gb/s, forget encoding overhead, forget that PCIe numbers are per direction, double-count by adding both directions, and, worst of all, confuse the PCIe generation of the link with the NVMe specification revision of the controller. This chapter makes the math explicit so you can derive every number yourself.

⚠️ Do not confuse

PCIe 4.0 (a PCI-SIG physical/link specification, 16 GT/s) and NVMe 1.4 / 2.0 / 2.4 (NVM Express command-set and controller specifications) are independent. A drive can implement NVMe 1.3 over a Gen4 link, or NVMe 2.x over a Gen3 link. lspci tells you the PCIe link; nvme id-ctrl (field VER) tells you the NVMe revision the controller claims.

6.2 Learning objectives

  • Explain GT/s, line encoding (8b/10b, 128b/130b, PAM4 + FLIT with FEC) and why the encoding changed.
  • Derive per-lane per-direction usable bandwidth for every generation, and scale to x4/x8/x16.
  • Estimate application-visible NVMe throughput after TLP and DLLP overhead.
  • Explain latency implications (serialization, FEC) and backward compatibility.
  • Validate a vendor bandwidth claim and spot marketing that sums both directions.

6.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 5 (lanes, embedded clock, encoding purpose).

6.4 Analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Each generation is a faster train on the same kind of track. But every train also carries some non-passenger cars: the engine and the guard's van (encoding and packet overhead). Early trains had 2 guard cars for every 8 passenger cars (8b/10b: 20% overhead). Later trains had 2 guard cars for every 128 passenger cars (128b/130b: ~1.5%). The newest trains pack passengers into fixed 256-seat carriages with a few seats reserved for repair crews (FLIT with FEC and CRC).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

"Guard cars" lump together two distinct overheads: line encoding (applies to every bit, below the packet layer) and packet framing/headers (per TLP, depends on payload size). The second one is often bigger and depends on your workload, not the generation.

6.5 Beginner: GT/s is not GB/s

GT/s (gigatransfers per second) counts symbols on the wire per lane. For Gen1–Gen5 (NRZ, two voltage levels) one transfer = one bit, so 16 GT/s = 16 Gbit/s raw. For Gen6+ (PAM4, four voltage levels) one symbol carries 2 bits; 64 GT/s is achieved at 32 GBaud. Raw bits include encoding overhead; you must remove it, then divide by 8 to get bytes.

BWlane,dir = R × E ÷ 8
  • BWlane,dir — usable bytes per second per lane per direction, after line encoding only (before TLP/DLLP overhead)
  • R — data rate in GT/s (bits per second per lane for NRZ generations; for Gen6+ the GT/s figure is already the bit rate)
  • E — encoding efficiency: 8/10 = 0.8 (8b/10b), 128/130 ≈ 0.984615 (128b/130b), ≈ 1.0 at the encoding level for Gen6 1b/1b FLIT mode (overhead moves into the FLIT's CRC/FEC bytes, see below)
  • ÷ 8 — bits to bytes

The same x4 column drawn to one linear scale. Each step roughly doubles the previous one; the visible exception is Gen2 → Gen3, where the rate rose only 1.6× (5 → 8 GT/s) but dropping 8b/10b for 128b/130b recovered the rest. derived

📘 Gen6 FLIT arithmetic, stated carefully

In PCIe 6.0 FLIT mode, a 256-byte FLIT carries 236 bytes of TLP content, 6 bytes of Data Link Layer payload (DLP, which carries the information DLLPs carried previously), 8 bytes of CRC, and 6 bytes of FEC verified. Whether you count DLP bytes as "useful" changes the efficiency between 236/256 = 92.2% and 242/256 = 94.5%; both numbers appear in public material derived. Crucially, FLIT mode also removes per-TLP framing tokens and per-TLP LCRC and uses a different TLP header format, so per-TLP overhead in FLIT mode is lower than in Gen5. Comparing Gen5 vs Gen6 efficiency requires including both effects. FLIT mode is also used at lower rates when both sides negotiate it in 6.0+ version.

6.7 Why the encoding changed

8b/10b (Gen1, Gen2)

Each 8-bit byte becomes a 10-bit symbol chosen from a table to guarantee transitions (for CDR) and DC balance (running disparity). Special "K" symbols (e.g. COM = K28.5) mark framing and ordered sets. Cost: 20% of the line rate.

128b/130b (Gen3–Gen5)

To reach 8 GT/s (instead of 10 GT/s that 8b/10b would have needed for ~2× Gen2 throughput), Gen3 adopted 130-bit blocks: a 2-bit sync header (01b = Data block, 10b = Ordered Set block) followed by 128 bits of payload. Data bytes are scrambled with a pseudo-random polynomial to provide transitions and spectral spreading; scrambling is statistical, not guaranteed like 8b/10b. Framing moved from K-symbols into tokens inside data blocks (STP, SDP, END Data Stream, EDB, IDL). Cost: 2/130 ≈ 1.54%.

PAM4 + FLIT (Gen6, Gen7)

Doubling NRZ to 64 GT/s would have required a ~32 GHz Nyquist frequency with unacceptable channel loss. PAM4 sends 2 bits per symbol at 32 GBaud, keeping Nyquist at 16 GHz like Gen5, but with three eyes each ~1/3 the height, so raw bit error rate is far worse (on the order of 10−6 first-bit error rate target vs 10−12 for NRZ generations verified). A lightweight FEC corrects most errors; a strong CRC detects the rest; Data Link Layer retry handles residual errors. Fixed-size FLITs make FEC and CRC practical.

6.8 Engineering: from link rate to NVMe throughput

Line rate after encoding is not what fio reports. Each TLP carries headers, and the link also carries DLLPs and periodic SKP ordered sets. For Gen3–Gen5 (non-FLIT) a TLP on the wire costs approximately:

Wire bytes per TLP ≈ framing(4) + sequence/DLL(2, inside the 4-byte STP token in 128b/130b) + header(12 or 16) + payload + ECRC(0 or 4) + LCRC(4)
  • framing — STP token (Gen3+) or STP + END symbols (Gen1/2); together with the sequence number about 6–8 bytes of DLL/PL overhead per TLP
  • header — 3DW (12 bytes) for 32-bit addresses and completions, 4DW (16 bytes) for 64-bit addresses
  • ECRC — optional end-to-end CRC (TD bit set)
  • LCRC — 32-bit link CRC, always present on TLPs in non-FLIT mode

Worked example (Gen4 x4 NVMe read): a 128 KiB read is delivered by the SSD as Memory Write TLPs into host memory (the SSD writes read data to the host). With Max Payload Size (MPS) = 256 bytes and 64-bit addresses (4DW header), each TLP carries 256 bytes using ≈ 256 + 16 + 8 = 280 wire bytes. Efficiency ≈ 256/280 = 91.4%. Subtract ~1–3% for Ack/UpdateFC DLLPs and SKP ordered sets impl. Usable ≈ 7.88 GB/s × 0.914 × ~0.98 ≈ 7.05 GB/s derived. Real Gen4 x4 drives quote ~7.0–7.4 GB/s sequential read, consistent with this ceiling. With MPS = 128 bytes efficiency drops to 128/152 ≈ 84%, ceiling ≈ 6.5 GB/s: MPS matters.

Payload per TLPHeaderWire bytesEfficiencyGen4 x4 ceilingGen5 x4 ceiling
64 B4DW8872.7%5.73 GB/s11.5 GB/s
128 B4DW15284.2%6.6313.3
256 B4DW28091.4%7.2014.4
512 B4DW53695.5%7.5215.0

Ceilings above are before DLLP/SKP overhead and assume a perfectly busy link derived. Writes are different: the SSD issues Memory Read requests to fetch host data, and data returns as Completions with Data (3DW header), split at Read Completion Boundary (RCB, 64 or 128 bytes) granularity and limited by MPS, plus the read requests consume the opposite direction. See Chapter 12.

6.9 Latency implications

  • Serialization: a 280-byte TLP takes 280 × 8 / (4 lanes × 16 Gb/s × 128/130) ≈ 35.6 ns on Gen4 x4; 71 ns on Gen3 x4; ~1.1 µs on Gen1 x1 (280 × 10 bits / 2.5 Gb/s) derived. Faster generations reduce per-packet latency but NVMe command latency (tens of µs, dominated by NAND) changes little — bandwidth improves much more than 4 KiB QD1 latency.
  • FEC in Gen6: adds a small fixed decode latency; PCI-SIG's design target was low single-digit nanoseconds uncertain (exact values are implementation-dependent).
  • Retimers add tens of ns each way impl.
  • Replays on a marginal link add round-trip delays and can dominate tail latency.

6.10 Compatibility

Higher-generation devices must support all lower rates; links train at 2.5 GT/s and upshift. Connectors (CEM card-edge, M.2, U.2) are mechanically compatible across generations within a form factor, but the electrical channel (board, riser, cable) may only be validated for lower speeds: the device and port can both be Gen5 while the channel limits the link to Gen4. FLIT mode is negotiated; Gen6 devices talking to Gen5 ports use non-FLIT 128b/130b at ≤32 GT/s.

6.11 Linux and verification

# PCIe link of controller nvme0 (speed, width)
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device/current_link_speed /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device/current_link_width
# MaxPayload / MaxReadReq actually configured (DevCtl), and supported (DevCap)
sudo lspci -vv -s $(basename $(readlink -f /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device)) | grep -E 'MaxPayload|MaxReadReq'
# NVMe specification revision the controller reports (a different thing!)
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i '^ver'
📭 What the spec does not say

The PCIe specification does not promise any application throughput; it defines signaling and protocol. Achieved throughput depends on MPS, MRRS, outstanding request limits (tags), completion credit sizing, root-complex memory bandwidth, IOMMU translation costs and SSD internals — all implementation-dependent.

6.12 Common mistakes

  • Quoting "Gen4 x4 = 64 Gb/s = 8 GB/s" (forgets encoding) or "16 GB/s" (adds both directions).
  • Assuming PAM4 64 GT/s means 128 Gb/s (it is 64 Gb/s at 32 GBaud).
  • Using 1 GB = 230 inconsistently with vendor 109.
  • Blaming the SSD for 5.7 GB/s on Gen4 x4 without checking MPS (64-byte or 128-byte MPS caps throughput).
  • Reporting "NVMe Gen4" — NVMe has revisions, PCIe has generations.

🧪 Lab 6.1 — Compute and validate your drive's ceiling SAFE

Objective: derive the theoretical sequential-read ceiling and compare with measurement. Setup: NVMe drive, fio, read-only test (fio --name=r --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=read --bs=128k --iodepth=32 --ioengine=libaio --direct=1 --readonly --runtime=30 --time_based). Steps: read speed/width and MPS; compute ceiling with the formula and table above; run fio. Questions: what fraction of the ceiling do you reach? Expected reasoning: 85–98% of the derived ceiling indicates the link is the limit; far below suggests the SSD or host is the limit.

Solution

For Gen4 x4 MPS 256: ceiling ≈ 7.2 GB/s before DLLP overhead, ≈ 7.0 after. A drive measuring 6.9 GB/s is link-bound; a drive measuring 5 GB/s on the same link is device- or host-bound (try higher iodepth, multiple jobs, check CPU).

Extension: repeat with --bs=4k and explain why GB/s drops (command-rate/IOPS limits and per-command overhead, not link encoding).

Quiz

  1. Gen3 x4 per-direction bandwidth after encoding?

    Answer

    4 × 8 × 128/130 ÷ 8 = 3.94 GB/s.

  2. Why did Gen3 choose 8 GT/s and not 10 GT/s?

    Answer

    128b/130b nearly eliminates encoding overhead, so 8 GT/s gives ~2× Gen2's usable bandwidth with lower frequency and channel loss than 10 GT/s.

  3. Does PCIe 5.0 imply NVMe 2.0?

    Answer

    No; independent specifications.

  4. What carries the old DLLP information in Gen6 FLIT mode?

    Answer

    The DLP bytes inside each FLIT.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Difference between GT/s and GB/s?
    Model answerGT/s is symbol rate per lane; GB/s is usable bytes after encoding, ×lanes, per direction.
  2. Intermediate Why does MPS change NVMe throughput?
    Model answerFixed per-TLP header/framing cost is amortized over payload; larger payload → higher efficiency.
  3. Advanced Why PAM4 at Gen6?
    Model answerTo double bit rate without doubling Nyquist frequency/channel loss; requires FEC due to higher raw BER.
  4. Advanced Why fixed-size FLITs?
    Model answerFEC and strong CRC operate on fixed blocks; retry granularity becomes per-FLIT; framing per TLP removed.
  5. Senior A customer sees 13 GB/s on Gen5 x4 and asks why not 15.75.
    Model answerExplain TLP efficiency at MPS, DLLP/SKP, host memory and IOMMU limits; derive ~14.4 ceiling at MPS 256; 13 is ~90% of practical ceiling.
💡 Senior insight

When a number disagrees with expectations, write the derivation down with every factor and its source. Disagreements almost always come from a hidden factor: direction, encoding, header size, MPS, units, or a link that is not running at the speed you assumed.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can derive per-lane, x4, x8, x16 bandwidth for Gen1–Gen7 with encoding.
  • I can compute TLP efficiency for a given MPS and header size.
  • I never confuse PCIe generation with NVMe revision.
  • I can explain why Gen6 uses PAM4, FLITs and FEC.
