7 PCIe Layer Model

← 6 PCIe Generations8 The Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM) →

7.0 Why this chapter exists

Every PCIe error message, every analyzer column and every AER bit belongs to a layer. If you know which layer generated an event, you know which layer's mechanisms to investigate. PCIe defines three layers — Transaction, Data Link, Physical — plus software above (configuration, device drivers) that the spec calls the software layer.

  • State the purpose, responsibilities, packet structures and error types of each layer.
  • Draw how a TLP grows as it passes down the stack and shrinks on the way up.
  • Map AER error bits to layers.
  • Explain what an analyzer can show at each layer and which layer's events are invisible to software.

Prerequisites: Chapter 5, Chapter 6.

🧒 Kid analogy for the whole stack

Sending a birthday present: You (Transaction Layer) write the card and wrap the gift, writing who it is for and whether you want a thank-you note back. The post office counter (Data Link Layer) stamps a tracking number, adds a tamper seal, and keeps a photocopy until the next post office confirms it arrived undamaged. The delivery van (Physical Layer) drives the box on the road, and the drivers of two vans first agree which lanes of the road they will use.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The tracking number and tamper seal are checked and removed at every hop (every link), not at the final destination; only the optional ECRC behaves like an end-to-end seal. And the "thank-you note" (completion) is a full separate transaction, not an acknowledgement — the post-office acknowledgement (Ack DLLP) is a different, per-link mechanism.

7.1 Physical Layer

🧒 Kid analogy

The road and the van drivers: they agree which lanes to use and how fast to drive, and they put "start" and "end" signs around every parcel so the receiver knows where one ends.

Purpose: move bits reliably enough (target BER ≤ 10−12 for NRZ generations) between two ports. Responsibilities: two sub-blocks. The electrical sub-block: drivers, receivers, equalization, CDR, receiver detection, electrical idle. The logical sub-block: encoding/scrambling, framing (STP/SDP/END tokens or K-symbols), byte striping and deskew, ordered sets (TS1, TS2, SKP, EIOS, EIEOS, FTS, SDS), and the LTSSM that trains and manages the link (Chapter 8). Packet structures: it does not originate TLPs or DLLPs; it originates ordered sets, which never pass to the Data Link Layer. SKP ordered sets are inserted periodically to compensate for clock differences between the two sides (elastic buffers add/remove SKP symbols).

Errors: Receiver Error (8b/10b disparity/symbol errors, 128b/130b sync header or framing token errors; reported as correctable), framing errors (which in 128b/130b force the link into Recovery), and link failures (link down → Surprise Down at the Data Link level). Trace visibility: an analyzer sees ordered sets, electrical idle, speed changes, LTSSM progression; software sees only summary registers (LnkSta, Link Status 2, equalization status, Receiver Error counts through AER).

7.2 Data Link Layer

🧒 Kid analogy

The post-office counter: numbers every parcel, seals it, keeps a copy, and throws the copy away only when the next office says "got numbers up to 57, all good". If a parcel arrives damaged, the next office says "Nak — resend after 56".

Purpose: reliable, in-order delivery of TLPs across one link. Responsibilities: assign a 12-bit sequence number to each TLP; append 32-bit LCRC; keep transmitted TLPs in a replay buffer until acknowledged; check received LCRC and sequence; send Ack/Nak DLLPs; replay on Nak or replay-timer expiry; exchange flow-control credit information (InitFC, UpdateFC DLLPs) on behalf of the Transaction Layer; carry power-management DLLPs; report link state (DL_Inactive, DL_Init, DL_Active) to the Transaction Layer. Packet structures: DLLPs (Gen1–5: 4 bytes of content + 16-bit CRC = 6 bytes, plus framing; Gen6 FLIT mode: carried in FLIT DLP bytes). Errors: Bad TLP (LCRC failure or bad sequence), Bad DLLP (CRC failure), Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover — all correctable because replay recovers them; Data Link Protocol Error and Surprise Down — uncorrectable. Trace visibility: analyzer sees sequence numbers, Ack/Nak, replays (duplicate sequence numbers), FC DLLPs. Software sees only AER counters/status. Details in Chapter 15.

7.3 Transaction Layer

🧒 Kid analogy

You, writing the letter: "To: memory address 0x1234_0000. From: SSD 03:00.0, request #21. Please send back 64 bytes." You only send it if the receiver has told you it has room in its mailbox (credits).

Purpose: end-to-end requests and completions between requesters and completers. Responsibilities: assembling and disassembling TLPs; split-transaction handling (match completions to outstanding requests by Requester ID + Tag); credit-based flow control (gate transmission by advertised credits); ordering rules; Traffic Class (TC) to Virtual Channel (VC) mapping; optional ECRC generation/check; poisoning (EP bit); address/ID routing in switches. Packet structures: TLPs — header (3 or 4 DW in non-FLIT mode), optional data payload, optional ECRC digest (Chapter 10). Errors: Poisoned TLP Received, ECRC Error, Unsupported Request (UR), Completer Abort (CA), Unexpected Completion, Completion Timeout, Malformed TLP, Receiver Overflow, Flow Control Protocol Error, ACS Violation; plus advisory variants. Trace visibility: analyzers decode headers fully; software sees AER header log (the offending TLP header captured on certain errors) — the single most valuable piece of evidence for transaction-layer errors.

7.4 Errors mapped to layers (AER view)

ErrorLayerAER class (default)Typical cause in NVMe systems
Receiver ErrorPhysicalCorrectableSignal integrity, marginal equalization
Bad TLP / Bad DLLPData LinkCorrectableLCRC/CRC failures from bit errors
Replay Timer Timeout / REPLAY_NUM RolloverData LinkCorrectableLost Acks, persistent errors; rollover triggers retraining
Data Link Protocol ErrorData LinkUncorrectable, fatalAck/Nak sequence outside valid range — design bug
Surprise DownData LinkUncorrectable, fatalLink lost unexpectedly (hot removal, power loss, PHY failure)
Poisoned TLPTransactionUncorrectable non-fatal (may be advisory)Data marked bad upstream (e.g. uncorrectable memory error)
Completion TimeoutTransactionUncorrectable non-fatalCompleter never answered (device hung, link reset, request lost)
Unsupported Request / Completer AbortTransactionUncorrectable non-fatal (often advisory)Access to unmapped address; BME off; device refusing request
Malformed TLPTransactionUncorrectable fatalLength vs payload mismatch, MPS exceeded, 4 KiB boundary crossing
Flow Control Protocol Error / Receiver OverflowTransactionUncorrectable fatalCredit accounting bug

Severity defaults are programmable via the AER Uncorrectable Error Severity register verified; "advisory non-fatal" handling for some UR/CA/poisoned cases is defined by the spec and depends on role (requester/completer) version.

7.5 Analyzer presentation vs protocol truth

📡 The four-step evidence chain
RAW EVENT          symbols/bits captured on the lanes (what physically happened)
    |
PROTOCOL DECODING  descrambling, framing, field extraction per the spec revision assumed
    |
ANALYZER UI        the tool's names, colors, grouping ("Read 64B", "Link Training", "Transaction")
    |
ENGINEER INTERPRETATION   your hypothesis about cause and effect

Every step can introduce error: a capture with bad probe signal integrity can invent errors that never happened on the real link; a decoder configured for the wrong link width or a non-FLIT decoder applied to FLIT traffic produces garbage; a UI may merge a request and its completions into one "transaction" row that hides a split completion or a duplicate; and the engineer may read a label ("Completion Timeout") as a wire event when it is the tool's inference from a missing packet. Before concluding, go back down the chain: what were the raw fields?

7.6 Linux view

# AER capability, status and logged header (per function)
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:04:00.0 | sed -n '/Advanced Error Reporting/,/^\s*Capabilities: \[/p'
# Kernel AER counters (if the kernel exposes them)
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/aer_dev_correctable
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/aer_dev_nonfatal
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:04:00.0/aer_dev_fatal
# Kernel messages from the AER driver
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'aer|pcieport'

Can prove: which error classes were reported and, for some errors, the logged TLP header. Cannot prove: how many replays occurred without error reports, exact timing, or whether a correctable error burst caused a latency spike.

7.7 Worked example: which layer?

A log shows "Correctable error: Bad TLP" every few seconds on the root port above an SSD, and the SSD shows "Receiver Error". Layer reasoning: Receiver Error (physical) at the SSD means the SSD's receiver saw symbol/framing errors in downstream traffic; Bad TLP at the root port means upstream TLPs arrived with bad LCRC. Both directions are affected → likely channel/connector/retimer issue rather than one transmitter. Transaction layer is unaffected because replay recovered every TLP — the cost is only bandwidth and latency.

🚀 Advanced: what FLIT mode changes in the layer model

In PCIe 6.0 FLIT mode the division of labor shifts version: the Physical Layer adds FEC over fixed 256-byte FLITs; the Data Link Layer protects and retries whole FLITs (FLIT CRC, FLIT sequence numbers) instead of individual TLPs with LCRC; DLLP information rides in dedicated DLP bytes of each FLIT; and the Transaction Layer uses a new header format with 14-bit tags and different field placement. Concepts — reliable in-order delivery per link, credits, ordering — survive; bit layouts do not. Any tool, decoder or mental shortcut built for 1.x–5.x must be re-validated for FLIT mode.

🧪 Lab 7.1 — Classify your system's PCIe errors by layer SAFE

Objective: build a per-port, per-layer error inventory. Prerequisites: Linux with AER enabled. Setup: none; read-only. Procedure:

  1. For each PCIe function, read aer_dev_correctable, aer_dev_nonfatal, aer_dev_fatal if present.
  2. Map each non-zero counter to Physical / Data Link / Transaction using the table in §7.4.
  3. For each NVMe device, pair its counters with its parent port's counters (the two ends of one link).
for d in /sys/bus/pci/devices/*; do
  f="$d/aer_dev_correctable"; [ -r "$f" ] || continue
  tot=$(awk '/TOTAL/{print $2}' "$f")
  [ "${tot:-0}" != "0" ] && { echo "== ${d##*/}"; cat "$f" | grep -v ' 0$'; }
done

Observations: which ports have errors; whether both ends of a link show errors. Questions: If only the SSD shows RxErr but the root port shows nothing, which direction of the link is affected? Expected reasoning: the receiver reports physical errors, so SSD RxErr means the downstream direction (RP transmitter → SSD receiver).

Solution

Physical errors are reported where they are received. SSD RxErr/BadTLP → problem in the root-port-to-SSD direction; RP BadTLP → SSD-to-RP direction; errors on both ends → shared element (connector, retimer, cable) or global cause (clocking, temperature). Transaction-layer errors (UR, CA, Completion Timeout) are logical and do not indicate signal problems.

Extension: log the counters hourly for a week and correlate with temperature and workload.

7.8 Common mistakes

  • Thinking Ack/Nak acknowledges the NVMe command or the read request. It acknowledges receipt of a TLP over one link.
  • Thinking LCRC protects end-to-end. It is regenerated at every switch; only ECRC is end-to-end.
  • Expecting ordered sets in a TLP-level trace view; many analyzer views hide them by default.
  • Treating correctable errors as harmless. They are recovered, but each costs a replay.

Quiz

  1. Which layer generates SKP ordered sets?

    Answer

    Physical.

  2. Which layer matches completions to requests?

    Answer

    Transaction (by Requester ID and Tag).

  3. Does a switch check LCRC? ECRC?

    Answer

    It checks and regenerates LCRC on every link; it may check ECRC only if it supports it but must forward ECRC unchanged.

  4. Why is Bad TLP correctable?

    Answer

    Replay retransmits the TLP; no data is lost.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Name PCIe's three layers.
    Model answerTransaction, Data Link, Physical.
  2. Intermediate What's in the replay buffer?
    Model answerCopies of transmitted, not-yet-acknowledged TLPs with their sequence numbers.
  3. Advanced What does the AER header log contain and why is it valuable?
    Model answerThe first 4 DW (or more with prefixes) of the TLP that caused certain errors; it identifies requester, address, tag, type.
  4. Senior An analyzer shows "Completion Timeout" at t=50ms. What do you verify?
    Model answerThat it's an analyzer inference from a missing completion; check if the completion appears later, if a link reset occurred, the tool's timeout setting, and capture point.
  5. Intermediate Which layer owns flow-control credits, and which layer carries them?
    Model answerThe Transaction Layer owns the meaning and gating of credits; the Data Link Layer carries them in InitFC/UpdateFC DLLPs.
  6. Advanced Why can a link be "up" (L0) yet unable to carry TLPs?
    Model answerThe DLL has not completed flow-control initialization (not DL_Active); PHY LinkUp alone is not enough.
  7. Advanced Where is ECRC checked in a switched path?
    Model answerAt the ultimate receiver (and optionally by switches that support checking); switches must forward it unchanged.
  8. Senior Errors appear only on the SSD side of a link. What does that tell you?
    Model answerThe direction toward the SSD is degraded: root port transmitter, channel, or SSD receiver/equalization — not the SSD's transmitter.
  9. Senior How do you justify a decoded conclusion to a reviewer?
    Model answerWalk from raw fields to decode to UI to interpretation, citing the spec section by topic name and stating what was not captured.
📌 Teach-back

Child: "the writer, the post office and the van." Junior: "TL makes requests and completions with credits and ordering; DLL guarantees per-link delivery with Seq#, LCRC, Ack/Nak and replay; PL trains the link and moves symbols." Senior: "each AER bit and analyzer event belongs to one layer; diagnose upward from physical evidence."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can draw the stack with what each layer adds and removes.
  • I can classify any AER error by layer.
  • I can explain LCRC vs ECRC and Ack vs Completion.
  • I can describe the RAW → DECODE → UI → INTERPRETATION chain and its failure points.

8 The Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM)

← 7 PCIe Layer Model9 PCIe Link Training in Depth →

8.1 Why this chapter exists

Before a single NVMe command can move, two physical-layer state machines — one in the root port, one in the SSD — must walk from "is anybody there?" to "fully operational link". The Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM) defines that walk and everything that happens later: retraining after errors, speed changes, low-power states and resets. When a drive is missing, flapping, slow to appear after boot, or stuck at Gen1, the LTSSM is where the story is written. Software normally sees only its outcome; an analyzer or a vendor debug register shows the path.

📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification, Physical Layer Logical Block, "Link Training and Status State Machine" section. REVISION: state names stable from 1.x to 6.x; Recovery.Equalization added in 3.0; FLIT-mode negotiation and L0p (a partial-width low-power state) added in 6.0 version. Timeout values below are those widely documented for 3.x–5.x; confirm against your revision before using them for compliance work.

  • Beginner: list the LTSSM top-level states and the normal power-up path Detect → Polling → Configuration → L0.
  • Intermediate: explain each substate's job, its exit conditions and its timeout.
  • Advanced: explain Recovery as the "repair shop" used for speed change, equalization, error recovery and L1 exit.
  • Senior: map symptoms (missing device, flapping, Gen1-only, slow boot) to the LTSSM state where the link is stuck.
  • Trace: read a synthetic LTSSM transition log and identify the first abnormal transition.
  • Debug/validation: know which registers expose LTSSM outcomes and which do not.

Prerequisites: physical architecture, layer model.

8.2 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Two kids in dark rooms connected by a tube. First each taps the tube to check someone is on the other side (Detect). Then they shout "hello hello hello" until they can both hear clearly (Polling). Then they agree "we'll use tubes 1 to 4 and you're kid number 0" (Configuration). Then they chat (L0). If the line gets crackly, they go back to saying "hello, can you hear me?" for a moment (Recovery). When bored, they doze (L0s / L1 / L2).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The kids decide things by talking; the LTSSM decides by counting consecutive identical ordered sets and by timeouts. There is no "conversation" with negotiation rounds as such: each side changes state when it has received N consecutive ordered sets with particular field values, or a timer fires. Also, both sides are not symmetric: the downstream port (root port or switch downstream port) leads link and lane numbering and equalization, the upstream port (the SSD) follows.

8.3 The state machine

#From → ToTrigger (simplified)Why it matters for NVMe
1Detect → PollingReceiver termination detected on lanes (Detect.Active)No detect = device invisible; parent port shows link down
2Polling → ConfigurationPolling.Active: ≥1024 TS1 sent and 8 consecutive TS1/TS2 received on all detected lanes; Polling.Configuration: 8 consecutive TS2 received, 16 TS2 sent after the first receivedBit lock, symbol/block lock, polarity resolved
3Configuration → L0Link and lane numbers agreed (Linkwidth.Start/Accept, Lanenum.Wait/Accept, Complete, Idle)Width decided here; DL layer starts InitFC after L0
4L0 → RecoverySpeed change request, re-equalization request, framing error (128b/130b), replay rollover, receiving TS1/TS2, retrain request (Retrain Link bit)The workhorse: Gen1→Gen4 upshift happens via this path

10L2 → DetectWake (beacon or WAKE#) and power restoreFull retrain on resume

Transition triggers are simplified summaries of the normative rules; numeric values are verified for 3.x–5.x-era documentation and should be re-confirmed per revision version.

8.4 State by state

Detect (Detect.Quiet, Detect.Active)

Transmitter in electrical idle. Detect.Quiet waits up to 12 ms (or until a lane leaves electrical idle). Detect.Active performs receiver detection: the transmitter changes its common-mode voltage and measures how fast the line charges. A terminated receiver on the far side (with the AC coupling capacitor) charges slowly; an open line charges fast. If receivers are detected on all lanes → Polling. If none → back to Quiet. If some lanes → wait and retry once, then go to Polling with the detected lanes only — this is where a broken lane first reduces width.

Polling (Polling.Active, Polling.Compliance, Polling.Configuration)

Both sides transmit TS1 ordered sets with PAD for link and lane numbers. Receivers achieve bit lock and symbol lock (8b/10b) or block alignment (128b/130b; but initial training is always at 2.5 GT/s so 8b/10b is used), resolve polarity inversion, and advertise supported data rates. Polling.Compliance is entered when a lane sees no TS but detected a receiver and a compliance condition exists — it transmits the compliance pattern used by test equipment. A device stuck sending compliance patterns in a real system is a known failure signature (e.g. a load-board or a damaged lane).

Configuration

The downstream port proposes link numbers in TS1 on all lanes (Linkwidth.Start), the upstream port echoes link numbers on lanes it accepts (Linkwidth.Accept), the downstream port proposes lane numbers (Lanenum.Wait/Accept), lane reversal is resolved, both sides exchange TS2 (Complete), then send logical idle (Idle). On exit to L0, the Physical Layer reports LinkUp = 1 and the Data Link Layer starts flow-control initialization (InitFC1, InitFC2 — Chapter 16). Only after FC initialization does the link become DL_Active and TLPs can flow; the Data Link Layer Link Active bit in the downstream port's Link Status register reflects this verified.

L0

Normal operation: TLPs, DLLPs, SKP ordered sets. The link is at whatever rate it was trained to; immediately after first training this is 2.5 GT/s.

Recovery

Recovery re-establishes bit/block lock and is used for: changing speed (Recovery.Speed), equalization at 8 GT/s and above (Recovery.Equalization), exiting L1, recovering from errors (e.g. framing errors, replay rollover), and as a path to Hot Reset, Disabled, Loopback, or Configuration. Substates: RcvrLock (send TS1, wait for 8 consecutive TS1/TS2), RcvrCfg (send TS2, wait for 8 consecutive TS2), Speed (electrical idle while switching rate), Equalization (phases 0–3, Chapter 9), Idle (send idle data, then L0). A healthy Recovery takes microseconds; a looping Recovery appears to software as throughput collapse, AER correctable errors, and sometimes as Link Bandwidth Management Status events.

L0s

Low-latency, per-direction standby: a transmitter with nothing to send enters electrical idle and exits by sending Fast Training Sequences (FTS) — the count N_FTS was advertised during training. Optional ASPM state; removed in FLIT mode (6.0) in favor of L0p version.

L1

Deeper link standby: both directions idle, reference clock may be gated (L1 PM Substates L1.1/L1.2 go further). Entry is a DLLP handshake; exit always goes through Recovery. Exit latency is reported in Link Capabilities (L1 Exit Latency) and checked by the OS against device acceptable latency before enabling ASPM.

L2 (and L2/L3 Ready, L3)

Main power removed with auxiliary power present (L2) or absent (L3, not an LTSSM state as such — the link is simply off). Return to operation always restarts from Detect.

Hot Reset

An in-band reset propagated by TS1 with the Hot Reset bit. The upstream component resets its logic (conventional reset semantics for the function) and the link retrains through Detect. Linux uses it via the bridge's Secondary Bus Reset bit ("bus reset") verified.

Disabled

Link deliberately shut down via the Link Disable bit of the downstream port; the far side sees TS1 with the Disable bit and then electrical idle. Used to power off or isolate a device.

Loopback

A loopback master sends data that the loopback slave retransmits unchanged; used for BER testing with test equipment. Not entered in normal operation.

8.5 Hardware and protocol view

🔧 Hardware

The LTSSM runs in the PHY/MAC logic of each port; it is hardware (often with firmware assistance in complex SerDes). Observable: ordered sets on the wire (analyzer, oscilloscope with decoding), LnkSta/LnkSta2 bits, some vendors' LTSSM state/history registers impl. Internal and generally unobservable: receiver equalizer adaptation values, CDR lock state, internal timers.

12.000 sL0 → Recovery.RcvrLockEntry cause not shown by this capture
12.000 s + 3 µsRecovery.Idle → L0Rate and width unchanged
(every ~1 s)same patternCould be L1 exits (ASPM) — normal; or error-induced recovery — abnormal. Need: was link in L1 before? any Nak/replay before entry? framing errors?

8.7 Linux view

# Downstream (parent) port: is the data link active? training in progress?
sudo lspci -vv -s 0000:00:01.1 | grep -E 'LnkSta:|LnkSta2:|LnkCtl:'
# ASPM policy and per-link ASPM state
cat /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy
sudo lspci -vv -s 0000:04:00.0 | grep -E 'ASPM|L1SubCtl'
# Hot-plug / link events
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'link (up|down)|pciehp|Surprise|retrain'

In LnkSta, "DLActive+" means Data Link Layer Link Active (only reported if the port supports Data Link Layer Link Active Reporting), "Training+" indicates the LTSSM is in Configuration/Recovery at the moment of reading, and "BWMgmt+/ABWMgmt+" flags (Link Bandwidth Management Status / Link Autonomous Bandwidth Status) indicate the link changed speed or width since last cleared verified. Cannot prove: how many recoveries occurred, or the current substate.

⚠️ Warning

Setting the Retrain Link bit (LnkCtl bit 5 of the downstream port) or Secondary Bus Reset via setpci interrupts I/O, can cause data loss for in-flight writes, and may hang a system whose root filesystem is on the device. Do this only on test machines, on non-boot devices, after unmounting.

8.8 Common mistakes

  • Thinking speed is negotiated in Polling. Rates are advertised there, but changes happen in Recovery after L0.
  • Equating "L1" with NVMe power states. ASPM L1 is a link state; NVMe Power States/APST are controller states; they are related only by policy.
  • Assuming Recovery means error. Recovery is also normal for speed change and L1 exit.
  • Reading LnkSta on the endpoint only: Data Link Layer Link Active and many status bits are meaningful only on downstream ports.

8.9 Five LTSSM failure patterns

#SymptomStuck wherePossible causesFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentConfidence
1Device never appearsDetect (no receiver)No power, missing device, broken RX terminationSlot power, presenceParent port DLActiveKnown-good deviceMedium
2Device never appears, parent port retriesDetect↔Polling loopPERST# held, REFCLK missing, TX brokenPERST# timingREFCLK presence / clock mode (SRIS vs common)Scope/analyzer on lanesMedium
3Link up but x1 or x2Configuration width reductionLane not detected or failing TS exchangeLnkSta width both endsSlot wiringSwap slots/devicesHigh for location
4Stuck at Gen1/Gen3Recovery.Speed/EqualizationEQ failure, BIOS cap, retimerLnkSta2 equalization bitsLnkCtl2 target speedForce lower target, step upMedium
5Drive disappears after idleL1 exit failure → Recovery → DetectASPM/L1SS bug, clock request issuedmesg link down after idleASPM stateBoot with pcie_aspm=off (test system)Medium-high if fixed

Quiz

  1. Which state follows Configuration on success?

    Answer

    L0.

  2. How does L1 exit?

    Answer

    Through Recovery, then L0.

  3. Where is a broken lane first excluded?

    Answer

    Detect (no receiver detected) or later in Polling/Configuration if TS exchange fails on it.

  4. Name four reasons to enter Recovery from L0.

    Answer

    Speed change, re-equalization, L1 exit (from L1), error recovery (framing error, replay rollover), retrain request, receipt of TS1/TS2.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What does LTSSM stand for and do?
    Model answerLink Training and Status State Machine; trains, maintains and power-manages the physical link.
  2. Beginner What is receiver detection?
    Model answerMeasuring line charge time after a common-mode step to see whether a terminated receiver is attached.
  3. Intermediate What's the difference between Hot Reset and Disabled?
    Model answerHot Reset resets the downstream component and retrains; Disabled turns the link off until the disable is cleared.
  4. Intermediate When does flow-control initialization happen?
    Model answerAfter the PHY reports LinkUp (L0); the DLL exchanges InitFC1/InitFC2 before DL_Active.
  5. Advanced Why might Recovery loop forever?
    Model answerFailure to reach 8 consecutive TS on all lanes at the new rate (equalization insufficient), rate fallback logic, persistent errors; implementations eventually fall back or go to Detect.
  6. Advanced How can ASPM interact badly with NVMe latency?
    Model answerL1 exit latency (µs) added to the first transaction after idle; at QD1 with sporadic I/O this inflates latency.
  7. Senior A drive appears on cold boot but not on warm reboot. Hypotheses?
    Model answerDevice not properly reset (PERST# not toggled on warm reset), firmware not ready within platform's wait time, link left in a state that requires power cycle; check timing between reset and enumeration, CRS handling.
  8. Senior What evidence distinguishes a normal L1-exit Recovery from an error Recovery?
    Model answerPreceding L1 entry DLLPs and electrical idle vs preceding Nak/replays/framing errors; AER correctable counts unchanged for L1 exits.
💡 Senior insight

Classify every "missing NVMe" ticket by the furthest LTSSM state reached. "Never detected", "detected but never L0", "L0 at Gen1 only", "L0 then lost". Each class has a different owner: board/power, clock/reset/firmware, signal integrity/equalization, power management/thermal.

  • I can explain each transition in the table and its trigger.
  • I can find the first abnormal transition in a synthetic LTSSM log.
  • I can distinguish normal Recovery (speed change, L1 exit) from error Recovery.
  • I know which registers reveal LTSSM outcomes and that substates are usually invisible to software.

9 PCIe Link Training in Depth

← 8 The Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM)10 Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs) →

9.1 Why this chapter exists

The LTSSM tells you which states exist; this chapter shows what is exchanged in them: the TS1 and TS2 training sequences, how lanes and speeds are negotiated, and the equalization procedure that makes 8 GT/s and faster possible. It ends with the lab the master curriculum requires: diagnosing a link that refuses to reach L0.

  • Describe TS1/TS2 fields and how they drive lane, width and speed negotiation.
  • Explain receiver detection and its failure modes.
  • Explain equalization phases 0–3, presets and coefficients, and when equalization reruns.
  • Diagnose training failures and link recovery events from evidence.

Prerequisites: Chapter 8.

🧒 Kid analogy

Training sequences are like name badges kids hold up repeatedly: "I'm on team PAD, seat PAD, I can run at speeds 1, 2, 3, 4". After a few rounds the leader writes team and seat numbers on the badges, everyone holds up their new badge 8 times in a row, and the game begins. Equalization is like adjusting a megaphone's bass and treble until the friend across the field hears each word clearly.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Badges are not "read once": receivers require consecutive identical ordered sets to filter noise. And in equalization the listener asks the talker to change the talker's transmitter settings — the megaphone is adjusted remotely by the person hearing it.

9.2 TS1 and TS2 ordered sets

Training Sequences are 16-symbol ordered sets sent on every lane. In 8b/10b mode (all initial training) the layout is:

Symbol0123456–15
FieldCOM (K28.5)Link Number (0–255 or PAD)Lane Number (0–31 or PAD)N_FTSData Rate IdentifierTraining ControlTS identifier: D10.2 (TS1) or D5.2 (TS2)
  • Link/Lane Number: PAD (K23.7) until the downstream port assigns numbers in Configuration.
  • N_FTS: number of Fast Training Sequences this receiver needs to exit L0s.
  • Data Rate Identifier: bit mask of supported rates (2.5, 5, 8, 16, 32 GT/s… plus 64 GT/s in 6.0) and a speed_change bit used in Recovery to request a rate change; also the autonomous-change indication version.
  • Training Control: bits for Hot Reset, Disable Link, Loopback, Disable Scrambling (8b/10b only), Compliance Receive.
  • TS identifier: distinguishes TS1 from TS2. In 128b/130b, TS ordered sets are carried in Ordered Set blocks; symbol 0 identifies TS1 (1Eh) or TS2 (2Dh), and symbols 6–9 carry equalization information (presets, coefficients, the transmitter's full-swing (FS) and low-frequency (LF) values) verified.

Why two kinds: TS1 means "I'm still training / proposing". TS2 means "I've accepted what I received and am ready to move on". Typical rule pattern: a substate exits when 8 consecutive TS2s with matching fields are received and enough TS2s (e.g. 16) have been sent after the first one was received — ensuring both sides advance together.

9.3 Receiver detection

Receiver detection is an analog measurement in Detect.Active: the transmitter steps its common-mode voltage; the time constant of the line depends on whether a receiver termination (DC impedance to ground at the far receiver, typically around 50 Ω single-ended during operation, with a specified high-impedance state when unpowered) is attached through the coupling capacitor. Failure modes: false negative (receiver present but not detected — wrong capacitor value, receiver not powered yet, retimer not ready) and false positive (detection on lanes that are routed to a connector with nothing behind it but some leakage path) impl.

9.4 Lane and width negotiation (Configuration)

Downstream Port (DSP)                       Upstream Port (USP, the SSD)
Linkwidth.Start:  TS1 Link=0 Lane=PAD  --->  on lanes 0..3
                                       <---  TS1 Link=0 Lane=PAD   (echo on lanes it accepts)
Linkwidth.Accept / Lanenum.Wait:
                  TS1 Link=0 Lane=0..3 --->
                                       <---  TS1 Link=0 Lane=0..3   (or reversed 3..0 → reversal)
Lanenum.Accept → Complete:
                  TS2 Link=0 Lane=n   <-->  TS2 Link=0 Lane=n       (8 rx / 16 tx)
Idle:             Idle data           <-->  Idle data → L0

If the USP returns PAD on lanes 2–3 (it cannot use them), the DSP re-proposes a narrower width (x2). If lane numbers come back reversed, the link uses lane reversal if either side supports it.

9.5 Speed negotiation

After first L0 at 2.5 GT/s, the downstream port (typically; either port can initiate) enters Recovery with the speed_change bit set in its TS1s and the highest common rate advertised. In Recovery.RcvrCfg both sides confirm with TS2 (speed_change set), enter Recovery.Speed (electrical idle while PLLs/CDR retune), and return to Recovery.RcvrLock at the new rate. For 8 GT/s and above, the first transition to each rate requires equalization. If RcvrLock cannot be achieved at the new rate within the timeout, the port falls back to the previous rate; implementations may retry or give up and stay low, which is how links end up "stuck at Gen3" impl. The platform can cap the target via the Target Link Speed field of Link Control 2.

9.6 Equalization phases 0–3

At 8 GT/s and above, channel loss closes the eye unless transmitter FIR coefficients (pre-cursor C−1, cursor C0, post-cursor C+1) and receiver equalizers are tuned for the specific channel. Equalization is a closed-loop procedure in Recovery.Equalization. Presets (P0–P10) are standard starting combinations of de-emphasis and preshoot verified.

PhaseWho leadsWhat happensExit condition
0DSP tells USPBefore the rate change, the DSP sends EQ TS2 at the lower rate carrying the transmitter preset (and receiver hint) the USP must use at the new rate. USP enters phase 0 at new rate transmitting with that preset.USP receives TS1s at new rate and moves to phase 1
1BothBoth ports transmit TS1 with their current presets and advertise FS/LF values so the other side can compute legal coefficient requests. Goal: a link good enough (BER ≈ 10−4) to exchange further requests.DSP may stop here if the link is good (equalization can be shortened by policy); otherwise phase 2
2USP adjusts DSP's TXThe USP (whose receiver sees the DSP's transmitter) requests new presets/coefficients from the DSP, evaluates its own receiver eye/BER for each, and picks the best. Iterative.USP satisfied, or timeout
3DSP adjusts USP's TXMirror of phase 2: the DSP requests settings for the USP's transmitter until the DSP's receiver is satisfied.DSP satisfied → Recovery.RcvrLock → L0 at the new rate; target BER ≤ 10−12

Equalization is performed separately for 8, 16 and 32 GT/s (each rate's settings differ). PCIe 5.0 added optional mechanisms to bypass intermediate-rate equalization and go directly to the highest rate, and to skip equalization when settings are already known version. Retimers participate in equalization on each of their two sub-links. Results are reported in Link Status 2 (Equalization 8.0 GT/s Complete, Phase 1/2/3 Successful, Link Equalization Request) and in the 16/32 GT/s extended capabilities verified. Software can request re-equalization (Perform Equalization bit in Link Control 3) followed by a retrain — expert use only.

9.7 Training failures and link recovery

FailureWhereSignatureTypical causes
No receiver detectedDetectParent link down, no TS everNo device, no power, broken RX lanes, wrong slot
No TS1 receivedPolling.ActiveDetect↔Polling loopReset held, no REFCLK, wrong clocking mode, device PHY not started
Partial lanesDetect/ConfigurationNarrow widthLane damage, routing, lane sharing
Speed change failsRecovery.Speed/RcvrLockFallback to lower rateChannel loss too high for new rate; retimer/firmware limits
Equalization failsRecovery.EqualizationPhase bits not set; rate stays lowerCoefficient search not converging; incompatible implementations
Unstable L0L0 ↔ RecoveryFrequent recovery, correctable errors, replaysMarginal equalization, thermal drift, crosstalk

Link recovery is the normal mechanism that keeps marginal links alive: the DLL triggers Recovery after REPLAY_NUM rollover (4 replays of the same TLP), the PHY on framing errors. Recovery is cheap (µs) compared to Detect (ms) and invisible to NVMe unless it repeats or fails.

9.8 Lane margining

PCIe 4.0 introduced Lane Margining at the Receiver: software can ask a receiver to shift its sampling point in time and voltage and report errors, measuring eye margin in-system version. Recent pciutils includes a margining utility (pcilmr) version; support depends on the device impl. Margining runs while the link is in L0 and can cause errors on the measured lane — treat as a CAUTION operation.

🧪 Lab 9.1 — Diagnose a link that refuses to reach L0 SAFE (paper/forensic lab)

Objective: from evidence, decide where training fails and propose the next experiment. Prerequisites: Chapters 5, 8, 9. Setup: you are given the synthetic evidence below from a server where a new Gen4 U.2 SSD is not visible.

Synthetic evidence pack
#SourceEvidence
E1lspci -tvSwitch downstream port 02:03.0 present; nothing below it
E2lspci -vv -s 02:03.0LnkSta: Speed 2.5GT/s, Width x0 (no link), DLActive- ; SltSta: Presence Detect+ ; Power Indicator On
E3journalctl -kpciehp: Slot(3): Card present; repeated "Link Down"/"No link" style messages
E4Analyzer on the slot (LTSSM view)Detect.Active: receivers detected lanes 0–3 → Polling.Active: DSP sends TS1; RX lanes show electrical idle; 24 ms timeout → Detect; repeating
E5Board documentationSlot clock configuration: SRIS enabled in BIOS for this backplane; SSD datasheet: "common clock only" (hypothetical)

Procedure: (1) Determine the furthest LTSSM state reached. (2) List hypotheses consistent with E1–E4. (3) Use E5 to rank. (4) Propose a disambiguating experiment that does not risk data.

Questions: Why does detection succeed while Polling fails? Which evidence rules out "no device"? What would you expect if PERST# were held?

Solution

(1) Furthest state: Polling.Active. Receivers were detected, so the SSD's receivers present termination — the device is physically present and at least partially powered (E2 presence detect agrees). (2) The SSD never transmits recognizable TS1: candidates are PERST# held asserted, missing or incompatible reference clock, SSD firmware/PHY not starting, broken TX pairs. (3) E5 shows a clocking mismatch: the backplane runs separate-reference independent-SSC (SRIS) while the SSD claims common-clock only — its CDR or elastic buffers cannot tolerate the frequency offset/SSC difference, or it never gets a REFCLK at all if the backplane does not route it in SRIS mode. Rank: clocking mismatch (highest), PERST# (check timing), TX lanes damaged (less likely on all four lanes). (4) Experiment: move the SSD to a slot configured for common clock (or change the backplane setting on a test system), or test a known SRIS-capable SSD in the same slot. If the known-good SRIS device trains and the original SSD trains in a common-clock slot, the conclusion is clock-mode incompatibility (high confidence). If PERST# were held, the device would typically keep its PHY in reset — the same TX silence — so a scope on PERST# distinguishes the two.

Extension: write the decision list for the four "furthest state reached" classes from Chapter 8's senior insight, with owner and first experiment for each.

🧪 Lab 9.2 — Read equalization outcomes on a real system SAFE

Objective: find equalization status for each Gen3+ link. Steps: sudo lspci -vv | grep -E '^[0-9a-f]|LnkSta2|EqualizationComplete'. Observations: for links at ≥8 GT/s, EqualizationComplete+ and Phase1+/2+/3+ are expected. Questions: what does a link at 16 GT/s with Phase3- imply?

Solution

Phase reporting can depend on the implementation and whether phases were skipped by policy (e.g. phases 2/3 bypassed if allowed) — a missing phase bit alone is not proof of failure; correlate with error counters and achieved rate. Also, the bits in Link Status 2 refer to 8 GT/s; 16 and 32 GT/s status lives in their extended capabilities, which lspci may decode depending on version.

Extension (EXPERT, test machine only): use lane margining (if supported) to compare eye margins between slots.

Quiz

  1. What distinguishes TS1 from TS2 in 8b/10b?

    Answer

    The identifier symbols 6–15: D10.2 for TS1, D5.2 for TS2.

  2. Which port tunes the DSP's transmitter in phase 2?

    Answer

    The USP (it evaluates the signal it receives from the DSP).

  3. Is equalization done once for all rates?

    Answer

    No, per rate (8, 16, 32 GT/s), with optional bypass mechanisms in newer revisions.

  4. What triggers Recovery after repeated replays?

    Answer

    REPLAY_NUM rollover in the Data Link Layer.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a TS1?
    Model answerA training ordered set carrying link/lane numbers, N_FTS, supported rates and training control, used during training.
  2. Intermediate Why are presets needed?
    Model answerTo start equalization from a known transmitter shape that likely gives an open-enough eye for phase 1 communication.
  3. Intermediate Why does every link start at 2.5 GT/s?
    Model answerUniversal compatibility; rate capabilities are exchanged during initial training and higher rates are reached via Recovery.
  4. Advanced What happens in Recovery.Speed?
    Model answerTransmitters go to electrical idle while both sides switch rate; then RcvrLock at new rate; failure leads to fallback.
  5. Advanced How do retimers affect equalization?
    Model answerThey split the link into two sub-links equalized separately and must pass/forward training per spec retimer rules; timeouts are extended.
  6. Senior Gen5 SSD trains at Gen5 in one server model, Gen4 in another. Approach?
    Model answerCompare channel (trace length, riser, retimer), BIOS EQ settings/presets, LnkCtl2, equalization status, margining; involve platform SI team with evidence.
  7. Senior What can't software know about training?
    Model answerSubstate history, coefficient values chosen, receiver adaptation, how close to failure the link is (except via margining).
📌 Teach-back

Child: "hold up badges until everyone agrees, then tune the megaphones." Junior: "TS1 proposes, TS2 confirms; width set in Configuration; speed raised in Recovery with equalization phases 0–3 per rate." Senior: "the furthest state reached and the equalization status separate platform, clock/reset and SI root causes."

PART V

PCIe Transaction Layer

Everything an NVMe controller does on the host side is a Transaction Layer Packet (TLP): the host's doorbell write, the controller's fetch of a 64-byte Submission Queue Entry, the PRP-list read, the data transfer, the 16-byte Completion Queue Entry, the MSI-X interrupt. This Part teaches TLPs from first principles, then field by field with bit positions, then the three rules that govern their behavior in flight: posted vs non-posted semantics, tag-based matching of split transactions, and ordering. It ends with a working Python decoder that you can feed synthetic headers and that shows every field in binary, hex and decimal.

📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification, Transaction Layer chapter. REVISION: header formats shown are the non-FLIT formats used in PCIe 1.x–5.x and in 6.x non-FLIT mode. PCIe 6.0 FLIT mode defines a different TLP header layout ("FLIT mode TLP headers") with 14-bit tags; it is not decoded here version. 10-bit tags (T9, T8 bits) exist since 4.0 version. OLDER VERSIONS: before 2.1 some header bits (TH, LN, AT usage, IDO) were reserved. SOURCE: PCI-SIG; NVMe usage of TLPs comes from the NVMe Base and PCIe Transport specifications, which define registers and data structures, not TLP formats.

10 Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs)

← 9 PCIe Link Training in Depth11 TLP Header Anatomy →

10.1 Why this chapter exists

If you can read TLPs, you can see NVMe working. Every claim an SSD or driver makes about "I submitted", "I fetched", "I completed", "I interrupted" can be checked against the TLPs on the link. This chapter answers: what is a TLP, why does it exist, what is it made of, and which TLP types matter — and then traces a whole NVMe read command as TLPs.

  • Beginner: define TLP, header, payload, digest, requester, completer.
  • Intermediate: list MRd, MWr, CfgRd/CfgWr, Cpl, CplD, Msg and AtomicOp, with posted/non-posted classification.
  • Advanced: map every step of an NVMe command to TLPs and directions.
  • Senior: apply TLP decoding safety: never infer a transaction from a label; separate PCIe normative, NVMe, implementation and analyzer-presentation facts.
  • Trace: read normal, slow, failed and ambiguous synthetic NVMe TLP traces.
  • Debug/validation: identify which missing TLP explains a stuck command.

Prerequisites: layer model, topology and routing.

10.2 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

A TLP is a letter in an envelope. The envelope (header) says what kind of letter it is ("please send me something" or "here's something for you"), who sent it, which question number it is, and where it goes. The contents (payload) are the actual data — only some letters have contents. A wax seal (digest/ECRC) can optionally prove nobody changed the letter on its whole journey.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Letters can be lost; TLPs essentially cannot (per-link replay recovers corruption — a missing completion means something failed, not that the post office misplaced it). Envelope sizes are strictly limited (payload ≤ Max Payload Size), and the "reply letter" to a read must quote the question number (Tag) and the asker's identity (Requester ID) exactly.

10.3 What a TLP is and why it exists

A Transaction Layer Packet is the unit by which PCIe carries a request or a completion between two functions, end to end, possibly through switches. It exists because PCIe is a split-transaction packet network: a read is not one bus cycle that holds the interconnect until data arrives; it is a request packet, and later one or more completion packets, with the link free for other traffic in between. TLPs carry everything a PCI bus cycle used to express (address, byte enables, command type) plus what a packet network needs (requester identity, tag, length, traffic class, attributes).

PartSizeContentsPresent when
Prefix(es)1 DW eachOptional TLP prefixes (e.g. PASID in end-end prefix form, vendor prefixes)Only if used (Fmt = 100b marks a prefix)
Header3 or 4 DW (12 or 16 bytes)Fmt, Type, TC, attributes, length, IDs, tag, address or completion fieldsAlways
Data payload0–1024 DW (0–4096 bytes), limited by MPSWrite data, completion data, atomic operandsFmt indicates "with data"
Digest (ECRC)1 DWEnd-to-end 32-bit CRC over header + data (invariant fields)TD = 1

The Data Link Layer then adds a sequence number and LCRC; the Physical Layer adds framing (Figure 7.1). A DW (doubleword) is 4 bytes.

10.4 Request / completion relationship

A requester issues a request TLP; a completer services it. For non-posted requests the completer must return completion TLP(s) carrying the requester's Requester ID and Tag so the requester can match them (Chapter 13). For posted requests no completion is returned (Chapter 12). Completions are ID-routed back to the requester.

10.5 The TLP types that matter

TLPFmt / TypePosted?CompletionNVMe use
Memory Read (MRd)000/001, 0 0000Non-postedCplD (one or more), or Cpl with error statusController fetches SQEs, PRP lists, SGL descriptors, write data from host memory; host reads registers (CSTS, CAP)
Memory Write (MWr)010/011, 0 0000PostedNoneHost doorbells and register writes (CC, AQA…); controller writes read data, CQEs, MSI-X messages
Config Read Type 0/1 (CfgRd0/1)000, 0 0100 / 0 0101Non-postedCplD or Cpl (UR/CRS)Enumeration, reading BARs, capabilities
Config Write Type 0/1 (CfgWr0/1)010, 0 0100 / 0 0101Non-postedCpl (no data)Programming BARs, Command register (Memory Space Enable, Bus Master Enable), MSI-X enable
Completion (Cpl)000, 0 1010——Completes config writes; reports errors (UR, CA) for reads
Completion with Data (CplD)010, 0 1010——Returns read data
Message (Msg/MsgD)001/011, 1 0rrrPostedNoneError messages (ERR_COR/NONFATAL/FATAL), legacy INTx assert/deassert, PM messages, Vendor Defined
AtomicOp (FetchAdd, Swap, CAS)010/011, 0 1100 / 0 1101 / 0 1110Non-postedCplD with original valueNot used by standard NVMe data path; used by accelerators/GPUs
I/O Read/Write000/010, 0 0010Non-postedCplD / CplLegacy; NVMe does not require I/O space (an optional I/O BAR exists for legacy index/data access) version

Type encodings verified for non-FLIT headers. "rrr" in Message Type is the routing sub-field (000 to RC, 001 by address, 010 by ID, 011 broadcast from RC, 100 local, 101 gathered to RC).

📌 Remember: MSI-X is a Memory Write

An NVMe interrupt in MSI-X mode is just a posted MWr of a 32-bit message data value to an address the host programmed into the MSI-X table. On a trace it looks like any other MWr; you recognize it only by its address (in the interrupt address range, e.g. FEExxxxxh on x86 impl) and context.

10.6 PCIe transaction lifecycle (conceptual model)

REQUEST CREATED      requester's TL forms header; needs a free tag (non-posted) and flow-control credits
      |
TLP TRANSMITTED      DLL assigns Seq#, LCRC, stores in replay buffer; PL frames and sends
      |
LINK DELIVERY        per hop: LCRC check, Ack/Nak, replay if needed; switches route and re-transmit
      |
COMPLETER PROCESSING completer decodes address/ID; executes (memory read, register access)
      |
COMPLETION           (non-posted only) completer forms Cpl/CplD with Requester ID + Tag, possibly split
      |
REQUESTER MATCHING   requester finds outstanding entry by Tag (+ID), checks Byte Count / Lower Address,
                     reassembles data, frees tag when Byte Count says the last completion arrived
📭 What this model is and is not

This six-step chain is a conceptual model conceptual of what the specification requires to be observable. It is not a literal universal internal implementation: a root complex may pipeline steps, split one CPU request into several TLPs, coalesce posted writes from a write-combining buffer into one TLP, or service a read from a cache; an SSD controller may prefetch SQEs before a doorbell is observed by firmware. The spec defines what goes on the link and the rules (ordering, completion, timeouts), not how chips organize work internally.

The six-step model above, drawn as one real journey. The NVMe SSD fetches a 64-byte Submission Queue Entry: it is the requester of a Memory Read, the root complex is the completer, and a switch sits in between. Watch which layer adds what, which hop routes by address and which by ID, and that every link hop is acknowledged separately. Values match the worked example in §10.7 synthetic.

Endpoint / requester (SSD)Host / root complex sideLink level (DLL, PL, DLLPs)Host memory
  1. The SSD's Transaction Layer builds the Memory Read request

    The controller wants SQ1 slot 5. Its Transaction Layer takes a free tag, records it in its outstanding-request table, checks it has a Non-Posted Header credit for the link, and forms a 4DW MRd header (64-bit address, so 16 bytes). An MRd carries no payload: only the header travels.

    Where: SSD Transaction Layer (requester)PCIe: not yet on the wire · MRd, 4DW header, Length 16 DW = 64 bytes
    Fmt/Type = 001b/0 0000 (MRd, 4DW) Requester ID = 0300h (03:00.0) Tag = 0Ah Length = 16 DW First/Last BE = 1111b/1111b Address = 1_2340_0140h (SQ1 base 1_2340_0000h + 5 × 64)
  2. The Data Link Layer adds a sequence number and LCRC

    The SSD's Data Link Layer prepends a 12-bit sequence number (in a 2-byte field) and appends a 32-bit LCRC computed over the sequence number and the TLP. It keeps a copy in its replay buffer until the other end of this link acknowledges it.

    Where: SSD Data Link LayerPCIe: link-local fields; they are stripped and regenerated at every hop
    Seq = 412h LCRC = 32-bit CRC (value not shown) Replay buffer: [412h: MRd Tag 0Ah]
  3. The Physical Layer frames, scrambles and transmits on Link A

    The Physical Layer marks the start of the packet (in 128b/130b an STP token, which also carries the TLP length; in 8b/10b STP and END symbols), scrambles the bytes, stripes them across the 4 lanes and serializes them toward the switch's downstream port.

    Where: SSD Physical Layer → Link APCIe: Yes, upstream (device → switch) · about 4 + 2 + 16 + 4 bytes on the wire
    Gen4 x4: ≈ 26 B × 8 / 63 Gb/s ≈ 3.3 ns to serialize (derived) The figure's STP/Seq split is conceptual: in 128b/130b the sequence number sits inside the 4-byte STP token.
  4. The switch checks the LCRC and returns an ACK DLLP

    The switch's downstream port checks LCRC and sequence order. Good, so its Data Link Layer sends an ACK DLLP naming sequence 412h (ACKs may be coalesced to cover several TLPs). The SSD then discards its replay copy. A bad LCRC would produce a NAK and a replay from the SSD instead (Chapter 15).

    Where: switch downstream port ↔ SSD Data Link LayersPCIe: Yes, downstream · ACK DLLP (8 bytes incl. framing), link-local, never forwarded
    ACK AckNak_Seq_Num = 412h SSD replay buffer: [ ] (empty)
  5. The switch routes the request by address and forwards it on Link 1

    Address 1_2340_0140h is not inside the down port's memory window (FE00_0000h–FE0F_FFFFh), so the request goes to the up port. The switch does not change the header (Requester ID, Tag and address are untouched) but its up port adds its own sequence number and LCRC for Link 1 and keeps its own replay copy. The root port then ACKs that hop.

    Where: inside the switch, then Link 1PCIe: Yes, upstream · same MRd, new Seq/LCRC on Link 1 · consumes NPH credit at the root port
    Link 1: Seq = 0C7h (switch's counter, unrelated to 412h) Root port → switch: ACK 0C7h
  6. The root complex reads host memory

    The root port's Transaction Layer decodes the address as system memory, passes it through the IOMMU (if enabled) and reads 64 bytes from RAM. This is the slowest part of the round trip and is invisible on the link.

    Where: root complex ↔ host memoryPCIe: No · host-internal memory access
    Reads 1_2340_0140h … 1_2340_017Fh (the 64-byte SQE, opcode 02h Read) In the §10.7 trace the whole round trip is 1290 − 540 = 750 ns.
  7. The root complex sends a Completion with Data

    The completer builds a CplD with a 3DW (12-byte) header, copying the Requester ID and Tag from the request, adding its own Completer ID, the Byte Count still owed and the Lower Address, followed by the 64 bytes of data. It sends it down Link 1 with its own sequence number and LCRC.

    Where: root complex → Link 1PCIe: Yes, downstream · CplD, 3DW header + 16 DW data
    Completer ID 0000h Requester ID 0300h Tag 0Ah Status SC (000b) Byte Count 64 Lower Address 40h Length 16 DW Link 1: Seq = 2A0h, then switch → root port: ACK 2A0h
  8. The switch routes the completion by ID

    Completions carry no address to route on. The switch reads the bus number from the Requester ID (03) and sends the TLP to the port whose secondary–subordinate bus range contains bus 03: the down port. It goes out on Link A with a fresh sequence number and LCRC.

    Where: inside the switch, then Link APCIe: Yes, downstream · same CplD, new Seq/LCRC on Link A
    Requester ID 0300h → bus 03 → down port (buses 03–03) Link A: Seq = 1B3h
  9. The SSD matches the completion to its request by tag

    After the SSD's Physical and Data Link Layers accept the packet, its Transaction Layer looks up Tag 0Ah (with its own Requester ID) in the outstanding-request table. Byte Count = 64 equals what is still owed, so this was the last completion: the tag is freed, the completion timer stopped and the SQE handed to the command processor.

    Where: SSD Transaction LayerPCIe: No further TLP · tag 0Ah may now be reused
    Lookup 0Ah → "64 B for SQ1 slot 5" → received 64 of 64 → done If no completion had come back: Completion Timeout (Chapter 12), not a retry.
  10. The SSD acknowledges the CplD on Link A

    The SSD's Data Link Layer ACKs sequence 1B3h so the switch can drop its replay copy. ACKs are per link: the root complex never learns, from ACKs, that the SSD received the data.

    Where: SSD → switch Data Link LayersPCIe: Yes, upstream · ACK DLLP, link-local
    ACK AckNak_Seq_Num = 1B3h Total for one SQE fetch: 2 TLPs end to end, 4 TLP transmissions (2 per link), 4 ACKs.

Only the Transaction Layer header crosses end to end unchanged. Sequence numbers, LCRCs, framing and ACKs exist per link and are rebuilt at every hop. That is why an analyzer on Link A and one on Link 1 show the same Tag 0Ah but different sequence numbers.

10.7 Worked example: one NVMe 4 KiB read, as TLPs

Assumptions synthetic: SSD at 03:00.0, BAR0 at FE000000h, doorbell stride 4 bytes (CAP.DSTRD = 0) so SQ1 tail doorbell is at BAR0 + 1000h + (2×1)×4 = 1008h and CQ1 head doorbell at 100Ch; SQ1 base at 1_2340_0000h; data buffer described by PRP1 = 1_5000_0000h (4 KiB, page aligned); MPS = 256 bytes; MSI-X vector address FEE00000h.

Synthetic trace — normal 4 KiB NVMe Read, captured on the SSD's link
#t (ns)DirTLPFieldsNVMe meaning
10↓MWr 3DW Len 1Addr FE001008h, data = 6 (bytes 06 00 00 00)SQ1 tail doorbell: new tail = 6
2540↑MRd 4DW Len 16Req 0300h Tag 0Ah Addr 1_2340_0140hFetch SQE slot 5 (5 × 64 = 140h)
31290↓CplD Len 16Cpl 0000h Req 0300h Tag 0Ah SC BC 64 LA 40hSQE delivered (opcode 02h Read)
4–19~75 µs…↑16 × MWr 4DW Len 64Addr 1_5000_0000h + n×100hRead data written into host buffer (16 × 256 B)
20+40↑MWr 4DW Len 4Addr = CQ1 base + slot × 1616-byte CQE posted (phase bit flipped)
21+30↑MWr 3DW Len 1Addr FEE00000h, data = vector messageMSI-X interrupt
22+2500↓MWr 3DW Len 1Addr FE00100ChCQ1 head doorbell after host consumed CQE

Ordering detail that makes this safe: rows 4–19, 20 and 21 are all posted writes from the same requester in TC0 without Relaxed Ordering, so they arrive in host memory in order — the CQE cannot become visible before the data, and the interrupt cannot overtake the CQE (Chapter 14).

39.8 µs↓CplD Tag 0Bh9.25 µs read latency vs ~0.75 µs normal. Candidate explanations: IOMMU translation miss, memory on remote NUMA node, root complex congestion, host power state exit. Not attributable from this link alone.

2↓Cpl (no data) Status UR Tag 11hRoot complex refuses: IOMMU fault (address not mapped for this requester) impl — some RCs return UR, others CA

10.8 TLP decoding safety

⚠️ Never infer a transaction solely from a label

An analyzer row labelled "Read" may be an MRd, a CfgRd, an IORd — or the tool's merged "transaction" view of an MRd and its CplDs. Decide using the evidence: Fmt, Type, Length, Requester ID, Completer ID, Address, Tag, byte enables, completion status, Byte Count, TC, attributes, payload, and context (what came before, which link, which direction). If a field is not in the capture (truncated header, filtered column, FLIT-mode decode unavailable), the correct statement is: "Insufficient trace evidence."

📡 Four worlds, one TLP

Take row 20 above. PCIe normative: it is a posted 4DW Memory Write of 4 DW, must follow earlier posted writes from the same requester (no RO). NVMe: the address is inside the I/O Completion Queue the host created; the 16 bytes are a CQE whose DW3 holds CID and phase tag. Implementation: whether the controller writes one CQE per TLP or coalesces several CQEs into one larger write is a controller choice. Analyzer presentation: the tool may label it "NVMe Completion" if it has NVMe decode enabled and knows the queue base addresses — a convenience inference, not wire truth.

10.9 Linux view

# Is the device allowed to issue TLPs to memory? (Bus Master Enable, Memory Space Enable)
sudo lspci -vv -s 0000:03:00.0 | grep -E 'Control:|Status:'
# MPS / MRRS that shape TLP sizes
sudo lspci -vv -s 0000:03:00.0 | grep -E 'DevCtl|MaxPayload'
# IOMMU faults (TLPs refused by translation)
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'DMAR|AMD-Vi|iommu.*fault'

Can prove: that the device is permitted to master, sizes configured, that translation faults happened. Cannot prove: individual TLPs or their timing — Linux has no TLP-level visibility without an analyzer.

🧪 Lab 10.1 — Narrate the TLPs of an NVMe write SAFE

Objective: predict the TLP sequence of an 8 KiB NVMe Write with PRP1 and PRP2 (two pages), MRRS = 512, MPS = 256. Steps: list every TLP, direction, type, length. Questions: how many MRd for data? How many CplD minimum?

Solution

Doorbell MWr ↓; SQE MRd ↑ (16 DW) + CplD ↓; data: 8192 / 512 = 16 MRd ↑ (each Len 128 DW), each returned as at least 2 CplD of 256 B (MPS) → ≥ 32 CplD ↓ (more if the completer splits at RCB boundaries); CQE MWr ↑; MSI-X MWr ↑; CQ head doorbell MWr ↓. No PRP list fetch because two pages fit in PRP1+PRP2. Requests are bounded by MRRS, completions by MPS.

Extension: repeat for 16 KiB (needs a PRP list → one extra MRd for the list).

Quiz

  1. Which TLP carries NVMe read data to the host?

    Answer

    Memory Write (posted) from the SSD to host memory.

  2. Which TLP carries NVMe write data to the SSD?

    Answer

    CplD responding to the SSD's Memory Reads.

  3. Is a Config Write posted?

    Answer

    No — non-posted; completed with Cpl.

  4. What field tells you a TLP has an ECRC?

    Answer

    TD = 1.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a TLP?
    Model answerTransaction Layer Packet: header, optional data and optional ECRC, carrying requests and completions end to end.
  2. Beginner Name a posted and a non-posted request.
    Model answerMWr posted; MRd non-posted.
  3. Beginner What is a CplD?
    Model answerCompletion with data, answering a read.
  4. Beginner Max TLP payload?
    Model answerFormat allows 4096 bytes; actual limit is the configured MPS.
  5. Beginner What is an MSI-X interrupt on the wire?
    Model answerA posted MWr.
  6. Intermediate Why split transactions?
    Model answerTo free the link while the completer works; enables many outstanding reads.
  7. Intermediate How does the SSD know a read finished?
    Model answerByte Count in the last completion equals remaining bytes of that completion.
  8. Intermediate What's MRRS vs MPS?
    Model answerMRRS bounds a read request's size; MPS bounds any TLP's payload.
  9. Intermediate Which TLPs does a host CSTS poll generate?
    Model answerMRd 1 DW ↓ and CplD ↑ from the SSD.
  10. Intermediate What do Messages do?
    Model answerSignal events (errors, INTx, PM, vendor) without address-mapped memory semantics.
  11. Advanced Can a root complex merge two CPU stores into one MWr?
    Model answerYes for write-combining memory types (implementation); not for UC MMIO like doorbells.
  12. Advanced How is a 4DW header distinguished from 3DW?
    Model answerFmt bit 0 (001/011 = 4DW).
  13. Advanced When can ECRC help where LCRC cannot?
    Model answerCorruption inside a switch's internal buffers between LCRC check and regeneration.
  14. Advanced What does EP=1 mean for the receiver?
    Model answerPayload is poisoned; must not be used as good data; error handling per policy.
  15. Advanced Why does the SQE fetch use a 4DW header in our trace?
    Model answerHost memory address above 4 GiB requires 64-bit addressing.
  16. Senior A tool labels a row "NVMe Read Cmd". How do you verify?
    Model answerCheck it's a CplD returning to the SSD's tag for an MRd into a known SQ address, decode the 64-byte payload: opcode 02h at byte 0.
  17. Senior Where in the TLP flow can a command get lost without any error?
    Model answerNowhere at PCIe level silently — but a doorbell to a wrong address can be accepted silently by the SSD (NVMe defines an Invalid Doorbell async event, which may not be enabled), and writes are posted so the host never learns.
  18. Senior Why are posted writes dangerous for error reporting?
    Model answerThe requester gets no completion; errors surface only via AER messages to the RC, asynchronously.
  19. Senior How do you prove data was written before CQE?
    Model answerShow both are MWr from the same requester, same TC, RO clear; ordering rules guarantee; analyzer shows sequence numbers in order.
  20. Senior What can't an analyzer on the SSD link tell you about IOMMU behavior?
    Model answerTranslation latency, page table state; it only sees the resulting completion delay or error status.
📌 Teach-back

Child: "letters with envelopes, some needing replies." Junior: "TLP = header + optional data + optional ECRC; MRd/CfgRd/CfgWr/AtomicOp are non-posted and get completions; MWr/Msg are posted." Senior: "NVMe is a choreography of MWr and MRd/CplD; correctness relies on posted ordering; decode from fields, never labels."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can list TLP types with Fmt/Type and posted/non-posted status.
  • I can write the full TLP sequence of an NVMe read and write.
  • I can identify the first missing TLP in a stuck-command trace.
  • I apply decoding safety and say "Insufficient trace evidence" when fields are missing.
  • I can separate PCIe normative, NVMe, implementation, and analyzer facts about a TLP.

11 TLP Header Anatomy

← 10 Transaction Layer Packets (TLPs)12 Posted vs Non-Posted Transactions (and Completions) →

11.1 Why this chapter exists

Analyzer GUIs, AER header logs (lspci prints them as four hex DWs), FPGA debug captures and simulation waveforms all hand you raw header DWs. This chapter teaches you to decode them by hand and with code, and tells you, for every field, what a wrong value looks like in practice.

  • Locate every non-FLIT header field by DW, byte and bit.
  • Decode MRd, MWr and CplD headers byte by byte in binary and hex.
  • Apply byte-enable, length, 4 KiB boundary, Byte Count and Lower Address rules.
  • Run and extend a Python teaching decoder.

Prerequisites: Chapter 10; binary/hex fluency.

🧒 Kid analogy

A header is a form with boxes in fixed places: box 1 says "what kind of letter", box 2 "how many pages", box 3 "who sent it", box 4 "question number", box 5 "address". Because the boxes are always in the same place, a machine can read it in a flash.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Some boxes change meaning depending on box 1 (completion headers reuse DW1–DW2 for completer ID, status and byte count), some boxes are split across bytes (Length is 10 bits spanning byte 2 and 3; tag bits T9/T8 live in byte 1), and the form changed in FLIT mode.

11.2 Byte order convention

Headers are transmitted byte 0 first. Within the header, the spec draws each DW with byte 0 on the left holding bits [31:24] of that DW — i.e. header fields read naturally as big-endian 32-bit words. Payload bytes, by contrast, are in address order: payload byte 0 is the byte at the lowest address. A little-endian host value 00000005h therefore appears in the payload as 05 00 00 00 verified.

11.3 DW0 — common to all TLPs

Bytebit 7bit 6bit 5bit 4bit 3bit 2bit 1bit 0
0Fmt[2:0]Type[4:0]
1T9TC[2:0]T8Attr[2] (IDO)LNTH
2TDEPAttr[1] (RO)Attr[0] (NS)AT[1:0]Length[9:8]
3Length[7:0]

T9/T8 are the upper tag bits for 10-bit tags (PCIe 4.0+); in older revisions those bit positions were reserved version. LN (Lightweight Notification) and TH (TLP Processing Hints) were added in 2.1-era revisions version.

1Requester ID [15:0] = Bus[7:0] | Device[4:0] | Function[2:0]Tag[7:0]Last DW BE[3:0] | First DW BE[3:0]
2 (3DW)Address[31:2] | PH[1:0] (or reserved)
2 (4DW)Address[63:32]
3 (4DW)Address[31:2] | PH[1:0] (or reserved)

DWByte 0Byte 1Byte 2Byte 3

Config requests are 3DW, Length = 1, TC0, attributes 0, Last DW BE = 0000 verified. Byte offset = (ExtReg << 8) | (Reg << 2), covering the 4 KiB extended configuration space.
