🧪 Lab 16.1 — Credit-gated link simulator SAFE

Objective: show how advertised data credits and credit-loop latency cap throughput.

def throughput(pd_credits, loop_ns, link_gbps=7.88, payload=256):
    tlp_ns = (payload + 24) / link_gbps        # wire time per TLP (bytes / (bytes/ns))
    per_tlp = payload // 16                      # PD credits per TLP
    t, cc, cl, returns, sent = 0.0, 0, pd_credits, [], 0
    while t < 200_000:                         # 200 us of simulated time
        while returns and returns[0][0] <= t:    # credits come back after loop_ns
            cl += returns.pop(0)[1]
        if cl - cc >= per_tlp:
            cc += per_tlp; sent += 1
            returns.append((t + loop_ns, per_tlp)); t += tlp_ns
        else:
            t = returns[0][0]                    # stall until next UpdateFC
    return sent * payload / t                    # GB/s
for credits in (128, 256, 512, 1024):
    print(credits, "PD credits:", round(throughput(credits, loop_ns=1000), 2), "GB/s")

Questions: at what credit count does throughput reach the link limit? How does doubling loop latency change it?

Solution

Throughput ≈ min(link, credits × 16 B / loop). With a 1 µs loop: 128 → ~2 GB/s, 256 → ~4.1 GB/s, 512 → link-limited ~7.2 GB/s (payload efficiency 256/280 of 7.88). Doubling the loop halves the credit-limited throughput — why buffers must scale with speed × latency (and why 6.0 added scaled credits).

Extension: add header credits and 64-byte TLPs to show header-bound behavior.

🧪 Lab 16.2 — Advanced: prove a shared-root-port credit bottleneck CAUTION

Objective: experimentally separate SSD limits from fabric credit limits. Prerequisites: two or more SSDs (test data only), read-only fio. Procedure: (1) measure each SSD alone; (2) run both under the same root port; (3) run both under different root ports; (4) vary block size (4 KiB vs 128 KiB) to shift header vs data pressure. Expected reasoning: if the pair under one RP loses more than its link sum would predict while the split pair scales, a shared fabric resource — possibly credits/buffers — limits; it cannot be attributed to credits specifically without an analyzer or uncore counters.

Solution

State the conclusion with its confidence: "shared upstream resource" (high) vs "credit buffer specifically" (low without DLLP evidence). This is the evidence discipline of Part IV–VI in one sentence.

Quiz

  1. Credits consumed by a CfgWr of 4 bytes?

    Answer

    1 NPH + 1 NPD.

  2. Credits consumed by a 512-byte CplD?

    Answer

    1 CplH + 32 CplD.

  3. What does an advertised value of 0 mean in InitFC?

    Answer

    Infinite credits.

  4. Why the "≤ half the range" check?

    Answer

    Safe comparison of wrapping modular counters.

  5. Which credits does an NVMe read-data stream use at the root port?

    Answer

    PH and PD.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is credit-based flow control?
    Model answerReceiver advertises buffer space; sender transmits only within it; no drops.
  2. Beginner Name the six credit types.
    Model answerPH, PD, NPH, NPD, CplH, CplD.
  3. Beginner Size of one data credit?
    Model answer16 bytes.
  4. Beginner Which DLLP returns credits?
    Model answerUpdateFC.
  5. Beginner What is backpressure?
    Model answerA full receiver stopping the sender via credits.
  6. Intermediate Why do endpoints advertise infinite completion credits?
    Model answerCompletions must never be blocked (deadlock avoidance); the requester pre-reserves space before issuing reads.
  7. Intermediate What's FC_INIT1 vs FC_INIT2?
    Model answerPhase 1 advertises; phase 2 confirms both sides recorded values.
  8. Intermediate How does MPS affect header credits?
    Model answerSmaller MPS → more TLPs per byte → more header credits.
  9. Intermediate Can posted traffic stall because NP credits are exhausted?
    Model answerNo, separate pools; posted must be able to pass.
  10. Intermediate Where do you see credit stalls?
    Model answerAnalyzer: idle gaps with pending traffic aligned to UpdateFC arrivals.
  11. Advanced Compute credits needed for 15.75 GB/s with 1.5 µs loop.
    Model answer15.75e9 × 1.5e-6 = 23.6 KB ≈ 1477 data credits — near the 12-bit (2047) limit; motivates scaled FC at higher speeds.
  12. Advanced What is Receiver Overflow?
    Model answerReceiver got more than it advertised — transmitter accounting bug; fatal by default.
  13. Advanced How do switches handle credits?
    Model answerEach port advertises its own buffers; credits are per link; internal arbitration maps ingress to egress.
  14. Advanced What did 6.0 change?
    Model answerScaled FC, FLIT-mode shared credit pools, DLP-carried FC info (version-dependent details).
  15. Advanced Header vs data starvation example?
    Model answerHigh-IOPS small writes/CQEs exhaust PH; large DMA exhausts PD.
  16. Senior Eight Gen4 SSDs behind a switch deliver 30% less than predicted. Plan.
    Model answerCompute uplink ceiling; check MPS; per-SSD solo vs group; analyzer on uplink for UpdateFC cadence; vendor switch buffer configuration; consider spreading across RPs.
  17. Senior How would you validate a new root port design's credit sizing?
    Model answerModel BW × loop latency for all widths/speeds/MPS, test with traffic generator at worst-case MPS and mixed classes, verify no gaps at line rate.
  18. Senior Can credits cause unfairness between SSDs?
    Model answerYes, via shared buffers and arbitration policies at switches/RC; implementation-dependent.
  19. Senior What evidence is needed before blaming flow control?
    Model answerDLLP-level capture showing gaps aligned with credit exhaustion; otherwise only "shared resource" can be claimed.
  20. Senior Why does a Gen5 SSD in a Gen5 slot behind a Gen4-era switch underperform?
    Model answerLink speed mismatch, buffers sized for lower BW × latency, header credits at high IOPS.
💡 Senior insight

Flow control problems never show up in error logs. If the link is healthy, the SSD is fast in isolation, and the CPU is idle, but bandwidth is missing — think credits and shared buffers, and go get DLLP-level evidence before you say so.

📌 Teach-back

Child: "tokens for space in the toy box." Junior: "six credit types, header = 1 per TLP, data = 16 B units; InitFC then UpdateFC; modular gating; 0 = infinite." Senior: "throughput ≤ credits × 16 B / loop latency; starvation and HOL blocking happen per class at shared ports; prove with DLLP timing."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute credits for any TLP.
  • I can run the modular gating example including wraparound.
  • I can derive the credit-limited throughput formula and apply it.
  • I can explain starvation, backpressure and HOL blocking in an NVMe topology.
  • I can state what Linux can and cannot show about credits.
  • I can cite the Flow Control sections of the PCIe Base Specification as the normative source.

16.11 Parts IV–VI summary

You now hold the full PCIe picture an NVMe engineer needs: a tree of point-to-point links (Ch 4) made of differential lanes (Ch 5) at generation-specific rates and encodings (Ch 6), organized in three layers (Ch 7), trained by the LTSSM with TS1/TS2 and equalization (Ch 8–9), carrying TLPs (Ch 10–11) that are posted or non-posted (Ch 12), matched by tags (Ch 13), constrained by ordering (Ch 14), delivered reliably by Ack/Nak and replay (Ch 15), and paced by credits (Ch 16). When something goes wrong, a useful heuristic (not an absolute rule) is to start at the bottom: is the link up and healthy? Are transactions completing? Only then move up into NVMe queues and commands.

Further reading: PCI Express Base Specification (Data Link Layer; Flow Control; Transaction Ordering); Linux Documentation/PCI/pcieaer-howto.rst. Next: the following Part of this book builds the NVMe controller on top of this PCIe foundation.

PART VII

PCIe Configuration

A PCIe link that has trained to L0 is a road with no addresses on it. Before a single NVMe command can travel, software must discover every device on that road, give every bridge a range of bus numbers, read every device's identity card (its configuration space), learn how big each device's register window is, carve those windows out of the physical address map, and finally switch on memory decoding and bus mastering. This Part walks that journey in three chapters: Chapter 17 — Enumeration (the depth-first walk and bus numbering), Chapter 18 — Configuration Space (decoding headers and capability lists by hand), and Chapter 19 — BARs and MMIO (sizing, assigning and using the doorway through which the NVMe driver reaches the controller's registers). By the end of the Part you will be able to read an lspci -vvv listing or a raw hex dump and say exactly what firmware and the OS did to the device — and what they forgot to do.

17 PCIe Enumeration

← 16 PCIe Flow Control18 Configuration Space →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG), configuration and enumeration model inherited from the PCI Local Bus Specification and PCI-to-PCI Bridge Architecture Specification. REVISION: concepts here are stable from PCIe 1.0 through 6.x/7.0 version; Flit-mode and 14-bit tag details do not change the enumeration algorithm. STATUS: current. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: conventional PCI had no Extended Configuration Space (only 256 bytes per function); PCIe added the 4 KiB space reachable through the Enhanced Configuration Access Mechanism (ECAM). SOURCE: PCI-SIG specifications (membership required for the normative text); Linux drivers/pci/probe.c as an openly readable implementation. Section numbers are intentionally not quoted.

17.1 Why this chapter exists

Every NVMe bring-up failure that ends in "the drive is not detected" is, at its root, an enumeration story. Either the link never reached L0, or a configuration read returned all-ones, or the bridge above the device did not forward the right bus numbers, or the Base Address Register (BAR) could not be placed, or the OS refused the device's resources. If you cannot narrate enumeration step by step, you will guess at these failures instead of localizing them. This chapter gives you that narration — from power-on to the moment the NVMe driver's probe() function runs — and teaches you to find the first step that went wrong.

17.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain what a Bus/Device/Function (BDF) number is and why software must discover devices rather than having them pre-listed.
  • Intermediate: perform a depth-first enumeration by hand on a topology with a switch, assigning Primary, Secondary and Subordinate bus numbers correctly.
  • Advanced: explain Type 0 vs Type 1 configuration requests, how a bridge decides to forward, convert, or reject them, and how Configuration Request Retry Status (CRS) interacts with slow-to-initialize devices.
  • Senior: reason about resource reallocation, hot-plug bus-number padding, ACPI and firmware hand-off, and why the OS may re-enumerate differently from firmware.
  • Trace analysis: recognise the signature of an enumeration scan in a protocol capture (bursts of CfgRd0/CfgRd1 at offset 00h, Unsupported Request completions for empty slots) and spot the first anomaly.
  • Debugging: map "device missing" symptoms to a layer: physical link, configuration routing, resource assignment, or driver binding.
  • Validation: design tests for enumeration robustness (cold boot, warm reset, hot-plug, CRS behaviour, slow firmware readiness).

17.3 Prerequisites

You should already understand the PCIe layer model and the Transaction Layer Packet (TLP) — in particular that configuration requests (CfgRd0, CfgRd1, CfgWr0, CfgWr1) are non-posted and complete with a Cpl or CplD (Cpl/CplD). You should know that the Link Training and Status State Machine (LTSSM) must reach L0 before any TLP flows. If those are shaky, revisit the PCIe fundamentals Part first. Inside this Part, the next stops are Chapter 18 and Chapter 19.

17.4 Story: the new apartment building

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine a postman who arrives at a brand-new town where nobody has house numbers yet. He starts at the post office (the Root Complex). He walks down the first street and knocks on every door: "Is anyone home?" If nobody answers, he moves on. If someone answers, he asks, "Who are you, and are you a gate to another street?" When he finds a gate, he walks through it, names the new street "Street 1", and keeps going deeper before returning. Each gate gets a little sign: "Streets 1 through 1 are behind me." When he has visited every street, he goes back and asks each household, "How big is your mailbox?" and then gives each one a real address in the town map. Only then can letters (memory reads and writes) be delivered.

🌍 Real-world analogy

A network administrator plugging in a new building of routers: she walks the cabling, assigns subnets to each router port (bus numbers to bridges), records which subnet range sits behind each router (Secondary..Subordinate), then hands out IP addresses to devices (BAR assignment). Routing then works by range checks — exactly how PCIe bridges forward configuration and memory requests.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

(1) Doors in PCIe do not answer with "nobody home" politely: a configuration read to an absent function is completed with Unsupported Request status by the bridge or Root Port, and the CPU typically sees FFFFh/FFFFFFFFh — the "all-ones" response. (2) The postman can find a house that says "come back later" (CRS) — a real device may still be booting its firmware. (3) House numbers (bus numbers) are assigned by the postman, but device numbers on a PCIe link are fixed by topology: a device directly below a Root Port or switch Downstream Port is device 0 (unless ARI is in use). (4) Addresses for mailboxes (BARs) are not chosen by the household — the household only states the size and alignment, and software picks the address.

17.5 Beginner view: what enumeration is

Enumeration is the process by which system software (platform firmware first, then usually the OS again) discovers every PCI Express function in the hierarchy, gives every bridge its bus-number range, sizes and assigns every BAR, and enables the functions it wants to use. It exists because PCIe, like PCI before it, is self-describing: the motherboard does not contain a list of what is plugged in. A slot could hold an NVMe SSD today and a network card tomorrow, and a switch could fan out to 24 drives in a storage enclosure. Software therefore discovers the topology at run time by issuing configuration reads and observing who answers.

17.5.1 Bus / Device / Function (BDF)

Every function is addressed in configuration space by a 16-bit Routing ID (called Requester ID when the function initiates a request, Completer ID when it completes one) verified:

Bits 15:8Bits 7:3Bits 2:0
Bus number (0–255)Device number (0–31)Function number (0–7)

Linux prints it as DDDD:BB:DD.F, for example 0000:01:00.0: PCI segment (domain) 0000, bus 01, device 00, function 0. Segments let a large server have more than 256 buses by giving each Root Complex (or each ECAM region) its own 256-bus space; the segment number is not carried in the TLP — it is a host-side concept. verified

  • Bus number — assigned by software during enumeration. Not burned into hardware. Bus 0 is the Root Complex's internal bus in the common case.
  • Device number — on a point-to-point PCIe link, the device below a Root Port or switch Downstream Port is device 0. The Downstream Port only forwards Type 0 configuration requests that target device 0 on its secondary bus (unless ARI forwarding is enabled). Devices other than 0 appear on a Root Complex's internal bus (integrated endpoints and Root Ports themselves) and on the internal virtual bus of a switch (one device number per Downstream Port).
  • Function number — a single physical device can expose up to 8 functions (e.g. a multi-port NIC). Function 0 must exist; software checks the multi-function bit (Header Type bit 7) of function 0 before probing functions 1–7.
🚀 Advanced: ARI

Alternative Routing-ID Interpretation (ARI, an extended capability, ID 000Eh) reinterprets the 8 bits of Device+Function as one 8-bit function number for devices directly below an ARI-capable Downstream Port. This allows up to 256 functions — needed for Single Root I/O Virtualization (SR-IOV) devices that expose many Virtual Functions. With ARI, "device number" stops being meaningful for that device. verified

The master journey requested for this chapter is: Firmware → Root Complex → Link → device detection → BDF → configuration space → BAR sizing → BAR assignment → Command register → bus mastering → driver. Here is that journey as a timeline with the evidence each step leaves behind.

17.7 Hardware view: who answers a configuration request

A configuration request is born in the Root Complex. The CPU never issues "a config TLP" directly; it performs a load or store to the ECAM window (or, on legacy x86, to I/O ports CF8h/CFCh), and the Root Complex converts that access into a configuration TLP verified. The Root Complex's ECAM decoder takes the address apart:

ECAM address = ECAM_base + (Bus << 20) + (Device << 15) + (Function << 12) + Register
  • ECAM_base — physical base of the configuration window, reported to the OS in the ACPI MCFG table (per segment and bus range).
  • Bus — 8 bits (0–255). Each bus takes 1 MiB of window.
  • Device — 5 bits (0–31). Each device takes 32 KiB.
  • Function — 3 bits (0–7). Each function takes 4 KiB.
  • Register — 12-bit byte offset (0–FFFh) into the function's 4 KiB configuration space.

A full 256-bus segment therefore needs a 256 MiB window. Firmware may describe a smaller bus range to save address space. derived

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""ECAM and legacy CF8h address calculators (pure arithmetic, no hardware access)."""

def ecam_addr(base, bus, dev, fn, reg):
    assert 0 <= bus < 256 and 0 <= dev < 32 and 0 <= fn < 8 and 0 <= reg < 4096
    return base + (bus << 20) + (dev << 15) + (fn << 12) + reg

def cf8_value(bus, dev, fn, reg):
    # Legacy mechanism reaches only the first 256 bytes, dword aligned.
    assert reg < 256 and reg % 4 == 0
    return (1 << 31) | (bus << 16) | (dev << 11) | (fn << 8) | (reg & 0xFC)

def bdf_from_rid(rid):
    return (rid >> 8) & 0xFF, (rid >> 3) & 0x1F, rid & 0x7

ECAM_BASE = 0xE000_0000          # synthetic: real base comes from the ACPI MCFG table
for bdf, reg in [((0x01, 0, 0), 0x000), ((0x01, 0, 0), 0x100), ((0x04, 0, 0), 0x034)]:
    b, d, f = bdf
    print(f"{b:02x}:{d:02x}.{f} reg {reg:03x}h -> ECAM {ecam_addr(ECAM_BASE, b, d, f, reg):#010x}")
print(f"CF8h value for 01:00.0 reg 10h = {cf8_value(1, 0, 0, 0x10):#010x}")
rid = (0x04 << 8) | (0 << 3) | 0
print(f"Requester ID {rid:#06x} -> bus {bdf_from_rid(rid)[0]:02x} dev {bdf_from_rid(rid)[1]:02x} fn {bdf_from_rid(rid)[2]}")
print(f"ECAM window for 256 buses = {256 * 32 * 8 * 4096 // (1 << 20)} MiB")

Output when run (pure arithmetic; the ECAM base is synthetic):

01:00.0 reg 000h -> ECAM 0xe0100000
01:00.0 reg 100h -> ECAM 0xe0100100
04:00.0 reg 034h -> ECAM 0xe0400034
CF8h value for 01:00.0 reg 10h = 0x80010010
Requester ID 0x0400 -> bus 04 dev 00 fn 0
ECAM window for 256 buses = 256 MiB

17.7.1 Type 0 vs Type 1 configuration requests

The Root Complex chooses a TLP type by comparing the target bus with the topology:

  • CfgRd0 / CfgWr0 (Type 0) — targets a function on the bus directly below the port issuing it. The receiving function consumes it.
  • CfgRd1 / CfgWr1 (Type 1) — targets a function on a bus further down. Each bridge (Root Port, switch port) compares the target bus with its own registers:
    • target bus == Secondary Bus Number → convert to Type 0 and send it down the link;
    • Secondary < target bus ≤ Subordinate Bus Number → forward downstream unchanged as Type 1;
    • otherwise → not for this bridge (it is not claimed by this branch).

This range check is why bus numbering must be contiguous and depth-first: every bridge must "own" exactly the range of bus numbers beneath it. verified

🔧 Hardware: what a switch looks like to software

A PCIe switch is not one device to software. It appears as a tree of PCI-to-PCI bridges: one Upstream Port (a Type 1 function on the bus below the Root Port) and an internal virtual bus with one Type 1 function per Downstream Port. A 1-upstream/3-downstream switch therefore consumes two levels of bus numbers before its endpoints: one for the internal bus, then one per Downstream Port. Engineers who forget the internal bus mis-predict BDFs every time.

17.8 The depth-first enumeration algorithm

next_bus = 0

scan_bus(bus):
    highest = bus
    for dev in 0..31:
        if read_cfg16(bus, dev, 0, 0x00) == 0xFFFF: continue       # no function 0 → no device
        nfuncs = 8 if (read_cfg8(bus, dev, 0, 0x0E) & 0x80) else 1   # multi-function bit
        for fn in 0..nfuncs-1:
            vid = read_cfg16(bus, dev, fn, 0x00)
            if vid == 0xFFFF: continue
            if vid == 0x0001: retry later                           # CRS software visibility (see 17.9)
            hdr = read_cfg8(bus, dev, fn, 0x0E) & 0x7F
            if hdr == 0x01:                                          # Type 1: a bridge
                next_bus += 1
                write_cfg8(bus, dev, fn, 0x18, bus)                  # Primary
                write_cfg8(bus, dev, fn, 0x19, next_bus)             # Secondary
                write_cfg8(bus, dev, fn, 0x1A, 0xFF)                 # Subordinate: temporarily "everything"
                sub = scan_bus(next_bus)                             # recurse first (depth-first)
                write_cfg8(bus, dev, fn, 0x1A, sub)                  # shrink to the real range
                highest = max(highest, sub)
            else:
                record endpoint; size its BARs later
    return highest

scan_bus(0)

Two details matter in real firmware impl: (1) hot-plug capable Downstream Ports often get extra bus numbers reserved ("bus padding") so a switch inserted later can be numbered without renumbering the whole tree; (2) Linux normally reads the bus numbers firmware programmed and only assigns new ones if they are missing or broken. Linux performs its own scan using the same principles (pci_scan_child_bus, pci_scan_bridge).

17.8.1 Worked walk with bus numbering

The following executable simulation applies the algorithm to a synthetic topology: a Root Complex with an integrated host bridge, Root Port A (an NVMe SSD directly attached) and Root Port B (a 3-port switch with two NVMe SSDs and one empty slot).

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Depth-first PCIe bus-numbering simulation (SYNTHETIC topology, no hardware access)."""

# Each node: ("bridge", name, [children]) or ("ep", name)
# Children of a bridge sit on the bridge's SECONDARY bus; device numbers are list positions.
TOPOLOGY = [  # devices on bus 0 (root complex internal bus)
    ("ep", "Host bridge"),                                   # 00:00.0
    ("bridge", "Root Port A", [("ep", "NVMe SSD #1")]),       # 00:01.0
    ("bridge", "Root Port B", [                               # 00:02.0
        ("bridge", "Switch Upstream Port", [
            ("bridge", "Switch Downstream Port 0", [("ep", "NVMe SSD #2")]),
            ("bridge", "Switch Downstream Port 1", [("ep", "NVMe SSD #3")]),
            ("bridge", "Switch Downstream Port 2", []),      # empty slot
        ]),
    ]),
]

next_bus = 0
rows = []

def scan_bus(bus, devices, depth):
    """Scan one bus; recurse into bridges depth-first. Returns highest bus number used."""
    global next_bus
    highest = bus
    for dev, node in enumerate(devices):
        bdf = f"{bus:02x}:{dev:02x}.0"
        if node[0] == "ep":
            rows.append((depth, bdf, node[1], "type 0", ""))
            continue
        _, name, children = node
        next_bus += 1
        secondary = next_bus
        # Real firmware temporarily programs subordinate = 0xFF so Type 1 config
        # requests for any deeper bus are forwarded while scanning below.
        idx = len(rows)
        rows.append([depth, bdf, name, "type 1", None])
        sub = scan_bus(secondary, children, depth + 1)
        rows[idx][4] = f"pri={bus:02x} sec={secondary:02x} sub={sub:02x}"
        highest = max(highest, sub)
    return highest

scan_bus(0, TOPOLOGY, 0)
print(f"{'BDF':8} {'header':7} {'bus registers':24} device")
for depth, bdf, name, hdr, regs in rows:
    print(f"{bdf:8} {hdr:7} {regs:24} {'  ' * depth}{name}")

Output:

BDF      header  bus registers            device
00:00.0  type 0                           Host bridge
00:01.0  type 1  pri=00 sec=01 sub=01     Root Port A
01:00.0  type 0                             NVMe SSD #1
00:02.0  type 1  pri=00 sec=02 sub=06     Root Port B
02:00.0  type 1  pri=02 sec=03 sub=06       Switch Upstream Port
03:00.0  type 1  pri=03 sec=04 sub=04         Switch Downstream Port 0
04:00.0  type 0                                 NVMe SSD #2
03:01.0  type 1  pri=03 sec=05 sub=05         Switch Downstream Port 1
05:00.0  type 0                                 NVMe SSD #3
03:02.0  type 1  pri=03 sec=06 sub=06         Switch Downstream Port 2
📌 Remember

Primary = the bus the bridge sits on. Secondary = the bus immediately below it. Subordinate = the highest-numbered bus anywhere below it. A Type 1 request is forwarded if Secondary ≤ target ≤ Subordinate, and converted to Type 0 at the bridge whose Secondary equals the target.

17.9 Readiness, CRS and the "device not ready yet" problem

An NVMe SSD contains a controller running firmware. After reset, that firmware may need time before it can answer configuration requests. PCIe provides Configuration Request Retry Status (CRS): the device may complete a configuration request with CRS status, meaning "try again" verified. What software sees depends on the Root Port's CRS Software Visibility enable (in the Root Control register of the PCI Express Capability):

  • Visibility disabled — the Root Complex re-issues the request itself (hardware retry); the CPU load may simply stall until the device answers or a platform timeout occurs impl.
  • Visibility enabled — for a read that includes the Vendor ID register, the Root Complex returns the special value 0001h in the Vendor ID field so software can poll without blocking verified. Linux uses this when available and waits up to a bounded time (on the order of a minute in current kernels) for the device to become ready impl.

Newer PCIe revisions add Readiness Notifications (Device Readiness Status and Function Readiness Status messages) and a Readiness Time Reporting capability so software need not guess version. Support is optional; capability discovery applies.

📭 What the spec does not say

The PCIe specification does not say how long a particular NVMe SSD's firmware takes to become ready, nor how long a given BIOS waits before giving up. A drive that is "missing only on cold boot" is frequently a readiness-timing interaction between a slow device and an impatient firmware — the evidence is the timestamp of the first CfgRd relative to link-up, and whether CRS completions were returned.

17.10 Protocol view: what travels on the link

TransactionDirectionPosted?CompletionMeaning during enumeration
CfgRd0Downstream (RC → device)Non-postedCplD (success) / Cpl with UR or CRSRead a register of a function on the bus directly below
CfgRd1DownstreamNon-postedSameRead a register of a function further down; converted to Type 0 at the right bridge
CfgWr0 / CfgWr1DownstreamNon-posted (unlike memory writes)Cpl (no data)Program bus numbers, BARs, Command register
Cpl with URUpstream——No function at that BDF (generated by the bridge/port above the empty slot or by a device lacking that function)
Cpl with CRSUpstream——Function exists but not ready yet

Configuration writes are non-posted: the writer waits for a completion. This is a deliberate safety property — software knows a BAR or bus-number write has taken effect before it issues the next request verified. A completion's Completer ID is captured by the device from the configuration requests it receives; this is how an endpoint learns its own bus/device number verified, which it then uses as Requester ID in its own memory reads (DMA).

Disambiguate with the Root Port's Link Status (Data Link Layer Link Active), its AER status (Surprise Down), hot-plug Slot Status (Presence Detect), and the timeline of any reset software issued.

17.12 Linux view

# Tree view: shows bridges and which BDFs hang below each Root Port / switch port
lspci -tv

# One device in detail: header, BARs ("Region"), capabilities, bus numbers on bridges
sudo lspci -vvv -s 01:00.0
sudo lspci -vvv -s 00:01.0        # bridge: look for "Bus: primary=00, secondary=01, subordinate=01"

# Kernel's enumeration narrative
sudo dmesg | grep -iE 'pci |pci_bus|ecam|mmconfig|bar [0-9]|bridge window'
sudo journalctl -k -b | grep -i nvme

# sysfs view of the same objects
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/{vendor,device,class}
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/resource       # start end flags per BAR
cat /proc/iomem | grep -i -A2 nvme
⚠️ Safety

Everything above is read-only. Commands such as echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/rescan, echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/…/remove, or setpci with a =value suffix change hardware state. Removing the device that holds your root filesystem will crash the system. Only do those in a VM or on a dedicated test machine (CAUTION LAB). Reading beyond the first 64 bytes of configuration space via sysfs requires root.

Illustrative, abbreviated lspci -tv shape for the synthetic topology (not captured from real hardware):

-[0000:00]-+-00.0  Host bridge
           +-01.0-[01]----00.0  Non-Volatile memory controller
           \-02.0-[02-06]----00.0-[03-06]--+-00.0-[04]----00.0  Non-Volatile memory controller
                                           +-01.0-[05]----00.0  Non-Volatile memory controller
                                           \-02.0-[06]--

The [02-06] notation is exactly Secondary–Subordinate. Reading the tree: Root Port 00:02.0 owns buses 2–6; the switch Upstream Port at 02:00.0 owns 3–6; its three Downstream Ports own 4, 5 and 6.

17.13 Code: how the Linux NVMe driver takes over after enumeration

Simplified from the shape of drivers/nvme/host/pci.c (names abbreviated; error handling removed; this is pseudocode, not compilable kernel code):

nvme_probe(pdev):
    dev = alloc(...)
    pci_enable_device_mem(pdev)          # Command.MSE = 1 (memory decode on)
    pci_set_master(pdev)                 # Command.BME = 1 (device may now DMA)
    dma_set_mask_and_coherent(&pdev->dev, DMA_BIT_MASK(64))
    pci_request_mem_regions(pdev, "nvme")   # claim BAR0 in /proc/iomem
    bar = ioremap(pci_resource_start(pdev, 0), size)   # kernel virtual mapping of BAR0
    cap = readq(bar + 0x00)              # NVMe CAP register (Chapter 24)
    pci_alloc_irq_vectors(pdev, 1, N, PCI_IRQ_ALL_TYPES)  # MSI-X preferred
    ... controller reset/enable, Identify, I/O queues ...

Notice the strict order: you cannot read CAP before MSE=1 (the device would not decode the address and the read returns all-ones or faults), and the device cannot fetch commands before BME=1 (its memory reads would be blocked by its own Command register). derived

17.14 Worked example: predicting BDFs before you boot

Problem. A server has one Root Port at 00:03.0 with a 1-upstream/4-downstream switch. Downstream Ports 0 and 2 have NVMe SSDs; ports 1 and 3 are empty. Firmware reserves no hot-plug padding. Bus numbers already used: 00 only. Predict every BDF and every bridge's (pri, sec, sub).

Solution. Root Port 00:03.0 gets sec = 1. Switch USP is 01:00.0 with sec = 2 (internal bus). DSPs are 02:00.0, 02:01.0, 02:02.0, 02:03.0. Depth-first: DSP0 sec = 3 → SSD at 03:00.0, sub = 3. DSP1 sec = 4, empty, sub = 4. DSP2 sec = 5 → SSD at 05:00.0, sub = 5. DSP3 sec = 6, sub = 6. USP sub = 6, Root Port sub = 6. Note that empty DSPs still consume a bus number — they are bridges and have a secondary bus whether or not anything is plugged in. derived

Twist. If firmware gives each hot-plug DSP 8 extra buses of padding, the second SSD moves from bus 05 to a much higher bus number. This is why BDFs are not stable identifiers across firmware settings — use serial numbers, NGUID/EUI-64, or physical slot numbers in automation.

17.15 Common mistakes

  • Assuming the device number on a PCIe link can be anything but 0 (without ARI).
  • Forgetting the switch internal bus when predicting BDFs.
  • Treating FFFFFFFFh as data. On PCIe, all-ones from a config read is almost always "no response".
  • Using BDF as a persistent drive identifier in test scripts.
  • Believing enumeration happens once. It can happen at boot, after hot-plug, after rescan, after a Secondary Bus Reset, and in VMs again inside the guest.
  • Issuing configuration requests immediately after a reset (no readiness wait) and interpreting failures as a dead device.

17.16 Debugging connection: five failure patterns

#SymptomPossible causesFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentLikely conclusion (confidence)
1SSD absent from lspci; Root Port presentLink never trained; device not powered; PERST# held; device in CRS foreverRoot Port Link Status: DLLLA bit, negotiated widthRoot Port Slot Status presence detect (if slot implemented)Move the drive to a known-good slot; analyzer on link: is there any training?No L0 → physical/link problem, not enumeration (high)
2SSD appears only after warm reboot, not cold bootDevice readiness slower than firmware's waitFirmware log timestamps; CRS handling settingDevice vendor's documented ready time implAdd delay in firmware setup (if available) or test with OS-level rescan after bootReadiness race (medium-high)
3Drives behind a switch missing, switch itself visibleBad Subordinate value; switch DSP link down; switch firmware/EEPROM configlspci -vvv on USP/DSPs: bus numbersDSP Link StatusRead config space of DSPs; if DSP link is up but endpoint missing, check bus rangesRouting range error vs downstream link failure (medium)
4Device enumerated but driver not bound; dmesg: "BAR 0: no space" / "can't assign"Bridge window too small; firmware did not reserve MMIO for hot-plug; 64-bit window missing/proc/iomem, bridge "Memory behind bridge" linesFirmware "Above 4G decoding" setting implBoot with pci=realloc (test system) and compareResource-assignment failure (high)
5BDF of SSD changes between bootsHot-plug bus padding, firmware version change, different slot populationlspci -tv diffsFirmware settings diffsRepeat boot with identical population and settingsExpected behaviour; fix the automation, not the system (high)
💡 Senior insight

When a device is "missing", resist starting in the driver. Ask, in order: Did the link train? (Root Port Link Status / analyzer) → Did a config read reach the device? (trace or Root Port AER UR counts) → Did it answer with data, UR, or CRS? → Did resource assignment succeed? (dmesg) → Did a driver match? (lspci -k). Each question has cheap, decisive evidence. Debugging by layer is ten times faster than debugging by intuition.

🏭 Implementation-dependent

Exact firmware scan order (some scan all functions of all devices; some stop early), bus padding policy, the readiness timeout, whether firmware leaves the NVMe controller enabled when handing off to the OS, and whether the OS reassigns resources are all implementation-dependent. Linux's behaviour also varies with kernel version and command-line options.

17.18 Labs

🧪 Lab 17.1 — Read your machine's PCIe tree SAFE

Objective: map every Root Port, switch and NVMe endpoint on a real or virtual machine, and reconstruct each bridge's (pri, sec, sub).

Prerequisites: Linux with pciutils; root for full output.

Setup: any Linux machine or VM. In QEMU, you can create an emulated NVMe device with -drive file=nvm.img,if=none,id=nvm -device nvme,serial=lab17,drive=nvm, optionally behind -device pcie-root-port,id=rp1 with bus=rp1 on the NVMe device (Q35 machine type).

Procedure: (1) Run lspci -tv. (2) For each bridge, run sudo lspci -vvv -s <bdf> and record the "Bus: primary=, secondary=, subordinate=" line. (3) Draw the tree with bus numbers. (4) Locate every device with class "Non-Volatile memory controller".

Observations: every endpoint's bus number must fall inside exactly one chain of nested bridge ranges.

Questions: Which bridges have empty secondary buses? Are any ranges padded (sub > sec although nothing is below)?

Solution / expected reasoning

Each bridge's range [sec, sub] must contain the ranges of all bridges below it. Padding appears as sub > sec with nothing below — usually on hot-plug capable ports (look for "HotPlug+" in the slot capabilities of that port). Empty Root Ports still have a secondary bus. In QEMU with a single root port you should see the NVMe device at 01:00.0 or similar depending on how many ports precede it.

Extension: write a script that parses lspci -vvv and validates the nesting automatically.

🧪 Lab 17.2 — Simulate depth-first numbering SAFE

Objective: modify the simulation in 17.8.1 to add hot-plug padding of N buses to every Downstream Port that is marked hot-plug capable.

Procedure: add a flag to bridge nodes; after recursing, set sub = max(sub, secondary + N) and bump next_bus accordingly. Rerun and compare BDFs.

Questions: Which endpoints change BDF? Does the Root Port's range grow?

Solution

Padding a port shifts the bus numbers of everything enumerated after it, not before it. The enclosing bridges' Subordinate values grow to include the padding. In the sample topology, padding DSP 0 by 4 moves SSD #3 from bus 05 to bus 09 and the Root Port's range from 2–6 to 2–10.

Extension: model a hot-plug event: insert a switch below a padded port and verify it can be numbered without touching other ranges.

🧪 Lab 17.3 — Remove and rescan a non-boot NVMe device in a VM CAUTION

Objective: observe enumeration messages live.

Setup: a VM whose root disk is not the NVMe device under test.

Procedure: (1) sudo dmesg -w in one terminal. (2) echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/remove. (3) echo 1 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/rescan. (4) Compare the messages to the timeline in 17.6.

Observations: you should see the PCI core report the device, its BAR assignment and the NVMe driver binding again.

Solution / expected reasoning

Remove detaches the driver and deletes the PCI device object; rescan re-reads configuration space below every bridge. The re-found device normally keeps its BDF because bus numbers on the bridge are unchanged. If BAR assignment messages appear, compare addresses with the earlier /proc/iomem — they may differ.

Extension: repeat with the NVMe namespace mounted and observe what the block layer and file system report (do this only in a disposable VM).

🧪 Lab 17.4 — Senior forensic lab: the missing drives SAFE

Objective: given synthetic trace 17.C plus this lspci fact — "switch USP 02:00.0: Bus: primary=02, secondary=03, subordinate=03" — produce a root-cause statement with evidence and confidence.

Model answer

Root cause: the switch Upstream Port's Subordinate Bus Number was programmed to 03h before the scan below it completed, so Type 1 requests for buses 4 and 5 were not forwarded and returned UR. Evidence: CfgWr at offset 18h with sub=03h (trace row 2.0), first UR on target bus 4 (row 3.4), lspci range 03–03. Confidence: high for the mechanism; whether the bug is in firmware code or a switch configuration EEPROM override is unknown without firmware source. Fix verification: after correction, USP range should read 03–06.

17.19 Exercises

🎯 Exercise
  1. Compute the ECAM address of register 104h of function 05:00.3 with ECAM base C000_0000h.
  2. A Root Port has sec=08h, sub=0Ch. For a CfgRd1 to bus 0Bh, what does it do? For bus 08h? For bus 0Dh?
  3. Decode Requester ID 3A11h into bus, device and function.
Answers

(1) C000_0000h + (05h<<20) + (0<<15) + (3<<12) + 104h = C050_3104h. (2) Bus 0Bh: forward as Type 1. Bus 08h: convert to Type 0. Bus 0Dh: not claimed — not forwarded downstream. (3) 3A11h = 0011_1010_0001_0001b: bus 3Ah, device 00010b = 2, function 001b = 1 → 3A:02.1.

Quiz

  1. Why does a Root Port normally only forward Type 0 configuration requests for device 0?

    Answer

    Because a PCIe link is point-to-point: only one device sits on the secondary bus of a Root Port or Downstream Port, and it is device 0. (ARI changes the interpretation of the device/function bits.)

  2. What value does software typically see when reading a configuration register of a non-existent function?

    Answer

    All ones (FFFFh for a 16-bit read, FFFFFFFFh for 32-bit), because the request completes with Unsupported Request and the Root Complex returns all-ones to the CPU.

  3. Why is Subordinate written as FFh during the descent?

    Answer

    So that the bridge forwards Type 1 requests for any deeper bus that will be numbered during the recursion; the final value is written once the deepest bus number is known.

  4. What does a Vendor ID read of 0001h mean when CRS Software Visibility is enabled?

    Answer

    The device answered with Configuration Request Retry Status — present but not ready. Software should retry later.

  5. Which two Command register bits must the NVMe driver set before it can talk to the controller and before the controller can fetch commands?

    Answer

    Memory Space Enable (bit 1) for MMIO register access, and Bus Master Enable (bit 2) so the device may issue memory requests (DMA).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a BDF and who assigns each part?
    Model answer

    Bus (8 bits, assigned by software during enumeration), Device (5 bits, determined by topology — 0 on a PCIe link), Function (3 bits, fixed by the device design). Together they form the Routing ID used in configuration requests and as Requester ID in TLPs the device sends.

  2. Beginner Why does PCIe need enumeration at all?
    Model answer

    Because the hierarchy is not known at design time; devices are self-describing and software must discover them, assign bus numbers and addresses, and enable them.

  3. Intermediate Explain the forwarding decision a bridge makes for a Type 1 configuration request.
    Model answer

    If the target bus equals Secondary, convert to Type 0 and send downstream; if it is greater than Secondary and at most Subordinate, forward unchanged; otherwise do not claim it.

  4. Intermediate How many bus numbers does a 1×4 switch consume below its Root Port, with no padding and nothing plugged in?
    Model answer

    Six: the Root Port's secondary bus (on which the Upstream Port sits), the switch's internal virtual bus (on which the four Downstream Ports sit), and one secondary bus per Downstream Port (four). Empty Downstream Ports still consume their secondary bus number.

  5. Advanced Why might an NVMe SSD be missing only after cold boot?
    Model answer

    Device readiness after power-on is slower than after warm reset (firmware load from NAND/NOR, self-tests); if platform firmware scans before readiness and does not honour CRS long enough, the device is missed. Evidence: timing of first CfgRd, CRS completions, firmware logs.

  6. Senior Your automation identifies drives by BDF and breaks after a BIOS update. What do you change and why?
    Model answer

    Switch to stable identifiers (controller serial number, namespace NGUID/EUI-64/UUID, physical slot via Slot Capabilities/ACPI). BDFs depend on enumeration order and padding policy and are not stable across firmware versions or population changes.

🧠 Teach-back

To a child: "The computer walks through every hallway knocking on doors, writes a number on each hallway, and then tells every room where its mailbox is." To a junior engineer: explain BDF, Type 0/1, and why bus numbering is depth-first. To a senior engineer: explain how CRS, padding and OS reallocation create time- and configuration-dependent enumeration results, and how you would prove which one caused a missing device.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute an ECAM address and decode a Requester ID without notes.
  • I can number buses depth-first for any topology including switches and empty ports.
  • I can identify an enumeration scan, UR responses and CRS in a trace.
  • I can list the steps between link-up and NVMe driver probe and name the evidence for each.
  • I can explain why "missing device" debugging starts at the link and walks up.
  • I can name which statements come from the PCIe specification and which are firmware/OS policy.

17.20 Summary, further reading and next

Enumeration is a depth-first walk that assigns bus numbers to bridges and discovers functions using non-posted configuration reads. BDF = software-assigned bus + topology-determined device + design-determined function. Bridges route Type 1 requests by Secondary/Subordinate ranges. Readiness (CRS) and resource assignment are the two most common sources of "device missing" problems after the link itself. The NVMe driver can only begin once Memory Space and Bus Master are enabled and BAR0 is mapped.

Further reading: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG) chapters on configuration space and the configuration transaction model; Linux kernel documentation Documentation/PCI/ (especially the PCI driver guide) and source drivers/pci/probe.c; ACPI specification (MCFG table, _CRS). Next: Chapter 18 — Configuration Space, where we decode each register the scan just read.

18 Configuration Space

← 17 PCIe Enumeration19 BARs and MMIO →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG); PCI Code and ID Assignment Specification (class codes, capability IDs); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (how an NVMe controller presents itself as a PCIe function). REVISION: header layouts are stable since PCI 2.x/PCIe 1.0; extended capabilities keep being added (e.g. physical-layer capabilities for 16/32/64 GT/s, Data Object Exchange, Integrity and Data Encryption) version. STATUS: current baseline for NVMe: NVMe over PCIe Transport Revision 1.4 within the NVMe 2.4 family (confirm on nvmexpress.org). OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: before NVMe 2.0, PCIe register requirements lived inside the single NVMe specification; since 2.0 they moved to the PCIe Transport specification. SOURCE: PCI-SIG specifications; nvmexpress.org; Linux include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h (openly readable register definitions).

18.1 Why this chapter exists

Configuration space is the device's identity card, control panel and feature catalogue in one 4 KiB structure. Every question you ask about a PCIe NVMe SSD — "what is it?", "is it allowed to DMA?", "what link speed did it negotiate?", "which interrupt vectors does it have?", "did it log an error?" — is answered by a field in configuration space. The master curriculum asks for something specific here: give hex dumps and teach the learner to decode them manually. By the end of this chapter you will decode a 256-byte dump by hand, walk a capability list, and cross-check your decoding against lspci -vvv.

18.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: name the fields of the common header (Vendor ID, Device ID, Command, Status, Revision ID, Class Code, Header Type) and say what each one is for.
  • Intermediate: decode a Type 0 and a Type 1 header from a raw little-endian hex dump.
  • Advanced: walk both the standard capability list (from offset 34h) and the extended capability list (from offset 100h), decoding PCI Express, MSI-X, Power Management and AER structures.
  • Senior: predict the consequences of wrong Command/Device Control settings (MPS/MRRS mismatch, Bus Master off, INTx disable with MSI-X off) and design validation checks for them.
  • Trace analysis: interpret CfgRd/CfgWr TLPs by register offset and byte enables.
  • Debugging: use Status and AER registers as first-line evidence for link and transaction errors.
  • Validation: verify that a device's configuration space conforms to required fields for an NVMe controller (class code, BAR0 type, MSI-X presence).

18.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 17 (BDF, ECAM, Type 0/1 configuration requests). Little-endian byte order: in a dump, the byte at the lowest address is the least significant byte of a multi-byte field. Hexadecimal and bit numbering (bit 0 = least significant).

18.4 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Every device carries a passport. The first page always looks the same for everyone: country (Vendor ID), name (Device ID), what kind of traveller it is (Class Code: "I am a storage device that speaks NVMe"), and a few switches the border guard can flip ("you may enter the country" = Memory Space Enable, "you may drive your own truck" = Bus Master Enable). After the first page come optional stamp pages — each stamp says "I can do power saving", "I can send interrupts as messages", "I keep an error diary". Each stamp says where the next stamp is, so you read them as a chain.

🌍 Real-world analogy

A server's BMC sensor table: a fixed header with identity fields, followed by a linked list of optional records whose type you check before interpreting the content. You never assume record 3 is "temperature" — you check its type ID.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A passport is read-only. Configuration space is not: many fields are writable control bits, some are "write 1 to clear" status bits, and some (BARs) behave strangely when written (they ignore address bits below their size). Also, the order of stamps (capabilities) is chosen by the device designer — two devices with identical features can list them in different orders and at different offsets.

18.5 Beginner view: the map of the 4 KiB

Offset rangeNameReachable throughContents
000h–03FhHeader (64 bytes)Legacy CF8h/CFCh and ECAMType 0 (endpoint) or Type 1 (bridge) layout
040h–0FFhPCI-compatible capability areaLegacy and ECAMLinked list of standard capabilities starting at the Capabilities Pointer (34h); device-specific registers
100h–FFFhPCIe Extended Configuration SpaceECAM onlyLinked list of extended capabilities always starting at 100h (AER, SR-IOV, ATS, LTR, L1 PM Substates, physical-layer capabilities, …)

All of this is configuration space: a separate address space reached by configuration TLPs. It is not the same as the NVMe controller registers (CAP, CC, CSTS…), which live in memory space behind BAR0 and are reached by Memory Read/Write TLPs — the subject of Chapter 19 and Chapter 24. Confusing the two is the single most common beginner mistake in this Part. verified

Here is the whole 4 KiB of configuration space on one page. On the left is the fixed 64-byte Type 0 header. The Capabilities Pointer at 34h starts a linked list of standard capabilities in 40h–FFh. A second linked list, the extended capabilities, always starts at 100h. Follow the arrows drawn in the pointer colour (see the legend): each one is a pointer to the next structure. Header and standard-capability values come from the synthetic dump in §18.9. synthetic

Type 0 header (fixed layout)Standard capability list (40h–FFh)Extended capability list (100h–FFFh)Pointer (Capabilities Pointer / Next)

FieldOffset/widthOwner (who writes)PurposeNVMe relevance

18.6.1 The Command register (04h)

BitNameMeaning in PCIeTypical NVMe value
0I/O Space EnableDecode I/O BARs0 (NVMe uses memory space; an optional I/O BAR is legacy/vendor-specific)
1Memory Space Enable (MSE)Respond to memory requests targeting the function's memory BARs1
2Bus Master Enable (BME)Allow the function to issue memory and I/O requests (DMA, MSI/MSI-X writes)1
3Special Cycle EnableNot applicable to PCIe (hardwired 0)0
4Memory Write and InvalidateNot applicable to PCIe0
5VGA Palette SnoopNot applicable to PCIe0
6Parity Error ResponseControls logging of Master Data Parity Error (poisoned TLP)Software choice
7Reserved (was IDSEL stepping)—0
8SERR# EnableAllows reporting of fatal/non-fatal errors as system errorsSoftware choice
9Fast Back-to-BackNot applicable to PCIe0
10Interrupt Disable1 = function must not assert INTx1 when MSI-X is in use
15:11Reserved—0
⚠️ Why BME matters for safety

Bus Master Enable is the gate that allows the device to originate DMA. Until BME = 1, an NVMe controller cannot fetch submission queue entries, read write-data, write read-data, post completion entries, or send MSI-X interrupt messages (which are memory writes). Clearing BME on a running controller stops all of that abruptly — Linux clears it on shutdown and in some error paths precisely to stop DMA. verified

18.6.2 The Status register (06h)

BitNameAccessMeaning
2:0Reserved—
3Interrupt StatusROINTx would be/is asserted (independent of Interrupt Disable)
4Capabilities ListRO1 = Capabilities Pointer at 34h is valid (always 1 for PCIe functions)
566 MHz CapableROConventional PCI only; 0
7Fast Back-to-Back CapableROConventional PCI only; 0
8Master Data Parity ErrorRW1CPoisoned TLP received as completion or sent as request, with Parity Error Response set
10:9DEVSEL TimingROConventional PCI only; 0
11Signaled Target AbortRW1CFunction completed a request with Completer Abort
12Received Target AbortRW1CFunction received a Completer Abort completion
13Received Master AbortRW1CFunction received an Unsupported Request completion
14Signaled System ErrorRW1CFunction sent ERR_FATAL/ERR_NONFATAL with SERR# Enable set
15Detected Parity ErrorRW1CFunction received a poisoned TLP (regardless of Parity Error Response)

RW1C means "read; write 1 to clear". Writing the value you just read back to Status clears every set error bit — a common debugging technique, but also a common way to destroy evidence before you recorded it. Record first, clear second.

18.6.3 Class Code: how the NVMe driver finds the device

The 24-bit Class Code is three bytes: Base Class at 0Bh, Sub-Class at 0Ah, Programming Interface at 09h verified. For an NVMe I/O controller on PCIe:

Byte 0Bh — Base ClassByte 0Ah — Sub-ClassByte 09h — Prog-IF
01h — Mass storage controller08h — Non-Volatile Memory controller02h — NVM Express

Linux's NVMe PCI driver includes a class match for PCI_CLASS_STORAGE_EXPRESS (= 010802h), so any compliant NVMe device binds to it even if its Vendor/Device IDs are unknown to the driver verified. Prog-IF 01h under the same sub-class corresponds to the older NVMHCI interface. Other Prog-IF values may be defined in newer PCI Code and ID Assignment revisions for other NVMe controller types — check that document rather than assuming version.

18.7 The Type 1 header (bridges: Root Ports, switch ports)

OffsetByte 3Byte 2Byte 1Byte 0
00h–0ChSame as Type 0 (Vendor/Device ID, Command/Status, Class/Revision, BIST/Header Type/Latency/Cache Line); Header Type = 01h
10hBAR0
14hBAR1
18hSecondary Latency TimerSubordinate Bus NumberSecondary Bus NumberPrimary Bus Number
1ChSecondary StatusI/O LimitI/O Base
20hMemory LimitMemory Base
24hPrefetchable Memory LimitPrefetchable Memory Base
28hPrefetchable Base Upper 32 Bits
2ChPrefetchable Limit Upper 32 Bits
30hI/O Limit Upper 16 BitsI/O Base Upper 16 Bits
34hReservedCapabilities Pointer
38hExpansion ROM Base Address
3ChBridge ControlInterrupt PinInterrupt Line
  • Memory Base/Limit (20h/22h): a 1 MiB-granular, 32-bit, non-prefetchable window. Bits 15:4 of each 16-bit register hold address bits 31:20. Memory requests whose address falls inside [Base, Limit+FFFFFh] are forwarded downstream. verified
  • Prefetchable Base/Limit (24h/26h plus upper 32 bits at 28h/2Ch): the 64-bit capable window where 64-bit prefetchable BARs of children are placed.
  • Bridge Control (3Eh): includes Secondary Bus Reset (bit 6) — writing it resets everything below the bridge (a "hot reset" of the link). Never toggle on a production system.
💡 Senior insight: NVMe BAR0 lives in the non-prefetchable window

Because NVMe register BARs are normally non-prefetchable (reads have side effects — e.g. reading a register must return current state, not a cached guess) and the classic non-prefetchable bridge window is only 32 bits wide, NVMe BAR0 is usually placed below 4 GiB even when it is a 64-bit BAR. A host with dozens of NVMe drives and small 32-bit MMIO space can run out of non-prefetchable window space. Firmware "Above 4G decoding" settings and newer approaches change what is possible impl. When dmesg says a BAR cannot be assigned, look at the bridge windows before blaming the device.

18.8 Capability lists

Both lists are singly linked. A standard capability starts with an 8-bit Capability ID and an 8-bit Next Pointer (00h ends the list). An extended capability starts with a 32-bit header: bits 15:0 Extended Capability ID, bits 19:16 Capability Version, bits 31:20 Next Capability Offset (000h ends the list). The extended list always starts at 100h; if 100h reads 0, there are no extended capabilities (and FFFFFFFFh there means the extended space is not accessible, e.g. no ECAM) verified.

Standard Cap IDNameWhy an NVMe engineer cares
01hPower ManagementD-state (D0/D3hot) of the PCIe function; distinct from NVMe power states (Chapter 24 and later power chapters)
05hMSIMessage Signalled Interrupts; up to 32 vectors; NVMe permits but prefers MSI-X
10hPCI ExpressDevice/Link capabilities, control and status: MPS, MRRS, link speed/width, FLR, error enables
11hMSI-XPer-queue interrupt vectors; the table lives in a BAR
09hVendor SpecificVendor-defined; content not standardized
Extended Cap IDNameWhy an NVMe engineer cares
0001hAdvanced Error Reporting (AER)Detailed correctable/uncorrectable error status, masks, severities, TLP header log
0003hDevice Serial Number64-bit PCIe-level serial (not the NVMe controller serial number in Identify)
000EhARIRouting for many functions (SR-IOV)
000FhATS (Address Translation Services)Device-side caching of IOMMU translations (Chapter 20)
0010hSR-IOVVirtual Functions — each VF can be an NVMe controller assigned to a VM
0018hLatency Tolerance Reporting (LTR)Platform power management latency hints
0019hSecondary PCI ExpressLane equalization control/status for 8 GT/s and above
001EhL1 PM SubstatesL1.1/L1.2 low-power link states — frequent source of client SSD link issues

Additional extended capabilities exist (e.g. physical-layer capabilities per speed, Lane Margining at the Receiver, Data Link Feature, Data Object Exchange) and the set grows with PCIe revisions version. A decoder must skip unknown IDs safely using the Next pointer rather than giving up.

18.8.1 PCI Express Capability (ID 10h) — the fields you will read weekly

Cap offsetRegisterKey fields (bits)
+00hCap ID / Next / PCI Express CapabilitiesCapability Version (3:0 of the 16-bit register at +02h); Device/Port Type (7:4): 0000b Endpoint, 0001b Legacy Endpoint, 0100b Root Port, 0101b Switch Upstream, 0110b Switch Downstream, 1001b Root Complex Integrated Endpoint; Slot Implemented (8); Interrupt Message Number (13:9)
+04hDevice CapabilitiesMax_Payload_Size Supported (2:0, 128 B << n); Extended Tag Field Supported (5); Role-Based Error Reporting (15); Function Level Reset Capability (28)
+08hDevice ControlCorrectable/Non-Fatal/Fatal/UR Reporting Enable (0–3); Enable Relaxed Ordering (4); Max_Payload_Size (7:5); Extended Tag Enable (8); Enable No Snoop (11); Max_Read_Request_Size (14:12); Initiate FLR (15, endpoints)
+0AhDevice StatusCorrectable/Non-Fatal/Fatal/Unsupported Request Detected (0–3, RW1C); Transactions Pending (5)
+0ChLink CapabilitiesMax Link Speed (3:0, index into Supported Link Speeds); Maximum Link Width (9:4); ASPM Support (11:10); Port Number (31:24)
+10hLink ControlASPM Control (1:0); Retrain Link (5, downstream ports); Common Clock Configuration (6)
+12hLink StatusCurrent Link Speed (3:0); Negotiated Link Width (9:4); Link Training (11); Slot Clock Configuration (12); Data Link Layer Link Active (13, if reporting capable)
+14h…+20hSlot / Root registersPresent only for ports with slots / Root Ports (hot-plug, presence detect, CRS Software Visibility)
+24h…+32hDevice Capabilities 2 / Control 2 / Link Capabilities 2 / Control 2 / Status 2Completion Timeout ranges and value; 10-bit tag support; Supported Link Speeds Vector; Target Link Speed (Link Control 2 bits 3:0); equalization status
MPS_bytes = 128 × 2Max_Payload_Size ; MRRS_bytes = 128 × 2Max_Read_Request_Size
  • Max_Payload_Size — 3-bit encoded field (000b=128 B … 101b=4096 B), Device Control bits 7:5. Limits data payload per TLP the function sends (and expects to receive). Must be set no larger than the smallest MPS supported along the path.
  • Max_Read_Request_Size — 3-bit field, Device Control bits 14:12, limits how many bytes one Memory Read Request from this function may ask for. Affects how an NVMe controller splits its DMA reads of write-data.

Link speed encoding in Current Link Speed / Max Link Speed: the value is an index into the Supported Link Speeds Vector in Link Capabilities 2; in practice 1 = 2.5 GT/s, 2 = 5.0, 3 = 8.0, 4 = 16.0, 5 = 32.0, 6 = 64.0 GT/s verified.

18.8.2 MSI-X Capability (ID 11h)

Cap offsetBits 31:16Bits 15:8Bits 7:0
+00hMessage Control: MSI-X Enable (15), Function Mask (14), Table Size (10:0, N−1)Next PointerCap ID = 11h
+04hTable Offset (31:3) | Table BIR (2:0) — which BAR holds the table and where
+08hPBA Offset (31:3) | PBA BIR (2:0) — Pending Bit Array location

Each MSI-X table entry is 16 bytes in memory space: Message Address (low 32), Message Upper Address, Message Data, Vector Control (bit 0 = Mask) verified. An interrupt is literally a posted Memory Write TLP, sent by the device to the address with the data from the entry. For NVMe this means each completion queue can be bound to its own vector (the Interrupt Vector field of Create I/O Completion Queue), and per-CPU queues can interrupt per-CPU vectors. The table is placed in a BAR — often BAR0 above the NVMe register and doorbell area, or a separate BAR impl.

18.8.3 Power Management Capability (ID 01h)

PMC (+02h) advertises supported D-states and PME support; PMCSR (+04h) holds PowerState (bits 1:0: 00b D0, 01b D1, 10b D2, 11b D3hot) and No_Soft_Reset (bit 3: if 1, D3hot→D0 does not reset the function's state) verified. These are PCI function power states, not NVMe power states (which are set with the Power Management feature via Set Features). Both exist, stack, and are frequently confused.

18.8.4 Advanced Error Reporting (extended ID 0001h)

AER offsetRegisterNotes
+00hExtended capability headerID 0001h, version, next offset
+04hUncorrectable Error Status (RW1C)bit 4 Data Link Protocol Error, 5 Surprise Down, 12 Poisoned TLP Received, 13 Flow Control Protocol Error, 14 Completion Timeout, 15 Completer Abort, 16 Unexpected Completion, 17 Receiver Overflow, 18 Malformed TLP, 19 ECRC Error, 20 Unsupported Request, 21 ACS Violation (and more in newer revisions)
+08hUncorrectable Error Mask1 = do not report
+0ChUncorrectable Error Severity1 = fatal, 0 = non-fatal
+10hCorrectable Error Status (RW1C)bit 0 Receiver Error, 6 Bad TLP, 7 Bad DLLP, 8 REPLAY_NUM Rollover, 12 Replay Timer Timeout, 13 Advisory Non-Fatal, 14 Corrected Internal Error, 15 Header Log Overflow
+14hCorrectable Error Mask
+18hAdvanced Error Capabilities and ControlFirst Error Pointer (4:0) — bit index of the first uncorrectable error; ECRC generation/check capable/enable
+1Ch–+28hHeader Log (4 DWs)Header of the TLP that caused the first logged uncorrectable error — gold for debugging
+2Ch…Root Error Command/Status, Error Source IDRoot Ports / Root Complex Event Collectors only

When a Completion Timeout is logged, the Header Log captures the header of the request that timed out (when supported) — from it you can recover the address, length and tag of the read that never completed. Linux prints AER events in dmesg via the AER driver with the decoded bit names and the header log. verified The details of when headers are logged for each error type are in the PCIe specification — check before relying on it.

18.8.5 SR-IOV (extended ID 0010h) in one paragraph

Single Root I/O Virtualization lets one Physical Function (PF) expose many Virtual Functions (VFs), each a lightweight PCIe function with its own BDF (via ARI and the First VF Offset / VF Stride fields), its own BARs (described collectively by VF BAR registers in the SR-IOV capability) and its own MSI-X. For NVMe, each VF is typically an NVMe controller that a hypervisor assigns to a VM; the NVMe specification's virtualization enhancements govern how controller resources (queues, interrupts) are shared between primary and secondary controllers version. Key fields: Total VFs, Num VFs, VF Enable, First VF Offset, VF Stride, VF Device ID.

18.9 Hex dump: decode it by hand

Below is a synthetic 256-byte-style dump of an NVMe function at 01:00.0, plus the first line of extended space. The Vendor/Device ID pair 1B36h:0010h is the ID used by QEMU's emulated NVMe controller, chosen so you can reproduce a similar device in Lab 18.2; every other value is invented for teaching and is not a capture of QEMU or any product. The format is the generic "offset: 16 bytes" layout used by many tools.

00: 36 1b 10 00 06 04 10 00 02 02 08 01 00 00 00 00
10: 04 00 a0 fe 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
20: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 f4 1a 00 11
30: 00 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0b 01 00 00
40: 01 50 03 00 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
50: 11 60 3f 80 00 20 00 00 00 30 00 00 00 00 00 00
60: 10 00 02 00 02 80 00 10 3f 28 00 00 44 0c 00 00
70: 40 00 44 10 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
100: 01 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

18.9.1 Manual decode, line by line

  1. 00h: bytes 36 1b → Vendor ID 1B36h (little-endian: low byte first). 10 00 → Device ID 0010h.
  2. 04h: 06 04 → Command 0406h = 0000_0100_0000_0110b: bit 1 MSE=1, bit 2 BME=1, bit 10 Interrupt Disable=1. 10 00 → Status 0010h: bit 4 Capabilities List=1, no error bits.
  3. 08h: 02 Revision 02h; 02 08 01 → Prog-IF 02h, Sub-Class 08h, Base Class 01h → Class Code 010802h = NVM Express.
  4. 0Ch: Header Type at 0Eh = 00h → Type 0, single-function.
  5. 10h: 04 00 a0 fe → BAR0 = FEA00004h. Bit 0 = 0 (memory), bits 2:1 = 10b (64-bit), bit 3 = 0 (non-prefetchable). Because it is 64-bit, BAR1 (14h) = 00000000h is the upper half. Address = 00000000_FEA00000h. The size is not visible here — sizing (Chapter 19) is required.
  6. 2Ch: Subsystem Vendor ID 1AF4h, Subsystem ID 1100h.
  7. 34h: Capabilities Pointer = 40h.
  8. 3Ch: Interrupt Line 0Bh (software scratch value), Interrupt Pin 01h = INTA#.
  9. 40h: 01 50 → Cap ID 01h (Power Management), next 50h. PMC = 0003h (version 3). PMCSR at 44h = 0008h: PowerState 00b = D0, No_Soft_Reset = 1.
  10. 50h: 11 60 → Cap ID 11h (MSI-X), next 60h. Message Control = 803Fh: bit 15 Enable = 1, bit 14 Function Mask = 0, Table Size = 3Fh → 64 vectors. Table = 00002000h → BIR 0, offset 2000h. PBA = 00003000h → BIR 0, offset 3000h.
  11. 60h: 10 00 → Cap ID 10h (PCI Express), next 00h (end of list). PCIe Capabilities register 0002h → version 2, Device/Port Type 0000b = PCI Express Endpoint.
  12. 64h: Device Capabilities 10008002h: MPS supported = 010b → 512 B; bit 15 Role-Based Error Reporting = 1; bit 28 FLR capable = 1.
  13. 68h: Device Control 283Fh = 0010_1000_0011_1111b: bits 3:0 = 1111b (all error reporting enabled), bit 4 Relaxed Ordering = 1, bits 7:5 = 001b → MPS 256 B, bit 11 No Snoop = 1, bits 14:12 = 010b → MRRS 512 B. Device Status at 6Ah = 0000h: no errors detected.
  14. 6Ch: Link Capabilities 00000C44h: bits 3:0 = 4 → max 16.0 GT/s, bits 9:4 = 04h → x4, bits 11:10 = 11b → L0s and L1 ASPM supported.
  15. 70h: Link Control 0040h: Common Clock Configuration = 1, ASPM Control = 00b (disabled). Link Status 1044h: Current Link Speed 4 (16.0 GT/s), Negotiated Width 4 (x4), bit 12 Slot Clock Configuration = 1, Link Training = 0.
  16. 100h: 01 00 02 00 → 00020001h: Extended Cap ID 0001h (AER), version 2, next 000h (end).

Now confirm with the executable decoder (it parses only the text above):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Decode a SYNTHETIC PCIe Type 0 configuration-space dump and walk its capability lists.
Pure parsing: it reads only the text below, never real hardware."""
import struct

DUMP = """
00: 36 1b 10 00 06 04 10 00 02 02 08 01 00 00 00 00
10: 04 00 a0 fe 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
20: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 f4 1a 00 11
30: 00 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0b 01 00 00
40: 01 50 03 00 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
50: 11 60 3f 80 00 20 00 00 00 30 00 00 00 00 00 00
60: 10 00 02 00 02 80 00 10 3f 28 00 00 44 0c 00 00
70: 40 00 44 10 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
100: 01 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
"""

cfg = bytearray(4096)
for line in DUMP.strip().splitlines():
    off, data = line.split(":")
    for i, byte in enumerate(data.split()):
        cfg[int(off, 16) + i] = int(byte, 16)

u8 = lambda o: cfg[o]
u16 = lambda o: struct.unpack_from("<H", cfg, o)[0]
u32 = lambda o: struct.unpack_from("<I", cfg, o)[0]
bit = lambda v, n: (v >> n) & 1
field = lambda v, hi, lo: (v >> lo) & ((1 << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1)

print(f"Vendor ID {u16(0x00):04x}h  Device ID {u16(0x02):04x}h")
cmd, sts = u16(0x04), u16(0x06)
print(f"Command {cmd:04x}h: IO={bit(cmd,0)} MEM={bit(cmd,1)} BusMaster={bit(cmd,2)} "
      f"SERR={bit(cmd,8)} INTxDisable={bit(cmd,10)}")
print(f"Status  {sts:04x}h: CapList={bit(sts,4)} RxMasterAbort={bit(sts,13)} DetParity={bit(sts,15)}")
cc = (u8(0x0B) << 16) | (u8(0x0A) << 8) | u8(0x09)
print(f"Revision {u8(0x08):02x}h  Class Code {cc:06x}h"
      + ("  -> mass storage / NVM / NVM Express" if cc == 0x010802 else ""))
ht = u8(0x0E)
print(f"Header Type {ht:02x}h: layout={ht & 0x7f} multifunction={bit(ht,7)}")

# BARs (Type 0 has six dword BAR slots at 10h..24h)
i = 0
while i < 6:
    off = 0x10 + 4 * i
    v = u32(off)
    if v == 0:
        i += 1
        continue
    if v & 1:
        print(f"BAR{i}: I/O at {v & ~0x3:#x}")
        i += 1
        continue
    kind, pref = field(v, 2, 1), bit(v, 3)
    if kind == 0b10:   # 64-bit: next BAR slot holds the upper dword
        addr = ((u32(off + 4) << 32) | (v & ~0xF)) & 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF
        print(f"BAR{i}/{i+1}: 64-bit memory at {addr:#x} prefetchable={pref}")
        i += 2
    else:
        print(f"BAR{i}: 32-bit memory at {v & ~0xF:#x} prefetchable={pref}")
        i += 1

print(f"Subsystem {u16(0x2C):04x}:{u16(0x2E):04x}  INTx pin {u8(0x3D)}  line {u8(0x3C)}")

NAMES = {0x01: "Power Management", 0x05: "MSI", 0x10: "PCI Express", 0x11: "MSI-X", 0x09: "Vendor Specific"}
ptr, seen = u8(0x34) & 0xFC, set()
print(f"Capabilities Pointer {u8(0x34):02x}h")
while ptr and ptr not in seen:          # 'seen' guards against a looping (corrupt) list
    seen.add(ptr)
    cid, nxt = u8(ptr), u8(ptr + 1) & 0xFC
    print(f"  [{ptr:02x}h] ID {cid:02x}h {NAMES.get(cid, 'unknown')} -> next {nxt:02x}h")
    if cid == 0x01:
        pmcsr = u16(ptr + 4)
        print(f"        PMCSR {pmcsr:04x}h PowerState=D{pmcsr & 3} NoSoftReset={bit(pmcsr,3)}")
    elif cid == 0x11:
        mc, tbl, pba = u16(ptr + 2), u32(ptr + 4), u32(ptr + 8)
        print(f"        MsgCtl {mc:04x}h Enable={bit(mc,15)} FuncMask={bit(mc,14)} "
              f"TableSize={field(mc,10,0) + 1} vectors")
        print(f"        Table BIR {tbl & 7} offset {tbl & ~7:#x}; PBA BIR {pba & 7} offset {pba & ~7:#x}")
    elif cid == 0x10:
        pcap = u16(ptr + 2)
        ptypes = {0: "PCIe Endpoint", 1: "Legacy Endpoint", 4: "Root Port",
                  5: "Switch Upstream Port", 6: "Switch Downstream Port", 9: "RCiEP"}
        print(f"        PCIe Cap version {field(pcap,3,0)} type {ptypes.get(field(pcap,7,4), '?')}")
        devcap, devctl = u32(ptr + 4), u16(ptr + 8)
        print(f"        DevCap MPS supported {128 << field(devcap,2,0)} B  FLR capable {bit(devcap,28)}")
        print(f"        DevCtl MPS {128 << field(devctl,7,5)} B  MRRS {128 << field(devctl,14,12)} B "
              f"RelaxedOrd {bit(devctl,4)} NoSnoop {bit(devctl,11)}")
        lcap, lsts = u32(ptr + 0x0C), u16(ptr + 0x12)
        speeds = {1: "2.5", 2: "5.0", 3: "8.0", 4: "16.0", 5: "32.0", 6: "64.0"}
        print(f"        LinkCap max {speeds.get(field(lcap,3,0))} GT/s x{field(lcap,9,4)}; "
              f"LinkSta now {speeds.get(field(lsts,3,0))} GT/s x{field(lsts,9,4)}")
    ptr = nxt

EXT = {0x0001: "Advanced Error Reporting", 0x0003: "Device Serial Number", 0x000E: "ARI",
       0x000F: "ATS", 0x0010: "SR-IOV", 0x0018: "LTR", 0x0019: "Secondary PCIe", 0x001E: "L1 PM Substates"}
off = 0x100
print("Extended capabilities (from 100h):")
while off:
    hdr = u32(off)
    if hdr in (0, 0xFFFFFFFF):
        break
    cid, ver, nxt = hdr & 0xFFFF, field(hdr, 19, 16), field(hdr, 31, 20) & 0xFFC
    print(f"  [{off:03x}h] ID {cid:04x}h {EXT.get(cid, 'unknown')} v{ver} -> next {nxt:03x}h")
    off = nxt

🐞 Debugging connection

From this one dump you can already answer several triage questions: the link is at full capability (16 GT/s x4 = max), so a performance problem is not a down-trained link; MSI-X is enabled with 64 vectors, so interrupt starvation is not caused by INTx fallback; MPS 256 B is below the 512 B supported — normal, because MPS must match the smallest along the path (check the Root Port); Device Status shows no detected errors at this moment; AER exists, so detailed error status is available at 104h/110h.

18.10 Procedure: reading any register correctly

The master curriculum's register-reading discipline applies to configuration registers as much as to NVMe registers:

  1. Locate the register (which capability, which offset — found by walking the list, never by hard-coding offsets that vary by device).
  2. Identify the width (8/16/32 bits) and read with a matching access size where side effects could matter.
  3. Identify the reset value (from the specification) to know what "untouched" looks like.
  4. Decode the fields with the bit ranges from the specification.
  5. Classify access (RO, RW, RW1C, RsvdP, RsvdZ, HwInit, ROS/RWS sticky) only when verified in the specification.
  6. Identify side effects (e.g. writing Initiate FLR resets the function; writing 1s to RW1C clears evidence).
  7. Identify sequencing rules (e.g. MSE off during BAR sizing; MSI-X table programmed before Enable).
  8. Identify related registers (Device Status ↔ AER status; Link Status ↔ Link Control 2 target speed).
  9. Identify the software owner (firmware? PCI core? driver?) to know who might change it behind your back.
  10. Identify hardware behaviour (what the device does when the field changes).
  11. Identify trace implications (which TLPs appear when this register is accessed or changes behaviour).
📘 Reserved fields

"RsvdP" (reserved and preserved) bits must be written back with the value read; "RsvdZ" bits must be written as zero. Software doing read-modify-write must respect these. Never assign meaning to reserved bits even if a particular device returns non-zero there.

18.11 Capability discovery: the universal rule

Before using any optional feature, determine whether the device reports support. This principle recurs throughout PCIe and NVMe:

FeatureWhere support is reportedWrong assumption → consequence
MSI-XPresence of Cap ID 11h; Table SizeProgramming vectors that don't exist → lost interrupts
FLRDevice Capabilities bit 28Writing Initiate FLR on a non-FLR device does nothing; recovery code hangs waiting
AERExtended Cap ID 0001hReading at a hard-coded offset returns unrelated data
10-bit tagsDevice Capabilities 2 (completer/requester support)Enabling requester tags the completer cannot handle → malformed/unexpected completions version
NVMe CMB, boot partitions, subsystem resetNVMe CAP.CMBS, CAP.BPS, CAP.NSSRS (Chapter 24)Writing NSSR on a controller that does not support it — no reset happens
NVMe optional commands/featuresIdentify Controller fields (OACS, ONCS, etc.)Sending an unsupported command → Invalid Command Opcode status

18.12 Protocol view: what configuration TLPs carry

A configuration request header carries the Requester ID, a Tag, the target Bus/Device/Function, the Extended Register Number (4 bits) and Register Number (6 bits) forming a 10-bit DWORD index (so offset = index × 4), and First DW Byte Enables selecting which bytes of the DWORD are accessed. Length is always 1 DW verified. A 16-bit read of the Command register at 04h is therefore a 1-DW CfgRd to register index 1 with byte enables 0011b; a read of Status (06h) uses byte enables 1100b.

18.13 Linux view and an illustrative lspci -vvv reading guide

sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -xxx        # 256-byte hex dump (root needed beyond 64 bytes)
sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -xxxx       # full 4 KiB extended space
sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -vvv        # decoded
sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -vvv -nn    # also numeric [vendor:device] and [class]
setpci -s 01:00.0 COMMAND         # read-only use: prints the Command register
setpci -s 01:00.0 CAP_EXP+12.w    # read Link Status via capability-relative name
sudo hexdump -C /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/config | head
⚠️ setpci writes

setpci with =value writes configuration space directly, bypassing the kernel's view. Writing the Command register can disable a live NVMe device (the root file system disappears); writing Bridge Control can reset everything below a port; writing Device Control can create MPS mismatches that cause fatal errors. Treat any setpci … = as an EXPERT LAB action on disposable hardware.

18.14 Code: reading configuration space safely from sysfs

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# READ-ONLY: reads /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/config. Root is needed to see past 64 bytes.
# Never open this file for writing on a live system.
import struct, sys
bdf = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "0000:01:00.0"
with open(f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/config", "rb") as f:
    cfg = f.read()
vid, did = struct.unpack_from("<HH", cfg, 0)
cls = cfg[0x0B] << 16 | cfg[0x0A] << 8 | cfg[0x09]
print(f"{bdf}: {vid:04x}:{did:04x} class {cls:06x} config bytes visible: {len(cfg)}")
if cls == 0x010802:
    print("This function is an NVM Express controller")

18.15 Worked example: decoding a Type 1 header fragment

Synthetic bytes at offsets 18h–2Fh of Root Port 00:02.0:

18: 00 02 06 00 f0 00 00 00 a0 fe b0 fe f1 ff 01 00
28: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
  • 18h = 00, 19h = 02, 1Ah = 06 → Primary 0, Secondary 2, Subordinate 6.
  • 1Ch = F0h, 1Dh = 00h → I/O Base > I/O Limit → I/O window disabled.
  • 20h = FEA0h → Memory Base bits 15:4 = FEAh → base FEA0_0000h; 22h = FEB0h → limit FEB0_0000h + F_FFFFh = FEBF_FFFFh. Non-prefetchable window FEA0_0000h–FEBF_FFFFh (2 MiB).
  • 24h = FFF1h, 26h = 0001h → Prefetchable Base (FFFh<<20) > Limit (000h<<20) → prefetchable window disabled. The low nibble 1h of both means "64-bit capable window".

Consequence: all downstream NVMe BAR0s must fit inside FEA0_0000h–FEBF_FFFFh. The SSD in 18.9 with BAR0 at FEA0_0000h, 16 KiB, fits. derived

18.16 Common mistakes

  • Looking for CC or CSTS in configuration space. They are in BAR0 memory space.
  • Hard-coding the offset of the PCI Express capability (e.g. "it's always at 70h"). Walk the list.
  • Reading a 64-bit BAR as two independent 32-bit BARs.
  • Forgetting little-endian order when reading a dump by eye.
  • Clearing RW1C status bits before recording them.
  • Confusing PCI D-states (PMCSR) with NVMe power states (Set Features), or PCIe Device Serial Number with the NVMe serial number.
  • Assuming Revision ID is the NVMe version (it is not; VS in BAR0 is).
