18.18 Zero-hallucination ledger

CategoryItems
verifiedHeader layouts; Command/Status bit meanings; class code 010802h; capability header formats; MSI-X structure; PMCSR PowerState; AER register order and listed bit positions; link speed encodings.
derivedThe manual decode results; bridge window consequences in 18.15; triage conclusions from the dump.
implCapability order and offsets; MSI-X table location; presence of optional capabilities; option ROM contents.
versionNew extended capabilities and new AER bits in later PCIe revisions; Prog-IF values for other NVMe controller types; NVMe virtualization details.
Check in the specExact access types (RO/RWS/RW1CS sticky variants) for each field you rely on; header logging rules per error type.
Never assumeFixed capability offsets; that a cleared Status means no past error; that lspci output formats are stable across versions.

18.19 Labs

🧪 Lab 18.1 — Decode a dump by hand, then verify SAFE

Objective: decode your own NVMe device's first 256 bytes by hand. Setup: sudo lspci -s <bdf> -xxx > dump.txt. Procedure: decode Vendor/Device, Command, Status, Class, BARs, then walk caps manually; then modify cfg_decode.py to read dump.txt (replace the DUMP string) and compare. Observations: record each capability ID and offset. Questions: Is MSI-X in BAR0 or another BAR? What is MPS vs MPS supported?

Expected reasoning

Your manual and automated decodes must agree; disagreements usually come from endianness or from forgetting that a 64-bit BAR consumes two slots. MPS is normally lower than or equal to the supported maximum because the whole path must agree. lspci output headers like "00:" use the same offset convention.

Extension: extend the decoder to print the extended capability names for every ID in your device and to decode the AER status registers.

🧪 Lab 18.2 — Compare an emulated NVMe with a real one SAFE

Setup: QEMU Q35 VM with -device nvme; optionally a physical NVMe SSD on the host. Procedure: run lspci -vvv in the guest and on the host. List capability chains side by side. Questions: Which capabilities does the emulated device omit? Why might link speed/width fields of an emulated device not reflect physical reality?

Expected reasoning

Emulated devices implement what the emulator's authors chose; link fields are emulated values, not a measured link. Real devices usually expose AER, LTR, L1 PM Substates and physical-layer capabilities that emulators may omit impl. Conclusion: use emulators for software-flow learning, not for link-level behaviour.

🧪 Lab 18.3 — Watch AER counters during a stress run CAUTION

Procedure: record lspci -vvv AER lines for the SSD and its Root Port; run a read-only fio workload against a scratch namespace; record again; compare. On kernels that expose them, also read /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/aer_dev_correctable. Questions: Did correctable errors increase? On which side of the link?

Expected reasoning

Receiver Errors/Bad TLPs are logged by the receiver: errors at the Root Port indicate problems on the device→host direction; errors at the SSD indicate host→device. A few correctable errors may be tolerable; a growing rate is a signal-integrity investigation.

🧪 Lab 18.4 — Senior forensic: Status = 2010h SAFE

Given synthetic trace 18.D, write the investigation plan with checkpoints and the evidence that would raise or lower your confidence that an IOMMU-unmapped DMA caused the bit.

Model answer

Record full state (Status, AER UESta at Root Port and device, dmesg IOMMU faults). Clear the RW1C bit. Reproduce the workload with IOMMU fault reporting visible. If the bit re-appears together with an IOMMU fault naming 01:00.0 and an address, confidence is high that a DMA to an unmapped IOVA occurred; then correlate the IOVA with the driver's mapping lifetime (Chapter 20). If the bit re-appears without IOMMU faults, consider a request to an address outside any host bridge window (UR from the Root Complex). If it never re-appears, the original event was probably during boot (e.g. firmware probing).

Quiz

  1. Where are the NVMe controller registers: in configuration space or memory space?

    Answer

    Memory space, behind BAR0 (MMIO). Configuration space only describes and controls the PCIe function.

  2. BAR0 reads 0000000Ch. What does it tell you?

    Answer

    Memory BAR (bit 0 = 0), 64-bit (bits 2:1 = 10b), prefetchable (bit 3 = 1), address not yet assigned (or assigned at 0 — unassigned in practice).

  3. Message Control = 001Fh in MSI-X. How many vectors, and is it enabled?

    Answer

    Table Size 1Fh → 32 vectors; Enable (bit 15) = 0 → not enabled.

  4. What does the extended capability header 14810001h mean?

    Answer

    ID 0001h (AER), version 1 (bits 19:16 = 1), next offset 148h (bits 31:20 = 148h).

  5. Why must you record Status before writing it back?

    Answer

    Error bits are RW1C; writing back the read value clears every set bit, erasing evidence.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is class code 010802h?
    Model answer

    Mass storage / Non-Volatile Memory controller / NVM Express — the class by which OSes bind a generic NVMe driver.

  2. Beginner Name three fields every PCI function has at the same offsets.
    Model answer

    Vendor ID (00h), Device ID (02h), Command (04h), Status (06h), Class Code (09h–0Bh), Header Type (0Eh).

  3. Intermediate How do you find the PCI Express capability?
    Model answer

    Check Status bit 4, read the Capabilities Pointer at 34h, follow Next pointers until Cap ID 10h, guarding against loops and malformed pointers.

  4. Intermediate What is the difference between MPS and MRRS?
    Model answer

    MPS bounds the payload of TLPs carrying data (writes and completions); MRRS bounds how much a single read request may ask for. MPS must be consistent along a path; MRRS is a per-requester choice affecting fairness and efficiency.

  5. Advanced What does the AER Header Log give you on a Completion Timeout?
    Model answer

    If logged for that error, the header of the request that timed out: address, length, tag, requester — letting you correlate with driver activity (e.g. which queue or PRP list fetch). Whether it is logged is error- and implementation-dependent; check the spec and device.

  6. Senior Design a configuration-space conformance check for an NVMe SSD.
    Model answer

    Class code 010802h; BAR0 memory, 64-bit, non-prefetchable as required by the transport spec (verify wording); capability list well-formed (no loops, all pointers DW-aligned, within range); PCI Express capability with Endpoint type; MSI-X present with table/PBA inside implemented BARs and non-overlapping with NVMe registers/doorbells; PM capability; AER present if claimed; FLR behaviour matches capability; all RW1C bits clear after reset; MPS/MRRS defaults within spec. Run across cold/warm/hot reset and after FLR.

🧠 Teach-back

Child: "The device has a passport with a fixed first page and a chain of stamps." Junior: decode the dump in 18.9 aloud. Senior: explain how Command, Device Control and AER together determine whether an NVMe DMA failure is a configuration problem, a link problem or an address-translation problem.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can decode a Type 0 and Type 1 header from a raw dump, respecting little-endian order.
  • I can walk standard and extended capability lists and skip unknown IDs safely.
  • I can decode Command, Status, Device Control, Link Status, MSI-X Message Control and AER status bits.
  • I can explain the difference between configuration space and BAR memory space with an NVMe example.
  • I can turn a dump into triage conclusions and state what each field can and cannot prove.
  • I can cite which document defines each field (PCIe Base, PCI Code and ID, NVMe PCIe Transport).

18.20 Summary, further reading and next

Configuration space = 64-byte header + standard capability list (from 34h) + extended capability list (from 100h). For NVMe the essentials are: Class Code 010802h, Command MSE/BME, BAR0 (64-bit memory), MSI-X capability, PCI Express capability (MPS, MRRS, link), and AER. Decode by walking, not by hard-coded offsets, and preserve evidence before clearing RW1C bits.

Further reading: PCI Express Base Specification (configuration space and capability chapters); PCI Code and ID Assignment Specification; NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (PCI header and capability requirements for NVMe controllers); Linux include/uapi/linux/pci_regs.h; man lspci, man setpci. Next: Chapter 19 — BARs and MMIO.

19 BARs and MMIO

← 18 Configuration Space20 DMA →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: PCI Express Base Specification (BAR format, bridge windows, memory request routing); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification Revision 1.4 and NVMe Base Specification Revision 2.4 (register map placed in memory space; doorbells; Controller Memory Buffer) version. STATUS: current baseline (confirm on nvmexpress.org and pcisig.com). OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: in NVMe 1.x the register map and PCI requirements were in one document; registers added in 2.0 (e.g. CRTO, NSSD) do not exist on 1.x controllers. SOURCE: PCI-SIG; NVM Express; Linux drivers/pci/setup-res.c, drivers/pci/probe.c (__pci_read_base) and drivers/nvme/host/pci.c.

19.1 Why this chapter exists

The NVMe driver controls the SSD by reading and writing registers: CAP to learn limits, CC to enable, CSTS to see readiness, AQA/ASQ/ACQ to locate the admin queues, and doorbells to announce work. All of those registers live inside a Base Address Register (BAR) window — a range of physical addresses that, once assigned, the device decodes as its own. This chapter explains how that window is sized, placed, enabled and used, and how a single CPU store becomes a PCIe Memory Write TLP that rings an NVMe doorbell. It is the bridge between PCIe configuration (Chapter 18) and NVMe registers (Chapter 24).

19.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain a BAR as "a numbered doorway into the device" and distinguish memory BARs from I/O BARs.
  • Intermediate: perform the BAR sizing algorithm for 32-bit and 64-bit BARs and compute size and alignment.
  • Advanced: explain prefetchable vs non-prefetchable, bridge windows, and why NVMe BAR0 is non-prefetchable.
  • Senior: reason about MMIO ordering (posted writes, read-to-flush), access width and atomicity, write-combining, and their effect on doorbell correctness and performance.
  • Trace analysis: identify MMIO MRd/MWr TLPs to BAR0 and decode the register offset from the address.
  • Debugging: diagnose all-ones register reads, BAR assignment failures and doorbell writes that "vanish".
  • Validation: test BAR sizing behaviour, reserved-region behaviour and access-width handling of a controller.

19.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 17 (where sizing fits in enumeration) and Chapter 18 (BAR fields at 10h–24h, Command register MSE). Memory Read (MRd) and Memory Write (MWr) TLPs; posted vs non-posted requests.

19.4 Story: a numbered doorway

🧒 Kid analogy

A BAR is a numbered doorway into the device. The device was built with a doorway of a fixed width — say 16 rooms wide — but no street number. The town planner (firmware) asks: "How wide is your doorway?" The device can't say the number directly, so they play a game: the planner writes "all the rooms!" (all ones) on the doorway sign; the device rubs out the parts of the number it can't use; what's left tells the planner how wide the doorway is. Then the planner paints a real street number on the doorway. From then on, anyone walking to that street number — the CPU — is actually walking into the device's rooms: room 0 is "what can you do" (CAP), room 14h is "start working" (CC), room 1000h is the bell (doorbell).

🌍 Real-world analogy

A company rents a block of extension numbers on a switchboard. It says "we need 100 consecutive extensions, aligned to a hundred" but not which ones; the telephone exchange assigns 4300–4399. Calls to those numbers ring inside the company; extension 4314 is always the same desk regardless of which block the company got.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Walking into a room has no side effect, but reading some device registers can (e.g. a read can clear a status in some devices — not typical for NVMe registers, but legal for devices in general — which is exactly why "non-prefetchable" exists). Also, a doorway only works once the device is told "open for visitors" (Command.MSE = 1), and the street (bridge windows above the device) must route visitors there.

19.5 Beginner view: the BAR register format

BitsMemory BARI/O BAR
00 = memory space indicator (RO)1 = I/O space indicator (RO)
2:1Type (RO): 00b = 32-bit decoder anywhere in 32-bit space; 10b = 64-bit decoder (uses this BAR and the next one); 01b reserved (was "below 1 MiB" in old PCI); 11b reservedbit 1 reserved, bits 31:2 address
3Prefetchable (RO)—
31:4Base address (RW above the size boundary, hard-wired 0 below it)—

The trick that makes sizing work: the device hard-wires to zero every address bit that lies inside its window. A 16 KiB window spans address bits 13:0, so bits 13:4 of the BAR always read 0 regardless of what is written; only bits 31:14 (and the upper BAR for 64-bit) are writable. All BAR sizes are powers of two and every BAR is naturally aligned to its size. verified

19.6 The BAR sizing algorithm

  1. Clear Command.MSE (and I/O Space Enable for I/O BARs) so that the transient all-ones address is not decoded. Otherwise, for a moment, the device claims an address range at the top of memory that might overlap real resources. verified
  2. Read and save the BAR's original value (and the upper BAR if 64-bit).
  3. Write FFFF_FFFFh to the BAR (and to the upper BAR if 64-bit).
  4. Read back. Mask off the low type bits (memory: lower 4 bits; I/O: lower 2 bits).
  5. Invert and add one: size = (~masked) + 1, computed across 64 bits for a 64-bit BAR.
  6. Restore the original value(s); restore Command.
size = (NOT (readback AND ~0xF)) + 1   (computed in the BAR's width: 32 or 64 bits)
  • readback — value read after writing all ones (for 64-bit: upper DWORD << 32 | lower DWORD).
  • 0xF — the four read-only type bits of a memory BAR (use 0x3 for an I/O BAR).
  • size — window size in bytes; also its required alignment.

19.6.1 Worked example: an NVMe BAR0 of 16 KiB

StepActionBAR0 (10h)BAR1 (14h)Reasoning
1Read originalFEA0_0004h0000_0000hMemory, type 10b (64-bit), non-prefetchable; address FEA0_0000h
2Write all ones← FFFF_FFFFh← FFFF_FFFFhCommand.MSE = 0 during this
3Read backFFFF_C004hFFFF_FFFFhBits 13:4 stuck at 0; type bits unchanged
4Mask low 4 bitsFFFF_C000hFFFF_FFFFh64-bit mask = FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_C000h
5Invert0000_0000_0000_3FFFh
6Add one0000_0000_0000_4000h = 16 384 bytes = 16 KiBAlignment 16 KiB
7Restore← FEA0_0000h← 0000_0000hType bits are RO; writing 0 there is harmless

The executable simulation below models a BAR register in software (hard-wiring the low bits exactly as hardware does) and runs the same algorithm for three BARs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""BAR sizing SIMULATION. A fake BAR register models how hardware hard-wires the low
address bits to zero; the sizing code is the same algorithm firmware/OS use."""

class FakeBar:
    def __init__(self, size, is64, prefetch):
        assert size & (size - 1) == 0 and size >= 16       # power of two, >= 16 bytes
        self.size, self.is64, self.pf = size, is64, prefetch
        self.addr = 0                                     # full 64-bit address latch
    def _flags(self):
        return (0b10 << 1 if self.is64 else 0) | (self.pf << 3)   # bit0=0 -> memory
    def read(self, upper=False):
        if upper:
            return (self.addr >> 32) & 0xFFFF_FFFF
        return (self.addr & 0xFFFF_FFFF & ~(self.size - 1)) | self._flags()
    def write(self, value, upper=False):
        mask = ~(self.size - 1) & 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF  # writable address bits only
        if not self.is64:
            mask &= 0xFFFF_FFFF
        if upper:
            new = (self.addr & 0xFFFF_FFFF) | (value << 32)
        else:
            new = (self.addr & ~0xFFFF_FFFF) | value
        self.addr = new & mask

def size_bar(bar):
    lo_orig = bar.read()
    if lo_orig & 1:
        raise ValueError("I/O BAR: mask with ~0x3 instead")
    is64 = ((lo_orig >> 1) & 0b11) == 0b10
    hi_orig = bar.read(upper=True) if is64 else 0
    # (Command.Memory Space Enable must be 0 while sizing -- see text.)
    bar.write(0xFFFF_FFFF)
    lo = bar.read()
    hi = 0xFFFF_FFFF
    if is64:
        bar.write(0xFFFF_FFFF, upper=True)
        hi = bar.read(upper=True)
    print(f"  read back lo={lo:#010x}" + (f" hi={hi:#010x}" if is64 else ""))
    mask = (hi << 32 | (lo & ~0xF)) & 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF
    if not is64:
        mask |= 0xFFFF_FFFF_0000_0000      # treat a 32-bit BAR as having all-ones upper bits
    size = ((~mask) & 0xFFFF_FFFF_FFFF_FFFF) + 1
    bar.write(lo_orig & ~0xF)               # restore original address
    if is64:
        bar.write(hi_orig, upper=True)
    return size, is64, (lo_orig >> 3) & 1

for desc, bar in [("NVMe BAR0 (16 KiB, 64-bit, non-prefetchable)", FakeBar(16 * 1024, True, 0)),
                  ("32-bit 1 MiB non-prefetchable", FakeBar(1 << 20, False, 0)),
                  ("64-bit 8 GiB prefetchable (e.g. a GPU)", FakeBar(8 << 30, True, 1))]:
    print(desc)
    size, is64, pf = size_bar(bar)
    print(f"  size = {size:#x} ({size // 1024} KiB) 64-bit={int(is64)} prefetchable={pf}")

Output:

NVMe BAR0 (16 KiB, 64-bit, non-prefetchable)
  read back lo=0xffffc004 hi=0xffffffff
  size = 0x4000 (16 KiB) 64-bit=1 prefetchable=0
32-bit 1 MiB non-prefetchable
  read back lo=0xfff00000
  size = 0x100000 (1024 KiB) 64-bit=0 prefetchable=0
64-bit 8 GiB prefetchable (e.g. a GPU)
  read back lo=0x0000000c hi=0xfffffffe
  size = 0x200000000 (8388608 KiB) 64-bit=1 prefetchable=1

Note the 8 GiB case: the lower DWORD reads back 0000_000Ch — all its address bits are inside the window — and the upper DWORD FFFF_FFFEh carries the size information. A 32-bit-only sizing routine would conclude "size = 16 bytes"! This is why a 64-bit BAR must be sized as a pair. derived

19.7 32-bit vs 64-bit, prefetchable vs non-prefetchable

PropertyMeaningConsequenceNVMe BAR0
32-bit (type 00b)Decoder only handles addresses below 4 GiBMust be placed below 4 GiB; competes for scarce 32-bit MMIO spaceNot the usual choice
64-bit (type 10b)Decoder handles 64-bit addresses; occupies two BAR slotsMay be placed anywhere — if the bridge windows above allow itRequired to be a 64-bit memory BAR by the NVMe PCIe transport register requirements (MLBAR/MUBAR naming) verified — confirm exact wording in your revision
Prefetchable (bit 3 = 1)Reads have no side effects; bytes may be merged/prefetched; writes may be mergedCan live in the bridge's prefetchable (64-bit capable) window; CPU may map it write-combiningNo
Non-prefetchable (bit 3 = 0)Reads may have side effects; accesses must be performed exactly as issuedMust live in the non-prefetchable window (32-bit only in the classic Type 1 header)Yes — register semantics

In NVMe terms, the registers at BAR0 are named MLBAR (Memory Register Base Lower Address, at 10h) and MUBAR (Memory Register Base Upper Address, at 14h) in the transport specification. The NVMe specification also defines an optional Index/Data Pair register mechanism at BAR2 for legacy I/O-space access to the registers version; modern hosts use the memory BAR. Other BARs may hold MSI-X tables, the Controller Memory Buffer (CMB) or Persistent Memory Region (PMR) — located through MSI-X BIR fields and CMBLOC.BIR / PMRCAP.BIR impl.

19.8 Placing the window: resource assignment

After sizing all BARs, firmware (or the OS) solves a packing problem: assign every BAR an address naturally aligned to its size, inside its parent bridge's window, and size each bridge window (1 MiB granularity for memory windows) to cover all children. Bridges are then programmed bottom-up so that memory requests are routed:

  • A Downstream-going MWr/MRd is forwarded by a bridge if its address lies within the bridge's Memory or Prefetchable window.
  • An Upstream-going request (DMA from the SSD) is forwarded by a bridge if its address lies outside its windows (i.e. not destined for a sibling below it) — peer-to-peer within a switch is possible when the address falls inside a sibling's window and the switch permits it (ACS may redirect it upstream) verified.

19.9 MMIO vs configuration access

AspectConfiguration accessMMIO (memory-mapped I/O) access
Address spaceConfiguration space (BDF + register)Memory space (physical address in a BAR window)
CPU mechanismLoad/store to ECAM window (or CF8h/CFCh)Load/store to the BAR address mapped uncached in the kernel
TLP typesCfgRd0/1, CfgWr0/1MRd, MWr (32- or 64-bit address format)
Writes posted?No — always completedYes — MWr is posted (no completion)
RoutingBy bus number (ID routing)By address (bridge windows)
Enabled byAlways available once the link is upCommand.MSE = 1 and a valid BAR assignment
Typical size1 DW per request1–2 DW for registers; larger for CMB/WC regions
NVMe useIdentity, enable bits, MSI-X capability, PCIe error stateCAP, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ, ACQ, doorbells, MSI-X table, CMB
PerformanceSlow path; not used in the I/O pathDoorbell writes are in the hot I/O path

19.9.1 What happens when the driver writes a doorbell

  1. The driver executes writel(tail, dbs + offset). dbs is a kernel virtual address produced by ioremap() of BAR0.
  2. The CPU's MMU translates the virtual address to the physical BAR address. The page is mapped uncacheable (UC) — no cache line is allocated, the store goes out as-is impl (architecture-specific memory types).
  3. The store reaches the Root Complex, which decodes the physical address as MMIO belonging to the Root Port's window and generates a MWr TLP: 1 DW payload, address = BAR0 + offset, Requester ID = the Root Complex.
  4. Bridges forward it downstream by address range. The SSD's BAR0 decoder claims it.
  5. Because MWr is posted, the CPU does not wait for any acknowledgement at the transaction level (the Data Link Layer still ACKs the TLP for reliability). The CPU continues immediately.
  6. The controller latches the new tail value and begins fetching submission queue entries by DMA (Chapter 20).
📡 Protocol: posted write ordering and the "read to flush" idiom

PCIe ordering rules let a later read not pass an earlier posted write in the same direction (with default attributes) verified. So if software must be sure a register write has arrived (for example before timing a delay), it reads any register of the same device: the read's completion cannot return before the earlier write was delivered. Linux drivers use this idiom (a read-back after write) in some reset and shutdown paths. Doorbell writes in the hot path deliberately avoid it — waiting a round-trip per I/O would cost microseconds.

⚠️ Access width

NVMe 64-bit registers (CAP, ASQ, ACQ, CMBMSC, …) may be accessed by hosts as two 32-bit accesses on platforms that lack atomic 64-bit MMIO; Linux uses lo_hi_readq/lo_hi_writeq helpers on such platforms. The NVMe specification defines the access rules for each register (for example which widths are required to be supported) — check the "register access" rules in your revision before relying on a particular behaviour version. Never use byte or word writes to doorbells; they are 32-bit registers.

19.10 Addressing safety: six addresses that are not the same

Engineers routinely lose days because two people say "the address" and mean different things. Never casually equate these:

Address kindWho uses itExample in our storyTranslated by
Virtual address (VA)CPU instructions in a process or the kernelKernel dbs pointer from ioremap(); user buffer pointer in fioCPU MMU page tables
Physical address (PA)CPU memory system after MMU translationFEA0_1008h (doorbell) or a DRAM page holding a submission queue—
DMA address / IOVAWhat the driver puts into PRPs, ASQ/ACQ, Create Queue commandsAn I/O virtual address returned by dma_map_*()IOMMU (if enabled) into PA; identity when no IOMMU
PCIe bus addressThe address field of a TLP on the linkThe address in the controller's MRd/MWr = the DMA address it was givenRoot Complex/IOMMU on the upstream side; usually identical to PA for MMIO downstream on common platforms impl
BAR addressThe bus address range the device decodesBAR0 = FEA0_0000hAssigned by firmware/OS; may differ from CPU PA on some non-x86 platforms with address offsets impl
Controller-local addressInside the SSD controller (SRAM, DRAM buffers, NAND addressing)Firmware's internal buffer for a 4 KiB blockController firmware — invisible to the host

An IOMMU may change the address a device must use: the same DRAM page has one PA but the device must present the IOVA. That is why NVMe PRP entries contain DMA addresses, not physical addresses, from the device's point of view verified.

19.11 Hardware view inside the SSD controller

Inside the controller, the PCIe endpoint core's BAR decoder compares the address of each incoming MRd/MWr against the BAR0 window and passes hits, with the offset, to a register block. The register block implements fixed registers (often in hardware), doorbell registers (often a small write-only RAM per queue whose writes trigger the queue manager), and possibly the MSI-X table. What happens after a doorbell write — how quickly the fetch engine reacts, whether doorbell writes are coalesced — is implementation-dependent and generally unobservable except through timing on a protocol analyzer.

📭 What the spec does not say

The NVMe specification defines what each register means and how the host shall use it; it does not specify how the controller implements decode, how long a register read takes, or how doorbell writes are internally queued. Latency numbers you see in a trace for MMIO reads are properties of a particular platform and controller.

19.12 Linux view

sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -vv | grep -i region       # BAR address, type, size
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/resource    # lines: start end flags (BAR0..BAR5, ROM, ...)
sudo grep -A3 -i 'nvme' /proc/iomem               # which driver claimed the region
ls -l /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/resource0 # the BAR0 file (mmap-able by root)
sudo dmesg | grep -E '01:00.0.*(BAR|reg 0x10)'     # sizing/assignment messages

Reading NVMe registers directly through resource0 is possible for root. The following is hardware-dependent and should be run only on a test machine:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
# CAUTION LAB: maps BAR0 of an NVMe device read-only and reads CAP, VS, CC, CSTS.
# Reading these registers has no side effects per the NVMe register definitions,
# but mapping device memory as root is a privileged operation. NEVER write here
# while the kernel nvme driver owns the device.
import mmap, os, struct, sys
bdf = sys.argv[1]                                   # e.g. 0000:01:00.0
fd = os.open(f"/sys/bus/pci/devices/{bdf}/resource0", os.O_RDONLY | os.O_SYNC)
m = mmap.mmap(fd, 4096, mmap.MAP_SHARED, mmap.PROT_READ)
rd32 = lambda off: struct.unpack_from("<I", m, off)[0]   # 32-bit accesses only
cap = rd32(0x00) | (rd32(0x04) << 32)
print(f"CAP={cap:#018x} VS={rd32(0x08):#010x} CC={rd32(0x14):#010x} CSTS={rd32(0x1C):#010x}")
⚠️ Safety note

Python's struct.unpack_from on an mmap is not guaranteed to perform a single 32-bit bus access on every platform/Python build impl. For reliable register work use a tool or a small C program with volatile 32-bit loads. Some kernels restrict resource mapping when lockdown is active. Writing any register (especially CC, NSSR or doorbells) behind the driver's back can corrupt queues and data.

19.14 Code: modelling BAR0 register decode

# Inside a (simplified) controller model: decode an incoming memory request
on_memory_request(tlp):
    if not cfg.command.MSE:                 return  # not decoded → upstream sees UR
    if not (BAR0 <= tlp.addr < BAR0 + 16 KiB): return  # not ours
    off = tlp.addr - BAR0
    if tlp.is_write:
        if off >= 0x1000:
            q, is_cq = divmod((off - 0x1000) // (4 << CAP.DSTRD), 2)
            ring_doorbell(q, is_cq, tlp.data)      # tail for SQ, head for CQ
        else:
            write_register(off, tlp.data, tlp.byte_enables)
    else:
        send CplD(read_register(off, tlp.length))

19.15 Common mistakes

  • Sizing a 64-bit BAR with only its lower DWORD.
  • Leaving Command.MSE = 1 while writing all ones to a BAR.
  • Assuming BAR addresses are stable across boots or rescans.
  • Mapping register BARs write-combining or cacheable — reads might be served stale, writes merged or reordered.
  • Expecting a completion for an MMIO write.
  • Putting a CPU physical address into a PRP when an IOMMU is active (should be a DMA address).
  • Assuming MSI-X table placement — always read BIR/offset.

19.16 Five failure patterns

#SymptomPossible causesFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentConclusion (confidence)
1dmesg: "BAR 0: no space for [mem size 0x00004000 64bit]"Bridge window too small; no 32-bit space left/proc/iomem windowsFirmware MMIO settingsRemove other devices / enable realloc on a test systemResource exhaustion (high)
2All register reads return all-ones but Vendor ID is fineMSE = 0; BAR unassigned; device in D3hotCommand; Region line "[disabled]" or "[virtual]"PMCSREnable via the driver path (not setpci) and retestDecode disabled (high)
3Doorbell writes have no effectWrong DSTRD in offset math; wrong BAR mapping; controller not enabled (CSTS.RDY=0)CAP.DSTRD, computed offsetAnalyzer: is the MWr on the link, at which address?Compare TLP address to BAR0 + expected offsetOffset bug vs controller state (medium-high)
4Intermittent stale register valuesMapping with wrong memory typeDriver's ioremap variantPAT/MTRR configuration implMap UC explicitly; compareMapping attribute bug (medium)
5Peer-to-peer DMA fails between two SSDs under one switchACS redirects P2P upstream; IOMMU blocks; not supported by the RCACS capability control on DSPsIOMMU fault logsTest P2P with ACS settings known; consult platform docsPlatform policy (medium)
💡 Senior insight

All-ones is the universal "something is not there" signature for both configuration reads and MMIO reads. Make it a reflex: when a register reads all-ones, first prove the device is still reachable (Vendor ID, link state), then prove decode is on (MSE, BAR), and only then believe the value. NVMe registers do have fields that can legitimately be all-ones in part, but a whole 32-bit FFFF_FFFFh in CSTS or CAP is never a healthy value.

19.18 Labs

🧪 Lab 19.1 — Size BARs on paper and in simulation SAFE

Objective: compute size from read-back values. Procedure: for each read-back pair, compute size and type: (a) FFFF_F000h (32-bit); (b) FFFE_000Ch / FFFF_FFFFh; (c) FFFF_FF01h (I/O). Then add each case to bar_size.py by constructing an appropriate FakeBar (or an I/O variant) and confirm.

Solution

(a) memory, 32-bit, non-prefetchable, size 4 KiB. (b) memory, 64-bit, prefetchable, mask FFFF_FFFF_FFFE_0000h → size 128 KiB. (c) I/O BAR, mask with ~3h → FFFF_FF00h → size 256 bytes.

Extension: write a function that packs a list of BARs into a window with natural alignment and reports the minimum bridge window size (1 MiB granular).

🧪 Lab 19.2 — Map BAR0 of an emulated NVMe device CAUTION

Setup: QEMU VM with an extra -device nvme that is not the boot disk. Procedure: run the hardware-dependent reader in 19.12 against its BDF; decode CAP with the decoder in Chapter 24. Compare VS with nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i ver.

Expected reasoning

VS read from BAR0 and the "ver" field of Identify Controller should agree in what they report (both encode the supported specification version, MJR.MNR.TER). CC.EN=1 and CSTS.RDY=1 because the kernel driver has enabled the controller.

🧪 Lab 19.3 — Senior forensic: the vanishing doorbell SAFE

Scenario (synthetic): a custom user-space driver rings SQ1 tail at BAR0+1008h, but the controller never fetches. CAP high DWORD = 0000_0002h. Task: find the bug.

Model answer

CAP.DSTRD = bits 35:32 = 2 → stride 4<<2 = 16 bytes. SQ1TDBL = 1000h + (2×1)×16 = 1020h, not 1008h. 1008h falls in the gap between SQ0TDBL (1000h) and CQ0HDBL (1010h) — a write to an undefined location. Fix: compute offsets from DSTRD. Confidence high; verify with an analyzer showing MWr at 1008h with no subsequent MRd of SQ1 memory.

Quiz

  1. Read-back after all-ones: FFFF_8004h, upper FFFF_FFFFh. Size?

    Answer

    Mask FFFF_FFFF_FFFF_8000h → size 8000h = 32 KiB; 64-bit, non-prefetchable.

  2. Why are register BARs non-prefetchable?

    Answer

    Because reads may have side effects or must reflect current state; the system must not speculatively read or merge accesses.

  3. Is an MMIO write to a doorbell acknowledged by a completion TLP?

    Answer

    No. MWr is posted. Only link-level ACK DLLPs acknowledge delivery across each link.

  4. Where are NVMe doorbells located?

    Answer

    In BAR0 starting at offset 1000h; SQyTDBL at 1000h + (2y)×(4<<DSTRD) and CQyHDBL at 1000h + (2y+1)×(4<<DSTRD).

  5. Name two address kinds that may differ for the same DRAM page.

    Answer

    Physical address and DMA address/IOVA (when an IOMMU is used); also the kernel virtual address.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a BAR?
    Model answer

    A configuration register that declares the type and size of an address window the device decodes, and holds the base address software assigns to it.

  2. Intermediate Walk me through BAR sizing for a 64-bit BAR.
    Model answer

    Disable decode, save both DWORDs, write all ones to both, read both, combine, mask the 4 type bits, invert, add one, restore both, re-enable decode.

  3. Intermediate MMIO vs config access?
    Model answer

    Config: ID-routed, non-posted CfgRd/CfgWr to configuration space; MMIO: address-routed MRd/MWr to BAR windows, writes posted. NVMe registers are MMIO.

  4. Advanced Why might a driver read back a register after writing it?
    Model answer

    To force earlier posted writes to complete before proceeding (ordering: the read completion cannot pass the earlier write), e.g. before a timed delay or before assuming a reset bit took effect.

  5. Senior Dozens of NVMe drives fail to get BARs in a dense server. What is your analysis?
    Model answer

    Non-prefetchable windows are 32-bit in Type 1 bridges; each drive's BAR0 (+ MSI-X, maybe CMB) needs space aligned within 1 MiB-granular bridge windows; with hot-plug reservation per port, 32-bit MMIO is exhausted. Options: firmware with larger MMIO hole, reducing per-port reservation, relying on 64-bit placement where the platform permits, or BIOS settings; verify with /proc/iomem and dmesg.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can size any BAR from read-back values, including 64-bit and I/O BARs.
  • I can explain prefetchable vs non-prefetchable and which window each lands in.
  • I can trace a doorbell write from writel() to an MWr TLP and to the controller.
  • I can name the six address kinds and who translates between them.
  • I can diagnose all-ones reads by layer.
  • I can compute NVMe doorbell offsets for any DSTRD.

19.19 Summary, further reading and next

A BAR is a numbered doorway: the device fixes its size and type, software chooses its address. Sizing exploits hard-wired zero bits; 64-bit BARs are sized as pairs. NVMe registers are MMIO in BAR0 (non-prefetchable, 64-bit), with doorbells at 1000h. MMIO writes are posted; reads are non-posted and can be used to flush. Address kinds differ: VA, PA, IOVA, bus address, BAR address, controller-local.

Further reading: PCIe Base Specification sections on BARs and Type 1 windows; NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (register mapping, MLBAR/MUBAR); Linux Documentation/driver-api/device-io.rst (MMIO accessors and ordering). Next: Chapter 20 — DMA, where the device starts reading and writing host memory.

PART VIII

DMA

Once the driver can reach the controller's registers (Part VII), the direction of most traffic reverses. In NVMe, the host CPU writes only a handful of registers per command — essentially one doorbell write to submit and one to acknowledge completions. Everything else — fetching the command, fetching the data pointer lists, moving the data, posting the completion, even raising the interrupt — is done by the controller as a bus master, reading and writing host memory with Direct Memory Access. This Part explains what DMA really is on PCIe, what addresses the device uses, how an IOMMU sits in the middle, and how to see and debug all of it.

20.1 Why this chapter exists

The master curriculum's DMA-safety rule is explicit: never describe DMA as "the SSD directly reads RAM" without qualification. Instead you must be able to say who initiates the transaction, which address is used, what translation may exist, what PCIe transaction represents it, how data returns, and what the controller may do internally. This chapter builds exactly that vocabulary, then follows one NVMe read command through every DMA it causes.

20.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain why DMA exists and contrast it with programmed I/O (CPU copying).
  • Intermediate: describe DMA in terms of source, destination, descriptors, scatter-gather lists and direction; map NVMe structures (SQ, CQ, PRP, SGL) onto those terms.
  • Advanced: explain IOMMU translation, IOVA, DMA masks, bounce buffering, cache coherency (snooping, No Snoop) and ATS.
  • Senior: diagnose DMA failures across layers: driver mapping lifetime, IOMMU faults, completion timeouts, poisoned data, ordering.
  • Trace analysis: identify device-initiated MRd/CplD and MWr TLPs and correlate them with an NVMe command.
  • Debugging: use IOMMU fault logs, AER and NVMe status to localize a DMA failure.
  • Validation: design tests for unaligned buffers, large transfers, PRP list boundaries and IOMMU on/off configurations.

20.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 19 (MMIO, posted writes, the six address kinds in 19.10); Chapter 18 (Command.BME, Device Control MPS/MRRS/Relaxed Ordering/No Snoop). TLP types MRd, MWr, CplD; Requester ID and Tag.

20.4 Story and analogies

🧒 Kid analogy

The teacher (CPU) could carry every book from the library to the classroom herself — but then she can't teach. Instead she writes a request slip, puts it in the request box, and rings a bell. The librarian (NVMe controller) comes over, reads the slip, walks to the classroom tables (RAM) and puts the books exactly on the table numbers written on the slip. When finished, the librarian puts a note in the answer box and taps the teacher's shoulder (interrupt). The teacher never carried a book.

🌍 Real-world analogies

Courier with a delivery manifest: the warehouse (host) prepares a manifest (descriptor) listing pick-up and drop-off addresses, possibly several drop-off points for one order (scatter-gather). The courier (DMA engine) does the driving. Gated community with a guard (IOMMU): the courier carries a visitor pass listing which houses it may enter; the guard translates "House 7 on my pass" to the real street address and turns the courier away from houses not on the pass.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

(1) The librarian does not "walk into" RAM — the controller requests memory transactions which the Root Complex performs against the memory system; the controller never sees DRAM directly. (2) For a read from host memory, data comes back as completions, possibly split into several CplD TLPs, and may arrive in a different order from requests with different tags. (3) The guard can also cache passes in the courier's pocket (ATS) — and then revoking a pass needs an explicit invalidation round-trip.

20.5 Beginner view: CPU copying vs DMA

AspectProgrammed I/O (CPU copies)DMA (device copies)
Who moves the dataCPU executes loads/stores to device registers or a data portDevice's DMA engine issues memory requests to host memory
CPU costProportional to bytes moved; each MMIO read is a slow round-trip (~µs-class)Small and roughly constant per command (build descriptor, ring doorbell, handle completion)
ThroughputLimited by uncached MMIO access rateLimited by link bandwidth, MPS/MRRS, device and memory system
ComplexitySimpleNeeds address mapping, coherency handling, buffer lifetime discipline
Historical exampleATA PIO modesBus-mastering IDE, AHCI, NVMe

At millions of I/Os per second and several GB/s per drive, programmed I/O is impossible: a CPU core would spend all its time in uncached MMIO accesses. NVMe was designed so that the CPU's per-command register work is just doorbell writes, and everything bulky is DMA. derived

20.7 Protocol view: what DMA looks like on PCIe

  • Device reads host memory: the controller sends a non-posted MRd (Requester ID = the controller's BDF, Tag, Address = DMA address, Length ≤ MRRS). The Root Complex reads memory and returns one or more CplD TLPs with Completer ID, the same Tag, a Byte Count and Lower Address so the requester can reassemble. Completions may be split at Read Completion Boundary (RCB, 64 or 128 bytes) aligned points, and each completion's payload is limited by MPS. verified
  • Device writes host memory: the controller sends posted MWr TLPs, each with payload ≤ MPS and not crossing a 4 KiB address boundary. No completion. verified
  • Device raises an interrupt: MSI-X is also an MWr — to the message address from the table entry with the message data. On x86 the address is in the FEEx_xxxxh range the Root Complex interprets as an interrupt impl (architecture-specific).
  • Ordering: posted writes from the device are not passed by later posted writes (unless Relaxed Ordering is set and permitted), and a completion cannot pass a posted write in the same direction by default. This is why a controller can write data (MWr), then the CQE (MWr), then the MSI-X (MWr), and the host is guaranteed to see the data before it sees the CQE — if Relaxed Ordering is not applied to the CQE write verified. The NVMe controller is responsible for using attributes that preserve this guarantee.
TLPs_for_write_data ≈ ⌈ transfer_bytes / MPS ⌉ (plus extra splits at 4 KiB boundaries)   |   MRd_requests ≈ ⌈ transfer_bytes / MRRS ⌉
  • transfer_bytes — bytes the controller moves for one command.
  • MPS — Max_Payload_Size in Device Control (e.g. 256 B).
  • MRRS — Max_Read_Request_Size in Device Control (e.g. 512 B).

Example: a 128 KiB NVMe read with MPS 256 B produces about 512 MWr TLPs of read-data; a 128 KiB NVMe write with MRRS 512 B produces about 256 MRd requests, answered by roughly 512 CplD (if the RC returns 256-byte completions — RC completion sizing is implementation-dependent). derived

20.8 Connecting to NVMe: one read command, every DMA

StepInitiatorAddress usedTranslationTLPData returnController internals impl
2 DoorbellCPUBAR0 + SQ1TDBL offset (physical MMIO address)CPU MMU (VA→PA)MWr ↓none (posted)Tail latched; fetch scheduled by arbitration
3–4 SQE fetchControllerSQ base IOVA + slot × 64IOMMUMRd ↑ / CplD ↓CplDMay fetch several SQEs in one request
5 PRP list fetchControllerPRP2 (pointer to a list)IOMMUMRd ↑ / CplD ↓CplDMay prefetch list entries lazily
6 Read-dataControllerPRP1, PRP list entriesIOMMUMWr ↑noneData from internal buffer after media read

For an NVMe write command, step 6 reverses: the controller issues MRd requests to the data buffer and receives CplD with the data. This is why NVMe write performance is sensitive to read-request latency through the Root Complex and to the number of outstanding tags the controller can use — Chapter on PCIe performance covers the arithmetic. derived

20.9 IOMMU, mapping and isolation

An Input-Output Memory Management Unit (IOMMU) sits between PCIe and the memory system in the Root Complex. For each incoming request it identifies the device (by Requester ID, optionally PASID), looks up that device's translation tables (a "domain"), translates the IOVA to a physical address and checks permissions. Untranslatable or forbidden requests are blocked and reported as faults; the device typically sees an error completion (for reads) or the write is dropped impl (exact behaviour is platform-specific).

  • Why: isolation (a buggy or malicious device cannot scribble over the kernel), virtualization (assign a device to a VM whose "physical" addresses are guest addresses), and addressing (devices with narrow DMA masks reach high memory).
  • Linux modes: translated DMA (default on many distributions), passthrough/identity (iommu=pt — DMA address equals physical address for host drivers), or IOMMU disabled. The NVMe driver code is identical in all modes because it uses the DMA API impl.
  • Cost: map/unmap per I/O and IOTLB misses add latency and CPU cost; IOTLB invalidation strategies (strict vs lazy/flush-queue) trade safety for speed.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Toy IOMMU SIMULATION: one flat IOVA->physical page table per device (Requester ID).
Real IOMMUs (Intel VT-d, AMD-Vi, Arm SMMU) use multi-level tables, caches (IOTLB),
and permission bits; this keeps only the idea. All addresses are synthetic."""
PAGE = 4096

class ToyIommu:
    def __init__(self):
        self.domains = {}                       # requester_id -> {iova_page: (phys_page, perms)}
        self.faults = []
    def map(self, rid, iova, phys, length, perms):
        dom = self.domains.setdefault(rid, {})
        for off in range(0, length, PAGE):
            dom[(iova + off) // PAGE] = ((phys + off) // PAGE, perms)
    def unmap(self, rid, iova, length):
        for off in range(0, length, PAGE):
            self.domains.get(rid, {}).pop((iova + off) // PAGE, None)
    def translate(self, rid, iova, is_write):
        entry = self.domains.get(rid, {}).get(iova // PAGE)
        need = "w" if is_write else "r"
        if entry is None or need not in entry[1]:
            self.faults.append((rid, iova, "write" if is_write else "read"))
            return None                          # request is blocked; the device sees an error
        return entry[0] * PAGE + iova % PAGE

io = ToyIommu()
NVME_RID = 0x0100                                # 01:00.0
# Driver maps a 3-page buffer that is physically scattered (an sg list):
for i, phys in enumerate([0x7_3A21_5000, 0x1_0F00_2000, 0x4_4410_9000]):
    io.map(NVME_RID, 0xFFFF_0000 + i * PAGE, phys, PAGE, "rw")
for iova in (0xFFFF_0000, 0xFFFF_1010, 0xFFFF_2FFF):
    print(f"device MWr to IOVA {iova:#x} -> phys {io.translate(NVME_RID, iova, True):#x}")
io.unmap(NVME_RID, 0xFFFF_1000, PAGE)            # driver unmapped too early (bug)
print("after early unmap:", io.translate(NVME_RID, 0xFFFF_1010, True))
print("other device using NVMe's IOVA:", io.translate(0x0400, 0xFFFF_0000, False))
for rid, iova, kind in io.faults:
    print(f"FAULT rid={rid >> 8:02x}:{(rid >> 3) & 0x1f:02x}.{rid & 7} {kind} iova={iova:#x}")

Output:

device MWr to IOVA 0xffff0000 -> phys 0x73a215000
device MWr to IOVA 0xffff1010 -> phys 0x10f002010
device MWr to IOVA 0xffff2fff -> phys 0x444109fff
after early unmap: None
other device using NVMe's IOVA: None
FAULT rid=01:00.0 write iova=0xffff1010
FAULT rid=04:00.0 read iova=0xffff0000

The simulation demonstrates the two classic IOMMU faults: a use-after-unmap by the device that owns the mapping (driver unmapped a buffer before the device finished — a real and serious bug), and a different device presenting an address that was never mapped for it (isolation working as intended).

20.9.1 ATS, PRI and PASID

Address Translation Services (ATS), an optional PCIe extended capability (ID 000Fh), lets a device ask the IOMMU (the Translation Agent) for a translation in advance and cache it in a device-side Address Translation Cache (ATC). The device then issues requests marked as already translated, saving IOMMU lookup latency. Software must invalidate the ATC when it changes mappings — an Invalidate Request message to the device, answered by an Invalidate Completion verified. Page Request Interface (PRI) lets a device request that missing pages be made resident (for shared-virtual-memory style use), and Process Address Space ID (PASID) tags requests with an address-space identifier so one function can serve several address spaces. Whether a given NVMe SSD implements ATS/PRI/PASID is implementation-dependent; it is uncommon in mainstream SSDs but appears in some data-centre and virtualization-focused designs. Capability discovery applies — check for the extended capabilities before assuming.

⚠️ Security note

Translated requests bypass the IOMMU lookup on the trusted assumption that the device's ATC is honest and up to date. Platforms therefore treat enabling ATS as a trust decision; Linux can refuse ATS for devices marked untrusted (e.g. externally exposed ports) impl.

20.10 Hardware view: coherency and attributes

  • Snooping: on most x86 platforms DMA is cache-coherent: device writes invalidate/update CPU caches and device reads see the latest CPU-written data. Many Arm platforms are also coherent for PCIe, but not all — the DMA API inserts cache maintenance where needed impl.
  • No Snoop attribute (TLP attribute bit, enabled by Device Control "Enable No Snoop"): tells the Root Complex it may skip snooping for that request. Only safe when software guarantees the data is not in CPU caches. Platforms may ignore it.
  • Relaxed Ordering attribute: allows a write to pass earlier writes. Good for bulk data, dangerous for the CQE that signals the data is complete — hence controllers must not apply it where ordering matters.
  • DMA mask: the number of address bits the device can generate. NVMe controllers use 64-bit addresses; drivers set a 64-bit mask, and the platform may still restrict addresses (IOMMU aperture, bounce buffers).

20.11 Linux view: the DMA API used by the NVMe driver

# Queue memory: long-lived, shared by CPU and device → coherent allocation
sq_cpu = dma_alloc_coherent(dev, depth * 64, &sq_dma, GFP_KERNEL)   # sq_dma goes into ASQ / Create SQ PRP1
cq_cpu = dma_alloc_coherent(dev, depth * 16, &cq_dma, GFP_KERNEL)

# Data buffers: per-request streaming mapping (block layer builds a scatterlist)
nents = blk_rq_map_sg(req, sgl)
n = dma_map_sg(dev, sgl, nents, rq_dma_dir(req))   # DMA_FROM_DEVICE for NVMe Read
build PRP1/PRP2 (+ PRP list in a DMA pool) or SGL from sg_dma_address/len
ring doorbell
... completion arrives ...
dma_unmap_sg(dev, sgl, nents, dir)                 # only after the CQE for this command
complete request to block layer
sudo dmesg | grep -iE 'iommu|dmar|amd-vi|smmu'       # IOMMU mode and faults
cat /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices/* 2>/dev/null | head   # (ls) which devices share a group
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/iommu_group/devices/
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0/iommu_group/type          # DMA, DMA-FQ, identity, ...
cat /proc/cmdline                                               # iommu=, intel_iommu=, amd_iommu= options

Illustrative, abbreviated shape of an IOMMU fault message (format differs per platform and kernel version; not real output): DMAR: [DMA Write] Request device [01:00.0] fault addr 0xffff1000 [fault reason …] …. What it can prove: a specific Requester ID presented a specific IOVA that the IOMMU refused. What it cannot prove: why the driver/device used that address.

📘 Specification discipline

Normative: PRP entries must be aligned per the rules in the NVMe Base Specification (PRP1 may have an offset; subsequent entries are memory-page aligned, page size set by CC.MPS); queue base addresses must be memory-page aligned (CC.MPS) and contiguous unless the controller supports non-contiguous queues (CAP.CQR = 0) verified. Optional: SGL support (reported in Identify Controller). Implementation-dependent: how many outstanding MRd the controller issues, prefetching of SQEs and PRP lists, completion coalescing. Version-dependent: SGL rules and related fields have been refined across revisions.

💡 Senior insight

In a DMA failure, ask "whose address was it?" before "what went wrong?". Every DMA address in an NVMe trace was produced by host software and handed to the controller through a structure you can inspect (ASQ/ACQ registers, Create Queue commands, the SQE, PRP lists). Trace the address back to the structure that delivered it, then to the code that wrote that structure. The controller is usually just the messenger.

20.13 Worked example: how many TLPs?

Problem: NVMe write of 64 KiB, buffer 4 KiB-aligned, MPS 256 B, MRRS 512 B, RCB 64 B, Root Complex returns completions of up to 256 B on 256 B boundaries synthetic. Count PCIe TLPs for data, excluding SQE/CQE/interrupt.

Solution: MRd requests = 64 KiB / 512 B = 128. Each 512 B read returns as 2 × 256 B CplD → 256 CplD. Total data-related TLPs = 384 (128 upstream MRd + 256 downstream CplD). Plus 1 SQE MRd + 1 CplD, 1 PRP-list MRd + CplD(s) (16 pages → PRP2 points to a list of 15 entries = 120 bytes), 1 CQE MWr, 1 MSI-X MWr, 2 doorbell MWr. derived

20.14 Common mistakes

  • Saying "the SSD reads RAM" without naming the MRd/CplD, the Requester ID, and the IOVA.
  • Putting virt_to_phys() results in PRPs instead of DMA-API addresses.
  • Touching a streaming buffer from the CPU while the device owns it.
  • Assuming coherency on every platform.
  • Unmapping buffers in timeout paths before the controller is disabled or the command is known aborted.
  • Thinking NVMe "read" generates MRd from the device for data (it generates MWr).

20.16 Labs

🧪 Lab 20.1 — Beginner: count DMA TLPs by reasoning SAFE

Objective: repeat 20.13 for a 4 KiB read, a 128 KiB read and a 1 MiB write (assume MDTS allows it) with MPS 128/256/512. Questions: how does MPS change header overhead?

Solution

4 KiB read: 32/16/8 MWr. 128 KiB read: 1024/512/256 MWr. 1 MiB write with MRRS 512: 2048 MRd; CplD count depends on RC completion size. Each TLP carries roughly 20–30 bytes of framing/header/LCRC overhead in non-Flit mode, so larger MPS improves efficiency. derived

🧪 Lab 20.2 — Intermediate: inspect IOMMU state SAFE

Procedure: run the read-only commands in 20.11; determine whether the NVMe device is in a translated or identity domain and which other devices share its IOMMU group. Questions: what does sharing a group imply for VM pass-through?

Expected reasoning

Devices in one group cannot be isolated from each other and must be assigned together. Domain type "identity" means DMA addresses equal physical addresses for host drivers.

🧪 Lab 20.3 — Advanced: extend the toy IOMMU SAFE

Procedure: add an IOTLB cache with N entries to iommu_sim.py, count misses for a sequential vs random IOVA pattern, then add ATS-style device-side caching and an invalidation call; show that forgetting the invalidation lets the device write to an unmapped page.

Solution sketch

With caching but no invalidation on unmap, a cached translation survives the unmap: the device write succeeds into a page that may now belong to someone else — exactly the hazard ATS invalidation exists to prevent.

🧪 Lab 20.4 — Senior forensic: trace 20.D SAFE

Write a root-cause hypothesis ranking with the evidence needed to confirm each, and a fix-verification plan.

Model answer

Rank (a) IOMMU-blocked read highest given the matching fault address; confirm by mapping the IOVA back to the driver's command (CID → PRP) and checking whether it was mapped at that time; (b) RC stall — would affect other devices too; check other devices' latency; (c) link loss — rejected by absence of link errors. Fix verification: after correcting the mapping lifetime, run the same workload with strict IOTLB invalidation and DMA debugging; expect zero faults and zero completion timeouts over a long soak.

Quiz

  1. Which TLP carries data for an NVMe Read command?

    Answer

    MWr from the controller to host memory.

  2. What must be true in the Command register before the controller can DMA?

    Answer

    Bus Master Enable (bit 2) = 1.

  3. Why are SQ/CQ rings allocated coherent while data buffers are streaming?

    Answer

    Rings are shared concurrently for the queue's lifetime; data buffers are owned by the device for one transfer and handed back.

  4. What does ATS add, and what new obligation does it create?

    Answer

    Device-side caching of translations; software must invalidate the device's ATC when mappings change.

  5. Why does the host see read-data before the CQE?

    Answer

    PCIe ordering: posted writes in the same direction are not reordered by default, so data MWr arrive before the CQE MWr if the controller does not use Relaxed Ordering for the CQE.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Why does DMA exist?
    Model answer

    To move bulk data without consuming CPU cycles on slow device accesses; the device's engine moves data while the CPU does other work.

  2. Beginner What is scatter-gather?
    Model answer

    Describing one transfer as multiple memory segments, because buffers are rarely physically contiguous; NVMe uses PRP lists or SGLs.

  3. Intermediate What is an IOVA?
    Model answer

    An I/O virtual address that the device uses and the IOMMU translates to a physical address, per device domain.

  4. Intermediate List every DMA for an NVMe 4 KiB read.
    Model answer

    SQE fetch (MRd/CplD), data MWr (4 KiB split by MPS), CQE MWr, MSI-X MWr. No PRP list (single page).

  5. Advanced How can an IOMMU reduce NVMe performance and what mitigations exist?
    Model answer

    Map/unmap CPU cost and IOTLB misses add latency; mitigations: passthrough for trusted host drivers, lazy invalidation (flush queues), larger pages, ATS where supported, batching.

  6. Senior A customer reports silent data corruption only with IOMMU disabled. How do you proceed?
    Model answer

    Hypothesis: a stray DMA (late write after unmap, wrong PRP) that the IOMMU normally blocks; enable the IOMMU in strict mode to convert silent corruption into faults with addresses; correlate fault IOVA with command history; check driver timeout/abort paths and PRP list construction; validate with DMA API debug; only then consider device firmware.

🧠 Teach-back

Child: the librarian carries the books, the teacher just writes slips. Junior: walk through Figure 20.1 naming the TLP and address at each arrow. Senior: explain how IOMMU mode, ordering attributes and buffer lifetime interact to produce either faults or silent corruption.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can describe any DMA by initiator, address, translation, TLP type, data return and internal behaviour.
  • I can draw the DMA sequence for NVMe read and write commands.
  • I can explain IOMMU, IOVA, ATS and when each matters.
  • I can compute TLP counts from transfer size, MPS and MRRS.
  • I can localize a DMA failure using BME, IOMMU logs, AER and NVMe status.
  • I can cite the documents that define each piece (PCIe Base, NVMe Base, platform IOMMU spec, Linux DMA API docs).

20.17 Summary, further reading and next

DMA moves data by device-initiated memory transactions: MRd/CplD to read host memory, MWr to write it, MWr for interrupts. NVMe makes the controller the bus master for commands, PRP lists, data, completions and interrupts; the host only rings doorbells. The addresses the controller uses are DMA addresses, possibly translated by an IOMMU, possibly cached by ATS. Buffer lifetime and ordering are where the hard bugs live.

Further reading: Linux Documentation/core-api/dma-api-howto.rst, dma-api.rst; PCIe Base Specification (ordering rules, ATS); Intel VT-d / AMD IOMMU / Arm SMMU architecture specifications; NVMe Base Specification (PRP/SGL). Next: Part IX — NVMe Architecture.

PART IX

NVMe Architecture

Parts VII and VIII gave you a PCIe function with a mapped BAR0 and permission to DMA. Now we put NVMe on top of it. This Part builds the complete mental model — host, driver, subsystem, controller, namespace, media — then explains how the NVM Express specification family has been reorganized since 2.0 into a base specification, command-set specifications and transport specifications, and finally goes deep into the controller as an object (state, properties, types) and into its registers bit by bit, ending with a step-by-step controller initialization you can execute in simulation. Chapters: 21 — What is NVMe?, 22 — NVMe 2.x Architecture, 23 — NVMe Controller, 24 — NVMe Registers.

21 What Is NVMe?

← 20 DMA22 NVMe 2.x Architecture →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Express Base Specification. REVISION: 2.4 (released as part of the NVMe 2.4 specification set announced 4 August 2026 — confirm on nvmexpress.org) version. STATUS: current baseline for this course. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.0 (2011) through 1.4 were single monolithic documents (with separate NVMe over Fabrics and NVMe-MI documents); 2.0 (2021) restructured the family (Chapter 22). SOURCE: https://nvmexpress.org/specifications/ ; https://nvmexpress.org/specification/nvm-express-base-specification/.

21.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineers who learn NVMe as "a faster SATA" or "a list of opcodes" get lost the moment a question involves two controllers, a shared namespace, a fabric transport, or a reset that affects more than one host. NVMe is an architecture — a set of objects (subsystem, controllers, namespaces, queues, ports) with defined relationships — plus a protocol carried by transports. This chapter builds the whole picture first, so that every later detail has a place to land.

21.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: state what NVMe is and name the chain Host → driver → subsystem → controller → namespace → media.
  • Intermediate: explain queue pairs, doorbells, admin vs I/O queues, and how NVMe differs from AHCI/SATA.
  • Advanced: distinguish protocol, command sets and transports; distinguish memory-based (PCIe) and message-based (fabrics) transport models.
  • Senior: reason about which object owns which state (queues belong to controllers; data belongs to namespaces; namespaces belong to the subsystem) and use that to predict the effects of resets and failures.
  • Trace analysis: place every NVMe-related transaction in a trace onto the object model.
  • Debugging / validation: know which Linux object (/dev/nvme0, /dev/nvme0n1, nvme-subsys0) corresponds to which NVMe object.

21.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 19 (BAR0, doorbells as MMIO) and Chapter 20 (DMA of SQEs, data, CQEs). Basic block-storage concepts: a Logical Block Address (LBA) and block size.

21.4 Story: the library, complete

🧒 Kid analogy

The school (host) has teachers (CPU cores). Each teacher has her own request box (Submission Queue) and answer box (Completion Queue) so teachers never fight over boxes. The giant library building is the NVM subsystem. Inside are one or more librarians at desks (controllers) — each desk serves visitors through its own doors. The library has sections (namespaces): "Section 1 — novels, numbered pages 0 to a billion". Behind the sections are the shelves and the warehouse (NAND media) that nobody visits directly. A librarian takes a slip from a box ("read pages 100–107 of section 1 into table 42"), fetches the books, puts them on the table, drops an answer slip, and taps the teacher.

🌍 Real-world analogy

A bank: the bank (subsystem) has several tellers (controllers), each with its own queues; customer accounts (namespaces) are held by the bank, not by a teller — any teller with access can serve an account; the vault (media) is behind everything. Closing one teller's window (controller reset) does not close the bank or delete accounts.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Controllers are not people with judgement — they process commands per the specification, in an order that is generally not guaranteed to match submission order. Namespaces are not just "sections": they have formats (LBA size, metadata), may be shared by controllers in different hosts, may be attached and detached, and may belong to different I/O command sets (block, zoned, key-value). The "warehouse" (flash translation layer, NAND) is entirely implementation-specific and outside the specification.

21.5 The complete mental model

ObjectWhat it isWho creates itState it ownsLinux representation
HostThe system issuing commands; identified by a Host Identifier (and Host NQN for fabrics)—Queues' memory, data buffersThe kernel; /etc/nvme/hostnqn (fabrics)
NVMe driverHost software implementing the protocolOSQueue bookkeeping, command IDs, timeoutsnvme, nvme-core modules
NVM subsystemThe entity containing controllers, namespaces, ports, media; identified by an NVM Subsystem NQN (SUBNQN)Product designNamespaces and their data, subsystem-wide features/sys/class/nvme-subsystem/nvme-subsys0
PortInterface through which controllers are reached (for PCIe: a PCIe port/function)Product design—PCI device (BDF)
ControllerThe interface between host and subsystem: processes commands from its queuesStatic (PCIe, typically) or dynamic (fabrics, on connect)Registers/properties, queues, features, log state, Controller ID (CNTLID)/dev/nvme0 (character device)
NamespaceA quantity of non-volatile storage formatted into logical blocks (or zones, or key-value pairs), identified by NSIDFactory or Namespace Management commandsData, format, protection info/dev/nvme0n1 (block), /dev/ng0n1 (generic char)

21.6 What existed before, and why NVMe is better

AspectAHCI (SATA host controller)NVMe over PCIe
Queues1 command list of up to 32 commands per portUp to 65 535 I/O queues, each up to 65 536 entries (bounded by CAP.MQES and controller limits) verified
Submission costSeveral register accesses, some uncached readsWrite SQE to host memory + one doorbell write (no register reads in the I/O path)
Completion signallingRead status registers to find which command finishedCQE in host memory with phase tag; no register read needed
InterruptsOne per port (MSI possible)MSI-X per completion queue → per-CPU affinity
LockingShared command list → contention across CPUsPer-CPU queues → lock-free submission
Interface to mediaDesigned for rotating disks (ATA command set)Designed for non-volatile memory; command sets for blocks, zones, key-value
Physical pathSATA link (6 Gb/s) behind an HBADirectly on PCIe (multiple lanes, Gen3–Gen6)

The core insight of NVMe: put all per-command state in host memory where the CPU accesses it at cache speed, make the device fetch it by DMA, and reduce CPU→device register traffic to doorbell writes, which are posted and cheap. derived

21.7 Protocol, command sets, transports

  • Protocol — the queueing model (SQ/CQ, doorbells or capsules), the 64-byte command and 16-byte completion formats, the admin command set, the controller state machine, features, log pages, asynchronous events, error reporting. Defined in the Base Specification.
  • I/O command sets — what I/O commands mean for a namespace of a given type: NVM Command Set (logical blocks: Read 02h, Write 01h, Flush 00h, Dataset Management 09h, Write Zeroes 08h, Verify 0Ch, Copy 19h…), Zoned Namespace (zones with sequential-write rules), Key Value, plus Computational Programs and Subsystem Local Memory command sets. Each namespace is associated with one I/O command set, identified by a Command Set Identifier (CSI) version.
  • Transports — how commands, data and completions move between host and controller: PCIe (memory-based: queues in host memory, DMA, MMIO doorbells), RDMA and TCP (message-based: commands and completions travel in capsules), and Fibre Channel (the FC mapping is defined by INCITS T11 as FC-NVMe, with NVMe-side requirements in NVMe documents) verified.
📡 Memory-based vs message-based

On PCIe, a "submission" is the host writing an SQE to its own memory and ringing a doorbell; the controller pulls the SQE. On fabrics, the host sends a command capsule (SQE plus optional in-capsule data) over the network; the controller sends back a response capsule containing the CQE. Same 64-byte command, same 16-byte completion, different delivery. Registers on PCIe correspond to properties on fabrics, accessed with Property Get/Set commands. verified

21.8 The command lifecycle in ten lines

  1. Application issues a read; the block layer picks the per-CPU hardware queue.
  2. Driver allocates a Command Identifier (CID), builds a 64-byte SQE (opcode 02h Read, NSID, SLBA in CDW10–11, NLB in CDW12, PRP1/PRP2 in DPTR bytes 24–39).
  3. Driver writes the SQE at SQ tail, advances tail, writes SQyTDBL.
  4. Controller fetches the SQE (MRd/CplD).
  5. Controller reads media (internal) and writes data (MWr) to PRP addresses.
  6. Controller writes a 16-byte CQE (DW2: SQ Head Pointer and SQ Identifier; DW3: CID, Phase Tag, Status) to the CQ.
  7. Controller sends MSI-X (unless coalesced/masked).
  8. Driver sees the new phase tag, matches CID to the request, checks status (SCT/SC, DNR, More).
  9. Driver writes CQyHDBL to release CQ entries; uses SQHD to know SQ slots are free.
  10. Block layer completes the request to the application.

21.9 Linux view

sudo nvme list                       # namespaces with their controller and model
sudo nvme list -v                    # subsystems → controllers → namespaces (newer nvme-cli)
sudo nvme list-subsys                # subsystem NQN, controllers, transport, address
ls /sys/class/nvme/ /sys/class/nvme-subsystem/ /sys/block/ | grep nvme
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | head -40   # controller identity (VID, SN, MN, FR, CNTLID, VER …)
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | head -30   # namespace size, capacity, LBA formats
cat /proc/interrupts | grep nvme          # per-queue vectors
⚠️ Naming trap

In Linux, nvme0n1 means "namespace 1 as seen through the subsystem/controller instance 0", but with native NVMe multipath the block device is attached to the subsystem and the controller numbers in the name may not match the controller actually used for I/O impl. Always confirm with nvme list -v or sysfs.

21.10 Common mistakes

  • "The SSD is the controller." The SSD is (usually) a subsystem containing one controller per PCIe function.
  • "Namespaces belong to controllers." They belong to the subsystem and are attached to controllers.
  • "NVMe means PCIe." NVMe is transport-independent; NVMe over PCIe is one transport.
  • "Commands complete in order." They need not; CID matching exists for this reason.
  • "VS in BAR0 tells me which features exist." It reports the specification version; individual features are discovered from CAP and Identify fields.

Quiz

  1. Name the six-link chain of the NVMe mental model.

    Answer

    Host → NVMe driver → NVM subsystem → controller → namespace → media.

  2. What is the difference between a command set and a transport?

    Answer

    A command set defines the meaning of I/O commands for a namespace type (blocks, zones, key-value…); a transport defines how commands/data/completions are delivered (PCIe, RDMA, TCP, FC).

  3. Why does NVMe avoid register reads in the I/O path?

    Answer

    MMIO reads are non-posted round trips costing on the order of a microsecond; NVMe puts completions in host memory with a phase tag instead.

  4. Which object does a controller reset destroy, and which does it not?

    Answer

    It destroys that controller's queues and volatile controller state; it does not delete namespaces or their data (which belong to the subsystem).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is NVMe?
    Model answer

    A host-controller interface and protocol for non-volatile storage, built around many paired submission/completion queues in host memory, with defined command sets and multiple transports.

  2. Intermediate Compare NVMe with AHCI.
    Model answer

    Many deep queues vs one 32-entry list; doorbell-only submission vs multiple register accesses; per-queue MSI-X vs per-port interrupts; designed for NVM vs rotating disks.

  3. Advanced How do registers on PCIe relate to properties on fabrics?
    Model answer

    The Base Specification defines controller properties; the PCIe transport maps them into BAR0 MMIO; fabrics access them with Property Get/Set commands.

  4. Senior Two hosts see the same namespace via different controllers. What can go wrong and what does NVMe provide?
    Model answer

    Concurrent writers can corrupt each other's data without coordination; NVMe provides reservations (and ANA for multipath access state), but correctness above blocks is the responsibility of a cluster-aware file system or application.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can draw Figure 21.1 from memory and explain each arrow.
  • I can say which object owns queues, which owns data, and which owns registers.
  • I can distinguish protocol, command set and transport with examples.
  • I can map Linux device nodes to NVMe objects.

21.11 Summary, further reading and next

NVMe = an object model (subsystem, controllers, namespaces, ports, queues) + a queueing protocol (Base Specification) + I/O command sets + transports. On PCIe, queues live in host memory, doorbells are MMIO, and the controller does all bulk movement by DMA. Further reading: NVMe Base Specification (theory of operation and architecture chapters); nvme-cli documentation. Next: Chapter 22 — NVMe 2.x Architecture.

22 NVMe 2.x Architecture

← 21 What Is NVMe?23 NVMe Controller →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: the NVMe specification family. REVISION SET: NVMe 2.4 set (announced 4 August 2026). STATUS: current baseline per the course brief — confirm every revision number on nvmexpress.org. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: 1.x monolithic base; 2.0 (June 2021) restructuring; 2.1 and later sets added documents and features. SOURCE: https://nvmexpress.org/specifications/ and the Revision Changes page https://nvmexpress.org/specification/nvm-express-revision-changes/.

22.1 Why this chapter exists

If you open "the NVMe spec" and search for the Read command, you will not find its full definition in the Base Specification — it lives in the NVM Command Set Specification. If you search the Base Specification for the doorbell stride formula, you may find it moved to the PCIe Transport Specification. Engineers trained on NVMe 1.4 routinely waste hours looking in the wrong document. This chapter is your map of the family: what each document owns, why the family was split, and how to find any answer.

22.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: list the documents in the NVMe specification family and what each covers.
  • Intermediate: explain why the family was modularized in 2.0 and how content from 1.4 maps to 2.x documents.
  • Advanced: use Command Set Identifiers, I/O Command Set discovery and controller types correctly.
  • Senior: judge whether a behaviour is base, command-set, or transport-specific, and which revisions of which documents a product must claim.
  • Validation: build a compliance matrix keyed by (document, revision, feature).

22.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 21 (protocol vs command set vs transport).

22.4 Story

🧒 Kid analogy

The library rule book got so thick nobody could carry it. So the librarians split it: one main rule book for how every library works (how to queue, how to ask questions, how to open and close), one small book per kind of section (novels, maps, puzzle boxes), and one small book per way of getting to the library (by road, by train, by boat). Now when a new kind of section opens, they write a new small book and don't reprint the main one.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The books are released together as a set with coordinated revision numbers, and they cross-reference each other heavily; you often need two or three of them open to answer one question (e.g. PRP rules in Base + Read command in NVM Command Set + doorbell layout in PCIe Transport).

22.5 The specification family (2.4 baseline)

DocumentBaseline revision versionOwnsTypical questions answered there
NVM Express Base Specification2.4Architecture (subsystem, controller, namespace, ports), queue model, command and completion formats, Admin Command Set, controller properties (registers), controller initialization and shutdown, reset types, features, log pages, asynchronous events, error/status codes, security, namespace management, virtualization, fabrics architecture (since 2.0)"What does CC.SHN do?", "What are the Identify CNS values?", "What is the status code for X?"
NVM Command Set Specification1.3Logical-block namespaces: Read, Write, Flush, Compare, Write Zeroes, Dataset Management, Verify, Copy, Write Uncorrectable; LBA formats, end-to-end protection, NVM-specific Identify structures"How is SLBA encoded?", "What does FUA mean for Write?"
Zoned Namespace (ZNS) Command Set Specification1.5Zones, zone states, Zone Append, Zone Management Send/Receive"When does a zone become Full?"

NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification1.4PCIe-specific mapping: register map in BAR0, doorbells and stride, PCI header/capability requirements, interrupts (MSI/MSI-X/INTx), memory-based queue rules, CMB/PMR specifics uncertain (some PCIe-related content remains in Base — check)"How do I compute a doorbell offset?", "Which BAR holds the registers?"
NVMe over RDMA Transport Specification1.3Capsule exchange over RDMA (RoCE, iWARP, InfiniBand)"How is in-capsule data sized?"

Notes: the Admin Command Set is not a separate document — it is part of the Base Specification verified. The Fibre Channel transport binding (FC-NVMe) is standardized by INCITS T11, not by NVM Express. Exact release dates of the SLM, Computational Programs and Boot documents should be checked on nvmexpress.org; they were added to the family after the 2.0 restructuring uncertain (dates not asserted here).

22.6 Why NVMe was modularized

  1. Size and navigability. By 1.4 the base document had grown very large, mixing PCIe-specific register details, block-storage command details and architecture. Readers needed only a fraction for any one task.
  2. Transport independence. NVMe over Fabrics was a separate document layered awkwardly on a PCIe-centric base. In 2.0 the fabrics architecture moved into the Base Specification and each transport got its own document — PCIe became "a transport" rather than "the" NVMe.
  3. Multiple I/O command sets. Zoned Namespaces and Key Value needed first-class status. Defining the block-storage commands in a separate NVM Command Set Specification made "an I/O command set" a pluggable concept, with discovery via I/O Command Set profiles and the Identify I/O Command Set data structure version.
  4. Independent evolution. A new command set (later: SLM, Computational Programs) or a transport change can be released without re-ratifying unrelated text; revisions of each document advance at their own pace (hence Base 2.4 alongside NVM 1.3 and ZNS 1.5).
  5. Cleaner compliance claims. A product can state exactly which documents and revisions it implements.
💡 Senior insight

The restructuring changed where things are written, not how a PCIe NVMe SSD works on the wire. A 1.4-era SSD and a 2.x SSD both use the same SQE/CQE formats, the same doorbells and the same admin queue registers. What changed for host software: new controller types, I/O Command Set selection in CC.CSS, new CAP/CC fields, new Identify CNS values, and the mental model that NVMe is transport-agnostic. When reading any statement, always ask: "Is this base, command-set, or transport?"

22.7 Mapping 1.4 knowledge to 2.x documents
