22.8 I/O Command Set discovery and selection

Since 2.0, a controller may support several I/O command sets. The host learns and selects them through a defined sequence version:

  1. Read CAP.CSS (bits 44:37). Bit 37 (in the CSS field: bit 0) = NVM Command Set supported; bit 43 (CSS bit 6) = one or more I/O Command Sets supported (I/O Command Set profiles); bit 44 (CSS bit 7) = no I/O command set supported (admin-only controller).
  2. Set CC.CSS (bits 6:4) before enabling: 000b = NVM Command Set; 110b = all supported I/O Command Sets (requires CAP.CSS bit 43); 111b = Admin Command Set only.
  3. If CC.CSS = 110b: issue Identify with the CNS value for the Identify I/O Command Set data structure to list supported command-set combinations, then select one with the I/O Command Set Profile feature (Set Features).
  4. For each namespace, discover its Command Set Identifier (CSI) via the Namespace Identification Descriptor list, and use I/O-command-set-specific Identify (CNS values that take a CSI) to read its type-specific structure. Commonly cited CSI values: 00h NVM, 01h Key Value, 02h Zoned Namespace; values for newer command sets: check the Base Specification.
📭 What must be checked in the specification

The exact CNS codes for "Identify I/O Command Set data structure" and the I/O-command-set-specific Identify variants, and the CSI values of SLM and Computational Programs command sets, must be taken from the current Base Specification — this course does not assert them.

Administrative controllerManagement-only: e.g. configuring namespaces, firmware, monitoring, without I/ONoPCIe or fabrics implCAP.CSS bit 44 (no I/O command set) set; host uses CC.CSS = 111b
Discovery controllerProvides Discovery log pages listing NVMe-oF subsystems/ports a host may connect toNoFabricsReached via the well-known discovery NQN; Get Log Page for the Discovery log

The Identify Controller data structure has a Controller Type field reporting which one you are talking to verified (check its byte offset in the Base Specification).

22.10 The 2.4 release highlights — what they are and where they belong

Per the announcement of the NVMe 2.4 set (4 August 2026), highlights include the following. This course states purpose only; details must be read in the normative documents.

HighlightPurpose (paraphrased)Likely homeRelevance to PCIe/NVMe trace analysis

PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem MigrationSupport migrating an NVM subsystem exported over PCIe (virtualization/live-migration scenarios)Base + PCIe Transport uncertainMedium for virtualization validation

⚠️ Truth policy

Do not infer command opcodes, field names or log identifiers for these features from this table. Read the 2.4 documents and the Revision Changes page; also check which Technical Proposals (TPs) and Engineering Change Notices (ECNs) were incorporated.

22.11 How to find any answer in the family

QuestionOpen firstThen
What does this register field mean?Base (controller properties)PCIe Transport for its BAR0 placement/access rules
What does this status code mean?Base (generic/command-specific status)Command-set spec for command-set-specific status values
How is a Read encoded?NVM Command SetBase for SQE common fields and PRP/SGL
What is this TLP for?PCIe Base (PCI-SIG)NVMe PCIe Transport for what the controller does with it
What changed in revision X?Revision Changes page; change list in the documentRatified TPs/ECNs
Is a feature mandatory?Requirements tables in the relevant spec (mandatory/optional per controller type)Identify fields that report support
📘 Normative language

"shall" = requirement; "should" = recommendation (a reasoned exception is allowed); "may" = permission/optional. Informative notes and examples are not requirements. Reserved fields must not be given meaning; vendor-specific fields are by definition not interoperable.

Quiz

  1. Which document defines the Identify admin command?

    Answer

    The NVM Express Base Specification (Admin Command Set is in Base).

  2. Which document defines the Write command's fields?

    Answer

    The NVM Command Set Specification (with common SQE fields from Base).

  3. What does CC.CSS = 111b select?

    Answer

    Admin Command Set only (no I/O command set).

  4. Name three reasons for the 2.0 restructuring.

    Answer

    Navigability/size, transport independence (fabrics in base, per-transport docs), first-class multiple I/O command sets, independent evolution, cleaner compliance.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is in the NVMe Base Specification?
    Model answer

    Architecture, queueing model, command/completion formats, Admin Command Set, properties/registers semantics, initialization/reset/shutdown, features, logs, errors, security, fabrics architecture.

  2. Intermediate How does a host discover which I/O command sets a controller supports?
    Model answer

    CAP.CSS bits, then (if I/O command sets supported) select CC.CSS=110b, Identify the I/O Command Set data structure, choose a profile via Set Features, discover per-namespace CSI through the namespace descriptor list.

  3. Advanced Why are command sets versioned separately from Base?
    Model answer

    So they can evolve independently; a ZNS change need not reissue Base; products claim combinations of revisions.

  4. Senior A customer asks whether your drive "supports NVMe 2.4". How do you answer precisely?
    Model answer

    Break it down: which Base revision the controller reports (VS), which mandatory features of that revision are implemented, which optional features (listed with Identify evidence), which command-set and transport revisions are claimed, and any compliance test results (e.g. interoperability test suites). "Supports 2.4" without that breakdown is not an engineering statement.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can list every document in the 2.4 family and what it owns.
  • I can say where any 1.4-era topic lives in 2.x.
  • I can explain CAP.CSS / CC.CSS and the I/O Command Set discovery flow.
  • I can distinguish I/O, administrative and discovery controllers.
  • I can describe the 2.4 highlights by purpose without inventing details.

22.14 Summary, further reading and next

NVMe 2.x is a family: Base (architecture + admin + properties), I/O command sets (NVM, ZNS, KV, SLM, Computational Programs), transports (PCIe, RDMA, TCP), NVMe-MI and Boot. Modularization made NVMe transport-agnostic and command-set-pluggable. Further reading: nvmexpress.org specification index and Revision Changes page; the "Changes" appendices in each document. 23 NVMe Controller

← 22 NVMe 2.x Architecture24 NVMe Registers →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Express Base Specification (architecture, controller model, resets, shutdown, Identify Controller); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (PCIe-specific reset interactions). REVISION: Base 2.4, PCIe Transport 1.4 version. STATUS: current baseline. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: controller types (I/O, administrative, discovery) are 2.0-era terminology; CRIME/ready-mode fields are 2.0+; Identify fields grow with every revision. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org.

23.1 Why this chapter exists

Most NVMe confusion in reviews and bug reports comes from mixing up two objects: the controller and the namespace. "The drive reset" — which object? "The namespace is read-only" — or is the controller in a degraded state? "Queue 3 belongs to namespace 1" — no, queues belong to controllers and can carry commands for any attached namespace. This chapter makes the controller a precise object with identity, properties, state and lifecycle, and separates it from the subsystem and namespace so cleanly that you will never mix them again.

23.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: define subsystem, controller, host and namespace and give one example of each on a real SSD.
  • Intermediate: explain controller properties, controller state (disabled, ready, shutdown, fatal) and how CC/CSTS express it.
  • Advanced: explain reset types (Controller Level Reset, NVM Subsystem Reset, PCIe Conventional Reset, Function Level Reset) and their scope; static vs dynamic controllers; primary/secondary controllers under SR-IOV.
  • Senior: predict the blast radius of an action (reset, format, namespace detach, firmware activation) by reasoning about which object owns which state.
  • Trace analysis: read a controller lifecycle from CC/CSTS accesses and admin commands in a trace.
  • Debugging/validation: design checks for controller identity, state transitions and reset scope.

23.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 21 (object model), Chapter 22 (controller types). Register names CC and CSTS are introduced here and dissected in Chapter 24.

23.4 Story

🧒 Kid analogy

The library (subsystem) has a front desk (controller). The desk has a light: off (disabled), blinking while it starts up, green (ready), orange while closing for the night (shutdown processing), and red (fatal — "something is badly wrong, call the manager"). The desk has its own in-tray and out-tray (queues). The books are in sections (namespaces) that belong to the library, not to the desk. If the desk closes and reopens, its trays are emptied — but no books are lost. If the whole library is reset, every desk closes at once.

🌍 Real-world analogy

A database server process (controller) serving connections (queues) to tables stored on disk (namespaces). Restarting the server process drops connections and in-flight transactions but not the tables. Two server processes can serve the same table (shared namespace) — and then you need locking (reservations).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

NVMe does not guarantee what happens to commands in flight at reset time beyond what the spec says (commands may or may not have been executed; the host must treat them as having unknown status). And "the library" might physically be one chip — the subsystem/controller split is architectural, not necessarily physical.

23.5.1 Controller vs namespace — the litmus tests

StatementAbout the controller or the namespace?Why
"Maximum queue entries is 1024"ControllerCAP.MQES is a controller property
"Block size is 4096 bytes"NamespaceLBA format is per namespace (Identify Namespace, FLBAS)
"Maximum transfer is 128 KiB"ControllerMDTS in Identify Controller (namespace-level limits may further apply in some command sets)
"Capacity is 1.92 TB"NamespaceNSZE/NCAP in Identify Namespace (the subsystem may report total NVM capacity separately)
"Firmware revision is X"Controller (reports it); firmware usually applies subsystem-wide implIdentify Controller FR; firmware slot log

"Queue 3 is full"ControllerQueues are controller objects; any attached namespace's commands may be in it
"Data is protected with PI type 1"NamespaceEnd-to-end protection is a namespace format property
"CSTS.CFS = 1"ControllerFatal status of this controller only (other controllers in the subsystem may be fine)
📌 Remember

Queues and registers → controller. Data and format → namespace. Namespaces belong to the subsystem and are attached to controllers. A command names its namespace with the NSID field (CDW1); the queue it travels on names the controller.

23.6 Controller properties

The Base Specification defines the controller's configuration and status as properties with offsets in a property address space (CAP at 00h, VS at 08h, CC at 14h, CSTS at 1Ch, NSSR at 20h, AQA at 24h, ASQ at 28h, ACQ at 30h, …). The PCIe transport maps that property space into BAR0 as MMIO registers (and adds the doorbells at 1000h and above); fabrics transports access properties with Property Get / Property Set commands verified. Some properties are PCIe-only (e.g. INTMS/INTMC for pin-based/MSI interrupt masking, doorbells, CMB/PMR registers) verified.

Property groupExamplesWho writesPurpose
Capabilities (RO)CAP, VS, CMBSZ, PMRCAP, CRTOControllerAdvertise limits and optional support
Configuration (RW)CC, AQA, ASQ, ACQ, INTMS/INTMC, CMBMSCHostConfigure before/at enable
Status (RO / RW1C)CSTS, CMBSTS, PMRSTSController (host clears certain bits)Report state
ActionsNSSR, doorbellsHostTrigger actions

StateCCCSTSWhat the host may doTrace signature
DisabledEN=0RDY=0Program AQA/ASQ/ACQ and CC fields; no commands processedMWr to 24h–37h, 14h
EnablingEN=1RDY=0Poll CSTS; wait up to CAP.TO × 500 ms (or CRTO-based timeouts in 2.x when applicable) versionRepeated MRd of 1Ch
ReadyEN=1RDY=1, CFS=0, SHST=00bSubmit admin and I/O commandsDoorbell MWr, DMA
Shutdown processingSHN=01b or 10bSHST=01bWait; no new commandsMRd of 1Ch polling
Shutdown completeSHN setSHST=10bSafe to remove power; to use again, reset (EN=0 then re-init)—

23.8 Resets and their scope

ResetTriggered byScopeQueuesNamespaces/dataPCIe config
Controller Level Reset (via CC.EN 1→0)Host writes CC.EN=0One controllerAll I/O queues deleted; admin queue resetUnaffected (committed data persists; in-flight commands' outcome unknown)Unaffected
Function Level Reset (FLR)Initiate FLR in PCIe Device ControlThe PCIe function → its controllerDeletedUnaffectedFunction's config state reset (BARs, Command) — host must restore
PCIe Conventional Reset (hot reset, link down, PERST#)Secondary Bus Reset, link disable, platformEverything below the portDeletedUnaffectedReset
NVM Subsystem ResetWrite 4E564D65h ("NVMe") to NSSR (if CAP.NSSRS=1), or subsystem power cycleAll controllers in the subsystemDeleted everywhereUnaffected; may activate pending firmware implFor PCIe, may cause link down/re-train verified (host must handle)

Notes verified (confirm wording in your revision): on a Controller Level Reset initiated by CC.EN 1→0 the Admin Queue registers (AQA, ASQ, ACQ) are not reset, while other controller state is; drivers reprogram them anyway for robustness. Persistent features (saveable) and namespace data survive all of these resets; volatile features return to defaults. CSTS.NSSRO ("NVM Subsystem Reset Occurred") lets the host detect that an NVM Subsystem Reset happened.

⚠️ Safety

NSSR affects every controller in the subsystem — on a dual-port SSD, the other host loses its queues too. Never use it as a "stronger reset" casually; it is an EXPERT LAB action on dedicated hardware.

23.9 Shutdown

  1. Host stops submitting I/O, optionally deletes I/O queues (good practice: delete SQs then CQs).
  2. Host writes CC.SHN = 01b (normal) or 10b (abrupt).
  3. Controller sets CSTS.SHST = 01b while processing, then 10b when complete — at which point volatile data the controller is responsible for (e.g. write cache content, internal metadata) has been made non-volatile per the specification's shutdown semantics.
  4. Host may now remove power. Linux waits for SHST=10b with a timeout (module parameter shutdown_timeout) impl.

Unsafe shutdowns (power lost before SHST=10b) are counted in the SMART / Health Information log (Unsafe Shutdowns) — a frequently used validation signal verified. NVMe 2.x adds subsystem-level shutdown (NSSD register, CAP.NSSS) and shutdown-type reporting (CSTS.ST) version.

23.10 Controller identity: Identify Controller essentials

FieldMeaningWhy you care
VID / SSVIDPCI Vendor ID / Subsystem Vendor ID (as reported in Identify)Match against config space; mismatch suggests reading the wrong device
SN / MN / FRSerial Number, Model Number, Firmware Revision (ASCII)Stable identifiers for automation; firmware version gating
MDTSMaximum Data Transfer Size, power of two in units of CAP.MPSMIN (0 = no limit)Driver splits larger I/O; test boundary cases
CNTLIDController IDDistinguish controllers within a subsystem; appears in logs and reservations
VERVersion (same encoding as VS)Cross-check with the VS register
CTRATTController attributes (bit flags for optional behaviours)Capability discovery
Controller TypeI/O, discovery or administrative (2.0+)Which commands are valid
OACS / ONCSOptional Admin / NVM Command SupportGate use of optional commands (namespace management, format, sanitize, DSM, write zeroes…)
SQES / CQESRequired and maximum SQ/CQ entry sizes (powers of two)Values to put in CC.IOSQES / CC.IOCQES (64 B / 16 B for NVM)
NNNumber of Namespaces (maximum valid NSID)Bounds namespace enumeration
SGLSSGL supportWhether the driver may use SGLs instead of PRPs
SUBNQNNVM Subsystem NQNIdentifies the subsystem; multipath grouping
CMICMulti-path I/O and namespace sharing capabilitiesWhether multiple controllers/ports exist and namespaces may be shared

The byte offsets of these fields are defined in the Identify Controller data structure; consult the Base Specification rather than memorized offsets, as later revisions add fields in previously reserved bytes version.

23.11 Deep dive: the subsystem

  • Ports — each PCIe port of a dual-port SSD is a separate PCIe function connected to a different host (or the same host for multipath). Each has its own BDF, BARs and controller.
  • Shared namespaces — the namespace's Identify data indicates whether it may be attached to multiple controllers (NMIC). Coordination is via reservations (Reservation Register/Acquire/Release/Report) verified.
  • Asymmetric Namespace Access (ANA) — reports per-controller access state for groups of namespaces (optimized, non-optimized, inaccessible, persistent loss, change) so multipath hosts pick paths verified.
  • Subsystem-wide actions — NVM Subsystem Reset, firmware activation (often), sanitize (affects all namespaces), subsystem shutdown (2.x).
  • Virtualization — with SR-IOV, a primary controller (on the PF) can manage secondary controllers (on VFs), assigning them queue and interrupt resources (Virtualization Management command) version.

23.12 Linux view

sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H | less      # -H decodes bit fields (OACS, ONCS, CMIC...)
sudo nvme list-subsys /dev/nvme0n1          # subsystem NQN, controllers, paths
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/{cntlid,state,transport,address,model,serial,firmware_rev}
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/subsysnqn
sudo nvme list-ctrl /dev/nvme0n1            # controllers that have this namespace attached (if supported)
sudo nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 --all          # allocated namespace IDs (requires namespace mgmt support)

The sysfs state attribute reports the driver's controller state machine (e.g. live, resetting, connecting, deleting, dead) — this is Linux's state, related to but not identical with the NVMe CC/CSTS state impl.

23.13 Code: a controller object model

class Subsystem:
    nqn; namespaces: dict[nsid → Namespace]; controllers: dict[cntlid → Controller]
    def nvm_subsystem_reset():
        for c in controllers: c.reset(level="subsystem")       # every controller loses queues
        set CSTS.NSSRO on each controller

class Controller:
    cntlid; regs (CAP, VS, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ, ACQ, ...); queues; attached: set[nsid]
    def reset(level):
        abort/forget outstanding commands  # host must treat them as status unknown
        delete I/O SQs/CQs; reset admin queue; CSTS.RDY = 0
        features: volatile → defaults; saveable → saved values
    def submit(cmd):
        if cmd.nsid not in attached and cmd needs a namespace: return Invalid Namespace or Format
        ...

class Namespace:
    nsid; format (LBA size, metadata, PI); data
    # survives every controller reset; changed only by Format/Sanitize/Write/Delete

💡 Senior insight

Before any destructive or disruptive action, write down its scope: one command, one queue, one controller, one namespace, all namespaces, the whole subsystem, the PCIe function, or everything below a port. Most production incidents involving NVMe maintenance are scope surprises, not protocol bugs.

CategoryItems
verifiedObject model; properties and PCIe mapping; CC.EN/CSTS.RDY handshake; SHN/SHST; NSSR value 4E564D65h; reset types; reservations and ANA exist; Identify Controller fields listed.

Never assumeThat a reset of one controller is invisible to other hosts (it may be, NSSR is not); that BDF ↔ controller ↔ namespace mapping is fixed.

23.17 Labs

🧪 Lab 23.1 — Map your objects SAFE

Procedure: using 23.12 commands, fill a table: subsystem NQN, controller(s) with CNTLID and BDF, namespaces with NSID, LBA size and capacity. Identify which facts came from Identify Controller and which from Identify Namespace.

Expected reasoning

A typical client SSD: one subsystem, one controller (CNTLID often 0 or 1 impl), one namespace (NSID 1). Facts like MDTS, SN, FR, SQES/CQES come from the controller; NSZE, LBA formats from the namespace.

🧪 Lab 23.2 — Controller reset in a VM CAUTION

Setup: QEMU VM with an extra (non-root) NVMe device. Procedure: sudo nvme reset /dev/nvme1 while watching dmesg -w; then check that nvme id-ns data and file contents on the namespace are unchanged. Questions: what was lost, what persisted?

Expected reasoning

Queues were torn down and re-created (driver messages), interrupts re-bound; namespace data and format persisted — demonstrating controller vs namespace ownership.

🧪 Lab 23.3 — Simulate scope SAFE

Implement the pseudocode model in 23.13 in Python with two controllers and a shared namespace; implement controller reset and NSSR; print which queues and outstanding commands are lost in each case.

Solution sketch

Controller reset clears only that controller's queue table; NSSR clears both and sets NSSRO on both; namespace dictionaries are untouched in both cases.

🧪 Lab 23.4 — Senior forensic: trace 23.D SAFE

Write the incident timeline and a prevention rule for maintenance on dual-port drives.

Model answer

Timeline: host A activated firmware with a reset that was subsystem-scoped; port 2 link reset; controller 2 lost queues; host B saw I/O errors, then recovered; NSSRO=1 on controller 2 and the firmware slot log confirm. Prevention: treat firmware activation and NSSR as subsystem-scope changes requiring coordination with every host attached to the subsystem (quiesce multipath, fail over, or schedule).

Quiz

  1. Does a Controller Level Reset erase namespace data?

    Answer

    No. It resets controller state and deletes queues; namespace data belongs to the subsystem.

  2. What value written to NSSR starts an NVM Subsystem Reset?

    Answer

    4E564D65h (ASCII "NVMe"), only if CAP.NSSRS = 1.

  3. Which register bits show shutdown progress?

    Answer

    CSTS.SHST: 00b normal operation, 01b processing, 10b complete.

  4. Is "maximum data transfer size" a namespace or controller property?

    Answer

    Controller (Identify Controller MDTS).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Controller vs namespace?
    Model answer

    Controller = command-processing interface with registers and queues; namespace = formatted storage addressed by NSID, owned by the subsystem and attached to controllers.

  2. Intermediate Walk through CC/CSTS during enable and shutdown.
    Model answer

    Enable: EN=0 → wait RDY=0 → program AQA/ASQ/ACQ and CC → EN=1 → wait RDY=1 within TO. Shutdown: SHN=01b → wait SHST=10b → power off or EN=0 to reuse.

  3. Advanced Compare FLR, Controller Level Reset and NSSR.
    Model answer

    CLR: one controller via CC.EN, config space intact. FLR: PCIe function reset incl. config state; controller reset implied. NSSR: all controllers of the subsystem; may cause PCIe link reset; NSSRO reports it.

  4. Senior How would you design a validation plan for reset robustness?
    Model answer

    Matrix of reset types × controller states (idle, heavy I/O, mid-admin command, during shutdown, during firmware download) × host topologies (single/dual port); checks: data integrity of committed writes, no stale completions after reset, correct NSSRO/AEN behaviour, ready-time within TO, feature persistence rules, AER cleanliness, unsafe-shutdown counters.

🧠 Teach-back

Child: the desk can close and reopen without losing library books. Junior: explain Figure 23.1 and the reset table. Senior: argue the blast radius of firmware activation on a dual-port drive in a multipath cluster.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can classify any property or statement as controller, namespace or subsystem.
  • I can draw the controller state diagram with CC/CSTS values.
  • I can explain each reset type's scope and effects.
  • I can interpret Identify Controller essentials and cross-check with registers.
  • I can read controller lifecycle events in a trace.

23.18 Summary, further reading and next

The controller is the command-processing interface with properties (registers), queues and state; the namespace is formatted storage owned by the subsystem; the subsystem contains both and defines the scope of subsystem-wide actions. CC and CSTS express controller state; resets differ in scope. Further reading: NVMe Base Specification (architecture, controller initialization, reset, shutdown, Identify Controller, reservations, ANA). Next: Chapter 24 — NVMe Registers.

📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVM Express Base Specification 2.4 (controller properties: definitions and semantics) and NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification 1.4 (memory-mapped placement in BAR0, doorbells, PCIe-only registers) version. STATUS: current baseline — confirm on nvmexpress.org. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.0–1.4 controllers lack 2.x fields (e.g. CAP.CRMS, CC.CRIME, CSTS.ST, NSSD, CRTO); CMB control registers (CMBMSC, CMBSTS…) and PMR registers arrived in 1.4; boot partition registers in 1.3. Reserved bits in an older controller read as 0. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org; Linux include/linux/nvme.h (openly readable register and field definitions).

24.1 Why this chapter exists

The register block in BAR0 is where the host and the controller first shake hands and where, when things go wrong, the controller says so (CSTS.CFS). Every NVMe bring-up, every reset, every "drive not ready" ticket and every driver port goes through these registers. The master curriculum demands depth: for each register — address, width, fields, purpose, reset behaviour, host interaction, controller interaction, trace consequences — without inventing field values. This chapter delivers that, then assembles the registers into the full controller initialization sequence and lets you execute it against a simulated controller.

24.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: name the registers at 00h–37h and the doorbell region, and say what each is for.
  • Intermediate: decode CAP, VS, CC, CSTS and AQA values by hand and with code.
  • Advanced: perform and justify every step of the controller initialization sequence; compute doorbell addresses for any DSTRD; reason about timeouts from CAP.TO.
  • Senior: diagnose initialization failures from a register trace; reason about reset behaviour and version differences; design register-level conformance tests.
  • Trace analysis: decode every MMIO TLP to BAR0 into a register access with meaning.
  • Validation: verify RO fields are stable, RW fields behave, invalid configurations are handled per spec.

24.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 19 (BAR0 and MMIO), Chapter 20 (queue memory is DMA memory), Chapter 23 (controller state).

24.4 Story

🧒 Kid analogy

The librarian's desk has a control panel. A brass plate you can only read (CAP: "I can hold 1024 slips per box, I need up to 20 seconds to wake up, my bells are 4 steps apart"). A version sticker (VS). A row of switches you set (CC: "start working", "use page size 4 KiB", "slips are 64 bytes"). Status lights (CSTS: ready, fatal, shutting down). Two hooks where you hang the addresses of the very first request box and answer box (ASQ, ACQ) and a dial for their sizes (AQA). And a long wall of bells (doorbells), one pair for each box pair.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The panel is not just read and set at leisure: some switches must only be changed while the desk is off (most CC fields with EN=0), some lights take time to change after you flip a switch (RDY after EN), and pressing the wrong bell (an invalid doorbell offset or value) is reported as an error event rather than ignored.

24.6 CAP — Controller Capabilities (00h, 64-bit, RO)

BitsFieldMeaningHost use
15:0MQES — Maximum Queue Entries SupportedLargest individual queue size, 0's based (value 3FFh = 1024 entries). Minimum value 1 (2 entries). Applies to I/O queues; admin queue limits are separate (AQA up to 4096 entries).Bound I/O queue sizes in Create I/O SQ/CQ
16CQR — Contiguous Queues Required1 = I/O queues must be physically contiguous (no PRP-list-described queues)Allocate contiguous queue memory (Linux always does)
18:17AMS — Arbitration Mechanism SupportedBit 17: Weighted Round Robin with Urgent Priority Class; bit 18: vendor specific. Round robin is always supported.Choose CC.AMS
23:19Reserved
31:24TO — TimeoutWorst-case time for CSTS.RDY to change after CC.EN changes, in 500 ms unitsHost timeout when polling RDY
35:32DSTRD — Doorbell StrideDoorbell spacing = 2(2+DSTRD) bytes (4 << DSTRD)Compute doorbell offsets
36NSSRS — NVM Subsystem Reset Supported1 = NSSR register implementedGate use of NSSR
44:37CSS — Command Sets SupportedBit 37: NVM Command Set; bit 43: one or more I/O Command Sets (2.0+); bit 44: No I/O Command Set (admin-only, 2.0+); others reservedChoose CC.CSS
45BPS — Boot Partition Support1 = boot partitions supportedGate BPINFO/BPRSEL use
47:46CPS — Controller Power ScopeScope of controller power management (version-dependent) versionInterpret power features
51:48MPSMIN — Memory Page Size MinimumMin page = 2(12+MPSMIN)Lower bound for CC.MPS
55:52MPSMAX — Memory Page Size MaximumMax page = 2(12+MPSMAX)Upper bound for CC.MPS
56PMRS — Persistent Memory Region Supported1 = PMR registers implementedGate PMR
57CMBS — Controller Memory Buffer Supported1 = CMB supported (and CMBMSC usable, 1.4+)Gate CMB
58NSSS — NVM Subsystem Shutdown Supported2.0+ versionGate NSSD
60:59CRMS — Controller Ready Modes SupportedBit 59: Controller Ready With Media; bit 60: Controller Ready Independent of Media (2.0+) versionChoose CC.CRIME; select timeout from CRTO
63:61Newer fields / reservedCheck the revision you implement against version
doorbell_stride_bytes = 4 × 2DSTRD ; page_bytes = 4096 × 2MPS ; ready_timeout_ms = TO × 500
  • DSTRD — CAP bits 35:32.
  • MPS — CC.MPS (bits 10:7), constrained by CAP.MPSMIN ≤ MPS ≤ CAP.MPSMAX.
  • TO — CAP bits 31:24.

Reset behaviour: RO; values are fixed by the implementation (some may reflect configuration such as SR-IOV state) impl. Host interaction: read once at probe (Linux reads CAP before any other register). Controller interaction: none at runtime. Trace consequence: one or two MRd at BAR0+0h/4h early in the driver probe; the values determine every later offset and timeout — always capture them when analysing a trace.

The executable decoder below reproduces this decode and also decodes VS, CC, CSTS examples and doorbell offsets:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Decode NVMe controller registers from SYNTHETIC values (no hardware access).
Field positions follow the NVMe Base Specification register definitions; fields
marked (2.x) were added in the 2.0-era revisions -- confirm against your revision."""

def f(v, hi, lo):
    return (v >> lo) & ((1 << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1)

def decode_cap(cap):
    css = f(cap, 44, 37)
    out = {
        "MQES  (15:0)  max queue entries": f"{f(cap,15,0)} (0's based) -> {f(cap,15,0) + 1} entries",
        "CQR   (16)    contiguous queues required": f(cap, 16, 16),
        "AMS   (18:17) arbitration supported": f"WRR+urgent={f(cap,17,17)} vendor={f(cap,18,18)}",
        "TO    (31:24) timeout": f"{f(cap,31,24)} x 500 ms = {f(cap,31,24) * 0.5:g} s",
        "DSTRD (35:32) doorbell stride": f"{f(cap,35,32)} -> {4 << f(cap,35,32)} bytes",
        "NSSRS (36)    subsystem reset supported": f(cap, 36, 36),
        "CSS   (44:37) command sets supported": f"{css:#04x}: NVM={css & 1} "
                        f"IOCS={(css >> 6) & 1} admin-only={(css >> 7) & 1}",
        "BPS   (45)    boot partitions": f(cap, 45, 45),
        "MPSMIN(51:48) min page size": f"{4096 << f(cap,51,48)} bytes",
        "MPSMAX(55:52) max page size": f"{4096 << f(cap,55,52)} bytes",
        "PMRS  (56)    persistent memory region": f(cap, 56, 56),
        "CMBS  (57)    controller memory buffer": f(cap, 57, 57),
        "CRMS  (60:59) ready modes (2.x)": f"with-media={f(cap,59,59)} independent={f(cap,60,60)}",
    }
    for k, val in out.items():
        print(f"  {k:42} {val}")

def decode_vs(vs):
    print(f"  VS {vs:#010x} -> NVMe {f(vs,31,16)}.{f(vs,15,8)}.{f(vs,7,0)}")

def decode_cc(cc):
    print(f"  CC {cc:#010x}: EN={f(cc,0,0)} CSS={f(cc,6,4):03b}b MPS={f(cc,10,7)} "
          f"({4096 << f(cc,10,7)} B) AMS={f(cc,13,11):03b}b SHN={f(cc,15,14):02b}b "
          f"IOSQES={f(cc,19,16)} ({1 << f(cc,19,16)} B) IOCQES={f(cc,23,20)} ({1 << f(cc,23,20)} B)")

def decode_csts(csts):
    shst = {0: "normal", 1: "shutdown in progress", 2: "shutdown complete", 3: "reserved"}
    print(f"  CSTS {csts:#010x}: RDY={f(csts,0,0)} CFS={f(csts,1,1)} "
          f"SHST={shst[f(csts,3,2)]} NSSRO={f(csts,4,4)} PP={f(csts,5,5)}")

def doorbell(qid, dstrd, completion):
    return 0x1000 + (2 * qid + (1 if completion else 0)) * (4 << dstrd)

CAP = 0x1A40_0830_2803_03FF        # synthetic, chosen for teaching
print(f"CAP = {CAP:#018x}")
decode_cap(CAP)
decode_vs(0x0002_0400)
decode_cc(0x0046_0001)              # EN=1, CSS=000b, MPS=0, IOSQES=6, IOCQES=4
decode_csts(0x0000_0001)
decode_csts(0x0000_0003)            # RDY=1 and CFS=1: fatal status
for q in (0, 1, 2):
    print(f"  queue {q}: SQ{q}TDBL @ {doorbell(q, 0, False):#06x}  CQ{q}HDBL @ {doorbell(q, 0, True):#06x}")
print(f"  with DSTRD=2: SQ1TDBL @ {doorbell(1, 2, False):#06x}")

Output:

CAP = 0x1a400830280303ff
  MQES  (15:0)  max queue entries            1023 (0's based) -> 1024 entries
  CQR   (16)    contiguous queues required   1
  AMS   (18:17) arbitration supported        WRR+urgent=1 vendor=0
  TO    (31:24) timeout                      40 x 500 ms = 20 s
  DSTRD (35:32) doorbell stride              0 -> 4 bytes
  NSSRS (36)    subsystem reset supported    1
  CSS   (44:37) command sets supported       0x41: NVM=1 IOCS=1 admin-only=0
  BPS   (45)    boot partitions              0
  MPSMIN(51:48) min page size                4096 bytes
  MPSMAX(55:52) max page size                65536 bytes
  PMRS  (56)    persistent memory region     0
  CMBS  (57)    controller memory buffer     1
  CRMS  (60:59) ready modes (2.x)            with-media=1 independent=1
  VS 0x00020400 -> NVMe 2.4.0
  CC 0x00460001: EN=1 CSS=000b MPS=0 (4096 B) AMS=000b SHN=00b IOSQES=6 (64 B) IOCQES=4 (16 B)
  CSTS 0x00000001: RDY=1 CFS=0 SHST=normal NSSRO=0 PP=0
  CSTS 0x00000003: RDY=1 CFS=1 SHST=normal NSSRO=0 PP=0
  queue 0: SQ0TDBL @ 0x1000  CQ0HDBL @ 0x1004
  queue 1: SQ1TDBL @ 0x1008  CQ1HDBL @ 0x100c
  queue 2: SQ2TDBL @ 0x1010  CQ2HDBL @ 0x1014
  with DSTRD=2: SQ1TDBL @ 0x1020

24.7 VS — Version (08h, 32-bit, RO)

Bits 31:16Bits 15:8Bits 7:0
MJR — Major VersionMNR — Minor VersionTER — Tertiary Version

Examples: 0001_0400h = 1.4.0; 0002_0000h = 2.0.0; 0002_0400h = 2.4.0. Purpose: reports the Base Specification version the controller complies with verified. Pitfall: VS tells you the revision claimed, not which optional features exist; feature support is in CAP and Identify. Older 1.0 controllers may report VS = 0 for features not defined then; host drivers treat VS as a hint and rely on capability fields. Trace: one MRd early in probe; Linux logs a warning for some version/feature mismatches impl.

24.8 INTMS / INTMC — Interrupt Mask Set / Clear (0Ch / 10h)

Each bit corresponds to an interrupt vector. Writing 1 to a bit in INTMS masks that vector; writing 1 to the same bit in INTMC unmasks it; reading either returns the current mask. These registers are for pin-based and MSI interrupts only: when MSI-X is used, masking is done in the MSI-X table's Vector Control, and host software shall not use INTMS/INTMC (access is undefined) verified (confirm wording). They do not exist as properties on fabrics. Trace consequence: on modern MSI-X systems you should never see accesses to 0Ch/10h in the I/O path; if you do, the host fell back to MSI/INTx — check why (MSI-X allocation failure, quirk).

24.9 CC — Controller Configuration (14h, 32-bit, RW)

BitsFieldValuesChange rules
0EN — Enable1: process commands; 1→0: Controller Level ResetHost waits for RDY to follow
3:1Reserved
6:4CSS — I/O Command Set Selected000b NVM Command Set; 110b All Supported I/O Command Sets (needs CAP.CSS bit 43); 111b Admin Command Set only (needs CAP.CSS bit 44 for admin-only controllers, or chosen when NVM also supported per spec rules) versionOnly when EN=0
10:7MPS — Memory Page SizePage = 2(12+MPS); must be within CAP.MPSMIN..MPSMAXOnly when EN=0
13:11AMS — Arbitration Mechanism Selected000b Round Robin; 001b WRR with Urgent Priority Class; 111b vendor specificOnly when EN=0
15:14SHN — Shutdown Notification00b none; 01b normal shutdown; 10b abrupt shutdown; 11b reservedWritten when shutting down
19:16IOSQES — I/O SQ Entry Size2n bytes; NVM Command Set requires 6 (64 B); must be within Identify SQES rangeBefore creating I/O SQs
23:20IOCQES — I/O CQ Entry Size2n bytes; 4 (16 B)Before creating I/O CQs
24CRIME — Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable2.0+; select ready mode if CAP.CRMS allows versionOnly when EN=0
31:25Reserved

Reset behaviour: 0000_0000h after a controller reset (all fields default) verified. Host interaction: one write with configuration fields, then a write setting EN (Linux writes them together in one store: e.g. 0046_0001h). Controller interaction: on EN 0→1 the controller validates configuration, reads AQA/ASQ/ACQ, initializes and sets RDY; on EN 1→0 it resets. On SHN it performs shutdown and reports via SHST. Trace consequence: MWr to BAR0+14h. A CC value with IOSQES=0/IOCQES=0 at enable is legal (they matter only when I/O queues are created) — but creating I/O queues with them unset fails (Linux sets them at enable).

🔧 Worked CC values

0046_0001h = IOCQES 4 (16 B), IOSQES 6 (64 B), SHN 00b, AMS RR, MPS 0 (4 KiB), CSS NVM, EN 1. During normal shutdown Linux writes the same value with SHN=01b → 0046_4001h. To reset: 0046_0000h.

24.10 CSTS — Controller Status (1Ch, 32-bit)

BitsFieldMeaningAccess
0RDY — Ready1: controller ready to process commands after CC.EN=1; 0 after CC.EN=0 completesRO
1CFS — Controller Fatal Status1: fatal error the controller cannot communicate through a completion; reset requiredRO
3:2SHST — Shutdown Status00b normal operation; 01b shutdown processing occurring; 10b shutdown processing complete; 11b reservedRO
4NSSRO — NVM Subsystem Reset OccurredSet when an NVM Subsystem Reset occurred; host clears by writing 1RW1C
5PP — Processing Paused1: controller paused command processing (e.g. during firmware activation without reset)RO
6ST — Shutdown Type2.0+: whether the shutdown reported by SHST is controller- or subsystem-scope versionRO
31:7Reserved

Host interaction: polled during enable, reset and shutdown; read in timeout handlers. Controller interaction: updated on state changes. Trace consequence: repeated MRd of BAR0+1Ch; the polling interval and duration tell you how long the controller took. A read of FFFF_FFFFh is not a status — it means the device is unreachable (Chapter 19).

24.11 NSSR — NVM Subsystem Reset (20h, 32-bit, optional)

Writing 4E564D65h ("NVMe" in ASCII, little-endian bytes 65 4D 56 4E) initiates an NVM Subsystem Reset if CAP.NSSRS = 1; other values have no effect. Reads return 0 (or the spec-defined value) verified. Effects: every controller in the subsystem is reset; on PCIe the link(s) may go down and retrain, so the host may see a surprise-down style event; CSTS.NSSRO is set afterwards. Trace consequence: one MWr to BAR0+20h followed by link recovery or Detect-to-L0 re-training on the analyzer and a full re-enumeration/re-init sequence. Linux: nvme subsystem-reset /dev/nvmeX (EXPERT, disruptive).

24.12 AQA, ASQ, ACQ — the admin queue registers

RegisterBitsFieldMeaning
AQA (24h, 32)11:0ASQS — Admin SQ Size0's based entries (min 1 → 2 entries, max FFFh → 4096 entries)
15:12Reserved
27:16ACQS — Admin CQ Size0's based entries (min 1, max FFFh)
31:28Reserved
ASQ (28h, 64)63:12ASQB — Admin SQ BaseMemory-page-aligned DMA address of the admin SQ (bits 11:0 reserved; alignment follows CC.MPS)
ACQ (30h, 64)63:12ACQB — Admin CQ BaseMemory-page-aligned DMA address of the admin CQ

The admin queues are always physically contiguous (no PRP list) and are fixed at queue ID 0. Reset behaviour: cleared by conventional/power-on resets; not reset by a Controller Level Reset initiated through CC.EN (verify against your revision) verified. Host interaction: written while EN=0, before enabling. Controller interaction: latched at EN 0→1. Trace consequence: MWr to 24h, 28h/2Ch, 30h/34h (possibly as 32-bit halves); then, after the first admin doorbell, the controller's first MRd must target exactly ASQ — the earliest proof that the host gave the right DMA address.

24.13 CMB, Boot Partition, PMR, NSSD, CRTO — the optional block

  • CMBLOC (38h): BIR (bits 2:0) selects the BAR holding the Controller Memory Buffer; OFST (bits 31:12) gives its offset in units of CMBSZ.SZU. CMBSZ (3Ch): support bits — SQS (bit 0, SQs in CMB), CQS (1), LISTS (2, PRP/SGL lists), RDS (3, read data), WDS (4, write data); SZU (11:8, size unit: 4 KiB × 16SZU); SZ (31:12, size in SZU units). In 1.4+, CMBMSC (50h) must enable the CMB memory space and set its controller base address before use version. A CMB lets queues or data live in device memory — the host then writes SQEs via MMIO (often write-combining) and the controller avoids a DMA fetch.
  • BPINFO/BPRSEL/BPMBL (40h–4Fh): read boot partitions (a small read-only-at-boot area) without enabling the controller — useful for early boot firmware version.
  • PMR registers (E00h–E1Bh): Persistent Memory Region — a byte-addressable persistent region exposed through a BAR impl support.
  • NSSD (64h): NVM Subsystem Shutdown (2.0+) — initiate a subsystem-scope shutdown with a defined value version (check spec for the value).
  • CRTO (68h): Controller Ready Timeouts (2.0+) — CRWMT (bits 15:0, ready-with-media timeout) and CRIMT (bits 31:16, ready-independent-of-media timeout), in 500 ms units; hosts use them instead of CAP.TO when the ready modes apply version.

24.14 Doorbells

SQyTDBL = 1000h + (2y) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD) ; CQyHDBL = 1000h + (2y + 1) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)
  • y — queue identifier (0 = admin).
  • CAP.DSTRD — doorbell stride field.
DoorbellBits 15:0Written whenController reaction
SQyTDBLSQT — new SQ tailHost has written one or more SQEsController may fetch entries from old tail to new tail − 1 (arbitration permitting)
CQyHDBLCQH — new CQ headHost has consumed CQEsController may reuse those CQ slots; may affect interrupt (re)assertion

Rules verified: queues are circular; full when tail + 1 == head (mod size), so one slot is always empty; the host must not write a tail that overruns the head or a head beyond the last posted CQE. Writing a doorbell for a non-existent queue, or an invalid value, is reported as an error via the Asynchronous Event mechanism (Error status: invalid doorbell register / invalid doorbell write value) if an Asynchronous Event Request is outstanding. Doorbells are write-only; reading them returns no meaningful value. Virtualized environments may use a Doorbell Buffer Config admin command (shadow doorbells) to reduce MMIO exits version.

📡 Why one slot is always empty

With head == tail meaning "empty", a completely full ring would also have head == tail. Reserving one slot makes "full" = (tail + 1) mod N == head. Hence a queue of MQES+1 entries holds at most MQES outstanding commands. derived

24.15 Controller initialization, step by step

StepActionWhyEvidence in a traceIf skipped or wrong
1Ensure CC.EN=0 and wait for CSTS.RDY=0Firmware/boot loader may have left the controller enabled; registers may only be configured when disabledMWr CC (EN=0), MRd CSTS loopWrites to AQA/ASQ/ACQ/CC fields while enabled have undefined/ignored effect; stale queues
2Program AQA, ASQ, ACQThe admin queue is the only queue defined by registersMWr 24h, 28h, 30hController fetches from wrong address → IOMMU faults/garbage; no completions
3Program CC configuration (CSS, MPS, AMS; IOSQES/IOCQES)Defines page size for PRPs/queue alignment, command set, arbitrationMWr 14h with EN=0 (or combined with step 4)RDY may never assert or controller may report error for invalid values
4Set CC.EN=1Start the controllerMWr 14h EN=1—
5Wait for CSTS.RDY=1 within CAP.TO (or CRTO)Controller needs time to initializeMRd 1Ch loopCommands submitted before RDY=1 may be ignored
6Identify Controller; (if CSS=110b) Identify I/O Command Set structure and select profileLearn MDTS, SQES/CQES, OACS/ONCS, NN, SGLS…Admin doorbell, SQE MRd, 4 KiB MWr, CQEDriver uses wrong limits
7Identify namespaces (active NS list CNS 02h; per-NS CNS 00h; descriptors CNS 03h)Learn namespaces, sizes, formats, CSISeveral Identify commandsMissing or wrongly sized block devices
8Set Features — Number of Queues (FID 07h)Request I/O queue count; the controller replies with what it allocatedSet Features SQE; CQE DW0 NSQA/NCQACreating more queues than allocated fails
9Configure interrupts (MSI-X vectors)Each I/O CQ needs a vector (if interrupts enabled)Config writes to MSI-X cap; table MWr in BARLost or misrouted completions
10Create I/O Completion Queues, then I/O Submission QueuesAn SQ must reference an existing CQ (CQID in CDW11)Admin 05h then 01hCreate SQ with a non-existent CQ → error status (Completion Queue Invalid)
11Submit Asynchronous Event Requests; configure features (AEN config, volatile write cache, APST, HMB…)Receive health/notice eventsAdmin 0Ch outstanding (no completion until an event)Host misses critical warnings

Deletion runs in reverse: Delete I/O SQ (00h) before Delete I/O CQ (04h). The ordering (CQ before SQ on creation, SQ before CQ on deletion) follows from the dependency: an SQ posts completions to its CQ verified.

Figure 24.1 lists the steps; Figure 24.2 shows who does each one and where it lands. The driver touches registers in BAR0 and its own RAM. The controller answers by changing CSTS and by reading and writing host memory with DMA. Click a step to follow it. Register offsets are real; CAP, CC and the addresses are the synthetic values used in this chapter. synthetic

Software (driver) starts itDevice (controller) starts itPCIe link
  1. Driver reads CAP

    Before touching anything, the driver reads the 64-bit Controller Capabilities register. It learns the largest queue size, how long to wait for ready, the doorbell stride and the allowed memory page sizes.

    Where: BAR0 + 00h (CAP)PCIe: Yes, both ways · MRd 8 B (or two 4-B reads) host → device, CplD back
    CAP = 1A40_0830_2803_03FFh MQES = 3FFh → up to 1024 entries per queue TO = 28h → 40 × 500 ms = 20 s maximum wait DSTRD = 0 → doorbells 4 bytes apart MPSMIN = 0 (4 KiB) · MPSMAX = 4 (64 KiB)
  2. Driver disables the controller and waits for RDY = 0

    Firmware or a boot loader may have left the controller running. The driver clears CC.EN and then reads CSTS again and again until RDY is 0. Admin queue registers may only be changed while the controller is disabled.

    Where: BAR0 + 14h (CC), then BAR0 + 1Ch (CSTS)PCIe: Yes · MWr 4 B host → device, then repeated MRd 4 B + CplD
    CC was 0046_0001h → driver writes 0046_0000h CSTS reads: 0000_0001h, 0000_0001h, 0000_0000h → RDY = 0, done
  3. Driver allocates the admin queues and a data buffer in RAM

    The driver takes page-aligned, DMA-able memory for the Admin Submission Queue, the Admin Completion Queue and a 4 KiB buffer for the Identify data. It zeroes the completion queue so every phase tag starts at 0.

    Where: Host memoryPCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    Admin SQ: 32 × 64 B = 2 KiB at 0x1_0000_0000 Admin CQ: 32 × 16 B = 512 B at 0x1_0000_1000 (zeroed) Identify buffer: 4 KiB at 0x1_0000_2000
  4. Driver programs AQA, ASQ and ACQ

    The admin queue is the only queue described by registers. AQA holds both sizes (0's based); ASQ and ACQ hold the bus addresses of the two rings.

    Where: BAR0 + 24h (AQA), 28h (ASQ), 30h (ACQ)PCIe: Yes · MWr host → device (4 B for AQA; 8 B or two 4-B writes each for ASQ and ACQ)
    AQA = 001F_001Fh → ACQS = 31, ASQS = 31 → 32 entries each ASQ = 0000_0001_0000_0000h ACQ = 0000_0001_0000_1000h
  5. Driver writes CC with EN = 1

    One write sets the configuration fields and enables the controller. IOSQES and IOCQES are only needed later for I/O queues, but Linux sets them here.

    Where: BAR0 + 14h (CC)PCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr 4 B (posted)
    CC = 0046_0001h IOCQES = 4 (16-B CQE) · IOSQES = 6 (64-B SQE) · SHN = 00b AMS = 000b (round robin) · MPS = 0 (4 KiB pages) · CSS = 000b (NVM) · EN = 1
  6. Controller initialises and sets CSTS.RDY = 1

    On EN going 0 → 1 the controller checks the configuration, latches AQA/ASQ/ACQ and gets ready. When it is ready it sets RDY. The driver sees it only by polling CSTS, and gives up after CAP.TO.

    Where: Inside the SSD; result visible in BAR0 + 1ChPCIe: Only the driver's MRd of CSTS. The controller's internal work does not cross the link.
    CSTS reads 0000_0000h … then 0000_0001h after a few ms RDY = 1 and CFS = 0 → admin queue is live CFS = 1 instead would mean a fatal controller error → reset
  7. Driver submits Identify Controller

    The driver writes a 64-byte Identify command (CNS = 01h) into slot 0 of the Admin SQ, then rings the SQ 0 tail doorbell. Only the doorbell value crosses the link.

    Where: Admin SQ slot 0; doorbell at BAR0 + 1000hPCIe: SQE write No · doorbell Yes, MWr 4 B host → device
    OPC = 06h · CID = 0 · NSID = 0 PRP1 = 0x1_0000_2000 · CDW10 = 0000_0001h (CNS = 01h) SQ0TDBL ← 1
  8. Controller fetches the command from the Admin SQ

    The controller reads 64 bytes at the ASQ address. This is the first DMA of the controller's life, and the first proof that ASQ was programmed correctly.

    Where: Host memory 0x1_0000_0000PCIe: Yes, both ways · MRd 64 B device → host, CplD 64 B back
    A wrong ASQ here shows up as an IOMMU fault or a fetch of garbage.
  9. Controller writes 4 KiB of Identify data, then the completion

    The controller writes the Identify Controller structure into the PRP1 buffer, then a 16-byte completion entry into slot 0 of the Admin CQ, then (if enabled) an interrupt message. The admin CQ uses interrupt vector 0.

    Where: 0x1_0000_2000 (data), 0x1_0000_1000 (CQE)PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr 4096 B split by Max Payload Size (e.g. 16 × 256 B), MWr 16 B, then the interrupt MWr
    CQE: CID = 0 · SQID = 0 · SQHD = 1 · P = 1 · Status = 0 (success)
  10. Driver reads the completion and rings the CQ 0 head doorbell

    The driver sees P = 1 in slot 0, matches CID 0, reads the Identify data (MDTS, SQES, CQES, number of namespaces…) and frees the slot by writing the CQ 0 head doorbell. Next come Set Features (Number of Queues) and creating I/O queues (Chapter 27).

    Where: Admin CQ slot 0; doorbell at BAR0 + 1004hPCIe: CQE read No · doorbell Yes, MWr 4 B host → device
    CQ0HDBL ← 1 Identify: MDTS = 5 → 2^5 × 4 KiB = 128 KiB per command (example)

CommandCDW10CDW11PRP1
Create I/O CQ (05h)QSIZE (31:16, 0's based) | QID (15:0)IV — interrupt vector (31:16) | IEN — interrupts enabled (1) | PC — physically contiguous (0)CQ base (or PRP list if PC=0 and CAP.CQR=0)

24.15.2 Execute the handshake in simulation

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""SIMULATION of the NVMe controller-enable handshake against a toy controller model.
The toy controller is synthetic: it becomes ready after a fixed number of polls and
checks a few of the rules a real controller enforces. No hardware is touched."""

CAP = 0x1A40_0830_2803_03FF          # synthetic CAP from the decode example

class ToyController:
    def __init__(self):
        self.regs = {"CC": 0, "CSTS": 1, "AQA": 0, "ASQ": 0, "ACQ": 0}   # left enabled by firmware
        self._countdown = 0
    def write(self, name, value):
        self.regs[name] = value
        if name == "CC":
            en = value & 1
            if not en:                         # disable: reset in progress
                self._countdown = 3
            else:
                aqa = self.regs["AQA"]
                ok = (aqa & 0xFFF) >= 1 and ((aqa >> 16) & 0xFFF) >= 1   # >= 2 entries each
                # Toy rule: bad admin-queue config -> never ready. What a REAL controller
                # does here is implementation-dependent (it may also report CSTS.CFS=1).
                self._countdown = 4 if ok else -1
    def read(self, name):
        if name == "CSTS" and self._countdown > 0:
            self._countdown -= 1
            if self._countdown == 0:
                want = self.regs["CC"] & 1
                self.regs["CSTS"] = (self.regs["CSTS"] & ~1) | want
        return self.regs[name]

def wait_rdy(ctrl, want, to_units):
    budget = to_units * 500                # CAP.TO is in 500 ms units; 1 poll = 1 ms here
    for ms in range(budget):
        csts = ctrl.read("CSTS")
        if csts & 2:
            raise RuntimeError("CSTS.CFS=1: controller fatal status -> reset path")
        if (csts & 1) == want:
            return ms
    raise TimeoutError(f"CSTS.RDY never reached {want} within {to_units * 0.5:g} s")

def enable(ctrl, asq_entries=32, acq_entries=32, asq=0x1_0000_0000, acq=0x1_0000_1000, mps=0):
    to = (CAP >> 24) & 0xFF
    mpsmin, mpsmax = (CAP >> 48) & 0xF, (CAP >> 52) & 0xF
    assert mpsmin <= mps <= mpsmax, "CC.MPS outside CAP.MPSMIN..MPSMAX"
    print("1. CC.EN=0 and wait for CSTS.RDY=0")
    ctrl.write("CC", ctrl.regs["CC"] & ~1)
    print(f"   RDY=0 after {wait_rdy(ctrl, 0, to)} polls")
    print("2. program AQA/ASQ/ACQ (sizes are 0's based)")
    ctrl.write("AQA", ((acq_entries - 1) << 16) | (asq_entries - 1))
    ctrl.write("ASQ", asq)
    ctrl.write("ACQ", acq)
    cc = (4 << 20) | (6 << 16) | (0 << 14) | (0 << 11) | (mps << 7) | (0 << 4)
    print(f"3. write CC={cc:#010x} (IOCQES=4, IOSQES=6, SHN=0, AMS=RR, MPS={mps}, CSS=NVM)")
    ctrl.write("CC", cc)
    print("4. set CC.EN=1")
    ctrl.write("CC", cc | 1)
    print(f"5. CSTS.RDY=1 after {wait_rdy(ctrl, 1, to)} polls -> admin queue usable")
    print("6. next: Identify Controller (CNS 01h), Identify namespaces, Set Features Number of Queues,")
    print("   Create I/O CQ (05h) then Create I/O SQ (01h), then Asynchronous Event Requests")

enable(ToyController())
print("--- same sequence with 1-entry admin queues (AQA fields = 0, invalid) ---")
try:
    enable(ToyController(), asq_entries=1, acq_entries=1)
except TimeoutError as e:
    print("   FAILED:", e)

Output:

1. CC.EN=0 and wait for CSTS.RDY=0
   RDY=0 after 2 polls
2. program AQA/ASQ/ACQ (sizes are 0's based)
3. write CC=0x00460000 (IOCQES=4, IOSQES=6, SHN=0, AMS=RR, MPS=0, CSS=NVM)
4. set CC.EN=1
5. CSTS.RDY=1 after 3 polls -> admin queue usable
6. next: Identify Controller (CNS 01h), Identify namespaces, Set Features Number of Queues,
   Create I/O CQ (05h) then Create I/O SQ (01h), then Asynchronous Event Requests
--- same sequence with 1-entry admin queues (AQA fields = 0, invalid) ---
1. CC.EN=0 and wait for CSTS.RDY=0
   RDY=0 after 2 polls
2. program AQA/ASQ/ACQ (sizes are 0's based)
3. write CC=0x00460000 (IOCQES=4, IOSQES=6, SHN=0, AMS=RR, MPS=0, CSS=NVM)
4. set CC.EN=1
   FAILED: CSTS.RDY never reached 1 within 20 s

The failure run illustrates the most common bring-up symptom — "RDY never becomes 1" — and why the host must bound its wait by CAP.TO rather than loop forever. What a real controller does with an invalid AQA is defined by the specification and the implementation; the toy model's choice is a teaching simplification synthetic.

24.16 Reading a register: the 11-step discipline applied to CSTS

  1. Locate: BAR0 + 1Ch (property offset 1Ch).
  2. Width: 32 bits; use a 32-bit read.
  3. Reset value: RDY = 0 after reset; other bits per spec.
  4. Decode: RDY(0), CFS(1), SHST(3:2), NSSRO(4), PP(5), ST(6).
  5. Access: RO except NSSRO (RW1C) — verified in the spec.
  6. Side effects: reading has none; writing 1 to NSSRO clears it.
  7. Sequencing: RDY follows CC.EN with delay ≤ TO; SHST follows CC.SHN.
  8. Related: CC (EN, SHN), CAP.TO, CRTO, NSSR, PCIe link state.
  9. Software owner: the NVMe driver (and only it, while bound).
  10. Hardware behaviour: controller updates on state changes.
  11. Trace implications: polling loops of MRd to 1Ch; all-ones means unreachable device.

💡 Senior insight

When reviewing a new driver or a firmware bring-up, demand a register trace of the first second: CAP/VS read, CC.EN=0 + RDY=0 wait, AQA/ASQ/ACQ, CC with EN=1, RDY wait, first doorbell, first SQE fetch address. Eight lines of evidence settle 80% of bring-up arguments: whether the host respected TO, whether the fetch address equals ASQ, whether the first CQE landed at ACQ, and how long each phase took.

24.21 Labs

🧪 Lab 24.1 — Beginner: decode your controller's registers SAFE

Procedure: run sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 (raw hex form) and decode CAP, VS, CC, CSTS, AQA by hand; then paste the raw CAP into cap_decode.py and compare. Questions: What is your stride? Your TO in seconds? Your MPS range? Is the current CC consistent with CAP?

Expected reasoning

Most client SSDs report DSTRD=0 and MPSMIN=0 impl; CC typically 0046_0001h under Linux (4 KiB pages, 64/16-byte entries). Check MPSMIN ≤ CC.MPS ≤ MPSMAX and that CSS selected is supported.

🧪 Lab 24.2 — Intermediate: compute doorbells and queue capacities SAFE

For DSTRD = 0, 1, 3 compute SQ5TDBL and CQ5HDBL. For a queue created with QSIZE = 3FFh, how many commands can be outstanding?

Solution

Stride 4/8/32 bytes. SQ5TDBL = 1000h + 10×stride = 1028h / 1050h / 1140h. CQ5HDBL = 1000h + 11×stride = 102Ch / 1058h / 1160h. QSIZE 3FFh → 1024 entries → at most 1023 outstanding (one slot empty).

🧪 Lab 24.3 — Advanced: break the simulation deliberately SAFE

Modify init_sim.py: (a) choose MPS = 5 (outside MPSMAX = 4); (b) skip step 1 (don't wait for RDY=0); (c) model CFS. Write down the symptom each produces and how a real driver should report it.

Solution sketch

(a) The assertion fires — a real host must validate CC against CAP before enabling. (b) The toy model may see RDY=1 left over from the previous enable and proceed with an unconfigured controller — a real race seen in drivers that skip the wait. (c) Make read("CSTS") return bit 1 set and confirm wait_rdy raises; real drivers must then reset and collect logs.

🧪 Lab 24.4 — Senior forensic: trace 24.C SAFE

Produce a root-cause report: symptom, first bad event, mechanism, evidence, confidence, fix, fix-verification.

Model answer

Symptom: first admin command timeout. First bad event: SQE fetch MRd to 4_3A21_5000h rejected by IOMMU. Mechanism: host wrote a CPU physical address into ASQ while the device's IOMMU domain is translated, so the address is not a valid IOVA. Evidence: ASQ register value, IOMMU fault naming 01:00.0 with that address, absence of CQE. Confidence: high. Fix: allocate the admin SQ with the DMA API and program its DMA handle. Verification: trace shows the first MRd targeting the DMA handle, CQE arrives, no IOMMU faults across 1000 reset cycles with IOMMU strict mode.

🎯 Exercise
  1. Decode CC = 0046_4001h.
  2. Decode CSTS = 0000_0009h.
  3. CAP low DWORD = 3C01_07FFh. Give MQES, CQR, AMS and TO.
  4. AQA = 003F_001Fh. Admin SQ and CQ sizes?
Answers

(1) EN=1, CSS=000b, MPS=0, AMS=RR, SHN=01b (normal shutdown requested), IOSQES=6, IOCQES=4. (2) RDY=1, CFS=0, SHST=10b (shutdown complete). (3) MQES=7FFh → 2048 entries; CQR=1; AMS bits 18:17 = 00b → only round robin; TO=3Ch=60 → 30 s. (4) ASQS=1Fh → 32 entries; ACQS=3Fh → 64 entries.

Quiz

  1. At which offset is CSTS and which bit means "fatal"?

    Answer

    1Ch; bit 1 (CFS).

  2. Units of CAP.TO?

    Answer

    500 milliseconds.

  3. Why must I/O CQs be created before I/O SQs?

    Answer

    Create I/O SQ names the CQ (CQID) it posts completions to; the CQ must exist.

  4. Are AQA sizes 0's based?

    Answer

    Yes — like MQES and Create Queue QSIZE.

  5. When should INTMS/INTMC be used?

    Answer

    Only with pin-based or MSI interrupts, never with MSI-X (use the MSI-X table mask bits).

  6. What value does NSSR require?

    Answer

    4E564D65h ("NVMe").

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Name the NVMe registers involved in enabling a controller.
    Model answer

    CAP (limits, TO), CC (configuration + EN), CSTS (RDY, CFS), AQA/ASQ/ACQ (admin queues).

  2. Beginner What is a doorbell?
    Model answer

    A write-only MMIO register per queue: SQ tail doorbell announces new commands, CQ head doorbell releases consumed completions.

  3. Intermediate Decode MPS and why it matters.
    Model answer

    CC.MPS sets the host memory page size (4 KiB × 2^MPS) used for PRP entries and queue alignment; must be within CAP.MPSMIN..MPSMAX and match the host's PRP construction.

  4. Intermediate What happens if the host doesn't wait for RDY=0 after EN=0?
    Model answer

    It may reconfigure or re-enable while the controller is still resetting; results are undefined — stale state, RDY seen from the previous enable, or failures.

  5. Advanced How do 2.x ready modes change initialization?
    Model answer

    CAP.CRMS advertises ready-with-media vs ready-independent-of-media; CC.CRIME selects; CRTO provides corresponding timeouts; with CRIME the controller may become ready before media is ready, and namespaces report readiness separately — hosts must handle namespace-not-ready conditions. Verify details in the spec.

  6. Senior Design a register conformance test suite.
    Model answer

    RO stability (CAP/VS identical across reads and resets); reserved bits read 0 and writes ignored; CC writes only effective when allowed; RDY transitions within TO across 1000s of cycles; SHN/SHST behaviour under load; NSSRO set/clear semantics; doorbell error events for invalid offsets/values; 32-bit split accesses of 64-bit registers; behaviour across FLR, hot reset, NSSR; version-gated fields absent on older VS.

🧠 Teach-back

Child: the control panel has a plate you read, switches you set, lights you watch, two hooks for the first boxes, and a wall of bells. Junior: walk Figure 24.1 and decode the synthetic CAP. Senior: explain how to prove from an eight-line register trace whether a bring-up failure is host configuration, DMA addressing, or device fault.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can reproduce the register map (00h–37h, doorbells) from memory.
  • I can decode CAP, VS, CC, CSTS, AQA by hand and with code.
  • I can perform and justify each step of initialization and name its evidence.
  • I can compute doorbell addresses for any DSTRD and queue ID.
  • I can diagnose RDY/CFS/doorbell failures from a register trace.
  • I can state which fields are version-dependent and where to verify them.

24.22 Summary, further reading and next

BAR0 holds the controller properties: CAP (limits and capabilities), VS, INTMS/INTMC (non-MSI-X masking), CC (configuration and enable), CSTS (ready/fatal/shutdown), NSSR, AQA/ASQ/ACQ (admin queues), optional CMB/BP/PMR/2.x registers, and doorbells from 1000h with stride 4<<DSTRD. Initialization is: disable and wait, program admin queues, configure, enable, wait for ready, Identify, request queues, create CQs then SQs, arm async events. Further reading: NVMe Base Specification (controller properties, controller initialization, shutdown, reset); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (register mapping and doorbells); Linux include/linux/nvme.h and drivers/nvme/host/pci.c (nvme_pci_enable, nvme_pci_configure_admin_queue). Next: the following Part takes the queues you just created and dissects submission and completion queue mechanics, commands and data pointers in depth.

PART X

NVMe Queues

Everything an NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) controller does for a host starts with a 64-byte entry appearing in a ring buffer in host memory and ends with a 16-byte entry appearing in another ring buffer. This Part teaches those rings so precisely that you can compute, by hand, the head, tail, phase tag and doorbell value for any moment in a trace. Chapter 25 builds the general model (producer, consumer, full/empty, phase), Chapter 26 brings up the one queue pair the controller knows about at reset (the Admin queue), Chapter 27 uses it to create I/O queues, and Chapter 28 dissects the doorbell write all the way down to the PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) Memory Write TLP (Transaction Layer Packet). If you can do the worked examples in this Part without looking, you can read 80% of an NVMe protocol trace.

📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Express Base Specification (queue model, SQE/CQE formats, status) and NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (doorbell registers, memory-based queues, PRP rules on PCIe). REVISION: Base 2.4, PCIe Transport 1.4 (course baseline, set released 4 Aug 2026). STATUS: current baseline version. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.x placed everything (including doorbells) in one base document; from 2.0 the specification library was split into Base + Command Set + Transport documents, so the same mechanism may be described in a different document depending on which revision you open. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications. Exact section numbers are deliberately not quoted here — look them up in the revision you hold.

25.1 Why this chapter exists

An NVMe device is fast for one structural reason: the host and the controller almost never wait for each other. They share circular queues in host memory; the host produces commands into a Submission Queue (SQ) and the controller produces results into a Completion Queue (CQ). Each side only tells the other "how far I have got" — with a doorbell register write in one direction and with a CQ entry (CQE) in the other. No locks are shared across the PCIe link. Every NVMe performance property (deep queues, per-CPU queues, interrupt steering, low latency) and almost every NVMe hang you will ever debug ("command timeout", "controller is down", "missing interrupt") is a consequence of this ring discipline. So we learn the rings first and the commands second.

25.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: name the SQ, CQ, Admin queue, I/O queue and say who produces and who consumes each.
  • Intermediate: compute the number of occupied slots, the empty condition and the full condition ((tail + 1) mod size == head) for any head/tail pair.
  • Advanced: step a CQ through a wrap and predict the phase tag value of every slot; explain why the phase tag removes the need for the host to read a controller register to find new completions.
  • Senior: given a partial trace, reconstruct each queue's head, tail and phase and identify the first event inconsistent with the ring rules.
  • Trace-analysis: map ring events to PCIe transactions (doorbell MWr, SQE MRd, CQE MWr, MSI-X MWr).
  • Debugging: distinguish "controller never fetched", "controller fetched but never completed" and "controller completed but host never noticed".
  • Validation: design tests for wrap-around, full-queue, phase inversion and SQHD feedback.

25.3 Prerequisites

You need: what MMIO (memory-mapped I/O) and DMA (direct memory access) are; that the NVMe controller registers live in BAR0 (Base Address Register 0) space; and that an MWr (Memory Write request) is posted while an MRd (Memory Read request) needs a CplD (Completion with Data). The controller registers CAP, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ and ACQ are used here and explained more in Chapter 26.

25.4 The story — the supermarket checkout

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine a supermarket with a round conveyor belt at the checkout. You (the host) put shopping baskets on the belt at the spot marked "next empty spot" — that spot is the tail. The cashier (the controller) picks baskets up from the spot marked "next basket to scan" — that is the head. The belt is round, so when you reach the end you start again at the beginning. You must never put a basket on a spot where the cashier has not yet taken the old basket away — so you always leave one spot empty, which is how you can tell "belt full" from "belt empty".

When you put baskets down you ring a little bell (the doorbell) and shout the number of your latest spot. The cashier does not keep looking at the belt — they wait for the bell.

When a basket is done, the cashier puts a receipt on a second round belt that comes back to you (the completion queue). Receipts printed on the first trip around are printed in blue ink; on the second trip around, red ink; then blue again. You know a receipt is new if its ink colour is the colour you expect for this trip. That ink colour is the phase tag.

🌍 Analogy mapping
SupermarketNVMeLives where
Basket conveyor beltSubmission Queue (array of 64-byte SQEs)Host memory (or optionally the Controller Memory Buffer)
Receipt beltCompletion Queue (array of 16-byte CQEs)Host memory
"Next empty spot" (where you put baskets)SQ tail — owned by hostHost variable; published via SQ Tail Doorbell
"Next basket to scan"SQ head — owned by controllerController internal; reported back in CQE.SQHD
Bell + shouted spot numberDoorbell register write (MMIO)BAR0 offset 1000h and above
Ink colour of receiptsPhase Tag bit (CQE DW3 bit 16)Each CQE
Basket ticket numberCommand Identifier (CID)SQE CDW0[31:16], echoed in CQE DW3[15:0]
Cashier shouting "done!"Interrupt (MSI-X message)A posted MWr to an address the host programmed
🧩 Where the analogy breaks
  • A supermarket cashier scans baskets in order. An NVMe controller fetches SQEs in order from one SQ but may complete them in any order. That is why every receipt must carry the basket's ticket number (CID) and SQ identifier.
  • Receipts are not tied to the basket's position on the belt. A CQ can serve several SQs; the controller writes the next free CQ slot, regardless of which SQ the command came from.
  • There are many checkouts (up to 65,535 I/O queue pairs in the specification limit; a real controller reports far fewer) and an extra "manager's desk" queue (the Admin queue) for store management rather than shopping.
  • The cashier does not physically remove the basket; "taking the basket" just means the controller has DMA-read the 64 bytes. The host learns that the slot is reusable only from the SQHD value in a later CQE.

25.5 Beginner view — the six words

Submission Queue (SQ): a fixed-size array of command slots. Completion Queue (CQ): a fixed-size array of completion slots. Producer: the side that writes new entries and advances the tail. Consumer: the side that reads entries and advances the head. Queue depth (size): number of slots. Phase tag: one bit in every CQE that flips meaning on every lap around the CQ.

QueueProducer (writes entries, owns tail)Consumer (reads entries, owns head)How the producer announces new tailHow the consumer announces new head
SQHost driverControllerMMIO write of tail to SQyTDBL verifiedSQ Head Pointer (SQHD) field in every CQE it posts verified
CQControllerHost driverNew entries carry the current phase tag value (no register) verifiedMMIO write of head to CQyHDBL verified
📌 Remember

The owner of an index is the side that advances it. The host owns SQ tail and CQ head; the controller owns SQ head and CQ tail. Each side learns the other's index only through the one feedback channel: doorbell (host→controller) or CQE fields (controller→host).

25.6 Engineering view — ring arithmetic

Let the queue have N slots numbered 0…N−1. Indices always wrap modulo N.

used = (tail − head) mod N     free = N − 1 − used
  • N — queue size in entries (the Create command and AQA fields encode N−1, a 0-based value).
  • head — index of the next entry the consumer will read.
  • tail — index of the next free slot the producer will write.
  • used — entries written but not yet consumed.
  • free — slots the producer may still fill; one slot is always sacrificed.
EMPTY ⇔ head == tail      FULL ⇔ (tail + 1) mod N == head
  • The full rule means a queue of N slots holds at most N − 1 outstanding entries verified. Without the sacrificed slot, head == tail would be ambiguous (empty or full?).

Worked numbers, N = 8:

headtailused = (tail−head) mod 8StateCan producer write?
000emptyyes (7 free)
253partially fullyes (4 free)
61(1−6) mod 8 = 3wrapped, 3 used (slots 6,7,0)yes (4 free)
327full: (2+1) mod 8 == 3no
077full: (7+1) mod 8 == 0no

The table gives the arithmetic; Figure 25.0a shows the same rules as pictures. One 8-slot Submission Queue goes through five moments, from creation to full. The host moves the tail, the controller moves the head. Watch the tail wrap from 7 to 0 in row D, and the one slot that must stay empty in row E. conceptual

Tail: the host advances it and announces it with the SQ tail doorbellHead: the controller advances it and reports it as SQHD in each CQESlot holds a command the controller has not consumed yet

25.6.1 The phase tag, precisely

The host cannot cheaply ask "what is your CQ tail?" — there is no CQ tail register the host reads in normal operation. Instead every CQE carries a Phase Tag (P) bit, DW3 bit 16 verified. The rules:

  1. Host allocates CQ memory and clears it to zero before creating the queue, so every slot initially has P = 0. (The specification requires the host to initialise the phase tags to 0 in a newly created CQ. verified)
  2. On the controller's first lap it writes every CQE with P = 1.
  3. When the controller's CQ tail wraps from N−1 to 0, it inverts the value it writes: second lap P = 0, third lap P = 1, …
  4. The host keeps an expected_phase, starting at 1, and inverts it whenever its CQ head wraps from N−1 to 0.
  5. Host rule: the CQE at CQ[head] is new iff CQE.P == expected_phase. Stop at the first slot where it differs.

25.6.2 Worked example — phase-tag flip across a wrap

CQ size N = 4. Host zeroed the memory. Trace the bit in every slot as completions arrive two at a time and the host consumes them.

StepEventSlot P values [0,1,2,3]ctrl tail / ctrl phasehost head / expectedHost decision
0Queue created, memory zeroed0,0,0,00 / 10 / 1slot0 P=0≠1 → nothing
1Controller posts CID 0, 11,1,0,02 / 10 / 1slots 0,1 new; slot 2 P=0 stop
2Host consumes, rings CQHDBL=21,1,0,02 / 12 / 1—
3Controller posts CID 2, 3; tail wraps 3→0 so ctrl phase inverts1,1,1,10 / 02 / 1slots 2,3 new (P=1)
4Host consumes 2,3; head wraps 3→0 so expected inverts; rings CQHDBL=01,1,1,10 / 00 / 0slot0 P=1 ≠ 0 → nothing new (correct! this is last lap's entry)
5Controller posts CID 4 with P=00,1,1,11 / 00 / 0slot0 P=0 == 0 → new; slot1 P=1 ≠ 0 stop

Step 4 is the whole point: without the phase bit, the host would see a fully valid-looking CQE (CID 0) in slot 0 and would complete it twice. derived

⚠️ Classic bug

A driver that forgets to zero CQ memory before Create I/O CQ, or reuses a CQ buffer after a controller reset without clearing it, will see "ghost completions" with P=1 on the first lap. The symptom is completions for CIDs the driver never issued, or double completion → use-after-free in the block layer. derived

25.7 Hardware view

🔧 What the silicon does
  • Queue memory is ordinary host DRAM allocated by the driver with a DMA-coherent allocator. The controller is given the base address (and for non-contiguous queues a PRP list) at creation time. With CAP.CQR = 1 the controller requires physically contiguous queues verified.
  • Doorbell registers are flip-flops/SRAM in the controller's BAR0 space. Writing them is cheap for the CPU (a posted write) and wakes the controller's fetch engine.
  • Fetch engine: when SQ tail (doorbell) ≠ internal SQ head, it issues MRd TLPs to read SQEs. Many controllers fetch several SQEs in one MRd (e.g. 64–512 bytes) impl.
  • Completion engine: writes 16-byte CQEs with MWr TLPs, then (optionally) the MSI-X message — itself just another MWr to the address the host programmed in the MSI-X table.
  • Arbitration: with many SQs, the controller chooses which SQ to fetch from by round robin (mandatory) or weighted round robin with urgent priority (optional, CAP.AMS) verified. Inside one SQ, fetch order is in order; execution and completion order are not guaranteed.

25.8 Specification view — the queue vocabulary

TermMeaningWhere encodedLabel
Admin SQ/CQ (queue ID 0)The single queue pair for management commands; exists from enable.AQA (sizes), ASQ, ACQ (base addresses)verified
I/O SQ/CQ (IDs 1…)Queues for command-set commands (Read, Write…); created by admin commands.Create I/O CQ (05h), Create I/O SQ (01h)verified
Queue sizeEntries; encoded 0-based. Minimum size is 2 entries. Max I/O size = CAP.MQES + 1; Admin max 4096.CAP.MQES bits 15:0; AQA.ASQS bits 11:0, AQA.ACQS bits 27:16verified
Physically Contiguous (PC)Queue lives in one contiguous region (PRP1 = base) or is described by a PRP list.CDW11 bit 0 of create commandsverified
Many-to-one mappingSeveral SQs may point to the same CQ; one SQ maps to exactly one CQ.Create I/O SQ CDW11.CQIDverified
SQ entry size / CQ entry size64 B / 16 B for NVM command set over PCIe. Encoded as power of two in CC.IOSQES/CC.IOCQES (6 and 4).CC, Identify Controller SQES/CQESverified
📭 What the spec does not say

It does not say how many SQEs a controller fetches per MRd, how quickly it reacts to a doorbell, which order it completes commands in, or how it splits internal resources across queues. All of that is impl and is exactly what makes two compliant SSDs behave very differently under the same workload.

25.9 Protocol view — what crosses the link for one command

 HOST (CPU + DRAM)                         PCIe link                     NVMe CONTROLLER
 -----------------                                                       ---------------
 1 write 64B SQE into SQ[tail] (DRAM, no PCIe traffic)
 2 tail = (tail+1) mod N
 3 MMIO store tail ---------------- MWr 4B  BAR0+SQyTDBL ------------>  doorbell latched
                                                                         4 compare tail vs head
 <------------------------------ MRd 64B (or more) SQ[head] ----------- 5 fetch SQE(s)
 root complex returns ----------- CplD 64B ---------------------------> 6 decode, execute
 <------------------------------ MRd/MWr data via PRP/SGL ------------- 7 data DMA
 <------------------------------ MWr 16B CQE at CQ[ctrl tail] -------- 8 post completion
 <------------------------------ MWr 4B MSI-X message ---------------- 9 interrupt (if enabled)
 10 ISR: read CQEs while P == expected
 11 MMIO store head --------------- MWr 4B  BAR0+CQyHDBL ------------>  CQ slots freed

Notice that only steps 3 and 11 are host-initiated PCIe transactions; everything else is controller-initiated DMA. That asymmetry is deliberate: posted writes from the CPU are cheap, reads across PCIe are expensive (hundreds of nanoseconds), so the host never reads device registers in the I/O fast path. derived

25.10 Queue analysis safety (how to reason about a queue in any trace)

🐞 Queue-analysis checklist

For every queue you analyse, write down a row with all ten items below. If the trace does not expose one, write "MISSING EVIDENCE" — do not guess.

ItemWhere you find itIf missing

Queue depthCreate CDW10[31:16]+1; AQA for adminLower bound = largest index seen + 1
HeadSQ: CQE.SQHD; CQ: CQyHDBL writesState "unknown"; never assume 0
TailSQ: SQyTDBL writes; CQ: count of CQE writesSame
Command identifierSQE CDW0[31:16]; CQE DW3[15:0]Match by order only with low confidence
PhaseCQE DW3 bit 16Infer from lap count
Memory locationASQ/ACQ registers; Create PRP1Match MRd/MWr addresses to ranges
Ownership of each slotDerived from head/tail—
ProducerFixed by queue type—
ConsumerFixed by queue type—
