Missing evidence: the lap count for this CQ since creation. Disambiguate by capturing from the Create I/O CQ command onward and counting CQE writes modulo N.

25.12 Linux view

# How many I/O queues did the driver create? (read-only)
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/            # one directory per blk-mq hardware context
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/0/cpu_list # which CPUs map to hw queue 0
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests
grep nvme /proc/interrupts           # one line per MSI-X vector; counts per CPU
nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x07 -H   # Number of Queues feature (FID 07h)
nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H         # CAP.MQES, CAP.CQR, CAP.DSTRD, AQA...
⚠️ Safety

All commands above only read. nvme show-regs maps BAR0 and reads registers; on some kernels it needs root and may be refused if the device is bound to another driver. Never use setpci or direct BAR writes to "poke" doorbells on a device that holds data.

What these prove: the number of hardware contexts, the CPU→queue mapping, and the interrupt distribution. What they cannot prove: real-time head/tail values or whether a particular CQE was written — for that you need a driver tracepoint (nvme:nvme_complete_rq, nvme:nvme_sq) or a protocol analyzer.

25.13 Code — an executable SQ/CQ simulator with doorbells and phase tags

The program below models one SQ/CQ pair, a host and a controller that communicate only through the shared rings and two doorbell values — exactly like the real thing. It implements the full/empty rules, SQHD feedback and phase inversion, and lets you inject the six classic faults required by this course: wrong tail, wrong queue ID, duplicate CID, CQ overflow (full CQ), stale phase and missing completion.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""nvme_qsim.py - teaching simulator for one NVMe SQ/CQ pair.
SIMULATION ONLY: models ring arithmetic, doorbells and phase tags.
It does not model PCIe, real controller timing or any real device."""
import random

class Ring:
    def __init__(self, size):
        assert size >= 2, "NVMe queues need at least 2 entries"
        self.size = size
        self.slots = [None] * size
        self.head = 0          # consumer index
        self.tail = 0          # producer index
    def empty(self):
        return self.head == self.tail
    def full(self):
        return (self.tail + 1) % self.size == self.head
    def used(self):
        return (self.tail - self.head) % self.size

class Controller:
    """Device side. Only sees memory + doorbell values the host gives it."""
    def __init__(self, sq, cq, sqid, faults):
        self.sq, self.cq, self.sqid = sq, cq, sqid
        self.sq_tail_db = 0     # last value host rang into SQyTDBL
        self.cq_head_db = 0     # last value host rang into CQyHDBL
        self.phase = 1          # controller's current CQ phase (starts at 1)
        self.cq_tail = 0
        self.faults = faults
        self.inflight_cids = set()
        self.log = []

    def ring_sq_doorbell(self, value, qid):
        if qid != self.sqid:
            self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] doorbell write for SQ{qid}: no such queue -> ignored "
                            "(real HW: undefined/async error 'Invalid Doorbell Write')")
            return
        if value >= self.sq.size:
            self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] SQ tail {value} >= size {self.sq.size}: invalid doorbell value")
            return
        self.sq_tail_db = value
        self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] SQ{qid}TDBL <- {value}")

    def ring_cq_doorbell(self, value):
        self.cq_head_db = value
        self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] CQ{self.sqid}HDBL <- {value}")

    def cq_full(self):
        return (self.cq_tail + 1) % self.cq.size == self.cq_head_db

    def run(self, budget=99):
        """Fetch commands between our SQ head and the doorbell tail, complete them."""
        done = 0
        while self.sq.head != self.sq_tail_db and done < budget:
            if self.cq_full():
                self.log.append("  [ctrl] CQ full (tail+1 == head) -> must stall, cannot post")
                return
            cmd = self.sq.slots[self.sq.head]
            self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] fetch SQ[{self.sq.head}] opcode={cmd['opc']:02X}h cid={cmd['cid']}")
            self.sq.head = (self.sq.head + 1) % self.sq.size
            status = 0x0000
            if cmd['nsid'] == 0:
                status = 0x000B          # zeroed slot = opcode 00h NSID 0 -> Invalid Namespace or Format
            elif cmd['cid'] in self.inflight_cids:
                status = 0x0003          # Generic SCT 0, SC 03h Command ID Conflict (detection is impl-dependent)
            if status == 0:
                self.inflight_cids.add(cmd['cid'])
            if status == 0 and cmd['cid'] in self.faults.get('drop_cid', ()):
                self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] (fault) cid={cmd['cid']} never completes (held/lost) - no CQE")
                done += 1
                continue
            phase = self.phase if not self.faults.get('stale_phase') else self.phase ^ 1
            cqe = {'dw0': 0, 'sqhd': self.sq.head, 'sqid': self.sqid,
                   'cid': cmd['cid'], 'p': phase, 'status': status}
            self.cq.slots[self.cq_tail] = cqe
            self.log.append(f"  [ctrl] post CQ[{self.cq_tail}] cid={cqe['cid']} P={phase} "
                            f"SQHD={cqe['sqhd']} status={status:04X}h -> MSI-X")
            self.cq_tail = (self.cq_tail + 1) % self.cq.size
            if self.cq_tail == 0:
                self.phase ^= 1          # wrap => invert phase for next pass
            self.inflight_cids.discard(cmd['cid']) if status == 0 else None
            done += 1

class Host:
    def __init__(self, depth, faults=None, cq_depth=None):
        self.faults = faults or {}
        self.sq, self.cq = Ring(depth), Ring(cq_depth or depth)
        self.sq.slots = [{'opc': 0x00, 'cid': 0, 'nsid': 0}] * depth   # zeroed SQ memory
        self.cq.slots = [{'p': 0}] * self.cq.size          # host zeroes CQ memory => P=0
        self.expected_phase = 1
        self.ctrl = Controller(self.sq, self.cq, 1, self.faults)
        self.next_cid = 0
        self.sq_head_seen = 0                        # learned from CQE.SQHD

    def submit(self, opc=0x02):
        if (self.sq.tail + 1) % self.sq.size == self.sq_head_seen:
            print("  [host] SQ full - cannot submit (tail+1 == head)")
            return False
        cid = self.next_cid
        if self.faults.get('dup_cid') and cid == 2:
            cid = 1                                   # fault: reuse an in-flight CID
        self.next_cid += 1
        self.sq.slots[self.sq.tail] = {'opc': opc, 'cid': cid, 'nsid': 1}
        self.sq.tail = (self.sq.tail + 1) % self.sq.size
        print(f"  [host] write SQE cid={cid} into SQ[{(self.sq.tail-1) % self.sq.size}], tail -> {self.sq.tail}")
        return True

    def doorbell(self):
        val = self.sq.tail
        if self.faults.get('wrong_tail'):
            val = (val + 1) % self.sq.size            # fault: one too far
        qid = self.faults.get('wrong_qid', 1)
        self.ctrl.ring_sq_doorbell(val, qid)

    def reap(self):
        n = 0
        while True:
            e = self.cq.slots[self.cq.head]
            if e['p'] != self.expected_phase:
                break                                  # not new yet
            print(f"  [host] reap CQ[{self.cq.head}] cid={e['cid']} status={e['status']:04X}h "
                  f"SQHD={e['sqhd']}")
            self.sq_head_seen = e['sqhd']
            self.cq.head = (self.cq.head + 1) % self.cq.size
            if self.cq.head == 0:
                self.expected_phase ^= 1
            n += 1
        if n:
            self.ctrl.ring_cq_doorbell(self.cq.head)
        else:
            print(f"  [host] no new CQE at CQ[{self.cq.head}] (expect P={self.expected_phase})")
        return n

def flush(ctrl):
    for line in ctrl.log:
        print(line)
    ctrl.log.clear()

def scenario(name, depth, rounds, per_round, faults=None, reap=True, cq_depth=None):
    print(f"=== {name} (SQ depth={depth}, CQ depth={cq_depth or depth}) ===")
    h = Host(depth, faults, cq_depth)
    for r in range(rounds):
        for _ in range(per_round):
            h.submit()
        h.doorbell(); flush(h.ctrl)
        h.ctrl.run(); flush(h.ctrl)
        if reap:
            h.reap(); flush(h.ctrl)
    print(f"  final: SQ head/tail={h.sq.head}/{h.sq.tail} CQ ctrl-tail={h.ctrl.cq_tail} "
          f"host-head={h.cq.head} host-phase={h.expected_phase} ctrl-phase={h.ctrl.phase}\n")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    scenario("normal: wrap twice, watch phase flip", 4, 4, 2)
    scenario("fault: wrong tail (one past real tail)", 4, 1, 1, {'wrong_tail': True})
    scenario("fault: doorbell rung for wrong queue id", 4, 1, 1, {'wrong_qid': 2})
    scenario("fault: duplicate CID while first copy still in flight", 8, 1, 3,
             {'dup_cid': True, 'drop_cid': (1,)})
    scenario("fault: host never reaps -> CQ full, controller stalls", 8, 1, 5, reap=False, cq_depth=4)
    scenario("fault: stale phase written by device", 4, 1, 1, {'stale_phase': True})
    scenario("fault: missing completion", 4, 1, 2, {'drop_cid': (0,)})

Output of python3 nvme_qsim.py (produced by actually running the program above; it is simulation output, not a device log):

=== normal: wrap twice, watch phase flip (SQ depth=4, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [host] write SQE cid=1 into SQ[1], tail -> 2
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 2
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=0 P=1 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=02h cid=1
  [ctrl] post CQ[1] cid=1 P=1 SQHD=2 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[0] cid=0 status=0000h SQHD=1
  [host] reap CQ[1] cid=1 status=0000h SQHD=2
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 2
  [host] write SQE cid=2 into SQ[2], tail -> 3
  [host] write SQE cid=3 into SQ[3], tail -> 0
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 0
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[2] opcode=02h cid=2
  [ctrl] post CQ[2] cid=2 P=1 SQHD=3 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[3] opcode=02h cid=3
  [ctrl] post CQ[3] cid=3 P=1 SQHD=0 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[2] cid=2 status=0000h SQHD=3
  [host] reap CQ[3] cid=3 status=0000h SQHD=0
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 0
  [host] write SQE cid=4 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [host] write SQE cid=5 into SQ[1], tail -> 2
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 2
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=4
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=4 P=0 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=02h cid=5
  [ctrl] post CQ[1] cid=5 P=0 SQHD=2 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[0] cid=4 status=0000h SQHD=1
  [host] reap CQ[1] cid=5 status=0000h SQHD=2
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 2
  [host] write SQE cid=6 into SQ[2], tail -> 3
  [host] write SQE cid=7 into SQ[3], tail -> 0
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 0
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[2] opcode=02h cid=6
  [ctrl] post CQ[2] cid=6 P=0 SQHD=3 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[3] opcode=02h cid=7
  [ctrl] post CQ[3] cid=7 P=0 SQHD=0 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[2] cid=6 status=0000h SQHD=3
  [host] reap CQ[3] cid=7 status=0000h SQHD=0
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 0
  final: SQ head/tail=0/0 CQ ctrl-tail=0 host-head=0 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: wrong tail (one past real tail) (SQ depth=4, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 2
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=0 P=1 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=00h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[1] cid=0 P=1 SQHD=2 status=000Bh -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[0] cid=0 status=0000h SQHD=1
  [host] reap CQ[1] cid=0 status=000Bh SQHD=2
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 2
  final: SQ head/tail=2/1 CQ ctrl-tail=2 host-head=2 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: doorbell rung for wrong queue id (SQ depth=4, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [ctrl] doorbell write for SQ2: no such queue -> ignored (real HW: undefined/async error 'Invalid Doorbell Write')
  [host] no new CQE at CQ[0] (expect P=1)
  final: SQ head/tail=0/1 CQ ctrl-tail=0 host-head=0 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: duplicate CID while first copy still in flight (SQ depth=8, CQ depth=8) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [host] write SQE cid=1 into SQ[1], tail -> 2
  [host] write SQE cid=1 into SQ[2], tail -> 3
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 3
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=0 P=1 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=02h cid=1
  [ctrl] (fault) cid=1 never completes (held/lost) - no CQE
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[2] opcode=02h cid=1
  [ctrl] post CQ[1] cid=1 P=1 SQHD=3 status=0003h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[0] cid=0 status=0000h SQHD=1
  [host] reap CQ[1] cid=1 status=0003h SQHD=3
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 2
  final: SQ head/tail=3/3 CQ ctrl-tail=2 host-head=2 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: host never reaps -> CQ full, controller stalls (SQ depth=8, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [host] write SQE cid=1 into SQ[1], tail -> 2
  [host] write SQE cid=2 into SQ[2], tail -> 3
  [host] write SQE cid=3 into SQ[3], tail -> 4
  [host] write SQE cid=4 into SQ[4], tail -> 5
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 5
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=0 P=1 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=02h cid=1
  [ctrl] post CQ[1] cid=1 P=1 SQHD=2 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[2] opcode=02h cid=2
  [ctrl] post CQ[2] cid=2 P=1 SQHD=3 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [ctrl] CQ full (tail+1 == head) -> must stall, cannot post
  final: SQ head/tail=3/5 CQ ctrl-tail=3 host-head=0 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: stale phase written by device (SQ depth=4, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 1
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=0 P=0 SQHD=1 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] no new CQE at CQ[0] (expect P=1)
  final: SQ head/tail=1/1 CQ ctrl-tail=1 host-head=0 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

=== fault: missing completion (SQ depth=4, CQ depth=4) ===
  [host] write SQE cid=0 into SQ[0], tail -> 1
  [host] write SQE cid=1 into SQ[1], tail -> 2
  [ctrl] SQ1TDBL <- 2
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[0] opcode=02h cid=0
  [ctrl] (fault) cid=0 never completes (held/lost) - no CQE
  [ctrl] fetch SQ[1] opcode=02h cid=1
  [ctrl] post CQ[0] cid=1 P=1 SQHD=2 status=0000h -> MSI-X
  [host] reap CQ[0] cid=1 status=0000h SQHD=2
  [ctrl] CQ1HDBL <- 1
  final: SQ head/tail=2/2 CQ ctrl-tail=1 host-head=1 host-phase=1 ctrl-phase=1

Reading the fault output

Injected faultHow it manifests in the modelHow it manifests on real hardware
Wrong tail (one past)Controller fetches a zeroed slot: opcode 00h (Flush) with NSID 0 → status 000Bh Invalid Namespace or Format, CID 0 completes twiceGarbage or stale SQE executed — could be a valid old Write replayed: silent corruption. Most dangerous fault. derived
Wrong queue IDDoorbell ignored, command never fetchedDoorbell to a non-existent queue: asynchronous error event possible; command times out
Duplicate CIDSecond copy completes with 0003h Command ID ConflictBehaviour impl: controller may detect it or may not; host may complete the wrong request
CQ fullController stalls after 3 posts with a 4-entry CQCompletions delayed; throughput collapse; looks like a slow drive
Stale phaseCQE written but host sees "nothing new"Timeout although analyzer shows the CQE MWr
Missing completionCID 0 never completes; later CIDs doSingle-command timeout; Abort then reset escalation

25.14 Command lifecycle (teaching model)

The following state chain is a teaching model conceptual. It is not a normative controller state machine; the specification defines the queue and completion rules, not a named internal state for each step.

CREATED ─► QUEUED ─► SUBMITTED ─► FETCHED ─► EXECUTING ─► DATA TRANSFER ─► MEDIA OPERATION
 (driver   (SQE in   (doorbell    (MRd of    (decoded)    (MRd/MWr via    (NAND read/
  builds    SQ slot)  rung)        SQE done)               PRP/SGL)         program; may
  request)                                                                  overlap DMA)
   ─► COMPLETED ─► CQE POSTED ─► INTERRUPT / POLL ─► DRIVER RETIREMENT
      (status      (MWr 16B     (MSI-X MWr or       (CID matched, request
       decided)     with P)      host polling)        ended, CQ head rung)
TransitionObservable on PCIe?Observable in Linux?
QUEUED→SUBMITTEDYes: doorbell MWrnvme:nvme_setup_cmd tracepoint (just before)
SUBMITTED→FETCHEDYes: MRd + CplD of SQ addressNo
EXECUTING / MEDIANo (internal)No
DATA TRANSFERYes: MWr (read cmd) / MRd (write cmd) to data pagesNo (unless IOMMU fault)
CQE POSTEDYes: MWr 16B to CQNo
INTERRUPTYes: MWr to MSI-X address/proc/interrupts counter
RETIREMENTYes: CQ head doorbell (maybe batched)nvme:nvme_complete_rq

25.15 Common mistakes

  • Believing a queue of N entries holds N commands. It holds N−1.
  • Encoding the size as N instead of N−1 in AQA or Create commands (0-based fields).
  • Thinking the host learns SQ progress from a register. It learns it only from CQE.SQHD.
  • Assuming completion order = submission order.
  • Expecting the phase tag to be 1 for "valid". It is valid when it matches the expected lap value.
  • Re-using CQ memory after a reset without zeroing it.
💡 Senior insight

When someone says "the drive hung", ask for four numbers per queue: last SQ tail doorbell value, last SQHD the host saw, last CQ head doorbell value, and the CQ slot/phase of the last CQE written. Ninety percent of "hangs" fall out of those four numbers: if tail ≠ SQHD and no MRd was seen, the controller never fetched; if a CQE was written but the CQ head never moved, the host lost the interrupt or misjudged the phase; if the CQ is full, the host is the bottleneck.

🧪 Lab 25.1 — Ring arithmetic by hand and in the simulator SAFE LAB

Objective: predict head/tail/phase for any sequence, then confirm with the simulator. Prerequisites: Python 3.8+. Setup: save the simulator as nvme_qsim.py.

  1. Without running anything, compute for SQ/CQ depth 4: after submitting and reaping 2 commands four times, what are the final SQ head/tail, CQ head, host expected phase and controller phase?
  2. Run the normal scenario and compare.
  3. Change depth to 5 and rounds to 3 with 3 commands per round. Predict where the phase flips.
  4. Add a scenario where the host reaps only every second round. Observe when the controller stalls.

Observations: list the CQ slot and P value of every posted CQE. Questions: why does P on slot 0 differ between lap 1 and lap 2? Why can the host only have 3 commands outstanding on a depth-4 SQ?

Solution

Depth 4, 8 commands total, two laps: SQ head/tail 0/0, CQ head 0, host expected phase 1 (flipped twice), controller phase 1 (flipped twice). With depth 5 and 3 per round the controller's tail goes 0→3→1 (wrap after 5 posts, phase becomes 0)→4; the first CQE with P=0 is the 6th completion, in slot 0. A depth-4 SQ: (tail+1) mod 4 == head when 3 are outstanding.

Extension: give the controller a random completion order (shuffle the fetched batch before posting) and confirm that the host still matches every CID.

🧪 Lab 25.2 — Read the queue layout of your own system SAFE LAB

Objective: relate blk-mq hardware contexts to NVMe I/O queues and MSI-X vectors. Setup: any Linux machine with an NVMe drive; read-only commands from §25.12.

  1. Count directories under /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/.
  2. Count nvme lines in /proc/interrupts.
  3. Run nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 7 -H and note NSQA/NCQA (0-based).

Questions: why is the number of vectors typically (I/O queues + 1)? Why may the number of hctx be smaller than NSQA+1?

Solution

Vector 0 is usually shared by the admin queue (and sometimes I/O queue 1); each I/O CQ has its own vector so completions interrupt the CPU that submitted. The driver creates at most min(controller-allocated queues, CPUs, module parameters) I/O queues; the controller may also allocate fewer than requested. Exact sharing policy is impl (Linux version dependent).

Extension: check /sys/module/nvme/parameters/poll_queues and write_queues — polled queues have no interrupt vector.

🎯 Exercise

A CQ of 32 entries. The host has head = 30, expected phase = 0. The controller writes 5 CQEs. List the slots, the P bit in each, and the host's head and expected phase afterwards. Answer: slots 30, 31 with P=0; wrap; slots 0, 1, 2 with P=1. Host head = 3, expected phase = 1.

Quiz

  1. An SQ has N = 64, head = 10, tail = 9. How many commands are outstanding?

    Answer

    (9 − 10) mod 64 = 63 = N − 1 → the queue is full.

  2. Who owns the CQ tail and how does the host learn it?

    Answer

    The controller. The host never reads it; it infers it by scanning CQEs whose phase tag matches its expected phase.

  3. Why does the host need CQE.SQHD?

    Answer

    It is the only way the host learns which SQ slots the controller has consumed and may be reused; without it the host cannot evaluate the SQ full condition.

  4. Can two SQs share one CQ? Can one SQ use two CQs?

    Answer

    Yes; no. Mapping is many SQs to one CQ.

  5. A CQE has P = 1 and the host expects 0. New or old?

    Answer

    Old (left over from the previous lap). The host stops scanning.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a queue pair in NVMe?
    Model answerAn SQ and the CQ it is associated with; the host submits to the SQ and the controller reports results in the CQ. The admin pair is QID 0; I/O pairs are created by admin commands.
  2. Beginner Why is one slot always left empty?
    Model answerSo that head == tail means only "empty"; full is tail + 1 == head.
  3. Intermediate Explain the phase tag and why it avoids an MMIO read.
    Model answerEach CQE's P bit equals the controller's lap parity; the host compares with its own expected lap parity, so it can find all new entries in its own memory (cache-friendly), with no PCIe read of a tail register, which would cost ~1 µs.
  4. Intermediate Why do NVMe drivers create one queue per CPU?
    Model answerEach CPU then owns its SQ tail and CQ head with no cross-CPU locking or cache-line bouncing, and the CQ's MSI-X vector can target the same CPU.
  5. Advanced The controller completes out of order. What breaks if the driver assumed in-order?
    Model answerIt would retire the wrong request (wrong buffer returned to the application) — data corruption visible above the block layer; CID matching is mandatory.
  6. Senior A customer shows an analyzer capture where the CQE was written but Linux timed out the I/O. What do you check?
    Model answerCQE phase vs the CQ's lap count since creation; CQ address vs the address the driver programmed (written to wrong memory/IOMMU fault?); MSI-X MWr presence and its address/data vs the MSI-X table; whether vector was masked; interrupt affinity/CPU offline; and whether CID/SQID in the CQE matches an outstanding request.
🎯 Teach-back

Explain the phase tag (1) to a child using the ink-colour story, (2) to a junior engineer with the N=4 table from §25.6.2, and (3) to a senior engineer as "lap parity that converts a shared-memory ring into a lock-free single-producer/single-consumer channel without tail publication".

📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?SQE 64 B / CQE 16 B; SQ produced by host, CQ by controller; full when (tail+1) mod N == head; phase tag in CQE DW3 bit 16 inverted per lap; host zeroes CQ before creation; SQHD feedback in CQE DW2. verified
What is derived?N−1 usable slots; ghost completions if CQ not zeroed; host needs no MMIO read to find new CQEs. derived
What is implementation-dependent?SQE fetch batching, completion order, reaction time to doorbells, internal arbitration beyond RR/WRR. impl
What is version-dependent?Location of queue/doorbell text (single 1.x document vs Base + PCIe Transport since 2.0). version
What must be checked in the specification?Exact normative wording on CQ initialisation and on invalid doorbell writes in the revision you test.
What should never be assumed?In-order completion; that a CQE with P=1 is new; that the host can read a CQ tail register.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute used/free/full/empty for any head, tail, N.
  • I can draw a CQ through two laps with correct P values.
  • I can state who owns each of the four indices and how each is published.
  • I can predict the PCIe transactions for a single command.
  • I ran the simulator and can explain the output of each fault scenario.
  • I can cite which specification document (Base vs PCIe Transport) describes queues vs doorbells in the revision I use.

25.16 Summary

NVMe is two kinds of rings in host memory plus two kinds of index publication: doorbell writes for the host's indices and CQE fields (SQHD, phase) for the controller's. Full is tail+1 == head, empty is head == tail, and the phase bit is lap parity. Everything else in this Part builds on that.

Further reading: NVM Express Base Specification 2.4 (queue model, completion entry); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification 1.4 (memory-based queues, doorbells); Linux drivers/nvme/host/pci.c (functions handling submission and nvme_cqe_pending-style phase checks; names vary by kernel version version). Next: Chapter 26 — the Admin queue.

26 The Admin Queue

← 25 Queue Architecture27 I/O Queues →

26.1 Why this chapter exists

At reset the controller knows about exactly one queue pair: the Admin Submission Queue and Admin Completion Queue (queue ID 0). Every other capability — learning what the controller is (Identify), reading its health (Get Log Page), configuring it (Set Features), and creating every I/O queue — is done by commands on this pair. If admin bring-up fails, nothing else exists. Understanding the exact register handshake that creates the admin queue is also the single best way to debug "controller never becomes ready" failures.

26.2 Learning objectives

  • Program AQA, ASQ and ACQ correctly, including the 0-based size encoding and alignment.
  • Sequence controller enable: CC.EN=0 → wait CSTS.RDY=0 → configure → CC.EN=1 → wait CSTS.RDY=1.
  • Explain why admin commands use PRPs (not SGLs) over PCIe and why admin commands are low-rate.
  • Issue Identify, Get Log Page, Get/Set Features conceptually and know which fields to fill.
  • Explain the queue-creation order (CQ before SQ) and deletion order (SQ before CQ).

Prerequisites: Chapter 25 (ring rules). Register definitions (CAP 00h, CC 14h, CSTS 1Ch, AQA 24h, ASQ 28h, ACQ 30h).

🧒 Kid analogy — the manager's desk

The supermarket has normal checkouts for shopping (I/O queues), but before the store opens, only the manager's desk exists. You go there to ask "what is this store?" (Identify), "show me the incident book" (Get Log Page), "open checkout number 3 and use belt number 3 for receipts" (Create I/O CQ/SQ), or "change the store temperature" (Set Features). The manager's desk is slow and you rarely use it, but nothing opens without it.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The manager's desk is not physically different hardware — the admin queue uses the same ring mechanics, doorbells (SQ0TDBL at 1000h, CQ0HDBL at 1000h + (4 << DSTRD)) and CQE format. What differs is its creation (registers, not commands), its command set (admin opcodes), and that it cannot be deleted.

26.3 Engineering — the registers that define the admin pair

Register (offset)BitsFieldMeaning
AQA (24h)11:0ASQSAdmin SQ size, 0-based (value 31 → 32 entries). Minimum 1 (2 entries) verified
AQA (24h)27:16ACQSAdmin CQ size, 0-based. 12-bit field → maximum 4096 entries verified
ASQ (28h, 64-bit)63:12ASQBAdmin SQ base; bits 11:0 must be zero (4 KiB aligned, more precisely aligned to the memory page size) verified
ACQ (30h, 64-bit)63:12ACQBAdmin CQ base; page aligned verified
CC (14h)0ENEnable
CC (14h)6:4CSSI/O command set selected (000b NVM; 110b all supported I/O command sets when CAP.CSS allows) version
CC (14h)10:7MPSMemory page size = 2^(12+MPS) bytes; must lie within CAP.MPSMIN…MPSMAX
CC (14h)13:11AMSArbitration: 000b round robin, 001b weighted round robin with urgent
CC (14h)15:14SHNShutdown notification
CC (14h)19:16 / 23:20IOSQES / IOCQESI/O SQ/CQ entry sizes as log2: 6 (64 B) and 4 (16 B)
CSTS (1Ch)0 / 1RDY / CFSReady / Controller Fatal Status
CAP (00h)15:0, 16, 31:24, 35:32MQES, CQR, TO, DSTRDMax queue entries (0-based), contiguous queues required, timeout (500 ms units), doorbell stride

26.4 Mechanism — bringing up the admin queue step by step

#Who actsWhat changesWhereEvidence on the wire / in Linux
1HostReads CAP (MQES, DSTRD, TO, MPSMIN/MAX, CSS)BAR0+00hMRd 8B (or 2×4B) + CplD
2HostIf CC.EN=1, writes CC.EN=0 and polls CSTS.RDY until 0 (bounded by CAP.TO × 500 ms)BAR0+14h, 1ChMWr to 14h, repeated MRd of 1Ch
3HostAllocates zeroed, page-aligned memory for admin SQ and CQDRAMnone
4HostWrites AQA = (ACQS−1)<<16 | (ASQS−1); ASQ, ACQ = bus addressesBAR0+24h, 28h, 30h3–5 MWr TLPs
5HostWrites CC: MPS, CSS, AMS, IOSQES=6, IOCQES=4, EN=1BAR0+14hMWr
6ControllerInitialises; sets CSTS.RDY=1 (or CFS=1 on failure)internalhost's MRd of 1Ch eventually returns RDY=1
7HostSubmits Identify Controller (CNS 01h) on SQ0 and rings SQ0TDBLBAR0+1000hMWr; then controller MRd of ASQ; MWr 4096 B to PRP1; MWr CQE to ACQ; MSI/MSI-X or INTx (admin interrupt)

Linux equivalent: the driver's controller-enable path waits on CSTS.RDY; failure shows as a kernel message about the controller not becoming ready within the CAP.TO-derived timeout version (exact text varies across kernel releases).

/* Admin queue bring-up (pseudocode; real drivers add barriers, timeouts, error paths) */
cap   = mmio_read64(bar0 + 0x00);
mqes  = (cap & 0xFFFF) + 1;            /* entries, from 0-based field              */
dstrd = (cap >> 32) & 0xF;
to_ms = ((cap >> 24) & 0xFF) * 500;

mmio_write32(bar0 + 0x14, cc & ~1);   /* CC.EN = 0                                */
wait_until((mmio_read32(bar0 + 0x1C) & 1) == 0, to_ms);

asq = dma_alloc_zeroed(64 * 32, PAGE_ALIGN);   /* 32-entry admin SQ                 */
acq = dma_alloc_zeroed(16 * 32, PAGE_ALIGN);   /* 32-entry admin CQ, P bits = 0     */
mmio_write32(bar0 + 0x24, (31 << 16) | 31);    /* AQA: ACQS=31, ASQS=31 (0-based)   */
mmio_write64(bar0 + 0x28, asq.bus_addr);
mmio_write64(bar0 + 0x30, acq.bus_addr);

cc = (4 << 20) | (6 << 16) | (0 << 11) | (0 << 7) | (0 << 4) | 1;
     /* IOCQES=4, IOSQES=6, AMS=RR, MPS=0 (4 KiB), CSS=NVM, EN=1 */
mmio_write32(bar0 + 0x14, cc);
wait_until(mmio_read32(bar0 + 0x1C) & 1, to_ms);   /* also check CFS (bit 1)     */

26.5 Specification — what makes the admin queue special

  • Queue ID 0 for both admin SQ and CQ; created by register writes at enable, not by commands; cannot be deleted verified.
  • Admin commands over PCIe use PRPs; SGLs are not supported for admin commands on the PCIe transport (PSDT shall be 00b) verified. (Fabrics transports differ version.)
  • Admin queue memory must be physically contiguous — there is no PRP list for ASQ/ACQ.
  • The Admin CQ receives completions of admin commands only, including Asynchronous Event Request completions, which arrive "late" (whenever an event happens).
  • Admin command set opcodes are separate from I/O command set opcodes: opcode 02h is Get Log Page on the admin queue and Read on an NVM I/O queue. The queue decides the opcode table.

26.6 The admin commands you use in the first second of life

OrderCommand (opcode)Key fieldsWhy
1Identify (06h), CNS 01hPRP1 → 4 KiB bufferLearn MDTS, SQES/CQES, VWC, SGLS, OACS, NN, version
2Set Features (09h), FID 07h Number of QueuesCDW11: NCQR[31:16], NSQR[15:0] 0-basedRequest I/O queue count; CQE DW0 returns allocated NCQA/NSQA (0-based) verified
3Create I/O CQ (05h) × nQID, QSIZE, PRP1, IV, IEN, PCCompletion rings with interrupt vectors
4Create I/O SQ (01h) × nQID, QSIZE, PRP1, CQID, QPRIO, PCSubmission rings bound to a CQ
5Identify CNS 02h, then CNS 00h per NSIDNSIDDiscover namespaces and their LBA formats
6Asynchronous Event Request (0Ch) × knonePark requests for future events (temperature, errors, namespace change)

Each command's full format is in Chapter 30.

26.6a Following one Identify Controller command end to end

The admin queue uses exactly the same ring mechanics as an I/O queue; only the queue number (0) and the command set differ. Here is the very first command most drivers send, Identify Controller, step by step. The admin queues are the ones set up in §24.15: Admin SQ at 0x1_0000_0000, Admin CQ at 0x1_0000_1000, and a 4 KiB buffer at 0x1_0000_2000. synthetic

Software starts itDevice starts itInside the SSD (not visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. Driver writes the 64-byte Identify command into Admin SQ slot 0

    The driver fills slot 0 of the Admin Submission Queue in RAM. Admin commands on PCIe always use PRPs, so PSDT = 00b and PRP1 points to the 4 KiB buffer.

    Where: Host memory, Admin SQ slot 0 (0x1_0000_0000 + 0 × 64)PCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    CDW0 = 0000_0006h → OPC 06h (Identify), FUSE 0, PSDT 00b, CID 0x0000 NSID = 0 (not used for CNS 01h) PRP1 = 0x1_0000_2000 PRP2 = 0 (4 KiB in one page) CDW10 = 0000_0001h → CNS = 01h (Identify Controller), CNTID = 0
  2. Driver rings the SQ 0 tail doorbell

    The driver writes the new tail (1) to the admin SQ tail doorbell. It means "slot 0 holds new work".

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 1000h (SQ0TDBL = 1000h + (2·0)·(4 << 0))PCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 1 Only this number crosses PCIe; the command is still in RAM.
  3. Controller fetches the command

    The controller sees the tail move from 0 to 1 and reads slot 0 from the address it latched from ASQ at enable time.

    Where: Host memory, Admin SQ slot 0PCIe: Yes, both ways · MRd 64 B (device → host), then CplD with 64 bytes
    The controller now knows: Identify, CNS 01h, put 4096 bytes at 0x1_0000_2000, CID 0. Its internal SQ 0 head moves to 1.
  4. Controller prepares the Identify Controller data

    The controller assembles the 4096-byte Identify Controller structure: vendor ID, serial number, model, firmware revision, MDTS, SQES/CQES, number of namespaces and many capability fields. How firmware stores and builds it is up to the design.

    Where: Inside the SSDPCIe: No. Nothing appears on the link during this step.
    Usually fast (microseconds to a few milliseconds) impl.
  5. Controller writes 4 KiB of Identify data into the host buffer

    The DMA engine writes the whole structure to PRP1. The CPU is not involved and does not know yet.

    Where: Host memory 0x1_0000_2000 … 0x1_0000_2FFFPCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr TLPs, each ≤ Max Payload Size (e.g. 16 × 256 B)
    Bytes 0–1 = PCI Vendor ID, 4–23 = serial number (ASCII), 24–63 = model number (ASCII), byte 77 = MDTS, byte 512 = SQES, byte 513 = CQES …
  6. Controller writes the 16-byte completion entry into Admin CQ slot 0

    It writes the completion into the next free slot of the Admin Completion Queue, with phase tag 1 because this is the first lap.

    Where: Host memory, Admin CQ slot 0 (0x1_0000_1000)PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 16 bytes
    DW0 = 0 (unused by Identify) DW2: SQHD = 1, SQID = 0 DW3: CID = 0x0000, P = 1, Status = 0 (success)
  7. Controller sends the interrupt

    The admin Completion Queue is tied to interrupt vector 0. With MSI-X this is a memory write to the address in MSI-X table entry 0. A driver may also simply poll the CQ during early bring-up.

    Where: Interrupt address/data from MSI-X table entry 0 (or MSI, or INTx)PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 4 bytes (MSI/MSI-X); INTx would be an Assert_INTx message
    PCIe ordering keeps the interrupt write behind the data and CQE writes.
  8. Driver reads the completion and the Identify data

    The driver checks P = 1 at Admin CQ slot 0, matches CID 0, sees status 0 and then parses the buffer. These numbers set the limits for everything that follows.

    Where: Host memory, Admin CQ slot 0 and the 4 KiB bufferPCIe: No. The CPU reads its own RAM.
    MDTS = 5 → max transfer 2^5 × 4 KiB = 128 KiB SQES = 66h → 64-B SQEs · CQES = 44h → 16-B CQEs · NN = 1
  9. Driver rings the CQ 0 head doorbell

    The driver tells the controller that slot 0 of the Admin CQ is free again.

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 1004h (CQ0HDBL = 1000h + (2·0+1)·(4 << 0))PCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 1 Next admin commands: Set Features (Number of Queues), then Create I/O CQ / SQ.

Compare with the I/O Read in Chapter 39: the same nine moves, but on queue 0, with an admin opcode, and with data that comes from the controller itself rather than from NAND.

🧪 Lab 26.1 — Decode your controller's CAP and admin config SAFE LAB

Objective: read and interpret CAP, CC, AQA without changing anything. Setup: root shell, nvme-cli.

sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H | less     # read-only register decode
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | egrep -i 'mdts|sqes|cqes|sgls|oacs|ver'
  1. Record MQES+1, DSTRD, TO×500 ms, MPSMIN.
  2. Record AQA and compute admin queue depths (add 1 to each field).
  3. Compute SQ0TDBL and CQ0HDBL offsets.

Questions: Why does Linux choose a fixed admin depth rather than the maximum? What would happen if MPS were set larger than the OS page size?

Solution

Admin traffic is low-rate; a small depth wastes no memory (Linux uses a fixed admin depth constant, version). MPS larger than the OS page size would make PRP construction impossible for buffers made of OS pages that are not MPS-aligned and contiguous — Linux sets MPS to match its page size (or the closest supported).

Extension: correlate the "nvme nvme0: … I/O queues" kernel message at boot (journalctl -k | grep nvme) with Set Features Number of Queues.

Quiz

  1. AQA = 003F001Fh. Sizes?

    Answer

    ACQS = 3Fh → 64-entry admin CQ; ASQS = 1Fh → 32-entry admin SQ.

  2. Can an admin command use an SGL on PCIe?

    Answer

    No. PSDT must be 00b (PRP) for admin commands over PCIe.

  3. Why create the I/O CQ before the I/O SQ?

    Answer

    Create I/O SQ names an existing CQID; if the CQ does not exist, the command fails with Completion Queue Invalid (command-specific status 00h).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What are AQA, ASQ, ACQ?
    Model answerAdmin Queue Attributes (sizes), Admin SQ Base Address, Admin CQ Base Address — the registers that define queue pair 0 before CC.EN is set.
  2. Intermediate Walk through controller enable.
    Model answerDisable, wait RDY=0, program AQA/ASQ/ACQ, program CC with MPS/CSS/AMS/entry sizes and EN=1, wait RDY=1 within CAP.TO, check CFS, then Identify.
  3. Advanced Why does an outstanding AER matter for debugging?
    Model answerErrors like invalid doorbell writes, SMART thresholds or namespace changes are reported only when an AER command is outstanding; a driver that never posts AERs is blind to these asynchronous events.
  4. Senior Device hangs during admin init only on one server model. Hypotheses?
    Model answerIOMMU/ACS differences blocking DMA to ACQ, interrupt remapping, MPS/page size mismatch, BIOS leaving device in a state (CC.EN=1) the driver doesn't reset correctly, power/link (ASPM) issues. Evidence: IOMMU faults, analyzer capture of ACQ writes, CSTS values.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?AQA ASQS[11:0]/ACQS[27:16] 0-based; ASQ 28h, ACQ 30h page-aligned; CC.EN/CSTS.RDY handshake; CAP.TO in 500 ms units; admin commands use PRPs on PCIe. verified
What is derived?Bring-up order and the evidence each step leaves on PCIe. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Time to RDY, admin command latency, behaviour while background tasks run. impl
What is version-dependent?CC.CSS encodings for multiple command sets (2.0+); fields added to Identify over revisions. version
What must be checked in the specification?Required CC fields for your command-set selection; CFS recovery requirements.
What should never be assumed?That RDY rises immediately; that FFFFFFFFh is a register value.

26.9 Summary

The admin queue pair is created by registers, uses PRPs, carries the commands that discover and configure the controller and that create I/O queues. Next: Chapter 27 — I/O queues.

27 I/O Queues

← 26 The Admin Queue28 Doorbells →

27.1 Why this chapter exists

The admin queue is for configuration; the I/O queues carry the actual reads and writes — millions per second on a modern SSD (Solid State Drive). Their number, depth, memory layout and interrupt binding decide whether a system scales across 128 CPUs or bottlenecks on one lock. This chapter teaches the two creation commands field by field, shows queue memory layouts (contiguous and PRP-described), explains the binding SQ→CQ→MSI-X vector→CPU, and treats the Command Identifier (CID) as the critical correlation key it is.

27.2 Learning objectives

  • Encode Create I/O Completion Queue (05h) and Create I/O Submission Queue (01h) in hex, including 0-based QSIZE.
  • Explain IV/IEN, PC and CQID/QPRIO fields and the errors returned when they are wrong.
  • Draw memory diagrams for a contiguous queue and for a non-contiguous queue described by a PRP list.
  • Explain CID uniqueness scope (per SQ) and how Linux encodes CIDs.
  • Choose queue count and depth with a quantitative argument (Little's law).

Prerequisites: Ch 25 ring model, Ch 26 admin queue. MSI-X (MSI-X, Message Signaled Interrupts – Extended) basics.

🧒 Kid analogy — opening checkouts

The manager opens new checkouts by writing two notes. The first note says "put a receipt belt here, 256 spots long, and when receipts arrive press buzzer number 3". The second note says "put a basket belt here, 256 spots long, and send its receipts to receipt belt number 3". You cannot connect a basket belt to a receipt belt that does not exist yet — so receipts belt first.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

"Buzzer number 3" is an MSI-X table index, not a CPU. The OS decides which CPU each vector interrupts (affinity). One receipt belt can collect receipts from several basket belts, and polled queues have no buzzer at all.

DPTRPRP1Queue baseIf PC=1: page-aligned base of contiguous memory. If PC=0: pointer to a PRP list describing the queue's pages (only if CAP.CQR = 0) verified

27.4.1 Worked encoding

Create I/O CQ 3, 1024 entries, contiguous at bus address 0x0000_0001_8000_0000, MSI-X vector 3, interrupts on. Then Create I/O SQ 3 of 1024 entries at 0x0000_0001_8004_0000 bound to CQ 3, medium priority.

CommandCDW0PRP1CDW10CDW11
Create I/O CQ0x00XX_0005 (CID XX)0x0000000180000000QSIZE 1023 = 0x3FF, QID 3 → 0x03FF0003IV=3, IEN=1, PC=1 → 0x00030003
Create I/O SQ0x00YY_00010x00000001800400000x03FF0003CQID=3, QPRIO=10b, PC=1 → 0x0003_0000 | (2<<1) | 1 = 0x00030005

Memory needed: CQ = 1024 × 16 B = 16 KiB; SQ = 1024 × 64 B = 64 KiB. derived

27.4.2 Who does what when a queue pair is created

The two commands above are ordinary admin commands, so they travel through the admin queue exactly like Identify in §26.6a. The figure follows the worked encoding: queue pair 3, 1024 entries each, CQ at 0x1_8000_0000 with MSI-X vector 3, SQ at 0x1_8004_0000. Watch step 7: the controller accepts the SQ only because CQ 3 already exists. That is the whole reason for "CQ first". synthetic

Software (driver) starts itDevice (controller) starts itPCIe link
  1. Driver allocates and zeroes the memory for I/O CQ 3

    The host, not the SSD, provides queue memory. The driver takes page-aligned DMA memory and clears it, so every phase tag starts at 0 and no old entry looks new.

    Where: Host memory 0x1_8000_0000PCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    1024 entries × 16 B = 16 KiB, physically contiguous (PC = 1) The OS has already programmed MSI-X table entry 3 for the CPU that will own this queue.
  2. Driver submits Create I/O Completion Queue (05h)

    The driver writes the command into Admin SQ slot 0 and rings the admin SQ tail doorbell.

    Where: Admin SQ slot 0; doorbell at BAR0 + 1000hPCIe: SQE write No · doorbell Yes, MWr 4 B host → device
    CDW0 = 0010_0005h → OPC 05h, CID 0x0010 PRP1 = 0x1_8000_0000 (queue base) CDW10 = 03FF_0003h → QSIZE 3FFh (1024 entries, 0's based), QID 3 CDW11 = 0003_0003h → IV 3, IEN 1, PC 1 SQ0TDBL ← 1
  3. Controller fetches the command and creates CQ 3

    The controller reads the SQE, checks the fields and stores the queue in its own internal table: base address, size and interrupt vector. Nothing is written to host memory yet.

    Where: Admin SQ slot 0, then inside the SSDPCIe: Yes · MRd 64 B device → host, CplD back. Creating the queue itself is internal.
    Checks (failure → SCT 1, command specific): QID 3 ≤ queues granted by Set Features Number of Queues, else 01h Invalid Queue Identifier QSIZE ≤ CAP.MQES, else 02h Invalid Queue Size IV 3 is a valid vector, else 08h Invalid Interrupt Vector
  4. Controller posts the completion into Admin CQ slot 0

    The controller writes a success CQE to the admin CQ and interrupts on vector 0. The driver reads it and frees the slot with the CQ 0 head doorbell. Only now does CQ 3 exist.

    Where: Admin CQ slot 0; then driver writes BAR0 + 1004hPCIe: Yes · MWr 16 B + interrupt MWr device → host; then MWr 4 B host → device (CQ0HDBL ← 1)
    CQE: CID 0x0010 · SQID 0 · SQHD 1 · P 1 · Status 0 (success)
  5. Driver allocates the memory for I/O SQ 3

    Same idea for the submission ring. It does not need its phase bits cleared (SQEs have none), but it must be DMA-able and page-aligned.

    Where: Host memory 0x1_8004_0000PCIe: No.
    1024 entries × 64 B = 64 KiB, physically contiguous (PC = 1)
  6. Driver submits Create I/O Submission Queue (01h) naming CQ 3

    The second admin command goes into Admin SQ slot 1. CDW11 carries CQID = 3: "send this SQ's completions to CQ 3".

    Where: Admin SQ slot 1; doorbell at BAR0 + 1000hPCIe: SQE write No · doorbell Yes, MWr 4 B host → device
    CDW0 = 0011_0001h → OPC 01h, CID 0x0011 PRP1 = 0x1_8004_0000 CDW10 = 03FF_0003h → QSIZE 1024 entries, QID 3 CDW11 = 0003_0005h → CQID 3, QPRIO 10b (medium), PC 1 SQ0TDBL ← 2
  7. Controller fetches it, finds CQ 3, creates SQ 3

    The controller looks up CQID 3 in its queue table. It is there (from step 3), so it records SQ 3 and binds it to CQ 3. Had the driver sent this command first, the lookup would fail.

    Where: Admin SQ slot 1, then inside the SSDPCIe: Yes · MRd 64 B device → host, CplD back. The binding is internal.
    If CQ 3 did not exist: SCT 1, SC 00h Completion Queue Invalid (DNR = 1) → this is why the CQ is always created first, and deleted last.
  8. Controller posts the second completion into Admin CQ slot 1

    Success again. The driver consumes it and writes CQ 0 head = 2. Queue pair 3 is now usable.

    Where: Admin CQ slot 1; then BAR0 + 1004hPCIe: Yes · MWr 16 B + interrupt device → host; MWr 4 B host → device (CQ0HDBL ← 2)
    CQE: CID 0x0011 · SQID 0 · SQHD 2 · P 1 · Status 0
  9. Driver starts I/O on the new queue pair

    The driver writes the first Read into SQ 3 slot 0 and rings SQ 3's own tail doorbell. From now on completions for SQ 3 land in CQ 3 and interrupt on vector 3, and the driver frees them with CQ 3's head doorbell.

    Where: SQ 3 slot 0; doorbell at BAR0 + 1018hPCIe: SQE write No · doorbell Yes, MWr 4 B host → device
    SQ3TDBL = 1000h + (2·3)·4 = 1018h ← 1 CQ3HDBL = 1000h + (2·3+1)·4 = 101Ch (used after the first completion)

27.5 Queue memory diagrams

27.6 Interrupt vectors and CPU binding

Each I/O CQ with IEN=1 names one interrupt vector. With MSI-X, the vector is an index into the MSI-X table in a BAR; each table entry holds a message address and data that the OS programmed (typically targeting one CPU's local APIC or equivalent). When the controller posts a CQE to that CQ and decides to interrupt, it issues a posted MWr with that address and data. verified (MSI-X mechanism per PCIe specification.)

 CPU0 ─┬─ SQ1 ─┐                                   MSI-X table (BAR)
       │       ├─► CQ1 ── IV=1 ─────────────────► entry 1: addr→CPU0, data→vec 0x41
 CPU1 ─┴─ SQ2 ─┘ (two SQs may share a CQ)
 CPU2 ─── SQ3 ───► CQ3 ── IV=3 ─────────────────► entry 3: addr→CPU2, data→vec 0x43
 poll ─── SQ9 ───► CQ9 ── IEN=0 (polled, no vector)
 admin─── SQ0 ───► CQ0 ── IV=0 ─────────────────► entry 0

Interrupt coalescing (Set Features FID 08h: aggregation threshold and time) lets the controller delay interrupts to batch completions; it improves throughput and CPU use at a latency cost verified. Whether and how precisely a controller honours it is impl. FID 09h (Interrupt Vector Configuration) can disable coalescing per vector.

27.7 Command Identifier (CID)

  • CID is 16 bits in CDW0[31:16], chosen by the host verified.
  • The pair (SQID, CID) must be unique among outstanding commands: a CID may be reused only after its CQE has been consumed verified. The same CID value may be in flight on two different SQs simultaneously.
  • The CQE echoes CID (DW3[15:0]) and SQID (DW2[31:16]); together they locate the original request.
  • Linux: the CID is derived from the blk-mq tag; newer kernels also place a small generation counter in the upper CID bits so a completion carrying a stale/bogus CID can be detected version (present since roughly the 5.15 era; verify in your kernel source).
🐞 Debugging connection

Kernel messages naming a CID and QID for a timeout are your bridge into an analyzer capture: find the SQE MRd on that queue whose CDW0[31:16] equals the CID, then look for the matching CQE MWr. If you find the SQE fetch but no CQE, the command is lost inside the controller; if you find neither, check the doorbell value.

27.8 Choosing queue count and depth

L = λ × W   (Little's law: outstanding = throughput × latency)
  • L — average number of commands in flight across the queues.
  • λ — target completion rate (IOPS).
  • W — average device latency per command (s).

Example: target 1,000,000 IOPS at 80 µs average 4 KiB read latency → L = 10⁶ × 80×10⁻⁶ = 80 commands in flight. Spread over 16 queues that is 5 per queue; a depth of 64–1024 per queue is ample. More depth than L does not raise throughput; it raises latency once the device saturates. derived

27.9 Deleting queues

Order matters: Delete I/O SQ (00h) first — the controller aborts outstanding commands on that SQ (status Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion, 08h) and posts their completions — then Delete I/O CQ (04h). Deleting a CQ that still has an SQ attached fails with Invalid Queue Deletion (command-specific 0Ch) verified.

🧪 Lab 27.1 — Encode creation commands SAFE LAB

Objective: encode CDW10/CDW11 by hand and verify with the decoder from Chapter 29 (run it with admin argument). Steps: (1) Encode Create I/O CQ QID 5, 256 entries, IV 5, PC=1. (2) Encode Create I/O SQ QID 5 bound to CQ 5, low priority. (3) Build a 64-byte hex dump and decode it.

Solution

CQ: CDW10 = 0x00FF0005, CDW11 = 0x00050003. SQ: CDW10 = 0x00FF0005, CDW11 = 0x00050007 (CQID 5, QPRIO 11b → bits 2:1 = 11 → 6, PC 1).

🧪 Lab 27.2 — Observe queue usage under fio CAUTION LAB

Objective: see per-queue interrupt counts change with CPU placement. Setup: a test drive or a file on a filesystem; use --readonly.

grep nvme0q /proc/interrupts > before.txt
taskset -c 2 fio --name=r --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --readonly --rw=randread \
    --bs=4k --iodepth=32 --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=10 --time_based
grep nvme0q /proc/interrupts > after.txt; diff before.txt after.txt
⚠️ Safety

Use --readonly and never point a write workload at a device containing data. Reads on a production disk add load; run on a test system.

Questions: which vector's count grew? Why?

Solution

The vector of the CQ mapped to CPU 2 (blk-mq maps CPU 2's submissions to the hardware queue whose cpu_list contains 2, and its CQ interrupt is affined to that CPU set).

Extension: repeat with --hipri on a kernel configured with poll queues and observe that interrupt counts barely move.

Quiz

  1. CDW10 = 0x007F0002 in a Create I/O SQ. Size and QID?

    Answer

    128 entries, QID 2.

  2. Can CID 0x0005 be outstanding on SQ1 and SQ2 at the same time?

    Answer

    Yes — uniqueness is per SQ.

  3. What happens to outstanding commands when their SQ is deleted?

    Answer

    They are aborted and completed with status Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion (generic 08h).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Which is created first, CQ or SQ, and why?
    Model answerCQ, because Create I/O SQ references an existing CQID.
  2. Intermediate What does PC=0 imply?
    Model answerThe queue is non-contiguous; PRP1 points to a PRP list of the queue's pages. Only allowed if CAP.CQR=0.
  3. Advanced How would you size queue depth for a latency-sensitive database?
    Model answerApply Little's law with the target IOPS and acceptable latency; keep depth just above the knee where throughput stops rising; deeper only adds queueing delay.
  4. Senior Why might a driver use polled queues for some I/O?
    Model answerAvoids interrupt overhead and wake-up latency for very low-latency devices; costs CPU spinning. Polled CQs are created with IEN=0.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?Create I/O CQ 05h / SQ 01h field layouts (QID, QSIZE 0-based, PC, IEN, IV, CQID, QPRIO); CQ before SQ; delete SQ before CQ; CID unique per SQ. verified
What is derived?Memory sizing; Little's-law queue depth; CID as trace correlation key. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Max queues allocated, MSI-X vector count, performance per queue, CID conflict detection. impl
What is version-dependent?NVMSETID in CDW12; Linux CID generation bits. version
What must be checked in the specification?Command-specific status codes for creation errors in your revision.
What should never be assumed?That NSQA equals what you requested; that IV equals a CPU number.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can encode both create commands in hex and decode their failure statuses.
  • I can draw contiguous and PRP-list queue memory and compute slot addresses.
  • I can trace SQ→CQ→IV→CPU for any queue on my system.
  • I can explain CID scope and use a CID to correlate a kernel timeout with a trace.

27.12 Summary

I/O queues are created by the admin queue, CQ first; they carry QID, 0-based size, contiguity, CQ binding and interrupt vector. CIDs are per-SQ correlation keys. Next: Chapter 28 — doorbells.

28 Doorbells

← 27 I/O Queues29 NVMe Command Structure →
📘 Source notes

Official specification: NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (doorbell registers, stride) and NVMe Base Specification (CAP.DSTRD, queue semantics). Revision: PCIe Transport 1.4 / Base 2.4 baseline. Establishes: doorbell location formula, that doorbell values are queue indices. Does not establish: the controller's internal reaction time, fetch size or batching policy (impl).

28.1 Why this chapter exists

The doorbell is the only moment in the I/O fast path where the host CPU talks to the device. Everything before it (building the SQE) is ordinary memory writes; everything after it is device-initiated DMA. Doorbell mistakes — wrong offset, wrong value, missing memory barrier, rung too often — produce the most confusing failures in NVMe: silent hangs, replayed commands, and mysterious throughput ceilings.

28.2 Learning objectives

  • Compute any doorbell offset from QID and CAP.DSTRD, and invert an offset back to a queue.
  • State exactly what value is written and what it means (index, not count).
  • Describe the nine-step flow and the PCIe TLP for the doorbell, including ordering rules that make it correct.
  • Explain doorbell batching, shadow doorbells and their trade-offs.
  • Diagnose doorbell faults from a trace.

Prerequisites: Ch 25, Ch 27; TLP header basics (TLP).

🧒 Kid analogy

The doorbell is the bell on the cashier's desk. Ringing it does not carry any baskets — it only carries one number: "my last basket is just before spot 7". The cashier then walks along the belt and picks up everything up to spot 7. Each checkout has its own bell, and each receipt belt has its own bell you ring to say "I've collected receipts up to spot 3".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The "number" is the next empty slot (new tail), not the number of new baskets. And ringing twice with the same number does nothing new; ringing with a number that skips past baskets you never placed makes the cashier scan empty or stale spots — a real bell does not cause that damage.

28.3 The doorbell register map

SQyTDBL offset = 1000h + (2y) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)
CQyHDBL offset = 1000h + (2y + 1) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)
  • y — queue identifier (0 = admin).
  • CAP.DSTRD — Doorbell Stride, CAP bits 35:32; stride in bytes = 2^(2+DSTRD) = 4 << DSTRD.
  • SQyTDBL — Submission Queue y Tail Doorbell; bits 15:0 = SQT (new tail).
  • CQyHDBL — Completion Queue y Head Doorbell; bits 15:0 = CQH (new head).
  • Offsets are relative to the start of the controller register space (BAR0/BAR1 pair) verified.

28.3.1 Worked numbers

DSTRDStrideSQ0TDBLCQ0HDBLSQ1TDBLCQ1HDBLSQ3TDBLCQ3HDBLSQ16TDBL
04 B1000h1004h1008h100Ch1000h+6×4 = 1018h1000h+7×4 = 101Ch1000h+32×4 = 1080h
18 B1000h1008h1010h1018h1000h+6×8 = 1030h1038h1100h
216 B1000h1010h1020h1030h1000h+6×16 = 1060h1000h+7×16 = 1070h1200h
92 KiB1000h1800h2000h2800h1000h+6×800h = 4000h4800h11000h

Inverse: given offset O ≥ 1000h, index k = (O − 1000h) / stride; y = k ≫ 1; if k is even it is SQyTDBL, if odd CQyHDBL. Example DSTRD = 0, O = 1034h → k = 13 → y = 6, odd → CQ6HDBL. derived

Why a stride? A larger stride lets each doorbell sit in its own cache line or page — useful for virtualization (map one queue's doorbell page into a guest) or for hardware that wants doorbells in separate address decoding regions. Most physical SSDs report DSTRD = 0 impl.

BAR size consequence: the BAR must be large enough to contain 1000h + 2 × (max QID + 1) × stride bytes. With DSTRD=0 and 128 queue pairs that is 1000h + 256 × 4 = 1400h — under 8 KiB, hence the common 16 KiB BAR0. derived

28.4 The nine-step flow, carefully

#StepActorMemory/register changedPCIe evidenceWhat can go wrong
1Host creates commandDriverLocal struct (CPU cache)noneWrong fields, CID reuse
2Host writes command into SQ[tail]Driver64 B of SQ memory (DRAM via cache)none (CPU store to own memory)Writing wrong slot; torn write if not complete before step 4
3Host updates SQ tailDriverHost variable tail = (tail+1) mod NnoneOff-by-one, no wrap
4Host writes doorbellCPU (MMIO store, after a write barrier)SQyTDBL = tailMWr, 1 DW, posted, to BAR0 + offsetMissing barrier → controller reads old SQE; wrong offset → wrong queue
5Controller noticesControllerInternal "SQ y tail" updated; work schedulednone (internal)Firmware bug: missed doorbell → stall until next ring
6Controller fetches commandController DMAinternal SQ head advancesMRd (64 B × k) → CplD from Root ComplexIOMMU blocks read (UR/CA), poisoned completion
7Controller executesController + mediaNAND, caches, mapping tablesdata DMA: MWr (Read cmd) or MRd/CplD (Write cmd)Media error, PRP fault
8Controller posts completionController DMACQ[ctrl tail] = CQE with P, SQHDMWr 16 BCQ full; wrong phase
9Controller interrupts host if configuredControllernone (message)MWr 1 DW to MSI-X address (if IEN=1, vector unmasked, coalescing permits)Masked vector, wrong affinity, coalescing delay

Then the host consumes CQEs (phase match) and writes CQyHDBL — another posted MWr — which returns CQ slots to the controller.

28.5 What happens at the TLP level

A doorbell write from a 64-bit host whose BAR0 is assigned 0x00000000_FE000000 (a 32-bit address, so a 3-DW header) with DSTRD = 0, ringing SQ3 with new tail 0x0015:

Header DWFieldValueNote
DW0Fmt / Type010b / 0 0000b3-DW header with data → Memory Write (MWr32)
DW0TC, attributes (RO, NS)0, typically 0Traffic class 0; strong ordering
DW0Length1 DW4-byte register write
DW1Requester IDRoot Port / host bridge BDFCPU-originated
DW1TaganyPosted request: no completion, tag not used for matching
DW1Last DW BE / First DW BE0000b / 1111bSingle-DW request: Last BE must be 0000b
DW2Address[31:2]FE001018hBAR0 + 1018h (SQ3TDBL at DSTRD 0)
DataDWbytes 15 00 00 00Little-endian 0x00000015: new tail 21

If BAR0 is above 4 GiB, the TLP is an MWr64 with Fmt = 011b and a 4-DW header. The doorbell write is posted: the CPU does not wait for the device; the write is complete from the CPU's point of view once it leaves the CPU's write path. verified (PCIe posted-write semantics).

28.5.1 Ordering — why the controller sees the new SQE, not the old one

  1. The SQE store (step 2) targets write-back cacheable DRAM; the doorbell store (step 4) targets uncacheable MMIO. The driver issues a write memory barrier between them (Linux: writel() includes the needed ordering on most architectures, plus explicit wmb()/dma_wmb() where required) so the SQE is globally visible before the doorbell leaves. impl (architecture-specific)
  2. When the controller's MRd for the SQE arrives at the Root Complex, coherent DMA reads observe the latest CPU store (snooped). On non-coherent platforms the driver must flush caches — a classic porting bug.
  3. In the other direction, PCIe ordering rules say a posted write may not pass an earlier posted write in the same direction (unless Relaxed Ordering is set). So data MWr → CQE MWr → MSI-X MWr arrive in that order, and when the interrupt fires the CQE and data are visible. verified (PCIe ordering rules); a controller using Relaxed Ordering for data must still guarantee data visibility before the CQE — how it does that is impl.

28.6 Doorbell economics: batching and shadow doorbells

  • Batching: writing SQEs for 8 requests then ringing once (tail += 8) costs one MMIO write instead of eight. Linux blk-mq passes a "last request in batch" hint so the NVMe driver can defer the doorbell (commit_rqs path) version. CQ head doorbells are likewise written once per batch of reaped CQEs.
  • Shadow doorbells (Doorbell Buffer Config, admin opcode 7Ch): optional feature for emulated/virtual controllers. The host writes tail/head values to a shadow buffer in memory and only performs the (expensive, VM-exit-causing) MMIO write when an "EventIdx" in another buffer says the controller needs one verified (optional; check OACS). It reduces VM exits for paravirtual NVMe.
  • Cost of an MMIO write: a posted write is cheap for the CPU (tens of ns to issue) but, in a VM without shadow doorbells, it traps to the hypervisor (µs). impl

28.7 Doorbell rules to remember

  • The value is an index in 0…N−1 — writing N or larger is an invalid doorbell write value verified.
  • The new SQ tail must not make the SQ appear to contain more than N−1 entries relative to the controller's head; the new CQ head must not move past the controller's tail (host would be "consuming" entries that do not exist) — both are invalid verified.
  • Writes to doorbells of queues that do not exist are invalid doorbell register writes; the controller may report them as an asynchronous error event verified.
  • Doorbell registers are write-oriented; reading them back is not a reliable way to learn queue state — do not design tools that depend on it uncertain (read behaviour is not something you should rely on across devices).
  • Bits 31:16 of a doorbell are reserved; write zero.

28.8 Code — doorbell calculator and decoder

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""doorbell.py - compute and invert NVMe doorbell offsets (offline, no device access)."""
def sq_tdbl(qid, dstrd): return 0x1000 + (2 * qid) * (4 << dstrd)
def cq_hdbl(qid, dstrd): return 0x1000 + (2 * qid + 1) * (4 << dstrd)

def which(offset, dstrd):
    stride = 4 << dstrd
    if offset < 0x1000 or (offset - 0x1000) % stride:
        return "not a doorbell (or misaligned for this DSTRD)"
    k = (offset - 0x1000) // stride
    return f"{'CQ' if k & 1 else 'SQ'}{k >> 1}{'HDBL' if k & 1 else 'TDBL'}"

for d in (0, 2):
    print(f"DSTRD={d}: SQ3TDBL={sq_tdbl(3, d):#x} CQ3HDBL={cq_hdbl(3, d):#x}")
for off in (0x1000, 0x1034, 0x1060, 0x1006):
    print(f"offset {off:#x} @DSTRD0 -> {which(off, 0)}")
DSTRD=0: SQ3TDBL=0x1018 CQ3HDBL=0x101c
DSTRD=2: SQ3TDBL=0x1060 CQ3HDBL=0x1070
offset 0x1000 @DSTRD0 -> SQ0TDBL
offset 0x1034 @DSTRD0 -> CQ6HDBL
offset 0x1060 @DSTRD0 -> SQ12TDBL
offset 0x1006 @DSTRD0 -> not a doorbell (or misaligned for this DSTRD)

🧪 Lab 28.1 — Doorbell arithmetic drill SAFE LAB

Objective: fluency in offset ↔ queue mapping. Steps: for DSTRD = 0, 1, 3 compute SQ7TDBL and CQ7HDBL; invert offsets 1078h (DSTRD 0), 1078h (DSTRD 1), 1100h (DSTRD 3).

Solution

DSTRD 0: 1038h / 103Ch. DSTRD 1: 1070h / 1078h. DSTRD 3 (stride 32): 1000h+14×20h = 11C0h / 11E0h. Inversions: 1078h@0 → k=30 → SQ15TDBL; 1078h@1 → k=15 → CQ7HDBL; 1100h@3 → k=8 → SQ4TDBL.

Extension: write a function that, given a list of (offset, value) doorbell writes and queue sizes, flags invalid values.

🧪 Lab 28.2 — Senior forensic: reconstruct queue state from doorbells SAFE LAB

Setup: synthetic doorbell log (DSTRD 0, SQ1/CQ1 N=8): 1008h=3, 100Ch=2, 1008h=6, 100Ch=3, 1008h=1, 100Ch=7. CQE writes seen: 7.

Questions: how many commands were submitted? Is any doorbell invalid? What is outstanding at the end?

Solution

Tail went 0→3→6→1 (wrapped): 3+3+3 = 9 commands. CQ head went 0→2→3→7 = 7 consumed, matching 7 CQE writes, so no head write is beyond the tail. Outstanding = 9 − 7 = 2 commands (submitted, not completed). Was the SQ ever over-full? After the third ring, host-side used = (1 − SQ head) mod 8; the controller head is unknown without SQHD values — record "missing evidence: SQHD of last CQE". If SQHD of the 7th CQE was ≥ 2, the SQ never exceeded 7 entries.

Quiz

  1. DSTRD = 2. Offset of CQ5HDBL?

    Answer

    1000h + 11 × 16 = 1000h + B0h = 10B0h.

  2. Is the doorbell MWr acknowledged by a completion TLP?

    Answer

    No, memory writes are posted. Link-level Ack DLLPs confirm delivery across each link, but no end-to-end completion exists.

  3. Host submits 3 commands, SQ tail was 6, N = 8. Value written?

    Answer

    (6+3) mod 8 = 1.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What does a doorbell write contain?
    Model answerA 16-bit queue index (new SQ tail or new CQ head) in a 32-bit register.
  2. Intermediate Derive the SQ3 doorbell offset with DSTRD=2.
    Model answer1000h + 6 × 16 = 1060h.
  3. Advanced Why can a missing write barrier cause the device to execute a stale command?
    Model answerThe MMIO doorbell may become visible to the device before the cached SQE store becomes visible to DMA; the device's MRd then returns the previous lap's content.
  4. Senior How do shadow doorbells work and when are they worth it?
    Model answerHost writes indices to memory; device publishes EventIdx; host rings the MMIO doorbell only when crossing EventIdx; it cuts VM exits for emulated controllers, irrelevant for bare-metal SSDs.
💡 Senior insight

In a protocol trace, the doorbell writes are your skeleton: filter on host-originated MWr to BAR0 ≥ 1000h first, decode each to (queue, index), and only then add device MRd/MWr around them. A clean doorbell skeleton tells you in minutes whether the host or the device stopped first.

📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?Doorbells start at 1000h; SQyTDBL = 1000h + 2y×(4<<DSTRD); CQyHDBL = 1000h + (2y+1)×(4<<DSTRD); values are 16-bit indices; MWr is posted. verified
What is derived?Inverse mapping offset→queue; BAR size bound; ordering argument data→CQE→MSI-X. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Doorbell-to-fetch latency, fetch size, shadow doorbell support (optional), barrier implementation per CPU architecture. impl
What is version-dependent?Doorbell Buffer Config availability; asynchronous error reporting details. version
What must be checked in the specification?Exact list of invalid doorbell conditions and how they are reported.
What should never be assumed?That doorbell reads return the last written value; that DSTRD is always 0.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute and invert doorbell offsets for any DSTRD.
  • I can describe the doorbell TLP header fields and why it is posted.
  • I can explain the ordering guarantees that make SQE→doorbell and data→CQE→MSI-X safe.
  • I can reconstruct queue occupancy from a doorbell log and say what evidence is missing.

28.11 Summary

Doorbells are posted 4-byte MMIO writes of a queue index at 1000h + (2y or 2y+1) × (4 << DSTRD). They are the only host-to-device traffic in the I/O path; ordering barriers make them correct and batching makes them cheap. Further reading: NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4 (doorbell registers, Doorbell Buffer Config); PCIe Base Specification (posted-write ordering). Next: Part XI — NVMe commands.

PART XI

NVMe Commands

A queue is just a conveyor belt; the commands are the baskets. This Part dissects the 64-byte Submission Queue Entry and the 16-byte Completion Queue Entry bit by bit (Chapter 29), then walks the Admin command set (Chapter 30) and the NVM I/O command set (Chapter 31), and finally follows a READ (Chapter 32), a WRITE (Chapter 33), a FLUSH (Chapter 34) and a Dataset Management deallocate (Chapter 35) end to end from the application down to NAND and back. You will build an executable decoder that turns a hex dump into a field table and a list of expected PCIe events.

29 NVMe Command Structure

← 28 Doorbells30 Admin Commands →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Express Base Specification (common command format, completion queue entry, status codes); NVM Command Set Specification (NVM-specific fields, e.g. Read/Write CDW10–15). REVISION: Base 2.4, NVM CS 1.3 (baseline, Aug 2026) version. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.x reserved DW1 of the CQE and CDW2–3 of most commands; later revisions gave some of these bits command-specific meanings (for example, extended protection-information fields). The Command Retry Delay (CRD) bits in the status field appeared in revision 1.4. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications.

29.1 Why this chapter exists

Every NVMe command, admin or I/O, Read or Identify, uses the same 64-byte envelope, and every result uses the same 16-byte envelope. Once you can decode those two envelopes from raw bytes, every protocol trace, every kernel tracepoint (nvme_setup_cmd prints CDW10–15), and every vendor debug dump becomes readable. This chapter is the Rosetta Stone for the rest of the book.

29.2 Learning objectives

  • Decode all 16 dwords of an SQE, including CDW0 subfields (opcode, FUSE, PSDT, CID).
  • Decode all 4 dwords of a CQE, including SQHD, SQID, CID, phase and the 15-bit status field.
  • Classify a status by Status Code Type (SCT) and Status Code (SC) and decide whether to retry (DNR, CRD).
  • Apply a disciplined 12-step procedure to read any unfamiliar command.
  • Run a decoder on a hex dump and predict the PCIe transactions the command will cause.

Prerequisites: Ch 25 (phase tag, SQHD), Ch 27 (CID scope), little-endian byte order.

🧒 Kid analogy — the request slip

Every request to the librarian is written on the same printed form with 16 boxes. Box 1 says what you want (the opcode) and your ticket number (CID). Box 2 says which library section (namespace). Boxes 7–10 say where your shelf at home is, so the librarian's helper can carry books straight there (data pointer). Boxes 11–16 are "special instructions" whose meaning depends on what you asked for. The answer slip is smaller: four boxes — a little answer, which belt position the librarian has reached, your ticket number, the ink colour and a "how did it go" code.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The form is binary, little-endian and position-based: the same bits in CDW10 mean "starting LBA" in a Read and "log page ID" in Get Log Page. Which meaning applies depends on the queue type (admin vs I/O) and the command set of the namespace — the form itself does not say.

The same picture for the 16-byte completion entry. The first two dwords depend on the command. The last two are fixed for every command: DW2 says which SQ and how far the controller has read it, DW3 says which command finished and how.

The 15-bit status field (DW3 bits 31:17), numbered here as status bits 14:0:

DW3 bitsStatus bitsFieldMeaning
24:177:0SC Status CodeMeaning depends on SCT
27:2510:8SCT Status Code Typesee table
29:2812:11CRD Command Retry Delay0 = no delay; 1–3 select CRDT1–3 from Identify Controller (units of 100 ms) version (1.4+)
3013M MoreMore status information available via Get Log Page (Error Information log)
3114DNR Do Not Retry1 = retrying the same command is expected to fail again

Quick decode trick: take DW3 bytes 14–15 as a 16-bit little-endian value V. Then P = V & 1, SC = (V >> 1) & FFh, SCT = (V >> 9) & 7, CRD = (V >> 12) & 3, M = (V >> 14) & 1, DNR = V >> 15. Example bytes 03 05 → V = 0503h → P=1, SC=81h, SCT=2 → Unrecovered Read Error. derived
