0/07hCommand Abort RequestedHost sent Abort for this CIDHost decision
0/08hCommand Aborted due to SQ DeletionDelete I/O SQ while command outstandingYes, on another queue
0/0BhInvalid Namespace or FormatNSID not active / 0 where requiredNo
0/0ChCommand Sequence ErrorFused pair broken, wrong orderNo
0/0Dh–11hSGL errors (Invalid SGL Segment Descriptor, Invalid Number of SGL Descriptors, Data SGL Length Invalid, Metadata SGL Length Invalid, SGL Descriptor Type Invalid)Malformed SGL (Ch 37)No
0/13hPRP Offset InvalidNon-zero offset where a page-aligned PRP is required (Ch 36)No
0/80hLBA Out of RangeSLBA+NLB beyond namespace sizeNo
0/82hNamespace Not ReadyNamespace temporarily unavailableYes (after delay)
0/83hReservation ConflictHost lacks reservation accessNo
2/80hWrite FaultMedia program failureMaybe
2/81hUnrecovered Read ErrorECC could not correctLimited
2/82h–84hEnd-to-end Guard / Application Tag / Reference Tag Check ErrorProtection information mismatchNo
2/85hCompare FailureCompare data mismatchNo (it is the answer)
2/87hDeallocated or Unwritten Logical BlockRead of deallocated LBA when the namespace is configured to report itNo

All codes verified against long-standing NVMe Base/NVM CS tables; confirm exact values in the revision you implement — new codes are appended over revisions version.

29.6 Reading an NVMe command — the 12-step procedure

  1. Identify the command set: admin queue → admin set; I/O queue → command set of the namespace (NVM, ZNS, KV …), selected via CC.CSS and the namespace's CSI.
  2. Identify the opcode (CDW0[7:0]) in that set's table.
  3. Identify the command format: which CDW10–15 layout applies (e.g. Read/Write layout).
  4. Identify mandatory fields (e.g. SLBA, NLB).
  5. Identify optional fields (FUA, LR, PRINFO, DSM hints) and whether the controller supports them.
  6. Identify data pointers: PSDT, PRP1/PRP2 or SGL1, MPTR; transfer direction.
  7. Identify namespace applicability: NSID meaning (specific, broadcast, unused).
  8. Identify prerequisites: queue exists, namespace attached, format supports PI, reservation held.
  9. Identify completion: what DW0 returns, which statuses are possible.
  10. Identify errors: field validation failures and their SCT/SC.
  11. Identify side effects: media change, cache flush, log updates, async events.
  12. Identify trace consequences: SQE fetch, data MRd/MWr counts and sizes, CQE, interrupt.
⚠️ Command decoding safety

Never infer semantics from the opcode alone. Before you write "this is a Read" check: (1) which command set the queue/namespace uses, (2) controller capabilities (Identify Controller ONCS, OACS…), (3) the Commands Supported and Effects log (LID 05h) for command-set support, (4) namespace context (CSI, LBA format, PI), (5) specification revision, and (6) that reserved fields are zero. Opcode 02h on a ZNS or KV namespace is decoded with that command set's table; opcode values at or above 80h may be vendor-specific in some ranges.

29.7 Code — an executable 64-byte command decoder

Input: a synthetic SQE hex dump (offset columns allowed). Output: a field table, command-set-specific interpretation, data pointer analysis, expected protocol events, plus CQE decoding. It is an offline teaching tool synthetic inputs.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""nvme_decode.py - teaching decoder for a 64-byte SQE and a 16-byte CQE.
EXECUTABLE, offline: it parses hex text only and touches no device.
Field names follow the NVMe Base / NVM Command Set layouts; always confirm
against the revision your device reports (Identify Controller VER / CAP)."""
import struct, sys

ADMIN = {0x00: "Delete I/O SQ", 0x01: "Create I/O SQ", 0x02: "Get Log Page",
         0x04: "Delete I/O CQ", 0x05: "Create I/O CQ", 0x06: "Identify",
         0x08: "Abort", 0x09: "Set Features", 0x0A: "Get Features",
         0x0C: "Asynchronous Event Request", 0x0D: "Namespace Management",
         0x10: "Firmware Commit", 0x11: "Firmware Image Download",
         0x80: "Format NVM", 0x84: "Sanitize"}
NVM = {0x00: "Flush", 0x01: "Write", 0x02: "Read", 0x04: "Write Uncorrectable",
       0x05: "Compare", 0x08: "Write Zeroes", 0x09: "Dataset Management",
       0x0C: "Verify", 0x19: "Copy"}
FUSE = ["normal", "fused: first command", "fused: second command", "reserved"]
PSDT = ["PRP", "SGL (MPTR = contiguous metadata buffer)",
        "SGL (MPTR = address of metadata SGL segment)", "reserved"]

def parse_hex(text):
    tok = text.replace(",", " ").split()
    tok = [t for t in tok if not t.endswith(":")]          # drop "0000:" offsets
    data = bytes(int(t, 16) for t in tok)
    return data

def bits(v, hi, lo):
    return (v >> lo) & ((1 << (hi - lo + 1)) - 1)

def decode_sqe(raw, queue="io", mps=4096):
    assert len(raw) == 64, f"SQE must be 64 bytes, got {len(raw)}"
    dw = struct.unpack("<16I", raw)
    opc, fuse, psdt, cid = bits(dw[0], 7, 0), bits(dw[0], 9, 8), bits(dw[0], 15, 14), bits(dw[0], 31, 16)
    table = ADMIN if queue == "admin" else NVM
    name = table.get(opc, "unknown/vendor-specific/other command set - CHECK SPEC")
    mptr = dw[4] | dw[5] << 32
    prp1 = dw[6] | dw[7] << 32
    prp2 = dw[8] | dw[9] << 32
    rows = [("CDW0[7:0]", "OPC", f"{opc:02X}h", f"{name} ({queue} queue)"),
            ("CDW0[9:8]", "FUSE", f"{fuse}", FUSE[fuse]),
            ("CDW0[15:14]", "PSDT", f"{psdt}", PSDT[psdt]),
            ("CDW0[31:16]", "CID", f"{cid:04X}h", "host-chosen tag, echoed in CQE DW3"),
            ("CDW1", "NSID", f"{dw[1]:08X}h",
             "broadcast (all namespaces)" if dw[1] == 0xFFFFFFFF else
             ("0 = not namespace-specific" if dw[1] == 0 else f"namespace {dw[1]}")),
            ("CDW2-3", "cmd-specific", f"{dw[2]:08X}h {dw[3]:08X}h", "reserved for many commands"),
            ("CDW4-5", "MPTR", f"{mptr:016X}h", "metadata pointer" if mptr else "unused"),
            ("CDW6-7", "PRP1/DPTR", f"{prp1:016X}h", f"page offset {prp1 % mps:#x}"),
            ("CDW8-9", "PRP2/DPTR", f"{prp2:016X}h", f"page offset {prp2 % mps:#x}")]
    for i in range(10, 16):
        rows.append((f"CDW{i}", "cmd-specific", f"{dw[i]:08X}h", ""))
    print(f"{'field':12} {'name':13} {'value':20} meaning")
    for r in rows:
        print(f"{r[0]:12} {r[1]:13} {r[2]:20} {r[3]}")
    if prp1 & 0x3:
        print("!! PRP1 bits 1:0 not zero - PRP entries must be dword aligned")
    if queue == "io" and opc in (0x01, 0x02, 0x05, 0x0C, 0x04, 0x08):
        slba = dw[10] | dw[11] << 32
        nlb = bits(dw[12], 15, 0) + 1
        print(f"\n{name}: SLBA={slba:#x} NLB={nlb} blocks (field holds {nlb-1}, 0-based) "
              f"LR={bits(dw[12],31,31)} FUA={bits(dw[12],30,30)} PRINFO={bits(dw[12],29,26):04b}")
        return {"opc": opc, "cid": cid, "slba": slba, "nlb": nlb, "prp1": prp1, "prp2": prp2}
    if queue == "io" and opc == 0x09:
        print(f"\nDSM: NR={bits(dw[10],7,0)+1} ranges, AD={bits(dw[11],2,2)} "
              f"IDW={bits(dw[11],1,1)} IDR={bits(dw[11],0,0)}; range list at PRP1")
    if queue == "admin" and opc == 0x06:
        cns = bits(dw[10], 7, 0)
        names = {0x00: "Identify Namespace (NSID)", 0x01: "Identify Controller",
                 0x02: "Active Namespace ID list"}
        print(f"\nIdentify CNS={cns:02X}h -> {names.get(cns,'other CNS - check spec')}, "
              f"CNTID={bits(dw[10],31,16)}; 4096-byte data buffer at PRP1")
    if queue == "admin" and opc == 0x02:
        lid = bits(dw[10], 7, 0)
        numd = (bits(dw[10], 31, 16) | bits(dw[11], 15, 0) << 16) + 1
        lids = {0x01: "Error Information", 0x02: "SMART / Health Information",
                0x03: "Firmware Slot Information"}
        print(f"\nGet Log Page LID={lid:02X}h ({lids.get(lid,'other - check spec')}), "
              f"RAE={bits(dw[10],15,15)}, NUMD={numd} dwords = {numd*4} bytes")
    if queue == "admin" and opc in (0x01, 0x05):
        print(f"\nCreate I/O {'SQ' if opc == 1 else 'CQ'}: QID={bits(dw[10],15,0)} "
              f"QSIZE={bits(dw[10],31,16)+1} entries (0-based field), PC={bits(dw[11],0,0)}, "
              + (f"CQID={bits(dw[11],31,16)} QPRIO={bits(dw[11],2,1)}" if opc == 1 else
                 f"IEN={bits(dw[11],1,1)} IV={bits(dw[11],31,16)}"))
    return {"opc": opc, "cid": cid}

SCT = {0: "Generic Command Status", 1: "Command Specific Status",
       2: "Media and Data Integrity Errors", 3: "Path Related Status", 7: "Vendor Specific"}
GEN_SC = {0x00: "Successful Completion", 0x01: "Invalid Command Opcode",
          0x02: "Invalid Field in Command", 0x03: "Command ID Conflict",
          0x04: "Data Transfer Error", 0x06: "Internal Error",
          0x07: "Command Abort Requested", 0x08: "Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion",
          0x0B: "Invalid Namespace or Format", 0x13: "PRP Offset Invalid",
          0x80: "LBA Out of Range"}
MEDIA_SC = {0x81: "Unrecovered Read Error", 0x80: "Write Fault"}

def decode_cqe(raw):
    assert len(raw) == 16, "CQE must be 16 bytes"
    dw0, dw1, dw2, dw3 = struct.unpack("<4I", raw)
    sf = bits(dw3, 31, 17)                     # 15-bit status field
    sc, sct = bits(sf, 7, 0), bits(sf, 10, 8)
    crd, more, dnr = bits(sf, 12, 11), bits(sf, 13, 13), bits(sf, 14, 14)
    meaning = (GEN_SC if sct == 0 else MEDIA_SC if sct == 2 else {}).get(sc, "see spec table")
    print(f"DW0={dw0:08X}h (command specific)  DW1={dw1:08X}h")
    print(f"SQHD={bits(dw2,15,0)} SQID={bits(dw2,31,16)} CID={bits(dw3,15,0):04X}h P={bits(dw3,16,16)}")
    print(f"Status: SCT={sct} ({SCT.get(sct,'reserved')}) SC={sc:02X}h ({meaning}) "
          f"CRD={crd} M={more} DNR={dnr}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # Synthetic Read: CID 0x0042, NSID 1, SLBA 0x1000, 32 x 512 B = 16 KiB, PRP list
    sqe = """
    0000: 02 00 42 00 01 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
    0010: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 34 12 01 00 00 00
    0020: 00 50 34 12 01 00 00 00 00 10 00 00 00 00 00 00
    0030: 1f 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00"""
    info = decode_sqe(parse_hex(sqe), queue="io")
    print("\nExpected protocol events (derived, PCIe transport):")
    print(" 1 host MWr 4 B -> BAR0 + SQyTDBL (posted)")
    print(" 2 ctrl MRd 64 B from SQ slot -> CplD 64 B")
    print(" 3 ctrl MRd PRP list (PRP2 is list pointer since >2 pages) -> CplD")
    print(" 4 ctrl MWr data to PRP1 page and listed pages (read = device writes host memory)")
    print(" 5 ctrl MWr 16 B CQE, then MWr MSI-X message (if enabled)")
    print(" 6 host MWr 4 B -> BAR0 + CQyHDBL")
    print("\n-- CQE --")
    decode_cqe(parse_hex("00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 05 00 01 00 42 00 01 00"))
    print("\n-- failed CQE --")
    decode_cqe(parse_hex("00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 06 00 01 00 43 00 03 05"))
    print("\n-- admin: Get Log Page, SMART/Health, 512 bytes --")
    glp = bytearray(64)
    struct.pack_into("<I", glp, 0, 0x0007 << 16 | 0x02)        # CID 7, opcode 02h
    struct.pack_into("<I", glp, 4, 0xFFFFFFFF)                 # NSID: controller-wide
    struct.pack_into("<Q", glp, 24, 0x0000000123456000)        # PRP1
    struct.pack_into("<I", glp, 40, (128 - 1) << 16 | 0x02)    # NUMDL=127, LID=02h
    decode_sqe(bytes(glp), queue="admin")

Read the expected events critically: the decoder knows the transfer is 32 × 512 B = 16 KiB and PRP1 is page-aligned, so 4 pages are touched, so PRP2 must be a PRP list pointer — the list itself must be fetched with an extra MRd. That inference is derived from the PRP rules of Chapter 36 and assumes a 512-byte LBA format; with a 4096-byte format the same NLB field would mean 128 KiB.

29.8 Fused operations

FUSE lets two adjacent SQEs in the same SQ execute as one atomic unit. The defined use is Compare (first) + Write (second): the write happens only if the compare matches — an atomic compare-and-write used by cluster filesystems/lock managers verified (support reported in Identify Controller FUSES). Rules: the two commands must be adjacent, have the same NSID and LBA range; if the first fails, the second is aborted with "Command Aborted due to Failed Fused Command" (0/09h); if a part is missing, 0/0Ah.

🧪 Lab 29.1 — Command status lab SAFE LAB

Objective: interpret synthetic completion entries: status, phase, CID, retry decision. Setup: the decoder above. Procedure: decode each 16-byte CQE (hex, little-endian) and fill the table.

#CQE bytesContext
100 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0a 00 02 00 10 00 00 00CQ2 host expects P=1
200 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0b 00 02 00 11 00 01 01Read on SQ2
300 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0c 00 02 00 12 00 01 80Write on SQ2
407 00 07 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 03 00 01 00Set Features FID 07h on admin
500 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0d 00 02 00 13 00 0f c5Read on SQ2
Solution
  1. V=0000h: P=0 ≠ expected 1 → not a new entry; stop scanning. Do not interpret the rest.
  2. V=0101h: P=1, SC=80h, SCT=0 → LBA Out of Range, DNR=0 (still not worth retrying: fix SLBA/NLB).
  3. V=8001h: P=1, SC=00h, SCT=0, DNR=1 → success with DNR set — DNR has no meaning on success; flag as suspicious device behaviour but treat as success.
  4. DW0=00070007h → NSQA=7, NCQA=7 (0-based) → 8 I/O SQs and 8 I/O CQs allocated. SQHD=1, SQID=0, CID 3, success.
  5. V=C50Fh: P=1, SC=87h, SCT=2 → Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block; M=1 (error log has more), DNR=1. Reading trimmed blocks with error reporting enabled.

Extension: write a function should_retry(cqe) using DNR, CRD and SCT, and justify each branch.

Quiz

  1. Which bytes of an SQE hold PRP2?

    Answer

    Bytes 32–39 (CDW8–9).

  2. CDW0 = 0x01234001. Decode.

    Answer

    OPC 01h, FUSE 00b, PSDT = bits 15:14 of 0x4001 = 01b (SGL, MPTR contiguous), CID 0x0123.

  3. Why does the CQE carry SQID?

    Answer

    Because several SQs may share one CQ, and CIDs are unique only per SQ.

  4. What does M=1 tell you?

    Answer

    More information is available in the Error Information log page (LID 01h).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner How big are SQEs and CQEs?
    Model answer64 and 16 bytes for NVMe over PCIe.
  2. Intermediate Where are PRP1 and PRP2, and when is DPTR an SGL?
    Model answerBytes 24–31 and 32–39; when PSDT is 01b or 10b, bytes 24–39 hold SGL descriptor 1.
  3. Advanced Explain SCT vs SC and give one example of each type.
    Model answerSCT selects the table; SC indexes it. Generic 02h Invalid Field; Command-specific 02h Invalid Queue Size (for Create); Media 81h Unrecovered Read Error; Path-related (ANA states).
  4. Senior A trace shows a command fetched with PSDT=11b. What happens and why does it matter?
    Model answerReserved encoding — controller should fail it with Invalid Field in Command; seeing it suggests host memory corruption or a mis-built SQE (e.g. CID written in the wrong half of CDW0).
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?SQE/CQE layouts; CDW0 OPC/FUSE/PSDT/CID; DPTR bytes 24–39; status field SCT/SC/CRD/M/DNR; generic and media status codes listed. verified
What is derived?The V-trick for decoding DW3 bytes 14–15; expected PCIe events from a decoded SQE. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Whether a controller detects CID conflicts or validates every reserved field. impl
What is version-dependent?CDW2–3 and CQE DW1 usage; CRD (1.4+); path-related SCT (1.4+); new status codes. version
What must be checked in the specification?Opcode meaning per command set; reserved-field rules per command.
What should never be assumed?That an opcode alone identifies the command; that DNR=0 means retry will succeed.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can decode any SQE/CQE hex dump by hand within two minutes.
  • I can classify any status and make a justified retry decision.
  • I can explain which fields are version-dependent.
  • I ran the decoder and modified it to decode at least one more command.

29.10 Summary

CDW0 (opcode/FUSE/PSDT/CID), NSID, MPTR, DPTR and CDW10–15 make up every command; DW0, SQHD/SQID, CID/P/Status make up every completion. Next: Chapter 30 — admin commands.

30 Admin Commands

← 29 NVMe Command Structure31 The NVM Command Set →

30.1 Why this chapter exists

Admin commands are how the host discovers, configures, monitors, updates and erases the device. They are low-rate but high-consequence: a wrong Format NVM or Sanitize destroys data, a wrong Firmware Commit can brick a device, and a missing Asynchronous Event Request hides errors. A senior engineer must know these commands' fields and side effects precisely.

30.2 Learning objectives

  • Recall the admin opcode table and classify each command as read-only, configuring or destructive.
  • Build Identify (CNS 00h, 01h, 02h) and Get Log Page (LID 01h, 02h, 03h) commands with correct NUMD.
  • Use Get/Set Features with SEL and SV; know key FIDs.
  • Explain Abort and AER semantics, firmware download/commit flow, namespace management/attachment, Format NVM and Sanitize.

Prerequisites: Ch 26, Ch 29.

🧒 Kid analogy

The manager's desk has a menu: "describe the store" (Identify), "show me a logbook" (Get Log Page), "change a setting / tell me a setting" (Set/Get Features), "cancel that order" (Abort), "call me if something happens" (Async Event Request), "install new store rules" (firmware), "build or remove a store section" (namespace management), "repaint and empty a section" (Format), "shred everything" (Sanitize).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

"Call me if something happens" is not a phone number left with the manager: it is a command that stays outstanding in the controller and completes only when an event occurs — possibly hours later. And "cancel that order" is only a best-effort request; the order may complete anyway.

The opcodes in the course's verified list (00h, 01h, 02h, 04h, 05h, 06h, 08h, 09h, 0Ah, 0Ch, 0Dh, 10h, 11h, 80h, 84h) are verified; the others (14h, 15h, 18h, 19h, 1Ah, 7Ch, 81h, 82h, 86h) are long-standing values you should still confirm in the revision you use version. The 2.4 release adds features (e.g. Restore Manufacturing Default Settings, rate limiting, voltage monitoring, post-quantum cryptography support for security protocols); read the 2.4 documents for their exact command/feature encodings — this book does not invent them version.

Key derived values: MDTS (Maximum Data Transfer Size) = 2^MDTS × minimum memory page size (CAP.MPSMIN); 0 = no limit. E.g. MDTS = 5, MPSMIN = 4 KiB → 128 KiB per command. LBA size = 2^LBADS of the format selected in FLBAS (LBADS = 9 → 512 B, 12 → 4096 B). verified

Worked: SMART log (512 bytes) → NUMD = 128 dwords → NUMDL = 127 = 7Fh → CDW10 = 0x007F0002 (with RAE=0) — the decoder output in §29.7 shows exactly this.

30.5.1 Get Log Page end to end: reading the SMART / Health log

A log page is a read in the device → host direction only: the driver sends a small command, and the controller answers by writing the log into a host buffer. Below is what nvme smart-log causes on the admin queue. It is the sixth admin command since enable, so it uses slot 5 and the doorbell values become 6. The flow is the same as Identify (§26.6a); what changes is the opcode, the 512-byte size and where the data comes from. synthetic

Software starts itDevice starts itInside the SSD (not visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. Driver writes the Get Log Page command into Admin SQ slot 5

    The 64-byte command says which log (LID), how many dwords (NUMD, 0's based) and where to put it (PRP1).

    Where: Host memory, Admin SQ slot 5 (0x1_0000_0000 + 5 × 64)PCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    CDW0 = 0005_0002h → OPC 02h (Get Log Page), CID 0x0005 NSID = FFFF_FFFFh (controller-wide health) PRP1 = 0x1_0000_3000 CDW10 = 007F_0002h → NUMDL 7Fh (128 dwords = 512 B), RAE 0, LID 02h CDW11 = 0 (NUMDU 0) · CDW12/13 = 0 (offset 0)
  2. Driver rings the SQ 0 tail doorbell

    The new tail is 6: slots 0–5 have been used since the queue was created.

    Where: BAR0 + 1000hPCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 6
  3. Controller fetches the command

    The controller reads slot 5 of the Admin SQ.

    Where: Host memory, Admin SQ slot 5PCIe: Yes, both ways · MRd 64 B device → host, CplD 64 B back
    Decoded: Get Log Page, LID 02h, 512 bytes, to 0x1_0000_3000, CID 5
  4. Controller takes a snapshot of its health counters

    Firmware fills the 512-byte SMART / Health Information structure from its internal counters and sensors. How fresh each value is depends on the design.

    Where: Inside the SSDPCIe: No.
    Composite temperature read from a sensor; wear and error counters from firmware tables impl
  5. Controller writes the 512-byte log into the host buffer

    The DMA engine writes the structure to PRP1. This is the only data movement of the whole command, and it goes device → host.

    Where: Host memory 0x1_0000_3000 … 0x1_0000_31FFPCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr TLPs (e.g. 2 × 256 B with Max Payload Size 256)
    Byte 0 critical warning · 1–2 composite temperature (K) · 3 available spare 5 percentage used · 32–47 data units read · 48–63 data units written 128–143 power-on hours · 144–159 unsafe shutdowns · 160–175 media errors
  6. Controller writes the completion into Admin CQ slot 5

    A normal 16-byte CQE. For Get Log Page, DW0 carries nothing the host needs here.

    Where: Host memory, Admin CQ slot 5 (0x1_0000_1000 + 5 × 16)PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 16 bytes
    CID 0x0005 · SQID 0 · SQHD 6 · P 1 · Status 0 (success)
  7. Controller sends the interrupt

    Admin completions use interrupt vector 0.

    Where: MSI-X table entry 0PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 4 bytes
    Ordered behind the 512-B data and the CQE.
  8. Driver reads the completion; the tool decodes the log

    The driver matches CID 5 with status 0 and hands the buffer to the caller (for example nvme smart-log), which decodes the little-endian fields.

    Where: Host memory, Admin CQ slot 5 and the 512-B bufferPCIe: No.
    byte 0 = 00h → no critical warning bytes 1–2 = 43 01 → 0143h = 323 K → about 50 °C byte 3 = 64h → 100 % spare left · byte 5 = 03h → 3 % of rated life used
  9. Driver rings the CQ 0 head doorbell

    Slot 5 of the Admin CQ is free again.

    Where: BAR0 + 1004hPCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 6

Host → device carries only the doorbells and the fetched 64-byte command; the 512 bytes of log data travel device → host. A larger log (e.g. Telemetry) uses the same flow with a bigger NUMD, an offset in CDW12/13, and possibly several commands.

30.6 Set Features (09h) / Get Features (0Ah)

CDW10 FID[7:0] selects the feature; Set Features CDW10 bit 31 SV (Save) asks to persist across resets (if the feature is saveable); Get Features CDW10 bits 10:8 SEL = 000b current, 001b default, 010b saved, 011b supported capabilities. Feature value is in CDW11 (and sometimes a data buffer); the current value comes back in CQE DW0.

FIDFeatureCDW11 / DW0 meaning
01hArbitrationBurst, low/medium/high priority weights
02hPower ManagementPS (power state), WH (workload hint)
04hTemperature ThresholdTMPTH (Kelvin), sensor select, over/under
06hVolatile Write CacheWCE bit 0 — enables the write cache (if present)
07hNumber of QueuesNSQR[15:0], NCQR[31:16] 0-based; DW0 returns allocated
08hInterrupt CoalescingTHR (aggregation threshold, 0-based), TIME (100 µs units)
09hInterrupt Vector ConfigurationIV, CD (coalescing disable)
0BhAsynchronous Event ConfigurationWhich events generate AENs
0ChAutonomous Power State TransitionAPSTE + table in data buffer

FIDs above verified as long-standing; newer FIDs (including those introduced with 2.4 features) must be read from the current spec version.

30.7 Abort (08h) and Asynchronous Event Request (0Ch)

  • Abort: CDW10 SQID[15:0] + CID[31:16] identify the victim. Abort is best-effort: the CQE DW0 bit 0 = 0 means the command was aborted, 1 means it was not verified. The victim, if aborted, completes with 0/07h Command Abort Requested. Abort Command Limit (ACL in Identify Controller, 0-based) caps concurrent aborts; exceeding it → command-specific 03h.
  • AER: no parameters. Up to AERL+1 may be outstanding. Completes when an event occurs; DW0 bits 2:0 Asynchronous Event Type (0 Error, 1 SMART/Health, 2 Notice, 6 I/O command set specific, 7 vendor), bits 15:8 Asynchronous Event Information, bits 23:16 Log Page Identifier to read. The host must read that log (without RAE) to clear the event and then re-submit an AER verified.

30.8 Firmware commands

  1. Firmware Image Download (11h): CDW10 NUMD (0-based dwords), CDW11 OFST (dword offset). Send the image in pieces; each piece must respect FWUG (Firmware Update Granularity) from Identify Controller.
  2. Firmware Commit (10h): CDW10 FS[2:0] slot, CA[5:3] commit action (000b replace, 001b replace and activate at next reset, 010b activate existing slot at next reset, 011b replace and activate immediately …), BPID[31] boot partition. Completion may say a reset is required (command-specific 0Bh / 10h / 11h etc.).
  3. Verify with Get Log Page LID 03h.
⚠️ Safety

Firmware commands are EXPERT operations. Only use vendor-supplied images, on test hardware, with power stability. Interrupting activation can leave a device unbootable.

30.9 Namespace management, attachment, Format NVM, Sanitize

  • Namespace Management (0Dh): SEL (CDW10[3:0]) 0h create (data buffer with NSZE, NCAP, FLBAS, …; CQE DW0 returns new NSID), 1h delete (NSID). Support in OACS bit 3.
  • Namespace Attachment (15h): SEL 0h attach, 1h detach; data buffer is a controller list. A created namespace is invisible until attached.
  • Format NVM (80h): CDW10 LBAF[3:0] (and upper bits 13:12 in newer revisions version), MSET[4], PI[7:5], PIL[8], SES[11:9] (0 none, 1 user data erase, 2 cryptographic erase). Changes LBA size → every LBA address the host knew changes meaning.
  • Sanitize (84h): SANACT[2:0] 001b exit failure mode, 010b block erase, 011b overwrite, 100b crypto erase; AUSE, OWPASS, OIPBP, NDAS. Affects all namespaces in the subsystem; runs in background; progress in Sanitize Status log (LID 81h) verified.
  • Security Send/Receive (81h/82h): transport for security protocols (e.g. TCG); SECP selects the protocol. Post-quantum cryptography support announced with the 2.4 release relates to security/authentication features — verify specifics in the 2.4 documents version.

30.11 Identify lab and Log page lab

🧪 Lab 30.1 — Identify lab SAFE LAB

Objective: separate controller identify, namespace identify and command-set-dependent information; never invent a field meaning. Setup: nvme-cli (read-only).

sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0            # CNS 01h
sudo nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0             # CNS 02h (active namespace list)
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0 -n 1          # CNS 00h
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -H       # human-readable LBA formats
sudo nvme ns-descs /dev/nvme0 -n 1       # CNS 03h (if supported)

Procedure: for each of these fields fill source (CNS), revision introduced (if you know; else "check spec"), width, interpretation, practical use: MDTS, VER, OACS, ONCS, VWC, SGLS, NN, NSZE, NUSE, FLBAS, LBADS of the current format, DLFEAT.

Observations: note which fields printed by nvme-cli are decoded by the tool vs raw.

Expected reasoning

MDTS (CNS 01h, 1 byte, power of two of MPSMIN units; sets max I/O size → Linux max_hw_sectors_kb). VER (CNS 01h, 4 bytes, MJR/MNR/TER). OACS (CNS 01h, 2 bytes, bitmap of optional admin commands: security, format, firmware, NS management, self-test, directives, doorbell buffer config …). ONCS (CNS 01h, bitmap of optional NVM commands: Compare, Write Uncorrectable, DSM, Write Zeroes, Save/Select in features, reservations, timestamp, verify, copy — bit assignments must be read from the spec). VWC (bit 0 = volatile write cache present; Flush broadcast support bits added in later revisions). SGLS (bitmap; bits 1:0 SGL support/alignment). NN (max NSID). NSZE/NUSE (CNS 00h, 8 bytes each, in LBAs). FLBAS (format index). LBADS (log2 LBA size). DLFEAT (what a read of deallocated blocks returns — key for Ch 35). Where you are not sure of a bit's position, write "check spec" — that is the correct answer.

Extension: compute max I/O size in bytes from MDTS and CAP.MPSMIN and compare with /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/max_hw_sectors_kb.

🧪 Lab 30.2 — Log page lab SAFE LAB

Objective: understand what a log page is, why it exists, how the host requests it and how the returned data is interpreted. Setup: nvme-cli.

sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0                       # LID 02h
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 16                 # LID 01h, 16 entries
sudo nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0                          # LID 03h
sudo nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 -i 2 -l 512 -b > smart.bin   # raw bytes (LID 2, 512 B)
xxd smart.bin | head

Procedure: (1) Check LPA in Identify Controller for which optional logs are supported. (2) Fetch SMART decoded and raw; locate composite temperature (bytes 1–2, Kelvin) and percentage used (byte 5) in the raw dump. (3) Fetch error log; check if any entries have non-zero error count and decode their status fields with the Ch 29 decoder.

Expected reasoning

Composite temperature K − 273 = °C. Percentage used may exceed 100. Error log entries with error count 0 are empty. Not every device supports per-namespace SMART or every optional LID — check LPA and the Commands Supported and Effects log before concluding "device broken" from a failed Get Log Page.

Extension: compute data written from "Data Units Written" (each unit = 1000 × 512 bytes) and compare to the drive's TBW rating.

Quiz

  1. Which CNS returns the list of active namespaces?

    Answer

    02h.

  2. Encode Get Log Page for the Error Information log, 4 entries of 64 bytes.

    Answer

    256 bytes = 64 dwords → NUMDL = 63 = 3Fh → CDW10 = 0x003F0001.

  3. Why must the host re-issue AERs?

    Answer

    Each AER completes once per event; without a new outstanding AER the controller cannot report further events.

  4. Which admin commands can destroy user data?

    Answer

    Format NVM, Sanitize, Namespace Management delete (and Firmware Commit indirectly by bricking). Treat them as EXPERT operations.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What does Identify Controller tell you?
    Model answerIdentity (VID, SN, MN, FR), limits (MDTS), supported features (OACS, ONCS, SGLS, VWC), number of namespaces, entry sizes.
  2. Intermediate Difference between Get Features SEL=000b and 010b?
    Model answerCurrent vs saved value; saved persists across resets if the feature is saveable.
  3. Advanced How do you safely abort a stuck command?
    Model answerSend Abort with SQID/CID; check DW0 bit 0; wait for the victim's completion; if none within the timeout, escalate to controller reset because Abort is best-effort.
  4. Senior Design a firmware update procedure for a fleet.
    Model answerCheck FRMW slots and FWUG, download in FWUG-aligned chunks, commit to an inactive slot with activate-at-reset, verify LID 03h, schedule reset with drained I/O, verify FR after reset, keep previous slot for rollback, monitor persistent event log and SMART after.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?Admin opcodes in the verified list; Identify CNS 00h/01h/02h; Get Log Page LID 01h/02h/03h and NUMD 0-based; AER DW0 format; Abort semantics. verified
What is derived?MDTS bytes; NUMD encodings; firmware update procedure ordering. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Log support beyond mandatory ones, telemetry formats, Sanitize/Format duration. impl
What is version-dependent?Opcodes/features/CNS values added after 1.4, including those tied to 2.4 announcements. version
What must be checked in the specification?Exact encodings of any 2.4 feature (rate limiting, voltage monitoring, restore manufacturing defaults, PQC).

  • I can encode Identify CNS 00h/01h/02h and Get Log Page 01h/02h/03h.
  • I can explain AER and Abort semantics including their limits.
  • I completed the Identify and Log page labs and wrote "check spec" where I was not sure.

30.13 Summary

Admin commands discover (Identify), observe (Get Log Page, Get Features, AER), configure (Set Features, queue and namespace management) and change (firmware, Format, Sanitize) the controller. Next: Chapter 31 — NVM command set.

31 The NVM Command Set

← 30 Admin Commands32 READ — End to End →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Command Set Specification. REVISION: 1.3 (course baseline, Aug 2026) version. STATUS: current. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: before NVMe 2.0 (2021) these commands were defined inside the single NVMe 1.x specification; field names are largely the same, but some fields (e.g. storage tags, 64-bit guard protection information, Copy formats) were added later. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specification/nvm-command-set-specification/.

31.1 Why this chapter exists

The NVM command set is the block-storage personality of NVMe: logical blocks addressed by LBA (Logical Block Address). Ninety-nine percent of the commands a production SSD sees are Read and Write; the remaining few — Flush, Write Zeroes, Dataset Management, Compare, Verify, Copy, reservations — carry outsized importance for correctness (durability, trim, clustering). This chapter gives you the opcode table and the shared Read/Write field layout used by most of them.

31.2 Learning objectives

  • Recall the NVM opcode table and each command's data direction.
  • Encode Read/Write CDW10–15 (SLBA, 0-based NLB, LR, FUA, PRINFO, DTYPE, DSM, DSPEC, PI tags).
  • Explain Write Zeroes, Compare, Verify, Write Uncorrectable and Copy and when to use them.
  • Explain reservations conceptually (register, acquire, release, report) and the Reservation Conflict status.
  • Check controller support (ONCS) before using optional commands.

Prerequisites: Ch 29, Ch 30 (Identify Namespace: LBA format).

🧒 Kid analogy — the numbered lockers

A namespace is a corridor of numbered lockers, each exactly the same size (the LBA size). "Read" means "bring me the contents of lockers 4096 to 4127"; "Write" means "put these things in those lockers"; "Write Zeroes" means "empty those lockers without me carrying anything"; "Compare" means "check those lockers contain exactly this"; "Flush" means "make sure everything you've been told to put in lockers is really locked in, not still in your hands".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Lockers on an SSD are virtual: an LBA has no fixed physical location. The FTL (Flash Translation Layer) remaps every write to a fresh NAND page, so "empty a locker" may only update a table.

A pattern worth noticing: bits 1:0 of the opcode encode data direction for most commands (01b host→controller, 10b controller→host, 00b none) — Write 01h, Read 02h, Compare 05h, DSM 09h — but do not decode direction from bits alone in production code; use the specification table. derived

Core fields (SLBA, NLB, PRINFO, FUA, LR, DSM, DSPEC, PI tags) verified; storage-tag/extended PI placements changed in NVM CS 1.0+ and may also use CDW2–3 version.

For a picture of these fields landing on namespace blocks and host pages, see Figure 32.1 in the next chapter.

bytes = (NLB + 1) × LBA_size      last LBA = SLBA + NLB
  • NLB — 0-based field value.
  • LBA_size — 2^LBADS of the namespace's active LBA format (512 or 4096 B typically), excluding metadata.
  • Constraint: SLBA + NLB < NSZE, else 0/80h LBA Out of Range; bytes ≤ MDTS limit, else 0/02h Invalid Field.

31.5 The other NVM commands

  • Write Zeroes (08h): same SLBA/NLB layout, no data pointer. Makes the range read as zeros. CDW12 bit 25 DEAC (deallocate) lets the controller deallocate instead of writing, if DLFEAT says deallocated blocks read as zero verified. Linux uses it for BLKZEROOUT / REQ_OP_WRITE_ZEROES.
  • Compare (05h): host supplies data; controller reads media and compares; mismatch → 2/85h Compare Failure. Used fused with Write (§29.8).
  • Verify (0Ch): controller reads and checks integrity (ECC, PI) without transferring data; error statuses as for Read. Useful for scrubbing without PCIe bandwidth.
  • Write Uncorrectable (04h): marks blocks so subsequent reads return Unrecovered Read Error until rewritten — for testing error paths. CAUTION: destroys data in range.
  • Copy (19h): copies one or more source ranges (in a descriptor list, formats selected by a field) to a destination SLBA inside the namespace, without host data transfer version (introduced around 2.0; formats extended later). Limits in Identify Namespace (MSSRL, MCL, MSRC).
  • Reservations: Register (a host registers a reservation key), Acquire (take a reservation of a given type — Write Exclusive, Exclusive Access, and their Registrants-Only / All-Registrants variants — or preempt), Release, Report (list holders). Other hosts' conflicting commands fail with 0/83h Reservation Conflict. Used by clustered/shared storage (SCSI-PR-like) verified.

31.6 Capability discovery before use

📌 Remember

Before using an optional command or field: check Identify Controller ONCS (optional NVM commands), FUSES, VWC, SGLS; Identify Namespace DLFEAT, DPC/DPS, RESCAP, NOWS/NPWG (preferred write granularity); and the Commands Supported and Effects log. A controller is allowed to return 0/01h Invalid Command Opcode for any optional command it does not implement.

🧪 Lab 31.1 — Encode NVM commands SAFE LAB

Objective: encode CDW10–13 for given requests (namespace with 4096-byte LBAs). (1) Read 64 KiB at byte offset 1 GiB with FUA. (2) Write 8 KiB at LBA 0x1_0000_0000 with LR. (3) Write Zeroes 1 MiB at LBA 0 with DEAC.

Solution

(1) LBA = 2^30/4096 = 0x40000; NLB = 16−1 = 15 → CDW10 = 0x00040000, CDW11 = 0, CDW12 = 0x4000000F (FUA bit 30). (2) CDW10 = 0x00000000, CDW11 = 0x00000001, CDW12 = 0x80000001 (LR bit 31, NLB 1). (3) 256 blocks → NLB 255; CDW12 = 0x020000FF (DEAC bit 25).

Extension: feed the encoded commands into the Ch 29 decoder.

🧪 Lab 31.2 — Which optional commands does my drive support? SAFE LAB
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H | sed -n '/oncs/,/fuses/p'
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0 -n 1 -H | egrep -i 'dlfeat|dps|dpc|rescap|nows|npwg'

Questions: does your drive support Write Zeroes, Verify, Copy, reservations? What does a read of a deallocated block return per DLFEAT?

Expected reasoning

Answer from the decoded ONCS bits only; consumer drives often lack reservations and Copy; DLFEAT bits 2:0 indicate whether deallocated blocks read as unspecified, zero or all-ones.

Quiz

  1. NLB = 0x00FF with 512-byte LBAs. Transfer size?

    Answer

    256 × 512 = 128 KiB.

  2. What does FUA mean on a Write?

    Answer

    The data must be on non-volatile media before the completion is posted (no reliance on a volatile cache).

  3. Which command checks data integrity without a data transfer?

    Answer

    Verify (0Ch).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner List the mandatory NVM commands.
    Model answerFlush, Write, Read.
  2. Intermediate Why is NLB 0-based?
    Model answerA zero-length transfer is meaningless, so the 16-bit field covers 1–65536 blocks.
  3. Advanced Write Zeroes vs DSM deallocate?
    Model answerWrite Zeroes guarantees subsequent reads return zeros (and may deallocate if DEAC and DLFEAT allow); DSM deallocate is advisory and reads of deallocated blocks return what DLFEAT says (possibly unspecified).
  4. Senior When would you set LR?
    Model answerIn redundant systems (RAID/erasure coding/replicas) where failing fast and reconstructing elsewhere beats waiting seconds for deep error recovery.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?NVM opcodes 00h/01h/02h/04h/05h/08h/09h/0Ch/19h; Read/Write SLBA, NLB 0-based, FUA bit 30, LR bit 31, PRINFO 29:26; Write Zeroes DEAC. verified
What is derived?Byte-length formula; error conditions for LBA range and MDTS. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Error-recovery effort under LR=0, Write Zeroes implementation, Copy performance. impl
What is version-dependent?Extended PI/storage tag fields; Copy descriptor formats; reservation details. version
What must be checked in the specification?ONCS bit positions; reservation opcodes in your revision.
What should never be assumed?That opcode bits always encode direction; that NLB is a byte count.

  • I can state direction and support indicator for every NVM opcode.

32 READ — End to End

← 31 The NVM Command Set33 WRITE — End to End →

32.1 Why this chapter exists

A single 16 KiB read touches about a dozen software and hardware layers and produces around 70 PCIe TLPs. When a read is slow or wrong, the bug can be in any of them. This chapter walks one read from pread() to wake-up and gives every layer its evidence, so you can bisect a latency or correctness problem instead of guessing.

32.2 Learning objectives

  • Name each layer in the read path and what it produces for the next.
  • Build the exact SQE for a 16 KiB read at LBA 0x1000 and predict every TLP.
  • Compute TLP counts from Max_Payload_Size and explain completion ordering.
  • Build a latency budget and identify which layer owns each microsecond.

Prerequisites: Ch 28, Ch 31; PRP basics (forward reference: Ch 36).

🧒 Kid analogy

You ask your teacher for a book. The teacher writes a request slip, drops it in the librarian's box and rings the bell. The librarian reads the slip, finds which shelf in the giant warehouse holds the book (the map), fetches it, and — instead of handing it to the teacher — walks straight to your desk and puts the pages there (DMA). Then she drops an "all done" note in the answer box and taps the teacher on the shoulder (interrupt).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The "pages on your desk" are spread across several desks (physical pages are not contiguous) and the librarian delivers them in small parcels (TLPs ≤ Max_Payload_Size) that may arrive in any order relative to each other only if Relaxed Ordering is used; with default ordering they arrive in order.

32.4 Worked example — 16 KiB at LBA 0x1000 with 4 KiB pages

Assumptions synthetic: namespace 1, 512-byte LBA format, MPS = 4 KiB (CC.MPS = 0), I/O queue 1 (DSTRD 0), CID 0x0042, the application buffer occupies four non-contiguous physical pages: 0x1_1234_0000, 0x1_1234_5000, 0x1_2000_0000, 0x1_0F00_3000. The driver allocates the PRP list from its own DMA pool, in a separate page at 0x1_7F00_0000 — a PRP list must never share memory with the data it describes (a read would overwrite the list while the controller may still be walking it).

  1. Size: 16384 / 512 = 32 blocks → NLB = 31 = 0x1F. (4 KiB LBA format: 4 blocks → NLB = 3.)
  2. Pages touched: buffer starts at offset 0 within the page → ceil((0 + 16384)/4096) = 4 pages.
  3. PRP1 = 0x1_1234_0000 (first page). Since more than 2 pages are touched, PRP2 = list pointer = 0x1_7F00_0000.
  4. PRP list (3 entries, 8 bytes each): [0] 0x1_1234_5000, [1] 0x1_2000_0000, [2] 0x1_0F00_3000.
SQE (little-endian bytes):
00: 02 00 42 00  01 00 00 00  00 00 00 00  00 00 00 00   CDW0 opc=02 CID=0042, NSID=1
10: 00 00 00 00  00 00 00 00  00 00 34 12  01 00 00 00   MPTR=0, PRP1=0x1_1234_0000
20: 00 00 00 7f  01 00 00 00  00 10 00 00  00 00 00 00   PRP2=0x1_7F00_0000, CDW10=SLBA lo=0x1000
30: 1f 00 00 00  00 00 00 00  00 00 00 00  00 00 00 00   CDW12 NLB=0x1F, FUA=0 LR=0 PRINFO=0

The same command drawn as a map: the left half of the SQE (SLBA, NLB) selects which blocks on the namespace; the PRP fields select which host pages the bytes go to. Block-to-page order is simple: the first 4 KiB of the transfer go to the page in PRP1, the next 4 KiB to PRP list entry [0], and so on. For the full doorbell → fetch → DMA → completion sequence, see Figure 39.0 (Read) and Figure 40.0 (Write); a Write uses exactly the same fields, only the data moves the other way.

Field written by the driver / pointerNamespace blocks on the SSDHost data pages

Variant with offset: if the buffer started at 0x1_1234_0200 (offset 0x200), PRP1 = 0x1_1234_0200 covers 4096 − 512 = 3584 bytes; remaining 12800 bytes need ceil(12800/4096) = 4 more pages → 5 pages total, list has 4 entries, and the last page receives only 12800 − 3×4096 = 512 bytes. derived

32.4.1 Expected TLPs (Max_Payload_Size 256 B, Read Completion Boundary 64 B)

#DirTLPCountWhy
1H→DMWr 1DW BAR0+1008h, data 0x…tail1SQ1 doorbell
2D→HMRd 64 B @ SQ1 slot1 (may be merged with neighbours)SQE fetch
3H→DCplD 64 B1—
4D→HMRd 24 B @ 0x1_7F00_00001PRP list (3 × 8 B); some controllers read more impl
5H→DCplD 24 B1—
6D→HMWr 256 B data16384 / 256 = 6416 per 4 KiB page; never crosses a 4 KiB boundary (PCIe rule)
7D→HMWr 16 B CQE @ CQ11after all data (ordering)
8D→HMWr 4 B MSI-X1vector of CQ1
9H→DMWr 1DW BAR0+100Ch1 (maybe batched)CQ1 head doorbell

Total ≈ 72 TLPs, of which 64 carry data. With MPS 512 B the data TLPs drop to 32. PCIe header/framing overhead with 256 B payload is roughly 20–30 bytes per TLP, ~8–10% derived.

32.6 Linux view

# Trace NVMe commands for 5 s (read-only tracing; requires root/tracefs)
cd /sys/kernel/tracing
echo 1 > events/nvme/nvme_setup_cmd/enable
echo 1 > events/nvme/nvme_complete_rq/enable
sleep 5; cat trace | head -40
echo 0 > events/nvme/nvme_setup_cmd/enable; echo 0 > events/nvme/nvme_complete_rq/enable

# Block-layer latency histogram (bpftrace one-liner style)
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue { @s[args->sector] = nsecs; }
  tracepoint:block:block_rq_complete /@s[args->sector]/ {
    @us = hist((nsecs - @s[args->sector]) / 1000); delete(@s[args->sector]); }'
⚠️ Safety

Enabling tracepoints is non-destructive but adds overhead on busy production systems; enable briefly. Writing to tracefs requires root. Tracepoint field names vary across kernel versions version.

🧪 Lab 32.1 — Follow one read through Linux CAUTION LAB

Objective: correlate a user read to an NVMe command. Setup: test system; root; nvme tracepoints. Procedure: (1) enable nvme_setup_cmd tracing; (2) run dd if=/dev/nvme0n1 of=/dev/null bs=16k count=1 skip=256 iflag=direct (reads byte offset 4 MiB); (3) find the Read command in the trace.

⚠️ Safety

if= must be the device and of=/dev/null. Swapping them destroys data. Double-check before pressing Enter.

Questions: what SLBA and NLB do you expect? Which QID? Why?

Solution

Offset 4 MiB = 8192 × 512 → SLBA 0x2000 with 512-byte LBAs (NLB 31) or 0x400 with 4 KiB LBAs (NLB 3). QID = the hardware queue mapped to the CPU dd ran on.

Extension: run with bs=1M and observe splitting at MDTS / max_sectors_kb.

🧪 Lab 32.2 — Senior forensic: count the TLPs SAFE LAB

Given: 128 KiB read, buffer offset 0x800, MPS(PCIe) = 512 B, NVMe MPS = 4 KiB, SQE fetched singly. Compute pages touched, PRP list entries, data TLPs, total TLPs.

Solution

Pages = ceil((2048 + 131072)/4096) = 33 → PRP1 + 32 list entries (256 B list). Data TLPs: the first page carries 2048 B → 4 TLPs; 31 full pages × 8 = 248; the last page carries 2048 B → 4; total 256. Plus doorbell, SQE MRd/CplD, PRP list MRd/CplD (CplD may be split at RCB), CQE, MSI-X, CQ doorbell ≈ 264.

Quiz

  1. For a read, who issues the data TLPs and of what type?

    Answer

    The controller issues MWr TLPs into host memory.

  2. Why can't a data TLP cross a 4 KiB address boundary?

    Answer

    PCIe forbids a memory request from crossing a 4 KiB boundary; so per-page splitting is natural.

  3. Why can a read complete "successfully" with garbage data?

    Answer

    Data MWrs are posted; if the IOMMU drops them the device is not told, so it reports success.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Describe the read path.
    Model answerApp → FS → block → driver → SQE → doorbell → fetch → FTL → NAND → DMA MWr → CQE → interrupt → completion.
  2. Intermediate Build the PRPs for 16 KiB at offset 0.
    Model answerPRP1 = page 0; PRP2 = list pointer; list = pages 1–3.
  3. Advanced Where does the time go in a 90 µs read?
    Model answerMostly media (NAND sense + ECC); a few µs host; ~2 µs DMA; use an analyzer gap between PRP fetch and first data MWr to measure device-internal time.
  4. Senior Silent corruption on reads only on one platform. Approach?
    Model answerCheck IOMMU faults, coherency, PRP construction for unusual alignments, Relaxed Ordering/ordering bugs, and compare analyzer data payloads to media contents; reproduce with pattern data and different buffer offsets.

33 WRITE — End to End

← 32 READ — End to End34 FLUSH →

33.1 Why this chapter exists

Writes reverse the data direction and add the hardest question in storage: when is data safe? A Write completion may mean "data is in a volatile cache" or "data is on NAND", depending on the write cache, FUA and power-loss protection. Durability bugs (lost writes after power loss) and write-latency spikes (garbage collection) both live here.

33.2 Learning objectives

  • Trace a Write: buffer → PRP/SGL → controller MRd → CplD → buffer in controller → NAND program → completion.
  • Count MRd requests from Max_Read_Request_Size and CplD from Read Completion Boundary.
  • Explain the volatile write cache, FUA and Flush, and what completion means in each configuration.
  • Explain NAND programming constraints (page program, block erase, write amplification) and their latency effects.

Prerequisites: Ch 32; MRRS (MRRS) and MPS (MPS).

🧒 Kid analogy

You want to store a box of drawings. The librarian walks to your desk and picks the drawings up herself (the device reads your memory). She may put them on her desk "to file later" (write cache) and tell you "done!" — fine, unless the lights go out before she files them. If you say "file it in the cabinet before telling me" (FUA) she does that first, which is slower.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Many enterprise SSDs have capacitors (power-loss protection) so "on her desk" is already safe; and the cabinet (NAND) can only be written in whole pages and erased in whole blocks, so filing even one drawing may cause a big re-shuffle (garbage collection).

33.3 Mechanism

#WhoWhatEvidence
1App/FSData in page cache (buffered) or user buffer (O_DIRECT); writeback creates biosblock:block_rq_issue (WS = sync write)
2DriverOpcode 01h, SLBA, NLB, FUA if REQ_FUA; DMA-map buffer (device will read it); PRP/SGLnvme_setup_cmd
3HostSQE → SQ, doorbellMWr
4ControllerFetch SQE, PRP listMRd/CplD
5Controller DMAMRd of data pages, each ≤ MRRS; Root Complex returns CplD split at RCB/MPSMRd/CplD pairs, tags in flight
6ControllerData into internal buffer (SRAM/DRAM); allocate new NAND location; update L2Pinternal
7ControllerIf write cache enabled and FUA=0: may post completion now. Else: program NAND (and wait), then completeCQE timing
8ControllerCQE + MSI-XMWr
9LaterBackground: program cached data, garbage collection, wear levellinglatency spikes on later commands

33.3.1 Worked TLP count — 16 KiB write, MRRS 512 B, MPS 256 B, RCB 64 B

Data reads: 16384 / 512 = 32 MRd requests (each within one 4 KiB page). Each 512 B request is answered by CplDs no larger than MPS = 256 B and split on RCB-aligned boundaries; for aligned addresses that is typically 2 CplD per MRd → 64 CplD derived (completer may split further impl). The controller needs enough outstanding tags (8-bit, or 10-bit if enabled) to keep the link busy: at 1 µs round trip and 7 GB/s, ~7 KB must be in flight ≈ 14 outstanding 512 B reads. derived

outstanding_reads ≥ (bandwidth × round_trip_latency) / MRRS
  • bandwidth — target bytes/s on the link.
  • round_trip_latency — MRd issue to last CplD (s).
  • MRRS — Max_Read_Request_Size in bytes.

33.4 Completion semantics

ConfigurationCompletion of Write (FUA=0) meansDurable after power loss?
No volatile write cache (VWC=0) or cache disabled (FID 06h WCE=0)Data on non-volatile mediaYes
Volatile cache enabled, FUA=0Data accepted, may be in volatile cacheNot guaranteed until Flush completes
Volatile cache enabled, FUA=1This command's data on non-volatile mediaYes (for this data only)
Power-loss protected cache (capacitors) — often reported as VWC=0Data in protected bufferYes impl

Linux reads VWC and sets the block queue's write-cache mode (/sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache: "write back" or "write through"); with write back, filesystems issue preflush/FUA (→ NVMe Flush and FUA bit) at journal commits. verified (behaviour of Linux block layer)

33.5 Flash programming in one paragraph

NAND is programmed in pages (e.g. 16 KiB) and erased in blocks (hundreds of pages); a page cannot be rewritten without erasing its whole block. So the FTL writes new data to a fresh page and marks the old one invalid; garbage collection later copies valid pages out of mostly-invalid blocks and erases them. The ratio NAND bytes written / host bytes written is write amplification (WA). Program times are hundreds of µs to ms for TLC/QLC; a controller hides them with parallelism across dies and with SLC caching. When the SLC cache fills or GC runs, write latency rises sharply. All figures impl.

WA = NAND_bytes_written / host_bytes_written
  • Host bytes: SMART "Data Units Written" × 512,000. NAND bytes: vendor-specific log only impl.

cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/write_cache

Expected reasoning

If write_cache = "write back", journal commits and fsync issue flushes (preflush) and/or FUA writes; if "write through", the block layer drops flushes. MRRS/MPS come from Device Control.

Extension: on a test device, measure 4 KiB sync write latency with fio --fsync=1 vs --fua-like workloads (--sync=1) and explain the difference.

🧪 Lab 33.2 — Steady-state write test EXPERT LAB

Objective: observe SLC-cache and GC effects. Setup: a dedicated, empty test SSD — all data will be destroyed.

fio --name=seqfill --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=write --bs=128k --iodepth=32 \
    --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --size=100% --write_bw_log=bw --log_avg_msec=1000
⚠️ Safety

Writes the entire device. Verify the device name with nvme list and serial number first. Never on a device with data.

Expected observations

A high-bandwidth plateau then a drop when the cache is exhausted; with random writes after fill, bandwidth drops further as GC runs. Exact shape impl.

Quiz

  1. In a Write, which side sends MRd TLPs?

    Answer

    The controller reads host memory.

  2. Does a Write completion guarantee durability?

    Answer

    Only if there is no volatile write cache (or it is disabled/protected) or FUA=1; otherwise a Flush is needed.

  3. Why can write failures on DMA be reported but read DMA failures not?

    Answer

    Write data is fetched with non-posted MRd (gets a completion status); read data is delivered with posted MWr (no completion).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is FUA?
    Model answerForce Unit Access: commit this command's data to non-volatile media before completing.
  2. Intermediate How many MRd for 64 KiB with MRRS 256?
    Model answer256.
  3. Advanced Explain write amplification and how DSM deallocate helps.
    Model answerGC copies valid data; deallocation tells the FTL data is invalid so it need not be copied.
  4. Senior A database sees periodic 50 ms write stalls. Plan?
    Model answerCorrelate with SMART temperature/throttle, GC (fill level, trim usage), flush frequency, interrupt coalescing; capture analyzer to separate host vs device time (gap before CQE vs before doorbell); test with over-provisioning.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?Write is opcode 01h; controller reads data with non-posted MRd; FUA semantics; VWC reporting and FID 06h. verified
What is derived?MRd/CplD counts; outstanding-read requirement; durability table. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Cache size, PLP, GC policy, SLC caching, program times. impl
What is version-dependent?Directive/stream fields; Linux write_cache handling. version
What must be checked in the specification?Exact durability wording for FUA and cache behaviour in NVM CS.
What should never be assumed?That completion means durable on every drive.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can trace a write's TLPs including tags and CplD splitting.
  • I can state what completion means for each cache configuration.
  • I can explain GC, WA and their latency signature.

33.8 Summary

Writes are device-read DMA, cached or programmed, with durability defined by VWC, FUA and Flush. Next: Chapter 34 — FLUSH.

34 FLUSH

← 33 WRITE — End to End35 Dataset Management (Deallocate / TRIM) →
📘 Source notes

Official specification: NVM Command Set Specification (Flush command) and NVMe Base Specification (Identify Controller VWC, Volatile Write Cache feature FID 06h). Revision: NVM CS 1.3 / Base 2.4 baseline. Establishes: Flush opcode 00h; that Flush commits data and metadata held in a volatile write cache to non-volatile media; NSID usage including broadcast where supported. Does not establish: how long a Flush takes, how a controller schedules it relative to other I/O, or whether a power-loss-protected drive does any work at all — those are impl.

34.1 Why this chapter exists

Flush is the shortest NVMe command (no data, no fields beyond NSID) and the most misunderstood. Databases, filesystems and hypervisors build their crash-consistency on it. Misunderstanding what it guarantees leads to either lost data (trusting completions that were only cached) or terrible performance (flushing on every write on a drive that does not need it).

34.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain what a volatile write cache is and what Flush does to it.
  • Intermediate: state precisely which writes a Flush covers and which it does not.
  • Advanced: map Linux REQ_PREFLUSH/REQ_FUA to NVMe Flush and FUA; explain when the block layer drops flushes.
  • Senior: reason about durability across multiple queues, namespaces and controllers; design a power-loss test.
  • Trace/debug/validation: identify Flush in a trace, measure its cost, and test that durability claims hold.

Prerequisites: Ch 33 (completion semantics), Ch 31.

🧒 Kid analogy — the homework tray

The teacher has an "in-tray" on her desk. When you hand in homework, she says "got it!" and drops it in the tray — fast. Later she files it in the big locked cabinet. If the school catches fire before filing, the tray burns. "Flush" is when you say: "please file everything that's in your tray right now into the cabinet, and tell me when you're done".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

(1) Homework handed in while she is filing may or may not be included — Flush only promises what was already completed when you asked. (2) Some teachers have a fireproof tray (power-loss protection): Flush then has nothing to do. (3) The cabinet is per-namespace; a Flush for one namespace says nothing about another, unless you use the broadcast NSID.

34.3 Vocabulary

TermPlain meaningEngineering meaningCommon confusion
Volatile write cache (VWC)A tray that is lost in a power cutController DRAM/SRAM holding written data not yet on NAND; Identify Controller VWC bit 0 = present"Has DRAM" ≠ "has volatile write cache" — DRAM may hold only mapping tables, or be power-loss protected
WCETray switched on/offVolatile Write Cache feature (FID 06h) bit 0 Write Cache EnableOnly meaningful if VWC present
Flush"File everything now"NVM opcode 00h; commits volatile cached data and metadata for the namespace(s) to non-volatile mediaNot a barrier on queues; does not order future commands
FUA"File this one before saying done"Per-command bit (Write/Read CDW12 bit 30)FUA affects only that command's data
PLPFireproof trayPower-loss protection: capacitors give time to save the cacheVendor feature, not an NVMe field; such drives typically report VWC=0 impl

34.4 Command format and guarantees

FieldValueNote
CDW0 OPC00hOn an I/O queue (00h on the admin queue is Delete I/O SQ!)
NSIDnamespace, or FFFFFFFFhBroadcast flushes all namespaces if supported; support for broadcast is reported in Identify Controller VWC bits 2:1 in newer revisions version
DPTR, CDW10–15reservedNo data transfer
QuestionAnswerLabel
What does Flush cover?Data and metadata of commands that completed before the Flush was submitted — they are on non-volatile media when Flush completes.verified (paraphrase; read the exact normative wording in NVM CS)
Writes outstanding at the same time?No guarantee either way. To include a write, wait for its completion before submitting Flush.derived
Does Flush order later commands?No. Commands submitted after Flush may execute before it completes.derived
Is it per queue?No — it is per namespace (or all). Writes completed on any queue to that namespace are covered.derived
No volatile cache present?Flush completes successfully with nothing to do.verified
Does Flush verify data?No. It does not re-read, and a later read can still hit an uncorrectable error.derived
Does it cover other controllers' writes to a shared namespace?The cache is a controller/subsystem implementation detail; check the spec text for multi-controller subsystems and do not assume.uncertain
📭 What the spec does not say

How long a Flush may take, whether it blocks other I/O, whether the controller flushes the whole cache or only the namespace's dirty data, and how a PLP device implements it. These are why Flush cost differs by 1000× across drives.

34.5 Architecture — who acts

 Application   fsync()/fdatasync()/O_DSYNC
     │
 Filesystem    journal commit: write log blocks → REQ_PREFLUSH | REQ_FUA on commit block
     │
 Block layer   blk-flush state machine: if queue is "write back": issue PREFLUSH as separate
     │         flush request; FUA passed if device supports it, else emulated with POSTFLUSH;
     │         if "write through": flush/FUA flags dropped
 NVMe driver   REQ_OP_FLUSH → SQE opcode 00h, NSID;  REQ_FUA → Write CDW12 bit 30
     │
 Controller    drain volatile cache for namespace → NAND program → update mapping persistently
     │
 CQE           success → data safe

Linux behaviour verified in principle; function names and flag handling evolve across kernel versions version.

34.5.1 The Flush on the wire, step by step

The stack above ends in one NVMe command. Below is that command on the same three-place picture used for Read and Write (Figure 39.0, Figure 40.0). Starting state: the volatile write cache is enabled, and three earlier Writes (W1–W3) on namespace 1 have already completed to the host, so their data may still be only in the cache. Click a step to follow it. synthetic

Software starts itDevice starts itInside the SSD (not visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. Software writes the 64-byte Flush command into the Submission Queue

    fsync() reaches the block layer as a flush request; the NVMe driver turns it into a Flush command in slot 5 of Submission Queue 1. It names only the namespace: no LBAs, no data pointer.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 5PCIe: No. The CPU writes its own RAM.
    Opcode = 00h (Flush, on an I/O queue) CID = 0x0031 NSID = 1 PRP1 = PRP2 = 0, CDW10–15 = 0 (reserved)
  2. Software rings the SQ tail doorbell

    Exactly as for a Read or Write: the new tail index tells the controller there is one more command.

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x1008PCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 6
  3. Device fetches the Flush command

    The controller reads slot 5 from host memory. This is the last PCIe traffic for a while: everything the Flush does happens inside the SSD.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 5PCIe: Yes, both ways. · MRd (device → host), then CplD with 64 bytes (host → device)
    Device now knows: "make everything completed so far on NSID 1 durable"
  4. Device drains its write cache into NAND

    Writes W1–W3 were already completed to the host earlier, but their data is still in the volatile write cache. The controller programs it into NAND and saves the mapping changes, so they would survive a power cut. This is the expensive part: it can take from almost nothing (cache empty, or power-loss-protected drive) to many milliseconds.

    Where: Inside the SSD (write cache → NAND)PCIe: No. On an analyzer the link is silent for this command.
    Dirty data: W1 (4 KiB) + W2 (64 KiB) + W3 (4 KiB) → programmed Writes still in flight when the Flush was submitted are not promised.
  5. Device writes the completion entry, only after the drain

    The Flush completion is posted only when the data covered by the Flush is on non-volatile media. Success here is the durability promise that the earlier Write completions did not give.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 5PCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 16 bytes
    CID = 0x0031 Status = 0 SQHD = 6
  6. Device sends the MSI-X interrupt

    As for every command, the interrupt is a memory write to the address in the MSI-X table entry for CQ1.

    Where: MSI-X addressPCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 4 bytes
    PCIe ordering keeps it behind the completion entry.
  7. Software reads the completion entry

    The driver matches CID 0x0031, sees success, completes the flush request; fsync() can return to the application.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 5PCIe: No.
    Status 0 → W1–W3 are durable.
  8. Software rings the CQ head doorbell

    The driver releases the completion slot.

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x100CPCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 6

On an analyzer a Flush is just doorbell, 64-byte fetch, a gap, CQE, interrupt. The length of the gap is the cost of the Flush, and it depends on how much dirty data the cache held.

34.6 Performance consequences

  • On a consumer drive with a large volatile cache, a Flush may need to program megabytes of data: milliseconds. An fsync-heavy workload (databases with synchronous commit, VMs with cache=none and barriers) becomes flush-bound.
  • On a PLP enterprise drive (VWC=0), Linux marks the queue write through; no Flush is sent; fsync cost is just the write latency.
  • Flush cost is roughly proportional to dirty cache content impl; frequent small flushes may each be cheap; rare large flushes expensive.
  • Flushes do not stop other queues' reads in the specification, but some controllers deprioritise or stall other I/O while draining impl — visible as read latency spikes coinciding with fsync.

34.9 Labs

🧪 Lab 34.1 — Beginner: find your durability model SAFE LAB

Procedure: run the read-only commands of Lab 33.1. Decide: does a completed write on this machine survive power loss without a flush? Solution:

Solution

If VWC=1 and WCE=1 → no; if VWC=0 → yes (assuming spec compliance); PLP claims require vendor documentation.

🧪 Lab 34.2 — Intermediate: watch flushes with blktrace CAUTION LAB
sudo blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 -o - | blkparse -i - | grep -E ' (F|FWS|FWFS) ' &
dd if=/dev/zero of=/mnt/test/f bs=4k count=100 oflag=dsync     # on a TEST filesystem

Questions: how many flush operations per dd block?

Solution

With O_DSYNC on a write-back queue, typically one preflush and/or FUA write per 4 KiB write (filesystem-dependent impl).

🧪 Lab 34.3 — Advanced: measure flush cost EXPERT LAB
fio --name=fsync --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --iodepth=1 \
    --direct=1 --fsync=1 --runtime=30 --time_based     # DESTROYS DATA on nvme1n1

Compare --fsync=1, --fsync=32 and no fsync.

Expected reasoning

IOPS should rise as flush frequency drops on a VWC drive; on a PLP drive the three are similar because no Flush is issued.

🧪 Lab 34.4 — Senior forensic: who lost the write? SAFE LAB

Given synthetic evidence: application log says "commit 991 durable" at t=10.000 s; blktrace shows Write(sector X) completion at 9.998 s, no flush events; device VWC=1, write_cache=write through (set by an admin script); power lost at 10.020 s; commit 991 missing.

Solution

The admin script told the block layer the device is write-through, so the block layer dropped the preflush/FUA. The data was in the device's volatile cache. Root cause: misconfiguration (host side), not the device. Confidence high, given VWC=1.

Quiz

  1. Does a Flush include a write submitted 1 µs before it but completed after it?

    Answer

    Not guaranteed.

  2. What does Flush do on a drive with no volatile cache?

    Answer

    Completes successfully; nothing to commit.

  3. Which Linux flag maps to NVMe FUA?

    Answer

    REQ_FUA.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is Flush for?
    Model answerTo make data in the volatile write cache durable.
  2. Beginner Opcode?
    Model answer00h in the NVM command set.
  3. Beginner Does it carry data?
    Model answerNo.
  4. Beginner What is FUA?
    Model answerPer-command durability.
  5. Beginner What is VWC?
    Model answerIdentify Controller field reporting a volatile write cache.
  6. Intermediate Flush vs FUA?
    Model answerFlush: everything previously completed in the namespace; FUA: only this command.
  7. Intermediate Why might Linux never send Flush?
    Model answerDevice reports no VWC, or the queue is configured write through.
  8. Intermediate What does Flush NSID FFFFFFFFh mean?
    Model answerAll namespaces, if supported.
  9. Intermediate Is Flush a barrier?
    Model answerNo; it does not order other commands.
  10. Intermediate How to include write W in a flush?
    Model answerWait for W's completion, then submit Flush.
  11. Advanced How does the block layer emulate FUA if unsupported?
    Model answerWrite followed by a post-flush.
  12. Advanced Flush and multiple queues?
    Model answerNamespace-scoped, covers completions from any queue.
  13. Advanced Why can Flush latency vary 1000×?
    Model answerDepends on dirty data, NAND program time, PLP, implementation.
  14. Advanced Flush in a VM?
    Model answerHypervisor must propagate it to the physical device depending on cache mode.
  15. Advanced How does a filesystem journal use Flush+FUA?
    Model answerPreflush before the commit block to persist journal data, FUA on the commit block.
  16. Senior Design a power-loss durability test.
    Model answerProgrammable power cut, writes with sequence numbers and checksums, record acknowledged-durable set, cut at random points, verify on restart that every acknowledged-durable record exists and no torn records are accepted; repeat thousands of times.
  17. Senior A PLP drive reports VWC=1. Implications?
    Model answerLinux will issue flushes (cost) though cheap on that device; verify vendor guidance; do not override write_cache without proof.
  18. Senior Flushes stall reads. Mitigations?
    Model answerBatch commits (group commit), separate namespaces/devices for logs, choose PLP devices, tune flush frequency.
  19. Senior What can't you infer from a fast Flush?
    Model answerThat data is durable — only a power-cut test can show the device honours it.
  20. Senior Multi-controller shared namespace durability?
    Model answerRead the specification for the subsystem's cache model; do not assume one controller's Flush covers another's completions without the normative text.

Child: the homework tray. Junior: VWC, completion semantics, Flush covers completed writes. Senior: durability contract across fs/block/driver/device, PLP, verification by power-cut testing.

34.10 Summary

Flush (00h) makes previously completed writes durable for a namespace; it is not a barrier and is free on drives without a volatile cache. Next: Chapter 35 — Dataset Management.

35 Dataset Management (Deallocate / TRIM)

← 34 FLUSH36 Physical Region Pages (PRP) →
📘 Source notes

Specification: NVM Command Set (Dataset Management command 09h, range format, DLFEAT in Identify Namespace; DSM limits in NVM-command-set-specific Identify Controller in newer revisions version). Establishes: command layout, range format, attributes (AD, IDW, IDR), read behaviour of deallocated blocks reported by DLFEAT. Does not establish: when the FTL actually reclaims space, the performance effect, or whether deallocation is immediate.

35.1 Why this chapter exists

An SSD cannot know a file was deleted — the filesystem just changes its own metadata. Without being told, the FTL keeps copying dead data during garbage collection, increasing write amplification, wearing NAND and slowing writes. Dataset Management with the Deallocate attribute (the NVMe equivalent of ATA TRIM / SCSI UNMAP) tells it. Misusing it causes performance stalls; misunderstanding its read-back semantics causes data-integrity bugs in software that assumed zeros.

35.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain why the SSD needs to know about deleted data.
  • Intermediate: encode a DSM command with N ranges and build the range list.
  • Advanced: explain DLFEAT, deallocated-read semantics and Write Zeroes vs DSM.
  • Senior: design a discard policy (online discard vs periodic fstrim) and diagnose discard-induced latency.
  • Trace/debug/validation: decode DSM in a trace including its 4 KiB payload fetch; test deallocate behaviour.

Prerequisites: Ch 31, Ch 33 (GC, WA).

🧒 Kid analogy — the moving company

A warehouse keeps your boxes. Every so often it must empty a room by moving every box that is still yours to another room. If you threw away half your toys but never told them, they carefully move broken toys forever. DSM-deallocate is a note: "boxes on shelves 100–355 are rubbish; don't bother moving them".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The note is advisory: the warehouse may throw the boxes out now, later, or partially. And if you later ask "what's on shelf 120?", the answer depends on the warehouse's stated policy (DLFEAT): maybe empty (zeros), maybe "unspecified" — not necessarily your old toy.

35.3 Command format

FieldBitsMeaning
CDW0 OPC7:009h
NSID—Namespace
DPTRPRP/SGLPoints to the range list (16 B × NR+1, ≤ 4096 B)
CDW10 NR7:0Number of Ranges, 0-based (0 → 1 range, 255 → 256 ranges)
CDW11 IDR0Integral Dataset for Read — hint: ranges are read as a unit
CDW11 IDW1Integral Dataset for Write — hint: written as a unit
CDW11 AD2Attribute – Deallocate: deallocate the ranges

35.3.1 Range format (16 bytes each)

BytesFieldMeaning
03:00Context AttributesHints: access frequency [3:0], access latency [5:4], sequential read range [8], sequential write range [9], write prepare [10], command access size [31:24] (in LBAs)
07:04Length in logical blocks1-based count (unlike NLB!) — a range of 256 LBAs has Length = 256
15:08Starting LBA64-bit

All verified long-standing layout. Note the asymmetry: NR and NLB are 0-based; range Length is 1-based. A classic bug: sending Length = n−1, leaving one block per range allocated.

35.4 Code — build a DSM range list

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""dsm_ranges.py - build and decode a Dataset Management range list (offline)."""
import struct

def build(ranges, ad=True):
    """ranges: list of (slba, nlb_count, context_attributes)."""
    assert 1 <= len(ranges) <= 256, "1..256 ranges per DSM command"
    buf = b"".join(struct.pack("<IIQ", ca, n, slba) for slba, n, ca in ranges)
    cdw10 = len(ranges) - 1                 # NR is 0-based
    cdw11 = (1 << 2) if ad else 0           # AD = Attribute - Deallocate
    return cdw10, cdw11, buf

def decode(buf):
    for i in range(len(buf) // 16):
        ca, n, slba = struct.unpack_from("<IIQ", buf, i * 16)
        print(f"  range {i}: SLBA={slba:#x} length={n} LBAs  CA={ca:#010x}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    # free three extents of a deleted file (4 KiB LBAs)
    cdw10, cdw11, buf = build([(0x10000, 256, 0), (0x48000, 2048, 0), (0x90010, 16, 0)])
    print(f"CDW10={cdw10:#010x} (NR={cdw10 + 1} ranges)  CDW11={cdw11:#010x} (AD=1)")
    print(f"payload {len(buf)} bytes, pointed to by PRP1:")
    for off in range(0, len(buf), 16):
        print(f"  {off:04x}: " + " ".join(f"{b:02x}" for b in buf[off:off + 16]))
    decode(buf)
CDW10=0x00000002 (NR=3 ranges)  CDW11=0x00000004 (AD=1)
payload 48 bytes, pointed to by PRP1:
  0000: 00 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 01 00 00 00 00 00
  0010: 00 00 00 00 00 08 00 00 00 80 04 00 00 00 00 00
  0020: 00 00 00 00 10 00 00 00 10 00 09 00 00 00 00 00
  range 0: SLBA=0x10000 length=256 LBAs  CA=0x00000000
  range 1: SLBA=0x48000 length=2048 LBAs  CA=0x00000000
  range 2: SLBA=0x90010 length=16 LBAs  CA=0x00000000

35.5 Semantics and the FTL

The range list built by the script above, followed into the drive: (1) the controller fetches the 48-byte list from host memory, (2) it removes the map entries for every LBA in the three ranges, (3) the NAND pages that held them become stale although nothing new was written, and (4) garbage collection later skips them. synthetic

Command written by softwareHost memoryDevice actsInside the SSD
  • What deallocation does: the controller may mark the mapping entries for those LBAs as unmapped and the corresponding physical pages as invalid impl.
  • Reads afterwards: governed by DLFEAT in Identify Namespace: bits 2:0 report whether deallocated blocks read as not reported/unspecified, all zeros, or all ones; DLFEAT also indicates whether Write Zeroes with DEAC is supported and guard field behaviour verified. If the namespace enables Deallocated or Unwritten Logical Block Error (DULBE, a feature), reads return 2/87h instead.
  • Guarantee: DSM deallocate is a hint about data you no longer need. If you need zeros, use Write Zeroes (with DEAC) and check DLFEAT — or write zeros.
  • Impact on GC: invalid pages need not be copied; WA falls, especially on nearly full drives. Example: block with 256 pages, 200 valid → GC copies 200; after trimming 150 of them → copies 50. derived
  • Performance: deallocation is metadata work. Large or frequent DSM commands can delay concurrent I/O on some controllers; Linux therefore offers online discard mount option vs periodic fstrim (batched, scheduled) impl.
  • Limits: max 256 ranges per command; per-range and per-command size limits may be reported (DMRL, DMRSL, DMSL) in newer revisions version. Linux exposes discard_max_bytes, discard_granularity in sysfs.

35.6 Hardware and protocol view

On the wire a DSM looks like a small write: doorbell → SQE fetch → controller MRd of the range list (48 bytes for 3 ranges, up to 4 KiB) → CQE. No user data moves. Everything interesting is internal and invisible to the analyzer; only latency (and later GC behaviour) is observable.

⚠️ Safety

blkdiscard and nvme dsm --ad destroy data in the given ranges immediately. fstrim only discards free filesystem space and is the safe tool. Never run blkdiscard on a device holding data.

35.10 Labs

🧪 Lab 35.1 — Beginner: does my stack pass discards? SAFE LAB

Run lsblk --discard; for every layer (partition, LVM, dm-crypt, filesystem) note DISC-GRAN/MAX.

Solution

Any layer with 0 in DISC-MAX blocks discards from reaching the NVMe device.

🧪 Lab 35.2 — Intermediate: encode DSM SAFE LAB

Free 1 GiB at byte offset 10 GiB on a 4 KiB-LBA namespace in ranges of max 256 MiB each. Give NR, CDW11 and the ranges.

Solution

SLBA0 = 10 GiB/4 KiB = 0x280000; 256 MiB = 65536 LBAs; 4 ranges: 0x280000, 0x290000, 0x2A0000, 0x2B0000, each Length 65536 (0x00010000). NR = 3; CDW11 = 0x4.

🧪 Lab 35.3 — Advanced: deallocated-read behaviour EXPERT LAB

On a scratch device: write a pattern to LBA 0–255, deallocate them (nvme dsm /dev/nvme1n1 -n 1 --ad -s 0 -b 256), read back. Compare with DLFEAT. Destroys data on the scratch device.

Expected reasoning

If DLFEAT says zeros, expect zeros. If "not reported", any result is legal — do not conclude a bug from old data.

🧪 Lab 35.4 — Senior forensic SAFE LAB

Synthetic: a database file has a 4 KiB hole of old content after a crash; trace shows DSM with NR=0x0F and a payload where range 15 overlaps the database extent; filesystem free-space map at that time did not include the extent.

Solution

The host sent a range that was not free: payload construction bug (stale entry or off-by-one in NR). Device behaved correctly. Evidence: decoded range vs free-space map. Confidence high.

Quiz

  1. NR field = 0. How many ranges?

    Answer

    One.

  2. Range Length = 8. How many LBAs?

    Answer

    Eight (1-based).

  3. Does DSM deallocate guarantee reads return zeros?

    Answer

    Only if DLFEAT says so.

  1. Beginner What is TRIM in NVMe?

    Model answer256.
  4. Beginner Range size?

  5. Beginner Why does trim help?

    Model answerIn host memory pointed to by DPTR.
