    Model answerIdentify Namespace field describing deallocated read behaviour and DEAC support.
  10. Intermediate Unit pitfalls?
    Model answerLBAs not bytes nor 512-byte sectors; Length 1-based.
  11. Advanced Write Zeroes with DEAC vs DSM?
    Model answerWrite Zeroes guarantees zeros; DSM is advisory.
  12. Advanced How can DSM hurt performance?
    Model answerMapping-table updates compete with I/O; large ranges block.
  13. Advanced What is DULBE?
    Model answerFeature making reads of deallocated blocks return an error.
  14. Advanced Trim through dm-crypt — security concern?
    Model answerReveals free-space patterns; hence opt-in.

    Model answerTracepoint/blktrace D events, analyzer DSM SQEs.
  16. Senior Discard policy for a write-heavy DB on QLC?
    Model answerPeriodic fstrim in quiet windows, over-provisioning, monitor WA via vendor logs.
  17. Senior Validating DSM in a controller?
    Model answerRange boundary tests, NR extremes, overlapping ranges, concurrency with writes to same LBAs, DLFEAT conformance, power loss mid-deallocate.

    Model answerNo ordering between concurrent commands; host must serialise if it cares.
  19. Senior Thin provisioning relation?

  • I can explain deallocated-read semantics with DLFEAT.

35.11 Summary

DSM (09h) with AD deallocates up to 256 ranges described in a 16-byte-per-range list; it is advisory, helps GC and WA, and its read-back semantics come from DLFEAT. Next: Part XII — PRP and SGL.

PART XII

PRP and SGL

The 64-byte command never carries user data; it carries directions to the data. NVMe has two direction formats: Physical Region Page entries (PRPs) — a list of page addresses — and Scatter Gather Lists (SGLs) — a list of (address, length) descriptors. Most data-corruption bugs and DMA faults that are not media errors trace back to wrong directions. Chapter 36 teaches PRPs with numbers you can compute by hand and an executable builder/validator; Chapter 37 teaches SGLs and compares the two; Chapter 38 is a forensic lab of valid and malformed cases.

36 Physical Region Pages (PRP)

← 35 Dataset Management (Deallocate / TRIM)37 Scatter Gather Lists (SGL) →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Base Specification (PRP entry and PRP list definitions, data pointer) and NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (PRPs are the required data-pointer mechanism for admin commands on PCIe) version. REVISION: Base 2.4 / PCIe Transport 1.4 baseline. OLDER VERSIONS: the PRP rules are essentially unchanged since NVMe 1.0; their location in the document set moved with the 2.0 restructuring. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org.

36.1 Why this chapter exists

Host memory given to I/O is a set of scattered physical pages; the controller needs the physical (or IOMMU-virtual, IOVA) address of every byte it will move. PRPs are NVMe's compact, page-oriented answer. They are simple enough to compute on paper, and strict enough that one wrong offset produces either a clean error (PRP Offset Invalid) or — far worse — silent data placement into the wrong memory.

36.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: explain PRP1, PRP2, PRP list, memory page size.
  • Intermediate: compute pages touched, PRP1 coverage, whether PRP2 is a data pointer or a list pointer, and list size.
  • Advanced: build chained PRP lists for large transfers and handle a PRP list starting at a non-zero offset.
  • Senior: diagnose DMA faults and corruption caused by malformed PRPs from a trace.
  • Trace: predict the controller's MRd of PRP lists and the data TLP addresses.
  • Debugging/validation: design a PRP conformance test matrix.

Prerequisites: Ch 29 (DPTR at bytes 24–39), Ch 32 (data DMA), IOMMU basics.

🧒 Kid analogy — the warehouse delivery note

A delivery company (the controller) must deliver 16 boxes of books to your house, but your house has no single empty room big enough: there's space in the kitchen, the attic, the garage and a bedroom. All rooms are the same size (a "page"). The delivery note has only two lines. Line 1 (PRP1): "first room, and you may start halfway into it" (an offset). Line 2 (PRP2): if only one more room is needed, "the second room"; if more rooms are needed, "the list of rooms is pinned on the fridge" — a PRP list. If the fridge list is full, its last line says "continued on the bathroom door" — chaining.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Only the first room may be entered halfway; every other room must be filled from its door (offset 0). The note never says how many boxes — that comes from the command (NLB × LBA size). And the "rooms" are addressed by bus addresses that may be translated by an IOMMU, not by physical location.

36.3 Vocabulary

TermPlainEngineeringCommon confusion
Memory page size (MPS)Room size2^(12 + CC.MPS) bytes, chosen by host within CAP.MPSMIN…MPSMAX; Linux normally 4 KiBNot PCIe Max_Payload_Size, which shares the acronym MPS
PRP entryOne room address64-bit address; low bits = offset within page; bits 1:0 must be 0 (dword aligned)Offset allowed only in specific positions
PRP1Line 1SQE bytes 24–31; first page, may have an offset—
PRP2Line 2SQE bytes 32–39; unused / second page / PRP list pointerIts meaning depends on transfer size and PRP1 offset
PRP listFridge noteA page (or part of a page) of 8-byte PRP entries, each page-alignedList pointer may be at an offset; list entries may not
Chaining"continued on"If more entries are needed than fit in the list page, the last entry of that page points to the next list pageOff-by-one: a full page holds MPS/8 − 1 data entries + 1 chain pointer

36.4 The rules

offset = PRP1 mod MPS     pages = ⌈(offset + length) / MPS⌉     PRP1 covers min(MPS − offset, length)
  • length — bytes to transfer = (NLB + 1) × LBA size (+ interleaved metadata if formatted so).
  • MPS — memory page size from CC.MPS.
  • pages — number of memory pages the transfer touches.
pagesPRP2PRP list
1Not used (reserved/ignored)none
2Address of the second page — offset must be 0none
≥ 3PRP list pointer (qword aligned; may have an offset in its page)pages − 1 entries, each page-aligned; chain if they do not fit
  • All PRP entries: bits 1:0 = 0 verified. Entries other than PRP1 that point to data: offset 0 verified. Violations may be reported as 0/13h PRP Offset Invalid verified; whether every controller checks every entry is impl.
  • Entries per list page = MPS / 8 = 512 for 4 KiB. If the list starts at offset o, the first list page holds (MPS − o)/8 entries derived.
  • The last entry in a list page is a chain pointer only if more entries remain after it; otherwise it is a data entry verified.
  • PRPs never describe more than the command's length; extra list entries are not read derived.
  • PRP lists for queue memory (Create I/O SQ/CQ with PC=0) follow the same entry format but describe queue pages, not data.

36.6 Code — PRP list builder, visualiser and validator

Inputs: page size, buffer start address, buffer length, and the addresses of the remaining pages. Outputs: PRP1, PRP2, the PRP list pages (with chaining), and validation of malformed pointers. Assumptions are stated in the docstring.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""prp_tool.py - build, visualise and validate NVMe PRP data pointers.
EXECUTABLE teaching tool (no device access). Assumptions, stated explicitly:
  * MPS = memory page size chosen by host in CC.MPS (4 KiB here);
  * data pages are given as a list of host physical/IOVA page addresses
    (they need NOT be contiguous - that is the point of PRPs);
  * PRP list pages come from a fake allocator starting at LIST_BASE;
  * rules modelled: PRP1 may carry an offset (dword aligned); every later
    data entry must be page aligned; PRP2 is a data pointer when exactly two
    pages are touched, a PRP-list pointer when more; the last slot of a full
    list page chains to the next list page."""
import math

MPS = 4096
LIST_BASE = 0x7F000000

def pages_touched(addr, length, mps=MPS):
    off = addr % mps
    return math.ceil((off + length) / mps)

def build(first_addr, length, more_pages, mps=MPS):
    """first_addr: address of first byte (may be unaligned).
    more_pages: page-aligned addresses of pages 2..n."""
    n = pages_touched(first_addr, length, mps)
    assert len(more_pages) >= n - 1, f"need {n-1} more pages, got {len(more_pages)}"
    data = more_pages[:n - 1]
    mem, lists = {}, []
    prp1, prp2 = first_addr, 0
    if n == 2:
        prp2 = data[0]
    elif n > 2:
        per = mps // 8                       # 512 entries per 4 KiB list page
        nxt = LIST_BASE
        prp2 = nxt
        remaining = list(data)
        while remaining:
            page = nxt
            if len(remaining) <= per:
                entries, remaining = remaining, []
            else:
                nxt = page + mps
                entries, remaining = remaining[:per - 1] + [nxt], remaining[per - 1:]
            mem[page] = entries
            lists.append(page)
    return {"n": n, "prp1": prp1, "prp2": prp2, "lists": lists, "mem": mem, "len": length}

def show(r, mps=MPS):
    off = r["prp1"] % mps
    print(f"transfer {r['len']} B, first offset {off:#x} -> {r['n']} page(s)")
    print(f"  PRP1 = {r['prp1']:#012x}  covers {min(mps - off, r['len'])} B")
    if r["n"] == 1:
        print("  PRP2 = unused (transfer fits in PRP1's page)")
    elif r["n"] == 2:
        print(f"  PRP2 = {r['prp2']:#012x}  DATA page (exactly two pages touched)")
    else:
        print(f"  PRP2 = {r['prp2']:#012x}  -> PRP LIST pointer")
        for p in r["lists"]:
            ents = r["mem"][p]
            last = ents[-1]
            chained = p != r["lists"][-1]
            print(f"    list page {p:#x}: {len(ents)} entries"
                  + (f", last entry {last:#x} = CHAIN to next list page" if chained else ""))
            for i, e in enumerate(ents[:3]):
                print(f"      [{i}] {e:#012x}")
            if len(ents) > 3:
                print(f"      ... [{len(ents)-1}] {ents[-1]:#012x}")

def validate(prp1, prp2, length, mem, mps=MPS):
    """Return list of problems a controller could reject (PRP Offset Invalid,
    Data Transfer Error) or that would silently corrupt data."""
    probs = []
    if prp1 & 3:
        probs.append("PRP1 bits 1:0 non-zero (must be dword aligned)")
    n = pages_touched(prp1, length, mps)
    if n == 2 and prp2 % mps:
        probs.append(f"PRP2 {prp2:#x} used as data pointer but has offset {prp2 % mps:#x} "
                     "-> expect 'PRP Offset Invalid' or wrong data placement")
    if n > 2:
        if prp2 & 7:
            probs.append(f"PRP list pointer {prp2:#x} not qword aligned")
        page = prp2 - (prp2 % mps)
        if page not in mem:
            probs.append(f"PRP2 {prp2:#x} points at memory that holds no PRP list "
                         "-> controller DMA-reads garbage (IOMMU fault / Data Transfer Error)")
        else:
            need = n - 1
            idx = (prp2 % mps) // 8
            per = mps // 8
            while need:
                ents = mem.get(page)
                if ents is None:
                    probs.append(f"chain points to {page:#x} which is not a list page"); break
                e = ents[idx] if idx < len(ents) else None
                if e is None:
                    probs.append("list ended early: fewer entries than pages"); break
                if idx == per - 1 and need > 1:
                    page, idx = e, 0          # chain entry
                    continue
                if e % mps:
                    probs.append(f"list entry {e:#x} has non-zero offset (must be page aligned)")
                need -= 1; idx += 1
    return probs or ["OK - structurally valid (does not prove the pages belong to this I/O)"]

if __name__ == "__main__":
    base = 0x112340000
    pages = [base + i * MPS for i in range(1, 600)]
    print("Case A: 16 KiB read, page-aligned buffer")
    show(build(base, 16384, pages))
    print("\nCase B: 16 KiB read, buffer starts at offset 0x200")
    show(build(base + 0x200, 16384, pages))
    print("\nCase C: 8 KiB, aligned (PRP2 is a data pointer)")
    show(build(base, 8192, pages))
    print("\nCase D: 2 MiB + 8 KiB aligned, list chaining")
    show(build(base, 2 * 1024 * 1024 + 8192, pages))
    print("\n--- validation of broken pointers ---")
    good = build(base, 16384, pages)
    print("good      :", validate(good["prp1"], good["prp2"], 16384, good["mem"]))
    print("unaligned :", validate(base + 0x800, base + 0x1800, 4096, {}))
    print("wrong list:", validate(base, 0x7F001000, 16384, good["mem"]))
    bad = {LIST_BASE: [base + 0x1000, base + 0x2010, base + 0x3000]}
    print("crossing  :", validate(base, LIST_BASE, 16384, bad))

36.7 Hardware view and protocol view

  • The controller must read PRP lists from host memory (MRd → CplD) before or while moving data; for long lists it may prefetch list pages and data in parallel impl.
  • Each data TLP is addressed inside one PRP page, so PRP pages map directly onto TLP address ranges; a page never produces a TLP crossing a 4 KiB boundary (PCIe rule).
  • With an IOMMU, PRP addresses are IOVAs; Linux maps the bio's pages via the DMA API and may coalesce them into contiguous IOVA ranges — the PRPs then look contiguous even though physical pages are not impl.
  • Linux builds PRP lists from DMA pools (a small pool of 256-byte lists and a page-sized pool); small lists therefore start at non-zero offsets within a page version.

36.10 Labs

🧪 Lab 36.1 — Beginner: PRPs by hand SAFE LAB

For MPS 4 KiB compute pages/PRP2/list size for: (a) 12 KiB at offset 0; (b) 12 KiB at offset 0xFFC; (c) 4 B at offset 0xFFC; (d) 64 KiB at offset 0x10.

Solution

(a) 3 pages → list, 2 entries. (b) ⌈(4092+12288)/4096⌉ = 4 → list, 3 entries; PRP1 covers 4 B. (c) 1 page (0xFFC+4 = 0x1000) → PRP2 unused. (d) ⌈(16+65536)/4096⌉ = 17 → list, 16 entries.

🧪 Lab 36.2 — Intermediate: extend the tool SAFE LAB

Add support for a PRP list starting at a non-zero offset (e.g. LIST_BASE + 0xF00) and check that the first list page then holds only 32 entries before chaining.

Solution sketch

Per-page capacity = (MPS − (addr mod MPS)) / 8; chain when remaining > capacity, putting the chain pointer in the last slot of that partial page.

🧪 Lab 36.3 — Advanced: PRP conformance matrix SAFE LAB

Design a validation test matrix for a controller's PRP handling: dimensions offset {0, 4, 0x200, MPS−4}, length {4, 512, MPS−offset, MPS, 2·MPS, 512·MPS, 513·MPS…}, list position {page start, mid-page, last 8 bytes}, malformed variants. State expected outcomes.

Expected reasoning

Valid cases: data placed exactly, no extra list reads beyond need. Malformed: 0/13h expected where offsets are illegal; for undetectable errors (wrong but aligned addresses) expect data in wrong place — must be caught by host-side checks, not the device.

🧪 Lab 36.4 — Senior forensic SAFE LAB

A capture shows: SQE Read NLB=0x3F (512 B LBAs → 32 KiB), PRP1 = 0x5_0000_0E00, PRP2 = 0x6_1000_0000. Controller then MRd 64 bytes at 0x6_1000_0000 and writes data to eight addresses from that list plus PRP1. Is this consistent?

Solution

Pages = ⌈(0xE00 + 32768)/4096⌉ = ⌈36352/4096⌉ = 9 → PRP1 + 8 list entries = 64 bytes. Consistent. The last page receives 32768 − 512 − 7×4096 = 3584 B.

Quiz

  1. When is PRP2 a list pointer?

    Answer

    When the transfer touches more than two memory pages.

  2. Which PRP entries may have a non-zero offset?

    Answer

    PRP1 (and the PRP list pointer, qword-aligned); not data entries after the first.

  3. How many data entries fit in a full 4 KiB list page that must chain?

    Answer

    511 + 1 chain pointer.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a PRP?
    Model answerA page-address entry telling the controller where data lives.
  2. Beginner Where are PRP1/PRP2?
    Model answerSQE bytes 24–31 and 32–39.
  3. Beginner What is the MPS used by PRPs?
    Model answerCC.MPS memory page size, not PCIe Max_Payload_Size.
  4. Beginner PRP for a 4 KiB aligned read?
    Model answerPRP1 only.
  5. Beginner Why alignment?
    Model answerFixed page arithmetic, simple hardware.
  6. Intermediate 1 KiB at 0xE00?
    Model answerTwo pages; PRP2 = second page.
  7. Intermediate Chaining rule?
    Model answerLast entry of a list page points to the next list page if more entries remain.
  8. Intermediate Who allocates PRP lists?
    Model answerThe host driver, in DMA-able memory.
  9. Intermediate What happens on wrong offset?
    Model answer0/13h if detected; otherwise mis-placed data.
  10. Intermediate PRPs and IOMMU?
    Model answerPRPs carry IOVAs that the IOMMU translates.
  11. Advanced Why can't the controller detect all PRP errors?
    Model answerAligned but wrong addresses are indistinguishable from correct ones.
  12. Advanced Effect of PRPs on PCIe efficiency?
    Model answerExtra list reads; page-bounded TLPs; scattered pages limit write-combining.
  13. Advanced Why might Linux prefer SGL above a threshold?
    Model answerLarge contiguous segments describe in one descriptor vs many PRPs.
  14. Advanced PRP list starting mid-page?
    Model answerAllowed (qword aligned); capacity reduced on that page.
  15. Advanced PRP with metadata?
    Model answerSeparate metadata uses MPTR (contiguous buffer) with PRPs.
  16. Senior Debug sporadic corruption at 2 MiB transfers.
    Model answerInspect chain entries; sweep sizes; compare analyzer data addresses to expected pages.
  17. Senior Design a PRP fuzzer.
    Model answerGenerate valid/invalid combos, check device status and memory canaries around pages.
  18. Senior Why are posted read-data writes dangerous with bad PRPs?
    Model answerDevice gets no error; corrupts arbitrary memory if IOMMU off.
  19. Senior Security implications?
    Model answerWithout IOMMU, a malicious/buggy device or bad PRP can DMA anywhere.
  20. Senior Validation evidence for a PRP fix?
    Model answerUnit tests of builder, offset/size fuzz, analyzer verification, DMA-API debug clean run.
🎯 Teach-back

Child: the two-line delivery note and the fridge list. Junior: the page-count formula and PRP2 rule. Senior: IOVA mapping, chaining, undetectable errors and validation strategy.

📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?PRP1/PRP2 locations; PRP entries dword aligned; only PRP1 data entry may have an offset; PRP2 data vs list rule; chaining via last entry; PRP Offset Invalid 0/13h; admin commands use PRP on PCIe. verified
What is derived?Page-count formula; entries per list page; list capacity at an offset. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Which violations a controller checks; list prefetch strategy. impl
What is version-dependent?Document location of PRP text; Linux DMA pool sizes. version
What must be checked in the specification?PRP list pointer alignment wording in your revision.
What should never be assumed?That an aligned PRP is a correct PRP.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute PRP1/PRP2/list for any address/length/MPS.
  • I can diagram chained lists and offset lists.
  • I can identify PRP list fetches and data TLPs in a trace.
  • I can debug PRP Offset Invalid and silent misplacement.
  • I can distinguish PRP from SGL and memory page size from Max_Payload_Size.
  • I can cite the Base/PCIe Transport specs for PRP rules.

36.11 Summary

PRP1 (with offset) + PRP2 (second page or list pointer) + page-aligned list entries with chaining describe any buffer; page count = ⌈(offset+length)/MPS⌉. Next: Chapter 37 — SGL.

37 Scatter Gather Lists (SGL)

← 36 Physical Region Pages (PRP)38 PRP/SGL Debugging Lab →

37.1 Why this chapter exists

PRPs assume page-granular buffers. Many real buffers are large contiguous regions (huge pages, RDMA memory) or byte-granular fragments. SGLs describe memory as (address, length) segments and add capabilities PRPs lack: discarding part of a read (bit bucket), arbitrary lengths, and — on fabrics — keyed remote memory. SGLs are mandatory on NVMe over Fabrics and optional on PCIe I/O commands (reported by Identify Controller SGLS) verified.

37.2 Learning objectives

  • Decode a 16-byte SGL descriptor: address, length, type, subtype.
  • Explain Data Block, Bit Bucket, Segment and Last Segment descriptors and the rules connecting them.
  • Walk a multi-segment SGL and compute the total length.
  • Compare PRP vs SGL and decide when each is preferable.

Prerequisites: Ch 36, Ch 29 (PSDT).

🧒 Kid analogy

Instead of "room numbers", the delivery note now says "put 4096 boxes starting at the kitchen door; put 8192 boxes starting at the garage; throw 512 boxes in the skip (bit bucket); for more instructions, read the note taped to the attic door (segment)".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

"Boxes" are bytes, the lengths are exact, and there are strict rules about where a "read more instructions" note may appear (only as the last descriptor in a segment).

37.3 Descriptor format

BytesFieldMeaning
07:00Address64-bit address (meaning per type)
11:08Length32-bit byte length
14:12Reserved / type-specificKeyed descriptors reuse bytes for a key (fabrics)
15SGL Identifierbits 7:4 Descriptor Type, bits 3:0 Descriptor Sub Type (0h Address, 1h Offset, Ah transport-specific…)
TypeNameAddress points toLength isRules
0hSGL Data BlockData bufferBytes of dataAny descriptor position
1hSGL Bit BucketReserved (not used)Bytes to discardValid for reads (controller→host): data is transferred to nowhere; not meaningful for writes
2hSGL SegmentNext SGL segment (array of descriptors)Bytes of that segment (multiple of 16)Must be the last descriptor of its segment
3hSGL Last SegmentFinal SGL segmentBytes of that segmentThe pointed-to segment must contain no Segment/Last Segment descriptors
4hKeyed SGL Data BlockRemote memory + keyBytesFabrics (RDMA) version
5hTransport SGL Data BlockTransport-definedBytesFabrics (e.g. TCP) version
FhVendor specific———

Types 0h–3h verified. SGL Descriptor 1 lives in SQE bytes 24–39 (DPTR) when PSDT = 01b/10b. The SGL's total data length must equal the command's transfer length, otherwise 0/0Fh Data SGL Length Invalid (the spec also allows controllers to accept longer SGLs if they report support — check SGLS) version. Other errors: 0/0Dh Invalid SGL Segment Descriptor, 0/0Eh Invalid Number of SGL Descriptors, 0/11h SGL Descriptor Type Invalid, 0/16h SGL Offset Invalid.

37.4 Code — SGL walker

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""sgl_walk.py - decode 16-byte NVMe SGL descriptors and walk a synthetic SGL.
EXECUTABLE teaching tool; memory is a Python dict, not a device."""
import struct

TYPES = {0x0: "Data Block", 0x1: "Bit Bucket", 0x2: "Segment",
         0x3: "Last Segment", 0x4: "Keyed Data Block (fabrics)",
         0x5: "Transport Data Block (fabrics)"}

def desc(raw):
    addr, length = struct.unpack_from("<QI", raw, 0)
    ident = raw[15]
    return {"addr": addr, "len": length, "type": ident >> 4, "sub": ident & 0xF}

def mk(addr, length, typ, sub=0):
    return struct.pack("<QI3xB", addr, length, (typ << 4) | sub)

def walk(sgl1, mem, total):
    """sgl1: 16-byte descriptor from SQE DPTR. mem: addr -> bytes of a segment."""
    d, moved, hops = desc(sgl1), 0, 0
    pending = [d]
    while pending:
        d = pending.pop(0)
        t = TYPES.get(d["type"], "RESERVED -> SGL Descriptor Type Invalid")
        if d["type"] in (0x0, 0x1):
            act = "transfer" if d["type"] == 0 else "discard (read only)"
            print(f"  {t:13} addr={d['addr']:#014x} len={d['len']:6} -> {act}")
            moved += d["len"]
        elif d["type"] in (0x2, 0x3):
            seg = mem.get(d["addr"])
            if seg is None or d["len"] % 16:
                print(f"  {t:13} addr={d['addr']:#x} len={d['len']} -> INVALID segment pointer/length")
                return
            n = d["len"] // 16
            print(f"  {t:13} addr={d['addr']:#014x} -> {n} descriptors")
            kids = [desc(seg[i*16:(i+1)*16]) for i in range(n)]
            if d["type"] == 0x3 and any(k["type"] in (2, 3) for k in kids):
                print("    !! Last Segment contains a segment descriptor -> invalid")
                return
            if any(k["type"] in (2, 3) for k in kids[:-1]):
                print("    !! segment descriptor not in last slot -> invalid")
                return
            pending = kids + pending
            hops += 1
        else:
            print(f"  {t}"); return
    verdict = "OK" if moved == total else f"MISMATCH (expected {total}) -> Data SGL Length Invalid"
    print(f"  total described = {moved} B over {hops} segment hop(s): {verdict}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    seg_a = mk(0x200000, 4096, 0) + mk(0x305000, 8192, 0) + mk(0x400000, 32, 3)
    seg_b = mk(0x90000, 512, 1) + mk(0x910000, 3584, 0)
    mem = {0x10000: seg_a, 0x400000: seg_b}
    print("Valid chain: SQE SGL1 = Segment -> Last Segment")
    walk(mk(0x10000, 48, 2), mem, 16384)
    print("Simple: SGL1 is a single Data Block (contiguous 16 KiB)")
    walk(mk(0x800000, 16384, 0), mem, 16384)
    print("Broken: length mismatch")
    walk(mk(0x800000, 12288, 0), mem, 16384)
Valid chain: SQE SGL1 = Segment -> Last Segment
  Segment       addr=0x000000010000 -> 3 descriptors
  Data Block    addr=0x000000200000 len=  4096 -> transfer
  Data Block    addr=0x000000305000 len=  8192 -> transfer
  Last Segment  addr=0x000000400000 -> 2 descriptors
  Bit Bucket    addr=0x000000090000 len=   512 -> discard (read only)
  Data Block    addr=0x000000910000 len=  3584 -> transfer
  total described = 16384 B over 2 segment hop(s): OK
Simple: SGL1 is a single Data Block (contiguous 16 KiB)
  Data Block    addr=0x000000800000 len= 16384 -> transfer
  total described = 16384 B over 0 segment hop(s): OK
Broken: length mismatch
  Data Block    addr=0x000000800000 len= 12288 -> transfer
  total described = 12288 B over 0 segment hop(s): MISMATCH (expected 16384) -> Data SGL Length Invalid

37.5 PRP vs SGL

AspectPRPSGL
GranularityMemory pages; only first entry offsetByte address + byte length (alignment per SGLS: none or dword)
Size of description for 1 MiB contiguousPRP1 + 255-entry list (2 KiB)One 16-byte Data Block in the SQE
Description for 256 scattered 4 KiB pages~2 KiB list256 × 16 = 4 KiB of descriptors
Support on PCIeMandatory; only option for admin commandsOptional for I/O commands (SGLS)
FabricsNot usedRequired (keyed/transport descriptors)
Discard part of readNoBit Bucket
Controller complexitySimple fixed arithmeticDescriptor parsing, variable-length segments
Linux useDefaultUsed for I/O when supported and average segment size ≥ sgl_threshold module parameter (default 32 KiB) version

🧪 Lab 37.1 — SGL support on your controller SAFE LAB
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H | grep -i -A6 sgls
cat /sys/module/nvme/parameters/sgl_threshold 2>/dev/null
Expected reasoning

SGLS bits 1:0 = 00b means no SGL support → Linux always uses PRPs. Many client SSDs report no SGL support impl.

🧪 Lab 37.2 — Build SGLs SAFE LAB

Using mk() from the walker, build (a) a valid SGL for a 12 KiB read made of 3 × 4 KiB non-contiguous buffers using one Last Segment; (b) an invalid one where a Segment descriptor is not last; run the walker on both.

Solution

(a) SGL1 = Last Segment @S len 48; S = three Data Blocks of 4096. (b) segment with [Segment, Data Block] → walker reports "segment descriptor not in last slot".

Quiz

  1. Which SGL type discards data?

    Answer

    Bit Bucket (1h).

  2. Where must a Segment descriptor appear?

    Answer

    As the last descriptor in its segment (or as SGL1 in the SQE).

  3. Can admin commands use SGLs on PCIe?

    Answer

    No.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner PRP vs SGL in one sentence?
    Model answerPRP lists pages; SGL lists address+length segments.
  2. Intermediate Why do fabrics require SGL?
    Model answerRemote memory needs keys/transport descriptors and byte-granular regions.
  3. Advanced When is SGL slower than PRP?
    Model answerMany small fragments, deep segment chains, controllers with slow descriptor parsing.
  4. Senior Validation plan for SGL?
    Model answerEach descriptor type, segment chaining positions, length mismatch, alignment per SGLS, bit bucket in reads, metadata SGL (PSDT 10b).
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?16-byte descriptor; types 0h Data Block, 1h Bit Bucket, 2h Segment, 3h Last Segment; PSDT selects SGL; SGL errors 0Dh–11h; SGL optional on PCIe I/O, not for admin. verified
What is derived?Total-length rule; segment placement rule; PRP vs SGL size comparison. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Descriptor parsing speed; support (SGLS) at all. impl
What is version-dependent?Keyed/transport descriptor types; excess-length support; Linux sgl_threshold. version
What must be checked in the specification?SGLS bit definitions and alignment requirements.
What should never be assumed?That every NVMe SSD supports SGLs.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can decode an SGL descriptor and walk a chain.
  • I can state the four core types and their placement rules.
  • I can choose PRP or SGL for a workload with reasons.

37.8 Summary

SGLs are byte-granular (address, length, type) descriptors chained by Segment/Last Segment, optional on PCIe I/O and essential on fabrics. Next: Chapter 38 — debugging lab.

38 PRP/SGL Debugging Lab

← 37 Scatter Gather Lists (SGL)39 The Most Important Chapter: An End-to-End NVMe Read →

38.1 Why this chapter exists

Knowing the rules is not the same as spotting their violation in a 64-byte hex dump at 2 a.m. This lab gives you valid and malformed data pointers. For each, decide: (1) is the command valid? (2) where is the data? (3) which DMA transactions should occur? (4) what failure might result? Use the PRP tool (Ch 36), the SGL walker (Ch 37) and the decoder (Ch 29).

38.2 Objectives

  • Classify PRP/SGL errors as detectable by the controller (error status) or undetectable (wrong placement).
  • Predict the exact MRd/MWr sequence for valid cases.
  • Attribute failures to host builder, IOMMU mapping, or controller.

All cases: MPS = 4 KiB, LBA = 512 B, Read unless stated, synthetic addresses synthetic.

🧪 Lab 38.1 — Ten cases SAFE LAB

Solutions
#Valid?Where is the dataExpected DMAFailure if any
1Yes0x2_0000_0000–0FFFSQE MRd; 16 × MWr 256 B (MPS 256); CQE—
2No, as built. Offset 0x400 with 8 KiB → ⌈(1024+8192)/4096⌉ = 3 pages → PRP2 must be a list pointer, so the controller interprets 0x2_0000_2000 as a list.Controller reads two 8-byte entries at 0x2_0000_2000 — which is (probably) the third data page, not a listMRd 16 B at 0x2_0000_2000 then MWr to whatever addresses those bytes containInvalid as built: the host treated PRP2 as the second data page. Result: garbage addresses → IOMMU fault or memory corruption. Lesson: always include the offset in the page count.
3No: 4 KiB at offset 0x800 → 2 pages → PRP2 is a data pointer and must have offset 0; 0x…1800 has offset 0x800Intended: 0x2_0000_0800–0FFF + 0x2_0000_1000–17FFController may fail before DMA0/13h PRP Offset Invalid if checked; if not checked, the second half lands at 0x…1800–1FFF (wrong place) impl
4Structurally valid (aligned) but semantically wrongController follows the other command's listMRd 24 B at 0x3_0000_1000; MWr into another request's pagesSilent corruption of another I/O's buffer; undetectable by the controller. Find by comparing PRP2 with driver's allocation (DMA-API debug, analyzer)

8No (logically): list overlaps the dataFor a Write, the controller reads the list, then reads data from page 0x2_0000_1000, which contains the list instead of user dataMRd list at 0x…1000; MRd data at the list's entriesWrong data written to media (list bytes); for a Read, the device would overwrite the list while walking it. Undetectable by the device.

10No: Bit Bucket in a Write (host→controller) has no meaning—MRd segment then errorSGL Descriptor Type Invalid (0/11h) or Invalid Field — exact status impl/version

38.4 Debugging method (use for every case)

  1. Decode SQE: opcode, NLB, PSDT, PRP1, PRP2 / SGL1.
  2. Compute transfer length (LBA format!) and pages (offset!).
  3. Decide PRP2's role; validate alignment of every entry.
  4. Read the list/segments as fetched by the controller (analyzer CplD), not as the driver intended.
  5. Map each data TLP address to a list entry; any TLP outside the expected set is the first bad event.
  6. Check IOMMU faults and completion status (UR/CA on MRd, 0/04h, 0/13h).
  7. Attribute: builder (host), mapping (IOMMU/DMA API), or controller (ignored a rule or mis-walked).
💡 Senior insight

The device can only reject what is syntactically wrong (offset bits, descriptor types, lengths). Everything semantically wrong — a well-aligned pointer to the wrong page — is silently honoured. That is why serious validation pairs a device-side test suite with host-side canaries (guard pages around buffers, DMA-API debugging, IOMMU strict mode).

Quiz

  1. Which malformed cases can a controller detect?

    Answer

    Offset/alignment violations (3, 5, 6), invalid SGL types/structure/lengths (10); not wrong-but-aligned pointers (2, 4, 7, 8).

  2. Why is case 2 dangerous although every address is aligned?

    Answer

    The host miscounted pages; the controller interprets a data page as a PRP list.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate How do you tell if PRP2 is a list pointer from a trace?
    Model answerCompute pages from PRP1 offset and length; if > 2 it is a list; confirm by MRd at PRP2.
  2. Advanced A read completes successfully but data is wrong only for unaligned buffers. Where do you look?
    Model answerPRP page-count and offset logic; compare to case 2/7 patterns.
  3. Senior How would you make such bugs impossible in a driver?
    Model answerSingle tested builder function, property-based tests against a reference model, DMA-API debug in CI, IOMMU strict mode in test, and analyzer-based regression on representative alignments.
📭 Zero-hallucination ledger
What is verified?The PRP/SGL rules from Chapters 36–37. verified
What is derived?Each case's validity, DMA sequence and failure mode. derived
What is implementation-dependent?Whether a given controller rejects or silently honours syntactic violations. impl
What is version-dependent?Status codes chosen for SGL violations. version
What must be checked in the specification?Your controller's documented validation behaviour.
What should never be assumed?That the device will catch host pointer bugs.
✅ Mastery gate

  • I can predict the DMA sequence for valid cases and the first bad event for invalid ones.
  • I can separate detectable from undetectable pointer errors.
  • I extended the validator for list-inside-data detection.

38.5 Summary

Validate data pointers in four steps — length, pages, roles, alignment — and remember the device cannot protect you from aligned-but-wrong addresses. Further reading: NVMe Base 2.4 (data pointer, PRP and SGL definitions, status codes); NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4; Linux drivers/nvme/host/pci.c PRP/SGL setup functions version.

PART XIII

End-to-End NVMe over PCIe

Up to now you have learned NVMe and PCIe as two separate machines: one that speaks in queues, commands and completion entries, and one that speaks in Transaction Layer Packets, credits and links. This part welds them together. You will follow a single 4 KiB read and a single 4 KiB write from the application's system call all the way through the doorbell, the command fetch, the data movement, the completion entry, the MSI-X interrupt and the final head-doorbell update — and you will learn to recognise every one of those steps as a specific packet, travelling in a specific direction, to a specific address region. This is the part that converts "I know NVMe" and "I know PCIe" into "I can read a trace of an SSD and tell you what it is doing and what went wrong".

39 The Most Important Chapter: An End-to-End NVMe Read

← 38 PRP/SGL Debugging Lab40 End-to-End NVMe Write →
📌 Remember

If you only ever master one chapter of this book, master this one. Every debugging session on a PCIe-attached SSD — a hang, a timeout, a performance cliff, a corrupted buffer, a missing interrupt — is a deviation from the sequence you will memorise here. When you know the normal sequence cold, the abnormal one jumps off the screen.

39.1 Why this chapter exists

Most engineers learn NVMe (Non-Volatile Memory Express) from the command-set point of view: a Read command has opcode 02h, a starting LBA (Logical Block Address) in CDW10–11, a block count in CDW12, and the data lands in the buffer described by PRP1/PRP2. Most engineers learn PCIe (Peripheral Component Interconnect Express) from the packet point of view: there are Memory Read requests, Memory Write requests, Completions with Data, and they flow over a layered link. Very few engineers can explain, without hesitation, which PCIe packets a single NVMe Read produces, who sends each one, in which order, to which address, and what evidence each one leaves behind. That gap is exactly where real bugs hide: a driver that rings the doorbell before the SQE (Submission Queue Entry) is visible in memory, a device that writes the CQE (Completion Queue Entry) before the data, an IOMMU (I/O Memory Management Unit) that blocks the device's DMA (Direct Memory Access), an MSI-X (Message Signalled Interrupts – Extended) vector that is masked. This chapter closes the gap.

39.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: list the 17 stages of an NVMe Read from application to application completion, in order, without notes.
  • Intermediate: for each stage, state whether it crosses the PCIe link, and if so the TLP (Transaction Layer Packet) type, direction (upstream/downstream), requester, completer, and address region (host DRAM, BAR0 doorbell, MSI-X address).
  • Advanced: explain why the CQE write cannot overtake the data writes under default PCIe ordering, why the SQE fetch is a non-posted request but the data delivery is posted, and how MPS (Max Payload Size), MRRS (Max Read Request Size) and RCB (Read Completion Boundary) change the number of TLPs.
  • Senior: given a partial trace with a missing step, reason about which layer stopped, what the first abnormal event is, and what capture would prove it.
  • Trace-analysis: label every packet in a synthetic read trace with the NVMe event it belongs to.
  • Debugging: map five failure symptoms (timeout, wrong data, no interrupt, AER error, all-ones reads) to the stage where they originate.
  • Validation: describe what a test must observe to prove a read completed correctly at both the NVMe and PCIe layers.

39.3 Prerequisites

You need: the NVMe queue model (SQ/CQ pairs, doorbells, phase tag), the 64-byte SQE and 16-byte CQE layouts, PRP (Physical Region Page) data pointers, the PCIe transaction layer (posted vs non-posted requests, completions, tags), and the idea of BARs (Base Address Registers) and MMIO (Memory-Mapped I/O). If any of those feel shaky, revisit the earlier parts of the book before continuing. Within this part, the companion chapters are Chapter 40 (write) and Chapter 41 (correlation); interrupts are detailed in Chapter 43.

39.4 The story: a library with a pneumatic tube

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine you live in a house (the host) next to a giant warehouse of books (the SSD). You want page 7 of a book. You write your request on a card and put it in your outbox tray in your own kitchen (the Submission Queue in host memory). Then you ring a little bell on the warehouse wall (the doorbell). The bell does not carry your card — it only says "there is new stuff in tray number 1, up to slot 5". The warehouse worker walks over, reaches into your kitchen and copies the card (command fetch). They go into the warehouse, find the book, copy the page and post the copy through your letterbox straight onto your table (data DMA). Then they drop a receipt into your inbox tray (Completion Queue) and ring your doorbell (MSI-X interrupt). You read the receipt, see "page 7 — done, OK", and tell the warehouse "I've read receipts up to slot 5" by ringing a second bell (CQ head doorbell).

🌍 Analogy

Engineering version: a restaurant where the waiter (driver) pins an order ticket to a rail inside the kitchen pass (SQ in host DRAM), taps a bell that tells the chef "the rail now has tickets up to position N" (doorbell MMIO write), the chef pulls the ticket (DMA read of SQE), cooks (media access), places the dish on the pass (DMA write of data), pins a "served" chit on a second rail (CQE write), then presses a buzzer in the dining room (MSI-X). The waiter clears chits and tells the chef which chits are cleared (CQ head doorbell).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

(1) In the analogy the chef "walks over"; in reality the controller issues PCIe Memory Read requests and waits for Completion TLPs — the fetch has latency, credits and can time out. (2) The doorbell is a single 32-bit register write; there is no handshake and no reply — it is a posted write, so the host has no idea whether it arrived. (3) The receipt (CQE) and the dish (data) travel on the same PCIe ordering rules; in a restaurant nothing prevents the chit arriving before the dish, but in PCIe, default ordering guarantees posted writes from the same requester are not reordered relative to each other. (4) The "buzzer" is itself just another memory write to a magic address; there is no separate wire.

39.5 The cast: who acts in an NVMe Read

ActorWhere it livesWhat it ownsWhat it can observe
ApplicationUser spaceBuffer (virtual addresses), file descriptorSystem-call return value, latency
Block layer (Linux blk-mq)Kernelstruct request / bio, tag, hardware context per CPURequest start/complete (blktrace, tracepoints)
NVMe driverKernel (nvme, nvme-core)SQ/CQ rings in DRAM, CID allocation, PRP list construction, doorbell writesCQE contents, timeouts, tracepoints nvme_setup_cmd/nvme_complete_rq
CPU + Root Complex (RC)SoC / chipsetConverts CPU stores to BAR addresses into downstream MWr TLPs; answers device MRd with CplD from DRAM; delivers MSI-X writes to interrupt controllerInternal; partially via AER on root ports
IOMMUBetween RC and memoryTranslates device-visible IOVA (I/O virtual addresses) to physical; enforces permissionsFault logs (e.g. DMAR faults on Intel, AMD-Vi events)
Switch (optional)Between RC and endpointRoutes TLPs by address/IDPer-port AER, counters (impl)
NVMe controllerSSD ASICDoorbell registers, queue state (internal copies of tail/head), command parser, DMA engines, MSI-X tableInternal logs, vendor telemetry
Media back end (FTL + NAND)SSDLogical-to-physical map, NAND dies, ECCSMART/Health log, vendor logs; generally unobservable from the bus

39.5a Who writes what: the block diagram

Before the detailed stages, here is the whole Read on one picture. There are three places: software (the driver, running on the host CPU), host memory (RAM, which only stores things and never starts anything) and the device (the SSD's controller, across the PCIe link). Click a step number, an arrow, or a list item to follow the command. The example reads 4 KiB (8 × 512-byte blocks) from LBA 0x1000 into a buffer at 0x1_2345_6000 using I/O queue 1, slot 3. synthetic

Software starts itDevice starts itInside the SSD (not visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. Software writes the 64-byte Read command into the Submission Queue

    The driver fills slot 3 of Submission Queue 1 in RAM.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 3 (address = SQ base + 3 × 64)PCIe: No. This is the CPU writing its own RAM.
    Opcode = 02h (Read) CID = 0x002A NSID = 1 SLBA = 0x1000 NLB = 7 (means 8 blocks = 4 KiB) PRP1 = 0x1_2345_6000 (where the data should go)
  2. Software rings the SQ tail doorbell

    The driver writes the new tail index into the SSD's SQ1 tail doorbell register. It means: "there is new work, up to (not including) slot 4".

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x1008PCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 4 Only this number crosses PCIe. The command is still sitting in RAM.
  3. Device fetches the command from host memory

    The controller sees tail moved from 3 to 4, so it reads slot 3. It sends a read request; the host's PCIe root complex answers with the 64 bytes.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 3PCIe: Yes, both ways. · MRd (device → host), then CplD with 64 bytes (host → device)
    The device now has the full command: "read 8 blocks from LBA 0x1000 into 0x1_2345_6000, call it CID 0x002A"
  4. Device reads the data from NAND flash

    The controller's flash translation layer maps LBA 0x1000 to a physical NAND page and reads it.

    Where: Inside the SSDPCIe: No. Nothing appears on the PCIe link during this step.
    Typically tens of microseconds. This is usually the slowest step.
  5. Device writes the 4 KiB of data into the host buffer

    The DMA engine writes the data straight into RAM at the address given in PRP1. The CPU is not involved.

    Where: Host memory, data buffer at 0x1_2345_6000PCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr packets (e.g. 16 × 256 bytes if Max Payload Size is 256)
    After this step the 4096 bytes are already in the application's buffer, but software does not know it yet.
  6. Device writes the 16-byte completion entry

    The controller writes a completion entry into the next free slot of Completion Queue 1. Software never writes completion entries; it only reads them.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 3 (address = CQ base + 3 × 16)PCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 16 bytes
    CID = 0x002A (which command finished) Status = 0 (success) Phase tag = 1 (new entry) SQID = 1 SQHD = 4 (device has read the SQ up to slot 4)
  7. Device sends the MSI-X interrupt

    The controller writes a small message to an address the CPU's interrupt controller watches. The CPU turns that into an interrupt and runs the driver's handler.

    Where: Interrupt address/data taken from the device's MSI-X tablePCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 4 bytes, to the MSI-X address
    An interrupt is just another memory write. PCIe ordering keeps it behind the data and completion writes, so they are already in RAM when it lands.
  8. Software reads the completion entry

    The interrupt handler reads CQ1 slot 3, checks the phase tag is the value it expects, matches CID 0x002A to the Read it sent, and sees status 0.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 3PCIe: No. The CPU reads its own RAM.
    Phase = 1 as expected → this is a new entry CID 0x002A → it is our Read Status 0 → success; wake the application, data is in the buffer
  9. Software rings the CQ head doorbell

    The driver writes the new head index into the CQ1 head doorbell. It means: "I have consumed entries up to slot 4, you may reuse those slots".

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x100CPCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 4 Without this, the completion queue would eventually look full to the device.

Software writes only three things: the command (step 1) and the two doorbells (steps 2 and 9). The device writes the data, the 16-byte completion entry and the interrupt message. Host memory never initiates anything.

39.6 The 17 stages — overview diagram

39.7 Stage by stage — the five views

Each stage below is described through five lenses demanded by this book: analogy, technical, hardware, protocol and trace appearance. Example parameters used throughout (all synthetic): I/O queue pair QID 3, SQ size 1024 entries, CQ size 1024 entries, CAP.DSTRD = 0 (doorbell stride 4 bytes), BAR0 at host physical address 0xF7A0_0000, SQ3 base IOVA 0x1_2340_0000, CQ3 base IOVA 0x1_2350_0000, data buffer IOVA 0x1_4000_0000 (4 KiB, page aligned), device BDF (Bus:Device.Function) 02:00.0 → Requester ID 0x0200, MPS = 256 bytes, MRRS = 512 bytes, MSI-X vector 4 for CQ3 with message address 0xFEE0_2000 and data 0x0000_0045 (x86-style, impl).

Stage 1 — Application request

Analogy: you decide you want page 7. Technical: the application calls pread(fd, buf, 4096, 7*4096) on an O_DIRECT file descriptor (or io_uring / libaio submit). With O_DIRECT the page cache is bypassed and the user buffer itself becomes the DMA target after pinning. Hardware: only the CPU is involved; the buffer may not even be resident yet. Protocol: none — no PCIe traffic. Trace appearance: nothing on a PCIe analyzer. In software, strace shows the system call, and bpftrace on syscalls:sys_enter_pread64 can timestamp it.

Stage 2 — Block request

Analogy: the house's secretary writes your wish onto a standard form. Technical: the filesystem maps file offset to device LBA; a bio is built and turned into a struct request by blk-mq, which picks a hardware queue (normally the one mapped to the submitting CPU) and allocates a tag. Hardware: CPU only. Protocol: none. Trace appearance: blktrace events Q (queued), G (get request), D (issued to driver) — the D timestamp is the last software event before the driver.

Stage 3 — Driver command creation

Analogy: the request is copied onto the warehouse's own card format. Technical: the driver chooses the SQ for this hardware context (SQ3), fills a 64-byte SQE: CDW0 = opcode 02h (Read), FUSE=00b, PSDT=00b (PRPs), CID = command identifier (Linux derives it from the blk-mq tag plus a generation counter in recent kernels — impl); NSID = 1; PRP1 = 0x1_4000_0000; PRP2 = 0 (a single 4 KiB page fits PRP1 alone); CDW10/11 = starting LBA; CDW12 bits 15:0 = NLB (number of logical blocks, zero-based) = 0 for one 4 KiB block on a 4 KiB-formatted namespace, or 7 for eight 512-byte blocks. The buffer has been DMA-mapped through the IOMMU, yielding the IOVA. Hardware: CPU writes into cacheable DRAM. Protocol: none yet. Trace appearance: Linux tracepoint nvme:nvme_setup_cmd records qid, cid, opcode, nsid and CDW10–15.

Stage 4 — Command memory

Analogy: the card is placed in the tray. Technical: the SQE is stored at SQ3_base + tail × 64. If the SQ were placed in a CMB (Controller Memory Buffer) instead, this store itself would be a PCIe write into device memory — a different trace shape (see the trace variants below). Hardware: the CPU store sits in cache; on most modern x86 platforms device DMA reads are cache-coherent (snooped), so no explicit flush is required, but a write memory barrier is required to order the SQE store before the doorbell store. Protocol: none for host-memory SQ. Trace appearance: invisible on the link. This is the first important negative-evidence trap: you can never "see" the SQE being written on a PCIe analyzer when the SQ lives in host DRAM — you only see the device reading it later.

Stage 5 — Submission queue tail update

Analogy: you count how many cards are in the tray now. Technical: driver increments its private tail: tail = (tail + 1) % qsize. The SQ is full when (tail + 1) % qsize == head, where head is learned from the SQHD field of returned CQEs. Hardware/Protocol: none yet. Trace: none.

Stage 6 — Doorbell

Analogy: ringing the bell. Technical: the driver writes the new tail value to the SQ3 Tail Doorbell register. Offset = 1000h + (2 × 3) × (4 << DSTRD) = 1000h + 24 = 1018h. With CAP.DSTRD = 0, the register sits at BAR0 + 0x1018 = 0xF7A0_1018. Linux writes it with writel(), preceded by a barrier so the SQE store is globally visible first. Linux may batch several SQEs and ring once (the bd->last hint) — impl. Hardware: the CPU issues an uncached (UC) store to the MMIO range; the store leaves the core, is claimed by the root complex because the address falls inside the root port's memory window, and becomes a TLP. Protocol: see stage 7. Trace: on a CPU-side tool (e.g. MMIO tracing in a hypervisor) the write is visible; on the link it becomes stage 7.

Stage 7 — PCIe Memory Write (doorbell TLP)

Analogy: the bell's sound travelling along the wire. Technical/Protocol: a MWr (Memory Write) request, 3DW header if the address is below 4 GiB (here it is), Length = 1 DW, First DW BE = 1111b, Last DW BE = 0000b, Requester ID = root port (e.g. 00:01.0 → 0x0008 — impl: some root complexes use 00:00.0), payload = tail value. It is posted: no completion will ever come back. It travels downstream. It consumes Posted Header and Posted Data flow-control credits on the link. Hardware: the endpoint's transaction layer decodes the address against BAR0, the controller latches the new tail. Trace appearance: one downstream MWr, 1 DW payload, address in BAR0 doorbell region. The payload equals the new tail — if you see tail values that skip or go backwards, suspect a driver bug or a lost/merged write.

⚠️ Warning

A posted doorbell write can be silently dropped if the device is in reset, if Memory Space Enable is cleared in the Command register, or if the link is down. The host's writel() returns immediately regardless. The first symptom is a command timeout 30 seconds later (Linux default nvme_core.io_timeout), not an error at the doorbell. Always correlate a timeout backwards to the doorbell.

Stage 8 — Controller command fetch decision

Analogy: the worker hears the bell and notes "tray 3 has one new card". Technical: the controller compares the new tail with its internal SQ head; entries between head and tail are pending. Fetch policy (how many SQEs per read, arbitration among SQs — round robin, weighted round robin with urgent priority) is controller-specific within the arbitration mechanism selected by CC.AMS. Hardware: doorbell write lands in a register file; firmware or a hardware queue manager schedules the fetch. Protocol: internal. Trace: the time gap between the doorbell MWr and the first fetch MRd is the controller's doorbell-to-fetch latency, typically sub-microsecond to a few microseconds (impl).

Stage 9 — DMA request

Analogy: the worker grabs a trolley. Technical: the DMA engine is programmed with source = SQ3_base + head × 64, length = 64 bytes (or a multiple if it fetches several SQEs at once, bounded by MRRS and by the ring wrap). Hardware: a tag is allocated from the device's outstanding-request pool (8-bit tags by default, 10-bit if enabled on both ends). Protocol/Trace: appears as stage 10.

Stage 10 — Memory Read TLP (SQE fetch)

Analogy: the worker's hand reaching into your kitchen. Protocol: MRd (Memory Read) request, 4DW header because the IOVA is above 4 GiB, Length = 16 DW (64 bytes), Requester ID = 0x0200 (the SSD), Tag = e.g. 0x11, address = 0x1_2340_0000 + head × 64. It is non-posted: it consumes Non-Posted Header credits and the device must keep the tag reserved until all completions arrive, or until the completion timeout fires. Direction: upstream. Hardware: the RC forwards to the IOMMU, which translates the IOVA; if no mapping exists the access is blocked and the device typically receives a completion with UR (Unsupported Request) or CA (Completer Abort) status — or, on some platforms, nothing useful — while the host logs an IOMMU fault (impl). Trace appearance: first upstream packet after the doorbell; address inside the SQ region.

Stage 11 — Completion with Data (SQE delivery)

Analogy: the copy of the card arrives in the worker's hand. Protocol: CplD (Completion with Data), downstream, Completer ID = root complex, Requester ID = 0x0200, Tag = 0x11 (matching), Status = SC (Successful Completion), Byte Count = 64, Lower Address = low 7 bits of the request address, payload 16 DW = the SQE. Because the request is 64-byte aligned and 64 bytes long, a single CplD is the usual result; a completer may legally split a read into multiple completions at RCB boundaries (64 or 128 bytes) — the requester must reassemble using Byte Count and Lower Address. Hardware: data comes from DRAM (or from CPU cache via snoop). Trace appearance: a CplD whose tag matches the MRd. The interval MRd→CplD is the host's memory read latency seen by the device, typically on the order of 0.5–2 µs on a direct-attached root port, more through switches or under IOMMU miss (impl).

📘 Spec

The PCIe Base Specification defines the Completion header fields (Completer ID, Completion Status, BCM, Byte Count, Requester ID, Tag, Lower Address) and the rules that a requester match completions by Requester ID + Tag (plus Function if Phantom Functions / extended tags are in use). The NVMe over PCIe Transport specification defines that the controller fetches SQEs from the SQ and posts CQEs; it does not mandate how many SQEs the controller reads per request.

Stage 12 — Flash operation

Analogy: the worker walks the warehouse aisles. Technical: the controller decodes opcode 02h, validates NSID, LBA range (else status 80h LBA Out of Range), and field values (else 02h Invalid Field). The FTL (Flash Translation Layer) maps the LBA to a physical NAND page; a NAND read (tR, tens of microseconds for TLC, less for SLC, impl) moves data into the die's page register, then onto the NAND channel into controller SRAM/DRAM, through LDPC/BCH ECC decode. If the LBA was never written (deallocated), the controller may return zeroes or a pattern per the DLFEAT reporting, without touching NAND. Hardware: NAND dies, channel controllers, ECC engine, internal buffer. Protocol: none on the PCIe link. Trace appearance: a silent gap on the PCIe link — no TLPs for this command. Other commands may be active in that gap.

Stage 13 — Data transfer (MWr to host buffer)

Analogy: the copy pushed through your letterbox, in several envelopes. Protocol: the controller issues MWr requests upstream to the PRP1 address. Each MWr payload is ≤ MPS (256 bytes here) and must not cross a 4 KiB address boundary. 4096 / 256 = 16 MWr TLPs, each 64 DW of payload, 4DW header (address above 4 GiB), Requester ID 0x0200, posted (no completion), consuming Posted credits. Hardware: IOMMU translates; RC writes into DRAM and invalidates/updates cache lines. Trace appearance: a burst of 16 upstream MWr packets to consecutive addresses 0x1_4000_0000, …_0100, …_0200 … _0F00.

N_MWr = ceil(transfer_bytes / MPS) (when start is MPS-aligned and no 4 KiB crossing)
  • transfer_bytes — data length of the command (NLB+1 × LBA size)
  • MPS — Max_Payload_Size programmed in Device Control (128–4096 bytes)
  • N_MWr — number of data-bearing write TLPs; unaligned starts add one partial TLP

Stage 14 — Completion entry (CQE write)

Analogy: the receipt in your inbox. Technical: the controller builds a 16-byte CQE: DW0 command-specific (0 for Read), DW1 reserved, DW2 = SQHD (new SQ head) bits 15:0 and SQID = 3 bits 31:16, DW3 = CID bits 15:0, Phase Tag bit 16, Status Field bits 31:17 (SC=00h, SCT=0 for success). It writes it to CQ3_base + cq_tail × 16. Protocol: one MWr, 4 DW payload, upstream, posted. Under default ordering (Relaxed Ordering attribute clear) a posted write may not pass an earlier posted write in the same direction, so the CQE cannot overtake the 16 data MWrs. Hardware: the controller's internal CQ tail and phase state advance; the phase it writes inverts every time the CQ wraps. Trace appearance: a 16-byte upstream MWr into the CQ region, immediately after the last data MWr.

🚀 Advanced

If the device sets Relaxed Ordering on data writes (allowed only if the host enabled it in Device Control), it must still ensure the CQE does not become visible before the data. Typical implementations send the CQE with RO clear, which forces it behind all earlier posted writes, or rely on a flush mechanism. Never assume — check the RO bit in the TLP Attr field in traces. A host bridge that mishandles RO is a classic source of "data corruption on fast completion" bugs (impl).

Stage 15 — MSI-X

Analogy: the buzzer. Technical: CQ3 was created with interrupt vector (IV) = 4 and IEN = 1 in the Create I/O CQ command. Unless coalescing defers it, the controller reads MSI-X table entry 4 (Message Address, Message Data, Vector Control) from its internal copy and, if the entry and the function are unmasked, sends the interrupt. Protocol: a MWr upstream, 1 DW payload = Message Data (0x45), to Message Address (0xFEE0_2000). On x86 that address range is decoded by the RC as an interrupt, not as DRAM (impl: platform interrupt architecture). Because it is a posted write behind the CQE write, the CQE is visible before the interrupt is delivered. Hardware: the interrupt controller (e.g. local APIC or interrupt remapping unit) raises the vector on the target CPU. Trace appearance: a 1 DW upstream MWr to a fixed, recurring address outside DRAM regions — recognisable because it repeats with the same address/data for every completion on that queue.

Stage 16 — Driver

Analogy: you read the receipt and tell the warehouse. Technical: the ISR (or a polling loop with io_uring IOPOLL) reads CQE at its own head index; it is new iff the Phase Tag equals the driver's expected phase. The driver issues a read barrier so the rest of the CQE is read after the phase bit, extracts CID to find the request, checks the status, updates SQ head from SQHD, advances its CQ head (flipping expected phase on wrap), and finally writes the CQ3 Head Doorbell at offset 1000h + (2×3+1) × 4 = 101Ch. Linux may process several CQEs before writing the head doorbell once. Protocol: the CQE read is a CPU memory read from DRAM — no PCIe. The head doorbell is a downstream MWr 1 DW, posted. Trace appearance: a downstream MWr to BAR0+0x101C some microseconds after the MSI-X message. Note the asymmetry: the SQ head never needs a doorbell — it comes back inside CQEs.

Stage 17 — Application completion

Analogy: you open the envelope and read page 7. Technical: blk_mq_complete_request → bio end → wake the waiting task / post an io_uring CQE (an io_uring CQE — not an NVMe CQE, another naming trap). The IOMMU mapping is torn down, and the pages unpinned. Protocol: none. Trace: blktrace C event; syscall return.

💡 Senior insight

Count the PCIe transactions for one 4 KiB read at MPS 256: 1 doorbell MWr + 1 MRd + 1 CplD + 16 data MWr + 1 CQE MWr + 1 MSI-X MWr + 1 CQ head doorbell MWr = 22 TLPs, plus Ack and UpdateFC DLLPs. Only 2 of them are downstream "control" writes; the protocol is deliberately device-driven. This is why NVMe scales: the host does a handful of uncached writes, everything else is device DMA into cacheable memory. Also note that with interrupt coalescing and doorbell batching, the per-command MSI-X and doorbells amortise away, approaching 1 MRd + 1 CplD + data + 1 CQE per command.

39.9 Sequence diagram: host vs device lanes

39.10 Timing budget

A representative latency budget for a 4 KiB random read on a modern TLC drive (all figures synthetic and impl; your platform will differ):

SegmentTypical order of magnitudeWhat dominates
Syscall + block layer + driver submit1–3 µsCPU path length, locking, IOMMU map
Doorbell MWr propagation< 0.5 µsRC and link latency
Doorbell → SQE fetch MRd0.2–2 µsController queue manager / firmware
MRd → CplD (SQE)0.5–2 µsDRAM latency, IOMMU walk on miss, switches
Command processing + FTL1–5 µsFirmware, L2P cache hit/miss
NAND tR + transfer + ECC30–100 µs (TLC), less for SLC/cache hitsMedia
Data MWr burst (4 KiB @ Gen4 x4)~0.6 µs on the wireLink bandwidth (~7.9 GB/s raw usable)
CQE + MSI-X< 0.5 µsOrdering, coalescing
Interrupt delivery + ISR + completion path1–5 µsInterrupt latency, context switch

The lesson: on the wire, a read is a tiny burst of control traffic, a long silence, and a data burst. If the silence is suspiciously long for a single command, the cause is almost always inside the device (media, firmware, garbage collection), not the link. If the gap between the doorbell and the fetch is long, suspect controller arbitration or a device stalled on something else. If the gap between the MSI-X and the head doorbell is long, suspect the host (interrupt affinity, CPU busy, softirq).

39.11 Variants that change the trace shape

VariantEffect on the TLP sequence
Transfer > 2 memory pages (e.g. 64 KiB, 4 KiB MPS page)PRP2 points to a PRP list: an extra MRd/CplD pair (or several) to fetch the list before data moves.
Transfer exactly 2 pagesPRP2 is a second data page pointer, no list fetch.
Buffer not page aligned (PRP1 offset ≠ 0)First data MWr is partial; total MWr count rises by one; PRP2 coverage changes.
SGL (Scatter Gather List) instead of PRPDescriptor fetches (MRd/CplD) for segments; data writes follow descriptors.
SQ in CMBStage 4 becomes a downstream MWr of 64 B (or write-combined bursts) into the CMB BAR; the SQE fetch MRd/CplD disappear from the link.
Interrupt coalescing (Feature 08h)One MSI-X per several CQEs; MSI-X may lag by up to the aggregation time.
Polling (io_uring IOPOLL, poll queues)No MSI-X MWr for that CQ (created with IEN=0); CQ head doorbells still occur.
Doorbell Buffer Config (shadow doorbells, used mainly with emulated controllers)Doorbell values written to host memory; MMIO doorbell only when the EventIdx says it is needed.
Larger MPS (e.g. 512 B)Fewer data MWr TLPs; better efficiency (header overhead amortised).
Address below 4 GiB3DW headers instead of 4DW.
HMB (Host Memory Buffer) in useExtra MRd/CplD (and MWr) traffic to the HMB region for L2P table segments, interleaved with the command.

39.12 Specification discipline

Applicable sources: NVMe Base Specification (queue model, SQE/CQE formats, status codes; baseline revision 2.4 in this book), NVM Command Set Specification (Read/Write semantics), NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (doorbells, register mapping, interrupts), PCIe Base Specification (TLP formats, ordering, completions, MSI-X). Confirm current revisions on nvmexpress.org and pcisig.com.

  • verified SQE is 64 bytes, CQE is 16 bytes (base sizes for NVMe over PCIe I/O queues); CQE DW3 holds CID, Phase Tag and Status; DW2 holds SQHD and SQID.
  • verified Doorbell offsets: SQ y Tail at 1000h + (2y)×(4 << CAP.DSTRD); CQ y Head at 1000h + (2y+1)×(4 << CAP.DSTRD).
  • verified MWr is posted, MRd is non-posted and answered by CplD; MSI-X is delivered as a memory write.
  • derived The CQE cannot become visible before the data under default ordering — derived from PCIe producer/consumer ordering rules for posted writes.
  • impl How many SQEs are fetched per MRd, fetch latency, use of Relaxed Ordering, interrupt address format.
  • version 10-bit tag support (PCIe 4.0+ optional), 14-bit tags in FLIT mode (PCIe 6.0), Gen6 FLIT framing change the low-level encoding but not the transaction sequence.
📭 What the spec does not say

The NVMe specification does not require the controller to process commands in submission order, to fetch SQEs one at a time, to post CQEs in command order, or to generate exactly one interrupt per CQE. Commands in the same SQ may complete out of order — that is why every CQE carries the CID. Anyone who builds a test that expects in-order completion is testing an implementation, not the protocol.

Reasoning: this trace cannot distinguish the hypotheses on its own — that is what makes it ambiguous. Disambiguate: check trace filter settings; look for an Asynchronous Event completion on the admin CQ; read CSTS (is CFS set?); check that the doorbell address actually maps to the intended queue (DSTRD!); replay the doorbell value.

39.14 Linux view

# Identify the device and its BAR0, MPS/MRRS, MSI-X
lspci -nn | grep -i "non-volatile"
sudo lspci -vvv -s 02:00.0 | grep -Ei "Region 0|MaxPayload|MaxReadReq|MSI-X|LnkSta"

# Queue / interrupt layout as seen by Linux
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/            # one dir per hardware queue
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/*/cpu_list
grep nvme /proc/interrupts            # one line per vector (admin+io queues)

# Per-command tracing (requires tracefs)
sudo sh -c 'echo 1 > /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/nvme_setup_cmd/enable'
sudo sh -c 'echo 1 > /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/nvme_complete_rq/enable'
sudo cat /sys/kernel/tracing/trace_pipe   # Ctrl-C to stop

# Issue exactly one 4 KiB O_DIRECT read to observe it end to end
sudo fio --name=one --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k \
     --direct=1 --ioengine=io_uring --iodepth=1 --number_ios=1 --readonly
⚠️ Safety

The commands above are read-only. --readonly makes fio refuse to write. Enabling tracepoints on a busy production system generates high volume; disable them afterwards (echo 0). Never point a write workload at a device holding data you care about.

What these outputs can prove: tracepoints prove the driver built a command with given CID/opcode and that a CQE with given status was consumed. What they cannot prove: which TLPs crossed the link, whether a doorbell was delivered, whether data landed before the CQE. Only a protocol analyzer (or device-internal logging) proves link-level events. This distinction — software evidence vs wire evidence — is the backbone of Chapter 47.

39.15 Code: a minimal submit/complete loop

// Submission (driver side) — pseudocode, single-producer queue
void submit_read(struct q *sq, u16 cid, u32 nsid, u64 slba, u16 nlb0, u64 prp1, u64 prp2) {
    struct sqe *e = &sq->ring[sq->tail];
    memset(e, 0, 64);
    e->cdw0  = 0x02 | (cid << 16);       // opcode Read, FUSE=0, PSDT=0 (PRP)
    e->nsid  = nsid;
    e->prp1  = prp1;  e->prp2 = prp2;     // bytes 24..39
    e->cdw10 = (u32)slba; e->cdw11 = (u32)(slba >> 32);
    e->cdw12 = nlb0;                      // zero-based block count
    sq->tail = (sq->tail + 1) % sq->size;
    wmb();                                // SQE globally visible BEFORE doorbell
    writel(sq->tail, sq->db);             // -> posted MWr on the link
}

// Completion (ISR side)
void cq_drain(struct q *cq, struct q *sq) {
    bool any = false;
    for (;;) {
        struct cqe *c = &cq->ring[cq->head];
        if (((c->dw3 >> 16) & 1) != cq->phase) break;  // not new yet
        rmb();                            // read rest of CQE after the phase bit
        u16 cid    = c->dw3 & 0xFFFF;
        u16 status = c->dw3 >> 17;        // SC[7:0] SCT[10:8] CRD[12:11] M[13] DNR[14]
        sq->head   = c->dw2 & 0xFFFF;      // SQHD
        complete(cid, status);
        if (++cq->head == cq->size) { cq->head = 0; cq->phase ^= 1; }
        any = true;
    }
    if (any) writel(cq->head, cq->db);   // CQ head doorbell -> posted MWr
}

39.16 Worked example: counting and addressing

Problem: CAP.DSTRD = 2, QID 5, 16 KiB read into a buffer at IOVA 0x8000_0800 (not page aligned), MPS = 128 B, memory page size (CC.MPS=0) 4 KiB. Compute: doorbell offsets, PRP entries, number of data MWr TLPs, header size.

Solution: stride = 4 << 2 = 16 bytes. SQ5 tail = 1000h + (2×5)×16 = 1000h + A0h = 10A0h; CQ5 head = 1000h + 11×16 = 10B0h. The buffer starts 0x800 into a page, so it spans 0x8000_0800 → 0x8000_47FF: pages 0x8000_0000 (2 KiB used), 0x8000_1000, 0x8000_2000, 0x8000_3000 and 0x8000_4000 (2 KiB used) = 5 pages. PRP1 = 0x8000_0800; more than 2 pages → PRP2 points to a PRP list containing 4 entries (0x8000_1000 … 0x8000_4000) → one extra MRd (32 bytes) + CplD. Data MWr count: 16384 / 128 = 128 TLPs; the start is 128-aligned (0x800) so no extra partial TLP. Addresses are below 4 GiB → 3DW headers. Total link TLPs ≈ 1 doorbell + 1 SQE MRd + 1 CplD + 1 PRP-list MRd + 1 CplD + 128 data MWr + 1 CQE + 1 MSI-X + 1 head doorbell = 136. Header+framing overhead per 128-byte TLP is significant — this is why MPS 128 costs bandwidth compared with 256 or 512.

39.17 Common mistakes

  • Believing the doorbell "contains" the command. It carries only a 16-bit index (in a 32-bit register).
  • Looking for the host's write of the SQE on the analyzer — it never crosses the link (unless the SQ is in the CMB).
  • Calling the CplD for the SQE fetch "the completion". It is a PCIe completion of a PCIe read; the NVMe completion is the CQE written later by an MWr.
  • Expecting a PCIe completion for the data write or for the doorbell. Both are posted.
  • Assuming in-order completion within a queue.
  • Forgetting the barrier between the SQE store and the doorbell (works on x86 by accident of strong ordering, fails on weakly ordered CPUs).
  • Reading the CQE fields before checking the phase bit, or without a read barrier after it.
  • Assuming one interrupt per command.
  • Computing doorbell offsets with stride 4 when CAP.DSTRD ≠ 0.
