39.19 Lab

🧪 Lab 39.1 — Observe one read end to end in software SAFE

Objective: correlate application, block, and NVMe driver events for a single read and identify the parts you cannot see without an analyzer.

Prerequisites: Linux with an NVMe drive, root, tracefs, fio, blktrace (optional).

Setup: enable nvme_setup_cmd and nvme_complete_rq tracepoints and block:block_rq_issue/block:block_rq_complete.

Procedure: (1) Start trace_pipe capture to a file. (2) Run the single-I/O fio read from §39.14. (3) Stop capture. (4) Find the issue, setup_cmd, complete_rq and rq_complete lines for your I/O. (5) Note qid and cid. (6) Look up which IRQ line in /proc/interrupts incremented.

Observations: timestamps of four software events; qid; cid; status 0; IRQ count change.

Questions: (a) Which of the 24 steps in §39.8 does each event correspond to? (b) What fraction of the measured latency lies between setup_cmd and complete_rq? (c) Which steps are invisible here?

Solution

(a) block_rq_issue ≈ step 2/3; nvme_setup_cmd ≈ step 4; nvme_complete_rq ≈ step 21–22; block_rq_complete ≈ step 24. (b) Typically the vast majority (often > 90%) — that interval contains the doorbell, fetch, media, data, CQE, interrupt. (c) Steps 7–20: all link traffic, controller-internal work and interrupt delivery are not individually visible; you see only their aggregate latency.

Extension: repeat with --hipri (polling) on a kernel with poll queues configured (nvme.poll_queues=N) and confirm that no IRQ counter increments.

🧪 Lab 39.2 — Decode a synthetic read trace SAFE

Objective: reconstruct the NVMe command from raw TLP fields.

Setup: given (synthetic) the CplD payload for tag 0x11, first 48 bytes in little-endian DWORDs: 00420002 00000001 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000 40000000 00000001 00000000 00000000 00001000 00000000.

Procedure: decode CDW0, NSID, PRP1, PRP2, CDW10–11.

Solution

CDW0 = 0x00420002 → opcode 02h (Read), FUSE 0, PSDT 0, CID = 0x0042. NSID = 1. CDW2–3 = 0, MPTR (bytes 16–23) = 0. PRP1 (bytes 24–31) = low DW 0x40000000, high DW 0x00000001 → 0x1_4000_0000. PRP2 (bytes 32–39) = 0. CDW10 = 0x00001000, CDW11 = 0 → SLBA = 0x1000 (4096). CDW12 (not shown) would hold NLB. Data MWrs should target 0x1_4000_0000 — check that they do.

Extension: write a 30-line Python script that decodes any 64-byte SQE hex dump.

39.20 Exercise

🎯 Exercise

For a 128 KiB read at MPS 512, page size 4 KiB, page-aligned IOVA above 4 GiB, MRRS irrelevant: (1) how many PRP list entries? (2) how many data MWr TLPs? (3) how many TLPs total, assuming one MSI-X and one CQ head doorbell? (4) If coalescing aggregates 8 completions per interrupt, what is the amortised MSI-X count per command?

Answer

(1) 32 pages; PRP1 covers page 0, PRP2 → list of 31 entries (248 bytes, fetched by one MRd if within one page). (2) 131072/512 = 256 MWr. (3) 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 1 + 256 + 1 + 1 + 1 = 264 (doorbell, SQE MRd, CplD, list MRd, list CplD — possibly split into 2 at RCB 128/64 — data, CQE, MSI-X, head doorbell). (4) 1/8.

Quiz

  1. Which TLP carries the 64-byte SQE across the link for a host-memory SQ?

    Answer

    A CplD (Completion with Data) sent by the root complex in response to the controller's MRd.

  2. Is the data delivery of an NVMe Read posted or non-posted?

    Answer

    Posted — MWr from device to host; no PCIe completion is returned.

  3. Why doesn't the host need to write an SQ head doorbell?

    Answer

    Only the controller consumes SQ entries; it reports its SQ head in the SQHD field of each CQE. There is no SQ head doorbell register.

  4. What guarantees the CQE is not visible before the data?

    Answer

    PCIe ordering: posted writes from the same requester (without RO) cannot pass earlier posted writes; the controller issues data writes before the CQE write.

  5. Compute the CQ 2 head doorbell offset with DSTRD = 0.

    Answer

    1000h + (2×2+1)×4 = 1014h.

  6. How does the driver know a CQE slot holds a new entry?

    Answer

    Its Phase Tag matches the driver's current expected phase, which flips each time the head wraps.

  7. On the analyzer you see a 1 DW upstream MWr to 0xFEE0_xxxx. What is it?

    Answer

    On x86 platforms, an MSI/MSI-X interrupt message (impl: address window is platform-defined).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Walk me through what happens when Linux issues a 4 KiB read to an NVMe SSD.
    Model answer

    Block layer builds a request; driver writes a 64 B SQE into the SQ in host memory and rings the SQ tail doorbell (MMIO MWr). Controller fetches the SQE (MRd/CplD), reads NAND, DMA-writes the data to the PRP buffer (MWr), writes a 16 B CQE to the CQ (MWr), sends MSI-X (MWr). Driver checks phase, completes the request, writes CQ head doorbell.

  2. Beginner What is a doorbell?
    Model answer

    A controller register in BAR0 (from 1000h) holding the SQ tail or CQ head index; writing it informs the controller of new submissions or freed completion slots.

  3. Intermediate Why does NVMe use device-side DMA fetch rather than MMIO pushes of commands?
    Model answer

    MMIO writes are uncached and slow for the CPU; DMA reads from cacheable memory let the CPU write commands at memory speed, batch submissions, and touch MMIO only once per batch. CMB is the exception that trades this for reduced latency.

  4. Intermediate How many TLPs does a 4 KiB read generate at MPS 256?
    Model answer

    About 22: doorbell MWr, MRd, CplD, 16 data MWr, CQE MWr, MSI-X MWr, head doorbell MWr — minus amortisation from batching/coalescing.

  5. Advanced What happens if the device uses Relaxed Ordering for the CQE write?
    Model answer

    The CQE could pass data writes, so the host could see the completion and read stale buffer contents. Devices must keep RO clear on the CQE (or otherwise guarantee ordering); RO is only usable if enabled in Device Control.

  6. Advanced A trace shows the doorbell and nothing else for 30 s. List hypotheses.
    Model answer

    Invalid doorbell value (async event), queue not created, controller hung/fatal (CSTS.CFS), doorbell to wrong offset (DSTRD), Memory Space disabled, capture filter/placement. Disambiguate with CSTS, admin CQ, trace config.

  7. Senior How would you prove whether a data corruption came from the SSD or the host?
    Model answer

    Capture the data MWr payload on the link and compare with the buffer contents and the known-good data; use end-to-end PI (protection information) if formatted; check IOMMU mapping lifetimes (use-after-unmap) and RO handling; check EP bits; reproduce with IOMMU strict mode.

  8. Senior Explain the tail-latency signature of a media stall vs a host interrupt stall.
    Model answer

    Media stall: long gap between CplD (SQE) and first data MWr; data/CQE/MSI-X then normal. Host stall: data, CQE, MSI-X on time, but long gap before head doorbell and software completion.

📌 Teach-back

To a child: "I put my wish in a tray, ring a bell, the warehouse takes my wish, puts the answer on my table, leaves a receipt, and buzzes me." To a junior engineer: describe the 24-step table, naming posted vs non-posted. To a senior engineer: explain ordering guarantees, amortisation (batching, coalescing), where latency is spent, and which steps are wire-visible.

39.21 Summary

An NVMe Read is a choreography of software steps (invisible to the link), a few host-initiated posted writes (doorbells), one device-initiated non-posted read per SQE batch (with CplD replies), a media gap, a posted data burst, a posted CQE write and a posted MSI-X write. The NVMe completion (CQE) and the PCIe completion (CplD) are completely different things. Every debugging question starts with: which step is the first that deviates?

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can recite the 17 stages and the 24-step table from memory.
  • I can draw the sequence diagram with correct directions and posted/non-posted labels.
  • I can compute doorbell offsets for any QID and DSTRD.
  • I can count TLPs for any transfer size, MPS, alignment.
  • I can identify, in a synthetic trace, the SQE fetch, data, CQE, MSI-X and doorbells.
  • I can name the first abnormal event in the slow, failed and ambiguous traces and say what evidence I'd collect next.
  • I can cite which specification defines each element (NVMe Base, NVM CS, PCIe transport, PCIe Base).

Further reading: NVMe Base Specification (queues, CQE, status); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification (doorbells, interrupts); PCIe Base Specification (transaction ordering, completions, MSI-X); Linux drivers/nvme/host/pci.c (nvme_queue_rq, nvme_irq, nvme_process_cq).

Next: Chapter 40 runs the same journey for a Write — where the data direction flips and the device becomes a heavy reader of host memory.

40 End-to-End NVMe Write

← 39 The Most Important Chapter: An End-to-End NVMe Read41 Command-to-TLP Correlation →

40.1 Why this chapter exists

A Write looks like a Read with the arrows flipped, and that intuition is half right and half dangerous. The control path (SQE, doorbell, fetch, CQE, MSI-X, head doorbell) is identical. The data path is not: for a Write the device must pull the data from host memory with non-posted MRd requests, each of which needs tags, Non-Posted credits, CplD responses and completion-timeout supervision. Writes therefore exercise the host's memory-read path far harder than reads do, they expose MRRS and RCB behaviour, and they bring in the volatile write cache, FUA (Force Unit Access) and Flush semantics — the source of most "I lost data after power loss" investigations.

40.2 Learning objectives

  • List the stages of a 4 KiB NVMe Write (opcode 01h) and mark which cross the link and in which direction.
  • Compute the number of MRd requests and CplD completions for a given size, MRRS and RCB.
  • Explain when the controller is allowed to post the CQE (before NAND program, with volatile write cache) and how FUA/Flush change that.
  • Recognise in a synthetic trace the data-fetch phase, tag usage and completion splitting.
  • Diagnose write-specific failures: completion timeout on data fetch, poisoned data, IOMMU read fault, write fault status, power-loss data loss.

40.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 39 (end-to-end read) — this chapter only details the differences; PCIe completions, tags and flow control from the PCIe part of the book.

40.4 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

This time you want the warehouse to store your drawing. You put the request card in the tray and ring the bell, just like before. But the worker can't take your drawing through the bell either: they must reach into your house again and ask "please hand me pieces 1, 2, 3 and 4 of the drawing", and you (your house's front door, the root complex) hand each piece back. When the worker has all the pieces safely in the warehouse's front desk tray (write cache), they can already give you a receipt — even if they haven't walked to the shelf yet.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The "front desk tray" (volatile write cache) loses its contents if power fails unless the drive has power-loss protection capacitors; the receipt (CQE) does not promise the drawing is on the shelf (NAND) unless you asked with FUA or later sent a Flush. Also, the worker's requests for pieces are numbered with tags, can be outstanding concurrently and can be answered out of order across different tags.

40.5 The differences at a glance

AspectRead (02h)Write (01h)
Data direction on the linkDevice → host, posted MWrHost → device, CplD in response to device MRd
Who initiates data movementDevice (writes)Device (reads)
Limits on TLP sizeMPS per MWrMRRS per MRd; completions limited by MPS (completer's) and split at RCB
Outstanding resourcePosted credits onlyTags + NP credits on device; completion buffer space; completion timeout
Media timing vs CQECQE after data has been read from mediaCQE may be posted once data is in controller buffer (VWC), before program
Typical error statusesUnrecovered Read Error (SCT 2h / SC 81h)Write Fault (SCT 2h / SC 80h), Namespace Write Protected (generic 20h), capacity exceeded
PCIe failure exposureUpstream posted pathHost memory read path (CTO, poisoned CplD, UR from IOMMU)

40.5a Who writes what: the block diagram

Here is the Write on the same three-place picture as the Read in Figure 39.0: software (the driver on the host CPU), host memory (RAM, which never starts anything) and the device (the SSD, across the PCIe link). The control steps are the same; the difference is step 4: the device must pull the data out of the host buffer by sending read requests (MRd), and the host's root complex answers with completions carrying the data (CplD). Click a step number, an arrow, or a list item to follow the command. The example writes 4 KiB (8 × 512-byte blocks) to LBA 0x1000 from a buffer at 0x1_2345_6000, using I/O queue 1, slot 3 (the master table below uses queue 3; only the doorbell offsets change). synthetic

Software starts itDevice starts itHost answers a device read (CplD)Inside the SSD (not visible on PCIe)PCIe link
  1. Software writes the 64-byte Write command into the Submission Queue

    The data to be written is already sitting in a host buffer. The driver fills slot 3 of Submission Queue 1 with a command that says where that buffer is and where on the namespace the data should go.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 3 (address = SQ base + 3 × 64)PCIe: No. This is the CPU writing its own RAM.
    Opcode = 01h (Write) CID = 0x002B NSID = 1 SLBA = 0x1000 NLB = 7 (means 8 blocks = 4 KiB) PRP1 = 0x1_2345_6000 (where the data comes FROM) FUA = 0
  2. Software rings the SQ tail doorbell

    The driver writes the new tail index into the SSD's SQ1 tail doorbell register: "there is new work, up to (not including) slot 4". Identical to the Read.

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x1008PCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 4 Neither the command nor the data has crossed PCIe yet.
  3. Device fetches the command from host memory

    The controller sees the tail move from 3 to 4 and reads slot 3: it sends a read request and the root complex answers with the 64 bytes.

    Where: Host memory, SQ1 slot 3PCIe: Yes, both ways. · MRd (device → host), then CplD with 64 bytes (host → device)
    The device now knows: "write 8 blocks at LBA 0x1000, take the data from 0x1_2345_6000, call it CID 0x002B"
  4. Device reads the 4 KiB of data from the host buffer

    This is the step that makes a Write different. The data must travel host → device, but the host never pushes it: the device's DMA engine sends read requests (MRd) for the buffer at PRP1, and the host's root complex answers each one with completions carrying the data (CplD). Each MRd is limited by Max_Read_Request_Size and holds a tag until all its CplDs have arrived.

    Where: Host memory, data buffer at 0x1_2345_6000PCIe: Yes, both ways. · MRd (device → host, no data) then CplD with the data (host → device)
    MRRS = 512 B → 8 MRd requests, tags 0x12–0x19 MPS = 256 B → 16 CplD × 256 B (two per request) The bytes in RAM are only read; the buffer is unchanged.
  5. Data lands in the controller's write cache

    The controller reassembles the 4 KiB in its buffer (the write cache, usually DRAM inside the SSD) and checks protection information if the namespace uses it. The NAND has not been touched yet.

    Where: Inside the SSDPCIe: No. Nothing appears on the PCIe link during this step.
    Volatile write cache present and enabled (VWC = 1, WCE = 1), FUA = 0 → the controller may complete the command now.
  6. Device writes the 16-byte completion entry

    The controller writes a completion entry into CQ1 slot 3. With a volatile write cache enabled and FUA = 0, this completion may be posted before the data is programmed into NAND: success means "accepted", not "durable". With FUA = 1, or with no volatile write cache, the controller posts it only after step 10 has finished for this data.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 3 (address = CQ base + 3 × 16)PCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 16 bytes
    CID = 0x002B Status = 0 (success) Phase tag = 1 SQID = 1 SQHD = 4
  7. Device sends the MSI-X interrupt

    The controller writes the interrupt message from its MSI-X table entry; the CPU runs the driver's handler. PCIe ordering keeps this write behind the completion entry.

    Where: Interrupt address/data taken from the device's MSI-X tablePCIe: Yes, device → host. · MWr, 4 bytes, to the MSI-X address
    Same mechanism as for a Read: an interrupt is just a memory write.
  8. Software reads the completion entry

    The handler checks the phase tag, matches CID 0x002B to the Write it sent, sees status 0 and completes the request; the application's write call returns.

    Where: Host memory, CQ1 slot 3PCIe: No. The CPU reads its own RAM.
    Phase = 1 as expected → new entry CID 0x002B → our Write; status 0 → success The buffer may now be reused by the application.
  9. Software rings the CQ head doorbell

    The driver writes the new head index into the CQ1 head doorbell so the device may reuse the consumed completion slots.

    Where: Device register at BAR0 + 0x100CPCIe: Yes, host → device. · MWr, 4 bytes (posted)
    Value written: 4
  10. Later: the cached data is programmed into NAND

    In the background the FTL picks a fresh NAND page, programs the data and updates its logical-to-physical map. Programming takes hundreds of microseconds to milliseconds and is invisible on PCIe. Until it finishes, a power loss on a drive without power-loss protection can lose this data, even though the host already saw success. A Flush command (or FUA on the Write) is how software asks for durability.

    Where: Inside the SSD (write cache → NAND)PCIe: No.
    Order with volatile write cache: 5 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 9 … 10 Order with FUA = 1 or no cache: 5 → 10 → 6 → 7 → 8 → 9

As for the Read, software writes only three things: the command (step 1) and the two doorbells (steps 2 and 9). The data does travel host → device, but the device fetches it: every data byte arrives in a CplD answering one of the device's own MRd requests.

N_MRd = ceil(bytes / MRRS) ; N_CplD ≥ Σ ceil(request_bytes / min(MPS_completer, ...)), split at RCB boundaries
  • MRRS — Max_Read_Request_Size in the requester's Device Control (128–4096 B)
  • MPS_completer — the completer cannot send a CplD payload larger than the link's MPS
  • RCB — Read Completion Boundary (64 or 128 B); a completer splitting a read must split at RCB-aligned addresses
🔧 Hardware

The number of tags a controller can keep outstanding, multiplied by MRRS, bounds the bytes in flight on the read path. With 8-bit tags (256) and MRRS 512 that's 128 KiB in flight — enough for Gen4 x4 at ~1–2 µs round trip. Gen5/Gen6 links and longer latencies (switches, retimers) push designs toward 10-bit tags (1024) — version: 10-bit tag requester/completer support is optional from PCIe 4.0 and must be enabled in Device Control 2. Write bandwidth that tops out well below link rate, with a trace showing the device stalls waiting for tags, is a classic signature.

40.7 Sequence diagram

40.8 Stage notes — the five views for the write-specific stages

Data fetch (MRd) — device → host

Analogy: "please pass me piece 3 of the drawing". Technical: the controller walks PRP1/PRP2 (or the PRP list it fetched) and issues reads no larger than MRRS that do not cross 4 KiB boundaries. Hardware: each request occupies a tag and reserves completion buffer space at the device (a requester must not issue a non-posted request unless it can accept all completions — completion credits are typically advertised as infinite by endpoints, so the requester self-limits). Protocol: MRd, 4DW header if above 4 GiB, Length in DW, First/Last BE all ones for aligned transfers. Trace: a train of upstream MRds with incrementing addresses and distinct tags.

Data delivery (CplD) — host → device

Analogy: pieces handed through the door. Technical: the completer returns one or more CplDs per request; Byte Count indicates remaining bytes including this completion; Lower Address gives the starting byte address low bits. Hardware: completions for the same request arrive in address order; completions for different tags may interleave. Protocol: CplD with Status SC; EP=1 marks poisoned data. Trace: pairs (or groups) of CplD with the same tag and decreasing Byte Count: 512, 256 for a 512-byte request split into two 256-byte completions.

Completion point

Technical: If the Volatile Write Cache is present and enabled (Feature 06h) and FUA=0, the controller may post the CQE as soon as the data is in its buffer. With FUA=1 (CDW12 bit 30) it must not complete until data is in non-volatile media. Drives with power-loss protection may report VWC not present because their buffer is effectively non-volatile (impl). Trace: the gap between the last CplD and the CQE MWr is short (µs) for cached writes and long (hundreds of µs or more) for FUA writes.

Reasoning: upstream and downstream are independent directions: ordering rules do not relate an upstream MWr to downstream CplDs. Is it a bug? Ambiguity resolved by mapping tags → command (requires device-internal logs or careful address correlation to PRPs). Also check the analyzer timestamp alignment between the two directions (probe skew).

40.10 Flush, FUA and durability

Host intentNVMe mechanismLinux mechanismWhen CQE means "durable"
Ordinary writeWrite, FUA=0REQ_OP_WRITEOnly if VWC absent or disabled
Durable single writeWrite, FUA=1REQ_FUA (if device advertises FUA support — Linux checks VWC/ONCS)Yes, for that write
Barrier for prior writesFlush (00h)REQ_PREFLUSH / fsyncYes, for all writes completed before the Flush was submitted
Disable cacheSet Features 06h WCE=0nvme set-feature -f 6 -v 0 (changes device state — caution)Every write
💡 Senior insight

On the PCIe link, a FUA write and a normal write look identical except for one bit inside the SQE payload of the CplD and the timing gap before the CQE. If you're investigating data loss after power failure, decode the SQE CDW12 bit 30 in captured CplDs and check whether Flush commands (opcode 00h on an I/O queue) were present before the power event. The absence of Flushes (in a complete capture) is strong evidence of a host/filesystem durability problem rather than an SSD bug.

40.11 Common mistakes

  • Expecting MWr from host to device for write data. The host never pushes I/O data (except into a CMB/PMR when used as a data buffer).
  • Treating each CplD as one request — multiple completions per request are normal.
  • Misreading Byte Count as "bytes in this TLP" — it is bytes remaining, including this one.
  • Assuming the CQE means data is on NAND.
  • Mapping the buffer DMA_FROM_DEVICE for a write (IOMMU permission fault).
  • Unmapping/reusing the buffer before the CQE (use-after-free DMA: device reads changed data).

40.12 Lab

🧪 Lab 40.1 — Count TLPs for writes of varying size SAFE

Objective: build intuition for MRRS/RCB effects without hardware. Setup: paper or a Python REPL. Procedure: for transfer sizes 512 B, 4 KiB, 16 KiB, 128 KiB and MRRS ∈ {128, 512, 4096}, completer max payload 256, RCB 64, compute MRd and minimum CplD counts. Observations: fill a table. Questions: which parameter dominates request count? which dominates completion count?

import math
def counts(size, mrrs, cpl_max=256):
    n_mrd = math.ceil(size / mrrs)
    n_cpl = sum(math.ceil(min(mrrs, size - i*mrrs) / cpl_max) for i in range(n_mrd))
    return n_mrd, n_cpl
for size in (512, 4096, 16384, 131072):
    for mrrs in (128, 512, 4096):
        print(size, mrrs, counts(size, mrrs))
Solution

MRRS dominates request count (e.g. 128 KiB: 1024 / 256 / 32 requests). The completer's max payload dominates completion count (128 KiB: 512 completions at 256 B regardless of MRRS ≥ 256; at MRRS 128 it's 1024 completions). Larger MRRS reduces tag and NP credit pressure, at the cost of potentially larger latency for other devices (fairness).

Extension: add RCB-split modelling for an unaligned start address (e.g. 0x...0020).

🧪 Lab 40.2 — Observe write cache and FUA in software CAUTION

Objective: observe latency difference between cached writes and FUA/flush writes. Setup: a scratch NVMe namespace with no valuable data. Procedure: nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i vwc; nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 6; run fio 4 KiB randwrite QD1 with and without --fsync=1; compare clat. Observations: latency with fsync significantly higher on drives without PLP. Questions: why can a drive with PLP show almost no difference?

⚠️ Safety

Write workloads destroy data on the target. Use only a dedicated test device or namespace. Do not change Feature 06h on a production system.

Solution

With PLP, the controller can treat its buffer as non-volatile and complete Flush/FUA quickly (or reports VWC not present). Without PLP, Flush forces NAND programming of cached data, adding hundreds of µs to ms.

Quiz

  1. Which TLP type carries write data across the link for an NVMe Write with host-memory buffers?

    Answer

    CplD (host → device), answering the controller's MRd requests.

  2. A 2 KiB MRd is answered by CplDs with Byte Count 2048, 1792, 1536… what is the payload of each?

    Answer

    256 bytes each (difference between successive Byte Counts).

  3. Which SQE bit requests FUA on a Write?

    Answer

    CDW12 bit 30.

  4. What PCIe error does the controller log if the host never answers a data MRd?

    Answer

    Completion Timeout (uncorrectable, default non-fatal) in its AER Uncorrectable Error Status.

  5. What does MRRS limit?

    Answer

    The maximum size of a single memory read request issued by that function.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner How does write data get from host to SSD?
    Model answer

    The SSD reads it: MRd requests to the PRP addresses, the root complex answers with CplD packets carrying the data.

  2. Intermediate Why might writes be slower than reads at the same queue depth on a deep PCIe topology?
    Model answer

    Non-posted reads need round trips; with limited tags/MRRS the device can't cover the bandwidth-delay product. Reads use posted writes, which stream without waiting.

  3. Advanced Explain how a write CQE can be correct while the data is lost after a power cut.
    Model answer

    VWC enabled, FUA=0, no Flush: CQE posted when data reached volatile buffer. Durability requires Flush or FUA, or PLP hardware.

  4. Senior You see a poisoned CplD on a write data fetch. Who is at fault and what do you capture next?
    Model answer

    Data was poisoned at or before the completer — host memory (uncorrectable ECC) or RC internal error. Capture machine-check/EDAC logs, root port AER, physical address; the SSD should fail the command (not write poisoned data) — check its status code.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can draw the write sequence and point out every non-posted request.
  • I can compute MRd/CplD counts from MRRS, MPS and RCB.
  • I can decode Byte Count and Lower Address in a completion series.
  • I can explain VWC, FUA and Flush and their effect on the CQE timing.
  • I can diagnose IOMMU-denied data fetch and tag starvation from traces.

Summary: writes share the control path with reads but invert the data path into device-initiated non-posted reads, making them sensitive to tags, MRRS, round-trip latency and host memory errors; the CQE timing depends on cache policy. Next: Chapter 41 — systematic correlation of NVMe commands with TLPs.

41 Command-to-TLP Correlation

← 40 End-to-End NVMe Write42 Interrupt Architecture: INTx, MSI and MSI-X →

41.1 Why this chapter exists

A protocol analyzer capture of a busy SSD contains millions of TLPs from dozens of queues and hundreds of in-flight commands. Nothing in a TLP header says "this belongs to NVMe command CID 0x0042 on queue 3". Correlation is an act of reasoning: you link a doorbell to a queue by address, a queue slot to an SQE fetch by address, an SQE to its data by PRP addresses, data to a CQE by CID and queue, and a CQE to an interrupt by vector. This chapter teaches that reasoning formally, and introduces the investigative rules — complete event model, timeline reconstruction, first-abnormal-event, negative evidence — used in every forensic lab of the remaining parts.

41.2 Learning objectives

  • Distinguish crisply: NVMe command, PCIe TLP, NVMe CQE, PCIe Completion TLP.
  • Build an address map (BAR0 doorbells, SQ/CQ rings, PRP lists, data buffers, MSI-X addresses) from initialization traffic.
  • Correlate each NVMe event to TLP type, direction, requester/completer, address region and tag.
  • Represent events using the complete event model and reconstruct expected vs observed timelines.
  • Apply the first-abnormal-event and negative-evidence rules.

41.3 The four things that are NOT interchangeable

📌 Remember

"Completion" means two unrelated things in this stack. A PCIe Completion (Cpl/CplD) answers a PCIe non-posted request within microseconds and lives only on the link. An NVMe Completion Queue Entry answers an NVMe command, may take milliseconds, and is carried to host memory inside a PCIe Memory Write — never inside a PCIe Completion.

NVMe CommandPCIe TLPNVMe CQEPCIe Completion TLP
LayerNVMe (command set / queue)PCIe transaction layerNVMe (queue)PCIe transaction layer
Size/format64-byte SQE3/4 DW header (+ prefixes) + 0–1024 DW payload (+ ECRC)16-byte entry3 DW header + optional data
IdentifierCID (16 bit) + SQIDRequester ID + Tag (for non-posted)CID + SQID (DW2/DW3)Requester ID + Tag of the request it answers; Completer ID
Lives inHost memory SQ (or CMB)On the wireHost memory CQOn the wire
Transported byCplD (answering the device's MRd), or MWr into CMB—MWr (device → host)—
Status—— (requests have none)SCT/SC, DNR, More, CRDSC, UR, CRS, CA
Time scaleµs to seconds lifetimens on wirewritten onceµs after request
Failure detectionDriver timeout (e.g. 30 s)LCRC/ECRC, Malformed, etc.Status ≠ 0Completion Timeout (50 µs–50 ms default range), status ≠ SC

41.4 The correlation chain

NVMe command (SQID, CID)
   ↕  queue location        SQ base + slot×64  (from Create I/O SQ PRP1 + slot index)
   ↕  controller access     MRd by device (ReqID = device BDF) to that address
   ↕  PCIe requester/completer  requester = device, completer = RC
   ↕  tag                   Tag in MRd = Tag in CplD (+ ReqID)
   ↕  data addresses        PRP1/PRP2/PRP list from the SQE payload → MWr (read) / MRd (write)
   ↕  completion            CQE MWr to CQ base + slot×16, payload CID + SQID
   ↕  interrupt             CQ's IV → MSI-X table entry → MWr to Message Address

Each link of the chain is learned from earlier traffic. You cannot correlate a mid-run capture unless you can reconstruct the setup: BAR0 address (from config space or lspci), CAP.DSTRD (from a CAP register read or the driver), queue base addresses (from Create I/O SQ/CQ admin commands — their PRP1 field), and MSI-X table contents (from host MMIO writes to the table, or by reading the BAR region).

Analyzer rows, kernel log lines, tracepoints and NVMe log entries all have different shapes. To reason across them, normalise every observation into one record type:

CONFIDENCEHigh/medium/low + whyHigh: address = SQ3 slot 0x42
🐞 Debugging

The EXPECTED_NEXT / ACTUAL_NEXT pair is the engine of diagnosis: every event creates an expectation, and the first event whose ACTUAL_NEXT differs from EXPECTED_NEXT is your first deviation. CONFIDENCE forces honesty — a correlation by address alone is weaker than by address + CID + timing.

41.7 Timeline reconstruction

Build every investigation as two aligned columns:

PhaseExpected timeline (normal read)Observed timeline (example incident)
T0 system stateCSTS.RDY=1, link L0 Gen4 x4, queues created, MSI-X enabledSame, but LnkSta shows Gen4 x2 (degraded width)
T1 first eventApp submits I/OSame
T2 requestSQE written, doorbell MWrDoorbell visible
T3 transportMRd/CplD for SQE within ~2 µsMRd visible; CplD after 1 replay (Nak seen)
T4 device actionMedia read 60–100 µs95 µs
T5 responseData MWr ×16Data MWr ×16, 3 replays
T6 completionCQE MWr, status 0CQE status 0
T7 software notificationMSI-X, ISR, head doorbellSame; total latency +4 µs

The comparison shows the NVMe layer is healthy; the link is not (degraded width, replays). The user-visible symptom ("slightly slow I/O") is far from the cause ("lane fault → width downgrade + bit errors").

🔍 Clock domains

Kernel timestamps, analyzer timestamps and device-internal logs run on different clocks. Align them with an anchor event visible in two domains (e.g. a doorbell MWr that also appears as an MMIO write in a hypervisor trace, or a distinctive admin command). Never compare raw timestamps across domains without an anchor and an error bar.

41.8 The first-abnormal-event rule

The first visible failure is not necessarily the root cause. Work backward: SYMPTOM → FIRST DEVIATION → PRECEDING CAUSE.

SYMPTOM          : "nvme0: I/O 66 QID 3 timeout" at t = 30 s (illustrative)
      ↑ backward
FIRST DEVIATION  : SQE fetch MRd (t = 0.7 µs) has no visible CplD
      ↑ backward
PRECEDING CAUSE? : at t = −2 s the IOMMU domain was switched (VFIO rebind),
                   SQ3 IOVA no longer mapped  → RC returns UR / drops request

The timeout is a symptom 30 seconds later; the first deviation is 0.7 µs after the doorbell; the cause predates the command entirely. An engineer who stops at the timeout will "fix" it by raising io_timeout.

41.9 The negative-evidence rule

Absence of an event is evidence only if (1) the event was expected and (2) the capture was complete enough to observe it. Never write "the device did not send the CQE". Write "no MWr to the CQ3 region is visible in the captured interval", then qualify with coverage: was the analyzer on the right link segment? Was the buffer full or filtered? Were both directions captured? Was the trigger window long enough? Was the CQ actually in host memory?

ClaimAcceptable only if…
"No doorbell was rung"Downstream direction captured, no filter on MWr, BAR0 address known, capture began before submission
"The device never fetched the command"Upstream MRd captured unfiltered for the whole interval, SQ base known, CMB not used for SQ
"No interrupt was sent"Upstream MWr to MSI address range captured, vector address known, no interrupt remapping change
"No error occurred"AER enabled and unmasked for that error, reporting enabled up to the root port, logs read before being cleared

41.10 Correlation worked example

Given (synthetic) these three upstream packets in a mixed trace with SQ1 base 0x1_0000_0000, SQ2 base 0x1_0001_0000, CQ1 base 0x1_0010_0000, CQ2 base 0x1_0011_0000 (1024-entry queues):

A: MRd  addr 0x1_0001_0FC0  len 32 DW tag 0x05
B: MWr  addr 0x1_0011_00A0  len 4 DW  payload DW2=0x0002_0040 DW3=0x0001_7A3F
C: MWr  addr 0xFEE0_1000    len 1 DW  payload 0x0000_0042

A: address − SQ2 base = 0xFC0 = slot 63; length 32 DW = 128 bytes → fetching SQ2 slots 63 and 64 (two SQEs in one request). B: address − CQ2 base = 0xA0 → CQ2 slot 10. DW2 = 0x0002_0040 → SQID 2, SQHD 0x40 (64); DW3 = 0x0001_7A3F → CID 0x7A3F, bit 16 Phase = 1, status bits 31:17 = 0 → success. The SQHD of 64 is consistent with slot 63 having been consumed. C: an MSI-X write; to know which CQ it signals, consult the MSI-X table: if entry 2 has address 0xFEE0_1000 and data 0x42, it's vector 2, which CQ2 was created with. Note that several vectors may share an address and differ only in data.

41.11 Common mistakes

  • Matching completions to requests by tag only (ignoring Requester ID) on topologies with several requesters.
  • Assuming one SQE per fetch MRd.
  • Correlating CQEs to commands by order instead of CID.
  • Comparing timestamps across clock domains without anchors.
  • Declaring absence without coverage.
  • Assuming tags are unique for all time — they are reused as soon as the request completes.

41.12 Lab

🧪 Lab 41.1 — Build the address map from initialization traffic SAFE

Objective: from a (synthetic) initialization trace, derive all addresses needed for correlation. Setup: given these downstream MWrs to BAR0 (base 0xF7A0_0000) and admin commands:

MWr F7A0_0024 = 0x001F_001F      (AQA)
MWr F7A0_0028 = 0x2_0000_0000    (ASQ, 2 DW)
MWr F7A0_0030 = 0x2_0001_0000    (ACQ, 2 DW)
MWr F7A0_0014 = 0x0046_0001      (CC)
Admin SQE: opcode 05h, PRP1 0x2_0100_0000, CDW10 0x03FF_0001, CDW11 0x0001_0003
Admin SQE: opcode 01h, PRP1 0x2_0200_0000, CDW10 0x03FF_0001, CDW11 0x0001_0001

Procedure: decode admin queue sizes, admin queue bases, CC fields, I/O CQ1 and SQ1 parameters (size, base, vector, contiguity, associated CQ).

Solution

AQA: ASQS = 0x1F → 32 entries, ACQS = 0x1F → 32 entries. ASQ base 0x2_0000_0000, ACQ base 0x2_0001_0000. CC = 0x0046_0001: EN=1, CSS (bits 6:4)=0 (NVM), MPS (10:7)=0 → 4 KiB pages, AMS=0, SHN=0, IOSQES (19:16)=6 → 64 B, IOCQES (23:20)=4 → 16 B. Create I/O CQ (05h): CDW10 QID=1, QSIZE=0x3FF → 1024 entries; CDW11 PC=1 (contiguous), IEN=1 (bit 1), IV (31:16)=1; base 0x2_0100_0000. Create I/O SQ (01h): QID 1, 1024 entries, CDW11 PC=1, QPRIO=0, CQID (31:16)=1; base 0x2_0200_0000. Doorbells: SQ1 tail 1008h, CQ1 head 100Ch (DSTRD 0 assumed — read CAP to confirm).

Extension: add MSI-X table programming MWrs and derive vector→address/data.

🧪 Lab 41.2 — Fill the event model for a failing command SAFE

Objective: practise EXPECTED_NEXT/ACTUAL_NEXT. Setup: use the "failed read: completion timeout on SQE fetch" trace in §39.13. Procedure: write one event-model record per row; fill EXPECTED_NEXT; mark the first mismatch; write CONFIDENCE with justification. Questions: what is the earliest event with a mismatch? what is missing from the evidence?

Solution

The MRd (tag 0x11) has EXPECTED_NEXT "CplD tag 0x11 within µs"; ACTUAL_NEXT "none visible; AER CTO ≈ 50 ms" — the first deviation. Missing: IOMMU fault log, root port AER registers, capture coverage on the RC side; confidence medium.

Quiz

  1. Which carries an NVMe CQE: a PCIe Completion or a PCIe Memory Write?

    Answer

    A PCIe Memory Write (posted, device → host).

  2. An MRd of 32 DW to an SQ ring — how many SQEs?

    Answer

    Two (128 bytes / 64).

  3. Which field links a CplD to its MRd?

    Answer

    Requester ID + Tag (Completer ID identifies the responder).

  4. Phrase correctly: the analyzer shows no CQE.

    Answer

    "No MWr to the CQ region is visible in the captured interval" — plus a statement of capture coverage.

  5. What admin command reveals an I/O CQ's base address and vector?

    Answer

    Create I/O Completion Queue (05h): PRP1 = base, CDW11 IV = vector.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What's the difference between an NVMe completion and a PCIe completion?
    Model answer

    NVMe CQE: 16-byte record reporting an NVMe command's outcome, written into host memory via MWr. PCIe Cpl/CplD: transaction-layer response to a non-posted request, matched by ReqID+Tag.

  2. Intermediate How do you find which NVMe queue a doorbell write targets?
    Model answer

    (offset − 1000h)/(4 << DSTRD) = index; even index → SQ (index/2), odd → CQ ((index−1)/2).

  3. Advanced Why can't you correlate a capture started mid-run, and how do you recover?
    Model answer

    Queue bases, vectors and BAR addresses were set up earlier. Recover from host side (driver debugfs/tracepoints, lspci, reading MSI-X table), or by inferring ring regions from repeating MRd/MWr address patterns, with lower confidence.

  4. Senior Explain the first-abnormal-event and negative-evidence rules with an example.
    Model answer

    As in §41.8–41.9: timeout symptom → missing CplD deviation → IOMMU remap cause; absence claims need coverage.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain the four-way distinction (command / TLP / CQE / Completion TLP) and draw the nesting.
  • I can derive an address map from an initialization trace.
  • I can tag every TLP in a mixed trace with queue, slot, CID and role.
  • I can fill complete event-model records and identify the first deviation.
  • I always phrase absence claims with coverage.

Next: Part XIV — how that final MWr becomes an interrupt.

PART XIV

Interrupts

An NVMe controller can complete millions of commands per second across dozens of queues. Telling the host about those completions — quickly, to the right CPU, without drowning it — is the job of the interrupt architecture. This part follows the evolution from shared level-triggered wires (INTx) to Message Signalled Interrupts (MSI) to MSI-X, and then dissects MSI-X down to the bytes of its table and pending-bit array, the masking rules, the queue-to-vector mapping NVMe uses, and NVMe's interrupt coalescing feature. You will finish able to recognise an interrupt on a PCIe trace, explain why one is missing, and tune interrupt behaviour for latency or throughput.

42 Interrupt Architecture: INTx, MSI and MSI-X

← 41 Command-to-TLP Correlation43 MSI-X in Depth (Deep-Dive Module: MSI and MSI-X) →

42.1 Why this chapter exists

Every completed NVMe command must eventually reach software. Software can poll the CQ (burning CPU) or be interrupted. PCIe offers three interrupt mechanisms inherited from PCI history, each with very different scalability. NVMe allows all three — the NVMe over PCIe transport supports pin-based (INTx), single and multiple MSI, and MSI-X — but real high-performance systems use MSI-X almost exclusively. Understanding why requires knowing what each mechanism physically is.

42.2 Learning objectives

  • Describe INTx virtual wires, MSI and MSI-X and their PCIe representation (Assert/Deassert messages vs memory writes).
  • Explain why MSI-X suits NVMe's per-queue, per-CPU model.
  • Explain NVMe INTMS/INTMC and why they do not apply to MSI-X.
  • Identify interrupt TLPs in a trace.

42.3 Prerequisites

Chapter 39's stage 15 (MSI-X in the end-to-end read); PCIe message TLPs and configuration space capabilities from earlier parts.

42.4 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

INTx is a single shared doorbell button for a whole apartment block: when it rings, the caretaker has to knock on every door to find who pressed it, and the bell keeps ringing until that person lets go. MSI is giving each flat a postcard with the caretaker's address printed on it — the flat drops the postcard in the post when it needs attention, and the postcard says which flat it is. MSI-X is giving each flat a whole book of differently addressed postcards — one for the plumber, one for the electrician, one for the caretaker — and a switch for each postcard to say "don't send this one right now".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

INTx in PCIe is not a wire at all: it is emulated with Assert_INTx/Deassert_INTx message TLPs that the switch/root port aggregate into a virtual level. And MSI "postcards" are memory writes travelling the same posted path as data — which is precisely why they order correctly behind earlier data writes, something no physical wire could guarantee.

42.5 The three mechanisms

Before the details, here are the three mechanisms side by side, each followed from the device to the CPU. The key difference is what the device sends: INTx sends a "line is now high / low" message that the host must turn back into a shared wire, while MSI and MSI-X send an ordinary memory write whose address and data the host chose in advance. conceptual

Device side / what the device sendsHost side (root complex, interrupt controller, CPU)PCIe link
INTx (legacy, pin-based)MSIMSI-X
Representation on PCIeAssert_INTx / Deassert_INTx messages (INTA–INTD), level semanticsMWr of 1 DW (data) to programmed addressMWr of 1 DW to per-vector address
CapabilityInterrupt Pin / Line in config header; Command reg bit 10 Interrupt Disable; Status reg bit 3 Interrupt StatusMSI capability (ID 05h)MSI-X capability (ID 11h) + table + PBA in a BAR
Vectors per function1 (shared)1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32 (power of two, contiguous data values)Up to 2048, independent
Address per vectorn/aOne address for all vectors; vectors differ in low data bitsIndependent address + data per vector
Per-vector maskingInterrupt Disable bit onlyOptional (if Per-Vector Masking Capable)Always (Vector Control bit 0) + Function Mask
Sharing / need to poll sourcesYes — ISR must check every possible sourceNo for single-source vectorsNo
Ordering with data writesNone — message path and data differ in semantics; driver must read device to flushOrdered (posted write)Ordered (posted write)
CPU affinitySingle targetLimited (one address)Per vector
📘 Spec

verified The NVMe over PCIe transport defines Interrupt Mask Set (INTMS, offset 0Ch) and Interrupt Mask Clear (INTMC, offset 10h) registers that let host software mask/unmask interrupt vectors when using pin-based or MSI interrupts; host software is not to use them when MSI-X is configured — MSI-X masking is done in the MSI-X table. NVMe also defines how pin-based interrupts aggregate across CQs. For exact normative wording, consult the transport specification.

42.6 Why NVMe strongly benefits from MSI-X

  • One vector per CQ: Linux creates one I/O queue pair per CPU (or per CPU group) and one vector per CQ, each with affinity to that CPU. The completion is handled on the CPU that submitted the I/O — cache-hot, lock-free.
  • No source polling: the vector itself identifies the CQ; the ISR scans only one CQ.
  • Scale: NVMe allows up to 65,535 I/O queues; MSI caps at 32 vectors, MSI-X at 2048. Controllers commonly expose 32–256 vectors (impl).
  • Independent masking: a vector can be masked (e.g. while its CPU goes offline) without affecting others.
  • Ordering: the interrupt MWr follows the CQE MWr on the same posted path; when the interrupt arrives the CQE is in memory — no "flushing read" required (INTx needs one).
💡 Senior insight

When an NVMe drive gets fewer vectors than queues (e.g. MSI-X table size 9 on a 64-CPU host), Linux reduces the number of I/O queues to match vectors, and several CPUs share each queue — you'll see it in /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/*/cpu_list. A "slow drive on big servers" complaint can be a vector-count limitation, not a media problem. Virtualised drives (SR-IOV VFs) are especially prone.

42.7 How each looks in a trace

Synthetic trace — the same completion signalled three ways
MechanismTLPs (upstream unless noted)Notes
INTxMWr CQE → Msg Assert_INTA … (host ISR reads CSTS/INTMS via MRd ↓/CplD ↑) … host writes INTMS ↓ … Msg Deassert_INTALevel semantics; extra MMIO reads; shared line
MSI (single)MWr CQE → MWr 1 DW to MSI address, data = base dataOne vector for all CQs: ISR must scan all CQs
MSI-XMWr CQE → MWr 1 DW to vector n address, data nDirectly identifies CQ

42.8 Linux view

sudo lspci -vvv -s 02:00.0 | grep -A3 -E "MSI:|MSI-X:"   # capability, Enable+/-, Count
grep -E "nvme" /proc/interrupts                           # per-vector counts per CPU
cat /proc/irq/<N>/effective_affinity_list                 # where vector N lands
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/msi_irqs/            # Linux IRQ numbers of vectors

Can prove: which mechanism is enabled, how many vectors are allocated, how many interrupts were delivered per vector/CPU. Cannot prove: whether a specific interrupt message was sent but lost, or why a vector is quiet (no completions vs masked vs remapping fault).

Quiz

  1. How is INTx carried on a PCIe link?

    Answer

    As Assert_INTx/Deassert_INTx message TLPs emulating a level-sensitive wire.

  2. Max vectors for MSI and MSI-X?

    Answer

    32 and 2048.

  3. Why does INTx need a flushing read?

    Answer

    The virtual-wire interrupt is turned into a CPU interrupt by the platform's interrupt controller on a path that is not guaranteed to be ordered with the device's earlier DMA writes reaching memory (and the line may be shared). A read of a device register cannot complete until earlier posted writes from the device ahead of the completion have been pushed through, so the ISR's MMIO read acts as a flush. MSI/MSI-X messages, being memory writes themselves, travel behind the data and need no such read.

  4. When should host software use INTMS/INTMC?

    Answer

    Only with pin-based or MSI interrupts — not MSI-X.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is MSI?
    Model answer

    An interrupt sent as a memory write of a data value to a special address, decoded by the platform as an interrupt.

  2. Intermediate Why does NVMe prefer MSI-X?
    Model answer

    Per-CQ vectors with independent address/data/mask allow per-CPU completion handling at scale.

  3. Advanced A server with 128 CPUs shows 16 NVMe queues. Why?
    Model answer

    Vector count or controller's Number of Queues (Feature 07h) limit; Linux maps several CPUs per queue.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain INTx, MSI, MSI-X and their trace appearance.
  • I can explain five reasons NVMe benefits from MSI-X.
  • I know when INTMS/INTMC apply.

43 MSI-X in Depth (Deep-Dive Module: MSI and MSI-X)

← 42 Interrupt Architecture: INTx, MSI and MSI-X44 NVMe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: NVMe Errors) →

43.1 Why this chapter exists

"The interrupt didn't fire" is one of the most common NVMe bring-up and virtualisation complaints. Diagnosing it requires knowing exactly where MSI-X state lives (config space capability, a table in a BAR, a pending-bit array in a BAR), which bits gate delivery, how masking produces pending bits rather than lost interrupts, how NVMe binds CQs to vectors, and how coalescing deliberately delays interrupts.

43.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: name the three pieces of MSI-X (capability, table, PBA) and what a vector is.
  • Intermediate: decode Message Control, Table Offset/BIR, PBA Offset/BIR and a 16-byte table entry.
  • Advanced: explain masking semantics (Function Mask, per-vector mask, pending bits) and NVMe interrupt coalescing (Feature 08h) and Interrupt Vector Configuration (Feature 09h).
  • Senior: diagnose lost/late interrupts across device, platform (interrupt remapping) and virtualisation layers.
  • Trace-analysis: identify MSI-X MWrs and table-programming MWrs; map them to CQs.
  • Debugging: apply five failure patterns.
  • Validation: design tests for masking/pending behaviour.

43.3 Kid story and analogy boundary

🧒 Kid analogy

The SSD has a phone book (MSI-X table) kept in its own drawer. Each page (entry) has a phone number (Message Address), a short secret word to say (Message Data), and a little "do not call" sticker (mask bit). When a mailbox (CQ) has a new letter, the SSD looks up that mailbox's page and calls the number, saying the secret word. If the page has the "do not call" sticker, the SSD writes a tick on a sticky-note board (PBA) instead, and calls as soon as the sticker is removed. There's also a big "nobody calls anybody" switch for the whole phone book (Function Mask).

🧩 Analogy boundary

Represents: table entry fields, mask, pending. Hides: that the "call" is a posted memory write subject to PCIe ordering and flow control; that the platform decides what the "phone number" means (APIC address, interrupt remapping handle); that the host programs the phone book with MMIO writes. Misleading when: you think the tick on the board is a counter — it's one bit per vector, so multiple masked events collapse into one pending interrupt.

43.4 Vocabulary

TermPlain meaningEngineering meaningRelated toCommon confusion
VectorOne interrupt "line"Index n into the MSI-X table; one (address, data, mask) tupleLinux IRQ number (different!)Vector index ≠ Linux IRQ number ≠ CPU vector number
MSI-X TablePhone bookArray of 16-byte entries in memory space of a BAR, at Table OffsetBIRIt's in a BAR, not config space
PBASticky notesPending Bit Array: 1 bit per vector, in QWORDs, in a BARMaskRead-only to software; writes are undefined-behaviour territory
BIRWhich drawerBAR Indicator Register: bits 2:0 of Table/PBA Offset register select BAR 0–5BARTable and PBA may be in different BARs
Function MaskMaster muteMessage Control bit 14; masks all vectorsPer-vector maskSetting it doesn't change per-vector bits
MSI-X EnableTurn system onMessage Control bit 15INTx/MSI disableWhen set, INTx and MSI must not be used
Table SizePages in bookMessage Control bits 10:0, encoded N−1VectorsValue 0x1F means 32 vectors
Interrupt coalescingWaiting to batch callsNVMe Feature 08h: aggregation threshold + timeFeature 09hNot a PCIe feature
Interrupt remappingSwitchboardIOMMU function translating MSI writes to validated interruptsIOMMUFaults appear in IOMMU logs, not AER

43.5 Architecture: where MSI-X state lives

43.5.1 MSI-X capability structure

Offset31 … 1615 … 87 … 0
+00hMessage Control (bit 15 MSI-X Enable, bit 14 Function Mask, bits 10:0 Table Size N−1)Next Capability PointerCapability ID = 11h
+04hTable Offset (bits 31:3, QWORD aligned) | Table BIR (bits 2:0)
+08hPBA Offset (bits 31:3, QWORD aligned) | PBA BIR (bits 2:0)

43.5.2 MSI-X table entry (16 bytes)

Entry offsetFieldNotes
+0hMessage Address (lower 32 bits)Bits 1:0 zero (DWORD aligned)
+4hMessage Upper Address0 → 3DW MWr header; non-zero → 4DW
+8hMessage DataPayload of the interrupt MWr
+ChVector ControlBit 0 = Mask Bit (1 after reset); other bits reserved (newer revisions define additional bits — version)

Entry n lives at BAR[TableBIR] + TableOffset + 16·n; pending bit n at BAR[PBABIR] + PBAOffset + (n/64)·8, bit n % 64.

43.5.3 Inputs, outputs, actors, state

ElementDetail
InputsInterrupt events from the controller (CQ has new entries, coalescing condition met); host MMIO writes programming the table; config writes to Message Control
OutputsUpstream MWr (1 DW) to the Message Address; PBA bits
ActorsNVMe driver, PCI core (allocates vectors), platform interrupt controller/IOMMU interrupt remapping, controller interrupt logic
StateEnable, Function Mask, per-vector Mask, Pending bits, NVMe coalescing counters/timers per vector
Memory/registersCapability (config), Table and PBA (BAR), NVMe Features 08h/09h, CQ's IV/IEN from Create I/O CQ
DependenciesBus Master Enable (Command register bit 2) must be set — MSI-X writes are memory writes issued by the function; Memory Space Enable for table access; INTx disabled when MSI-X enabled

43.6 Mechanism step by step

The table below lists every actor. First, the same story as a picture: one I/O completion on queue 3 turning into an interrupt on CPU 3, plus what happens when a vector is masked. Click a step number, an arrow or a list item. All addresses and data values are synthetic (the address format shown is x86-style). synthetic

Software / host starts itDevice starts itInside the SSD (not on the PCIe link)PCIe link
  1. Software programs MSI-X table entry 3

    At probe time the PCI core reads the MSI-X capability in config space (Table Size, Table BIR and Offset), sets MSI-X Enable with Function Mask, then writes each table entry it wants in the BAR: Message Address, Message Data, and finally Vector Control with Mask = 0. The address and data are chosen by the platform's interrupt code so that the write will reach a chosen CPU.

    Where: BAR0 + Table Offset + 3 × 16 (table entry 3)PCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr to the table (plus CfgWr to Message Control)
    entry 3: Address = 0xFEE0_3000 Upper Address = 0 Data = 0x0024 Vector Control = 0 (unmasked) (values synthetic; the address format is platform-defined)
  2. Driver binds CQ 3 to vector 3 with Create I/O CQ

    The NVMe driver sends the admin command Create I/O Completion Queue (opcode 05h). Its CDW11 carries the Interrupt Vector (IV, bits 31:16) and Interrupts Enabled (IEN, bit 1). From now on the controller knows: "completions on CQ 3 are signalled through MSI-X vector 3". The admin CQ always uses vector 0.

    Where: admin SQ entry in host memory, fetched by the controllerPCIe: Yes · doorbell MWr, then the controller fetches the 64-byte SQE (MRd/CplD)
    Create I/O CQ: QID = 3, QSIZE = 255 (256 entries) CDW11: IV = 3, IEN = 1, PC = 1 (physically contiguous)
  3. Controller writes the completion entry to CQ 3

    An I/O on SQ 3 finishes. The controller writes its 16-byte completion entry into the next slot of CQ 3 in host memory, with the phase tag flipped to show it is new.

    Where: host memory, CQ 3 slot 2PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 16 bytes
    CQE: CID = 0x0107 SQID = 3 SQHD = 3 Status = 0 P = 1
  4. Controller looks up vector 3 and decides whether to signal now

    Inside the SSD, the controller finds which vector CQ 3 uses (vector 3) and applies interrupt coalescing if the host enabled it: with Feature 08h it may wait until THR+1 completions have accumulated or TIME × 100 µs has passed. Then it checks MSI-X Enable = 1, Function Mask = 0 and entry 3's Mask = 0, and reads entry 3's address and data.

    Where: inside the SSD (vector state, coalescing counters, MSI-X table)PCIe: No. Nothing appears on the link while the controller decides.
    Coalescing off (Linux default): signal at once. With THR = 3, TIME = 1: signal after 4 CQEs or 100 µs, whichever first.
  5. Controller sends the interrupt: a memory write of Data to Address

    The interrupt is just a posted 4-byte memory write, sent upstream like any DMA write. Because it uses the same posted path, it cannot overtake the CQE write from step 3, so the CQE is already in RAM when the interrupt fires. Bus Master Enable must be set, or the device may not send it at all.

    Where: the Message Address from table entry 3 (an interrupt address, not RAM)PCIe: Yes, device → host · MWr, 1 DW, payload = Message Data
    MWr Requester ID = 02:00.0 Address = 0xFEE0_3000 Data = 0x0000_0024
  6. The platform turns the write into an interrupt on CPU 3

    The root complex recognises the interrupt address. If interrupt remapping (IOMMU) is on, it checks the requester ID and translates the message; the APIC then interrupts CPU 3. The NVMe handler for vector 3 reads CQ 3 only, processes entries while the phase tag matches, and writes the CQ 3 head doorbell.

    Where: host interrupt controller, then CPU 3PCIe: Only the final CQ head doorbell (MWr, host → device)
    /proc/interrupts: the count for the nvme0q3 line goes up on CPU 3
  7. If the vector is masked: the controller sets the pending bit instead

    Suppose vector 4 has Mask = 1 (for example while its CPU is going offline) when its CQ gets a new entry. The controller must not send the message. It sets bit 4 in the Pending Bit Array (PBA) and keeps the message waiting. The CQE itself is still written normally.

    Where: PBA in the BAR (read-only to software)PCIe: No message is sent while masked
    Entry 4: Mask = 1 → PBA bit 4 = 1
  8. When software unmasks, the pending message is sent

    When software later writes Mask = 0 for entry 4, the controller sees the pending bit, sends the MWr with entry 4's address and data, and clears the pending bit. Whether the controller re-checks that the CQ still has unprocessed entries first is implementation-dependent.

    Where: table entry 4 (unmask) → interrupt address of entry 4PCIe: Yes · host MWr to Vector Control, then device MWr 1 DW
    Host writes Vector Control[4] = 0 Device sends MWr 0x0025 → 0xFEE0_4000, PBA bit 4 = 0

Coalescing note: coalescing (Feature 08h) changes only when step 5 happens, never where the message goes. It trades fewer interrupts for added latency, and the admin CQ is never coalesced. A vector can be exempted with Feature 09h (Coalescing Disable).

#Who actsWhat changesWhereEvidence

2PCI coreSets Function Mask + Enable (masked while programming)Message ControlConfig write (CfgWr0 TLP)
3PCI core / IRQ domainAllocates Linux IRQs, writes address/data per entryMSI-X table in BARDownstream MWr to table region
4PCI coreClears per-vector masks for requested vectors; clears Function MaskTable + Message ControlMWr + CfgWr
5NVMe driverAdmin CQ uses vector 0 (by NVMe convention admin CQ interrupts on vector 0); Create I/O CQ with IV=n, IEN=1Controller queue stateAdmin SQE CDW11
6ControllerCQE posted to CQ bound to vector nHost memoryMWr CQE

📘 Spec discipline

verified Normative (PCIe Base): capability layout, table entry layout, mask bit reset value of 1, pending-bit behaviour (a masked vector's message is held pending and sent when unmasked if still pending), Table Size encoding, max 2048. verified Normative (NVMe): Create I/O CQ carries IV and IEN; Feature 08h Interrupt Coalescing; Feature 09h Interrupt Vector Configuration with Coalescing Disable. impl: number of vectors, table placement in BAR, message address/data format (platform), whether the controller re-evaluates an interrupt condition or only latches pending. informative: The NVMe spec does not mandate one vector per CQ; several CQs may share a vector.

43.7 Queue-to-vector mapping

CPU0 ── SQ1/CQ1 ── IV=1 ── table[1] → addr/data targeting CPU0
CPU1 ── SQ2/CQ2 ── IV=2 ── table[2] → … CPU1
 …
CPUn ── SQn+1/CQn+1 ── IV=n+1 ── table[n+1] → … CPUn
Admin SQ0/CQ0 ─────── IV=0 ── table[0] (often shared with I/O queue 1 in Linux — impl)
Poll queues (IEN=0) ── no vector

Linux's nvme driver uses managed IRQ affinity: vectors are spread across CPUs at allocation; when a CPU goes offline, its managed vector is shut down after its queue drains (impl, kernel-version dependent).

43.8 Interrupt coalescing (NVMe Feature 08h)

CDW11 bitsFieldMeaning
15:08Aggregation Time (TIME)Maximum delay in 100 µs increments; 0 = no delay-based coalescing
07:00Aggregation Threshold (THR)Minimum number of CQEs to aggregate per vector, zero-based (0 → 1 entry)

The controller sends an interrupt when either the threshold of completions accumulates or the aggregation time elapses since the first unsignalled completion (spec describes the intent; exact timing impl). The setting applies to all I/O-queue vectors; Feature 09h (Interrupt Vector Configuration) CDW11 bits 15:0 select a vector and bit 16 Coalescing Disable (CD) exempts it. The admin CQ vector is not coalesced.

interrupts/s ≈ min(IOPS_per_vector / (THR+1), …) bounded below by 1 / (TIME × 100 µs) when traffic is light
  • THR — zero-based aggregation threshold
  • TIME — aggregation time in 100 µs units
  • IOPS_per_vector — completions per second on CQs mapped to this vector
⚠️ Latency trade-off

With TIME = 1 (100 µs) and QD1 workloads, a coalescing controller can add up to ~100 µs to every I/O — doubling the latency of a fast read. Linux does not enable NVMe coalescing by default. Tune only with measurement. nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 8 -H is read-only; set-feature changes device behaviour (caution).

Reasoning: link evidence says the device sent it; host evidence says software didn't run. Candidates: interrupt remapping rejected it (stale entry after VM migration/affinity change — check IOMMU fault log), address/data stale (host reprogrammed the table but the device used a cached copy — device bug), the capture point is upstream of a switch that dropped it (unlikely). This is a cross-layer gap between "PCIe delivered" and "CPU received".

43.10 Linux view

sudo lspci -vvv -s 02:00.0 | grep -A2 "MSI-X"
#  Capabilities: [b0] MSI-X: Enable+ Count=33 Masked-       (illustrative)
#        Vector table: BAR=0 offset=00002000
#        PBA: BAR=0 offset=00003000
grep nvme /proc/interrupts | head
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H   # interrupt coalescing (read-only)
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x09 -c 1 -H  # vector 1 configuration (read-only)
# Reading table/PBA memory directly requires mapping the BAR (e.g. /sys/.../resource0)
# - read-only inspection only; writing would corrupt interrupt state.
⚠️ Safety

Never write MSI-X table entries or Message Control by hand (setpci or resource mmap) on a live system: you can mask the interrupt of the boot disk and hang the machine. Treat all of these as read-only inspection.

43.12 Labs

🧪 Lab 43.1 (beginner) — Map vectors to queues and CPUs SAFE

Objective: derive the queue/vector/CPU map. Prerequisites: Linux, NVMe drive. Setup/Procedure: run the commands in §43.10; list nvme lines in /proc/interrupts; read effective_affinity_list for each; read /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/*/cpu_list. Observations: number of vectors, queues, CPUs per queue. Questions: is vector count = I/O queues + 1? Which vector serves the admin queue? Expected reasoning: Linux names vectors nvme0q0, nvme0q1…

Solution

Typically nvme0q0 is admin (vector 0), nvme0q1..qN are I/O; poll queues have no vector. Mismatch indicates vector limits or poll/read queue configuration (nvme.poll_queues, nvme.write_queues).

Extension: run fio pinned to one CPU and confirm only that vector increments.

🧪 Lab 43.2 (intermediate) — Decode an MSI-X capability dump SAFE

Setup (synthetic): capability bytes at 0xB0: 11 C0 20 80 | 00 20 00 00 | 00 30 00 00. Procedure: decode.

Solution

Cap ID 11h; next pointer C0h; Message Control (little-endian bytes 20 80) = 0x8020 → Enable=1, Function Mask=0, Table Size field 0x020 → 33 vectors. Table Offset/BIR = 0x0000_2000 → BIR 0, offset 2000h. PBA = 0x0000_3000 → BIR 0, offset 3000h. Entry 5 at BAR0+2050h; pending bit 5 in QWORD at BAR0+3000h.

🧪 Lab 43.3 (advanced) — Coalescing model SAFE

Objective: simulate interrupt rate and added latency vs THR/TIME. 

import random
def simulate(iops, thr0, time_units, dur_s=1.0):
    thr = thr0 + 1; tmax = time_units * 100e-6
    t = 0.0; pending = []; irqs = 0; added = []
    while t < dur_s:
        t += random.expovariate(iops); pending.append(t)
        if len(pending) >= thr or (tmax and t - pending[0] >= tmax):
            irqs += 1; added += [t - p for p in pending]; pending = []
    return irqs, sum(added)/max(1, len(added))
for thr0, tu in [(0,0),(3,1),(7,2),(15,4)]:
    print(thr0, tu, simulate(200_000, thr0, tu))

Questions: how does added latency scale with THR at high IOPS vs low IOPS?

Solution

At high IOPS the threshold triggers first: added latency ≈ (THR)/2 inter-arrival times (small). At low IOPS the timer dominates: added latency approaches TIME×100 µs. (This simple model only checks the timer on arrivals — a real controller has an independent timer; extend accordingly.)

Extension: add an independent timer event.

🧪 Lab 43.4 (senior forensic) — The silent vector SAFE

Given (synthetic): timeouts on QID 7 only; /proc/interrupts for nvme0q7 stopped incrementing at 10:02:13; at 10:02:12 the kernel log shows CPU 6 offline then online; trace shows CQEs on CQ7 and no MWr to vector 7 address; PBA bit 7 = 1; Vector Control 7 = 1. Questions: What happened? Device or host? What fix?

Solution

The vector was masked during CPU offline (managed IRQ shutdown) and never unmasked when the CPU returned — host-side bug/race (high confidence: PBA proves the device latched the interrupt correctly). Fix: kernel update/patch for the affinity/hotplug path; workaround: avoid hotplug, reset controller.

43.13 Interview questions

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is an MSI-X vector?
    Model answer

    An entry in the MSI-X table: address, data and mask; the device sends an MWr of the data to the address.

  2. Beginner Where is the MSI-X table?
    Model answer

    In a memory BAR, located by Table BIR and Offset from the capability.

  3. Beginner What does the PBA do?
    Model answer

    Records pending interrupts for masked vectors.

  4. Beginner How does an NVMe CQ choose its vector?
    Model answer

    IV field in Create I/O CQ CDW11, with IEN=1.

  5. Beginner Max MSI-X vectors?
    Model answer

    2048.

  6. Intermediate Decode Message Control 0xC01F.
    Model answer

    Enable=1, Function Mask=1, 32 vectors.

  7. Intermediate What does Feature 08h do?
    Model answer

    Configures interrupt aggregation threshold and time for I/O vectors.

  8. Intermediate Why must Bus Master Enable be set for MSI-X?
    Model answer

    Interrupt messages are memory writes the function initiates as a bus master.

  9. Intermediate What's the reset value of a vector's mask bit?
    Model answer

    1 (masked).

  10. Intermediate Can several CQs share a vector?
    Model answer

    Yes; the ISR must then scan all those CQs.

  11. Advanced Why does the CQE become visible before the ISR runs?
    Model answer

    Both are posted writes from the same requester; the interrupt cannot pass the CQE under default ordering.

  12. Advanced What happens to multiple events while a vector is masked?
    Model answer

    They collapse into one pending bit; one message on unmask.

  13. Advanced How does interrupt remapping change the meaning of Message Address/Data?
    Model answer

    Address/data become a handle into the IOMMU's remapping table, validated against the source ID.

  14. Advanced How would you test pending-bit behaviour?
    Model answer

    Mask vector, generate completions, read PBA (expect set), unmask, expect exactly one message and PBA clear.

  15. Advanced What is Coalescing Disable?
    Model answer

    Feature 09h bit 16 per vector, exempting it from Feature 08h.

  16. Senior A VM sees periodic 30 s timeouts after live migration. Approach?
    Model answer

    Check posted-interrupt/remapping state, table restore, PBA; correlate timestamp with migration; test with polling.

  17. Senior Design interrupt strategy for 2 M IOPS at low CPU.
    Model answer

    Per-CPU queues, MSI-X affinity, moderate coalescing for throughput queues, CD on latency queues, poll queues for hipri, NAPI-like hybrid polling.

  18. Senior Prove whether a missing interrupt is device or host.
    Model answer

    Analyzer at device link: MWr seen → host; not seen with PBA set → masked; not seen and PBA clear and CQE present → device bug (if coalescing excluded).

  19. Senior Why might vector count limit performance?
    Model answer

    Fewer queues than CPUs → shared queues, locking, cross-CPU completions, cache misses.

  20. Senior When is polling better than MSI-X?
    Model answer

    Ultra-low latency, high-IOPS dedicated cores where interrupt overhead dominates; costs CPU.

📌 Teach-back

Child: phone book with do-not-call stickers and a sticky-note board. Junior: capability → table/PBA in BAR → entry fields → CQ IV mapping. Senior: ordering vs CQE, masking/pending semantics, coalescing trade-offs, remapping and virtualisation failure modes.

✅ Mastery gate
  • Explain: capability, table, PBA, vector, masking, coalescing.
  • Diagram: Figure 43.1 from memory.
  • Identify in trace: table programming, interrupt MWr, coalescing gaps.
  • Debug: the five failure patterns.
  • Distinguish: MSI vs MSI-X vs INTx; PCIe masking vs NVMe INTMS/INTMC; vector vs IRQ number.
  • Cite: PCIe Base (MSI-X), NVMe Base (Features 08h/09h), NVMe over PCIe transport (interrupts).

Next: Part XV — Error handling.

PART XV

Error Handling

Errors on an NVMe SSD live on at least three floors of the building. On the top floor, the NVMe controller reports command outcomes in the 15-bit status field of every CQE, keeps an Error Information log, raises asynchronous events, and — in the worst case — declares itself fatally broken through CSTS.CFS. On the middle floor, the PCIe transaction and data link layers detect malformed, poisoned, unexpected and missing packets and classify them as correctable, uncorrectable non-fatal or uncorrectable fatal. Underneath, the physical layer suffers receiver errors that the data link layer quietly repairs with replays. AER (Advanced Error Reporting) is the instrument panel for the PCIe floors. This part teaches each floor, then — the real skill — how to correlate them so you can tell a software bug from a driver bug, an NVMe protocol error, a PCIe transaction error, a link problem, a firmware bug or a failing NAND die.

44 NVMe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: NVMe Errors)

← 43 MSI-X in Depth (Deep-Dive Module: MSI and MSI-X)45 PCIe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: PCIe Errors) →

44.1 Why this chapter exists

Every NVMe command ends with a status. Most of the time it is zero. When it isn't, the exact Status Code Type (SCT) and Status Code (SC), plus the DNR (Do Not Retry) and More bits, tell the host whether the command was malformed, rejected for a state reason, failed by the media, aborted, or failed because of a path problem — and whether retrying could help. Misreading status (e.g. treating "Invalid Field" as a media failure, or retrying a DNR error forever) causes wrong RMAs, data loss and endless retry storms. Beyond per-command status, NVMe has controller-level mechanisms — asynchronous events, the Error Information log, SMART/Health critical warnings, and the Controller Fatal Status bit — that you must read alongside.

44.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: locate the status field in a CQE and decode SCT/SC for success, invalid opcode, invalid field, LBA out of range.
  • Intermediate: classify status codes into generic, command specific, media and data integrity, path related; interpret DNR, More, CRD.
  • Advanced: use the Error Information log, Asynchronous Event Requests and SMART critical warnings to build a controller-level error picture; understand abort and CFS handling.
  • Senior: design retry/escalation policy; separate host-induced from device-induced statuses.
  • Trace-analysis: decode status from a captured CQE MWr payload.
  • Debugging: apply the five failure patterns.
  • Validation: design negative tests that elicit specific statuses safely.

44.3 Kid story and analogy boundary

🧒 Kid analogy

Every receipt the warehouse gives you has a stamp. Green "OK". Blue stamps mean "you filled the card wrong" (no such book type, a box ticked that makes no sense, a card number you already used). Orange stamps are "that particular kind of request didn't work" (the shelf you asked to build is the wrong size). Red stamps mean "the book itself is damaged" (we couldn't read page 7). Purple means "the road to that warehouse is blocked". And there's a small "don't bother asking again" box that is ticked when retrying won't help. If the whole warehouse catches fire, it doesn't stamp anything — it hangs a big sign on the door (CSTS.CFS).

🧩 Analogy boundary

Represents: SCT categories, DNR. Hides: that status can only be delivered if the controller is healthy enough to write a CQE; that some failures produce no CQE (timeouts); that statuses are command-set specific (the same SC value means different things under different SCTs and command sets). Misleading when: you assume a "red stamp" always means the SSD's NAND is failing — some media/data-integrity codes (e.g. end-to-end guard check errors) may reflect host-supplied protection information mismatches.

44.3a Where NVMe errors surface: the map

An NVMe controller has exactly four ways to tell the host that something went wrong. They differ in who writes the evidence, where it ends up and how software has to go and get it. Keep this map in mind for the rest of the chapter: sections 44.4–44.9 explain each row in detail. conceptual

Device writes it (crosses PCIe)Inside the SSD (not on PCIe)Software reads itLands in host memory

44.4 The status field

CQE Dword 3: bits 15:0 CID, bit 16 Phase Tag, bits 31:17 Status Field (SF). Inside the 15-bit SF:

SF bitCQE DW3 bitFieldMeaning
7:024:17SC — Status CodeSpecific code within the type
10:827:25SCT — Status Code Type0 Generic, 1 Command Specific, 2 Media and Data Integrity, 3 Path Related, 4–6 reserved, 7 Vendor Specific
12:1129:28CRD — Command Retry DelaySelects one of CRDT1–3 from Identify Controller (in 100 ms units) if host supports it
1330M — MoreMore status information available in the Error Information log
1431DNR — Do Not RetryRetrying the identical command is expected to fail
🔍 Linux status notation

Linux prints NVMe status as the 15-bit SF value shifted down (i.e. (DW3 >> 17)), so 0x281 = SCT 2, SC 81h (Unrecovered Read Error), and 0x4002 = DNR set, SCT 0, SC 02h (Invalid Field in Command). On a trace, the raw DW3 of a CQE MWr is (SF << 17) | (P << 16) | CID: Unrecovered Read Error with P=1, CID 0x0042 → 0x0503_0042.

CategoryHow it manifestsHost action

44.7 Error Information log (Log Identifier 01h)

Each entry is 64 bytes; the controller keeps up to ELPE+1 entries (Identify Controller Error Log Page Entries, zero-based). Entries record (verified field set; exact byte offsets — consult the Base spec):

  • Error Count — 64-bit unique, incrementing identifier (0 = invalid entry).
  • Submission Queue ID and Command ID — which command (FFFFh if not command-related).
  • Status Field — the status that was (or would have been) returned, including Phase Tag position conventions.
  • Parameter Error Location — byte and bit within the SQE that caused an Invalid Field — invaluable for host bugs.
  • LBA and Namespace — first LBA affected.
  • Vendor Specific Information Available, Transport Type, Command Specific Information, Transport Type Specific Information.
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 16        # last 16 entries (read-only)
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0              # media_errors, num_err_log_entries, critical_warning
sudo nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=0x01 --log-len=1024   # raw bytes
🏭 Implementation-dependent

Which errors a controller records in the Error log is partly implementation-defined: some log every non-zero status, some only selected ones. Many consumer drives log host-caused Invalid Field errors from probing commands (e.g. the OS querying an unsupported log page), producing large num_err_log_entries counts that are not health problems. Always read the entries before concluding.

44.8 Asynchronous events

The host keeps one or more Asynchronous Event Request commands (admin opcode 0Ch) outstanding; they have no timeout. When something happens, the controller completes one with DW0 describing the event:

DW0 bitsFieldValues
2:0Asynchronous Event Type0 Error status, 1 SMART/Health status, 2 Notice, 6 I/O Command specific status, 7 Vendor specific
15:8Asynchronous Event InformationType-specific (e.g. for Error: 00h write to invalid doorbell register, 01h invalid doorbell write value, 02h diagnostic failure, 03h persistent internal error, 04h transient internal error, 05h firmware image load error; for Notice: namespace attribute changed, firmware activation starting, …)
23:16Log Page IdentifierLog page to read to clear the event (e.g. 01h Error, 02h SMART, 04h Changed Namespace List)

Events of a type are masked until the host reads the indicated log page (with RAE clear). Async events are the only way a controller tells the host about errors that are not tied to a command — notably a bad doorbell write, which otherwise would just silently be ignored.

🐞 Debugging

When a doorbell write seems to "do nothing", look for an async event with type 0 / info 00h or 01h on the admin CQ. If your driver doesn't keep AERs outstanding (custom/bring-up drivers often don't), you've thrown away the controller's only way to tell you.

44.9 Abort and Controller Fatal Status

Abort (08h): CDW10 = SQID (15:0) and CID (31:16) of the target. Abort is best effort: completion DW0 bit 0 = 1 means the command was not aborted. The aborted command, if aborted, completes with SCT0/07h. Linux sends Abort on I/O timeout, then escalates to controller reset if the Abort itself times out.

CSTS.CFS (bit 1): the controller sets Controller Fatal Status when it cannot communicate through its normal mechanisms — no further CQEs are expected. Host response is a controller reset; if CSTS reads as 0xFFFFFFFF the issue is not CFS but that the device isn't answering MMIO at all (link down, surprise removal, reset in progress) — a PCIe-floor problem.
