44.13 Labs

🧪 Lab 44.1 (beginner) — Decode CQE DW3 values SAFE

Objective: decode raw CQE status. Setup: values (synthetic): 0x0001_0010, 0x8005_0011, 0x0101_0012, 0x0503_0013, 0x8004_0014. Procedure: SF = DW3 >> 17; P = bit 16; CID = low 16 bits.

Solution

(1) CID 0x10, P=1, success. (2) DW3>>17 = 0x4002 → DNR=1, SCT0, SC 02h Invalid Field; P=1; CID 0x11. (3) 0x0101_0012 >> 17 = 0x80 → SCT0 SC80h → LBA Out of Range (NVM); P=1; CID 0x12. (4) 0x0503_0013 >> 17 = 0x281 → SCT2 SC81h Unrecovered Read Error; P=1. (5) 0x8004_0014 >> 17 = 0x4002 → DNR, Invalid Field; P=0 — phase 0 is legal after a wrap.

Extension: write a decoder that prints names for the codes in §44.5.

🧪 Lab 44.2 (intermediate) — Read error logs safely SAFE

Procedure: run the read-only commands in §44.7; correlate error entries' SQID/CID with any dmesg messages; classify each entry host vs device.

Solution

Entries with SQID 0 and status Invalid Field/Invalid Log Page are typically host probes (e.g. tools querying unsupported log pages). Entries on I/O queues with SCT 2 are media-related. Entries with SQID FFFFh are not command-related.

🧪 Lab 44.3 (advanced) — Elicit an Invalid Field error safely CAUTION

Objective: generate a known host error without risking data. Setup: test system. Procedure: issue a Get Log Page for an unsupported vendor log ID via nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=0xC7 --log-len=512 (read-only admin command); observe the returned status and new Error log entry.

Solution

Expected: SCT1/09h Invalid Log Page or SCT0/02h Invalid Field (implementation may vary); Error count increments if the controller logs it. Demonstrates host-induced errors in the log.

Extension: compare behaviour across two drive models.

🧪 Lab 44.4 (senior forensic) — Is it the drive? SAFE

Given (synthetic): app reports checksum mismatch; NVMe statuses all success; namespace formatted with PI type 1; no E2E errors; error log empty; dmesg shows IOMMU faults from 02:00.0 at nearby times.

Solution

PI would have caught media/device corruption of the data with E2E check errors (82h/84h). Success with corruption plus IOMMU faults points to host-side DMA mapping problems (buffer reuse/unmapped) or app bugs. Confidence medium; next evidence: IOMMU strict mode reproduction, data capture of MWr payloads.

Quiz

  1. Which SCT is "Media and Data Integrity Errors"?

    Answer

    2h.

  2. What does DNR mean?

    Answer

    Do Not Retry — the same command is expected to fail again.

  3. Linux prints status 0x2281. Decode.

    Answer

    More=1, SCT 2, SC 81h — Unrecovered Read Error, details in Error log.

  4. How does the controller report a write to an invalid doorbell?

    Answer

    Asynchronous event, type Error (0), info 00h, if an AER command is outstanding.

  5. CSTS reads 0xFFFFFFFF. Is CFS set?

    Answer

    Can't tell — the read failed (device unreachable); all-ones is a PCIe-level symptom.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Where is the status in a CQE?
    Model answer

    DW3 bits 31:17.

  2. Beginner Difference between Invalid Opcode and Invalid Field?
    Model answer

    Opcode unsupported vs supported command with bad parameter.

  3. Beginner What is the Error Information log?
    Model answer

    Log 01h, 64-byte entries with count, SQID, CID, status, parameter location, LBA, NSID.

  4. Beginner What is an AER command in NVMe?
    Model answer

    Asynchronous Event Request (0Ch) — not PCIe AER; a parked command completed when an event occurs.

  5. Beginner What's CFS?
    Model answer

    CSTS bit 1 Controller Fatal Status.

  6. Intermediate How should retry logic treat DNR and CRD?
    Model answer

    DNR=1: don't retry; else retry, honouring CRD delays (CRDT) if ACRE enabled.

  7. Intermediate Why might num_err_log_entries be huge on a healthy drive?
    Model answer

    Host probing produces logged invalid-field/log errors.

  8. Intermediate What causes Command Aborted due to SQ Deletion?
    Model answer

    Deleting an SQ with outstanding commands — normal during reset/teardown.

  9. Intermediate How do E2E PI errors help localise corruption?
    Model answer

    Guard/ref tags verify data integrity and LBA association across the path.

  10. Intermediate What's the Parameter Error Location?
    Model answer

    Byte/bit in the SQE responsible for an invalid-field error.

  11. Advanced What's the Linux recovery ladder on timeout?
    Model answer

    Abort → controller reset → remove device if reset fails (impl-dependent details).

  12. Advanced When is an Abort considered successful?
    Model answer

    Completion DW0 bit 0 = 0 and the target completes with 07h; otherwise not aborted.

  13. Advanced Data Transfer Error: where to look?
    Model answer

    PCIe AER on device/root port, IOMMU faults, poisoned TLPs.

  14. Advanced How are async events re-armed?
    Model answer

    Read the indicated log page (RAE=0) and submit a new AER command.

  15. Advanced What's DLFEAT and its relation to 87h?
    Model answer

    Deallocate features describe read behaviour for deallocated blocks; error 87h reported when configured (DULBE).

  16. Senior Design an error-handling policy for a storage array.
    Model answer

    Classify by SCT; retry transient (non-DNR) with backoff; rebuild from redundancy on 81h; quarantine on repeated; reset on CFS; correlate with AER and SMART.

  17. Senior How do you prove an RMA is justified?
    Model answer

    Reproducible media errors at device LBAs, SMART trends, telemetry, clean PCIe/host evidence.

  18. Senior Why can't status alone tell you who's at fault?
    Model answer

    Same status may stem from host data/PI, transport, or device; need cross-layer evidence.

  19. Senior How do you handle a controller that silently stops completing?
    Model answer

    Timeouts → check CSTS (CFS vs all-ones), AER, link; reset ladder; capture telemetry.

  20. Senior What's risky about retrying writes blindly?
    Model answer

    Semantics (e.g. ordering, atomicity, reservations) and wasting time on DNR errors; masking a deeper fault.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can decode any CQE DW3 into CID, P, SC, SCT, CRD, M, DNR.
  • I can name 10+ generic, 5 command-specific and 5 media status codes.
  • I can read and classify Error log entries.
  • I can explain async events and CFS.
  • I can distinguish host-caused, transport-caused and device-caused statuses.

45 PCIe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: PCIe Errors)

← 44 NVMe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: NVMe Errors)46 AER — Advanced Error Reporting (Deep-Dive Module: AER) →

45.1 Why this chapter exists

PCIe was designed so that most physical-layer imperfections never reach software: LCRC (Link CRC) and the Ack/Nak replay protocol repair corrupted TLPs transparently. When errors do reach software, PCIe classifies them by who detected them and how bad they are. Understanding the classes — correctable, uncorrectable non-fatal, uncorrectable fatal — and the individual errors (Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout, Receiver Error, Completion Timeout, Unsupported Request, Completer Abort, Malformed TLP, Poisoned TLP, ECRC, Surprise Down…) lets you tell a marginal link from a broken driver from a dead device.

45.2 Learning objectives

  • Classify every major PCIe error into correctable / non-fatal / fatal and name the layer that detects it.
  • Explain which errors are "symptoms" (replays, completion timeouts) vs "causes".
  • Explain how errors are signalled (ERR_COR, ERR_NONFATAL, ERR_FATAL messages), and how baseline (Device Status) and advanced (AER) reporting differ.
  • Interpret error patterns in synthetic traces.
  • Apply five failure patterns.

45.3 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Letters between two towns travel on a road with a postman. If rain smudges a letter, the receiving post office says "send that again please" and nobody else ever hears about it — that's a correctable error; the post office just keeps a tally. If a letter arrives addressed to a house that doesn't exist, the post office says "unsupported!" — the letter is lost but the road is fine: uncorrectable non-fatal. If the bridge collapses, no letters get through at all: uncorrectable fatal.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Severity of most uncorrectable errors is programmable (via the AER Severity register), not inherent; "non-fatal" refers to the link's reliability, not the impact on your application — a non-fatal Completion Timeout can still hang your NVMe command and crash a filesystem. And some correctable errors (Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover) are the early warning of a bridge about to collapse.

45.4 Error classes

ClassDefinitionHardware handled?MessageTypical software response
CorrectableDetected and corrected by hardware, no information lostYes (e.g. replay)ERR_CORCount, rate-monitor; act on trends
Uncorrectable non-fatalTransaction affected, link still reliableNo — a transaction failedERR_NONFATALDevice driver error handler; recovery possibly without link reset
Uncorrectable fatalLink or device integrity compromisedNoERR_FATALLink/slot reset (Secondary Bus Reset), driver re-init; DPC may contain

The same classification as a tree. Read it top-down: first "did the hardware fix it?", then "can the link still be trusted?". Each leaf names an example error and the layer (or role) that detects it. conceptual

45.5 The master error table

ErrorLayerDetected byClass (default severity)What it meansTypical root causes

Completion TimeoutTransactionRequesterUncorrectable, non-fatalNon-posted request got no (complete) completion in timeLost completion, unreachable completer, IOMMU drop, device hung, link retraining
Completer AbortTransactionCompleterUncorrectable, non-fatalCompleter couldn't complete a request it otherwise supports (internal violation)Access-rule violation, device internal error

Uncorrectable Internal ErrorInternalComponentUncorrectable, fatalInternal non-correctable faultDevice hardware
📘 Spec

verified The error list and default severities above reflect the PCIe Base Specification's AER Uncorrectable Error Severity register defaults (Data Link Protocol, Surprise Down, Flow Control Protocol, Receiver Overflow, Malformed TLP and Uncorrectable Internal Error default to fatal; others non-fatal). Severity is programmable. Newer revisions add errors (e.g. related to TLP prefixes, IDE, FLIT mode) — version; consult the current Base spec for the full list.

45.6 Requester vs completer errors

For a non-posted request, errors split by role: the completer detects UR and CA and returns a completion with that status (and logs the error, possibly as advisory); the requester detects Completion Timeout and receives the UR/CA completion status, and logs Unexpected Completion if a completion matches nothing. For NVMe this matters because the device is the requester for all data-path reads (SQE fetch, write data, PRP lists). So a host-side problem servicing the device's reads appears in the device's AER registers as Completion Timeout — the SSD is reporting the host's failure.

📌 Remember

"The SSD logged a Completion Timeout" usually means "the SSD asked the host for something and the host never answered". Treat it as host/topology-side evidence first.

45.7 Signalling paths

Endpoint detects error
  ├─ updates Device Status (CED/NFED/FED/URD)         [baseline, always]
  ├─ updates AER status bits (if AER implemented)      [advanced]
  ├─ if not masked and reporting enabled (Device Control bits 0-3, SERR# for fatal/non-fatal on bridges):
  │     sends Msg ERR_COR / ERR_NONFATAL / ERR_FATAL upstream (Requester ID = itself)
  └─ root port receives message
        ├─ Root Error Status records (first/multiple, source ID)
        ├─ if Root Error Command enables → interrupt to OS (AER service driver)
        └─ (optional) DPC trigger on fatal/non-fatal → contain link

DPC (Downstream Port Containment): an optional capability on downstream ports that, on an uncorrectable error, disables the link to stop traffic (protecting data integrity), lets software recover the port, and makes subsequent requests to the device complete with UR/all-ones. Linux supports DPC and Error Disconnect Recover (EDR) — impl/platform-dependent.

45.10 Lab

🧪 Lab 45.1 — Classify errors from descriptions SAFE

Procedure: for each scenario, give error name, class, detecting component: (a) SSD sends 512 B MWr to a root port with MPS 256; (b) host's DRAM reports UE while serving an SSD read; (c) SSD replays a TLP 4 times; (d) host reads BAR0 while SSD is in D3hot; (e) switch internal SRAM bit flip on a forwarded TLP with ECRC.

Solution

(a) Malformed TLP, fatal (default), root port. (b) Poisoned TLP Received (CplD EP=1), non-fatal, SSD. (c) REPLAY_NUM Rollover, correctable, SSD transmitter (then Recovery). (d) Unsupported Request (memory requests in D3hot are not supported), non-fatal, SSD as completer; host sees UR completion → all-ones. (e) ECRC Error, non-fatal, final receiver (if ECRC check enabled).

Quiz

  1. Which errors are corrected by the data link layer replay?

    Answer

    Bad TLP (LCRC/sequence), with Replay Timer Timeout / REPLAY_NUM Rollover as related correctable events.

  2. Who detects a Completion Timeout?

    Answer

    The requester.

  3. What's the default severity of Malformed TLP?

    Answer

    Fatal.

  4. What does EP=1 mean?

    Answer

    Poisoned — the data payload is known to be corrupt.

  5. Why is ECRC useful if LCRC exists?

    Answer

    LCRC is per link and regenerated at every hop; ECRC covers end-to-end, detecting corruption inside switches.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Three PCIe error classes?
    Model answer

    Correctable, uncorrectable non-fatal, uncorrectable fatal.

  2. Intermediate UR vs CA?
    Model answer

    UR: request not supported by completer; CA: supported but completer failed to complete it due to a violation/internal error.

  3. Advanced Why might a correctable error storm hurt performance?
    Model answer

    Replays consume bandwidth and add latency; interrupts per error cost CPU; may lead to retraining/downgrades.

  4. Senior Device reports CTO, root port reports nothing. Next steps?
    Model answer

    Check IOMMU, switch ports' AER, whether the request reached the RC (analyzer upstream of switch), completion routing (BDF changes), ACS.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can fill the master error table from memory with class and detector.
  • I can explain why the SSD logs host-caused completion timeouts.
  • I can describe ERR_* message flow and DPC.
  • I can classify MPS-mismatch, poisoned, UR and ECRC scenarios.

46 AER — Advanced Error Reporting (Deep-Dive Module: AER)

← 45 PCIe Errors (Deep-Dive Module: PCIe Errors)47 Error Correlation Across Layers →

46.1 Why this chapter exists

Baseline PCIe error reporting (four bits in Device Status) tells you that a correctable, non-fatal, fatal or unsupported-request error happened. AER tells you which error, which was first, how it was classified, and — crucially — logs the header of the offending TLP, which turns an anonymous error into a forensic artefact: requester, tag, address, length, type. In NVMe debugging the AER header log is often the single piece of evidence that ties a PCIe error to a specific NVMe queue or buffer.

46.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: list the AER registers and what each holds.
  • Intermediate: decode Uncorrectable/Correctable Status and Mask values bit by bit; explain Severity.
  • Advanced: decode a 4-DW Header Log into a TLP and map it to an NVMe action; use First Error Pointer; read root port Root Error Status and Error Source Identification.
  • Senior: plan masking/severity policy; know when AER evidence is incomplete (masked, overflow, cleared by OS).
  • Trace-analysis: match an AER header log to a TLP in a capture.
  • Debugging: read AER from Linux logs/sysfs and lspci safely.
  • Validation: design error-injection validation (e.g. via platform error injection or aer-inject on test systems).

46.3 Kid story and analogy boundary

🧒 Kid analogy

Every room in the house has a logbook by the door. When something goes wrong, the room ticks a box on a checklist ("muddy letter", "letter for a person who doesn't live here", "nobody answered my question"). Some boxes are taped over (masked) so ticking them doesn't call anyone. Each box also says whether it's a "call the parent now" box or "just tell them later" (severity). The room photocopies the envelope of the bad letter (header log) and writes which box was ticked first. The parent's room (root port) keeps a master logbook: "I got a message from room 2:00.0 about a serious problem".

🧩 Analogy boundary

Represents: status, mask, severity, header log, root collection. Hides: that there's only room for one (or a few, if multiple-header recording is supported) envelope photocopies; that status bits are sticky (survive some resets) and RW1C (cleared by writing 1); that masking a bit still records status in many cases but suppresses signalling. Misleading when: you assume the logbook is complete — OS drivers clear AER status after reading it, so by the time you run lspci the evidence may be gone.

23–26MC Blocked TLP, AtomicOp Egress Blocked, TLP Prefix Blocked, Poisoned TLP Egress BlockedNon-fatal (Prefix Blocked: non-fatal)—

Bits 0 (formerly Training Error / Undefined) and others not listed are reserved or revision-specific — version. Default severity register value is commonly 0x0006_2030 (bits 4, 5, 13, 17, 18 fatal) plus bit 22 in components implementing it (derived from the defaults listed).

46.5.2 Correctable Error Status/Mask bit map

BitErrorLinux short name
0Receiver ErrorRxErr

46.6 Mechanism step by step

The table below is the general recipe. Here it is as one concrete story: the SSD (at 02:00.0) asks host memory for data, the answer never comes, and the error travels to the OS. Click a step number, an arrow or a list item. Bus numbers, tags and register values are synthetic. synthetic

Software (OS) starts itDevice (SSD) starts itInside one component (not on the link)PCIe link
  1. The SSD sends a read request that is never answered

    The SSD's DMA engine is the requester here: it asks host memory for data (for example the next command or write data) with a non-posted Memory Read. Something on the host side drops it (an IOMMU fault, a hung root complex, a link retrain at the wrong moment), so no completion ever comes back.

    Where: SSD → root port → host memoryPCIe: Yes, device → host · MRd, 64 bytes; the CplD that should come back never arrives
    MRd Requester ID = 02:00.0 Tag = 0x12 Address = 0x1_2345_6000 Length = 16 DW
  2. The completion timer expires and the SSD sets its AER bits

    After the completion-timeout interval (its range is chosen in Device Control 2) the SSD gives up on tag 0x12. It sets Uncorrectable Error Status bit 14 (Completion Timeout), sets First Error Pointer to 14, and sets Non-Fatal Error Detected in its Device Status. A Completion Timeout has no received TLP to copy, so the Header Log is often empty unless the device supports logging the request header for timeouts (newer revisions).

    Where: SSD config space: AER capability + PCIe capabilityPCIe: No. Register changes only.
    Uncorrectable Error Status = 0x0000_4000 (bit 14) Severity bit 14 = 0 → non-fatal · Mask bit 14 = 0 → report it
  3. The SSD sends ERR_NONFATAL to the root port

    Because the error is unmasked, its severity bit says non-fatal, and Non-Fatal Error Reporting is enabled in Device Control, the SSD sends an error message upstream. The message carries the SSD's ID, but not which error it was: the details stay in the SSD's registers.

    Where: SSD → (switches) → root portPCIe: Yes, device → host · Msg ERR_NONFATAL, routed to the root complex
    Msg Requester ID = 02:00.0 Code = ERR_NONFATAL
  4. The root port records who sent it

    The root port sets "ERR_FATAL/NONFATAL Received" (bit 2) and "Non-Fatal Error Messages Received" (bit 5) in Root Error Status and, because this is the first such message, stores the sender's ID in Error Source Identification bits 31:16. A second message before software clears these would set the "Multiple" bit instead of overwriting the ID.

    Where: root port AER capability (Root Error Status, Error Source ID)PCIe: No. Root port internal.
    Root Error Status = 0x0000_0024 (bits 2 and 5) Error Source ID [31:16] = 0x0200 → bus 02, device 00, function 0
  5. The root port interrupts the CPU

    Root Error Command bit 1 (Non-Fatal Error Reporting Enable) is set, so the root port raises its own interrupt (the port's MSI or MSI-X vector). The kernel's AER port service handler runs. On firmware-first platforms the firmware would get this event instead, and the OS would later receive an APEI/GHES record.

    Where: root port → host interrupt controller → CPUPCIe: No. The root port is inside the root complex.
    /proc/interrupts: the count on the root port's "aer" / "PCIe PME, aer" line goes up
  6. The AER driver reads the registers

    The handler reads Root Error Status and Error Source ID from the root port, then uses the source ID to read the SSD's AER capability over the link: Uncorrectable Status, Mask, Severity, First Error Pointer and Header Log.

    Where: root port config space (local), SSD config space (remote)PCIe: Yes, host → device · CfgRd Type 1/0 (and CplD back) for the SSD's registers
    SSD: UE Status = 0x0000_4000, Severity = 0x0006_2030, FEP = 14 Header Log = 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000
  7. The AER driver writes the kernel log

    It decodes the bits into names and prints them: severity, which device, which error, whether it was the first error. This is the evidence an engineer later finds in dmesg or journal. The exact wording varies by kernel version.

    Where: kernel ring buffer (dmesg), AER statistics in sysfsPCIe: No
    pcieport 0000:00:1c.0: AER: Uncorrected (Non-Fatal) error received: 0000:02:00.0 nvme 0000:02:00.0: [14] CmpltTO (First) (illustrative wording, synthetic)
  8. Recovery: driver callbacks, reset, clear the bits

    The AER core calls the NVMe driver's error handlers. For a non-fatal error the driver usually resets the controller (or the core resets the link), the NVMe driver re-initialises queues and retries or fails the affected I/O, and the AER driver clears the status bits by writing 1s to them (RW1C) in both the SSD and the root port. The NVMe command whose data was lost may still end with an I/O error.

    Where: NVMe driver, SSD BAR0 (controller reset), SSD and root port config spacePCIe: Yes, host → device · CfgWr (RW1C clears), MWr to CC for the controller reset
    CfgWr SSD UE Status ← 0x0000_4000 (write 1 to clear) CfgWr root port Root Error Status ← 0x0000_0024 nvme nvme0: resetting controller → I/O resumes

If the severity bit for Completion Timeout had been set to 1, step 3 would send ERR_FATAL instead and recovery would normally reset the link. If the error had been masked, steps 3–8 would not happen at all, but the status bit from step 2 would still be set and visible with lspci.

#Who actsWhat changesWhereEvidence
1Receiver/requester/completer logic in the functionDetects error EFunction—
2FunctionSets Uncorrectable/Correctable Status bit E (even if masked, per spec for most errors)AER capStatus register
3FunctionIf uncorrectable, unmasked and no prior unhandled error: sets First Error Pointer = E, stores header in Header LogAER capFEP, Header Log
4FunctionSets Device Status error bit (CED/NFED/FED/URD)PCIe caplspci DevSta
5FunctionIf unmasked and Device Control reporting enabled: sends ERR_COR or ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_FATAL (by severity) upstreamLinkMsg TLP on analyzer
6Switch portsForward message upstream (bridges may convert/log per their control)Switch—
7Root portRoot Error Status bits; Error Source ID if firstRoot port AERRoot Error Status
8Root portIf Root Error Command enables: interrupt (MSI/MSI-X/INTx of root port)Host/proc/interrupts (aer)
9OS AER driverReads root + source device AER, logs, clears (RW1C), calls driver error handlers (error_detected, mmio_enabled, slot_reset, resume)Kerneldmesg, sysfs counters
10Platform (optional)Firmware-first: platform firmware handles AER and reports via APEI/GHESFirmwareDifferent log format (impl)
🏭 Implementation-dependent

On many servers AER is firmware-first: the BIOS/UEFI owns the AER registers (OS not granted control via _OSC), handles errors, and reports to the OS through APEI/GHES records. Then Linux logs look different and the OS may never see raw registers. Know which mode your platform uses before interpreting the absence of AER logs.

46.7 Decoding the Header Log

The Header Log holds the first 4 DW of the TLP header (for a 3DW header, DW3 is undefined/zero). Decode DW0 with the standard fields:

DW0 bits31:2928:242322:2019181716151413:1211:109:0
FieldFmtTypeT9TCT8Attr[2]LNTHTDEPAttr[1:0]ATLength (DW)
DW0 byte 0TLP
00h / 20hMRd 3DW / 4DW
40h / 60hMWr 3DW / 4DW
04h / 44hCfgRd0 / CfgWr0
0Ah / 4AhCpl / CplD
30h–37h / 70h–77hMsg / MsgD (routing in low 3 bits)

Requests DW1: Requester ID [31:16], Tag [15:8], Last DW BE [7:4], First DW BE [3:0]. DW2 (3DW) address [31:2]; for 4DW, DW2 = address [63:32], DW3 = address [31:2]. Completions DW1: Completer ID [31:16], Completion Status [15:13] (000 SC, 001 UR, 010 CRS, 100 CA), BCM [12], Byte Count [11:0]. DW2: Requester ID [31:16], Tag [15:8], Lower Address [6:0].

Worked decode 1 — Poisoned completion seen by the SSD

Device 02:00.0 AER Uncorrectable Status = 0x0000_1000   (bit 12 Poisoned TLP)
Header Log: 4A004010 00000040 02002A00 00000000

DW0 = 0x4A004010: byte 0 = 4Ah → CplD; bit 14 EP = 1 (poisoned); Length = 0x010 = 16 DW = 64 bytes. DW1 = 0x0000_0040: Completer ID 0000 (root complex), status 000 (SC), Byte Count 0x040 = 64. DW2 = 0x0200_2A00: Requester ID 0x0200 = 02:00.0 (the SSD itself), Tag 0x2A, Lower Address 0. Interpretation: a 64-byte read by the SSD came back poisoned — exactly an SQE fetch size (or a 64-byte PRP list/data chunk). Correlate tag 0x2A at that time in a trace, or the SQ base address, to identify which. Cause direction: host memory or RC (the poison was applied upstream). Next evidence: host MCE/EDAC logs.

Worked decode 2 — Malformed TLP at the root port

Root port 00:01.1 AER Uncorrectable Status = 0x0004_0000 (bit 18 Malformed TLP), severity fatal
Header Log: 60000040 020000FF 00000001 40000000

DW0: byte 0 = 60h → MWr 4DW; Length 0x040 = 64 DW = 256 bytes. DW1: Requester 0x0200 (the SSD), Tag 00 (writes may carry any tag), BEs FF. Address = 0x1_4000_0000 → data buffer region (read data DMA). Interpretation: 256-byte write rejected as malformed — check root port MPS: if 128, the SSD was misconfigured with MPS 256 (or ignored its setting). Next evidence: lspci -vvv DevCtl MaxPayload on both ends.

Worked decode 3 — Unsupported Request at the SSD

Device 02:00.0 AER Uncorrectable Status = 0x0010_0000 (bit 20 UR)
Header Log: 00000001 00000C0F F7A0001C 00000000

DW0: MRd 3DW, Length 1 DW. DW1: Requester 0x0000 (host RC), Tag 0x0C, First BE F. DW2: address 0xF7A0_001C = BAR0 + 1Ch = CSTS. Interpretation: the host read CSTS and the SSD answered UR — the SSD was not accepting memory requests (e.g. in D3hot, Memory Space Enable clear, or mid-reset). The host saw a UR completion → returned all-ones to the CPU → driver sees CSTS = 0xFFFFFFFF. Symptom or cause? Symptom of a power/reset state problem.

Worked decode 4 — Completion Timeout

Status bit 14 set; Header Log usually not meaningful for CTO (no received TLP). Newer components may advertise Completion Timeout Prefix/Header Log Capable and log the request header (version). Without it, correlate by time and by the device's outstanding request types — a trace is needed.

46.8 Linux view

sudo lspci -vvv -s 02:00.0 | sed -n '/Advanced Error Reporting/,/HeaderLog/p'
#   UESta: DLP- SDES- TLP- FCP- CmpltTO- CmpltAbrt- UnxCmplt- RxOF- MalfTLP- ECRC- UnsupReq- ACSViol-
#   UEMsk: ...   UESvrt: DLP+ SDES+ ... MalfTLP+ ...
#   CESta: RxErr- BadTLP- BadDLLP- Rollover- Timeout- AdvNonFatalErr-
#   AERCap: First Error Pointer: 00, ECRCGenCap- ECRCGenEn- ECRCChkCap- ECRCChkEn-
#   HeaderLog: 00000000 00000000 00000000 00000000            (illustrative)
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/aer_dev_correctable   # per-error counters
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/aer_dev_nonfatal
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/aer_dev_fatal
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:00:01.1/aer_rootport_total_err_cor
sudo journalctl -k | grep -i -E "aer|pcie bus error"
Illustrative, abbreviated dmesg lines (format approximates Linux AER driver output; IDs replaced; not from a real system)
pcieport 0000:00:01.1: AER: Uncorrected (Non-Fatal) error message received from 0000:02:00.0
nvme 0000:02:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrectable (Non-Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Requester ID)
nvme 0000:02:00.0:   device [vvvv:dddd] error status/mask=00004000/00400000
nvme 0000:02:00.0:    [14] CmpltTO
pcieport 0000:00:01.1: AER: Corrected error message received from 0000:02:00.0
nvme 0000:02:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Correctable, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID)
nvme 0000:02:00.0:   device [vvvv:dddd] error status/mask=00000001/0000e000
nvme 0000:02:00.0:    [ 0] RxErr

Reading the lines: "status/mask=00004000/00400000" → status bit 14 (Completion Timeout); mask bit 22 (Uncorrectable Internal Error masked by default). "00000001/0000e000" → Receiver Error; mask bits 13–15 default-masked. The "(Requester ID)" / "(Receiver ID)" annotation tells you whether the logging agent was acting as requester or receiver. Can prove: which error bits were set at the time the OS read them, source device. Cannot prove: errors that were masked, cleared by firmware-first handling, or that occurred on devices without AER; which NVMe command was affected (needs header/trace correlation).

⚠️ Safety

setpci can write AER mask/severity registers; doing so on a production system can hide real errors or turn a correctable condition into a system-wide fatal recovery. Use read-only lspci and sysfs. Tools like aer-inject require a kernel module and are for test systems only.

46.9 Protocol view and trace view

Error messages are Msg TLPs routed to the Root Complex, codes ERR_COR (30h), ERR_NONFATAL (31h), ERR_FATAL (33h) (verified message codes), Requester ID = reporting function.

Synthetic trace — normal: correctable error reported

Reasoning: two endpoints under one switch both reporting non-fatal errors at the same time suggests a shared upstream cause — check the switch's upstream/downstream port AER. The root's single Source ID can mislead you into blaming 03:00.0 alone.

46.11 Labs

🧪 Lab 46.1 (beginner) — Read AER state safely SAFE

Objective: locate AER in lspci and sysfs. Procedure: run §46.8 commands for the NVMe device and its root port (lspci -tv to find it). Observations: is AER present? which bits set? counters? Questions: are any errors masked that you'd want unmasked?

Solution

Most systems show zeros. Default masks: Uncorrectable Internal Error; correctable Advisory Non-Fatal, Corrected Internal, Header Log Overflow. Counters in sysfs accumulate since boot even after status is cleared.

🧪 Lab 46.2 (intermediate) — Decode status/mask words SAFE

Given: UE status 0x0010_4000, CE status 0x0000_1041. Procedure: decode.

Solution

UE: bit 14 Completion Timeout, bit 20 Unsupported Request. CE: bit 0 Receiver Error, bit 6 Bad TLP, bit 12 Replay Timer Timeout. Interpretation: noisy link plus at least one transaction failure; ask whether the CTO followed a retrain.

🧪 Lab 46.3 (advanced) — Header log decoding drill SAFE

Given: (a) 4A000010 00000040 02001100 00000000 logged as Unexpected Completion at 02:00.0; (b) 40000001 0000000F F7A01018 00000000 logged as UR at 02:00.0.

Solution

(a) CplD, 16 DW, not poisoned; Completer 0000, BC 64; Requester 0200, tag 0x11. The SSD got a completion for tag 0x11 it no longer expected — typical after the device already timed out that request (late completion) → correlate with an earlier CmpltTO. (b) MWr 3DW, 1 DW, Requester 0000, tag 00, First BE F, address 0xF7A0_1018 = SQ3 tail doorbell. A doorbell write was rejected as UR: the device was not accepting memory writes (in reset/D3hot/MSE clear) → the doorbell was lost; expect an NVMe timeout later.

🧪 Lab 46.4 (senior) — AER forensics lab SAFE

Objective: answer the six forensic questions from a full evidence pack. Device topology (synthetic):

00:00.0 Root Complex
 └─ 00:01.1 Root Port (MPS 256)
     └─ 01:00.0 Switch upstream port
         ├─ 02:00.0 Switch downstream port ── 03:00.0 NVMe SSD A
         └─ 02:01.0 Switch downstream port ── 04:00.0 NVMe SSD B

AER status: 03:00.0 UESta = 0x0000_4000 (CmpltTO), no header; 04:00.0 clean; 02:00.0 (downstream port) UESta = 0x0001_0000 (Unexpected Completion), Header Log 4A000010 00000040 03001F00 00000000; root port Root Error Status = 0x0000_0024, Error Source ID [31:16] = 0x0300.

Trace (synthetic, captured between 02:00.0 and 03:00.0):

Synthetic trace — SSD A link
tDirPacketDetail
0↓MWrSQ2 tail doorbell
0.6 µs↑MRdtag 0x1F, 16 DW, SQ2 slot
0.6 µs – 50 ms——no CplD tag 0x1F visible on this link
50 ms↑Msg ERR_NONFATALfrom 0300
(none)——no CplD for 0x1F ever visible on this link

Questions: 1. What error occurred? 2. Which TLP is implicated? 3. Which requester? 4. Which completer? 5. Symptom or cause? 6. What additional evidence is needed?

Solution

1. SSD A reported a Completion Timeout; the switch downstream port 02:00.0 reported an Unexpected Completion. 2. The SQE-fetch MRd with tag 0x1F (16 DW) from 03:00.0. The header logged at 02:00.0 is a CplD with Requester ID 0x0300 and tag 0x1F, byte count 64 — the completion for that very request. 3. Requester: 03:00.0 (SSD A). 4. Completer: the root complex (Completer ID 0000). 5. The CTO is a symptom. The completion did come back but was rejected at the switch's downstream port as unexpected — so it never reached the SSD. Why would a switch port consider a completion for 03:00.0 unexpected? Possibilities: the completion arrived after the port considered the request expired (unlikely — switches don't time out), or more plausibly the completion was routed by ID to a bus number that doesn't match the port's secondary/subordinate bus range at that moment — e.g. bus numbers were reprogrammed (hot-plug rescan) or the completion carried a corrupted Requester ID. Given the logged Requester ID 0x0300 is correct, check the port's bus number registers and any recent re-enumeration. 6. Evidence needed: switch port config (secondary/subordinate bus), timeline of hot-plug/rescan events, a capture on the upstream side of the switch to see when the CplD arrived, root port AER (0x24 = ERR_FATAL/NONFATAL received + non-fatal messages), switch vendor counters. Confidence in "switch-side routing/state problem rather than SSD fault": medium.

Extension: rewrite the conclusion if the logged Requester ID had been 0x0400 (SSD B).

46.12 Interview questions

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What does AER add over baseline error reporting?
    Model answer

    Per-error status, masks, severity, first error pointer, header log, root error collection.

  2. Beginner What is the Header Log?
    Model answer

    The first 16 bytes of the header of the TLP associated with the first logged uncorrectable error.

  3. Beginner How do you clear an AER status bit?
    Model answer

    Write 1 to it (RW1C).

  4. Beginner Where are root-level AER registers?
    Model answer

    Root ports/RCECs: Root Error Command, Root Error Status, Error Source Identification.

  5. Beginner What's the difference between NVMe AER and PCIe AER?
    Model answer

    NVMe Asynchronous Event Request (command) vs PCIe Advanced Error Reporting (capability).

  6. Intermediate What does severity control?
    Model answer

    Whether an uncorrectable error is signalled as ERR_FATAL or ERR_NONFATAL.

  7. Intermediate Why might the header log be zero for a CTO?
    Model answer

    No TLP was received; CTO header logging is an optional newer capability.

  8. Intermediate What is First Error Pointer?
    Model answer

    Bit index of the first uncorrectable error recorded; ties the header log to that error.

  9. Intermediate What does "Multiple ERR_COR Received" mean?
    Model answer

    More correctable messages arrived after the first was logged; the source ID only identifies the first.

  10. Intermediate What is firmware-first?
    Model answer

    Platform firmware owns AER handling and reports through APEI/GHES.

  11. Advanced Decode header DW0 0x4A004010.
    Model answer

    CplD, EP=1, 16 DW.

  12. Advanced Why would masking Surprise Down be done?
    Model answer

    During intentional link-down operations (hot-plug, resets) to avoid fatal reporting of an expected event.

  13. Advanced What are Linux PCI error recovery callbacks?
    Model answer

    error_detected, mmio_enabled, slot_reset, resume (and reset_prepare/done for resets).

  14. Advanced How does DPC relate to AER?
    Model answer

    DPC uses uncorrectable error detection at a downstream port to disable the link and contain errors; AER still provides details.

  15. Advanced How do you map a header log to an NVMe command?
    Model answer

    Requester/tag/address → SQ/CQ/PRP region from address map → slot → CID via SQE or trace.

  16. Senior What's your policy for correctable error thresholds?
    Model answer

    Rate-based alerting per link, correlate with temperature/ASPM/speed, schedule maintenance before fatal; avoid per-event paging.

  17. Senior Why is AER evidence often incomplete?
    Model answer

    Masking, firmware-first, OS clears status, single header slot, first-source-only, devices without AER.

  18. Senior How do you validate AER handling?
    Model answer

    Error injection (platform EINJ, aer-inject, analyzer/exerciser injection) on test systems; verify logging and recovery paths.

  19. Senior Two devices report errors simultaneously. What do you suspect?
    Model answer

    Common upstream component (switch, root port, power, clock).

  20. Senior When would you change severity defaults?
    Model answer

    Rarely; e.g. to downgrade a known benign error on specific hardware after root-cause, with documented risk.

📌 Teach-back

Child: logbooks with taped boxes and envelope photocopies. Junior: registers, bits, header decode. Senior: evidence completeness, firmware-first, cross-device reasoning, recovery flows.

✅ Mastery gate
  • Explain every AER register and bit listed.
  • Diagram the reporting path endpoint → switch → root port → OS.
  • Decode any header log into a TLP and map it to NVMe activity.
  • Debug with the five patterns; recognise firmware-first.
  • Distinguish AER (PCIe) from NVMe Asynchronous Events.
  • Cite: PCIe Base Specification AER capability.

Next: Chapter 47 — putting all error floors together.

47 Error Correlation Across Layers

← 46 AER — Advanced Error Reporting (Deep-Dive Module: AER)48 NVMe Reset (Deep-Dive Module: Reset, NVMe Side) →

47.1 Why this chapter exists

A user says "the SSD is broken". The SSD vendor says "our drive is fine". The platform team says "PCIe is healthy". Everyone may be honest and wrong, because each looked at one floor. This chapter trains you to distinguish software issue vs driver issue vs NVMe issue vs PCIe transaction issue vs link issue vs firmware issue vs media issue with explicit decision trees, an error correlation matrix, a "what would you capture" ladder, multi-layer failure cases, and a safe error-injection lab.

47.2 Learning objectives

  • Assign any error observation to a layer with a stated confidence.
  • Use decision trees starting from the five common symptoms.
  • Know what each evidence source can and cannot prove.
  • Diagnose multi-layer failures where one layer looks healthy and another fails.
  • Run simulated error injection and diagnose the results.

47.3 Analogy

🌍 Analogy

A package didn't arrive. Was the order form wrong (software), did the clerk mistype it (driver), did the warehouse reject it (NVMe), did the courier lose the parcel at a depot (PCIe transaction), was the road flooded (link), did the warehouse robot crash (firmware), or was the item itself broken on the shelf (media)? Each has a different paper trail: order history, clerk's notes, warehouse rejection slip, courier tracking, road reports, robot logs, inventory quality reports.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In real systems the layers share timing and resources: a flooded road (link errors) can make the warehouse robot (firmware) hit an internal timeout and report "internal error" — so a firmware symptom can have a link cause. Layer boundaries are where causality crosses, not where it stops.

47.4 The layers and their evidence

47.6 Decision trees

Tree A — "I/O timed out"

I/O timeout (driver)
├─ Read CSTS
│   ├─ 0xFFFFFFFF ──► device unreachable ─► check LnkSta, AER/DPC on root port, lspci presence
│   │                   ├─ link down / Surprise Down ─► LINK or POWER (or intentional reset)
│   │                   └─ link up, config reads OK, BAR reads all-ones ─► Memory Space disabled / D3 / reset ─► DRIVER/PM
│   ├─ CFS=1 ─► FIRMWARE (controller fatal) ─► reset, collect telemetry
│   └─ RDY=1, CFS=0 ─► controller alive
│        ├─ CQE present in memory with valid phase? (driver debug / timeout handler message)
│        │    └─ yes ─► INTERRUPT path ─► MSI-X mask/PBA, affinity, remapping (DRIVER/PLATFORM)
│        ├─ device AER CmpltTO? ─► PCIe TRANSACTION (host didn't answer device reads) ─► IOMMU, switch
│        ├─ async event on admin CQ (invalid doorbell)? ─► DRIVER (doorbell offset/value)
│        └─ nothing ─► FIRMWARE hang on command or MEDIA stall ─► vendor telemetry, retry same LBA

Tree B — "Command returned an error status"

Non-zero status
├─ SCT 0 (generic)
│   ├─ 01h/02h/0Bh/0Ch/13h ─► HOST (software/driver) ─► Error log PEL, Identify capabilities
│   ├─ 03h ─► DRIVER (CID reuse)
│   ├─ 04h ─► TRANSPORT ─► AER, IOMMU
│   ├─ 06h ─► FIRMWARE (± transport) ─► telemetry, AER internal errors
│   ├─ 07h/08h ─► HOST ACTION (abort/teardown) ─► why was it aborted? (timeout upstream)
│   └─ 80h–84h (NVM) ─► HOST/CONFIG (range, capacity, reservations, format state)
├─ SCT 1 ─► HOST misuse of a specific command (check command semantics)
├─ SCT 2 ─► MEDIA (81h/80h) or DATA INTEGRITY (82h–84h: host PI vs device)
├─ SCT 3 ─► PATH (multipath/ANA)
└─ SCT 7 ─► VENDOR ─► vendor docs

Tree C — "Wrong data, success status"

Corruption with success
├─ PI enabled and no E2E errors? ─► device path likely clean ─► HOST: buffer reuse, IOMMU lifetime, app bug
├─ Same LBA reads differently over time? ─► MEDIA/FIRMWARE (silent corruption) ─► rare; capture data MWr payloads
├─ Corruption pattern = stale previous contents? ─► CQE before data (ordering/RO), or ignored error status ─► check RO, check status handling
└─ Corruption = shifted/other LBA data? ─► wrong PRP/LBA ─► DRIVER/FIRMWARE ─► decode SQE from trace

47.7 Multi-layer failure cases

CaseWhat looks healthyWhat failsHow to separate the layers
1. PCIe healthy, NVMe failsNo AER, link at full speed/width, all TLPs well-formedReads return 81h at a cluster of LBAs; SMART media_errors climbingClean transport + reproducible LBA-specific status → media. Confirm with error log LBAs and SMART trends.
2. NVMe healthy, PCIe failsEvery CQE that arrives has status 0; controller logs cleanRxErr storm, Gen4→Gen3 downgrade, throughput halved, occasional CTOCorrectable errors and LnkSta prove link; NVMe layer is a victim. Reseat/retimer/slot swap test.
3. Both healthy, software misuseNo AER, status 0 everywhereDatabase corruption after power lossNo Flush/FUA in captured command stream (complete capture) + VWC enabled → host durability bug.
4. Both healthy, software misuse (DMA)No AER, status 0Random 4 KiB blocks of garbage in filesIOMMU strict mode reveals faults on unmapped IOVAs → buffer freed before completion.
5. Link cause, firmware symptomDriver fineStatus 06h Internal Error occasionallyError times align with Recovery events/replays; firmware's internal DMA timeout triggered by link stalls. Fix link; errors vanish.
6. Power management cause, PCIe symptomWorks under loadUR/CTO only after idleCorrelate with APST/ASPM transitions; disable each separately (test system).

47.9 Error-injection lab (simulated)

🧪 Lab 47.1 — Simulated error injection and diagnosis SAFE

Objective: inject faults into a model of the end-to-end read and practise diagnosing them from the resulting synthetic evidence — without touching hardware. Prerequisites: Python 3. Setup: the simulator below produces an event list (simplified event model) and evidence (AER, status, logs) for a single 4 KiB read under a chosen fault.

FAULTS = ["none", "missing_completion", "invalid_opcode", "invalid_prp",
          "unsupported_request", "completion_timeout", "malformed", "link_recovery"]

def simulate(fault):
    ev, aer, status, log = [], {}, None, []
    t = 0.0
    def e(dt, d, typ, info):
        nonlocal t; t += dt; ev.append((round(t, 2), d, typ, info))
    e(0, "dn", "MWr", "SQ3 tail doorbell")
    if fault == "unsupported_request":            # device not accepting memory requests
        aer["dev"] = "UnsupReq, header=MWr 3DW BAR0+1018h"
        log.append("t=30s nvme: I/O timeout QID3 (illustrative)")
        return ev, aer, status, log
    e(0.6, "up", "MRd", "SQE fetch tag 0x11")
    if fault in ("missing_completion", "completion_timeout"):
        aer["dev"] = "CmpltTO"
        if fault == "missing_completion":
            log.append("IOMMU fault: read 0x123401080 not mapped (illustrative)")
        log.append("t=30s nvme: I/O timeout QID3 (illustrative)")
        return ev, aer, status, log
    e(0.9, "dn", "CplD", "tag 0x11 SQE" + (" opcode 0xFF" if fault == "invalid_opcode" else ""))
    if fault == "invalid_opcode":
        status = "SCT0/SC01h DNR"
    elif fault == "invalid_prp":
        status = "SCT0/SC13h PRP Offset Invalid DNR"
    else:
        if fault == "link_recovery":
            e(10, "--", "LTSSM", "Recovery entered (REPLAY_NUM rollover)")
            aer["dev"] = "Rollover, BadTLP (correctable)"
        e(60, "up", "MWr x16", "data")
        if fault == "malformed":
            aer["rootport"] = "MalfTLP fatal, header=MWr 4DW len 64DW"
            log.append("AER fatal -> link reset, I/O error (illustrative)")
            return ev, aer, status, log
        status = "success"
    e(0.1, "up", "MWr", "CQE " + status)
    e(0.05, "up", "MWr", "MSI-X")
    e(3, "dn", "MWr", "CQ3 head doorbell")
    return ev, aer, status, log

import random
f = random.choice(FAULTS)
ev, aer, status, log = simulate(f)
for x in ev: print(x)
print("AER:", aer, "\nNVMe status:", status, "\nlogs:", log)
# Diagnose before printing f!
# print("injected:", f)

Procedure: run the simulator 10 times; for each run, before revealing the injected fault, write (1) first abnormal event, (2) layer, (3) symptom vs cause, (4) next evidence you would request, (5) confidence.

Observations: keep a table of your diagnoses vs the truth.

Questions: Which two faults produce nearly identical evidence? What extra evidence separates them? Why does "invalid_opcode" produce no data TLPs? Why does "link_recovery" still end with success?

Solution

"missing_completion" and "completion_timeout" both show an MRd without CplD and CmpltTO at the device; only the IOMMU fault log (or a capture at the RC side) separates "host refused" from "completion lost in fabric". "invalid_opcode": controller rejects at parse, posts CQE with SCT0/01h — no data phase; layer = host/driver (or a corrupted SQE — check the CplD payload against what the driver wrote). "invalid_prp": host/driver bug, DNR. "unsupported_request": the doorbell itself was rejected (device in D3hot/reset/MSE clear) — no fetch at all; first abnormal event is the UR logged against the doorbell; timeout is a symptom 30 s later. "malformed": data MWr exceeded root port MPS → fatal at root port → link reset; cause is configuration. "link_recovery": correctable; replays/retrain recovered transparently — I/O succeeded with added latency; layer = link; evidence is the correctable counters.

Extension: add faults "poisoned_cpld", "msix_masked" and "cqe_before_data (RO bug)"; generate an ambiguous variant where the capture misses the upstream direction, and practise negative-evidence phrasing.

47.10 Worked example: the 3 a.m. page

Observations (synthetic): database reports I/O errors at 03:12:44; dmesg shows "I/O … QID 7 timeout, aborting", then an abort attempt that itself times out, then a controller reset (exact message wording is impl/kernel-version dependent); after reset the drive works. AER: root port logged Receiver Errors (correctable) at a low rate for weeks; no uncorrectable errors were logged at or around 03:12:44. SMART clean. LnkSta Gen4 x4.

Analysis: timeline T0 (weeks of RxErr — background), T1 03:12:14 (30 s before timeout — the command was submitted), T2 timeout, T3 abort, T4 reset recovers. First abnormal event in the evidence: the command at 03:12:14 that never completed. Was it fetched? Unknown — no trace (negative evidence: we cannot say it wasn't). Hypotheses: (a) firmware hang on that command (reset fixes; no CFS though), (b) lost interrupt (CQE present? — the driver would have reported completion in the timeout handler; it didn't), (c) lost doorbell due to link error (RxErr on the downstream direction would cause replay, not loss — the DLL guarantees delivery unless the link fails). Conclusion: most likely firmware (medium confidence); background RxErr probably unrelated but should be fixed. Next evidence: vendor telemetry captured after the event (Telemetry Host-Initiated log), firmware version vs known errata, and enabling nvme tracepoints for the next occurrence.

Quiz

  1. CSTS reads 0xFFFFFFFF. Which layer first?

    Answer

    PCIe/link/power/reset state — the MMIO read itself failed.

  2. Status 04h Data Transfer Error — which evidence next?

    Answer

    AER on device and ports, IOMMU faults.

  3. Corruption with PI enabled and no E2E errors suggests?

    Answer

    Host-side problem (buffer lifetime, app), since device path is PI-protected.

  4. Can a link problem cause an NVMe Internal Error status?

    Answer

    Yes — e.g. firmware internal timeouts triggered by link stalls; correlate timing.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate How do you tell a driver bug from a device bug on an invalid-field status?
    Model answer

    Error log Parameter Error Location + decode the SQE as fetched (trace CplD) vs what the driver intended; if the fetched SQE is valid per spec, device bug.

  2. Advanced Walk through the decision tree for timeouts.
    Model answer

    CSTS all-ones vs CFS vs alive; CQE present → interrupts; AER CTO → transport; async events → doorbell; else firmware/media.

  3. Senior Describe a case where every layer looked healthy yet data was lost.
    Model answer

    Missing Flush/FUA with VWC enabled and power loss; proven by command stream and VWC settings.

  4. Senior How do you avoid blaming the first visible error?
    Model answer

    Build an expected vs observed timeline, look backwards for earlier deviations, state confidence, apply negative-evidence discipline.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can place any observation in the correlation matrix with justification.
  • I can walk all three decision trees from memory.
  • I can explain the six multi-layer cases.
  • I can state what each evidence source can and cannot prove.
  • I diagnosed at least 8/10 simulated injections correctly.

Next: Part XVI — Power and reset.

PART XVI

Power and Reset

Resets and power transitions are where state goes to die — and where many of the hardest bugs live. An NVMe SSD has state at several levels: NVMe controller registers and queues, the NVM subsystem shared by controllers, the PCIe function's configuration space, the link's training state, and the physical power rails. Each reset type and each power state wipes a different subset of that state, takes a different amount of time, and leaves different evidence. This part teaches you, for every reset and every power transition, exactly what is lost, what survives, what the host must rebuild, and how to recognise each one in a trace or a log.

48 NVMe Reset (Deep-Dive Module: Reset, NVMe Side)

← 47 Error Correlation Across Layers49 PCIe Reset →

48.1 Why this chapter exists

When an NVMe command times out, Linux's escalation ends in a controller reset. When firmware is updated, activation may need a reset. When the system shuts down, the controller must be told so that it can flush its caches and mark itself clean — otherwise the next boot may see an "unsafe shutdown" and spend time rebuilding mapping tables. Each of these is a different NVMe mechanism: Controller Reset (CC.EN 1→0), NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR), and Shutdown (CC.SHN / CSTS.SHST). Confusing them causes lost data, hung reboots and "drive disappeared" incidents.

48.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: state what CC.EN, CSTS.RDY, CC.SHN, CSTS.SHST and NSSR do.
  • Intermediate: list the state destroyed and preserved by a controller reset; write the re-initialisation sequence.
  • Advanced: explain outstanding command handling, CAP.TO timing, NSSR scope and its PCIe side effects; distinguish normal vs abrupt shutdown.
  • Senior: design a robust reset/recovery ladder and reason about lost commands.
  • Trace-analysis: recognise reset and re-init sequences on the link.
  • Debugging/validation: five failure patterns; validate reset correctness.

48.3 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

A controller reset is the warehouse manager blowing a whistle: every worker drops what they're holding, all the trays except the main office tray are thrown away, and work starts again only when the manager says "ready". Shutdown is closing time: workers finish putting things on shelves, lock up, and hang a sign "closed properly". NVM subsystem reset is turning off the power to the whole warehouse complex, including the other managers' buildings next door.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Dropped work isn't reported: commands outstanding at a controller reset simply never get CQEs — the host has to know to treat them as aborted. And "closed properly" (SHST complete) does not by itself mean power is off; the host decides what happens next (power off, D3, keep running).

48.4 Registers involved

Register (offset)FieldBitsMeaning
CAP (00h)TO31:24Worst-case time for RDY to change after EN changes, in 500 ms units
CAP (00h)NSSRS36NVM Subsystem Reset supported
CC (14h)EN0Enable; 1→0 = controller reset
CC (14h)SHN15:14Shutdown Notification: 00 none, 01 normal, 10 abrupt
CSTS (1Ch)RDY0Ready
CSTS (1Ch)CFS1Controller Fatal Status
CSTS (1Ch)SHST3:2Shutdown Status: 00 normal operation, 01 shutdown processing occurring, 10 shutdown processing complete
CSTS (1Ch)NSSRO4NVM Subsystem Reset Occurred (RW1C)
CSTS (1Ch)PP5Processing Paused
NSSR (20h)NSSRC31:0Write 4E564D65h ("NVMe") to initiate NVM Subsystem Reset
AQA/ASQ/ACQ (24h/28h/30h)——Admin queue attributes/bases — preserved across controller reset

48.5 Controller Reset (CC.EN 1 → 0)

Effects (verified in substance; consult Base spec "Controller Reset" for normative text):

  • The controller stops processing commands; all I/O SQs and CQs are deleted; outstanding commands are not completed (the host treats them as aborted).
  • Controller registers return to their reset values except the admin queue registers (AQA, ASQ, ACQ), which are retained; CSTS.RDY goes to 0 within CAP.TO.
  • Internal controller state (Set Features values that are not saved, Asynchronous Event state, etc.) resets; persistent namespace data is unaffected; writes already completed remain subject to cache rules (a reset is not a power loss, but a host should Flush before a deliberate reset if durability matters).
  • The PCIe function, its configuration space, BARs, MSI-X configuration and the link are not reset by CC.EN alone.

Re-initialisation sequence:

// Controller reset + re-init (host side)
cc = mmio_read32(CC); cc &= ~CC_EN; mmio_write32(CC, cc);   // MWr to BAR0+14h
wait_until(mmio_read32(CSTS) & RDY == 0, CAP.TO * 500 ms);   // MRd/CplD polling
// all I/O queues are gone; outstanding CIDs -> fail/requeue in software
mmio_write32(AQA, (acqs-1) << 16 | (asqs-1));               // optional: retained, but reprogram
mmio_write64(ASQ, asq_iova); mmio_write64(ACQ, acq_iova);
mmio_write32(CC, CSS | MPS | AMS | IOSQES(6) | IOCQES(4) | EN);
wait_until(mmio_read32(CSTS) & RDY == 1, CAP.TO * 500 ms);
if (CSTS & CFS) escalate();                                    // PCIe-level reset
identify_controller();                                         // re-validate (FW may have changed)
set_features(NUM_QUEUES 07h);                                  // re-negotiate
for each queue: create_io_cq(qid, iv), create_io_sq(qid, cqid); // CQs first, then SQs
submit_async_event_requests(AERL+1 or fewer);
restore_features();   // e.g. APST (0Ch), coalescing (08h), VWC (06h), HMB (0Dh) if used
resubmit_or_fail(outstanding_requests);
⚠️ Host Memory Buffer

If the controller uses an HMB (Feature 0Dh), the host must keep the HMB memory intact and mapped until the controller is reset or the HMB disabled; after a controller reset the host re-enables it. Freeing HMB memory while the device may still access it is a classic use-after-free DMA hazard (derived).

48.6 Outstanding commands — the lost-command problem

At the moment of reset, a command can be in any of these states; the host cannot generally tell which:

State at resetHas data moved?Media effectHost treatment
In SQ, not fetchedNoNoneResubmit safe
Fetched, not startedNoNoneResubmit safe
Read in progressPartially into host bufferNoneResubmit (buffer contents undefined until success)
Write in progressPartially fetchedMay be partially written (atomicity rules — AWUN/AWUPF — define what's guaranteed)Resubmit; upper layers must tolerate torn writes beyond atomic size
Completed, CQE posted but not consumedYesDoneCQE is lost with CQ deletion; host may resubmit — idempotent for read/write, not for e.g. some admin commands
💡 Senior insight

The dangerous cases are non-idempotent commands (Firmware Commit, Format, Sanitize, Namespace Management, reservation commands) and writes whose completion was lost. Robust hosts poll the CQ one last time before resetting (Linux's timeout handler does check for a completed CQE), and upper layers must use FUA/Flush and journalling, not assumptions about which writes landed.

48.7 NVM Subsystem Reset (NSSR)

If CAP.NSSRS = 1, writing 4E564D65h to NSSR (20h) resets the whole NVM subsystem — every controller in it, on every port. After it, CSTS.NSSRO = 1 tells hosts it happened. Because the subsystem includes the PCIe port logic on many designs, the PCIe link may go down and retrain (impl) — the root port may log Surprise Down unless masked, and Linux must handle the device as if it had been reset at the PCIe level (re-restore config space). Linux exposes it as nvme subsystem-reset.

⚠️ Safety

nvme reset and nvme subsystem-reset interrupt all I/O on the device; on a boot or root device this can crash or hang the system. Use only on dedicated test devices.

48.8 Shutdown

TypeCC.SHNController doesHost waits forUse
Normal01bCompletes/flushes internal work, saves metadata, marks cleanCSTS.SHST = 10b (time guided by RTD3E in Identify Controller and host timeout; Linux nvme_core.shutdown_timeout)Power off, reboot, suspend-to-power-off
Abrupt10bMinimal processing to reach a safe state quicklyCSTS.SHST = 10bImminent power loss; time-critical

Recommended order (normal shutdown): stop new I/O → wait for or abort outstanding commands → delete I/O SQs, then I/O CQs → set CC.SHN = 01b → poll SHST until 10b → (optionally) clear EN, transition to D3hot/D3cold or power off. To restart after shutdown, the host performs a controller reset/enable sequence. Newer specification revisions also define NVM-subsystem-level shutdown — version.

🔍 Evidence

SMART/Health log "Unsafe Shutdowns" counter increments when the controller lost power without a completed shutdown. A rising unsafe-shutdown count with no known power failures implicates the host's shutdown path (timeouts too short, platform cuts power early).

Here is the whole "clean stop, then restart" sequence on one picture: a normal shutdown, then a controller reset, then re-initialisation. The strip at the bottom shows how the four register fields change; values that just changed are highlighted. Click a step number, an arrow or a list item. synthetic

Software (driver) starts itInside the SSD (not on the PCIe link)Host memoryPCIe link
  1. Stop new I/O and delete the I/O queues

    The driver stops accepting new requests, waits for (or aborts) outstanding commands, then sends Delete I/O Submission Queue (00h) for every I/O SQ, followed by Delete I/O Completion Queue (04h) for every I/O CQ. SQs go first because each SQ points at a CQ.

    Where: admin SQ in host memory; the controller fetches and executes the commandsPCIe: Yes · doorbell MWr, SQE fetch (MRd/CplD), CQE MWr for each admin command
    Delete I/O SQ 1..8, then Delete I/O CQ 1..8 (8 queue pairs, synthetic)
  2. Request a normal shutdown: CC.SHN = 01b

    The driver reads CC, sets the Shutdown Notification field (bits 15:14) to 01b (normal) and writes it back. EN stays 1.

    Where: CC register at BAR0 + 14hPCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes
    CC: 0x0046_0001 → 0x0046_4001 (SHN = 01b; EN = 1)
  3. The controller starts shutdown processing: SHST = 01b

    The controller reports "shutdown processing occurring" in CSTS.SHST and starts its work: finishing anything in flight, writing its volatile cache and mapping tables to NAND, and recording a clean shutdown.

    Where: inside the SSD; CSTS at BAR0 + 1ChPCIe: No. Internal work; nothing is sent.
    CSTS: SHST = 01b, RDY = 1
  4. The controller finishes: SHST = 10b

    When everything is safe, the controller sets SHST = 10b (shutdown processing complete). How long this takes is device-specific; Identify Controller RTD3E gives a hint, and the host also has its own timeout.

    Where: CSTS at BAR0 + 1ChPCIe: No
    CSTS: SHST = 10b, RDY = 1 (e.g. 180 ms after step 2, synthetic)
  5. The driver polls CSTS until SHST = 10b

    The driver reads CSTS in a loop. Each read is a full round trip over PCIe. If SHST does not reach 10b before the host's timeout, the host gives up; the next power-up will count an unsafe shutdown in the SMART log.

    Where: CSTS at BAR0 + 1ChPCIe: Yes · MRd (host → device), CplD with 4 bytes (device → host), repeated
    reads: 0x0000_0005 (SHST=01b, RDY=1) … 0x0000_0009 (SHST=10b, RDY=1)
  6. Controller reset: CC.EN = 0

    To use the device again (instead of powering it off), the host performs a controller reset by clearing CC.EN (and SHN). This is the same reset used for error recovery.

    Where: CC at BAR0 + 14hPCIe: Yes, host → device · MWr, 4 bytes
    CC: 0x0046_4001 → 0x0046_0000 (EN = 0, SHN = 00b)
  7. The controller resets: RDY → 0

    The controller drops all I/O queue state and any outstanding commands, returns its registers to reset values except AQA, ASQ and ACQ, and clears CSTS.RDY within CAP.TO. SHST returns to 00b. Config space, BARs, MSI-X and the PCIe link are not touched.

    Where: inside the SSD; CSTSPCIe: No
    CSTS: RDY = 0, SHST = 00b (CAP.TO = 0x28 → wait up to 20 s)
  8. Wait for RDY = 0, then enable again

    The driver polls CSTS until RDY = 0. It (re)writes AQA, ASQ and ACQ (they were kept, but drivers usually write them anyway), then writes CC with the queue entry sizes, memory page size and EN = 1.

    Where: AQA 24h, ASQ 28h, ACQ 30h, CC 14hPCIe: Yes · MRd/CplD polls, then MWr to each register
    AQA = 0x001F_001F (32-entry admin queues) CC = 0x0046_0001 (IOCQES=4, IOSQES=6, EN=1)
  9. The controller becomes ready: RDY = 1

    The controller initialises and sets CSTS.RDY = 1. The driver's polling sees it. If instead CSTS.CFS = 1, or RDY never comes within CAP.TO, the driver escalates to a PCIe-level reset (Chapter 49).

    Where: CSTSPCIe: MRd/CplD polls only
    CSTS: 0x0000_0001 (RDY = 1, CFS = 0, SHST = 00b)
  10. Rebuild: Identify, features, queues, async events

    The driver sends Identify Controller (firmware may have changed), Set Features Number of Queues (07h), creates each I/O CQ and then its SQ, submits Asynchronous Event Requests, restores other features (APST, coalescing, write cache) and resubmits or fails the requests that were stopped in step 1.

    Where: admin queue, then I/O queuesPCIe: Yes · normal admin-command traffic
    Create I/O CQ 1..8 (IV 1..8), then Create I/O SQ 1..8 (CQID 1..8)

An error-recovery reset skips steps 1–5: the driver goes straight to step 6, and any command that was outstanding is lost without a completion (see 48.6).

48.12 Lab — Reset lab

🧪 Lab 48.1 — Reset lab: which state must be rebuilt? SAFE

Objective: from a synthetic event log covering normal init, reset, teardown, re-init and a lost command, determine what the host must rebuild and which command was lost. Setup (synthetic log):

t=0.000  CC.EN=1, RDY=1; Identify; Set Features 07h -> 4 SQ / 4 CQ granted
t=0.010  Create I/O CQ 1..4 (IV 1..4); Create I/O SQ 1..4; 4x AER armed
t=0.020  Set Features 08h (THR=3, TIME=1); Set Features 0Ch APST enabled
t=5.000  SQ2: Write CID 0x0101 LBA 0x1000 NLB 7   (doorbell seen)
t=5.000  SQ2: Write CID 0x0102 LBA 0x2000 NLB 7   (doorbell seen)
t=5.001  CQ2: CQE CID 0x0101 status 0             (MWr seen; host has NOT processed CQ2 yet)
t=5.002  host: CC.EN=0  (timeout recovery on another queue)
t=5.015  CSTS.RDY=0
t=5.020  CC.EN=1 ... RDY=1
t=5.400  Identify; Set Features 07h; Create CQ1..4; Create SQ1..4; AER armed
t=5.410  (no Set Features 08h / 0Ch issued)

Procedure: list every piece of state destroyed by the reset; mark which the host rebuilt; identify missing rebuild steps; classify CID 0x0101 and 0x0102.

Questions: (1) What did the reset destroy? (2) What did the host forget? (3) What is the status of CIDs 0x0101 and 0x0102? (4) What changes in observed behaviour after the reset?

Solution

(1) All I/O SQs/CQs and their contents (including the unprocessed CQE for 0x0101), outstanding commands, queue doorbell state, AER commands, non-saved feature values (Interrupt Coalescing, APST, etc.), async event masks. Admin queue registers were retained; PCIe config/MSI-X were not touched. (2) Coalescing (08h) and APST (0Ch) were not restored — they reverted to defaults. (3) 0x0101: completed by the device, but its CQE was destroyed before the host consumed it → host sees it as outstanding → must resubmit (write is idempotent: same data to same LBA). 0x0102: unknown — may be partially written; must resubmit; durability only after Flush/FUA. (4) Interrupt rate changes (no coalescing → more interrupts, lower latency) and power behaviour changes (no APST → higher idle power): "performance changed after a reset" is a classic symptom of features not restored.

Extension: add an HMB and decide when the host may free it.

Quiz

  1. Which registers survive CC.EN 1→0?

    Answer

    AQA, ASQ, ACQ (admin queue attributes and bases).

  2. What value initiates NSSR?

    Answer

    4E564D65h ("NVMe") written to offset 20h, if CAP.NSSRS=1.

  3. Which SHST value means shutdown complete?

    Answer

    10b.

  4. How long may the host wait for RDY?

    Answer

    CAP.TO × 500 ms.

  5. Order to create queues after reset?

    Answer

    CQs before the SQs that reference them.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What does a controller reset do?
    Model answer

    Stops the controller, deletes I/O queues, drops outstanding commands, resets registers except admin queue registers; host re-enables and rebuilds.

  2. Intermediate Difference between shutdown and reset?
    Model answer

    Shutdown prepares for power loss (flush, mark clean) and is reported via SHST; reset reinitialises the controller and discards in-flight work.

  3. Advanced Why might NSSR cause a Surprise Down?
    Model answer

    Subsystem reset can reset PCIe port logic, dropping the link.

  4. Senior Design a recovery ladder.
    Model answer

    Poll CQ → Abort → controller reset → FLR → hot reset (SBR) → slot power cycle → remove device; with feature restore and command replay rules at each step.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can write the reset and re-init sequence with timing.
  • I can list destroyed vs preserved state.
  • I can reason about lost commands and idempotency.
  • I can explain normal vs abrupt shutdown and unsafe-shutdown evidence.

49 PCIe Reset

← 48 NVMe Reset (Deep-Dive Module: Reset, NVMe Side)50 Power Management (Deep-Dive Module: Power Management) →

49.1 Why this chapter exists

When an NVMe controller reset is not enough — the controller is fatal, MMIO returns all-ones, or the link is broken — recovery moves down to PCIe-level resets. They are blunter: they reset configuration space (BARs, Command register, MSI-X enable, MPS/MRRS settings), may retrain the link and may take hundreds of milliseconds. Knowing which reset resets what is essential to recover a device without rebooting, and to avoid making things worse.

49.2 Learning objectives

  • Define Conventional Reset (Cold, Warm, Hot) and Function Level Reset, plus Link Disable and Secondary Bus Reset as triggers.
  • State what each reset affects (function state, link, sticky bits) and timing rules after reset.
  • Explain the relationship between PCIe resets and NVMe controller state.
  • Recognise resets in traces (LTSSM transitions, CRS completions, config re-programming).

49.3 Analogy

🌍 Analogy

A cold reset is unplugging the whole building. A warm reset is pressing the building's big red reset button with power still on (PERST#). A hot reset is a message sent down the road telling the next building to reset itself. An FLR resets just one office in a building that houses several companies, leaving the road open.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Hot reset is not addressed to one device: it propagates to everything below the port that issued it. And FLR does not reset the shared link or other functions, but an NVMe subsystem may still be shared with other functions or ports — FLR's scope is the function's controller only.

49.4 Reset types

ResetCategoryTriggerScopeLinkSticky bits
Cold resetConventional (Fundamental)Main power applied/re-appliedWhole componentRetrains from DetectReset (power lost)
Warm resetConventional (Fundamental)PERST# asserted with power on (platform mechanism — impl)Whole componentRetrains from DetectPreserved if Vaux maintained (sticky semantics) — impl
Hot resetConventional (in-band)TS1/TS2 with Hot Reset bit from upstream port; software sets Secondary Bus Reset (Bridge Control bit 6) on the downstream portAll components below that portGoes through Hot Reset LTSSM state then DetectPreserved
Link down / Link DisableResults in reset of downstream componentsLink Control bit 4 (Link Disable) on downstream port, or loss of linkBelow the portDisabled → Detect when re-enabledPreserved
Function Level Reset (FLR)Function-specificDevice Control bit 15 (Initiate FLR), if Device Capabilities bit 28 (FLR Capable)One functionUnaffectedPreserved; link-related and some other registers not reset
📘 Spec — timing rules

verified (substance; see PCIe Base for exact conditions): after a Conventional Reset, software must wait at least 100 ms before sending configuration requests to a device below a port supporting ≤ 5 GT/s; for ports supporting > 5 GT/s, wait 100 ms after link training completes (Data Link Layer Link Active). A device may answer configuration requests with Configuration Request Retry Status (CRS) while initialising, for up to 1 s after reset; software with CRS Software Visibility enabled sees a special value (Vendor ID 0001h) when reading. After FLR, software waits 100 ms before accessing the function (unless Readiness Notifications/Immediate Readiness say otherwise — version). After D3hot → D0, a 10 ms recovery time applies.

The rows of the table can be pictured as boxes inside boxes: a wider reset includes the effect of every narrower one inside it, and costs the host a longer recovery. Orange boxes are NVMe-defined resets, purple ones are PCIe-defined. conceptual

PCIe-defined resetNVMe-defined reset

AER sticky statusKeptKeptKeptCold: lost; warm: kept if Vaux (impl)
LinkUpUpRetrainedRetrained
Other functions on deviceUnaffectedUnaffectedResetReset

🐞 Debugging

After any PCIe-level reset, the OS must restore config space (BARs, Command register Memory Space + Bus Master enable, MSI-X, MPS/MRRS, ASPM, LTR, L1 substates) before the NVMe driver touches BAR0. If restore is skipped or partial, the first MMIO read of CAP returns all-ones (Memory Space disabled → UR) or the first DMA fails (Bus Master disabled → the device can't issue requests). Many "device dead after reset" bugs are restore bugs, not device bugs.

49.8 Linux view

cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:02:00.0/reset_method      # e.g. "flr bus" (kernel-dependent)
sudo lspci -vvv -s 02:00.0 | grep -E "FLReset|DevCtl|LnkSta|LnkCtl2"

⚠️ Safety

echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/…/reset, echo 1 > …/remove and setpci writes to Bridge Control/Link Control are disruptive operations. They can take a boot disk away, hang the machine or trigger fatal error handling. Use only on test devices that are not mounted, and preferably via the driver (nvme reset) for controller-level resets.

Quiz

  1. Which resets are Conventional Resets?

    Answer

    Cold, warm (Fundamental Resets) and hot reset.

  2. How is FLR initiated?

    Answer

    Device Control bit 15 (Initiate Function Level Reset), if FLR capable.

  3. Does FLR retrain the link?

    Answer

    No.

  4. What does CRS mean?

    Answer

    Configuration Request Retry Status — device not ready; retry the config request.

  5. Does a controller reset (CC.EN) reset MSI-X configuration?

    Answer

    No — PCIe config/MSI-X untouched; only NVMe controller state.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Compare FLR and SBR for recovering an NVMe SSD.
    Model answer

    FLR: function only, link stays up, no effect on siblings; SBR: everything below the port, link retrains, more thorough (resets PCIe logic) but broader impact.

  2. Advanced Why wait 100 ms after reset?
    Model answer

    Spec-mandated time for device initialisation before config requests; CRS covers longer init up to 1 s.

  3. Senior A device recovers only after a cold power cycle. What does that tell you?
    Model answer

    State survives warm/hot/FLR: sticky or always-powered logic, firmware stuck in a state not reset by PERST#, or PHY needing full power-on; escalate to vendor with that evidence.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can fill the reset-effects table from memory.
  • I can describe SBR step by step and the post-reset timing rules.
  • I can recognise resets and CRS in traces.
  • I can choose the right reset rung for a given failure.
