50 Power Management (Deep-Dive Module: Power Management)

← 49 PCIe Reset50A Capstone: One Incident, Every Layer →

50.1 Why this chapter exists

A laptop NVMe SSD may spend 99% of its life idle; a data-centre SSD may never be idle at all. Power management lets one design serve both — but it stacks three independent power-control systems on top of each other: NVMe power states (PS0…PSn, chosen by the host or autonomously via APST), PCIe link power states (ASPM L0s/L1 and L1 substates) and PCIe device power states (D0, D3hot, D3cold). Each saves power by adding wake-up latency, and each has failure modes: drives that never wake, links that throw errors on L1 exit, firmware that loses state in deep sleep. A large fraction of consumer NVMe bug reports on Linux are power-management quirks. This chapter makes the stack and its trade-offs explicit.

50.2 Learning objectives

  • Beginner: name the three power systems and their states.
  • Intermediate: read Power State Descriptors (MP, ENLAT, EXLAT, NOPS); configure/inspect Feature 02h and APST (0Ch); explain Linux nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us.
  • Advanced: explain ASPM L0s/L1, L1.1/L1.2, LTR, CLKREQ#, D3hot vs D3cold, PME and their latency budgets.
  • Senior: diagnose wake failures by separating power, link, controller and driver causes; tune for latency vs power.
  • Trace-analysis: recognise power transitions on the link (PM DLLPs, electrical idle, LTSSM L1 entry/exit, PME messages).
  • Debugging/validation: five failure patterns, power-state lab.

50.3 Kid story and analogy boundary

🧒 Kid analogy

The warehouse has three ways to save electricity. Inside, the manager can dim the lights in steps — bright, dim, very dim, off (NVMe power states); in the "off" steps nobody works, and it takes a while to switch lights back on. The road to your house can close one lane, or put up a barrier that takes a moment to lift (link L0s, L1). And the whole warehouse can go into night mode — doors locked except for the night bell (D3hot) — or be switched off at the mains (D3cold), which means a full morning start-up before anyone can help you.

🧩 Analogy boundary

Represents: three independent mechanisms, latency to wake. Hides: that the host and device must agree on some of these (ASPM must be enabled at both link ends, L1 substates need CLKREQ# and LTR), and that autonomous transitions (APST, ASPM) happen without host commands — there's no request on the wire you can point to. Misleading when: you assume a "dimmed" warehouse is also a closed road: NVMe PS and PCIe link states are independent; a drive in PS4 may have its link in L0 if ASPM is disabled, and a drive in PS0 may have its link in L1 between I/Os.

50.4 Vocabulary

TermPlainEngineeringCommon confusion
PS0…PSnLight levelsNVMe power states; up to 32 (Identify Controller NPSS, zero-based); each described by a 32-byte Power State DescriptorHigher number ≠ always lower power — check MP
Operational / Non-operationalWorking / not workingNOPS bit in descriptor; I/O not processed in non-operational states (controller returns to an operational state to process I/O)Admin commands may be processed without leaving the state (check spec)
ENLAT / EXLATTime to dim / brightenEntry / Exit Latency in µsSum is the worst-case added latency of a round trip
APSTAutomatic dimmerAutonomous Power State Transition, Feature 0Ch, table of idle timeouts → target stateHost sets the policy, device executes
ASPMLane closingActive State Power Management of link (L0s, L1) without software interventionIndependent of D-state transitions
L1.1 / L1.2Barrier with/without guardL1 PM Substates: further power reduction with CLKREQ#; L1.2 turns off common-mode voltage keepersExit latency much larger in L1.2
LTR"I can wait this long"Latency Tolerance Reporting message from device to platformUsed to decide L1.2 entry (threshold)
D0 / D3hot / D3coldDay / night / mains offPCI device power states (PMCSR PowerState); D3cold = main power removedD3hot keeps config space accessible; memory space not
PMEWake-up bellPower Management Event message / WAKE#Not an interrupt by itself
L2/L3 ReadyReady for mains offLink state after PME_Turn_Off / PME_TO_Ack handshake before power removal—

50.5 Architecture: the three-level stack

50.6 NVMe power states

50.6.1 Power State Descriptor (Identify Controller, 32 bytes each)

FieldMeaning
MP (Maximum Power) + MXPS (scale)Max power in this state (0.01 W units, or 0.0001 W when MXPS=1)
NOPSNon-Operational Power State: 1 = I/O not processed in this state
ENLATEntry Latency (µs)
EXLATExit Latency (µs)
RRT, RRL, RWT, RWLRelative Read/Write Throughput/Latency rankings
IDLP/IPS, ACTP/APW/APSIdle power and active power with scales/workload
Illustrative descriptor table for a client SSD (synthetic values)
PSMPNOPSENLAT (µs)EXLAT (µs)Comment
08.0 W000Full performance
15.5 W000Capped performance
23.5 W000Further capped
30.05 W120002000Light sleep
40.005 W1600014000Deep sleep (often relies on L1.2)

50.6.2 Host-controlled transitions — Feature 02h

Set Features 02h (Power Management) CDW11 bits 4:0 = PS, bits 7:5 = Workload Hint. Get Features 02h returns the current state. If the host submits I/O while the controller is in a non-operational state, the controller transitions to an operational state to process it (verified in substance — consult the Base spec "Power Management" section for exact rules).

50.6.3 APST — Feature 0Ch

Identify Controller APSTA bit indicates support. Set Features 0Ch: CDW11 bit 0 APSTE (enable) and a 256-byte data buffer of 32 entries (one per power state, 8 bytes each):

Entry bitsFieldMeaning
7:3ITPS — Idle Transition Power StateState to move to after the idle time, when in the state this entry describes
31:8ITPT — Idle Time Prior to TransitionMilliseconds of idle before transition (0 = disabled for this entry)

APST transitions go only to non-operational states. The device returns to the last operational state when work arrives, paying EXLAT.

50.6.4 Linux: nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us

Linux builds the APST table automatically: it considers non-operational states whose ENLAT + EXLAT ≤ the latency tolerance (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us, commonly 100000 µs by default — version/kernel-dependent) and picks idle timeouts proportional to the state's latency (impl — the heuristic has changed across kernel versions). Setting the parameter to 0 disables APST. A per-device override exists via /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/power/pm_qos_latency_tolerance_us. Quirk tables (e.g. NVME_QUIRK_NO_DEEPEST_PS, NVME_QUIRK_NO_APST) disable states known to be broken on specific models.

sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H | sed -n '/^ps /,$p'      # power state descriptors
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -E "npss|apsta"
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x02 -H              # current power state
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0c -H              # APST table (read-only)
cat /sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/default_ps_max_latency_us
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/power/pm_qos_latency_tolerance_us

50.7 PCIe link power: ASPM and L1 substates

StateEntryExit latency (order of magnitude)Notes
L0——Active
L0sPer direction, transmitter idle short time< 1 µs to a few µsGen3+ links often don't use it; optional in newer spec revisions (version); not supported in FLIT mode
L1 (ASPM)Both sides agree via PM DLLPs (PM_Active_State_Request_L1 / PM_Request_Ack)Few µs to tens of µsReported in LnkCap L1 Exit Latency
L1.1CLKREQ# deasserted; common-mode maintainedTens of µsL1 PM Substates capability (ext cap ID 001Eh)
L1.2Also common-mode off; uses LTR thresholdTens to hundreds of µs (T_POWER_ON, Common_Mode_Restore_Time)Biggest savings, biggest risk
L2 / L3After PME_Turn_Off / PME_TO_Ack, L2/L3 Ready, power removedFull re-trainUsed with D3cold

ASPM is enabled per link end in Link Control bits 1:0 (01 L0s, 10 L1, 11 both). Endpoint Device Capabilities report acceptable L0s/L1 latencies; software should enable ASPM only where exit latencies along the path fit. Linux: /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy (default, performance, powersave, powersupersave), boot option pcie_aspm=off, and per-link controls under /sys/bus/pci/devices/…/link/ on recent kernels (version).

🔧 Hardware

L1.2 requires the CLKREQ# sideband signal to be wired correctly on the board and supported at both ends, and correct T_POWER_ON / Common_Mode_Restore_Time programming. A board that advertises L1.2 but wires CLKREQ# incorrectly produces devices that "fall off the bus" after idle — the link cannot exit L1.2 cleanly and the root port logs Surprise Down or the device stops responding.

50.8 PCIe device power: D-states

D-stateAccessibleLinkContextReturn to D0
D0EverythingL0 / ASPM statesFull—
D1/D2Optional, rarely used by NVMeL1Device-specificShort
D3hotConfig space only; memory/IO requests → URL1 (entered via PM_Enter_L1 DLLP)Preserved if No_Soft_Reset=1; otherwise device resets on D3hot→D0 (internal reset, config must be restored)Write PMCSR to D0, wait 10 ms
D3coldNothing (power off)L2 (with Vaux) or L3Lost (except Vaux-powered sticky/PME)Power on, full reset, enumeration restore, NVMe init
📘 Spec

verified PMCSR (Power Management Control/Status, in the PM capability, ID 01h) bits 1:0 PowerState (00 D0, 01 D1, 10 D2, 11 D3hot); bit 3 No_Soft_Reset; bit 8 PME_En; bit 15 PME_Status. 10 ms recovery time after D3hot → D0 before accessing the function. NVMe RTD3R / RTD3E in Identify Controller report the expected resume and entry latency for "runtime D3" (power removal) in µs — these are the NVMe-side numbers for D3cold-style power-off.

🏭 Implementation-dependent

How Linux handles system suspend for NVMe depends on platform: on many client platforms with s2idle, the driver keeps the controller in D0 and relies on an NVMe non-operational power state plus ASPM L1.2, instead of a full shutdown (because shutdown + power-off costs RTD3R on resume). Platform firmware (ACPI _DSD "StorageD3Enable" and similar) may request D3. The exact policy changes by kernel version and platform.

50.9 Latency trade-offs

added_latency_first_IO ≈ EXLAT(NVMe PS) + L1.x exit latency (+ D3hot→D0 10 ms + controller re-init, if applicable)
  • EXLAT — exit latency of the current NVMe non-operational state
  • L1.x exit — link exit latency (L1, L1.1 or L1.2)
  • D-state term — only if runtime PM put the function into D3

Example (synthetic): PS4 EXLAT 14 ms + L1.2 exit 70 µs → the first read after idle takes ~14 ms instead of ~80 µs. For a desktop, fine; for a database with a 5 ms SLO, unacceptable — disable deep APST states with default_ps_max_latency_us (e.g. 5000) on that system.

50.10 Mechanism: APST idle → sleep → wake

Figure 50.1 shows the three layers side by side; this timeline shows them working together over one idle period and one wake-up. The time axis is not to scale (idle lasts seconds, the wake-up only milliseconds), and all numbers are the synthetic values from the descriptor table in 50.6. synthetic

1DriverSets APST table (Feature 0Ch)ControllerAdmin command; get-feature

3ControllerEnters ITPS (e.g. PS3)ControllerGet Features 02h (host can query — wakes? admin processing allowed)
4Link (both ends)ASPM L1 entry (PM DLLP handshake), then L1.2 if LTR/threshold allowLinkAnalyzer: PM DLLPs, electrical idle; LTR message earlier

9ControllerNormal command processing—Normal trace shape thereafter

50.11 Synthetic traces

Reasoning: with the link proven healthy and the doorbell visible, the candidates are controller (firmware stuck in a non-operational state) or driver (doorbell to wrong offset). Disambiguate: disable APST (latency 0) and retest — if the problem vanishes, it's power-state firmware (common reason for Linux quirk entries).

50.13 Labs

🧪 Lab 50.1 (beginner) — Inventory the power stack SAFE

Objective: record all three layers' configuration for your drive. Procedure: run the read-only commands in §50.6.4; sudo lspci -vvv -s <nvme> | grep -E "LnkCap|LnkCtl|L1SubCap|L1SubCtl1|PME|Status: D"; cat /sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy; cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<bdf>/power/control. Observations: NPSS, PS table, APST enabled, ASPM enabled states, L1 substates enabled, D-state, runtime PM. Questions: what's the worst-case wake latency on your system?

Solution

Sum the EXLAT of the deepest APST-enabled state and the L1.x exit latency; add D3 resume if runtime PM puts the device in D3. Many laptops: ~10–20 ms; servers often have APST/ASPM disabled → microseconds.

🧪 Lab 50.2 (intermediate) — Measure first-I/O-after-idle latency CAUTION

Objective: observe APST exit latency in software. Setup: test system; read-only I/O. Procedure: run a 4 KiB O_DIRECT read, sleep N seconds (N = 0.05, 0.5, 2, 10), read again, record latency; repeat with nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0 (boot parameter; reboot required).

for s in 0.05 0.5 2 10; do
  sleep "$s"
  sudo fio --name=w --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k --direct=1 \
       --ioengine=psync --number_ios=1 --readonly --output-format=terse \
       | awk -F';' -v s="$s" '{print "idle", s, "s: clat_us", $16}'
done
⚠️ Safety

The fio job is read-only (--readonly). Changing kernel parameters affects power/battery and must be done on a test machine. The terse-output field index for completion latency varies by fio version — verify against fio --terse-version documentation before trusting the number.

Solution

Expect latency to jump once idle exceeds the APST ITPT for a non-operational state (e.g. ~100 ms → +EXLAT). With APST disabled, latency stays flat (but idle power rises).

🧪 Lab 50.3 (advanced/senior) — Power-state lab: active → idle → low power → wake → failure SAFE

Objective: distinguish power, link, controller and driver issues in a synthetic incident. Given (synthetic timeline):

Synthetic composite timeline
tSourceEvent
10:00:00.000workloadActive: 20k IOPS
10:00:05.000workloadIdle begins
10:00:05.100device (inferred)APST: PS0 → PS3 (ITPT 100 ms)
10:00:05.1xxanalyzerLink: L1 entry, then L1.2
10:00:07.100device (inferred)APST: PS3 → PS4 (ITPT 2000 ms)
10:05:00.000analyzerRoot port: CLKREQ# asserted; Recovery; L0 reached in 75 µs
10:05:00.000075analyzer↓ MWr SQ4 tail doorbell
10:05:00.000075 → 10:05:30analyzerNo upstream TLP from device in captured interval; link stays L0; DLLP Acks for the doorbell seen; UpdateFC DLLPs continue
10:05:30dmesg (illustrative)nvme nvme0: I/O tag 12 (…) QID 4 timeout, aborting
10:05:30analyzer↓ MWr admin SQ0 doorbell (Abort); no fetch
10:06:00dmesg (illustrative)controller reset; ↓ MRd CSTS → CplD 0x0000_0001 (RDY=1, CFS=0)
10:06:00+analyzerCC.EN=0 → RDY=0 → EN=1 → RDY=1; I/O resumes

Questions: (1) Power issue, link issue, controller issue or driver issue? (2) What's the first abnormal event? (3) What evidence rules out the link? (4) What rules out the driver? (5) What experiment confirms? (6) Mitigation?

Solution

(1) Controller (firmware) issue in leaving a non-operational power state — a power-management-triggered controller bug. (2) The absence of any device response after the doorbell at 10:05:00.000075 — phrased as "no upstream TLP visible in the captured interval" (capture covered both directions, link in L0, so coverage is good). (3) Link exited L1.2 to L0 promptly, DLLP Acks for the doorbell prove the device's data link layer received it; flow control continues — the link layer is alive. (4) The doorbell targeted SQ4's tail offset with a plausible value (verify), the admin Abort doorbell was also ignored (two different queues), and a controller reset fixed it without driver changes; CSTS shows no CFS — the controller wasn't "fatal", it was unresponsive. (5) Disable APST deep states (default_ps_max_latency_us below PS4's ENLAT+EXLAT) and run the same idle/wake pattern — failure should disappear; then re-enable only PS4 to confirm it's PS4-specific; check for firmware updates/errata. (6) Firmware update; until then, limit APST (kernel parameter or quirk). Confidence: medium-high.

Extension: rewrite the timeline so that the link fails to exit L1.2 instead, and list what evidence changes (Surprise Down, LTSSM Detect, CSTS all-ones).

50.14 Interview questions

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Name the three power-management layers of an NVMe SSD.
    Model answer

    NVMe power states, PCIe link states (ASPM), PCIe device states (D-states).

  2. Beginner What is APST?
    Model answer

    Autonomous Power State Transition: the controller moves to non-operational states after configured idle times.

  3. Beginner What does NOPS mean?
    Model answer

    Non-operational: I/O not processed in that state.

  4. Beginner D3hot vs D3cold?
    Model answer

    D3hot: powered, config accessible; D3cold: main power removed.

  5. Beginner What is ASPM?
    Model answer

    Hardware-autonomous link power saving (L0s, L1) during idle.

  6. Intermediate How does Linux choose APST states?
    Model answer

    Non-operational states with ENLAT+EXLAT ≤ default_ps_max_latency_us; timeouts by heuristic.

  7. Intermediate What's in a power state descriptor?
    Model answer

    MP, NOPS, ENLAT, EXLAT, relative throughput/latency, idle/active power.

  8. Intermediate What does L1.2 need on the board?
    Model answer

    CLKREQ# routing, LTR support, correct T_POWER_ON/common mode restore timing.

  9. Intermediate Why does a memory read to a D3hot device fail?
    Model answer

    In D3hot only configuration requests are supported; memory requests get UR.

  10. Intermediate What's RTD3R?
    Model answer

    RTD3 Resume Latency (Identify Controller): expected time to resume from power-off runtime D3.

  11. Advanced How do PM DLLPs negotiate L1?
    Model answer

    Downstream component requests (PM_Active_State_Request_L1), upstream acknowledges (PM_Request_Ack) after blocking new TLPs; both go to electrical idle.

  12. Advanced What's LTR used for?
    Model answer

    Device reports tolerable latency so platform can choose deeper states (e.g. L1.2 threshold, package C-states).

  13. Advanced Why might s2idle keep NVMe in D0?
    Model answer

    Faster resume and lower complexity using NVMe PS + L1.2 instead of full shutdown and RTD3R.

  14. Advanced How does the trace show an APST exit?
    Model answer

    Doorbell→fetch gap ≈ EXLAT; often preceded by link L1.x exit.

  15. Advanced Effect of No_Soft_Reset=0 on D3hot→D0?
    Model answer

    Function undergoes internal reset; config must be restored; NVMe sees a controller-level reset.

  16. Senior Tuning for a latency-SLO database server?
    Model answer

    Limit APST (latency budget), disable L1.2 or ASPM if exits exceed SLO, runtime PM off, measure p99.

  17. Senior How do you separate power vs link vs controller vs driver for a wake failure?
    Model answer

    Link state/AER/LTSSM for link; DLLP Acks + no device response for controller; config restore/timing for driver; ablation (APST off, ASPM off, runtime PM off) one at a time.

  18. Senior Why do Linux quirk tables exist for NVMe PS?
    Model answer

    Some firmware/boards fail in deep states; quirks disable them per model.

  19. Senior How does thermal throttling interact with power states?
    Model answer

    Device may lower performance autonomously (thermal management temperatures, HCTM) independent of host-selected PS; shows as throughput drop with SMART temperature evidence.

  20. Senior What evidence proves a device was in a deep state when it failed?
    Model answer

    Idle duration vs APST table, link L1.2 in trace, get-feature 02h before failure (if captured), doorbell→fetch gap patterns; otherwise only inferred — state confidence.

📌 Teach-back

Child: dimming lights, closing road lanes, night mode and mains off. Junior: PS descriptors, APST table, ASPM states, D-states and the commands to inspect them. Senior: latency budget formula, platform/firmware/driver interactions, ablation-based diagnosis.

✅ Mastery gate
  • Explain the three layers and their controls.
  • Diagram Figure 50.1 and the APST wake sequence.
  • Identify in a trace: L1 entry/exit, doorbell→fetch gap from EXLAT.
  • Debug the five failure patterns and the power-state lab.
  • Distinguish NVMe PS from link states from D-states.
  • Cite: NVMe Base (Power Management, APST features), PCIe Base (PM capability, ASPM, L1 PM Substates, LTR).

50A Capstone: One Incident, Every Layer

← 50 Power Management (Deep-Dive Module: Power Management)51 PCIe Ordering — Who May Overtake Whom →

50A.1 Why this capstone exists

Parts XIII–XVI gave you the normal end-to-end sequence, interrupts, three floors of errors, resets and power states. Real incidents use all of them at once. This capstone presents a single synthetic incident and walks through a full investigation using the complete event model, timeline reconstruction, the first-abnormal-event rule and the negative-evidence rule.

50A.2 The incident (synthetic)

A storage server reports a burst of I/O errors on one NVMe drive at 02:14, followed by the drive disappearing and reappearing 40 seconds later. The application team wants to RMA the drive.

Synthetic evidence pack (abbreviated; dmesg lines illustrative)
TimeSourceObservation
01:00–02:13sysfs countersRoot port 00:03.0 aer_rootport_total_err_cor rising ~5/min; device RxErr
02:13:50BMCChassis fan profile change; inlet temp +6 °C
02:14:02.110dmesgAER: Corrected error: BadTLP, Timeout (Replay) from 02:00.0 — burst of ~400 in 1 s
02:14:02.900dmesgAER: Uncorrected (Non-Fatal) from 02:00.0: CmpltTO
02:14:03.0NVMe (later from error log)Error log entries: SQID 5, CID 0x00A1, status SCT0/04h Data Transfer Error
02:14:03.4dmesgLink down on 00:03.0 (DPC triggered on uncorrectable error)
02:14:03.4dmesgnvme0: controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff (illustrative)
02:14:04–02:14:43dmesgDPC recovery; link retrains at Gen4 x4 → later Gen3 x4; controller re-init; I/O resumes
02:14:44SMARTmedia_errors 0; critical_warning 0; temperature 61 °C; unsafe shutdowns +0

50A.3 Investigation

Step 1 — Build the expected timeline

Normal: I/O with clean link, rare correctable errors, no uncorrectable errors, link at Gen4 x4.

Step 2 — Observed timeline and first deviation

The background RxErr since 01:00 is a pre-existing deviation (low rate). The first sharp deviation is the burst of BadTLP/Replay Timeouts at 02:14:02.110. Working backwards: what preceded it? The BMC fan/temperature change at 02:13:50. Hypothesis: a marginal link (already showing RxErr) crossed a threshold with temperature change.

Step 3 — Layer assignment

EventLayerCause or symptom?
RxErr backgroundLink (PHY)Early cause indicator
BadTLP/Replay burstLink (DLL)Cause (proximate)
CmpltTO on devicePCIe TLSymptom (completions delayed/lost during link trouble/Recovery)
NVMe 04h Data Transfer ErrorNVMeSymptom (device converted transport failure into NVMe status)
DPC link downPCIe portContainment action (by design)
CSTS all-onesDriver viewSymptom of containment
Link retrain at Gen3LinkCorroborates signal-integrity problem at Gen4
SMART cleanMedia/FWNegative evidence against media failure (good coverage: SMART counts media errors reliably)

Step 4 — Negative evidence check

"No media errors" is supported (SMART media_errors and error log show only transport status). "The drive's PHY is at fault" vs "the slot/riser/retimer is at fault" cannot be separated with this evidence — both ends of the link are candidates. Phrase it: "The evidence localises the fault to the physical link between root port 00:03.0 and device 02:00.0; it does not identify which side."

Step 5 — Disambiguating experiments

  • Swap the drive into a known-good slot and put a known-good drive in this slot (A/B swap): follow the errors.
  • Run at forced Gen3 to confirm margin-dependent behaviour (test window).
  • Check retimer/riser seating and firmware; check thermal profile.
  • If available, use lane margining (PCIe 4.0+ Lane Margining at the Receiver — version) to quantify eye margin per lane.

Step 6 — Conclusion

Do not RMA the drive on this evidence. The incident is a link-layer (signal integrity) fault, likely aggravated by temperature, that propagated up as PCIe completion timeouts, NVMe Data Transfer Errors, DPC containment and a controller reset. Confidence: medium-high for "link layer"; low for "which side". Next step: A/B swap.

💡 Senior insight

Notice how every layer told the truth from its own point of view: the NVMe controller correctly reported a Data Transfer Error, the driver correctly saw an unreachable controller, the AER driver correctly logged a completion timeout, and DPC correctly contained the link. The root cause lives where none of the error messages point directly — in the trend of corrected errors that nobody alerted on. Build monitoring on correctable-error rates.

✅ Mastery gate — Parts XIII–XVI
  • I can narrate the end-to-end read and write and count their TLPs.
  • I can correlate any NVMe event with its TLP type, direction, address region and tag.
  • I can explain MSI-X structure, masking, pending bits and coalescing.
  • I can decode NVMe status, AER status and AER header logs.
  • I can run the decision trees and assign layers with confidence levels.
  • I can list what each reset and power state destroys and what must be rebuilt.
  • I always identify the first abnormal event and phrase absence claims with coverage.
PART XVII

Advanced PCIe

You already know what a Transaction Layer Packet (TLP) is, how a link trains, and how an NVMe command turns into memory reads and writes. This part opens the hood on the rules that make that traffic correct under stress: who may overtake whom (ordering), how answers to reads come back (completion rules), how a sender knows the receiver has room (flow-control credits), how a 32 GT/s or 64 GT/s link makes its electrical eye open (equalization), how errors are logged and contained (AER and DPC), and how one physical SSD pretends to be many (SR-IOV). Every chapter ends with the same question a senior engineer always asks: what would this look like in a trace, and what would I suspect when it breaks?

51 PCIe Ordering — Who May Overtake Whom

← 50A Capstone: One Incident, Every Layer52 Completion Rules — How Answers Come Back →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG), Transaction Ordering section and its ordering table. REVISION: the rules discussed here have been stable in spirit since PCIe 1.x; Relaxed Ordering (RO) comes from PCI-X heritage, ID-Based Ordering (IDO) was added in the 2.x era, and FLIT-mode (6.0+) changes the packet framing but not the producer/consumer intent. STATUS: normative. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: the exact cell entries of the ordering table (especially the “Yes / No / Y/N” sub-cases for RO and IDO) were refined across revisions — read the table in the revision your silicon claims. SOURCE: PCI-SIG members’ specification library. version

51.1 Why this chapter exists

An NVMe SSD finishes a 4 KiB read by doing three things on the wire, all of them posted Memory Write (MWr) TLPs going upstream: it writes the data into the host buffer, it writes a 16-byte Completion Queue Entry (CQE) into the host Completion Queue (CQ), and it writes an MSI-X (Message Signaled Interrupt – Extended) message. Software trusts that when it sees the CQE’s phase tag flip, the data is already in memory. Nothing in NVMe itself enforces that. PCIe ordering rules do. If you do not understand ordering you cannot explain the most frightening class of storage bug: the one where the completion arrives, the checksum fails, and five seconds later the same buffer is correct.

  • Beginner: name the three ordering classes (Posted, Non-Posted, Completion) and say which TLPs belong to each.
  • Intermediate: state the producer/consumer guarantee and show why “data write, then CQE write, then MSI-X write” is safe by default.
  • Advanced: explain Relaxed Ordering (Attr[1]), ID-Based Ordering (Attr[2]) and No Snoop (Attr[0]) and which NVMe writes may safely use them.
  • Senior: reason about deadlock avoidance (why posted writes must be able to pass non-posted requests) and about ordering across switches and the Root Complex.
  • Trace analysis: given a synthetic trace, identify whether a CQE could have become visible before its data.
  • Debugging / validation: design an experiment that distinguishes an ordering violation from a host-side cache or driver bug.

Prerequisites. TLP types and headers (MRd, MWr, CplD — see glossary TLP, MWr, MRd, CplD); the NVMe completion path (CQE, phase tag, MSI-X). Flow control is covered next door in Chapter 53; you need it to understand why ordering and deadlock are linked.

51.2 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine a one-lane mountain road from the library (the SSD) to the school (the host). The librarian sends a truck full of books (the data), then a postcard saying “your books arrived” (the CQE), then rings the school bell (the interrupt). Because the road is one lane and nobody overtakes, by the time the postcard arrives the books are already on the teacher’s desk. Now imagine the road gets a passing lane, and the postcard truck is small and fast. If it is allowed to overtake, the teacher reads “your books arrived”, looks at the desk, and finds… nothing. Ordering rules are the traffic law that says which trucks may use the passing lane.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Real PCIe has several independent “lanes” per direction in the logical sense (separate buffers for Posted, Non-Posted and Completion traffic, per Virtual Channel), the rules differ by pair of packet classes, and some overtaking is mandatory (to avoid deadlock), not merely permitted. Also, “arrived” really means “became visible to a reader of that memory”, which involves the Root Complex and CPU cache coherency, not just the wire.

51.3 Beginner view — three classes of traffic

ClassExamplesNeeds an answer?NVMe example
Posted (P)Memory Write (MWr), Messages (Msg/MsgD), MSI/MSI-X writes (which are MWr)No — fire and forgetDoorbell write host→SSD; data/CQE/MSI-X writes SSD→host
Non-Posted (NP)Memory Read (MRd), I/O Read/Write, Configuration Read/Write (CfgRd/CfgWr), AtomicOpsYes — a Completion must returnSSD reading an SQE or PRP list or write-data from host memory; host reading a BAR register
Completion (Cpl)Cpl (no data), CplD (with data), locked variantsIt is the answerRoot Complex returning SQE bytes to the SSD; SSD returning CSTS register value to the CPU

verified These three classes and their membership are defined by the PCIe Base Specification; each Virtual Channel keeps them in separate flow-control buffers (Chapter 53).

51.4 Engineering view — the rules that matter

The ordering table in the PCIe Base Specification is a grid of “row = later TLP, column = earlier TLP, may the later one pass the earlier one?”. Each cell says No (must not pass), Yes (must be allowed to pass — required for deadlock freedom) or Y/N (permitted, not required). You do not need to memorise every cell. You need the five rules that drive real bugs:

  1. Posted must not pass Posted (default, Relaxed Ordering clear). A later MWr may not overtake an earlier MWr in the same direction. verified This is what makes “data, then CQE, then MSI-X” safe.
  2. Posted must be able to pass Non-Posted. A write must never get stuck behind a read that cannot complete. verified This is the deadlock-avoidance rule: if a read’s completion depends on a write getting through (for example, through a bridge), blocking writes behind reads could lock the fabric.
  3. Non-Posted must not pass Posted (default). A read issued after a write must not overtake it, so a read “flushes” earlier writes in the same direction. verified Drivers rely on this: a read of a device register after an MMIO write guarantees the write has reached the device (the classic “posted write flush” pattern).
  4. Completion must not pass Posted (default). A read completion travelling in the same direction as earlier writes may not overtake them. verified This is the producer/consumer guarantee for “write data, then let the consumer read a flag”.
  5. Completions for the same request stay in address order. When a read is answered by several CplD TLPs (split at Read Completion Boundaries), they return in increasing address order. verified (Details in Chapter 52.)

51.5 The attribute bits

AttributeHeader bitMeaning when setEnabled bySafe for NVMe?
No Snoop (NS)Attr[0]Hardware need not snoop CPU caches for this transaction; software guarantees coherencyDevice Control register “Enable No Snoop” bitimpl Only if the host platform and driver manage cache coherency for those buffers. Linux NVMe does not ask for it; devices should not set it unless enabled.
Relaxed Ordering (RO)Attr[1]This TLP may pass earlier Posted TLPs (and a completion with RO may pass earlier writes)Device Control register “Enable Relaxed Ordering” bitderived Safe on data writes, because they may reorder among themselves. Unsafe on the CQE write, because a CQE with RO set could pass its own data. The MSI-X write must not pass the CQE either.
ID-Based Ordering (IDO)Attr[2] (header bit placement version-dependent)Ordering only enforced between TLPs from the same Requester/Completer IDDevice Control 2 “IDO Request Enable” / “IDO Completion Enable”impl Useful in switches with many functions (e.g. SR-IOV VFs) so one function’s traffic is not blocked behind another’s.
⚠️ Warning — the RO trap

Some platforms have had errata where Relaxed Ordering was unsafe or slow in the Root Complex, and operating systems have quirk lists that clear the Enable Relaxed Ordering bit for devices below specific root ports. impl Never conclude “the SSD violated ordering” until you have checked (a) the Device Control register value the OS actually programmed (lspci -vvv shows RlxdOrd+/- and NoSnoop+/- under DevCtl), and (b) the Attr bits in the captured TLP header.

51.6 Hardware view

🔧 Hardware

Inside the SSD controller, the DMA engine that streams read data and the completion engine that posts CQEs are often separate blocks. A correct design either funnels both into a single in-order posted queue toward the PCIe core, or tags the data writes with RO and keeps the CQE strictly ordered behind them. Inside the Root Complex, writes may be committed to memory through multiple paths (different memory controllers, different coherency agents). The Root Complex must still honour PCIe ordering for what a consumer can observe. impl How it does that (write-combining buffers, coherency fences) is not visible in a PCIe trace.

51.7 Protocol and trace view

Synthetic trace — normal 4 KiB read completion path (upstream, single VC, MPS = 256 B)
#Time (ns, relative)DirTLPAddressLenAttr (NS/RO/IDO)Note
10↓MWrBAR0+1008h1 DW0/0/0SQ1 tail doorbell
2610↑MRdSQ1 slot 516 DW0/0/0Fetch 64-byte SQE
31 020↓CplD—16 DW0/0/0SQE returned
4–1958 000–59 900↑MWr ×16buffer+0 … +F00h64 DW each0/1/0Data, RO set (permitted)
2060 050↑MWrCQ1 slot 54 DW0/0/0CQE, RO clear — cannot pass 4–19
2160 120↑MWrMSI-X address1 DW0/0/0Interrupt
Synthetic trace — failed: CQE marked Relaxed Ordering
#Time (ns)DirTLPAddressAttr (NS/RO/IDO)Note
4–1958 000–59 900↑MWr ×16buffer+…0/1/0Data
2060 050↑MWrCQ1 slot 50/1/0CQE with RO set — now permitted to pass data in the Root Complex
2160 120↑MWrMSI-X0/1/0Interrupt also RO
—host————Application checksum mismatch, rare, load-dependent; re-read of buffer is correct
🔍 Reading the failed trace

The wire order of TLPs 4–21 still looks perfect: the CQE was transmitted after the data. That is the trap. Ordering is about what the Root Complex is allowed to do after receipt. With RO set on the CQE write, the Root Complex may commit it to memory before the last data write is visible. An analyzer on the link cannot show you the inside of the Root Complex; it can only show you that the device gave permission to reorder. That is enough to file the bug. derived

Synthetic trace — ambiguous: MMIO write flushed by read
#DirTLPAddressNote
1↓MWrBAR0+14h (CC)Driver sets CC.EN = 0
2↓MRdBAR0+1Ch (CSTS)Driver polls CSTS.RDY
3↑CplD—CSTS.RDY = 1 (still ready)

Is TLP 3 a bug? No. The read (NP) could not pass the write (P), so the device had received CC.EN = 0 before it answered — but the specification gives the controller time to transition CSTS.RDY to 0 (bounded by CAP.TO). Ordering guarantees arrival, not completion of the side effect. derived

51.8 Linux view

# Which ordering attributes may this function use? (read-only)
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:3b:00.0 | grep -E 'DevCtl:|DevCtl2:|RlxdOrd|NoSnoop|IDO'
# Walk the path to the root port: each bridge has its own DevCtl
lspci -tv
# Kernel quirks that disable RO appear in the boot log on some platforms
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'relaxed|ordering'

What this proves: whether the function was allowed to set RO/NS/IDO. What it cannot prove: whether the device actually set the bits in a given TLP (you need a protocol analyzer), or how the Root Complex handled them.

51.9 Worked example — is this design safe?

A firmware engineer proposes: “To speed up completions, the CQE write engine will run on a separate PCIe virtual channel (VC1) from the data engine (VC0).” Analysis: ordering rules apply within a Virtual Channel (and traffic class mapping); there is no ordering between VCs. verified So the CQE on VC1 may become visible before data on VC0. The design is unsafe unless the device explicitly waits for data to be committed — which a posted write cannot report. derived The engineer would have to issue a zero-length or ordinary read after the data writes (a read completion cannot pass the writes) before sending the CQE, which costs latency. Most NVMe devices simply use one VC. impl

51.10 Common mistakes

  • Believing wire order equals visibility order. It does only for the default (strong) ordering case.
  • Assuming an MMIO write has taken effect when it returns to the CPU. Posted writes return immediately; use a read-back to flush.
  • Assuming ordering holds across different Requester IDs when IDO is enabled.
  • Blaming the SSD for a stale buffer when the driver forgot a DMA sync / memory barrier on a non-coherent platform.
  • Forgetting that peer-to-peer traffic through a switch follows the same rules but different paths.

51.11 Debugging connection — five failure patterns

SymptomPossible causesFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentConfidence
Rare data miscompare right after completion; data correct on re-readCQE/MSI-X with RO; driver missing barrier; IOMMU/cache issueDevCtl RO enable on device and bridgesCapture TLP Attr bits of CQE writesDisable RO via OS quirk/setting (lab only) and rerun stressMedium-high if Attr[1]=1 on CQE
System hang under mixed peer-to-peer read/writePosted traffic blocked behind non-posted in a non-compliant bridgeIs P blocked while NP outstanding? (analyzer)Credit state for P vs NPStop peer reads; does hang disappear?Medium
Register value read back looks stale after writeExpected side-effect latency, not orderingSpec timing for that registerRepeat read with delayPoll with bounded timeoutHigh

Throughput drops when RO disabledRoot Complex serialises writesCompare with RO onPlatform errataA/B test on same linkImplementation-dependent
💡 Senior insight

Ordering bugs are statistical. They hide at low queue depth and appear under exactly the conditions that make the Root Complex reorder: many outstanding writes, multiple memory channels, remote NUMA memory. When you see “rare, load-dependent, self-healing corruption”, put ordering on the suspect list before media errors, and prove or disprove it with Attr bits in the trace.

🧪 Lab 51.1 — Ordering audit of a synthetic capture SAFE

Objective: classify every TLP in a 30-line synthetic capture and decide whether any consumer could observe a CQE before its data. Setup: paper or spreadsheet; the two synthetic traces above. Steps: (1) label each TLP P/NP/Cpl; (2) mark Attr bits; (3) for each CQE, list the earlier posted writes to the same buffer; (4) decide “may pass?” using the five rules. Observations: the normal trace has RO only on data. Questions: What changes if the CQE goes on VC1? What if the data writes target a peer device instead of host memory?

Solution

Normal trace: no CQE may pass its data because CQE has RO = 0 and is in the same VC. Failed trace: TLP 20 may pass any of 4–19 in the Root Complex. VC1 variant: no ordering relationship exists between VCs, so unsafe. Peer target: ordering still holds along the path, but visibility depends on the peer’s internal behaviour — implementation-dependent.

Extension: write a 30-line script that ingests a CSV of TLPs and flags any MWr to a CQ address with Attr[1]=1.

Quiz

  1. Why must Posted requests be able to pass Non-Posted requests?

    Answer

    To avoid deadlock: if a read cannot complete until some write gets through, blocking writes behind reads could lock the fabric permanently.

  2. Which NVMe write is it safe to mark Relaxed Ordering?

    Answer

    Data writes into host buffers (they may reorder among themselves). Not the CQE and not the MSI-X write that follows it.

  3. Why does reading CSTS after writing CC “flush” the CC write?

    Answer

    Non-Posted requests must not pass Posted requests in the same direction, so the read reaches the device after the write. The completion therefore proves the write arrived (not that its effect finished).

  4. Does an analyzer on the SSD link prove that the host observed data before the CQE?

    Answer

    No. It proves transmit order and attribute bits. Visibility inside the Root Complex and memory system is not observable on that link.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What are the three PCIe ordering classes?
    Model answerPosted (MWr, Msg), Non-Posted (MRd, CfgRd/Wr, IORd/Wr, AtomicOps), Completion (Cpl, CplD).
  2. Intermediate Explain producer/consumer ordering using an NVMe read.
    Model answerThe SSD (producer) writes data then writes the CQE flag; both posted, same VC, no RO on the CQE, so the CQE cannot pass the data. The CPU (consumer) sees the flag only after the data is visible.
  3. Advanced What does IDO buy you in an SR-IOV device?
    Model answerTraffic from different Requester IDs (different VFs) need not be ordered with respect to each other, so a stalled VF does not head-of-line-block another VF’s writes.
  4. Senior A customer reports rare silent corruption only on one server model. How do you approach it?
    Model answerCheck platform RO errata and quirks, compare DevCtl settings across models, capture Attr bits on CQE/MSI-X writes, run A/B with RO disabled, and correlate with NUMA placement; only then suspect media.
📌 Summary

Posted writes in one VC stay in order unless RO says otherwise; reads and completions do not overtake earlier writes; writes must be able to overtake reads. NVMe’s “data → CQE → interrupt” correctness rests entirely on these rules. A trace shows permission to reorder, not reordering itself.

Teach-back: explain to a child why the postcard must not overtake the book truck; to a junior why RO is fine on data but not on the CQE; to a senior why ordering and flow-control deadlock are the same design problem.

Further reading: PCIe Base Specification, Transaction Ordering; your SSD controller’s DMA engine documentation; Linux drivers/pci/quirks.c (search for relaxed ordering). Next: Chapter 52 — Completion Rules.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can classify any TLP into P / NP / Cpl.
  • I can state the five practical ordering rules from memory and justify each.
  • I can explain why the CQE write must not carry RO.
  • I can point to the Attr field in a TLP header and read NS/RO/IDO.
  • I can explain what a link-level trace can and cannot prove about visibility.

52 Completion Rules — How Answers Come Back

← 51 PCIe Ordering — Who May Overtake Whom53 Flow Control and Credits →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification — Completion rules, Completion Timeout mechanism, Read Completion Boundary (RCB), Device Control / Device Control 2 registers. STATUS: normative. VERSION NOTES: Configuration Request Retry Status (CRS) was renamed Request Retry Status (RRS) in later revisions, which also allow it for some non-configuration cases version; 10-bit tags are optional from 4.0, and 14-bit tags appear with FLIT mode in 6.0 version.

52.1 Why this chapter exists

Every time an NVMe controller fetches a Submission Queue Entry (SQE), a PRP list, or the data of a write command, it issues a Memory Read (MRd) and waits for a Completion with Data (CplD). Every time the CPU reads a controller register, the controller must answer with a CplD. If completions are split, late, mis-tagged or carry an error status, the NVMe layer sees stalls, timeouts or controller fatal status — and the root cause is invisible unless you can read completion headers. This chapter teaches you to read them.

  • Decode Completer ID, Requester ID, Tag, Completion Status, Byte Count and Lower Address.
  • Explain the Read Completion Boundary and predict how a read will be split.
  • Explain Completion Timeout ranges and what happens when one fires.
  • Distinguish UR, CA, CRS/RRS and Successful Completion and attribute each to a layer.
  • Recognise Unexpected Completions and tag aliasing in a trace.

Prerequisites: Chapter 51 (ordering), TLP header basics, MRRS and MPS.

🧒 Kid analogy — the library request desk

You hand the librarian a request slip with a ticket number (the Tag) and your name (the Requester ID). The librarian may bring the books back in several trips, but always with your ticket number and always in page order. If the book does not exist, you get a slip saying “no such book” (Unsupported Request). If the librarian is broken, you get “I can’t do this” (Completer Abort). If the library is still opening, you get “come back later” (Retry Status). If nobody comes back at all, after a while you give up (Completion Timeout).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In PCIe the requester must have pre-reserved buffer space for the answer — there is no “I’ll wait at the desk” without room for the books. And “giving up” (timeout) is a hardware mechanism with programmable ranges, not patience.

52.2 Completion header fields

DWBits 31:24Bits 23:16Bits 15:8Bits 7:0
0Fmt / Type (Cpl or CplD), TC, Attr, TD, EP, Length (non-FLIT layout)
1Completer ID (Bus/Device/Function)Completion Status (3 bits), BCM (1 bit), Byte Count[11:8]Byte Count[7:0]
2Requester IDTag[7:0] (extended tag bits elsewhere when 10-bit tags in use)R, Lower Address[6:0]

verified for the classic (non-FLIT) 3-DW completion header. In FLIT mode the header layout differs version — use the 6.x specification for exact bit positions.

FieldOwner / creatorPurposeDebug use
Requester ID + TagCopied from the request by the completerLets the requester match the answer to its outstanding requestMismatch ⇒ Unexpected Completion at the requester
Completer IDCompleterIdentifies who answeredShows which function/bridge generated a UR/CA
Completion StatusCompleter000b SC, 001b UR, 010b CRS/RRS, 100b CAError localisation
Byte CountCompleterBytes remaining to satisfy the request, including this completion (4096 encoded as 0)Detect missing or extra split completions
Lower AddressCompleterLow 7 bits of the starting byte address of this completion’s dataVerify RCB splitting
EP (poisoned)Completer or forwarding elementData is known badPoisoned TLP error at the receiver (AER)

52.3 Splitting: Read Completion Boundary (RCB)

A completer may return a read in several CplD TLPs. Each must not exceed the Max Payload Size of the path, and split points (other than the first and last) must fall on naturally aligned RCB boundaries. Root Complexes have an RCB of 64 or 128 bytes (reported in the Link Control register’s RCB bit for the root port); endpoints mirror the setting. verified

N_cpl ≥ ⌈ (A_start mod RCB + L) / min(MPS, chosen chunk) ⌉   (lower bound; completer may split at any RCB multiple)
  • N_cpl — number of completion TLPs
  • A_start — starting byte address of the read
  • RCB — Read Completion Boundary (64 or 128 B)
  • L — requested length in bytes (≤ MRRS)
  • MPS — Max Payload Size programmed on the path

Worked example

The SSD reads a 512-byte PRP list at host address 0x1_2340_0FC0 with MRRS = 512 and MPS = 256, RCB = 64. The Root Complex may answer: CplD #1 covers 0FC0–0FFF (64 bytes, ends at a 64-byte boundary, Byte Count 512, Lower Address 40h), CplD #2 covers 1000–10FF (256 bytes, Byte Count 448, Lower Address 00h), CplD #3 covers 1100–11BF (192 bytes, Byte Count 192, Lower Address 00h). synthetic Another legal answer uses more, smaller completions — the choice is implementation-dependent impl; the constraints (address order, RCB-aligned splits, ≤ MPS, Byte Count arithmetic) are not.

52.4 Completion Timeout

The requester runs a timer per outstanding non-posted request. If no completion (or not all completions) arrives in time, it logs a Completion Timeout — an uncorrectable error, by default non-fatal — and frees the tag. Device Control 2 lets software choose a range; Device Capabilities 2 reports which ranges are supported (Ranges A–D) and whether timeout disable is supported. The default range is 50 µs to 50 ms. verified

🏭 Implementation-dependent

What the NVMe controller does after a Completion Timeout on an SQE fetch or on write-data fetch is not defined by PCIe. Many controllers set CSTS.CFS (Controller Fatal Status); some retry; some complete the affected command with an internal error status. Your controller’s datasheet decides.

52.5 Error statuses by layer

StatusTypical causeLayerNVMe consequence
UR — Unsupported RequestAddress outside any BAR; IOMMU blocks DMA (some Root Complexes return UR); function in D3hot; Bus Master Enable clearTransaction / platformSQE or data fetch fails; controller may go fatal
CA — Completer AbortCompleter violated its own programming model or internal errorCompleter internalSame
CRS / RRSDevice not ready to answer configuration requests after resetConfig / initEnumeration delay; with CRS Software Visibility the read of Vendor ID returns 0001h
Poisoned (EP=1)Uncorrectable memory error in host DRAM on a DMA readData integrityController should not write poisoned data to media; behaviour impl-dependent
Unexpected CompletionCompletion with no matching outstanding request (late after timeout, wrong tag, wrong RID)TransactionLogged as AER uncorrectable (often advisory non-fatal)

52.7 Linux view

sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:3b:00.0 | grep -E 'DevCap2|DevCtl2|CmpltTO|MaxPayload|MaxReadReq|RCB'
# AER counters exposed by the kernel (read-only files)
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/aer_dev_nonfatal
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/aer_dev_fatal
journalctl -k | grep -i -E 'AER|Completion Timeout|Unsupported Request'

Illustrative, abbreviated lspci lines will show fields such as CmpltTO ranges and MaxPayload/MaxReadReq. They prove configuration; they do not prove what happened on the wire.

52.8 Common mistakes and failure patterns

SymptomPossible causesEvidenceFirst / second checkLikely conclusion

💡 Senior insight

When an NVMe controller dies, look backward in the trace for the last non-successful completion it received. A single UR on a PRP fetch explains a controller fatal far more often than a firmware bug does. And always check Byte Count arithmetic: a completer that miscounts produces data that looks “correct but shifted”.

🧪 Lab 52.1 — Predict the completion split SAFE

Objective: compute legal completion sequences. Setup: RCB = 64 B, MPS = 128 B. Steps: for reads of (a) 256 B at 0x...000, (b) 200 B at 0x...0F0, (c) 4096 B at 0x...F80 with MRRS = 4096, list one legal sequence with Byte Count and Lower Address per completion. Questions: what is the minimum number of completions for (c)?

Solution

(a) Two completions of 128 B: first BC 256 / LA 00h, second BC 128 / LA 80h (low 7 bits of 0x…080). (b) 0F0–0FF (16 B, BC 200, LA 70h), 100–17F (128 B, BC 184, LA 00h), 180–1B7 (56 B, BC 56, LA 00h). (c) F80–FFF (128 B, BC 0 meaning 4096, LA 00h because 0xF80 has its low 7 bits clear), then 31 further 128-byte completions; minimum 32 completions because each is capped at MPS = 128 B. Lower Address is always the low 7 bits of that completion’s starting byte address.

Extension: repeat with RCB = 128 and explain why Root Complexes report RCB.

Quiz

  1. Who generates the Completion Status field?

    Answer

    The completer (the function that serviced the request), or an intermediate element that terminated the request (e.g. a bridge returning UR).

  2. What does Byte Count 0 mean in a CplD?

    Answer

    4096 bytes remaining (the 12-bit field encodes 4096 as 0).

  3. Is a Completion Timeout correctable?

    Answer

    No, it is an uncorrectable error (default severity non-fatal, programmable in AER).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Which TLPs require completions?
    Model answerNon-posted: memory reads, I/O and config requests, AtomicOps.
  2. Intermediate Why may a 4 KiB read return as many TLPs?
    Model answerEach completion is capped by MPS and splits are allowed at RCB boundaries; the completer chooses.
  3. Advanced How would you detect tag aliasing with 10-bit tags enabled on only one side?
    Model answerCheck Device Control 2 10-bit Tag Requester Enable and the completer’s 10-bit Tag Completer Supported; look for completions whose upper tag bits differ from the request; correlate with Unexpected Completion logs.
  4. Senior The controller sets CFS after a UR. Is the controller wrong?
    Model answerNot necessarily; PCIe does not dictate NVMe recovery. Determine why the host returned UR (IOMMU, BME cleared by error recovery, bad PRP). The NVMe behaviour is implementation-dependent; the root cause is upstream.
📌 Summary

Completions carry Requester ID + Tag for matching, Completion Status for error attribution, Byte Count and Lower Address for split reassembly. Splits respect MPS and RCB and stay in address order. Timeouts are requester-side, programmable, and their NVMe-level consequence is implementation-dependent.

53 Flow Control and Credits

← 52 Completion Rules — How Answers Come Back54 Equalization — Opening the Eye at 8 GT/s and Beyond →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification — Flow Control (Transaction Layer), Data Link Layer InitFC/UpdateFC DLLPs. STATUS: normative. VERSION NOTES: Scaled Flow Control (larger credit fields with a scale factor) was introduced to support higher bandwidth-delay products version; FLIT mode in 6.0 adds shared credit pools alongside dedicated credits version. The counter rules below are for the classic (non-FLIT, unscaled) case.

53.1 Why this chapter exists

PCIe never drops a TLP because a buffer is full. Instead, the receiver advertises how much buffer space it has, in credits, and the transmitter is forbidden to send a TLP unless enough credits are available. When credits run dry, the link goes quiet even though both sides are healthy. Most “mysteriously low NVMe throughput” investigations that end at the PCIe layer end here.

  • List the six credit types and what each counts.
  • Explain InitFC1/InitFC2 and UpdateFC DLLPs.
  • Apply the credit gating rule and compute credit-limited throughput.
  • Recognise credit starvation in a trace and distinguish it from a slow device.

Prerequisites: ordering classes, DLLPs (DLLP, FC), Ack/Nak.

🧒 Kid analogy — parking tickets

The school car park gives the library six kinds of parking tickets: big-truck tickets and small-car tickets, for three different car parks (deliveries, requests, answers). The library may only send a vehicle if it holds a ticket for that car park. When the school empties a space, it mails a ticket back (UpdateFC). If the school is slow to mail tickets back, the library’s trucks wait at the gate even though the road is empty.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Tickets are not individual objects; they are running counters that wrap around. The receiver does not “mail back tickets”; it periodically advertises the total it has ever freed, and the sender computes the difference. And a sender may be told “infinite credits” (advertised as 0), meaning no tickets are needed at all for that type.

53.2 Credit types

TypeCountsUnitConsumed by
PHPosted Request headers1 per TLPMWr, Msg
PDPosted Request data1 credit = 16 bytes (4 DW)MWr payload, MsgD payload
NPHNon-Posted Request headers1 per TLPMRd, CfgRd/Wr, IORd/Wr, AtomicOps
NPDNon-Posted data16 bytesCfgWr, IOWr, AtomicOp payloads
CplHCompletion headers1 per TLPCpl, CplD
CplDCompletion data16 bytesCplD payload

verified Credits are kept per Virtual Channel. Header credit fields are 8 bits and data credit fields 12 bits in unscaled flow control; an advertised value of 0 means infinite. Endpoints are generally required to advertise infinite completion credits for requests they issue, since a requester must reserve space for completions before issuing a read uncertain — confirm the exact rule and its exceptions in the revision you use.

53.3 Initialisation and update

During Data Link Layer initialisation (link reaches DL_Active), each side sends InitFC1 then InitFC2 DLLPs for P, NP and Cpl, per VC0 (other VCs when enabled). After that, the receiver sends UpdateFC DLLPs as it frees buffer space. verified

Send allowed ⇔ (CREDIT_LIMIT − (CREDITS_CONSUMED + CUMULATIVE_CREDITS_REQUIRED)) mod 2FieldSize ≤ 2FieldSize / 2
  • CREDIT_LIMIT — most recent value advertised by the receiver (from InitFC/UpdateFC)
  • CREDITS_CONSUMED — credits consumed by TLPs sent since init (modular)
  • CUMULATIVE_CREDITS_REQUIRED — credits this TLP needs (1 header, ⌈payload/16⌉ data)
  • FieldSize — 8 for headers, 12 for data (unscaled)

verified (form of the gating rule from the specification’s flow-control model; confirm FieldSize when Scaled Flow Control is enabled).

53.4 Credit-limited throughput

BW_max ≈ (Credits_D × 16 B) / RTT_FC
  • BW_max — sustainable payload bandwidth for one credit type
  • Credits_D — data credits advertised (buffer size / 16)
  • RTT_FC — round-trip time from sending a TLP until the UpdateFC that returns its credits is processed (wire, receiver processing, UpdateFC scheduling)

Worked example

A Gen4 x4 link carries ≈ 7.9 GB/s raw after 128b/130b encoding (16 GT/s × 4 lanes × 128/130 ÷ 8). derived Suppose a switch port advertises 128 PD credits (2 KiB) and the credit loop RTT is 600 ns. BW_max ≈ 2048 B / 600 ns ≈ 3.4 GB/s. The NVMe SSD streaming reads (posted writes upstream) would be capped well below link speed. synthetic numbers chosen for teaching. Doubling the buffer or halving the RTT doubles the ceiling. This is why Scaled Flow Control and larger receive buffers appear as speeds rise.

53.5 Hardware view

🔧 Hardware

Credit buffers are SRAM inside the Transaction Layer of each port. Switches have a set per port per VC. Root ports often advertise generous posted credits because host writes from devices are the bulk direction. The SSD itself must reserve completion buffer space for every MRd it has outstanding; this, together with the number of tags, bounds how much write data it can prefetch from host memory. impl

Gaps alone do not prove starvation. You must reconstruct the credit counters from InitFC/UpdateFC and TLP sizes: if the counter shows ample credit during the gap, the device was idle, not blocked. derived

53.7 Linux view and its limits

# Link speed/width and MPS are visible; credit state is NOT exposed by standard Linux tools
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:3b:00.0 | grep -E 'LnkSta:|MaxPayload'
# Measure the symptom instead
sudo fio --name=seqread --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=read --bs=128k --iodepth=64 \
     --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=30 --time_based --readonly
⚠️ Safety

The fio command above uses --readonly and reads only. Never run write workloads against a device that holds data you care about.

Credit counters are internal to ports. Some switches expose vendor-specific debug counters impl; otherwise a protocol analyzer that decodes DLLPs is the only direct evidence.

53.8 Failure patterns

SymptomCausesEvidenceDisambiguating experimentConfidence
Sequential read throughput plateaus below link rateUpstream posted credit starvation; MPS too small; host memory bandwidthGaps gated by credit limitMove SSD to root port directly (bypass switch)Medium
Writes slow, reads fineSSD runs out of tags / completion buffer for data fetch; MRRS smallFew outstanding MRdIncrease MRRS (lab system), compareMedium

Link hangs with outstanding readsNP credits never returned (deadlock in a bridge)NP gated, P still flowingCheck ordering rule P-passes-NP complianceMedium
💡 Senior insight

Bandwidth-delay product is the single most useful mental model in PCIe performance. Credits, tags, MRRS and NVMe queue depth are all the same idea at different layers: “how much can be in flight before I must wait for an acknowledgement?” If any one of them is smaller than bandwidth × latency, it becomes the bottleneck.

🧪 Lab 53.1 — Credit counter simulation SAFE

Objective: simulate the gating rule. Setup: Python 3.

FIELD = 12                      # data credit field width (unscaled)
MOD = 1 << FIELD
limit, consumed = 256, 0         # InitFC advertised 256 PD credits (4 KiB)
def can_send(payload):
    need = -(-payload // 16)     # ceil(payload/16)
    return ((limit - (consumed + need)) % MOD) <= MOD // 2
sent = 0
while can_send(256):
    consumed = (consumed + 16) % MOD
    sent += 1
print("TLPs sent before gating:", sent)   # expect 16
limit = (limit + 64) % MOD                 # UpdateFC returns 64 credits
print("after update can send:", can_send(256))

Questions: why does modular arithmetic handle wrap-around? What happens if the receiver advertises 0? Extension: add RTT and compute throughput.

Solution

Counters wrap; comparing the modular difference against half the range distinguishes “ahead” from “behind”. An advertised 0 means infinite — the real implementation skips gating for that type; this toy code would mis-handle it, which is exactly the bug class to watch for.

Quiz

  1. How many PD credits does a 256-byte MWr consume?

    Answer

    16 (256 / 16) plus 1 PH credit.

  2. Which DLLPs carry credit information?

    Answer

    InitFC1, InitFC2 (initialisation) and UpdateFC (runtime), each per class (P, NP, Cpl) and per VC.

  3. What does an advertised credit value of 0 mean?

    Answer

    Infinite credits for that type.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Why does PCIe use credits instead of retransmitting on overflow?
    Model answerCredits guarantee the receiver always has space, so the Data Link Layer replay mechanism only handles bit errors, not congestion; this keeps latency deterministic and avoids loss.
  2. Senior Throughput is 60% of link rate behind a switch but 95% direct. Walk me through it.
    Model answerCompare posted credits advertised by the switch upstream port vs root port, measure UpdateFC latency, check MPS on all hops, check switch egress contention from other devices, compute bandwidth-delay product.
📌 Summary

Six credit types, per VC, initialised by InitFC and replenished by UpdateFC; a TLP may only be sent if its header and data credits are available. Credit-limited bandwidth ≈ buffer / round-trip time. Gaps in a trace mean starvation only if counter reconstruction says so.

Next: Chapter 54 — Equalization.

✅ Mastery gate

  • I can reconstruct credit counters from a DLLP trace.
  • I can compute a credit-limited bandwidth ceiling and explain how to raise it.
  • I can distinguish starvation from idleness with evidence.

54 Equalization — Opening the Eye at 8 GT/s and Beyond

← 53 Flow Control and Credits55 Advanced Error Handling — AER, DPC and Recovery →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification — Physical Layer electrical sub-block, LTSSM Recovery.Equalization substate, Secondary PCI Express Extended Capability (8 GT/s lane equalization control), Physical Layer 16 GT/s / 32 GT/s / 64 GT/s Extended Capabilities, Lane Margining at the Receiver. STATUS: normative. VERSION NOTES: equalization first became mandatory for 8 GT/s (Gen3); each higher rate (16, 32, 64 GT/s) has its own equalization procedure and preset tables; later revisions add options to skip or shorten equalization when previously learned settings are trusted version. Gen6 uses PAM4 signalling with FLIT mode and FEC; Gen7 (128 GT/s, specification released 2025) continues PAM4 version.

54.1 Why this chapter exists

An NVMe SSD that trains to Gen4 x4 instead of Gen5 x4, or that trains to Gen5 and then logs thousands of correctable Receiver Errors, is almost always an equalization or signal-integrity story. You will never decode a TLP that explains it. You need to know how the two ends tune their transmitters, where the result is recorded, and what you can and cannot see from software.

  • Explain inter-symbol interference (ISI) and why channel loss grows with frequency.
  • Describe transmitter de-emphasis/pre-shoot: pre-cursor, cursor, post-cursor coefficients and presets.
  • Walk through equalization Phases 0–3 and who tunes whom.
  • Read Link Status 2 equalization bits and interpret “Equalization Complete / Phase N Successful”.
  • Diagnose speed downgrades and correctable-error storms caused by poor equalization.

Prerequisites: LTSSM states (LTSSM: Detect, Polling, Configuration, L0, Recovery), encoding (8b/10b, 128b/130b), Chapter 53 for why replay storms hurt throughput.

🧒 Kid analogy — shouting across a canyon

Two friends shout numbers across a canyon. Every shout echoes, and the echo of “seven” smears into the next word “three”. So each friend learns to shout the start of a word louder and soften the tail, so the echo matters less. They try different shouting styles (presets), and the listener says “try a bit more emphasis” until every number is heard clearly. Then they swap roles.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The receiver also has its own equalizer (CTLE, DFE) that it tunes privately; only transmitter settings are negotiated in-band. And the “listener’s feedback” is not a perceptual judgement but an implementation-specific figure of merit (eye height/width, error counts) that the specification does not define.

54.2 Engineering view

At 8 GT/s and above the PCB trace, connector and package attenuate high frequencies far more than low ones. A long run of identical bits followed by a transition is smeared by ISI. The transmitter compensates with a 3-tap FIR filter: a pre-cursor coefficient (C−1), the cursor (C0), and a post-cursor coefficient (C+1). Combinations are summarised as presets P0–P10, each defining pre-shoot and de-emphasis in dB. verified (preset count and table values per rate: check the electrical chapter of your revision).

Equalization is run inside the LTSSM’s Recovery.Equalization substate when the link changes to a rate that needs it (8 GT/s, then separately 16, 32, 64 GT/s). Software can request re-equalization via Link Control 3 “Perform Equalization”, and a port can request it via the “Link Equalization Request” status. verified The algorithm each receiver uses to evaluate coefficients is impl.

54.3 Hardware view

🔧 Hardware

Each lane has its own transmitter FIR and receiver CTLE/DFE. Equalization is per lane, so one bad lane (damaged connector pin, crosstalk) can force the entire link down in speed or width. Retimers participate in equalization on each of their link segments, which multiplies the number of phases that can fail. M.2 and U.2/E3.S SSDs behind long backplanes with retimers are the classic hard case.

sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:00:1c.0 | grep -E 'LnkCap:|LnkSta:|LnkSta2|LnkCtl2|Equalization'
# Illustrative, abbreviated fields you may see in LnkSta2: EqualizationComplete+ EqualizationPhase1+ ...

Recent Linux kernels print a message when a link is running below its capability (wording varies by version) version. Lane margining tools exist (open-source and vendor) but margining is intrusive on some platforms. impl

⚠️ Safety

Do not use setpci to write Link Control 2 (Target Link Speed) or Link Control 3 (Perform Equalization) on a system disk. A failed retrain can drop the link and take the root filesystem with it. Do such experiments only on a lab system with the test SSD not mounted. CAUTION

54.6 Failure patterns

SymptomPossible causesFirst checkSecond checkExperiment

💡 Senior insight

Correctable errors are not “free”. Each Bad TLP or Bad DLLP triggers a replay; enough replays turn a 14 GB/s link into a 9 GB/s link with no uncorrectable error ever logged. Always read correctable counters before blaming SSD firmware for throughput.

🧪 Lab 54.1 — Link health survey SAFE

Objective: inventory every NVMe link’s capability vs status. Steps: (1) lspci -tv to find the path; (2) for each SSD and its root port, record LnkCap speed/width, LnkSta speed/width, LnkSta2 EQ bits; (3) read aer_dev_correctable before and after a 10-minute read-only fio run. Observations: mismatches, rising counters. Questions: which mismatches are policy (BIOS limit) and which are failures?

Solution

If LnkCtl2 Target Link Speed is below LnkCap, it is policy. If target equals capability but status is lower, training/EQ failed or fell back. Rising Receiver Error counts with stable speed indicate marginal SI.

Extension: repeat after warming the system; plot counter rate vs temperature from nvme smart-log.

Quiz

  1. In which phase does the upstream port tune the downstream port’s transmitter?

    Answer

    Phase 2.

  2. Is the receiver’s figure of merit standardised?

    Answer

    No; how a receiver evaluates coefficients is implementation-dependent.

  3. Why is equalization not needed at 2.5 and 5 GT/s?

    Answer

    Those rates use fixed de-emphasis that is sufficient for their channel loss; adaptive negotiation was introduced with 8 GT/s.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate What are presets and coefficients?
    Model answerCoefficients are the FIR tap weights (pre-cursor, cursor, post-cursor); presets are named standard combinations used as starting points and in Phase 0/1.
  2. Senior A Gen5 SSD works on one motherboard and downgrades to Gen4 on another. How do you separate device and platform?
    Model answerCompare LnkSta2 per-phase status, use lane margining on both, swap with a known-good device on the bad board and the suspect device on a good board, check retimers and BIOS presets; collect LTSSM trace with an interposer if available.
📌 Summary

Equalization tunes transmitter FIR coefficients per lane in four phases inside Recovery.Equalization, separately for each rate from 8 GT/s. Software sees the outcome (status bits, speed/width, error counters, margining), not the algorithm.

55 Advanced Error Handling — AER, DPC and Recovery

← 54 Equalization — Opening the Eye at 8 GT/s and Beyond56 SR-IOV — One SSD, Many Controllers →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: PCI Express Base Specification — Error Signaling and Logging, Advanced Error Reporting (AER) Extended Capability, Downstream Port Containment (DPC) Extended Capability; Linux kernel PCI error recovery documentation (Documentation/PCI/pci-error-recovery.rst, pcieaer-howto.rst). STATUS: normative (PCIe) and informative (Linux). VERSION NOTES: DPC was added as an ECN to 3.x and integrated later; error types have been added over revisions (e.g. ACS Violation, Poisoned TLP Egress Blocked, DMWr-related) version.

55.1 Why this chapter exists

When an NVMe drive is surprise-removed, its link flaps, or its firmware returns a malformed TLP, the platform must decide: log and continue, reset the link, or crash. AER is how errors are reported and logged; DPC is how a downstream port stops a sick device from poisoning the rest of the system; the OS error-recovery framework is how the NVMe driver gets a chance to recover. If you work on enterprise SSDs, hot-plug, or fleet reliability, you will read AER logs weekly.

  • Classify errors: correctable, uncorrectable non-fatal, uncorrectable fatal; and by layer.
  • Read AER registers: status, mask, severity, header log, first error pointer, Root Error Status, Error Source ID.
  • Explain DPC triggering, containment and release.
  • Follow the Linux recovery flow: error_detected → mmio_enabled/slot_reset → resume, and what the NVMe driver does.
  • Diagnose surprise removal vs link instability vs device-internal error.

Prerequisites: completion statuses, link health, AER, ECRC, LCRC.

🧒 Kid analogy — the fire alarm and the fire door

Every room has a smoke detector that writes in a notebook what happened (AER logging). Small problems — burnt toast — are written down and everyone keeps working (correctable). Bigger problems ring the alarm at the head office (the root port). For a real fire, the hallway has a fire door (DPC) that slams shut automatically so the fire cannot spread, even before the head office decides what to do. Afterwards, the caretaker (the OS) checks the room, cleans up, and reopens the door.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

After DPC closes the “door”, the device behind it is effectively gone: in-flight requests to it are completed with error status by the port, and the device sees its link go down, which typically resets it. The “room” does not keep its state. Also, the notebook (header log) only records the first error of its kind in detail.

55.2 Error classes

ClassExamples (AER bit names)Message sent upstreamTypical layer
CorrectableReceiver Error, Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Replay Timer Timeout, Advisory Non-Fatal, Corrected Internal Error, Header Log OverflowERR_CORPhysical / Data Link
Uncorrectable non-fatal (default severity)Poisoned TLP Received, Completion Timeout, Completer Abort, Unexpected Completion, Unsupported Request, ECRC Error, ACS ViolationERR_NONFATALTransaction
Uncorrectable fatal (default severity)Data Link Protocol Error, Surprise Down, Flow Control Protocol Error, Receiver Overflow, Malformed TLP, Uncorrectable Internal ErrorERR_FATALData Link / Transaction / internal

verified for the classes and the bit names listed. Default severities are programmable through the Uncorrectable Error Severity register; check your platform’s firmware settings, which often change them impl.

55.3 AER registers

RegisterPurposeDebug note
Uncorrectable Error Status / Mask / SeverityWhich errors occurred; which are masked; fatal vs non-fatalMasked errors still may set status bits, but do not signal
Correctable Error Status / MaskSame for correctablePlatforms often mask some (e.g. Advisory Non-Fatal) impl
Advanced Error Capabilities and ControlFirst Error Pointer, ECRC generation/check enable, multiple header recordingFirst Error Pointer says which status bit was first
Header Log (4 DW; larger with TLP prefix log)Header of the TLP that caused the first logged errorDecode it: it names the requester, address, tag
Root Error Command / Status, Error Source IdentificationOn root ports: which function sent ERR_COR / ERR_(NON)FATALSource ID = BDF of reporter

55.4 Downstream Port Containment

When triggered, the downstream port transitions its link to a disabled state and sets DPC Trigger Status and Trigger Reason. While contained, requests targeting the device are completed by the port (typically UR or an all-ones read response at the CPU) impl. Software (Linux pcieport DPC service) handles the interrupt, runs driver recovery callbacks, then clears Trigger Status to release the link. Enhanced DPC (eDPC) adds Root Port Programmed I/O (RP PIO) error handling for CPU-originated non-posted requests. verified at concept level; the exact Linux log wording is version.

55.5 Linux recovery and the NVMe driver

// Conceptual flow of PCI error recovery as seen by a driver (Linux pci_error_handlers)
on AER uncorrectable or DPC event at a port:
    for each affected driver: state = err_handler.error_detected(dev, channel_state)
        // NVMe: normal_frozen  -> quiesce queues, return NEED_RESET
        //       perm_failure  -> mark controller dead, return DISCONNECT
    if link was reset (fatal or DPC): reset_link / secondary bus reset
    for each driver: err_handler.slot_reset(dev)    // NVMe: restore config, re-init controller
    for each driver: err_handler.resume(dev)        // NVMe: restart I/O, requeue
if any step returns DISCONNECT: device is removed; I/O fails upward

The Linux NVMe PCI driver implements these callbacks verified (see drivers/nvme/host/pci.c, nvme_err_handler). Exact behaviour and timeouts vary with kernel version version.

journalctl -k | grep -E 'AER|DPC|pcieport|nvme'      # error events and recovery
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/ | grep aer       # aer_dev_correctable, aer_dev_fatal, aer_dev_nonfatal
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/aer_dev_correctable
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:3b:00.0 | sed -n '/Advanced Error Reporting/,/^\s*Capabilities/p'
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:00:1c.0 | sed -n '/Downstream Port Containment/,/^\s*Capabilities/p'
⚠️ Safety

Error injection (the kernel aer_inject facility, or a platform’s firmware/ACPI error-injection interfaces) is an EXPERT-level activity: it can cause device removal, data loss and kernel panics. Use it only on disposable lab systems with no mounted filesystems on the target. EXPERT
