💡 Senior insight

Always decode the Header Log. “Uncorrectable non-fatal: Unsupported Request” is noise until you see it was a memory read from the SSD to an address outside the IOMMU mapping, at which point it is a driver bug with a precise address. And always ask which component reported: the Error Source ID often points at the root port, not the device.

🧪 Lab 55.1 — Decode an AER header log SAFE

Objective: decode a synthetic Header Log captured at a root port that logged Malformed TLP: 40000040 3b0001ff 3fe5a000 00000000 (illustrative). The root port and SSD both have MPS = 128 bytes. Steps: decode Fmt/Type, Length, Requester ID, Tag, byte enables and address. Questions: what kind of TLP is this? Who sent it? Why is it malformed?

Solution

DW0 40000040: Fmt 010b (3-DW header with data), Type 00000b ⇒ MWr with 32-bit address; Length 040h = 64 DW = 256 bytes. DW1 3b0001ff: Requester ID 3B00h (bus 3Bh, device 0, function 0 — the SSD), Tag 01h, Last DW BE Fh, First DW BE Fh. DW2 3FE5A000h is the address. DW3 is not part of a 3-DW header and carries no meaning here. The payload (256 B) exceeds the programmed MPS (128 B), which is a Malformed TLP condition at the receiver. Next questions: is the SSD’s DevCtl MPS really 128 (did firmware ignore it, or did software reprogram MPS after the device cached a value)? Lesson: the error name says “malformed”; only the decoded header says “payload larger than MPS, from the SSD”.

Extension: repeat with a 4-DW MRd header and identify the 64-bit address.

Quiz

  1. Which message does a device send for a Completion Timeout with default severity?

    Answer

    ERR_NONFATAL.

  2. What does DPC do that AER alone does not?

    Answer

    It contains the error in hardware by disabling the link at the downstream port, preventing further corrupted traffic before software reacts.

  3. Why do MMIO reads return all ones after a surprise removal?

    Answer

    The request fails (UR/containment) and the Root Complex synthesises an all-ones value for the CPU load; the driver must treat all ones in CSTS as “device gone”.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Name three correctable errors.
    Model answerReceiver Error, Bad TLP, Bad DLLP (also Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover).
  2. Advanced How do Linux NVMe and PCI core cooperate on a fatal error?
    Model answerPCI core calls error_detected, the NVMe driver freezes queues and requests reset; core resets the link; slot_reset re-initialises; resume restarts I/O; any failure leads to removal.
  3. Senior Should hot-plug NVMe platforms enable DPC on ERR_NONFATAL?
    Model answerTrade-off: containment on non-fatal improves isolation but turns recoverable events (e.g. a single UR) into full device resets; policy depends on workload, OS recovery maturity, and whether the error type is truly per-transaction.
📌 Summary

AER classifies, logs and signals; DPC contains; OS recovery callbacks restore. Decode the Header Log, identify the reporter, and map the error to its layer before deciding whose bug it is.

56 SR-IOV — One SSD, Many Controllers

← 55 Advanced Error Handling — AER, DPC and Recovery57 SMART / Health Information →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: PCI Express Base Specification — Single Root I/O Virtualization and Sharing (SR-IOV) Extended Capability, Alternative Routing-ID Interpretation (ARI); NVMe Base Specification 2.4 — Virtualization Enhancements (primary/secondary controllers, flexible resources, Virtualization Management command). STATUS: optional features. VERSION NOTES: SR-IOV was historically a separate PCI-SIG specification and is now part of the Base specification; NVMe virtualization enhancements were introduced in NVMe 1.3 and carried forward version. SOURCE: pcisig.com, nvmexpress.org/specifications.

56.1 Why this chapter exists

Cloud hosts give each virtual machine (VM) its own NVMe controller by exposing SR-IOV Virtual Functions (VFs) and passing them through. The VM’s guest driver talks directly to hardware queues — no hypervisor in the data path. To debug or validate this you need to know what is a PCIe concept (PF, VF, routing ID, VF BARs), what is an NVMe concept (primary controller, secondary controller, flexible queue and interrupt resources), and what is entirely implementation-specific (how bandwidth is shared, how isolation is enforced internally).

  • Explain Physical Function (PF) and Virtual Function (VF) and how VF Routing IDs are computed.
  • Read the SR-IOV capability: TotalVFs, InitialVFs, NumVFs, First VF Offset, VF Stride, VF Device ID, VF BARs, VF Enable.
  • Map PF/VF to NVMe primary/secondary controllers and flexible resources (VQ, VI).
  • Enable VFs on Linux and assign them to VMs safely.
  • Diagnose common SR-IOV failures: VF not appearing, VF controller not ready, interrupt starvation, IOMMU group issues.

Prerequisites: BDF and config space (BDF, BAR), MSI-X, NVMe queues (SQ, CQ), IOMMU (IOMMU), IDO.

🧒 Kid analogy — one kitchen, many serving windows

A restaurant has one big kitchen (the SSD) and one head chef (the PF). The owner opens several little serving windows (VFs), each with its own order slot and its own bell. Customers at window 3 cannot see window 5’s orders. The head chef decides how many cooks and order slots each window gets (flexible resources) and can close a window for maintenance.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The windows share the same stove (NAND, controller cores, PCIe link), so a greedy window can slow others unless the device enforces QoS — and how it does so is not defined by SR-IOV. Also the windows share the storage only if namespaces are attached to several controllers; by default each VF sees only what the PF administrator attaches to it.

56.2 PCIe view

SR-IOV capability fieldOwnerMeaning
TotalVFsDevice (RO)Max VFs the PF can expose
InitialVFsDevice (RO)VFs initially associated (relevant for some migration models)
NumVFsSoftware (RW)How many VFs to enable
First VF Offset, VF StrideDevice (RO, may depend on NumVFs)RID of VF n = PF RID + First VF Offset + (n−1) × VF Stride
VF Device IDDeviceDevice ID the VFs report (Vendor ID of a VF reads FFFFh; software uses PF’s)
VF BAR0–5, System Page SizeDevice + softwareOne BAR range is carved into NumVFs equal slices
VF Enable, VF MSESoftwareTurn VFs on; enable VF memory space

verified RID formula and field meanings. ARI (Alternative Routing-ID Interpretation) lets one device use up to 256 functions in the function number space, which large VF counts need. verified

56.3 NVMe view — primary and secondary controllers

In NVMe virtualization, the PF’s controller is a primary controller and each VF’s controller is a secondary controller. The primary controller manages flexible resources: Virtual Queue resources (VQ) and Virtual Interrupt resources (VI), which are assigned to secondary controllers before they are brought online. The admin command Virtualization Management (admin opcode 1Ch) assigns resources and sets secondary controllers online/offline. Identify returns a Primary Controller Capabilities structure and a Secondary Controller List. verified at concept level; confirm exact CNS values and field layouts in Base 2.4 version.

// Typical bring-up order (conceptual; check device documentation)
1. PF driver loaded; read Primary Controller Capabilities (total VQ/VI flexible, granularity)
2. Virtualization Management: assign VQ resources to secondary controller k
3. Virtualization Management: assign VI resources to secondary controller k
4. Enable VFs at the PCIe level (sriov_numvfs = N)          // VF config spaces appear
5. Virtualization Management: set secondary controller k Online
6. Attach namespace(s) to controller k (Namespace Attachment)
7. Pass VF to VM; guest NVMe driver enables controller (CC.EN=1) normally
🏭 Implementation-dependent

Whether steps 2–5 must happen before or after VF Enable, whether resources can be changed while a VF is enabled, whether a device supports private (fixed) resources only, and how bandwidth/IOPS are partitioned among VFs, all vary by product. Some devices pre-assign resources and need no Virtualization Management at all.

56.4 Linux view

cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/sriov_totalvfs
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/sriov_numvfs
sudo lspci -vvv -s 0000:3b:00.0 | sed -n '/SR-IOV/,/^\s*Capabilities/p'
sudo nvme primary-ctrl-caps /dev/nvme0         # Primary Controller Capabilities (nvme-cli)
sudo nvme list-secondary /dev/nvme0            # Secondary Controller List
ls -l /sys/kernel/iommu_groups/*/devices | grep 3b:00
⚠️ Safety — CAUTION

Writing sriov_numvfs and running nvme virt-mgmt change device configuration. On some devices changing resources resets controllers or detaches namespaces. Do it only on a lab SSD with no mounted filesystems; never on a boot disk.

# LAB ONLY — example enablement (device-specific; consult vendor documentation first)
echo 0 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/sriov_numvfs
sudo nvme virt-mgmt /dev/nvme0 --cntlid=2 --rt=0 --act=8 --nr=4   # assign VQ resources (example values)
sudo nvme virt-mgmt /dev/nvme0 --cntlid=2 --rt=1 --act=8 --nr=2   # assign VI resources
echo 2 | sudo tee /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:3b:00.0/sriov_numvfs
sudo nvme virt-mgmt /dev/nvme0 --cntlid=2 --act=9                 # set secondary online

Action and resource-type codes in this example follow nvme-cli’s documented options; verify them against nvme virt-mgmt --help on your version and the Base specification. version

Is VF1’s slowdown a bug? SR-IOV specifies isolation of configuration and address spaces, not performance isolation. NVMe offers mechanisms that may help (e.g. NVM Sets, Endurance Groups, and in 2.4 the announced Rate Limiting feature — see Chapter 20.1), but whether and how a device enforces QoS is impl.

💡 Senior insight

Draw two boundaries on every SR-IOV whiteboard: the PCIe boundary (config space, RIDs, BARs, MSI-X tables, IOMMU) and the NVMe boundary (controller IDs, queues, namespaces, resources). Most customer escalations are on the line between them: the PCIe side says “VF exists”, the NVMe side says “controller offline”. Live migration of such controllers is exactly what the 2026 “PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration” topic sits next to.

🧪 Lab 56.1 (Extended Lab 47) — Conceptual PF/VF topology SAFE

Objective: build a paper model of an SR-IOV NVMe SSD and classify each property as specification-defined (PCIe or NVMe) or implementation-specific. Prerequisites: this chapter. Setup: PF at 3b:00.0, First VF Offset = 1, VF Stride = 1, NumVFs = 4, VF BAR0 size 16 KiB, flexible VQ total 64, VI total 32.

  1. Identity: compute each VF’s BDF.
  2. Resources: split VQ/VI so VF1 gets twice the queues of the others; remember each controller needs an admin queue pair.
  3. Isolation: list what isolates VF1 from VF2 (RID-based IOMMU, separate BAR slices, separate controllers) and what does not (NAND, link bandwidth).
  4. Queues and interrupts: how many I/O queue pairs can VF1’s guest create? How many MSI-X vectors?
  5. Virtualization: what changes if NumVFs becomes 8 with the same BAR?

Observations: identity and address isolation are PCIe-defined; queue/interrupt resources are NVMe-defined; performance isolation is implementation-specific.

Solution

BDFs 3b:00.1–3b:00.4. VF BAR0 region = 4 × 16 KiB = 64 KiB carved contiguously. A split such as VF1 = 24 VQ, VF2–4 = 13/13/14 VQ (total 64), VI 12/7/7/6 (total 32) — exact granularity per Primary Controller Capabilities. Whether VQ counts include the admin queue is defined in the Base spec’s virtualization section — check it; this is a classic off-by-one. With NumVFs = 8, First VF Offset/Stride may change (they are allowed to depend on NumVFs) and BAR slices double in count; check System Page Size alignment.

Extension (intermediate): on a real lab SSD, read primary-ctrl-caps and list-secondary and fill your model with real values. Advanced: design a test that measures noisy-neighbour impact. Senior forensic: given a guest log showing controller not ready, enumerate the evidence needed from the host to locate the fault.

Quiz

  1. What is VF 3’s RID if PF = 3b:00.0, offset 4, stride 2?

    Answer

    RID offset = 4 + 2×2 = 8 ⇒ function 8, which requires ARI ⇒ with ARI the RID is bus 3Bh, function number 8 (displayed as 3b:01.0 in non-ARI notation).

  2. Which NVMe command assigns flexible resources?

    Answer

    Virtualization Management (admin opcode 1Ch).

  3. Does SR-IOV guarantee performance isolation?

    Answer

    No; it defines functional separation. Performance isolation is implementation-dependent.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a VF?
    Model answerA lightweight PCIe function created by a PF via the SR-IOV capability, with its own RID, BAR slice and MSI-X, sharing the device’s hardware.
  2. Intermediate Why does a VF’s Vendor ID read FFFFh?
    Model answerThe SR-IOV design makes several VF config fields read-only or not implemented to save hardware; software identifies VFs through the PF’s SR-IOV capability.
  3. Advanced Primary vs secondary controller?
    Model answerThe primary controller (on the PF) manages flexible resources and secondary controller state; secondary controllers (on VFs) are ordinary NVMe controllers from the guest’s view once online.
  4. Senior How would you validate VF isolation?
    Model answerNegative tests: VF DMA to addresses outside its IOMMU domain must fault; namespace not attached must be invisible; reset of one VF must not affect another; performance tests with noisy neighbours; error injection on one VF and check others continue.
📌 Summary

PCIe SR-IOV creates functions; NVMe virtualization turns them into resourced, online controllers; namespace attachment gives them storage; performance isolation is up to the device.

Teach-back: child — serving windows; junior — RID formula and resource assignment; senior — the PCIe/NVMe boundary and migration implications. Next: Part XVIII — NVMe Advanced Features.

  • I can describe primary/secondary controller resource flow.

  • I can separate PCIe-defined, NVMe-defined and implementation-specific behaviour.
  • I can debug “VF present but controller not ready”.
PART XVIII

NVMe Advanced Features

The core of NVMe — queues, doorbells, PRPs, reads and writes — is only the skeleton. Real products are distinguished by the features layered on top: how they report health, how they carve capacity into namespaces, how they expose zones, key-value stores and on-drive compute, how they are managed by a baseboard management controller over a side channel, and how they are booted before any operating system exists. Each chapter in this part is anchored to the August 2026 NVMe 2.4 specification set (Base 2.4, NVM Command Set 1.3, ZNS 1.5, Key Value 1.4, Subsystem Local Memory 1.3, Computational Programs 1.3, NVMe-MI 2.2, Boot 1.4 — revision numbers per the course brief; confirm each on nvmexpress.org/specifications before relying on them).

57 SMART / Health Information

← 56 SR-IOV — One SSD, Many Controllers58 Namespaces — Carving the Subsystem →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVM Express Base Specification. REVISION: 2.4 (August 2026 set). RELEVANT TOPIC: Get Log Page (admin opcode 02h), SMART / Health Information log page (Log Identifier 02h), Error Information log page (Log Identifier 01h), Asynchronous Event Request (admin opcode 0Ch), Temperature Threshold feature. STATUS: the SMART / Health log is mandatory for controllers that support the NVM Command Set (confirm the mandatory/optional matrix for your controller type in 2.4). OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: Critical Warning bits and Endurance Group fields were added over 1.x revisions; per-namespace SMART support is optional. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications. version

57.1 Why this chapter exists

Fleet operators decide whether to retire, migrate or keep a drive based almost entirely on one 512-byte log page. Validation engineers must prove that every counter in it moves correctly. Support engineers receive it as the first artefact in every escalation. Misreading it — confusing data units with bytes, treating Percentage Used as “percent until failure”, or ignoring Unsafe Shutdowns — leads to wrong conclusions with real money attached.

  • Beginner: name the key fields and what physical phenomenon each reflects.
  • Intermediate: convert data units to bytes, Kelvin to Celsius, and compute write amplification inputs.
  • Advanced: map Critical Warning bits to asynchronous events and thresholds.
  • Senior: design a fleet health policy that distinguishes wear, thermal, power and media problems.
  • Trace: recognise the Get Log Page command and its data transfer in a PCIe/NVMe trace.
  • Debug/validation: design tests that move each counter predictably.

Prerequisites: admin queue and Get Log Page basics, CQE status fields, NAND wear concepts, FTL.

🧒 Kid analogy — the car dashboard and the logbook

A car has a dashboard: temperature gauge, fuel (spare blocks), odometer (data written), engine-hours (power-on hours), and warning lights (critical warnings). It also has a logbook of times someone turned the key off without parking properly (unsafe shutdowns) and of times the engine misfired (media errors). The SMART log is the SSD’s dashboard plus logbook.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

An odometer is exact; Percentage Used is a vendor estimate based on the device’s own endurance model. The “fuel gauge” (Available Spare) is not linear with remaining life. And warning lights in NVMe can trigger an asynchronous message to the host, which a car dashboard cannot.

Before the field-by-field table, here is where the numbers come from and how they reach you. The controller keeps its own sensors and counters, summarises them in one log page, and hands that page over only when software asks with Get Log Page. Critical warnings are the exception: the controller can push those to the host as an asynchronous event, provided the driver has left Asynchronous Event Request commands waiting.

Host software starts itController starts itInside the controller (not on PCIe)PCIe link

57.2 The SMART / Health Information log (LID 02h)

BytesFieldUnit / encodingMeaning and pitfalls
0Critical Warningbit fieldBit 0 available spare below threshold; bit 1 temperature above an over-temperature threshold or below an under-temperature threshold; bit 2 NVM subsystem reliability degraded (significant media or internal errors); bit 3 media placed in read-only mode; bit 4 volatile memory backup device failed; bit 5 Persistent Memory Region became read-only or unreliable (newer revisions). Any set bit may generate an asynchronous event if enabled.
2:1Composite TemperatureKelvin (16-bit)A single “representative” temperature chosen by the controller; °C = K − 273. How it is composed from sensors is impl.
3Available Sparepercent (0–100)Normalised remaining spare capacity.
4Available Spare ThresholdpercentWhen Available Spare falls below this, Critical Warning bit 0 sets.
5Percentage Usedpercent, may exceed 100 (saturates at 255)Vendor estimate of life consumed relative to rated endurance. 100 means rated endurance reached, not that the drive has failed.
6Endurance Group Critical Warning Summarybit fieldSummary of critical warnings in Endurance Groups (when supported).
47:32Data Units Read128-bit count of units of 1000 × 512 bytesHost data read, rounded up; one unit = 512 000 bytes. Excludes metadata.
63:48Data Units Writtensame unitHost data written. Not NAND writes — write amplification is not visible here.
79:64Host Read CommandscountCommands completed (by command set definition of “read”).
95:80Host Write CommandscountSame for writes.
111:96Controller Busy TimeminutesTime with commands outstanding to I/O queues.
127:112Power CyclescountNumber of power cycles.
143:128Power On HourshoursWhether non-operational power-state time is included is impl/version.
159:144Unsafe ShutdownscountPower lost without a prior shutdown notification (CC.SHN) completing.
175:160Media and Data Integrity ErrorscountUnrecovered data integrity errors (e.g. uncorrectable ECC, end-to-end protection check failures).
191:176Number of Error Information Log EntriescountLifetime count of entries created in the Error Information log (LID 01h).
195:192Warning Composite Temperature TimeminutesTime above warning threshold (WCTEMP).
199:196Critical Composite Temperature TimeminutesTime above critical threshold (CCTEMP).
215:200Temperature Sensor 1–8Kelvin, 2 bytes each0 = sensor not implemented.

verified — this layout has been stable across NVMe 1.x and 2.x; confirm field presence and reserved ranges in Base 2.4 before writing a parser. All multi-byte fields are little-endian.

57.3 Conversions

Bytes = DataUnits × 1000 × 512
  • DataUnits — Data Units Read or Written (128-bit integer)
  • 1000 × 512 — the fixed unit defined by the specification (512 000 bytes)
T(°C) = T(K) − 273     WAF ≈ NAND_bytes_written / (DataUnitsWritten × 512 000)
  • T(K) — Composite Temperature in Kelvin
  • WAF — write amplification factor
  • NAND_bytes_written — only available from vendor-specific logs impl

Worked example

A drive reports Data Units Written = 61 035 157 and Power On Hours = 8 760. Bytes written = 61 035 157 × 512 000 ≈ 31.25 × 1012 bytes ≈ 31.25 TB (decimal) over one year, i.e. ≈ 85.6 GB/day. If the drive is a 3.84 TB device rated 1 drive-write-per-day for 5 years (≈ 7 008 TB), this is ≈ 0.45% of rated endurance per year — but Percentage Used might still read 2% or 3% because it reflects NAND wear including write amplification. synthetic numbers. The lesson: never compute Percentage Used yourself from Data Units Written.

57.4 Protocol and trace view

Get Log Page is admin opcode 02h; CDW10 carries the Log Page Identifier (bits 7:0) and the lower Number of Dwords (NUMDL); CDW11 the upper (NUMDU); CDW12/13 the Log Page Offset; the NSID selects controller-wide (FFFFFFFFh or 0 per support) or per-namespace scope. verified

57.5 Linux view

sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0                 # decoded SMART/Health log
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0 -o json         # machine-readable
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 16           # Error Information log entries
sudo nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=2 --log-len=512 --raw-binary | xxd | head
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x04 -H    # Temperature Threshold feature
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x0b -H    # Asynchronous Event Configuration
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/hwmon*/temp1_input 2>/dev/null   # kernel hwmon (milli-°C), if present

What it proves: the controller’s self-report at that instant. What it cannot prove: the internal cause of a counter change, NAND write volume, or whether a value is computed correctly (that requires controlled tests).

💡 Senior insight

Trend, do not snapshot. A single SMART read tells you little; deltas per day of Media Errors, Unsafe Shutdowns, Available Spare and Percentage Used, correlated with firmware version and slot, tell you almost everything a fleet needs. Store the raw 512 bytes, not just a decoded subset — new fields appear with new revisions.

🧪 Lab 57.1 — Move every counter CAUTION

Objective: validate that counters move as specified. Setup: a disposable lab SSD, no mounted filesystems. Steps: (1) save raw SMART log; (2) read exactly 1 GB with dd if=/dev/nvme1n1 of=/dev/null bs=1M count=1000 iflag=direct; (3) save log, compute Data Units Read delta (expect ≈ 2 048 units: 1 048 576 000 / 512 000); (4) issue a clean shutdown, then a hard power-off (lab PSU), compare Unsafe Shutdowns; (5) watch Composite Temperature under sustained read load. Observations: deltas, rounding. Questions: why might the delta differ slightly? Why does a write test require extra caution?

Solution

Rounding up per unit and background reads by OS tools (partition probing) add small deltas. Write tests destroy data and consume endurance; they must target a disposable device. Unsafe Shutdowns increments only on the hard power-off.

Extension: write a parser for the raw 512-byte log in Python and compare against nvme smart-log -o json.

Quiz

  1. How many bytes is one Data Unit?

    Answer

    1000 × 512 = 512 000 bytes.

  2. Composite Temperature reads 0x0150. What is it in °C?

    Answer

    0x150 = 336 K ⇒ 63 °C.

  3. Can Percentage Used exceed 100?

    Answer

    Yes; values above 254 are reported as 255.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Name five SMART fields.
    Model answerCritical Warning, Composite Temperature, Available Spare, Percentage Used, Data Units Written (also Power On Hours, Unsafe Shutdowns, Media Errors).
  2. Intermediate How does the host learn about a critical warning without polling?
    Model answerOutstanding Asynchronous Event Requests complete with a SMART/Health event when enabled in Asynchronous Event Configuration; the host then reads the log.
  3. Advanced Why is WAF not computable from the SMART log alone?
    Model answerIt reports host writes only; NAND writes are in vendor logs.
  4. Senior Design a retirement policy.
    Model answerCombine Critical Warning (immediate), Available Spare vs threshold trend, Media Error rate, Percentage Used projection, thermal history, firmware cohort; avoid single-threshold decisions on vendor estimates.
📌 Summary

The SMART / Health log (LID 02h) is a 512-byte self-report: warnings, temperatures in Kelvin, spare, wear estimate, host traffic in 512 000-byte units, power history, and error counts. Treat estimates as estimates, trend deltas, and confirm field layout per revision.

58 Namespaces — Carving the Subsystem

← 57 SMART / Health Information59 Zoned Namespaces (ZNS) →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe Base Specification 2.4 (Namespace Management admin opcode 0Dh, Namespace Attachment admin opcode 15h, Identify CNS values, Changed Namespace List log) and NVM Command Set 1.3 (Identify Namespace data structure for NVM: NSZE, NCAP, NUSE, FLBAS, LBA Format list). STATUS: Namespace Management and Attachment are optional (Identify Controller OACS bit 3 reports support). VERSION NOTES: since NVMe 2.0 the Identify data is split between command-set-independent and command-set-specific structures, and the I/O Command Set (CSI) concept was introduced version.

58.1 Why this chapter exists

A namespace is the thing your OS calls /dev/nvme0n1. It is a range of logical blocks with a format, a size and a set of controllers allowed to access it. Multi-tenant arrays, SR-IOV (see Chapter 56), multipath, and every “why does my drive show 0 bytes” bug lead here.

  • Define NSID, NSZE, NCAP, NUSE and their ordering NSZE ≥ NCAP ≥ NUSE.
  • Read the LBA format list (LBADS, MS, RP) and FLBAS.
  • Explain thin provisioning and capacity accounting (TNVMCAP/UNVMCAP).
  • Execute and trace the create → attach → rescan → use → detach → delete flow.
  • Understand shared namespaces and the Namespace Attribute Changed event.

Prerequisites: Identify command (admin 06h), LBA, controller ID (CNTLID).

🧒 Kid analogy — the library sections

A huge library (NVM subsystem) can be divided into sections (namespaces): “Science, 2 shelves”, “Stories, 5 shelves”. Each section has its own shelf numbering starting at 0 (LBAs). The head librarian decides which reading rooms (controllers) get a key to each section (attachment). A section can be labelled “5 shelves” but only have books on 3 (thin provisioning).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Namespaces are logical; there is no fixed physical shelf behind them. The FTL places data anywhere on NAND. Also, a namespace can be attached to several controllers at once (shared), which needs reservations or a cluster file system to be safe.

58.2 Size fields

FieldBytes (Identify Namespace, NVM)Meaning
NSZE — Namespace Size7:0Total size in logical blocks (LBA 0 … NSZE−1)
NCAP — Namespace Capacity15:8Max blocks that may be allocated at once; < NSZE implies thin provisioning
NUSE — Namespace Utilization23:16Blocks currently allocated (deallocate/trim may reduce it if supported)
NSFEAT24Bit 0 THINP (thin provisioning supported) and other feature bits
NLBAF25Number of LBA formats (0’s based)
FLBAS26Formatted LBA size: index of the active LBA format (+ metadata placement bit)
LBAF0…from 128, 4 bytes eachMS (metadata size), LBADS (log2 of data size, e.g. 9 = 512, 12 = 4096), RP (relative performance)

verified for the classic offsets; the format index field was extended to allow more than 16 formats in 2.0-era revisions version.

Capacity_bytes = NSZE × 2LBADS
  • NSZE — namespace size in logical blocks
  • LBADS — LBA data size exponent of the active format

58.3 Management and attachment flow

Create: the host sends Namespace Management with a data structure containing at least NSZE, NCAP, FLBAS and (optionally) DPS, NMIC (shared bit) and, for other command sets, the CSI-specific fields. The controller allocates an NSID and returns it in CQE Dword 0. Attach: Namespace Attachment with a Controller List (count + list of CNTLIDs). Notify: each affected controller posts a Namespace Attribute Changed asynchronous event and updates the Changed Namespace List log (LID 04h). Rescan: the host reads Identify (CNS 02h active NSID list; CNS 00h per NSID) and creates block devices. verified

Identify CNSReturns
00hIdentify Namespace (NVM-specific, for an active NSID)
01hIdentify Controller
02hActive Namespace ID list
03hNamespace Identification Descriptor list (EUI64, NGUID, UUID, CSI)
10hAllocated Namespace ID list
11hIdentify Namespace for an allocated NSID
12hControllers attached to an NSID
13hAll controllers in the subsystem

verified long-standing CNS values; 2.x added CSI-specific variants — check the 2.4 CNS table.

58.4 Linux view

sudo nvme list
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -E '^(oacs|nn|mnan|tnvmcap|unvmcap|cntlid)'
sudo nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 --all          # allocated NSIDs
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H | grep -E 'nsze|ncap|nuse|flbas|LBA Format'
sudo nvme list-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -n 1         # controllers attached to NSID 1
⚠️ Safety — CAUTION / destructive

The commands below destroy data. Run only on a lab SSD, after unmounting, never on the boot device.

# LAB ONLY: create a 100 GiB (4 KiB format) namespace and attach it to controller 0
sudo nvme create-ns /dev/nvme1 --nsze=26214400 --ncap=26214400 --flbas=1   # flbas index is device-specific
sudo nvme attach-ns /dev/nvme1 --namespace-id=2 --controllers=0x0          # use the NSID returned and your CNTLID
sudo nvme ns-rescan /dev/nvme1
# teardown
sudo nvme detach-ns /dev/nvme1 --namespace-id=2 --controllers=0x0
sudo nvme delete-ns /dev/nvme1 --namespace-id=2

26 214 400 blocks × 4 096 B = 100 GiB. Which FLBAS index is 4 KiB differs per device — read the LBA Format list first. impl

58.6 Failure patterns

SymptomCausesFirst checkSecond checkConclusion

💡 Senior insight

Namespace bugs are almost always state-machine bugs: allocated vs active, attached vs visible to the OS, formatted vs advertised. Draw the state of each NSID on each controller, then compare with what the host believes. Most escalations end in “the host never rescanned” or “a detach raced with I/O”.

🧪 Lab 58.1 — Namespace state table SAFE

Objective: build the state of every NSID on a subsystem with two controllers. Steps: using read-only commands (list-ns --all, list-ns, list-ctrl -n, id-ns), fill a table NSID × controller with {unallocated, allocated-inactive, attached}. Questions: which NSIDs are allocated but invisible? Solution approach: anything in the allocated list and absent from every controller’s active list is allocated-inactive.

Solution

Expected reasoning: CNS 10h (allocated) minus union of CNS 02h (active per controller). On a single-controller consumer SSD without OACS bit 3, every namespace is fixed and attached; the table has one column of “attached”.

Extension (CAUTION): on a lab SSD with namespace management, create two namespaces with different LBA formats and measure 4 KiB random-read latency on each.

Quiz

  1. Order NSZE, NCAP, NUSE.

    Answer

    NSZE ≥ NCAP ≥ NUSE.

  2. Which command makes a namespace visible to a controller?

    Answer

    Namespace Attachment (15h) with SEL = attach.

  3. LBADS = 12; NSZE = 1 000 000. Capacity?

    Answer

    4 096 000 000 bytes (≈ 4.1 GB).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is an NSID?
    Model answerA 32-bit identifier of a namespace within the subsystem; 0 is invalid for I/O and FFFFFFFFh is the broadcast value.
  2. Intermediate What is thin provisioning in NVMe terms?
    Model answerNCAP < NSZE (NSFEAT THINP): the namespace addresses more blocks than can be allocated simultaneously.
  3. Senior How do you safely resize capacity for a VM backed by a VF?
    Model answerQuiesce, detach from the secondary controller, delete/create (or use a resize mechanism if supported in the revision), attach, guest rescan; reason about data migration and AEN delivery to the guest.
📌 Summary

Namespaces are created (0Dh), attached (15h), announced (AEN + LID 04h) and discovered (Identify). Size is NSZE × 2LBADS; NCAP and NUSE add allocation semantics. Every NSID has a state per controller.

  • I can run and trace the full lifecycle on a lab SSD.
  • I can diagnose “namespace not visible”.
  • I can explain shared namespaces and their risks.

59 Zoned Namespaces (ZNS)

← 58 Namespaces — Carving the Subsystem60 Key Value Command Set →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Zoned Namespace Command Set Specification. REVISION: 1.5 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm on nvmexpress.org). STATUS: optional I/O command set (CSI for ZNS). OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: ZNS 1.0 was published with NVMe 1.4-era TP 4053; later revisions refined zone attributes, limits and reporting version. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications. Linux: Documentation/block/zoned and kernel zoned block device docs.

59.1 Why this chapter exists

A conventional SSD hides NAND’s erase-before-write nature behind an FTL that remaps every write, which costs DRAM, over-provisioning and write amplification. ZNS exposes the truth: the namespace is divided into zones that must be written sequentially and reset as a whole. The host takes over data placement, and in return the device can be cheaper, more predictable and more durable. The price is a strict state machine that the host must respect — and that you must be able to debug.

  • Define zone, zone size, zone capacity, write pointer, ZSLBA.
  • Draw the zone state machine with all seven states and the transitions caused by writes and Zone Management Send actions.
  • Explain active and open resource limits.
  • Explain Zone Append and why it exists.
  • Diagnose invalid-write and resource-limit errors from traces.

Prerequisites: namespaces, FTL, NAND erase blocks, ZNS.

🧒 Kid analogy — the warehouse aisles

A warehouse has many long aisles (zones). Workers must fill each aisle from the front to the back, one box after another, never skipping a spot. A pointer on the floor (write pointer) shows where the next box goes. When an aisle is full, nobody can add more until the whole aisle is emptied at once (reset). Only a limited number of aisles may have their lights on and workers in them at the same time (open zones). If you are in a hurry, you can hand a box to the foreman and say “put it at the end of aisle 7 and tell me where it went” (zone append).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A zone’s writable capacity may be smaller than its address span (zone capacity < zone size), so the “aisle” has a painted-off end you can never use. Zones can also become read-only or offline because of media failure — the warehouse can lose an aisle by itself. And “open” is an accounting state, not necessarily a physical one.

59.2 Vocabulary

TermPlain meaningEngineering meaningCommon confusion
Zonean aislecontiguous LBA range [ZSLBA, ZSLBA + zone size)not the same as one NAND block
Zone size (ZSZE)aisle lengthLBAs per zone, uniform in a namespace, from the ZNS LBA format extensionvs capacity
Zone capacity (ZCAP)usable lengthwritable LBAs in the zone, ≤ zone size, per zone descriptorwriting past ZCAP is an error even if < zone size
Write pointer (WP)the floor arrownext LBA that may be written in a sequential-write-required zoneWP is invalid in Full/RO/Offline states
Active zoneaisle in usezone in Implicitly Opened, Explicitly Opened or ClosedClosed still counts as active
Open zonelights onzone in Implicitly or Explicitly Openedlimits are separate (MOR vs MAR)
Zone Append“put it at the end”write command targeting ZSLBA; device chooses LBA = WP and returns it in the completionnot a host-chosen LBA

59.3 The zone state machine

FromTriggerToResource effect
EmptyWrite / Zone Append to the zoneImplicitly Opened+1 active, +1 open (may fail with Too Many Active/Open Zones)
EmptyOpen Zone actionExplicitly Opened+1 active, +1 open
Implicitly OpenedClose Zone action, or controller closes it to free an open resourceClosed−1 open (stays active)
Explicitly OpenedClose Zone action (controller does not implicitly close it)Closed−1 open
ClosedWriteImplicitly Opened+1 open
ClosedOpen Zone actionExplicitly Opened+1 open
IO / EO / ClosedWP reaches zone capacity, or Finish Zone actionFullreleases active (and open)
IO / EO / Closed / FullReset Zone actionEmptyWP = ZSLBA, releases resources
Read OnlyOffline Zone actionOfflineterminal for host

59.4 Commands

CommandPurposeNotes
Write (NVM opcode 01h)Write at exactly WPWrite to LBA ≠ WP ⇒ Zone Invalid Write; crossing zone ⇒ Zone Boundary Error
Zone AppendWrite at WP chosen by deviceSLBA field = ZSLBA; assigned LBA returned in the completion; size bounded by the Zone Append Size Limit
Zone Management SendActions: Open, Close, Finish, Reset, Offline, Set Zone Descriptor Extension“Select All” applies to all zones in eligible states
Zone Management ReceiveReport Zones: list of zone descriptors (type, state, attributes, ZCAP, ZSLBA, WP)filter by state; partial report option
Read (02h)Read any written LBAReads above WP: behaviour defined by namespace setting (e.g. read across zone boundaries, unwritten data) — check spec

The ZNS-specific opcodes (Zone Management Send, Zone Management Receive, Zone Append) are defined in the ZNS command set specification; widely used values are 79h, 7Ah and 7Dh respectively verified — confirm against ZNS 1.5. Status names (Zone Boundary Error, Zone Is Full, Zone Is Read Only, Zone Is Offline, Zone Invalid Write, Too Many Active Zones, Too Many Open Zones, Invalid Zone State Transition) are command-specific statuses defined there; read their codes from the specification rather than from memory.

59.5 Why Zone Append exists

With ordinary writes, the host must issue exactly one write per zone at a time at the WP, because NVMe does not guarantee command execution order: two queued writes to the same zone may be processed out of order and the second becomes a Zone Invalid Write. That forces queue depth 1 per zone. Zone Append lets many writes to the same zone be outstanding; the device serialises them and reports where each landed. derived from NVMe’s lack of inter-command ordering. Linux’s block layer historically used per-zone write locking (mq-deadline) for regular writes and zone append for file systems such as btrfs and zonefs. version (kernel behaviour changes; newer kernels add zone write plugging).

59.7 Linux view

cat /sys/block/nvme0n2/queue/zoned              # host-managed
cat /sys/block/nvme0n2/queue/chunk_sectors      # zone size in 512-byte sectors
cat /sys/block/nvme0n2/queue/max_open_zones /sys/block/nvme0n2/queue/max_active_zones
sudo blkzone report /dev/nvme0n2 | head         # util-linux
sudo nvme zns id-ns /dev/nvme0n2 -H             # ZNS Identify Namespace (MAR, MOR, LBAFE)
sudo nvme zns report-zones /dev/nvme0n2 -d 8    # first 8 zone descriptors

Linux exposes ZNS namespaces as zoned block devices; the NVMe driver’s acceptance criteria (for instance requiring Zone Append support or power-of-two zone sizes) are version-dependent kernel policy, not specification requirements.

💡 Senior insight

ZNS moves the FTL’s hardest problem — garbage collection — into host software. When performance is bad on ZNS, the device is rarely the first suspect; look at the host’s zone allocation policy (how many zones are open, how data with different lifetimes is mixed). When correctness is bad, it is almost always the WP: compare the host’s idea of WP with Report Zones after every anomaly.

🧪 Lab 59.1 (Extended Lab 48) — Warehouse model and invalid-write diagnosis SAFE

Objective: build a software model of zones, write pointers and states; then diagnose an invalid write. Prerequisites: Python 3. Setup: the simulation below.

class Zone:
    def __init__(s, zslba, size, cap):
        s.zslba, s.size, s.cap = zslba, size, cap
        s.wp, s.state = zslba, "EMPTY"
class ZNS:
    def __init__(s, nzones=8, size=0x1000, cap=0xC00, mar=4, mor=2):
        s.z = [Zone(i*size, size, cap) for i in range(nzones)]
        s.size, s.mar, s.mor = size, mar, mor
    def count(s, states): return sum(z.state in states for z in s.z)
    def write(s, slba, nlb, append=False):
        z = s.z[slba // s.size]
        if z.state in ("FULL", "READ_ONLY", "OFFLINE"): return "Zone Is " + z.state.title(), None
        if append and slba != z.zslba: return "Invalid Field", None
        start = z.wp if append else slba
        if start != z.wp: return "Zone Invalid Write", None
        if start + nlb > z.zslba + z.cap: return "Zone Boundary Error", None
        if z.state == "EMPTY" and s.count({"IMP_OPEN","EXP_OPEN","CLOSED"}) >= s.mar:
            return "Too Many Active Zones", None
        if z.state in ("EMPTY","CLOSED") and s.count({"IMP_OPEN","EXP_OPEN"}) >= s.mor:
            return "Too Many Open Zones", None   # simplified: real devices may implicitly close
        if z.state in ("EMPTY","CLOSED"): z.state = "IMP_OPEN"
        z.wp += nlb
        if z.wp == z.zslba + z.cap: z.state = "FULL"
        return "Success", start
    def reset(s, zslba):
        z = s.z[zslba // s.size]; z.wp, z.state = z.zslba, "EMPTY"

d = ZNS()
print(d.write(0x0, 8))            # Success, 0
print(d.write(0x10, 8))           # Zone Invalid Write (WP is 0x8)
print(d.write(0x0, 8, append=True))  # Success, 8
print(d.write(0x1000, 8), d.write(0x2000, 8))  # second hits open limit (MOR=2)
  1. Map each warehouse concept to a model field (aisle → Zone, floor arrow → wp, lights on → open states, empty the aisle → reset).
  2. Run the script; explain each result.
  3. Diagnose: a host log shows “Zone Invalid Write at SLBA 0x10”; what single piece of evidence settles whether the host or device is wrong?
  4. Add a finish() and a close() method and the implicit-close behaviour.
Solution

The decisive evidence is the zone’s write pointer at the time of the command (Report Zones immediately after, plus the history of successful writes). If WP = 0x8 and SLBA = 0x10, the host skipped LBAs — host bug (often reordering). If WP = 0x10 but the device rejected, the device is wrong. The real specification also lets the controller implicitly close an Implicitly Opened zone instead of failing with Too Many Open Zones; whether it does is part of normative rules plus implementation choice — check the ZNS spec and device documentation.

Extension (advanced): add Read Only/Offline injection and verify your host code migrates data. Senior forensic: given only completion statuses and timestamps from a crash, reconstruct the WP of three zones.

Quiz

  1. Name the seven zone states.

    Answer

    Empty, Implicitly Opened, Explicitly Opened, Closed, Full, Read Only, Offline.

  2. Does a Closed zone count against the active limit?

    Answer

    Yes. Active = IO + EO + Closed.

  3. Where does the host learn the LBA used by a Zone Append?

    Answer

    In the completion queue entry for that command.

  4. Why can zone capacity be smaller than zone size?

    Answer

    So zone size can be a convenient (e.g. power-of-two) address span while capacity matches the device’s physical erase unit structure.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a write pointer?
    Model answerThe next LBA that may be written in a sequential-write-required zone.
  2. Intermediate Conventional namespace vs ZNS?
    Model answerConventional allows random writes and the device FTL remaps; ZNS requires sequential writes per zone and explicit resets, moving placement and GC to the host.
  3. Advanced Why does Linux need special handling for zoned writes?
    Model answerBecause the block layer and NVMe may reorder; it must serialise per-zone writes or use zone append.
  4. Senior How would you validate a ZNS device’s state machine?
    Model answerEnumerate every (state, action) pair from the spec’s transition table, including illegal ones expecting Invalid Zone State Transition; test resource limits at MAR/MOR boundaries; power-loss tests for WP consistency; concurrency tests with append.

Teach-back: child — warehouse aisles; junior — WP and states; senior — why ZNS shifts GC and how to prove a WP bug.

📌 Summary

ZNS zones are written sequentially at the write pointer, tracked through seven states, limited by active/open resources, and recycled by reset. Zone Append removes the QD-1-per-zone limit. Most bugs are WP disagreements between host and device.

  • I can cite the ZNS command set specification and its revision for these facts.

60 Key Value Command Set

← 59 Zoned Namespaces (ZNS)61 Computational Programs →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Key Value Command Set Specification. REVISION: 1.4 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm on nvmexpress.org). STATUS: optional I/O command set, selected by Command Set Identifier (CSI). OLDER VERSIONS: KV 1.0 was published with the NVMe 2.0 family (2021) when the specification was refactored into a base plus command sets version. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications.

60.1 Why this chapter exists

Many applications do not want blocks at all; they want “store this value under this key” and “give me the value for that key”. Today they run a key-value engine (an LSM-tree such as RocksDB) on a file system on a block SSD that runs an FTL — three layers of mapping, each with its own write amplification. The KV command set lets the device expose keys and values directly, potentially collapsing those layers. Whether it helps is workload- and implementation-dependent; understanding the interface lets you evaluate it honestly.

  • Explain the KV namespace concept and how it differs from an LBA namespace.
  • Describe Store, Retrieve, Delete, Exist and List at the conceptual level.
  • Compare KV and block storage on mapping, atomicity, write amplification and tooling.
  • Identify what the KV specification defines and what is left to the device.

Prerequisites: namespaces and CSI; NVMe command/completion format.

🧒 Kid analogy — the coat check

A block SSD is a wall of numbered lockers: you must remember which locker numbers hold your coat. A key-value SSD is a coat check: you hand over your coat (value) and say a name (key). Later you say the name and get your coat back. You do not care which hook it hangs on.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Keys have a strict maximum length, values have device-reported limits, there is no built-in range query beyond the List command’s semantics, and the device still runs an internal index and garbage collection — the mapping did not disappear, it moved.

60.2 Engineering view

OperationConceptData movementSpec / implementation boundary
Storewrite value under key; options control whether the key must already exist or must not existhost → device (value in the data buffer)options and atomicity defined in KV spec; internal placement impl
Retrieveread value for a keydevice → hostbehaviour when buffer is smaller than the value: check spec (partial returns and reported value size)
Deleteremove key and valuenonewhen space is reclaimed impl
Existdoes this key exist?none (status only)defined in spec
Listenumerate keysdevice → host (key list)ordering semantics: read the spec, do not assume sorted order

verified command names. Key length is bounded by the specification (the original release allowed keys up to 16 bytes, carried with the command) version; maximum value size and number of keys are reported by the device impl. Opcodes and status codes: read them from the KV specification — do not reuse NVM command set opcodes by analogy.

60.3 KV vs block

The difference in one picture: on the left the host must remember where its data lives (which LBAs); on the right the host only remembers names, and the device keeps the index. The mapping did not disappear: it moved into the device.

AspectBlock (NVM command set)Key Value
AddressingLBA + lengthkey (bytes)
Unitfixed-size logical blockvariable-size value
Host mappingfile system / KV engine maps names to LBAsdevice maps keys to media
Ecosystemuniversal (file systems, RAID, tools)application-specific libraries, passthrough
Failure “not found”no such concept (any LBA readable)key-not-found status
DebuggingLBA traces, blktracecommand-level traces; no block-layer view

Truncation or bug? If the completion reports a value size larger than the buffer, the host must re-issue with a larger buffer (or offset, if supported). Check how the KV spec defines partial retrieval before calling it a defect. derived

💡 Senior insight

Evaluate KV by end-to-end write amplification and tail latency against a tuned LSM on a block SSD with the same NAND — not by interface elegance. And plan the operational story: backup, replication, encryption and monitoring tools all assume blocks or files.

Quiz

  1. Name the five KV operations.

    Answer

    Store, Retrieve, Delete, Exist, List.

  2. Does KV eliminate the device’s mapping table?

    Answer

    No; it moves key→media mapping into the device and may remove host-side mapping layers.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Why does a KV command set exist?
    Model answerTo let applications that think in keys and values avoid stacked mapping layers (KV engine → file system → FTL), potentially reducing write amplification, CPU and latency.
  2. Senior How would you validate KV atomicity?
    Model answerPower-loss during Store of large values; verify after restart that each key returns either old or new value per spec guarantees, never a mix; repeat for overwrite and delete.

61 Computational Programs

← 60 Key Value Command Set62 Subsystem Local Memory (SLM) →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Computational Programs Command Set Specification, used together with the Subsystem Local Memory Command Set Specification (Chapter 62). REVISION: Computational Programs 1.3 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm). STATUS: optional I/O command set. OLDER VERSIONS: both command sets were first released in January 2024 version (confirm date on nvmexpress.org). SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications; the SNIA Computational Storage Architecture is a related but separate document.

61.1 Why this chapter exists

Moving a terabyte from SSD to host DRAM to filter out 1% of it wastes PCIe bandwidth, host memory bandwidth and CPU time. Computational storage runs the filter next to the data and sends back only the result. NVMe’s Computational Programs command set is the standard interface for that: programs live in a compute namespace, operate on data staged in subsystem local memory, and are managed and executed with NVMe commands.

  • Explain computational storage and the data-locality argument with a bandwidth calculation.
  • Distinguish device-defined (preloaded) and downloadable programs.
  • Describe the program lifecycle: load, activate, execute, results.
  • Explain the relationship between compute namespaces, memory namespaces (SLM) and NVM namespaces.

Prerequisites: namespaces, CSI; PCIe bandwidth (Chapter 53).

🧒 Kid analogy — the factory beside the mine

A mine (NVM namespace) produces tons of rock. Trucking all the rock to the city (host) to extract a few grams of gold is slow and expensive. So you build a small factory (compute engine) next to the mine, with its own loading yard (subsystem local memory). The factory has some machines that came installed (preloaded programs) and you can ship in new machines (downloaded programs). Only the gold goes to the city.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The factory is small: compute engines inside SSDs are much weaker than host CPUs, so offload helps only when data reduction is large or host resources are the bottleneck. Also, the “yard” must be explicitly filled and emptied with commands — the factory does not dig the mine by itself.

61.2 Data-locality arithmetic

T_host ≈ D / BW_link + D / R_host     T_offload ≈ D / BW_internal + D / R_dev + (s·D) / BW_link
  • D — bytes to scan
  • BW_link — effective PCIe bandwidth to host
  • R_host / R_dev — processing rate of host CPU / device compute engine
  • BW_internal — media-to-SLM bandwidth inside the device
  • s — selectivity (fraction of data returned)

Worked example synthetic: D = 1 TB, BW_link = 7 GB/s, R_host = 20 GB/s (several cores), BW_internal = 10 GB/s, R_dev = 4 GB/s, s = 0.01. Simplifying as pipelined (time = slowest stage): host path ≈ 1 TB / 7 GB/s ≈ 143 s; offload ≈ 1 TB / 4 GB/s ≈ 250 s. Offload is slower here — but it frees the host CPU and PCIe link for other work. With 8 such SSDs on a shared x16 uplink (≈ 28 GB/s), the host path needs 8 TB / 28 GB/s ≈ 286 s of uplink time and 8 TB / 20 GB/s ≈ 400 s of CPU time, so it takes ≈ 400 s, while the eight devices offload in parallel in ≈ 250 s and return only 80 GB. derived The value of computational storage is usually aggregate and system-level.

61.3 Architecture

61.4 Lifecycle

  1. Discover: identify compute namespaces and their programs (device-defined programs are present from manufacture/firmware; downloadable program slots may exist).
  2. Load (downloadable programs): transfer a program image to a program slot. Program type/format is specified per program type; image contents are impl.
  3. Activate: make a program executable.
  4. Stage data: copy data from an NVM namespace into SLM ranges (SLM command set), or write host data into SLM.
  5. Define memory ranges: describe which SLM ranges a program may use (memory range sets).
  6. Execute: run the program with parameters; completion returns program status.
  7. Collect: read results from SLM to host.

verified lifecycle concepts; command names (e.g. Load Program, Program Activation Management, Execute Program, Memory Range Set Management) and their fields must be read from Computational Programs 1.3 — this course deliberately does not reproduce field layouts.

📭 What the spec does not say

The specification does not define what a program’s instruction set is (that depends on program type, e.g. a device-specific format or a standard such as eBPF if a vendor chooses it), how fast it runs, how it is sandboxed internally, or how compute and I/O share device resources. Security of downloaded code is a system design concern; check how the spec ties program loading to security mechanisms and access control.

Conceptual trace — normal: filter offload

Long-running compute collides with host command timeouts designed for I/O. Whether the program was slow, or the host timeout policy is wrong for compute, must be decided by the program’s expected run time. derived

61.6 Failure patterns

SymptomCausesFirst checkConclusion

💡 Senior insight

The NVMe rule that commands are unordered is the number-one correctness trap in computational storage: “copy, then execute, then read” is three independent commands. The host must chain them by waiting for completions (or use mechanisms the spec provides for dependency, if any — check). Validation should deliberately submit them back-to-back at high queue depth to expose hosts that assume order.

Quiz

  1. Where does a program read its input data?

    Answer

    From Subsystem Local Memory ranges (memory namespace), not directly from LBAs.

  2. Preloaded vs downloaded program?

    Answer

    Preloaded (device-defined) programs ship with the device; downloadable programs are loaded by the host into program slots and activated.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Why move compute toward data?
    Model answerTo cut data movement over PCIe and host memory; benefits grow with data reduction and with many devices sharing host links.
  2. Senior What validation risks are unique to computational storage?
    Model answerCommand-ordering assumptions, long execution vs timeouts, isolation between programs/tenants, security of downloaded code, resource contention with I/O, error reporting from inside programs.

62 Subsystem Local Memory (SLM)

← 61 Computational Programs63 NVMe Management Interface (NVMe-MI) →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Subsystem Local Memory Command Set Specification. REVISION: 1.3 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm). STATUS: optional I/O command set; memory namespaces. RELATIONSHIP: designed to be used with Computational Programs (Chapter 61), but it is a separate command set. version

62.1 What SLM is and why it exists

Subsystem Local Memory is memory inside the NVM subsystem (for example DRAM on the SSD) exposed as a memory namespace that is accessed with NVMe commands — byte-addressed rather than LBA-addressed. It exists to give computational programs a workspace and to let hosts move data between NVM namespaces and that workspace without crossing PCIe. verified concept.

🧒 Kid analogy

SLM is the factory’s loading yard from the previous chapter: a place right next to the mine where rock can be piled up for the machines, and from which the finished gold is loaded onto trucks.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

SLM is not host memory, not mapped into the CPU’s address space by this command set, and (unless stated otherwise) volatile — contents may be lost on reset or power loss. Do not confuse it with the Controller Memory Buffer (CMB) or Persistent Memory Region (PMR), which are exposed through PCIe BARs.

62.2 Access

verified operation concepts; exact command names, addressing fields and alignment rules are in SLM 1.3 — read them there.

Where SLM sits, and which steps cross PCIe: only the host's Memory Write (inputs) and Memory Read (results) do. Staging bulk data from an NVM namespace into SLM and running a program on it stay inside the subsystem. The numbers follow the copy → execute → read workflow.

Host → subsystem over PCIeSubsystem → host over PCIeInside the subsystem (no PCIe payload)

Quiz

  1. How is SLM addressed?

    Answer

    As a memory namespace accessed by NVMe commands with byte-oriented addressing, not as LBAs and not via a BAR.

  2. Why can computational programs not just use the CMB?

    Answer

    CMB is a host-visible BAR region for queues/data; SLM is a namespace designed to be operated on by programs and filled by internal copies, with its own command set semantics.

Interview questions

  1. Advanced Explain the relationship between SLM and Computational Programs.
    Model answerSLM provides memory namespaces that hold program inputs/outputs; data is staged from NVM namespaces by copy, programs in compute namespaces operate on memory ranges, hosts read results from SLM. Two command sets, one workflow.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can define SLM and its three basic operations.
  • I can distinguish SLM, CMB, PMR, HMB.
  • I can explain the copy → execute → read workflow and its ordering hazard.

Next: Chapter 63 — NVMe-MI.

63 NVMe Management Interface (NVMe-MI)

← 62 Subsystem Local Memory (SLM)64 NVMe Boot →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe Management Interface Specification, revision 2.2 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm); DMTF Management Component Transport Protocol (MCTP) Base Specification (DSP0236), MCTP SMBus/I2C Transport Binding (DSP0237), MCTP PCIe VDM Transport Binding (DSP0238). STATUS: optional. OLDER VERSIONS: NVMe-MI 1.0 (2015), 1.1, 1.2; 2.0 aligned with the NVMe 2.0 refactoring version. SOURCE: nvmexpress.org; dmtf.org.

63.1 Why this chapter exists

In a data centre, a Baseboard Management Controller (BMC) must see drive temperature, health and inventory even when the host OS is crashed, not installed or not trusted. NVMe-MI defines how a management controller talks to an NVMe subsystem out-of-band (over a side-band bus such as SMBus/I2C, or over PCIe using MCTP vendor-defined messages), and also how host software can send the same management messages in-band through the NVMe admin queue.

  • Distinguish in-band and out-of-band management paths.
  • Explain MCTP, its bindings, and NVMe-MI as an MCTP message type.
  • Name the categories of NVMe-MI commands: MI commands, tunnelled NVMe admin commands, PCIe commands (where supported).
  • Explain discovery, monitoring, configuration, firmware update and enclosure management use cases.
  • Diagnose common BMC-to-drive failures.

Prerequisites: SMART log, admin commands, I2C/SMBus basics, NVMe-MI.

🧒 Kid analogy — the janitor’s back door

The teacher (host CPU) talks to the library (SSD) through the main door (PCIe + NVMe queues). The building janitor (BMC) has a key to a small back door (SMBus) and can check the thermostat, read the logbook and even swap a light bulb (firmware), even when the classroom is locked or the teacher is asleep.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The “back door” can also be a logical path over the main PCIe link (MCTP over PCIe VDM), and the janitor and teacher can step on each other’s toes: concurrent configuration from BMC and host must be coordinated, which the spec addresses only partly.

63.2 Architecture

PathTransportWorks when host OS down?Notes
Out-of-band, side-bandMCTP over SMBus/I2C (DSP0237)Yes (if drive powered, aux power)low bandwidth; common on servers; physical bus addressing and ARP considerations
Out-of-band, over PCIeMCTP over PCIe Vendor Defined Messages (DSP0238)Yes if link up (BMC on PCIe hierarchy)VDM TLPs routed by ID/to root; higher bandwidth
In-bandNVMe-MI Send / NVMe-MI Receive admin commandsNosame MI messages tunnelled through the admin queue

verified NVMe-MI is carried as an MCTP message type; MCTP base/bindings are DMTF standards. The legacy “basic management command” (a simple SMBus block read of health data) is described in an informative appendix of NVMe-MI version.

Exact command names and which admin commands may be tunnelled out-of-band are defined in NVMe-MI 2.2; confirm there. version

# In-band: nvme-cli can send some NVMe-MI messages through the admin queue (support varies by version/device)
sudo nvme admin-passthru --help | head -5    # passthrough exists; prefer dedicated subcommands where present
# Out-of-band: Linux has an MCTP networking stack (AF_MCTP) and the libnvme "mi" library used by tools such as nvme-cli;
# availability depends on kernel config and platform wiring.
ip link | grep -i mctp

Linux MCTP support and libnvme-mi exist version; whether your platform exposes an MCTP interface to the drives is impl.

💡 Senior insight

Out-of-band management is where electrical, firmware and policy problems meet: a drive that is perfect in-band can be “unmanageable” because of a backplane SMBus mux, a 3.3 V aux rail, or an address plan. Always validate the management path on the exact chassis, with all slots populated.

Quiz

  1. Name two out-of-band transports for NVMe-MI.

    Answer

    MCTP over SMBus/I2C and MCTP over PCIe VDM.

  2. How does host software reach NVMe-MI in-band?

    Answer

    Through NVMe-MI Send / Receive admin commands on the admin queue.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is a BMC?
    Model answerA baseboard management controller: an independent processor on the server board for monitoring and control, working even when the host is off or crashed.
  2. Senior How would you validate NVMe-MI on a new server?
    Model answerAddress plan and mux tests with all slots populated, aux-power-only tests, concurrency with heavy host I/O, firmware update via BMC with recovery tests, error injection on the bus, consistency of in-band vs out-of-band data.

  • I can explain MCTP’s role vs NVMe-MI’s role.
  • I can list five use cases and their mechanisms.
  • I can debug “BMC can’t see the drive”.

Next: Chapter 64 — NVMe Boot.

64 NVMe Boot

← 63 NVMe Management Interface (NVMe-MI)65 The NVMe-oF Mental Model →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe Boot Specification, revision 1.4 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm); UEFI Specification (NVM Express Pass Thru Protocol, device paths); ACPI. STATUS: optional. SCOPE NOTE: booting from a local NVMe-over-PCIe SSD is handled by platform firmware (UEFI NVMe driver) and has worked for years without the NVMe Boot Specification; the Boot Specification primarily addresses booting over NVMe over Fabrics, including how pre-OS firmware passes its fabric configuration to the operating system version.

64.1 Why this chapter exists

Diskless servers and cloud instances want to boot from a remote NVMe/TCP target. Before the OS runs, UEFI firmware must connect to the target, read the boot loader and kernel, and then hand over to an OS that must reconnect to the same namespace without losing its root file system. That handoff is what the NVMe Boot Specification standardises, through a firmware table the OS reads.

  • Explain the pre-OS environment and the UEFI role for local NVMe boot.
  • Explain NVMe-oF boot and the NVMe Boot Firmware Table (NBFT) handoff concept.
  • Trace the boot sequence and identify failure points.

Prerequisites: controller initialisation (CC.EN, CSTS.RDY), NVMe-oF mental model (forward link — read Chapter 65 first if new).

🧒 Kid analogy — the relay baton

The morning caretaker (UEFI) unlocks the school, fetches the timetable from the faraway library (remote target), and starts the day. When the teacher (OS) arrives, the caretaker hands over a note: “we are using library X, room Y, with this key” (NBFT). Without the note the teacher would not know where the timetable came from.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The OS does not continue the caretaker’s connection; it builds its own new connections using the information in the table. Any secrets (authentication keys) in the handoff require careful protection — what the spec allows in the table must be checked, not assumed.

64.2 Local NVMe (PCIe) boot

  1. Platform firmware enumerates PCIe, finds class code 01h/08h/02h (mass storage / NVM / NVMe).
  2. UEFI NVMe driver initialises the controller (admin queues, CC.EN = 1, wait CSTS.RDY), identifies namespaces, creates I/O queues.
  3. UEFI exposes block I/O and the NVM Express Pass Thru Protocol; device paths include an NVMe namespace node.
  4. Boot manager reads the EFI System Partition and loads the boot loader.
  5. OS loader calls ExitBootServices; the OS NVMe driver resets and re-initialises the controller.

verified class code 010802h for NVMe; UEFI protocol names per UEFI specification.

64.3 NVMe-oF boot

sudo nvme nbft show                      # nvme-cli: decode NBFT if firmware published one
ls /sys/firmware/acpi/tables/ | grep -i nbft
journalctl -b | grep -i -E 'nvme|nbft|nvmf'

💡 Senior insight

Boot failures split cleanly at the handoff: everything before ExitBootServices is firmware, everything after is OS. Collect evidence on both sides (firmware log, NBFT dump, initramfs listing) before guessing.

Quiz

  1. Is the NVMe Boot Specification required to boot from a local M.2 NVMe SSD?

    Answer

    No; local boot relies on UEFI’s NVMe support. The Boot Specification addresses fabrics boot and handoff.

  2. What does the OS do with the controller after taking over from UEFI (local boot)?

    Answer

    Its driver resets and re-initialises the controller with its own queues.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate What is transport-aware boot?
    Model answerPre-OS firmware that knows how to reach NVMe over a given transport (e.g. TCP) and records that configuration for the OS.
