  • I can explain the NBFT handoff purpose.
  • I can split a boot failure into firmware vs OS side with evidence.

Next: Part XIX — NVMe over Fabrics.

PART XIX

NVMe over Fabrics

NVMe was designed around shared memory: queues live in host RAM, the controller reads them by DMA, and a doorbell write across PCIe says “look now”. NVMe over Fabrics (NVMe-oF) keeps the command set, the queue-pair model, the namespaces and the status codes, and replaces the shared-memory transport with messages — capsules — carried by RDMA or TCP. This part teaches what stays the same, what changes, and how to debug the new layers. Baseline: NVMe Base 2.4 (which contains the fabrics architecture), NVMe over TCP Transport 1.3, NVMe over RDMA Transport 1.3, NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4 (revision numbers per the August 2026 set — confirm on nvmexpress.org).

65 The NVMe-oF Mental Model

← 64 NVMe Boot66 NVMe/TCP →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe Base Specification 2.4 (NVMe over Fabrics architecture, capsules, Fabrics commands, discovery, NQNs); transport binding specifications for PCIe (1.4), RDMA (1.3) and TCP (1.3). VERSION NOTES: NVMe-oF was a separate specification (1.0 in 2016, 1.1 in 2019) until the NVMe 2.0 refactoring (2021) moved the architecture into the Base specification and the bindings into transport specifications version.

65.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineers who know NVMe over PCIe often bring the wrong instincts to fabrics: they look for doorbells, PRPs and MSI-X, and find none. Engineers who know networking look for “a storage protocol inside TCP” and miss that it is still NVMe queue semantics. This chapter builds the bridge so the next three chapters make sense.

  • State precisely what is common to all NVMe transports and what each transport binds differently.
  • Explain capsules (command capsule = SQE + optional data/SGLs; response capsule = CQE).
  • Compare command delivery, data transfer, completion and notification across PCIe, RDMA and TCP.
  • Explain why fabrics need explicit Connect, NQNs and keep-alive.

Prerequisites: NVMe queues and SQE/CQE format (SQ, CQE), PRP and SGL; namespaces.

🧒 Kid analogy — same order form, different delivery

The library uses the same order form everywhere. In the school building (PCIe) you drop the form in a box on the librarian’s desk and ring a bell. For a library in another town you mail the form in an envelope (capsule) by express courier (RDMA) or by the regular postal service (TCP). The librarian fills orders the same way; only the delivery changes.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

With PCIe, the librarian reaches into the school’s memory directly (DMA). With TCP, nobody reaches into anyone’s memory; every byte travels as a message. RDMA is in between: the remote librarian can read and write registered parts of the school’s memory, with permission keys.

65.2 What remains the same

  • Command set semantics: Read, Write, Flush, Identify, Get Log Page, and their status codes. verified
  • The SQE (64 bytes) and CQE (16 bytes) structures, with fabrics-specific use of some fields (e.g. SGLs are mandatory for data descriptions; PRPs are not used). verified
  • The subsystem → controller → namespace hierarchy, NSIDs, Asynchronous Events, reservations, ANA (Asymmetric Namespace Access) for multipath.
  • Queue-pair model: admin queue (QID 0) plus I/O queues.

65.3 What changes

AspectNVMe over PCIeNVMe over RDMANVMe over TCP
Queue locationhost memory (or CMB); controller DMAseach side’s memory; SQE delivered in a capsuleeach side’s memory; capsule in a TCP stream
Command notificationdoorbell MWrRDMA SEND of command capsuleCapsuleCmd PDU
Data descriptionPRP or SGLSGL (Keyed SGL Data Block: address + length + key) or in-capsuleSGL (transport data block) or in-capsule
Data movementcontroller DMA (MRd/MWr TLPs)target-initiated RDMA READ / RDMA WRITEH2CData / C2HData PDUs; R2T to solicit write data
CompletionCQE MWr to host CQ + phase tagRDMA SEND of response capsuleCapsuleResp PDU (or SUCCESS flag on last C2HData where enabled)
Notification to hostMSI-X interruptRDMA completion queue event at the host NICsocket receive; no NVMe-level interrupt
Controller registersMMIO in BAR0Property Get / Property Set fabrics commandssame
Association setupenumeration + CC.ENRDMA CM connect + Fabrics Connect command per queueTCP connect + ICReq/ICResp + Fabrics Connect per queue
Livenesslink state, CSTSKeep Alive command + transportKeep Alive + TCP
IdentityPCIe BDFNQN (NVMe Qualified Name) of host and subsystemsame

verified structure of the comparison; field-level details belong to the transport specifications.

65.4 Capsules

65.5 Fabrics commands

Fabrics command (opcode 7Fh, FCTYPE)Purpose
Connect (01h)create the admin or an I/O queue association; carries host NQN, subsystem NQN, Host Identifier, requested CNTLID (FFFFh for the dynamic controller model)
Property Get (04h) / Property Set (00h)read/write controller properties (CAP, VS, CC, CSTS…) instead of MMIO
Authentication Send (05h) / Receive (06h)in-band authentication (DH-HMAC-CHAP)
Disconnect (08h)tear down an I/O queue (newer revisions) version

verified for Connect, Property Get/Set and Authentication FCTYPE values; confirm in Base 2.4.

💡 Senior insight

On PCIe, the transport is “invisible” and reliable: if a TLP is lost the link retries it. On fabrics, the transport has its own failure modes (packet loss, congestion, path failover, TLS errors) that surface to NVMe as timeouts and reconnects. Every NVMe-oF debug session starts by deciding: is this an NVMe problem or a transport problem?

Quiz

  1. Why are PRPs not used on fabrics?

    Answer

    PRPs are host physical page pointers meaningful only to a DMA engine with direct memory access; fabrics need descriptors meaningful to the transport (RDMA keys, TCP offsets), hence SGLs.

  2. How does a fabrics host read CSTS?

    Answer

    Property Get fabrics command on the admin queue.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate What stays the same between NVMe/PCIe and NVMe/TCP?
    Model answerCommand sets, SQE/CQE structures, queue-pair model, subsystem/controller/namespace model, status codes, log pages.
  2. Senior Where does latency come from in NVMe/TCP vs PCIe?
    Model answerNetwork stack processing, copies, NIC interrupts, switch hops, R2T round trips for writes, and TCP congestion control — none of which exist in a PCIe doorbell/DMA path.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can fill the “what changes” table from memory.
  • I can define command and response capsules.
  • I can explain Connect, Property Get/Set and keep-alive.

Next: Chapter 66 — NVMe/TCP.

66 NVMe/TCP

← 65 The NVMe-oF Mental Model67 NVMe/RDMA →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe over TCP Transport Specification, revision 1.3 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm). STATUS: transport binding. VERSION NOTES: NVMe/TCP was ratified in 2018 (TP 8000) and first published within NVMe-oF 1.1; TLS support and secure channel concatenation were added in later TPs version. PORTS: 4420 is the IANA-assigned port commonly used for NVMe-oF I/O; 8009 for the NVMe/TCP discovery service verified.

66.1 Why this chapter exists

NVMe/TCP runs on any Ethernet with an ordinary NIC and Linux kernel, which makes it the most widely deployed fabrics transport. Debugging it means reading a packet capture where NVMe commands are hidden inside a TCP byte stream as PDUs. This chapter teaches the PDU types, the command/data/completion paths, and the performance and failure patterns.

  • List the PDU types and their directions.
  • Decode the 8-byte common header (PDU-Type, FLAGS, HLEN, PDO, PLEN).
  • Trace read and write commands, including R2T and in-capsule data.
  • Explain header and data digests and when to enable them.
  • Diagnose connection, digest, R2T and timeout problems.

Prerequisites: Chapter 65; TCP fundamentals (stream, segments, retransmission).

🧒 Kid analogy — a phone call with forms

Two offices keep a phone line open (TCP connection). First they say hello and agree on rules (ICReq/ICResp). Then one reads out order forms (CapsuleCmd). For a delivery order, the other says “send me pages 1–4 now” (R2T) and the first reads them out (H2CData). For a fetch order, the other reads the pages back (C2HData) and then says “done, status OK” (CapsuleResp).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

TCP is a byte stream: PDUs are not aligned to TCP segments, one segment can carry many PDUs, one PDU can span many segments. A capture tool must reassemble the stream to find PDU boundaries using PLEN.

66.2 PDU types

Type valuePDUDirectionPurpose
00hICReqhost → controllerInitialize Connection Request: PDU format version, host PDU data alignment, digest enable requests, maximum outstanding R2Ts
01hICRespcontroller → hostInitialize Connection Response: controller PDU data alignment, digest settings, MAXH2CDATA (max data per H2CData PDU)
02hH2CTermReqhost → controllerhost terminates connection due to fatal transport error
03hC2HTermReqcontroller → hostcontroller terminates connection due to fatal transport error
04hCapsuleCmdhost → controllercommand capsule: 64-byte SQE + optional in-capsule data
05hCapsuleRespcontroller → hostresponse capsule: 16-byte CQE
06hH2CDatahost → controllerwrite data, sent in response to an R2T
07hC2HDatacontroller → hostread data; LAST_PDU flag; optional SUCCESS flag to omit CapsuleResp
09hR2Tcontroller → hostReady to Transfer: solicits a range of write data (offset + length, transfer tag)

verified PDU names and type values (08h is not used for these PDUs). Field layouts beyond the common header: read the TCP transport specification.

Byte 0Byte 1Byte 2Byte 3Bytes 4–7
PDU-TypeFLAGS (e.g. HDGSTF, DDGSTF, LAST_PDU, SUCCESS — meaning depends on type)HLEN (header length)PDO (PDU data offset)PLEN (total PDU length incl. header, digests, padding)

The common header is 8 bytes; it is followed by the PDU-specific header (e.g. the 64-byte SQE for CapsuleCmd), an optional header digest (CRC32C, 4 bytes), optional padding up to PDO, data, and an optional data digest (CRC32C). verified

66.3 Paths

  READ (8 KiB)                               WRITE (64 KiB, not in-capsule)
  Host                    Controller          Host                    Controller
   | CapsuleCmd (Read)  ----> |                | CapsuleCmd (Write) ----> |
   |                           | media read     |                          | buffer alloc
   | <---- C2HData (0..8K, LAST)|                | <---- R2T (off 0, 32K)  |
   | <---- CapsuleResp (CQE)   |                | H2CData (0..32K)  ----> |
   |                           |                | <---- R2T (off 32K,32K) |
                                                | H2CData (32K..64K)----> |
                                                |                          | media write
                                                | <---- CapsuleResp (CQE) |

Small writes can carry data in the CapsuleCmd itself (in-capsule data), avoiding the R2T round trip, if the controller’s in-capsule data size allows. verified The number of R2Ts and their sizes are controller choices bounded by MAXR2T and MAXH2CDATA impl.

The table and ASCII sketch above list the PDUs. The step-through below puts them in order on one I/O queue connection: TCP setup, the NVMe/TCP handshake (ICReq/ICResp), the Fabrics Connect, and then one 4 KiB Read. It assumes the admin queue connection (QID 0) already exists and its Connect returned controller ID 5. Values follow the synthetic trace in 66.5. synthetic

Host / initiator sends itController / target sends itInside the target (not on the wire)
  1. Host opens a TCP connection to the target

    The host connects to the target's I/O port (4420 here). NVMe/TCP uses one TCP connection per NVMe queue, so this connection will carry only I/O queue 1.

    Where: TCP layer of both machinesWire: Yes, host → target first · TCP SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK (no NVMe bytes yet)
    t = 0 µs host 198.51.100.7:51234 → target 192.0.2.10:4420
  2. Host sends ICReq

    The first PDU on any NVMe/TCP connection is the Initialize Connection Request. The host states the PDU format version, the data alignment it wants (HPDA), whether it wants header and data digests, and how many R2Ts it allows outstanding.

    Where: First PDU in the host → target byte streamWire: Yes, host → target · ICReq, PDU type 00h
    t = 90 µs PFV 0 · HPDA 0 · HDGST off · DDGST off
  3. Target answers with ICResp

    The target confirms the digest settings and gives its own data alignment (CPDA) and MAXH2CDATA: the largest data chunk the host may put in one H2CData PDU.

    Where: First PDU in the target → host byte streamWire: Yes, target → host · ICResp, PDU type 01h
    t = 140 µs CPDA 0 · digests off · MAXH2CDATA = 128 KiB
  4. Host sends the Fabrics Connect command

    A CapsuleCmd carries the 64-byte Connect command plus 1 KiB of in-capsule data (host NQN, subsystem NQN, host ID). For an I/O queue the host asks for QID 1 and names the controller ID it got on the admin queue.

    Where: CapsuleCmd PDU on the I/O connectionWire: Yes, host → target · CapsuleCmd, PDU type 04h (SQE + in-capsule data)
    t = 200 µs Connect · QID 1 · SQSIZE per host policy · CNTLID 5 hostnqn nqn.2014-08.org.nvmexpress:uuid:… · subnqn nqn.2026-01.org.example:lab-subsys1
  5. Target accepts: Connect CapsuleResp

    The CapsuleResp carries the 16-byte completion for the Connect. Status 0 means the queue exists and I/O may start. A wrong NQN or a host that is not allowed shows up here as a non-zero status.

    Where: CapsuleResp PDUWire: Yes, target → host · CapsuleResp, PDU type 05h (16-byte CQE)
    t = 420 µs Status 0 (success) · I/O queue 1 is live on this connection
  6. Host sends the Read command capsule

    The nvme-tcp driver wraps the normal 64-byte Read SQE in a CapsuleCmd. There is no doorbell and no fetch: sending the capsule is the submission.

    Where: CapsuleCmd PDU on I/O queue 1Wire: Yes, host → target · CapsuleCmd 04h, 8-byte common header + 64-byte SQE
    t = 9 000 µs Opcode 02h (Read) · CID 0x0012 · NSID 1 SLBA 0x1000 · NLB 0 (one 4 KiB block)
  7. Target reads the data from its media

    The target passes the Read to its backing storage (a local NVMe SSD, for example) and waits for the data.

    Where: Inside the target systemWire: No. Nothing for this command crosses the network during this step.
    Here ≈ 95 µs, mostly media time
  8. Target sends the data in a C2HData PDU

    The 4 KiB arrive at the host in one C2HData PDU. CCCID ties it to command 0x0012, DATAO is the offset inside the transfer and LAST_PDU marks the final data PDU for this command.

    Where: C2HData PDU; the host copies the payload into the request's bufferWire: Yes, target → host · C2HData, PDU type 07h, 4096 data bytes
    t = 9 095 µs CCCID 0x0012 · DATAO 0 · DATAL 4096 · flags LAST_PDU
  9. Target sends the CapsuleResp

    The completion arrives as a CapsuleResp with the CQE. The driver matches CID 0x0012 and completes the block request. (If the SUCCESS flag was set on the last C2HData, this PDU is omitted.)

    Where: CapsuleResp PDUWire: Yes, target → host · CapsuleResp 05h, 16-byte CQE
    t = 9 097 µs CID 0x0012 · status 0 · total ≈ 97 µs on the wire for this Read

Compare with PCIe (Figure 39.0): there the device fetches the command and writes the data into host memory itself. Over TCP the target can only send PDUs; the host's driver receives them and copies the data into place.

A Write is different: the target, not the host, decides when data may be sent. The host sends the command, the target answers with one R2T (Ready to Transfer) per chunk it can accept, and the host sends exactly that chunk in an H2CData PDU. Here a 64 KiB Write without in-capsule data is accepted in two 32 KiB chunks, as in the sketch above. synthetic

Host / initiator sends itController / target sends itInside the target (not on the wire)
  1. Host sends the Write command capsule

    The 64-byte Write SQE goes in a CapsuleCmd. The data is too large for in-capsule data, so the capsule carries the command only.

    Where: CapsuleCmd PDU on an I/O queue connectionWire: Yes, host → target · CapsuleCmd 04h, SQE only
    t = 0 µs Opcode 01h (Write) · CID 0x0013 · NSID 1 SLBA 0x2000 · NLB 15 (16 × 4 KiB = 64 KiB)
  2. Target reserves buffer space

    Before it asks for data, the target needs somewhere to put it. How much it reserves at once is an implementation choice.

    Where: Inside the targetWire: No.
    Here: buffers in 32 KiB pieces impl
  3. Target sends R2T for the first 32 KiB

    The R2T names the command (CCCID), gives the transfer a tag (TTAG), and says which part of the data it wants: offset R2TO and length R2TL.

    Where: R2T PDUWire: Yes, target → host · R2T, PDU type 09h
    t ≈ RTT after step 1 CCCID 0x0013 · TTAG 1 · R2TO 0 · R2TL 32768
  4. Host sends that 32 KiB in H2CData

    The host sends exactly the requested range. 32 KiB fits in one PDU because MAXH2CDATA is 128 KiB, so this single PDU is also the last one for TTAG 1 and carries LAST_PDU.

    Where: H2CData PDUWire: Yes, host → target · H2CData, PDU type 06h, 32768 data bytes
    CCCID 0x0013 · TTAG 1 · DATAO 0 · DATAL 32768 · LAST_PDU
  5. Target sends R2T for the next 32 KiB

    With MAXR2T = 1 only one R2T may be outstanding, so the second one comes after the first chunk has arrived. Each R2T costs another network round trip.

    Where: R2T PDUWire: Yes, target → host · R2T 09h
    CCCID 0x0013 · TTAG 2 · R2TO 32768 · R2TL 32768
  6. Host sends the second 32 KiB

    The final chunk arrives; the target now holds all 64 KiB.

    Where: H2CData PDUWire: Yes, host → target · H2CData 06h, 32768 data bytes
    CCCID 0x0013 · TTAG 2 · DATAO 32768 · DATAL 32768 · LAST_PDU
  7. Target commits the data

    The target writes the data to its backing storage (or to a cache it is allowed to acknowledge from).

    Where: Inside the targetWire: No.
    Where the data must be before completion depends on the target and its write cache settings impl
  8. Target sends the CapsuleResp

    The CQE in the CapsuleResp completes command 0x0013. Compared with the Read, the host waited for two extra target → host round trips (the R2Ts).

    Where: CapsuleResp PDUWire: Yes, target → host · CapsuleResp 05h, 16-byte CQE
    CID 0x0013 · status 0 Small writes that fit the in-capsule data size skip steps 3–6 entirely

66.4 Performance

T_write ≈ RTT (CapsuleCmd→R2T) + Σ(H2CData serialization) + t_media + RTT/2 (CapsuleResp)
  • RTT — network round-trip time
  • H2CData serialization — bytes / link rate per data PDU
  • t_media — controller processing and media time

Writes pay at least one extra half round trip for the R2T compared with reads unless in-capsule data is used. CPU cost per I/O (copies, checksums, interrupts) often limits IOPS before the network does; digests add CRC32C computation (offloaded by some NICs) impl.

66.6 Linux view

sudo nvme discover -t tcp -a 192.0.2.10 -s 8009          # read discovery log (no connection to I/O ctrl)
sudo nvme list-subsys                                      # show connected subsystems and paths
cat /etc/nvme/hostnqn                                      # this host's NQN
sudo tcpdump -i eth1 -w nvme.pcap 'tcp port 4420'          # capture; Wireshark has an NVMe/TCP dissector
journalctl -k | grep -E 'nvme.*(tcp|reconnect|keep-alive|digest)'
# LAB: connect to a test target (creates block devices on this host)
sudo nvme connect -t tcp -a 192.0.2.10 -s 4420 -n nqn.2026-01.org.example:lab-subsys1
sudo nvme disconnect -n nqn.2026-01.org.example:lab-subsys1
⚠️ Safety

Connecting to a production target from a lab host can expose shared namespaces to a second writer. Use a dedicated test subsystem with host-NQN access control. Packet captures contain data; treat them as sensitive.

💡 Senior insight

Map every NVMe/TCP I/O queue to its TCP connection (one connection per queue) and analyse them separately. An apparently random latency spike usually belongs to one connection that hit retransmission — averaged across queues it looks like a storage problem.

Quiz

  1. Which PDU solicits write data?

    Answer

    R2T (09h), sent by the controller.

  2. What do HLEN, PDO and PLEN tell you?

    Answer

    Header length, offset of data within the PDU, and total PDU length — enough to find the next PDU in the stream.

  3. Can a read finish without a CapsuleResp?

    Answer

    Yes, if the SUCCESS flag mechanism is enabled/used on the last C2HData PDU; otherwise a CapsuleResp follows.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner List the NVMe/TCP PDU types.
    Model answerICReq, ICResp, H2CTermReq, C2HTermReq, CapsuleCmd, CapsuleResp, H2CData, C2HData, R2T.
  2. Intermediate Why use digests if TCP has checksums?
    Model answerTCP’s 16-bit checksum is weak and does not cover corruption inside NICs, offload engines or middleboxes after checksum verification; CRC32C end-to-end digests catch those.
  3. Advanced How do you find PDU boundaries in a capture?
    Model answerReassemble the TCP stream and walk PDUs using PLEN from each common header, starting from ICReq.
  4. Senior A customer sees 2× write latency over TCP vs RDMA. Explain and propose fixes.
    Model answerR2T round trip(s), stack copies, interrupt handling; fixes: in-capsule data for small writes, larger R2T/MAXH2CDATA, more queues, busy-poll, NIC offloads, CPU affinity.
✅ Mastery gate
  • I can list PDU types with values and directions.
  • I can decode a common header and walk a stream.
  • I can draw read and write PDU sequences including R2T.
  • I can separate NVMe failures from TCP failures with evidence.

67 NVMe/RDMA

← 66 NVMe/TCP68 Fabric Architecture and Discovery →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe over RDMA Transport Specification, revision 1.3 per the August 2026 set (course brief — confirm). RELATED: InfiniBand Architecture Specification and RoCE annexes (IBTA), iWARP RFCs (IETF). STATUS: transport binding. version

67.1 Why this chapter exists

RDMA (Remote Direct Memory Access) lets a NIC read and write registered memory on another machine without involving that machine’s CPU in the data path. NVMe/RDMA uses this to keep the “controller moves the data” spirit of PCIe NVMe across a network, giving the lowest-latency fabrics transport — at the cost of specialised networks and configuration.

  • Explain RDMA verbs at a conceptual level: SEND/RECEIVE, RDMA READ, RDMA WRITE.
  • Explain queue pairs and the mapping of NVMe queues to RDMA QPs.
  • Explain memory registration and keyed SGLs.
  • Trace NVMe reads and writes over RDMA.
  • Recognise RDMA transport failures (lossless network, PFC, retries).

Prerequisites: Chapter 65.

🧒 Kid analogy — the robot arm with a permission card

Before the library in the other town may take books from your shelf, you give it a permission card for one shelf (memory registration and key). Then its robot arm can reach over the network and take exactly those books (RDMA READ) or put books on that shelf (RDMA WRITE), without you lifting a finger. Messages like “please do this order” and “done!” are still mailed as letters (SEND).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The permission card is a 32-bit key plus address range checked by the NIC hardware; it can be invalidated, and stale keys are a security and correctness hazard. Also, RoCE networks usually need lossless Ethernet configuration (PFC/ECN) to perform well — the robot arm hates dropped packets.

67.2 Mechanism

NVMe stepRDMA operationWho initiates
Submit commandSEND of command capsule (consumes a pre-posted RECEIVE at the target)Host
Read data (controller → host)RDMA WRITE into host buffer described by Keyed SGL (address, length, key)Target
Write data (host → controller)RDMA READ from host buffer described by Keyed SGL, or in-capsule dataTarget
CompleteSEND of response capsule (optionally with invalidate of the host key)Target

Each NVMe queue pair (admin or I/O) maps to one RDMA queue pair (QP); connections are established with the RDMA connection manager, then the Fabrics Connect command is sent over that QP. verified concept; field and descriptor formats in the RDMA transport specification.

The table above in one picture. Watch who starts each data movement: the host only SENDs command capsules. For a Read the target pushes data into host memory with RDMA WRITE; for a Write the target pulls data out of host memory with RDMA READ. Neither touches the host CPU. The Read uses the values of the normal trace in 67.3. synthetic

Host CPU / driver starts itTarget starts itHost memory answers through the host RNIC (no CPU)Inside the target
  1. Host registers the data buffer

    Before sending the command, the driver registers the destination buffer with its RDMA NIC (RNIC). Registration pins the pages and returns a key; only a peer that presents this key may access this address range.

    Where: Host: driver and its RNICWire: No. Registration is local to the host.
    Buffer 0x7f3a_1c00_0000, 16 384 bytes, remote write allowed key = 0x1a2b3c4d
  2. Host SENDs the Read command capsule

    The 64-byte Read SQE travels in a command capsule by RDMA SEND. It consumes a RECEIVE buffer the target posted earlier. The data pointer is a keyed SGL: address, length and key of the buffer from step 1.

    Where: Host QP → target QPWire: Yes, host → target · RDMA SEND (command capsule)
    t = 0.0 µs Read · CID 0x0021 · NSID 1 · SLBA 0x4000 · 16 KiB SGL: keyed {{addr 0x7f3a_1c00_0000, len 16384, key 0x1a2b3c4d}}
  3. Target RDMA WRITEs the data into host memory

    After reading its media, the target issues RDMA WRITE with the address and key from the SGL. The host RNIC checks the key and places the 16 KiB straight into the buffer. The host CPU does nothing.

    Where: Host memory, registered bufferWire: Yes, target → host · RDMA WRITE, 16 384 bytes
    t = 14.0 µs 16 KiB to 0x7f3a_1c00_0000 with key 0x1a2b3c4d
  4. Target SENDs the response capsule

    The 16-byte CQE travels back by SEND. It can ask the host RNIC to invalidate the key at the same time, so the buffer can no longer be reached remotely.

    Where: Target QP → host QP; the driver sees a receive completionWire: Yes, target → host · SEND (with invalidate)
    t = 14.6 µs CID 0x0021 · status 0 · key 0x1a2b3c4d invalidated
  5. Host SENDs the Write command capsule

    For a Write the host registers its source buffer (with remote read allowed) and SENDs the command capsule. Small writes may instead carry the data in the capsule itself (in-capsule data).

    Where: Host QP → target QPWire: Yes, host → target · RDMA SEND (command capsule)
    Write · CID 0x0022 · SLBA 0x8000 · 16 KiB SGL: keyed {{addr 0x7f3a_1c00_8000, len 16384, key 0x5e6f7a8b}}
  6. Target issues RDMA READ

    The target pulls the data when it has room for it, by sending an RDMA READ request naming the host address, length and key.

    Where: Target RNIC → host RNICWire: Yes, target → host · RDMA READ request
    Read 16 384 bytes at 0x7f3a_1c00_8000, key 0x5e6f7a8b
  7. Host memory returns the data

    The host RNIC checks the key, reads the buffer by DMA and sends the bytes back as RDMA READ responses. The host CPU is not involved. A stale or wrong key fails here with a remote access error (see the failed trace in 67.3).

    Where: Host memory → targetWire: Yes, host → target · RDMA READ response, 16 384 bytes
    The only data movement of the Write; started by the target, served by the host RNIC
  8. Target commits the data

    The target writes the data to its media or to a cache it may acknowledge from.

    Where: Inside the targetWire: No.
    Timing and durability point depend on the target impl
  9. Target SENDs the response capsule

    The CQE completes command 0x0022. The host can now deregister the buffer; doing so before this point is the classic bug behind remote access errors.

    Where: Target QP → host QPWire: Yes, target → host · SEND (response capsule)
    CID 0x0022 · status 0

Same pattern as PCIe NVMe: the controller side moves the data (there with PCIe DMA, here with RDMA WRITE and RDMA READ). Compare NVMe/TCP (Figures 66.1 and 66.2), where the host must send write data in H2CData PDUs when asked by R2T.

💡 Senior insight

In NVMe/RDMA the data path is driven by the target: it pulls write data and pushes read data. That mirrors PCIe NVMe (the controller does DMA) and is why RDMA latency approaches local NVMe. It also means a host-side memory lifecycle bug shows up as a remote error on the target’s operation — look at both sides.

Quiz

  1. Which RDMA operation moves data for an NVMe Write command (non-in-capsule)?

    Answer

    RDMA READ, issued by the target against the host’s registered buffer.

  2. What three things does a keyed SGL descriptor carry?

    Answer

    Address, length and key (remote access key).

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate What is memory registration and why is it needed?
    Model answerPinning and mapping a buffer in the NIC with access rights and a key so remote peers can access it via RDMA without CPU involvement and without accessing unauthorised memory.
  2. Senior RoCEv2 vs TCP for NVMe-oF in a large cloud?
    Model answerRoCE: lower latency and CPU, needs lossless/congestion-managed fabric and RDMA NICs; TCP: universal, simpler operations, higher CPU and latency; choice depends on scale, operational maturity and hardware.
✅ Mastery gate

  • I can explain QPs, registration and keyed SGLs.
  • I can diagnose remote access and retry-exceeded errors.

68 Fabric Architecture and Discovery

📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENT: NVMe Base Specification 2.4 — NVM subsystem model, NQN format, discovery controller, Discovery Log Page (Log Identifier 70h), Asymmetric Namespace Access (ANA). Discovery enhancements (centralized discovery controllers, discovery information management, automated discovery over IP) were added via technical proposals ratified around 2021–2022 version.

68.1 The hierarchy

68.2 Discovery

A discovery controller is a special controller (in a discovery subsystem with the well-known NQN nqn.2014-08.org.nvmexpress.discovery, or a unique NQN for newer discovery models) that supports only what is needed to return the Discovery Log Page. Each log entry describes how to reach one subsystem port: transport type (TRTYPE), address family (ADRFAM), subsystem type, port ID, controller ID, transport address (TRADDR), transport service ID (TRSVCID, e.g. 4420), subsystem NQN and transport-specific attributes. verified

host:
  connect to discovery controller (e.g. TCP 192.0.2.10:8009, NQN = well-known discovery NQN)
  Get Log Page LID 70h  -> entries[]
  for e in entries matching policy:
      connect admin queue to e.TRADDR:e.TRSVCID, subnqn = e.SUBNQN
      Identify controller / namespaces; create I/O queues (one connection per queue)
  optionally keep discovery association (persistent) for change notifications

Centralized Discovery Controllers (CDC) aggregate many subsystems in large IP fabrics; hosts and subsystems register with them (Discovery Information Management) and mDNS-based automated discovery can locate discovery controllers version — confirm the current model and names in Base 2.4.

68.3 Multipath and ANA

A namespace can be reachable through several controllers/ports. Asymmetric Namespace Access (ANA) reports per-group states (optimized, non-optimized, inaccessible, persistent loss, change) via an ANA log page so hosts choose paths. Linux native NVMe multipath presents one block device per namespace across paths. verified

cat /sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/multipath
sudo nvme list-subsys -v
sudo nvme ana-log /dev/nvme1

68.4 Interoperability (Extended topic 97)

A standard interface does not eliminate implementation bugs. Every NVMe deployment is a chain, and an interoperability failure can sit in any link or between two links:

Link in the chainTypical interop issueEvidence
Host application ↔ OSassumes write ordering or atomicity NVMe doesn’t giveapplication logs, fsync patterns
OS ↔ driverquirk tables, timeout defaults, queue countskernel version, module parameters
Driver ↔ PCIe platformMSI-X, IOMMU, ASPM, RO quirkslspci -vvv, IOMMU faults
Platform ↔ controllerlink training, equalization, power statesLnkSta, AER counters
Controller ↔ firmwareoptional feature support differs across firmware revisionsIdentify Controller (FR), feature support bits
Firmware ↔ mediawear, read disturb, retentionSMART, vendor logs
Host ↔ fabric ↔ targetNQN format, digests, MAXH2CDATA, KATO, TLS versionsPDU captures, connect status
💡 Senior insight

Interoperability bugs live in “optional” and “may”. When two compliant implementations fail together, list every optional feature and every “may” behaviour each one exercises, and test them pairwise. Then check which revision each side claims (VS register / Identify), because they may be reading different specifications.

🧪 Lab 68.1 (Extended Lab 49) — PCIe path vs TCP path side by side CAUTION

Objective: compare one 4 KiB read over local NVMe/PCIe and over NVMe/TCP. Prerequisites: two Linux machines (or one with loopback), a disposable SSD, the Linux nvmet target (configfs). Setup: export a test namespace with nvmet-tcp on port 4420 with host NQN restriction; on the host, connect with nvme connect. Procedure: (1) run fio --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 --readonly against the local device and against the remote one; (2) capture tcpdump on the TCP path; (3) fill the table below. Observations / table:

DimensionPCIe pathTCP path
Command transportSQE in host memory, doorbell MWr, controller MRdCapsuleCmd PDU in TCP stream
Data transportcontroller MWr TLPs into PRP/SGL buffersC2HData PDU(s), copied by stack (or zero-copy where supported)
CompletionCQE MWr + phase tag + MSI-XCapsuleResp PDU (or SUCCESS flag)
Network layersPCIe transaction/data link/physicalNVMe/TCP PDU → TCP → IP → Ethernet (+ target’s own PCIe to its SSD)
Failure modesAER, completion timeout, link down, CFSconnection loss, digest error, KATO expiry, retransmission, target-side PCIe errors
Measured QD1 latency(your value)(your value)

Questions: how many PCIe transactions occur on the target machine for one remote read? Where are the two extra copies (if any)? Which layer adds most latency?

Solution

The target performs the same local PCIe NVMe sequence (doorbell, SQE fetch, data MWr, CQE, interrupt) against its SSD, then sends PDUs. The remote read therefore contains a complete local read plus network round trip and stack processing; typical added latency is tens of microseconds on a LAN (implementation- and environment-dependent). Expected reasoning: decompose latency into host stack, wire, target stack, target local NVMe.

Extension: enable data digest and measure CPU cost; introduce 1% packet loss with tc netem (lab only) and observe reconnects.

Quiz

  1. What is in a Discovery Log Page entry?

    Answer

    Transport type, address family, subsystem type, port ID, controller ID, transport address, service ID, subsystem NQN, transport-specific attributes.

  2. What is the well-known discovery NQN?

    Answer

    nqn.2014-08.org.nvmexpress.discovery

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Walk the hierarchy host → namespace.
    Model answerHost (host NQN) reaches a target port over a fabric, connects to a subsystem (subsystem NQN), which creates a controller (CNTLID) for the association; the controller exposes attached namespaces (NSIDs).
  2. Senior Design discovery for 10 000 hosts.
    Model answerCentralized discovery controllers with registration, zoning/access policy, persistent discovery connections for change notification, mDNS or DHCP-based bootstrap, redundancy for the CDC itself.

  • I can explain discovery and decode discovery entries.
  • I can explain ANA multipath.
  • I can compare the PCIe and TCP paths across five dimensions.
  • I can list interop risk points along the chain.

PART XX

2026 NVMe 2.4 Updates

On August 4, 2026, NVM Express, Inc. announced the NVMe 2.4 specification set. This part is the course’s modern-update section. It is deliberately written as a reading and verification guide, not as a feature encyclopedia: for each highlighted capability it tells you what problem it addresses, which documents to open, what a validation engineer should look for, and — equally important — what you cannot conclude from a press release. Field layouts, opcodes and status codes of new 2.4 features are intentionally not reproduced here; you must read them in the normative text.

SOURCE: NVM Express press release of August 4, 2026 (nvmexpress.org, News / Press Releases) and the specifications library at nvmexpress.org/specifications. version — individual sub-specification revision numbers are taken from the course brief; confirm each on nvmexpress.org before citing them in a report.

📭 Source notes — read this first
  • Official source: NVM Express announcement dated August 4, 2026; nvmexpress.org/specifications (each specification’s PDF and its revision history / list of incorporated ratified Technical Proposals (TPs) and Engineering Change Notices (ECNs)).
  • What the announcement establishes: that a 2.4 set was released; that it emphasises security, manageability, sustainability and support for AI, cloud, enterprise and client storage; and that it highlights Post-Quantum Cryptography, PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration, Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting and Restore Manufacturing Default Settings.
  • What it does not establish: command opcodes, data structure layouts, log identifiers, feature identifiers, status codes, mandatory/optional status, which controller types must support a feature, or the exact algorithms used. None of these are stated in this course. Every one must be read in the normative specification.
  • Accessed/verified: the course baseline was fixed in August 2026. If you are reading this later, check for 2.4 errata/ECNs and later revisions.

20.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Every year, engineers receive a press release, skim five bullet points, and then — months later — confidently describe “how feature X works” in a design review, based on a guess. This chapter trains the opposite habit. You will learn a repeatable method for absorbing a new revision: read the announcement for intent, read the revision history for scope, read the normative sections for behaviour, then decide how it affects your product, your tests and your traces.

  • Beginner: name the five highlighted 2.4 capabilities and explain each one’s purpose in one sentence.
  • Intermediate: identify which specification documents you must open to study each capability.
  • Advanced: produce a “what is verified / what must be checked” sheet for each capability.
  • Senior: assess impact on a product roadmap, test plan and interoperability matrix without over-claiming.
  • Trace analysis: predict which capabilities can plausibly appear in a PCIe or NVMe command trace, and which have no necessary wire signature.
  • Debugging: recognise when a field anomaly may stem from a host and device implementing different revisions.
  • Validation: design validation thought experiments that do not depend on invented details.

Prerequisites: SR-IOV and NVMe virtualization (Ch 56), health monitoring (Ch 57), NVMe-MI (Ch 63), NVMe/TCP (Ch 66), and the spec-reading discipline of shall / should / may.

🧒 Kid story — the new rulebook for the football league

Every summer the football league publishes a new rulebook. The newspaper headline says: “New rules on safer helmets, team transfers, checking the stadium lights, limiting how fast players may run onto the pitch, and a reset button for the scoreboard.” A smart coach does not change tactics from the headline. She gets the rulebook, finds the exact pages, reads what is required and what is allowed, checks which rules apply to her league division, and only then trains the team.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A sports rulebook applies to everyone at once. NVMe features are mostly optional and are advertised by each device through capability fields, so two “NVMe 2.4” devices may support completely different subsets. A controller reporting a 2.4 version value is not a promise that it implements any particular new feature. Also, a single feature may be split across several documents (Base, a transport, NVMe-MI).

20.1.3 The method — twelve questions per feature

For every new capability we answer the same twelve questions. Where the honest answer is “read the spec”, we say so and tell you exactly what to look for.

  1. What existed before?
  2. What changed?
  3. Why was it needed?
  4. What problem does it solve?
  5. Which specification contains it?
  6. Which revision introduced or updated it?
  7. Is it mandatory or optional?
  8. What hardware/software is affected?
  9. How could it appear in traces?
  10. How would a validation engineer test it?
  11. What could go wrong?
  12. Why should a senior engineer care?

20.1.4 Post-Quantum Cryptography (PQC)

#QuestionAnswer (with evidence label)
1What existed before?NVMe already had security mechanisms that depend on public-key cryptography in some form: for example in-band authentication for fabrics (DH-HMAC-CHAP, which uses Diffie-Hellman groups), TLS for NVMe/TCP, and device security protocols reached through Security Send/Receive. verified that these mechanisms exist in recent revisions; derived that classical public-key algorithms are among their building blocks.
2What changed?The 2.4 announcement highlights Post-Quantum Cryptography. verified (announcement). Which mechanisms gained PQC options, and with which algorithms, must be read in the specification. uncertain
3Why was it needed?A sufficiently large quantum computer would break today’s widely used public-key schemes (RSA, elliptic-curve and finite-field Diffie-Hellman). Data recorded now could be decrypted later (“harvest now, decrypt later”), and storage devices have long service lives. NIST published its first PQC standards (FIPS 203 ML-KEM, FIPS 204 ML-DSA, FIPS 205 SLH-DSA) in August 2024. verified (NIST).
4What problem does it solve?Lets NVMe security mechanisms remain trustworthy against future quantum-capable adversaries; supports organisations with PQC migration mandates. derived
5Which specification?Open the NVMe Base Specification 2.4 first (security and authentication sections) and the NVMe over TCP Transport 1.3 (TLS-related content). Check NVMe-MI 2.2 if management-path security is in scope. Confirm against the revision history — do not assume which documents changed. uncertain
6Which revision?Highlighted with the 2.4 set (Aug 4 2026). Whether earlier TPs laid groundwork: check the revision history. version
7Mandatory or optional?Not stated in the announcement. Most new NVMe capabilities are optional and advertised by capability bits, but you must read the requirement language. uncertain
8Affected hardware/softwareController security firmware and crypto engines; host authentication stacks (e.g. Linux nvme-auth, nvme-cli, TLS libraries/keyrings), fabric targets, key-management systems. derived
9Trace appearanceNo necessary PCIe-level signature: PQC changes the content of security exchanges, not TLP types. Over fabrics, authentication/TLS handshakes may carry larger messages (PQC keys and signatures are generally larger than elliptic-curve ones — verified property of the NIST algorithms). Exact message formats: read the spec. Do not fabricate a trace.
10ValidationThought experiments: negotiate PQC vs classical between mixed-capability host/target; verify fallback policy matches the spec’s rules; measure handshake time and message sizes; negative tests with corrupted signatures; interop matrix across host stacks.
11What could go wrong?Downgrade to classical algorithms when policy forbids it; buffer sizes too small for larger keys; handshake timeouts tuned for classical crypto; interoperability gaps between early implementations. derived
12Why care (senior)?Crypto agility becomes a product requirement with a long tail: devices shipped in 2026 may still be in service when PQC is mandatory. Architecture must allow algorithm updates via firmware without breaking interop.

20.1.5 PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration

#QuestionAnswer
1BeforeVirtualised hosts expose NVMe to guests through SR-IOV VFs (Ch 56) or software emulation. Direct-assigned devices are hard to live-migrate because state lives in the device. Recent NVMe revisions added infrastructure aimed at live migration of controllers version — identify which revision and which mechanisms in the revision history rather than relying on memory.
2What changedThe 2.4 announcement highlights “PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration”. verified (name). Its mechanics are not described here. uncertain
3–4Why / problemCloud operators need to move running workloads (maintenance, load balancing) without stopping I/O for long, even when storage is presented over PCIe. The feature name indicates migration of an NVM subsystem that is exported over PCIe. derived from the name; confirm the definition of “exported NVM subsystem” in Base 2.4.
5SpecificationNVMe Base 2.4 (architecture, admin commands, data structures) and possibly NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4 (PCIe-specific behaviour). Verify both. uncertain
6–7Revision / mandatoryHighlighted in 2.4; requirement level must be read. uncertain
8AffectedControllers supporting virtualization, hypervisors (VFIO-style passthrough, migration drivers), orchestration software, possibly DPUs/smart NICs that export storage. derived
9TracesAt NVMe command level, migration control would appear as admin commands and their data transfers on the managing function. At PCIe level, any state transfer is ordinary MRd/MWr traffic; there is no new TLP type to look for. A guest-visible pause may show as a gap in the guest’s I/O and a resumption on a different physical path. Do not invent command names.
10ValidationThought experiments: migrate under QD 128 mixed I/O; verify no lost, duplicated or reordered-in-violation completions; verify outstanding commands’ fate per spec; verify namespaces, reservations and AEN state after migration; abort migration mid-way; power loss during migration.
11What could go wrongLost in-flight commands; stale doorbell values; interrupt vector mismatch after resume; dirty-page tracking misses DMA writes; security boundary violations between tenants. derived
12SeniorMigration features move the hardest correctness problems (in-flight state, ordering, idempotency) into the boundary between hypervisor and device. Your test plan must cover the protocol’s failure states, not just the happy path.

20.1.6 Voltage Monitoring

#QuestionAnswer
1BeforeNVMe exposes temperatures (Composite Temperature, sensors), power states, and in recent revisions additional power-related reporting; supply voltage visibility typically came from platform/BMC sensors or vendor-specific logs. derived / impl
2What changedThe 2.4 announcement highlights Voltage Monitoring. verified (name). What is measured, granularity, units and reporting path: read the spec. uncertain
3–4Why / problemSupply-voltage excursions cause brown-out resets, unsafe shutdowns and latent reliability issues; correlating device events with voltage requires device-side visibility. Supports manageability and fleet reliability. derived
5SpecificationBase 2.4 (log pages/features/health reporting) and NVMe-MI 2.2 (out-of-band monitoring). Verify where it is defined and whether both paths expose it. uncertain
6–7Revision / mandatoryHighlighted in 2.4; requirement level must be read.
8AffectedController firmware and sensing hardware; host monitoring tools (nvme-cli plugins, telemetry pipelines); BMC firmware.
9TracesIf read via an admin command, it looks like any Get Log Page / Get Features exchange (Ch 57); out-of-band it appears as NVMe-MI messages over MCTP. No PCIe physical-layer signature is implied — the feature reports voltage, it does not change electrical behaviour.
10ValidationThought experiment: vary supply voltage with a programmable lab supply within the device’s rated range; check reported values track the reference meter within the device’s stated accuracy; check any threshold/event behaviour defined in the spec; compare in-band vs out-of-band values. EXPERT — voltage margining can damage hardware.
11What could go wrongUnit or scaling errors in host parsers; stale values; disagreement between BMC sensors and device reports due to measurement point differences. derived
12SeniorGives fleet teams a new correlation axis for “unexplained” resets and Unsafe Shutdown increments — if, and only if, sampling and reporting semantics are understood.

20.1.7 Rate Limiting

#QuestionAnswer
1BeforeNVMe offered building blocks for performance isolation (NVM Sets, Endurance Groups, I/O determinism, arbitration settings) but multi-tenant QoS was largely implementation-specific or host-enforced (e.g. Linux cgroups io controllers). derived
2What changedThe 2.4 announcement highlights Rate Limiting. verified (name). What is limited (commands, bandwidth, something else), at what scope (controller, namespace, host, other), and how limits are configured: read the spec. uncertain
3–4Why / problemNoisy neighbours in shared SSDs (see the SR-IOV noisy-neighbour trace in Ch 56) and predictable service levels for cloud and AI workloads. derived
5–7Spec / revision / mandatoryExpect Base 2.4; verify whether command-set or transport documents are involved; requirement level per spec.
8AffectedController schedulers; hypervisors/orchestrators that set limits; host drivers that must react to throttled behaviour.
9TracesConfiguration would appear as admin commands. Enforcement would appear as timing — longer command latency, spaced completions — not as a new packet type. A trace alone cannot distinguish rate limiting from thermal throttling or garbage collection; you need configuration state and device reporting.
10ValidationThought experiment: configure a limit, drive load above it, measure achieved rate and latency distribution; verify other tenants are unaffected; change limit under load; verify persistence across resets per spec.
11What could go wrongHost timeouts triggered by intentional throttling; unfairness at small time scales; interactions with host-side QoS producing double throttling. derived
12SeniorStandardised QoS changes how latency anomalies must be triaged: “the device is slow” may be policy, not fault. Make limit state part of every performance bug report.

20.1.8 Restore Manufacturing Default Settings

#QuestionAnswer
1BeforeConfiguration could be changed through many features (Set Features with Save, namespace management, power and thermal settings, MI configuration), while Sanitize (84h) and Format NVM (80h) address user data. Returning a repurposed drive to a known configuration often required vendor tools. derived
2What changedThe 2.4 announcement highlights Restore Manufacturing Default Settings. verified (name). Which settings are restored, whether namespaces or data are affected, and how it interacts with security state: read the spec. uncertain
3–4Why / problemDevice reuse and redeployment (sustainability, circular economy), consistent baselines for testing and support, recovery from misconfiguration. derived (the announcement emphasises sustainability).
5–7Spec / revision / mandatoryExpect Base 2.4; check NVMe-MI 2.2 for out-of-band invocation. Requirement level per spec.
8AffectedController firmware; provisioning and decommissioning tools; data-centre asset workflows.
9TracesInvocation appears as a command exchange; effects appear afterwards as changed Identify/Get Features values and possibly resets. No PCIe signature beyond ordinary traffic and any reset the spec requires.
10ValidationThought experiment: change every saveable setting; invoke the restore; verify each setting against documented defaults; verify user data handling exactly as specified (do not assume erase); verify behaviour with security locked; power loss during restore.
11What could go wrongOperators assuming it sanitises data (or that it doesn’t); host caches of feature values becoming stale; restoring settings that break the current platform (e.g. power limits). derived
12SeniorAny “reset to defaults” is a data-governance question. Write decommissioning procedures that cite exact spec behaviour, and keep Sanitize as the data-destruction step unless the spec says otherwise.

20.1.10 Reading section — “What changed from NVMe 2.3 to 2.4?”

🎯 Guided reading
  1. Collect sources. Download the 2.3 and 2.4 versions of the Base specification and every sub-specification you care about from nvmexpress.org/specifications. Save the August 4 2026 announcement.
  2. Read the revision histories first. Each specification lists changes and incorporated TPs/ECNs. Build a spreadsheet: document, TP/ECN identifier, title, one-line summary, sections touched.
  3. Map highlights to TPs. For each of the five highlighted features, find the TP(s) that introduced it and the sections they modified.
  4. Classify each change with the revision-diff method (Ch 20.3): added feature, changed field, changed behaviour, changed error handling, interoperability implication, validation requirement.
  5. Find requirement words. In each new section, highlight every “shall”, “should”, “may”. Note which controller types (I/O, administrative, discovery) each requirement applies to.
  6. Write the “cannot infer” list. For each feature, list three things you expected to find but did not — those are implementation-dependent and must not appear in your design docs as facts.

20.1.11 What is verified, derived, implementation- and version-dependent

CategoryContent
verifiedThe 2.4 set was announced Aug 4 2026; it highlights the five named features; emphasis on security, manageability, sustainability and AI/cloud/enterprise/client storage.
derivedProblem statements (why each feature helps), likely affected components, and the absence of new PCIe TLP types for these features.
implHow each device implements the features, performance impact, which optional subsets are supported.
versionEverything about 2.4 vs earlier; sub-spec revision numbers; any later errata.
Must be checked in the specOpcodes, structures, IDs, status codes, requirement levels, scope, interactions with reset, security and virtualization.
Never assumeThat a 2.4-reporting device supports any new feature; that Restore Manufacturing Defaults erases data; that Rate Limiting is per-namespace; that PQC replaces classical algorithms rather than adds options; that migration requires SR-IOV.

⚠️ No fabricated wire traces

None of the five features necessarily has a distinctive PCIe packet signature. This course therefore does not show “a PQC TLP” or “a migration DLLP”. If you see such a thing in training material, treat the material as unreliable.

💡 Senior insight

The strongest engineers are not the ones who know the newest feature first; they are the ones who can say precisely which sentence of which revision supports their claim — and who label everything else as unknown. Make “source and revision” a mandatory field in your bug templates.

Quiz

  1. Name the five capabilities highlighted in the Aug 4 2026 announcement.

    Answer

    Post-Quantum Cryptography, PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration, Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting, Restore Manufacturing Default Settings.

  2. A controller reports VS = 2.4. Does it support Rate Limiting?

    Answer

    Unknown. Check the capability fields defined by the specification for that feature.

  3. Should you expect a new TLP type for PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration?

    Answer

    No basis for that. Control would use NVMe commands; any data movement is ordinary PCIe traffic. Confirm in the spec.

  4. Does Restore Manufacturing Default Settings erase user data?

    Answer

    Cannot be inferred from the name or the announcement. Read the normative description.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is post-quantum cryptography and why might storage care?
    Model answerPublic-key algorithms designed to resist quantum attacks; storage devices and their authentication/encryption key exchanges live for years, so long-lived data and trust anchors need protection against future attacks.
  2. Intermediate How would you find what changed between 2.3 and 2.4?
    Model answerRead each specification’s revision history and the incorporated TP/ECN list, map highlights to TPs, then read the affected normative sections and classify changes.
  3. Advanced How would you test a migration feature without knowing its internals in advance?
    Model answerDefine invariants independent of the mechanism (no lost/duplicated completions, consistent namespace and reservation state, bounded pause, security isolation), then read the spec to add mechanism-specific tests.
  4. Senior A product manager wants to claim “NVMe 2.4 compliant” on the datasheet. What do you say?
    Model answerSpecify which documents and revisions, which optional features are supported, and how compliance was tested (e.g. formal compliance programs); avoid implying support of all 2.4 features.

Teach-back: to a child — “the new rulebook headline vs the rulebook pages”; to a junior — the twelve questions for one feature; to a senior — how version skew causes interop failures and how to prevent claims without evidence.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain the purpose of each of the five 2.4 highlights without inventing mechanisms.
  • I can name which documents to open for each and why.
  • I can list, for each feature, three things that cannot be inferred from the announcement.
  • I can explain why none of them implies a new PCIe packet type.
  • I can cite the Aug 4 2026 announcement and nvmexpress.org/specifications as sources.

20.2.5 Version-control rule applied

🧪 Lab 20.2.1 — Verify the baseline yourself SAFE

Objective: independently confirm every row of 20.2.2. Steps: (1) open nvmexpress.org/specifications; (2) record each document’s title, revision and date from its title page; (3) find the August 4 2026 announcement and record the five highlights verbatim (short quotes only); (4) mark any discrepancy with this course; (5) check for ECNs/errata issued after August 2026. Questions: did any document keep its previous revision number? Are there documents in the set that the course does not cover (e.g. other transports)?

Solution

Expected reasoning: the official library is authoritative; where it differs from the course, the library wins and the course should be corrected. Documents outside this course’s list (for example a Fibre Channel binding defined by INCITS) are out of scope, not non-existent.

Extension: write a one-page “baseline memo” for your team citing each document and date.

20.3 Revision Labs — 2026 Features, Version Compatibility and the Revision-Diff Method

← 20.2 2026 Release Verification72.1 What Is New in NVMe? →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe 2.4 set (Aug 4 2026) and at least one earlier revision of each document you study (e.g. the 2.3 set, or NVMe 1.4 for long-range comparison). SOURCE: nvmexpress.org/specifications (current and archived revisions). Historical introduction points below are labelled version; confirm each in the revision history of the document concerned.

20.3.1 Why this chapter exists

Products ship with firmware written against one revision, drivers written against another, and test suites written against a third. The labs here turn “read the new spec” into a disciplined, repeatable procedure that produces artefacts your team can review.

  • Run a structured reading of every 2026 highlight (Lab 50).
  • Build and use a version-compatibility feature matrix (Lab 55).
  • Apply the six-step revision-diff method to any change (Lab 56).

20.3.2 The revision-diff method (Extended topic 56)

For every revision change you study, answer six questions and record the evidence (document, revision, section title — not invented section numbers):

StepQuestionTypical evidenceWhy it matters
1Added feature?new section, new capability bit, new command/log/featurenew optional surface area: needs capability-gated host code
2Changed field?previously reserved bits now defined; field widened; meaning refinedold parsers may misread; reserved-bit checks in tests must change
3Changed behaviour?“shall” sentences added/removed/rewordedfirmware conformance; host assumptions
4Changed error handling?new status codes; new conditions for existing codeshost error paths and retry logic
5Interoperability implication?negotiation, defaults, backwards-compatibility notesmixed-revision deployments
6Validation requirement?new tests, changed expected results, compliance program updatestest plans and certification
📌 Spec-reading discipline

shall = requirement; should = recommendation (deviation allowed with reason); may = permission/option. Informative notes, examples and rationale do not create requirements. Reserved fields: senders set to zero and receivers typically ignore them, as the document’s conventions specify — read the conventions section of each document rather than assuming identical rules everywhere.

Solution guidance

A good submission cites document + revision + section title for every claim, keeps short quotes only, and has a populated “not specified” column for each feature. A submission that contains opcodes or field offsets without citations fails the lab, even if those values turn out to be right — the point is evidence.

PART LXXIII

An Important Distinction: NVMe, PCIe, and NVMe over PCIe

The learner studies two technologies that are connected but independent. NVMe defines storage protocol semantics. PCIe provides the transport/interconnect in the PCIe deployment. NVMe over PCIe defines the binding between them. Collapsing the three into one concept is the root of many wrong diagnoses.

73.1 Three Things, Not One

← 72.1 What Is New in NVMe?69 Linux PCIe Inspection →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG); NVM Express Base Specification 2.4 (NVM Express); NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification 1.4 (NVM Express) — revisions per course brief. STATUS: separate standards bodies and documents. verified

73.1.1 Why this chapter exists

“The NVMe link is down”, “the PCIe command failed”, “NVMe TLP” — these phrases are common and wrong. Each mixes layers. When an engineer mixes layers, they also mix owners, tools and specifications, and spend days in the wrong document. This chapter draws the boundaries sharply.

  • State which specification owns each concept from link training to namespaces.
  • Explain what the NVMe over PCIe transport binding adds.
  • Attribute symptoms to the correct layer and document.
🧒 Kid analogy — language, road, and the rule for posting letters

NVMe is a language for asking a library for books. PCIe is a road. “NVMe over PCIe” is the rule that says: “when you use that road, put your request in this box at this address and ring this bell.” You could speak the same language over a different road (a phone line — TCP), and you could drive other things on the same road (graphics cards, network cards).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The binding is more than a mailbox rule: it decides that queues live in memory the device reaches by DMA, that registers sit in a BAR, that interrupts are MSI/MSI-X, and how PRPs describe memory. Those choices shape NVMe’s performance profile on PCIe deeply.

73.1.2 Who owns what

ConceptOwner documentNot owned by
Link training, equalization, LTSSM, lanes, speedsPCIe Base (PCI-SIG)NVMe
TLPs, DLLPs, flow control, ordering, completionsPCIe BaseNVMe
Configuration space, BARs, capabilities, class codePCIe Base (class code 010802h value assigned for NVMe)—
AER, DPC, ASPM, L1 substates, SR-IOVPCIe BaseNVMe (NVMe virtualization builds on SR-IOV)
Register map in BAR0 (CAP, VS, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ, ACQ, doorbells)NVMe Base defines registers/properties; NVMe over PCIe defines their memory-mapped placement and doorbellsPCIe
PRP lists, MSI-X usage by NVMeNVMe Base / NVMe over PCIe transportPCIe defines MSI-X itself
SQE/CQE format, opcodes, status codes, namespaces, logs, featuresNVMe Base + command setsPCIe
Capsules, PDUs, RDMA mappingNVMe TCP / RDMA transportsPCIe

The precise split of register definitions between Base and the PCIe transport document changed with the 2.0 refactoring version; check both when citing.

73.1.3 Correcting common phrases

Wrong phraseWhat is meantCorrect layer
“The NVMe link is down”PCIe link (LTSSM not in L0) — or a fabric connectionPCIe / transport
“NVMe TLP”a PCIe MWr/MRd carrying NVMe data or a doorbellPCIe TLP carrying NVMe payload
“PCIe command failed”an NVMe command completed with error status, or a PCIe request got UR/CAdecide which!
“The SSD timed out”NVMe command timeout (host driver) or PCIe Completion Timeout (root port)NVMe vs PCIe — different timers, different logs
“NVMe error in AER”a PCIe error reported by the NVMe device’s functionPCIe

73.1.4 Traces — the same event at three layers

Synthetic trace — one failed read seen per layer
LayerObservationOwning spec
Applicationread() returns EIOOS
NVMeCQE status: data transfer error (SCT generic) for CID 0x31NVMe Base
PCIeController’s MRd for PRP list got UR completionPCIe Base
PlatformIOMMU fault for that addressplatform / OS

The first abnormal event is at the PCIe layer, caused by the platform; the NVMe status is a consequence and the application error a further consequence. Reading only the NVMe status would point at the SSD. derived

73.1.5 Failure attribution exercise

🎯 Exercise — which layer, which document?
  1. Link trains at Gen3 instead of Gen4.
  2. Namespace shows 0 capacity.
  3. CSTS reads FFFFFFFFh.
  4. CQE phase tag never flips although doorbell writes are seen in the trace.
  5. Correctable Receiver Errors increase.
  6. Zone Invalid Write.
  7. NVMe/TCP connection reset after digest error.
Answers

(1) PCIe physical/LTSSM — PCIe Base. (2) NVMe namespace/format — NVMe Base + NVM CS. (3) PCIe accessibility (device gone/contained) observed through an NVMe register — PCIe first. (4) Binding/controller: doorbell reached the device (PCIe ok); controller did not fetch/complete — NVMe over PCIe + controller implementation. (5) PCIe physical — PCIe Base. (6) ZNS command set. (7) NVMe/TCP transport.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Is NVMe a kind of PCIe?
    Model answerNo. NVMe is a storage protocol; PCIe is one interconnect it can run over, via the NVMe over PCIe transport binding. NVMe also runs over TCP and RDMA.
  2. Intermediate What does the NVMe over PCIe binding define?
    Model answerHow NVMe controller registers and doorbells are memory-mapped in a BAR, that queues and data buffers live in memory accessed by device DMA, PRP usage, and MSI/MSI-X interrupt usage, among others.
  3. Senior Why does keeping these layers separate matter for a debug team?
    Model answerIt decides which evidence to collect (LTSSM/TLP vs NVMe command/CQE), which owner to engage (platform, PCIe IP, controller firmware, driver), which specification to cite, and prevents consequence-as-cause errors.
📌 Summary

NVMe = storage semantics. PCIe = interconnect. NVMe over PCIe = the binding. Always name the layer, the owner and the document when you describe a symptom.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can place any concept in this book into the correct layer and document.
  • I never say “NVMe TLP” or “NVMe link” without qualification.
  • I can trace one failure through all three layers and identify the first abnormal event.

Further reading: PCI Express Base Specification (pcisig.com); NVM Express Base Specification 2.4 and NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification 1.4 (nvmexpress.org/specifications); NVM Express announcement of August 4, 2026.

PART XXI

Linux Practicals

Everything so far has been theory, specification and synthetic traces. This Part puts your hands on a real Linux machine — safely. You will learn to read what the kernel and the device already expose: the PCIe configuration space through lspci and sysfs, the NVMe controller through nvme-cli, and the history of what went wrong through dmesg and journalctl. The rule for the whole Part is simple: read first, write never — unless you know exactly what the write does, on a machine you are allowed to break, with data you are willing to lose. Every command table in this Part has two columns that matter more than the command itself: what this proves and what this cannot prove.

69 Linux PCIe Inspection

← 73.1 Three Things, Not One70 Linux NVMe Inspection →

69.1 Why this chapter exists

When an NVMe drive is "slow", "missing" or "flaky", the first question a senior engineer asks is not about NVMe at all. It is: did the PCIe link come up the way it should, and is the device configured the way the driver expects? On Linux, the answers already sit in the PCI Express configuration space of every device and every port above it. lspci, setpci and /sys/bus/pci are the three windows onto that space. Engineers who cannot read them waste days on analyzers and firmware logs to discover something that one lspci -vv line would have told them: the drive trained at x2 instead of x4, or at 8 GT/s instead of 16 GT/s.

  • Beginner: list PCIe devices, find your NVMe controller, and identify its Bus/Device/Function (BDF) and vendor/device IDs.
  • Intermediate: read Link Capabilities vs Link Status, Max Payload Size (MPS), Max Read Request Size (MRRS), MSI-X state, and Advanced Error Reporting (AER) status bits from lspci -vv.
  • Advanced: walk the topology with lspci -tv and sysfs to find the upstream port that limits the link, and decode raw config space with lspci -xxxx and the Lab 1 parser.
  • Senior: state precisely what config-space inspection proves and what it can never prove, and decide when to escalate to a protocol analyzer.
  • Validation: build a read-only "link health snapshot" that can be compared before and after a test run.

Prerequisites. Configuration space layout, capability lists, Base Address Registers (BAR), link training (LTSSM) and the PCIe Capability structure from the PCIe Parts of this book; the programming lab that parses config hex is Lab 1 in Chapter 72.

69.2 Story: the building inspector

🧒 Kid analogy

Imagine a huge apartment building. Every apartment has a little sign-board by its door: who lives there, how many rooms they have, how wide their front door is, and whether the door is currently stuck half-open. A building inspector walks the corridors reading every sign-board. She never goes inside and never moves the furniture — she only reads. lspci is that inspector. The sign-boards are each device's configuration space. The corridors are the PCIe bridges and switches. If a sign says "my door is 4 people wide" but "today only 2 people can pass", the inspector has found a problem without opening a single door.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Real sign-boards cannot lie or go stale, but config-space values are written by firmware, by the BIOS/UEFI, by the kernel and by the device itself, at different times. A "status" bit may be sticky (it records something that happened hours ago and stays set until cleared — many AER bits behave this way), and some registers change dynamically (link speed can change after a Recovery). Also, reading certain registers is not always side-effect free on broken hardware, and reading the extended space needs root. The inspector reads a snapshot, never a movie.

69.3 Beginner: the commands and what each one is for

Before the command table, a map. Each tool looks at one layer of the I/O stack, so the first debugging skill is picking the tool that sees the layer you suspect. Arrows show what a tool observes, not the path its request takes (nvme-cli and lspci both go through the kernel to reach the device).

Host software layersPCIe linkDeviceTool observes this layer

The PCI utilities package (pciutils) provides lspci (list and decode) and setpci (read and write individual registers). Both read the same data the kernel exposes through /sys/bus/pci/devices/<domain:bus:dev.fn>/config. As an unprivileged user you typically see only the first 64 bytes (the standard header); the capability lists — where everything interesting lives — need root.

CommandWhat it revealsWhat it provesWhat it cannot provePrivilege / safety
lspciOne line per function: BDF, class name, vendor and device name from the local pci.ids databaseThe function enumerated: config reads to it succeeded at boot or rescanThat a driver bound, that the link is healthy, or that the name is right (the name database may be stale)User; read-only
lspci -nnSame, plus numeric [class] and [vendor:device] IDsExact IDs the kernel matches drivers against; class 0108 with prog-if 02 = NVMeProduct revision or firmware version (use nvme id-ctrl)User; read-only
lspci -v / -vv / -vvvDecoded header, BARs (with sizes the kernel recorded), every capability: PM, MSI/MSI-X, PCIe (DevCap/DevCtl/LnkCap/LnkSta/LnkCtl2...), AER, etc.; "Kernel driver in use"Negotiated link speed/width at the moment of reading; MPS/MRRS programmed; which error-status bits are latchedLink stability over time, how many Recoveries occurred, whether any TLP was replayed, or anything about NVMe queuesRoot for capabilities ("access denied" otherwise); read-only
lspci -xHex dump of the first 64 bytes (standard header)Raw values exactly as read, independent of the decoderAnything in capabilities beyond 0x40User
lspci -xxxHex dump of the full 256-byte legacy config spaceRaw capability list contentsExtended capabilities (AER, DSN, L1 PM Substates, physical-layer 16/32 GT/s caps...)Root. Note: on some old devices, reading undefined registers was reported to misbehave — pciutils documents this as a caution
lspci -xxxxHex dump of the 4096-byte extended config spaceRaw extended capability chain; input for the Lab 1 parserAnything about the past except sticky status bitsRoot; read-only; same caution as above
lspci -tvTree view: root complex → root ports → switches → endpoints, with namesTopology: which port your SSD hangs from, whether a switch is in the pathPhysical slot wiring, retimers (normally invisible to software), cable qualityUser
lspci -s 01:00.0 / -d 144d:Restrict output to one BDF / one vendor(:device)——Combine with other flags
lspci -kKernel driver in use and candidate modulesWhich driver owns the function (e.g. nvme, vfio-pci)That the driver initialized the controller successfully (check dmesg)User
lspci -DAlways print the PCI domain (segment) numberDisambiguates multi-segment servers—User
lspci -PPShow the path of bridges leading to each device (pciutils 3.6+ version)The exact upstream chain—User
# Find the NVMe controllers (class 0108) with numeric IDs
lspci -nn -d ::0108

# Full decode of one controller (root needed to see capabilities)
sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -vv

# The topology above it
lspci -tv

# Raw 4 KiB config space, saved for offline parsing (Lab 1)
sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -xxxx > nvme0-cfg.hex
📌 Remember

-d ::0108 filters by class (the vendor:device:class filter syntax is available in reasonably recent pciutils version). If your version rejects it, use lspci -nn | grep 0108.

69.4 Engineering: reading lspci -vv for an NVMe controller

Below is an illustrative, abbreviated excerpt in the general shape that recent pciutils prints. It is synthetic: the IDs are placeholders and field order and wording vary by pciutils version. Use it to learn where to look; compare against your own machine.

01:00.0 Non-Volatile memory controller [0108]: Example Corp NVMe SSD [abcd:0001] (rev 01) (prog-if 02 [NVM Express])

        Vector table: BAR=0 offset=00002000
        PBA: BAR=0 offset=00003000

        DevCap: MaxPayload 512 bytes, PhantFunc 0, Latency L0s unlimited, L1 unlimited
        DevCtl: CorrErr+ NonFatalErr+ FatalErr+ UnsupReq+
                RlxdOrd+ ExtTag+ PhantFunc- AuxPwr- NoSnoop-
                MaxPayload 256 bytes, MaxReadReq 512 bytes
        DevSta: CorrErr+ NonFatalErr- FatalErr- UnsupReq- AuxPwr- TransPend-
