FieldMeaningHealthy NVMe expectationRed flag and next step
Control: Mem+ BusMaster+Memory Space Enable and Bus Master Enable in the Command registerBoth + when the nvme driver owns the deviceBusMaster- with driver bound: the device cannot DMA — every SQE fetch would fail. Check driver probe errors in dmesg
Region 0 ... [size=16K]BAR0 assignment and size (size comes from the kernel's resource record, not a fresh sizing write)Non-prefetchable 64-bit memory BAR holding NVMe registers and doorbells[disabled] or [virtual] or unassigned: resource allocation failed (BIOS, hot-plug, bridge window too small)
MSI-X: Enable+ Count=NMSI-X capability: vectors available, enabled, function maskEnable+ Masked-; Count ≥ number of I/O queues the driver wantsEnable- while driver loaded: running on legacy INTx or MSI — performance and interrupt-loss risk (Failure Library Chapter 84)
DevCap MaxPayload vs DevCtl MaxPayloadCapability vs programmed MPSProgrammed MPS equals the smallest MPS supported along the path (OS/BIOS policy) implMPS 128 on a modern platform caps efficiency (see Chapter 90); mismatched MPS across a path can cause Malformed TLPs
MaxReadReqMRRS: largest read the device may request (affects write-to-SSD traffic, where the SSD reads host memory)512 B–4 KiB typical implVery small MRRS (128 B) inflates MRd count for writes
LnkCap vs LnkStaMaximum speed/width the device supports vs currently negotiatedEqual, or limited by the upstream port's LnkCap(downgraded): compare the port above; see Failure Library width/speed downgrade
LnkCtl2 Target Link SpeedSpeed the port aims for; software may have capped itEqual to the max of both endsA capped target speed explains a "downgrade" that is really a policy setting
DevSta: CorrErr+A correctable error was detected since last clearIdeally -; occasional set bits are not alarming by themselvesLook at CESta and the AER counters in sysfs; trend over time matters more than one bit
UESta / CEStaAER uncorrectable / correctable status bits (sticky until cleared by software)All -, or the kernel's AER handler has cleared them after loggingCmpltTO+, MalfTLP+, UnsupReq+: transaction-layer problem; RxErr+ BadTLP+: signal integrity / link layer
Kernel driver in useWhich driver bound the functionnvme (or vfio-pci when passed to a VM / user-space driver)Missing: the driver failed probe or is not loaded
💡 Senior insight

The single most valuable two-line comparison in PCIe debugging is endpoint LnkCap/LnkSta vs root-port LnkCap/LnkSta. If the root port's LnkCap says 8 GT/s, your "Gen4 SSD at Gen3" is not a fault at all — it is the platform. If both say 16 GT/s and LnkSta says 8 GT/s, something during equalization or Recovery decided to fall back, and that is a signal-integrity investigation. Always read both ends before you write a bug report.

69.5 Topology: lspci -tv and sysfs paths

The tree view is how you find the port above your device. Illustrative shape (synthetic):

-[0000:00]-+-00.0  Host bridge
           +-01.0-[01]----00.0  NVMe controller (the SSD)
           +-01.1-[02-05]----00.0-[03-05]--+-00.0-[04]----00.0  NVMe controller
           |                               \-08.0-[05]----00.0  NVMe controller
           \-1f.0  ISA bridge

Read it as: root port 00:01.0 has secondary bus 01, and on that bus sits the SSD 01:00.0. Root port 00:01.1 leads to bus 02 where a switch upstream port 02:00.0 lives; its downstream ports 03:00.0 and 03:08.0 lead to buses 04 and 05. The switch matters for debugging because every TLP crosses an extra pair of links and an extra store-and-forward or cut-through stage, and because the switch can be a capture point itself (see Chapter 78).

sysfs encodes the same path in its directory names, which makes it scriptable:

# Full path from the root complex to the device
readlink -f /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0
#  -> /sys/devices/pci0000:00/0000:00:01.0/0000:01:00.0

# Upstream port of the device = parent directory
basename "$(dirname "$(readlink -f /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:01:00.0)")"

# Link state, both ends, without root
for d in 0000:00:01.0 0000:01:00.0; do
  p=/sys/bus/pci/devices/$d
  echo "$d now=$(cat $p/current_link_speed) x$(cat $p/current_link_width)" \
       "max=$(cat $p/max_link_speed) x$(cat $p/max_link_width)"
done

69.6 sysfs: the PCI files that matter

Path under /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/ContentProvesCannot prove / caution
vendor, device, class, revision, subsystem_vendorIDs as hexIdentity, scriptable—
current_link_speed, current_link_width, max_link_speed, max_link_widthDecoded LnkSta / LnkCapNegotiated vs capable, readable without rootSnapshot only; a link that flaps between reads looks fine
configBinary config space (64 B as user, full as root)Raw values (xxd it)Writable by root — writing here is as dangerous as setpci
resource, resource0BAR ranges (text) / mmap-able BAR0Where NVMe registers are mappedresource0 mmap gives raw register access; touching doorbells while the driver runs corrupts queues. Do not.
driver (symlink)Bound driverWhich driver owns it—
numa_node, local_cpulistNUMA localityWhich CPUs are "near" the device — essential for performance runs-1 means unknown / single node
msi_irqs/One entry per allocated MSI/MSI-X vector (IRQ number)How many vectors the driver gotThat interrupts actually arrive (use /proc/interrupts deltas)
aer_dev_correctable, aer_dev_nonfatal, aer_dev_fatalPer-error-type counters maintained by the kernel AER driver versionError history since boot, by type — better than one sticky bitOnly errors the OS was notified of; firmware-first platforms may handle errors before Linux sees them impl
power/runtime_status, power_stateRuntime PM state, D-stateWhether the device is suspendedLink power state (ASPM L1/L1.x) is not shown here
reset, remove, rescan, enableWrite-only control files—Destructive/disruptive. Writing triggers a function reset, hot-removal or re-enumeration. Lab-only.

69.7 setpci: reading single registers — and why writing is dangerous

setpci addresses registers by offset or by name, with a width suffix .b, .w or .l. Capability-relative names such as CAP_EXP (the PCI Express capability) and ECAP_AER let you avoid hard-coding offsets that differ between devices (check man setpci for the names your version supports version).

# READS ONLY. No "=" sign anywhere means no write.
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 VENDOR_ID.w DEVICE_ID.w      # identity
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 COMMAND.w                      # bit1 Mem, bit2 BusMaster
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 CAP_EXP+0x08.w                 # Device Control (MPS bits 7:5, MRRS 14:12)
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 CAP_EXP+0x0c.l                 # Link Capabilities
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 CAP_EXP+0x12.w                 # Link Status (speed 3:0, width 9:4)
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 ECAP_AER+0x04.l                # AER Uncorrectable Error Status
sudo setpci -s 01:00.0 ECAP_AER+0x10.l                # AER Correctable Error Status

Decoding CAP_EXP+0x12.w = 1043: bits 3:0 = 3 → 8 GT/s; bits 9:4 = 4 → x4; bit 12 = 1 → slot clock configuration. Compare with Link Capabilities bits 3:0 (max speed) and 9:4 (max width).

⚠️ Warning — setpci writes

Any setpci argument containing = is a write to live hardware. A single wrong write can: disable Memory Space or Bus Master (the device vanishes from the driver's view mid-I/O, causing timeouts and possible data loss), change MPS to a value the path does not support (Malformed TLPs, fatal errors), retrain or disable the link (the root filesystem disappears if it lives on that drive), or clear AER status that someone else needed as evidence. Rules: never write on a production system; never write to the device holding your OS; know the register's semantics from the specification, including RW1C ("write 1 to clear") bits; record the old value first; and prefer the kernel's own interfaces (sysfs, driver parameters) over raw writes. This book does not ask you to perform any setpci write.

69.8 Specification and hardware view

📘 Specification

The register layout lspci decodes is defined by the PCI Express Base Specification (Type 0/1 headers, capability structures, extended capabilities starting at offset 100h). verified Offsets used above inside the PCI Express Capability: Device Capabilities +04h, Device Control +08h, Device Status +0Ah, Link Capabilities +0Ch, Link Control +10h, Link Status +12h, Device Control 2 +28h, Link Capabilities 2 +2Ch, Link Control 2 +30h, Link Status 2 +32h. Inside AER: Uncorrectable Status +04h, Mask +08h, Severity +0Ch, Correctable Status +10h, Correctable Mask +14h. Always confirm against the specification revision your platform implements.

🔧 Hardware

Every config read by lspci becomes a configuration-read request (CfgRd0 to the endpoint, or ECAM memory reads that the root complex converts into configuration TLPs impl). That means an analyzer on the link will see your lspci — useful as a deliberate trigger marker, and a reason not to run monitoring loops of lspci during a sensitive capture. A device that has dropped off the link returns all-ones (ff) for every config read; lspci then shows !!! Unknown header type 7f or similar.

69.9 Debugging connection

🐞 Debugging

Config space is the first stop for: device missing (enumerated or not?), slow sequential throughput (width/speed downgrade, MPS 128), interrupts misbehaving (MSI-X disabled or masked), and error storms (AER status bits). It is the wrong tool for: intermittent link Recovery (you need counters or an analyzer), latency outliers (you need block-layer tracing), or "which command failed" (you need NVMe logs). See the decision tree in Chapter 80.

69.10 Common mistakes

  • Running lspci -vv without root and concluding "the device has no AER capability" — the output said Capabilities: <access denied>.
  • Reading only the endpoint's LnkSta and blaming the SSD for a speed the root port could never reach.
  • Treating one latched CorrErr+ as a fault. Correctable errors are designed to be corrected; their rate is the signal.
  • Copy-pasting a setpci line from a forum that contains =.
  • Assuming lspci names are authoritative: the pci.ids file maps IDs to names and may be outdated; IDs are the truth.
🧪 Lab 69.1 — H1/H2/H3: identify the device, read config space, identify BARs SAFE

Classification: non-destructive · read-only · production-safe (reads only; root needed for full decode).

Objective: produce a one-page "PCIe identity card" for one NVMe controller.

Setup: any Linux machine with an NVMe SSD; pciutils installed.

  1. H1 — lspci -nn -d ::0108; record BDF, vendor:device, revision.
  2. H2 — sudo lspci -s <BDF> -vv; record Command bits, MSI-X state, DevCap/DevCtl MPS, MRRS, LnkCap, LnkSta, AER status lines.
  3. H2b — sudo lspci -s <BDF> -xxxx > cfg.hex; run python3 lab01_cfgspace.py cfg.hex (Chapter 72) and check that its decode agrees with lspci.
  4. H3 — cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/0000:<BDF>/resource; identify BAR0 start/end; compute its size.
  5. Repeat steps 2 for the upstream port (find it with readlink -f).

Observations to record: device and port speeds/widths; programmed MPS on both; any AER bits set.

Questions: (1) Is the link at the maximum both ends support? (2) Is MPS identical on port and endpoint? (3) How large is BAR0 and why is it at least 0x1000 + doorbell space?

Solution / expected reasoning

(1) Compare min(port LnkCap, device LnkCap) with LnkSta; equality is healthy. (2) MPS must be configured consistently along a path; Linux commonly programs a common value per hierarchy (policy is configurable with the pci=pcie_bus_* kernel parameters version). (3) NVMe controller registers occupy offsets 00h–FFFh and doorbells begin at 1000h with stride 4 << CAP.DSTRD; with N queue pairs you need 1000h + 2·N·stride bytes; vendors round BAR0 up (16 KiB is common) and may place MSI-X tables in the same BAR impl.

Extension: write a shell script that prints a CSV row per NVMe device: BDF, port BDF, cur/max speed and width for both, MPS, MSI-X count. Run it before and after a stress test and diff.

Quiz

  1. Which flag shows extended capabilities such as AER in hex?

    Answer

    -xxxx (as root). -xxx stops at 256 bytes; extended capabilities start at offset 100h.

  2. LnkSta shows 16GT/s x2 on a x4-capable SSD whose root port is x4-capable. Name three plausible causes.

    Answer

    Lanes failing detect/training (damaged lane, bad connector, cable/riser), a slot physically wired x2 despite a x4 port configuration (bifurcation/BIOS setting), or a retimer/redriver issue. Confirm with port LnkCap, platform documentation, and if needed an analyzer capture of training.

  3. Why can lspci not tell you that the link went through Recovery 300 times last night?

    Answer

    Config space shows current state and some sticky status bits, not event counts. Recovery history needs AER counters, vendor-specific counters, platform telemetry or an analyzer.

  4. Which setpci commands in this chapter write to hardware?

    Answer

    None. A write always contains = (e.g. REG.w=VALUE).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner How do you find the PCIe address and IDs of an NVMe SSD on Linux?
    Model answer

    lspci -nn and look for class [0108], or nvme list plus /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/address. Report domain:bus:device.function and vendor:device.

  2. Intermediate What is the difference between DevCap MaxPayload and DevCtl MaxPayload?
    Model answer

    DevCap is what the function supports; DevCtl is what software programmed. Only the programmed value governs the maximum TLP payload the function may send.

  3. Advanced An SSD is fine on one server but shows (downgraded) on another identical server. Walk through your triage.
    Model answer

    Compare both ends' LnkCap/LnkSta/LnkCtl2 on both servers; check BIOS/firmware versions and slot configuration; check AER counters for RxErr/BadTLP; swap the drive between servers to see whether the problem follows the drive or the slot; if it follows the slot, capture link training with an analyzer or use lane-margining tools if supported.

  4. Senior What can config-space inspection never tell you, and how do you close that gap?
    Model answer

    Temporal behavior (event counts, Recovery frequency, latency), traffic contents, and anything inside the controller. Close it with AER/telemetry counters, NVMe logs, block-layer tracing, and a protocol analyzer with a well-defined trigger.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can find any NVMe device's BDF, IDs, and upstream port in under a minute.
  • I can explain every field in the lspci table of §69.4 and what would make it a red flag.
  • I can read Link Status with setpci and decode it by hand.
  • I can state three things config space proves and three it cannot.
  • I never run a setpci line containing = without knowing the register's spec definition.

Teach-back. Child: "the computer reads every device's name tag and door size." Junior: "lspci decodes config space; compare LnkCap and LnkSta on both ends." Senior: "config space is a scoped snapshot; it localizes static misconfiguration fast but cannot show temporal or traffic-level behavior."

Summary. lspci/sysfs reveal identity, topology, negotiated link parameters, programmed payload sizes, interrupt mode and latched errors. They prove static state, not dynamic behavior. setpci reads are safe; writes are a lab-only, expert activity. Next: the NVMe controller itself, through nvme-cli.

70 Linux NVMe Inspection

← 69 Linux PCIe Inspection71 Kernel Logs: dmesg and journalctl →

70.1 Why this chapter exists

PCIe inspection tells you the road is open. NVMe inspection tells you what the controller says about itself: who it is, what it supports, how healthy it is, and what errors it has recorded. nvme-cli wraps the admin commands you studied earlier (Identify 06h, Get Log Page 02h, Get Features 0Ah) and sends them through the kernel driver's passthrough interface. Most of what you need is read-only; a small but dangerous subset of nvme-cli commands destroys data or changes firmware.

  • Beginner: list controllers and namespaces; map nvme0, nvme0n1, the PCIe BDF and the subsystem.
  • Intermediate: interpret the key Identify Controller and Identify Namespace fields (MDTS, SQES/CQES, NN, ONCS, LBA formats) and the SMART / Health log.
  • Advanced: read the Error Information log and correlate its SQID/CID entries with kernel timeouts; read features (Number of Queues, Interrupt Coalescing, APST).
  • Senior: classify every nvme-cli subcommand as read-only, state-changing, or destructive before running it.
  • Validation: snapshot NVMe health before/after a test and compute deltas.

Prerequisites: admin queue and admin opcodes; Identify; Get Log Page; Features; namespace concepts; Chapter 69.

70.2 Story

🧒 Kid analogy

The library (the SSD) has a front desk (the controller). You can ask the desk polite questions on special "office" forms: "What is your name? How many rooms do you have? How tired are you? What went wrong recently?" The desk answers on paper and nothing in the library changes. But some office forms say things like "throw away every book and repaint the shelves" — those forms (format, sanitize) are real, and the desk will obey them. Learn to read the form's title before you hand it over.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A real librarian might ask "are you sure?"; the controller does not. nvme-cli may print a warning or ask for confirmation for some destructive commands version, but you must not rely on that. Also, "polite questions" are not always free: an admin command still occupies the admin queue, and on a hung controller even an Identify can time out.

70.3 Device naming

NameWhat it isWhere
/dev/nvme0Character device for controller 0 — target for admin commandsAdmin passthrough
/dev/nvme0n1Block device for namespace 1 as seen through controller/subsystem 0Filesystems, fio
/dev/nvme0n1p1Partition 1 of that namespace—
/dev/ng0n1Generic character device per namespace (for passthrough I/O; newer kernels) versionio_uring passthrough
nvme-subsys0Subsystem object (groups controllers sharing namespaces; multipath)/sys/class/nvme-subsystem/
⚠️ Naming is not stable

With native NVMe multipath, the n1 in nvme0n1 follows the subsystem instance, and controller numbering can change between boots. Scripts that format or write must identify the target by serial number / WWID (/dev/disk/by-id/), never by nvmeX alone.

70.4 The command table

CommandUnderlying operationWhat it provesWhat it cannot proveSafety
nvme listEnumerates controllers/namespaces via sysfs + IdentifyWhich namespaces exist, model, serial, firmware, capacity, LBA sizeHealth, link stateRead-only
nvme list-subsysReads subsystem topology from sysfsSubsystem NQN, controllers and transport paths (pcie address), path stateThat I/O over each path worksRead-only
nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 (-H for decoded bits)Identify, CNS 01hCapabilities: MDTS, SQES/CQES, NN, OACS, ONCS, VWC, power states, sanitize/format support, firmware slots, versionThat optional features work; it states supportRead-only
nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 (-H)Identify, CNS 00hSize/capacity/utilization, LBA formats (FLBAS, LBAF list), protection info, metadataPhysical NAND layoutRead-only
nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0Get Log Page, Log ID 02hCritical warnings, temperature, spare, % used, data units, media errors, error-log entry count, unsafe shutdownsRoot cause of any counter; internal vendor telemetryRead-only
nvme error-log /dev/nvme0Get Log Page, Log ID 01hRecent error entries: error count, SQID, CID, status field, parameter error location, LBA, NSIDErrors the host never sent (link-level), older entries beyond the log depthRead-only
nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=N --log-len=LGet Log Page, arbitrary Log IDRaw log contents (firmware slot 03h, commands supported 05h, self-test 06h, telemetry, vendor logs)Meaning of vendor-specific logs without documentationRead-only for standard logs. Some logs have a "retain asynchronous event" / clear semantics uncertain — check the log's definition
nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 7 -HGet Features (FID 07h Number of Queues)Queues granted; similarly 02h Power Mgmt, 08h Interrupt Coalescing, 0Ch APST, 06h Volatile Write CacheRuntime effect of the featureRead-only
nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0Log 03hActive firmware slot and revisionsFirmware qualityRead-only
nvme self-test-log /dev/nvme0Log 06hResults of past device self-tests—Read-only (starting a test is a separate, state-changing command)
nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -HReads controller registers (CAP, VS, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ, ACQ...) via BAR mappingCC.EN, CSTS.RDY/CFS, CAP.TO, CAP.DSTRD, CAP.MQESDoorbell contents (write-only from host) or queue stateRead-only, needs root; maps BAR0 — avoid on a controller in a fragile state impl
sudo nvme list
sudo nvme list-subsys
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H | less
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H | less
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 | head -60
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x07 -H      # Number of Queues
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x08 -H      # Interrupt Coalescing
sudo nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=0x03 --log-len=512   # Firmware Slot log, raw
cat /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/{model,serial,firmware_rev,address,state,transport}

Field (nvme-cli name)MeaningWhy it matters in debugging
vid, ssvid, sn, mn, frPCI vendor IDs, serial, model, firmware revisionEvery bug report needs mn+fr; redact sn when sharing (data safety)

oacsOptional Admin Command Support bits (format, firmware, namespace mgmt, self-test...)Whether a command should be accepted; Invalid Opcode otherwise
sqes, cqesRequired/maximum SQ and CQ entry sizes as powers of two (NVM: 64 B / 16 B → 6 / 4)The driver programs CC.IOSQES/IOCQES from these
nnMaximum namespace ID / number of namespacesNamespace scans
oncsOptional NVM Command Support (Compare, Write Uncorrectable, DSM, Write Zeroes, Verify, Copy...)Whether discard/TRIM (DSM) is available
vwcVolatile Write Cache presentFlush semantics and power-loss behavior
npss, power state table (ps 0..n)Number of power states, max power, entry/exit latencies, non-operational flagAPST and latency spikes on idle→active transitions
apstaAutonomous Power State Transition supportPower-management-related latency/failure investigations

70.6 Interpreting Identify Namespace

FieldMeaningDebug use
nsze, ncap, nuseSize, capacity, utilization in logical blocksLBA Out of Range errors: compare SLBA+NLB with nsze
flbasIndex of the LBA format in use (plus metadata-at-end bit)Determines the LBA size
lbaf N : ms:M lbads:D rp:R (in use)LBA formats: metadata bytes, data size 2D (9 → 512 B, 12 → 4 KiB), relative performanceConverting NLB to bytes in traces; 512 B vs 4 KiB alignment issues
dps, dpcEnd-to-end data protection settings/capabilitiesProtection-information errors

70.7 Interpreting the SMART / Health log

FieldMeaningHow to use it
critical_warningBit field: spare below threshold, temperature, reliability degraded, read-only mode, volatile backup failed (and newer bits) versionAny non-zero value is a stop-and-investigate condition
temperatureComposite temperatureCorrelate with throughput drops (throttling)
available_spare, available_spare_thresholdRemaining spare capacity, % (normalized)Endurance trend
percentage_usedVendor estimate of life used; may exceed 100Trend, not an exact gauge impl
data_units_read/writtenIn thousands of 512-byte units (1 = 512,000 bytes), rounded upDeltas before/after a test verify the workload really reached the device
host_read_commands, host_write_commandsCommands completedDelta ÷ test duration ≈ average IOPS seen by the device
controller_busy_timeMinutes with I/O outstandingCoarse utilization
power_cycles, power_on_hours, unsafe_shutdownsLifetime countersUnsafe-shutdown increments after a "hang" = power was cut without shutdown notification
media_errorsUnrecovered data integrity errors detectedNon-zero delta during a test → media-layer investigation
num_err_log_entriesLifetime count of error-log entriesDelta tells you whether new errors were logged; then read error-log
warning_temp_time, critical_comp_timeMinutes above thresholdsThermal explanation for performance variance

70.8 Interpreting the Error Information log

Each entry carries an error_count (a unique, incrementing number), sqid, cmdid, status_field, parm_err_location (byte/bit in the command that caused the error, if applicable), lba, nsid and vendor info. The log is a circular buffer of a device-specific depth (Identify Controller elpe = entries minus one). Entries with error_count 0 are empty.

🐞 Correlation recipe

The kernel's timeout message names the queue (QID) and tag/command id. The error log names sqid and cmdid. If they match and the status field is, for example, Unrecovered Read Error, you have tied a host-visible failure to a controller-reported media event. If the error log is empty, the controller did not consider the command errored — that pushes suspicion toward the transport (lost doorbell, lost completion, interrupt path). Note that the Linux driver's CID encoding may include a generation counter in upper bits on newer kernels version, so match on what the log line actually prints.

70.9 Commands that change state or destroy data

⚠️ DESTRUCTIVE — read before you type

nvme format (Format NVM, 80h) erases every LBA in the namespace — or, depending on the controller's format attributes, all namespaces. nvme sanitize (84h) irreversibly destroys all user data in the entire NVM subsystem and may run for a long time and continue after a reset. nvme write, write-zeroes, write-uncor, dsm --ad (deallocate/TRIM) overwrite or discard data. nvme delete-ns / create-ns destroy namespaces. nvme fw-download + fw-commit change firmware (a bad image or interrupted activation can brick the drive). nvme reset, subsystem-reset and set-feature change live controller state. Never run these on a production system or on a drive holding data you want, and never on a device addressed as nvmeX without verifying its serial number first.

ClassExamplesRule
Read-onlylist, list-subsys, id-ctrl, id-ns, smart-log, error-log, fw-log, get-log (standard logs), get-feature, show-regsSafe on production, preferably during low load
State-changing, non-destructiveset-feature (e.g. APST, interrupt coalescing), device-self-test (starts a test), resetLab or maintenance window; record previous values
Destructiveformat, sanitize, write*, dsm deallocate, delete-ns, fw-commitLab only, dedicated scratch drive, double-check serial

70.10 Linux sysfs and module parameters for NVMe

PathWhat it shows
/sys/class/nvme/nvme0/{model,serial,firmware_rev,state,address,transport,cntlid,subsysnqn}Identity and controller state (live, resetting, connecting, dead...)
/sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/{logical_block_size,max_hw_sectors_kb,max_sectors_kb,nr_requests,scheduler}Block-layer limits (max_hw_sectors_kb reflects MDTS)
/sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/One directory per hardware queue (blk-mq hctx) with its cpu_list
/sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/io_timeout, admin_timeoutHost command timeouts (seconds; io_timeout default 30 version)
/sys/module/nvme_core/parameters/default_ps_max_latency_usAPST policy cap (0 disables APST)
/sys/module/nvme/parameters/{poll_queues,write_queues}Polled and dedicated write queue counts
/proc/interrupts (grep nvme)Per-vector interrupt counts per CPU — deltas show which queues are active
🧪 Lab 70.1 — H4–H7: controller, namespaces, SMART, error log SAFE

Classification: non-destructive · read-only · production-safe.

Objective: build an NVMe "health card" and a before/after delta tool.

  1. H4 — nvme id-ctrl -H: record mn, fr, ver, mdts, sqes/cqes, oncs, vwc, npss, apsta.
  2. H5 — nvme list, nvme id-ns -H: record nsze, flbas and the in-use LBA format.
  3. H6 — nvme smart-log twice, 10 minutes apart during normal use; compute deltas of data units and host commands.
  4. H7 — nvme error-log: count non-empty entries; for each, decode SCT/SC (use Lab 4's tables).
  5. Compute the MDTS in bytes: 2^mdts × CAP.MPSMIN page (MPSMIN from show-regs; commonly 4 KiB).
Solution / expected reasoning

Example reasoning: mdts=9 with 4 KiB minimum page → 2 MiB per command; max_hw_sectors_kb should be ≤ 2048. Data-unit delta of 1,000 → about 512 MB moved. If num_err_log_entries grew but your application saw no errors, the errors may belong to commands the kernel retried successfully, to admin commands (e.g. an unsupported Get Log Page issued by a monitoring tool), or to other hosts on a shared subsystem — check sqid (0 = admin queue).

Extension: write a Python script that runs these commands with -o json (nvme-cli JSON output) and diffs two snapshots.

Quiz

  1. Which device node do you pass to id-ctrl, and which to id-ns?

    Answer

    Controller character device /dev/nvme0 for id-ctrl; a namespace (e.g. /dev/nvme0n1) for id-ns (or the controller plus -n NSID).

  2. smart-log shows data_units_written grew by 2000 during your test. How many bytes?

    Answer

    2000 × 1000 × 512 = 1,024,000,000 bytes (≈1.02 GB), subject to rounding.

  3. An error-log entry shows sqid 0. What does that tell you?

    Answer

    The failing command was on the admin queue — often a tool probing an unsupported log or feature, not your I/O workload.

  4. Name three nvme-cli subcommands that destroy data.

    Answer

    format, sanitize, write / write-zeroes / dsm deallocate / delete-ns (any three).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is the difference between /dev/nvme0 and /dev/nvme0n1?
    Model answer

    Controller (admin) character device vs namespace block device.

  2. Intermediate Why does a 1 MiB fio block size appear as several NVMe commands in a trace?
    Model answer

    The block layer splits requests above max_sectors_kb/max_hw_sectors_kb, which derive from MDTS and driver limits.

  3. Advanced A drive logs media_errors increments but the application never saw an I/O error. Explain.
    Model answer

    Errors on reads that were retried successfully, on background or internal operations, on other namespaces/hosts, or on reads issued by tools; the counter is subsystem-wide and lifetime. Correlate with error-log entries and kernel messages.

  4. Senior How do you make destructive nvme-cli operations safe in an automated validation lab?
    Model answer

    Target by serial/WWID, never by nvmeX; an allow-list of lab serials; dry-run mode that prints resolved targets; refuse if the device hosts a mounted filesystem or the root disk; log before/after id-ctrl/fw-log; require explicit per-run confirmation token.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can map nvme0 ↔ nvme0n1 ↔ PCIe BDF ↔ subsystem NQN.
  • I can explain mdts, sqes/cqes, oncs, flbas/lbaf, and the main SMART fields.
  • I can correlate an error-log entry with a kernel timeout line.
  • I can classify any nvme-cli command as read-only, state-changing or destructive.

Summary. nvme-cli exposes Identify, logs and features; it proves what the controller reports, not what happened on the link. Next: the kernel's own narrative — logs.

71 Kernel Logs: dmesg and journalctl

← 70 Linux NVMe Inspection72 Programming Labs 1–5: Parsers and Decoders →

71.1 Why this chapter exists

Config space and NVMe logs are snapshots. The kernel log is a timeline: enumeration, driver probe, link events, AER reports, NVMe timeouts, aborts, resets, removals. For most field failures it is the only evidence you will ever get, so you must learn to read it precisely — and to know which events it can never contain.

  • Beginner: retrieve kernel messages for the current and previous boot; filter for nvme, pcieport, AER.
  • Intermediate: recognize the message families for link errors, AER, NVMe timeouts, aborts, resets and controller failure.
  • Advanced: order events into a causal hypothesis chain without confusing correlation for causation.
  • Senior: know the blind spots: firmware-first error handling, rate-limited messages, lost logs on crash, timestamp caveats.
  • Validation: automatically extract a failure timeline (Lab 10) from a saved log.

Prerequisites: Chapter 69, Chapter 70, AER and the Linux NVMe driver's timeout path from earlier Parts.

🧒 Kid analogy

The kernel log is the ship's logbook. The captain writes "12:03 — heard a strange noise from engine 2", "12:05 — engine 2 restarted". The logbook only has what the crew noticed and bothered to write down. If the noise happened while everyone was asleep, or the page got wet, it is not in the book — but the noise still happened.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Some "crew members" (platform firmware in firmware-first error handling) may fix a problem and never tell the captain. Some messages are rate-limited, so the 1,000th identical noise is not written down. And the logbook itself lives in RAM: a hard hang can lose the last pages unless the journal is persistent or a serial/netconsole is attached.

71.2 Retrieving the log

CommandPurposeCaveat
dmesgKernel ring buffer since boot (seconds since boot)Ring buffer may have wrapped on a long-running noisy system; may require root (kernel.dmesg_restrict)
dmesg -THuman wall-clock timestampsComputed from boot time; can be wrong after suspend/resume — prefer raw seconds when correlating
dmesg -l err,warnFilter by levelAER corrected errors may be logged at lower levels — do not filter them out by accident
dmesg -wFollow liveUse during a lab run in a second terminal
journalctl -kKernel messages from the systemd journalSame content, plus persistence if configured
journalctl -k -b -1Kernel messages from the previous bootRequires persistent journal (/var/log/journal); essential after a crash/reboot
journalctl -k --since "10 min ago" -o short-monotonicTime-bounded, monotonic timestampsMonotonic time matches dmesg seconds
journalctl -k -g 'nvme|AER|pcieport'Regex filter (journalctl --grep) versionNeeds a journalctl built with pattern support; otherwise pipe to grep -E
sudo dmesg --level=err,warn,info | grep -E 'nvme|pcieport|AER|DPC|pciehp'
sudo journalctl -k -b -1 -o short-monotonic | grep -E 'nvme|AER|pcieport'   # previous boot
sudo journalctl -k -b > kern-$(date +%Y%m%d-%H%M).txt                         # save evidence

71.3 Message families you must recognize

The excerpts below are illustrative and synthetic, written in the general shape of messages printed by recent Linux kernels. Exact wording varies by kernel version and driver version; never grep for an entire sentence in production tooling — match stable fragments.

A. Link bandwidth / training

nvme 0000:01:00.0: 15.752 Gb/s available PCIe bandwidth, limited by 8.0 GT/s PCIe x2 link at 0000:00:01.0 (capable of 63.012 Gb/s with 16.0 GT/s PCIe x4 link)

Meaning: at probe time the kernel compared the device's capability with the narrowest link on the path and found a limitation, naming the limiting port. Proves: a static bandwidth limit exists at probe time. Cannot prove: why (platform design vs failed lanes) or whether it changes later.

B. Link errors (AER correctable)

pcieport 0000:00:01.0: AER: Corrected error received: 0000:01:00.0
nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Corrected, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID)
nvme 0000:01:00.0:   device [abcd:0001] error status/mask=00000001/00002000
nvme 0000:01:00.0:    [ 0] RxErr

Meaning: the device's receiver saw a physical-layer error (e.g. framing/decode problems) that the link recovered from, typically via Data Link Layer replay. Status bit 0 = Receiver Error. BadTLP (bit 6) and BadDLLP (bit 7) point at LCRC failures; Rollover (8) and Timeout (12) at the replay mechanism. Proves: link-level errors occurred and were corrected. Cannot prove: data loss (there was none at the transaction level) or which side's transmitter is weak — the reporting side is the receiver.

C. AER uncorrectable

pcieport 0000:00:01.0: AER: Uncorrected (Non-Fatal) error received: 0000:01:00.0
nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Non-Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Requester ID)
nvme 0000:01:00.0:   device [abcd:0001] error status/mask=00004000/00000000
nvme 0000:01:00.0:    [14] CmpltTO
nvme 0000:01:00.0: AER:   TLP Header: 20000010 01002aff 00000001 10010080

Meaning: bit 14, Completion Timeout, detected by the SSD acting as requester: a read it issued (here the logged header decodes — with Lab 2 — as a 64-byte MRd, tag 0x2a, to an address that may be an SQ slot) never completed. When a TLP header is logged, decode it: it is often the best single clue in the whole log. Non-fatal uncorrectable errors are typically followed by the driver's error-recovery callbacks; fatal ones by a link reset.

D. NVMe timeout, abort, reset

nvme nvme0: I/O tag 23 (1017) opcode 0x2 (Read) QID 3 timeout, aborting
nvme nvme0: I/O tag 23 (1017) opcode 0x2 (Read) QID 3 timeout, reset controller
nvme nvme0: Abort status: 0x0
nvme0n1: I/O Cmd(0x2) @ LBA 123456, 8 blocks, I/O Error (sct 0x3 / sc 0x71)
blk_update_request: I/O error, dev nvme0n1, sector 123456 op 0x0:(READ) flags 0x0 phys_seg 1 prio class 0

Meaning: the host's timer (io_timeout) expired for a read on hardware queue 3. The driver's escalation (abort the command, then reset the controller) is version-dependent version. The "I/O Error" line with SCT/SC is printed by newer kernels on error completions; SCT 3h is Path Related status; SC 71h in that type is "Command Aborted By Host", which the Linux driver assigns itself to requests it cancels during a controller reset verify against your kernel source — so this line may describe the host's cleanup, not something the device reported. Always check whether a status came from a real CQE or was synthesized by the driver. Proves: the host did not observe a completion in time. Cannot prove: whether the device never received the command, received it and stalled, posted a CQE that the host missed, or raised an interrupt that was lost. That is exactly the ambiguity Labs 6–8 and the analyzer resolve.

E. Controller failure / surprise removal

nvme nvme0: controller is down; will reset: CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff
nvme nvme0: Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x1
nvme nvme0: Removing after probe failure status: -19
nvme 0000:01:00.0: frozen state error detected, reset controller
pcieport 0000:00:01.0: pciehp: Slot(1): Link Down
pcieport 0000:00:01.0: DPC: containment event, status:0x1f01 source:0x0000
  • CSTS=0xffffffff, PCI_STATUS=0xffff: register reads returned all-ones — the device is not answering on the link at all (link down, device reset, power loss). This is a PCIe-layer observation, not an NVMe status.
  • CSTS=0x1 while trying to reset: RDY stuck at 1 — controller not responding to CC.EN=0 within CAP.TO; firmware hang suspicion.
  • CSTS bit 1 (CFS, Controller Fatal Status) set: the controller itself declared a fatal internal error.
  • frozen state error detected: the PCI error-recovery framework told the NVMe driver the channel is frozen (typically after a fatal AER or DPC event).
  • pciehp ... Link Down, DPC: containment event: hot-plug saw link loss; Downstream Port Containment isolated the port after an uncorrectable error.

71.4 What logs prove — and their blind spots

EvidenceProvesBlind spot
AER messagesThe OS was notified of these errors, with BDF and typeFirmware-first platforms may consume errors; masked errors are not reported; storms are rate-limited
NVMe timeout messageNo completion was processed by the host in io_timeoutWhere the chain broke (doorbell, fetch, media, CQE, interrupt)
CSTS=0xffffffffMMIO reads returned all-onesWhy the device left the link
Absence of messagesNothing the kernel chose to printLots: corrected errors handled silently, analyzer-only events (replays, Recovery)
dmesg timestampsOrder of messages on this hostExact time of hardware events (message is printed after detection and handling); relation to analyzer time (needs a sync marker)
💡 Senior insight — create a sync marker

To align a kernel log with an analyzer capture, generate a recognizable, harmless event on the link and log it at the same time: for example a setpci read of a specific register (appears as a configuration read on the analyzer) immediately followed by echo MARK-1 | sudo tee /dev/kmsg. The configuration read in the trace and the MARK-1 line in dmesg anchor both clocks to within the latency of the script.

🧪 Lab 71.1 — H10 (part 1): build a failure timeline from a saved kernel log SAFE

Classification: non-destructive · read-only · production-safe (offline analysis).

Objective: turn raw log text into an ordered, layered timeline.

  1. Save a log: journalctl -k -b -o short-monotonic > kern.txt (or use the synthetic sample in Lab 10).
  2. Run python3 lab10_aer.py kern.txt (Chapter 73).
  3. Mark the first abnormal line, the first uncorrectable line and the first NVMe-visible line.
  4. For each, write: Observation / Inference / Hypothesis (Chapter 79).
Solution (for the synthetic sample)

First abnormal: corrected RxErr at 812.112 s (physical layer, receiver = SSD). First uncorrectable: Completion Timeout at 901.001 s with the SSD as requester. First NVMe-visible: I/O timeout at 931.1 s — exactly ~30 s after the Completion Timeout, matching the default io_timeout. Inference: the SSD's read of host memory (possibly an SQE fetch or write-data fetch) never completed, so the SSD could not progress the command; the host noticed 30 s later. Hypotheses: completions lost on a marginal link (supported by earlier RxErr/replay timeouts), a root-complex/IOMMU issue blocking the read, or a device bug declaring timeout too early. Evidence needed: analyzer capture of the MRd and whether a CplD ever appeared; IOMMU fault messages; Completion Timeout range settings (DevCtl2).

Quiz

  1. Why prefer monotonic timestamps over dmesg -T when correlating?

    Answer

    -T converts using an assumed boot time and can drift across suspend/resume; monotonic seconds are what the kernel actually recorded.

  2. CSTS=0xffffffff. Is this an NVMe status?

    Answer

    No. It means MMIO reads returned all-ones: the device is not responding on PCIe (link down/reset/power). Investigate the PCIe layer first.

  3. Corrected RxErr is reported by device 01:00.0. Whose receiver saw the error?

    Answer

    01:00.0's own receiver (downstream direction traffic). The weak side could be the port's transmitter, the channel, or the device's receiver.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate The log shows an NVMe timeout but no AER messages. What does that exclude?
    Model answer

    Very little. It excludes OS-reported AER errors — not firmware-first handled errors, masked errors, or non-PCIe causes (controller hang, lost interrupt, host software). It shifts but does not settle suspicion.

  2. Senior How do you preserve kernel evidence for a hang that requires a power cycle?
    Model answer

    Persistent journal, serial console or netconsole, pstore/ramoops where available, and an external analyzer or BMC log; also capture NVMe telemetry logs after reboot if supported.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can retrieve kernel logs for current and previous boot and filter them safely.
  • I can classify a line as link, AER, NVMe timeout/abort/reset, or controller failure.
  • I can state what each class proves and cannot prove.
  • I can create a sync marker between host log and analyzer.

Summary. Kernel logs give an ordered host-side narrative of detected events. Read them by family, decode logged TLP headers, and keep a strict line between what was observed and what you infer. Next: write the tools that turn hex and logs into understanding.

PART XXII

Programming Labs

Reading a hex dump by eye is a rite of passage; doing it a thousand times is a waste of a career. In this Part you write the small, sharp tools that senior PCIe/NVMe engineers keep in their personal toolbox: a config-space parser, a TLP header decoder, SQE and CQE decoders, a PRP walker, a transaction timeline builder, a CID correlator, missing-completion and completion-timeout detectors, and an AER log analyzer. Every program is Python 3 standard library only, runs on any normal Linux machine, and is shown together with the output it actually produced when this book was built — on synthetic inputs. One C example shows the same decoding discipline in a systems language.

72 Programming Labs 1–5: Parsers and Decoders

← 71 Kernel Logs: dmesg and journalctl73 Programming Labs 6–10: Timelines, Correlation and Anomaly Detection →

72.1 Why this chapter exists

Analyzer software decodes for you — until it does not: a new spec revision, a vendor-specific field, a log line, a customer's hex paste in an email, or a capture exported to CSV. The engineer who can turn bytes into meaning with twenty lines of code is never blocked. Writing the decoder also forces you to know every field boundary, which is the real point.

  • Beginner: run each lab, read its output, and match fields with the specification tables from earlier Parts.
  • Intermediate: modify the decoders (add a capability, a status code, an opcode) and feed them your own data.
  • Advanced: use the decoders as building blocks for the timeline tools of Chapter 73.
  • Senior: explain the safety boundaries: which code touches hardware (none here), which parses offline, which simulates.
  • Validation: turn each decoder's checks (alignment, malformed fields) into automated assertions on captured data.

Prerequisites: Python 3.8+, comfort with bit shifts and masks; Chapter 69; the TLP, SQE, CQE and PRP chapters earlier in the book.

72.2 The three kinds of code — never mix them up

KindLabel used in this bookTouches hardware?Labs
Simulationdata-kind="simulation"No — generates synthetic events/memory in Python objects5, 6, 7, 8, 9 (trace generator), performance models
Offline parsingdata-kind="executable"No — reads text/hex you saved earlier with read-only commands1, 2, 3, 4, 10
Real hardware accessdata-kind="hardware-dependent"YesNone in this Part. Saving input with lspci -xxxx or journalctl is read-only inspection, done by you, outside the scripts
⚠️ Safety boundary

None of these programs open /dev/mem, mmap resource0, write config, or issue NVMe passthrough commands. Do not "extend" them to do so. Writing to controller registers or doorbells from user space while the kernel driver owns the device corrupts queue state and can lose data. A script that safely drives a controller from user space (e.g. through VFIO) must be designed for it, own the device exclusively, and be run on a lab machine with a scratch drive — that is outside the scope of these labs.

🧒 Kid analogy

A secret-decoder ring: the letters of a coded message are just bytes; the ring tells you which letters go together and what they mean. These labs are you building the decoder ring yourself, so you can read any message, even ones the shop-bought ring does not know.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A decoder ring is always right. Your decoder is only as right as your reading of the specification — and the bytes may themselves be corrupt, truncated, byte-swapped or from a different spec revision. Good decoders validate and warn, not just print.

🧪 Lab 1 — Parse PCIe configuration-space hex SAFE

Classification: offline parsing · non-destructive · production-safe. File: lab01_cfgspace.py.

Objective: decode a Type 0 header, BARs, the capability chain (PM, MSI-X, PCI Express) and the extended chain (AER) from lspci -xxx/-xxxx text.

Setup: Python 3. Optional real input: sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -xxxx > dev.hex (read-only).

Key ideas: config space is little-endian; capability pointers are byte offsets with the low two bits reserved; the standard chain lives below 100h and the extended chain starts at 100h with 32-bit headers (ID 15:0, version 19:16, next 31:20); a loop guard prevents a corrupt chain from hanging the parser; BAR sizes cannot be read from a dump because sizing requires writing all-ones — the parser deliberately never does that.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 1 - Parse PCIe configuration-space hex (OFFLINE PARSING, read-only).

Input : text in the format printed by `lspci -xxx` / `lspci -xxxx`
        ("OFF: b0 b1 ... b15"). Missing rows are treated as zero.
Output: decoded Type 0 header, BARs, capability chains, link status.
The script never touches hardware. Feed it a saved file:
        sudo lspci -s 01:00.0 -xxxx > dev.hex   # read-only, needs root
        python3 lab01_cfgspace.py dev.hex
"""
import sys, struct

SAMPLE = """\
000: cd ab 01 00 06 04 10 00 01 02 08 01 00 00 00 00
010: 04 00 60 fe 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
020: 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 cd ab 01 00
030: 00 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 0b 01 00 00
040: 01 50 03 00 08 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
050: 11 70 20 80 00 20 00 00 00 30 00 00 00 00 00 00
070: 10 00 02 00 c2 8f 00 10 30 20 00 00 44 0c 00 00
080: 40 00 43 10 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
090: 00 00 00 00 10 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 1e 00 00 00
0a0: 04 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
100: 01 00 02 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 30 20 46 00
110: 41 00 00 00 00 20 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00
"""  # SYNTHETIC: placeholder vendor ID ABCD, not a real product.

CAP_NAMES = {0x01: "Power Management", 0x05: "MSI", 0x10: "PCI Express",
             0x11: "MSI-X", 0x09: "Vendor Specific", 0x0D: "Bridge Subsys VID"}
ECAP_NAMES = {0x0001: "AER", 0x0002: "Virtual Channel", 0x0003: "Device Serial Number",
              0x000B: "Vendor Specific Ext", 0x000D: "ACS", 0x000E: "ARI",
              0x0010: "SR-IOV", 0x0018: "LTR", 0x0019: "Secondary PCIe",
              0x001E: "L1 PM Substates", 0x0026: "Physical Layer 16.0 GT/s",
              0x0027: "Lane Margining at Receiver"}
SPEED = {1: "2.5 GT/s", 2: "5 GT/s", 3: "8 GT/s", 4: "16 GT/s", 5: "32 GT/s", 6: "64 GT/s"}
PAYLOAD = {i: 128 << i for i in range(6)}          # 000b=128 ... 101b=4096

def parse_hex(text):
    buf = bytearray(4096)
    top = 0
    for line in text.splitlines():
        if ":" not in line:
            continue
        off_s, data = line.split(":", 1)
        try:
            off = int(off_s.strip(), 16)
        except ValueError:
            continue
        vals = [int(x, 16) for x in data.split()]
        buf[off:off + len(vals)] = bytes(vals)
        top = max(top, off + len(vals))
    return bytes(buf[:max(256, top)]), top

u8 = lambda b, o: b[o]
u16 = lambda b, o: struct.unpack_from("<H", b, o)[0]
u32 = lambda b, o: struct.unpack_from("<I", b, o)[0]

def decode_header(b):
    print(f"Vendor:Device      {u16(b,0):04x}:{u16(b,2):04x}")
    cmd, sts = u16(b, 4), u16(b, 6)
    print(f"Command  {cmd:04x}   MemSpace={cmd>>1&1} BusMaster={cmd>>2&1} INTxDisable={cmd>>10&1}")
    print(f"Status   {sts:04x}   CapList={sts>>4&1} MasterAbort={sts>>13&1} SERR={sts>>14&1} ParityErr={sts>>15&1}")
    cls = (b[11], b[10], b[9])
    note = " (Mass storage / NVM / NVMe I/O controller)" if cls == (1, 8, 2) else ""
    print(f"Class    {cls[0]:02x}{cls[1]:02x}{cls[2]:02x}{note}   Rev {b[8]:02x}")
    htype = b[0x0E]
    print(f"Header type {htype & 0x7f} multifunction={htype >> 7}")
    if htype & 0x7f != 0:
        print("Not a Type 0 header (bridge?) - BAR decode below covers BAR0/1 only")
    i = 0
    while i < 6:
        raw = u32(b, 0x10 + 4 * i)
        if raw == 0:
            i += 1
            continue
        if raw & 1:
            print(f"BAR{i}: I/O  0x{raw & ~3:x}")
            i += 1
            continue
        typ = (raw >> 1) & 3
        pref = (raw >> 3) & 1
        addr = raw & ~0xF
        if typ == 2:
            addr |= u32(b, 0x14 + 4 * i) << 32
            print(f"BAR{i}/{i+1}: 64-bit memory 0x{addr:x} prefetchable={pref}")
            i += 2
        else:
            print(f"BAR{i}: 32-bit memory 0x{addr:x} prefetchable={pref}")
            i += 1
    print("(BAR *size* is NOT in config space dumps: sizing needs a write of all-1s,"
          " which this script deliberately never does. Use `lspci -vv` or sysfs resource.)")

def walk_caps(b):
    ptr, seen, caps = b[0x34] & 0xFC, set(), {}
    while ptr and ptr not in seen and ptr < 256:
        seen.add(ptr)
        cid, nxt = b[ptr], b[ptr + 1] & 0xFC
        caps[cid] = ptr
        print(f"  cap @0x{ptr:02x} id 0x{cid:02x} {CAP_NAMES.get(cid, '?')}  next 0x{nxt:02x}")
        ptr = nxt
    if ptr in seen:
        print("  !! capability loop detected - corrupt dump or broken device")
    return caps

def decode_msix(b, p):
    mc = u16(b, p + 2)
    t, pba = u32(b, p + 4), u32(b, p + 8)
    print(f"MSI-X: vectors={(mc & 0x7FF) + 1} enable={mc >> 15} function_mask={mc >> 14 & 1}"
          f" table=BAR{t & 7}+0x{t & ~7:x} PBA=BAR{pba & 7}+0x{pba & ~7:x}")

def decode_pcie(b, p):
    pcap = u16(b, p + 2)
    print(f"PCIe cap version {pcap & 0xF}, device/port type {pcap >> 4 & 0xF}")
    devcap, devctl = u32(b, p + 4), u16(b, p + 8)
    print(f"DevCap  MPS supported {PAYLOAD[devcap & 7]} B")
    print(f"DevCtl  MPS={PAYLOAD[devctl >> 5 & 7]} B  MRRS={PAYLOAD[devctl >> 12 & 7]} B"
          f"  RelaxedOrd={devctl >> 4 & 1} NoSnoop={devctl >> 11 & 1} ErrReportEn={devctl & 0xF:04b}")
    lcap, lsta = u32(b, p + 0x0C), u16(b, p + 0x12)
    mspd, mw = lcap & 0xF, lcap >> 4 & 0x3F
    cspd, cw = lsta & 0xF, lsta >> 4 & 0x3F
    print(f"LnkCap  max {SPEED.get(mspd, mspd)} x{mw}   ASPM support={lcap >> 10 & 3:02b}")
    print(f"LnkSta  now {SPEED.get(cspd, cspd)} x{cw}   training={lsta >> 11 & 1} slotclk={lsta >> 12 & 1}")
    lctl2 = u16(b, p + 0x30)
    print(f"LnkCtl2 target speed {SPEED.get(lctl2 & 0xF, lctl2 & 0xF)}")
    if cspd < mspd or cw < mw:
        print("  !! DOWNGRADED vs device capability. Next: compare with the PORT above"
              " (its LnkCap may be the limit), slot wiring, retimer, LTSSM history.")
    dctl2 = u16(b, p + 0x28)
    print(f"DevCtl2 completion-timeout value field={dctl2 & 0xF:x}h disable={dctl2 >> 4 & 1}")

UNCOR = {4: "DLP", 5: "SurpriseDown", 12: "PoisonedTLP", 13: "FCP", 14: "CmpltTO",
         15: "CmpltAbrt", 16: "UnxCmplt", 17: "RxOverflow", 18: "MalfTLP",
         19: "ECRC", 20: "UnsupReq", 21: "ACSViol"}
CORR = {0: "RxErr", 6: "BadTLP", 7: "BadDLLP", 8: "Rollover", 12: "Timeout",
        13: "AdvNonFatalErr", 14: "CorrIntErr", 15: "HdrLogOvfl"}

def bits(v, names):
    return [n for bit, n in names.items() if v >> bit & 1] or ["-"]

def walk_ecaps(b):
    if len(b) <= 256:
        print("Extended space not in dump (use lspci -xxxx as root)")
        return
    ptr, seen = 0x100, set()
    while ptr and ptr not in seen and ptr + 4 <= len(b):
        seen.add(ptr)
        hdr = u32(b, ptr)
        if hdr in (0, 0xFFFFFFFF):
            break
        eid, ver, nxt = hdr & 0xFFFF, hdr >> 16 & 0xF, hdr >> 20
        print(f"  ecap @0x{ptr:03x} id 0x{eid:04x} v{ver} {ECAP_NAMES.get(eid, '?')}")
        if eid == 0x0001:
            us, cs = u32(b, ptr + 4), u32(b, ptr + 0x10)
            print(f"    AER UncorrStatus {us:08x} {bits(us, UNCOR)}  sev {u32(b, ptr + 0x0C):08x}")
            print(f"    AER CorrStatus   {cs:08x} {bits(cs, CORR)}  mask {u32(b, ptr + 0x14):08x}")
        ptr = nxt

def main():
    text = open(sys.argv[1]).read() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else SAMPLE
    b, top = parse_hex(text)
    decode_header(b)
    print("Capabilities:")
    caps = walk_caps(b)
    if 0x11 in caps: decode_msix(b, caps[0x11])
    if 0x10 in caps: decode_pcie(b, caps[0x10])
    print("Extended capabilities:")
    walk_ecaps(b)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()

Output on the built-in synthetic sample (synthetic, produced by running the script):

Header type 0 multifunction=0
BAR0/1: 64-bit memory 0xfe600000 prefetchable=0

  cap @0x70 id 0x10 PCI Express  next 0x00
