DevCtl2 completion-timeout value field=0h disable=0
Extended capabilities:
  ecap @0x100 id 0x0001 v2 AER
    AER UncorrStatus 00000000 ['-']  sev 00462030
    AER CorrStatus   00000041 ['RxErr', 'BadTLP']  mask 00002000

Observations: the sample device is capable of 16 GT/s x4 but runs at 8 GT/s x4; MPS is programmed to 256 although 512 is supported; AER shows latched RxErr and BadTLP.

Questions: (1) Which byte offsets hold the class code and why is it printed "010802"? (2) Why does BAR0/1 decode as one 64-bit BAR? (3) What do RxErr+BadTLP together suggest, combined with the speed downgrade?

Solution

(1) Offsets 09h (prog-if 02h), 0Ah (subclass 08h), 0Bh (base class 01h); printed most-significant first: mass storage / non-volatile memory / NVMe. (2) BAR0 bits 2:1 = 10b mark a 64-bit memory BAR, so BAR1 holds address bits 63:32. (3) Physical-layer errors (Receiver Error) and LCRC failures (Bad TLP) are both consistent with marginal signal integrity; a link that equalizes poorly at 16 GT/s may fall back to 8 GT/s. It is a hypothesis — the downgrade could also be policy (check LnkCtl2 target and the port's LnkCap). Here LnkCtl2 targets 16 GT/s, so policy is less likely.

Extension: add decoding for the MSI capability (05h), Device Serial Number (0003h — redact before sharing), and L1 PM Substates (001Eh). Add a --json output.

🧪 Lab 2 — Decode a TLP header SAFE

Classification: offline parsing. File: lab02_tlp.py.

Objective: decode 3DW/4DW non-Flit TLP headers: Fmt/Type, TC, attributes, TD, EP, Length, Requester/Completer IDs, 10-bit Tag, byte enables, address, completion status, byte count, lower address. Flag obvious malformations.

Key ideas: header DWs are transmitted big-endian (byte 0 is the most significant byte of DW0 as conventionally printed); Length = 0 encodes 1024 DW; Tag bits 9 and 8 live in DW0 byte 1 (T9 at bit 23, T8 at bit 19) when 10-bit tags are enabled; a memory request whose upper address DW is zero must use the 3DW format; 1-DW requests must have Last DW BE = 0000b. verified for the PCIe non-Flit header layout. Gen6 Flit-mode TLPs use a different header format and are not handled.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 2 - Decode a PCIe TLP header (OFFLINE PARSING, non-Flit / Gen1-5 format).

Input: header DWs as big-endian hex words, exactly as most analyzers and the
AER "TLP Header:" log line present them (byte 0 = most significant byte of DW0).
Flit-mode (Gen6) headers use a different layout and are NOT handled here.
"""
import sys

FMT = {0: "3DW no data", 1: "4DW no data", 2: "3DW with data", 3: "4DW with data", 4: "TLP prefix"}
CPL_STATUS = {0: "SC (Successful)", 1: "UR (Unsupported Request)",
              2: "CRS (Config Request Retry)", 4: "CA (Completer Abort)"}

def tlp_kind(fmt, typ):
    if typ == 0b00000: return "MRd" if fmt in (0, 1) else "MWr"
    if typ == 0b00001: return "MRdLk"
    if typ == 0b00010: return "IORd" if fmt == 0 else "IOWr"
    if typ == 0b00100: return "CfgRd0" if fmt == 0 else "CfgWr0"
    if typ == 0b00101: return "CfgRd1" if fmt == 0 else "CfgWr1"
    if typ == 0b01010: return "Cpl" if fmt == 0 else "CplD"
    if typ == 0b01011: return "CplLk" if fmt == 0 else "CplDLk"
    if typ >> 3 == 0b10: return "Msg" if fmt in (0, 1) else "MsgD"
    return f"?type={typ:05b}"

def bdf(rid):
    return f"{rid >> 8:02x}:{rid >> 3 & 0x1f:02x}.{rid & 7}"

def decode(dws):
    d0 = dws[0]
    fmt, typ = d0 >> 29 & 7, d0 >> 24 & 0x1F
    t9, tc, t8 = d0 >> 23 & 1, d0 >> 20 & 7, d0 >> 19 & 1
    attr2, th = d0 >> 18 & 1, d0 >> 16 & 1
    td, ep, attr, at = d0 >> 15 & 1, d0 >> 14 & 1, d0 >> 12 & 3, d0 >> 10 & 3
    length = d0 & 0x3FF or 1024           # 0 encodes 1024 DW
    kind = tlp_kind(fmt, typ)
    out = {"kind": kind, "fmt": FMT.get(fmt, "?"), "TC": tc, "TD(ECRC)": td,
           "EP(poisoned)": ep, "RO": attr >> 1 & 1, "NS": attr & 1, "IDO": attr2,
           "TH": th, "AT": at}
    if fmt & 2 or kind in ("MRd", "MRdLk", "IORd", "CfgRd0", "CfgRd1"):
        out["length_DW"] = length
    hdr_dw = 4 if fmt in (1, 3) else 3
    if len(dws) < hdr_dw:
        raise ValueError(f"need {hdr_dw} DWs, got {len(dws)}")
    d1, d2 = dws[1], dws[2]
    if kind.startswith(("MRd", "MWr", "IO", "Cfg")):
        tag = (t9 << 9) | (t8 << 8) | (d1 >> 8 & 0xFF)
        fbe, lbe = d1 & 0xF, d1 >> 4 & 0xF
        out.update(requester=bdf(d1 >> 16), tag=tag, first_BE=f"{fbe:04b}", last_BE=f"{lbe:04b}")
        if kind.startswith("Cfg"):
            out.update(target=bdf(d2 >> 16), reg=f"0x{d2 & 0xFFC:03x}")
        else:
            addr = ((d2 << 32) | (dws[3] & ~3)) if hdr_dw == 4 else (d2 & ~3)
            out["address"] = f"0x{addr:x}"
            if hdr_dw == 4 and d2 == 0:
                out["WARNING"] = "4DW header with addr[63:32]=0 is not allowed for memory requests (malformed)"
            # byte count actually transferred (for MRd/MWr)
            if length == 1:
                out["note"] = "1-DW request: last_BE must be 0000"
                if lbe != 0:
                    out["WARNING"] = "length==1 but Last DW BE != 0 (malformed)"
    elif kind.startswith("Cpl"):
        out.update(completer=bdf(d1 >> 16), status=CPL_STATUS.get(d1 >> 13 & 7, "reserved"),
                   BCM=d1 >> 12 & 1, byte_count=(d1 & 0xFFF) or 4096,
                   requester=bdf(d2 >> 16),
                   tag=(t9 << 9) | (t8 << 8) | (d2 >> 8 & 0xFF),
                   lower_addr=f"0x{d2 & 0x7F:02x}")
    elif kind.startswith("Msg"):
        out.update(requester=bdf(d1 >> 16), msg_code=f"0x{d1 & 0xFF:02x}", routing=f"{typ & 7:03b}")
    return out

EXAMPLES = {  # SYNTHETIC headers built for teaching
    "upstream data write (NVMe read data to host)": "60000040 01000eff 00000001 2a3b4000",
    "SQE fetch read, 64 B, 64-bit address":       "20000010 01002aff 00000001 10010080",
    "completion with data for tag 0x2a":          "4a000010 00000040 01002a00",
    "UR completion":                               "0a000000 00002004 01003100",
    "poisoned write":                              "40004001 0000000f fe601008",
}

if __name__ == "__main__":
    items = {"argv": " ".join(sys.argv[1:])} if len(sys.argv) > 1 else EXAMPLES
    for name, hexs in items.items():
        dws = [int(x, 16) for x in hexs.split()]
        print(f"== {name}: {hexs}")
        quiet = {"TC", "TD(ECRC)", "EP(poisoned)", "RO", "NS", "IDO", "TH", "AT"}
        fields = [f"{k}={v}" for k, v in decode(dws).items() if not (k in quiet and v == 0)]
        print("   " + ", ".join(fields))

Output (synthetic headers):

== upstream data write (NVMe read data to host): 60000040 01000eff 00000001 2a3b4000
   kind=MWr, fmt=4DW with data, length_DW=64, requester=01:00.0, tag=14, first_BE=1111, last_BE=1111, address=0x12a3b4000
== SQE fetch read, 64 B, 64-bit address: 20000010 01002aff 00000001 10010080
   kind=MRd, fmt=4DW no data, length_DW=16, requester=01:00.0, tag=42, first_BE=1111, last_BE=1111, address=0x110010080
== completion with data for tag 0x2a: 4a000010 00000040 01002a00
   kind=CplD, fmt=3DW with data, length_DW=16, completer=00:00.0, status=SC (Successful), BCM=0, byte_count=64, requester=01:00.0, tag=42, lower_addr=0x00
== UR completion: 0a000000 00002004 01003100
   kind=Cpl, fmt=3DW no data, completer=00:00.0, status=UR (Unsupported Request), BCM=0, byte_count=4, requester=01:00.0, tag=49, lower_addr=0x00
== poisoned write: 40004001 0000000f fe601008
   kind=MWr, fmt=3DW with data, EP(poisoned)=1, length_DW=1, requester=00:00.0, tag=0, first_BE=1111, last_BE=0000, address=0xfe601008, note=1-DW request: last_BE must be 0000

Questions: (1) Which direction does the first TLP travel and what NVMe operation produces it? (2) The SQE-fetch MRd has tag 42; which TLP answers it and how do you know? (3) What would an analyzer do with the poisoned write, and what should the completer do?

Solution

(1) Upstream (device → host): an MWr from requester 01:00.0 carrying 256 bytes (64 DW) of read data into host memory — the data phase of an NVMe Read. (2) The CplD with requester 01:00.0 and tag 42 (0x2a), byte count 64 — matched on (Requester ID, Tag), never on address (completions have no address, only Lower Address bits). (3) EP=1 marks the payload poisoned; analyzers flag it; the receiver must not use the data as good and handles it as a Poisoned TLP error per its error-handling configuration.

Extension: accept an AER "TLP Header:" log line directly; add Message code names (e.g. PM, error messages); add a check that a CplD's Length matches Byte Count and Lower Address for the final completion.

🧪 Lab 3 — Parse an NVMe command (SQE) SAFE

Classification: offline parsing. File: lab03_sqe.py (also used as a library by Labs 6–9).

Objective: decode the 64-byte SQE: CDW0 (opcode 7:0, FUSE 9:8, PSDT 15:14, CID 31:16), NSID, MPTR, PRP1/PRP2 (DPTR, bytes 24–39), CDW10–15; derive SLBA, NLB (0-based!) and byte count for I/O commands; flag destructive opcodes.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 3 - Parse a 64-byte NVMe Submission Queue Entry (OFFLINE PARSING).
Input: 64 bytes as hex (little-endian memory image, as it sits in the SQ ring
and as it appears in the payload of the CplD that returns an SQE fetch)."""
import struct, sys

ADMIN = {0x00: "Delete I/O SQ", 0x01: "Create I/O SQ", 0x02: "Get Log Page",
         0x04: "Delete I/O CQ", 0x05: "Create I/O CQ", 0x06: "Identify", 0x08: "Abort",
         0x09: "Set Features", 0x0A: "Get Features", 0x0C: "Async Event Request",
         0x0D: "Namespace Management", 0x10: "Firmware Commit",
         0x11: "Firmware Image Download", 0x80: "Format NVM", 0x84: "Sanitize"}
NVM = {0x00: "Flush", 0x01: "Write", 0x02: "Read", 0x04: "Write Uncorrectable",
       0x05: "Compare", 0x08: "Write Zeroes", 0x09: "Dataset Management",
       0x0C: "Verify", 0x19: "Copy"}
DESTRUCTIVE = {("admin", 0x80), ("admin", 0x84), ("admin", 0x0D), ("admin", 0x10),
               ("io", 0x01), ("io", 0x04), ("io", 0x08), ("io", 0x09)}

def build_sqe(opcode, cid, nsid=1, prp1=0, prp2=0, cdw10=0, cdw11=0, cdw12=0,
              cdw13=0, cdw14=0, cdw15=0, psdt=0, fuse=0):
    """Helper used by the synthetic traces in Labs 6-9."""
    cdw0 = opcode | (fuse << 8) | (psdt << 14) | (cid << 16)
    return struct.pack("<IIQQQQIIIIII", cdw0, nsid, 0, 0, prp1, prp2,
                       cdw10, cdw11, cdw12, cdw13, cdw14, cdw15)

def parse_sqe(raw, queue="io", lba_size=512):
    if len(raw) != 64:
        raise ValueError("SQE must be exactly 64 bytes")
    cdw0, nsid, cdw2, cdw3, mptr, dptr1, dptr2 = struct.unpack_from("<IIIIQQQ", raw, 0)
    cdw10_15 = struct.unpack_from("<6I", raw, 40)
    opc = cdw0 & 0xFF
    d = {"opcode": f"0x{opc:02x} {(ADMIN if queue == 'admin' else NVM).get(opc, 'vendor/other')}",
         "fuse": cdw0 >> 8 & 3, "psdt": ["PRP", "SGL(buf)", "SGL(seg)", "rsvd"][cdw0 >> 14 & 3],
         "cid": cdw0 >> 16, "nsid": nsid, "mptr": f"0x{mptr:x}",
         "prp1/sgl": f"0x{dptr1:x}", "prp2/sgl": f"0x{dptr2:x}",
         "cdw10..15": " ".join(f"{x:08x}" for x in cdw10_15)}
    if queue == "io" and opc in (0x01, 0x02, 0x05, 0x08, 0x0C, 0x04):
        slba = cdw10_15[0] | (cdw10_15[1] << 32)
        nlb = (cdw10_15[2] & 0xFFFF) + 1           # 0-based field!
        d.update(slba=slba, nlb=nlb, bytes=nlb * lba_size,
                 fua=cdw10_15[2] >> 30 & 1, lr=cdw10_15[2] >> 31 & 1)
    if queue == "admin" and opc == 0x06:
        d["cns"] = f"0x{cdw10_15[0] & 0xFF:02x}"
    if queue == "admin" and opc == 0x02:
        numd = ((cdw10_15[1] & 0xFFFF) << 16 | cdw10_15[0] >> 16) + 1
        d.update(log_id=f"0x{cdw10_15[0] & 0xFF:02x}", log_bytes=numd * 4)
    if (queue, opc) in DESTRUCTIVE:
        d["SAFETY"] = "data-modifying/destructive opcode - never replay on real media"
    if opc != 0 and d["psdt"] == "PRP" and dptr1 & 3:
        d["WARNING"] = "PRP1 not dword aligned (invalid)"
    return d

if __name__ == "__main__":
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        raw = bytes.fromhex("".join(sys.argv[2:]))
        print(parse_sqe(raw, queue=sys.argv[1]))
        sys.exit()
    # SYNTHETIC example: Read 8 LBAs (4 KiB with 512 B LBAs) at LBA 0x1000, CID 0x0017
    rd = build_sqe(0x02, cid=0x17, nsid=1, prp1=0x12a3b4000, cdw10=0x1000, cdw12=7)
    print("hex:", rd.hex())
    for k, v in parse_sqe(rd).items():
        print(f"  {k:10s} {v}")
    idf = build_sqe(0x06, cid=0x1, nsid=0, prp1=0x7f000000, cdw10=0x01)
    print("Identify:", parse_sqe(idf, "admin")["opcode"], "CNS", parse_sqe(idf, "admin")["cns"])

Output (synthetic):

hex: 02001700010000000000000000000000000000000000000000403b2a010000000000000000000000001000000000000007000000000000000000000000000000
  opcode     0x02 Read
  fuse       0
  psdt       PRP
  cid        23
  nsid       1
  mptr       0x0
  prp1/sgl   0x12a3b4000
  prp2/sgl   0x0
  cdw10..15  00001000 00000000 00000007 00000000 00000000 00000000
  slba       4096
  nlb        8
  bytes      4096
  fua        0
  lr         0
Identify: 0x06 Identify CNS 0x01

Questions: (1) CDW12 is 7; why does the decoder say 8 blocks? (2) Where would you find this SQE on a PCIe analyzer? (3) Why can the same CID appear on two different SQs at the same time?

Solution

(1) NLB is a 0-based count. 7 means 8 logical blocks; with 512-byte LBAs, 4096 bytes. Off-by-one here is a classic driver and decoder bug. (2) In the payload of the CplD that answers the controller's MRd to the SQ slot address (SQ base + slot × 64). The host writes the SQE to memory with ordinary CPU stores, which do not appear on the PCIe link. (3) CIDs are only required to be unique among outstanding commands within one SQ; the correlation key is (SQID, CID).

Extension: decode SGL descriptors when PSDT ≠ 00b; decode Create I/O SQ/CQ (QID, QSIZE 0-based, PC, IEN, IV, CQID).

🧪 Lab 4 — Decode a Completion Queue Entry SAFE

Classification: offline parsing. Files: lab04_cqe.py, cqe_decode.c.

Objective: decode the 16-byte CQE: DW0 command-specific, DW2 SQ Head Pointer (15:0) and SQ Identifier (31:16), DW3 CID (15:0), Phase Tag (16), Status Field (31:17: SC 24:17, SCT 27:25, CRD 29:28, More 30, DNR 31); implement the phase-tag "is this entry new?" rule.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 4 - Decode a 16-byte NVMe Completion Queue Entry (OFFLINE PARSING)."""
import struct, sys

GENERIC_SC = {0x00: "Successful Completion", 0x01: "Invalid Command Opcode",
              0x02: "Invalid Field in Command", 0x03: "Command ID Conflict",
              0x04: "Data Transfer Error", 0x06: "Internal Error",
              0x07: "Command Abort Requested", 0x0B: "Invalid Namespace or Format",
              0x13: "Invalid PRP Offset", 0x80: "LBA Out of Range",
              0x81: "Capacity Exceeded", 0x82: "Namespace Not Ready"}
MEDIA_SC = {0x80: "Write Fault", 0x81: "Unrecovered Read Error",
            0x85: "Compare Failure", 0x86: "Access Denied"}
SCT = {0: "Generic", 1: "Command Specific", 2: "Media & Data Integrity",
       3: "Path Related", 7: "Vendor Specific"}

def build_cqe(cid, sqid, sqhd, phase=1, sc=0, sct=0, dnr=0, more=0, dw0=0):
    status = sc | (sct << 8) | (more << 13) | (dnr << 14)   # 15-bit Status Field (DW3[31:17])
    dw3 = cid | (phase << 16) | (status << 17)
    return struct.pack("<IIII", dw0, 0, sqhd | (sqid << 16), dw3)

def parse_cqe(raw):
    dw0, dw1, dw2, dw3 = struct.unpack("<IIII", raw)
    sc, sct = dw3 >> 17 & 0xFF, dw3 >> 25 & 7
    table = MEDIA_SC if sct == 2 else GENERIC_SC if sct == 0 else {}
    return {"dw0": f"0x{dw0:08x}", "sqhd": dw2 & 0xFFFF, "sqid": dw2 >> 16,
            "cid": dw3 & 0xFFFF, "phase": dw3 >> 16 & 1,
            "sct": f"{sct} {SCT.get(sct, 'reserved')}",
            "sc": f"0x{sc:02x} {table.get(sc, '(see spec table)')}",
            "crd": dw3 >> 28 & 3, "more": dw3 >> 30 & 1, "dnr": dw3 >> 31 & 1,
            "ok": sc == 0 and sct == 0}

def is_new(raw, expected_phase):
    """Host-side rule: an entry is new only if its phase tag equals the phase
    the host currently expects; the expected phase flips on each CQ wrap."""
    return parse_cqe(raw)["phase"] == expected_phase

if __name__ == "__main__":
    samples = [build_cqe(0x17, 1, 0x0005),
               build_cqe(0x18, 1, 0x0006, sc=0x81, sct=2, dnr=1),
               build_cqe(0x19, 1, 0x0007, sc=0x80, sct=0),
               build_cqe(0x1a, 1, 0x0008, phase=0)]
    if len(sys.argv) > 1:
        samples = [bytes.fromhex("".join(sys.argv[1:]))]
    for raw in samples:
        p = parse_cqe(raw)
        print(raw.hex(), "->", p, "| new for phase=1:", is_new(raw, 1))

Output (synthetic):

00000000000000000500010017000100 -> {'dw0': '0x00000000', 'sqhd': 5, 'sqid': 1, 'cid': 23, 'phase': 1, 'sct': '0 Generic', 'sc': '0x00 Successful Completion', 'crd': 0, 'more': 0, 'dnr': 0, 'ok': True} | new for phase=1: True
00000000000000000600010018000385 -> {'dw0': '0x00000000', 'sqhd': 6, 'sqid': 1, 'cid': 24, 'phase': 1, 'sct': '2 Media & Data Integrity', 'sc': '0x81 Unrecovered Read Error', 'crd': 0, 'more': 0, 'dnr': 1, 'ok': False} | new for phase=1: True
00000000000000000700010019000101 -> {'dw0': '0x00000000', 'sqhd': 7, 'sqid': 1, 'cid': 25, 'phase': 1, 'sct': '0 Generic', 'sc': '0x80 LBA Out of Range', 'crd': 0, 'more': 0, 'dnr': 0, 'ok': False} | new for phase=1: True
0000000000000000080001001a000000 -> {'dw0': '0x00000000', 'sqhd': 8, 'sqid': 1, 'cid': 26, 'phase': 0, 'sct': '0 Generic', 'sc': '0x00 Successful Completion', 'crd': 0, 'more': 0, 'dnr': 0, 'ok': True} | new for phase=1: False

The same decode in C, with explicit byte assembly so that it is endian-independent:

/* cqe_decode.c - decode a 16-byte NVMe CQE given as 32 hex chars (OFFLINE).
 * Build: cc -O2 -Wall -o cqe_decode cqe_decode.c
 * Run:   ./cqe_decode 00000000000000000600010018000385
 * Byte order: the CQE sits in host memory little-endian; we assemble DWs
 * explicitly from bytes so the program is correct on any host endianness. */
#include <stdio.h>
#include <stdint.h>
#include <string.h>

static int hexbyte(const char *s, uint8_t *out) {
    unsigned v;
    if (sscanf(s, "%2x", &v) != 1) return -1;
    *out = (uint8_t)v;
    return 0;
}

int main(int argc, char **argv) {
    uint8_t b[16];
    uint32_t dw[4];
    if (argc != 2 || strlen(argv[1]) != 32) {
        fprintf(stderr, "usage: %s <32 hex chars>\n", argv[0]);
        return 2;
    }
    for (int i = 0; i < 16; i++)
        if (hexbyte(argv[1] + 2 * i, &b[i])) { fprintf(stderr, "bad hex\n"); return 2; }
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
        dw[i] = (uint32_t)b[4*i] | (uint32_t)b[4*i+1] << 8 |
                (uint32_t)b[4*i+2] << 16 | (uint32_t)b[4*i+3] << 24;
    printf("DW0 (cmd specific) 0x%08x\n", dw[0]);
    printf("SQHD %u  SQID %u\n", dw[2] & 0xffff, dw[2] >> 16);
    printf("CID 0x%04x  P %u\n", dw[3] & 0xffff, (dw[3] >> 16) & 1);
    printf("SC 0x%02x  SCT %u  CRD %u  M %u  DNR %u\n",
           (dw[3] >> 17) & 0xff, (dw[3] >> 25) & 7, (dw[3] >> 28) & 3,
           (dw[3] >> 30) & 1, dw[3] >> 31);
    return ((dw[3] >> 17) & 0x7ff) ? 1 : 0;   /* non-zero exit on error status */
}
$ cc -O2 -Wall -o cqe_decode cqe_decode.c && ./cqe_decode 00000000000000000600010018000385
DW0 (cmd specific) 0x00000000
SQHD 6  SQID 1
CID 0x0018  P 1
SC 0x81  SCT 2  CRD 0  M 0  DNR 1
$ echo $?
1

Questions: (1) The last sample has phase 0 while the host expects 1. What does that mean? (2) Why does a CQE carry SQHD? (3) DNR=1 on the media error: what should the host do?

Solution

(1) The entry is stale (left from the previous pass around the ring); the host must stop consuming. The expected phase inverts each time the host's head wraps. (2) SQHD tells the host how far the controller has consumed the SQ, so the host knows which SQ slots are free — there is no other SQ-head feedback channel. (3) Do Not Retry: retrying the same command is expected to fail again; report the error upward (the block layer surfaces an I/O error).

Extension: add Command Specific status codes for Create I/O SQ (e.g. Invalid Queue Identifier) after checking the spec tables; write a CQ ring scanner that walks a memory image of the CQ and stops at the first stale phase.

🧪 Lab 5 — Interpret PRP addresses SAFE

Classification: simulation (fake host memory). File: lab05_prp.py.

Objective: compute the exact list of (address, length) DMA segments a controller derives from PRP1, PRP2 and a transfer length — including PRP lists and chained list pages — and detect invalid PRPs.

Key ideas: PRP1 may have a dword-aligned offset; all subsequent data PRP entries must be page-aligned (offset 0) with page size from CC.MPS; when the transfer needs more than two pages PRP2 is a PRP list pointer; the last entry of a full list page points to the next list page. Whether the controller reports Invalid PRP Offset, Data Transfer Error or something else for a specific violation is defined by the specification's status rules and controller behavior — consult the spec for the exact code impl.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 5 - Interpret PRP addresses (SIMULATION on a fake host memory dict).
Implements the PRP rules for a transfer of `length` bytes with memory page
size `mps` (CC.MPS, typically 4 KiB):
  * PRP1 may carry an offset (dword aligned); it covers up to the page end.
  * If the rest fits in one more page, PRP2 is that page's address.
  * Otherwise PRP2 points to a PRP List; list entries are page-aligned page
    addresses; the LAST slot of a full list page chains to the next list page.
"""
import struct

class FakeHostMemory:
    def __init__(self):
        self.qwords = {}
    def write_list(self, addr, entries):
        for i, e in enumerate(entries):
            self.qwords[addr + 8 * i] = e
    def read_qword(self, addr):
        if addr not in self.qwords:
            raise LookupError(f"controller would DMA-read unmapped 0x{addr:x}")
        return self.qwords[addr]

def walk_prps(prp1, prp2, length, mem, mps=4096):
    """Return [(addr, nbytes)] the controller would DMA, or raise on violation."""
    if prp1 & 3:
        raise ValueError("PRP1 must be dword aligned")
    off = prp1 & (mps - 1)
    first = min(length, mps - off)
    segs, remaining = [(prp1, first)], length - first
    if remaining == 0:
        return segs
    if remaining <= mps:                       # exactly two pages: PRP2 is a page
        if prp2 & (mps - 1):
            raise ValueError("PRP2 used as data page must have zero offset (Invalid PRP Offset)")
        return segs + [(prp2, remaining)]
    if prp2 & 7:
        raise ValueError("PRP list pointer must be qword aligned")
    entries_per_page = mps // 8
    ptr = prp2
    slot = (ptr & (mps - 1)) // 8              # list may start mid-page
    while remaining:
        entry = mem.read_qword(ptr)
        last_slot = slot == entries_per_page - 1
        if last_slot and remaining > mps:      # chain to the next list page
            ptr, slot = entry, 0
            continue
        if entry & (mps - 1):
            raise ValueError(f"PRP entry 0x{entry:x} has non-zero offset")
        n = min(mps, remaining)
        segs.append((entry, n))
        remaining -= n
        ptr += 8
        slot += 1
    return segs

def demo(title, prp1, prp2, length, mem, mps=4096):
    print(f"--- {title}: length={length} prp1=0x{prp1:x} prp2=0x{prp2:x}")
    try:
        for a, n in walk_prps(prp1, prp2, length, mem, mps):
            print(f"    DMA 0x{a:010x} .. +{n}")
    except (ValueError, LookupError) as e:
        print("    ERROR:", e)

if __name__ == "__main__":
    mem = FakeHostMemory()
    demo("4 KiB, page aligned (PRP2 unused)", 0x1_2000_0000, 0, 4096, mem)
    demo("4 KiB, PRP1 offset 0x200 -> spills into PRP2", 0x1_2000_0200, 0x1_3000_0000, 4096, mem)
    pages = [0x1_4000_0000 + 0x1000 * i for i in range(4)]
    mem.write_list(0x7000_0000, pages)
    demo("20 KiB -> PRP2 is a list pointer", 0x1_3F00_0000, 0x7000_0000, 20480, mem)
    # chained list: mps 4 KiB holds 512 entries; build a 2.1 MiB transfer
    big = [0x2_0000_0000 + 0x1000 * i for i in range(540)]
    mem.write_list(0x7100_0000, big[:511] + [0x7200_0000])   # last slot chains
    mem.write_list(0x7200_0000, big[511:])
    segs = walk_prps(0x1_FFFF_F000, 0x7100_0000, 4096 * 541, mem)
    print(f"--- chained list: {len(segs)} segments, last at 0x{segs[-1][0]:x}")
    demo("BUG: PRP2 data page with offset", 0x1_2000_0200, 0x1_3000_0100, 4096, mem)
    demo("BUG: list pointer to unmapped memory", 0x1_2000_0000, 0x7700_0000, 16384, mem)

Output (synthetic):

--- 4 KiB, page aligned (PRP2 unused): length=4096 prp1=0x120000000 prp2=0x0
    DMA 0x0120000000 .. +4096
--- 4 KiB, PRP1 offset 0x200 -> spills into PRP2: length=4096 prp1=0x120000200 prp2=0x130000000
    DMA 0x0120000200 .. +3584
    DMA 0x0130000000 .. +512
--- 20 KiB -> PRP2 is a list pointer: length=20480 prp1=0x13f000000 prp2=0x70000000
    DMA 0x013f000000 .. +4096
    DMA 0x0140000000 .. +4096
    DMA 0x0140001000 .. +4096
    DMA 0x0140002000 .. +4096
    DMA 0x0140003000 .. +4096
--- chained list: 541 segments, last at 0x20021b000
--- BUG: PRP2 data page with offset: length=4096 prp1=0x120000200 prp2=0x130000100
    ERROR: PRP2 used as data page must have zero offset (Invalid PRP Offset)
--- BUG: list pointer to unmapped memory: length=16384 prp1=0x120000000 prp2=0x77000000
    ERROR: controller would DMA-read unmapped 0x77000000

Trace view: on the link, a PRP list shows up as an extra MRd from the SSD (reading the list from host memory) before the data MWr (for a Read) or data MRd (for a Write). A 20 KiB read therefore has: SQE fetch MRd/CplD, PRP list MRd/CplD (32 bytes for 4 entries), then 20 KiB of data MWr. If the list pointer is bad, you see the list MRd answered by a UR/CA completion, or a DMA fault logged by the IOMMU — and no data.

Questions: (1) Why does a 4 KiB transfer with PRP1 offset 0x200 need PRP2? (2) How many list pages does a 2.1 MiB transfer need with 4 KiB pages? (3) A trace shows data MWr to the right pages but one page is shifted by 0x100. Which PRP rule might the host have violated?

Solution

(1) Only 4096 − 0x200 = 3584 bytes fit before the page boundary; the remaining 512 bytes go to the page named by PRP2. (2) 541 pages: PRP1 covers one; 540 entries remain; the first list page holds 511 data entries plus one chain pointer, the second holds the remaining 29 — two list pages. (3) A non-first PRP entry with a non-zero offset; a conforming controller should reject it, a non-conforming one may DMA to the wrong place — data corruption with "successful" status. Verify with the PRP list contents (MRd/CplD payload) in the trace.

Extension: add an SGL walker (Data Block, Segment, Last Segment descriptors) and a visualizer that prints an ASCII memory map of pages touched.

💡 Senior insight

Decoders earn trust through cross-checks, not through printing. Every decoder in this Part has at least one consistency rule (capability loop guard, 4DW-with-zero-upper-address, Last BE rule, PRP offset rule, phase tag). When you write your own, add the rule first, then the pretty-printing. The rule is what finds bugs at 3 a.m.

Quiz

  1. Why must an SQE decoder add 1 to CDW12[15:0]?

    Answer

    NLB is a 0-based value: 0 means one logical block.

  2. Which two fields correlate a PCIe completion to its request?

    Answer

    Requester ID and Tag (the completion echoes both; it carries the Completer ID too, but matching uses Requester ID + Tag).

  3. Why can BAR sizes not be extracted from an lspci -xxxx dump?

    Answer

    The size is discovered by writing all-ones and reading back the mask; a dump only contains the programmed base address. The kernel records sizes during enumeration and exposes them via lspci -vv and sysfs resource.

  4. What is the phase tag of the first pass through a freshly created CQ?

    Answer

    The host initializes CQ memory with phase 0 entries (zeroed), and the controller writes phase 1 on the first pass; the host expects 1 first.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain every shift and mask in Labs 1–4 without looking at the code.
  • I can compute PRP segments for any (PRP1, PRP2, length) by hand and validate with Lab 5.
  • I can state which of my scripts are simulation, offline parsing or hardware access.

73 Programming Labs 6–10: Timelines, Correlation and Anomaly Detection

← 72 Programming Labs 1–5: Parsers and Decoders74 Protocol Trace Academy: Rules of Evidence →

73.1 Why this chapter exists

Decoding one TLP is a skill; reconstructing an NVMe command from forty TLPs interleaved with thirty others is the job. This chapter builds a small, honest version of what protocol analyzers call a "transaction view" and what debug engineers do in their heads: group link events into commands, measure each phase, and find where a command's chain broke.

  • Beginner: read a normalized TLP event table and point at doorbell, SQE fetch, data, CQE and interrupt.
  • Intermediate: build per-command phase timelines and correlate by (SQID, CID).
  • Advanced: classify missing completions by the furthest stage reached; separate PCIe completion timeout from NVMe command timeout.
  • Senior: account for capture coverage (capture end, filtering, interrupt coalescing) before declaring anything "missing".
  • Validation: run these detectors over every capture in a regression suite.

73.2 Shared model: trace_common.py (queue simulator S8)

The generator below produces a SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE: one I/O queue pair (QID 1), 4 KiB reads, MPS 256, a doorbell stride of 4 bytes (CAP.DSTRD = 0), and fault injection by CID. The classify() function is the heart of NVMe-over-PCIe trace reading: it turns an address into a meaning using only what you would know from configuration (BAR0, queue base addresses from Create I/O SQ/CQ commands, the MSI-X table).

"""trace_common.py - shared SYNTHETIC trace model for Labs 6-9 (SIMULATION).
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE - NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE.
Every event is one TLP as an analyzer would decode it, normalised to a schema:
  t_ns, dir ('DN' = host->device, 'UP' = device->host), kind, addr, nbytes, tag, payload
"""
from dataclasses import dataclass
from lab03_sqe import build_sqe, parse_sqe
from lab04_cqe import build_cqe, parse_cqe

BAR0, DSTRD, MPS = 0xFE60_0000, 0, 256
SQ_BASE, CQ_BASE, QSIZE = 0x1_1001_0000, 0x1_1002_0000, 64
MSIX_ADDR = 0xFEE0_0000
DATA_BASE = 0x1_2000_0000

@dataclass
class Ev:
    t_ns: int
    dir: str
    kind: str
    addr: int = 0
    nbytes: int = 0
    tag: int = -1
    payload: bytes = b""

def sq_tail_db(qid):  return BAR0 + 0x1000 + (2 * qid) * (4 << DSTRD)
def cq_head_db(qid):  return BAR0 + 0x1000 + (2 * qid + 1) * (4 << DSTRD)

def classify(ev, qid=1):
    """Turn an address into an NVMe meaning - the core of NVMe-over-PCIe trace reading."""
    a = ev.addr
    if ev.kind == "MWr" and a == sq_tail_db(qid):   return "SQ%d tail doorbell" % qid
    if ev.kind == "MWr" and a == cq_head_db(qid):   return "CQ%d head doorbell" % qid
    if ev.kind == "MRd" and SQ_BASE <= a < SQ_BASE + 64 * QSIZE:
        return "SQE fetch slot %d" % ((a - SQ_BASE) // 64)
    if ev.kind == "MWr" and CQ_BASE <= a < CQ_BASE + 16 * QSIZE:
        return "CQE post slot %d" % ((a - CQ_BASE) // 16)
    if ev.kind == "MWr" and a & ~0xFFFFF == MSIX_ADDR: return "MSI-X interrupt"
    if ev.kind == "MWr" and ev.dir == "UP":         return "data to host (read payload)"
    if ev.kind == "CplD":                           return "completion with data"
    return "other"

def gen_trace(n=4, faults=(), media_ns=60_000):
    """Generate a synthetic NVMe Read trace on I/O queue 1.
    faults (cid in hex, e.g. 'slow:0x12'): 'nocqe:', 'nocpl:' (SQE-fetch CplD lost), 'slow:',
            'nomsix:', 'dupcid'."""
    f = set(faults)
    ev, t, tag = [], 1_000, 0x20
    for i in range(n):
        cid = 0x10 + i if not ("dupcid" in f and i == n - 1) else 0x10
        slot, buf = i, DATA_BASE + i * 0x1000
        sqe = build_sqe(0x02, cid, 1, prp1=buf, cdw10=0x8000 + 8 * i, cdw12=7)
        ev.append(Ev(t, "DN", "MWr", sq_tail_db(1), 4, payload=(slot + 1).to_bytes(4, "little")))
        ev.append(Ev(t + 400, "UP", "MRd", SQ_BASE + 64 * slot, 64, tag))
        if f"nocpl:{cid:#x}" not in f:
            ev.append(Ev(t + 1_100, "DN", "CplD", 0, 64, tag, sqe))
            tm = t + 1_100 + (8_000_000 if f"slow:{cid:#x}" in f else media_ns)
            for k in range(4096 // MPS):
                ev.append(Ev(tm + 32 * k, "UP", "MWr", buf + MPS * k, MPS))
            tc = tm + 32 * (4096 // MPS) + 100
            if f"nocqe:{cid:#x}" not in f:
                ev.append(Ev(tc, "UP", "MWr", CQ_BASE + 16 * slot, 16,
                             payload=build_cqe(cid, 1, (slot + 1) % QSIZE)))
                if f"nomsix:{cid:#x}" not in f:
                    ev.append(Ev(tc + 150, "UP", "MWr", MSIX_ADDR, 4, payload=b"\x01\0\0\0"))
                    ev.append(Ev(tc + 2_500, "DN", "MWr", cq_head_db(1), 4,
                                 payload=((slot + 1) % QSIZE).to_bytes(4, "little")))
        t += 3_000
        tag += 1
    return sorted(ev, key=lambda e: e.t_ns)

def print_trace(evs, qid=1):
    print(" #   time(us)  dir  kind  addr          len  tag  meaning")
    for i, e in enumerate(evs):
        tag = f"{e.tag:#04x}" if e.tag >= 0 else "  - "
        print(f"{i:3d} {e.t_ns/1000:9.3f}  {e.dir:3s}  {e.kind:4s}  {e.addr:#012x} {e.nbytes:4d} {tag} {classify(e, qid)}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print_trace(gen_trace(2))

🔍 What to notice
  • The host's SQE store is invisible; the first link event of a command is the doorbell MWr (4 bytes, downstream).
  • The SQE travels downstream inside a CplD — because the SSD pulled it with an MRd.
  • Commands overlap: CID 0x11's data streams while CID 0x10's completion and the host's CQ head doorbell go by. Any tool that assumes "one command at a time" fails on real traffic.
  • The MSI-X interrupt is just an MWr to an address in the 0xFEE00000 range on x86 platforms impl — an analyzer only knows it is an interrupt if it knows the MSI-X table contents.
🧪 Lab 6 — Build an NVMe transaction timeline SAFE

Classification: offline / simulation. File: lab06_timeline.py.

Objective: group TLPs into per-command transactions and compute phase durations: doorbell→fetch, fetch→SQE arrival, SQE→first data (≈ controller + media time), data duration, data→CQE, CQE→interrupt.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 6 - Build an NVMe transaction timeline from TLP events (OFFLINE / SIMULATION).
Groups TLPs into per-command transactions using ONLY information visible on
the link: doorbell writes, SQE-fetch MRd + tag-matched CplD (whose payload
is the SQE), data MWr addresses matched to PRP1, CQE payloads, MSI-X writes."""
from trace_common import gen_trace, classify, Ev, SQ_BASE, CQ_BASE, MSIX_ADDR
from lab03_sqe import parse_sqe
from lab04_cqe import parse_cqe

def build_timeline(evs):
    pending_mrd = {}            # tag -> MRd event (SQE fetch)
    cmds = {}                   # (sqid, cid) -> dict of phase timestamps
    by_buf = {}                 # PRP1 page -> key
    last_cqe_key, db_t = None, None
    for e in evs:
        role = classify(e)
        if role.startswith("SQ") and "doorbell" in role:
            db_t = e.t_ns
        elif role.startswith("SQE fetch"):
            pending_mrd[e.tag] = (e, db_t)
        elif e.kind == "CplD" and e.tag in pending_mrd:
            mrd, dbt = pending_mrd.pop(e.tag)
            sqe = parse_sqe(e.payload)
            key = (1, sqe["cid"])
            if key in cmds and "cqe" not in cmds[key]:
                cmds[key].setdefault("anomaly", []).append("CID reused while outstanding")
            cmds[key] = {"doorbell": dbt, "fetch": mrd.t_ns, "sqe": e.t_ns,
                         "opcode": sqe["opcode"], "prp1": int(sqe["prp1/sgl"], 16)}
            by_buf[int(sqe["prp1/sgl"], 16) & ~0xFFF] = key
        elif role.startswith("data"):
            key = by_buf.get(e.addr & ~0xFFF)
            if key:
                c = cmds[key]
                c.setdefault("data_first", e.t_ns)
                c["data_last"] = e.t_ns
                c["bytes"] = c.get("bytes", 0) + e.nbytes
        elif role.startswith("CQE"):
            q = parse_cqe(e.payload)
            key = (q["sqid"], q["cid"])
            c = cmds.setdefault(key, {"anomaly": ["CQE for unknown command"]})
            c["cqe"], c["status"] = e.t_ns, q["sc"]
            last_cqe_key = key
        elif role == "MSI-X interrupt" and last_cqe_key:
            cmds[last_cqe_key].setdefault("irq", e.t_ns)
    return cmds, pending_mrd

def show(cmds):
    us = lambda a, b: f"{(b - a) / 1000:8.2f}" if a is not None and b is not None else "     n/a"
    print("SQID CID   db->fetch fetch->sqe sqe->data data dur data->cqe cqe->irq  total(us)  status")
    for (sq, cid), c in sorted(cmds.items(), key=lambda kv: kv[1].get("doorbell", 0)):
        g = c.get
        print(f"{sq:4d} {cid:#05x} {us(g('doorbell'), g('fetch'))} {us(g('fetch'), g('sqe'))}"
              f"  {us(g('sqe'), g('data_first'))} {us(g('data_first'), g('data_last'))}"
              f" {us(g('data_last'), g('cqe'))} {us(g('cqe'), g('irq'))}"
              f"  {us(g('doorbell'), g('cqe'))}  {g('status', 'NO CQE')} {g('anomaly', '')}")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    cmds, orphan = build_timeline(gen_trace(4, faults=["slow:0x12"]))
    show(cmds)
    print("unanswered SQE fetch tags:", [hex(t) for t in orphan])

Output with CID 0x12 injected as "slow" (synthetic):

SQID CID   db->fetch fetch->sqe sqe->data data dur data->cqe cqe->irq  total(us)  status
   1 0x010     0.40     0.70     60.00     0.48     0.13     0.15     61.71  0x00 Successful Completion 
   1 0x011     0.40     0.70     60.00     0.48     0.13     0.15     61.71  0x00 Successful Completion 
   1 0x012     0.40     0.70   8000.00     0.48     0.13     0.15   8001.71  0x00 Successful Completion 
   1 0x013     0.40     0.70     60.00     0.48     0.13     0.15     61.71  0x00 Successful Completion 
unanswered SQE fetch tags: []

Questions: (1) Which phase explains CID 0x12's 8 ms? Which layer owns it? (2) Why is "data dur" 0.48 µs for 4 KiB, and what does that imply about link bandwidth for this synthetic trace? (3) What assumption does the tool make when attributing data MWr to a command?

Solution

(1) SQE→first data: the controller had the command and produced no data for 8 ms — controller/media domain (e.g., internal contention, garbage collection, read retry), not PCIe and not host. (2) 16 × 256 B over 0.48 µs ≈ 8.5 GB/s payload — the generator's spacing is idealized; with a real Gen4 x4 link the floor is roughly 0.55–0.6 µs (see Chapter 90). A good engineer sanity-checks synthetic or decoded timing against physics. (3) That the data buffer page equals PRP1's page. Real commands with PRP lists span many pages; a real tool must expand PRP lists (Lab 5) to build an address→command map, and must handle buffer reuse over time.

Extension: handle PRP lists by parsing the list MRd/CplD; output a Gantt-style text chart; detect interrupt coalescing (one MSI-X after several CQEs).

🧪 Lab 7 — Correlate command IDs with completions SAFE

Classification: offline / simulation. File: lab07_correlate.py.

Objective: match each submitted command (seen as SQE payload) with its CQE by (SQID, CID); detect CID reuse while outstanding and completions for unknown commands.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 7 - Correlate command IDs with completions (OFFLINE / SIMULATION).
Key rule: a CID is unique only among OUTSTANDING commands of ONE submission
queue, so the correlation key is (SQID, CID) - never CID alone."""
from trace_common import gen_trace, classify
from lab03_sqe import parse_sqe
from lab04_cqe import parse_cqe

def correlate(evs):
    outstanding, done, problems = {}, [], []
    fetch_tags = set()
    for e in evs:
        role = classify(e)
        if role.startswith("SQE fetch"):
            fetch_tags.add(e.tag)
        elif e.kind == "CplD" and e.tag in fetch_tags:
            fetch_tags.discard(e.tag)
            s = parse_sqe(e.payload)
            key = (1, s["cid"])
            if key in outstanding:
                problems.append(f"t={e.t_ns/1e3:.3f}us CID {s['cid']:#x} submitted again while "
                                f"still outstanding (host bug: Command ID Conflict risk)")
            outstanding[key] = e.t_ns
        elif role.startswith("CQE"):
            q = parse_cqe(e.payload)
            key = (q["sqid"], q["cid"])
            if key not in outstanding:
                problems.append(f"t={e.t_ns/1e3:.3f}us completion for {key} that is not outstanding")
                continue
            done.append((key, (e.t_ns - outstanding.pop(key)) / 1e3, q["sc"]))
    return done, outstanding, problems

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for faults in ([], ["dupcid"]):
        done, left, probs = correlate(gen_trace(4, faults))
        print(f"faults={faults}")
        for k, lat, sc in done:
            print(f"   SQ{k[0]} CID {k[1]:#06x}  sqe->cqe {lat:7.2f} us  {sc}")
        print("   still outstanding at capture end:", list(left))
        for p in probs:
            print("   PROBLEM:", p)

Output (synthetic; second run injects a host CID reuse bug):

faults=[]
   SQ1 CID 0x0010  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   SQ1 CID 0x0011  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   SQ1 CID 0x0012  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   SQ1 CID 0x0013  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   still outstanding at capture end: []
faults=['dupcid']
   SQ1 CID 0x0010  sqe->cqe   51.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   SQ1 CID 0x0011  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   SQ1 CID 0x0012  sqe->cqe   60.61 us  0x00 Successful Completion
   still outstanding at capture end: []
   PROBLEM: t=11.100us CID 0x10 submitted again while still outstanding (host bug: Command ID Conflict risk)
   PROBLEM: t=71.712us completion for (1, 16) that is not outstanding

Questions: (1) In the faulty run, why is CID 0x10's latency reported as 51.61 µs, and is that number true? (2) What would a controller be allowed to do when it sees a duplicate CID? (3) Why is the key (SQID, CID) and not CID alone?

Solution

(1) The second submission of CID 0x10 overwrote the first in the outstanding map; the first CQE was then attributed to the second submission, yielding an impossible latency. The number is an artifact — exactly the kind of wrong conclusion a host bug produces in naive tooling. (2) The spec defines a "Command ID Conflict" generic status; whether a controller detects every conflict is implementation-dependent impl. Host software must never issue it. (3) CIDs are unique per SQ; different SQs may use the same CID concurrently.

Extension: also verify that CQE SQHD values advance monotonically (mod queue size) and never pass the last doorbelled tail.

🧪 Lab 8 — Detect a missing completion SAFE

Classification: offline / simulation. File: lab08_missing.py.

Objective: for every command that never fully completed, report the furthest stage reached and what that implies; refuse to conclude when the capture ended too soon.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 8 - Detect a missing NVMe completion and say WHERE the chain broke.
Classification uses the furthest stage reached on the link. The capture end
time matters: a command submitted 5 us before capture end is not 'missing'."""
from trace_common import gen_trace
from lab06_timeline import build_timeline

STAGES = ["doorbell", "fetch", "sqe", "data_first", "cqe", "irq"]
VERDICT = {
    "fetch": "SQE fetch MRd sent but no CplD: PCIe completion problem (host/RC side or tag loss)",
    "sqe": "SQE delivered but no data/CQE: controller-internal stall (media, FW, or command hang)",
    "data_first": "Data moved but no CQE: controller failed to post completion (FW) or CQ full",
    "cqe": "CQE posted but no MSI-X seen: interrupt path (MSI-X mask/config/coalescing)",
}

def find_missing(evs, capture_end_ns, grace_ns=1_000_000):
    cmds, orphan_tags = build_timeline(evs)
    report = []
    for key, c in cmds.items():
        if "cqe" in c and "irq" in c:
            continue
        reached = [s for s in STAGES if s in c][-1]
        age = capture_end_ns - c.get("doorbell", 0)
        if age < grace_ns:
            report.append((key, "INCONCLUSIVE - submitted too close to capture end"))
        else:
            report.append((key, f"stopped after '{reached}': {VERDICT.get(reached, '?')}"))
    for tag, (mrd, _) in orphan_tags.items():
        report.append((("?", "?"), f"MRd tag {tag:#x} @ {mrd.t_ns/1e3:.3f}us never completed; "
                                   "CID unknown because the SQE never arrived"))
    return report

if __name__ == "__main__":
    evs = gen_trace(5, faults=["nocqe:0x11", "nocpl:0x13", "nomsix:0x12"])
    end = evs[-1].t_ns + 5_000_000           # capture kept running 5 ms after last TLP
    for key, msg in find_missing(evs, end):
        print(f"SQ{key[0]} CID {key[1] if isinstance(key[1], str) else hex(key[1])}: {msg}")

Output with three injected faults (synthetic):

SQ1 CID 0x11: stopped after 'data_first': Data moved but no CQE: controller failed to post completion (FW) or CQ full
SQ1 CID 0x12: stopped after 'cqe': CQE posted but no MSI-X seen: interrupt path (MSI-X mask/config/coalescing)
SQ? CID ?: MRd tag 0x23 @ 10.400us never completed; CID unknown because the SQE never arrived

Questions: (1) For each finding, name the owning layer. (2) CID 0x12's CQE exists on the link, yet the host will time it out. How? (3) Why is the orphan MRd reported without a CID?

Solution

(1) 0x11: controller (data moved, no CQE — firmware or CQ-full condition; check whether the host's CQ head doorbells left room). 0x12: interrupt path (MSI-X masked, vector misprogrammed, interrupt remapping, coalescing threshold never reached). Orphan tag: PCIe transaction layer — the root complex never answered the SQE fetch. (2) The host only processes the CQ when an interrupt (or poll) prompts it; without the MSI-X the CQE sits unseen until the timeout handler polls and may then "find" it — Linux can log that a completion was found during timeout handling version. (3) The CID lives inside the SQE, which never arrived; the analyzer only knows "a 64-byte read of SQ slot N went unanswered" — and slot N maps to a command only via the host's own records.

Extension: accept a coverage dict (capture start/end, filters active, directions captured) and downgrade conclusions accordingly — the Trace Coverage Rule from Chapter 74.

🧪 Lab 9 — Detect a completion timeout SAFE

Classification: offline / simulation. File: lab09_cpl_timeout.py.

Objective: track every Non-Posted request by (Requester ID, Tag), accumulate partial completions until the byte count is satisfied, flag tag reuse, unexpected completions and requests older than a timeout; separately age NVMe commands against the host io_timeout.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 9 - Detect PCIe completion timeouts and NVMe command timeouts (OFFLINE).
Two different clocks, two different owners:
  * PCIe Completion Timeout: a Non-Posted request (MRd) whose CplD does not
    return within the requester's configured range (Device Control 2). The
    REQUESTER (here: the SSD fetching an SQE or write data) detects it.
  * NVMe command timeout: the HOST driver's timer (Linux nvme_core io_timeout,
    default 30 s) on a submitted command with no CQE.
Matching key for PCIe completions: (Requester ID, Tag). Tags may be reused
only after the previous request with that tag has fully completed."""
from trace_common import gen_trace, Ev

def pcie_completion_check(evs, timeout_ns=50_000_000, requester="01:00.0"):
    open_tags, findings, lat = {}, [], []
    for e in evs:
        if e.kind == "MRd" and e.dir == "UP":
            if e.tag in open_tags:
                findings.append(f"t={e.t_ns/1e3:.3f}us tag {e.tag:#x} REUSED while outstanding "
                                f"(protocol violation by requester)")
            open_tags[e.tag] = {"t": e.t_ns, "want": e.nbytes, "got": 0}
        elif e.kind in ("CplD", "Cpl") and e.dir == "DN":
            o = open_tags.get(e.tag)
            if o is None:
                findings.append(f"t={e.t_ns/1e3:.3f}us Unexpected Completion tag {e.tag:#x}")
                continue
            o["got"] += e.nbytes
            if o["got"] >= o["want"]:
                lat.append(e.t_ns - o["t"])
                del open_tags[e.tag]
    end = evs[-1].t_ns
    for tag, o in open_tags.items():
        age = end - o["t"]
        state = "TIMED OUT" if age > timeout_ns else f"open {age/1e3:.1f}us (< timeout, inconclusive)"
        findings.append(f"tag {tag:#x} MRd @ {o['t']/1e3:.3f}us {state}; got {o['got']}/{o['want']} B")
    return lat, findings

def nvme_timeout_check(cmd_submit_ns, cmd_cqe_ns, now_ns, io_timeout_s=30):
    out = []
    for key, t0 in cmd_submit_ns.items():
        t1 = cmd_cqe_ns.get(key, now_ns)       # no CQE yet: age it against "now"
        if (t1 - t0) > io_timeout_s * 1e9:
            out.append((key, (t1 - t0) / 1e9))
    return out

if __name__ == "__main__":
    evs = gen_trace(4, faults=["nocpl:0x12"])
    evs.append(Ev(evs[-1].t_ns + 60_000_000, "DN", "MWr", 0, 0))   # capture continues 60 ms
    lat, f = pcie_completion_check(evs)
    print(f"completed MRd: {len(lat)}, max read latency {max(lat)/1e3:.2f} us")
    for x in f:
        print("FINDING:", x)
    # host side: CID 0x12 submitted at ~7 us, no CQE after 31 s
    print("NVMe commands past io_timeout:", nvme_timeout_check({(1, 0x12): 7_000}, {}, now_ns=31_000_000_000))

Output (synthetic):

completed MRd: 3, max read latency 0.70 us
FINDING: tag 0x22 MRd @ 7.400us TIMED OUT; got 0/64 B
NVMe commands past io_timeout: [((1, 18), 30.999993)]
📘 Specification

The PCIe Completion Timeout mechanism and its programmable ranges are configured through Device Control 2 (value field bits 3:0, disable bit 4) with supported ranges advertised in Device Capabilities 2. The default range is commonly described as 50 µs to 50 ms confirm the exact wording in your PCIe Base Specification revision. A completion may legally be split into several CplDs (at Read Completion Boundary multiples); a detector must sum byte counts rather than expect exactly one completion per request — as this lab does.

Questions: (1) Which agent detects a PCIe Completion Timeout and which agent detects an NVMe I/O timeout? (2) Why does a PCIe completion timeout on an SQE fetch eventually surface as an NVMe timeout? (3) Why does the lab treat an open request younger than the timeout as "inconclusive"?

Solution

(1) The PCIe requester (here the SSD) detects completion timeout and may report it via AER; the host driver detects NVMe command timeouts with its own timer. (2) Without the SQE, the controller cannot execute the command and never posts a CQE; the host's io_timeout (default 30 s) eventually fires. Expect AER CmpltTO from the SSD, then ~30 s later an NVMe timeout — as in Chapter 71's sample. (3) Capture end is not proof of absence; the completion may arrive after the capture stopped.

Extension: model the Read Completion Boundary: split each CplD into 64- or 128-byte pieces and verify Lower Address and Byte Count progress correctly.

🧪 Lab 10 — Analyze AER logs SAFE

Classification: offline parsing of saved log text. File: lab10_aer.py.

Objective: extract AER events from kernel logs, decode status registers into named bits and layers, count per device, find the first uncorrectable error and what preceded it — while explicitly refusing to equate "preceded" with "caused".

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Lab 10 - Analyze AER logs (OFFLINE PARSING of saved kernel log text).
Usage:  journalctl -k -b > kern.txt   (read-only)   ;  python3 lab10_aer.py kern.txt
The parser is deliberately tolerant: AER message wording differs across
kernel versions, so it keys on stable fragments ("severity=", "type=",
"error status/mask=") and reports lines it could not classify."""
import re, sys
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

UNCOR = {4: "Data Link Protocol", 5: "Surprise Down", 12: "Poisoned TLP",
         13: "Flow Control Protocol", 14: "Completion Timeout", 15: "Completer Abort",
         16: "Unexpected Completion", 17: "Receiver Overflow", 18: "Malformed TLP",
         19: "ECRC", 20: "Unsupported Request", 21: "ACS Violation"}
CORR = {0: "Receiver Error", 6: "Bad TLP", 7: "Bad DLLP", 8: "REPLAY_NUM Rollover",
        12: "Replay Timer Timeout", 13: "Advisory Non-Fatal", 14: "Corrected Internal",
        15: "Header Log Overflow"}
LAYER = {"Receiver Error": "Physical", "Bad TLP": "Data Link", "Bad DLLP": "Data Link",
         "REPLAY_NUM Rollover": "Data Link", "Replay Timer Timeout": "Data Link",
         "Data Link Protocol": "Data Link", "Surprise Down": "Data Link/Physical",
         "Completion Timeout": "Transaction", "Unsupported Request": "Transaction",
         "Poisoned TLP": "Transaction", "Malformed TLP": "Transaction",
         "Completer Abort": "Transaction", "Unexpected Completion": "Transaction",
         "ECRC": "Transaction", "Receiver Overflow": "Transaction",
         "Flow Control Protocol": "Data Link"}

SAMPLE = """\
[  812.112233] pcieport 0000:00:1c.0: AER: Corrected error received: 0000:01:00.0
[  812.112240] nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Corrected, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID)
[  812.112244] nvme 0000:01:00.0:   device [abcd:0001] error status/mask=00000001/00002000
[  812.112248] nvme 0000:01:00.0:    [ 0] RxErr
[  815.400101] pcieport 0000:00:1c.0: AER: Corrected error received: 0000:01:00.0
[  815.400110] nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Corrected, type=Data Link Layer, (Transmitter ID)
[  815.400114] nvme 0000:01:00.0:   device [abcd:0001] error status/mask=00001000/00002000
[  901.000500] pcieport 0000:00:1c.0: AER: Uncorrected (Non-Fatal) error received: 0000:01:00.0
[  901.000510] nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Uncorrected (Non-Fatal), type=Transaction Layer, (Requester ID)
[  901.000514] nvme 0000:01:00.0:   device [abcd:0001] error status/mask=00004000/00000000
[  901.000520] nvme 0000:01:00.0:    [14] CmpltTO
[  931.100000] nvme nvme0: I/O tag 23 (1017) opcode 0x2 (Read) QID 3 timeout, aborting
"""  # SYNTHETIC, written to resemble common Linux AER/NVMe log shapes; wording varies by kernel.

TS = re.compile(r"^\[\s*(\d+\.\d+)\]")
DEV = re.compile(r"(\d{4}:[0-9a-f]{2}:[0-9a-f]{2}\.[0-7])")
STAT = re.compile(r"error status/mask=([0-9a-f]{8})/([0-9a-f]{8})")
SEV = re.compile(r"severity=([^,]+), type=([^,]+)")

def decode(status, mask, uncorrectable):
    table = UNCOR if uncorrectable else CORR
    return [(table.get(b, f"bit{b}"), bool(mask >> b & 1)) for b in range(32) if status >> b & 1]

def analyze(text):
    events, unknown, sev, last_ts = [], [], None, None
    per_dev = defaultdict(Counter)
    for line in text.splitlines():
        m = TS.search(line)
        ts = float(m.group(1)) if m else None
        if (s := SEV.search(line)):
            sev = s.group(1)
            continue
        if (s := STAT.search(line)):
            dev = DEV.search(line).group(1)
            st, mk = int(s.group(1), 16), int(s.group(2), 16)
            unc = sev is not None and sev.startswith("Uncorrected")
            for name, masked in decode(st, mk, unc):
                layer = LAYER.get(name, "?")
                events.append((ts, dev, sev, name, layer, masked))
                per_dev[dev][name] += 1
            continue
        if "timeout" in line and "nvme" in line:
            events.append((ts, "nvme", "driver", "NVMe command timeout", "NVMe/driver", False))
        elif "AER" in line or "PCIe Bus Error" in line:
            continue
        elif line.strip() and not re.search(r"\]\s+\S+ \S+:\s+\[\s*\d+\]", line):
            unknown.append(line)
    return events, per_dev, unknown

if __name__ == "__main__":
    text = open(sys.argv[1]).read() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else SAMPLE
    events, per_dev, unknown = analyze(text)
    for ts, dev, sev, name, layer, masked in events:
        print(f"{ts:10.3f}  {dev:14s} {str(sev):26s} {name:22s} layer={layer}{' (masked bit set)' if masked else ''}")
    first_unc = next((e for e in events if e[2] and str(e[2]).startswith("Uncorrected")), None)
    if first_unc:
        prior = [e for e in events if e[0] < first_unc[0]]
        print(f"\nFirst uncorrectable at {first_unc[0]:.3f}s: {first_unc[3]}; "
              f"{len(prior)} earlier corrected event(s) - correlation, not proof of causation.")
    print("Per-device counts:", {d: dict(c) for d, c in per_dev.items()})
    if unknown:
        print("Unclassified lines (review by hand):", *unknown, sep="\n  ")

Output on the synthetic sample (synthetic):

   812.112  0000:01:00.0   Corrected                  Receiver Error         layer=Physical
   815.400  0000:01:00.0   Corrected                  Replay Timer Timeout   layer=Data Link
   901.001  0000:01:00.0   Uncorrected (Non-Fatal)    Completion Timeout     layer=Transaction
   931.100  nvme           driver                     NVMe command timeout   layer=NVMe/driver

First uncorrectable at 901.001s: Completion Timeout; 2 earlier corrected event(s) - correlation, not proof of causation.
Per-device counts: {'0000:01:00.0': {'Receiver Error': 1, 'Replay Timer Timeout': 1, 'Completion Timeout': 1}}

Questions: (1) Why does the parser decode the status register rather than trusting the [14] CmpltTO line? (2) The second corrected event has no bit-name line in the sample. Did the parser still classify it? (3) What is the most useful next evidence?

Solution

(1) The register value is the ground truth the kernel read; named lines vary across versions and may be omitted. Decoding both and comparing is even better. (2) Yes — from status/mask=00001000, bit 12 = Replay Timer Timeout. (3) The logged TLP header of the uncorrectable error (decode with Lab 2), AER counters in sysfs over time, and an analyzer capture triggered on the completion-timeout signature.

Extension (S12 — forensic report generator): emit an HTML report: a header with system identity (redacted serials), a timeline table with layer colors, per-device counts, first-abnormal-event highlight and an "Observations / Inferences / Hypotheses" section with empty slots for the engineer to fill.

73.3 Putting it together: what these tools can and cannot do

ToolCan establishCannot establish
Timeline (Lab 6)Phase durations for each command as seen on the linkWhat happened inside the controller during the long phase
Correlation (Lab 7)Submit/complete pairing, CID protocol violationsHost-internal reasons (driver bug vs memory corruption)
Missing completion (Lab 8)The furthest link-visible stageAnything if the capture was filtered or ended early
Completion timeout (Lab 9)Unanswered Non-Posted requests by tagWhy the completer did not answer (needs host-side evidence)
AER analyzer (Lab 10)OS-reported error history by device/type/layerErrors handled in firmware or masked; causality

Quiz

  1. Where does the SQE appear on the PCIe link?

    Answer

    As the payload of a CplD flowing host→device in answer to the controller's MRd of the SQ slot.

  2. A CQE MWr is present but the host times out. Name two link-visible checks.

    Answer

    Is there an MSI-X MWr after it (to the right address/data)? Did the CQE land in the CQ slot the host expects with the right phase tag?

  3. Why must completion matching sum byte counts?

    Answer

    Completers may split a read into multiple CplDs; the request is satisfied only when all bytes have returned.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Describe how you would reconstruct an NVMe read from a PCIe trace.
    Model answer

    Find the SQ tail doorbell MWr; find the controller's MRd to the SQ slot and the matching CplD by tag; parse the SQE (opcode, CID, PRP, LBA); find PRP list fetches if any; find data MWr to the PRP pages; find the CQE MWr in the CQ ring with matching SQID/CID and phase; find the MSI-X MWr; find the host's CQ head doorbell.

  2. Senior Your missing-completion detector flags 200 commands in a 2-second capture. What do you check before filing a bug?
    Model answer

    Capture coverage: end time vs submission times, active filters (were CQ writes or MSI-X filtered out?), both directions captured, buffer overflow or dropped packets, correct queue base addresses (queues may have been re-created after a reset), interrupt coalescing, polled queues (no MSI-X by design).

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain each step of classify() and which configuration knowledge it needs.
  • I can classify a stuck command by its furthest stage and name the owning layer.
  • I can distinguish PCIe completion timeout from NVMe command timeout in one sentence each.
  • I always state capture coverage before calling something missing.

Summary. Group first, measure second, conclude last — and only within the coverage of your evidence. Next: the Protocol Trace Academy, where you apply these habits to full trace labs.

PART XXIII

Trace Analysis Laboratory — the Protocol Trace Academy

A trace is the closest thing a hardware engineer has to a time machine — but only for the slice of time, the direction, and the packet types it actually recorded. This Part is a gym. Chapter 74 gives you the rules of evidence (coverage, synthetic vs real traces, normalization, diffing, golden traces) and a ten-level skill ladder. Chapters 75 and 76 are full trace labs written to one template, from "read this table" to "write the bug report and the regression test". Every trace in this Part is labelled SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE; none imitates any vendor's screen.

74 Protocol Trace Academy: Rules of Evidence

← 73 Programming Labs 6–10: Timelines, Correlation and Anomaly Detection75 Trace Labs I: Beginner and Intermediate →

74.1 Why this chapter exists

Most wrong root causes are not caused by ignorance of the protocol; they come from over-trusting a trace: concluding "the completion never came" when the capture stopped too early, "the device never sent the interrupt" when the filter hid MSI-X writes, or "the link error caused the timeout" because one happened before the other. This chapter installs the habits that prevent those mistakes.

  • Beginner: read a trace table column by column and say what each row is.
  • Intermediate: state a trace's coverage and its limitations before analysing it.
  • Advanced: normalize traces into an event schema, group them into transactions and diff against a golden trace.
  • Senior: run the full ladder from packet reading to regression-test design; write evidence-graded bug reports.
  • Trace-analysis objective: find the first abnormal event, not the loudest one.
  • Validation objective: maintain versioned golden traces and automatic first-divergence detection.
🧒 Kid analogy

A trace is a security-camera recording of one hallway. It shows everyone who walked through that hallway while the camera was on. If the camera only records people wearing red (a filter), or was switched off at 3 o'clock (capture end), or faces only one way (one direction), then "nobody came" really means "nobody the camera could see came".

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A camera records pixels; an analyzer records decoded symbols. If the analyzer cannot lock onto the signal (bad probing, unsupported speed, electrical idle exit it misses), it may silently miss or mis-decode packets — the recording itself can be wrong, not just incomplete.

74.2 The Trace Coverage Rule

Every trace lab — and every real bug report — must state:

Coverage itemWhy it mattersExample statement
Capture startEvents before start (e.g. link training, queue creation) are absent, so addresses may be unexplainable"Capture starts 2 s after driver load; queue creation not captured."
Capture endAnything "missing" may simply be after the end"Capture ends on buffer-full, 1.2 ms after trigger."
Timestamp completenessGaps, wrap-around, or per-direction clocks distort latency math"Single time base, 1 ns resolution, no gaps reported."
FilteringFiltered packet types cannot be argued from absence"DLLPs and SKP ordered sets filtered out; all TLPs kept."
Decoder omissionsDecoder may not recognize a new spec feature or vendor message"Analyzer decoder version does not decode 14-bit tags."
Directions capturedOne-direction captures cannot show requests and their completions together"Both upstream and downstream captured."

74.3 Synthetic and real trace rules

⚠️ Synthetic trace rule

Every invented trace in this book is labelled SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE and marked synthetic. Timings are plausible orders of magnitude chosen for teaching, not measurements of any product. Do not cite them as data.

Real trace rule. If you use a real trace (in training or a bug report), record: its source; the capture tool and its software/firmware version; whether it is public or confidential; known limitations (probe point, filters, buffer size); and redact confidential content: serial numbers, possibly vendor/device IDs, host names, file paths, proprietary payload bytes (user data can appear in data TLPs!), and customer identity. A trace of a Read command contains the data that was read — treat captures of production systems as potentially containing customer data.

74.4 The trace table schema used in this Part

ColumnMeaning
TimeRelative time (µs) from the trigger or the first row; same time base for both directions
DirDN = downstream (root port → device), UP = upstream (device → root port)
LayerPHY (ordered sets, link state), DLL (DLLPs: Ack/Nak/UpdateFC), TL (TLPs)
TypeMRd, MWr, CplD, Cpl, CfgRd0, Msg, Ack, Nak, UpdateFC, TS1/TS2, EIOS...
Requester / CompleterBDF of requester (for requests) and completer (for completions); RC = root complex (00:00.0 in these labs), EP = 01:00.0
AddressMemory address for requests; "—" for completions
TagTransaction tag for Non-Posted requests and their completions; DLL sequence numbers shown as "seq N" for Ack/Nak
LengthPayload bytes (or requested bytes for MRd)
MeaningThe NVMe-level interpretation — the column you are learning to fill in

The common system configuration for the labs unless stated otherwise: endpoint 01:00.0 (NVMe SSD) under root port 00:01.0; BAR0 = 0xFE600000; CAP.DSTRD = 0 (doorbell stride 4 B), so SQ0 tail doorbell = 0xFE601000, CQ0 head = 0xFE601004, SQ1 tail = 0xFE601008, CQ1 head = 0xFE60100C; I/O SQ1 base 0x1_1001_0000, I/O CQ1 base 0x1_1002_0000 (64 entries each); MSI-X message address 0xFEE00000 impl; MPS 256 B; LBA size 512 B.

74.5 The analyzer skill ladder (Levels 0–10)

LevelSkillProof of skillPractised in

7Form root-cause hypothesesSeveral, ranked, each falsifiableTL-5 onwards
8Prove/disprove hypothesesDesign the disambiguating experimentTL-6 onwards
9Write a bug reportObservation/inference/hypothesis/evidence structure with coverage statementTL-9
10Design the regression testA test that fails before the fix and passes after, automaticallyAll solutions

74.6 Trace normalization: deterministic first, reasoning second

Raw captures come in proprietary formats, with analyzer-specific columns, and with traffic you do not care about. Before any human — or any AI assistant — reasons about a trace, convert it deterministically:

raw capture (vendor file)
   │  export with vendor software (CSV/text) — see Chapter 78
   ▼
normalized event schema   {t_ns, dir, layer, kind, req, cpl, addr, tag, len, status, payload?}
   │  classify addresses using configuration knowledge (BAR0, queue bases, MSI-X table)
   ▼
transaction groups        (Requester ID, Tag) pairs; NVMe commands keyed by (SQID, CID)
   │  order by time, compute phases
   ▼
timeline                  per command: doorbell, fetch, data, CQE, interrupt, head doorbell
   │  rules + golden-trace diff
   ▼
anomalies                 first divergence, missing stages, timeouts, protocol violations
💡 Senior insight — why deterministic normalization comes before LLM reasoning

A language model (or a tired human) reading 50,000 raw rows will pattern-match, skip, and occasionally invent a matching completion that is not there. A 100-line deterministic script never invents a row, produces the same answer every time, and can be reviewed and regression-tested. Use deterministic code for counting, matching and ordering; use human or AI reasoning for interpreting the reduced, verified anomaly list — and keep the reduced list as the citation for every claim.

74.7 Trace diffing and golden traces

A golden trace is a capture of a known-good transaction that is versioned (device firmware, host kernel, analyzer software), reproducible (scripted workload), labelled (what operation, what config), configuration-documented (Gen, width, MPS, MRRS, queue count, interrupt coalescing) and known-good (passed functional checks). Diffing a failing capture against the golden trace aligns: initialization, command submission, queue activity, TLP sequences, completions and interrupts — and highlights the first divergence.

The script below normalizes two synthetic traces and diffs them in two ways. Note how the raw-sequence diff is noisy because commands overlap, while the transaction-grouped diff pinpoints the missing stage:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Trace normalization + good-vs-bad diff (OFFLINE / SIMULATION).
raw events -> normalized schema -> transaction-role tokens -> alignment -> first divergence.
Normalization removes things that legitimately differ between runs (timestamps,
absolute buffer addresses, tag values) so that only BEHAVIOUR is compared."""
import difflib
from trace_common import gen_trace, classify

def normalize(evs):
    toks = []
    for e in evs:
        role = classify(e)
        if role.startswith("data"):
            role = "data"                       # collapse addresses
        elif "slot" in role:
            role = role.rsplit(" ", 1)[0]       # drop ring slot index
        toks.append(f"{e.dir}:{e.kind}:{role}:{e.nbytes}")
    # collapse runs of identical data TLPs into one token with a count
    out = []
    for t in toks:
        if out and out[-1][0] == t:
            out[-1][1] += 1
        else:
            out.append([t, 1])
    return [f"{t} x{n}" if n > 1 else t for t, n in out]

def first_divergence(golden, test):
    sm = difflib.SequenceMatcher(a=golden, b=test, autojunk=False)
    for op, a0, a1, b0, b1 in sm.get_opcodes():
        if op != "equal":
            return op, a0, golden[a0:a1], test[b0:b1]
    return None

def transaction_diff(golden_evs, test_evs):
    """Group into per-command transactions FIRST, then compare stage sequences.
    Overlapping commands make raw-sequence diffs noisy; grouped diffs are not."""
    from lab06_timeline import build_timeline
    stages = ["doorbell", "fetch", "sqe", "data_first", "cqe", "irq"]
    g, _ = build_timeline(golden_evs)
    t, _ = build_timeline(test_evs)
    for key in sorted(g, key=lambda k: g[k].get("doorbell", 0)):
        gs = [s for s in stages if s in g[key]]
        ts = [s for s in stages if s in t.get(key, {})]
        if gs != ts:
            missing = [s for s in gs if s not in ts]
            return key, gs, ts, missing[0]
    return None

if __name__ == "__main__":
    golden = normalize(gen_trace(3))
    bad = normalize(gen_trace(3, faults=["nocqe:0x11"]))
    print(f"golden {len(golden)} tokens, test {len(bad)} tokens")
    d = first_divergence(golden, bad)
    if d:
        op, idx, g, b = d
        print(f"FIRST DIVERGENCE at golden token #{idx} ({op}):")
        print("   context :", golden[max(0, idx - 2):idx])
        print("   golden  :", g)
        print("   test    :", b)
    r = transaction_diff(gen_trace(3), gen_trace(3, faults=["nocqe:0x11"]))
    if r:
        key, gs, ts, first_missing = r
        print(f"TRANSACTION DIFF: SQ{key[0]} CID {key[1]:#x}: golden {gs}")
        print(f"                                test   {ts}")
        print(f"   first missing stage: {first_missing}")
golden 23 tokens, test 18 tokens
FIRST DIVERGENCE at golden token #14 (replace):
   context : ['UP:MWr:data:256 x4', 'DN:MWr:CQ1 head doorbell:4']
   golden  : ['UP:MWr:data:256 x12', 'UP:MWr:CQE post slot:16', 'UP:MWr:MSI-X interrupt:4', 'UP:MWr:data:256 x4', 'DN:MWr:CQ1 head doorbell:4', 'UP:MWr:data:256 x12']
   test    : ['UP:MWr:data:256 x28']
TRANSACTION DIFF: SQ1 CID 0x11: golden ['doorbell', 'fetch', 'sqe', 'data_first', 'cqe', 'irq']
                                test   ['doorbell', 'fetch', 'sqe', 'data_first']
   first missing stage: cqe
🔍 Lesson

Normalization removed timestamps, tags and buffer addresses (which legitimately differ between runs) and collapsed runs of data TLPs. Even so, interleaving makes the sequence diff point at "data x12 vs data x28" — technically the first divergence, but not a useful one. Grouping by transaction first yields: CID 0x11 stopped after data; CQE missing. Always diff at the level of meaning you want to conclude about.

74.8 Data safety when sharing traces

ItemRiskAction
Data TLP payloadsUser data, file contents, keysStrip payload columns or zero them in exports; share headers only
Identify data (SN, model, firmware)Ties trace to a customer or unreleased productRedact SN; share model/firmware only if permitted
Vendor/device IDs, DSN capabilityUnreleased product identificationReplace with placeholders when confidential
Host names, paths, BMC logsInfrastructure detailsRedact
Vendor-specific log pages, proprietary annotationsNDA materialShare only under the applicable agreement

Quiz

  1. Name the six coverage items every trace analysis must state.

    Answer

    Capture start, capture end, timestamp completeness, filtering, decoder omissions, directions captured.

  2. Why can an SQE be absent from a trace even when the device executed the command?

    Answer

    The capture may have started after the fetch, a filter may hide CplDs, or the SQ may live in the Controller Memory Buffer (CMB), in which case the host writes it with MWr to the device and no fetch MRd occurs.

  3. What five properties make a trace "golden"?

    Answer

    Versioned, reproducible, labelled, configuration-documented, known-good.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I state coverage before analysis, every time.
  • I can describe the normalization pipeline and why it precedes interpretation.
  • I can explain why transaction-level diffs beat raw-sequence diffs.
  • I know what to redact before sharing a trace.

🧪 Trace Lab TL-1 — Anatomy of a healthy 4 KiB read (Beginner) SAFE

Scenario. You run fio --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 and trigger the analyzer on the first MWr to the SQ1 tail doorbell.

Background. NVMe over PCIe: host writes the SQE into host memory, rings the doorbell; the controller fetches the SQE, reads media, writes data into host memory (MWr), writes the CQE, raises MSI-X; the host consumes the CQE and writes the CQ head doorbell.

CoverageCapture from trigger −1 µs to +200 µs; both directions; DLLPs filtered; single time base; TLP decoder complete for this traffic.

t=0.42     SQE fetch MRd ─┐ 0.71 µs round trip

Questions. (1) Fill in the Meaning column. (2) Which rows are Posted, which Non-Posted? (3) What does the CQ head doorbell value tell the controller? (4) Where does the 4 KiB data payload's latency go?

Hints

Doorbell offsets: 1000h + (2y)·4 for SQy tail and 1000h + (2y+1)·4 for CQy head. MRd is the only Non-Posted request type here.

Solution

Meanings: 1 SQ1 tail doorbell (value 1: one new SQE); 2 SSD fetches SQ1 slot 0 (64 B); 3 root complex returns the SQE (opcode 02h, CID 0x0010) — Level 1: requester 01:00.0, completer 00:00.0; 4–19 read data, 16 × 256 B = 4096 B to the PRP1 buffer; 20 CQE into CQ1 slot 0 (CID 0x0010, SQHD 1, phase 1, status 0); 21 MSI-X interrupt; 22 host CQ1 head doorbell = 1 (slot 0 consumed).

Posted vs Non-Posted: MWr rows are Posted (no completion); row 2 MRd is Non-Posted and is answered by row 3.

CQ head doorbell: it frees CQ slots for reuse; without it the controller eventually sees a full CQ and must stop posting.

Latency: ~1.1 µs submission, ~62.8 µs inside the device (media read dominates), ~0.5 µs data transfer, ~0.3 µs completion+interrupt, ~4.5 µs host processing until the head doorbell (the application already had its data earlier, at ISR time).

First abnormal event: none — this is the golden reference for TL-2…TL-9. Regression test: store this normalized trace as golden; require all stages present in order per command.

💡 Senior insight

Memorize the shape: tiny DN write, small UP read, small DN completion, long silence, burst of UP writes, one small UP write to the CQ, one tiny UP write to the interrupt address, tiny DN write. Abnormal traces are recognisable first as a shape violation — a missing burst, a silence in the wrong place.

Follow-up challenge. Redraw the trace for QD=4 with a single doorbell write of tail=4. How many SQE-fetch MRds might you see? (Answer: implementation-dependent — one 256-byte MRd fetching four SQEs, or four 64-byte MRds impl.)

🧪 Trace Lab TL-2 — Admin Identify during initialization (Beginner) SAFE

Scenario. Capture driver load. You trigger on the first write to BAR0 offset 14h (CC).

Background. Initialization: host programs AQA/ASQ/ACQ, sets CC.EN=1, polls CSTS.RDY, then submits Identify Controller (CNS 01h) on the admin queue.

Questions. (1) Decode AQA and CC. (2) What is row 5 and who is the requester? (3) The capture ends with CSTS still 0. Is the controller broken?

Hints

AQA holds ACQS (27:16) and ASQS (11:0), both 0-based. CC.IOCQES (23:20) and IOSQES (19:16) are powers of two. CAP.TO is in 500 ms units.

Solution

(1) AQA: 32-entry admin SQ and CQ (0x1F = 31, 0-based). CC = 0x00460001: EN=1, CSS=0 (NVM command set), MPS=0 (4 KiB pages), IOSQES=6 (64 B), IOCQES=4 (16 B). (2) Row 5 is the host (root complex as requester, 00:00.0) reading CSTS at 1Ch; the device answers with CplD — MMIO reads are Non-Posted requests to the device. (3) Not proven. CAP.TO = 0x14 × 500 ms = 10 s is the maximum time the host must wait for RDY; the capture is only 1 ms long. Coverage limits the conclusion. First abnormal event: none within coverage.

Regression test: measure CC.EN=1 → CSTS.RDY=1 time over 100 power cycles; fail if any exceeds CAP.TO or a product-specific budget.

Follow-up challenge. Extend the capture and draw the admin SQ0 doorbell, the SQE fetch at 0x7E00_0000, the 4 KiB Identify data MWr to 0x7F00_0000, the CQE at 0x7E01_0000. Which address range would an analyzer user put in a filter to see only admin traffic?

🧪 Trace Lab TL-3 — A 16 KiB write: MRRS splits and split completions (Intermediate) SAFE

Scenario. Sequential write, 16 KiB per command. The team asks why the analyzer shows "so many reads" for a write workload.

Background. For an NVMe Write, the SSD reads the data from host memory. Each MRd is at most MRRS bytes; the root complex may return each in several CplDs (at Read Completion Boundary multiples, at most MPS each).
