Questions. (1) What is row 4 and why 24 bytes? (2) How many MRds and CplDs carry the 16 KiB, and why? (3) The CQE arrives only ~10 µs after the data. Did the data reach NAND? (4) Check Byte Count on rows 9–10.

Hints

PRP1 covers the first page. A CplD may not exceed MPS. Byte Count in a completion is the bytes remaining including this completion.

Solution

(1) The PRP list fetch: PRP2 points to a list; the remaining 3 pages need 3 entries × 8 B = 24 B. (2) 16384 / 512 = 32 MRds (MRRS); each 512 B answered by 2 × 256 B CplDs (MPS) → 64 CplDs. (3) Not necessarily: a CQE for a write means the controller accepted the data per its rules — with a volatile write cache enabled, data may still be in cache; durability needs FUA or Flush impl. (4) Row 9 Byte Count = 512 (all bytes remaining, including this 256), row 10 Byte Count = 256 — the requester knows the request is complete when Byte Count equals the payload length of the final completion.

First abnormal event: none. Insight: "many reads during writes" is normal. Regression test: count MRd = ceil(bytes/MRRS) and CplD ≥ ceil(bytes/MPS) for scripted writes; alert if MRRS shrinks after a BIOS update.

💡 Senior insight

Write throughput depends on the read-request pipeline: number of outstanding MRds (tags) × MRRS ÷ round-trip time. A platform with long completion latency needs more outstanding tags to fill the link — one reason 10-bit tags matter at Gen5 and beyond.

Follow-up challenge. Recompute rows for MRRS 4096: how many MRds, and does the CplD count change?

🧪 Trace Lab TL-4 — Nak, replay and Recovery in the middle of a read (Intermediate) SAFE

Scenario. Benchmark shows small, periodic throughput dips. AER counters show occasional corrected errors. You capture with DLLPs and ordered sets enabled.

Background. The Data Link Layer protects TLPs with LCRC and sequence numbers; the receiver Acks good TLPs and Naks a bad one; the transmitter replays from its replay buffer. Repeated failures (replay timer or REPLAY_NUM rollover) trigger link Recovery (retraining).

Questions. (1) Interpret rows 4–7. (2) What is row 10 and what does it cost? (3) Is any NVMe-visible data lost? (4) Which side's receiver is failing, and which transmitter could be at fault?

Hints

Nak carries the sequence number of the last good TLP. TS1/TS2 ordered sets during L0 imply the LTSSM entered Recovery.

Solution

(1) Root-port receiver detected the LCRC error on seq 101; it Naks with seq 100 (last good); the SSD replays 101 and 102; Ack 102 acknowledges both. (2) TS1/TS2 exchange = LTSSM Recovery (retraining/re-equalization or just re-lock); traffic stalls ~1.3 µs here (synthetic). Whether Recovery followed a Nak directly depends on the cause (e.g. receiver lost lock) impl. (3) No: replay is lossless at the transaction layer; the cost is time. (4) The root-port receiver (upstream direction); the SSD transmitter, the channel (connector, retimer, trace) or the root-port receiver equalization are candidates.

First abnormal event: row 2, the first TLP with bad LCRC — not the Nak (a consequence) and not the Recovery (an escalation).

Hypotheses: H1 marginal channel at 16 GT/s; H2 SSD transmitter equalization preset; H3 root-port receiver issue; H4 power/thermal noise. Evidence: error rate vs temperature; same SSD in another slot; another SSD in this slot; force 8 GT/s and see errors disappear; lane margining (if supported) per lane.

Root cause (for this lab): undetermined by trace alone — the trace localizes the direction and layer (upstream, physical/data link). Corrective action: swap experiments, then hardware fix (channel) or equalization tuning. Regression test: 24-hour stress with AER correctable counters sampled per minute; threshold on rate, plus zero Recovery events per hour target.

💡 Senior insight

Small periodic dips often correlate with replay bursts; but correlation is not causation. Prove it by removing the replays (lower speed, different slot) and showing the dips vanish, or by measuring that replay time × frequency accounts for the lost throughput.

Follow-up challenge. Compute the throughput lost if each replay costs 0.3 µs and Recovery 1.5 µs, with one replay per 20 µs and one Recovery per second.

Quiz

  1. In TL-1, which row is the first evidence the controller knows about the command?

    Answer

    Row 2 (its SQE-fetch MRd). Row 1 proves the host rang; row 2 proves the device acted on it.

  2. In TL-3, why are there CplDs but no data MWr?

    Answer

    It is a Write: data flows host→device as completions to the device's MRds.

  3. In TL-4, what is the first abnormal event?

    Answer

    The TLP received with an LCRC error (row 2).

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can annotate a healthy read and write trace without hints.
  • I can decode AQA/CC values from MWr payloads.
  • I can explain Nak/replay/Recovery from a DLLP-enabled capture and name the first abnormal event.

These labs add ambiguity: incomplete coverage, multiple probe points, host-side evidence, and failures whose first abnormal event is far from the loudest one. Same template as Chapter 75; same configuration unless stated (§74.4).

🧪 Trace Lab TL-5 — Read fails with "Data Transfer Error" (Advanced) SAFE

Scenario. After a driver change, ~1 in 106 large reads fails with an I/O error. The kernel log shows an IOMMU fault near each failure.

Background. With an IOMMU, device DMA addresses are I/O virtual addresses (IOVAs). A DMA to an unmapped IOVA is blocked by the root complex; the requester typically receives an unsuccessful completion (for reads) or the write is dropped (for posted writes) impl.

Gen / widthGen4 x4Device01:00.0, IOMMU enabled

CoverageBoth directions; TLPs only; triggered on "completion status ≠ SC"; 100 µs pre-trigger, 100 µs post-trigger.
# illustrative, synthetic host log (wording varies by platform/kernel)

nvme0n1: I/O Cmd(0x2) @ LBA 0x3a2000, 128 blocks, I/O Error (sct 0x0 / sc 0x4)
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · TL-5 PRP list fetch blocked
#Time µsDirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
1−40.2DNTLMWr00:00.0—FE601008—4SQ1 tail = 23
2−39.8UPTLMRd01:00.0—1_1001_05800x6164SQE fetch slot 22
3−39.1DNTLCplD01:00.000:00.0—0x6164SQE Read CID 0x222, PRP2 = FFF0_1000
4−0.6UPTLMRd01:00.0—FFF0_10000x7c120PRP list fetch (15 entries)
50.0DNTLCpl01:00.000:00.0—0x7c0status UR — trigger
61.9UPTLMWr01:00.0—1_1002_0160—16CQE CID 0x222, SCT 0 SC 04h
72.0UPTLMWr01:00.0—FEE0_0000—4MSI-X

Questions. (1) Why is row 4 the first abnormal event rather than row 5? (2) Who decided the read had failed and how did it report? (3) List hypotheses for why IOVA 0xFFF0_1000 was unmapped. (4) What does the 38-µs gap between rows 3 and 4 suggest?

Hints

Compare the PRP list pointer in the SQE with the IOMMU fault address. Think about the lifetime of the PRP list page in the driver.

Solution

(1) Row 4 is the first event touching an invalid address — the request itself was already wrong; row 5 is the platform's (correct) reaction. Strictly, the true "first abnormal" fact is in row 3: the SQE carried a bad pointer — the trace cannot tell when it became bad. (2) The root complex/IOMMU blocked the DMA and returned UR; the controller then completed the command with Generic status 04h (Data Transfer Error) — a reasonable, implementation-chosen status impl. (3) H1 driver freed/unmapped the PRP list page before the device fetched it (use-after-unmap race); H2 the list was allocated from a pool whose IOVA mapping was torn down (e.g. after a reset); H3 IOVA arithmetic bug for lists crossing a page boundary; H4 IOMMU invalidation race. (4) The controller fetched the PRP list late (only when it was ready to transfer data) — devices may fetch lists lazily impl, which widens any host race window.

Evidence: instrument the driver to log map/unmap of PRP list pages with timestamps; check whether the failing commands' lists cross a page boundary; run with IOMMU in strict vs lazy invalidation modes. Root cause (lab answer): driver change released the PRP-list DMA mapping on a timeout-path cleanup that raced with normal completion. Corrective action: tie the list's lifetime to the request's completion. Regression test: stress 64 KiB–1 MiB reads with forced random timeouts and IOMMU strict mode for 24 h; zero DMAR faults allowed.

💡 Senior insight

The link was healthy; the controller behaved correctly; the bug was in host memory management. PCIe traces are often the tool that exonerates the device by showing exactly what address it was told to use.

Follow-up. How would the same bug look without an IOMMU? (Hint: the device reads whatever is in that physical page — possibly garbage PRP entries — and may DMA data to random memory: silent corruption. The IOMMU converted silent corruption into a clean error.)

🧪 Trace Lab TL-6 — The completion that nobody heard (Advanced) SAFE

Scenario. A single queue occasionally stalls for exactly 30 s; then I/O resumes. Kernel log: nvme nvme0: I/O 17 QID 5 timeout, completion polled (illustrative).

Background. MSI-X vectors can be masked per vector (table entry Mask bit) or for the whole function (Function Mask). A masked vector sets its Pending bit instead of sending the message; unmasking later sends the pending message verified for MSI-X semantics.

Gen / widthGen4 x4Device01:00.0, 33 MSI-X vectors; QID 5 → vector 5
Expected opRead CID 0x0011 on QID 5Initial stateHost CPU affinity for vector 5 being changed by irqbalance at about the time of the stall
CoverageBoth directions; TLPs; 40 s segmented capture with filter = "everything to/from QID 5 ranges + MSI-X address range + BAR0 writes".
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · TL-6 masked vector
#TimeDirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
10.000000 sDNTLMWr00:00.0—FE60202C—4MSI-X table entry 2, Vector Control: Mask = 1
20.000004 sDNTLMWr00:00.0—FE601028—4SQ5 tail doorbell
30.000065 sUPTLMWr01:00.0—(CQ5 slot)—16CQE CID 0x11, success
40.000066 s——(none)—————no MSI-X MWr follows
50.0001 sDNTLMWr00:00.0—FE60205C—4MSI-X table entry 5, Vector Control: Mask = 1
60.0001 sDNTLMWr00:00.0—FE602058/50—4+8entry 5 new data/address (affinity change)
7———(missing)——FE60205C——no unmask write for entry 5 in 30 s
830.0001 sDNTLMRd00:00.0—FE60001C0x094timeout handler reads CSTS
930.0003 sDNTLMWr00:00.0—FE60102C—4CQ5 head doorbell (completion polled)

Questions. (1) The MSI-X table lives in BAR0 at offset 2000h with 16-byte entries. Decode rows 1, 5, 6. (2) Is the device at fault for not sending the interrupt? (3) Why is row 4's "absence" trustworthy here but would not be in a capture filtered differently?

Hints

Entry n is at 2000h + 16n: Message Address low +0, high +4, Data +8, Vector Control +0Ch. Rows 1 and 5 differ.

Solution

(1) Row 1: entry 2 (2000h + 20h + 0Ch = 202Ch) masked — irrelevant to QID 5, a distractor; real traces have many. Row 5: entry 5 (2000h + 50h + 0Ch = 205Ch) masked; row 6 reprograms entry 5's address/data — the host is moving the vector to another CPU. Row 7: no unmask of entry 5 follows within the capture.

(2) Look at the ordering: the CQE (row 3) and the missing interrupt (row 4) come before the mask write of row 5. Two explanations fit: (a) vector 5 was already masked before capture start (an earlier affinity change outside coverage; row 5 is a repeated mask), in which case the device correctly withheld the message and set its Pending bit; or (b) the device failed to send an interrupt for an unmasked vector. The trace alone cannot decide, because coverage starts at row 1. Disambiguating evidence: read the Pending Bit Array (PBA, BAR0+3000h here) after the stall — bit 5 set supports (a); extend the capture start earlier to catch the first mask write; check host tracing of the affinity-change path. A masked vector must not send its message, so under (a) the device is not at fault.

(3) The filter explicitly included the MSI-X address range and all BAR0 writes; with a filter that excluded the interrupt address range, absence would mean nothing.

Root cause (lab answer): explanation (a), confirmed by PBA bit 5 = 1 and an extended capture: the host interrupt-affinity update path masked the vector and an error path skipped the unmask. Corrective action: fix the unmask path; regression test: stress I/O while forcing affinity changes every 10 ms for 1 h; assert no I/O exceeds 1 s; check PBA bits clear at end.

💡 Senior insight

Exactly-30-second stalls are a fingerprint: something waited for the default io_timeout. "Completion polled" means the CQE was already there — the interrupt path, not the device's command execution, is the suspect. Distractor rows (entry 2) are normal in real traces; disciplined address decoding beats intuition.

Follow-up. Design an analyzer trigger that fires when a CQE MWr is not followed by an MSI-X MWr within 10 µs (a "sequence + timer" trigger, if your analyzer supports it version).

🧪 Trace Lab TL-7 — Completion timeout behind a switch: two probe points (Senior) SAFE

Scenario. SSDs behind a PCIe switch report AER Completion Timeout every few hours under heavy mixed load. Two analyzers (or one multi-link analyzer) capture: Probe A on the switch downstream link to the SSD, Probe B on the switch upstream link to the root port. Clocks are aligned via a shared reference/ cross-trigger impl.

Gen / widthGen4 x4 (A), Gen4 x16 (B)DeviceSSD 04:00.0 behind switch DSP 03:00.0
Expected opSQE fetch, tag 0x2aInitial state8 SSDs at QD 64 each, mixed 70/30
CoverageA and B both directions; TLPs + DLLPs; trigger on ERR_NONFATAL message from 04:00.0; 60 ms pre-trigger.
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · TL-7 merged view (A = SSD link, B = upstream link)
#Time msProbe/DirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
10.0000A UPTLMRd04:00.0—2_0400_0A800x2a64SQE fetch
20.0003B UPTLMRd04:00.0—2_0400_0A800x2a64forwarded by switch
30.0011B DNTLCplD04:00.000:00.0—0x2a64RC answered — on time
40.0012B UPDLLAck———seq—switch acknowledged receipt
50.0011–50.0A DNTL(none for tag 0x2a)———0x2a—CplD never forwarded to the SSD
60.0015…A DNTLCplD04:00.000:00.0—0x2b,0x2c……other tags forwarded normally
750.2A UPTLMsg04:00.0————ERR_NONFATAL (Completion Timeout) — trigger

Questions. (1) Which component owns the failure? (2) With only Probe A, what would you have concluded? (3) List three switch-internal mechanisms that could drop or misroute a completion. (4) What else must you check before blaming the switch?

Solution

(1) The switch: it received (and Acked) the CplD on its upstream port but never transmitted it on the downstream port. (2) "The root complex never answered" — wrong owner. Single-probe captures localize to a link, not a component. (3) Completion routing by Requester ID mis-programmed (bus number ranges), internal buffer/credit accounting bug under mixed load, error containment (e.g. internal parity error dropping the packet), tag-tracking bug for 10-bit tags impl. (4) Probe coverage (did Probe A's analyzer drop packets? check its buffer/overflow indications), that 0x2a's CplD on B really has Requester ID 04:00.0 (not a different function), switch error counters/logs, switch firmware version, and whether the switch reported its own AER error.

Corrective action: escalate to switch vendor with both captures and configuration; workaround candidates (lower load, firmware update). Regression test: mixed-load soak on all downstream ports with completion-timeout counters per SSD; zero tolerated.

💡 Senior insight

Placing probes is a hypothesis test. Probe A answers "did the SSD receive it?"; Probe B answers "did the switch receive it?". Together they bracket a single component. Before purchase or setup, ask what question each probe point answers.

Follow-up. If a switch offers its own internal capture/trace feature (Chapter 78), what would you capture to confirm the drop inside the switch?

🧪 Trace Lab TL-8 — The doorbell that rang the wrong bell (Senior) SAFE

Scenario. A new user-space test harness (lab-only, device bound to vfio-pci) works on SSD model A but on model B no I/O command ever completes; the admin queue works.

Background. Doorbell address: SQy tail = 1000h + (2y)·(4 << CAP.DSTRD); CQy head = 1000h + (2y+1)·(4 << CAP.DSTRD). Model A has DSTRD = 0; model B has DSTRD = 1 (8-byte stride).

Gen / widthGen4 x4DeviceModel B, CAP.DSTRD = 1
Expected opRead on QID 1, CID 1Initial stateAdmin queue live; one Asynchronous Event Request (AER cmd, opcode 0Ch) outstanding with CID 0x7F
CoverageBoth directions; all TLPs; 1 s.
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · TL-8 wrong doorbell stride
#Time µsDirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
10.0DNTLMWr00:00.0—FE601008—4value 0x00000001 — intended "SQ1 tail = 1"
23.5UPTLMWr01:00.0—(admin CQ slot 9)—16CQE: CID 0x7F (the AER command), SQID 0, DW0 = 0x00010000
33.6UPTLMWr01:00.0—FEE0_0000—4MSI-X vector 0 (admin)
4———(none)—————no SQE fetch from I/O SQ1 within 1 s

Questions. (1) With DSTRD = 1, which register is at 1008h? (2) Decode DW0 of the asynchronous event completion: event type in bits 2:0, event information in bits 15:8, log page identifier in bits 23:16. (3) Why does the admin queue still work?

Hints

Stride = 8 bytes: SQ0 tail 1000h, CQ0 head 1008h, SQ1 tail 1010h, CQ1 head 1018h.

Solution

(1) 1008h is the admin CQ (CQ0) head doorbell. The harness wrote "head = 1" to the admin CQ — an invalid value if the host had not consumed entries accordingly. (2) DW0 = 0x00010000: event type 0 (Error status), event information 00h, log page 01h (Error Information). Under the spec's asynchronous event information for error status, the values distinguish "write to invalid doorbell register" and "invalid doorbell write value" — check the exact encoding table in the base specification revision you use verify code-point. Whether and how a controller reports an invalid doorbell write is controller behavior governed by the spec and may vary impl. (3) Admin SQ0 tail is at 1000h for any stride; only queues y ≥ 1 or the CQ0 head move with DSTRD.

Root cause: harness hard-coded a 4-byte stride instead of computing 4 << CAP.DSTRD. Corrective action: derive all doorbell offsets from CAP. Regression test: run the harness against devices (or an emulator such as a configurable virtual NVMe device) with DSTRD = 0, 1 and 2; assert I/O completes and no asynchronous error events are logged.

💡 Senior insight

Absence of activity after a doorbell is a doorbell-addressing problem until proven otherwise. Always decode the doorbell address against this device's CAP, and keep an outstanding Asynchronous Event Request — the controller will often tell you what you did wrong.

🧪 Trace Lab TL-9 — Capstone: resume failure becomes a reset loop SAFE

Scenario. Laptop-class platform: after resume from a low-power state, the SSD disappears ~15 % of the time. Logs show repeated controller resets, then removal. You must deliver a bug report (Level 9) and a regression test (Level 10).

Gen / widthGen4 x4 (capable)Device01:00.0; on resume the platform removed main power (D3cold) impl
Expected opLink retrain, config restore, controller re-init, admin queue setup, CC.EN=1, RDY=1Initial stateDevice had lost all register state (D3cold)
CoverageBoth directions; TLPs + link-state events (ordered-set summaries); capture armed before suspend; trigger on link up; 3 s post-trigger.
# illustrative, synthetic host log excerpt (wording varies)
[ 4120.551] nvme nvme0: 8/0/0 default/read/poll queues
[ 4122.553] nvme nvme0: Device not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=0x2
[ 4122.560] nvme nvme0: Removing after probe failure status: -19
SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · TL-9 resume sequence
#Time msDirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
10.0bothPHYlink up—————L0 at 2.5 GT/s x4 after Detect/Polling/Configuration
20.8bothPHYRecovery—————speed change → L0 at 16 GT/s
3101DNTLCfgWr0 ×N00:00.001:00.0—…4config restore: BAR0, Command (Mem+, BusMaster+), MSI-X, DevCtl
4102DNTLMRd00:00.0—FE60001C0x014read CSTS → 0x00000000
5102.3DNTLMWr00:00.0—FE600014—4CC = 0x00460001 (EN=1) — before AQA/ASQ/ACQ were written
6102.4DNTLMWr ×300:00.0—FE600024/28/30—4/8/8AQA, ASQ, ACQ written — after enable
7103…2100DN/UPTLMRd/CplD00:00.001:00.0FE60001C…4CSTS polled: 0x00000002 (CFS=1, RDY=0)
82102————————host gives up; device removed

Questions. (1) Find the first abnormal event and justify it. (2) Which layer owns the problem? (3) Why only 15 % of resumes? (4) Write the bug report skeleton. (5) Design the regression test.

Solution

(1) Row 5: CC.EN=1 written while AQA/ASQ/ACQ hold reset values (zero). The spec's initialization sequence requires configuring the admin queue registers before setting CC.EN to 1 verified (initialization order). Rows 1–4 are healthy: the link trained to full speed and config restore succeeded. (2) Host driver / platform resume path (NVMe register programming order), not PCIe. CSTS.CFS=1 (row 7) is the controller's reaction — how a controller reacts to enable-without-queues is implementation-dependent impl. (3) Hypothesis: the resume path assumes register state is preserved (true after D3hot without reset, false after D3cold); the platform chooses D3cold only sometimes (e.g. depending on how long it slept or on a platform policy) impl. Evidence: correlate failures with the platform's power-state decision (logs/ACPI tracing) and with sleep duration.

(4) Bug report skeleton: Title: NVMe controller fatal status after resume when device enters D3cold: CC.EN set before admin queue registers. Environment: platform/BIOS, kernel version, SSD model/FW (SN redacted), link Gen4 x4. Coverage: capture armed before suspend; both directions; TLP + link-state; no filters on BAR0 traffic. Observations: rows 1–8 with times. Inferences: link and config restore healthy; register order violated. Hypotheses ranked: H1 resume path skips full re-init after D3cold (high); H2 controller firmware loses AQA writes (low — disproved: writes are visible on the link after CC). Evidence requested: driver trace of resume path; ACPI power-state decisions. Impact: data unavailability, potential data loss for unflushed writes. Reproduction rate: 15 % over 200 cycles.

(5) Regression test: 1,000 suspend/resume cycles forcing D3cold, and 1,000 forcing D3hot; assert after each resume: device present, CSTS.RDY=1 with CFS=0 within CAP.TO, a read-verify of a known pattern succeeds; on failure, auto-save kernel log and analyzer trigger.

💡 Senior insight

In resume bugs, the loud events (removal, reset loop) arrive seconds after the decisive one. Read forward from the last known-good state (link up, config restored) rather than backward from the crash.

76.1 The 45-lab catalog

The full Academy contains 45 trace exercises: 10 beginner, 10 intermediate, 10 advanced, 10 senior and 5 capstone. The nine labs above (TL-1…TL-9) are written out in full; the catalog below gives each remaining exercise as a compact case — scenario and the key synthetic trace signature — with the expected reasoning hidden. Expand each into the full template as practice: invent the rows that would show the signature, state coverage, and write the regression test.

Beginner (B1–B10)

IDScenario / trace signatureQuestionAnswer
B1= TL-1 healthy 4 KiB readAnnotate every rowSee TL-1
B2= TL-2 controller enableDecode AQA/CCSee TL-2
B3CfgRd0 to 01:00.0 offset 000h, CplD data 0001abcdWhat was read and what is the answer?
Answer

Vendor ID/Device ID dword: vendor ABCDh, device 0001h (little-endian register, printed as DW).

B4CfgRd0 to 02:00.0 answered by Cpl with status CRS during bootMeaning?
Answer

Configuration Request Retry Status: the device is not ready yet after reset; software retries. Normal briefly after reset; abnormal if it persists beyond the allowed time.

B5MWr 4 B to FE60100C with value 3 after three CQE MWrsWhat is it?
Answer

CQ1 head doorbell: host consumed three CQEs (head now 3).

B6MRd 256 B from SQ1 slot 4 after doorbell value 8What happened?
Answer

Controller fetched four SQEs (slots 4–7) in one request — legal batching impl.

B7Read of 8 KiB: 32 MWr of 256 B to two different 4 KiB pagesHow were the pages described?
Answer

Two pages → PRP1 and PRP2 (no list), if PRP1 is page-aligned.

B8Flush command: doorbell, SQE fetch, no data, CQE ~2 ms laterWhy no data and why slow?
Answer

Flush has no data transfer; the controller commits its volatile write cache to media before completing.

B9UpdateFC DLLPs every few µs in both directionsAbnormal?
Answer

No: receivers return flow-control credits as buffers free.

B10Electrical idle ordered sets, then no traffic for 2 ms, then TS1sWhat happened?
Answer

Link entered a low-power state (e.g. L1 via ASPM) and exited through Recovery. Normal if ASPM is enabled; check exit latency impact.

Intermediate (I1–I10)

IDScenario / trace signatureQuestionAnswer
I1= TL-3 write with MRRS splits—See TL-3
I2= TL-4 Nak/replay/Recovery—See TL-4
I3Read CQE status SCT 2h SC 81h, DNR=1Layer and host action?
Answer

Media: Unrecovered Read Error; do not retry; report error; check SMART media_errors delta.

I4One MSI-X MWr after every 8 CQEsBug?
Answer

Likely interrupt coalescing (Feature 08h); verify with get-feature. Adds latency by design.

I5CQE phase bit 0 in slots 0–3 after a wrap on a 64-entry CQCorrect?
Answer

Yes: the phase inverts on each pass; second pass writes phase 0.

I6LnkSta-equivalent: link trained at x2 (TS show lanes 2–3 no detect)First check?
Answer

Physical lanes 2–3: connector, riser, slot wiring/bifurcation; compare port LnkCap.

I7Data MWr of 128 B although device supports 512 BWhy?
Answer

Programmed MPS is 128 (path minimum or BIOS policy).

I8Dataset Management (09h) command with 4 KiB MRd for range list, then CQEWhat was fetched?
Answer

The range descriptor list (16 bytes per range) describing LBAs to deallocate.

I9Two SSDs, identical traces, one 20 % slower: its MWrs are spaced widerFirst suspicion?
Answer

Flow-control credit starvation upstream (UpdateFC cadence) or lower link speed; compare DLLPs and LnkSta.

I10Get Log Page 02h: 512 B MWr to host bufferWhich log?
Answer

SMART / Health Information (512 bytes).

Advanced (A1–A10)

IDScenario / trace signatureQuestionAnswer
A1= TL-5 PRP list blocked by IOMMU—See TL-5
A2= TL-6 masked vector—See TL-6
A3CplD with EP=1 for a write-data pull; CQE status Data Transfer ErrorOrigin?
Answer

Host side marked the data poisoned (e.g. memory ECC uncorrectable); the SSD refused poisoned data. Check host memory error logs.

A4MWr from SSD to address beyond any PRP of outstanding commandsSignificance?
Answer

Stray DMA — device bug or stale PRP use; with IOMMU it faults, without it corrupts memory. High severity.

A5Abort command (08h) submitted for CID 0x30; CQE for Abort arrives; CQE for 0x30 arrives with status "Command Abort Requested"Sequence correct?
Answer

Yes; both complete. Abort is best-effort: the target may also complete normally impl.

A6SQE fetch MRds slow down (2 µs → 20 µs RTT) only when GPU traffic peaksLayer?
Answer

Shared fabric/root complex contention; not the SSD. Evidence: completion latency vs other devices' load.

A7Unexpected Completion error: CplD with tag 0x15 arrives 70 ms after MRd tag 0x15 timed outStory?
Answer

Completer was very slow; requester already timed out and released the tag; late completion is "unexpected". Root cause is the slow completer.

A8Malformed TLP reported by RC: MWr with payload 512 B while MPS=256Owner?
Answer

Transmitter (SSD) violated programmed MPS — or MPS was changed under it. Check DevCtl on both ends at failure time.

A9CQE written to CQ slot 0 while host expects slot 40Possible cause?
Answer

Controller and host disagree on CQ state, e.g. after a reset/re-create the controller restarted at 0 while the host did not; or queue size mismatch.

A10LTR messages and L1.2 entry right before a latency spikeProof needed?
Answer

Correlation only; prove by disabling L1 substates and comparing latency distributions.

Senior / debug (S1–S10)

IDScenario / trace signatureQuestionAnswer
S1= TL-7 switch drops completion—See TL-7
S2= TL-8 doorbell stride—See TL-8
S3Capture shows CQE missing; analyzer status shows "buffer overflow — packets dropped"Conclusion?
Answer

None about the CQE: coverage invalid. Re-capture with filters or segmented capture.

S4Host timeouts every ~8 h; trace shows CQE and MSI-X fine, but host CQ head doorbell stops advancingOwner?
Answer

Host software: interrupt arrived but the completion path did not run or did not finish (stuck CPU, softirq starvation, lock). Check CPU stalls, /proc/interrupts deltas.

S5Write data CplDs arrive out of address order across tagsBug?
Answer

No: completions for different tags may be reordered; within one request, completions arrive in address order.

S6After FW update, Identify shows new FR, but read latency p99 doubled; trace shows SQE→data gap distribution widerLayer?
Answer

Controller/firmware internals; link and host unchanged. Provide distributions before/after to vendor.

S7Surprise Down error after hot-unplug test, followed by host hangExpected vs bug?
Answer

Surprise Down is expected on unplug; host hang is a bug in the removal path (outstanding I/O not cancelled), not in the SSD.

S8Two hosts share a dual-port SSD; reservation conflict status on oneLayer?
Answer

NVMe reservations (command-set semantics), not transport. Check reservation report.

S9Replay rate rises with SSD temperatureNext experiment?
Answer

Controlled heating/cooling with fixed workload; check thermal throttling separately; consider transmitter equalization margin vs temperature.

S10Analyzer decoder labels a TLP "unknown type" on a Gen6 captureInterpretation?
Answer

Decoder limitation possible (Flit mode, new header formats); check analyzer software version before calling the device non-compliant.

IDScenarioDeliverableKey reasoning
C1= TL-9 resume reset loopBug report + regression testSee TL-9
C2"Read occasionally takes 10 seconds" — the cross-layer lab of Chapter 80Owner layer with evidence
Answer

See Chapter 80 §80.6.

C3Throughput 30 % below spec on Gen5 x4; trace shows MPS 128, 10-bit tags disabled, completion RTT 1.8 µsBandwidth model explaining the gap
Answer

MPS 128 caps payload efficiency at ~84 %; for writes, outstanding read-request limit × MRRS / RTT may cap throughput below link rate. Compute both with Chapter 90 and Little's law.

C4Firmware activation without reset: some commands time out during activationTest plan
Answer

Measure command latency during activation; check the controller's advertised maximum time for activation; verify host timeouts exceed it; capture CSTS.PP (processing paused) if supported version.

C5Silent data corruption reported by an application checksumEvidence plan across layers
Answer

Capture data TLPs for the corrupted LBA (payload compare), check EP/ECRC, PRP correctness (stray DMA), IOMMU logs, end-to-end protection information, host memory errors; reproduce with a known pattern write/read-verify tool.

PART XXIV

Protocol Analyzer Training (Teledyne LeCroy–class Workflows)

Teledyne LeCroy is one of the best-known makers of PCIe/NVMe protocol analyzers, and many teams say "the LeCroy" the way people say "the Xerox". This Part teaches the workflow and concepts shared by hardware protocol analyzers of that class — capture, trigger, filters, views, timestamps, link state, error views, traffic analysis — and the reasoning path from symptom to root-cause hypothesis. It deliberately does not reproduce any product's menus, button names or screen layouts: those differ between product generations and software versions. Whenever this Part says "most analyzers can…", treat it as version-dependent and verify against the documentation for the exact analyzer hardware, firmware and software version you use.

77 Protocol Analyzer Workflows: From Symptom to Hypothesis

← 76 Trace Labs II: Advanced, Senior and Capstone — plus the 45-Lab Catalog78 Capture Files, PEX, and Portable Trace Evidence →

77.1 Why this chapter exists

A protocol analyzer is the only instrument that shows what actually crossed the link, symbol by symbol, in both directions, with nanosecond timestamps. It is also expensive, intrusive (you must insert something into the channel), limited in memory, and only as useful as the trigger you set. Teams that own analyzers but lack the workflow fill buffers with gigabytes of irrelevant idle traffic and still miss the event. This chapter teaches the workflow.

77.2 Learning objectives (deep-dive module)

  • Beginner: explain what an analyzer captures, the difference between capture-time filtering and display filtering, and what a trigger is.
  • Intermediate: configure a capture conceptually: speed/width, probe, buffer, trigger position, trigger condition; navigate packet, transaction and NVMe-command views.
  • Advanced: design sequence/timer triggers for "A not followed by B" failures; reason about lock, de-skew, scrambling and training capture requirements.
  • Senior: choose probe points as hypothesis tests; state analyzer limitations in every report.
  • Trace-analysis: go from symptom → trace region → first abnormal event → reconstructed transaction → hypothesis.
  • Debugging: distinguish device fault, host fault, channel fault and analyzer artefact.
  • Validation: build repeatable capture recipes and golden traces for regression.

77.3 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy — the wildlife camera

A nature photographer wants a picture of a shy fox. She cannot film the forest all year — her memory card is small. So she puts a camera on the fox's path (probe placement), tells it to start recording when something fox-sized moves (trigger), keeps the last 10 seconds before the movement too (pre-trigger buffer), and ignores leaves blowing (filter). Back home, she watches the clip frame by frame (packet view), groups frames into "fox enters, sniffs, leaves" (transaction view), and decides what the fox was doing (hypothesis).

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Represents: limited memory, triggers, pre-trigger history, filters, placement. Hides: that the camera itself is part of the path — an interposer changes the electrical channel and can create or hide errors; that the analyzer must understand the scene (lock to the bit stream, de-skew lanes, descramble, know queue addresses) to decode anything; and that what you see is a decoded interpretation, not raw truth. Misleading when: you believe "the camera saw no fox, so no fox passed" — filters, lock loss, buffer overflow and decoder limitations all produce false absences.

77.4 Vocabulary

TermPlain meaningEngineering meaningRelated toCommon confusion
InterposerA pass-through adapter with tapsBoard inserted between slot and device (CEM slot, M.2, U.2/U.3, EDSFF form factors) that routes signals to the analyzerProbe, channel loss"Transparent" — it adds loss/reflections; at Gen5+ it can change link behavior impl
Mid-bus probeA probe clipped onto a board footprintProbe attached to a dedicated footprint on the PCB tracesBoard designRequires the footprint to be designed in
Lock"I can hear you"Analyzer's receivers achieve bit/symbol/block lock on each laneTraining, equalizationLock can fail silently mid-capture
De-skewLining up the lanesAligning per-lane arrival differences so multi-lane packets reassemble correctlyLane-to-lane skewBad de-skew looks like corrupted packets on the analyzer only
DescramblingUndoing the mixingGen1–5 scramble data with an LFSR; analyzer must track scrambler state (learned during training) implTraining captureStarting capture mid-stream may prevent decode on some tools
Trigger"Start/stop here"Condition marking the reference point in the bufferPre/post-triggerThe trigger event is not necessarily the first abnormal event
Pre-trigger %How much history to keepFraction of buffer reserved for events before the triggerBuffer sizeToo little history hides the cause
Capture (hardware) filterDon't record leavesPackets excluded before storage — gone foreverBuffer efficiencyConfused with display filter
Display filterHide leaves while watchingPackets stored but hidden in a viewViewsExports may include or exclude hidden rows depending on settings version
Packet viewEvery framePer-TLP/DLLP/ordered-set decoded listLab 2—
Transaction viewQuestion + answer togetherRequests grouped with their completions (by Requester ID + Tag)Split transactionsGrouping fails if completions were filtered or lost
NVMe command viewWhole story of one commandDoorbell, SQE fetch, PRP fetch, data, CQE, interrupt grouped per commandLab 6Requires queue configuration knowledge (see 77.9)
Link/state viewRoad statusLTSSM states, speed/width changes, ordered sets, electrical idleLTSSMLow-level views may be hidden by default
Error viewList of bad framesLCRC/symbol/framing errors, malformed packets, protocol violations detected by the analyzerAERAnalyzer-detected errors ≠ errors the receiver detected
Traffic analysisCounting and timingBandwidth per direction, latency histograms, outstanding-request countsPerformanceStatistics over filtered data are biased
Cross-triggerCameras that tell each otherTrigger in/out signals shared with scopes, other analyzers, or host GPIOTime alignmentCable delays and clock domains must be accounted for

77.5 Architecture: inputs, outputs, actors, state

ActorRoleEvidence it leaves
Host/root port, deviceGenerate traffic (unaware of the analyzer if the probe is passive)The traffic itself; their own logs
Probe/interposerElectrical tapChanged channel characteristics (measurable as error rates with vs without)
Analyzer hardwareLock, decode, trigger, filter, storeCapture file; lock-loss/overflow indications
Analyzer softwareDecode, group, display, exportViews, statistics, exports — interpretation layer, version-dependent
EngineerChooses placement, trigger, filters; interpretsCapture recipe and notes — part of the evidence

77.6 Mechanism: one capture, step by step

StepWho actsWhat changesWhereEvidence
1. Power down, insert interposer/probeEngineerChannel now includes the probeSlot / boardLab notes; photo
2. Configure capture: speed(s), width, lanes, clocking mode, buffer, pre-trigger %Engineer → analyzerAnalyzer receiver settingsAnalyzerSaved capture settings (keep with the trace!)
3. Define trigger and capture filtersEngineerTrigger state machineAnalyzerTrigger definition
4. Arm, then power on / start workloadEngineerAnalyzer follows training (learns lane map, scrambling, equalization)AnalyzerLink/state view shows Detect…L0
5. Traffic flows; analyzer stores into the circular bufferHost, deviceBuffer fills/wrapsAnalyzer memoryBuffer fill indicator

7. Upload, decode, viewSoftwareDecoded database builtWorkstationCapture file; views

77.7 Triggers: the art of catching the fox

Trigger type (generic)Use it forExample
Packet pattern (type + field match)Specific operationsMWr to the SQ5 tail doorbell address; CplD with status ≠ SC; any TLP with EP=1
ErrorLink-level problemsLCRC error, symbol/framing error, malformed TLP, Nak DLLP
Link stateTraining/power issuesEntry into Recovery; speed change; electrical idle; L1 entry
Sequence (A then B)Multi-step conditionsDoorbell to SQ1 then MRd to an address outside known queues
Counter (Nth occurrence)Rare repeatsThe 1000th Nak
Timer / "A not followed by B within T"Missing responsesCQE MWr not followed by MSI-X within 10 µs; MRd tag not completed within 1 ms
External trigger inHost-detected symptomsHost script toggles a GPIO when it logs an NVMe timeout (beware: 30 s late — needs a deep buffer or segmented capture)
MessageError signallingERR_COR/ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_FATAL message TLPs

Availability of sequence, timer and "not followed by" triggers, and their depth, varies by analyzer model and software version version.

💡 Senior insight — trigger on the earliest observable deviation

Host symptoms (timeouts) arrive seconds late. Instead of triggering on the symptom, trigger on the earliest link-visible precursor you can define: an unsuccessful completion, an ERR_* message, a Recovery entry, or a timer trigger on a missing response. Set pre-trigger large enough to contain the precursor's cause; if the buffer cannot hold that much, use capture filters to drop bulk data payload TLPs (keep headers if the tool supports header-only capture version).

77.8 Filters and the capture buffer

  • Capture filters drop traffic before storage: e.g. drop idle/skip ordered sets, drop data MWr payloads, keep only one device's traffic behind a switch. What you drop cannot be argued from later. Record filters in the coverage statement (§74.2).
  • Display filters only hide rows; they are safe, but exports and statistics might honor them — check before exporting.
  • Buffer arithmetic: a Gen4 x4 link carrying ~7 GB/s of read data in one direction fills a buffer quickly. Example: with a hypothetical 8 GB buffer and both directions at high load, the window is on the order of one second, less with storage overheads derived. A 30-second NVMe timeout cannot be fully captured unfiltered; use filters, segmented capture (many short captures around repeated triggers), or trigger on a precursor.
  • Segmented capture (if supported): many small trigger-centred windows — ideal for intermittent failures.

77.9 Views and their limits

ViewAnswersLimitations
Link / raw symbolTraining sequence, speed changes, equalization phases, electrical idle, per-lane errorsHuge; needs capture of training to make sense
Packet (TLP/DLLP)Exact headers, sequence numbers, CRC status, timestampsNo grouping; easy to drown
Transaction / split transactionRequest ↔ completion pairing; latency per requestMissing completions show as orphans; filtered completions look missing
NVMe command viewPer-command reconstruction (doorbell → CQE)Needs queue base addresses and sizes, usually learned from Create I/O SQ/CQ admin commands. If capture began after queue creation, the tool may need manual configuration or cannot decode impl. SQ in CMB, or HMB traffic, may be decoded differently or not at all version
Error viewWhat the analyzer considered erroneousAnalyzer-detected ≠ device-detected; lock loss produces fake errors
Traffic statisticsBandwidth, IOPS, latency histograms, outstanding requestsBiased by filters; window may be too short to represent steady state
Hierarchy / topologyDevices discovered via config cycles in the captureOnly what was enumerated during the capture
📭 What the analyzer does not see

Host CPU stores to memory (SQE writes), controller-internal activity (FTL, NAND, firmware scheduling), host software (interrupt handling, block layer), and — if PCIe Integrity and Data Encryption (IDE) is enabled — the contents of encrypted TLP data version. Behind a switch, an analyzer on one link sees only that link.

77.10 The four-step method (the heart of this chapter)

Step 1 — From symptom to trace region

Translate the symptom into a link-visible signature and a time relation. "I/O timeout on QID 3" → signature: a command on SQ3 whose CQE never appears; time relation: the doorbell is ~30 s before the host log line. Choose: trigger (unsuccessful completion? timer trigger on missing CQE?), pre-trigger depth, filters. If you already have a long capture: search for the doorbell writes to SQ3 in the window 30 s ± 1 s before the logged time (needs a sync marker — Chapter 71).

Step 2 — Identify the first abnormal event

Walk forward from the last known-good state and compare each stage with the golden shape (TL-1). The first abnormal event is the earliest observation that deviates from expected behavior within coverage. It is frequently quieter than the trigger: a malformed field, a missing Ack, a late completion.

Step 3 — Reconstruct the transaction

Group everything belonging to the affected command: doorbell, SQE fetch (and its CplD payload: opcode, CID, PRPs), PRP list fetches, data, CQE, MSI-X, head doorbell. For PCIe-level problems, group request ↔ completion pairs by Requester ID + Tag, including split completions. Write the reconstructed timeline down.

Step 4 — Formulate root-cause hypotheses

For the stage where the chain broke, list the components that own that stage (Chapter 80), rank them by evidence, and for each define the experiment that would falsify it. A hypothesis that no experiment could disprove is not yet useful.

77.11 Trace views of the module: normal, slow, failed, ambiguous

SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · four outcomes of the same read, transaction-level summary
CaseDoorbellSQE fetch RTTSQE→dataCQEMSI-XReading
Normal0 µs0.7 µs62 µs64.5 µs64.6 µsGolden shape
Slow0 µs0.7 µs4.1 ms4.1 ms4.1 msDevice-internal delay; link fine
Failed0 µsno CplD———Completion missing for SQE fetch → transaction layer upstream of device
Ambiguous0 µs0.7 µs—— (capture ended at 2 ms)—Inconclusive: coverage too short to call it missing

77.12 Hardware view and safe practice

⚠️ Safe hardware practice

Inserting an interposer is lab-only, requires powering down the system (unless the setup is explicitly designed for hot-plug), ESD precautions, and mechanical care with high-speed connectors. It is non-destructive to data but not production-safe: the extra channel loss can cause link degradation, and removing a drive's host from service to probe it is an operational decision. Never probe a system whose drives hold the only copy of important data.

🏭 Implementation-dependent

Whether an analyzer requires capturing link training to decode (scrambler and lane state), supports lane reversal/polarity inversion, SRIS/SRNS clocking, Gen5/Gen6 rates, FLIT mode, 10/14-bit tags, IDE, or NVMe command decoding for a given spec revision depends on the analyzer model, licenses and software version. Check the release notes before the lab day, not during it.

77.13 Five analyzer failure patterns

#SymptomPossible causesFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentLikely conclusion (confidence)
1Many LCRC errors in analyzer, none in AERAnalyzer lock/de-skew problem; probe marginalAnalyzer lock-loss indicatorsAER counters on both endsSame workload, different probe/cable; or compare error timestamps with Nak DLLPs (real errors cause Naks)No Naks → analyzer artefact (high)
2Link fails to reach Gen4 only with interposer installedInterposer channel lossWithout interposer: LnkStaInterposer spec for the rateSwap interposer type/lengthProbe-induced (high if it disappears without it)
3NVMe view shows no commands, packet view shows trafficDecoder lacks queue config (capture began after Create I/O SQ/CQ)Is Create I/O SQ/CQ in the capture?Decoder settingsCapture from driver load, or configure queue addresses manually implDecoder limitation (high)
4"Missing" completionsFilters, overflow, one direction captured, real lossCoverage statementBuffer overflow indicatorRe-capture without filters, shorter windowDepends — never conclude before coverage check
5Latency in analyzer ≠ latency in fioDifferent endpoints of measurement (link vs syscall)What each measuresHost-side tracing (blktrace/bpftrace)Latency budget decomposition (Chapter 87)Both correct, different scopes (high)

77.14 Labs

🧪 Lab 77.1 — Paper capture plan (Beginner) SAFE

Objective: write a capture plan without touching hardware. Procedure: for the symptom "random-read p99.9 spikes to 5 ms every few seconds", write: probe point, speed/width, buffer, pre-trigger %, trigger, capture filters, display filters, metadata to record, coverage statement template. Questions: what is your trigger, and why not "every read"?

Solution

Example: interposer at the SSD slot; capture both directions; filter out data payloads (keep headers) if supported; trigger: timer trigger "SQE-fetch CplD for SQ n not followed by data MWr within 2 ms" or, if unsupported, segmented captures triggered on MSI-X with a host-side marker for slow I/Os; pre-trigger ≥ 5 ms. Triggering on every read fills the buffer with normal reads and gives no anchor.

🧪 Lab 77.2 — Coverage audit of an exported capture (Intermediate) SAFE

Objective: given the synthetic export in Chapter 78's normalizer, list what you can and cannot conclude. Solution sketch in Chapter 78's lab.

🧪 Lab 77.3 — Trigger design for a missing interrupt (Advanced) CAUTION

Classification: lab-only hardware (interposer), non-destructive to data, read workload only. Objective: catch TL-6-like failures. Procedure: define a sequence/timer trigger "MWr into CQ ring range, not followed by MWr to MSI-X address range within 20 µs"; run a read-only fio workload; force interrupt affinity changes from the host. Questions: what if your analyzer lacks "not followed by" triggers?

Solution

Fallbacks: external trigger from a host-side watchdog (bpftrace program that detects a request older than 100 ms and toggles a GPIO or writes a marker that produces a recognizable config read), with a deep pre-trigger; or segmented capture triggered on every CQ5 MWr with short windows and offline post-processing (Lab 8 detector).

🧪 Lab 77.4 — Senior forensic: is it the device, the host, the channel, or the analyzer? SAFE

Objective: for each of the five failure patterns above, write the one-paragraph argument you would send to a skeptical colleague, including coverage and confidence. Extension: turn the arguments into a checklist that gates every analyzer-based bug report in your team.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Capture filter vs display filter?
    Model answer

    Capture filters drop data before storage (irrecoverable); display filters hide stored data.

  2. Beginner Why keep pre-trigger data?
    Model answer

    The cause precedes the trigger; the trigger is usually a consequence.

  3. Beginner Why must the analyzer see both directions?
    Model answer

    Requests and completions, data and Acks, travel in opposite directions; one direction cannot show a transaction.

  4. Intermediate Why might an NVMe command view be empty?
    Model answer

    The decoder lacks queue base addresses because queue creation happened before capture start.

  5. Intermediate How do you align analyzer time with dmesg?
    Model answer

    Sync marker: a recognizable link event generated by a host script that also logs to /dev/kmsg.

  6. Intermediate What does an interposer change?
    Model answer

    The electrical channel (loss, reflections), potentially link training results and error rates.

  7. Advanced How do you capture a failure whose host symptom appears 30 s later?
    Model answer

    Trigger on an earlier precursor, filter bulk payloads, segmented capture, or deep buffer with external trigger and large pre-trigger.

  8. Advanced Analyzer shows LCRC errors but no Naks follow. Interpretation?
    Model answer

    Likely analyzer-side decode error (lock/de-skew/probe), since the real receiver would Nak a bad TLP.

  9. Advanced What changes when IDE is enabled?
    Model answer

    TLP data is encrypted/integrity-protected; the analyzer can show headers and timing but not payload contents (unless provided keys in a supported workflow uncertain).

  10. Senior How do you choose probe points behind a switch?
    Model answer

    Each probe answers "did the packet reach this link?"; bracket the suspected component (TL-7).

  11. Senior What goes in an analyzer-based bug report?
    Model answer

    Capture recipe (probe, settings, trigger, filters), coverage statement, analyzer/software versions, first abnormal event, reconstructed transaction, ranked hypotheses, requested evidence, redactions.

  12. Senior When is an analyzer the wrong tool?
    Model answer

    When the problem is above the link (host scheduling, filesystem) or inside the controller, or when cheaper evidence (logs, counters) already localizes it.

Teach-back. Child: "a smart camera that starts recording when the fox appears." Junior: "set trigger, pre-trigger and filters; then find the first abnormal event and group the transaction." Senior: "an analyzer trace is scoped, decoded evidence from one probe point; its value depends on the placement and trigger hypothesis and on stating its coverage."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can write a complete capture plan (placement, trigger, filters, buffer, metadata) for any symptom in the Failure Library.
  • I can explain lock, de-skew and why training capture may matter.
  • I can execute the four-step method and name the first abnormal event.
  • I can tell device fault, host fault, channel fault and analyzer artefact apart with evidence.
  • I never name product-specific UI features without checking the documentation for that version.
PART XXV

PEX and Proprietary Capture-File Training

Captures outlive the lab bench: they are mailed to vendors, archived with bug reports, and reopened years later. This Part covers the file side — what a proprietary capture file is, how to identify and preserve it, what can be inspected without vendor software, how to export it into portable form, and what is lost in conversion. It also covers captures and diagnostics that come from PCIe switches (for example Broadcom PEX-family switches) rather than from external analyzers.

78 Capture Files, PEX, and Portable Trace Evidence

← 77 Protocol Analyzer Workflows: From Symptom to Hypothesis79 The Debugging Framework: Observation, Inference, Hypothesis, Evidence, Root Cause →

78.1 Why this chapter exists

"Can you look at this .pex file?" is a common request. The honest answer begins with questions: which tool and version produced it, what was captured, and do we have the software to decode it? Engineers who guess — or who trust a "converter" of unknown provenance — corrupt evidence. Engineers who know the difference between a file container and decoded protocol content handle captures like forensic evidence.

  • Beginner: distinguish a capture file from an export; record a capture's metadata.
  • Intermediate: identify the producing tool and version safely; preserve chain of custody.
  • Advanced: export to portable formats and normalize with a reviewed mapping; validate the conversion.
  • Senior: explain what is lost in conversion and how that limits conclusions; handle switch-generated captures.
  • Trace-analysis / Debugging / Validation: keep conversions deterministic, reproducible and documented.

78.2 What "PEX" may mean

UsageWhat it refers toTruth label
File extension .pexCommonly associated with PCIe trace files saved by Teledyne LeCroy PCIe protocol-analysis softwareuncertain — widely reported in practice; confirm with the documentation of the software version that produced your file. Other tools may use other extensions, and extensions alone prove nothing
"PEX" switchesBroadcom (formerly PLX Technology) PCIe switch product families named PEX…; some provide on-chip diagnostic/performance/error-logging or capture features accessible through vendor toolsimpl — feature sets vary by device family and are documented (often under NDA) by the vendor
🧒 Kid analogy — the sealed diary

A capture file is a diary written in a secret alphabet, inside a locked box. You can weigh the box, read the label on it, and photocopy it (safely, without opening). To read the diary you need the key and the alphabet book — the vendor's software. If someone gives you a typed copy (an export), it is easier to share, but the typist may have skipped pages or misread smudges.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A capture file is not just text in a secret alphabet: it may contain raw per-lane symbol data, analyzer state, decoder settings, bookmarks and annotations, and an index database built by the software. "Reading" it means re-running a decoder whose output depends on the software version and settings — two versions can produce different decoded views from the same file.

78.3 Five things people call "the trace"

LayerWhat it isWho can read itFidelity
Raw packets / symbolsWhat the analyzer hardware recorded: per-lane symbols/blocks, timestamps, error flagsVendor software (sometimes partially exportable)Highest (within capture coverage)
File containerThe proprietary file that packages raw data plus metadata (settings, trigger, version info)Vendor software; generic tools see bytes onlyHighest; format undocumented publicly in general
Analyzer databaseIndex/decoded structures the software builds (sometimes as sidecar files) for fast viewsThe same software version familyDerived; may need rebuild on version change
Decoded protocol contentThe interpreted view: TLP fields, transactions, NVMe commandsShown in vendor softwareDepends on decoder version and configuration
Exported CSV/text/XMLA projection of the decoded content into a portable fileAnyoneLossy: selected columns, maybe filtered, maybe truncated payload, timestamp precision and base may change

78.4 Why capture formats are proprietary

  • They encode hardware-specific raw data (lane mapping, per-lane timestamps, analyzer error flags) that only make sense with that hardware's design.
  • They evolve with every software release (new protocol generations, new decoders, new metadata).
  • They embody vendor intellectual property (decoding pipeline, indexing).
  • Consequence: there is generally no public, official parser for such files; this book does not point to any, and you should be skeptical of unofficial converters — they may silently misinterpret data. If your vendor offers an SDK, automation API or command-line export for your version, use that and record its version version.

78.5 Identifying the producing tool and version — safely

# Work on a COPY. Never open the only original in tools that might "upgrade" it.
cp -p capture_0612.pex /evidence/work/
sha256sum capture_0612.pex > capture_0612.pex.sha256     # chain of custody
ls -l --time-style=full-iso capture_0612.pex               # size, mtime
file capture_0612.pex                                       # usually just "data"
xxd capture_0612.pex | head -16                             # header bytes (do not guess meanings)
strings -n 8 capture_0612.pex | head -40                    # readable strings may name tool/version

What you may learn: readable product or version strings, sometimes the capture date or the analyzer model. What you must not do: infer field layouts from a few bytes and write a "parser". The reliable sources are: the vendor software's file/capture information dialog (generic description; names vary), the lab notebook of whoever captured it, and sidecar files saved alongside (settings, notes).

78.6 Metadata that must travel with every capture

CategoryItems
InstrumentAnalyzer model, hardware/firmware version, software version used to capture and to export, licenses/decoders enabled
ProbeType (interposer form factor, mid-bus), placement (which link), cable lengths
LinkExpected and observed speed/width, lane reversal/polarity, clocking (common/SRIS), Flit mode, ASPM state
CaptureBuffer size, pre-trigger %, trigger definition, capture filters, segmentation, start/end time, overflow/lock-loss indicators
DecoderNVMe decode settings (queue bases if manually set), spec revision assumed
DUT / hostBDFs, device model and firmware (SN redacted), host platform/BIOS, kernel version, driver parameters, workload command line
CorrelationSync markers used, host log file names and hashes
HandlingSHA-256 of original, who captured, who has copies, confidentiality class

78.7 Exporting to a portable representation

  1. Open the capture (copy) in the vendor software version recorded in metadata (or a compatible later one — note any differences).
  2. Clear display filters, or deliberately set them and record them.
  3. Export packet-level rows with at least: timestamp (absolute or relative — record which), direction/link, packet type, requester ID, completer ID, address, tag, length, completion status, error flags, and header bytes if available. Exclude payload bytes unless needed and permitted.
  4. Export the vendor tool's own statistics (counts per packet type) for validation.
  5. Write a metadata JSON sidecar (§78.6).
  6. Normalize with a reviewed mapping (below) and compare counts.
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""normalize_export.py - map an analyzer's TEXT/CSV EXPORT to the normalized schema.
OFFLINE PARSING of a file you exported with the vendor's own software.
It does NOT read proprietary capture files: decoding those requires the
vendor's tools. Column names differ between tools and versions, so the
mapping lives in a small dict you edit after looking at the export header."""
import csv, io, json, sys, hashlib

SCHEMA = ["t_ns", "dir", "layer", "kind", "req", "addr", "tag", "len", "status"]

# Edit this mapping for YOUR export (keys = your column names). Example only.
MAPPING = {"Time Stamp": "t_ns", "Link Dir": "dir", "Packet": "kind",
           "Req ID": "req", "Address": "addr", "Tag": "tag",
           "Length": "len", "Status": "status"}
TIME_UNIT_NS = {"ns": 1, "us": 1_000, "ms": 1_000_000, "s": 1_000_000_000}
DIR_MAP = {"Upstream": "UP", "Downstream": "DN", "UP": "UP", "DN": "DN"}
DLL_KINDS = {"Ack", "Nak", "UpdateFC", "InitFC1", "InitFC2", "PM"}

def parse_time(text, default_unit="ns"):
    text = text.strip().replace(",", "")          # beware locale decimal commas!
    for unit in ("ns", "us", "ms", "s"):
        if text.endswith(unit):
            return round(float(text[:-len(unit)]) * TIME_UNIT_NS[unit])
    return round(float(text) * TIME_UNIT_NS[default_unit])

def normalize(fh, mapping=MAPPING):
    rows, problems = [], []
    reader = csv.DictReader(fh)
    missing = [c for c in mapping if c not in (reader.fieldnames or [])]
    if missing:
        problems.append(f"export lacks expected columns {missing} - wrong mapping or tool version?")
    for n, raw in enumerate(reader, 2):
        ev = {mapping[k]: v.strip() for k, v in raw.items() if k in mapping and v is not None}
        try:
            ev["t_ns"] = parse_time(ev["t_ns"])
            ev["dir"] = DIR_MAP.get(ev.get("dir", ""), "?")
            ev["layer"] = "DLL" if ev.get("kind") in DLL_KINDS else "TL"
            ev["addr"] = int(ev["addr"], 16) if ev.get("addr") else None
            ev["tag"] = int(ev["tag"], 16) if ev.get("tag") else None
            ev["len"] = int(ev["len"]) if ev.get("len") else 0
        except (KeyError, ValueError) as e:
            problems.append(f"line {n}: cannot normalize ({e}) -> kept out, review by hand")
            continue
        rows.append({k: ev.get(k) for k in SCHEMA})
    rows.sort(key=lambda r: r["t_ns"])
    return rows, problems

SAMPLE = """Time Stamp,Link Dir,Packet,Req ID,Address,Tag,Length,Status
0.000 us,Downstream,MWr,00:00.0,FE601008,,4,
0.420 us,Upstream,MRd,01:00.0,110010000,20,64,
1.130 us,Downstream,CplD,01:00.0,,20,64,SC
1.200 us,Upstream,Ack,,,,,
63.900 us,Upstream,MWr,01:00.0,120000000,,256,
bogus,Upstream,MWr,01:00.0,120000100,,256,
"""  # SYNTHETIC export, column names invented for this example

if __name__ == "__main__":
    data = open(sys.argv[1], newline="").read() if len(sys.argv) > 1 else SAMPLE
    print("sha256 of input:", hashlib.sha256(data.encode()).hexdigest()[:16], "... (record for chain of custody)")
    rows, problems = normalize(io.StringIO(data))
    counts = {}
    for r in rows:
        counts[r["kind"]] = counts.get(r["kind"], 0) + 1
    print("per-type counts (compare with the vendor tool's own statistics):", counts)
    for r in rows[:4]:
        print(json.dumps(r))
    for p in problems:
        print("PROBLEM:", p)

Output on the built-in synthetic export (column names invented for the example — your tool's will differ):

sha256 of input: adce953798ef543f ... (record for chain of custody)
per-type counts (compare with the vendor tool's own statistics): {'MWr': 2, 'MRd': 1, 'CplD': 1, 'Ack': 1}
{"t_ns": 0, "dir": "DN", "layer": "TL", "kind": "MWr", "req": "00:00.0", "addr": 4267708424, "tag": null, "len": 4, "status": ""}
{"t_ns": 420, "dir": "UP", "layer": "TL", "kind": "MRd", "req": "01:00.0", "addr": 4563468288, "tag": 32, "len": 64, "status": ""}
{"t_ns": 1130, "dir": "DN", "layer": "TL", "kind": "CplD", "req": "01:00.0", "addr": null, "tag": 32, "len": 64, "status": "SC"}
{"t_ns": 1200, "dir": "UP", "layer": "DLL", "kind": "Ack", "req": "", "addr": null, "tag": null, "len": 0, "status": ""}
PROBLEM: line 7: cannot normalize (could not convert string to float: 'bog') -> kept out, review by hand
⚠️ Conversion caveats
  • Dropped layers: exports often omit DLLPs, ordered sets and link-state events unless explicitly selected.
  • Timestamps: precision may be reduced; time base may be relative to trigger; per-direction or per-link clocks may be merged with unknown alignment.
  • Filters: active display filters may silently apply to exports.
  • Locale: decimal commas and thousands separators break naive parsers (the normalizer strips commas — check that this is correct for your locale!).
  • Truncation: payload columns may be truncated; long captures may be split into multiple files.
  • Version drift: column names and enumerations change across software versions — the mapping is versioned with the export.
  • Validation: per-type counts after normalization must equal the vendor tool's statistics for the same range; unparseable rows must be reported, never dropped silently (as the script does).

78.8 Captures and diagnostics from PCIe switches

Some PCIe switches — Broadcom PEX-family devices among them — provide diagnostic capabilities such as per-port error counters, performance/traffic counters, and in some families an internal packet-capture or trace facility, accessible through vendor management tools or in-band/out-of-band interfaces impl. The details (which families, buffer sizes, trigger options, file formats) are vendor documentation, frequently under NDA, so this book does not describe them. Conceptually:

AspectExternal link analyzerSwitch-internal capture / counters
IntrusivenessInterposer changes channelNo added channel; may perturb switch firmware/management load impl
Physical-layer visibilitySymbols, ordered sets, trainingTypically limited to counters/states the switch exposes
CoverageOne link per probePotentially many ports at once, as seen inside the switch
BufferLarge external memoryUsually small on-chip memory
TimestampsAnalyzer time baseSwitch clock; alignment with host/analyzer needs markers
Best forProving what crossed a specific linkBracketing faults inside the switch (TL-7), fleet-wide counters without hardware access
💡 Senior insight

In TL-7 a switch-internal view would answer "was the completion received on the upstream port and was it ever queued for the downstream port?" — the exact gap between the two external probes. When a switch is in the path, ask its vendor early which diagnostic features exist for your part and firmware; they can save weeks.

78.9 Data safety and sharing

A capture of a production host may contain user data in TLP payloads, encryption keys in transit (if not IDE-protected), file contents, and identifiers. Before sharing: export headers only where possible; zero or remove payloads; redact serial numbers (Identify data, DSN capability), host names and paths; and keep the original under access control with its hash. Share the original proprietary file only with parties who need it and are permitted to see it (e.g. the vendor under NDA).

78.10 Five capture-file failure patterns

#SymptomCause candidatesFirst checkDisambiguating stepConclusion (confidence)
1File will not openVersion mismatch, truncated transfer, missing sidecar filesHash vs original; sizeOpen with the recorded software versionUsually version/transfer (high)
2Export has fewer packets than the tool's statisticsDisplay filter applied, range limitedFilter stateExport with filters cleared, compare countsFilter (high)
3Latencies differ between colleagues' analysesDifferent time base or decoder versionsMetadataRe-export both with recorded settingsTooling difference (medium-high)
4NVMe decode differs between versionsDecoder updates / spec revision assumptionsRelease notesDecode with both, diff normalized outputVersion-dependent decode (high)
5Vendor says "we can't see the error in your file"Capture filters dropped it; wrong probe point; file is an export not a captureCoverage statementSend original capture + recipeEvidence handling (high)
🧪 Lab 78.1 — Evidence intake for an unknown capture (Beginner→Senior) SAFE

Classification: read-only inspection of files; non-destructive; production-safe.

Objective: receive a capture file from a colleague and produce an intake record.

  1. Copy, hash, record size and timestamps.
  2. strings/xxd inspection — note any tool/version strings; write "unknown" rather than guessing.
  3. Request missing metadata (§78.6) from the sender.
  4. Open in vendor software (if available) and export with cleared filters; save statistics.
  5. Normalize with normalize_export.py using a mapping written for that export; compare counts.
  6. Write a coverage statement (§74.2) and a redaction plan.

Questions: In the synthetic sample, which conclusion is impossible? What would you ask the sender?

Solution

With one malformed row dropped (reported), five events, and an unknown capture window, you cannot conclude anything about missing completions or interrupts. Ask for: analyzer/software version, filters (was MSI-X traffic kept?), capture start/end, probe point, and the original capture.

Extension: add a JSON metadata validator that refuses to run analysis scripts if required metadata fields are missing.

Quiz

  1. Name the five representations of "a trace".

    Answer

    Raw packets/symbols, file container, analyzer database, decoded protocol content, exported CSV/text/XML.

  2. Why compute a hash before anything else?

    Answer

    Chain of custody: proves later analyses used the unmodified original.

  3. What can a switch-internal capture show that an external analyzer on one link cannot?

    Answer

    Traffic at multiple ports/internal points simultaneously — e.g. whether a packet received upstream was queued for a downstream port.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate A customer sends a CSV export and says the device dropped a completion. Response?
    Model answer

    Ask for the original capture, tool versions, filters and probe point; an export cannot prove absence.

  2. Senior Someone found an open-source converter for your analyzer's file format. Use it?
    Model answer

    Only as a cross-check, after validating against vendor exports on known captures; never as sole evidence. Record its version and validation results.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can explain container vs decoded content vs database vs export vs raw packets.
  • I never invent a file format or parser; I use vendor tools and validate exports by counts.
  • I attach complete metadata and a coverage statement to every capture I share.
  • I can explain what a switch-internal capture adds and what it lacks.

Summary. Treat captures as forensic evidence: preserve, identify, export deterministically, validate, redact, and state what the representation can and cannot show. Next: the debugging method that turns evidence into root cause.

PART XXVI

Debugging Methodology

Protocol knowledge tells you what should happen. Methodology is what gets you from "it hangs sometimes" to a fix that provably works. This Part makes one habit automatic: separate what you observed from what you inferred from what you merely suspect, and do not call anything a root cause until evidence has eliminated the alternatives.

79 The Debugging Framework: Observation, Inference, Hypothesis, Evidence, Root Cause

← 78 Capture Files, PEX, and Portable Trace Evidence80 Decision Tree, Debugging by Layer, Evidence Escalation and the Cross-Layer Lab →

79.1 Why this chapter exists

The most expensive debugging mistakes are not technical. They are: fixing the first plausible cause and declaring victory; confusing "happened before" with "caused"; reasoning from a trace whose coverage nobody checked; and changing three things at once. A framework is a defence against your own cleverness.

  • Beginner: label every statement in a bug discussion as observation, inference or hypothesis.
  • Intermediate: walk the 12-step framework from symptom to regression test.
  • Advanced: design eliminating experiments that change exactly one variable.
  • Senior: grade confidence explicitly and write reports others can audit.
  • Debugging / validation: every fix ships with a regression test that failed before the fix.

Prerequisites: Trace Academy rules, kernel logs.

79.2 The framework

StepQuestionTypical artefactClassic failure
1 SymptomWhat exactly did someone observe, where, how often?Reproduction rate, exact error text, environmentAccepting "it's slow" without numbers
2 TimelineWhat happened in which order, on one time base?Merged log/trace timeline with sync markersMixing clocks
3 Expected behaviorWhat should have happened?Golden trace, spec sequenceSkipping — then nothing looks abnormal
4 First deviationEarliest observation that departs from expectedMarked row / log lineChoosing the loudest event
5 LayerWhich layer owns the stage where the deviation occurred?Layer table (Ch 80)Assigning by reporting component instead of owning component
6 EvidenceWhat evidence exists / can be collected for that layer?Logs, counters, capturesCollecting everything instead of what discriminates
7 HypothesesWhat could cause this deviation?Ranked list, each falsifiableOnly one hypothesis
8 EliminationWhich experiment kills which hypothesis?One-variable experiments, swap testsChanging several variables at once
9 Root causeWhich surviving hypothesis explains all observations?Causal chain, confidenceIgnoring observations that don't fit
10 FixWhat change removes the cause (not the symptom)?Patch, config, hardware changeIncreasing a timeout to hide a hang
11 Regression testWhat automatically fails without the fix?Test that reproduces the trigger conditionTest that passes on the broken build too
12 Golden updateDoes the golden reference need an update?New versioned golden traceGolden traces silently drifting

79.3 The five habits

HabitDefinitionExample statement
ObservationWhat we actually know: directly recorded, with source and scope"dmesg at 931.100 s: I/O tag 23 QID 3 timeout." "Trace (both directions, no filters, 0–2 s): no CplD for MRd tag 0x2a."
InferenceWhat logically follows from observations and protocol rules"Since the SQE was never delivered, the controller could not have executed CID 0x17."
HypothesisWhat might be happening; must predict something testable"The switch drops completions under mixed load — predicts the CplD is visible upstream but not downstream."
EvidenceWhat would prove or disprove the hypothesis"A second probe on the upstream link during the next failure."
Root causeThe most likely explanation after elimination, with confidence"Switch firmware drops CplD when … (high confidence: reproduced 5/5, fixed with FW x.y, regression passes)."
🧒 Kid analogy — the detective notebook

A good detective's notebook has three columns: "I saw" (muddy boots by the door), "So" (someone came in from the garden), "Maybe" (the gardener? the dog-walker?). She never writes "the gardener did it" in the first column. And before arresting anyone she checks: did the dog-walker have muddy boots too?

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In engineering you can usually re-run the crime: reproduce the failure under controlled changes. That makes elimination far stronger than in detective stories — and makes skipping it inexcusable.

79.4 Worked exercise: the slow Gen5 drive

Symptom: "New Gen5 SSD reaches only 6.8 GB/s sequential read; datasheet says ~14 GB/s."

CategoryStatements
Observationfio seqread 128k QD32 numjobs=1: 6.8 GB/s. lspci -vv on the SSD: LnkCap Speed 32GT/s, Width x4, LnkSta Speed 16GT/s (downgraded), Width x4; on the root port: LnkCap Speed 16GT/s. CPU usage of the fio thread 100 %.
InferenceThe link is Gen4 x4 because the root port only supports 16 GT/s → payload ceiling ~7 GB/s (Chapter 90). The observed 6.8 GB/s is consistent with the link ceiling. CPU 100 % is a second potential limit.
HypothesesH1 platform Gen4 port limits link (strong); H2 single fio job CPU-bound (possible); H3 drive thermally throttling (weak: no data).
EvidenceMove drive to a Gen5-capable port (H1); run numjobs=4 with the same total QD (H2); log temperature and throughput over 10 min (H3).
Root causeAfter moving to a Gen5 port: 13.1 GB/s with numjobs=4, 9.5 GB/s with numjobs=1 → H1 primary, H2 secondary. Confidence high (two one-variable experiments).

79.5 Correlation is not causation (performance causality)

Latency rose after a PCIe Recovery event. Did the Recovery cause it? Possible structures: (a) Recovery → stall → latency (causal); (b) a third factor causes both — e.g. temperature raises both link errors and NAND read-retry rates; (c) coincidence in a noisy system. Evidence for causality: temporal precision (latency spike begins within microseconds of the Recovery, not seconds); mechanism (Recovery duration explains the spike's magnitude); intervention (removing Recovery — lower speed, better channel — removes spikes); dose-response (more Recoveries → proportionally more spikes). Require at least intervention before claiming cause.

79.6 Device-specific limitations

🏭 Implementation-dependent

Two NVMe SSDs that expose the same standard interface may differ in firmware, NAND type and generation, controller architecture, DRAM or HMB-based mapping caches, internal scheduling, garbage-collection policy, thermal behavior and power management. Standard-visible behavior (latency distributions, throughput curves) is the output of all of these. Do not infer internal architecture — "it must be GC", "the cache is 8 GB" — from external behavior without evidence such as vendor telemetry, controlled preconditioning experiments, or vendor confirmation. Say "consistent with" rather than "is".

79.7 Analyzer and log limitations as evidence rules

  • A trace is evidence with scope: filtering, capture gaps, dropped packets, timestamp limits, decoder limits, version-dependent UI, proprietary annotations (Chapter 77).
  • A log is evidence of what was detected and printed, not of everything that happened (Chapter 71).
  • A counter is evidence of how many, not when — sample it over time.
  • Absence of evidence counts only within proven coverage.

79.8 Bug report template

TITLE        : <layer>: <observable failure> when <condition>
ENVIRONMENT  : platform/BIOS, kernel, driver params, device model + FW (SN redacted), link Gen/width/MPS
REPRODUCTION : workload command, rate (k/N runs), time to failure
COVERAGE     : evidence sources, capture start/end, filters, directions, versions
OBSERVATIONS : numbered, each with source + timestamp
FIRST DEVIATION : which observation, why it is the first
INFERENCES   : each citing observation numbers and the rule applied
HYPOTHESES   : ranked; for each: prediction, evidence for/against, status (open/eliminated)
ROOT CAUSE   : (or "not yet determined") + confidence + remaining doubts
FIX / WORKAROUND : what changed
REGRESSION TEST  : how it fails before / passes after
ATTACHMENTS  : logs + hashes, exports + metadata, golden trace reference

79.9 Debugging exercises

🎯 Exercise 79.1 — Classify the statements SAFE

Label each: (a) "The SSD is overheating." (b) "smart-log temperature: 352 K at 10:02, 341 K at 09:50." (c) "Throughput dropped 40 % at 10:01." (d) "Thermal throttling would reduce throughput." (e) "The drive firmware throttles at 350 K."

Answer

(a) hypothesis; (b) observation (352 K ≈ 79 °C); (c) observation (needs source: fio log?); (d) inference from general knowledge — but becomes a hypothesis about this case; (e) a claim about implementation — unverified unless from vendor documentation or WCTEMP + throttling counters (impl).

🎯 Exercise 79.2 — Full framework on a reset loop SAFE
