Symptom: after a firmware update on a lab drive, the host logs a controller reset every ~2 minutes. dmesg shows I/O ... timeout, reset controller each time, no AER. smart-log: num_err_log_entries unchanged. Error log: empty. Write Observation / Inference / Hypothesis / Evidence / Root cause.

Model answer

Observation: periodic timeouts (≈120 s), resets succeed, no AER, no new error-log entries, began after FW update. Inference: link-level errors unlikely to be reported (no AER); controller did not consider any command errored; commands are not completing within io_timeout (30 s), i.e. something stalls ≥30 s every 2 min — or completions are not noticed. Hypotheses: H1 new FW stalls during a periodic internal task (e.g. background operation) >30 s; H2 interrupt delivery broken for one vector after FW change (CQEs posted, not signalled); H3 APST/power-state transition in new FW has long exit latency; H4 host-side change coincident with FW update. Evidence: kernel message "completion polled" would support H2; disable APST (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0, lab only) for H3; analyzer: does the CQE exist before the timeout? (H1 vs H2); roll back FW keeping host identical (H4). Root cause: chosen only after these; report confidence.

🎯 Exercise 79.3 — Spot the causality error SAFE

"We saw 12 corrected Receiver Errors last night and the database had 3 latency spikes; therefore the link causes the spikes." Critique.

Answer

No temporal alignment shown (do the spikes coincide within microseconds–milliseconds with errors?), no mechanism magnitude (a corrected error costs a replay of ~µs, not ms), no intervention. Likely coincidence or common cause; collect per-event timestamps and test by eliminating errors.

Quiz

  1. At which step do hypotheses first appear?

    Answer

    Step 7, after the first deviation, layer and available evidence are established.

  2. What makes a hypothesis useful?

    Answer

    It predicts an observation that an experiment can confirm or refute.

  3. Why must the regression test fail before the fix?

    Answer

    Otherwise it does not exercise the failure condition and proves nothing.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate How do you avoid changing multiple variables?
    Model answer

    Plan experiments as a table: baseline, one change per run, repeat enough to beat variance; record everything else as fixed.

  2. Senior A manager wants a root cause today; you have two surviving hypotheses. What do you report?
    Model answer

    Both, ranked, with the evidence for each, the experiment and time needed to decide, and a safe interim mitigation that works under both.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I separate observation, inference and hypothesis in every written analysis.
  • I can walk all 12 steps for any failure in the library.
  • I demand intervention evidence before asserting causality.
  • I can write a bug report using the template.

80 Decision Tree, Debugging by Layer, Evidence Escalation and the Cross-Layer Lab

← 79 The Debugging Framework: Observation, Inference, Hypothesis, Evidence, Root Cause81 Failure Library I: Physical and Data Link Layer →

80.1 Why this chapter exists

With twelve layers between an application and a NAND die, knowing where to look next is half the job. This chapter gives a diagnostic heuristic (decision tree), a layer-by-layer table, an evidence-escalation ladder, and a cross-layer capstone.

  • Intermediate: use the decision tree to choose the next check.
  • Advanced: map symptoms to layers with typical evidence and next checks.
  • Senior: plan evidence escalation: what each additional source makes possible, and its cost.

80.2 The debugging decision tree

⚠️ A heuristic, not a law

This tree orders checks from cheapest/most fundamental to most specific. Real failures can involve several layers simultaneously, and some evidence (e.g. a lost interrupt) appears healthy at lower layers. Use it to choose the next check, not to conclude.

80.3 Debugging by layer

LayerTypical symptomEvidenceTypical next check
ApplicationSlow requests, errors returned to userApp logs, request tracingDoes the I/O reach the kernel? (strace/syscall latency)
Filesystemfsync latency, journal stalls, ENOSPC, corruption reportsFS logs, /proc/fs stats, fsckRaw-device test to bypass FS
Block layerQueueing delay, request merging/splitting, scheduler effectsiostat -x, blktrace/btt, /sys/block/*/queueCompare Q2D (queue→dispatch) vs D2C (dispatch→complete)
DriverTimeouts, resets, wrong queue mapping, interrupt handlingdmesg, driver tracepoints (nvme:*), /proc/interruptsIs the completion visible in the CQ? (polled message, tracepoints)
NVMe (command set / controller)Error status, namespace not ready, slow commandsCQE status, error log, SMART, telemetryDecode SCT/SC; correlate SQID/CID with error log
Transport (NVMe over PCIe)Doorbell/queue misuse, PRP/SGL errors, CMB issuesAnalyzer NVMe view, Async EventsDoorbell addresses vs CAP.DSTRD; PRP rules
PCIe TransactionUR/CA, Completion Timeout, Malformed, PoisonedAER uncorrectable, logged TLP header, analyzer transaction viewDecode TLP header; check MPS/MRRS, IOMMU, routing
PCIe Data LinkReplays, Bad TLP/DLLP, replay timeouts, rolloversAER correctable, analyzer DLLP viewError rate trend; temperature; slot swap
PCIe PhysicalNo link, downtraining, Receiver Errors, Recovery stormsLnkSta, LTSSM capture, lane marginingPort vs device LnkCap; channel/connector; force lower speed
FirmwareHangs, CFS, regressions after update, long latency tailsfw-log, CSTS, vendor telemetry, reproduction vs FW versionFW A/B test on identical host
MediaUnrecovered read errors, read-retry latency, wear-outSMART media_errors, error log (SCT 2h), vendor logsSame-LBA reproducibility; rewrite-and-reread test (lab drive only)

80.4 "What would you capture?" — evidence escalation

If you have…You can knowYou still cannot knowCost
OS logs onlyHost-detected events and their order: timeouts, resets, AER reports, removalsWhere the command chain broke; device internals; unreported link eventsFree
+ NVMe logs (SMART, error log, features, telemetry)Whether the controller saw errors, media health, temperature, configurationTiming on the link; transport-level lossLow
+ PCIe analyzerExactly what crossed the probed link: doorbells, fetches, data, CQEs, interrupts, replays, trainingController-internal reasons; host-internal processing; other linksHigh (hardware, setup, lab access)
+ Controller firmware logs (vendor)Internal state machines, media operations, error recovery stepsHost side; depends on vendor support/NDAMedium–high (vendor engagement)
+ Hardware signals (scope on PERST#, power rails, refclk; thermal sensors)Power integrity, reset timing, clock problems, electrical marginsProtocol meaning (combine with analyzer via cross-trigger)High (probing, expertise)
💡 Senior insight — escalate deliberately

Each step up the ladder should answer a question the previous step raised. "We captured everything" is not a plan; "the OS log shows a Completion Timeout from the SSD as requester, so we need the analyzer to see whether the root complex ever sent the CplD" is.

80.5 Practice: what would you capture?

ProblemFirst evidenceEscalate to
Drive missing after bootlspci (enumerated?), dmesg probe errorsAnalyzer on link training (does it reach L0?); scope on PERST#/power
Periodic 30 s stallsdmesg timeout lines, "completion polled"?Analyzer with CQE-not-followed-by-MSI-X trigger
Throughput 50 % lowLnkSta, MPS, fio CPU usage, NUMAAnalyzer traffic statistics (payload sizes, outstanding requests)
Rare unrecovered read errorsError log + SMART media_errorsVendor FW logs; same-LBA tests on a lab copy
Corrected error stormsAER counters per device over time, temperatureAnalyzer DLLP view; lane margining; hardware swap

80.6 Cross-layer lab: "Read occasionally takes 10 seconds"

🧪 Lab 80.1 — Which layer owns the 10-second read? SAFE

Classification: offline analysis of synthetic evidence; non-destructive.

Scenario. A database reports that roughly once an hour a single 16 KiB read takes about 10 s. No application errors. You have four evidence sources (synthetic).

1. OS log (journalctl -k, the hour around one event at 14:02:11):

13:41:07 nvme 0000:01:00.0: AER: Corrected error received: 0000:01:00.0
13:41:07 nvme 0000:01:00.0: PCIe Bus Error: severity=Corrected, type=Physical Layer, (Receiver ID)
13:41:07 nvme 0000:01:00.0:    [ 0] RxErr
(no nvme timeout, reset or I/O error messages between 13:00 and 15:00)

2. NVMe logs (before/after the hour): smart-log media_errors unchanged (0 → 0); num_err_log_entries unchanged; temperature 318–321 K; percentage_used 2 %. Feature 05h (Error Recovery) Time-Limited Error Recovery field = 0 (no limit) impl.

3. PCIe trace (segmented captures triggered by a host bpftrace watchdog that marks any read older than 1 s):

SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · Lab 80.1 slow read
Time sDirLayerTypeRequesterCompleterAddressTagLenMeaning
0.000000DNTLMWr00:00.0—FE601010—4SQ2 tail doorbell
0.0000004UPTLMRd01:00.0—(SQ2 slot 17)0x4464SQE fetch
0.0000011DNTLCplD01:00.000:00.0—0x4464Read, CID 0x91, SLBA 0x2F00_1000, NLB 31
0.000100————————expected data by ~100 µs (golden); none
0.0001–9.97bothTL/DLL…—————other commands on other queues complete normally; no Nak, no Recovery, no error TLPs
9.971000UPTLMWr ×6401:00.0—(PRP pages)—25616 KiB data
9.971400UPTLMWr01:00.0—(CQ2 slot)—16CQE CID 0x91, status success
9.971550UPTLMWr01:00.0—FEE0_0000—4MSI-X

4. Performance counters: iostat -x 1 shows r_await spike to ~10,000 ms for one interval, %util normal; CPU idle 70 %; blktrace for the request: Q→D 4 µs, D→C 9.97 s. Over a week, the slow reads always hit LBAs in the range 0x2F00_0000–0x2F10_0000 (data written ~11 months ago, rarely read).

Questions. (1) Which layer owns the delay? (2) What role does the 13:41 RxErr play? (3) What is the most likely mechanism, and how confident can you be? (4) What experiment would raise confidence? (5) What mitigation and regression test do you propose?

Hints

Use blktrace phases to split host from device. Use the trace to split link from controller. Use the LBA pattern.

Solution

Observations: host queueing 4 µs, device time 9.97 s (blktrace D→C); on the link, the SQE was fetched within ~1 µs, data appeared after 9.97 s, no link-level errors in the capture window, other queues progressed; CQE status success; no media_errors increment; slow reads cluster on old, rarely-read LBAs; one corrected RxErr 21 minutes earlier.

Inferences: host software and PCIe transport are not the owners (the command reached the controller promptly; the link carried other traffic normally). The delay lies inside the controller between SQE receipt and data transfer: controller firmware / media layer. Success status with no media-error increment means the data was eventually recovered.

(2) The RxErr is a distractor: 21 minutes earlier, corrected, and the slow command's capture shows no link errors. Correlation without temporal or mechanistic link.

(3) Hypothesis (medium confidence): media-level error recovery on aged data (e.g. extensive read-retry / soft-decode steps on cells whose charge drifted), allowed to run long because no time-limited error recovery is configured. This is consistent with the evidence but the internal mechanism is not observable via the standard interface impl. Alternatives: firmware internal lock/contention affecting that LBA range; background operation on the same die.

(4) Experiments: on a lab copy (never production): read the slow range repeatedly — is it consistently slow? Rewrite the range and re-read — does latency normalize? Request vendor telemetry / read-retry counters (vendor-specific logs). If supported, set a time-limited error recovery value on a lab drive and observe whether the command now fails fast with an error instead of succeeding late.

(5) Mitigation: application/storage-level: background scrubbing (periodic reads) or vendor-recommended data refresh; configure time-limited error recovery where appropriate for redundant systems (fail fast, read from replica) impl. Regression test: a scrub job plus a latency SLO monitor on p99.99 per LBA region; in qualification, an aging test (retention bake per vendor guidance) followed by full-range read latency histogram with a maximum-latency threshold.

Owner layer: NVMe controller firmware/media.

Quiz

  1. In the decision tree, what comes after "command status is successful"?

    Answer

    Interrupt/completion delivery to the host, then software processing.

  2. blktrace shows Q→D = 9 s, D→C = 80 µs. Which half owns the delay?

    Answer

    The host side before dispatch (block layer queueing, scheduler, tag exhaustion) — not the device.

  3. What new knowledge does controller firmware logging add over a PCIe analyzer?

    Answer

    Internal state: why the controller was slow or failed (media operations, internal errors), which the link cannot show.

Interview questions

  1. Advanced Walk the decision tree for "device occasionally disappears".
    Model answer

    Link: does it go down (pciehp Link Down, DPC, Surprise Down)? If yes, physical/power/reset investigation with analyzer training capture and scope on power/PERST#. If the link stays up but CSTS reads all-ones, the device stopped responding — firmware/hardware hang. Escalate accordingly.

  2. Senior Which evidence would you collect first for a fleet-wide intermittent issue and why?
    Model answer

    Cheap, scalable evidence: kernel logs, AER counters, SMART/error-log deltas, FW versions, platform versions — to find correlations by population; then targeted analyzer captures on a reproducing unit.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can use the decision tree to pick the next check and explain why it is a heuristic.
  • I can map any symptom to layer, evidence and next check.
  • I can justify each evidence escalation by the question it answers.
  • I solved the cross-layer lab and can defend the owner layer with observations.
PART XXVII

Failure Library

A troubleshooting encyclopedia of 30 failure patterns, organized from the wire upward: physical and data link (Chapter 81), transaction layer and AER (Chapter 82), NVMe (Chapter 83), and system-level interrupts, performance, power and reset (Chapter 84). Every entry uses the same card: symptoms · likely layers · trace signature · Linux evidence · NVMe evidence · PCIe evidence · first check · disambiguating experiment · likely root causes · remediation · regression test. Trace signatures are synthetic descriptions of what an analyzer would typically show; status-code names follow the NVMe Base Specification — confirm exact code points in the revision you work with.

81 Failure Library I: Physical and Data Link Layer

← 80 Decision Tree, Debugging by Layer, Evidence Escalation and the Cross-Layer Lab82 Failure Library II: Transaction Layer and AER →

81.1 Why this chapter exists — and how to use the library

Under pressure you need pattern recognition plus discipline. The cards give you the pattern; the "first check" and "disambiguating experiment" rows enforce the discipline (Chapter 79). Use them as starting hypotheses, never as conclusions: every card's "likely root causes" are ranked by typical frequency in practice, which is impl-dependent and varies by platform.

  • Recognize each link-level failure from Linux, NVMe and PCIe evidence.
  • Name the first check and the experiment that separates the top two causes.
  • Propose remediation and a regression test.
🧒 Kid analogy — the doctor's symptom book

A doctor's book says "fever + rash + sore throat: maybe A, maybe B; first take temperature, then do test X to tell them apart". It does not say "it is A". This library is that book for SSD links and queues.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Patients rarely let you swap their organs; you can swap drives, slots, cables and firmware. Use swap experiments generously — they are the cheapest disambiguators in hardware debugging.

F1 — Link never reaches L0

SymptomsDevice absent from lspci; or present only after rescan; BIOS does not see the drive
Likely layersPhysical (power, reset, refclk, lanes), device firmware boot
Trace signatureReceiver detect repeatedly; TS1s without progressing to TS2/Configuration; or no electrical activity from the device at all; LTSSM cycling Detect ↔ Polling
Linux evidenceNothing for the device; port may log pciehp ... Link Down or nothing; lspci -vv on the root port: LnkSta shows training or Width x0 / DLActive- (if Data Link Layer Link Active reporting is supported)
NVMe evidenceNone (controller never reachable)
PCIe evidencePort Link Status; port AER (Surprise Down if it was up before)
First checkPower and seating; same drive in a known-good slot; another drive in this slot
Disambiguating experimentSwap test (fails with drive or with slot?); analyzer/scope: is PERST# deasserted, refclk present, does the device transmit TS1?
Likely root causesBad connector/riser/cable; missing refclk or wrong clocking mode (SRIS vs common); PERST# timing; device firmware not booting (dead drive); slot disabled/bifurcation misconfigured in BIOS
RemediationHardware repair/replacement; BIOS slot/bifurcation fix; clocking configuration; RMA drive
Regression test500 cold boots + 500 warm resets: device enumerates at expected speed/width every time

F2 — Intermittent link Recovery

SymptomsThroughput dips, latency blips, sometimes no visible symptom; occasionally escalates to link down
Likely layersPhysical (signal integrity, equalization, clocking), Data Link
Trace signatureL0 → Recovery (TS1/TS2) → L0, often preceded by bad LCRC TLPs, Naks, or receiver errors; possibly speed change attempts
Linux evidenceAER correctable RxErr/BadTLP/Replay Timer Timeout; rising aer_dev_correctable
NVMe evidenceUsually none (lossless recovery); latency tail
PCIe evidenceLink Status 2/equalization status bits (if exposed), Lane Error Status in Secondary PCIe extended cap
First checkCorrectable error rate vs time and temperature; which side reports (receiver side)
Disambiguating experimentForce lower speed (lab) — errors vanish? Swap slot/drive/cable; lane margining per lane if supported
Likely root causesMarginal channel (loss, crosstalk, connector), poor equalization presets, retimer issues, refclk jitter/SSC mismatch, power noise
RemediationChannel fix, retimer firmware/config, equalization tuning by platform vendor, clocking fix
Regression test24–72 h stress across temperature corners; Recovery count and correctable error rate below threshold

F3 — Width downgrade

SymptomsSequential throughput roughly halves (x4 → x2) or quarters; kernel "limited by ... x2 link" message
Likely layersPhysical lanes, slot wiring/bifurcation
Trace signatureDuring Configuration, lanes 2–3 fail detect or never send TS with matching link/lane numbers; link forms x2
Linux evidenceLnkSta Width x2 vs LnkCap x4; probe-time bandwidth message
NVMe evidenceNone
PCIe evidencePort and device LnkCap/LnkSta; Lane Error Status
First checkPort LnkCap width and platform slot documentation (is the slot physically x2?)
Disambiguating experimentSwap drive and slot; inspect connector; analyzer training capture to see which lanes fail
Likely root causesSlot wired x2 or bifurcated; damaged/dirty lanes; riser/cable fault; lane reversal unsupported in a particular routing
RemediationCorrect slot/BIOS setting; hardware repair
Regression testBoot-time check script comparing width to expected inventory; alert on mismatch

F4 — Speed downgrade

SymptomsThroughput ceiling at a lower generation's value; (downgraded) in lspci
Likely layersPhysical (equalization), policy (target speed), platform capability
Trace signatureSpeed change attempts via Recovery, equalization phases failing, fallback to lower rate; or no attempt at all (policy)
Linux evidenceLnkSta speed < min(port, device LnkCap); LnkCtl2 target speed
NVMe evidenceNone
PCIe evidenceLnkCtl2 target, Link Status 2 equalization-complete bits version
First checkPort LnkCap and LnkCtl2 target on both ends (policy or capability?)
Disambiguating experimentIf target speed is max: capture training to see equalization failure vs no attempt; swap slot/drive
Likely root causesPlatform limit (not a fault); BIOS speed cap; channel too lossy for the rate; retimer config; device EQ bug
RemediationBIOS setting, channel improvement, firmware updates
Regression testExpected-speed check after every boot/resume/reset in qualification

F5 — Receiver errors

SymptomsAER corrected RxErr messages; possibly no user-visible effect
Likely layersPhysical
Trace signatureAnalyzer symbol/framing errors on one direction; followed by Nak or Recovery
Linux evidence[ 0] RxErr, reporting device identifies the receiving side; aer_dev_correctable
NVMe evidenceNone
PCIe evidenceAER Correctable Status bit 0 (sticky until cleared)
First checkRate and direction (which device reports)
Disambiguating experimentSwap the transmitter side component; temperature sweep; lower speed
Likely root causesChannel margin, transmitter EQ, receiver CDR, interposer (if probing!)
RemediationAs F2; remove interposer and compare
Regression testError-rate threshold over a long soak

F6 — Bad DLLP

SymptomsCorrected BadDLLP errors; occasionally sluggish flow control
Likely layersData Link (CRC on DLLPs), Physical underneath
Trace signatureDLLPs (Ack/UpdateFC) with CRC errors; missing Acks lead to replay timer expiry
Linux evidenceAER correctable bit 7 BadDLLP
NVMe evidenceNone
PCIe evidenceAER status; analyzer DLLP view
First checkCo-occurrence with RxErr/BadTLP (common physical cause)
Disambiguating experimentSame as F2/F5
Likely root causesSignal integrity; rarely a DLLP generation bug
RemediationAs F2
Regression testAs F2

F7 — Replay: timeouts and REPLAY_NUM rollover

SymptomsCorrected Replay Timer Timeout / REPLAY_NUM Rollover; throughput dips; rollovers trigger Recovery
Likely layersData Link
Trace signatureTLPs transmitted, no Ack within replay timer, same sequence numbers retransmitted; after repeated replays, Recovery
Linux evidenceAER bits 12 (Timeout) / 8 (Rollover) reported by the transmitter
NVMe evidenceLatency tail
PCIe evidenceAER; analyzer shows missing/bad Acks in the opposite direction
First checkAre Acks lost (opposite-direction errors) or never sent (receiver problem)?
Disambiguating experimentCapture both directions: look for corrupted Acks vs absent Acks
Likely root causesReverse-direction signal integrity; receiver that cannot keep up / bug; misconfigured Ack latency timer impl
RemediationFix reverse channel; firmware fix
Regression testSoak with replay counters (if accessible) or AER rates

Quiz

  1. Replay Timer Timeout is reported by which side?

    Answer

    The transmitter of the unacknowledged TLPs.

  2. LnkSta x2 on an x4 device. First check?

    Answer

    The port's LnkCap and the platform's slot wiring/bifurcation.

82 Failure Library II: Transaction Layer and AER

← 81 Failure Library I: Physical and Data Link Layer83 Failure Library III: NVMe Queues, Commands, Media and Firmware →

Transaction-layer failures change what software sees: data that never arrives, requests that are refused, payloads marked bad. Unlike most link errors they are uncorrectable and propagate up as NVMe errors, timeouts or containment events.

  • Decode the logged TLP header of each uncorrectable error.
  • Identify requester vs completer responsibility.
  • Choose between configuration, routing, IOMMU and device bugs.

F8 — Malformed TLP

SymptomsUncorrectable (often fatal by default severity) error; link reset or DPC containment; device disappears
Likely layersTransaction (transmitter bug or configuration mismatch)
Trace signatureTLP whose fields violate rules: payload > MPS, Length vs actual payload mismatch, 4DW header with zero upper address, crossing a 4 KiB boundary in a memory request, invalid byte enables
Linux evidenceAER Uncorrected MalfTLP, logged TLP header (decode with Lab 2), DPC/link reset messages
NVMe evidenceSubsequent timeouts/reset
PCIe evidenceReceiver's AER Header Log; DevCtl MPS on both ends
First checkDecode the header log; compare payload size with MPS programmed at the receiver
Disambiguating experimentRead MPS on every device in the path at failure time; reproduce with MPS forced to the path minimum (lab)
Likely root causesMPS mismatch after hot-plug or reconfiguration; transmitter bug splitting at wrong boundary; switch bug
RemediationConsistent MPS policy; firmware fix
Regression testHot-plug and MPS-variation matrix with large transfers; zero MalfTLP

F9 — Completion timeout

SymptomsAER CmpltTO; NVMe command timeouts ~io_timeout later; data transfer errors
Likely layersTransaction (completer, routing, switch), sometimes IOMMU/root complex, sometimes Data Link (lost completions after link issues)
Trace signatureNon-Posted request (MRd) with no CplD for its (Requester ID, Tag) within the timeout range; possibly a late CplD flagged as Unexpected Completion
Linux evidence[14] CmpltTO from the requester (the SSD for DMA reads; the root port for MMIO reads); TLP header may be logged
NVMe evidenceTimeouts, Data Transfer Error statuses
PCIe evidenceDevCtl2 timeout range; AER
First checkWho is the requester? Decode the address: SQ, PRP list, data buffer, or an MMIO register?
Disambiguating experimentTwo-probe capture (TL-7) to localize where the completion is lost; IOMMU fault logs; check whether the completer was in a low-power or reset state
Likely root causesCompletion dropped in a switch/RC; completer hung; completion timeout value too short for the platform; device in D3/reset while host accessed MMIO
RemediationFirmware fix in the component that loses it; adjust timeout range (with care); fix power-management ordering
Regression testMixed-load soak with completion-timeout counters; Lab 9 detector over captures

F10 — Unsupported Request (UR)

SymptomsDMA failures, IOMMU faults, NVMe Data Transfer Errors; or host MMIO reads returning all-ones
Likely layersTransaction (address decode), IOMMU, host driver
Trace signatureRequest answered by Cpl with status UR (Non-Posted), or a Posted write silently dropped with error logged at the completer
Linux evidenceAER UnsupReq; DMAR/AMD-Vi IOMMU fault lines
NVMe evidenceCQE status Data Transfer Error or similar impl
PCIe evidenceAER header log contains the offending address
First checkDecode address; is it a valid, mapped IOVA / BAR address?
Disambiguating experimentInstrument DMA map/unmap; run with IOMMU strict mode; compare with IOMMU passthrough (lab)
Likely root causesUse-after-unmap (TL-5), wrong IOVA, BAR not assigned / Memory Space disabled, device accessing after reset
RemediationDriver lifetime fixes; resource assignment fix
Regression testIOMMU-strict stress with fault injection on timeouts

F11 — Poisoned transaction

SymptomsAER PoisonedTLP; NVMe write fails or read data flagged; host memory error logs (machine check)
Likely layersHost memory subsystem or device internal memory errors, forwarded as poisoned data
Trace signatureTLP with EP=1 (CplD to the SSD for write data, or MWr from the SSD for read data)
Linux evidenceAER PoisonedTLP, EDAC/MCE memory errors
NVMe evidenceError status on the affected command; possibly controller internal error logs
PCIe evidenceEP bit in header log
First checkDirection: who generated the poisoned TLP?
Disambiguating experimentCorrelate with host memory errors (host origin) vs device internal error counters (device origin)
Likely root causesUncorrectable DRAM error on host; device internal SRAM/DRAM error
RemediationReplace faulty memory; device RMA
Regression testMemory test; device burn-in with data verification

F12 — AER storm / uncorrectable error with containment

SymptomsThousands of AER messages; system sluggish; device reset/containment (DPC); possible removal
Likely layersAny; storm usually physical (corrected) or a repeating transaction error
Trace signatureContinuous error condition plus ERR_COR/ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_FATAL messages upstream
Linux evidenceRate-limited AER lines; DPC containment events; error-recovery callbacks ("frozen state", reset)
NVMe evidenceTimeouts during recovery; controller re-initialization
PCIe evidenceAER counters, header logs, DPC status
First checkFirst error in the storm (earliest timestamp) and its type
Disambiguating experimentMask correctable reporting temporarily (lab) to see if the system stabilizes — confirms storm-induced load vs real fault effects
Likely root causesPhysical layer degradation; device stuck repeating an erroneous request; misconfigured severity
RemediationFix underlying cause; error-rate thresholds; platform firmware-first policy review
Regression testError injection (where the platform supports it) with recovery validation

Quiz

  1. Which field of an AER message most directly localizes a transaction-layer bug?

    Answer

    The logged TLP header (address, requester, tag, type).

  2. Completion timeout reported by the root port: what kind of access failed?

    Answer

    A host-initiated Non-Posted request — typically an MMIO read or config read to the device.

83 Failure Library III: NVMe Queues, Commands, Media and Firmware

← 82 Failure Library II: Transaction Layer and AER84 Failure Library IV: Interrupts, Performance, Power and Reset →

NVMe-layer failures live in the contract between host memory structures (queues, PRPs, SGLs) and controller behavior. Your best tools are the Lab 3–8 decoders, the error log, and an analyzer that saw queue creation.

  • Locate the broken stage of the command chain.
  • Use CQE status, error log and Async Events as first-class evidence.
  • Separate host data-structure bugs from controller bugs from media problems.

F13 — Missing NVMe completion

SymptomsI/O ... timeout, aborts, resets; application hangs ~30 s
Likely layersAny stage: doorbell, fetch, controller, CQE posting, interrupt, host processing
Trace signatureChain stops at a stage (Lab 8 classification): no fetch / fetch without CplD / SQE without data / data without CQE / CQE without MSI-X
Linux evidenceTimeout line with QID and tag; "completion polled" variant indicates CQE existed
NVMe evidenceError log (often empty); CSTS (CFS?); Abort result
PCIe evidenceAER CmpltTO (fetch stage), UR (bad address)
First checkKernel message variant; AER around the doorbell time (≈ timeout − 30 s)
Disambiguating experimentAnalyzer with Lab 8 classification; or polled-queue experiment (lab: nvme.poll_queues) to bypass interrupts
Likely root causesController FW hang for a command type; lost interrupt (F24); CQ full due to host not updating head; SQE fetch completion lost (F9)
RemediationFix the owning stage
Regression testLong soak with mixed opcodes; Lab 8 detector on sampled captures; zero timeouts

F14 — Queue corruption

SymptomsRandom Invalid Opcode / Invalid Field errors; wrong data returned; controller fatal
Likely layersHost memory management (driver), DMA coherency, rarely controller
Trace signatureSQE CplD payload containing garbage (unexpected opcode, NSID, PRPs); CQE written to unexpected slot
Linux evidenceError completions with odd status; KASAN/memory corruption reports in debug kernels
NVMe evidenceError log with parameter error location pointing at corrupted fields
PCIe evidenceSQE payload in CplD
First checkDecode the fetched SQE: is it what the host intended to write (driver trace)?
Disambiguating experimentDriver-side logging of SQE contents at submission vs SQE as fetched; debug kernel (KASAN); IOMMU strict
Likely root causesMissing memory barrier before doorbell (SQE not visible when fetched); buffer reuse; non-coherent DMA mapping misuse
RemediationCorrect ordering (write SQE, barrier, then doorbell); lifetime fixes
Regression testStress on weakly-ordered architectures with SQE checksum validation in a test driver

F15 — Wrong doorbell

SymptomsNo I/O completes on some queues; Async Event errors; controller fatal on some devices
Likely layersHost driver/harness (doorbell offset computation)
Trace signatureDoorbell MWr to an address that is not the intended queue's register; no SQE fetch follows (TL-8)
Linux evidenceTimeouts; for in-kernel driver rare (bug would be universal)
NVMe evidenceAsynchronous Event: error status (invalid doorbell register / write value) impl
PCIe evidenceDoorbell address vs 1000h + (2y [+1]) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)
First checkRead CAP.DSTRD (nvme show-regs) and recompute doorbell offsets
Disambiguating experimentRun harness on devices with different DSTRD
Likely root causesHard-coded stride; queue ID mix-up (SQ vs CQ)
RemediationCompute from CAP
Regression testEmulated devices with DSTRD 0/1/2

F16 — Wrong queue pointer (tail/head)

SymptomsCommands executed twice or never; stale CQEs consumed; Invalid Doorbell Write Value events
Likely layersHost driver queue accounting
Trace signatureDoorbell value beyond queue size; tail moving backwards; SQE fetch of slots never written; CQ head doorbell ahead of posted CQEs
Linux evidenceDuplicate completions, "invalid id" style driver warnings version
NVMe evidenceAsync Event error; CQE SQHD inconsistent with host view
PCIe evidenceDoorbell payloads sequence; SQ fetch addresses
First checkPlot doorbell values over time per queue: monotonic modulo size?
Disambiguating experimentVary queue size (e.g. 2, 3, 64, 1024 entries) to expose wrap bugs; check the "one slot empty" full-queue rule
Likely root causesOff-by-one on wrap; 0-based QSIZE confusion; missing phase flip on wrap
RemediationFix accounting
Regression testQueue-size sweep with millions of wraps; Lab 7 correlator must report zero anomalies

F17 — Invalid PRP

SymptomsInvalid PRP Offset / Invalid Field / Data Transfer Error statuses; or silent corruption
Likely layersHost driver PRP construction; IOMMU
Trace signaturePRP entries with non-zero offsets beyond PRP1; list pointer to unmapped memory; data MWr to unexpected pages
Linux evidenceI/O errors; IOMMU faults
NVMe evidenceCQE status; error log parameter location (PRP field)
PCIe evidencePRP list CplD payload; UR completions
First checkDecode SQE PRPs and list contents with Lab 5
Disambiguating experimentUnaligned-buffer I/O tests (O_DIRECT with various offsets); transfer sizes around page and list boundaries
Likely root causesOffset arithmetic bug; list chaining bug at 512-entry boundary; buffer not page-aligned when assumed
RemediationFix builder; validate PRPs in debug builds
Regression testSize/offset sweep (4 KiB × n ± 512 B, list-chaining sizes) with data verification

F18 — Invalid SGL

SymptomsSGL-related error statuses (e.g. SGL descriptor type invalid, data SGL length invalid, invalid number of SGL descriptors); Invalid Field when SGLs unsupported
Likely layersHost SGL construction; controller SGL support
Trace signatureSQE PSDT ≠ 00b; SGL segment fetch MRds; descriptor contents inconsistent with transfer length
Linux evidenceI/O errors; driver choosing SGL vs PRP depends on size thresholds and device support version
NVMe evidenceIdentify Controller SGLS field (support); CQE status
PCIe evidenceSGL segment CplD payloads
First checkDoes the controller support SGLs for this command set (SGLS)?
Disambiguating experimentForce PRP path (driver parameter, lab) — errors disappear?
Likely root causesUsing SGLs on a controller that lacks support; descriptor length sum ≠ transfer length; wrong descriptor type/subtype
RemediationHonor SGLS; fix descriptor builder
Regression testSGL descriptor matrix (data block, segment, last segment, bit bucket if supported)

F19 — Controller fatal (CSTS.CFS)

SymptomsAll I/O stops; driver resets controller; may recover or loop
Likely layersController firmware/hardware; host register misuse (TL-9)
Trace signatureMMIO read of CSTS returns CFS=1; I/O activity ceases; sometimes preceded by host writes violating init order
Linux evidencecontroller is down; will reset: CSTS=0x3-style messages (bit 1 = CFS); note CSTS=0xffffffff means device not responding (different!)
NVMe evidenceTelemetry log (controller-initiated) if supported; vendor logs
PCIe evidenceLink healthy (distinguishes from surprise down)
First checkCSTS value: CFS vs all-ones
Disambiguating experimentReproduce with captured host register sequence; FW A/B
Likely root causesFirmware assert; internal hardware error; illegal host programming
RemediationFW fix; host init-order fix
Regression testStress + reset-injection suite; telemetry collection automated

F20 — Media error

SymptomsRead I/O errors on specific LBAs; long-latency reads (successful after retries)
Likely layersMedia (NAND), controller ECC/error recovery
Trace signatureNormal link traffic; CQE with SCT 2h (Media and Data Integrity), e.g. Unrecovered Read Error; or long SQE→data gap (Lab 80.1)
Linux evidenceI/O error, dev nvme0n1, sector …; critical medium error messages
NVMe evidenceSMART media_errors increment; error log entry with LBA; critical_warning bits
PCIe evidenceNone abnormal
First checkError log LBA and status; SMART deltas
Disambiguating experimentLab copy only: re-read the LBA; rewrite and re-read; check whether the error is persistent
Likely root causesAged/worn NAND, retention loss, read disturb, defect
RemediationRestore data from redundancy; rewrite; replace drive if spare/critical warnings
Regression testNot a code regression — monitoring: SMART thresholds, scrub schedule
⚠️ Data safety

Never "test" a media error by writing to the LBA on a production drive — rewriting destroys the evidence and possibly the only copy of data. Work on lab drives or on images.

F21 — Namespace error

SymptomsInvalid Namespace or Format; Namespace Not Ready; namespace missing after management operations; write-protected namespace errors
Likely layersNVMe namespace management, host configuration, multipath
Trace signatureSQE with NSID not attached to this controller; CQE generic error status
Linux evidenceMissing nvme0nX; rescan messages; I/O errors
NVMe evidenceIdentify active namespace list (CNS 02h), namespace attachment state, Changed Namespace List log (04h)
PCIe evidenceNone
First checknvme list-ns / id-ns for the NSID; was a namespace operation performed?
Disambiguating experimentRescan; compare active NS list across controllers of the subsystem
Likely root causesNamespace detached/deleted; format in progress; host using stale NSID; write protection state
RemediationCorrect attachment; wait for readiness; refresh host view
Regression testNamespace create/attach/detach cycles with I/O running (lab drives only)

F22 — Firmware issue

SymptomsNew behavior after FW update: timeouts, latency shifts, CFS, feature changes; activation failures
Likely layersController firmware; update process
Trace signatureSame host traffic, different device timing or responses compared with golden trace on old FW
Linux evidenceCorrelates with fw update date; fw-log active slot change
NVMe evidencefw-log, Identify FR, Firmware Commit status (e.g. activation requiring reset)
PCIe evidenceUsually none; link-level FW changes possible
First checkGolden trace diff old vs new FW with identical host
Disambiguating experimentA/B FW on same hardware, same host, same workload; bisect FW versions if available
Likely root causesFW regression; incompatible feature default change; interrupted activation
RemediationVendor fix; roll back (if permitted by FW slot/rollback policy)
Regression testQualification suite with golden-trace comparison per FW release
⚠️ Firmware changes

Firmware download/commit is state-changing and can render a drive unusable if interrupted or if the image is wrong. Lab-only, vendor-approved images, verified power, and a recovery plan.

84 Failure Library IV: Interrupts, Performance, Power and Reset

← 83 Failure Library III: NVMe Queues, Commands, Media and Firmware85 Performance Fundamentals: Latency, IOPS, Throughput and Their Limits →

System-level failures are where layers interact: interrupts cross PCIe, the platform's interrupt remapping and the OS; performance depends on everything; power management and reset touch the link, the controller and the driver at once.

  • Diagnose interrupt-path failures with MSI-X table/PBA evidence.
  • Separate performance limits by resource (link, controller, media, CPU, queueing).
  • Debug power-state and reset/resume sequences.

F23 — MSI-X problem (configuration)

SymptomsAll I/O completions slow or only via polling; fewer queues than expected; interrupts land on one CPU
Likely layersHost interrupt allocation, MSI-X capability, platform interrupt remapping
Trace signatureMSI-X MWr to unexpected address/data; no MSI-X MWr at all with legacy INTx Assert/Deassert messages instead
Linux evidencelspci -vv MSI-X Enable-/Count; /proc/interrupts; driver log "x/y/z default/read/poll queues"
NVMe evidenceGet Features Number of Queues (07h); Interrupt Vector Configuration (09h)
PCIe evidenceMSI-X capability, table contents via host debug interfaces
First checkMSI-X enabled and vectors allocated = queues
Disambiguating experimentBoot with different nvme queue parameters; check platform interrupt-remapping logs
Likely root causesVector exhaustion; remapping failure; virtualization config
RemediationKernel/platform configuration
Regression testBoot-time checks on vector counts; per-queue interrupt delta test

F24 — Interrupt loss

SymptomsExact io_timeout stalls with "completion polled"; per-queue hangs
Likely layersHost interrupt management (mask/unmask, affinity), platform, rarely device
Trace signatureCQE MWr not followed by MSI-X MWr (masked vector or device omission) — TL-6
Linux evidenceTimeout + polled message; affinity changes at the time
NVMe evidenceInterrupt Coalescing feature (rule it out)
PCIe evidenceMSI-X Vector Control mask bits; PBA pending bits
First checkIs the CQE present when the timeout fires?
Disambiguating experimentPin IRQ affinity (stop irqbalance) — stalls vanish? PBA read after stall
Likely root causesMask without unmask in affinity path; interrupt remapping race; device not sending for unmasked vector
RemediationFix host path or device FW
Regression testAffinity-churn stress (TL-6)

F25 — High latency

Symptomsp99/p99.9 far above expectation; average may look fine
Likely layersHost queueing, CPU scheduling, controller (GC, read retry), power states, link recovery
Trace signatureLong phases in Lab 6 timeline: SQE→data (device), CQE→head doorbell (host)
Linux evidenceblktrace Q2D vs D2C; fio clat percentiles; CPU stats
NVMe evidenceTemperature, controller busy time, APST states
PCIe evidenceRecovery/ASPM exit events at spike times
First checkSplit host vs device time (blktrace D2C)
Disambiguating experimentDisable APST/ASPM (lab), precondition drive, isolate CPUs, compare distributions
Likely root causesQueue depth too high (queueing), background device work, power-state exit latency, CPU contention
RemediationTune QD, power policy, CPU isolation; vendor FW
Regression testLatency SLO test with percentiles and repeatability (Chapter 88)

F26 — Low throughput

SymptomsBandwidth below expectation
Likely layersLink (speed/width/MPS), controller/NAND limits, host CPU, insufficient concurrency, NUMA
Trace signatureGaps between data TLPs (credit starvation or device pacing); small payloads (MPS); few outstanding reads (writes)
Linux evidenceLnkSta, MPS, fio CPU usage, numa_node, iostat util
NVMe evidenceThermal throttling counters, MDTS
PCIe evidenceAnalyzer bandwidth statistics; UpdateFC cadence
First checkCompute the ceiling (Chapter 90) and required concurrency (Little's law)
Disambiguating experimentIncrease QD/jobs; move to local NUMA node; check for CPU-bound jobs
Likely root causesDowngraded link; insufficient QD; single-thread CPU limit; device steady-state write limit
RemediationFix link; tune workload; accept device limit
Regression testThroughput matrix (bs × QD × jobs) with tolerance bands

F27 — Queue-depth instability

SymptomsIOPS oscillates; latency grows superlinearly with QD; throughput collapses at high QD
Likely layersController scheduling, host block layer (tag exhaustion), workload generator
Trace signatureBursty doorbells; outstanding commands at device plateau then latency climbs
Linux evidencenr_requests, blk-mq tags; fio iodepth histogram
NVMe evidenceNumber of queues; MQES (max queue entries)
PCIe evidenceOutstanding MRd counts for writes (tags)
First checkPlot IOPS and latency vs QD (Little's law consistency)
Disambiguating experimentRepeat with preconditioned steady state; vary numjobs vs iodepth at constant total outstanding
Likely root causesDevice saturation (more QD only adds queueing delay); host tag limits; GC interference
RemediationOperate at the knee of the curve
Regression testQD sweep with knee detection

F28 — Power-management issue

SymptomsLatency spikes after idle; timeouts after idle; device disappears after idle (some platforms)
Likely layersNVMe power states (APST), PCIe link states (ASPM L1, L1 substates), device D-states
Trace signatureElectrical idle / L1 entry, then exit via Recovery when traffic resumes; first command after idle slow
Linux evidenceAPST settings (nvme get-feature -f 0x0c), ASPM policy (/sys/module/pcie_aspm/parameters/policy), LnkCtl ASPM
NVMe evidencePower state table entry/exit latencies; current power state (Feature 02h)
PCIe evidenceL1 PM Substates capability and control; LTR values
First checkDo problems correlate with idle periods?
Disambiguating experimentLab: disable APST (nvme_core.default_ps_max_latency_us=0) and/or ASPM (pcie_aspm=off) — one at a time
Likely root causesExit latency larger than advertised; platform/device incompatibility in L1.2; firmware bug in deep power state
RemediationQuirk/policy limit; FW fix
Regression testIdle/active cycling test with latency histogram on first I/O after idle

F29 — Reset loop

SymptomsRepeated "resetting controller" messages; eventually removal
Likely layersController (does not become ready), host init sequence, link
Trace signatureCC.EN 1→0, CSTS.RDY polling, CC.EN=1, RDY never 1 (or CFS=1); repeated
Linux evidenceDevice not ready; aborting reset, CSTS=…; Removing after probe failure
NVMe evidenceCAP.TO; CSTS values; telemetry
PCIe evidenceLink up and stable (else see F1/F2)
First checkCSTS value during the loop; link state
Disambiguating experimentPower-cycle vs controller reset vs function-level reset — which recovers? Capture host register sequence (TL-9)
Likely root causesFirmware stuck; host enabling before configuring admin queues; device needs longer than CAP.TO
RemediationFW fix; host ordering fix; quirk
Regression testReset-injection loop: 10,000 controller resets with I/O

F30 — Resume failure

SymptomsAfter suspend/resume: device missing, timeouts, or reset loop; intermittent
Likely layersPlatform power sequencing, link retraining, driver resume path, controller re-init
Trace signatureLink retraining at resume (Detect…L0), config restore CfgWr, NVMe register restore; deviation at the first wrong step (TL-9)
Linux evidenceResume timeline in kernel log; previous-boot journal if the system crashed
NVMe evidenceCSTS after resume; unsafe_shutdowns increment (power lost without notification?)
PCIe evidenceLnkSta after resume; AER Surprise Down
First checkWhich power state did the device actually reach (D3hot vs D3cold)?
Disambiguating experimentForce each path (platform settings) and compare failure rates
Likely root causesDriver assumes preserved state; device FW slow to boot after power loss; link training issue at resume
RemediationFull re-init path; quirk for delays; platform fix
Regression testThousands of suspend/resume cycles per power path with data verification

84.1 Library index by symptom

You see…Start with
Device missingF1, F30, F29
Throughput lowF3, F4, F26, F27
Latency tailF25, F28, F2, F20 (read retry)
30-second stallsF13, F24, F9
I/O errors with statusF20, F21, F17, F18
AER messagesF5–F12
Repeated resetsF29, F19, F12

Quiz

  1. CSTS=0x3 vs CSTS=0xffffffff — which library entries?

    Answer

    0x3 = RDY+CFS → F19 (controller fatal). All-ones → device not responding on the link → F1/F2/F30 territory.

  2. Exactly 30 s stall with "completion polled": which entry?

    Answer

    F24 interrupt loss (CQE existed; interrupt did not lead to processing).

  3. Why is "rewrite the LBA" not a valid first experiment for F20 on production?

    Answer

    It destroys data and evidence; use lab drives or images.

Interview questions

  1. Senior Pick any three failures from the library and explain how you'd separate them with one experiment each.
    Model answer

    E.g. F13 vs F24: polled queues (lab) — if stalls vanish, the interrupt path is guilty. F2 vs F25: force a lower link speed — if tail latency persists, the link was not the cause. F26 link vs CPU: run more jobs on other cores — if throughput scales, CPU-bound.

✅ Mastery gate — Failure Library
  • For each of F1–F30 I can name the first check and a disambiguating experiment from memory.
  • I can map a raw kernel log excerpt to library entries in under five minutes.
  • I can write the regression test for any entry.
PART XXVIII

Performance Engineering

Performance is where protocol knowledge meets arithmetic. This Part teaches the vocabulary (latency, IOPS, throughput, queue depth, outstanding commands, CPU overhead, PCIe/controller/NAND bandwidth, tail latency), the equations that tie them together (above all Little's law), the latency budget of a single I/O, benchmarking discipline with fio, the causality rules that keep performance claims honest, and finally the exact PCIe bandwidth arithmetic for Gen3 through Gen6 links. All numbers labelled synthetic are teaching values, not measurements of any product.

85 Performance Fundamentals: Latency, IOPS, Throughput and Their Limits

← 84 Failure Library IV: Interrupts, Performance, Power and Reset86 Little's Law and Queue Depth →

85.1 Why this chapter exists

"This SSD does 1.5 million IOPS" is meaningless without block size, read/write mix, queue depth, number of jobs, latency percentiles, preconditioning state and platform. Engineers who cannot decompose a performance number into its resources cannot tell whether a result is a device limit, a link limit, a CPU limit, or an artefact of the test.

85.2 Learning objectives (deep-dive module 53)

  • Beginner: define latency, IOPS, throughput, queue depth, and convert between IOPS and bandwidth.
  • Intermediate: explain why sequential and random workloads behave differently and why queue depth matters.
  • Advanced: identify the bottleneck resource from a set of measurements (link, controller, NAND, CPU, queueing).
  • Senior: explain why high IOPS can coexist with bad latency and why high bandwidth can hide latency problems; defend claims with causality evidence.
  • Trace-analysis: derive per-phase latency and link utilization from a PCIe trace.
  • Debugging: map a performance symptom to Failure Library entries F25–F27.
  • Validation: design repeatable benchmarks with defined percentiles and tolerance bands.

85.3 Story and analogy

🧒 Kid analogy — the pizza kitchen

A pizza shop gets phone orders. Latency is how long you wait for your pizza. IOPS is how many pizzas leave per minute. Throughput is how many kilograms of pizza leave per minute (big pizzas = more kilograms for the same count). Queue depth is how many orders are in the kitchen at once. With one order at a time, the ovens sit idle while the cook rolls dough; with ten orders at once, every oven is busy — more pizzas per minute. But with a hundred orders at once, the ovens are already full, so new orders just wait on the counter: pizzas per minute stop growing, while your personal wait keeps growing.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Represents: concurrency, service time, queueing, saturation. Hides: an SSD has many parallel "ovens" (NAND dies/planes) whose availability depends on where the data lives; writes are absorbed by caches and later cost background work (garbage collection); the delivery road (PCIe) has its own capacity and overhead per trip; the phone operator (CPU) can be the bottleneck. Misleading when: you assume every order takes the same time — storage service times have long tails (read retries, GC, power-state exits).

85.5 Core equations

Throughput = IOPS × BlockSize
  • Throughput — payload bytes per second (B/s)
  • IOPS — completed I/O operations per second
  • BlockSize — bytes per I/O
L = λ · W (Little's law — Chapter 86)
  • L — average number of outstanding I/Os
  • λ — average completion rate (IOPS) in steady state
  • W — average latency (s)
IOPSmax ≤ min( Nparallel / S , BWlink,eff / bytesper IO on link , Cores × IOPSper core , device limit )
  • Nparallel/S — internal parallel units divided by service time per I/O (media-bound ceiling)
  • BWlink,eff — effective link payload bandwidth; bytesper IO on link includes TLP and NVMe overhead (Ch 90)
  • IOPSper core — CPU-bound ceiling per core for the software stack
Utilization ρ = λ / μ ; for a simple single-server queue (M/M/1, illustrative) W = 1 / (μ − λ)
  • μ — service rate capacity (IOPS the resource can do flat out)
  • ρ — fraction of capacity in use; as ρ → 1, waiting time grows without bound. Real SSDs are many-server systems with non-exponential service times; the formula illustrates the shape, not exact values conceptual

85.6 Architecture: where performance is decided

85.7 Sequential vs random

AspectSequential (e.g. 128 KiB)Random (e.g. 4 KiB)
Typical limiting resourceLink bandwidth or NAND/controller bandwidthMedia parallelism and per-command overhead; CPU at very high IOPS
Per-command overhead shareSmall (SQE fetch, CQE, interrupt amortized over 128 KiB)Large (same fixed costs per 4 KiB)
Device internalsRead-ahead and striping across dies work well; large writes fill pages efficiently implEach read may hit any die; collisions on the same die serialize; small random writes increase FTL and GC work
QD needed to saturateLow-moderate (each command already spans many dies)High (need many independent commands to keep dies busy)
Metric to reportGB/s plus latencyIOPS plus latency percentiles

85.8 Why queue depth matters

At QD1, a device with dozens of independent NAND dies uses one at a time: IOPS ≈ 1/W. Raising QD lets independent commands overlap, so IOPS rises roughly linearly — until a resource saturates. Past the knee, more QD adds only queueing delay: IOPS flat, latency rising in proportion (Little's law). The knee is the operating point you usually want.

SYNTHETIC TEACHING DATA — QD sweep, 4 KiB random read, one device
QDIOPSMean latency µsL = IOPS × WReading
112,500801.0Media service time dominates
449,00081.64.0Linear region
32380,0008431.9Still near linear
128950,000135128Near knee: latency starts climbing
5121,000,000512512Saturated: 4× QD bought 5 % IOPS and 3.8× latency

85.9 Why high IOPS can still have bad latency — and high bandwidth can hide latency problems

  • High IOPS, bad latency: IOPS is a rate; latency is per request. At saturation (QD 512 above), IOPS is at its maximum while every request waits behind hundreds of others. Also, averages hide tails: 99 % fast requests and 1 % at 2 ms produce a fine mean and IOPS, but a database waiting on many reads per transaction hits the slow 1 % constantly.
  • High bandwidth hiding latency: large sequential transfers with deep queues keep the link full even if each command takes milliseconds; GB/s looks perfect. The same device may be terrible for small synchronous I/O (fsync-heavy logs). Bandwidth tests also amortize per-command problems (a slow doorbell path, a power-state exit) that dominate QD1 latency.
💡 Senior insight

Always report three numbers together: the rate (IOPS or GB/s), the concurrency (outstanding I/Os), and the latency distribution (p50/p99/p99.9). Any two let you check the third with Little's law; a mismatch means the measurement is wrong or the system is not in steady state.

85.10 Percentiles: computing and reading the tail

The model below draws 200,000 synthetic read latencies (~80 µs typical, 1 % delayed by 0.5–2 ms, 0.05 % by 20 ms) and computes percentiles; it also contains the Little's law helper and the latency budget used in Chapter 87.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Performance models (SIMULATION): Little's law, percentiles, latency budget.
All numbers are SYNTHETIC teaching values, not measurements of any product."""
import random, statistics

def littles(L=None, lam=None, W=None):
    """L = lambda * W. Give any two, get the third (units: ops, ops/s, s)."""
    if L is None:   return lam * W
    if lam is None: return L / W
    return L / lam

def percentile(sorted_vals, p):
    k = (len(sorted_vals) - 1) * p / 100
    lo, hi = int(k), min(int(k) + 1, len(sorted_vals) - 1)
    return sorted_vals[lo] + (sorted_vals[hi] - sorted_vals[lo]) * (k - lo)

def synthetic_latencies(n=200_000, seed=7):
    """Mostly ~80 us reads, 1% hit a 'GC-like' 2 ms stall, 0.05% hit 20 ms."""
    r = random.Random(seed)
    out = []
    for _ in range(n):
        x = r.gauss(80, 8)
        u = r.random()
        if u < 0.0005:   x += 20_000
        elif u < 0.0105: x += r.uniform(500, 2_000)
        out.append(max(x, 20))
    return sorted(out)

BUDGET = [  # (component, microseconds) - SYNTHETIC 4 KiB random read, QD1
    ("application + syscall", 1.5), ("block layer / blk-mq", 1.0),
    ("NVMe driver: build SQE, ring doorbell", 0.5), ("doorbell MWr reaches device", 0.5),
    ("SQE fetch (MRd + CplD round trip)", 1.0), ("controller FW: decode, FTL lookup", 3.0),
    ("NAND read (tR) + ECC decode", 60.0), ("data DMA 4 KiB over Gen4 x4", 0.6),
    ("CQE write + MSI-X", 0.5), ("interrupt -> completion -> wake app", 4.0)]

def show_budget(budget):
    tot = sum(v for _, v in budget)
    for name, v in sorted(budget, key=lambda x: -x[1]):
        print(f"  {name:40s} {v:6.1f} us  {100*v/tot:5.1f}%")
    print(f"  {'TOTAL':40s} {tot:6.1f} us -> QD1 ceiling {1e6/tot:,.0f} IOPS")
    return tot

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Little: QD32 @ 80us ->", f"{littles(L=32, W=80e-6):,.0f} IOPS")
    print("Little: 1M IOPS @ 100us needs L =", littles(lam=1e6, W=100e-6))
    print("Little: 500k IOPS at QD256 -> W =", f"{littles(L=256, lam=500e3)*1e6:.0f} us")
    lat = synthetic_latencies()
    print(f"mean {statistics.fmean(lat):.1f}  p50 {percentile(lat,50):.1f}  p95 {percentile(lat,95):.1f}"
          f"  p99 {percentile(lat,99):.1f}  p99.9 {percentile(lat,99.9):.1f}  p99.99 {percentile(lat,99.99):.1f} us")
    print("Budget A (TLC-like media):"); show_budget(BUDGET)
    fast = [(n, 8.0 if n.startswith("NAND") else v) for n, v in BUDGET]
    print("Budget B (media 8 us, e.g. low-latency media/cache hit):"); show_budget(fast)
    poll = [(n, 1.0 if n.startswith("interrupt") else v) for n, v in fast]
    print("Budget C (B + polled completion):"); show_budget(poll)

Read the tail: the mean (≈100 µs) is pulled up by rare stalls; p50 and p95 look healthy; p99 jumps to ~0.6 ms and p99.9 to ~2 ms because 1 % of requests are slow; the 0.05 % 20 ms stalls appear only at p99.99. A test of 10,000 I/Os would barely see them — tail percentiles need enough samples (rule of thumb: at least ~100× the inverse of the tail fraction you want to report, e.g. ≥106 samples for a stable p99.99 derived).

85.11 Performance lab: find the bottleneck

🧪 Lab 85.1 — Four synthetic workloads, four bottlenecks SAFE

Classification: paper/simulation exercise. Objective: classify each case as queue saturation, bandwidth limitation, latency (service-time) limitation, or CPU limitation. Link: Gen4 x4 (≈7.0 GB/s effective, Ch 90).

CaseWorkloadResult (synthetic)Extra observations
A128 KiB seq read, QD32, 1 job6.9 GB/s, mean lat 600 µsCPU 25 %
B4 KiB rand read, QD112,000 IOPS, mean 83 µs, p99 95 µsDevice idle most of the time
C4 KiB rand read, QD256 × 4 jobs1.0 M IOPS, mean 1.02 ms, p99 2.5 msSame IOPS at QD64 × 4 jobs with 250 µs
D4 KiB rand read, QD128, 1 job420,000 IOPS, mean 300 µsfio thread at 100 % of one core; 4 jobs give 1.0 M IOPS
Solution

A — bandwidth limitation: 6.9 GB/s ≈ link effective ceiling; Little check: 6.9e9/131072 ≈ 52.6k IOPS × 600 µs ≈ 31.6 ≈ QD32 ✓. B — latency (service-time) limitation: QD1 means IOPS = 1/W ≈ 12k; the device has spare parallelism. C — queue saturation: IOPS identical at lower QD; extra outstanding I/Os only wait (1.0e6 × 1.02 ms ≈ 1020 ≈ 1024 outstanding ✓). D — CPU limitation: one submitting core saturated; outstanding = 420k × 300 µs = 126 ≈ QD128 ✓, but scaling jobs raises IOPS, proving the limit was host-side.

Quiz

  1. A device does 400k IOPS at 4 KiB. Throughput?

    Answer

    400,000 × 4096 B = 1.64 GB/s (1.53 GiB/s).

  2. Why is QD1 4 KiB random-read IOPS ≈ 1/latency?

    Answer

    Only one I/O is ever outstanding; Little's law with L = 1 gives λ = 1/W.

  3. Why can a 7 GB/s sequential result coexist with poor database performance?

    Answer

    Bandwidth with deep queues hides per-request latency and tails; databases are often latency-bound on small I/O.

86 Little's Law and Queue Depth

← 85 Performance Fundamentals: Latency, IOPS, Throughput and Their Limits87 The Latency Budget and Tail Latency →

86.1 Why this chapter exists

Little's law is the single most useful equation in storage performance. It is exact for long-run averages of any stable system — no assumptions about distributions — and it turns three hard-to-reason-about quantities into one line of arithmetic.

  • State and apply L = λ·W with correct units.
  • Compute the concurrency needed for a target IOPS and latency.
  • Use the law to sanity-check benchmark output and detect broken measurements.
  • Apply it inside the PCIe layer: outstanding read requests (tags) needed to fill a link.
🧒 Kid analogy — the water slide

If 2 kids per minute go down a slide (λ) and each ride takes 3 minutes from top of the stairs to the splash (W), then on average 6 kids are on the stairs-and-slide at any moment (L = 2 × 3). Want more kids per minute without making the slide faster? You must allow more kids on it at once.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

The law holds for averages over long, stable periods. It does not say anything about percentiles, and it does not hold over a short window where the queue is growing or draining (e.g. the first second of a benchmark, or during a GC storm).

86.2 The law

L = λ · W
  • L — mean number of I/Os in the system (outstanding: submitted, not completed)
  • λ — mean throughput of completions (IOPS), equal to arrival rate in steady state
  • W — mean time each I/O spends in the system (latency at the same measurement boundary as L)
📘 Boundary rule

L and W must be measured at the same boundary. If W is fio's completion latency (clat, from submission to completion), L is the number in flight between those points. If W is the device-side D2C time from blktrace, L is the number dispatched to the device. Mixing boundaries produces nonsense.

86.3 Worked examples

#GivenFindArithmeticResult
1QD32 (1 job), W = 80 µsIOPSλ = L/W = 32 / 80×10−6400,000 IOPS (1.64 GB/s at 4 KiB)
2Target 1,000,000 IOPS at W = 100 µsOutstanding neededL = 106 × 10−4100 outstanding (e.g. 4 jobs × QD25, or 4 × 32 with headroom)
3500,000 IOPS measured at QD256Mean latencyW = 256 / 5×105512 µs — most of it queueing if service time is ~80 µs
4numjobs = 4, iodepth = 32, W = 120 µsIOPSL = 128; λ = 128 / 120 µs≈1.07 M IOPS (if submission keeps queues full)
5Sequential 128 KiB, target 14 GB/s, W = 400 µsOutstandingλ = 14e9/131072 = 106,812 IOPS; L = λ × 4×10−4≈43 outstanding commands
6fio reports 300k IOPS, mean clat 50 µs, iodepth 64Consistency checkL = 3×105 × 5×10−5 = 1515 ≠ 64: queue is not being kept full (submission-bound, or iodepth_batch settings) — investigate

The tube below makes Example 1 visible. A new command enters every 2.5 µs (λ = 400 000 per second) and each stays 80 µs (W). Count the commands inside at any instant: 80 ÷ 2.5 = 32. That count is L, the queue depth the device sees. The lower bars compare Example 3 on its own time scale: the device cannot complete faster, so the extra 224 outstanding commands only add waiting time.

86.4 Little's law inside PCIe: outstanding read requests

For writes, the SSD pulls data with MRds. To sustain a payload bandwidth B with read-completion round-trip time R and request size MRRS:

Noutstanding MRd = B × R / MRRS
  • B — target pull bandwidth (B/s)
  • R — MRd → last CplD round-trip time (s)
  • MRRS — bytes per read request

Example derived: Gen4 x4 ≈ 7.06 GB/s, R = 1 µs, MRRS = 512 B → N ≈ 13.8 outstanding requests; at R = 2 µs (a busy root complex or a switch in the path) → ≈27.6. At Gen5 x4 with R = 2 µs: ≈55 outstanding. This is why tag space (8-bit, 10-bit tags) and MRRS matter for write throughput at higher generations — the device must have enough tags and internal buffering to keep that many requests in flight.

86.5 Lab: calculate the expected concurrency

🧪 Lab 86.1 — Little's law workbook SAFE

Classification: calculation; optional real run with read-only fio. Objective: predict, then measure, concurrency.

  1. Predict IOPS at QD 1, 4, 16, 64 for a device with 80 µs service time and a saturation limit of 800k IOPS (assume latency stays 80 µs until saturation, then grows as L/λmax).
  2. Optional (lab machine, read-only job, see Chapter 88): run the sweep and feed fio's JSON to fio_summary.py to check L ≈ IOPS × mean.
  3. Explain any mismatch.
Solution

QD1: 12.5k; QD4: 50k; QD16: 200k; QD64: 800k (exactly at the limit, W = 80 µs). QD128 would stay at 800k with W = 160 µs. Mismatches in real runs: submission overhead (CPU), interrupt coalescing, non-steady state, device internal parallelism lower than assumed, or latency rising before saturation due to die collisions (random addresses map to the same die).

Quiz

  1. Does Little's law tell you the p99?

    Answer

    No — only means.

  2. What happens to W if you double QD on a saturated device?

    Answer

    It roughly doubles, because λ cannot grow.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can apply L = λW in both directions with correct units and boundaries.
  • I can check any benchmark output for Little's-law consistency.
  • I can compute outstanding PCIe read requests needed for a write bandwidth.

87 The Latency Budget and Tail Latency

← 86 Little's Law and Queue Depth88 Benchmarking Discipline with fio →

87.1 Why this chapter exists

A latency number without a breakdown cannot be improved. The latency budget assigns every microsecond of one I/O to a component — software, driver, queue, PCIe, controller, media, completion, interrupt — so that you know which one to attack and what improvement is even possible.

  • Build an end-to-end latency budget for a 4 KiB read.
  • Identify the dominant component; change one component and recompute.
  • Explain where tail latency comes from in each component.

The executable version of this budget is in perf_models.py (Chapter 85); its output shows three variants: A (TLC-like media, 60 µs) where media is 83 % of the total; B (media 8 µs, e.g. a low-latency media type or a controller cache hit) where the total falls to 20.6 µs and media is only 39 % — the interrupt/wake path (19 %) and controller (15 %) now matter; C (B + polled completion) where replacing interrupt-driven completion with polling trims another 3 µs.

87.3 Which component dominates? Change one and recompute

🧪 Lab 87.1 — Latency budget lab SAFE

Classification: simulation. Steps: (1) Identify the dominant component in budget A. (2) Halve the PCIe-related items (doorbell, fetch, data, completion: 2.6 µs → 1.3 µs, e.g. a faster generation) and recompute. (3) Instead, halve the media time. (4) Which change is worth engineering effort for a QD1 database log workload? (5) Edit perf_models.py to add a 25 µs "L1.2 exit latency" component on the first I/O after idle and compute its effect.

Solution

(1) Media, 60 of 72.6 µs. (2) 72.6 → 71.3 µs: 1.8 % better — a faster link barely matters for QD1 4 KiB reads. (3) 72.6 → 42.6 µs: 41 % better. (4) Media/controller (or caching) for budget A; once media is fast (budget B), software and interrupt paths become worthwhile targets. (5) First-after-idle I/O becomes ~97.6 µs (+34 %): power-state exit is a classic tail contributor (Failure Library F28).

87.4 Where tails come from

SourceMechanismSignatureHow to confirm
QueueingWaiting behind other I/OsTail grows with QDQD sweep; Little's law

Quiz

  1. In budget A, by how much would a Gen5 link (halving transfer times) improve QD1 latency?

    Answer

    Less than 2 % — the link contributes only ~2.6 µs.

  2. When does the host software path become the dominant term?

    Answer

    When media and controller latencies shrink to a few microseconds (low-latency media, cache hits), as in budgets B and C.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can build a latency budget from evidence (blktrace + analyzer) and name the dominant term.
  • I can predict the effect of improving any single component.
  • I can list tail-latency sources and the test that confirms each.

88 Benchmarking Discipline with fio

← 87 The Latency Budget and Tail Latency89 Performance Causality, Bottleneck Forensics and the Performance Mastery Module →

88.1 Why this chapter exists

Most published SSD comparisons are irreproducible because nobody recorded the preconditioning state, the queue depth, the CPU placement, or the temperature. A benchmark is an experiment; it needs a hypothesis, controlled variables, repetitions and an error bar. fio is the standard Linux tool; this chapter teaches safe, interpretable fio usage.

  • Write fio jobs that state block size, mix, QD, jobs, engine, direct I/O, runtime and ramp.
  • Run read-only jobs safely; know which jobs destroy data.
  • Interpret fio output: IOPS, BW, slat/clat/lat, percentiles, CPU, IO depth distribution, util.
  • Apply benchmarking discipline: warm-up, steady state, cache, thermal, power, repeatability.
⚠️ DESTRUCTIVE — fio writes destroy data

Any fio job with rw=write, randwrite, rw/readwrite, randrw, trim/randtrim/trimwrite pointed at a raw device (filename=/dev/nvme0n1) overwrites or discards data on that device including partition tables and filesystems. Run write jobs only on a dedicated scratch drive with nothing you want to keep, verified by serial number. For read jobs, add readonly=1 as a safety net: fio then refuses to run write or trim workloads. Even read-only benchmarks load production systems — run them in maintenance windows.

88.2 Job file examples

# read-jobs.fio — READ-ONLY jobs (safe for data; still loads the system)
[global]
filename=/dev/nvme0n1     ; raw namespace: bypasses filesystem and page cache with direct=1
readonly=1                ; safety net: fio refuses writes/trims
ioengine=io_uring         ; or libaio
direct=1                  ; O_DIRECT: no page cache
time_based=1
ramp_time=30              ; warm-up excluded from results
runtime=120
group_reporting=1
norandommap=1
randrepeat=0
percentile_list=50:90:99:99.9:99.99
numa_cpu_nodes=0          ; pin to the SSD's NUMA node (check /sys/.../numa_node); needs fio built with libnuma

[randread-4k-qd32]
rw=randread
bs=4k
iodepth=32
numjobs=1
stonewall                 ; run jobs one after another, not concurrently

[randread-4k-qd1-latency]
rw=randread
bs=4k
iodepth=1
numjobs=1
stonewall

[randread-4k-qd32x4]
rw=randread
bs=4k
iodepth=32
numjobs=4
stonewall

[seqread-128k-qd32]
rw=read
bs=128k
iodepth=32
numjobs=1
stonewall
# write-jobs.fio — DESTRUCTIVE. SCRATCH DRIVE ONLY. Verify the serial first:
#   nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvmeX | grep -E '^(sn|mn)'
[global]
filename=/dev/disk/by-id/nvme-EXAMPLE_SCRATCH_SERIAL   ; by-id path, never a bare nvmeXn1
ioengine=io_uring
direct=1
group_reporting=1
percentile_list=50:99:99.9:99.99

[precondition-seq]        ; fill the drive twice sequentially before random-write tests
rw=write
bs=128k
iodepth=32
loops=2
stonewall

[randwrite-4k-qd32]
rw=randwrite
bs=4k
iodepth=32
numjobs=4
time_based=1
ramp_time=60
runtime=600               ; long enough to reach steady state on many drives (verify by plotting)
stonewall

[randrw-70-30-4k]

rwmixread=70
bs=4k
iodepth=32
numjobs=4
time_based=1
runtime=600
stonewall
sudo fio read-jobs.fio --output-format=json+ --output=read.json
python3 fio_summary.py read.json

88.3 Interpreting fio output

Illustrative, abbreviated text output for the randread-4k-qd32 job (synthetic numbers; exact layout varies by fio version):

randread-4k-qd32: (groupid=0, jobs=1): err= 0: pid=4242
  read: IOPS=395k, BW=1543MiB/s (1618MB/s)(181GiB/120001msec)
    slat (nsec): min=730, max=48211, avg=1450.20, stdev=410.11
    clat (usec): min=11, max=9876, avg=80.41, stdev=31.70
     lat (usec): min=12, max=9878, avg=81.88, stdev=31.72
    clat percentiles (usec):
     | 50.00th=[   77], 90.00th=[  102], 99.00th=[  141],
     | 99.90th=[  611], 99.99th=[ 2442]
  cpu          : usr=12.51%, sys=38.22%, ctx=..., majf=0, minf=...
  IO depths    : 1=0.1%, 2=0.1%, 4=0.1%, 8=0.1%, 16=0.1%, 32=100.0%, >=64=0.0%
Disk stats (read/write):
  nvme0n1: ios=47400000/0, ..., util=99.62%
FieldMeaningWhat to check
IOPS, BWCompletion rate and payload bandwidth (MiB/s and MB/s both shown)BW = IOPS × bs; quote units correctly
slatSubmission latency (time to submit to the kernel)Large slat → CPU/submission bottleneck
clatCompletion latency: submission → completionThe device+stack latency; use its percentiles
latTotal latency ≈ slat + clat—
PercentilesDistribution of clatTail behavior; sample count adequate for p99.99?
cpuUser/system CPU of the job~100 % of one core per job → CPU-bound
IO depthsDistribution of submitted depthShould be at the configured depth; otherwise queue not kept full
utilFraction of time the device had I/O outstanding100 % does not mean saturated for SSDs (parallel device) — it only means "never idle"

Interpretation of the example: 395k IOPS × 80.4 µs ≈ 31.8 outstanding ≈ iodepth 32 → consistent (Little's law). p50 77 µs and p99 141 µs are tight; p99.9 611 µs and p99.99 2.4 ms reveal a tail affecting ~0.1–1 % of I/Os — worth investigating with the tail sources of Chapter 87. System CPU 38 % of one core: not CPU-bound at this rate. Output of the summary tool on equivalent synthetic JSON:

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""fio_summary.py - summarize `fio --output-format=json` results (OFFLINE PARSING).
Also checks Little's law consistency: outstanding ~= IOPS x mean latency.
Usage: fio job.fio --output-format=json > out.json ; python3 fio_summary.py out.json"""
import json, sys

SAMPLE = {"jobs": [{"jobname": "randread-4k-qd32", "job options": {"iodepth": "32"},
           "read": {"iops": 395_000.0, "bw": 1_580_000,          # bw in KiB/s
                    "clat_ns": {"mean": 80_400.0, "percentile": {
                        "50.000000": 77_312, "99.000000": 140_288,
                        "99.900000": 610_304, "99.990000": 2_441_216}}}}]}
# SYNTHETIC numbers in the shape of fio JSON (field names as used by fio's JSON output)

def summarize(doc):
    for job in doc["jobs"]:
        for d in ("read", "write"):
            st = job.get(d)
            if not st or not st.get("iops"):
                continue
            iops, mean_s = st["iops"], st["clat_ns"]["mean"] / 1e9
            pct = st["clat_ns"].get("percentile", {})
            qd = int(job.get("job options", {}).get("iodepth", 1))
            L = iops * mean_s
            print(f"{job['jobname']} {d}: {iops:,.0f} IOPS, {st['bw'] * 1024 / 1e9:.2f} GB/s, "
                  f"mean {mean_s * 1e6:.1f} us")
            print("   percentiles (us): " + ", ".join(f"p{float(k):g}={v / 1000:.0f}"
                                                     for k, v in sorted(pct.items(), key=lambda kv: float(kv[0]))))
            print(f"   Little's law: IOPS x mean = {L:.1f} outstanding vs iodepth {qd} per job"
                  + ("  (consistent)" if abs(L - qd) / qd < 0.15 else "  (CHECK: submission-side gaps or extra queueing)"))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    summarize(json.load(open(sys.argv[1])) if len(sys.argv) > 1 else SAMPLE)
randread-4k-qd32 read: 395,000 IOPS, 1.62 GB/s, mean 80.4 us
   percentiles (us): p50=77, p99=140, p99.9=610, p99.99=2441
   Little's law: IOPS x mean = 31.8 outstanding vs iodepth 32 per job  (consistent)

88.4 The benchmarking discipline checklist

ItemWhyPractice
Warm-upInitial seconds include queue ramp, CPU frequency ramp, cachesramp_time; discard first minutes
Steady stateWrite performance of a fresh (FOB) drive is far higher than after GC debt accumulates implPrecondition (e.g. 2× capacity sequential, then random); plot IOPS over time until stable; industry methodology exists (e.g. SNIA's Solid State Storage Performance Test Specification)
Workload definitionResults are meaningless without itRecord bs, rw/mix, QD, numjobs, engine, direct, range, runtime
Block sizeChanges the limiting resourceSweep 4k…1M when characterizing
Queue depthDetermines concurrency and latencySweep; report the knee
Read/write mixWrites create background work affecting readsTest mixes your application uses
Filesystem vs raw deviceFS adds metadata, journaling, alignment effectsRaw for device characterization; FS for application realism; never compare across
Cache effectsPage cache serves reads from RAM; device caches serve recent writesdirect=1; working set ≫ device cache; avoid re-reading just-written data unless intended
Thermal effectsThrottling reduces performance over minutesLog SMART temperature during runs; control airflow
Power statesAPST/ASPM affect latency, especially at low loadRecord policy; test both if relevant
CPU/NUMA placementRemote NUMA access and IRQ placement change resultsPin jobs near the device; record IRQ affinity
RepeatabilitySingle runs hide variance≥3–5 runs; report mean ± spread; investigate outliers instead of deleting them
VersionsKernel, fio, FW, BIOS change resultsRecord all in the result file
🧪 Lab 88.1 — H8/H9: safe read workload and performance observation CAUTION

Classification: non-destructive (read-only with readonly=1) · write-incapable by configuration · lab or maintenance window (loads the system).

Objective: run the read job file, verify Little's law, and observe QD scaling.

  1. Snapshot nvme smart-log (temperature, data units read).
  2. Run read-jobs.fio with JSON output.
  3. Run fio_summary.py; check consistency for each job.
  4. Snapshot smart-log again; verify data_units_read delta ≈ bytes read / 512,000.
  5. Watch /proc/interrupts deltas for nvme vectors during the run (which queues are used?).

Questions: (1) Does QD32×4 scale IOPS over QD32×1? Why or why not? (2) Did temperature rise? (3) Which job has the worst p99.9 and why?

Solution / expected reasoning

(1) If one job was CPU-bound or the device has spare parallelism, ×4 jobs increases IOPS; if the device was already saturated, IOPS stays and latency rises ~4×. (2) Sustained reads heat the controller; compare with WCTEMP. (3) Usually the deepest-queue job (queueing) — or QD1 if power-state exits dominate at low load. The SMART delta check proves the I/O reached the device (not a cache).

89 Performance Causality, Bottleneck Forensics and the Performance Mastery Module
