89.1 Why this chapter exists

The previous chapters give tools; this one gives judgement: how to prove what limits performance, how to avoid causal fallacies, what Linux tools can and cannot show, and how performance problems look in traces.

89.2 Linux performance evidence

ToolShowsProvesCannot prove
iostat -x 1Per-device r/s, w/s, rkB/s, await, aqu-sz, %utilRates and average latency/queue size at the block layerPercentiles; device internals; %util ≠ saturation for SSDs
blktrace + bttPer-request events (Q, G, I, D, C) and phase statisticsHost vs device split (Q2D vs D2C)What the device did during D2C
perf (record/top/stat)CPU profiles, cycles per I/OCPU hotspots, CPU-bound conditionsDevice-side causes
bpftraceCustom latency histograms at kernel tracepoints/kprobes (e.g. block request issue/complete, nvme tracepoints)Distributions at precise boundaries; outlier captureLink-level events
/proc/interruptsInterrupt counts per vector per CPUWhich queues/CPUs are active; IRQ distributionInterrupt latency
nvme smart-logTemperature, data units, busy timeThermal and volume contextFine-grained timing
PCIe analyzerLink utilization, per-phase times, payload sizes, creditsLink-level limits and device response timesHost software time
# Block-layer latency histogram for one device (read-only tracing; needs root and bpftrace)
sudo bpftrace -e '
tracepoint:block:block_rq_issue    /args->dev == $1/ { @start[args->sector] = nsecs; }
tracepoint:block:block_rq_complete /@start[args->sector]/ {
    @usecs = hist((nsecs - @start[args->sector]) / 1000); delete(@start[args->sector]); }' \
  $(( (259 << 20) | 0 ))   # dev_t encoding is kernel-internal (major<<20|minor); verify for your system
# Simpler and version-independent: sudo blktrace -d /dev/nvme0n1 -o - | blkparse -i - | head

The bpftrace one-liner is version-dependent (tracepoint argument names and dev_t encoding vary); prefer published tools (e.g. biolatency from the bcc/bpftrace tool collections) where available.

89.3 Causality rules for performance claims

  1. Temporal precision: the cause must precede the effect at the right time scale (µs events cannot explain second-long stalls without a mechanism).
  2. Magnitude: the cause must be large enough (a 1 µs replay cannot explain a 2 ms tail).
  3. Intervention: removing the cause removes the effect, everything else fixed.
  4. Dose-response: more cause → proportionally more effect.
  5. Alternative exclusion: common causes (temperature, background work) ruled out.
🏭 Device-specific limitations

Do not attribute a curve to "GC", "SLC cache exhaustion" or "die collisions" by shape alone. Those are plausible mechanisms for many SSDs, but firmware, NAND type, controller architecture, caches, scheduling and thermal policies differ, and the standard interface exposes none of them directly. Say "consistent with write-cache exhaustion; vendor confirmation or telemetry needed".

89.4 Performance in traces: normal, slow, failed, ambiguous

SYNTHETIC TEACHING TRACE — NOT A REAL DEVICE CAPTURE · link-level view of a 128 KiB sequential read stream (Gen4 x4, MPS 256)

#SymptomPossible causesEvidenceFirst checkSecond checkDisambiguating experimentLikely conclusion (confidence)

89.6 Labs by level

🧪 Lab 89.1 — Senior forensic: "the new server is slower" SAFE

Classification: analysis of supplied synthetic data. Scenario: identical SSD model; old server 1.05 M IOPS (4 KiB randread, 4 jobs × QD64); new server 640k IOPS. New server data: LnkSta 16GT/s x4 (same as old); fio jobs at 100 % CPU each; numa_node of SSD = 1; fio pinned to node 0; /proc/interrupts shows all nvme vectors on node-1 CPUs; mean clat 390 µs (old: 240 µs).

Questions: Observation / inference / hypothesis / evidence / root cause?

Solution

Observation: same link; jobs CPU-saturated; cross-NUMA placement; higher latency. Inference: Little's law: 256 outstanding / 390 µs ≈ 656k ✓ consistent; the extra latency is spent on host side (CPU-bound jobs, remote memory, cross-node interrupts), not the device (same model, same link). Hypothesis: NUMA misplacement + CPU saturation. Evidence: rerun pinned to node 1 (numa_cpu_nodes=1); blktrace D2C should be similar on both servers. Root cause (expected): benchmark placement, not hardware. Confidence high after the pinned rerun recovers IOPS.

Interview questions — performance (module 53)

  1. Beginner Convert 250k IOPS at 8 KiB to GB/s.
    Model answer

    250,000 × 8192 = 2.05 GB/s.

  2. Beginner What is queue depth?
    Model answer

    Maximum outstanding I/Os per submitter; actual outstanding may be lower.

  3. Beginner Why report percentiles?
    Model answer

    Averages hide tails that dominate user-visible latency.

  4. Beginner Why use direct=1?
    Model answer

    Bypass the page cache so the device is measured, not RAM.

  5. Beginner What does fio's clat measure?
    Model answer

    Completion latency from submission to completion.

  6. Intermediate State Little's law and use it to check fio output.
    Model answer

    L = λW; IOPS × mean latency should ≈ total outstanding (iodepth × jobs).

  7. Intermediate Why does sequential need lower QD than random to saturate?
    Model answer

    Each large command already spans many dies/pages; random small I/Os need many independent commands for parallelism.

  8. Intermediate What is the effect of MPS 128 vs 256 on Gen4 x4 throughput?
    Model answer

    Efficiency ~84 % vs ~91 % → ~6.5 vs ~7.1 GB/s ceilings (Ch 90 model).

  9. Intermediate Why precondition before write tests?
    Model answer

    To measure steady state instead of fresh-drive behavior with empty caches and no GC debt.

  10. Intermediate %util is 100 %. Is the SSD saturated?
    Model answer

    Not necessarily; it only shows the device always had work. Check whether IOPS grows with QD.

  11. Advanced How many outstanding MRds sustain 14 GB/s writes at 2 µs RTT, MRRS 512?
    Model answer

    14e9 × 2e-6 / 512 ≈ 55.

  12. Advanced Distinguish device-bound from host-bound latency.
    Model answer

    blktrace D2C vs Q2D/total; CPU profiles; analyzer device response times.

  13. Advanced Why can interrupt coalescing raise throughput but hurt latency?
    Model answer

    Fewer interrupts reduce CPU overhead per I/O, but completions wait for the threshold or timer.

  14. Advanced How many samples for a trustworthy p99.99?
    Model answer

    On the order of 106 or more, and repeated runs to estimate variance.

  15. Advanced What does a QD sweep knee tell you?
    Model answer

    The concurrency where the bottleneck saturates; beyond it, latency grows with no IOPS gain.

  16. Senior A vendor claims 14 GB/s on Gen5 x4. Is it plausible?
    Model answer

    Yes, near the ~14.1–14.7 GB/s effective ceiling with MPS 256–512 — leaves almost no margin; verify MPS, platform and measurement units (GB vs GiB).

  17. Senior Latency spikes coincide with AER corrected errors. What do you do?
    Model answer

    Check temporal precision and magnitude, then intervene (lower speed or fix channel) to test causality; consider common causes.

  18. Senior Design a performance regression gate for firmware releases.
    Model answer

    Fixed hardware, preconditioning, matrix of workloads, ≥5 repetitions, percentile-based tolerances with statistical tests, thermal logging, golden traces for latency phases.

  19. Senior When is a faster PCIe generation pointless?
    Model answer

    When media/controller latency or CPU dominates (QD1 4 KiB, Ch 87) or when the device's internal bandwidth is below the old link's ceiling.

  20. Senior How do you explain tail latency to a product manager?
    Model answer

    The slowest 1 in 1,000 requests; a page load that needs 100 storage reads hits it ~10 % of the time.

Teach-back. Child: "more orders in the kitchen help until the ovens are full; after that you just wait longer." Junior: "rate × latency = outstanding; find the saturated resource." Senior: "every performance claim is a causal claim; show the bottleneck by intervention, report concurrency and percentiles, and respect device-specific unknowns."

✅ Mastery gate — Performance engineering
  • I can derive IOPS/BW/latency/concurrency from any two of them.
  • I can classify a result as bandwidth-, latency-, queue- or CPU-limited with evidence.
  • I can write safe fio jobs and interpret every field of the output.
  • I can build a latency budget and predict the effect of a change.
  • I apply the five causality rules before claiming a performance root cause.

90 PCIe Bandwidth Calculations

← 89 Performance Causality, Bottleneck Forensics and the Performance Mastery Module29 Validation Engineering: From Requirement to Evidence →

90.1 Why this chapter exists

"Gen5 x4 is 16 GB/s" is the most repeated half-truth in storage. The raw signaling rate is not what your application gets: line encoding, TLP framing and headers, DLLPs and ordered sets, NVMe's own traffic (SQE fetches, CQEs, interrupts) and the device's internal limits all take their share. This chapter does the arithmetic explicitly so you can tell a link limit from a device limit.

  • Separate raw signaling rate, encoding efficiency, protocol efficiency, effective payload bandwidth and device limitation.
  • Compute TLP efficiency for MPS 128/256/512 including framing and header overhead.
  • Work Gen3 x4, Gen4 x4, Gen5 x4, Gen5 x8 and Gen6 x4 end to end.
  • Compute per-I/O link bytes for NVMe reads, and the write-direction (completion) efficiency.
🧒 Kid analogy — moving boxes on a conveyor

A conveyor belt moves 16 slots per second. Every 130 slots, 2 are used for "start marker" labels (encoding). Every box needs a shipping label and a tape strip (header and framing) that also take belt space — a small box wastes more belt on labels than a big one. Now and then, the belt carries "got it!" notes going back (DLLPs). What arrives at the end is fewer useful kilograms than the belt's slot rate suggests.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

PCIe is full duplex: two belts in opposite directions, each with its own budget; acknowledgements for one direction ride on the other. And the factory at the end (the SSD) may simply not be able to fill the belt.

90.2 The four layers of bandwidth

BWraw = (GT/s per lane) × lanes / 8 [GB/s, per direction]
  • GT/s — transfers per second per lane: 2.5, 5, 8, 16, 32, 64 for Gen1–6 verified (Gen7 128 GT/s version); for Gen1–5 one transfer = one bit; Gen6 PAM4 carries 2 bits per symbol at 32 GBaud = 64 GT/s
  • /8 — bits to bytes
BWencoded = BWraw × Eenc , Eenc = 8/10 (Gen1–2), 128/130 (Gen3–5), 236/256 TLP bytes per flit (Gen6 Flit mode)
  • Eenc — encoding efficiency. Gen6 Flit mode: each 256-byte flit carries 236 bytes of TLP space plus data-link payload, CRC and FEC bytes (commonly described as 6 DLP + 8 CRC + 6 FEC) version — verify against the PCIe 6.x specification
ETLP = MPS / (MPS + H + F)
  • MPS — payload bytes per TLP (Max Payload Size, when transfers are large and aligned)
  • H — TLP header bytes: 12 (3DW) or 16 (4DW, 64-bit address); NVMe data to host memory usually uses 64-bit addresses → 16
  • F — per-TLP framing and link protection: Gen3–5: 4-byte STP token (includes sequence number) + 4-byte LCRC = 8; Gen1–2: STP 1 + sequence 2 + LCRC 4 + END 1 = 8; optional ECRC adds 4. Gen6 Flit: no per-TLP LCRC/framing (protection is per flit), header format differs — approximated here as 16 B per TLP approximation
BWeff ≈ BWencoded × ETLP × (1 − d)
  • d — fraction of link time for DLLPs (Ack/Nak, UpdateFC) and ordered sets (SKP) in the data direction; modelled as 2 % for Gen3–5 and 0 for Gen6 Flit (DLLP information travels inside flits) — an assumption; real values depend on Ack/UpdateFC policies and traffic in the other direction impl
⚠️ Never present theoretical bandwidth as guaranteed

BWeff is a ceiling for payload on the link. Application throughput is further limited by the device (controller and NAND), the host (CPU, memory, root complex), NVMe protocol traffic, and the workload's concurrency. Use these numbers to find which limit you are hitting, not to promise results.

90.3 TLP efficiency by MPS

MPSBytes on link per TLP (Gen3–5, 64-bit MWr)ETLPCompletion (CplD, 3DW header, 20 B overhead)
128 B128 + 16 + 8 = 1520.8421128/148 = 0.8649
256 B256 + 24 = 2800.9143256/276 = 0.9275
512 B512 + 24 = 5360.9552512/532 = 0.9624

90.4 Worked example: Gen4 x4

  1. Raw: 16 GT/s × 4 lanes / 8 = 8.000 GB/s per direction.
  2. Encoding 128b/130b: 8.000 × 128/130 = 7.877 GB/s.
  3. TLP overhead at MPS 256: 7.877 × 256/280 = 7.202 GB/s.
  4. DLLP/ordered-set allowance 2 %: 7.202 × 0.98 = 7.058 GB/s effective payload.
  5. Same at MPS 128: 7.877 × 0.8421 × 0.98 = 6.501 GB/s; at MPS 512: 7.374 GB/s.

NVMe per-I/O overhead (4 KiB random read, device → host direction). Upstream bytes per I/O at MPS 256: data 16 TLPs × 280 B = 4480; CQE MWr 16 + 24 = 40; MSI-X MWr 4 + 24 = 28 (if not coalesced); the SQE-fetch MRd header also travels upstream: 24. Total 4572 B → efficiency 4096/4572 = 0.896. Link-only ceiling: 7.877 × 0.98 × 109 / 4572 ≈ 1.69 M IOPS (6.92 GB/s of 4 KiB payload) — above most devices' 4 KiB random-read capability, so random-read IOPS is usually device-limited, not link-limited, at Gen4 x4 derived.

90.5 Worked example: Gen5 x4

  1. Raw: 32 × 4 / 8 = 16.000 GB/s.
  2. Encoded: 16 × 128/130 = 15.754 GB/s.
  3. MPS 256: 15.754 × 0.9143 × 0.98 = 14.115 GB/s; MPS 128: 13.001; MPS 512: 14.747.
  4. 4 KiB read link-only ceiling (MPS 256): ≈ 3.38 M IOPS.

90.6 All requested configurations

Generated by the calculator below (derived model, GB/s = 109 B/s per direction):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""PCIe bandwidth estimator (DERIVED MODEL - teaching estimates, not guarantees).
Layers of loss, applied in order:
  1. line encoding        8b/10b (Gen1-2), 128b/130b (Gen3-5), Flit 236/256 TLP bytes (Gen6)
  2. TLP framing+header   per-TLP bytes around each payload chunk of <= MPS
  3. DLLP / ordered sets  modelled as a fixed fraction (assumption, see text)
Units: GB/s = 1e9 bytes/s, per direction."""
GEN = {  # GT/s per lane, encoding efficiency, per-TLP non-payload bytes (64-bit MWr, no ECRC)
    1: (2.5, 8 / 10, 2 + 1 + 16 + 4 + 1),     # STP + seq(2) + hdr16 + LCRC4 + END ~ 24 B
    2: (5.0, 8 / 10, 24),
    3: (8.0, 128 / 130, 4 + 16 + 4),            # STP token 4 B (incl. seq) + hdr 16 + LCRC 4
    4: (16.0, 128 / 130, 24),
    5: (32.0, 128 / 130, 24),
    6: (64.0, 236 / 256, 16),                   # flit: CRC/FEC/DLP live in the flit; ~16 B hdr (approx.)
}

def raw_GBps(gen, lanes):
    gt, enc, _ = GEN[gen]
    return gt * lanes / 8                     # 1 bit per transfer per lane (PAM4 Gen6: 64 GT/s still = 64 Gb/s)

def encoded_GBps(gen, lanes):
    gt, enc, _ = GEN[gen]
    return gt * enc * lanes / 8

def tlp_eff(gen, mps):
    return mps / (mps + GEN[gen][2])

def effective_GBps(gen, lanes, mps=256, dllp_os_frac=None):
    if dllp_os_frac is None:                  # Gen6 flit already carries DLLP info in-flit
        dllp_os_frac = 0.0 if gen >= 6 else 0.02
    return encoded_GBps(gen, lanes) * tlp_eff(gen, mps) * (1 - dllp_os_frac)

def per_io_bytes(io_bytes, mps, gen):
    """Upstream link bytes for one NVMe READ of io_bytes (device -> host)."""
    ovh = GEN[gen][2]
    n = -(-io_bytes // mps)
    data = io_bytes + n * ovh
    cqe = 16 + ovh                             # CQE MWr
    msix = 4 + ovh                             # MSI-X MWr (if not coalesced)
    sqe_req = ovh                              # MRd header for the SQE fetch travels upstream too
    return data + cqe + msix + sqe_req

if __name__ == "__main__":
    print("Gen x  | raw GB/s | after encoding | eff MPS128 | MPS256 | MPS512  (2% DLLP/OS allowance Gen3-5, 0% Gen6)")
    for g, w in [(3, 4), (4, 4), (5, 4), (5, 8), (6, 4)]:
        print(f"G{g} x{w} | {raw_GBps(g, w):8.3f} | {encoded_GBps(g, w):14.3f} | "
              + " | ".join(f"{effective_GBps(g, w, m):6.3f}" for m in (128, 256, 512)))
    print("\nTLP efficiency (Gen3-5 non-flit, 24 B/TLP):",
          {m: round(tlp_eff(4, m), 4) for m in (128, 256, 512)})
    for g in (4, 5):
        for m in (128, 256, 512):
            b = per_io_bytes(4096, m, g)
            enc = encoded_GBps(g, 4) * 0.98
            print(f"G{g}x4 MPS{m}: 4KiB read uses {b} B upstream -> eff {4096/b:.4f}, "
                  f"link-only ceiling {enc*1e9/b/1e6:.2f} M IOPS, {enc*4096/b:.2f} GB/s")

The same numbers as a chart, all on one GB/s scale. Two things stand out. MPS matters more than people expect: going from 128 to 512 is worth about 13 % on the Gen3–5 links (about 9 % in the Gen6 flit approximation). And Gen5 x8 and Gen6 x4 have the same raw rate; Gen6 loses more to flit overhead but less per TLP, so the two land within a few percent of each other. derived

90.7 The write direction: read requests and completions

For NVMe writes, the payload flows host → device as CplDs answering the SSD's MRds. Completion size is chosen by the completer (root complex) within MPS and Read Completion Boundary rules impl. Effective downstream ceiling at Gen4 x4 (2 % allowance):

CplD payloadE (20 B overhead)Gen4 x4 GB/sGen5 x4 GB/s
64 B (RCB-sized completions)0.7625.8811.76
128 B0.8656.68—
256 B0.9287.1614.32
512 B0.9627.4314.86

Plus the concurrency requirement from Chapter 86: outstanding MRds = BW × RTT / MRRS. A platform that splits completions into 64-byte pieces and has a long round trip can make write throughput link-protocol-limited well below the read ceiling.

90.8 Bandwidth lab

🧪 Lab 90.1 — Raw vs protocol vs effective vs device SAFE

Classification: calculation; optional read-only measurement. Tasks: (1) Run pcie_bw.py; add an ecrc=True option (+4 B per TLP) and recompute Gen5 x4 MPS 256. (2) Compute the 128 KiB sequential-read per-I/O efficiency at Gen4 MPS 256. (3) A Gen4 x4 SSD measures 6.9 GB/s seq read, 5.1 GB/s seq write. Which is link-limited? (4) Optional: measure your own drive with the read job of Chapter 88 and compare with the ceiling for its LnkSta and MPS.

Solution

(1) E = 256/284 = 0.9014 → 15.754 × 0.9014 × 0.98 ≈ 13.92 GB/s (−1.4 %). (2) 512 data TLPs × 280 = 143,360 + 40 + 28 + 24 = 143,452 B per I/O → 0.914 efficiency → ~7.05 GB/s; per-command overhead is negligible for large I/O. (3) Reads at 6.9 ≈ 98 % of the 7.06 ceiling → link-limited. Writes at 5.1 are well below any write-direction ceiling (5.9–7.4) → most likely device-limited (NAND program bandwidth) — or completion-size/concurrency-limited; check CplD sizes on an analyzer to be sure. (4) Expect 85–98 % of the ceiling for a link-bound device.

Quiz

  1. Why is Gen5 x4 not "16 GB/s" for applications?

    Answer

    128b/130b encoding, TLP header/framing overhead (MPS-dependent), DLLPs/ordered sets, NVMe command traffic, and device limits reduce it to ~14 GB/s or less.

  2. Per-TLP overhead for a 64-bit MWr at Gen4?

    Answer

    4 B STP token + 16 B header + 4 B LCRC = 24 B (no ECRC).

  3. Does doubling MPS from 256 to 512 double bandwidth?

    Answer

    No: efficiency rises from ~91.4 % to ~95.5 % — about +4.5 %.

  4. Gen6 uses PAM4 at 64 GT/s. Raw x4 bandwidth?

    Answer

    64 × 4 / 8 = 32 GB/s per direction before flit overhead.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Walk me through the effective bandwidth of Gen4 x4 with MPS 256.
    Model answer

    8 GB/s raw → ×128/130 = 7.88 → ×256/280 = 7.20 → minus ~2 % DLLP/SKP ≈ 7.06 GB/s.

  2. Advanced Why can writes be slower than reads at the protocol level on the same link?
    Model answer

    Writes need Non-Posted MRds with round trips and enough outstanding tags; completions may be split into small RCB-sized pieces with 20 B overhead each.

  3. Senior When would you recommend Gen5 x8 for a single SSD?
    Model answer

    Only if the device's internal bandwidth exceeds the Gen5 x4 ceiling (~14 GB/s) for the target workload, or for multi-function/aggregated designs; otherwise lanes are wasted.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can compute raw, encoded and effective bandwidth for any Gen/width/MPS from memory.
  • I can compute per-I/O link bytes for NVMe reads including CQE, MSI-X and SQE fetch.
  • I can explain write-direction efficiency and the outstanding-request requirement.
  • I never state theoretical link bandwidth as application throughput.

Summary. Bandwidth is a stack of efficiencies: raw rate × encoding × TLP efficiency × link-maintenance allowance, then NVMe overhead and finally the device's own limits. Compute each layer and compare with measurements to find which one binds. This completes the Linux, lab, trace, analyzer, debugging, failure and performance Parts of the journey.

PART XXIX

Validation Engineering

Everything you have learned so far — enumeration, registers, queues, doorbells, Transaction Layer Packets, completions, interrupts, power and errors — becomes useful to a team only when someone turns it into evidence. Validation engineering is the discipline of converting a requirement into a stimulus, an expected behaviour, an observable piece of evidence and a pass/fail decision, and then doing that systematically, across a matrix of configurations, with negative, stress and recovery cases, and with regression protection after every fix. This Part teaches you to write a validation plan that a senior reviewer would sign, to design a test matrix that does not explode combinatorially, to reproduce intermittent failures deliberately, and to treat every fixed bug as a permanent test.

29 Validation Engineering: From Requirement to Evidence

DOCUMENTS: NVM Express (NVMe) Base Specification, NVM Command Set Specification, NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification, PCI Express (PCIe) Base Specification; Zoned Namespace (ZNS) Command Set for the ZNS rows. REVISIONS (course baseline, August 2026): NVMe Base 2.4, NVM Command Set 1.3, PCIe Transport 1.4, ZNS 1.5 version. STATUS: current per the course brief — confirm on nvmexpress.org before you cite them in a real plan. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.x (single monolithic document; command sets and transport were not yet separate documents), and any revision before a feature was introduced. SOURCE NOTES: this chapter cites register names, opcodes and log identifiers that are long-established; it deliberately does not cite section numbers. Each test card below names the requirement in paraphrase and tells you which document owns it, so that you look up the normative sentence yourself.

29.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineers who understand a protocol but cannot validate it produce opinions. Engineers who can validate it produce evidence. In an SSD program, the validation team is where the specification, the firmware, the host driver and the board meet: they decide whether a product ships, and their test logs and traces are the raw material of every root-cause investigation. The skills in this chapter — writing a requirement precisely, choosing the observable that proves it, designing a matrix, isolating intermittent failures — are the same skills you use when you debug. A debug session is simply a validation test whose result surprised you.

  • Beginner objective: explain the difference between a requirement, a test, an expected result and evidence, and write one complete test card for NVMe controller enable.
  • Intermediate objective: build test cards with negative, stress and recovery variants for queue creation, read/write integrity, flush, error handling and MSI-X (Message Signalled Interrupts – Extended).
  • Advanced objective: design a test matrix over PCIe generation × link width × Max_Payload_Size × queue depth × block size × power state, compute its full size and reduce it with pairwise and risk-based selection.
  • Senior objective: write a test plan that a program manager, a firmware lead and a PCIe architect can all sign, with explicit exit criteria and a regression strategy.
  • Trace-analysis objective: recognise normal, slow, failed and ambiguous outcomes of a validation test in a synthetic trace and identify the first abnormal event.
  • Debugging objective: convert an intermittent failure into a deterministic reproduction using stress, reset, power-cycle and workload-dependent methods, and record what each method proves.
  • Validation objective: close every fixed defect with a regression test that would have caught it, plus neighbouring cases.

Prerequisites. You should already be comfortable with the controller registers (CAP, CC, CSTS, AQA, ASQ, ACQ), the Submission Queue / Completion Queue model (SQ, CQ, CQE), memory requests and completions (MRd, MWr, CplD), Physical Region Page (PRP) data pointers, MSI-X, and PCIe Advanced Error Reporting (AER). If any of these is shaky, revisit the earlier Parts first; this chapter assumes them and uses them as building blocks. The automated tools you will later build in Chapter 34 consume the evidence formats introduced here.

29.2 Story, analogy and where it breaks

🧒 Kid analogy — the bridge inspector

Imagine a new footbridge in a park. The builder says "it is strong". The bridge inspector does not argue; she writes on a clipboard: "Requirement: the bridge holds 50 children at once. Setup: a calm day, the bridge dry. Stimulus: 50 children walk on and stand still. Expected: the middle sags less than 2 cm. Evidence: a laser ruler reading. Pass if under 2 cm." Then she does sneaky things: one heavy cart instead of children (negative test), children jumping for an hour (stress test), and checking the bridge springs back after they leave (recovery test). She tests on a hot day and a frosty day, with the bridge wet and dry (the test matrix). When a bolt breaks and is replaced, she reruns the exact test that broke it, and the tests nearby (regression).

🌍 Engineering analogy — the driving examiner

A driving examiner has a fixed checklist (requirements), a route (setup and stimulus), observable behaviours (mirror checks, stopping distance), a scoring rule (pass/fail) and deliberate surprises (the emergency stop is a negative/stress test). The examiner never writes "drove well"; she writes "stopped within the line at the junction on Elm Street". That specificity is what makes a validation result reproducible and arguable.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A bridge or a driver is observed directly. An SSD is observed through narrow windows: registers you can read, log pages the firmware chooses to populate, PCIe packets an analyzer can capture, and host-side timings. Much of the device (NAND management, internal queues, firmware scheduling) is generally unobservable. Also, a bridge does not change between inspections; firmware does, and so does the host kernel. Validation of an SSD is therefore always "evidence about a specific firmware, on a specific platform, with a specific driver, at a specific time" — and must record all four.

29.3 Vocabulary

TermPlain meaningEngineering meaningAdjacent termsCommon confusion
RequirementWhat must be trueA testable statement traced to a source: a specification "shall", a product requirement document, or a customer specificationSource, traceabilityTreating a "should" as a "shall", or a vendor datasheet target as a spec requirement
Device Under Test (DUT)The thing being checkedThe exact drive + firmware revision + slot + platform combinationConfiguration, SKUWriting "the SSD" without firmware and platform identifiers
StimulusWhat you doThe command sequence, register writes, workload or physical event appliedTest step, workloadMixing setup (preconditions) with stimulus (the thing under test)
OracleHow you know the right answerThe mechanism that decides expected behaviour: spec rule, reference model, golden data, previous firmwareExpected resultUsing "it did not crash" as the oracle

29.4 The nine-field test card

Every feature, without exception, gets the same nine fields. The discipline is boring on purpose: boring templates make omissions visible.

#FieldQuestion it answersBad exampleGood example
1RequirementWhat must be true, and who says so?"Reset works""After host clears CC.EN to 0, CSTS.RDY transitions to 0 within the CAP.TO window." Source: NVMe Base, controller reset/initialization rules (look up the normative sentence).
2SetupWhat state and configuration before the test?"Drive installed""Controller enabled (CSTS.RDY=1), 4 I/O queue pairs created, no outstanding commands, firmware X.Y, Gen4 x4, kernel driver unbound (test uses a user-space harness)"
3StimulusExactly what do we do?"Reset it""MMIO write CC with EN=0, other fields unchanged; poll CSTS every 1 ms"
4Expected behaviourWhat should happen, per the oracle?"Should be fine""CSTS.RDY reads 0 before CAP.TO × 500 ms elapses; CSTS.CFS stays 0"
5Observable evidenceWhat artifact proves it?"Looks OK""Timestamped log of every CSTS read; analyzer capture of the CC MWr and subsequent MRd/CplD pairs on CSTS"
6Pass/failThe decision rule, numerically"No errors""PASS iff RDY=0 observed at t ≤ CAP.TO×500 ms and CFS=0 throughout"
7Negative testWhat invalid input/sequence, and what correct error?—"Write CC.EN=1 with an MPS value outside CAP.MPSMIN..MPSMAX; expect the controller not to become ready normally (exact behaviour: check spec), no hang of the link"
8Stress testSame thing, many times / under load—"10 000 enable/disable cycles with I/O in flight on 4 queues before each disable; check data integrity after every 100 cycles"
9Recovery testDoes it come back clean?—"After disable during I/O, re-initialize admin queue, recreate I/O queues, verify all previously acknowledged writes read back correctly"
📌 Remember

A negative test passes only when the DUT fails correctly: the right status code type and status code, no corruption of unrelated state, no link-level side effects, and an unchanged ability to process the next valid command.

29.5 Architecture of a validation setup

Actors: the harness (decides what to run and judges results), the host (executes stimulus through a driver), the DUT, and optional observers (interposer + analyzer, thermal chamber, programmable power supply). State: DUT configuration (firmware, namespaces, features set), host configuration (kernel, driver parameters, IOMMU mode), link state (generation, width, ASPM). Interfaces: PCIe (packets), MMIO (registers), admin/I/O commands, log pages, OS logs. Dependencies: a test is only as good as its oracle; a performance test is only as good as its preconditioning; a trace is only as good as its trigger.

29.6 Hardware, protocol and specification views

🔧 Hardware view — what participates and what you can see
  • Must participate: Root Port (or switch downstream port), the link, the NVMe controller's PCIe function, its BAR0 register file, its DMA engine, host memory for queues and data.
  • May participate: PCIe switch, retimers, IOMMU, interposer, power-loss-protection capacitors, thermal sensors, out-of-band management (NVMe-MI over SMBus/I2C or VDM).
  • Observable: config space, BAR registers, CQE contents, log pages, Linux kernel messages, timings, and — with an analyzer — every TLP and DLLP on the link.
  • Generally unobservable: internal SRAM/DRAM caches, NAND program/erase scheduling, internal retry, firmware task scheduling. Vendor debug logs may expose some of it impl.
📡 Protocol view — the transactions a validation test produces

Every NVMe test reduces to a small vocabulary of PCIe transactions: host MWr to BAR0 (register writes and doorbells, posted — no completion), host MRd to BAR0 (register reads, answered by CplD from the device), device MRd to host memory (SQE fetch, PRP list fetch, write-data fetch, answered by CplD from the Root Complex), device MWr to host memory (read data, CQEs, MSI-X messages). Ordering matters: PCIe ordering rules keep a CQE MWr from passing the data MWrs issued before it in the same direction under default ordering attributes, which is why "data before completion" is visible in correct traces derived. Errors appear as completion status (UR, CA), poisoned TLPs (EP bit), AER messages, or NVMe status in the CQE.

📘 Specification discipline for validation
  • Normative behaviour ("shall") becomes a pass/fail requirement.
  • Recommended behaviour ("should") becomes a warning-level finding, not a failure, unless your product requirements upgrade it.
  • Optional behaviour ("may", or features gated by a capability bit) is tested only if the DUT advertises it — and then it must behave as specified. Your plan must read the capability first (CAP, Identify Controller, Identify Namespace) and select tests accordingly.
  • Implementation-dependent behaviour (latency, which internal error produces which vendor-specific log entry) is measured and characterised, never "failed" against the spec.
  • Version-dependent behaviour: record which revision your requirement came from; a 2.x-only feature on a device reporting an older Version register (VS, offset 08h) is not a defect.

📭 What the specification does not say

The NVMe and PCIe specifications define behaviour, formats and many timing limits, but they do not give you a validation plan, a performance target, an error-injection method, a minimum soak duration, or a pass threshold for correctable PCIe errors per hour. Those come from product requirements, customer specifications, compliance programs (for example plugfests and integrator lists) and your organisation's quality policy. Never write "spec requires 0 correctable errors" — write which document set that target.

29.8 Four worked test cards

29.8.1 Controller enable after reset

TEST  NVME-CTRL-EN-001   Controller enable from reset
REQ   NVMe Base: controller initialization sequence; CSTS.RDY semantics; CAP.TO bound
SETUP CSTS.RDY == 0 (after CC.EN=0 completed); admin queues allocated in host memory,
      page-aligned; driver unbound; analyzer trigger = MWr to BAR0+14h (CC)
STIM  1. read CAP (00h), VS (08h)          -> record MQES, TO, DSTRD, MPSMIN/MAX, CSS
      2. write AQA (24h) = ACQS<<16 | ASQS  (both 0-based)
      3. write ASQ (28h), ACQ (30h)       -> 64-bit base addresses
      4. write CC (14h): MPS, CSS, AMS, IOSQES=6, IOCQES=4, then EN=1
      5. poll CSTS (1Ch) every 1 ms
EXP   CSTS.RDY == 1 at t <= CAP.TO * 500 ms; CSTS.CFS == 0
EVID  host log of each poll with timestamp; analyzer: CC MWr, CSTS MRd/CplD sequence
PASS  RDY observed within bound AND first admin command (Identify, CNS=01h) succeeds
NEG   a) MPS outside [MPSMIN, MPSMAX]   b) ASQ not aligned as required
      c) EN=1 while RDY still 1 from previous enable (illegal host sequence)
      -> expect no link hang; exact controller reaction: read the spec + record
STRESS 10 000 cycles of disable(with I/O in flight)/enable; latency histogram of RDY
RECOV after each cycle: recreate I/O queues, verify last-acknowledged data pattern

29.8.2 I/O queue creation and deletion ordering

Requirement: an I/O Submission Queue is associated with an existing I/O Completion Queue at creation; a CQ cannot be deleted while an SQ still uses it. Stimulus: Create I/O CQ (05h) with QID=1, QSIZE (0-based), PC=1, IEN=1, IV=1; then Create I/O SQ (01h) with QID=1, CQID=1. Negative cases and the evidence you expect:

Negative stimulusExpected CQE status (name; confirm code in spec table)Also check
Create SQ with CQID that does not existCompletion Queue Invalid (Command Specific)No SQ created: a later doorbell to that SQ is ignored / errors
QID = 0 or above the number of queues granted by Set Features Number of QueuesInvalid Queue IdentifierExisting queues unaffected
QSIZE larger than CAP.MQES (0-based) or 0Invalid Queue Size—
IV larger than the MSI-X vectors availableInvalid Interrupt VectorMSI-X table unchanged
Delete I/O CQ while its SQ existsInvalid Queue DeletionSQ still processes I/O
Physically-contiguous flag cleared when CAP.CQR=1Invalid Field in Command (generic) — verify for your revision—

29.8.3 Flush and the volatile write cache

First read Identify Controller's Volatile Write Cache (VWC) field: if no volatile cache is present, Flush is still a valid command but the power-loss experiment cannot distinguish behaviour. If a cache is present and enabled (Get Features, Volatile Write Cache feature), the experiment is: write a unique pattern (LBA number + generation counter in each block), issue Flush, wait for its CQE, cut power with a programmable supply, power on, read back. Every block whose write and subsequent Flush completed must contain the new pattern. Blocks written after the last Flush may contain old or new data — but never a torn mixture of unrelated data, unless the product's atomicity rules allow it (check Identify fields for atomic write unit sizes version).

⚠️ Safety

Power-cut testing is an EXPERT LAB activity: use a dedicated, non-production drive in a dedicated test host, with a controllable supply or a relay-switched riser. Never on a drive whose data you need, and never on a laptop's internal SSD.

29.8.4 MSI-X routing

Requirement: completions on CQ n are signalled with the vector given in that CQ's IV field (when IEN=1). Evidence ladder: (1) /proc/interrupts counters per nvme vector increase in proportion to I/O submitted on each CPU/queue; (2) analyzer shows an MWr to the MSI-X message address/data for that vector after each CQE MWr (or after a coalesced batch); (3) masking the vector in the MSI-X table sets its Pending Bit Array bit, and unmasking delivers the pending message. A failure where the CQE is written but no interrupt MWr follows points to the interrupt path; a failure where the interrupt arrives but the host does not reap points to the host (phase tag / CQ head handling).

29.9 Test matrix design and combinatorial explosion

Every dimension multiplies. With six dimensions of three values each, the full factorial has 36 = 729 configurations. Add firmware (3 builds), OS (2 kernels), temperature (3 points) and duration (2): 729 × 36 = 26 244 runs. At 30 minutes each that is about 1.5 years of a single station.

Nfull = ∏i=1..k vi     Npairwise ≥ v(1) × v(2)
  • k — number of dimensions
  • vi — number of values in dimension i
  • v(1), v(2) — the two largest value counts (a pairwise suite must cover every pair of their values, so it can never be smaller than their product)
IDPCIe genWidthMPSQueue depthBlock sizePower stateWhy this row is high-value
M01Gen4 (16 GT/s)x4256 B324 KiBPS0Baseline: most common client configuration; golden reference for every other row
M02Gen5 (32 GT/s)x4512 B256128 KiBPS0Maximum bandwidth; exposes credit and tag exhaustion
M03Gen3 (8 GT/s)x4128 B14 KiBAPST onLatency path with power transitions between commands (exit-latency bugs)
M04Gen4x2256 B321 MiBPS0Degraded width; large transfers split by MRRS/MPS; PRP lists
M05Gen4x1128 B2564 KiBPS0Severe link bottleneck with deep queues: timeouts and fairness
M06Gen5x4256 B1512 BAPST onSub-4 KiB I/O on 512 B-formatted namespace; low-QD wake latency at max speed
M07Gen4x4256 B128mixed 4K/128K 70/30 R/WPS0 → PS3 → PS0 cyclingPower-state changes under mixed load
M08Gen3x4256 B32128 KiBL1.2 enabled (ASPM)Link power management + NVMe idle; L1 exit latency vs completion timeout

The executable script below computes the full factorial for a six-dimension example and greedily builds a pairwise (all-pairs) cover: every value of every dimension appears together with every value of every other dimension at least once.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""matrix.py - full-factorial size vs. greedy pairwise (all-pairs) reduction.
Executable, standard library only. Dimensions are a SYNTHETIC teaching example."""
import itertools

DIMS = {
    "gen":   ["Gen3", "Gen4", "Gen5"],
    "width": ["x1", "x2", "x4"],
    "mps":   [128, 256, 512],
    "qd":    [1, 32, 256],
    "bs":    ["4K", "128K", "1M"],
    "ps":    ["PS0", "PS3", "APST"],
}

def all_pairs(dims):
    names = list(dims)
    uncovered = set()
    for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(len(names)), 2):
        for va in dims[names[a]]:
            for vb in dims[names[b]]:
                uncovered.add((a, va, b, vb))
    tests = []
    candidates = list(itertools.product(*dims.values()))
    while uncovered:
        def gain(c):
            return sum((a, c[a], b, c[b]) in uncovered
                       for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(len(c)), 2))
        best = max(candidates, key=gain)
        tests.append(best)
        for a, b in itertools.combinations(range(len(best)), 2):
            uncovered.discard((a, best[a], b, best[b]))
    return names, tests

if __name__ == "__main__":
    full = 1
    for v in DIMS.values():
        full *= len(v)
    names, tests = all_pairs(DIMS)
    print(f"full factorial: {full} configurations")
    print(f"pairwise cover: {len(tests)} configurations")
    print(" | ".join(f"{n:>5}" for n in names))
    for t in tests[:6]:
        print(" | ".join(f"{str(x):>5}" for x in t))
    print("...")

Output of running it (real output of the script; the dimensions are synthetic):

full factorial: 729 configurations
pairwise cover: 15 configurations
  gen | width |   mps |    qd |    bs |    ps
 Gen3 |    x1 |   128 |     1 |    4K |   PS0
 Gen3 |    x2 |   256 |    32 |  128K |   PS3
 Gen3 |    x4 |   512 |   256 |    1M |  APST
 Gen4 |    x1 |   128 |    32 |  128K |  APST
 Gen4 |    x2 |   256 |     1 |    1M |   PS0
 Gen5 |    x1 |   128 |   256 |    1M |   PS3
...

How senior engineers choose high-value tests

  1. Risk first. Weight cells by (probability of a defect) × (impact). New firmware features, recently changed code, unusual hardware (x1, Gen5 retimers), and boundaries (QD=1, max QD, minimum and maximum transfer sizes, MPS edges) get more cells.
  2. Pairwise as a floor, not a ceiling. Most interaction defects involve one or two factors; pairwise gives broad coverage cheaply. Add 3-way coverage only for factors known to interact (MPS × transfer size × PRP alignment).
  3. Boundaries and equivalence classes. Instead of all block sizes, choose 512 B, 4 KiB, one size that is not a power of two (e.g. 12 KiB), MDTS, and MDTS + 1 (negative).
  4. Customer configurations are mandatory cells, regardless of what the reduction algorithm says.
  5. Duration is a dimension. Short runs find functional bugs; long runs find leaks, wear-related and thermal behaviour.
  6. Keep a golden baseline cell (M01) that runs on every build: it is your regression canary and your performance reference.

29.10 The test plan template

TEST PLAN: <feature / product / firmware release>
1  IDENTIFICATION     plan id, version, author, reviewers, date, change log
2  SCOPE              features in scope; explicitly OUT of scope (and why)
3  SOURCES            spec documents + revisions (e.g. NVMe Base 2.4, NVM CS 1.3,
                      PCIe transport 1.4, PCIe Base rev used by platform);
                      product requirement doc ids; customer spec ids
4  DUT & PLATFORM     drive SKU, firmware build(s), capacity, namespace format;
                      host CPU, chipset/root port, BIOS, kernel, driver, IOMMU mode;
                      slot (CPU-attached vs chipset), adapters, risers, retimers
5  CAPABILITY READ    CAP, VS, Identify Controller/Namespace dumps stored as artifacts;
                      the plan selects optional tests from these, not from datasheets
6  TEST CATALOGUE     one 9-field card per test (requirement..recovery), each with id
7  MATRIX             dimensions, values, reduction method, mandatory cells, total runs
8  ORACLES            data-pattern scheme, reference model, golden traces, thresholds
9  INSTRUMENTATION    host logging, nvme log pages captured before/after, analyzer
                      trigger/filter plan, power meter, thermal chamber
10 ENTRY CRITERIA     builds available, stations calibrated, smoke suite green
11 EXIT CRITERIA      e.g. 100% of P0 tests pass; no open severity-1 defects;
                      every waived failure has a signed rationale
12 RISKS              station shortage, analyzer availability, flaky tests, unknown
                      firmware behaviour; mitigation for each
13 DEFECT WORKFLOW    how failures are triaged, reproduced, filed with evidence
14 REGRESSION POLICY  which suite runs per build / nightly / release
15 SCHEDULE           station-hours per section, critical path
16 SIGN-OFF           validation lead, firmware lead, platform lead, PM

Synthetic trace — ambiguous: CSTS reads all ones
#t (ms)EventMeaning
10MWr CC EN=1enable
21host log: CSTS = FFFFFFFFhno analyzer on the link. Could be: (a) link down — Root Port synthesised all-ones for a failed read; (b) a completion with UR/CA the platform converted to all-ones; (c) the device really returned FFFFFFFFh (not a sensible CSTS)

Disambiguating the last trace: read the Vendor ID through config space. If it also returns FFFFh, the function is not reachable (link down, device in reset, surprise removal): check lspci -vvv LnkSta on the Root Port and the kernel log for AER / link-down messages. If config space is fine but BAR reads are all ones, suspect memory decode (Command register Memory Space Enable cleared, BAR reprogrammed) or a completion error path. An analyzer would settle it immediately: either a CplD with real data, a Cpl with UR/CA status, or no completion at all (completion timeout).

29.12 Failure reproduction

MethodWhen to useHowEvidence gainedPitfall
DeterministicFailure seen with a known command/sequenceReplay exact command sequence with same data and configurationProves causality from sequence; enables bisection of firmware buildsHidden state (cache, wear, temperature) differs between replay and original
StressRare failure under loadIncrease QD, concurrency, queue count, mix; reduce think timeRaises failure rate so experiments become cheap; reveals race windowsStress can create a different failure that you then mistake for the original
IntermittentLow and random rateRun N iterations, record per-iteration evidence, compute rate with confidence intervalA rate you can compare before/after a fixDeclaring "fixed" after zero failures in fewer runs than statistically meaningful
Long-runFailure after hours/daysSoak with periodic checkpoints (SMART log, error log, latency percentiles)Time-dependence: leaks, counters wrapping, thermal, wearNo intermediate snapshots, so you only know "it died eventually"
Power-cycleFailures at boot/enumeration or after power lossProgrammable supply, controlled off-time, cold vs warmInitialization races, link training margins, PLP behaviourOff-time too short: capacitors keep parts of the device alive
ResetFailures after error recoveryLoop CC.EN toggles, FLR, hot reset, NSSR (if supported)Distinguishes which reset scope clears the faultDriver resets something you did not intend; log every reset type
Workload-dependentOnly with a specific applicationCapture block trace (blktrace) of the app, replay with fio or a replay toolSeparates "this access pattern" from "this application"Replay timing differs; preserve inter-arrival times when relevant
n ≥ ln(α) / ln(1 − p)
  • n — number of clean consecutive runs needed after a fix
  • p — failure probability per run measured before the fix
  • α — accepted chance of seeing zero failures even though the bug is still present (e.g. 0.05)

Worked example. Before the fix the failure occurred in 3 of 200 runs, so p ≈ 0.015. For α = 0.05: n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.985) ≈ 2.996/0.01511 ≈ 198.2, so about 199 clean runs are needed before you can claim, at roughly 95% confidence, that the per-run failure rate dropped below the original derived. Fifteen clean runs prove almost nothing.

29.13 Regression engineering

  1. Reproduce the original failure on the unfixed build; record its rate and evidence.
  2. Capture a baseline: traces, logs, performance of the neighbouring cells.
  3. Apply the fix (one change at a time; record build ids).
  4. Rerun the original test for the number of iterations the statistics require.
  5. Run neighbouring cases: same feature at other matrix cells; same code path through other commands.
  6. Run stress on the fixed path.
  7. Compare traces: the fixed trace should differ from the failing trace exactly at the first abnormal event, and match the baseline elsewhere. Unexpected differences elsewhere are new findings.
  8. Record evidence and add the test permanently to the regression suite, tagged with the defect id.
💡 Senior insight

A fix without a test that failed before and passes after is an opinion. A fix with such a test but without neighbouring cases is a patch. A fix with both plus a trace diff that shows the first abnormal event disappeared — and nothing else changed — is engineering.

29.14 Linux view: safe inspection for validation evidence

# Identity and link (SAFE, read-only)
lspci -nn -d ::0108                      # list NVMe-class functions (class 0108)
sudo lspci -vvv -s 03:00.0               # LnkCap/LnkSta, MaxPayload, MaxReadReq, AER, MSI-X
nvme list
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0             # VWC, NPSS, MDTS, SGLS, firmware revision, etc.
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1             # LBA formats, capacity
# Health and error evidence before/after every test (SAFE)
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0
sudo nvme fw-log /dev/nvme0              # firmware slot information
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x02 # power management (current power state)
journalctl -k --since "-10 min" | grep -iE "nvme|aer|pcie"
grep nvme /proc/interrupts               # per-vector MSI-X counts
Output categoryCan proveCannot prove
LnkSta speed/widthCurrent negotiated link at the time of readingThat the link never retrained during the test (sample before and after; watch AER/recovery evidence)
SMART / health logCounter deltas (media errors, unsafe shutdowns, temperature)Which command caused a counter change
Error Information logCommands the controller chose to log, with status and locationErrors the controller did not log; host-side timeouts
Kernel logDriver's view: timeouts, resets, AER reportsWhat happened on the link between log lines
/proc/interruptsInterrupts delivered per vectorWhether an interrupt was required but missed
🏭 Implementation-dependent

Reset latency, enable-to-ready time, interrupt coalescing defaults, APST transition behaviour, which errors populate the Error Information log, and performance all vary by controller, firmware, driver, OS, platform and analyzer. To establish them for a specific system you need: the exact firmware and driver versions, the Identify data, repeated measurements with a stated distribution (not a single number), and — for timing claims at the link — analyzer timestamps rather than host timestamps.

29.15 Verified, derived, implementation- and version-dependent

StatementLabel
CC is at offset 14h, CSTS at 1Ch, CAP at 00h; CSTS.RDY is bit 0 and CSTS.CFS bit 1verified
CAP.TO is expressed in 500 ms units and bounds the host's wait for RDYverified
A negative test must check side effects as well as statusderived from the requirement that unrelated state is unaffected
Typical enable-to-ready time of a given driveimpl
Availability of a given feature (e.g. a 2.4-era feature) on a deviceversion + impl
"Pairwise finds most interaction defects"uncertain — an empirical observation from software testing literature, not a law; validate on your own defect history

Must be checked in the specification: exact reaction to an invalid CC configuration; whether a field is reserved, obsolete or defined in your target revision; exact status codes for each negative test; reset scopes and what each one clears. Never assume: that a "PASS" on one firmware applies to the next build; that host timestamps represent link timing; that a command which failed "correctly" left no side effects.
