29.17 Labs

🧪 Lab 29.1 — Capability-driven plan skeleton SAFE

Objective: produce a test plan section 5 (capability read) and select optional tests from real capability data. Prerequisites: a Linux host with any NVMe drive, or a QEMU VM with an emulated NVMe controller (see Chapter 32). Setup: install nvme-cli. Procedure: run nvme id-ctrl, nvme id-ns, lspci -vvv and save them as artifacts; build a table "feature → advertised? → field that told you → tests selected". Observations: note VWC, NPSS, SGLS, ONCS (optional NVM commands), FRMW, and link capability. Questions: Which optional commands will you not test, and why? Which fields did you have to look up in the spec to interpret?

Solution / expected reasoning

A good answer ties each selection to a field (e.g. "ONCS shows Write Zeroes supported → include WZ tests; SGLS indicates no SGL support → SGL tests out of scope, negative test: PSDT selecting SGL must be rejected with an appropriate status"). It also notes that the meaning of each bit must be read from the Identify Controller data structure table in the revision the device reports via VS.

Extension: write a script that diffs two id-ctrl outputs (two firmware builds) and flags capability changes that require plan updates.

🧪 Lab 29.2 — Negative-test suite on emulated NVMe SAFE

Objective: exercise queue-creation negative tests without risk. Setup: QEMU guest with an emulated NVMe device backed by a scratch image file. Procedure: using nvme admin-passthru inside the VM, send Create I/O SQ (opcode 01h) with a CQID that does not exist, and Delete I/O CQ (04h) for a queue the kernel driver is using (expect refusal while the SQ exists). Observations: CQE status printed by nvme-cli. Questions: Did the guest kernel's queues continue to work after each negative command?

Solution

Expected: Command Specific status for an invalid CQ and invalid deletion; existing I/O keeps working (run a short fio read afterwards). Recording that "existing I/O kept working" is what makes this a complete negative test. Note that emulated behaviour proves the test logic, not the behaviour of a physical controller.

Extension: wrap the commands in a script that emits a JSON verdict per card.

🧪 Lab 29.3 — Data-integrity soak on a spare drive CAUTION

Objective: run a verifying workload and interpret the evidence. Setup: a spare, non-production drive with no needed data. Procedure: fio --name=v --filename=/dev/nvme1n1 --rw=randwrite --bs=4k --iodepth=32 --size=8G --verify=crc32c --do_verify=1 --direct=1; capture SMART and error logs before and after. Observations: verify errors (should be zero), SMART deltas. Questions: What exactly does fio's verify prove, and what does it not prove about power-loss behaviour?

Solution

It proves read-back equals what was written within the run (no miscompare in the steady state). It does not prove persistence across power loss, nor behaviour of the volatile cache, nor correctness under other queue depths. Add the power-loss experiment (Expert) for that.

⚠️ Warning

Writing to a raw block device destroys its contents. Double-check the device name with nvme list and lsblk; never point fio at a mounted or system disk.

🧪 Lab 29.4 — Senior forensic lab: the marginal pass SAFE

Objective: write a validation finding from the "slow" synthetic trace in §29.11. Procedure: produce a one-page finding with the root-cause template headings (observed symptom, evidence, first abnormal event, expected vs actual, layer, candidates, eliminated, likely cause, confidence, additional evidence, recommendation, regression test). Question: is a 9.8 s ready time a defect?

Solution

Against the spec bound it is a pass; against product risk it is a finding. Expected reasoning: "Evidence: RDY at 9.8 s with CAP.TO=20 (10 s). Expected: ≤ 10 s (met). Risk: hosts with shorter internal timeouts (implementation-dependent) may fail; margin 2%. Additional evidence: distribution over 1 000 cycles, conditions (after clean vs unsafe shutdown). Recommendation: characterise; if the tail exceeds the bound, it becomes a defect. Regression: enable-time histogram as a tracked metric." Confidence about defect status: LOW until distribution is known.

🎯 Exercise

Write complete nine-field cards for (a) Write Zeroes and (b) Get Log Page for the SMART/Health log (Log Identifier 02h). For (b) the negative test should include an invalid log page identifier and an out-of-range offset if your revision supports log page offsets version.

Quiz

  1. Why does a negative test that returns an error not automatically pass?

    Answer

    It must return the correct status, leave unrelated state untouched, and leave the controller able to process subsequent valid commands. Any of those failing is a defect.

  2. Six dimensions with 3, 3, 3, 4, 3, 2 values: how many full-factorial configurations, and what is a lower bound on a pairwise suite?

    Answer

    3×3×3×4×3×2 = 648. Lower bound: product of the two largest = 4×3 = 12.

  3. Where does a performance target come from: the NVMe specification or elsewhere?

    Answer

    Elsewhere — product requirements or customer specifications. The NVMe specification defines behaviour, not product performance.

  4. Before a fix, a failure occurred in 1 of 100 runs. Roughly how many clean runs are needed for ~95% confidence the fix changed something?

    Answer

    n ≥ ln(0.05)/ln(0.99) ≈ 298.1, so about 299 runs.

  5. CSTS reads FFFFFFFFh. Name the first two checks.

    Answer

    Read Vendor ID via config space (is the function reachable?) and check the Root Port link status / kernel log for link-down or AER messages.

  6. Why must the plan read CAP and Identify data before selecting tests?

    Answer

    Optional features are tested only if advertised; selection based on a datasheet risks testing unsupported features (false failures) or skipping supported ones (coverage holes).

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is the difference between verification and validation?
    Model answer

    Verification asks "did we build it to the specification?" (conformance to documented requirements); validation asks "did we build the right thing for its use?" (fitness for the customer's purpose). SSD teams often use "validation" for both; a good engineer says which one a test addresses.

  2. Beginner What are the nine fields of a test card?
    Model answer

    Requirement, setup, stimulus, expected behaviour, observable evidence, pass/fail, negative test, stress test, recovery test.

  3. Beginner Which Linux commands give you safe before/after evidence for an NVMe test?
    Model answer

    nvme smart-log, nvme error-log, nvme id-ctrl, lspci -vvv, kernel log via journalctl -k, and /proc/interrupts.

  4. Beginner What is a flaky test and why is "rerun until green" dangerous?
    Model answer

    A non-deterministic test; rerunning hides a real race in either the DUT or the harness. Measure its failure rate and investigate.

  5. Beginner Why record firmware revision with every result?
    Model answer

    Behaviour is a property of the firmware build as much as of the hardware; without it a result cannot be reproduced or compared.

  6. Intermediate Design negative tests for Create I/O SQ.
    Model answer

    Non-existent CQID, QID 0 or beyond granted queues, QSIZE 0 or larger than MQES+1 entries, non-contiguous when CAP.CQR requires contiguous, duplicate QID. For each: expected status, no side effects, existing queues keep working.

  7. Intermediate How would you test that Flush works?
    Model answer

    Only meaningful if a volatile write cache is present/enabled: unique patterns, Flush, wait for completion, controlled power cut, read back; blocks covered by the completed Flush must be durable.

  8. Intermediate What evidence separates an interrupt-path failure from a host reaping failure?
    Model answer

    Analyzer: CQE MWr present but no MSI-X MWr → interrupt path; MSI-X MWr present but host times out → host. Without an analyzer: /proc/interrupts counters and driver tracing.

  9. Intermediate Why does performance testing need preconditioning?
    Model answer

    A fresh-out-of-box drive performs differently (no garbage collection pressure); steady state after a defined fill workload gives reproducible numbers. The procedure is implementation-dependent and usually follows an industry test specification.

  10. Intermediate What does a test plan's "out of scope" section protect against?
    Model answer

    Implicit assumptions of coverage. Stating that, e.g., SR-IOV is out of scope makes the gap visible and reviewable.

  11. Advanced How do you reduce a 26 000-run matrix to something runnable without losing important coverage?
    Model answer

    Pairwise as baseline, 3-way for known interacting factors, mandatory customer cells, boundary/equivalence classes, risk weighting toward changed code, long-duration runs only on a few representative cells, golden baseline cell on every build.

  12. Advanced How do you prove an intermittent failure is fixed?
    Model answer

    Measure the pre-fix rate, compute the clean-run count for a chosen confidence, run it, and confirm with a trace diff that the first abnormal event is gone; run neighbouring cells and stress.

  13. Advanced What makes host timestamps unsuitable for link-level latency claims?
    Model answer

    They include CPU scheduling, interrupt latency, driver path and clock-source effects; analyzer timestamps are taken at the link.

  14. Advanced A test passes alone but fails in suite order. Approach?
    Model answer

    Treat it as state leakage; dump features/namespace/power state before each test; bisect the predecessor list; fix the harness or file the device defect if the state should have been reset.

  15. Advanced Which tests change when a new spec revision adds a field in a formerly reserved area?
    Model answer

    Tests that wrote/checked that reserved area (old hosts write 0 — check the new default meaning), new positive tests for the field, interoperability tests between old hosts and new devices and vice versa.

  16. Senior What exit criteria would you sign for a firmware release?
    Model answer

    All P0 cards pass on mandatory cells; no open severity-1; every waiver signed with rationale and risk; regression suite green on the final build id; performance within tolerance of the baseline; known issues documented for customers.

  17. Senior How do you decide where to spend analyzer time?
    Model answer

    On failures whose layer cannot be determined from host and device logs, on timing claims at the link, and on golden-trace baselines for regression diffing; not on tests that already have clear evidence.

  18. Senior A customer reports a failure you cannot reproduce. What do you ask for?
    Model answer

    Exact platform/BIOS/kernel/driver/firmware, workload and timing, logs from both host and drive (SMART, error, telemetry if supported), frequency, and conditions (temperature, power events); then build a reproduction ladder matching their configuration.

  19. Senior How do you prevent validation from becoming a test-count metric?
    Model answer

    Report requirement and risk coverage with evidence quality, defect escape rates, and time-to-root-cause; not raw test counts.

  20. Senior When is a marginal pass worse than a fail?
    Model answer

    When it hides a tail that will fail in the field (different hosts, temperatures, ageing). A fail gets fixed; a marginal pass gets shipped. Report margins, not just verdicts.

💡 Teach-back

To a child: "We check a bridge by deciding what it must do, making it do that, and writing down proof, and we also try to trick it." To a junior engineer: "Every feature gets nine fields; the evidence field is the most important, and negative tests must check side effects." To a senior engineer: "Our plan is capability-driven, risk-weighted pairwise with mandatory customer cells, with statistically justified reproduction counts and trace-diff regression gates."

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can write a complete nine-field card for any NVMe feature in this chapter's catalogue without looking.
  • I can draw the validation setup and say what each observer can and cannot prove.
  • I can compute a full-factorial size, a pairwise lower bound, and a clean-run count after a fix.
  • I can identify the first abnormal event in each of the four synthetic traces and explain the ambiguous one's disambiguation.
  • I can distinguish a spec requirement from a product requirement and cite which document owns each test row.
  • I can describe the eight regression steps and explain why trace diffing belongs in them.

29.18 Summary, further reading, next

Summary. Validation converts requirements into evidence: nine fields per feature, capability-driven selection, a reduced but risk-weighted matrix, explicit reproduction methods with statistical stopping rules, and regression that ends in trace diffs. Further reading: the NVMe Base Specification sections on controller initialization, queue management and status codes; the NVM Command Set for I/O commands; the NVMe over PCIe Transport specification for register mapping and doorbells; the PCIe Base Specification for error handling and power management (obtain the revision your platform implements through PCI-SIG); nvme-cli and fio documentation. Next: validation depends on reading specifications precisely — Chapter 30 teaches how.

PART XXX

Specification Reading School

The NVMe Base Specification, the command-set and transport specifications, and the PCI Express Base Specification together run to thousands of pages. Nobody reads them like a novel. Senior engineers read them like lawyers read statutes and like detectives read evidence: they know which words are binding, which are explanation, which fields are reserved for the future, which behaviour is left to the implementer, and which revision a sentence came from. This Part teaches that skill explicitly — with a keyword guide, procedures for reading registers, commands and state machines, a revision-diff method, a cross-specification matrix and a reusable worksheet — so that you never again cite a forum post where a "shall" should be.

30 How to Read a 1000-Page Specification

← 29 Validation Engineering: From Requirement to Evidence30B Cross-Specification Mapping, Revisions and the Limits of a Specification →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: NVMe Base Specification; NVM Command Set Specification; NVMe over PCIe Transport Specification; PCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG). REVISIONS: NVMe Base 2.4, NVM CS 1.3, PCIe Transport 1.4 (course baseline, set released 4 August 2026) version; the PCIe Base revision is whichever your platform and device claim (PCIe 5.0/6.0 era; Gen7 128 GT/s specification released 2025 version). STATUS: confirm on nvmexpress.org and pcisig.com. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: NVMe 1.x was one monolithic document; from 2.0 the material is split into a library (Base + command sets + transports + management + boot). SOURCE NOTES: this chapter teaches method. It quotes no section numbers; register offsets and field positions shown are long-established and labelled verified; anything else is labelled.

30.1 Why this chapter exists

Most protocol misunderstandings in industry are not caused by ignorance of a fact but by a misreading: a "should" treated as a "shall", a 0-based field read as 1-based, a reserved bit assumed to be zero on read, a sentence from an informative note quoted as a requirement, a field that changed meaning between revisions, or a behaviour assumed to be standard when it is explicitly implementation-specific. Each of these produces wrong drivers, wrong firmware, wrong tests and wrong root causes. Reading discipline is cheaper than any of them.

  • Beginner: distinguish normative from informative text and interpret shall / should / may, reserved, obsolete and vendor-specific.
  • Intermediate: decode a register table, a command format and an error table using a repeatable procedure; maintain a field dictionary.
  • Advanced: read a state machine and turn it into a diagnostic tree; map a concept across Base, command-set, transport and PCIe documents.
  • Senior: read revision changes and derive interoperability and validation consequences; write source notes that state what a source does and does not establish.
  • Trace-analysis: link every decoded trace field to the table that defines it (trace mapping).
  • Debugging: recognise when a debate is really about an ambiguous or version-dependent sentence, and resolve it with the primary source.
  • Validation: turn each normative sentence into a test card (Chapter 29).

Prerequisites: controller registers (CAP, CC, CSTS), the 64-byte Submission Queue Entry and 16-byte Completion Queue Entry (CQE), and the PCIe Transaction Layer (TLP). The validation chapter (29) motivates why precise reading matters.

30.2 Story, analogy, and where it breaks

🧒 Kid analogy — the board-game rule book

A new board game comes with a thick rule book. Some sentences are rules ("You must roll before moving"). Some are tips ("You should keep your gold hidden"). Some are choices ("You may trade with a neighbour"). Some boxes are greyed out: "Reserved for the expansion pack" — you must not put anything there, because the expansion will use it. Some pages are stories about how the game was invented; fun, but not rules. When friends argue, you settle it by pointing at the exact rule sentence — and checking it is the same edition of the rule book everyone is using.

🌍 Engineering analogy — building codes

A building code contains mandatory requirements, recommended practices, informative commentary and referenced standards. An inspector cites the clause and edition. A contractor who builds to the commentary instead of the clause, or to last decade's edition, fails inspection. A specification works the same way: it binds conformance claims, not opinions.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Game rules and building codes are written for humans in a single domain. Protocol specifications bind two or more independent implementers (host and device, requester and completer), and many sentences are written from one side's viewpoint ("the controller shall…", "host software should…"). A requirement on the controller does not automatically imply a requirement on the host, and vice versa. Also, a specification frequently delegates to another specification (NVMe to PCIe), so the answer may live in a document the first one only references.

30.3 Anatomy of a large specification

Part of the documentNormative?How to use itTypical trap
Front matter, revision history, change listNo (but authoritative about what changed)Find revision, ratified changes, incorporated technical proposalsSkipping it and assuming your old notes are current
Introduction / overview / theory of operationMostly informativeBuild the mental model; read firstQuoting an overview paragraph as a requirement
Conventions, definitions, keywords, notationNormative for interpretationRead once carefully; re-read when in doubtAssuming notation from another spec (e.g. bit numbering, 0-based values)
Normative body (requirements, data structures, registers, commands)YesRead with the procedures in §30.7–30.10Reading one table without the surrounding requirements and footnotes
Tables and figuresUsually normative for the structure they define; check notesField dictionary entries come from hereMissing a footnote that changes meaning under a condition
Notes, examples, rationaleInformativeUnderstanding, not conformanceTreating an example value as required
Annexes / appendicesEither — each annex says whichCheck its labelAssuming all annexes are informative
Referenced documentsNormative where the text says compliance requires themFollow references to the owning specExpecting the NVMe document to define PCIe packet details

30.4 Truth policy and source hierarchy

This book, and your notebook, should follow one policy: a statement is presented as normative fact only if it is established by an official specification, official standards documentation, official vendor documentation, official kernel documentation or another identified primary source. When sources disagree, use this priority:

RankSourceUse forNever use for
1Current official NVM Express specificationsNVMe behaviour, structures, status codesPCIe link/packet detail it only references
2Current official PCI-SIG specifications available to youTLP/DLLP formats, ordering, errors, LTSSM, power managementNVMe command semantics
3Official Linux kernel documentation/sourceWhat Linux does (driver timeouts, reset flow, sysfs)What the spec requires
4Device/controller vendor documentationImplementation-dependent behaviour of that productGeneralising to other devices
5Protocol-analyzer vendor documentationWhat the tool decodes and how it timestampsProtocol requirements
6Peer-reviewed papers, standards publicationsMeasurements, methodsNormative claims
7High-quality technical booksExplanation and intuitionRevision-specific detail
8Community material (forums, blogs)Leads and intuition onlyAnything you will cite in a defect or a design review
LabelMeaningExample
verifiedDirectly supported by a cited sourceCSTS is at offset 1Ch
derivedLogically follows from verified factsWith DSTRD=0, SQ1 tail doorbell is at 1008h
syntheticInvented for teachingEvery trace in this book unless marked otherwise
implVaries by vendor/device/firmware/OSEnable-to-ready time
versionChanges with specification revisionPresence of a field in a formerly reserved area
uncertainInsufficient evidenceAnything you have not yet checked

Every specification-level page in your notebook starts with the same header: SPECIFICATION BASELINE — DOCUMENT / REVISION / RATIFICATION DATE / STATUS / OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER / SOURCE, and ends with SOURCE NOTES — official specification / revision / relevant topic / accessed-verified date / what this source establishes / what it does not establish. Write "unknown" rather than leaving a field blank, and never write a section number you did not read in the actual document.

30.5 Normative keyword guide

Specifications define their own keywords in a conventions section. The table summarises how these words are conventionally used in NVM Express and PCI-SIG documents and how to treat them in engineering work. It is a reading aid, not a legal interpretation: when precision matters, re-read the document's own definitions uncertain in edge cases.

Keyword / markerConventional meaningTreat in validation asTreat in design asCommon misreading
shall / shall notMandatory requirement for a conforming implementationPass/fail requirementMust implement exactlyAssuming a "shall" on the controller binds the host too
should / should notRecommendation; strongly preferred but deviation is permittedWarning-level finding unless product requirements upgrade itDo it unless you have a documented reasonFailing a device for a "should"; or ignoring every "should"
mayPermitted; optional behaviourTest only if supported/advertised; then test it fullyYour choice; host must tolerate either choiceHost software assuming the "may" behaviour always occurs (or never occurs)
mandatory / optional (feature tables)Whether support is required for conformance in a given context (e.g. I/O controller vs admin controller vs discovery controller)Capability-driven test selectionProduct feature listIgnoring the controller-type column
ReservedSet aside for future definition. Writers conventionally clear reserved fields to 0; readers should not depend on their value. The exact host/controller obligations are stated in the document's conventions — read them for your revision versionNegative test: non-zero reserved fields (check what the spec allows the controller to do)Write 0; ignore on read; never store meaning thereUsing reserved bits for private flags; asserting reserved reads as 0
RsvdP / RsvdZ (PCIe register attributes)RsvdP: reserved and preserved — software must preserve the value read when writing. RsvdZ: reserved and zero — software must write 0 verifiedRead-modify-write checks in driver reviewCorrect RMW sequencesWriting 0 to a RsvdP field
ObsoletePreviously defined, no longer defined in this revision; the field/value is kept from reuse so old implementations do not collideDo not require it; old devices may still implement itDo not implement in new designs unless needed for legacy compatibilityTreating obsolete as "reserved and free to reuse"
Vendor specificRange/field whose meaning is defined by the vendorOut of spec scope; vendor docs onlyDocument it for your customersDecoding a vendor-specific log with another vendor's tool
Implementation specific / implementation dependentSpec permits implementations to differCharacterise, do not failDocument your choiceWriting "the spec says latency is X"
IgnoredReceiver does not act on the valueWrite junk, verify no effect (if the spec allows any value)Do not decodeConfusing "ignored" with "reserved"
Note / Example / RationaleInformativeContext for understandingNot a requirementCopying example values into firmware defaults
0's based (NVMe notation)Value N means N+1 (e.g. queue size, number of logical blocks)Boundary tests at 0 and maxOff-by-one review itemTreating NLB=7 as 7 blocks (it is 8)
📌 Remember

Ask three questions of every sentence: Who is bound (controller, host, requester, completer, switch)? How strongly (shall, should, may)? Under what condition (if a capability is set, if a feature is enabled, in which revision)?

30.6 Terminology, abbreviations and notation

Build your field dictionary from the very first page. Every abbreviation gets an entry, because the same letters mean different things in different documents: AER is Advanced Error Reporting in PCIe but Asynchronous Event Request in NVMe; MPS is Max_Payload_Size in PCIe Device Control but Memory Page Size in NVMe CC; CA is Completer Abort in PCIe; CQ means Completion Queue only in NVMe.

NotationMeaningPitfall
1Ch, 0x1CHexadecimal (NVMe uses the "h" suffix)Reading 10h as ten
01bBinaryReading 10b as ten or as hex
[31:16], "bits 31:16"Bit range, most significant firstOff-by-one width (16 bits, not 15)
Byte/Dword numberingNVMe data structures are little-endian; PCIe TLP headers are transmitted with byte 0 first and bit 7 most significant within each byteDecoding an analyzer header dump with the wrong byte order
CDW10 … CDW15Command Dwords at byte offsets 40–63 of the SQECounting CDW0 as byte 4
2^(12+MPS)NVMe memory page size from CC.MPSConfusing with PCIe Max_Payload_Size
CAP.TO in 500 ms unitsTimeout encodingUsing the raw value as milliseconds

30.7 Reading a register

  1. Locate the register (document, offset, which space: PCI config space, BAR0 MMIO, or a capability structure).
  2. Identify width (32/64-bit) and whether it must be accessed atomically or as two halves.
  3. Identify the reset value and which reset sets it.
  4. Decode each field: bits, name, meaning, units, 0-based or not.
  5. Classify access type (RO, RW, RW1C, RWS, HwInit, …) only as stated in the table legend — never by guess.
  6. Identify side effects of reads and writes (e.g. a doorbell write starts work; a write-1-to-clear clears status).
  7. Identify sequencing rules (must be written before/after another register, only while disabled).
  8. Identify related registers and capability gates.
  9. Identify the software owner (who writes it: driver, firmware, BIOS).
  10. Identify hardware behaviour (what the controller does on change).
  11. Identify trace implications (what TLP and timing you expect).

Worked example: Controller Configuration (CC, offset 14h)

Bits31:252423:2019:1615:1413:1110:76:43:10
FieldReservedCRIME versionIOCQESIOSQESSHNAMSMPSCSSReservedEN

Applying the procedure: (1) BAR0 offset 14h, 32-bit verified. (4) EN enables the controller; CSS selects the I/O command set(s); MPS gives memory page size 2^(12+MPS); AMS selects the arbitration mechanism; SHN requests shutdown (01b normal, 10b abrupt); IOSQES/IOCQES give I/O queue entry sizes as powers of two (6 → 64 bytes, 4 → 16 bytes). (5) Read the access legend for each field in your revision. (7) Sequencing: several fields are only to be changed while the controller is disabled — read the exact rule. Bit 24 is an example of version dependence: older revisions show it reserved; later revisions define it (Controller Ready Independent of Media Enable) — so a driver written to an older revision writes 0 there, which must remain a valid, backward-compatible choice. (11) Trace: a single 1-DW MWr to BAR0+14h; enabling is followed by CSTS polling reads.

⚠️ Do not invent access semantics

If a table legend says a field is RW, do not assume it is readable back with the same value under all conditions, and do not assume the write takes effect immediately. If you cannot find the statement, write "unknown" in your field dictionary.

30.8 Reading a command definition

  1. Identify the command set (Admin, NVM, ZNS, KV, …) and owning document.
  2. Identify the opcode.
  3. Identify the command format (common 64-byte SQE plus command-specific dwords).
  4. Identify mandatory fields.
  5. Identify optional fields and the capability that gates each.
  6. Identify data pointers (PRP or SGL per PSDT; metadata pointer) and direction.
  7. Identify namespace applicability (NSID used? broadcast value allowed?).
  8. Identify prerequisites (feature enabled, namespace attached, controller state).
  9. Identify completion content (DW0/DW1 command-specific results).
  10. Identify errors (generic and command-specific status codes).
  11. Identify side effects (log pages updated, asynchronous events, state changes).
  12. Identify trace consequences (SQE fetch, data direction, CQE, interrupt).

Worked example: NVM Read (opcode 02h)

StepFindingSource / label
1–2NVM Command Set, I/O command, opcode 02hNVM CS verified
3Common format: CDW0 (opcode, FUSE, PSDT, CID), NSID (bytes 4–7), MPTR (16–23), DPTR (24–39), CDW10–15Base verified
4SLBA in CDW10–11; NLB (0's based) in CDW12 bits 15:0NVM CS verified
5FUA (CDW12 bit 30), Limited Retry (bit 31), protection-information fields, directives, dataset-management hints — each gated by capabilities/formatNVM CS; check your revision version
6Device writes into host memory described by PRP1/PRP2 (or SGL); direction = controller → hostderived
7Requires a valid active NSIDNVM CS
8Namespace attached and controller ready; I/O queues createdBase
9CQE DW0/DW1 generally not used for Read results; status in DW3check NVM CS
10e.g. LBA Out of Range, Invalid Namespace or Format, Unrecovered Read Error (media), Data Transfer ErrorBase/NVM CS status tables
11Error Information log entry on failure (if the controller logs it); SMART counters (data units read)Base
12SQE fetch MRd → device MWrs to PRP pages → CQE MWr → MSI-X MWrderived

30.9 Reading a state machine

  1. List the states.
  2. Identify each state's entry condition.
  3. Identify each exit condition.
  4. Identify events that cause transitions.
  5. Identify timers.
  6. Identify error transitions.
  7. Identify recovery paths.
  8. Map each state/transition to trace evidence.
  9. Identify impossible transitions (they become assertions in your analyzer scripts).
  10. Build a diagnostic tree.

Worked example: controller shutdown handshake

StepResult for the shutdown handshake
StatesNormal (00b), Processing (01b), Complete (10b); 11b reserved
Entry/exitHost write of CC.SHN ≠ 00b starts shutdown; controller sets SHST=10b when complete
TimersHost waits a bounded time; the controller may report an expected shutdown latency in Identify Controller (RTD3 entry latency) — check field and revision version
ErrorsSHST stuck at 01b; CFS set; link down before complete
Trace evidenceMWr to CC (14h) with SHN; repeated MRd to CSTS (1Ch) with SHST transitioning in the CplD data
Impossible transitions00b → 10b without the host having written SHN (assert in your script); SHST changing while the controller is unreachable (reads of all-ones are not state)
Diagnostic treeSHST never leaves 00b → was the CC write seen on the link? → yes: controller ignored/delayed; no: host path. SHST stuck 01b → time vs reported latency → media/cache flush issue impl vs host too impatient

30.10 Reading tables, bitfields, error tables and references

Tables: read the caption, every column header, every footnote, and the sentences immediately before and after; a table often defines structure while a nearby sentence defines a condition ("this field is valid only if…"). Bitfields: record bits, width, units, 0-based-ness, reset value, attribute; then write one positive and one boundary test. Error tables: NVMe status is a pair (Status Code Type, Status Code) plus flags (More, Do Not Retry); generic status codes (SCT 0h) apply to many commands; command-specific codes (SCT 1h) are only meaningful for the command that defines them; media and data-integrity errors are SCT 2h; path-related SCT 3h; vendor specific SCT 7h verified. Read the conditions under which each code is returned, not just the name. References: when the text says "see …" or refers to another document, follow it and record the chain in your cross-reference map — a requirement may only be complete after two hops.

30.11 Maintaining the specification notebook system

30.13 Source-based question generator (for this chapter's topic: controller initialization)

TypeQuestions
SOURCE-LOOKUP (10)1 What offset is AQA? 2 Which CC bits encode MPS? 3 What unit is CAP.TO in? 4 Which CAP field limits queue entries, and is it 0-based? 5 What does CSTS.CFS indicate? 6 What value enables NSSR, and when is NSSR supported? 7 Which CC field selects command sets? 8 What are the SHN encodings? 9 Which register holds the admin CQ base address? 10 Where is the doorbell stride defined?
SYNTHESIS (10)11 Why must ASQ/ACQ be programmed before EN=1? 12 Why is the queue size field 0-based? 13 How do MPSMIN/MPSMAX constrain PRP construction? 14 Why does doorbell stride exist? 15 How do CAP.CSS and CC.CSS interact? 16 Why might a controller take longer to become ready after unsafe shutdown? 17 Which reset scopes clear which state? 18 How does CRIME (where defined) change the enable sequence? 19 Why is CSTS read rather than CC to know readiness? 20 How does the Version register influence driver behaviour?
TRACE (5)21 What TLP writes CC? 22 What completion carries CSTS? 23 How do you detect "no completion" vs "UR"? 24 What is the first device-initiated TLP after the first admin doorbell? 25 How do you tell a CSTS poll from a doorbell write on the analyzer?
DEBUG (5)26 RDY never sets — first three checks? 27 CFS=1 after enable — next evidence? 28 All-ones register reads — layer? 29 Identify returns zeros — PRP or controller? 30 Enable works on one platform, not another — what differs?
DESIGN (2)31 Design a driver enable routine robust to slow controllers. 32 Design firmware so that the controller reports readiness only when it can safely accept admin commands, and explain what evidence proves it.
📭 What the specification does not say

It does not tell you how long a particular controller takes to become ready (only the bound it reports), how firmware schedules internal work, how a protocol analyzer displays things, or how fast a product is. It also does not interpret itself: when two sentences seem to conflict, the specification's own errata and later revisions — or the standards body — resolve it, not a forum thread.

🏭 Implementation-dependent

"This behaviour may vary by controller, firmware, driver, OS, platform, or analyzer." To establish it for a given system you need: the exact versions of each, repeated measurements, the Identify data that bounds it, and preferably a link-level trace.

🧪 Lab 30.1 — Build a field dictionary for CAP SAFE

Objective: practise the register procedure. Setup: the NVMe Base Specification (free download from nvmexpress.org) and any Linux host or QEMU VM. Procedure: (1) fill the field dictionary for every CAP field; (2) run sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H (read-only register dump; availability depends on the nvme-cli version and kernel access to BAR impl); (3) decode CAP by hand from the raw value and compare with nvme-cli's decoding. Questions: which fields are 0-based? which use units? which did your nvme-cli version decode differently from your reading?

Solution / expected reasoning

MQES is 0-based; TO is in 500 ms units; DSTRD gives stride 2^(2+DSTRD) bytes; MPSMIN/MPSMAX are exponents (2^(12+n)). Any disagreement with the tool is resolved by the specification table of the revision the device reports in VS — tools can lag behind specification revisions.

Extension: add a "revision introduced" column, filled only from revision-history evidence.

🧪 Lab 30.2 — Keyword hunt SAFE

Objective: classify ten sentences from the Base specification's queue-management text as shall/should/may, identify who is bound and under which condition. Procedure: copy the sentences into your notebook (short quotes), fill a three-column table (bound party, strength, condition). Question: which of them could a host violate, and how would you observe it?

Solution

Expect a mix of host obligations (e.g. ordering of queue creation) and controller obligations (e.g. status returned for invalid parameters). Host violations are observed in traces as commands sent in the wrong order or invalid fields; controller violations as wrong status or missing completion.

Quiz

  1. A sentence says "the controller should complete the command within X". Is exceeding X a spec violation?

    Answer

    No — "should" is a recommendation; it is a finding, and may be a product-requirement failure if your PRD adopts X.

  2. NLB = 0 in a Read command means how many blocks?

    Answer

    One (0's based).

  3. Difference between RsvdP and RsvdZ?

    Answer

    RsvdP: preserve the read value when writing (read-modify-write). RsvdZ: write zero.

  4. Why is "obsolete" not the same as "reserved"?

    Answer

    Obsolete marks something that once had meaning; old implementations may still use it, so it is not freely reusable and new hosts must tolerate it.

  5. Which document defines the doorbell stride and doorbell register offsets for PCIe-attached controllers?

    Answer

    The NVMe register map (CAP.DSTRD and doorbell offsets) — in the 2.x library the PCIe-specific register mapping is in the NVMe over PCIe Transport specification, while doorbell semantics are in the Base specification; check how your revision splits it version.

  6. What does AER mean in the NVMe document vs the PCIe document?

    Answer

    NVMe: Asynchronous Event Request (admin opcode 0Ch). PCIe: Advanced Error Reporting capability.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner What is the difference between normative and informative text?
    Model answer

    Normative text defines conformance requirements; informative text (notes, examples, overviews, rationale) explains but does not bind.

  2. Beginner How should software treat reserved fields?
    Model answer

    Write them with the value the conventions require (typically 0), do not depend on their value when reading, and never store private meaning in them; check the document's conventions for the exact rule.

  3. Intermediate Walk me through reading a new admin command definition.
    Model answer

    The 12-step command procedure: set, opcode, format, mandatory/optional fields and gates, data pointers, namespace use, prerequisites, completion content, errors, side effects, trace consequences.

  4. Intermediate How do you avoid off-by-one bugs from specifications?
    Model answer

    Mark 0-based fields and units in the field dictionary; write boundary tests at 0 and max; review code with the dictionary.

  5. Advanced Two engineers disagree about whether a controller may return a status in a situation. How do you resolve it?
    Model answer

    Find the normative sentences (both sides), check revision, conventions, footnotes and referenced sections; record what the source establishes and does not; if still ambiguous, check errata/later revisions or escalate to the standards body; meanwhile make the host tolerant of both.

  6. Advanced How do you convert a state diagram into analyzer assertions?
    Model answer

    List impossible transitions and timer bounds; encode each as a rule over observed register reads or packets; flag violations as candidate first abnormal events.

  7. Senior How would you onboard a team to a new specification revision?
    Model answer

    Revision-diff workshop (added/changed fields, behaviour, errors, interoperability, validation impact), update field dictionaries and command matrices, flag driver/firmware code touching changed areas, add tests, and document "what we do not yet know".

  8. Senior What does a good source note contain?
    Model answer

    Document, revision, topic, verification date, what it establishes, and explicitly what it does not establish.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can classify any sentence by bound party, strength and condition.
  • I can apply the register, command and state-machine procedures to an unfamiliar definition.
  • I can fill the worksheet for a topic and write correct source notes without inventing section numbers.
  • I can explain reserved, RsvdP, RsvdZ, obsolete, vendor specific and implementation specific with an example of each.
  • I maintain a field dictionary and command matrix and can show them.

Summary. Read structure first, then conventions, then normative text with its tables and footnotes; classify every sentence; record everything in a notebook with source notes; never invent section numbers or access semantics. Next: Chapter 30B maps concepts across documents and teaches revision diffs.

30B Cross-Specification Mapping, Revisions and the Limits of a Specification

← 30 How to Read a 1000-Page Specification31 The Official-Document Reading Plan →
📘 Specification baseline

DOCUMENTS: the NVM Express library (Base 2.4; NVM CS 1.3; ZNS 1.5; KV 1.4; SLM 1.3; Computational Programs 1.3; PCIe transport 1.4; RDMA 1.3; TCP 1.3; NVMe-MI 2.2; Boot 1.4) and the PCIe Base Specification version. STATUS: per the course brief (set released 4 August 2026); confirm each sub-revision on nvmexpress.org. SOURCE NOTES: the matrix below states which document covers each concept — derived from the published scope of each document — not specific section numbers.

30B.1 Why this chapter exists

No single document defines an NVMe read on a PCIe SSD. The Base specification defines the queue model and command processing; the NVM Command Set defines Read; the PCIe transport specification defines how the controller's registers and doorbells map onto a PCIe function; the PCIe Base specification defines the packets that actually carry everything; the operating system defines what software does. Engineers who confuse these owners cite the wrong document, test the wrong thing, and argue past each other.

  • Map any NVMe/PCIe concept to the documents that own it, and refuse to populate a cell no source covers.
  • Apply the six-point revision-diff method and derive validation consequences.
  • State what a specification does not guarantee, and what evidence would establish implementation-dependent behaviour.
  • Verify a new release's highlighted features without inventing details.

Prerequisites: Chapter 30.

🧒 Kid analogy — the school with many rule books

A school has a school rule book (how classes work), a maths department book (how maths tests are marked), a bus company book (how the bus to school runs) and a city traffic code (how every vehicle on every road behaves). "How do I get my maths test back?" touches all four. If you only read the maths book, you will never learn why the bus was late.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

School rule books rarely conflict; protocol documents are layered so that the lower one (PCIe) knows nothing about the upper (NVMe). A PCIe completion timeout is a PCIe event; the NVMe command timeout that follows is a host-driver policy. Neither document defines the other.

Cross-spec check for NVMe READ: Base (queue, SQE format, CQE, status) → NVM Command Set (Read opcode 02h, SLBA/NLB, errors) → NVMe over PCIe Transport (doorbell mapping, PCIe-specific data-pointer rules, interrupts) → PCIe Base (MWr/MRd/CplD, ordering, MPS/MRRS, errors) → OS/driver (queue selection, timeouts, retries). Do not imply the NVMe specification alone defines the TLPs you see.

30B.3 What the specification does not say, and implementation-dependent behaviour

📭 What the specification does not guarantee
  • Internal NAND management algorithms (garbage collection, wear levelling, read-retry).
  • Proprietary firmware scheduling and internal queue arbitration beyond the defined arbitration mechanisms.
  • Undocumented controller optimisations (prefetch, write coalescing).
  • Protocol-analyzer user-interface behaviour, decode naming, or timestamp methods.
  • Vendor-specific performance, latency, or power numbers beyond what the device reports.
  • How many TLPs a given transfer is split into (bounded by MPS, MRRS, page boundaries; the exact split is the device's choice).
  • Operating-system timeouts, retry policies, and recovery escalation.
🏭 Implementation-dependent — and how to establish it
BehaviourVaries byEvidence needed for a specific system
Data TLP sizes for a 128 KiB readcontroller, MPS setting, platformAnalyzer capture + lspci DevCtl MaxPayload
SQE fetch batchingcontroller firmwareAnalyzer: MRd lengths after doorbells with multiple new entries
Interrupt coalescing defaultscontroller, driverGet Features (Interrupt Coalescing) + interrupt counts per CQE
Command timeout and retryOS/driver version and parametersKernel source/doc for that version; module parameters; logs
Read latency distributioneverythingfio latency percentiles with stated workload, preconditioning, temperature, firmware

30B.4 Version control rule and revision awareness

Never describe a modern feature as if it existed in an older revision; never use an old command layout as though it were necessarily current. The largest structural change to learn is the move from NVMe 1.x (one monolithic document including the PCIe register interface and NVM I/O commands) to the 2.0 library, which separated the Base specification from command-set specifications (NVM, ZNS, KV, …) and transport specifications (PCIe, RDMA, TCP) version. Older references to "the NVMe spec, section X" therefore often point to material that now lives in a different document.

The revision-diff method

  1. Added feature — what new capability exists, which capability bit or field advertises it, which document owns it.
  2. Changed field — new fields in formerly reserved space; widened fields; renamed fields; new encodings in existing fields.
  3. Changed behaviour — a "may" that became "shall", new conditions, new ordering rules.
  4. Changed error handling — new status codes, new conditions for existing codes, new log pages or events.
  5. Changed interoperability implication — what an old host does with a new device (writes 0 to the new field; ignores new events) and what a new host does with an old device (must check capability before using).
  6. Changed validation requirement — tests added, retired (obsolete), or modified.

The script below diffs two field dictionaries that you built from two revisions (sample content is synthetic and refers to an invented register, so nothing in it asserts real specification text):

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""revdiff.py - diff two field dictionaries you built from two spec revisions
(executable, stdlib only). The dictionaries are YOUR notebook entries; the sample
content is SYNTHETIC (invented register 'XREG') so nothing here asserts real spec text."""
OLD = {  # "register.field": (bits, attribute, meaning)
    "XREG.EN":   ("0",     "RW", "enable"),
    "XREG.MODE": ("3:1",   "RW", "mode select; 000b/001b defined"),
    "XREG.RSV":  ("31:4",  "reserved", ""),
}
NEW = {
    "XREG.EN":   ("0",     "RW", "enable"),
    "XREG.MODE": ("3:1",   "RW", "mode select; 000b/001b/010b defined"),
    "XREG.LIM":  ("7:4",   "RW", "rate limit (new)"),
    "XREG.RSV":  ("31:8",  "reserved", ""),
}

def diff(old, new):
    rows = []
    for k in sorted(set(old) | set(new)):
        a, b = old.get(k), new.get(k)
        if a is None:
            rows.append(("ADDED", k, b, "new field: old hosts write 0 here (was reserved) -> check default behavior"))
        elif b is None:
            rows.append(("REMOVED", k, a, "field gone/obsolete: new devices may ignore it -> retire tests"))
        elif a != b:
            what = [n for n, x, y in zip(("bits", "attr", "meaning"), a, b) if x != y]
            rows.append(("CHANGED", k, (a, b), f"changed {what}: interoperability + new negative tests"))
    return rows

if __name__ == "__main__":
    for kind, key, val, impl in diff(OLD, NEW):
        print(f"{kind:<8} {key:<10} -> {impl}")
ADDED    XREG.LIM   -> new field: old hosts write 0 here (was reserved) -> check default behavior
CHANGED  XREG.MODE  -> changed ['meaning']: interoperability + new negative tests
CHANGED  XREG.RSV   -> changed ['bits']: interoperability + new negative tests

Verifying the 2026 release highlights without inventing details

The August 2026 NVM Express release announcement highlights Post-Quantum Cryptography, PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration, Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting, and Restore Manufacturing Default Settings verified (per the course brief). For each, a disciplined reader records only this until the normative text is read:

HighlightPurpose (paraphrase of announced intent)Where to lookWhat you must verify in the normative textCannot be inferred from the announcement
Post-Quantum CryptographySecurity algorithms resistant to quantum attack for NVMe security featuresBase 2.4 and security-related sections/referenced standardsWhich features use it; capability reporting; command/field changesAlgorithms, key sizes, performance impact
PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem MigrationMoving an exported NVM subsystem (virtualisation/cloud use)Base 2.4, PCIe transport 1.4Actors, states, commands, error handlingDowntime, implementation complexity
Voltage MonitoringReporting supply-voltage information for manageabilityBase 2.4 / NVMe-MI 2.2Data structures, units, access pathsAccuracy, sampling rate
Rate LimitingLimiting rates of some activity (e.g. for multi-tenant fairness)Base 2.4What is limited, configuration, reportingGranularity, enforcement method
Restore Manufacturing Default SettingsReturning configurable settings to factory defaultsBase 2.4 / NVMe-MI 2.2Scope (which settings, data or not), command, safetyWhether user data is affected
🧪 Lab 30B.1 — Version-compatibility lab SAFE

Objective: compare an older and a newer revision. Setup: download NVMe 1.4 (monolithic) and the current Base + NVM CS + PCIe transport. Procedure: build a feature matrix for ten topics you know (CC fields, CAP fields, Identify Controller fields you use, Read command fields, status codes for Read). For each row record: present in old? in new? changed? owning document in each. Questions: What is common? What changed? What must be checked before relying on it? What cannot be assumed about a device that reports VS=1.4?

Solution / expected reasoning

Common: core register offsets, SQE/CQE sizes, Read/Write layout. Changed: document ownership (I/O commands moved to the NVM CS), some formerly reserved bits now defined (for example CC bit 24 in 2.x), new log pages/features. Must check: capability bits before using any newer feature. Cannot assume: that a 1.4 device implements 2.x-defined fields, or that it ignores non-zero values written there.

30B.5 Official-document reading order

  1. NVMe overview and specification index (what exists, current revisions).
  2. Base specification architecture (theory of operation, queue model, controller types).
  3. NVM Command Set.
  4. NVMe over PCIe Transport.
  5. Relevant PCIe documentation (Transaction Layer, ordering, errors, power management, LTSSM).
  6. Advanced command sets (ZNS, KV, SLM, Computational Programs).
  7. Management (NVMe-MI) and Boot.
  8. Fabrics transports (RDMA, TCP).

Return to the Base specification repeatedly: each pass through another document will send you back with sharper questions. Chapter 31 turns this order into a detailed plan.

Quiz

  1. Which document would you cite for the MRd tag field?

    Answer

    The PCIe Base Specification — NVMe documents do not define TLP formats.

  2. Which document defines the Read command's SLBA field in the 2.x library?

    Answer

    The NVM Command Set specification.

  3. Give two examples of things no specification guarantees.

    Answer

    Garbage collection behaviour; analyzer UI/decode naming; product performance; OS timeouts.

  4. Name the six revision-diff questions.

    Answer

    Added feature, changed field, changed behaviour, changed error handling, interoperability implication, validation requirement.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Which specifications are involved in an NVMe read on a PCIe SSD?
    Model answer

    Base, NVM Command Set, NVMe over PCIe Transport, PCIe Base; plus the OS driver's behaviour, which no spec defines.

  2. Advanced A new revision defines a field in formerly reserved space. What risks exist for deployed hosts and devices?
    Model answer

    Old hosts write 0 (must be a safe default); old devices may not ignore non-zero values from new hosts unless the conventions require it; new hosts must check capabilities. Add interoperability tests in both directions.

  3. Senior How do you present a newly announced feature to your organisation before the spec is fully digested?
    Model answer

    State the announced purpose, affected documents, what is verified versus unknown, what must be read, and a plan with owners — and resist speculating about implementation details.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can fill the cross-reference matrix row for any new concept and leave cells empty where no source covers it.
  • I can perform a revision diff and list validation consequences.
  • I can write a "what the spec does not say" and an "implementation-dependent" box for any topic.

PART XXXI

Reading Plan

A structured, track-based plan for reading the official documents themselves: what to read first, what to skip on the first pass, which tables to memorise, which diagrams to redraw, which commands to try and which trace patterns to look for. Four tracks — Base, Commands, Transport, Advanced — plus a PCIe companion track.

31 The Official-Document Reading Plan

← 30B Cross-Specification Mapping, Revisions and the Limits of a Specification32 Building a Safe NVMe/PCIe Lab →
📘 Specification baseline

Base 2.4, NVM CS 1.3, PCIe transport 1.4, ZNS 1.5, KV 1.4, SLM 1.3, Computational Programs 1.3, NVMe-MI 2.2, Boot 1.4, RDMA 1.3, TCP 1.3 version — confirm current revisions on nvmexpress.org/specifications/ before you start; NVM Express publishes the specifications free of charge. PCIe Base specifications are distributed by PCI-SIG (membership or purchase); use the revision your hardware implements.

31.1 Why this chapter exists

Reading thousands of pages without a plan produces exhaustion and false confidence. Each track below states the prerequisite chapters in this book, the exact purpose, what to skip initially, what to highlight, the tables to memorise, the diagrams to redraw, the commands to test and the trace patterns to look for. Use the worksheet from Chapter 30 for every session.

  • Follow a sequenced plan through the NVMe library and the PCIe companion material.
  • Know what to skip on a first pass and when to come back.
  • Connect each reading session to a hands-on command and a trace pattern.
🧒 Kid analogy — climbing with base camps

Climbers do not run up a mountain. They walk to base camp, rest, learn the terrain, then climb to the next camp. Each track is a camp: you stop, practise (labs), and only then climb on. And climbers go back down to base camp to acclimatise — just as you return to the Base specification.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Mountains do not change between expeditions; specifications do. Re-check revisions at the start of each track.

Exact purposeOwn the architecture: controller types, queue model, register semantics, initialization/reset/shutdown, admin command set, data pointers, status reporting, logs, features, asynchronous events, namespaces.

nvme write, write-zeroes and dsm destroy data. Use a VM disk image or a dedicated spare drive (CAUTION LAB). See Chapter 32.

Track D is chosen by role: a client-SSD validation engineer gets more value from deeper Base/NVM/PCIe reading and power management than from KV; a cloud storage engineer needs ZNS, NVMe-MI, virtualization and fabrics. Write down your role-based choice and revisit it each quarter.

🧪 Lab 31.1 — Reading-session ritual SAFE

Objective: make one 90-minute session productive. Procedure: (1) 5 min: fill the worksheet header and the question; (2) 50 min: read with keyword classification; (3) 20 min: run the matching read-only command and map output fields to tables; (4) 15 min: update field dictionary, command matrix, cross-reference map, and write three source-based questions. Question: which part did you skip and why?

Expected reasoning

A productive session ends with artifacts (dictionary rows, questions) and at least one link between a table and real output. If you only read, the session was input without consolidation.

Quiz

  1. Which track contains the doorbell offset formula for PCIe-attached controllers?

    Answer

    Track C (PCIe transport), with semantics from Track A (Base).

  2. Why skip fabrics chapters in your first Base pass?

    Answer

    They add a different transport model; on PCIe they are not needed for the core queue/command model and would dilute the first pass.

  3. Which trace pattern distinguishes a Write from a Read?

    Answer

    Write: device-issued MRd of host data with CplD back; Read: device-issued MWr of data to host.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Where do you get the NVMe specifications, and which do you read first?
    Model answer

    nvmexpress.org; the Base specification's overview and theory of operation, then registers/initialization and queues.

  2. Senior How would you plan spec training for a new validation team?
    Model answer

    Tracks A–C for everyone with hands-on labs and artifacts; role-based Track D; weekly source-based questions; revision-diff sessions when new revisions are released; mastery gates rather than attendance.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I have completed Tracks A–C with a field dictionary, command matrix and cross-reference map.
  • I can name the tables to memorise for each track and reproduce the register map and opcode lists from memory.
  • I have chosen and justified my Track D documents.

Summary. Read in tracks, with artifacts and hands-on checks, returning to Base often. Next: a safe place to do all those hands-on checks — Chapter 32, the lab environment.

PART XXXII

Lab Environment

You learn protocols with your hands, but hands can destroy data. This Part builds a graded lab: zero-risk emulation in a virtual machine, read-only inspection of real hardware, cautious experiments on a spare drive in a dedicated test host, and expert-only destructive work. Every activity in this book carries one of three labels — SAFE, CAUTION, EXPERT — and this Part defines them precisely.

32 Building a Safe NVMe/PCIe Lab

← 31 The Official-Document Reading Plan33A Projects 1–6: Models, Decoders and Simulators →
📘 Baseline

Tools change faster than specifications. Commands below are real for current mainstream Linux distributions, QEMU, nvme-cli and fio, but option names and output formats are version- and impl-dependent: check --help and man pages for your installed versions. Output shown is illustrative and abbreviated, never authoritative.

32.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineers lose data in labs for three reasons: they run a destructive command on the wrong device, they run an experiment on a machine they also depend on, or they did not know a command was destructive. This chapter removes all three: a classification of every activity, a recommended set of environments and hardware, and setup recipes that let you do most of this book's labs with zero risk.

  • Classify any lab activity as SAFE, CAUTION or EXPERT and apply the matching precautions.
  • Build a QEMU virtual machine with emulated NVMe controllers and namespaces for zero-risk experiments.
  • Set up a dedicated physical test host with a spare SSD, adapters and (optionally) an analyzer.
  • Use Linux kernel tracing, nvme-cli, fio and offline trace files as evidence sources.

Prerequisites: basic Linux shell; the validation mindset from Chapter 29.

🧒 Kid analogy — the science classroom

In a science class, reading the thermometer is always allowed (SAFE). Heating water needs goggles and a teacher nearby (CAUTION). Mixing chemicals that could explode is done only by the teacher, behind a glass screen, with a fire extinguisher ready (EXPERT). And the very first experiments are done with pretend chemicals in a computer game — that is the virtual machine.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In a classroom you can see the danger. In a lab, /dev/nvme0n1 and /dev/nvme1n1 look identical, device numbering can change between boots, and a destructive command gives no warning. The danger is invisible; your procedure must make it visible.

32.2 Safety levels

LevelDefinitionExamplesRequired precautions
SAFE LABRead-only inspection; offline analysis; emulationlspci -vvv, lspci -tv, nvme list, nvme id-ctrl, nvme id-ns, nvme smart-log, nvme error-log, nvme get-log, nvme get-feature, dmesg, journalctl -k, reading sysfs, Python on trace files, anything inside a VM on a scratch imageNone beyond normal care (some reads need root)
CAUTION LABOperations that can affect a device or its data, or the running systemfio/dd writes to a raw device, nvme write/write-zeroes/dsm, nvme set-feature, sysfs reset/remove/rescan, unbinding drivers, SPDK setup (takes the device away from the kernel), changing ASPM policySpare, non-production drive with no needed data; dedicated test host; verify the device by serial number before every run; backups irrelevant because nothing on it matters
EXPERT LABPotentially destructive or irreversiblenvme format, nvme sanitize, namespace delete/create, firmware download/commit, setpci writes, power-cut testing, error injection, writing BAR registers from user spaceAll CAUTION precautions plus: written procedure, second person review where available, known recovery path (e.g. vendor tool for firmware recovery), accept that the drive may be permanently damaged
⚠️ Never on production drives

Never run CAUTION or EXPERT activities on a drive that holds an operating system, personal data, or anything you or anyone else needs — including "just a quick test". Never on a laptop's only SSD. Never on a server in service. Identify target drives by serial number (nvme list, nvme id-ctrl | grep -i sn), not by device name, because names can change between boots.

32.3 Environment tiers

TierWhat it can teachWhat it cannot teach
0 OfflineDecoding, correlation, statistics, report writing on synthetic or exported tracesReal timing, real device behaviour
1 QEMUNVMe command semantics, queue setup, admin commands, namespace management, error paths, even destructive commands — with zero risk; driver behaviour on a real kernelPCIe physical/link layer, real TLP timing, real firmware behaviour, performance (emulation is a software model impl)
2 Real host (read-only)Real capabilities, link status, logs, healthAnything requiring writes
3 Test host + spare SSDReal I/O behaviour, performance, error handling, resets, power statesLink-level packets (unless Tier 4)
4 + analyzerEvery TLP/DLLP, ordered sets, LTSSM, precise timingFirmware internals

32.4 Tier 1: QEMU with emulated NVMe (zero risk)

QEMU emulates an NVMe controller as a PCI device (on mainstream builds the device model is called nvme, with separate nvme-ns devices for additional namespaces) version. The guest kernel's real NVMe driver binds to it, so you exercise genuine driver code paths, nvme-cli and fio — while every "destructive" command only modifies an image file on the host.

# On the HOST (not inside the guest). Creates two scratch images; touches no real disk.
qemu-img create -f qcow2 guest-os.qcow2 20G        # or reuse a cloud image as the OS disk
qemu-img create -f raw   nvme-ns1.img   4G
qemu-img create -f raw   nvme-ns2.img   1G

qemu-system-x86_64 -enable-kvm -m 4G -smp 4 -cpu host \
  -drive file=guest-os.qcow2,if=virtio \
  -drive file=nvme-ns1.img,if=none,id=ns1,format=raw \
  -drive file=nvme-ns2.img,if=none,id=ns2,format=raw \
  -device nvme,id=nvme0,serial=LAB0001 \
  -device nvme-ns,drive=ns1,bus=nvme0,nsid=1 \
  -device nvme-ns,drive=ns2,bus=nvme0,nsid=2 \
  -nographic
# Options and sub-option names vary by QEMU version: check
#   qemu-system-x86_64 -device nvme,help    and    -device nvme-ns,help

Inside the guest (all SAFE, because the targets are image files):

lspci -nn | grep -i 0108          # emulated controller, class 0108
sudo nvme list                    # serial LAB0001, two namespaces
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -H   # human-readable decode of Identify Controller
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 -H
sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H # CAP/VS/CC/CSTS/AQA... if supported by your nvme-cli
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x07 -H   # Number of Queues

Useful QEMU features for learning impl (availability depends on QEMU version): trace events for the NVMe device model (e.g. enabling events matching pci_nvme* with QEMU's -trace option) give you a host-side log of each command the emulated controller processes — a software "analyzer" for the NVMe layer; zoned namespaces can be enabled on nvme-ns devices in recent versions for ZNS labs; SR-IOV emulation exists in recent versions for virtualization labs.

📭 What emulation does not show

An emulated controller has no PCIe link: no LTSSM, no DLLPs, no flow-control credits, no real TLP timing. Its latency and error behaviour are those of a software model. Use it to learn command semantics and driver behaviour; never to characterise a product.

32.5 Tier 2: physical system, read-only

lspci -tv                              # topology: root ports, switches, endpoints
sudo lspci -vvv -s <BDF>               # capabilities, LnkCap/LnkSta, DevCtl MaxPayload/MaxReadReq, AER
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/<domain:BDF>/  # current_link_speed, current_link_width, max_link_speed ...
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/<domain:BDF>/current_link_speed
sudo nvme list
sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0
journalctl -k -b | grep -iE "nvme|pcieport|aer"
cat /proc/interrupts | grep nvme
⚠️ setpci is not read-only by default

setpci can read (setpci -s BDF CAP_EXP+12.w) but also write configuration registers (anything with =value). A write can disable memory decoding, change link control, or hang the system. Treat any setpci write as EXPERT, on a test host only.

32.6 Tier 3–4: recommended hardware for a dedicated test bench

ItemWhyNotes and pitfalls
Spare NVMe SSD(s)The DUT you are allowed to destroyInexpensive M.2 2280 drives are fine for learning; label them physically with "TEST — DATA WILL BE DESTROYED" and record serial numbers. Different vendors' drives reveal implementation-dependent behaviour.
Dedicated test hostIsolation: a crash, hang or wrong command cannot hurt your work machineDesktop with CPU-attached M.2 or x16 slots; firmware setup that allows link-speed limiting and ASPM control impl; boot from a separate SATA/USB disk so the NVMe DUT is never the boot device.
M.2-to-PCIe x4 adapter cardPuts an M.2 drive in a standard slot; easier access and hot-swap of the card in a powered-off systemPassive adapters are simple; check lane wiring (x4) and that the slot provides x4 electrically.
U.2 (SFF-8639) adapter/cableFor enterprise 2.5" drivesNeeds proper power; cable quality matters at Gen4/Gen5.
PCIe riser / extenderMechanical access, room for probesRisers degrade signal integrity; at Gen4/Gen5 they can cause link errors or down-training. Use only qualified risers and check LnkSta and AER counters after inserting one — a riser can create the bug you are hunting.
Switchable power (relay / programmable supply)Power-loss and power-cycle testsEXPERT. Control off-time; capacitors hold charge.
Heatsink / fan / thermocoupleThermal reproducibilityThrottling changes performance and timing; log temperature from the SMART log.
Interposer + protocol analyzer (optional)Link-level visibilityExpensive; form-factor specific (M.2, U.2, CEM); the interposer itself adds a channel and can affect margins at high speeds. Learn on exported or synthetic captures first.
Avoid: USB-to-NVMe enclosures—A bridge chip translates to USB mass-storage protocols; the host does not see the NVMe controller directly, so most NVMe admin commands and all PCIe observation are unavailable or translated impl.

32.7 Software tools

ToolUseSafety
nvme-cliAdmin commands, logs, features, raw passthroughRead subcommands SAFE; format/sanitize/fw/ns-delete EXPERT; write/passthru CAUTION or EXPERT depending on the command
fioWorkloads, latency percentiles, verifyReads SAFE-ish (can still stress the system); writes to raw devices CAUTION
Linux NVMe driverReal host behaviour; module parameters such as I/O and admin timeouts, poll queues implChanging parameters is CAUTION (affects all NVMe devices on the host)
Kernel tracing (tracepoints, trace-cmd, perf, bpftrace)Per-command events from the driver (e.g. the nvme tracepoint group with setup/complete events) implSAFE (observation), though high-rate tracing has overhead
blktrace / blkparse, iostatBlock-layer timing and queueingSAFE
SPDK (Storage Performance Development Kit)User-space NVMe driver; its identify/perf tools show controller behaviour without the kernel driverCAUTION: its setup script unbinds devices from the kernel driver — make sure the boot disk and any needed disk are excluded
Python (stdlib)Offline decoders, simulators, summarizers (Projects in Ch 33A/33B)SAFE
# Kernel tracing of NVMe commands (SAFE observation; event names/fields vary by kernel)
sudo ls /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/          # see which events YOUR kernel has
sudo trace-cmd record -e nvme -- sleep 5          # record while a workload runs
sudo trace-cmd report | head
# bpftrace: count submitted commands per opcode (field names: check with
#   sudo bpftrace -lv 'tracepoint:nvme:*' )
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:nvme:nvme_setup_cmd { @ops[args->opcode] = count(); }'

32.8 Offline trace files

Keep a library of trace files with provenance: who captured, which tool and version, DUT and firmware, platform, trigger, and a hash of the raw file. Export to a neutral format (CSV/JSON) for your own tools, but keep the original. Label every file as real, synthetic, excerpted or reconstructed; a synthetic file must never be renamed into the "real" folder. The analyzer's export format is impl — write a column mapping per tool version (Project 9).

32.9 Bench procedure (the pre-flight checklist)

  1. Confirm the activity's safety level.
  2. Confirm the host is the dedicated test host and the boot disk is not the DUT.
  3. Identify the DUT by serial number; record firmware revision.
  4. Capture "before" evidence: lspci -vvv, id-ctrl, smart-log, error-log.
  5. Start observers (kernel trace, analyzer trigger) before stimulus.
  6. Run; capture "after" evidence; store everything with a run id.
🧪 Lab 32.1 — Zero-risk NVMe in QEMU SAFE

Objective: create a VM with an emulated NVMe controller and two namespaces; practise "destructive" commands safely. Setup: §32.4. Steps: (1) inside the guest list controllers and namespaces; (2) run nvme id-ctrl -H and note OACS (optional admin commands) and ONCS; (3) sudo nvme format /dev/nvme0n2 — destructive on real hardware, harmless here; (4) re-read id-ns and smart-log. Observations: what changed after format? Questions: why is this command EXPERT on real hardware but SAFE here?

Solution

The format only rewrites the host-side image file backing namespace 2; nothing physical is touched. On real hardware it erases user data and can take long, change LBA format, and fail in ways that need vendor recovery. Expected observations: namespace data reads back as zeros/deallocated pattern impl; counters may change.

Extension: enable QEMU's NVMe trace events and correlate guest nvme-cli commands with the host-side trace lines.

🧪 Lab 32.2 — Inventory a real machine SAFE

Objective: read-only inventory. Steps: topology (lspci -tv), link (LnkCap vs LnkSta), MaxPayload/MaxReadReq, MSI-X count, NVMe identify, health. Question: is your drive running at its capable speed and width? If not, which component limits it?

Solution

Compare drive LnkCap with the Root Port's LnkCap and the LnkSta; the link trains to the lower common capability, and can be down-trained by signal-integrity problems or firmware settings. A chipset-attached slot may also share upstream bandwidth.

🧪 Lab 32.3 — First workload on a spare drive CAUTION

Objective: run a read-only-then-write fio sequence on a dedicated spare. Steps: verify serial; random read QD1 and QD32 (--rw=randread --readonly); then random write with verify on the raw device. Questions: how did latency percentiles change between QD1 and QD32, and why?

Solution

QD32 increases throughput and increases per-command latency due to queueing (Little's Law: outstanding = throughput × latency). Absolute values are implementation-dependent.

🧪 Lab 32.4 — Firmware-slot inspection and controlled reset EXPERT

Objective: observe reset effects on a spare drive in the test host. Steps: read nvme fw-log (SAFE); then trigger a controller reset with nvme reset /dev/nvmeX and a function reset via sysfs (echo 1 > /sys/bus/pci/devices/<BDF>/reset) while no workload runs; observe kernel log and re-read Identify. Questions: what did each reset clear? What would change if I/O were in flight?

Solution

Controller reset reinitialises the NVMe controller (queues recreated by the driver); a function-level reset also resets PCIe function state and the OS restores config space. With I/O in flight, commands are aborted and retried or failed by the driver — implementation-dependent. Firmware download/commit are deliberately not part of this lab: they need a vendor-approved image and recovery path.

⚠️ Warning

Resets of the wrong device can take a running system's disk offline. Triple-check the BDF and serial; never run on a host whose boot disk is NVMe on the same controller.

Quiz

  1. Classify: nvme smart-log, nvme sanitize, fio --rw=randwrite on /dev/nvme1n1, setpci ... =0.

    Answer

    SAFE; EXPERT; CAUTION; EXPERT.

  2. Why identify a drive by serial number rather than device name?

    Answer

    Device names depend on enumeration order and can change between boots or after hot-plug.

  3. What can QEMU's emulated NVMe not teach?

    Answer

    PCIe link behaviour (LTSSM, DLLPs, credits, real TLP timing), real firmware behaviour, product performance.

  4. Why avoid USB enclosures for NVMe labs?

    Answer

    A bridge translates the protocol; the host does not talk NVMe/PCIe to the drive directly.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner How would you start learning NVMe commands without risking data?
    Model answer

    QEMU VM with emulated NVMe on image files; nvme-cli inside the guest; then read-only inspection of real hardware.

  2. Intermediate What could a PCIe riser do to your experiment?
    Model answer

    Degrade signal integrity, cause correctable errors, replays, recovery or down-training — changing the behaviour under test. Verify link status and error counters with and without it.

  3. Senior Design a lab policy for a new team.
    Model answer

    Three safety levels with examples, dedicated test hosts, labelled spare drives tracked by serial, pre-flight checklist, evidence capture before/after, reviewed procedures for EXPERT activities, and a rule that production hardware is never a DUT.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I have a working QEMU VM with emulated NVMe and can run every SAFE lab in this book.
  • I can classify any command by safety level and explain why.
  • I can list the hardware for a test bench and the pitfall of each item.

Next: use the lab to build things — Part XXXIII, project-based learning.

PART XXXIII

Project-Based Learning

Twelve projects take you from a mental model to a senior-level protocol-debugging assistant. Each project has requirements, an architecture, milestones, expected output, tests and acceptance criteria, failure cases and extension ideas — and a runnable starter in standard-library Python. Every starter in this Part was executed to produce the output shown beside it; all inputs are synthetic unless stated otherwise.

33A Projects 1–6: Models, Decoders and Simulators

← 32 Building a Safe NVMe/PCIe Lab33B Projects 7–12: From DMA to a Debugging Assistant →

33A.1 Why this chapter exists

Reading creates familiarity; building creates understanding. When you write a TLP decoder, you discover that Length 0 means 1024 DW; when you simulate a completion queue, you discover why the phase tag exists. Each project is small enough to finish in a weekend and connected to the next, so that by Project 12 you have a toolkit.

  • Build executable models of the NVMe command lifecycle, PCIe configuration space, TLP headers, SQEs, queues and doorbells.
  • Write acceptance tests that encode specification rules.
  • Practise labelling: every input marked synthetic, every rule traced to a document.

Prerequisites: Python 3; the earlier Parts on PCIe configuration space, TLPs, NVMe queues and doorbells; Chapter 32 for where to run things. Glossary: TLP, BAR, SQ, CQ, PRP, BDF.

🧒 Kid analogy — building a model railway

You understand trains better after building a model railway: you have to decide where the signals go, what happens when two trains want the same track, and how the station knows a train arrived. Our projects are model railways for NVMe and PCIe.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A model is only as true as its rules. A simulator that is wrong teaches wrong lessons confidently. That is why every project has tests derived from the specification, and why simulations are labelled simulation, not truth.

#ProjectBuilds onKey skillEst. effort
1NVMe mental model—Actors and evidence of each lifecycle step4 h
2Config-space decoder—Type 0 header, BARs, capability list6 h
3TLP decoder—Header bitfields, Fmt/Type, completions8 h
4NVMe command decoder1SQE layout, opcodes, 0-based fields6 h
5SQ/CQ simulator4Ring arithmetic, phase tag, full/empty8 h
6Doorbell simulator5Address map, stride, invalid writes4 h
7DMA / PRP simulator4PRP rules, page crossing, TLP splitting8 h
