Every fault falls in the HMB region described by the previous descriptor list — never a random address, never a PRP, never the current list. This pattern, repeated across two independent failures, is the strongest evidence in the bundle.

S4. Root cause

Hidden root cause (official): SSD firmware R1.07 caches the HMB segment table internally when the HMB is first enabled after a controller enable (CC.EN 0→1) and does not reload it when the HMB is disabled (EHM = 0) and re-enabled (EHM = 1, MR = 0) with a new descriptor list while the controller remains enabled. After Set Features HMB EHM = 0 completes successfully, the firmware also continues to treat the old segments as valid on the next enable. Consequently, after resume the device accesses host memory that the host legitimately released after the disable completed. On this platform the IOMMU blocks those accesses (UR completions, dropped writes); the firmware then fails commands whose logical-to-physical map segments reside in the HMB (Internal Error, then stalls), and in the second incident hits an internal assertion leading to CSTS.CFS.

Why resets “fix” it: a controller reset clears the firmware’s cached table; the next HMB enable (D35, D39-reset) is the first after CC.EN 0→1 and is therefore honoured. The bug re-arms at the next suspend cycle where the driver chooses new memory.

Why some queues kept working (Likely): commands whose mapping segments were cached in device SRAM or whose LBAs were not mapped through HMB-resident segments did not need HMB reads. SQ 1, 2, 4 traffic in that window was a small working set (developer tools) — consistent but not proven.

Why the second failure looks different (Possible → needs vendor confirmation): in the second incident the first stale access was a write-back of a dirty map segment combined with reads; firmware error handling diverged into an assertion path. Same root cause, different symptom — a common pattern.

S5. Confidence and evidence

ClaimConfidenceEvidence
Device accessed HMB memory after HMB disable completedConfirmedD28 completion at 600.0010; H9/H11/H14 addresses in L1; IOMMU faults G
The accesses follow the previous descriptor list, not random corruptionStrong evidenceS3 table, two incidents, 100% of faulting addresses
Firmware does not reload descriptors on re-enable without controller resetStrong evidenceH6 shows device fetched L2 descriptors yet used L1; post-reset enable works (perf L rows)
Link errors are not causalStrong evidenceSingle correctable replay at L1.2 exit, no subsequent errors, faults 70 ms later with clean link
The Unrecovered Read Error at ~410 s is unrelatedLikelyPredates suspend; different SCT; single occurrence
Firmware assertion explains CFS in incident 2PossibleTiming; needs telemetry/vendor log

To reach Confirmed on the root cause: vendor reproduces with a scripted sequence (enable HMB list A → disable → free A → enable list B without reset → I/O) on R1.07, and confirms the code path; or obtain controller-initiated telemetry from incident 2.

S6. Hypotheses eliminated

  • Signal integrity / L1.2 exit: eliminated as root cause — replay succeeded, no Bad TLP/Receiver Errors after, faults are address-specific.
  • Host driver freed HMB while still enabled: eliminated — free happened after EHM = 0 completed successfully (D28 → 600.0012); the specification expects the controller to stop using HMB memory once the disable completes derived (consult the HMB feature description in the Base specification for normative wording).
  • Bad PRPs from host: eliminated — faulting addresses do not match any SQE PRP (SQE H8 PRP1 differs) and match HMB lists exactly.
  • Power-state restore lost config (D3hot): eliminated — PMCSR No_Soft_Reset = 1; Command, Device Control, MSI-X unchanged; admin commands worked immediately (H5, H6).
  • APST: not involved in the failure window (device was in PS0 via explicit Set Features).

S7. Workaround and fix

  • Workaround (host): on resume for this device/firmware, either (a) re-enable HMB with the same memory and list and MR = 1 (keep HMB memory allocated across suspend), or (b) perform a controller reset before re-enabling HMB. Option (a) avoids the bug at the cost of 64 MiB reserved during suspend.
  • Permanent fix (device firmware): on every Set Features HMB with EHM = 0, quiesce and invalidate all HMB segment references before posting the completion; on every EHM = 1, (re)fetch the descriptor list and rebuild the segment table; if MR = 0 treat contents as undefined.
  • Hardening (host): optionally add an IOMMU-fault-to-device correlation in the driver to log “DMA to released HMB region” explicitly.

S8. Regression test

for cycle in range(500):
    run_random_io(duration_s=5, qd=32, working_set="large")   # forces HMB map use
    set_features_hmb(ehm=0); assert ok
    old = hmb.memory; hmb.release(old)                       # IOMMU unmap
    poison_and_unmap_check(old)                              # any DMA here must fault
    hmb.memory = alloc_new_region(size=64*MiB)               # different addresses
    set_features_hmb(ehm=1, mr=0, list=hmb.build_list()); assert ok
    run_random_io(duration_s=5, qd=32, verify=True)
    assert iommu_faults(device) == 0
    assert controller_resets() == 0 and not csts().cfs
# Variants: with D3hot/L1.2 cycle between disable and enable; MR=1 path; HMDLEC 1..max

Pass criteria: zero IOMMU faults, zero resets, zero data mismatches over 500 cycles on fixed firmware; the test must fail on R1.07 within a few cycles (proves the test detects the bug).

Extension: modify the scenario so that the IOMMU is in passthrough mode. What would happen instead of faults? (Answer sketch: the stale DMA would silently read/write memory that the host may have reallocated — potential host memory corruption with no fault logged. This is why IOMMU translation is valuable for debugging and safety.)

💡 Senior insight

The decisive step was not decoding packets — it was building the address-attribution table (S3). Investigations often turn on a single join between two evidence sources (here: IOMMU fault addresses ⨝ HMB descriptor lists). Always ask “what other record contains this address/ID/tag?”

✅ Mastery gate
  • I identified H9 as the first abnormal event before opening the solution.
  • I correctly classified the Replay Timer Timeout and the Unrecovered Read Error as decoys, with reasons.
  • My bug report contained a regression test that would fail on the buggy firmware.

Next: Part XL — Engineering Bug Report Training.

PART XL

Engineering Bug Report Training

A root cause that nobody can act on is worth very little. The bug report is the product of an investigation: it transfers evidence, reasoning and next steps to people who were not in the room — firmware teams, platform vendors, managers, the engineer who will hit the same bug in three years. This part gives a template, a fully worked excellent report, and a poor report dissected line by line.

40.1 Writing Bug Reports That Get Bugs Fixed

← 39.1 Capstone Investigation47.1 The A–F Assessment Framework →

40.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Most escalations stall not because the bug is hard but because the report is unusable: no versions, no reproduction, no first abnormal event, conclusions without evidence, or evidence without conclusions. A reader on the receiving end must be able to answer three questions in under a minute: What failed? Where is the proof? What do you want me to do?

40.1.2 Learning objectives

  • Fill every section of the standard template with precise, verifiable content.
  • State the first abnormal event with a pointer to the exact evidence row.
  • Separate observation, inference and recommendation; label confidence.
  • Write a regression test that fails on the buggy build and passes on the fix.
  • Critique a poor report and rewrite it.

Prerequisites: Part XV (Error handling), the capstone, scenario method in 38.1.

🧒 Kid analogy

If you tell a doctor “I feel bad”, they can’t help much. If you say “since Tuesday, my left knee hurts when I climb stairs, not when I walk on flat ground, and it is swollen here”, they can. A bug report is telling the engineer exactly where it hurts, when, and how you know.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A patient is not expected to diagnose. An engineering bug report is expected to contain your diagnosis — but clearly separated from the observations, so the reader can disagree with the diagnosis while still trusting the data.

40.1.3 The template

SectionWhat goes in itQuality test
TitleSymptom + trigger + scope, ≤ 100 chars. Avoid blame words.Could someone search for this title and find it when they hit the same symptom?
EnvironmentSystem type, topology (root port → switch → device), slot, retimers, cables, IOMMU mode, BIOS version.Could another lab rebuild the setup?
HardwareDevice model, hardware revision, serial(s) affected, quantity tested/failed.Failure rate expressed as n/N.
FirmwareDevice firmware revision (Identify FR / firmware slot log), platform firmware, retimer/switch firmware.Exact strings, not “latest”.
OSKernel version and config relevant options, driver version, relevant module parameters, tool versions (nvme-cli, fio).Includes non-default parameters.
PCIe generationCapability and negotiated speed at both ends; how it was measured.LnkCap vs LnkSta both stated.
Link widthCapability and negotiated width.Same.
NVMe revisionVS register value; command sets in use; relevant optional features enabled (HMB, APST, VWC, PI).Distinguishes NVMe revision from PCIe generation.
Reproduction stepsNumbered, minimal, deterministic where possible, with commands and parameters; time-to-repro and repro rate.A stranger can reproduce without asking questions.
Expected resultWhat should happen, with the basis (spec behaviour, previous firmware, other device).Says why it is expected.
Actual resultWhat happened, user-visible and low-level.Factual, no interpretation.
Trace evidenceAttached captures/logs with names, time ranges, analyzer settings, and annotated excerpts.Every claim points to a row/line/file.
First abnormal eventThe earliest deviation from expected behaviour, with timestamp, layer and evidence row.One event, not a list.
Root causeMechanism, with confidence label; eliminated hypotheses with reasons.Explains all observations, including the odd ones.
WorkaroundSafe mitigation with cost and scope.Says what it costs (performance, power).
Permanent fixProposed change and owner.Names the owner (host, device, platform).
Regression testTest that fails before the fix and passes after; pass criteria; duration.Proven to fail on the buggy build.

40.1.4 A fully worked excellent report

📘 Context

The following report is synthetic. The host component is a fictional user-space NVMe driver named udrv; the device and platform are placeholders. It illustrates the style; it is not a record of a real defect.

📝 Report UDRV-1342 SAFE

Title

Read of exactly 513 pages (e.g. 2 MiB at non-page-aligned buffer) returns wrong data in last page; PRP list page overwritten — udrv 5.4

Environment

Server “LAB-R2” (synthetic), root port 0000:80:03.0 direct-attached to SSD in U.2 bay 3, no switch, no retimer. IOMMU disabled for udrv (VFIO no-IOMMU mode for the lab — note this hides DMA faults). BIOS 2.14.

Hardware

SSD model “X-3200” (placeholder), HW rev B; 3/3 units reproduce. Different SSD model “Y-800”: 0/2 reproduce (see Root cause for why).

Firmware

SSD firmware 4.2.1 (slot 1, active). Platform BMC 1.9.

OS

Kernel 6.x (vendor build), hugepages 2 MiB × 1024, udrv 5.4.0 commit 9f3c2e1 (synthetic), fio 3.x with udrv ioengine.

PCIe generation / link width

Device LnkCap 16 GT/s x4; root port LnkCap 32 GT/s x16 (bifurcated x4); LnkSta 16 GT/s x4 on both ends, measured with lspci -vvv before and after the test.

NVMe revision

VS = 0001_0400h (1.4). CAP.MPSMIN = 0 (4 KiB); CC.MPS = 0. MDTS = 0 (no limit reported). PRPs used (SGLs not supported by X-3200 for I/O). Y-800 reports MDTS = 9 (2 MiB).

Reproduction steps

  1. Write a known pattern: fio --ioengine=udrv --rw=write --bs=2M --size=1G --verify_pattern=0xA5A5… with page-aligned buffers.
  2. Read back with buffer offset 512 B: --rw=read --bs=2M --iomem_align=512 --verify=pattern (the unaligned buffer spans 513 pages).
  3. Observe verification failures. Repro rate: 100% of 2 MiB reads with offset ∉ {0}; 0% with offset 0.
  4. Minimal reproducer: udrv_test prp_boundary --pages=513 (attached) — fails in 1 iteration.

Expected result

All 2 MiB reads return the written pattern. Basis: identical reads with aligned buffers succeed; the PRP rules (first entry may carry an offset; list entries page-aligned; a list page’s last entry is a chain pointer only when more entries follow) allow this transfer.

Actual result

The last 512 bytes of the user buffer contain stale data; the CQE reports success (SC 00h). Occasionally a subsequent unrelated command fails with Invalid Field or a Data Transfer Error.

Trace evidence

Capture udrv1342_cap1 (analyzer, both directions, headers + first 64 B of payload, 16 GT/s x4 interposer; failure reproduced with interposer present). Annotated excerpt:

Synthetic excerpt — 2 MiB read with 512-byte buffer offset
#DirTLPAddressLenNote
12↑MRdSQE @ 2_0000_3C4016 DWSQE: opc 02h, NLB 1FFh (512 blocks × 4 KiB = 2 MiB), PRP1 = 3_1000_0200, PRP2 = 2_4000_0000 (list)
14↑MRd ×82_4000_0000 …128 DW eachDevice reads the full list page (512 entries, MRRS 512)
15↓CplD ×16—64 DW eachEntry 511 = 2_4000_1000 (points to a second list page)
16–8205↑MWr ×81903_1000_0200 … per list64 DWData writes to pages in entries 0–510
8206↑MWr ×22_4000_1000 …64 DWDevice writes the last 512 B of data into address 2_4000_1000 — the second list page — treating entry 511 as a data page
8208↑MWrCQE4 DWSC 00h

Calculation: buffer offset 512 B → PRP1 covers 4096 − 512 = 3584 B; remaining 2 MiB − 3584 B = 2093568 B = 511 full pages + 512 B → 512 more pages → 512 list entries. 512 entries fit exactly in one 4 KiB list page (512 × 8 B), so no chain pointer is needed; entry 511 must be a data pointer derived. udrv wrote a chain pointer in entry 511 and placed the last data page pointer in the second list page.

First abnormal event

Row 14–15: the PRP list fetched by the device contains a chain pointer in entry 511 although exactly 512 entries are required. This is a host-side construction error; row 8206 is its consequence. Note: the trace marks row 8206 as first-bad because it is the first visible misbehaviour on the wire; the report identifies the earlier list content (rows 14–15) as the first abnormal event because the list was already wrong when fetched.

Root cause

Confirmed (code inspection + trace + fix verified): prp_build() in udrv/src/prp.c chains when remaining_entries >= entries_per_page instead of > entries_per_page. The off-by-one triggers only when exactly 512 entries are needed (513 pages touched). Y-800 does not reproduce because its MDTS (2 MiB) causes udrv to split the I/O, so no single command needs 512 entries.

Eliminated: device PRP handling bug (device behaviour matches the PRP rules given the list it received); memory corruption (pattern reproducible and address-exact); link errors (no AER, no Nak in capture).

Secondary effect (Strong evidence): the device wrote user data into udrv’s second PRP list page, which is pooled and reused; later commands that use that pool page as a list read garbage entries, explaining sporadic Invalid Field / Data Transfer Errors.

Workaround

Set udrv.max_io_size=1M (forces splitting) — cost: ~3% lower sequential throughput at QD1, none measurable at QD8+.

Permanent fix

Owner: udrv maintainers. Change comparison to strict greater-than; add assertion that a list page’s last slot holds a chain pointer only if entries remain. Patch udrv!2211 attached.

Regression test

udrv_test prp_boundary: for page counts {1, 2, 3, 511, 512, 513, 514, 1024, 1025, 1026} × buffer offsets {0, 8, 512, 4088} × read/write, verify data and verify PRP list structure by a software model. Fails on 5.4.0 (513 pages, offset ≠ 0), passes with patch; runtime 40 s; added to CI.

40.1.5 A poor report, critiqued

⚠️ The bad report (synthetic)

Title: SSD broken!!!
Description: Our SSD keeps failing on the new servers. We get I/O errors and AER. The firmware is buggy, probably a PCIe issue with Gen4. We tried a lot of things. Logs attached (dmesg.txt). Please fix ASAP, customer is angry. Also performance is bad.
Steps: Run our workload.
Expected: Works.
Actual: Doesn’t work.

ProblemWhy it hurtsRewrite
Title “SSD broken!!!”Unsearchable, emotional, no symptom/trigger“Write I/O timeouts within 1 h at QD ≥ 32 on Gen4 x4, platform P-9, FW 3.1 — 4/10 units”
“keeps failing”No rate, no count, no time base“4 of 10 drives, mean time to failure 42 min under workload W”
“I/O errors and AER”Which errors? Which AER type, which reporter?Quote the status codes (SCT/SC) and the AER type + BDF that logged it, with timestamps
“firmware is buggy, probably PCIe Gen4”Two contradictory conclusions without evidence; blames before localisingMove to Root cause with confidence label, or remove; state evidence for each hypothesis
“We tried a lot of things”Information destroyed — the reader will repeat themList each experiment with result: “Gen3 forced: still fails (3/3)”, “other slot: fails”
“Logs attached (dmesg.txt)”No time window, no annotations, no versionsAttach logs with the relevant line ranges quoted and explained
Missing environment/firmware/OS/linkCannot reproduce; cannot correlate with known issuesFill every template field
“Run our workload”Non-reproduciblefio job file or recorded trace replay, with parameters
“Expected: works / Actual: doesn’t”Zero information“Expected: all writes complete < 1 s (QoS spec)”; “Actual: 14 writes time out at 30 s, controller reset”
“Also performance is bad”Second unrelated issue mixed inFile separately with its own measurements
No first abnormal event, no regression testNobody knows where to start or how to verify a fixProvide both, even if provisional
💡 Senior insight

Write the “First abnormal event” section first. If you cannot fill it, your investigation is not finished — the report is a status update, and should be titled as such.

🎯 Exercise

Rewrite the bad report into a complete report using invented-but-consistent synthetic details for Scenario 6 (“reads work, writes time out”) from 38.1. Then exchange with a peer and score each other’s reports using the quality-test column.

Quiz

  1. Why must the “Actual result” section avoid interpretation?

    Answer

    So the reader can trust the observation even if they disagree with your diagnosis. Mixing interpretation in makes the data look biased and forces the reader to re-derive the facts.

  2. What makes a regression test trustworthy?

    Answer

    It demonstrably fails on the buggy build and passes on the fixed build, has explicit pass criteria and bounded runtime, and covers the boundary conditions around the bug (neighbouring values), not just the single failing case.

  3. The capstone’s report should name which owner for the permanent fix?

    Answer

    The device firmware team (HMB re-enable handling), with an optional host workaround owned by the driver team.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I wrote a complete report for the capstone with every template section filled.
  • My report’s first abnormal event references an exact evidence row.
  • I critiqued and rewrote the bad report.
PART XLVII

Testing the Learner

Reading creates an illusion of understanding. Testing breaks the illusion. Every chapter in this book is meant to end with six categories of assessment — A Recall, B Understanding, C Application, D Debugging, E Senior thinking, F Lab — with answers hidden behind collapsible sections. This part defines each category, shows how to write good items, and provides a full sample set you can reuse as a model.

47.1 The A–F Assessment Framework

← 40.1 Writing Bug Reports That Get Bugs Fixed48.1 Review Checkpoints and Major Assessments →

47.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Different questions test different levels of knowledge. Recall without understanding fails at the first debugging task; understanding without recall is slow. A balanced end-of-chapter set (5 Recall, 5 Understanding, 5 Application, 3 Debugging, 2 Senior thinking, 1 Lab) exercises the whole ladder.

47.1.2 Learning objectives

  • Classify questions into categories A–F and explain what each measures.
  • Write items that cannot be answered by pattern-matching a sentence in the text.
  • Use collapsible answers and delayed self-checking to avoid illusion of competence.
CategoryCount per chapterMeasuresGood item stemWeak item stem
A. Recall5Facts, offsets, names“At what BAR0 offset is CSTS?”“Is CSTS important?”
B. Understanding5Mechanism, why“Why does the CQ need a phase tag when the host could read a controller register?”“Define phase tag.”
C. Application5Use in new situation“Compute PRP entries for a 20 KiB read at offset 0x200.”“What is a PRP list?”
D. Debugging3Reason from symptoms“Doorbell seen, no SQE fetch. Three hypotheses?”“What is debugging?”

F. Lab1Hands-onObserve and explain a real or simulated artefact“Read more about X.”

47.1.3 Sample set — topic: NVMe queues and doorbells

A. Recall (5)

  1. What is the size of an SQE and a CQE?

    Answer

    64 bytes and 16 bytes (standard sizes configured via CC.IOSQES = 6 and CC.IOCQES = 4, i.e. 2^6 and 2^4).

  2. Where does the doorbell region start in BAR0?

    Answer

    Offset 1000h.

  3. Which register field gives the maximum queue entries supported?

    Answer

    CAP.MQES, bits 15:0, zero-based.

  4. Which bit of CQE DW3 is the phase tag?

    Answer

    Bit 16.

  5. Opcode of Create I/O Completion Queue?

    Answer

    05h (admin).

B. Understanding (5)

  1. Why is a queue with N slots able to hold only N−1 outstanding entries?

    Answer

    Because head == tail means empty; if all N were used, full would also be head == tail, which is ambiguous. Full is defined as (tail + 1) mod N == head.

  2. Why does the host update the CQ head doorbell at all?

    Answer

    So the controller knows which CQ slots are free; without it the controller would eventually consider the CQ full and stop posting.

  3. Why can many SQs share one CQ but not vice-versa?

    Answer

    Each SQ is bound to exactly one CQ at creation (CQID field); a CQ is just a destination. Sharing lets a CPU collect completions from several SQs (e.g. different priorities) in one place.

  4. Why is the doorbell write posted, and what does that imply for error reporting?

    Answer

    It is a Memory Write, which PCIe defines as posted: no completion returns, so the host cannot know from the write itself whether it arrived. Errors appear via AER or by the absence of subsequent device activity.

  5. Why does the controller report SQHD in each CQE?

    Answer

    To tell the host how far it has consumed the SQ so the host can reuse slots — the host has no other cheap way to know.

C. Application (5)

  1. CAP.DSTRD = 2. Offset of CQ 3 head doorbell?

    Answer

    Stride = 4 << 2 = 16 B. Offset = 1000h + (2×3+1)×16 = 1000h + 112 = 1070h.

  2. Host wants 256-entry I/O queues. What value goes in QSIZE?

    Answer

    255 (FFh), zero-based.

  3. SQ size 16, head 14, tail 3. How many commands outstanding? How many free slots?

    Answer

    (3 − 14) mod 16 = 5 outstanding (slots 14, 15, 0, 1, 2). Free usable = 16 − 1 − 5 = 10.

  4. Host consumed CQEs in slots 1022, 1023, 0, 1 of a 1024-entry CQ. Expected phase after?

    Answer

    Phase flips when the head wraps from 1023 to 0; if it was 1 before, it is now 0. New head = 2; write 2 to the CQ head doorbell.

  5. Number of Queues Set Features returned DW0 = 0003_0007. How many I/O SQs and CQs may the host create?

    Answer

    Bits 15:0 = NSQA = 7 → 8 SQs; bits 31:16 = NCQA = 3 → 4 CQs (both zero-based).

D. Debugging (3)

  1. Analyzer shows SQ tail doorbell writes but no SQE fetches. Hypotheses?

    Answer

    Bus Master Enable cleared; controller not enabled/ready (CSTS.RDY = 0) or in fatal state; doorbell written to wrong offset (stride) or wrong queue ID that doesn’t exist; tail value invalid (≥ queue size) → controller flags invalid doorbell and ignores; device lacks NP credits/tags; link problems. Check Command register, CSTS, doorbell offset vs CAP.DSTRD, AER, async events.

  2. The host sees CQEs but they all appear “old” after a reset. What went wrong?

    Answer

    Host reset its expected phase to 1 but did not clear CQ memory, which still holds entries with phase 1 from before — the host consumes stale entries. Or vice versa: memory zeroed but expected phase left at 0. Fix: zero CQ memory on (re)creation and reset phase to 1.

  3. Completion latency is fine but throughput collapses when 8 SQs share a 64-entry CQ. Why?

    Answer

    CQ fills; the controller stops posting until head advances; SQ processing stalls. Size CQ for the sum of outstanding commands or reduce sharing.

E. Senior thinking (2)

  1. Should a driver write the SQ doorbell for every command or batch? Discuss.

    Answer

    Batching reduces MMIO writes (each is an uncached posted write — costly in virtualised environments and at very high IOPS) but adds latency for the first command in a batch. Linux uses a “last request in plug/batch” hint to ring once. Shadow doorbells (Doorbell Buffer Config) reduce MMIO exits in VMs. The decision depends on latency targets and virtualisation.

  2. Design-review question: a firmware engineer proposes allowing the controller to post CQEs out of order across SQs sharing a CQ. Is that a problem?

    Answer

    Completion order is not guaranteed in NVMe — commands may complete in any order, and hosts must match by SQID/CID. So it is permitted; review should instead focus on fairness and starvation, and on whether any host software wrongly assumes ordering (bug-for-bug compatibility risk).

🧪 F. Lab — Inspect queue registers SAFE

Objective: read CAP, compute doorbell stride, and relate queue count to the driver’s configuration.

Steps:

sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H | head -40      # decode CAP, CC, CSTS, AQA
sudo nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x07 -H        # Number of Queues
ls /sys/block/nvme0n1/mq/ | wc -l                  # blk-mq hardware queues
grep nvme /proc/interrupts | head

Questions: Does the number of mq directories match the number of I/O queues granted? Which CPUs map to which vectors?

Solution

Usually the driver creates up to min(CPUs, granted queues) default queues, plus optional read/poll queues if configured — counts may differ by kernel version version. Each I/O queue’s vector appears in /proc/interrupts; affinity lists show CPU mapping. CAP.DSTRD is commonly 0 on physical devices impl.

Extension: repeat inside a VM with an emulated NVMe controller and compare CAP and queue counts.

📌 Remember

Answer before you open. If you opened an answer before committing to your own, mark that item as “not yet learned” and revisit it at the next spaced checkpoint.

PART XLVIII

Spaced Learning

Memory decays on a predictable curve; retrieval practice at expanding intervals flattens it. This part defines the review checkpoints placed after every five chapters and the major assessments placed after every ten, and gives a complete sample checkpoint.

48.1 Review Checkpoints and Major Assessments

← 47.1 The A–F Assessment Framework49.1 The Ten Phases →

48.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Without scheduled review, Part IV’s LTSSM states will be gone by the time you read traces in later parts. Spaced checkpoints force retrieval exactly when forgetting begins, and connect earlier material to new material.

48.1.2 Learning objectives

  • Follow a review schedule with expanding intervals (1 day, 3 days, 7 days, 21 days, 60 days).
  • Run a checkpoint: reflection prompts, 10 quick, 5 application, 3 trace, 1 design question.
  • Use major assessments every ten chapters to decide whether to advance.

48.1.4 Sample Review Checkpoint RC-7 (end-to-end flow + interrupts)

📌 Reflection prompts (write 3–5 sentences each)
  • What did we learn? List the PCIe transactions of one read and one write.
  • What connects? How do MSI-X writes relate to the posted-write ordering rules learned in the Transaction Layer chapters?
  • What remains unclear? Write the one question you would ask an expert. Look it up before the next checkpoint.

10 quick questions

  1. Direction of the SQE fetch MRd?

    Answer

    Upstream: device → host.

  2. Is an MSI-X message posted or non-posted?

    Answer

    Posted (it is a Memory Write).

  3. What TLP returns SQE bytes to the device?

    Answer

    Completion with Data (CplD).

  4. Size of one MSI-X table entry?

    Answer

    16 bytes.

  5. Which field links a CQ to an MSI-X vector?

    Answer

    IV (Interrupt Vector) in Create I/O CQ CDW11, with IEN set.

  6. For a Write, who issues MRds for data?

    Answer

    The device (controller) as requester.

  7. What signals a new CQE to a polling host?

    Answer

    The phase tag matching the expected phase.

  8. Which register bit masks all MSI-X vectors of a function?

    Answer

    Function Mask in MSI-X Message Control.

  9. What happens to an interrupt while its vector is masked?

    Answer

    Its PBA pending bit is set; the message is sent when unmasked.

  10. Which NVMe feature configures interrupt coalescing?

    Answer

    Feature 08h (Interrupt Coalescing); per-vector disable via Feature 09h.

5 application questions

  1. Count TLPs (both directions, excluding DLLPs) for a 16 KiB page-aligned read using a PRP list, MPS 256, one interrupt, one CQ doorbell.

    Answer

    Doorbell MWr 1; SQE MRd 1 + CplD ≥1; PRP list MRd 1 (3 entries, 24 B) + CplD 1; data MWr 16384/256 = 64; CQE MWr 1; MSI-X MWr 1; CQ head doorbell MWr 1. Total ≈ 71 (assuming single CplDs).

  2. Same for a 16 KiB write with MRRS 512.

    Answer

    Doorbell 1; SQE MRd+CplD 2; list MRd+CplD 2; data MRd 32 + CplD ≥ 64 (256-B max each); CQE 1; MSI-X 1; CQ doorbell 1. ≈ 104.

  3. Estimate link time for 64 data MWrs of 256 B at Gen4 x4 (≈ 7.88 GB/s raw, ~24 B overhead per TLP).

    Answer

    64 × 280 B ≈ 17.9 KB → ≈ 2.3 µs derived.

  4. The host processes 6 CQEs per interrupt on average at 600 K IOPS. Interrupt rate?

    Answer

    100 K interrupts/s.

  5. If coalescing time is 100 µs and QD is 1, worst added latency?

    Answer

    Up to ~100 µs per I/O if the threshold is never reached — coalescing hurts QD1.

3 trace questions

  1. MWr to FEE0_xxxx appears before the CQE MWr. Is that possible? Is it a bug?

    Answer

    It is a device bug if it happens for the same completion: the interrupt must follow the CQE so the host finds it. Ordering of posted writes ensures that if the device sends the CQE first, it arrives first. Check that both are for the same vector/queue.

  2. A CQE MWr with 4 DW payload goes to address ending in …08. Abnormal?

    Answer

    Yes — CQEs are 16-byte aligned slots; an address ending in 8 suggests a wrong base or entry size (e.g. device thinks CQE size differs from CC.IOCQES).

  3. Two MSI-X MWrs with identical address/data 2 µs apart, but only one CQE. Explanation?

    Answer

    Possibly the second is for another CQ sharing the same vector, a spurious interrupt, or a CQE that the analyzer filter hid. Check vector sharing and filters before calling it a bug.

1 design question

  1. Design an interrupt strategy for a storage server with 64 CPUs and 16 NVMe drives, targeting low p99 at moderate load and high throughput at peak.

    Answer

    Per-CPU queues per drive limited by MSI-X vectors (e.g. 16–32 per drive), managed affinity aligned with NUMA locality of each drive’s root port, adaptive coalescing (low threshold at low load), optional polling queues for latency-critical tenants, monitor interrupt rate and p99; justify trade-offs.

When mentoring, diagnose the phase a person is in from the errors they make: confusing PCIe and NVMe completions is a Phase 5 gap; blaming the device from an AER type is a Phase 8 gap.

PART LIX

12-Month Study Plan

A year-long plan for a working engineer studying 6–10 hours per week. Each month has four weekly goals, a deliverable you can show someone, and links to the parts of the book that carry the material. The plan assumes one evening lab session and one weekend block per week, following the weekly lab format.

59.1 Month-by-Month Plan

← 50.1 The Dependency Map60.1 Day-by-Day Plan →

59.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Ambitious learners fail by sprinting through Parts I–X in three weeks and then stalling at traces. A paced plan with deliverables spreads load, builds artefacts (parsers, notes, reports) you will use later, and inserts the spaced checkpoints from Part XLVIII.

59.1.2 Learning objectives

  • Commit to a realistic schedule with measurable weekly goals.
  • Produce twelve deliverables that together form a portfolio.
  • Reach rubric level 7 (Senior) by month 12.
🧪 Equipment assumptions

A Linux machine with at least one NVMe SSD you can afford to wipe (for CAUTION/EXPERT labs only), nvme-cli, pciutils, fio, Python 3. An analyzer is not required — synthetic traces cover trace skills; real analyzer time is a bonus in months 7–11.

PART LXI

Weekly Lab Format

Every study week follows the same eight-step loop — Read, Understand, Draw, Implement, Observe, Analyze, Debug, Explain. The loop guarantees that each concept passes through text, diagram, code, real data, trace and speech.

61.1 The Eight-Step Weekly Loop

← 60.1 Day-by-Day Plan62.1 Two Audiences, Two Grades →

61.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Without a fixed loop, learners default to reading. The loop forces production: a drawing, a program, an observation, a debugged trace and a spoken explanation every week.

StepActivityTimeOutputExample (week on PRPs)
ReadOfficial specification sections for the topic (cite document + revision you used)60–90 minNotes with normative statements quoted in your own notes, marked with document/revisionNVMe Base / NVMe over PCIe transport sections on PRP; note revision
UnderstandThe textbook chapter60 minSummary in 10 linesPart XII
DrawArchitecture / data-structure diagram from memory30 minDiagram photo or SVGSQE → PRP1/PRP2 → list page → chained list page
ImplementSmall parser or simulator2 hCode with testsPRP builder + validator

ExplainTeach-back (kid + senior)30 minRecording or written script, self-graded“Why does a 2 MiB unaligned transfer need 513 pages?”
📭 What the spec does not say

The specifications define behaviour, not how to learn it. When the Read step points to “official specification sections”, use the current documents from nvmexpress.org and pcisig.com that you have access to, and record the revision you used. Do not rely on section numbers quoted from memory.

PART LXII

Teach-Back Method

At the end of every major chapter, you explain the concept twice: as if to a 10-year-old, and as if to a senior hardware engineer. Both explanations are graded. Weak intuition and weak technical precision are flagged separately because they need different remedies.

62.1 Two Audiences, Two Grades

← 61.1 The Eight-Step Weekly Loop63.1 Levels 0–8 →

62.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Explaining to a child tests whether you have a mental model; explaining to an expert tests whether the model is precise and complete. Many engineers pass one and fail the other.

62.1.2 The prompts

🧒 Prompt 1

“Explain this concept as if you are teaching it to a 10-year-old.”

🔧 Prompt 2

“Explain it as if you are presenting to a senior hardware engineer.”

62.1.3 Grading rubric

ScoreKid explanation (intuition)Senior explanation (precision)
0Jargon only, or wrong pictureVague, incorrect, or only analogies
1Analogy present but misleading in an important way; no limits statedCorrect terms, missing mechanism or direction/ownership
2Clear analogy covering the main mechanismCorrect mechanism, registers/packets named, direction and owner clear
3Clear analogy + states where it breaksAdds evidence (how to observe), edge cases, version/impl labels
PatternDiagnosisRemedy
Kid 3, Senior ≤ 1Good intuition, weak technical explanationReturn to register/packet chapters; decode exercises; rewrite with field names
Kid ≤ 1, Senior 3Technical but weak intuition (memorised mechanism)Analogy library; draw the concept; explain why each step exists
Both ≤ 1Concept not learnedRepeat chapter; smaller pieces
Both ≥ 2LearnedAdvance; revisit at next spaced checkpoint

62.1.4 Worked example — the doorbell

🧒 Kid version (scores 3)

“Imagine a restaurant where you write your order on a slip and pin it on a board by the kitchen. The cook can’t watch the board all the time, so after pinning slips you ring a little bell. The bell doesn’t say what you ordered — it just says ‘new slips are up to here’. The cook then walks over and reads the slips. Where it breaks: in a real computer the cook reads slips really fast by itself (DMA), and the bell is a number — the position of the newest slip — not just a ring.”

🔧 Senior version (scores 3)

“The SQ tail doorbell is a 32-bit write-only register in BAR0 at 1000h + 2y × (4 << CAP.DSTRD). The host writes the new tail index after placing SQEs in host memory, with a write barrier before the MMIO so the SQE stores are visible first. On the wire it is a 1-DW posted MWr downstream. The controller then issues MRds for 64-byte SQEs from SQ base + index × 64, CplDs return them. A tail ≥ queue size or a write to a non-existent queue is an invalid doorbell write, which the controller may report as an asynchronous event. Shadow doorbells (Doorbell Buffer Config) can replace most MMIO in virtualised setups version. To verify: analyzer filter on BAR0+1000h range; correlate with the subsequent MRd address.”

⚠️ Weak example (Kid 1, Senior 1)

“The doorbell is how NVMe sends commands to the SSD over PCIe.” — Wrong: the doorbell does not carry the command; it carries an index. Precise and intuitive explanations both fix this misconception.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I have recorded teach-backs for doorbell, DMA, TLP, PRP, MSI-X, CQE and AER.
  • Each has both scores ≥ 2; at least four have both = 3.

PART LXIV

Final Senior Engineer Exam

A six-hour simulated exam in twelve parts (A–L) covering PCIe architecture, NVMe architecture, TLP decoding, command decoding, queue analysis, DMA analysis, trace reconstruction, AER debugging, performance, architecture design, 2026 feature analysis and a senior incident investigation. Answers are sealed in collapsible blocks. Grade with the rubric; certification needs level 7+ on Parts G, H and L and ≥ 75% overall.

64.1.2 Part A — PCIe architecture

Part A

  1. A1. Explain the three PCIe layers and give one error detected at each.

    Answer

    Transaction Layer: TLP creation/consumption, flow control accounting, ordering; errors: Unsupported Request, Completion Timeout, Malformed TLP, ECRC error, Poisoned TLP. Data Link Layer: sequence numbers, LCRC, Ack/Nak, replay, DLLPs; errors: Bad TLP, Bad DLLP, Replay Timer Timeout, REPLAY_NUM Rollover, Data Link Protocol Error. Physical Layer: encoding, framing, scrambling, LTSSM, equalization; errors: Receiver Error, link training failures, Surprise Down (reported via DLL state).

  2. A2. Why can a Gen3 link at 8 GT/s carry nearly as much data per lane as a Gen2 link at 10 GT/s would?

    Answer

    Gen2 uses 8b/10b (80% efficiency) so 5 GT/s → 4 Gb/s; Gen3 uses 128b/130b (~98.5%) so 8 GT/s → ~7.88 Gb/s. A hypothetical 10 GT/s 8b/10b link would give 8 Gb/s — similar to Gen3. The encoding change let Gen3 nearly double usable bandwidth without doubling the rate.

  3. A3. What is the purpose of the Configuration state of the LTSSM?

    Answer

    Establish link and lane numbering, negotiate width, handle lane reversal and polarity (polarity is handled in Polling), and verify both ends agree via TS1/TS2 ordered sets before entering L0.

  4. A4. A switch sits between root port and SSD. Which agent regenerates LCRC, and what protects data integrity across the switch’s internals?

    Answer

    Each link’s transmitter regenerates LCRC (the switch checks on ingress and regenerates on egress). Internal switch paths are protected by switch-internal mechanisms (implementation-dependent) and end-to-end by ECRC if enabled; NVMe PI provides end-to-end protection at the storage level.

64.1.3 Part B — NVMe architecture

Part B

  1. B1. Define NVM subsystem, controller, namespace, and NVM set / endurance group in one sentence each.

    Answer

    Subsystem: the collection of controllers, namespaces and media sharing one NQN. Controller: the host-facing interface that processes commands through queues. Namespace: a formatted quantity of NVM addressed by NSID and LBAs. Endurance group: a set of media with shared endurance management; NVM set: a partition of media within an endurance group for isolation (introduced around 1.4 version).

  2. B2. What does VS = 0002_0000h mean, and what must you still check to know the feature set?

    Answer

    Major 2, minor 0, tertiary 0 → NVMe Base 2.0. Features are mostly optional: check Identify Controller (OACS, ONCS, LPA, FRMW, SGLS, CTRATT, etc.), supported log pages, Commands Supported and Effects log, and the command set specs in use.

  3. B3. Explain why NVMe was split into Base, command set and transport specifications, and name the document you would read for doorbell register layout in NVMe over PCIe.

    Answer

    To evolve command sets and transports independently (2.0 family). Doorbell/register mapping for PCIe: the NVMe over PCIe Transport specification (plus Base for controller register definitions) — confirm the current revision on nvmexpress.org.

  4. B4. Explain the difference between Admin, I/O, and Fabrics command sets in terms of queues.

    Answer

    Admin commands go on the admin queue (QID 0); I/O commands on I/O queues for a selected I/O command set; Fabrics commands (Connect, Property Get/Set, Authentication) are used by NVMe over Fabrics transports to establish queues and access properties, since no PCIe BAR exists there.

64.1.4 Part C — TLP decoding

Part C

  1. C1. Decode: DW0 = 0x2000_0010, DW1 = 0x0200_2CFF, DW2 = 0x0000_0001, DW3 = 0x0230_1000.

    Answer

    Fmt 001 = 4-DW header, no data; Type 00000 → MRd 64-bit. Length 10h = 16 DW = 64 B. DW1: Requester ID 0200h = bus 02, dev 0, fn 0; Tag 2Ch; Last BE Fh, First BE Fh. Address = 0000_0001_0230_1000. Interpretation: device 02:00.0 reading 64 B at 1_0230_1000 — a likely SQE fetch (64 B, from a queue address).

  2. C2. Decode: DW0 = 0x4A00_0010, DW1 = 0x0000_0040, DW2 = 0x0200_2C00.

    Answer

    Fmt 010 (3-DW, with data), Type 01010 → CplD. Length 16 DW. DW1: Completer ID 0000h, status bits 15:13 = 000 (SC), BCM 0, Byte Count = 040h = 64. DW2: Requester ID 0200h, Tag 2Ch, Lower Address = 00h. This completes C1’s request with all 64 bytes.

  3. C3. A CplD has Byte Count = 0x100 and Length = 0x20 DW. What do you conclude?

    Answer

    This completion carries 128 B but 256 B remain including this one → at least one more completion for this tag will follow (128 B). Not an error.

  4. C4. A TLP has Fmt 011, Type 00000, Length 1, address FEE0_3000 with data 0000_0024. What is it likely to be and how do you confirm?

    Answer

    4-DW MWr with data — an MSI/MSI-X message on x86 (address in FEEx_xxxx range) impl. Confirm by reading the device’s MSI-X table entries (address/data) and matching data 0024h to a vector. Note a 4-DW header with an address below 4 GiB is unusual (hardware normally uses 3-DW for 32-bit addresses) — worth noting as possibly a decoder display convention or a device quirk.

  5. C5. What do First DW BE = 0h with Length = 1 indicate for an MRd?

    Answer

    A zero-length read: commonly used as a flush to ensure prior posted writes have reached the destination. The completion returns one DW of undefined data.

64.1.5 Part D — NVMe command decoding

SQE (little-endian dwords): CDW0 = 0x0123_0002, NSID = 0x0000_0001, CDW2–3 = 0, MPTR = 0, PRP1 = 0x0000_0001_3A41_7200, PRP2 = 0x0000_0001_3A42_0000, CDW10 = 0x0010_0000, CDW11 = 0x0000_0000, CDW12 = 0x4000_0003, CDW13 = 0, CDW14 = 0, CDW15 = 0.

Part D

  1. D1. Opcode, CID, FUSE, PSDT?

    Answer

    Opcode 02h (Read), FUSE 0, PSDT 0 (PRPs), CID = 0x0123.

  2. D2. SLBA, number of blocks, FUA?

    Answer

    SLBA = CDW11:CDW10 = 0x0000_0000_0010_0000. NLB = 3 → 4 blocks. CDW12 bit 30 = 1 → FUA set. (Bit 31 LR = 0.)

  3. D3. With 4 KiB LBA format and 4 KiB memory page size, is the PRP usage valid?

    Answer

    Transfer 16 KiB starting at offset 0x200 in page 1_3A41_7000: PRP1 covers 4096 − 512 = 3584 B; remaining 12800 B spans 4 more pages (3 full + 512 B), i.e. 4 more entries → PRP2 must point to a PRP list, not a data page. Here PRP2 = 1_3A42_0000; whether it is a list cannot be known from the SQE alone — the device will treat it as a list pointer because more than one page remains. If the host intended it as a single data page, it is a host bug. Check memory at PRP2.

  4. D4. The CQE for this command has DW3 = 0x0285_0123 (assume current phase 0). Decode.

    Answer

    CID 0x0123; upper 16 bits 0x0285 → P = bit 16 = 1. The host expects phase 0, so this entry is not new — it is a stale entry from the previous pass and must not be consumed at all. If it were new (expected phase 1): Status = 0x0285 >> 1 = 0x0142: SC = 42h, SCT = 1 (command specific) — interpret against the command-specific status table for Read in the NVM Command Set (do not guess). Trick: check phase before decoding anything.

  5. D5. Encode a Write Zeroes for NSID 1, SLBA 0x2000, 256 blocks, deallocate requested.

    Answer

    CDW0 opcode 08h + CID; NSID 1; CDW10 = 0x0000_2000; CDW11 = 0; CDW12 = NLB 0x00FF with DEAC bit (bit 25) = 1 → 0x0200_00FF; no data pointer. Confirm DEAC support via Identify Namespace DLFEAT / Identify Controller ONCS version.

64.1.6 Part E — Queue analysis

Part E

  1. E1. SQ size 64. Host tail history: 10, 20, 63, 5. Controller SQHD history in CQEs: 8, 19, 60. How many commands outstanding at the end?

    Answer

    Tail 5 after wrap; head 60 → (5 − 60) mod 64 = 9 outstanding (slots 60–63, 0–4).

  2. E2. A host writes tail = 64 to a 64-entry queue. What should happen?

    Answer

    Invalid doorbell value (must be 0–63). The controller may report an Invalid Doorbell Write Value asynchronous event (error type), and behaviour of the queue is undefined/ignored for that write. Host bug.

  3. E3. CQ size 256, head 255, expected phase 1. Next CQE slot and expected phase after consuming it?

    Answer

    Consume slot 255 with phase 1; head wraps to 0; expected phase becomes 0.

  4. E4. Why might a controller stop fetching from an SQ that has pending entries while other SQs proceed?

    Answer

    Its CQ is full (head doorbell not advanced), arbitration priorities (WRR with urgent queues starving low), controller per-queue limits, or the SQ was deleted/invalid. Check CQ head doorbells first.

64.1.7 Part F — DMA analysis

Part F

  1. F1. List every DMA operation the controller performs for a 64 KiB write using a PRP list, in order.

    Answer

    SQE fetch (MRd 64 B) → PRP list fetch (MRd; 15 entries × 8 B if PRP1 page-aligned → 120 B) → write-data fetch MRds (64 KiB / MRRS) → (media program, internal) → CQE write (MWr 16 B) → MSI-X (MWr). Order of list fetch vs data fetch may interleave impl.

  2. F2. Why is an IOMMU fault for a write-direction DMA (device → memory) harder to notice than for a read?

    Answer

    Posted writes get no completion; the device believes the write succeeded and completes the command with success. Only the IOMMU log shows it. A read fault produces an error completion or timeout the device must handle.

  3. F3. A device DMAs read data to PRP1 + 0x1000 although PRP1 has offset 0x200 and PRP2 is a list. Is it wrong?

    Answer

    Yes. After the first page portion (from PRP1 to the end of its page), subsequent data must go to the page addresses from the list. Writing to PRP1’s page + 0x1000 (the physically next page) assumes contiguity — a device PRP-walk bug, or the list entry happens to equal that address (check the list).

  4. F4. What host-side condition can make DMA correct on the wire but data still wrong in the application?

    Answer

    Non-coherent DMA without proper cache maintenance (on non-coherent platforms), the host reading the buffer before completion (race), buffer reuse after timeout/abort while DMA still in flight, or bounce-buffer (swiotlb) copy errors.

64.1.8 Part G — Trace reconstruction

Exam trace G — reconstruct what happened (BAR0 = FC00_0000, DSTRD = 0; SQ1 base 8_0000_0000; CQ1 base 8_0001_0000; MSI-X vector 1 address FEE0_2000 data 0x41)
#t (µs)DirTLPAddressLen / dataTag
10.0↓MWrFC00_10081 DW: 0x0000_0007—
20.4↑MRd8_0000_014032 DW0x31
30.9↓CplD—32 DW0x31
41.3↑MRd2_1000_0000128 DW0x32
51.3↑MRd2_1000_0200128 DW0x33
61.9↓CplD ×4—64 DW each0x32, 0x33
744.0↑MWr ×163_0000_0000…64 DW each—
844.6↑MWr8_0001_00604 DW—
944.7↑MWrFEE0_20001 DW: 0x41—
1051.0↑MWr8_0001_00704 DW—
1151.1↑MWrFEE0_20001 DW: 0x41—
1253.0↓MWrFC00_100C1 DW: 0x0000_0008—

Part G

  1. G1. What did row 1 do and how many commands were submitted (assume previous tail 5)?

    Answer

    FC00_1008 = 1000h + 2×1×4 → SQ 1 tail doorbell, new tail 7 → 2 commands (slots 5, 6).

  2. G2. Explain row 2.

    Answer

    Device MRd of 32 DW = 128 B starting at 8_0000_0140: offset 140h / 64 = slot 5, so the device fetched two 64-byte SQEs (slots 5 and 6) in one read — exactly the newly submitted commands. Fetching several SQEs per read is common but not required impl. The CplD (row 3) carries both SQEs; decode them to learn opcodes and CIDs before interpreting rows 4–7.

  3. G3. What are rows 4–7? Is it a read or a write?

    Answer

    Rows 4–6: device MRds of 1 KiB total from 2_1000_0000 — write-data fetch for a 1 KiB write (or a PRP list read — 1 KiB list = 128 entries, unlikely here). Row 7: 16 MWrs × 256 B = 4 KiB to 3_0000_0000 — read data. So likely one 1 KiB write (or 2×512 B) and one 4 KiB read. Decode the SQE payloads in row 3 to confirm.

  4. G4. Why are there two interrupts (rows 9 and 11) and one CQ head doorbell?

    Answer

    Each CQE triggered an MSI-X (no coalescing). The host handled both before ringing the CQ 1 head doorbell once with head 8 (FC00_100C = CQ 1 head) → it consumed slots 6 and 7. Consistent.

  5. G5. Write a three-sentence reconstruction.

    Answer

    The host submitted SQEs to SQ 1 and rang the doorbell (tail 7). The controller fetched two SQEs, executed a small write (1 KiB fetched from host) and a 4 KiB read (data written to 3_0000_0000), posting two CQEs to CQ 1 slots 6–7, each followed by an MSI-X on vector 1. The host consumed both and advanced CQ head to 8. Observed: all TLPs; inferred (label derived): which command was the write and which the read — confirm by decoding the SQEs in row 3.

64.1.9 Part H — AER debugging

Exam item H — AER register snapshot (root port 00:02.0 above SSD 03:00.0)
AgentUncorrectable StatusUncorrectable SeverityCorrectable StatusHeader Log
Root port0000_40000006_20300000_00410000_0001 0000_00FF FC00_001C 0000_0000
SSD0000_00000006_20300000_0000—

Part H

  1. H1. Decode the root port uncorrectable status and its severity.

    Answer

    0x4000 = bit 14 = Completion Timeout. Severity register 0006_2030: bits 4, 5, 13, 17, 18 set (DLP, Surprise Down, FC Protocol, Receiver Overflow, Malformed TLP = fatal); bit 14 clear → Completion Timeout is non-fatal.

  2. H2. Decode the correctable status.

    Answer

    0x41 = bit 0 Receiver Error + bit 6 Bad TLP.

  3. H3. The header log is shown. What request timed out, and who issued it?

    Answer

    DW0 0000_0001 → Fmt 000, Type 0 → MRd 3-DW, length 1. DW1 0000_00FF → Requester 0000 (root complex/CPU), tag 00, BE Fh/Fh… (FF = last BE F, first BE F). Address FC00_001C → BAR0 + 1Ch = CSTS. So a CPU read of the NVMe CSTS register got no completion. Note: header logging for Completion Timeout is not guaranteed on every implementation impl.

  4. H4. Combine: what is your leading hypothesis and next steps?

    Answer

    The device stopped responding to MMIO (hung, in reset, or link issue). Correctable Receiver Errors and Bad TLPs suggest link marginality preceding it — possibly the link went through Recovery or the device’s receiver is struggling; but the SSD’s own AER is clean (if it is accessible at all — reading it may itself be unreliable). Next: check LnkSta/DLL Link Active, look for Surprise Down, read device config space (all ones?), check correctable error rate history, NVMe driver logs for timeouts preceding the CSTS read (the CSTS read is usually part of timeout handling — so the original failure is earlier). Confidence: Likely device unresponsive; cause Unknown pending evidence.

64.1.10 Part I — Performance debugging

Part I

  1. I1. A Gen4 x4 drive delivers 3.3 GB/s sequential read at QD 32, 128 KiB. Spec sheet says 7 GB/s. LnkSta: 16 GT/s x4. MPS 128. What do you suspect and why?

    Answer

    MPS 128 reduces efficiency to roughly 128/(128+24) ≈ 84% → ~6.6 GB/s ceiling, not 3.3. So MPS alone does not explain halving. Look at host side: single-thread fio CPU-bound? IOMMU strict mode? Drive in thermal throttling? Spec sheet measured with different conditions? Also check if the drive has an x4 link but the root port shares bandwidth via a switch upstream at x2. Measure per-layer.

  2. I2. 4 KiB random read at QD1: 85 µs average; at QD 32: 380 K IOPS. Compute average latency at QD 32 and comment.

    Answer

    32 / 380 000 = 84 µs — same as QD1. Latency did not grow with QD, meaning the device scales well with parallelism up to QD 32 (not yet saturated). Push to higher QD to find the knee.

  3. I3. p99.9 latency spikes of 5 ms every ~10 s during sustained random writes. Hypotheses?

    Answer

    Device GC/metadata flush, write cache flush cycles, thermal throttling steps, host writeback bursts (if via filesystem), SLC cache exhaustion periods. Check SMART temperature over time, test with direct I/O, vary fill level, look at the device’s periodicity vs host timers.

  4. I4. Interrupt rate is 900 K/s at 1 M IOPS and CPU is saturated. Two fixes?

    Answer

    Enable interrupt coalescing (moderate threshold/time) or use polling queues for high-QD workloads; ensure affinity so interrupts land on submitting CPUs; batch CQ head doorbells. Measure p99 impact.

64.1.11 Part J — Architecture design

Part J

  1. J1. Design host-side queue/interrupt topology for a 2-socket server with 8 NVMe drives (4 per socket), 128 CPUs, latency-sensitive DB plus batch analytics.

    Answer

    NUMA-local placement: DB threads on the socket of their drives; per-CPU I/O queues limited by vectors; separate poll queues for DB latency-critical I/O; WRR priority if supported (DB high, analytics low) or cgroup I/O controls; coalescing tuned per queue; monitor cross-socket traffic. Trade-offs: memory/vectors vs isolation.

  2. J2. Specify the minimum observability a new SSD controller must expose for field debugging.

    Answer

    Accurate Error Information log (SQID, CID, LBA, parameter location), Persistent Event Log, telemetry (host- and controller-initiated) with versioned decoders, link event counters (Recovery entries, replays), timestamp synchronised to host, thermal/throttle history, firmware activation history. Justify each by a failure class it helps diagnose.

  3. J3. Should a JBOF use one x16 upstream for 24 x4 drives? Discuss.

    Answer

    Oversubscription 96 lanes → 16 (6:1). Acceptable if workloads are capacity/IOPS-bound with low aggregate bandwidth; unacceptable for sequential-heavy workloads. Also consider failure domain (one upstream link), DPC behaviour, and switch latency. Alternatives: dual upstreams, multiple switches, higher gen upstream.

  4. J4. Design a validation matrix for APST.

    Answer

    Dimensions: each power state entry/exit, idle-time thresholds around transitions, I/O arrival during transition, combined with ASPM L1/L1.2 enabled/disabled, D3hot cycles, temperature extremes, firmware activation, host latency tolerance settings. Measure first-I/O latency, errors, link events. Include negative tests (non-operational state + admin commands).

64.1.12 Part K — 2026 NVMe feature analysis

Part K

  1. K1. Name the five highlights announced with the NVMe 2.4 specification set (August 2026) and the purpose of each, labelling what you know vs what you would check.

    Answer

    Post-Quantum Cryptography (purpose: resistance of security protocols to future quantum attacks); PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration (moving exported subsystems across hosts/contexts); Voltage Monitoring (visibility into supply voltage conditions); Rate Limiting (controlling resource/throughput consumption); Restore Manufacturing Default Settings (standard return to factory configuration). Known: names and announced purposes version. To check: which documents carry each (Base 2.4, transport 1.4, MI 2.2…), the exact commands/log pages/features, and optionality.

  2. K2. A vendor claims “NVMe 2.4 compliant”. What questions do you ask?

    Answer

    Which documents and revisions (Base, NVM CS, transport, MI); which optional features implemented; compliance testing evidence (e.g. interoperability/compliance programs); VS value reported; behaviour with hosts expecting earlier revisions.

  3. K3. How would you teach a 1.4-era engineer about the 2.x restructuring in two minutes?

    Answer

    See Teach-back 106: the monolith split into Base + command sets + transports; new command sets (ZNS, KV, later SLM/computational programs); features like FDP and live migration in 2.1-era; 2.4 adds the listed highlights. Always cite document + revision.

  4. K4. What is the risk of using a protocol analyzer decoder older than the device’s spec revision?

    Answer

    New opcodes, log pages, fields or reserved bits now defined may be decoded as reserved/invalid or mislabelled, leading to false anomalies or missed ones. Label such decodes uncertain and verify against the spec.

64.1.13 Part L — Senior incident investigation

🧠 Incident brief

After a fleet kernel upgrade, 0.3% of servers with SSD model Q report a once-per-day I/O error “Data Transfer Error” on writes larger than 512 KiB. No AER errors. IOMMU logs show nothing. Old kernel: zero errors. Same drive firmware. Only servers with a specific CPU stepping are affected.

Exam trace L — failing 768 KiB write (excerpt)
#DirTLPAddressLenTagStatus
1↑MRdSQE16 DW0x101
2↓CplD—16 DW0x101SC
3↑MRd ×24PRP list + data…128 DW0x102–0x119
4↓CplD ×46—64 DW0x102–0x118SC
5↓CplD—64 DW0x119SC, EP = 1
6↓CplD—64 DW0x119SC
7↑MWrCQE4 DW—Data Transfer Error

Part L

  1. L1. What is the first abnormal event and its layer?

    Answer

    Row 5: a CplD with the poisoned (EP) bit — Transaction Layer, originated by the completer (root complex/memory subsystem). The device correctly refuses poisoned data and fails the command.

  2. L2. Why no AER entries, and why might that be a configuration issue?

    Answer

    Poisoned TLP received may be masked in the device’s AER Uncorrectable Mask, or the platform handles errors firmware-first and logs elsewhere (BMC/SEL), or advisory non-fatal handling suppresses reporting impl. Check masks and platform logs — the absence of AER is not absence of error.

  3. L3. What does the kernel-upgrade correlation suggest, given the CPU stepping dependence?

    Answer

    The new kernel may change memory placement or DMA buffer allocation patterns (e.g. larger contiguous buffers, different NUMA placement, new use of a memory feature) that exercise a CPU-stepping-specific erratum or a marginal memory region, causing poisoned reads (memory ECC uncorrectable surfaced as poison). Or a kernel change in RO/ordering settings. Hypotheses: Possible until platform logs (machine check / memory error records) correlate.

  4. L4. Plan the investigation and write the first abnormal event section of your report.

    Answer

    Plan: gather platform error logs (machine checks, memory ECC, firmware-first records) at failure times; map the poisoned address (from the request with tag 0x119 → PRP entry → physical page) to DIMM/channel; check whether failing addresses cluster; bisect kernel changes on affected stepping; consult CPU errata with vendor; test the old kernel with forced large buffers. First abnormal event: “At t=…, the root complex returned a poisoned CplD (EP=1) for device MRd tag 0x119 (address …, part of PRP entry N of write CID …); the device completed the command with Data Transfer Error as expected. Layer: host memory subsystem/root complex (Transaction Layer origin). Confidence: Confirmed (trace row 5).”

📌 Scoring

Total 100 points. Pass: ≥ 75 overall, and level 7 behaviours on G3/G5 (separating observed from inferred rather than forcing a story), H4 (recognising the CSTS read is part of timeout handling), L1–L4 (evidence-based chain with labels).

PART LXV

Final Project — NVMe PCIe Forensic Investigation Platform

Build a system that ingests PCIe traces, NVMe logs, AER logs, Linux logs, configuration-space dumps, Identify data and SMART data; normalises, decodes and correlates them; builds a timeline; detects anomalies; identifies the first abnormal event; generates hypotheses with evidence; and produces a root-cause report in HTML. It is the tool you wished you had during the capstone.

65.1 Forensic Platform: Requirements, Architecture, Milestones, Grading

← 64.1 The Exam100 Final Master Rubric →

65.1.1 Why this chapter exists

Building the tool forces you to formalise everything you do implicitly when reading traces: what a doorbell looks like, how a CQE maps to an SQE, what “first abnormal” means. It turns tacit skill into explicit, testable rules — the hallmark of principal-level work.

65.1.2 Learning objectives

  • Design normalized schemas for heterogeneous evidence.
  • Implement decoders for TLPs, SQEs, CQEs, register dumps and AER.
  • Implement correlation (doorbell → fetch → data → CQE → interrupt) and anomaly rules.
  • Generate a report with evidence links and confidence labels.

Prerequisites: Part V, X, XI, XII, XIII, XV, and the capstone.

65.1.3 Requirements

R2Normalize timestamps to one timeline with per-source offset and uncertaintyMustConfigurable offsets; events sorted; uncertainty shown

65.1.4 Architecture

65.1.5 Schemas

Event {
  id:          string            # "trace:H9", "log:2400.1203#1"
  t:           float             # seconds on unified timeline
  t_err:       float             # uncertainty (s) from clock alignment
  source:      enum[trace, kernel_log, aer, cfg_dump, nvme_log, smart, identify, register]
  provenance:  {file, row_or_line}
  label:       enum[observed, decoded, derived, hypothesis, synthetic]
  layer:       enum[phy, dll, tl, nvme_queue, nvme_cmd, driver, platform, media]
  kind:        string            # "MRd", "CplD", "doorbell", "cqe", "msix", "iommu_fault", "ltssm"
  fields:      map               # decoded fields
  refs:        list[event_id]    # correlation links
}
QueueCtx { qid, type: sq|cq, base, size, cqid?, vector?, created_at, deleted_at? }
CommandLife { sqid, cid, opcode, submit_evt, fetch_evt, data_evts[], cqe_evt?, irq_evt?,
              status?, latency?, anomalies[] }
Anomaly { id, rule, t, layer, severity, evidence: list[event_id], explanation }
Hypothesis { id, statement, supports: list[evidence], contradicts: list[evidence],
             confidence: enum[confirmed, strong, likely, possible, unknown], tests: list[str] }

65.1.6 Parser architecture

  • Source adapters (one per format) produce raw records with provenance; no interpretation.
  • Decoders are pure functions: decode_tlp(bytes) → fields, decode_sqe(64B), decode_cqe(16B), decode_aer(regs), decode_cap(u64). Each references spec tables with revision tags.
  • Context builder scans config writes (BARs, Command, MSI-X), admin commands (Create CQ/SQ, Set Features) and register writes (AQA/ASQ/ACQ, CC) to build a time-versioned context: “at time t, BAR0 = …, SQ3 base = …, HMB list = …”.
  • Classifier uses the context to label MMIO writes as doorbells/CC writes, device MRds as SQE/PRP-list/data/HMB fetches, MWrs as data/CQE/MSI-X.

65.1.7 Command lifecycle state machine

  SUBMITTED ──(SQE fetch covering slot)──▶ FETCHED ──(data MRd/MWr in PRP ranges)──▶ DATA_MOVING
      │                                       │                                         │
      │ (timeout without fetch)               │ (timeout)                              ▼
      ▼                                       ▼                                 CQE_POSTED ──(MSI-X)──▶ SIGNALLED
  ANOMALY:not_fetched                 ANOMALY:not_completed                          │                     │
                                                                                    └──(host CQ head ≥ slot)──▶ CONSUMED
  Any state ──(controller reset / queue delete)──▶ ABORTED_BY_RESET

65.1.8 Correlation algorithm

def correlate(events, ctx):
    pending_fetch = {}            # (sqid, slot) -> CommandLife
    outstanding_reads = {}        # (requester_id, tag) -> MRd event
    for e in sorted(events, key=lambda e: e.t):
        c = ctx.at(e.t)
        if e.kind == "MWr" and c.is_doorbell(e.addr):
            q, kind = c.doorbell_target(e.addr)
            if kind == "sq_tail":
                for slot in c.sq[q].slots_between(c.sq[q].tail, e.data):
                    pending_fetch[(q, slot)] = CommandLife(sqid=q, submit_evt=e)
                c.sq[q].tail = e.data
            else:
                c.cq[q].host_head = e.data; mark_consumed(c, q, e)
        elif e.kind == "MRd":
            outstanding_reads[(e.req_id, e.tag)] = e
            for q, slots in c.sq_slots_covered(e.addr, e.length_bytes):
                for s in slots:
                    life = pending_fetch.pop((q, s), None)
                    if life: life.fetch_evt = e
        elif e.kind in ("CplD", "Cpl"):
            req = outstanding_reads.get((e.req_id, e.tag))
            if req is None: flag(e, "unexpected_completion")
            elif e.status != "SC": flag(e, f"completion_{e.status}", refs=[req])
            if e.fields.get("EP"): flag(e, "poisoned", refs=[req])
            if req and e.byte_count == e.length_bytes: outstanding_reads.pop((e.req_id, e.tag))
        elif e.kind == "MWr" and c.is_cq_slot(e.addr):
            cqe = decode_cqe(e.payload)
            life = find_life(cqe.sqid, cqe.cid)
            if not life: flag(e, "cqe_without_command")
            elif cqe.phase != c.cq_expected_phase(e.addr): flag(e, "phase_mismatch")
            else: life.cqe_evt = e
        elif e.kind == "MWr" and c.is_msix(e.addr, e.data):
            link_irq(e, c.vector_of(e.addr, e.data))
        elif e.kind == "MWr" or e.kind == "MRd":
            if not c.addr_in_known_region(e.addr):    # PRP ranges, queues, HMB lists
                flag(e, "dma_outside_known_regions")
        if e.kind == "iommu_fault":
            region = c.region_history(e.addr)          # e.g. "HMB list L1, freed at 600.0012"
            flag(e, "iommu_fault", note=region)
    for life in all_lives(): check_timeouts(life)

65.1.9 Anomaly rules (excerpt)

RuleConditionLayerSeverity
R-UR-CPLCpl with UR/CA status to a device MRdTLHigh
R-POISONEP = 1 on any TLPTLHigh
R-CTOMRd without completion within configured windowTLHigh
R-STALE-DMADMA to a region whose lifetime ended (freed HMB, deleted queue, unmapped PRP)NVMe/driverCritical
R-DB-RANGEDoorbell value ≥ queue size or to non-existent queueNVMe queueHigh
R-NOFETCHSQ tail advanced, no fetch within N µsNVMeMedium
R-NOCQEFetched, no CQE within timeoutNVMeHigh
R-PHASECQE phase inconsistent with slot wrap countNVMeHigh
R-REPLAYNak/replay or correctable AERDLL/PHYLow (context)
R-LINKDOWNLTSSM leaves L0 to Detect, or Surprise DownPHYCritical
R-CFSCSTS.CFS = 1 or CSTS reads all-onesNVMe/PCIeCritical

First abnormal event = the earliest anomaly with severity ≥ High whose evidence is observed (not derived), after suppressing anomalies explained as consequences of an earlier one (e.g. R-NOCQE after R-UR-CPL on the same command). Low-severity anomalies are reported as context and candidate decoys.

⚠️ Truth policy for the tool

Spec tables in the tool must carry their source document and revision. Do not fill tables from memory for fields you have not verified; mark them “unverified” so reports show reduced confidence.

FINAL MASTERY

Master Rubric, Transformation and Teach-Back Capstones

The last stretch is about proof. A learner is not senior because they read this book or memorised 500 definitions. They are senior when they can demonstrate accurate mental models, specification literacy, version awareness, evidence-based debugging, trace reconstruction, cross-layer reasoning, performance reasoning, validation planning, clear communication and uncertainty management — on demand, in front of someone else. This part defines the master rubric, maps the kid-to-senior transformation, sets five teach-back capstones with layer-by-layer grading, and ends with the final certification checklist.

100.1 Why this chapter exists
