101.2 One concept through all seven stages — “completion”

StageHow they describe a completion
Kid“The librarian brings back the book and says ‘done!’”
Beginner“The SSD puts a note in the completion queue.”
Junior“A 16-byte CQE with CID, SQID, SQHD, status and phase is written to the CQ, then an interrupt fires.”
Intermediate“The CQE arrives as a posted MWr from the device; it is different from a CplD, which answers the device’s own MRds.”
Advanced“In this trace the CQE MWr at row 8 is to CQ1 slot 6; phase 1; CID matches the SQE fetched at row 3.”
Senior“The CQE never appeared; the first abnormal event is the UR completion to the PRP list fetch 40 µs earlier.”
Principal“To prove it, we’ll replay the same SQE with a valid list and with an unmapped list on a test host and compare; and we’ll add a driver assertion that validates PRP list pages are mapped before ringing the doorbell.”

102–106 Teach-Back Capstones

← 101 Kid-to-Senior Transformation★ Final Certification →

102.0 How these are run

Record yourself (audio or video) or write a script, without notes, then grade with the per-layer tables below. Each layer scores 0 (missing/wrong), 1 (vague), 2 (correct), 3 (correct + evidence/edge case). Pass threshold: no layer below 2, average ≥ 2.5. Model answers are sealed.

102. First teach-back — “Explain NVMe Read from application to NAND and back.”

LayerMust mentionScore 3 adds
Softwareread()/io_uring, VFS/filesystem (or direct I/O), block layer request, driverPage cache bypass with O_DIRECT; request splitting by MDTS/max_sectors
QueuePer-CPU SQ selected; slot at tail; CQ pairedQueue full handling; CID allocation
Command64-byte SQE: opcode 02h, CID, NSID, PRP1/PRP2, SLBA, NLB (zero-based)PRP list when > 2 pages; FUA/PI flags
DoorbellMMIO write of new tail to SQ tail doorbell (1000h + 2y × stride)Write barrier before MMIO; batching
PCIePosted MWr downstream; device MRd for SQE; CplD returns itCredits, tags, MPS/MRRS/RCB effects
TLPHeader fields (Fmt/Type, Length, Requester ID, Tag, Address)3-DW vs 4-DW, ordering
DMADevice writes data to PRP pages via MWrsIOMMU translation; split by MPS
ControllerFetches, parses, schedules, FTL lookup LBA → physicalHMB/DRAM map caches; arbitration
MediaNAND page read (tR), ECC/LDPC decode, retry if neededRead-retry/soft decode latency; die parallelism
Completion16-byte CQE with CID, SQID, SQHD, status, phase via posted MWr — after dataOrdering guarantee data-before-CQE; RO caveat
InterruptMSI-X MWr to vector address/data; ISR consumes CQEs; CQ head doorbell; request completion to appCoalescing; polling alternative; affinity
Model answer (abridged script)

“The application calls read() on a file opened with O_DIRECT. The filesystem maps the file offset to LBAs and the block layer builds a request, splitting it to fit the device’s limits. The NVMe driver picks the submission queue owned by the current CPU, allocates a command identifier and fills a 64-byte SQE: opcode 02h Read, NSID 1, starting LBA, number of blocks minus one, and PRP entries pointing to the physical (IOMMU-mapped) pages of the user buffer — a PRP list if more than two pages. It places the SQE at the queue tail in host memory, issues a write barrier, and writes the new tail to the SQ tail doorbell in BAR0. That MMIO write travels as a posted Memory Write TLP down the PCIe link. The controller sees the doorbell, issues a Memory Read TLP for 64 bytes at the SQ slot; the root complex returns a Completion with Data carrying the SQE. The controller parses it, looks up the logical-to-physical mapping in its FTL, issues NAND page reads to the right dies, waits tR, moves data through ECC decoding, then DMAs the data into host memory as Memory Write TLPs to the PRP addresses, each up to Max Payload Size. Then it writes a 16-byte CQE — CID, SQ ID, SQ head, status success, current phase — into the CQ with another posted write, which PCIe ordering keeps behind the data. Then it sends the MSI-X message — a Memory Write to the vector’s address with its data — which becomes a CPU interrupt. The driver’s handler sees the phase bit flip, reads the CQE, matches the CID to the request, completes it, writes the CQ head doorbell, and the block layer wakes the application, whose buffer already contains the data.”

103. Second teach-back — “Explain why a PCIe Completion TLP is not the same thing as an NVMe Completion Queue Entry.”

DimensionPCIe Completion TLP (Cpl/CplD)NVMe CQE
LayerPCIe Transaction LayerNVMe (above the transport)
Answers whatA non-posted PCIe request (MRd, CfgRd/Wr, I/O)An NVMe command (SQE)
Who sends itThe completer of that request — can be host (root complex) or deviceAlways the NVMe controller
How it travelsIs itself a TLP type (Fmt/Type Cpl or CplD)Carried as payload of a posted Memory Write TLP into host memory
Matching keyRequester ID + TagSQID + CID
StatusSC, UR, CRS, CASCT/SC, DNR, More, CRD
Count per NVMe ReadSeveral (e.g. CplD for SQE fetch, PRP list)Exactly one
Model answer

“They live at different layers and answer different questions. A PCIe completion answers a single PCIe non-posted request; it is matched by requester ID and tag and its status is about the transaction (successful, unsupported request, completer abort). In an NVMe read, the host sends CplDs to the device — for example to return the SQE the device fetched. The NVMe CQE answers an entire NVMe command; it is a 16-byte data structure the controller writes into host memory, and on the wire it is the payload of a Memory Write, not a Completion TLP. So in a normal NVMe read you see CplDs flowing toward the device and exactly one CQE carried in an MWr toward the host. Confusing them leads to wrong conclusions — like thinking a UR completion means the NVMe command failed (it means a PCIe request failed, which may or may not later cause the command to fail).”

104. Third teach-back — “Explain how you would debug a missing NVMe completion.”

Required elementWhat to checkEvidence source
Queue inspectionSQ tail/head, CQ head, expected phase, CQ fullnessDriver debug, memory dump, CQE SQHD values
Command trackingWhich SQID/CID, when submitted, any duplicate CIDsDriver logs, block tracing
DoorbellWas the tail doorbell written, correct offset and valueAnalyzer MWr to BAR0 doorbell range
ControllerCSTS.RDY/CFS, controller still alive, firmware stateMMIO read of CSTS; telemetry
DMASQE fetched? PRP list fetched? data moved? any UR/CA/EP?Analyzer MRd/CplD; IOMMU fault log
CompletionCQE written? to which address? phase? CID?Analyzer MWr to CQ range; CQ memory dump
InterruptMSI-X sent? masked? vector address/data correct? delivered?Analyzer; MSI-X table/PBA; /proc/interrupts
PCIe evidenceLink state, Recovery, Nak/replay, credits, AERLnkSta, AER registers, analyzer DLLPs
LogsKernel messages, NVMe error log, async eventsdmesg/journalctl, nvme error-log
Hypothesis eliminationRanked list, discriminating tests, confidence labelsYour notes and the report
Model answer

“First, identify the exact command: SQID, CID, submit time. Second, check whether the system is alive: read CSTS — all ones means the device is off the bus; CFS means controller fatal. Third, check the host’s view: is the CQE already in CQ memory with the right phase (lost interrupt or host bug) — polling the CQ answers that cheaply. If not, walk the pipeline on the wire: doorbell written with the right offset and value; SQE fetched (MRd covering the slot and a successful CplD); PRP list fetched if needed; data moved; CQE written — if it was written elsewhere, compare with the CQ base from Create I/O CQ; MSI-X sent with the right address/data and not masked. The first missing or wrong step is the first abnormal event. Then look at the layer of that step: UR completions point to addressing or IOMMU; no fetch after doorbell points to Bus Master, controller state or credits; CQE present but ignored points to phase or CQ mapping. At each step I keep alternatives and look for the evidence that eliminates them — e.g. link Recovery events or AER around the time, async events, error log. Finally I label confidence and design one experiment to confirm.”

105. Fourth teach-back — “What would you look for first in a protocol-analyzer trace (e.g. a Teledyne LeCroy capture) when a system reports an NVMe timeout?”

📭 Tool-neutral note

This answer describes an investigative sequence that applies to any PCIe protocol analyzer, including Teledyne LeCroy tools. It deliberately does not reproduce any vendor’s screens, menu names or exact view formats; consult the analyzer’s own documentation for how to perform each step.

StepConcrete actionWhy first / what it rules out
0Validate the capture: both directions present, link speed/width as expected, no buffer overflow gaps, triggers and filters recorded, interposer did not change behaviourPrevents conclusions from missing data
1Get the timed-out command’s QID and CID and the host timestamp from the kernel log; align host time with trace time using a marker or a known event (e.g. controller reset CC write)Gives the search key
2Compute that queue’s SQ tail doorbell address (BAR0 from config writes + 1000h + 2y × stride); find doorbell writes in the window before the timeout start (30 s earlier by default in Linux impl)Did the submission reach the device?
3Find the device MRd covering the SQE slot; decode the returned SQE; confirm CID and opcodeDid the controller fetch it? Is the SQE what the host intended?
4Follow data movement: PRP list fetch, data MRds (write) or MWrs (read); check every completion status, EP bit, and outstanding tagsLocates DMA/IOMMU/completion problems
5Search for the CQE MWr with matching SQID/CID into the CQ range; check phase and addressDistinguishes “device never completed” from “host never noticed”
6Search for the MSI-X MWr for that CQ’s vector after the CQELost/masked interrupt
7In the same window check link health: LTSSM transitions (Recovery, L1 exits), Naks/replays, UpdateFC progress, ERR_COR/ERR_NONFATAL/ERR_FATAL message TLPsTransport-layer causes and context
8Look at the host’s reaction: Abort command, CSTS reads, CC.EN writes; make sure you do not mistake recovery traffic for the causeSeparates cause from consequence
9State the first abnormal event, its layer, and the next evidence neededOutput of the analysis
⚠️ Not accepted

“I would look for errors in the trace.” — generic, no search key, no ordering. Also not accepted: starting from the end (the reset) and working backwards without first locating the specific command.

106. Fifth teach-back — “Explain NVMe 2.4 to a senior engineer who knows NVMe 1.4.”

📘 Specification baseline for this answer

DOCUMENT: NVM Express specification set. REVISION: Base 2.4 with NVM Command Set 1.3, ZNS 1.5, KV 1.4, SLM 1.3, Computational Programs 1.3, NVMe over PCIe Transport 1.4, RDMA 1.3, TCP 1.3, NVMe-MI 2.2, Boot 1.4 (per course brief). RATIFICATION DATE: set released August 4, 2026 per press coverage. STATUS: current at time of writing — confirm on nvmexpress.org. OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: 1.4 (2019) and every 2.x revision. SOURCE: NVM Express announcements; consult the documents themselves for any normative detail.

ThemeWhat a 1.4 engineer needs to hearLabel
StructureFrom 2.0 the single document became a library: Base spec + I/O command set specs (NVM, ZNS, KV, later others) + transport specs (PCIe, RDMA, TCP) + NVMe-MI + Boot. Register/doorbell mapping for PCIe now sits in the PCIe transport spec; Read/Write details in the NVM Command Set spec.version
Command setsZoned Namespaces and Key Value became first-class command sets; Subsystem Local Memory and Computational Programs command sets were added later in the 2.x line.version
Data placement and enduranceEndurance groups and NVM sets (1.4) continued; Flexible Data Placement was added in the 2.x era as a host-hint placement mechanism.version confirm exact revision
Virtualisation and migrationLive migration support arrived in the 2.x line; 2.4 highlights PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration.version
SecurityKey-per-I/O and authentication features developed in 2.x; 2.4 highlights Post-Quantum Cryptography.version
Manageability and sustainability2.4 highlights Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting, and Restore Manufacturing Default Settings.version purposes only
What did not changeQueue model, 64-byte SQE / 16-byte CQE, phase tag, controller registers CAP/CC/CSTS/AQA/ASQ/ACQ, doorbells from 1000h, core admin and NVM opcodes.verified
Practical impactCite document + revision in every bug report; update analyzer decoders and nvme-cli; check Identify fields for optional features rather than assuming from VS; test interop with hosts written against older revisions.derived
Model answer (script)

“If you learned NVMe at 1.4, the fundamentals you know still hold: the queue pairs, 64-byte commands and 16-byte completions, phase tags, the controller registers and doorbells, and the core admin and NVM opcodes. What changed is mostly around them. First, the specification is now a family: since 2.0 there is a Base specification, separate I/O command set documents — NVM, Zoned Namespaces, Key Value and newer ones like Subsystem Local Memory and Computational Programs — and separate transport documents for PCIe, RDMA and TCP. When you cite behaviour, cite the right document and revision. Second, the 2.x line added capabilities in placement, virtualisation and security — Flexible Data Placement, live migration, per-I/O keys among them; I’d check the exact revision of each before quoting it. Third, the 2.4 set released in August 2026 highlights Post-Quantum Cryptography, PCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration, Voltage Monitoring, Rate Limiting and a standard way to Restore Manufacturing Default Settings. I can tell you their purposes; for mechanisms — new commands, log pages, feature identifiers — we should read the 2.4 documents rather than guess. Practically: update your tools’ decoders, never infer feature support from the version register alone, and always state which revision you are reasoning from.”

✅ Mastery gate
  • All five teach-backs recorded; no layer below 2; average ≥ 2.5.
  • Teach-back 105 contains a concrete numbered sequence with a search key.
  • Teach-back 106 labels every 2.x feature with its revision context or as “to confirm”.

PART LI

One Concept, Many Views

The back-matter of this book begins with a consolidation exercise. Eight core mechanisms — Doorbell, Read, Write, Completion, DMA, PRP, TLP and MSI-X — are each shown through twelve lenses, from the story an 8-year-old would understand all the way to the question a principal engineer would ask in an interview. If you can move up and down this ladder for every concept without losing the thread, you understand the system rather than its vocabulary.

R1 One Concept, Many Views

← ★ Final CertificationR2 The Analogy Library →

R1.1 Why this chapter exists

Most confusion in NVMe Express (NVMe) and Peripheral Component Interconnect Express (PCIe) work is not caused by missing facts; it is caused by switching levels without noticing. An engineer says "the completion arrived" and means a PCIe Completion-with-Data Transaction Layer Packet (TLP); a colleague hears "the NVMe Completion Queue Entry (CQE) was posted". Both are right about something different. This chapter forces every core concept through the same twelve views so that you can always name which view you are speaking from.

  • Explain each of eight core mechanisms at child, beginner, engineer, hardware, specification, memory, packet, trace, debugging, performance and interview levels.
  • Identify, for any statement about a mechanism, which view it belongs to.
  • Recognise when two people are describing the same event from two different views.
  • Use the "view ladder" as a debugging checklist: a failure must be localised in at least the memory, packet and trace views before a root cause is claimed.

Prerequisites. This is a review chapter. You should have worked through PCIe fundamentals (Part IV), the Transaction Layer (Part V), DMA (Part VIII), NVMe queues (Part X), NVMe commands (Part XI), PRP and SGL (Part XII), the end-to-end flow (Part XIII) and interrupts (Part XIV).

R1.2 Story: the twelve windows of one house

Imagine a house with twelve windows. A child looking through the kitchen window sees a family eating dinner. An electrician looking through the basement window sees wiring and a fuse box. A city planner looking at the house on a map sees a rectangle on a lot. All three are looking at the same house. If the electrician tells the child "the house is a 200-amp service", the child is confused — not because the statement is wrong, but because it is said from a window the child is not standing at. Every concept in this book is a house with twelve windows.

🌍 Analogy

The views are like map layers in a navigation app: satellite, terrain, traffic, transit. Turning a layer on does not change the city; it changes what you can see and therefore what questions you can answer.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Map layers are rendered from one consistent database. Engineering views are not automatically consistent: the specification view says what must happen, the trace view shows what did happen, and the difference between them is exactly where bugs live. Never assume the views agree — check.

📌 Remember

Rows 1 (intuition) and 3 (evidence) are the ones engineers skip. Skipping row 1 makes you brittle when the vocabulary changes; skipping row 3 makes you confident without proof.

R1.3 View 1 of 8 — Doorbell

ViewDoorbell
1. KidThe teacher puts request slips in a box, then rings a little bell so the librarian knows "there are new slips — up to slip number 6".
2. AnalogyA restaurant ticket rail: the waiter clips orders to the rail (the queue), then hits the service bell once (the doorbell). The bell carries no order details; it only says "look at the rail".
3. BeginnerAfter the driver writes one or more commands into a Submission Queue (SQ) in host memory, it writes the new tail index into a special controller register. That write is the doorbell.
4. EngineerEach SQ has a Submission Queue Tail Doorbell (SQyTDBL) and each Completion Queue (CQ) a Completion Queue Head Doorbell (CQyHDBL). The host writes the SQ tail to publish new entries and the CQ head to release consumed CQ slots. The value is an index, not a pointer, and not a count.
5. HardwareDoorbells live in the controller's Base Address Register 0 (BAR0) memory-mapped I/O (MMIO) space starting at offset 1000h. A write lands in a register file inside the controller front-end, which typically triggers a fetch engine. Some controllers coalesce rapid doorbell writes impl.
6. SpecificationOffsets: SQyTDBL = 1000h + (2y × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)); CQyHDBL = 1000h + ((2y+1) × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)) verified. Writing an invalid value (for example a tail beyond queue size) is an error the controller may report via an asynchronous event version — check the base spec's doorbell error definitions.
7. MemoryThe doorbell itself is device memory (MMIO), not host RAM. The SQ entries it refers to are in host RAM (or in the Controller Memory Buffer, CMB, if used). Ordering matters: the SQE store must be globally visible before the doorbell MMIO write — Linux uses write barriers for this.
8. PCIe packetOne Memory Write (MWr) TLP, usually 1 DW payload, host → device, posted (no PCIe completion). If BAR0 is mapped below 4 GiB the TLP uses a 3-DW header; above 4 GiB a 4-DW header.
9. TraceA downstream MWr from the Root Port to the SSD with address = BAR0 + 1000h + k and a small value. Recognise it by address range (inside BAR0, ≥ 1000h) and size (4 bytes), then confirm by what follows: an SQE fetch (MRd) from the device within microseconds.
10. DebuggingNo MRd after a doorbell → controller not enabled, wrong offset (DSTRD misread), wrong BAR, write dropped (Unsupported Request), or the command was already fetched. MRd but with wrong address → SQ base programmed wrongly. Tail value wraps incorrectly → driver ring arithmetic bug.
11. PerformanceEach doorbell is an uncached MMIO write: cheap for the CPU (posted) but it is a PCIe transaction and may cost the device a fetch. Batching (one doorbell for many SQEs) reduces doorbells per I/O. Shadow doorbells (Doorbell Buffer Config) reduce VM exits in virtualised controllers version.
12. Interview"Why is the doorbell a tail index rather than a 'go' bit?" — Because an index lets the host publish many entries with one write and lets the controller compute how many are new (tail − head mod size), with no read-modify-write and no lock between host and device.

R1.4 View 2 of 8 — Read command

ViewNVMe Read (opcode 02h)
1. Kid"Please bring me pages 4096 to 4103 of book number 1 and put them on table 7."
2. AnalogyA warehouse pick order: item location (LBA), quantity (NLB+1), and the delivery dock (PRP address in host RAM).
3. BeginnerThe host asks the SSD to copy logical blocks from flash into host memory. The SSD does the copying itself and then reports success.
4. Engineer64-byte SQE: opcode 02h, Command Identifier (CID), Namespace ID (NSID), data pointer (PRP1/PRP2 or SGL), Starting LBA in CDW10–11, Number of Logical Blocks (NLB, zero-based) in CDW12 bits 15:0.
5. HardwareController fetches SQE, translates LBA → physical NAND location via the Flash Translation Layer (FTL), issues NAND page reads, decodes ECC, moves data via its DMA engine to host memory, then writes the CQE.
6. SpecificationRead is defined by the NVM Command Set specification; the SQE framing, CQE and queues by the Base specification; the doorbell/MMIO mapping by the PCIe Transport specification version (post-2.0 document split).
7. MemorySQE in SQ memory; destination buffer described by PRPs (possibly a PRP list page); CQE written into CQ memory; all in host RAM unless CMB is used.
8. PCIe packetHost→dev MWr (doorbell); dev→host MRd (SQE fetch, 64 B); host→dev CplD (SQE data); [dev→host MRd + CplD for a PRP list]; dev→host MWr × N (data, each ≤ Max Payload Size); dev→host MWr (16-byte CQE); dev→host MWr (MSI-X).
9. TraceDirection is the giveaway: read data travels upstream as writes. A Read command produces device-originated MWr TLPs carrying data.
10. DebuggingData MWr present but CQE missing → controller stuck after DMA or CQ full. CQE with status Unrecovered Read Error (SCT 2h, SC 81h) → media error, check Error Information log. Data landing at wrong address → PRP construction bug or IOMMU mapping problem.
11. PerformanceSmall random reads are latency/IOPS bound (NAND tR dominates); large sequential reads are link bound. Upstream efficiency depends on MPS (header overhead per MWr).
12. Interview"Why does an NVMe read generate PCIe writes?" — Because PCIe transactions are named from the requester's point of view; the SSD's DMA engine is the requester pushing data into host memory.

R1.5 View 3 of 8 — Write command

ViewNVMe Write (opcode 01h)
1. Kid"Here are new pages on table 3 — please copy them into book number 1 at page 100."
2. AnalogyA courier collection: the courier (controller) comes to your house (host RAM) and picks up parcels, rather than you carrying them to the depot.
3. BeginnerThe SSD fetches the data from host memory and stores it. "Success" means the controller accepted the data per its durability rules — not necessarily that it is on NAND yet.
4. EngineerSame SQE layout as Read with opcode 01h. Optional Force Unit Access (FUA, CDW12 bit 30) requires data to be in non-volatile media before completion. Without FUA and with a volatile write cache enabled, Flush (00h) is needed for durability.
5. HardwareDMA engine issues reads to host memory, data enters controller SRAM/DRAM buffers (or Host Memory Buffer metadata path), firmware schedules NAND program operations later. Power-loss protection capacitors are an impl feature.
6. SpecificationNVM Command Set defines Write, FUA, LBA ranges; Base defines Volatile Write Cache feature and Flush semantics; Identify Controller VWC field says whether a volatile cache exists.
7. MemorySource buffer in host RAM must remain valid and unchanged until the CQE is seen. Reusing it early is a classic data-corruption bug.
8. PCIe packetDoorbell MWr; SQE fetch MRd/CplD; data fetch: dev→host MRd requests (each ≤ Max Read Request Size), host→dev CplD responses (split at Read Completion Boundary); CQE MWr; MSI-X MWr.
9. TraceWrite data travels downstream as completions (CplD). Count bytes in CplD TLPs whose tags match the device's MRd requests.
10. DebuggingMRd with no CplD → Completion Timeout at the device (AER uncorrectable). CplD with status Unsupported Request (UR) → IOMMU blocked or bad address. CQE "Write Fault" (SCT 2h, SC 80h) → media/program failure.
11. PerformanceWrites are often faster than reads at low QD (cache absorbs), slower at steady state (garbage collection). Read-request tag count and round-trip time bound fetch bandwidth.
12. Interview"When is a write durable?" — After completion if FUA was set or no volatile write cache is present/enabled; otherwise after a subsequent Flush completes. Anything else is implementation-specific behaviour.

R1.6 View 4 of 8 — Completion (CQE)

ViewNVMe Completion Queue Entry
1. KidThe librarian writes "slip 17 done, all fine" on a card and drops it into the answer box.
2. AnalogyA parcel delivery receipt with a tracking number: it refers back to the order, says whether it succeeded, and has a coloured stamp that changes every round so old receipts are not mistaken for new ones (phase tag).
3. BeginnerA small record written by the controller into host memory telling the driver which command finished and whether it worked.
4. Engineer16 bytes. DW0 command-specific result; DW1 reserved/command-specific; DW2 SQ Head Pointer (SQHD, bits 15:0) and SQ Identifier (SQID, bits 31:16); DW3 CID (15:0), Phase tag P (bit 16), Status field (31:17: SC, SCT, CRD, More, DNR).
5. HardwareController's completion engine tracks CQ tail and phase internally; it writes the CQE via DMA, then (if enabled and not coalesced) sends the MSI-X message.
6. SpecificationBase specification defines CQE layout, phase tag inversion on wrap, and status code types (0h Generic, 1h Command Specific, 2h Media and Data Integrity, 3h Path Related, 7h Vendor Specific) verified.
7. MemoryCQ ring in host RAM, physically contiguous (or PRP-list described if CAP.CQR=0 allows non-contiguous). The driver detects new entries by comparing the phase bit with its expected phase.
8. PCIe packetOne dev→host MWr with a 16-byte payload (often), sometimes multiple CQEs in one larger MWr if the controller batches impl.
9. TraceAn upstream MWr whose address falls inside the known CQ ring. Decode payload: CID matches the SQE CID; SQID matches the SQ; SQHD shows controller fetch progress.
10. DebuggingPhase not toggling on wrap → driver hangs reading stale entries. CQE written but no interrupt → MSI-X masked or vector mis-programmed. Status DNR=1 → retrying is pointless.
11. PerformanceInterrupt coalescing (Feature 08h) trades latency for CPU; polling (io_uring/hipri) avoids interrupts at the cost of CPU spinning.
12. Interview"How does the driver know a CQE is new without a register read?" — Phase tag: the controller writes the current phase; the driver's expected phase flips each time the head wraps.

R1.7 View 5 of 8 — DMA

ViewDirect Memory Access
1. KidThe librarian has a trolley and is allowed to walk into the classroom and put books directly on the tables, so the teacher does not have to carry them.
2. AnalogyA trusted delivery driver with a building access badge: allowed into specified rooms only (IOMMU), without the receptionist (CPU) escorting every parcel.
3. BeginnerThe device itself reads and writes host memory; the CPU only prepares addresses and is told at the end.
4. EngineerBus mastering: the function's Command register Bus Master Enable bit must be set. The device issues MRd/MWr TLPs with I/O virtual addresses (IOVAs) which the IOMMU translates to physical addresses.
5. HardwareController DMA engines with descriptor processors (PRP/SGL walkers), tag allocators for outstanding reads, and write-combining buffers.
6. SpecificationPCIe Base defines memory requests/completions, ordering rules and attributes (Relaxed Ordering, No Snoop). NVMe defines only the data-pointer structures (PRP/SGL) that tell the controller where to DMA.
7. MemoryLinux DMA API (dma_map_sg, etc.) produces bus addresses. Cache coherency on x86 is hardware-maintained for snooped transactions; No-Snoop changes that impl.
8. PCIe packetDevice-originated MRd (with Tag), host CplD (same Tag), device-originated MWr (posted).
9. TraceLook at Requester ID: DMA TLPs carry the SSD's Bus/Device/Function (BDF) as requester. Host MMIO writes carry the root's ID.
10. Debuggingdmesg "DMAR fault"/"IO_PAGE_FAULT" style messages impl → IOMMU denied. UR completions to device reads → address not mapped. Data corruption with no errors → wrong IOVA, stale mapping, or buffer reuse.
11. PerformanceOutstanding-read concurrency (tags) × MRRS / RTT bounds read-DMA bandwidth. IOMMU IOTLB misses add latency.
12. Interview"Is DMA a copy?" — It is a transfer done by the device, not by the CPU. The CPU never touches the bytes; that is the point.

R1.8 View 6 of 8 — PRP

ViewPhysical Region Page entries
1. KidThe teacher gives the librarian a list of table numbers: "put the first part on table 7, the next on table 12, the next on table 3".
2. AnalogyA parcel split across several numbered lockers; the note lists locker numbers in order. If the list is long, the note says "remaining locker numbers are on the sheet in locker 40".
3. BeginnerPRPs are addresses of memory pages that together form the data buffer.
4. EngineerPRP1 may have a page offset; every later entry must be page-aligned (memory page size = 2^(12+CC.MPS)). If the transfer spans ≤2 pages, PRP2 is the second page; if more, PRP2 points to a PRP list; the last entry of a full list page chains to the next list page.
5. HardwareA PRP walker in the controller fetches list pages via MRd and generates per-page DMA descriptors.
6. SpecificationDefined in the Base specification. PRP entries have bits 1:0 cleared (dword aligned). PRPs are mandatory for PCIe admin commands; SGLs are optional for I/O commands (Identify Controller SGLS) verified.
7. MemoryScatter-gather of non-contiguous 4 KiB pages is natural for user buffers; the PRP list itself is one more page the driver allocates (Linux uses a DMA pool).
8. PCIe packetExtra dev→host MRd (+CplD) for the PRP list page(s) before data DMA. Data TLPs never cross a page boundary described by different PRPs.
9. TraceAn MRd shortly after the SQE fetch whose address equals PRP2 → list fetch. Its length tells you how many entries the controller read up-front impl.
10. DebuggingStatus "PRP Offset Invalid" or "Invalid Field" → misalignment. Data written to wrong page → off-by-one in list building or confusion of PRP2-as-data vs PRP2-as-list.
11. PerformanceList fetch adds a round-trip to large I/Os; SGLs with one large descriptor can avoid it; the CMB can host lists closer to the device.
12. Interview"8 KiB transfer starting 512 bytes into a page — how many PRPs?" — It touches 3 pages, so PRP1 (with offset) + PRP2 pointing to a list of 2 entries.

R1.9 View 7 of 8 — TLP

ViewTransaction Layer Packet
1. KidA truck on the highway with a label: "deliver to address X, carrying 64 bytes, tracking number 42".
2. AnalogyA shipping container: standard header (destination, type, size), optional cargo, and a seal (CRC) checked at every hop.
3. BeginnerThe unit in which PCIe moves a request or a response between two devices.
4. Engineer3-DW or 4-DW header (Fmt, Type, TC, Attr, TD, EP, Length, Requester ID, Tag, byte enables, address — or for completions Completer ID, status, byte count, lower address), optional payload, optional ECRC. The Data Link Layer adds sequence number and LCRC.
5. HardwareBuilt by the transaction-layer logic of the PCIe controller IP; buffered against flow-control credits; replayed from the retry buffer if a NAK or timeout occurs.
6. SpecificationPCI Express Base Specification (PCI-SIG). Gen6 adds FLIT mode with a different header format and 14-bit tags version.
7. MemoryA memory TLP's address is a bus address. It may be translated by the IOMMU (upstream) or decoded by BARs (downstream).
8. PCIe packetIt is the packet view. Posted (MWr, Msg), non-posted (MRd, Cfg, I/O), completions (Cpl, CplD).
9. TraceAnalyzers decode TLPs per direction; header fields reveal requester, tag, length. Higher-level NVMe decoding is an analyzer inference built on top.
10. DebuggingMalformed TLP, poisoned (EP=1) TLP, ECRC error, UR/CA completions — each points to a different layer of fault.
11. PerformanceEfficiency = payload / (payload + ~20–24 B overhead) before DLLP traffic; bigger MPS = better efficiency, at a latency/buffer cost.
12. Interview"Is an NVMe command one TLP?" — No. One NVMe I/O typically produces 5+ TLPs in different directions, and none of them is the command; one of them carries the command's 64 bytes as completion data.

R1.10 View 8 of 8 — MSI-X

ViewMessage Signalled Interrupts — Extended
1. KidThe librarian presses a button that lights up a specific lamp on the teacher's desk — lamp number 3 means "look at answer box 3".
2. AnalogyA text message to a specific phone number (the vector address) with a short code (data). It says "you have mail", not what the mail contains.
3. BeginnerThe device interrupts the CPU by writing a small value to a special address; there is no interrupt wire.
4. EngineerMSI-X capability (ID 11h) points to a table in a BAR. Each 16-byte entry has Message Address (64-bit), Message Data, and Vector Control (mask). NVMe binds each CQ to an Interrupt Vector (IV) in Create I/O CQ CDW11.
5. HardwareDevice's interrupt logic writes Message Data to Message Address; the platform interrupt controller (x86 local APIC / interrupt remapping) turns it into a CPU interrupt.
6. SpecificationMSI-X is PCIe/PCI; NVMe defines INTMS/INTMC (used for pin/MSI, not MSI-X), CQ-to-vector mapping, and interrupt coalescing.
7. MemoryThe table and Pending Bit Array (PBA) live in device BAR space; the target address is an interrupt-controller address, not RAM.
8. PCIe packetA dev→host 1-DW MWr. On x86 the address is in the 0xFEExxxxx range impl.
9. TraceAn upstream MWr to an address outside all RAM buffers, 4 bytes, often immediately after a CQE write. Only by matching the address against the MSI-X table do you prove it is an interrupt.
10. DebuggingCQEs present, no interrupts → vector masked (Vector Control bit 0), Function Mask set, MSI-X Enable clear, or IRQ affinity offline. Interrupt storm → CQ head doorbell not updated.
11. PerformancePer-CPU queues + per-queue vectors give locality; coalescing reduces interrupt rate.
12. Interview"Can an MSI-X write overtake the CQE write?" — Both are posted writes from the same requester in the same traffic class; PCIe ordering prevents a posted write from passing an earlier posted write (unless Relaxed Ordering is set on the earlier one), which is why the CQE is visible when the interrupt arrives.

R1.11 Cross-view consistency check

A strong engineer can pick any row from any table and say which row of another table it interacts with. For example, the "Trace" row of Read (data as upstream MWr) is produced by the "Hardware" row of DMA and bounded by the "Performance" row of TLP (MPS efficiency). Practise drawing these links.

Conceptual trace — the eight concepts appearing in one 4 KiB read (offset 0, one page)
#DirectionTLPConcept(s) visible
1Host → DevMWr 4 B to BAR0+1008hDoorbell (SQ1 tail, DSTRD=0)
2Dev → HostMRd 64 BDMA (SQE fetch)
3Host → DevCplD 64 BRead command bytes carried as PCIe completion data
4Dev → HostMWr 256 B × 16 (MPS 256)DMA + PRP (destination page from PRP1) + TLP efficiency
5Dev → HostMWr 16 B to CQ ringCompletion (CQE)
6Dev → HostMWr 4 B to 0xFEExxxxxMSI-X
7Host → DevMWr 4 B to BAR0+100ChDoorbell (CQ1 head)

R1.12 Common mistakes

  • Answering a "trace" question with a "specification" answer ("the spec says the controller fetches the SQE") instead of evidence ("I see MRd tag 2Ah to SQ base + 0x180").
  • Using the kid view in a design review — analogies are for intuition, not for argument.
  • Skipping the memory view: most data-corruption bugs live in buffer lifetime and address translation, not in packets.
  • Treating the performance view as separate from correctness: a coalescing setting that makes latency exceed a timeout is a correctness bug.
🐞 Debugging connection

When you open a bug, write one sentence per view for the failing mechanism, starting at the trace view and working outward. The first view where you cannot write a confident sentence is where your investigation should go next.

💡 Senior insight

Seniors switch views deliberately and announce it: "From the packet view, the doorbell was delivered; from the controller-firmware view we have no evidence it was processed." That one sentence prevents an hour of people arguing past each other.

🧪 Lab R1.1 — Build your own twelve-view card SAFE

Objective: produce a twelve-view table for a concept not covered above: Identify (admin opcode 06h).

Setup: a Linux machine with an NVMe SSD and nvme-cli; no writes are performed.

sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | head -40     # controller identity (Identify CNS 01h)
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | head -30     # namespace identity (Identify CNS 00h)
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 -o binary | xxd | head   # raw 4096-byte structure

Steps: (1) For each of the twelve views, write one or two sentences. (2) For the packet view, predict which TLPs carry the 4096-byte Identify data and in which direction. (3) For the memory view, state who allocates the 4 KiB buffer.

Observations: fields such as MDTS, SGLS, VWC, and OACS in the output.

Questions: Why does Identify use a data buffer instead of returning data in the CQE?

Solution

Identify returns a 4096-byte data structure — far more than the 4-byte DW0 of a CQE — so the controller DMA-writes it into a host buffer described by PRP1/PRP2. Packet view: SQE fetch (MRd/CplD), then upstream MWr TLPs totalling 4096 bytes (e.g. 16 × 256 B at MPS 256), then the CQE MWr and an MSI-X MWr (admin CQ uses vector 0). The driver allocates the buffer (in Linux the core allocates and maps it for the admin command).

Extension: repeat for Get Log Page (02h), noting that NUMDL/NUMDU specify a dword count.

🎯 Exercise

Take the statement "the interrupt arrived before the data". Classify which views it could come from, and explain why, from the PCIe ordering view, this would be surprising (and which attribute could make it legal).

Answer

Trace view (most likely: analyzer timestamps) or Linux view (driver tracepoints). Data MWr and MSI-X MWr are both posted from the same requester; a posted write may not pass an earlier posted write unless the earlier one had Relaxed Ordering set. If the data TLPs carried RO, a fabric could in principle reorder them relative to the interrupt write; well-behaved controllers avoid RO on the CQE/MSI path impl. More commonly, the "observation" is an artefact of capturing on a different link than where ordering is enforced or of timestamp granularity.

Quiz

  1. In which direction does the data of an NVMe Write travel, and in which TLP type?

    Answer

    Host → device, in CplD TLPs responding to the device's MRd requests.

  2. Which view would contain the phrase "CAP.DSTRD"?

    Answer

    Specification (and hardware/register) view.

  3. What single packet-level property best distinguishes a doorbell write from an MSI-X write?

    Answer

    Direction plus address: doorbells are downstream writes into BAR0 ≥ 1000h; MSI-X writes are upstream writes to an address from the MSI-X table.

  4. Why is a CQE not a PCIe completion?

    Answer

    A CQE is NVMe data written into host memory by a posted MWr; a PCIe completion answers a non-posted request (MRd/Cfg) and is matched by Requester ID + Tag.

Interview questions

  1. Beginner Explain an NVMe read to a non-engineer, then to a firmware engineer.
    Model answer

    Non-engineer: "The computer leaves a note in a shared tray and rings a bell; the drive reads the note, copies the requested data straight into the computer's memory and leaves a 'done' card." Firmware engineer: SQE fetch after SQ tail doorbell; LBA → FTL lookup; NAND reads with ECC; DMA via PRPs to host; CQE post with phase; MSI-X per CQ vector.

  2. Senior Which views would you use to prove a buffer-reuse corruption bug?
    Model answer

    Memory (buffer lifetime vs CQE time), trace (timestamp of the device CplD/MWr touching that address vs timestamp of the CPU's reuse — via tracepoints), and Linux (block layer request completion). Packet errors would be absent; the proof is a timeline showing reuse before completion.

📌 Teach-back

Pick one concept. Explain it in 30 seconds to a child, 2 minutes to a junior, and 5 minutes to a senior. Record yourself. If the senior version contradicts the child version, fix the child version — it hid something important.

R1.13 Summary

Each concept has at least twelve legitimate views. The packet and trace views are where evidence lives; the specification view is where obligations live; the kid and analogy views are where intuition lives. Mixing them silently causes most misunderstandings.

Further reading: the end-to-end chapter (Part XIII) and the trace laboratory (Part XXIII). Next: the analogy library.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can fill all twelve views for Doorbell, Read, Write, CQE, DMA, PRP, TLP, MSI-X from memory.
  • Given any sentence about one of them, I can name its view.
  • I can explain why read data is upstream MWr and write data is downstream CplD.
  • I can explain why a CQE and an MSI-X are ordered.
PART LII

Real-World Analogy Library

One analogy everywhere breeds one misconception everywhere. This library offers more than forty analogies drawn from twelve domains — library, school, warehouse, airport, railway, postal system, restaurant, factory, highway, hospital, bank and delivery service — each mapped to a precise engineering concept and each followed by the point at which it stops being accurate.

R2 The Analogy Library

← R1 One Concept, Many ViewsR3 Things Engineers Commonly Get Wrong About NVMe and PCIe →

R2.1 Why this chapter exists

Analogies are compression: they let you carry a mechanism in your head cheaply. But every compression loses information, and the loss is not random — each analogy systematically hides particular details. By using several analogies for the same concept and by writing down where each one breaks, you train yourself to notice the hidden detail before it bites you in a trace.

  • Use at least two different analogies for each core concept.
  • State precisely what each analogy maps and what it hides.
  • Choose an analogy appropriate to the audience (executive, junior engineer, customer).
  • Detect when an analogy is being used as an argument rather than as an explanation.

Prerequisites: R1 One Concept, Many Views.

🧒 Kid analogy

A toy model aeroplane helps you understand a real one — wings, tail, wheels — but you cannot fly in it. Every analogy here is a toy model: great for learning the shape, useless for carrying passengers.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Some toy models are deliberately wrong in scale (a wider wing so it is easy to see). Engineering analogies are often wrong in time scale: human-world actions take seconds; PCIe events take nanoseconds, and that changes which effects dominate (for example, round-trip latency dominating over transfer time).

R2.2 How to read the library

Each row lists: the domain, the analogy, the engineering concept it maps, what maps well, and where the analogy stops being accurate. Analogies are numbered A1–A48 so other chapters and your own notes can cite them.

R2.3 Library and school analogies

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A1Librarian fetches books from the stacksNVMe controller executing readsAn agent with its own knowledge of where things are (FTL) serves requestsA librarian serves one patron at a time; a controller has dozens of NAND dies working in parallel, completing out of order.
A2Request slips in a boxSubmission Queue entriesFixed-format requests, processed laterThe SQ is a ring with head/tail indices; slips are not "removed" — slots are reused after the controller reports SQ head.
A3Answer box with stamped cardsCompletion Queue + phase tagEach card refers to a slip number (CID)Cards are not removed by reading; the driver must tell the controller (CQ head doorbell) which slots it consumed.
A4Library sections (fiction, science)NamespacesSeparate address spaces with own size and formatSections share the same librarian and corridors — namespaces share controller resources, so one busy namespace affects another's latency.
A5Library catalogue indexFlash Translation Layer mapping tableLogical → physical lookupThe catalogue does not move books on its own; the FTL constantly relocates data (garbage collection, wear levelling).
A6Class register taken at start of dayPCIe enumeration (config reads of Vendor ID)Discover who is present, assign seats (bus numbers)Enumeration also sizes and assigns memory windows (BARs) — a register doesn't give pupils addresses.
A7Teacher's raised-hand signalLegacy INTx interruptA shared "attention" lineINTx is level-sensitive and virtual wires are emulated by Assert/Deassert messages on PCIe; MSI-X has replaced it for NVMe in practice.
A8Homework drop trayHost Memory Buffer (HMB)The device borrows space it does not ownHMB is host DRAM lent by the driver under rules (Set Features); the device must not assume it survives resets.

R2.4 Warehouse and factory analogies

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A9Warehouse pick listRead command (SLBA, NLB, PRPs)Location, quantity, destination dockQuantity is zero-based in NVMe: NLB = 7 means 8 blocks.
A10Forklifts working different aislesNAND channels and diesParallelism scales with independent workersNAND operations on one die serialise and have asymmetric times (read ≪ program ≪ erase).
A11Shelves you must empty before re-stockingNAND erase-before-writeCannot overwrite in placeErase granularity (block) is much larger than write granularity (page) — a shelf analogy hides that ratio.
A12Re-packing half-empty palletsGarbage collectionValid items moved to free whole palletsGC competes with host I/O for the same dies and causes latency spikes; a warehouse can hire more forklifts, an SSD cannot.
A13Extra empty floor spaceOver-provisioningMore free space → less re-packingOP is invisible to the host and its effect on write amplification is non-linear.
A14Assembly line stationsPCIe layers (Transaction, Data Link, Physical)Each station adds/removes its own wrappingLayers also interact in reverse (Ack/Nak and flow-control feedback), which a one-way line hides.
A15Quality inspector at each stationLCRC checked per link hopErrors caught at each hop and redone locallyLCRC is regenerated by each switch; end-to-end protection needs ECRC — a per-station inspector says nothing about the whole route.
A16Factory gate with badge readerIOMMUOnly authorised destinations reachableThe IOMMU also translates addresses; a gate does not rename rooms.
A17Kanban cards limiting work in progressFlow-control creditsSender may only send when receiver has roomCredits are per type (Posted/Non-Posted/Completion, header vs data); one exhausted type can stall while others flow.

R2.5 Airport and railway analogies

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A18Air traffic control assigning runwaysRoot Complex routing / switch portsCentral authority, routes by destinationPCIe switches route by address/ID ranges programmed at enumeration, not by real-time decisions.
A19Boarding pass with seat numberTag in a non-posted requestMatching a response to a requestTags are reused as soon as the completion returns; a boarding pass is unique per flight.
A20Baggage split across beltsCompletion splitting at RCBOne request, several partial deliveriesPartial completions for one request arrive in address order; luggage can come in any order.
A21Railway signalling blocksFlow control between link partnersTrain may enter a block only if it is freeCredits are advertised and returned by UpdateFC DLLPs; trains do not send "block free" telegrams back.
A22Train coupling test at departureLink training (LTSSM)Agreeing on parameters before runningLTSSM includes equalization at high speeds — tuning the track itself — and can re-enter Recovery during operation.
A23More tracks between citiesLink width (x1/x4/x16)Bandwidth scales with lanesOne TLP is striped across all lanes; it is not "one train per track".
A24Faster trainsHigher generation (GT/s)More data per secondFaster lanes need equalization, retimers and stricter channel loss budgets; and latency per TLP barely changes.
A25Conductor re-sending a missed telegramAck/Nak replayLost message re-sent automaticallyReplay is from a retry buffer in sequence-number order; NAK means "replay everything after sequence N".

R2.6 Postal system, delivery service and highway analogies

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A26Posting a letter (no reply expected)Posted write (MWr)Sender continues without waitingNo delivery confirmation at all at the transaction level; Ack DLLPs only confirm the next hop.
A27Registered letter requiring replyNon-posted request (MRd, CfgWr)Sender waits for a responseMissing replies trigger Completion Timeout, typically after tens of µs to seconds depending on the configured range impl.
A28Postal code routingAddress routing through switchesHierarchical decodeCompletions are routed by ID (bus/device/function), not by address.
A29Return-to-sender stampUnsupported Request completion"No such address here"A UR for a posted write produces no completion; the error is reported by the receiver via AER/ERR_* message instead.
A30Tracking numberCommand Identifier (CID)Correlate request and resultCID is unique only per SQ among outstanding commands; the pair (SQID, CID) is the real key.
A31Courier collects from your doorstepDevice-initiated DMA read (for Write cmd)Receiver fetches the goodsThe courier needs the house to answer the door each time (CplD per MRd); latency-bound for small items.
A32Delivery van drops parcel and texts youRead data MWr + MSI-XDelivery then notificationThe text is guaranteed to arrive after the parcel only because PCIe ordering rules require it — a real courier text can overtake.
A33Highway lanes and toll boothsLanes + per-TLP overheadEach vehicle pays a fixed toll regardless of loadOverhead is in bytes per packet, and bigger payloads amortise it — trucks don't get cheaper per kg that way at a real toll.
A34Traffic jamCredit starvation / head-of-line blockingUpstream backs upPCIe ordering lets some types bypass blocked ones (e.g. posted writes may pass blocked non-posted requests) to avoid deadlock.
A35Ring road with numbered exitsCircular queue indexingIndices wrap aroundFull vs empty disambiguation: a ring of N slots holds at most N−1 entries.

R2.7 Restaurant, hospital and bank analogies

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A36Ticket rail + service bellSQ + doorbellBell carries no order detailsThe doorbell carries a number (new tail); a bell does not say how many tickets were added.
A37Many waiters, one kitchenMultiple CPUs, multiple SQs, one controllerNo lock contention between waitersArbitration (round robin or weighted) decides which SQ the kitchen serves next.
A38Dishes leave the kitchen in any orderOut-of-order completionFast orders finish firstThe driver must never assume CQE order equals SQE order.
A39Hospital triageWeighted Round Robin with Urgent priority classPriority between queuesOptional feature (CAP.AMS); many controllers support only round robin impl.
A40Patient chart with vital signsSMART / Health Information logPeriodic health summaryCounters are cumulative and some are vendor-interpreted; a "normal" chart does not prove the link is healthy.
A41Emergency department incident reportAER error log (header log)Records first error and contextRecords the symptom at the detecting port, not the cause; the faulty party may be elsewhere.
A42Hospital ward isolationDownstream Port Containment (DPC)Isolate a failing link to protect the restDPC brings the link down; recovery requires software to re-enable, and in-flight I/O fails.
A43Bank teller window numbersQueue IDs (QID)Each window has its own lineAdmin queue is QID 0 and must exist first; I/O queues are created by admin commands.
A44Bank vault with dual controlSanitize / crypto eraseIrreversible, controlled operationSanitize continues across resets and its completion is reported via a log; it is not one atomic moment.
A45Bank cheque with amount in words and digitsCRC/ECC redundancyRedundant encoding detects errorsCRC detects; ECC (LDPC) corrects. The cheque only detects.
A46Branch managers with delegated authoritySR-IOV PF and VFsVFs act independently for routine workVFs share the physical link and media; PF controls resources (e.g. via Virtualization Management).

R2.8 Extra analogies for advanced topics

#AnalogyMaps toWhat maps wellWhere it stops being accurate
A47Notebook you may only write at the end ofZNS zone + write pointerSequential writes; reset to reuseZone Append lets the device pick the position and return it; an ordinary notebook doesn't tell you the page number afterwards.
A48A diner bringing their own chefComputational Programs command setCode runs near the dataThe program runs within device-defined compute namespaces and memory (SLM); safety, resource and lifetime rules are specified version.
A49Building maintenance panelNVMe-MI (out-of-band management)Separate access path for managementNVMe-MI can be carried over SMBus/I2C or PCIe VDM using MCTP; it can also be tunnelled in-band.
A50Moving house with the furniture still in usePCIe Exported NVM Subsystem Migration (NVMe 2.4)Relocating a live resourceExact mechanism is defined only in the 2.4 normative text; do not infer details from the analogy version.

R2.9 Choosing an analogy for an audience

AudienceBest domainsAvoid
Children, outreachLibrary, school, restaurantBank (abstract), highway credit rules
ExecutivesHighway (bandwidth), warehouse (GC, OP)Detailed postal routing
New-hire engineersPostal (posted vs non-posted), railway (flow control)Any analogy without the "breaks" column
Customers in escalationHospital (triage, chart, incident report)Analogies that imply blame
⚠️ Warning

An analogy used in a root-cause discussion is a red flag. "The queue is like a traffic jam, so we need more lanes" is not evidence that link bandwidth is the bottleneck. Replace analogy with measurement before deciding.

R2.10 Worked example — three analogies for flow control

Railway (A21) explains that the sender waits for permission. Kanban (A17) explains that permission is a finite number of tokens. Traffic jam (A34) explains the symptom when tokens run out. None of them explains that credits are separate for Posted, Non-Posted and Completion classes, or that headers and data have separate credit counts. Hence the engineering fact must be learned directly: a device starved of Non-Posted Header credits cannot issue new MRd requests even while it happily sends MWr TLPs.

R2.11 Common mistakes

  • Using one analogy family for everything (all "library") — the learner then assumes libraries' properties (one librarian, in-order service) apply.
  • Omitting the "breaks" statement — the hidden detail becomes the learner's belief.
  • Mixing analogies mid-sentence ("the truck rings the doorbell") — produces a chimera nobody can reason with.
🐞 Debugging connection

When a junior's hypothesis is wrong, ask which analogy they were using. Very often the error is exactly the "breaks" column of that analogy (e.g. assuming CQEs arrive in order because "the restaurant serves in order").

💡 Senior insight

The best engineers carry several deliberately incompatible models and know which one to consult. The analogy library is a training ground for that habit.

🧪 Lab R2.1 — Analogy stress test SAFE

Objective: find the breaking point of an analogy using a real measurement.

Setup: Linux, an NVMe SSD with a scratch file on a mounted filesystem, fio. Reads only.

# read-only random 4 KiB reads against an existing file, QD 1 then QD 32
fio --name=qd1 --filename=/mnt/scratch/testfile --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=1 \
    --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=20 --time_based --readonly
fio --name=qd32 --filename=/mnt/scratch/testfile --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=32 \
    --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=20 --time_based --readonly

Steps: compare IOPS and mean latency. The "one librarian" analogy (A1) predicts IOPS stays roughly constant with QD. The "forklifts" analogy (A10) predicts scaling.

Questions: Which analogy survived? At what QD did scaling stop, and which analogy explains that?

Solution

IOPS typically rises strongly from QD1 to QD32 impl, falsifying A1 and supporting A10. Scaling stops when die-level parallelism or controller processing saturates; Little's law (L = λW) shows latency then rises with QD at constant IOPS — the traffic-jam analogy (A34) now applies.

Extension: add a sequential write job in parallel and observe read tail latency (GC / write interference, A12).

Quiz

  1. Why does the "registered letter" analogy fit MRd but not MWr?

    Answer

    MRd is non-posted and requires a completion; MWr is posted with no completion.

  2. What does the "tracking number" analogy hide about CID?

    Answer

    CIDs are only unique per SQ among outstanding commands; (SQID, CID) is the unique key.

  3. Which analogy best explains why GC hurts latency, and what does it hide?

    Answer

    Re-packing pallets (A12); it hides that GC competes for the very same dies serving host reads.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate Give two analogies for MSI-X and explain where each breaks.
    Model answer

    Text message (breaks: content is only a vector code, not the result; ordering with data is guaranteed by PCIe, not by a phone network). Desk lamp per CQ (breaks: lamps can be shared by multiple CQs; vector masking and coalescing change when it lights).

  2. Senior When would you refuse to use an analogy?
    Model answer

    When arguing a root cause, approving a design or writing a spec interpretation; analogies there substitute narrative for evidence.

📌 Teach-back

Choose three analogies from different domains for "completion timeout" and teach the concept using all three, ending with the engineering definition and the "breaks" statement for each.

R2.12 Summary

Analogies accelerate learning and decelerate debugging if trusted too much. Always pair them with their boundary. Next: Things engineers commonly get wrong, and analogy safety and the mastery loop.

✅ Mastery gate
  • For each core concept I can give two analogies from different domains.
  • For each analogy I use, I can state its boundary unprompted.
  • I can name one decision I would never justify by analogy.
PART LIII

Things Engineers Commonly Get Wrong

Forty-two misconceptions about NVMe and PCIe, each with the reality, why it matters, and — most importantly — how to prove the reality on a real system or in a trace. This part also contains the analogy-safety rules, the mastery loop, counterexample training and layer-confusion training: the habits that stop misconceptions forming in the first place.

R3 Things Engineers Commonly Get Wrong About NVMe and PCIe

← R2 The Analogy LibraryR4 Analogy Safety and the Mastery Loop →

R3.1 Why this chapter exists

Misconceptions are not random ignorance; they are stable wrong models that survive because they usually predict the right answer. They fail exactly in the corner cases where bugs live. This chapter collects the most common ones encountered in validation, driver and firmware teams, and gives each a concrete disproof.

  • Recognise 42 common misconceptions in your own and others' reasoning.
  • State the correct model in one or two sentences each.
  • Design an experiment or trace check that demonstrates the correct model.
  • Explain the engineering consequence of each misconception.

Prerequisites: R1, the NVMe architecture (Part IX) and PCIe transaction layer (Part V).

🧒 Kid analogy

Many people think the Great Wall of China is visible from the Moon with the naked eye. It sounds right and gets repeated, but it's false. Engineering has its own "Great Wall" myths — they sound right, get repeated, and someone has to check.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

A trivia myth costs nothing. An engineering myth costs weeks: a team that believes "AER tells you the root cause" will replace the wrong component.

R3.2 Layer and identity misconceptions

#MisconceptionRealityWhy it mattersHow to prove
M1NVMe is the same thing as PCIe.NVMe is a storage interface/command architecture; PCIe is one transport (others: RDMA, TCP, Fibre Channel). verifiedErrors must be assigned to the right layer: a PCIe Completion Timeout is not an NVMe command timeout.nvme list -v on an NVMe/TCP host shows NVMe controllers with no PCIe device; lspci shows PCIe devices that are not NVMe.
M2M.2 means NVMe.M.2 is a form factor/connector; M.2 cards may be SATA or PCIe (NVMe or, historically, AHCI). verifiedBuying or debugging the wrong thing; a SATA M.2 never shows in nvme list.Check lsblk -o NAME,TRAN (sata vs nvme) and the keying (B/M) of the module.
M3PCIe is the NVMe protocol.PCIe carries memory reads/writes; NVMe meaning (SQE, CQE, doorbell) is assigned by addresses and data structures in memory.An analyzer's "NVMe decode" is an inference; if it misses the queue setup, it mislabels traffic.Start a capture after queues are created and observe the analyzer showing only raw MRd/MWr.
M4The NVMe command set is the same as the transport.Since NVMe 2.0, command sets (NVM, ZNS, KV, ...) and transports (PCIe, RDMA, TCP) are separate specifications. versionReading only the base spec leaves out Read/Write details (NVM CS) and doorbell mapping (PCIe transport).Open the specification index at nvmexpress.org and list the documents.
M5The controller is the namespace.A controller is the interface that processes commands; a namespace is a quantity of non-volatile storage. One controller can have many namespaces; a namespace can be shared by controllers.Namespace-level errors (format, capacity) vs controller-level (CSTS.CFS) need different recovery.nvme list-ns /dev/nvme0 and nvme list-subsys.
M6A queue is the same as a doorbell.A queue is a ring in memory; a doorbell is a register holding one index for it."Queue is broken" may mean memory corruption or doorbell misaddressing — different fixes.Dump SQ memory (debugfs/driver instrumentation in a lab) and compare to doorbell writes in a trace.
M7The doorbell write contains the command.It contains only the new tail index (or CQ head). The command is fetched by the controller via DMA.Looking for command fields in a 4-byte MWr wastes hours.In a trace, decode the doorbell payload: a small integer < queue size.
M8DMA is a CPU copy.The device masters the bus and moves the data; the CPU does not touch payload bytes.CPU utilisation is not proportional to bytes moved; cache effects differ.Compare perf CPU cycles for large direct I/O vs memcpy of the same size.
M9A TLP is the same as an NVMe command.One command produces several TLPs; the SQE bytes travel inside a CplD.Counting TLPs ≠ counting commands; throughput analysis goes wrong.Count TLPs per command in a synthetic or real capture of a single 4 KiB read.
M10A Completion TLP is an NVMe Completion Queue Entry.A PCIe completion answers a non-posted request; a CQE is a 16-byte structure written by a posted MWr.Misreading "completion timeout" as "command timed out".Find CQE writes: they are upstream MWr into the CQ address range, not Cpl/CplD.
M11PCIe completion and NVMe completion mean the same.Different layers, different matching keys (Requester ID+Tag vs SQID+CID).Wrong layer = wrong fix.Show both in one trace: CplD for SQE fetch, MWr for CQE.
M12PCIe generation is the NVMe revision."Gen4" is a PCIe link speed; "NVMe 2.0" is a spec revision. They are independent.A Gen5 drive can implement an older NVMe revision and vice versa.lspci -vvv LnkSta vs nvme id-ctrl VER field.
M13SSD latency is PCIe latency.Link/transaction latency is a small part (sub-µs to a few µs derived); media access and firmware dominate (tens of µs for NAND reads impl).Upgrading the link does not fix media-bound latency.Measure QD1 4 KiB latency on the same SSD at Gen3 vs Gen4 link: small change.
M14AER identifies the root cause.AER reports what a port detected; the cause may be the link partner, the channel, the firmware or software.Replacing a "reporting" component wastes time.Correlate AER header log with a trace; often the first error is elsewhere.

R3.3 Queue, command and data misconceptions

#MisconceptionRealityWhy it mattersHow to prove
M15CQEs come back in submission order.The controller may complete commands in any order.Drivers that assume order corrupt state.Mix 4 KiB and 1 MiB reads at QD>1; log CIDs in completion order.
M16NLB is the number of blocks.NLB is zero-based: NLB=0 means one block.Off-by-one data corruption or "LBA Out of Range".Decode CDW12 of a 4 KiB read on 512 B format: NLB=7.
M17An LBA is 512 bytes.LBA size is set by the namespace's active LBA format (commonly 512 B or 4 KiB, optionally with metadata).Byte offsets computed with the wrong size.nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 → flbas, lbaf entries ("in use").
M18Queue size N holds N commands.Full when head == tail+1 (mod N): at most N−1 entries outstanding.Overrun corrupts the ring.Ring arithmetic exercise with N=4.
M19The host writes both head and tail for every queue.Host writes SQ tail and CQ head; the controller reports SQ head inside CQEs (SQHD) and owns CQ tail.Misplaced writes cause invalid-doorbell errors.Check doorbell offsets in a trace: only SQyTDBL and CQyHDBL.
M20The phase tag is a status bit.It marks newness; status is in bits 31:17 of DW3.Misinterpreting P=0 as failure.Decode the second pass of a CQ: P=0, status 0 = success.
M21Submission queues live on the SSD.Normally in host memory; optionally in the CMB.Explains why SQE fetch is a device MRd.Trace shows MRd from the device to SQ base.
M22CID is globally unique.Unique per SQ among outstanding commands.Correlating by CID alone across queues merges different commands.Find two in-flight commands with the same CID on different SQs.
M23PRP entries can point anywhere at byte granularity.Only PRP1 may have an offset; others must be page-aligned (except the first entry's offset rule).Invalid-field errors or silent corruption.Construct a misaligned PRP2 in a simulator; observe status.
M24SGLs are always supported.Optional for I/O commands over PCIe; check Identify Controller SGLS.Driver must fall back to PRPs.nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -i sgls.
M25Completion means data is on NAND.Only with FUA, a non-volatile/absent write cache, or after Flush.Data loss on power failure.nvme get-feature /dev/nvme0 -f 0x06 (Volatile Write Cache) and Identify VWC.
M26Deallocate (TRIM) erases data immediately.It marks LBAs as deallocated; read-back behaviour is reported in DLFEAT; physical erase happens later.Not a security erase.Compare DSM deallocate with Sanitize semantics.
M27nvme format is a harmless refresh.It destroys data in the namespace (optionally with secure erase).Irreversible.Read the command description; never run it on a disk with data.
M28More queues always means more performance.Beyond one per CPU (or per core group) gains vanish; resource cost rises.Over-allocation wastes memory/vectors.Vary nr_poll_queues/io queues in a lab; plot IOPS.
M29Higher queue depth is always better.Past saturation, more QD only adds latency (Little's law).Tail latency SLOs violated.fio QD sweep: IOPS plateaus, latency rises linearly.

R3.4 Link, error, reset and performance misconceptions

#MisconceptionRealityWhy it mattersHow to prove
M30A posted write is confirmed delivered.No end-to-end acknowledgement. Ack DLLPs confirm only receipt by the next link partner.Flush-by-read patterns exist because of this.Trace: Ack DLLP for a doorbell comes from the switch, not the endpoint, when a switch is present.
M31An Ack DLLP means the command completed.Ack is Data Link Layer acknowledgement of TLP sequence numbers.Layer confusion in trace review.Ack precedes any controller activity.
M32"x4 Gen4" gives 8 GB/s of user data.16 GT/s × 4 × 128/130 ≈ 7.88 GB/s raw after encoding; TLP/DLLP overhead reduces it further (~85–92% derived).Unrealistic performance targets.Formula in R12; sequential read fio test.
M33If lspci shows Gen4 x4 capability, the link runs at Gen4 x4.LnkCap is capability; LnkSta is current. Links can down-train or be in low power.Hidden half-bandwidth links.sudo lspci -vvv -s <bdf> | grep -E 'LnkCap|LnkSta'.
M34Correctable errors are harmless.They are corrected, but rising rates indicate a marginal channel and precede uncorrectable errors or down-training.Early warning ignored.Track AER correctable counters in sysfs (aer_dev_correctable) over time.
M35Completion Timeout means the SSD is dead.It means a non-posted request got no completion in time: could be the requester's view of a hung completer, a lost TLP, a surprise down, or a misconfigured timeout.Premature RMA.Check which side logged it (requester), then the link state and the partner's logs.
M36A reset is a reset.Conventional (cold/warm), Hot Reset, FLR, NVM Subsystem Reset, Controller Reset (CC.EN 1→0) have different scopes.Choosing too small a reset leaves state; too big a reset loses others' I/O.Reset scope table in Part XVI; observe what lspci config survives.
M37MSI-X interrupt delivers the completion.The interrupt says "look at CQ"; the CQE is already in memory.Debugging interrupts when CQEs are wrong (or vice versa).Polling mode (io_uring with hipri) completes I/O with no interrupts.
M38Interrupt coalescing is free throughput.Fewer interrupts, but added completion latency.QD1 latency regressions.Set Features 08h in a lab and measure QD1 latency.
M39A Gen5 SSD is always faster than Gen4 for applications.Only if the workload is link-bound (large sequential at high QD).Wasted upgrade budget.Compare random 4 KiB QD1 on both.
M40A healthy SMART log means a healthy link.SMART reports device/media health; link errors appear in AER and PCIe status registers.Link issues missed.Compare nvme smart-log with AER counters.
M41An SR-IOV VF is an independent physical device.VFs share the physical link, controller hardware and media; resources are assigned by the PF.Noisy-neighbour effects and reset scope.Load one VF and measure another VF's latency.
M42An analyzer decode is ground truth.The decode is the analyzer's interpretation; the raw symbols/TLPs are the evidence, and probe placement matters.Mis-decodes treated as device bugs.Check the raw header bytes behind every decoded field you rely on.

R3.5 Deep dive: why M10/M11 matter so much

In a typical 4 KiB read at least three TLPs could be called "completion": the CplD that returns the SQE bytes to the controller, the MWr that writes the CQE, and the MSI-X MWr that "signals completion". Only the second is the NVMe completion. If a status report says "completion missing", ask: missing at which layer? A missing CplD (PCIe) produces a Completion Timeout logged by the device (the requester of the SQE fetch); a missing CQE (NVMe) produces an I/O timeout in the host driver (Linux logs a timeout and typically aborts/resets); a missing MSI-X with a present CQE produces a stalled queue that a poll would rescue.

Synthetic trace — three different "completions" in one command (synthetic example for teaching)
t (ns)DirTLPKey fieldsWhich completion?
0↓MWr 32baddr FEA01008h, data 0000_0003hnone (SQ1 tail doorbell)
820↑MRd 64blen 16 DW, tag 11h, addr 1_2F40_2080hrequest for SQE
1460↓CplDtag 11h, BC 64, status SCPCIe completion
61200↑MWr 64b × 16256 B each, datanone (DMA)
62050↑MWr 64b16 B into CQ1, CID 0042h, P=1, status 0NVMe completion (CQE)
62110↑MWr 32baddr FEE0_0000h, data 0000_0041hinterrupt ("go look")

R3.6 Common mistakes when correcting misconceptions

  • Replacing one absolute with another ("AER is useless") — AER is valuable evidence of where something was detected.
  • Correcting the words but not the experiment — learners only abandon a misconception when they see the disproof.
🐞 Debugging connection

At the start of a debugging session, scan this table against the team's current hypothesis. If the hypothesis depends on any misconception here, stop and run the "How to prove" check first.

💡 Senior insight

When a misconception keeps recurring on a team, it is usually built into a tool, a dashboard label, or a document — e.g. a log column called "completion" that mixes PCIe and NVMe events. Fix the artefact, not just the people.

🧪 Lab R3.1 — Disprove five misconceptions on your machine SAFE

Objective: gather first-hand evidence against M2, M12, M17, M24 and M33.

lsblk -o NAME,TRAN,MODEL                       # M2: transport per block device
sudo nvme id-ctrl /dev/nvme0 | grep -E '^ver|^sgls|^mdts'   # M12, M24
sudo nvme id-ns /dev/nvme0n1 | grep -E 'flbas|lbaf'         # M17
BDF=$(basename "$(readlink -f /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device)")
sudo lspci -vvv -s "$BDF" | grep -E 'LnkCap:|LnkSta:'        # M33

Observations: record VER (e.g. 0x20000 = 2.0), SGLS bits, active LBA format, LnkCap vs LnkSta.

Questions: Is your link running at capability? Does VER correlate with the PCIe generation?

Solution

VER is an NVMe revision encoding (MJR in bits 31:16, MNR 15:8, TER 7:0) and has no relationship with the PCIe link speed reported in LnkSta. A mismatch between LnkCap and LnkSta may indicate a slot limit, down-training or power management; confirm by checking the upstream port's LnkCap as well.

Extension: record AER correctable counters before and after a 10-minute sequential read.

Quiz

  1. A CQE has P=0 and status 0. Did the command fail?

    Answer

    No. P only distinguishes passes through the ring; status 0 is success.

  2. Who logs a PCIe Completion Timeout for an SQE fetch?

    Answer

    The requester of the MRd — the SSD's function — not the host.

  3. What is the maximum number of outstanding entries in a 64-entry SQ?

    Answer

    63.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate "Our Gen5 upgrade didn't improve database latency." Explain.
    Model answer

    Database random reads at low QD are media/firmware latency bound; link transfer time for 4 KiB at Gen4 x4 is ~0.5 µs versus tens of µs NAND access. Gen5 halves only the transfer component.

  2. Senior A colleague says "AER shows the SSD's port logged Unsupported Request, so the SSD is broken." Respond.
    Model answer

    UR logged at the SSD means the SSD received a request it doesn't support — e.g. host MMIO to an unclaimed address, or a config access to a non-existent function. The suspect is the requester (often host software). Inspect the header log to see the offending TLP.

📌 Teach-back

Pick five misconceptions and explain each with the disproof experiment, not just the correct statement.

R3.7 Summary

Most misconceptions are layer confusions (M1–M14, M30–M31), off-by-one/ownership errors (M16–M22), or optimism about performance (M28–M32, M39). Each has a cheap disproof. Next: analogy safety and the mastery loop.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can state the reality for any misconception number given.
  • I have personally run at least five "how to prove" checks.
  • I can identify the three different "completions" in a trace.

R4 Analogy Safety and the Mastery Loop

← R3 Things Engineers Commonly Get Wrong About NVMe and PCIeR5 Counterexample Training →

R4.1 Why this chapter exists

The previous chapters used analogies freely and catalogued misconceptions. This chapter turns both into method: rules for using analogies safely, and a twelve-step loop (plus three supporting tests) that every concept in the book should pass through before you claim to know it.

  • Apply the analogy-boundary rule: what maps, what does not, what is hidden.
  • Run any concept through the 12-step mastery loop.
  • Explain any concept at three levels that remain mutually recognisable.
  • Pass the five-question depth test and the trace-based mastery test for a mechanism.

Prerequisites: R2, R3.

R4.2 Child analogy safety — the analogy boundary

Analogies are for intuition, not normative truth. After every analogy write an Analogy boundary block with three parts:

  1. Maps well — the relationships that genuinely correspond.
  2. Does not map — properties of the analogy that are false for the engineering object.
  3. Hidden detail — the engineering fact the analogy conceals and which you must learn directly.
🧒 Kid analogy

The doorbell: the teacher rings a bell to tell the librarian new request slips are in the box.

🧩 Analogy boundary

Maps well: notification is separate from content; one ring can announce several slips. Does not map: it is not a physical bell, not a sound, not a "ring now"; it is a number — the new tail index. Hidden detail: the real operation is a host MMIO write (a posted PCIe Memory Write TLP) to a controller register at BAR0 + 1000h + (2y × (4 << CAP.DSTRD)); it must be ordered after the SQE store, and the controller then fetches SQEs by DMA.

AnalogyMaps wellDoes not mapHidden detail
Interrupt = librarian phones the teacherAsynchronous notificationA phone call carries a message; MSI-X carries only a vector codeOrdering with the CQE write; masking; coalescing; vector-to-CQ mapping
TLP = truckHeader (label), payload (cargo)Trucks travel independently; TLPs obey ordering rules and flow-control creditsRetry buffer and sequence numbers in the Data Link Layer
Tag = tracking numberMatches response to requestTracking numbers are unique foreverTags recycle; 8-, 10- or 14-bit width limits outstanding reads
Namespace = library sectionSeparate logical spaceSections have walls; namespaces share controller and mediaPerformance interference; per-namespace LBA format
PCIe = fast roadPoint-to-point, lanesRoads are shared buses; PCIe links are dedicated point-to-point serial linksPackets striped across lanes; per-link LCRC

R4.3 The twelve-step mastery loop

Every concept must be learned through: intuition, terminology, structure, mechanism, example, counterexample, trace, lab, failure, recovery, explanation by the learner, and assessment. Here is the loop applied fully to the Completion Queue phase tag.

StepPhase tag worked through the loop
1 IntuitionThe answer cards change colour every lap of the box, so yesterday's cards can't be mistaken for today's.
2 TerminologyPhase Tag (P), DW3 bit 16 of the CQE; "expected phase" kept by the host.
3 StructureCQ memory initialised to zero; controller writes P=1 on the first pass, P=0 on the second, and so on.
4 MechanismHost reads the CQE at head; if P == expected, it is new; on head wrap to 0, the host inverts expected.
5 ExampleCQ of 4 entries: pass 1 writes P=1 into slots 0–3; pass 2 writes P=0 into slot 0 — host expected phase is now 0, so it is new.
6 Counterexample"P=1 means a new entry" is false on the second pass. A driver that hard-codes P=1 hangs after the first wrap.
7 TraceSuccessive CQE MWrs to slot 0 a lap apart show DW3 bit 16 alternating.
8 LabIn a queue simulator (pseudocode below), run 10 laps and assert alternation.
9 FailureDriver forgets to zero the CQ before Create I/O CQ: stale P=1 values from a previous use look "new" → phantom completions.
10 RecoveryController reset, reinitialise CQ memory to zero, recreate queues; abort/requeue in-flight commands.
11 ExplainLearner teaches it in 60 seconds using a two-lap whiteboard sketch.
