12 AssessGiven a CQ dump and the head index, learner identifies which entries are new.
// Phase-tag simulator (language-neutral pseudocode)
N = 4; cq = [ {p:0} ] * N; ctrl_tail = 0; ctrl_phase = 1
host_head = 0; host_phase = 1
function controller_post(cid):
    cq[ctrl_tail] = {cid: cid, p: ctrl_phase}
    ctrl_tail = (ctrl_tail + 1) % N
    if ctrl_tail == 0: ctrl_phase ^= 1          // phase inverts on wrap
function host_poll():
    while cq[host_head].p == host_phase:
        consume(cq[host_head].cid)
        host_head = (host_head + 1) % N
        if host_head == 0: host_phase ^= 1
    write_cq_head_doorbell(host_head)
// Assert: for 10 laps every posted cid is consumed exactly once.

R4.4 Three-level explanation requirement

The same concept must be recognisable across all three levels. Example: Completion Timeout.

LevelExplanation
1 — ChildYou sent a letter asking for something and promised to wait. If no answer comes after a long time, you give up and tell a grown-up.
2 — Junior engineerA requester that sends a non-posted request (MRd, config, I/O) starts a timer. If no completion with the matching Requester ID and Tag arrives within the configured Completion Timeout range, it logs an uncorrectable error (AER Completion Timeout status bit) and treats the request as failed.
3 — Senior engineerTimeout ranges are programmed in Device Control 2 (with supported ranges advertised in Device Capabilities 2) verified. The error is typically non-fatal by default severity impl; its consequence depends on what the request was: a timed-out SQE fetch in the SSD may lead to a controller fatal status, while a timed-out host MMIO read returns all-ones to software. Root cause candidates: completer hang, lost TLP after unrecovered link error, surprise down, ACS/routing misconfiguration, or a completer whose own downstream access is stalled. Prove with a trace showing the request, absence of completion, and link state.

Check: the child's "letter", the junior's "non-posted request" and the senior's "MRd with tag" are the same thing — recognisable at all three levels.

R4.5 The five-question depth test

After every major concept ask: What? Why? How? What happens if it fails? How would you prove what happened? Worked for MSI-X:

QuestionModel answer (MSI-X)
What?An interrupt delivered as a PCIe memory write to an address/data pair taken from a per-vector table in device BAR space.
Why?To give each queue its own vector (per-CPU locality), avoid shared level-triggered pins, and order interrupts behind data writes.
How?Driver programs table entries, enables MSI-X in the capability's Message Control; NVMe binds CQs to vectors at Create I/O CQ; the controller writes Message Data to Message Address after posting a CQE.
Failure?Masked vector → pending bit set, no interrupt → I/O timeouts despite CQEs present. Wrong address → IOMMU interrupt-remapping fault or interrupt to wrong CPU.
Prove?Read /proc/interrupts counts for the nvme vectors; a trace showing CQE MWr without subsequent MSI-X MWr; read the PBA in a lab with care (read-only).

R4.6 The trace-based mastery test

For every major mechanism, the learner must identify in a trace: start, trigger, request, response, completion, side effect, expected next event, actual next event, anomaly.

Synthetic trace — Create I/O Completion Queue (admin) with an anomaly
#t (µs)DirEventDetail
10.0↓MWrBAR0+1000h (admin SQ tail) ← 5
20.9↑MRd64 B at ASQ+4×64, tag 03h
31.5↓CplDtag 03h; SQE opcode 05h, QID 1, QSIZE 1023, PC=1, IEN=1, IV=1
46.2↑MWrCQE to ACQ slot 4: CID 0004h, status 0, P=1
56.3↑MWrMSI-X vector 0
68.0↓MWrBAR0+1004h (admin CQ head) ← 5
79.1↓MWrBAR0+1008h (SQ1 tail) ← 1 — but no Create I/O SQ was ever issued
8——(nothing)no MRd follows
ElementAnswer
StartRow 1, admin SQ tail doorbell
TriggerDriver submits Create I/O CQ
RequestRow 2 MRd (SQE fetch)
ResponseRow 3 CplD carrying the SQE
CompletionRow 4 CQE (status success)
Side effectRow 5 interrupt; I/O CQ 1 now exists
Expected next eventA Create I/O SQ (opcode 01h) admin command naming CQID 1
Actual next eventRow 7 doorbell for SQ1 that does not exist
AnomalyDoorbell write to a non-existent queue; controller ignores it and may raise an asynchronous event for an invalid doorbell version. Root cause candidate: driver skipped/failed Create I/O SQ — confirm from driver logs.
⚠️ Warning

Passing the five-question test with textbook answers but failing the trace test means the knowledge is verbal, not operational. The trace test is the gate.

🧪 Lab R4.1 — Run the full loop on Get Log Page SAFE

Objective: take Get Log Page (02h) through all twelve steps plus the three tests.

sudo nvme smart-log /dev/nvme0          # Log Identifier 02h
sudo nvme error-log /dev/nvme0 -e 4     # Log Identifier 01h, first 4 entries
sudo nvme get-log /dev/nvme0 --log-id=0x02 --log-len=512 | head

Steps: write the loop table; predict the TLP sequence for a 512-byte log; identify one failure (e.g. log length exceeding what the controller supports) and its status code.

Solution

Packet prediction: doorbell MWr ↓, SQE MRd ↑/CplD ↓, data MWr ↑ totalling 512 B (e.g. 2 × 256 B), CQE MWr ↑, MSI-X ↑. Failure: requesting an unsupported Log Identifier returns Invalid Log Page (command-specific status) or Invalid Field in Command — check the base spec for the exact code in your revision version.

Extension: compare numd dword arithmetic: NUMD = (bytes / 4) − 1 (zero-based).

Quiz

  1. Name the three parts of an analogy boundary.

    Answer

    Maps well; does not map; hidden detail.

  2. Which mastery-loop step is most often skipped, and why is it dangerous?

    Answer

    Counterexample (step 6) — without it, the learner's model is never tested at its edges.

Interview questions

  1. Senior Explain FLR at three levels in under three minutes.
    Model answer

    Child: "turn one appliance off and on without unplugging the house". Junior: Function Level Reset, initiated by setting Initiate FLR in Device Control; resets one function's internal state and config (mostly) without affecting the link or other functions. Senior: software must quiesce DMA, wait the required time before config access, restore config; for NVMe, controller state and queues are lost and must be rebuilt; for SR-IOV PF, FLR also affects VFs; outstanding transactions are discarded.

📌 Teach-back

Teach the phase tag using the simulator; ask your listener to predict P in slot 2 on lap 3.

R4.7 Summary

Analogy boundaries prevent misconceptions; the loop, the three-level requirement, the five questions and the trace test convert understanding into operational skill. Next: counterexample training.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I write analogy boundaries automatically.
  • I can complete the trace mastery table for any admin command.
  • My three-level explanations are mutually recognisable.

R5 Counterexample Training

← R4 Analogy Safety and the Mastery LoopR6 Layer-Confusion Training →

R5.1 Why this chapter exists

A rule you have never seen fail is a rule you do not understand. For every important concept this chapter gives a naive interpretation that sounds right, a concrete situation where it is wrong, and the evidence that exposes it.

  • Recognise 20 naive interpretations that fail in practice.
  • Construct a counterexample for a new rule on demand.
  • Use counterexamples as test cases in validation plans.

Prerequisites: R4.

🌍 Analogy

"All swans are white" was a perfectly good rule in Europe until black swans were observed in Australia. One observation is enough to falsify a universal rule.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In engineering, many "rules" are true for your device and false in general (implementation-dependent). The counterexample may not exist on your bench yet — it exists in the specification's permission space.

R5.2 The counterexample catalogue

#Naive interpretationCounterexampleEvidence that exposes it
C1Every Memory Read Completion means the NVMe command completed.A CplD may answer the controller's SQE fetch, PRP list fetch, or Write-data fetch — all mid-command.Match the CplD tag to its MRd; check MRd address against SQ/PRP/data buffers.
C2Every upstream MWr is read data.CQE writes and MSI-X messages are also upstream MWr.Address classification against CQ ring and MSI-X table.
C3Every downstream MWr is a doorbell.Host writes to CMB (SQEs in CMB), MSI-X table programming, CC/AQA writes are also downstream MWr.Offset within BAR0: doorbells ≥ 1000h; controller registers < 1000h; MSI-X table at its BIR/offset.
C4The interrupt vector number equals the queue number.Linux commonly maps admin + I/O queue 1 to vectors in a particular way, and vectors can be shared impl.Create I/O CQ CDW11 IV field in the SQE fetched for that command.
C5Link Up means the device is usable.Link in L0 but controller CSTS.RDY=0 or CSTS.CFS=1.Read CSTS; nvme driver logs.
C6A successful CQE means the data is correct.End-to-end protection disabled + silent DMA to wrong IOVA = success with wrong data.Application checksum; enable protection information if supported.
C7No AER errors means the link is clean.AER may be disabled, not reported to OS (firmware-first), or masked.Check AER capability presence, mask registers, and platform firmware policy.
C8A bigger MPS is always better.Large TLPs increase latency for other traffic and require larger buffers; MPS is limited by the smallest in the path.DevCtl MaxPayload across hierarchy; latency of small reads under load.
C9MRRS = transfer size.Device may issue smaller requests than MRRS; completer may split into RCB-aligned completions.Trace MRd lengths and CplD Byte Count/Lower Address sequences.
C10Tags are unique per transaction for all time.Tags are reused immediately after completion.Same tag used twice within microseconds for different addresses.
C11If the CQE says success, PCIe had no errors.Correctable errors with replay happened silently; the command succeeded.AER correctable status; Replay counters if exposed.
C12Abort command cancels the command.Abort is best-effort; the target may complete normally; Abort's own CQE DW0 bit 0 indicates whether it was not aborted.Both CQEs: aborted command status (Command Abort Requested) or normal; Abort DW0.
C13Writing CC.EN=0 resets everything.Does not reset PCIe config state or the link; doesn't affect other functions.Config space unchanged; LnkSta unchanged.
C14Deallocated LBAs read back as zero.Read behaviour is reported by DLFEAT; may be unspecified/vendor.Identify Namespace DLFEAT.
C15QD1 latency = device latency.Includes software stack, interrupt delivery, scheduler wakeups.Compare interrupt vs polled completion latency.
C16A switch is transparent to timing.Adds store-and-forward or cut-through latency and its own Ack/Nak and flow control per link.Analyzer on both sides of the switch.
C17If nvme list shows the drive, MSI-X works.Admin commands may complete by polling during early init in some drivers impl; failures show later under I/O./proc/interrupts counters per nvme queue.
C18Poisoned TLP means the link corrupted the data.EP=1 is set by the source to forward known-bad data (e.g. uncorrectable memory error); the link CRC passed.LCRC fine, EP bit set in header; source error logs.
C19Recovery state means a failure.Recovery is entered for normal speed changes and L1 exit too.LTSSM trace showing Recovery around a planned speed change.
C20Sequential host writes are sequential on NAND.FTL may interleave across dies; other writes and GC intervene.Not visible from host; vendor tools/telemetry only impl.

R5.3 Worked counterexample in depth (C1)

Naive claim: "In the capture I see a Completion with Data right after the doorbell, so the command finished in 600 ns." Disproof: the doorbell is downstream MWr; the controller then requests the SQE with MRd; the CplD 600 ns later is the root complex returning the 64-byte SQE to the controller. The command has only just started. Evidence: the CplD's Requester ID is the SSD's BDF (it is a completion to the SSD), its Tag matches the SSD's MRd, Byte Count is 64, and its payload decodes as an SQE whose CID will later appear in a CQE.

🎯 Exercise — Build your own counterexamples

For each rule, construct a counterexample: (a) "The controller always fetches exactly one SQE per doorbell." (b) "A Read command always generates at least one MWr." (c) "The CQ head doorbell is written once per CQE."

Answer

(a) Controllers may fetch multiple SQEs in one MRd (e.g. 128 or 256 bytes) when tail advanced by several entries impl; also zero fetches if the tail equals the already-fetched head. (b) A Read that fails before data transfer (LBA Out of Range) produces a CQE MWr but no data MWr; and a Read with a CMB destination may keep data inside the device BAR impl. (c) Drivers batch: Linux processes several CQEs then writes the head once.

🧪 Lab R5.1 — Counterexample hunting with tracepoints SAFE

Objective: show that completions arrive out of order (counterexample to "in-order" rule).

sudo sh -c 'echo 1 > /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/nvme_setup_cmd/enable'
sudo sh -c 'echo 1 > /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/nvme_complete_rq/enable'
# run a mixed-size read-only fio job in another terminal, then:
sudo head -50 /sys/kernel/tracing/trace
sudo sh -c 'echo 0 > /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/enable'

Observation: per queue (qid), the order of cmdid in completions differs from setup order.

Solution

With mixed sizes and QD > 1, small reads overtake large reads. If you see strictly in-order completions, increase mixing (bs=4k and bs=1m jobs on the same CPU) — note that the tracepoint names are those in current mainline kernels; older kernels may differ version.

Extension: derive per-command latency by pairing setup and complete events on (qid, cmdid).

Quiz

  1. Give a counterexample to "a poisoned TLP means bad link".

    Answer

    Source forwarded data it knew was corrupt (e.g. memory ECC uncorrectable) — LCRC was valid.

  2. Why does C12 matter in timeout handling?

    Answer

    Because the original command may still complete; the driver must handle both CQEs and not reuse the CID/buffer until both resolve.

Interview questions

  1. Senior Give a counterexample to "doorbells are always 4-byte writes".
    Model answer

    Doorbell registers are 32-bit, but a host might (incorrectly or via a write-combining mapping) emit a merged write covering several doorbells; behaviour for such accesses is a spec question — check what the transport spec says about register access widths and treat anything beyond as implementation-dependent.

💡 Senior insight

Turn every counterexample into a regression test: a validation suite that encodes the black swans is worth more than one that re-confirms white ones.

📌 Teach-back

Pick three counterexamples and explain how you would observe each one on a real system.

R5.4 Summary

Rules about traces are usually usually-true. Counterexamples teach you which evidence turns "usually" into "in this case". Next: layer-confusion training.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can produce a counterexample for any rule in this chapter without looking.
  • I have converted two counterexamples into concrete test cases.

R6 Layer-Confusion Training

← R5 Counterexample TrainingR7 Trace Correlation →

R6.1 Why this chapter exists

The single most expensive class of reasoning error in NVMe/PCIe work is putting an observation in the wrong layer. These drills deliberately pair look-alike concepts from different layers until telling them apart becomes automatic.

  • Distinguish nine canonical pairs of confusable concepts.
  • Classify mixed statements by layer: application, block, driver, NVMe, PCIe Transaction, Data Link, Physical, media.
  • Rewrite ambiguous bug reports to be layer-explicit.

Prerequisites: R3; the PCIe layer model (Part IV).

🧒 Kid analogy

"I got a letter" could mean the envelope arrived, or you read what's inside, or you did what it asked. Envelope, message and action are different things.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In PCIe/NVMe there are more than three nested "envelopes" (Physical framing, DLL sequence/LCRC, TLP header, NVMe structure), and the same word ("completion", "reset", "queue") names different things at different layers.

R6.2 The nine canonical pairs

PairConcept A (layer)Concept B (layer)Discriminating test
1NVMe command (NVMe)PCIe TLP (PCIe TL)Does it have an opcode/CID (NVMe) or Fmt/Type/Tag (PCIe)?
2NVMe CQE (NVMe)PCIe Completion TLP (PCIe TL)CQE is payload of an MWr into CQ memory; Cpl/CplD answers a non-posted request.
3Doorbell (NVMe register / MMIO)Command (NVMe structure in memory)Doorbell = 4-byte index in BAR0; command = 64 bytes in SQ memory.
4Controller (NVMe entity)Namespace (NVMe storage entity)Controller has registers and queues; namespace has NSID, size, LBA format.
5Queue entry (NVMe memory)Packet (PCIe)An entry is persistent in memory; a packet exists only in flight.
6DMA operation (device behaviour)PCIe transaction (PCIe TL)One 128 KiB DMA = many TLPs; one MRd may serve part of one DMA.
7Interrupt (MSI-X / platform)Completion (NVMe CQE)Interrupt can be absent (polling) while completion exists; coalescing = 1 interrupt for N CQEs.
8PCIe reset (link/function)NVMe controller reset (CC.EN)PCIe resets affect config/link; CC.EN=0 resets only NVMe controller state.
9NVMe revision (spec version)PCIe generation (link speed)VS register vs Link Status speed field.

R6.3 Drill set A — classify the statement

For each statement, name the layer(s) and, if it mixes layers incorrectly, rewrite it.

  1. "The read completed with a UR."
  2. "The SSD NAKed our doorbell."
  3. "Namespace 2 went into fatal status."
  4. "The link reset cleared the CQ."
  5. "Gen5 adds support for ZNS."
  6. "The interrupt had status Invalid Field."
  7. "Our 1 MiB write was a single TLP."
  8. "After FLR the namespace data was lost."
Answers
  1. Mixed. If "read" means a PCIe MRd: "the MRd received a Completion with status UR" (PCIe TL). If it means the NVMe Read command: NVMe commands don't complete with UR; perhaps a device MRd during it got UR → the controller reports a data transfer error status in the CQE.
  2. Mixed. NAK is a DLLP indicating a TLP with bad LCRC/sequence (DLL); it is not a rejection of the doorbell's meaning. Rewrite: "the link partner NAKed the TLP carrying the doorbell; replay succeeded/failed."
  3. Wrong entity. CSTS.CFS (Controller Fatal Status) belongs to a controller, not a namespace.
  4. Partly right but imprecise. A link-level reset (Hot Reset, conventional) resets the function, so the NVMe controller loses queue state; the CQ memory in host RAM is not "cleared" — it is abandoned and must be reinitialised by the driver.
  5. Wrong. ZNS is an NVMe command set; PCIe generation is irrelevant.
  6. Wrong. MSI-X carries only message data; status is in the CQE.
  7. Impossible. Max TLP payload is MPS (≤ 4096 bytes per the spec maximum verified); a 1 MiB write is many TLPs (and many MRd/CplD pairs).
  8. Wrong layer for "lost": FLR resets the controller; non-volatile namespace data persists. Data in a volatile write cache not yet flushed may be lost impl.

R6.4 Drill set B — PCIe reset vs NVMe reset

ResetLayerInitiated byLink retrains?NVMe queues lost?Config space preserved?
Conventional (cold, PERST#)Platform/PCIePower/PERST# assertionYesYesNo
Hot ResetPCIe linkSecondary Bus Reset bit on upstream bridge, or TS1/TS2 Hot ResetYesYesNo
Function Level ResetPCIe functionInitiate FLR bit in Device ControlNoYesMostly no (function's config reset; link-related fields kept) verified
NVM Subsystem ResetNVMe subsystemWrite 4E564D65h ("NVMe") to NSSR (if CAP.NSSRS)May (implementation and transport dependent) implYesTransport-dependent
Controller ResetNVMe controllerCC.EN 1→0NoYesYes

R6.5 Drill set C — rewrite the bug report

Original: "Drive times out on completion after reset, interrupts look broken, Gen4 issue?"

Layer-explicit rewrite

"After a Controller Reset (CC.EN 1→0→1) initiated by the Linux nvme driver's timeout handler, the first I/O command on qid 3 produced no CQE within the block-layer timeout (30 s default impl). PCIe: link stayed in L0 at 16 GT/s x4 (LnkSta), no AER errors logged at the root port or endpoint. NVMe: CSTS.RDY=1, CSTS.CFS=0. Interrupts: /proc/interrupts count for the qid-3 vector did not increase. Unknown: whether a CQE was written (no trace). Next step: poll the CQ memory via a debug build or capture the link to see whether the controller fetched the SQE." — Notice "Gen4 issue" is removed: there is no evidence linking link speed to the symptom.

🎯 Exercise — layer labelling of a timeline

Label each event with its layer: (1) TS1 ordered sets; (2) InitFC1-P DLLP; (3) CfgRd0 to offset 0; (4) MWr CC=00460001h; (5) CSTS.RDY becomes 1; (6) Identify Controller CQE; (7) block device nvme0n1 appears; (8) mkfs runs.

Answer

(1) Physical/LTSSM; (2) Data Link (flow-control init); (3) PCIe Transaction (configuration); (4) PCIe TL carrying an NVMe register write; (5) NVMe controller state; (6) NVMe admin; (7) Linux block layer; (8) application/filesystem.

🧪 Lab R6.1 — Find each layer's evidence on your system SAFE
BDF=$(basename "$(readlink -f /sys/class/nvme/nvme0/device)")
cat /sys/bus/pci/devices/$BDF/current_link_speed /sys/bus/pci/devices/$BDF/current_link_width  # Physical
ls /sys/bus/pci/devices/$BDF/ | grep -i aer                                                   # PCIe error reporting
sudo nvme show-regs /dev/nvme0 -H 2>/dev/null | head -30   # NVMe registers (may need a recent nvme-cli)
cat /sys/block/nvme0n1/queue/nr_requests                                                       # block layer
grep nvme /proc/interrupts | head                                                              # interrupts

Questions: which layer could you not observe at all from Linux? (Answer: Data Link — Ack/Nak/UpdateFC are invisible without an analyzer; only aggregated error counters surface.)

Solution notes

show-regs reads BAR0 via sysfs resource mapping; on some systems it requires the device to be unbound or fails under lockdown impl. If it fails, use nvme id-ctrl for the VER field instead.

Quiz

  1. Which reset preserves the PCIe link and config space but loses NVMe queues?

    Answer

    Controller Reset (CC.EN 1→0).

  2. Is "DMA" a layer?

    Answer

    No — it is a device behaviour expressed as PCIe memory transactions.

Interview questions

  1. Intermediate "Is an Ack DLLP sent for an MSI-X write?"
    Model answer

    Yes — every TLP, including the MSI-X MWr, is acknowledged by the link partner's Data Link Layer; that says nothing about the interrupt being serviced.

💡 Senior insight

Insist on layer-explicit language in bug trackers. A template field "Layer where symptom observed / Layer where cause suspected" pays for itself in the first escalation.

📌 Teach-back

Explain the nine pairs to a colleague using only the discriminating test column.

R6.6 Summary

Same words, different layers. Always say which layer. Next: the trace correlation exercise.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I score 8/8 on Drill set A.
  • I can fill the reset table from memory.
  • I can rewrite any ambiguous bug report to be layer-explicit.
PART LV

Trace Correlation Exercise

Packet type alone never tells you what a packet means. This part starts with the six-line trace from the course brief, then gives a full synthetic multi-command trace with interleaved TLPs and DLLPs, and asks you to correlate every packet to its NVMe purpose — with an answer key that shows the evidence chain for each conclusion.

R7 Trace Correlation

← R6 Layer-Confusion TrainingR8 Evidence-Based Debugging →

R7.1 Why this chapter exists

Protocol analyzers show TLPs; engineers need NVMe meaning. The gap between them is filled by correlation: matching addresses against known structures (BARs, queue rings, PRP buffers, MSI-X table), matching tags between requests and completions, and matching CIDs between SQEs and CQEs. This chapter trains that skill and, equally important, the discipline of saying "unknown" when the evidence is missing.

  • Classify each TLP in a trace as doorbell, SQE fetch, PRP fetch, data DMA, CQE, interrupt, register access or unrelated.
  • State the evidence used for each classification and the evidence still missing.
  • Reconstruct per-command timelines from interleaved traffic of multiple commands.
  • Compute command latency components from timestamps.

Prerequisites: R1, R6, end-to-end flow (Part XIII), trace laboratory (Part XXIII).

🧒 Kid analogy

You watch a busy post office through a window. You see envelopes going in and out, but you can't read them. To know which envelope is a birthday card, you look at the address, the size, who sent it and when — and sometimes you just can't tell.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In a trace you can read the envelope contents (payload) — but the meaning of the contents depends on setup you may not have captured (which address is the CQ, which vector is which). Context capture is as important as packet capture.

R7.2 Warm-up: the six-line trace

Synthetic trace — the course-brief warm-up (no addresses given)
TEvent
100Memory Write
110Memory Write
130Memory Read
140Completion with Data
150Memory Write
160MSI-X Message

Questions: Which could be a doorbell? Which could be DMA? Which could be a CQ update? Which could be an interrupt? What additional evidence is required?

Answer and discussion
TCould beCould also beEvidence needed
100Doorbell (if host→device into BAR0 ≥ 1000h)Read-data DMA (if device→host); CQE write; CMB write; MSI-X table programming; register write (CC)Direction, address, length, requester ID
110Second doorbell (another queue, or CQ head)Same alternatives as T=100Same; plus value relative to queue size
130SQE fetch (device→host, 64 B, into SQ ring)PRP list fetch; Write-data fetch; host MMIO read of a register (host→device)Direction, address vs SQ base, length
140Completion carrying the SQECompletion carrying write data or PRP list; or the device answering a host register readTag + Requester ID match to T=130; Byte Count; payload decode
150CQE write (16 B into CQ ring) or read-data DMAAnything upstream-postedAddress vs CQ base; length 16; payload CID
160InterruptAn analyzer that labels "MSI-X" has already correlated the address with the MSI-X table — verify it captured the table programmingAddress/data match MSI-X table entry; vector mapped to the CQ

Without direction, address, length, tag and setup context, every answer is "possible" at best. Notice also the timing: 30 time units between doorbell and CQE is far too short for a NAND read — if these were nanoseconds, the CQE at T=150 is more likely an error completion (e.g. invalid field) or an admin command that needs no media access. Packet type alone is not evidence.

R7.5 Questions

  1. Classify every row (doorbell / SQE fetch / SQE delivery / register access / PRP list / data / CQE / interrupt / link-layer).
  2. Decode the two SQEs (rows 8 and 9): opcode, CID, NSID, PRP1, PRP2, SLBA, NLB, transfer size.
  3. Why does command B need row 12 but command A does not?
  4. Row 10 is a "Completion with Data" travelling upstream. Is it part of either NVMe command?
  5. Which command completes first, and is that a problem?
  6. Compute, for each command, doorbell-to-CQE latency and the data-transfer time.
  7. Check rows 22 and 27: are the SQHD values consistent with the doorbells?
  8. List what you cannot conclude from this trace alone.

23MSI-X vector 2Address/data match MSI-X table entry 2Confirmed
24CQ2 head doorbell, head=31000h + (2·2+1)·4 = 1014hConfirmed
25–26Read data for A, 2 pages, 16 × 256 B eachAddresses = PRP1, PRP2 of SQE AConfirmed
27CQE for A on CQ1 slot 7CQ1 base + 7×16 = 70h; CID 0021h, SQID 1Confirmed
28MSI-X vector 1Table entry 1Confirmed
29CQ1 head doorbell, head=81000h + 3·4 = 100ChConfirmed
2 — SQE decodes
FieldA (row 8)B (row 9)
DW00021_0002h → CID 0021h, FUSE 0, PSDT 0 (PRP), opcode 02h Read0035_0001h → CID 0035h, opcode 01h Write
NSID11
PRP11_3A5C_2000h1_4410_0000h
PRP21_3A5C_3000h (second data page)1_2F40_A000h (pointer to PRP list)
SLBA (CDW10–11)8000h1_0000h
NLB (CDW12[15:0])0Fh → 16 blocks × 512 B = 8 KiB1Fh → 32 blocks × 512 B = 16 KiB
3 — Why only B needs a PRP list

A spans exactly two 4 KiB pages: PRP1 + PRP2 (as a data pointer) suffice. B spans four pages: PRP1 covers page 0, so PRP2 must point to a list of the remaining three entries. The 24-byte list read confirms the controller fetched exactly three entries impl (some controllers read a whole list page).

4 — Row 10

No. It is the SSD answering the host's register read (row 7). Requester ID 0000h (host), Completer 0100h (SSD). It is a counterexample to "every CplD is DMA" and to "every completion belongs to a command".

5 — Completion order

B (submitted second, on SQ2) completes at 14.8 µs; A at 66.3 µs. Out-of-order completion across queues is normal; even within one queue it is allowed. A write can complete early when absorbed by a write cache impl; a read must wait for media (tR plus transfer).

6 — Latency arithmetic
  • A: doorbell t=0 → CQE t=66 300 ns ⇒ 66.3 µs device-side latency. Data transfer: 61 000 → 66 100 ns ≈ 5.1 µs for 8 KiB on the wire as seen here (the interval includes gaps; the link time for 8 KiB at ~7 GB/s effective would be ~1.2 µs derived, so the controller is pacing the transfer — e.g. from NAND buffers).
  • B: doorbell t=150 → CQE t=14 800 ns ⇒ 14.65 µs. Data fetch 2 600 → 9 300 ns ≈ 6.7 µs for 16 KiB. Fetch is round-trip bound: each MRd waits ~600–700 ns for its CplD; only 8 MRd per page in flight.
  • Host-side: MSI-X → CQ head doorbell 1.34 µs (B) and 1.54 µs (A) — ISR + completion processing time.
7 — SQHD consistency

Row 22 DW2 = 0002_0009h → SQID 2, SQHD 9: the controller has consumed SQ2 up to tail 9 — consistent with row 3. Row 27 DW2 = 0001_0004h → SQID 1, SQHD 4 — consistent with row 1. DW3 bit 16 (P) = 1 in both, matching expected phase 1.

8 — What cannot be concluded
  • Whether B's data reached NAND (write cache; durability unknown without FUA/Flush/VWC info).
  • Why the host read CSTS (row 7) — driver intent is not visible on the wire.
  • Whether the read data is correct — the trace shows bytes moved, not their correctness versus the stored data.
  • Which CPU handled each interrupt.
  • Anything about the other direction's Acks we did not list (the capture shows only some DLLPs).

R7.7 A broken variant

Synthetic trace — variant with a fault (find the first bad event)
#t (ns)DirPacketFields
10↓MWrFEA0_1010h ← 9
2760↑MRdtag 11h, 1_2F40_6200h, 16 DW
31340↓CplDtag 11h, SQE Write CID 0035h, PRP2 1_2F40_A000h
41900↑MRdtag 12h, 1_2F40_A000h, 6 DW
52500↓CplDtag 12h, entries 4410_1000, 5000_7000, 4410_3000 (high DW 1)
62600↑MRd × 16pages 0, 1 fetched normally
75000↑MRdtag 23h, 1_5000_7000h, 128 DW
85600↓Cpl (no data)tag 23h, status UR
95700—(no further MRd for page 2/3)
109000↑MWrCQE CQ2: CID 0035h, SCT 0h, SC 04h (Data Transfer Error), DNR 0
119060↑MWrMSI-X vector 2
Analysis

The first abnormal event is the UR completion at row 8 — but the first bad decision may be earlier: the PRP list entry 1_5000_7000h (row 5) is not mapped for the device in the IOMMU, or is wrong. Evidence chain: (1) row 7 address equals the second list entry; (2) row 8 UR from the root complex means the address was not accepted (IOMMU fault or unclaimed address impl); (3) the controller aborts the data transfer and reports a Data Transfer Error (Generic Command Status 04h) verified. Confidence: Strong evidence that the PRP entry was invalid for DMA; Likely an IOMMU mapping bug; to confirm, find the matching IOMMU fault message in the kernel log and the driver's mapping for that page.

🐞 Debugging connection

The first abnormal packet and the first wrong state are often different events. Here the wrong state (a bad list entry in memory) existed at row 5; the packet symptom appeared at row 8.

💡 Senior insight

Always capture enumeration and queue creation, or at least dump BARs, queue bases and the MSI-X table from the host before starting a mid-run capture. Correlation without context degrades every "confirmed" to "possible".

🧪 Lab R7.1 — Build a correlator SAFE

Objective: write a small program that ingests the trace table (CSV) plus setup context, and classifies each row.

ctx = { bar0: 0xFEA00000, dstrd: 0, ssd_rid: 0x0100,
        sq: {1: (0x12F402000, 64), 2: (0x12F406000, 64)},
        cq: {1: (0x12F404000, 64), 2: (0x12F408000, 64)},
        msix: {(0xFEE00000, 0x24): 1, (0xFEE02000, 0x25): 2} }
outstanding = {}               # (requester, tag) -> MRd row
def classify(r):
    if r.kind == "MWr" and r.dir == "down" and in_range(r.addr, ctx.bar0 + 0x1000, ctx.bar0 + 0x2000):
        idx = (r.addr - ctx.bar0 - 0x1000) // (4 << ctx.dstrd)
        return ("SQ%d tail doorbell" % (idx // 2)) if idx % 2 == 0 else ("CQ%d head doorbell" % (idx // 2))
    if r.kind == "MRd":
        outstanding[(r.req, r.tag)] = r
        for q,(base,n) in ctx.sq.items():
            if in_range(r.addr, base, base + 64*n): return "SQE fetch SQ%d slot %d" % (q, (r.addr-base)//64)
        return "DMA read (data or PRP list) - check PRP context"
    if r.kind in ("Cpl", "CplD"):
        req = outstanding.pop((r.req, r.tag), None)
        return "completion for row %s" % (req.row if req else "UNKNOWN - unexpected completion")
    if r.kind == "MWr" and r.dir == "up":
        if (r.addr, r.data) in ctx.msix: return "MSI-X vector %d" % ctx.msix[(r.addr, r.data)]
        for q,(base,n) in ctx.cq.items():
            if in_range(r.addr, base, base + 16*n): return "CQE CQ%d slot %d" % (q, (r.addr-base)//16)
        return "DMA write (read data) - check PRP context"
    return "other / link layer"

Questions: how does your correlator handle a CplD split into two (BC 512 then BC 256)? How should it treat an MRd whose tag is reused before its completion arrives?

Solution

Keep the outstanding entry until the completion with Byte Count equal to the remaining bytes arrives (BC counts remaining bytes, so the last completion has BC = its own length). A reused tag before completion is a protocol violation by the requester — flag it as an anomaly rather than overwriting the entry.

Extension: add PRP-awareness by decoding SQEs from CplD payloads and registering their PRP ranges.

Quiz

  1. Why do the read-data TLPs for A use 4-DW headers?

    Answer

    The target addresses are above 4 GiB (1_3A5C_xxxxh), requiring 64-bit addressing.

  2. What does BC 512 in the first CplD for a 512-byte MRd tell you?

    Answer

    512 bytes remain including this completion; since its payload is 256 B, another completion with BC 256 must follow.

Interview questions

  1. Senior An analyzer labels a TLP "NVMe Completion" but you see no CQ creation in your capture. What do you do?
    Model answer

    Treat the label as the tool's inference. Check the raw address against queue bases obtained from the host (driver debug output or a capture of queue creation). Until verified, downgrade the classification to "possible".

📌 Teach-back

Walk a colleague through rows 1, 5, 8, 22, 23 of the full trace, stating evidence and confidence for each.

R7.8 Summary

Correlation = context + addresses + tags + CIDs + timing. Packet type alone is never enough. Next: evidence-based debugging.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I can classify all 29 rows with evidence without the key.
  • I can find the first bad event and the first wrong state in the broken variant.
  • I have a working correlator for at least doorbells, SQE fetches, CQEs and MSI-X.
PART LVI

Evidence-Based Debugging

Every root-cause conclusion must carry a confidence label and must point to its evidence. This part defines the five confidence levels, the evidence hierarchy, the root-cause statement template, and walks through a complete investigation.

R8 Evidence-Based Debugging

← R7 Trace CorrelationR9 Specification Safety →

R8.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineering organisations lose more time to confident wrong conclusions than to hard bugs. A conclusion with an honest "Likely" invites the next experiment; a wrong "Confirmed" shuts investigation down. This chapter standardises how certainty is expressed and earned.

  • Apply the labels Confirmed, Strong evidence, Likely, Possible, Unknown correctly.
  • Rank evidence by strength and independence.
  • Write root-cause statements that cite evidence and state what would falsify them.
  • Plan the cheapest experiment that raises confidence by one level.

Prerequisites: debugging methodology (Part XXVI), error handling (Part XV), R7.

🌍 Analogy

A court distinguishes "beyond reasonable doubt" from "balance of probabilities" and from "suspicion". Each verdict requires a different evidence standard, and the standard is stated openly.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In engineering you can usually re-run the crime: reproduce, instrument and experiment. Confidence should rise over time through experiments, not just through argument.

R8.2 The five confidence labels

LabelMeaningMinimum evidenceTypical example
ConfirmedCause demonstrated; mechanism understood; fix removes symptom; reverting fix restores it.Direct observation of the faulty event + controlled reproduction (on/off).Trace shows driver writing doorbell before SQE store visible; adding barrier removes failure in 10 000 runs; removing it brings it back.
Strong evidenceDirect observation points to the cause; no on/off experiment yet.Primary evidence (trace, register dump, header log) directly showing the faulty event.AER header log at the root port captures the exact TLP rejected as Unsupported Request (e.g. a DMA write to an unmapped address); trace shows the same TLP.
LikelyBest explanation of indirect evidence; alternatives less consistent.Multiple consistent indirect observations.Errors correlate with temperature and one slot; swapping slots moves errors.
PossibleConsistent with evidence but not specifically supported.No contradicting evidence."Firmware bug in GC could cause the latency spikes."
UnknownInsufficient evidence to discriminate.—Single occurrence, no logs.

R8.3 Evidence hierarchy

  1. Direct protocol evidence captured at the right place: analyzer trace at the failing link, with context.
  2. Hardware-latched state: AER status and header log, CSTS, LnkSta, error logs read soon after the event.
  3. Controlled reproduction with on/off variable.
  4. Software logs: dmesg, tracepoints, driver debug messages (subject to timing and loss).
  5. Statistical correlation: fleet data, temperature/slot/firmware patterns.
  6. Expert intuition: hypothesis generator only — never evidence.
⚠️ Warning

Two pieces of evidence derived from the same source are not independent. A dmesg line and a dashboard alert both generated from the same AER interrupt count as one observation.

R8.4 The root-cause statement template

SYMPTOM:          what was observed, where, when, how often
LAYER (symptom):  physical | data link | transaction | NVMe | driver | block | app | media
FIRST BAD EVENT:  earliest observed deviation from expected behaviour (with evidence ref)
CAUSE:            mechanism, stated so it could be falsified
LAYER (cause):    ...
CONFIDENCE:       Confirmed | Strong evidence | Likely | Possible | Unknown
EVIDENCE:         numbered list, each with source + timestamp + what it shows
ALTERNATIVES:     other hypotheses + why they rank lower
FALSIFIER:        observation that would disprove the cause
NEXT EXPERIMENT:  cheapest step to raise confidence one level
SPEC REFERENCE:   document + revision (+ section title if verified), or "none needed"

R8.5 Worked investigation — intermittent I/O timeouts

Report: "nvme nvme0: I/O 123 QID 4 timeout, aborting" appears about once per day on one server; followed by a controller reset; workload resumes.

StepActionResultConfidence after
1Read dmesg around eventTimeout on QID 4 only; no AER linesUnknown (layer: NVMe/driver symptom)
2Check AER is reported to OSAER capability present, OS-native AER enabled; correctable counters non-zero and rising daily at endpointPossible: link marginality
3Check /proc/interrupts for QID-4 vector across eventsCount continues to increase after the event — interrupts work in generalPossible (no change)
4Enable nvme tracepoints; catch next eventCommand submitted; no completion tracepoint until abort; other queues finePossible: lost CQE, lost interrupt, or device hang on that command
5Add polling of CQ memory in a debug build when timeout firesCQE is present in CQ memory with correct phaseStrong evidence: completion written, notification lost
6Analyzer on the link, trigger on driver timeout (GPIO/marker)CQE MWr present; no MSI-X MWr after itStrong evidence: device did not send the interrupt
7Inspect interrupt coalescing settingAggregation threshold 8, time 100 µs set by a tuning scriptLikely: coalescing timer bug in device firmware when queue goes idle with < threshold entries
8Disable coalescing (on/off test, 2 weeks each)0 events off; 13 events onConfirmed (the trigger); device-firmware mechanism still Likely pending vendor confirmation

Notice the correlated "rising correctable errors" (step 2) was a red herring: true, but unrelated. Without step 5–6 the team might have replaced cables.

R8.6 Anti-patterns

  • Upgrade-as-diagnosis: "we updated firmware and it went away" — without a revert test, this is Likely at best (the trigger may simply be rarer).
  • Last-log fallacy: blaming the final error message; often a consequence (reset) of the first error.
  • Single-occurrence certainty: one capture is an anecdote.
  • Spec-as-evidence: "the spec requires the device to do X, so the device did X" — the spec states obligations, not observations.
💡 Senior insight

Separate the confidence in the trigger from the confidence in the mechanism. You can be Confirmed that disabling coalescing removes the symptom while only Likely about why. Both labels belong in the report.

🧪 Lab R8.1 — Label a real report SAFE

Objective: take a past bug from your own tracker (or the case above) and rewrite its conclusion with the template.

Steps: list every piece of evidence, mark its source and independence, assign confidence, write a falsifier.

Checklist for a good answer

Every claim cites evidence; at least one alternative hypothesis is listed; a falsifier is specific (an observation, not "if it happens again"); the confidence label matches the hierarchy in R8.3.

Quiz

  1. You have an AER header log identifying the specific TLP that was rejected as Unsupported Request, but no reproduction. Label?

    Answer

    Strong evidence (for "this TLP was rejected at this port"); why it was sent remains Possible/Unknown until further evidence. Note that a Completion Timeout is not associated with a received TLP, so do not expect a header log for it — the evidence for timeouts comes from traces.

  2. Is "the vendor said it's a known firmware issue" evidence?

    Answer

    It is a hypothesis with some authority; raise confidence only when the vendor's described mechanism matches your observations and a fix passes an on/off test.

Interview questions

  1. Principal How do you stop a war-room converging on the wrong cause?
    Model answer

    Require confidence labels and evidence references on the whiteboard; keep an alternatives list alive; assign someone to try to falsify the leading hypothesis; prefer the cheapest discriminating experiment over debate.

📌 Teach-back

Explain the difference between "Strong evidence" and "Confirmed" using the worked investigation.

R8.7 Summary

Confidence is earned by evidence and stated openly. Next: specification safety.

✅ Mastery gate
  • Every conclusion I write carries one of the five labels.
  • I can name the next experiment that raises a given conclusion one level.
PART LVII

Specification Safety

Never hallucinate a specification. This part teaches how to cite, how to separate normative text from interpretation, and how to handle revisions honestly.

R9 Specification Safety

← R8 Evidence-Based DebuggingR10 The Final Reference Matrix →

R9.1 Why this chapter exists

Specifications are long, revised, and sometimes membership-restricted. It is tempting — for humans and for AI tools — to fill gaps with plausible text: an invented section number, a paraphrase presented as a quotation, a feature described as if it existed in an older revision. Each such fabrication can propagate into test plans and designs. This chapter defines the rules this book follows and that you should follow.

  • Cite specifications by document and revision, and by section only when verified.
  • Distinguish normative requirements, informative text, and interpretation.
  • Recognise version-dependent behaviour and say so.
  • Avoid claiming knowledge of proprietary documents not consulted.

Prerequisites: the specification-reading school (Part XXX).

🧒 Kid analogy

If you tell your friend "the rulebook says page 12 allows it", you had better have looked at page 12. Making up page numbers is how arguments — and games — go wrong.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Game rulebooks rarely change; specifications have revisions, errata, and Engineering Change Notices/Technical Proposals. "The rulebook" must always mean "which edition".

R9.2 The rules

  1. Consult the official document when exact normative behaviour matters.
  2. Cite document name + revision (+ section title/number only if you have it in front of you).
  3. Never invent quotations. Paraphrase and say "paraphrased".
  4. Never fabricate section numbers — section numbering changes between revisions (NVMe 2.0 reorganised the entire document set).
  5. Separate normative text ("shall", "shall not", "should", "may" carry defined meanings in the conventions sections of these specs) from informative notes and from your interpretation.
  6. State revision context for every feature introduced after 1.0.
  7. Do not pretend to have read a proprietary analyzer manual, a vendor datasheet under NDA, or a PCI-SIG member document you did not consult.
  8. Label implementation-dependent behaviour impl and unknowns uncertain.

R9.3 Zero-hallucination template

SPECIFICATION BASELINE:
  DOCUMENT:   NVM Express Base Specification
  REVISION:   2.4  (course baseline; confirm current at nvmexpress.org)
  DATE:       released August 2026 per NVM Express announcement of 4 Aug 2026
  STATUS:     current baseline for this course
  OLDER VERSIONS THAT MAY DIFFER: 1.x (single document), 2.0–2.3
  SOURCE:     https://nvmexpress.org/specifications/
CLAIM:        <statement>
CLAIM TYPE:   normative | informative | interpretation | implementation-dependent
EVIDENCE:     <section title as printed, if verified> | "not verified - check spec"
CONFIDENCE:   verified | derived | uncertain

R9.4 Safe and unsafe statements

UnsafeWhySafe rewrite
"Section 5.12.1.3 says the controller shall abort all commands."Fabricated section, invented quotation."The Base specification's description of Controller Reset (consult the Controller Reset subsection in the revision you are using) requires outstanding commands to be aborted; paraphrased, not quoted."
"NVMe 1.2 supports ZNS."Anachronism."ZNS was ratified as a technical proposal in 2020 and is a separate command set specification from NVMe 2.0 onward version."
"PCIe Gen6 latency is 2 ns lower."Unsourced numeric claim."Gen6 FLIT mode adds FEC; any latency impact is implementation-dependent — measure."
"NVMe 2.4's Rate Limiting caps IOPS per host at a register value."Invents mechanism details."NVMe 2.4 announced a Rate Limiting capability; read the 2.4 normative text for its mechanism — this book does not describe it beyond its stated purpose."
"The analyzer's manual says it timestamps at the first symbol."Unconsulted proprietary document."Timestamp reference point is tool-specific; check your analyzer's documentation."

R9.5 Reading normative language

NVMe and PCIe specifications define conventions for requirement keywords near their beginning. In both, "shall" denotes a mandatory requirement, "should" a recommendation, and "may" a permission verified. Optional features are discovered via capability fields (CAP, Identify, PCIe capability registers) — so a statement "the device supports X" must be checked against the reported capability, not assumed from the spec.

R9.6 Version awareness

QuestionWhere the answer lives
Which NVMe revision does this controller claim?VS register / Identify Controller VER
Which command sets?CAP.CSS, Identify I/O Command Set data structures version
Which PCIe speeds?Link Capabilities (Max Link Speed) and Link Capabilities 2 (Supported Link Speeds Vector)
Is a feature optional?The spec's feature tables; OACS/ONCS/etc. in Identify Controller
What changed between revisions?NVM Express revision-changes page; ratified technical proposals list
📭 What the spec does not say

Specifications rarely specify latency, internal firmware algorithms, NAND management, garbage-collection policy, or analyzer behaviour. Any statement about those is implementation-dependent by default.

🏭 Implementation-dependent

How a controller sizes SQE fetches, coalesces doorbells, orders data vs CQE writes within ordering rules, and allocates tags — all vendor choices.

🧪 Lab R9.1 — Audit a document SAFE

Objective: take any internal design document or blog post about NVMe and mark every specification claim as verified/derived/impl/version/uncertain.

What to look for

Section numbers without revision; quotations without quotation marks or sources; numbers (latency, bandwidth) without method; features attributed to the wrong revision; "always/never" claims about optional features.

Quiz

  1. You remember a section number from a 1.4 document. May you cite it for 2.4?

    Answer

    No — 2.0 reorganised the documents; verify in the 2.4 text.

  2. Does "may" in a spec mean the device will do it?

    Answer

    No — it permits; capability fields or testing tell you whether it does.

Interview questions

  1. Senior A test plan cites "spec requirement" for a behaviour you can't find. What do you do?
    Model answer

    Ask for document, revision and section; search the normative text; if absent, reclassify the test as "implementation expectation" with an owner, or remove it. Never fail a device against an imaginary requirement.

📌 Teach-back

Rewrite three unsafe statements from your notes using the template.

R9.7 Summary

Cite exactly, quote rarely, label always. Next: the final reference matrix.

✅ Mastery gate
  • I never write a section number I have not seen in the revision I cite.
  • I can classify a claim as normative, informative, interpretation or implementation-dependent.
PART LVIII

Final Reference Matrix

One table that answers, for each major topic: which specification governs it, which layer it lives in, what is observable in a trace, which Linux tool exposes it, and where in this book it is taught.

R10 The Final Reference Matrix

← R9 Specification SafetyR11 The Final Mental Model →

R10.1 How to use the matrix

When you meet an unfamiliar problem, find its topic row: the specification columns tell you where normative answers live; the layer column tells you which vocabulary to use; the trace column tells you what evidence to capture; the Linux column tells you what you can check without an analyzer. Specification ownership reflects the post-2.0 NVMe document split version; when in doubt, search all three NVMe documents.

  • Locate the governing document for any topic in under a minute.
  • Choose the right observation tool for a topic.

Prerequisites: all main parts; this is a reference.

🌍 Analogy

An airport departures board: one row per flight, columns for gate, time, status. You do not read it top to bottom; you look up your row.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Topics are not independent flights: errors touch every column at once, and the matrix gives the primary home only.

PART LXXIV

The Final Mental Model

One picture of the whole stack — from an application's read() call to NAND and back — and a narrative that explains every arrow.

R11 The Final Mental Model

← R10 The Final Reference MatrixR12 Mathematics Appendix →

R11.1 Why this chapter exists

By the end of the book you should be able to hold the entire path in your head and explain each transition: who acts, what crosses which boundary, in which direction, and what evidence each step leaves. This chapter is that picture.

  • Draw the complete stack from memory.
  • For every arrow, name the actor, mechanism, data moved, and the observable evidence.
  • Locate any failure on the picture.

Prerequisites: everything; especially Part XIII.

🧒 Kid analogy

A letter's journey: you write it, put it in an envelope, drop it in the box, the postman collects it, it rides a truck, it's sorted, delivered, read, answered — and the answer comes back the same way. Every step has a person and a bag.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

In the real stack the "answer" doesn't retrace the outbound path: data goes up by DMA writes, the completion by a different write, and the "doorbell" goes down separately. The paths are asymmetric.

R11.2 Every arrow, explained

R11.3 Narrative

An application asks for bytes. The filesystem translates "file, offset" into "device, LBA" — the last moment the request has any notion of a file. The block layer turns the bio into a request bound to the submitting CPU's hardware context, which in the NVMe driver corresponds to one SQ/CQ pair. The driver now speaks NVMe: it makes the buffer device-visible (an IOVA via the IOMMU), describes it with PRPs, fills a 64-byte SQE, and publishes it with a single tail-index write. That write is the only thing that crosses PCIe from host to device at submission time; the command itself stays in host memory until the controller pulls it across with a Memory Read — whose answer, a PCIe Completion with Data, is the moment the NVMe command first touches the link. The controller interprets the command, looks up its mapping table, wakes NAND dies, corrects bit errors, and moves the data using its own DMA engine, emitting Memory Writes towards host memory (for reads) or Memory Reads (for writes). When it has decided the outcome, it writes a 16-byte CQE whose phase bit announces "new", and then — ordered behind that write by PCIe's posted-write ordering — sends an MSI-X Memory Write that becomes a CPU interrupt. The driver reads the CQE, matches the CID, releases the CQ slot with a head-doorbell write, unmaps the buffer, and hands the status up. The application's read returns.

At no point is "the NVMe command" a packet; at no point is "the completion" a PCIe completion; at no point did the CPU copy the payload. If you can say why each of those three sentences is true, you hold the model.

🐞 Debugging connection

Place any symptom on the figure: an I/O timeout is "arrow 15 or 16 or 17 did not happen (or was not noticed)"; a Completion Timeout logged by the device is "arrow 11/13 MRd had no CplD"; a link down-train lives at arrow 10. Then use the evidence row for that arrow.

💡 Senior insight

The asymmetric paths explain most performance behaviour: submission is cheap (one posted write), the controller's pull of SQEs and write data is latency-sensitive (round trips), and completion is cheap again (posted writes). Optimisations target the round trips: CMB for SQEs, bigger MRRS, more tags, fewer PRP list fetches.

🧪 Lab R11.1 — Observe every arrow you can without an analyzer SAFE
sudo bpftrace -e 'tracepoint:nvme:nvme_setup_cmd { @s[args->cid] = nsecs; }
  tracepoint:nvme:nvme_complete_rq /@s[args->cid]/ { @lat_us = hist((nsecs - @s[args->cid]) / 1000); delete(@s[args->cid]); }'
# in another terminal: a read-only fio job; Ctrl-C bpftrace afterwards

Note: tracepoint field names vary between kernel versions version; inspect /sys/kernel/tracing/events/nvme/nvme_setup_cmd/format first. CIDs repeat across queues, so a robust script keys on (qid, cid).

What you learn

The histogram covers arrows 4–17 (driver submit to driver completion). Comparing it with fio's completion latency isolates arrows 1–3 and 18–20 (software above the driver).

Quiz

  1. Which arrow first puts the NVMe command bytes on the PCIe link?

    Answer

    Arrow 11: the CplD answering the controller's SQE fetch.

  2. Which arrows are posted writes?

    Answer

    6–10 (doorbell), read-data DMA in 13, 15 (CQE), 16 (MSI-X), 18 (CQ head doorbell).

Interview questions

  1. Principal Draw the stack and mark where you would add instrumentation to separate software latency from device latency.
    Model answer

    Tracepoints at arrows 4 and 17 give driver-to-driver; an analyzer gives doorbell-to-MSI-X (arrows 9–16), isolating device+link time; the difference is root complex/interrupt delivery. fio clat minus the tracepoint interval gives the block/FS/app software overhead.

📌 Teach-back

Draw Figure R11.1 from memory on a whiteboard and narrate all twenty arrows in under ten minutes.

R11.4 Summary

The whole book in one picture: down by software and one posted write, across by device-initiated reads, back by posted writes and an interrupt. Next: the mathematics appendix.

PART XLV

Mathematics Appendix

Every formula used in this book, collected in one place: link bandwidth per PCIe generation with encoding overhead, TLP efficiency, IOPS and throughput, Little's law, queue depth sizing, latency percentiles and tail amplification, utilisation, write amplification, endurance (DWPD/TBW), LBA and byte conversions, doorbell offsets, PRP entry counts, tag budgets and error-rate arithmetic. Each formula defines its variables, explains itself in plain English, and is followed by a worked example.

R12 Mathematics Appendix

← R11 The Final Mental ModelR13 Example Data Appendix →

R12.1 Why this chapter exists

Engineers argue less when they compute more. Most performance disagreements end the moment someone writes the right formula with the right variables. Most configuration bugs (wrong doorbell offset, wrong NLB, wrong PRP count) are arithmetic. This appendix is the reference.

  • Compute effective PCIe bandwidth for any generation and width.
  • Estimate TLP efficiency for a given MPS and header size.
  • Use Little's law to relate queue depth, IOPS and latency.
  • Compute percentiles and reason about tail amplification.
  • Compute write amplification, TBW and DWPD.
  • Compute LBA/byte conversions, doorbell offsets, PRP entry counts, MDTS limits and tag budgets.

Prerequisites: PCIe physical layer (Part IV), performance engineering (Part XXVIII).

🧒 Kid analogy

If a bus holds 40 children and comes every 10 minutes, then at most 240 children per hour can ride it. You don't need to watch the bus all day to know that — you can work it out. Formulas let you know limits without watching.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Real systems have many "buses" in series (software, link, controller, media), and the slowest stage — which may change with workload — sets the limit. Formulas give bounds; measurements tell you which bound you hit.

R12.2 Bandwidth per PCIe generation

BW_lane (bytes/s) = R × E / 8 ; BW_link = BW_lane × W
  • R — raw signalling rate per lane in GT/s (2.5, 5, 8, 16, 32, 64; Gen7 128 version).
  • E — encoding efficiency: 8/10 for Gen1–2 (8b/10b), 128/130 for Gen3–5 (128b/130b). Gen6 uses PAM4 signalling (64 GT/s means 32 GBaud × 2 bits) and FLIT mode; for a TLP-byte bound use the fraction of each 256-byte flit available to TLPs (236/256) derived.
  • W — link width in lanes (1, 2, 4, 8, 16).
  • /8 — bits to bytes.

Plain English: each lane carries R billion symbols per second; encoding spends some of them on overhead; multiply by lanes. This is per direction — PCIe is full duplex.

GenGT/sEncodingPer lane (MB/s)x1x4x8x16 (GB/s)
12.58b/10b2500.251.002.004.00
258b/10b5000.502.004.008.00
38128b/130b984.60.983.947.8815.75
416128b/130b1969.21.977.8815.7531.51
532128b/130b3938.53.9415.7531.5163.02
664PAM4 + FLIT (1b/1b) with FEC/CRC in flit~7375 (TLP bytes) derived7.429.559.0118.0

Worked example: Gen4 x4: 16 × 128/130 / 8 = 1.969 GB/s per lane; × 4 = 7.88 GB/s per direction. That is the ceiling before TLP/DLLP overhead.

⚠️ Warning

Marketing "GB/s" numbers for PCIe are often bidirectional totals or raw rates. Always ask: per direction? before or after encoding? before or after protocol overhead?

R12.3 TLP efficiency

η_TLP = P / (P + O) ; O ≈ F + H + LCRC (+ ECRC)
  • P — payload bytes per TLP (≤ MPS for writes/completions).
  • H — header bytes: 12 (3 DW) or 16 (4 DW, 64-bit address).
  • F — framing + sequence number: Gen1–2: STP(1) + seq(2) + END(1) = 4; Gen3–5: 4-byte STP token that includes the sequence number derived.
  • LCRC — 4 bytes; ECRC — 4 bytes when TD=1.

Plain English: each packet pays a fixed tax; bigger packets amortise it. For non-FLIT links O ≈ 20 bytes (3-DW) or 24 bytes (4-DW).

MPS / payloadη (4-DW, O=24)η (3-DW, O=20)
128 B84.2%86.5%
256 B91.4%92.8%
512 B95.5%96.2%

Worked example: Gen4 x4 read-data stream at MPS 256 with 64-bit addresses: 7.88 × 0.914 ≈ 7.20 GB/s. Subtract a few percent for Ack and UpdateFC DLLPs (8 bytes each including framing derived), SKP ordered sets and the opposite-direction completions; realistic sequential-read ceilings land around 6.8–7.1 GB/s impl.

R12.4 IOPS and throughput

Throughput = IOPS × S
  • IOPS — completed I/Os per second.
  • S — bytes per I/O.

Worked example: 1 000 000 IOPS × 4096 B = 4.096 GB/s. Conversely, a link-bound ceiling of 7.2 GB/s supports at most 7.2e9 / 4096 ≈ 1.76 M IOPS of 4 KiB reads — beyond that the link, not the media, is the limit derived.

R12.5 Little's law and queue depth

L = λ × W ⇒ QD = IOPS × latency
  • L — average number of items in the system (outstanding I/Os = effective queue depth).
  • λ — average arrival (= completion, in steady state) rate, I/Os per second.
  • W — average time each item spends in the system (latency), seconds.

Plain English: if 400 000 requests finish every second and each takes 80 µs, then on average 32 are in flight. It holds for any stable system regardless of arrival distribution (Little, 1961).

Worked examples:

  • QD 32, mean latency 80 µs ⇒ IOPS = 32 / 80e-6 = 400 000.
  • Target 1 M IOPS with 100 µs latency ⇒ need QD = 1e6 × 1e-4 = 100 outstanding across all queues.
  • Saturation: if IOPS plateaus at 800 k, increasing QD from 64 to 128 raises latency from 80 µs to 160 µs — the "more QD only adds latency" regime.
💡 Senior insight

Little's law applies to every subsystem boundary: to the tags in flight on the link, to commands inside the controller, to requests in the block layer. Applying it per boundary tells you where requests are actually waiting.

R12.6 Utilisation and queueing delay

U = λ × S_t ; W ≈ S_t / (1 − U) (M/M/1 model)
  • U — utilisation of a single server (0…1).
  • S_t — mean service time of the server.
  • W — mean time in system including queueing.

Plain English: as a resource approaches 100% busy, waiting time explodes. At 50% busy you wait about 2× the service time; at 90%, 10×; at 99%, 100×.

Worked example: a die with 60 µs read service time receiving 12 000 reads/s: U = 12 000 × 60e-6 = 0.72 ⇒ W ≈ 60 / 0.28 ≈ 214 µs. M/M/1 assumes exponential arrivals/service — real SSDs deviate; use it for intuition, not prediction conceptual.

R12.7 Latency percentiles and tail amplification

p-th percentile (nearest-rank) = x_(k), k = ⌈ p/100 × N ⌉
  • x_(k) — k-th smallest of N sorted samples.
  • p — percentile (e.g. 99).
  • N — number of samples.

Worked example: 20 sorted latencies (µs): 70, 71, 72, 72, 73, 74, 75, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79, 80, 82, 85, 88, 95, 110, 240, 1900. Median (p50): k = 10 → 77 µs. p90: k = 18 → 110 µs. p95: k = 19 → 240 µs. p99: k = ⌈19.8⌉ = 20 → 1900 µs. The mean is 177 µs — dominated by one outlier, which is why means are poor latency summaries. Tools differ in interpolation method impl; with 20 samples, p99 is just "the maximum".

P(at least one slow) = 1 − (1 − q)^n
  • q — probability a single I/O exceeds the threshold (e.g. 0.01 for p99).
  • n — number of independent I/Os a request fans out to.

Worked example: a database query touching 100 pages on independent I/Os, each with a 1% chance of exceeding p99: 1 − 0.99^100 ≈ 63.4% of queries see at least one p99-slow I/O. Tail latency at the device becomes typical latency for the application (Dean and Barroso, "The Tail at Scale").

R12.8 Write amplification

WAF = NAND bytes written / host bytes written
  • NAND bytes written — including GC relocation, metadata, and parity; available only via vendor telemetry/logs impl.
  • host bytes written — from SMART Data Units Written (each unit = 1000 × 512 bytes).

Worked example: host wrote 100 TB; NAND programmed 250 TB ⇒ WAF = 2.5. Sequential workloads on a fresh drive approach 1.0; small random overwrites at high fill levels with little over-provisioning can exceed 3–5 impl.

TBW ≈ C × PE / WAF (approximate endurance)
  • C — raw capacity (or user capacity as a simplification).
  • PE — rated program/erase cycles of the NAND.

Worked example: 3.84 TB, PE 3000, WAF 2.5 ⇒ ≈ 4608 TB written. Vendors specify TBW under defined workloads (JEDEC JESD218/JESD219 methodology); your WAF may differ derived.

R12.9 DWPD and TBW

TBW = DWPD × C × 365 × Y ; DWPD = TBW / (C × 365 × Y)
  • DWPD — drive writes per day (full-capacity writes per day over the warranty).
  • C — user capacity (TB).
  • Y — warranty years.

Worked example: 3.84 TB, 1 DWPD, 5 years ⇒ 3.84 × 365 × 5 = 7008 TB ≈ 7.0 PB TBW. A 600 TBW, 1 TB, 5-year client drive ⇒ DWPD = 600 / (1 × 1825) ≈ 0.33.

SMART check: Percentage Used (byte 5 of the Health log) is a vendor estimate of life consumed; can exceed 100 verified.

R12.10 LBA ↔ bytes

byte_offset = SLBA × B ; bytes = (NLB + 1) × B ; capacity = NSZE × B
  • SLBA — Starting LBA (CDW10–11, 64-bit).
  • NLB — Number of Logical Blocks, zero-based (CDW12[15:0]).
  • B — LBA data size = 2^LBADS from the active LBA format (e.g. LBADS 9 → 512, 12 → 4096).
  • NSZE — Namespace Size in LBAs (Identify Namespace).

Worked examples: 4 KiB read on 512 B format: NLB = 4096/512 − 1 = 7. On 4 KiB format: NLB = 0. Byte offset 1 GiB on 512 B format: SLBA = 2^30 / 512 = 2 097 152 = 20_0000h. Max per command by NLB field alone: 65 536 blocks (32 MiB at 512 B) — but MDTS usually limits lower.

MaxTransfer = 2^MDTS × 2^(12 + CAP.MPSMIN)
  • MDTS — Identify Controller byte 77; 0 means no limit reported.
  • CAP.MPSMIN — minimum memory page size exponent.

Worked example: MDTS = 5, MPSMIN = 0 ⇒ 32 × 4096 = 128 KiB per command.

R12.11 Doorbell offsets

SQyTDBL = 1000h + (2y) × (4 << DSTRD) ; CQyHDBL = 1000h + (2y + 1) × (4 << DSTRD)
  • y — queue identifier (0 = admin).
  • DSTRD — CAP bits 35:32, doorbell stride exponent.
Queue ySQ tail (DSTRD=0)CQ head (DSTRD=0)SQ tail (DSTRD=1)CQ head (DSTRD=1)
01000h1004h1000h1008h
11008h100Ch1010h1018h
21010h1014h1020h1028h
31018h101Ch1030h1038h
161080h1084h1100h1108h

Reverse: given offset X ≥ 1000h: idx = (X − 1000h) / (4 << DSTRD); y = idx / 2; SQ if idx even, CQ if odd.

R12.12 Ring arithmetic

entries_pending = (tail − head + N) mod N ; full ⇔ (tail + 1) mod N = head
  • N — queue size in entries (QSIZE + 1, since QSIZE is zero-based).

Worked example: N = 64, head = 60, tail = 3 ⇒ pending = (3 − 60 + 64) mod 64 = 7. Memory: SQ = N × 64 B (64 entries = 4 KiB); CQ = N × 16 B (64 entries = 1 KiB). Queue size limit: N ≤ CAP.MQES + 1.

R12.13 PRP entry count

pages = ⌈ (o + L) / PS ⌉ ; list entries n = pages − 1 (when pages > 2)
list pages = 1 if n ≤ E ; else ⌈ (n − 1) / (E − 1) ⌉ , E = PS / 8
  • o — byte offset of the buffer start within its first page (PRP1 offset).
  • L — transfer length in bytes.
  • PS — memory page size = 2^(12 + CC.MPS).
  • E — PRP entries per list page (8 bytes each); when a list page is not the last, its final entry chains to the next list page.
Case (PS = 4 KiB)pagesPRP1PRP2List entriesList pages
4 KiB, o = 01dataunused00
4 KiB, o = 5122data (offset)data page 200
8 KiB, o = 5123data→ list21
128 KiB, o = 032data→ list311
2 MiB, o = 0512data→ list5111
4 MiB, o = 01024data→ list10232 (511 + chain, then 512)

Check the 4 MiB case: ⌈1022 / 511⌉ = 2. First list page holds 511 data entries + 1 chain pointer; second holds the remaining 512.

R12.14 TLP counts per I/O

N_dataTLP ≥ ⌈ L / MPS ⌉ (aligned) ; N_MRd ≥ ⌈ L / MRRS ⌉ ; N_CplD per MRd ≥ ⌈ MRRS / C ⌉
  • L — bytes; MPS — Max Payload Size; MRRS — Max Read Request Size; C — completer's completion chunk size (≥ RCB, ≤ MPS) impl.

Worked example: a 4 KiB NVMe Read at MPS 256 with PRP1 only: 1 doorbell + 1 SQE MRd + 1 CplD + 16 data MWr + 1 CQE MWr + 1 MSI-X + 1 CQ-head doorbell = 22 TLPs. A 4 KiB Write at MRRS 512 and 256-byte completions: 1 + 1 + 1 + 8 MRd + 16 CplD + 1 + 1 + 1 = 30 TLPs.

R12.15 Tag budget (outstanding reads)

N_tags ≥ BW × RTT / MRRS
  • BW — target read bandwidth (B/s).
  • RTT — request-to-completion round trip (s).
  • MRRS — bytes per read request.

Plain English: to keep the pipe full you need enough reads in flight to cover the round trip (bandwidth-delay product).

Worked examples: Gen4 x4, 7.88 GB/s, RTT 1 µs, MRRS 512 ⇒ ≈ 15.4 tags — 8-bit tags (256) are plenty. Gen5 x16, 63 GB/s, RTT 2 µs, MRRS 512 ⇒ ≈ 246 tags — at the 8-bit limit, which is why 10-bit tags (Gen4+, optional) and 14-bit tags in Gen6 FLIT mode exist derived.

R12.16 Bit-error arithmetic

errors/s ≈ R_bits × W × BER
  • R_bits — bit rate per lane (bits/s); W — lanes; BER — bit error ratio.

Worked example: 16 Gb/s per lane, x4, BER 1e-12 ⇒ 0.064 errors/s ≈ one every 16 s across the link. Each detected error typically costs a NAK + replay (a correctable error). The PCIe specification's BER target for Gen3–5 is 10⁻¹² verified; Gen6 relies on FEC because the raw PAM4 BER is far higher version.

R12.17 Timeouts and timing fields

T_ready_max = CAP.TO × 500 ms

Worked example: CAP.TO = 3Ch (60) ⇒ host should wait up to 30 s for CSTS.RDY to change after toggling CC.EN.

Interrupt rate ≈ IOPS_per_vector / A (with aggregation threshold A, if the timer does not fire first)

Worked example: 200 k IOPS on one vector with threshold 8 ⇒ ≈ 25 k interrupts/s; each completion waits up to the aggregation time when traffic is light.

R12.18 Power and energy (bonus)

Energy per I/O = P_active / IOPS

Worked example: 8 W at 800 k IOPS ⇒ 10 µJ per I/O. At QD1, 15 k IOPS and 5 W ⇒ 333 µJ per I/O: efficiency depends strongly on load derived.

R12.19 Common mistakes

  • Using GT/s as GB/s; forgetting encoding; forgetting per-direction.
  • Forgetting NLB and QSIZE are zero-based.
  • Applying Little's law to a non-steady system (warm-up, bursts).
  • Averaging percentiles across servers (p99 of p99s is not a p99).
  • Mixing TB (10¹²) and TiB (2⁴⁰): 1 TB ≈ 0.909 TiB.
🐞 Debugging connection

When measured throughput is far below the formula ceiling, compute the intermediate bounds: link (R12.2–3), tags (R12.15), Little's law (R12.5) and media. The first bound you hit is the bottleneck hypothesis.

🧪 Lab R12.1 — Check the formulas against your SSD SAFE
# Large sequential read (read-only) to measure link-bound throughput
sudo fio --name=seq --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=read --bs=1m --iodepth=32 \
    --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=20 --time_based --readonly
# Small random reads at several depths to test Little's law
for qd in 1 4 16 64; do
  sudo fio --name=r$qd --filename=/dev/nvme0n1 --rw=randread --bs=4k --iodepth=$qd \
      --ioengine=io_uring --direct=1 --runtime=15 --time_based --readonly \
      --output-format=terse | awk -F';' '{print "'"$qd"'", $8, $40}'
done
⚠️ Warning

Use --readonly and --rw=read/randread only. Pointing a write job at a raw device destroys data. The terse field positions shown are illustrative; check your fio version's terse format documentation before relying on column numbers version.

Questions: Does IOPS × mean latency ≈ QD? How close is sequential throughput to the R12.3 estimate for your LnkSta?

Solution

Little's law should hold within a few percent at steady state (QD here is per job; fio's own latency includes software overhead consistently). Sequential throughput usually lands at 85–92% of the encoded link rate when link-bound; well below that indicates media/controller limits or a down-trained link.

Quiz

  1. Gen3 x8 per-direction encoded bandwidth?

    Answer

    8 × 128/130 / 8 × 8 = 7.88 GB/s.

  2. QD 16, 200 k IOPS. Mean latency?

    Answer

    16 / 200 000 = 80 µs.

  3. CQ head doorbell for queue 5, DSTRD 0?

    Answer

    1000h + 11 × 4 = 102Ch.

  4. 12 KiB transfer starting at offset 0 with 4 KiB pages: PRP layout?

    Answer

    3 pages: PRP1 = page 0, PRP2 → list with 2 entries.

Interview questions

  1. Senior Our Gen5 x4 SSD reads at 9 GB/s. Is that link-bound?
    Model answer

    Ceiling ≈ 15.75 GB/s encoded, ≈ 14.3 GB/s after MPS-256 overhead. 9 GB/s is ~63% — not link-bound; look at controller/media parallelism, QD, tag limits or MRRS-related fetch efficiency (for writes), and confirm LnkSta shows 32 GT/s x4.

  2. Principal Derive why 10-bit tags became necessary.
    Model answer

    Bandwidth-delay product: at Gen5 x16 (~63 GB/s) with µs-scale RTT and 512-byte reads, required outstanding requests approach or exceed 256 — the 8-bit tag space. Longer RTT through switches/retimers makes it worse.

📌 Teach-back

Explain Little's law with a fio QD sweep plot, then use it to predict latency at QD 128.

R12.20 Summary

Bandwidth = rate × encoding × lanes; efficiency = payload / (payload + overhead); QD = IOPS × latency; tails amplify with fan-out; endurance = capacity × cycles / WAF; NLB and QSIZE are zero-based; doorbells are 1000h + index × stride. Next: example data appendix.

R13.1 Why this chapter exists

Decoding real bytes is the core skill of protocol work. This appendix gives you a consistent synthetic system — one SSD at BDF 01:00.0 with BAR0 at FEA0_0000h — and decodes every structure byte by byte, so that you can practise and check your own decoders.

  • Decode PCI configuration space headers and walk capability lists.
  • Decode NVMe controller registers, SQEs and CQEs from hex.
  • Decode TLP headers from hex.
  • Recognise the little-endian layout of NVMe structures versus the big-endian presentation of TLP header bytes.

Prerequisites: configuration (Part VII), NVMe registers (Part IX), commands (Part XI), TLPs (Part V).

📌 Labelling

Synthetic example for teaching. Source: invented for this book. Assumptions: x86-64 host, 4 KiB pages, 512-byte LBA format, DSTRD = 0, MPS 256 B, MRRS 512 B. Expected behaviour: as decoded. Vendor ID ABCDh is a placeholder chosen for illustration and should not be read as identifying any real vendor.

🌍 Analogy

A language textbook's worked translations: you see the foreign sentence, the word-by-word gloss, and the meaning.

🧩 Where the analogy breaks

Byte order is "grammar" that changes between structures: NVMe structures and PCIe register contents are little-endian in memory, while TLP headers are conventionally shown most-significant byte first, in transmission order.

R13.2 PCI configuration space header (type 0)

Synthetic: lspci -xxx style dump (offset: bytes, little-endian)
00: cd ab 01 23 06 04 10 00 00 02 08 01 10 00 00 00
10: 04 00 a0 fe 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 00

30: 00 00 00 00 40 00 00 00 00 00 00 00 ff 01 00 00
OffsetRegisterRawDecode
00hVendor ID / Device IDABCDh / 2301hPlaceholder IDs (FFFFh would mean "no function")
04hCommand0406hbit 1 Memory Space Enable, bit 2 Bus Master Enable, bit 10 Interrupt Disable (INTx off — MSI-X in use)
06hStatus0010hbit 4 Capabilities List present
08hRevision ID00h—

0ChCache Line Size10h16 DW = 64 B (legacy, informational on PCIe)
0EhHeader Type00hType 0 (endpoint), single-function
10hBAR0 (low)FEA0_0004hbit 0 = 0 memory; bits 2:1 = 10b 64-bit; bit 3 = 0 non-prefetchable; base FEA0_0000h
14hBAR0 (high)0000_0000hUpper 32 bits of the 64-bit BAR
2ChSubsystem Vendor/IDABCDh / 0001hPlaceholder
34hCapabilities Pointer40hFirst capability at 40h
3ChInterrupt Line / PinFFh / 01hLine unassigned; INTA# declared

BAR sizing (derived): software writes FFFF_FFFFh to BAR0 low and reads back e.g. FFFF_C004h ⇒ size = ~(FFFF_C000h) + 1 = 16 KiB (with the upper BAR also written all-ones). The BAR must cover registers (0–FFFh), doorbells (from 1000h) and here the MSI-X table and PBA.

MSI-X decode: Message Control 8020h: bit 15 MSI-X Enable = 1; bit 14 Function Mask = 0; bits 10:0 Table Size = 20h ⇒ 33 vectors (N−1 encoding). Table Offset/BIR 0000_2000h: BIR = 0 (BAR0), offset 2000h ⇒ table at FEA0_2000h. PBA at FEA0_3000h.

R13.4 PCI Express capability registers

Register (offset in cap)RawDecode
Device Control (+08h)293Fhbits 3:0 error reporting enables (Correctable, Non-Fatal, Fatal, UR) = 1; bit 4 Relaxed Ordering enable; bits 7:5 = 001b MPS 256 B; bit 8 Extended Tag enable; bit 11 No Snoop enable; bits 14:12 = 010b MRRS 512 B
Link Capabilities (+0Ch)0000_0C44h (other fields omitted)bits 3:0 = 4 → max 16 GT/s; bits 9:4 = 4 → max x4; bits 11:10 = 11b ASPM L0s and L1 supported
Link Status (+12h)1044hbits 3:0 = 4 → current 16 GT/s; bits 9:4 = 4 → x4; bit 12 Slot Clock Configuration
Link Status (degraded variant)1023hcurrent speed 3 → 8 GT/s, width 2 → x2: down-trained relative to capability — investigate slot, retimer, channel

Speed encoding for Current Link Speed: value n indexes the Supported Link Speeds Vector; for typical devices 1 = 2.5, 2 = 5, 3 = 8, 4 = 16, 5 = 32, 6 = 64 GT/s verified.

Register (offset from 100h)RawDecode
Uncorrectable Error Status (+04h)0010_0000hbit 20 Unsupported Request Error
Uncorrectable Error Severity (+0Ch)0046_2030h (example)bit 20 = 0 → UR reported as Non-Fatal; bits 4, 5, 13, 17, 18 = 1 (Fatal: DL Protocol, Surprise Down, FC Protocol, Receiver Overflow, Malformed TLP); bit 22 (Uncorrectable Internal Error) shown Fatal
Correctable Error Status (+10h)0000_10C0hbit 6 Bad TLP, bit 7 Bad DLLP, bit 12 Replay Timer Timeout
Adv. Error Capabilities & Control (+18h)0000_0014hbits 4:0 First Error Pointer = 14h = 20 → UR was first
Header Log (+1Ch…+28h)4000_0001h 0000_000Fh FEA0_7000h 0000_0000hLogged TLP header: MWr 3DW, length 1, Requester 0000h, FBE Fh, address FEA0_7000h — a host write beyond the BAR's decoded registers (byte 0 of the header shown in bits 31:24 of the first DW — confirm in your spec revision)

Other uncorrectable status bits for reference: 4 Data Link Protocol Error, 5 Surprise Down, 12 Poisoned TLP, 13 Flow Control Protocol Error, 14 Completion Timeout, 15 Completer Abort, 16 Unexpected Completion, 17 Receiver Overflow, 18 Malformed TLP, 19 ECRC Error, 20 Unsupported Request, 21 ACS Violation. Correctable: 0 Receiver Error, 6 Bad TLP, 7 Bad DLLP, 8 REPLAY_NUM Rollover, 12 Replay Timer Timeout, 13 Advisory Non-Fatal verified.
